## Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent

## The Letters

## The Alphabet

a. Sigma (not capital) at the end of a word is written s, elsewhere s1. Thus, seismo/s earthquake.
b. The names in parentheses, from which are derived those in current use, were given at a late period, some as late as the Middle Ages. Thus, epsilon means ‘simple e,’ upsilon ‘simple u,’ to distinguish these letters from ai, oi, which were sounded like e and u.
c. Labda is a better attested ancient name than lambda.

§2
The Greek alphabet as given above originated in Ionia, and was adopted at Athens in 403 B.C. The letters from A to T are derived from Phoenician and have Semitic names. The signs *u to *w were invented by the Greeks. From the Greek alphabet are derived the alphabets of most European countries. The ancients used only the large letters, called majuscules (capitals as *e, uncials as [Eunc ]); the small letters (minuscules), which were used as a literary hand in the ninth century, are cursive forms of the uncials.
a. Before 403 B.C. in the official Attic alphabet E stood for e, h, spurious ei (6), O for o, w, spurious ou (6), H for the rough breathing, *x*s for *c, *f*s for *y. *l was written for g, and [lins ] for l. Thus:

*e*d*o*x*s*e*n*t*e*i*b*o[lins ]*e*i*k*a*i*t*o*i*d*e*m*o*ie)/docen th=| boulh=| kai\ tw=| dh/mw|.

*x*s*u*l*l*r*a*f*e*s*x*s*u*n*e*l*r*a*f*s*a*ncuggrafh=s cune/grayan.

*e*g*i*t*e*d*e*i*o*n*e*n*a*i*a*g*o*t*o*a*r*l*u*r*i*oe)pith/deion ei)=nai a)po\ tou= a)rguri/ou.

§3
In the older period there were two other letters: (1) *v: vau=, uau, called digamma (i.e. double-gamma) from its shape. It stood after e and was pronounced like w. v was written in Boeotian as late as 200 B.C. (2) ϟ: ko/ppa, koppa, which stood after p. Another s, called san, is found in the sign [sampi ], called sampi, i.e. san + pi. On these signs as numerals, see 348.

§3 D
Vau was in use as a genuine sound at the time the Homeric poems were composed, though it is found in no Mss. of Homer. Many apparent irregularities of epic verse (such as hiatus, 47 D.) can be explained only by supposing that v was actually sounded. Examples of words containing v are: a)/stu town, a)/nac lord, a(nda/nw please, ei)/kw give way (cp. weak), ei)/kosi twenty (cp. viginti), e(/kastos each, e(kw/n willing, e)/lpomai hope (cp. voluptas), e)/oika am like, e(/o, oi(=, e(/ him, e(/c six, e)/pos word, ei)=pon said, e)/rgon, e)/rdw work, e(/nnu_mi clothe, fr. ves-nu_mi (cp. vestis), e)re/w will say (cp. verbum), e(/speros evening (cp. vesper), i)/on violet (cp. viola), e)/tos year (cp. vetus), h(du/s sweet (cp. suavis), i)dei=n (oi)=da) know (cp. videre, wit), i)/_s strength (cp. vis), i)_te/a willow (cp. vitis, withy), oi)=kos house (cp. vicus), oi)=nos wine (cp. vinum), o(/s his (123), o)/xos carriage (cp. veho, wain). Vau was lost first before o-sounds (o(ra/w see, cp. be-ware). v occurred also in the middle of words: kle/vos glory, ai)vei/ always, o)/vis sheep (cp. ovis), klhvi/s key (Dor. kla_i+/s, cp. clavis), ce/nvos stranger, *divi/ to Zeus, kalvo/s beautiful. Cp. 20, 31, 37 D., 122, 123.

## Vowels and Diphthongs

§4
There are seven vowels: a, e, h, i, o, u, w. Of these e and o are always short, and take about half the time to pronounce as h and w, which are always long; a, i, u are short in some syllables, long in others. In this Grammar, when a, i, u are not marked as long (a_, i_, u_) they are understood to be short. All vowels with the circumflex (149) are long. On length by position, see 144.
a. Vowels are said to be open or close according as the mouth is more open or less open in pronouncing them, the tongue and lips assuming different positions in the case of each.

§5
A diphthong (di/fqoggos having two sounds) combines two vowels in one syllable. The second vowel is i or u. The diphthongs are: ai, ei, oi, a_|, h|, w|; au, eu, ou, hu, and ui. The i of the so-called improper diphthongs, a_|, h|, w|, is written below the line and is called iota subscript. But with capital letters, i is written on the line (adscript), as *t*h*i *w*i*d*h*i = th=| w)|dh=| or *)widh=| to the song. All diphthongs are long.
a. In a|, h|, w| the i ceased to be written about 100 B.C. The custom of writing i under the line is as late as about the eleventh century.

§5 D
A diphthong wu occurs in New Ionic (w(uto/s the same from o( au)to/s 68 D., e)mwutou= of myself = e)mautou= 329 D., qwu=ma = qau=ma wonder). Ionic has hu for Attic au in some words (Hom. nhu=s ship).

§6

ei, ou are either genuine or spurious (apparent) diphthongs (25). Genuine ei, ou are a combination of e + i, o + u, as in lei/pw I leave (cp. le/loipa I have left, 35 a), ge/nei to a race (49), a)ko/louqos follower (cp. ke/leuqos way). Spurious ei, ou arise from contraction (50) or compensatory lengthening (37). Thus, e)fi/lei he loved, from e)fi/lee, qei/s placing from qent-s; e)fi/loun they loved from e)fi/leon, plou=s voyage from plo/os, dou/s giving from dont-s.

§7
The figure of a triangle represents the relations of the vowels and spurious diphthongs to one another.
From a_ to i and from a^ to ou the elevation of the tongue gradually increases. w, o, ou, u are accompanied by rounding of the lips.

§8

Diaeresis.—A double dot, the mark of diaeresis (diai/resis separation), may be written over i or u when these do not form a diphthong with the preceding vowel: proi+/sthmi I set before, nhi+/ to a ship.

§8 D
In poetry and in certain dialects vowels are often written apart which later formed diphthongs: pa/is (or pa/i+s) boy or girl, *phlei+/dhs son of Peleus, e)u/ (or e)u+/) well, *)ai/dhs (or *)ai+/dhs) Hades, ge/nei+ to a race.

## Breathings

§9
Every initial vowel or diphthong has either the rough (‘) or the smooth (’) breathing. The rough breathing (spiritus asper) is pronounced as h, which is sounded before the vowel; the smooth breathing (spiritus lenis) is not sounded. Thus, o(/ros hóros boundary, o)/ros óros mountain.

§9 D
The Ionic of Asia Minor lost the rough breathing at an early date. So also before r (13). Its occurrence in compounds (124 D.) is a relic of the period when it was still sounded in the simple word. Hom. sometimes has the smooth where Attic has the rough breathing in forms that are not Attic: *)ai+/dhs (*(/a_idhs), the god Hades, a)=lto sprang (a(/llomai), a)/mudis together (cp. a(/ma), h)e/lios sun (h(/lios), h)w/s dawn (e(/ws), i)/_rhc hawk (i(e/ra_c), ou)=ros boundary (o(/ros). But also in a)/maca wagon (Attic a(/maca). In Laconian medial s became ( (h): e)ni/_ka_e( = e)ni/_khse he conquered.

§10
Initial u (u^ and u_) always has the rough breathing.

§10 D
In Aeolic, u, like all the other vowels (and the diphthongs), always has the smooth breathing. The epic forms u)/mmes you, u)/mmi, u)/mme (325 D.) are Aeolic.

§11
Diphthongs take the breathing, as the accent (152), over the second vowel: ai(re/w hairéo I seize, ai)/rw aíro I lift. But a|, h|, w| take both the breathing and the accent on the first vowel, even when i is written in the line (5): a)/|dw = *)/aidw I sing, a(/|dhs = *(/a_idhs Hades, but *ai)nei/a_s Aeneas. The writing a)i/dhlos (*)ai/dhlos) destroying shows that ai does not here form a diphthong; and hence is sometimes written ai+ (8).

§12
In compound words (as in proora=n to foresee, from pro/ + o(ra=n) the rough breathing is not written, though it must often have been pronounced: cp. e)ce/dra_ a hall with seats, Lat. exhedra, exedra, polui/stwr very learned, Lat. polyhistor. On Attic inscriptions in the old alphabet (2 a) we find *e*u*h*o*r*k*o*n eu)o(/rkon faithful to one's oath.

§13
Every initial r has the rough breathing: r(h/twr orator (Lat. rhetor). Medial rr is written r)r( in some texts: *pu/r)r(os Pyrrhus.

§14
The sign for the rough breathing is derived from H, which in the Old Attic alphabet (2 a) was used to denote h. Thus, HO o( the. After H was used to denote h, one half ([rough ]) was used for h (about 300 B.C.), and, later, the other half ([smooth]) for the smooth breathing. From [rough ] and [smooth] come the forms ‘and’.

## CONSONANTS

§15
The seventeen consonants are divided into stops (or mutes), spirants, liquids, nasals, and double consonants. They may be arranged according to the degree of tension or slackness of the vocal chords in sounding them, as follows:
a. Voiced (sonant, i.e. sounding) consonants are produced when the vocal chords vibrate. The sounds are represented by the letters b, d, g (stops), l, r (liquids), m, n, g-nasal (19 a) (nasals), and z. (All the vowels are voiced.) r with the rough breathing is voiceless.
b. Voiceless (surd, i.e. hushed) consonants require no exertion of the vocal chords. These are p, t, k, f, q, x (stops), s (spirant or sibilant), and y and c.
c. Arranged according to the increasing degree of noise, nearest to the vowels are the nasals, in sounding which the air escapes without friction through the nose; next come the semivowels [uglide] and [iglide] (20 a), the liquids, and the spirant s, in sounding which the air escapes with friction through the cavity of the mouth; next come the stops, which are produced by a removal of an obstruction; and finally the double consonants.

§16

Stops (or mutes). Stopped consonants are so called because in sounding them the breath passage is for a moment completely closed. The stops are divided into three classes (according to the part of the mouth chiefly active in sounding them) and into three orders (according to the degree of force in the expiratory effort).

Classes

Labial (lip sounds)pbf

Dental (teeth sounds)tdq

Palatal (palate sounds)kgx

Orders

Smoothptk

Middlebdg

Roughfqx
a. The dentals are sometimes called linguals. The rough stops are also called aspirates (lit. breathed sounds) because they were sounded with a strong emission of breath (26). The smooth stops are thus distinguished from the rough stops by the absence of breathing. ( (h) is also an aspirate. The middle stops owe their name to their position in the above grouping, which is that of the Greek grammarians.

§17

Spirants.—There is one spirant: s (also called a sibilant).
a. A spirant is heard when the breath passage of the oral cavity is so narrowed that a rubbing noise is produced by an expiration.

§18

Liquids.—There are two liquids: l and r. Initial r always has the rough breathing (13).

§19

Nasals.—There are three nasals: m (labial), n (dental), and g-nasal (palatal).
a. Gamma before k, g, x, c is called g-nasal. It had the sound of n in think, and was represented by n in Latin. Thus, a)/gku_ra (Lat. ancora) anchor, a)/ggelos (Lat. angelus) messenger, sfi/gc sphinx.
b. The name liquids is often used to include both liquids and nasals.

§20

Semivowels.—i, u, the liquids, nasals, and the spirant s are often called semivowels. ([iglide] becoming z, and v are also called spirants.)
a. When i and u correspond to y and w (cp. minion, persuade) they are said to be unsyllabic; and, with a following vowel, make one syllable out of two. Semivocalic i and u are written [iglide] and [uglide]. Initial [iglide] passed into ( (h), as in h(=par liver, Lat. jecur; and into z in zugo/n yoke, Lat. jugum (here it is often called the spirant yod). Initial [uglide] was written v (3). Medial [iglide], [uglide] before vowels were often lost, as in ti_ma/-（[iglide]) w I honour, bo（[uglide]）-o/s, gen. of bou=-s ox, cow (43).
b. The form of many words is due to the fact that the liquids, nasals, and s may fulfil the office of a vowel to form syllables (cp. bridle, even, pst). This is expressed by l?o?, m?o?, n?o?, r?o?, s?o?, to be read ‘syllabic l,’ etc., or ‘sonant l’ (see 35 b, c).

§21

Double Consonants.—These are z, c, and y. z is a combination of sd (or ds) or di (26). c is written for ks, gt, xt; y for ps, bs, fs.

## ANCIENT GREEK PRONUNCIATION

§23
The pronunciation of Ancient Greek varied much according to time and place, and differed in many important respects from that of the modern language. While in general Greek of the classical period was a phonetic language, i.e. its letters represented the sounds, and no heard sound was unexpressed in writing (but see 108), in course of time many words were retained in their old form though their pronunciation had changed. The tendency of the language was thus to become more and more unphonetic. Our current pronunciation of Ancient Greek is only in part even approximately correct for the period from the death of Pericles (429 B.C.) to that of Demosthenes (322); and in the case of several sounds, e.g. z, f, x, q, it is certainly erroneous for that period. But ignorance of the exact pronunciation, as well as long-established usage, must render any reform pedantical, if not impossible. In addition to, and in further qualification of, the list of sound equivalents in 1 we may note the following:

§24

Vowels.—Short a, i, u differed in sound from the corresponding long voweis only in being less prolonged; e and o probably differed from h and w also in being less open, a difference that is impossible to parallel in English as our short vowels are more open than the long vowels. a^: as a in Germ. hat. There is no true ă in accented syllables in English; the a of idea, aha is a neutral vowel. e: as é in bonté; somewhat similar is a in bakery. h: as ê in fête, or nearly as e in where. i^: nearly as the first e in meteor, eternal. o: as o in Fr. mot, somewhat like unaccented ŏ in obey or phonetic (as often sounded). w: as o in Fr. encore. Eng. ō is prevailingly diphthongal (o^{u}). u was originally sounded as u in prune, but by the fifth century had become like that of Fr. tu, Germ. thür. It never had in Attic the sound of u in mute. After u had become like Germ. ü, the only means to represent the sound of the old u (oo in moon) was ou (25). Observe, however, that, in diphthongs, final u retained the old u sound.

§24 D
In Lesbos, Boeotia, Laconia, possibly in Ionia, and in some other places, u was still sounded oo after it became like Germ. ü in Attic.

§25

Diphthongs.—The diphthongs were sounded nearly as follows:

ai as in Cairoau as ou in outhu as ēh’-oo

ei as in veineu as e (met) + oo (moon)wu as ōh’-oo

oi as in soilou as in ourangui as in Fr. huit
In a|, h|, w| the long open vowels had completely overpowered the i by 100 B.C., so that i ceased to be written (5 a). The i is now generally neglected in pronunciation though it may have still been sounded to some extent in the fourth century B.C.—The genuine diphthongs ei and ou (6) were originally distinct double sounds (ĕh’-i, ŏh’-oo), and as such were written *e*i, *o*u in the Old Attic alphabet (2 a): *e*g*e*i*d*e e)peidh/, *t*o*u*t*o*n tou/twn. The spurious diphthongs ei and ou (6) are digraphs representing the long sounds of simple e (French é) and original u. By 400 B.C. genuine ei and ou had become simple single sounds pronounced as ei in vein and ou in ourang; and spurious ei and ou, which had been written E and O (2 a), were now often written *e*i and *o*u. After 300 B.C. ei gradually acquired the sound of ei in seize. eu was sounded like eh’-oo, hu and wu like ēh’-oo, ōh’-oo, pronounced rapidly but smoothly. ui is now commonly sounded as ui in quit. It occurred only before vowels, and the loss of the i in u(o/s son (43) shows that the diphthongal sound was disliked.

§26

Consonants.—Most of the consonants were sounded as in English (1). Before i, k, g, t, s never had a sh (or zh) sound heard in Lycia (*luki/a_), Asia (*)asi/a_). s was usually like our sharp s; but before voiced consonants (15 a) it probably was soft, like z; thus we find both ko/zmos and ko/smos on inscriptions. —z was probably = zd, whether it arose from an original sd (as in *)aqh/naze, from *)aqhna（n）s-de Athens-wards), or from dz, developed from dy (as in zugo/n, from (d）yugo/n, cp. jugum). The z in zd gradually extinguished the d, until in the Hellenistic period (p. 4) z sank to z (as in zeal), which is the sound in Modern Greek.—The aspirates f, q, x were voiceless stops (15 b, 16 a) followed by a strong expiration: p^{h}, t^{h}, k^{h} as in upheaval, hothouse, backhand (though here h is in a different syllable from the stop). Thus, feu/gw was p(eu/gw, qe/lw was t(e/lw, e)/xw was e)/-k(w. Cp. e)f' w(=| for e)p（i\) (w=|, etc. Probably only one h was heard when two aspirates came together, as in e)xqro/s (e)kt(ro/s). After 300 A.D. (probably) f, q, and x became spirants, f being sounded as f (as in *fi/lippos Philip), q as th in theatre, x as ch in German ich or loch. The stage between aspirates and spirants is sometimes represented by the writing pf (= pf), tq, kx, which are affricata.—The neglect of the h in Latin representations of f, q, x possibly shows that these sounds consisted of a stop + h. Thus, Pilipus = *fi/lippos, tus = qu/os, Aciles = *)axilleu/s. Modern Greek has the spirantic sounds, and these, though at variance with classical pronunciation, are now usually adopted. See also 108.

§26 D
Aeolic has sd for z in u)/sdos (o)/zos branch). In late Laconian q passed into s (shri/on = qhri/on wild beast). In Laconian and some other dialects b became a spirant and was written for v. d became a spirant in Attic after Christ.

§28
Difference in quantity between Attic and Epic words is due chiefly either to (1) metrical lengthening, or to (2) different phonetic treatment, as kalvo/s, tinvw become Epic ka_lo/s fair, ti/_nw I pay (37 D. 1), Attic ka^lo/s, ti^/nw.

§28 D
Metrical lengthening.—Many words, which would otherwise not fit into the verse, show in the Epic ei for e, ou (rarely oi) for o, and a_, i_, u_ for a, i, u. Thus, ei)na/lios in the sea for e)na/lios, ei)arino/s vernal for e)arino/s, u(pei/roxos eminent for u(pe/roxos, ei)lh/louqa have come for e)lh/louqa, ou)lo/menos destructive, accursed for o)lo/menos, ou)/rea mountains from o)/ros, *ou)lu/mpoio of Olympus from *)/olumpos. o before a vowel appears as oi in pnoih/ breath. Similarly, h)ga/qeos very holy for a)ga/qeos; but h)nemo/eis windy (from a)/nemos) has the h of u(ph/nemos under the wind (29), and tiqh/menos placing (for tiqe/menos) borrows h from ti/qhmi.
A short syllable under the rhythmic accent (‘ictus’) is lengthened metrically: (1) in words having three or more short syllables: the first of three shorts (ou)lo/menos), the second of four shorts (u(pei/roxos), the third of five shorts (a)perei/sia boundless); (2) in words in which the short ictus syllable is followed by two longs and a short (*ou)lu/mpoio). A short syllable not under the rhythmic accent is lengthened when it is preceded and followed by a long; thus, any vowel preceded by v (pnei/w breathe = pnevw), i or u before a vowel (proqu_mi/_h|si zeal).

§29
The initial short vowel of a word forming the second part of a compound is often lengthened: strathgo/s general (strato/s army + a)/gein to lead 887 d).

§30

Attic h, a_.—Attic has h for original a_ of the earlier period, as fh/mh report (Lat. fāma). Ionic also has h for original a_. Doric and Aeolic retain original a_ (fa/_ma_).
a. This is true also of the a_ which is the result of early compensative lengthening, by which -ans-, -asl-, -asm-, and -asn- changed to -a_s-, -a_l-, -a_m-, and -a_n-. (See 37 b.) But in a few cases like ta/_s for ta/ns, and in pa=sa for pa/nsa (113) where the combination ans arose at a later period, a_ was not changed to h. u(fa=nai for u(fh=nai to weave follows tetra=nai to pierce.
b. Original a_ became h after u, as fuh/ growth. In some words, however, we find a_.

§30 D. 1
Doric and Aeolic retain original a_, as in ma=lon apple (cp. Lat. mālum, Att. mh=lon), ka=ruc herald (Att. kh=ruc). But Doric and Aeolic have original h when h interchanges with e, as in ti/qhmi I place, ti/qemen we place, ma/_thr ma_te/ra mother, poimh/n poime/ni shepherd.
2. Ionic has h after e, i, and r. Thus, geneh/, skih/, h(me/rh.

§31
In Attic alone this h was changed back to a_:
1. When preceded by a r; as h(me/ra_ day, xw/ra_ country. This appears to have taken place even though an o intervened: as a)kro/a_ma a musical piece, a)qro/a_ collected.
EXCEPTIONS: (a) But rvh was changed to rh: as ko/rh for korvh maiden. (b) Likewise rh, when the result of contraction of rea, remained: as o)/rh from o)/rea mountains. (c) And rsh was changed to rrh: as ko/rrh for ko/rsh (79) one of the temples.
2. When preceded by e or i: as genea/_ generation, skia/_ shadow.
This change takes place even when the h is the result of the contraction of ea: as u(gia= healthy, e)ndea= lacking, for u(gih= from u(gie（s）a, e)ndeh= from e)ndee（s）a; also, if originally a v intervened, as ne/a_ for neva_ young (Lat. nova).
EXCEPTIONS: Some exceptions are due to analogy: u(gih= healthy, eu)fuh= shapely (292 d) follow safh= clear.

§32
In the choruses of tragedy Doric a_ is often used for h. Thus, ma/_thr mother, yu_xa/_ soul, ga= earth, du/sta_nos wretched, e)/ba_n went.

§33
The dialects frequently show vowel sounds that do not occur in the corresponding Attic words.

§33 D

a for e: i(aro/s sacred, *)/artamis (for *)/artemis), tra/pw turn Dor.; e for a: qe/rsos courage Aeol., e)/rshn male, o(re/w see, te/sseres four ( = te/ttares) Ion.; a for o: dia_kati/oi (for dia_ko/sioi) 200 Dor., u)pa/ under Aeol.; o for a: stro/tos (strato/s) army, o)/n (a)na/) up Aeol., te/tores (te/ttares) four Dor.; e for h: e(/sswn inferior (h(/ttwn) Ion.; e for o: *)ape/llwn Dor. (for e(sti/a_), xru/_sios (xru/_seos) golden Aeol., qio/s god Boeot., kosmi/w arrange Dor.; u for a: pi/sures four (te/ttares) Hom.; u for o: o)/numa name Dor., Aeol., a)pu/ from Aeol.; w for ou: w)=n accordingly Ion., Dor.

§34

Transfer of Quantity.—ho, ha often exchange quantities, be coming ew, ea_. Thus, lho/s (Epic la_o/s folk) becomes lew/s, as po/lhos becomes po/lews of a city; teqnho/tos teqnew=tos dead; basilh=a basile/a_ king.

§34 D
Often in Ionic: *)atrei+/dew from earlier *)atrei+/da_o son of Atreus, i(ke/tew from i(ke/ta_o suppliant. This ew generally makes a single syllable in poetry (60). The ho intermediate between a_o and ew is rarely found.

§35

Qualitative Vowel Gradation.—In the same root or suffix we find an interchange among different vowels (and diphthongs) similar to the interchange in sing, sang, sung.
a. This variation appears in strong grades and in a weak grade (including actual expulsion of a vowel—in diphthongs, of the first vowel). Thus, fe/r-w I carry, fo/r-o-s tribute, fw/r thief, far-e/-tra_ quiver, di/-f r-o-s chariot (twocarrier), lei/p-w I leave, le/-loip-a I have left, lip-ei=n to leave. The interchange is quantitative in fo/r-o-s fw/r (cp. 27).
b. When, by the expulsion of a vowel in the weak grade, an unpronounceable combination of consonants resulted, a vowel sound was developed to render pronunciation possible. Thus, ra or ar was developed from r between consonants, as in pa-tra/-si from ṛatr-si (262); and a from n, as in au)to/-ma-to-n for au)to-mṇ-ton automaton (acting of its own will), cp. me/n-o-s rage, me/-mon-a I yearn. So in o)nomai/nw name for o)nomṇ-[iglide]w; cp. o)/noma.
c. A vowel may also take the place of an original liquid or nasal after a consonant; as e)/lu_sa for e)lu_sṃ. This r, l, m, n in b and c is called sonant liquid or sonant nasal.

## COMPENSATORY LENGTHENING

§37
Compensatory lengthening is the lengthening of a short vowel to make up for the omission of a consonant.

The short vowelsaeiou

are lengthened toa_eii_ouu_

Thus the formsta/n-se)-men-sae)klin-sato/nsdeiknunt-s

becometa/_se)/meinae)/kli_natou/sdeiknu/_s

theI remainedI leanedtheshowing
a. Thus are formed ktei/nw I kill for kten-[iglide]w, fqei/rw I destroy for fqer-[iglide]w, do/teira giver for doter-[iglide]a, kli/_nw I lean for klin-[iglide]w, o)lofu/_rw I lament for o)lofur-[iglide]w.
b. a becomes h in the s-aorist of verbs whose stems end in l, r, or n, when not preceded by i or r. Thus, e)fan-sa becomes e)/-fhna I showed, but e)peran-sa becomes e)pe/ra_na I finished. So selh/vh moon for selas-nh (se/las gleam).
c. The diphthongs ei and ou due to this lengthening are spurious (6).

§37 D
1. Ionic agrees with Attic except where the omitted consonant was v, which in Attic disappeared after a consonant without causing lengthening. Thus, cei=nos for ce/nos stranger, ei(/neka on account of (also in Dem.) for e(/neka, ou)=ros boundary for o(/ros, kou=ros boy for ko/ros, mou=nos alone for mo/nos. These forms are also used generally in poetry.
2. Doric generally lengthens e and o to h and w: ch=nos, w(=ros, kw=ros, mw=nos. So mw=sa muse from monsa for mont[iglide]a, tw/s for to/ns the, h)mi/ am for e)smi, xhli/oi 1000 for xeslioi, Ionic xei/lioi. (In some Doric dialects v drops as in Attic (ce/nos, o(/ros); and ans, ons may become a^s, os: despo/ta^s lords, to/s the.)
3. Aeolic has ais, eis (a genuine diphth.), ois from ans, ens, ons. Thus, pai=sa all (Cretan pa/nsa, Att. pa=sa), lu/_oisi they loose from lu/_onti. Elsewhere Aeol. prefers assimilated forms (e)/menna, e)/klinna, ce/nnos, e)/nneka, o)/rros, e)/mmi, xe/llioi). But single n, r are also found, as in ko/ra_, mo/nos. Aeolic has fqe/rrw, kli/nnw, o)lofu/rrw; cp. 37 a.

§38

a_ arises from ai upon the loss of its i (43) in a)_ei/ always (from ai)ei/), a)_eto/s eagle (ai)eto/s), kla/_ei weeps (klai/ei), e)la/_a_ olive-tree (e)lai/a_, cp. Lat. oliva).
a. This change took place only when ai was followed by v (ai)vei/, ai)veto/s from a)vietos, klaivei from klaviei, 111, 128) or i (*qhba_i/s the Thebaïd from *qhbaii/s); and only when v or i was not followed by o.

## SHORTENING, ADDITION, AND OTHER VOWEL CHANGES

§39

Shortening.—A long vowel may be shortened before another long vowel: basile/wn from basilh/wn of kings, new=n from nhw=n of ships, teqnew/s from teqnhw/s dead.

§39 D
In the Ionic genitive of Â stems (214 D. 8) -ewn is from -hwn out of -a_wn. So in Ionic basile/a from basilh=a king. So even before a short vowel in Hom. h(/rw^os, h(/rw^i hero (cp. 148 D. 3).

§40
A long vowel before i, u, a nasal, or a liquid + a following consonant was regularly shortened: na^u=s from original na_us ship, e)mi/gen from e)-migh-nt were mixed. The long vowel was often introduced again, as Ion. nhu=s ship.

§41

Addition.—a, e, o are sometimes prefixed before l, m, r, v (prothetic vowels). Thus, a)-lei/fw anoint with oil, li/pos fat; e)-ruqro/s red (cp. Lat. ruber), e)-ei/kosi from e)-（v）ei/kosi; o)-mo/rgnu_mi wipe; e)-xqe/s and xqe/s yesterday, i)/-ktis weasel (ktide/h weasel-skin helmet) are doubtful cases.

§42

Development.—A medial vowel is sometimes developed from l or n between two consonants; thus al, la; ar, ra; an (35 b). Also (rarely) in forms like Ion. ba/ragxos = Att. bra/gxos hoarseness.

§43

Disappearance.—The i and u of diphthongs often disappear before a following vowel. Thus, u(o/s from ui(o/s son, bo-o/s genitive of bou=-s ox, cow. i and u here became semivowels ([iglide], [uglide]), which are not written. Cp. 148 D. 3.

§43 D
So in Hdt. ke/etai for kei/etai lies, baqe/a for baqei=a deep.

§44

a. The disappearance of e before a vowel is often called hyphaeresis (u(fai/resis omission). Thus Ionic nosso/s chick for neosso/s, o(rth/ for e(orth/ festival; a)dew=s fearlessly for a)dee/ws. Here e was sounded nearly like y and was not written.

§44 a. D
Cp. Hom. qeoi/ A 18 (one syllable). i becomes [iglide] in Hom. po/lios (two syllables)
*f 567. i rarely disappears: dh=mon for dh/mion belonging to the people M 213.
b. The disappearance of a short vowel between consonants is called syncope (sugkoph/ cutting up). Thus pi/_ptw fall for pi-pet-w, patro/s father for pate/ros. Syncopated forms show the weak grade of vowel gradation (35, 36).

§45

Assimilation.—A vowel may be assimilated to the vowel standing in the following syllable: bibli/on book from bubli/on (bu/blos papyrus).
a. On assimilation in distracted verbs (o(ro/w see, etc.), see 643 ff., 652.

## EUPHONY OF VOWELS

## CONTACT OF VOWELS AND HIATUS

§46
Attic more than any other dialect disliked the immediate succession of two vowel sounds in adjoining syllables. To avoid such succession, which often arose in the formation and inflection of words, various means were employed: contraction (48 ff.), when the vowels collided in the middle of a word; or, when the succession occurred between two words (hiatus), by crasis (62 ff.), elision (70 ff.), aphaeresis (76), or by affixing a movable consonant at the end of the former word (134).

§47
Hiatus is usually avoided in prose writers by elision (70 ff.); but in cases where elision is not possible, hiatus is allowed to remain by different writers in different degrees, commonly after short words, such as w)=, ei), h)/, kai/, mh/, and the forms of the article.

§47 D
Hiatus is allowed in certain cases.
1. In epic poetry: a. After i and u: a)/coni a)mfi/s, su/ e)ssi.
b. After a long final syllable having the rhythmic accent: moi e)qe/lousa ([macrdot]˘˘[macrdot]˘).
c. When a long final syllable is shortened before an initial vowel (weak , or improper, hiatus): a)kth=| e)f' u(yhlh=| ([macrdot]˘˘[macrdot]¯[macrdot]).
d. When the concurrent vowels are separated by the caesura; often after the fourth foot: a)ll' a)/g' e)mw=n o)xe/wn e)pibh/seo, | o)/fra i)/dhai; very often between the short syllables of the third foot (the feminine caesura): as, a)ll' a)ke/ousa ka/qhso, | e)mw=| d' e)pipei/qeo mu/_qw|; rarely after the first foot: au)ta\r o( e)/gnw A 333.
e. Where v has been lost.
2. In Attic poetry hiatus is allowable, as in 1 c, and after ti/ what? eu)= well, interjections, peri/ concerning, and in ou)de\ (mhde\) ei(=s (for ou)dei/s, mhdei/s no one).

## CONTRACTION

§48
Contraction unites in a single long vowel or diphthong two vowels or a vowel and a diphthong standing next each other in successive syllables in the same word.
a. Occasion for contraction is made especially by the concurrence of vowel sounds which were once separated by s, [uglide] (v), and [iglide] (17, 20 a).
The following are the chief rules governing contraction:

§49
(I) Two vowels which can form a diphthong (5) unite to form that diphthong: ge/nei+ = ge/nei, ai)do/i+ = ai)doi=, klh/i+qron = klh=|qron.

§50
(II) Like Vowels.—Like vowels, whether short or long, unite in the common long; ee, oo become ei, ou (6): ge/raa = ge/ra_, file/hte = filh=te; e)fi/lee = e)fi/lei, dhlo/omen = dhlou=men.
a. i is rarely contracted with i (o)fi + idion = o)fi/_dion small snake) or u with u (u(/_s son in inscriptions, from u(（i）u/s = ui(o/s, 43).

§50 D

i + i = i_ occurs chiefly in the Ionic, Doric, and Aeolic dative singular of nouns in -is (268 D.), as in po/lii = po/li_; also in the optative, as in fqi-i_-to = fqi=to.

§51
(III) Unlike Vowels.—Unlike vowels are assimilated, either the second to the first (progressive assimilation) or the first to the second (regressive assimilation).
a. An o sound always prevails over an a or e sound: o or w before or after a, and before h, forms w. oe and eo form ou (a spurious diphthong, 6). Thus, ti_ma/omen = ti_mw=men, ai)do/a = ai)dw=, h(/rwa = h(/rw, ti_ma/w = ti_mw=, dhlo/hte = dhlw=te; but file/omen = filou=men, dhlo/eton = dhlou=ton.
b. When a and e or h come together the vowel sound that precedes prevails, and we have a_ or h: o(/rae = o(/ra_, ti_ma/hte = ti/_ma=te, o)/rea = o)/rh.
c. u rarely contracts: u + i = u_ in i)xqu/_dion from i)xqui/dion small fish; u + e strictly never becomes u_ (273).

§52
(IV) Vowels and Diphthongs.—A vowel disappears before a diphthong beginning with the same sound: mna/ai = mnai=, file/ei = filei=, dhlo/oi = dhloi=.

§53
A vowel before a diphthong not beginning with the same sound generally contracts with the first vowel of the diphthong; the last vowel, if i, is subscript (5): ti_ma/ei = ti_ma=|, ti_ma/oimen = ti_mw=|men, lei/peai = lei/ph|, memnhoi/mhn = memnw/|mhn.
a. But e + oi becomes oi: file/oi = filoi=; o + ei, o + h| become oi: dhlo/ei = dhloi=, dhlo/h| = dhloi=.

§54
Spurious ei and ou are treated like e and o: ti_ma/ein = ti_ma=n, dhlo/ein = dhlou=n, ti_ma/ousi = ti_mw=si (but ti_ma/ei = ti_ma=| and dhlo/ei = dhloi_, since ei is here genuine; 6).

§55
(V) Three Vowels.—When three vowels come together, the last two unite first, and the resulting diphthong may be contracted with the first vowel: thus, ti_ma=| is from ti_ma-h| out of ti_ma-e（s）ai; but *perikle/ous from *perikle/eos.

§55 D
In Hom. dei=os of fear from de/e（s）-os the first two vowels unite.

§56
Irregularities.—A short vowel preceding a or any long vowel or diphthong, in contracts of the first and second declensions, is apparently absorbed (235, 290): xru/_sea = xru_sa= (not xru_sh=), a(plo/a = a(pla= (not a(plw=), by analogy to the a which marks the neuter plural, xru_se/ais = xru_sai=s. (So h(me/as = h(ma=s to show the -as of the accus. pl.) Only in the singular of the first declension does ea_ become h (or a_ after a vowel or r): xru_se/a_s = xru_sh=s, a)rgure/a| = a)rgura=|. In the third declension eea becomes ea_ (265); iea or uea becomes ia_ (ua_) or ih (uh). See 292 d.
Various special cases will be considered under their appropriate sections.

§57
The contraction of a long vowel with a short vowel sometimes does not occur by reason of analogy. Thus, nhi+/ (two syllables) follows nho/s, the older form of new/s (275). Sometimes the long vowel was shortened (39) or transfer of quantity took place (34).

§58
Vowels that were once separated by s or [iglide] (20) are often not contracted in dissyllabic forms, but contracted in polysyllabic forms. Thus, qe（s）o/s god, but *qouku_di/dhs Thucydides (qeo/s + ku=dos glory).

N.—The forms of r(i_go/w shiver contract from the stem r(i_gw- (yielding w or w|).

§59 D
Attic contracts more, Ionic less, than the other dialects. The laws of contraction often differ in the different dialects.
1. Ionic (Old and New) is distinguished by its absence of contraction. Thus, plo/os for plou=s voyage, tei/xea for tei/xh walls, o)ste/a for o)sta= bones, a)oidh/ for w)|dh/ song, a)ergo/s for a)_rgo/s idle. The Mss. of Hdt. generally leave ee, eh uncontracted; but this is probably erroneous in most cases. Ionic rarely contracts where Attic does not: o)gdw/konta for o)gdoh/konta eighty.
2. eo, ew, eou generally remain open in all dialects except Attic. In Ionic ew is usually monosyllabic. Ionic (and less often Doric) may contract eo, eou to eu: seu= from se/o of thee, fileu=si from file/ousi they love.
3. ao, a_o, aw, a_w contract to a_ in Doric and Aeolic. Thus, *)atrei/da_ from *)atrei/da_o, Dor. gela=nti they laugh from gela/onti, xwra=n from xwra/_wn of countries. In Aeolic oa_ = a_ in ba_qo/enti (Ion. bwqo/enti) = Att. bohqou=nti aiding (dative).
4. Doric contracts ae to h; ah to h; aei, ah| to h|. Thus, ni/_kh from ni/_kae conquer! o(rh=| from o(ra/ei and o(ra/h|; but a_e = a_ (a(/_lios from a)_e/lios, Hom. h)e/lios sun).
5. The Severer (and earlier) Doric contracts ee to h, and oe, oo to w. Thus, filh/tw from filee/tw, dhlw=te from dhlo/ete, i(/ppw from i(/ppo-o (230 D.); the Milder (and later) Doric and N. W. Greek contract to ei, and ou. Aeolic agrees with the Severer Doric.

## SYNIZESIS

§60
In poetry two vowels, or a vowel and a diphthong, belonging to successive syllables may unite to form a single syllable in pronunciation, but not in writing. Thus, be/lea missiles, po/lews city, *phlhi+a/dew son of Peleus, xru_se/w| golden. This is called Synizēsis (suni/zhsis settling together).

§61
Synizesis may occur between two words when the first ends in a long vowel or diphthong. This is especially the case with dh/ now, h)/ or, h)= (interrog.), mh/ not, e)pei/ since, e)gw/ I, w)= oh; as h)= ou' O 18.
a. The term synizesis is often restricted to cases where the first vowel is long. Where the first vowel is short, e, i were sounded nearly like y; u nearly like w. Cp. 44 a. The single syllable produced by synizesis is almost always long.

## CRASIS

§62
Crasis (kra=sis mingling) is the contraction of a vowel or diphthong at the end of a word with a vowel or diphthong beginning the following word. Over the syllable resulting from contraction is placed a ' called corōnis (korwni/s hook), as ta)/_lla from ta\ a)/lla the other things, the rest.
a. The coronis is not written when the rough breathing stands on the first word: o( a)/nqrwpos = a(/_nqrwpos.
b. Crasis does not occur when the first vowel may be elided. (Some editors write ta)/lla, etc.)

§63
Crasis occurs in general only between words that belong together; and the first of the two words united by crasis is usually the less important; as the article, relative pronoun (o(/, a(/), pro/, kai/, dh/, w)=. Crasis occurs chiefly in poetry.
a. It is rare in Hom., common in the dialogue parts of the drama (especially in comedy), and frequent in the orators.

§64

p, t, k become f, q, x when the next word begins with the rough breathing (124): th=| h(me/ra| = qh)me/ra| the day, kai\ oi( and the = xoi' (68 c).

§65
Iota subscript (5) appears in the syllable resulting from crasis only when the first syllable of the second word contains an i: e)gw\ oi)=da = e)gw)=|da I know (but tw=| o)rga/nw| = tw)rga/nw| the instrument, 68 a).

§66
The rules for crasis are in general the same as those for contraction (48 ff.). Thus, to\ o)/noma = tou)/noma the name, o( e)n = ou(n, w)= a)/ner = w)=ner oh man, pro\ e)/xwn = prou)/xwn excelling, to\ i(_ma/tion = qoi)ma/tion the cloak (64), a(\ e)gw/ = a(_gw/.
But the following exceptions are to be noted (67-69):

§67
A diphthong may lose its final vowel: oi( e)moi/ = ou(moi/, soi e)sti/ = sou)sti/, mou e)sti/ = mou)sti/. Cp. 43, 68.

§68
The final vowel or diphthong of the article, and of toi/, is dropped, and an initial a of the next word is lengthened unless it is the first vowel of a diphthong. The same rule applies in part to kai/.
a. Article.—o( a)nh/r = a(_nh/r, oi( a)/ndres = a(/_ndres, ai( a)gaqai/ = a(_gaqai/, h( a)gh/qeia = a(_lh/qeia, tou= a)ndro/s = ta)_ndro/s, tw=| a)ndri/ = ta)_ndri/, o( au)to/s = au(to/s the same, tou= au)tou= = tau)tou= of the same.
b. toi/.—toi\ a)/ra = ta)/_ra, me/ntoi a)/n = menta)/_n.
c. kai/.—(1) ai is dropped: kai\ au)to/s = kau)to/s, kai\ ou) = kou', kai\ h( = xh', kai\ oi( = xoi', kai\ i(keteu/ete = xi)_keteu/ete and ye beseech (64). (2) ai is contracted chiefly before e and ei: kai\ e)n = ka)_n, kai\ e)gw/ = ka)_gw/, kai\ e)s = ka)_s, kai\ ei)=ta = ka)=|ta (note however kai\ ei) = kei', kai\ ei)s = kei)s); also before o in kai\ o(/te = xw)/te. kai\ o(/pws = xw)/pws (64).
N.—The exceptions in 68 a-c to the laws of contraction are due to the desire to let the vowel of the more important word prevail: a(/_nhr, not w(nhr, because of a)nh/r.

§68 D
Hom. has w)/ristos = o( a)/ristos, wu)to/s = o( au)to/s. Hdt. has ou(/teros = o( e(/teros, w(nh/r = o( a)nh/r, w(utoi/ = oi( au)toi/, tw)uto/ = to\ au)to/, tw)utou= = tou= au)tou=, e(wutou= = e(/o au)tou=, w(=ndres = oi( a)/ndres. Doric has kh)pi/ = kai\ e)pi/.

§69
Most crasis forms of e(/teros other are derived from a(/teros, the earlier form: thus, o( e(/teros = a(/_teros, oi( e(/teroi = a(/_teroi; but tou= e(te/rou = qou)te/rou (64).

## ELISION

§70
Elision is the expulsion of a short vowel at the end of a word before a word beginning with a vowel. An apostrophe (') marks the place where the vowel is elided.
a)ll' (a\) a)/ge, e)/dwk' (a) e)nne/a, e)f' (= e)pi\) e(autou= (64), e)/xoim' (i) a)/n, ge/noit' (o) a)/n.
a. Elision is often not expressed to the eye except in poetry. Both inscriptions and the Mss. of prose writers are very inconsistent, but even where the elision is not expressed, it seems to have occurred in speaking; i.e. o(/de ei)=pe and o(/d' ei)=pe were spoken alike. The Mss. are of little value in such cases.

§71
Elision affects only unimportant words or syllables, such as particles, adverbs, prepositions, and conjunctions of two syllables (except peri/, a)/xri, me/xri, o(/ti 72 b, c), and the final syllables of nouns, pronouns, and verbs.
a. The final vowel of an emphatic personal pronoun is rarely elided.

§72
Elision does not occur in
a. Monosyllables, except such as end in e (te/, de/, ge/).
b. The conjunction o(/ti that? (o(/t' is o(/te when).
c. The prepositions pro/ before, a)/xri, me/xri until, and peri/ concerning (except before i).
d. The dative singular ending i of the third declension, and in si, the ending of the dative plural.
e. Words with final u.

§72 D
Absence of elision in Homer often proves the loss of v (3), as in kata\ a)/stu X 1. Epic admits elision in sa/ thy, r(a/, in the dat. sing. of the third decl., in -si and -ai in the personal endings, and in -nai, -sqai of the infinitive, and (rarely) in moi/, soi/, toi/. a)/na oh king, and a)/na = a)na/sthqi rise up, elide only once, i)de/ and never. Hdt. elides less often than Attic prose; but the Mss. are not a sure guide. peri/ sometimes appears as pe/r in Doric and Aeolic before words beginning with other vowels than i. o)cei=) o)du/nai *l 272. Cp. 148 D. 1.

§73
Except e)sti/ is, forms admitting movable n (134 a) do not suffer elision in prose. (But some cases of e in the perfect occur in Demosthenes.)

§73 D
In poetry a vowel capable of taking movable n is often cut off.

§74

ai in the personal endings and the infinitive is elided in Aristophanes; scarcely ever, if at all, in tragedy; its elision in prose is doubtful. oi is elided in tragedy in oi)/moi alas.

§75
Interior elision takes place in forming compound words. Here the apostrophe is not used. Thus, ou)dei/s no one from ou)de\ ei(=s, kaqora/w look down upon from kata\ o(ra/w, meqi/_hmi let go from meta\ i(/_hmi (124).
a. o(di/_, touti/_ this are derived from the demonstrative pronouns o(/de, tou=to + the deictic ending i_ (333 g).
b. Interior elision does not always occur in the formation of compounds. Thus, skhptou=xos sceptre-bearing from skhpto + oxos (i.e. soxos). Cp. 878.
c. On the accent in elision, see 174.

§75 D

Apocope (a)pokoph/ cutting off) occurs when a final short vowel is cut off before an initial consonant. In literature apocope is confined to poetry, but in the prose inscriptions of the dialects it is frequent. Thus, in Hom., as separate words and in compounds, a)/n, ka/t, pa/r (a)p, u(p rarely) for a)na/, kata/, para/ (a)po/, u(po/). Final t is assimilated to a following consonant (but katqanei=n to die, not kaqqanei=n, cp. 83 a); so final n by 91-95. Thus, a)lle/cai to pick up, a)\m po/non into the strife; ka/bbale threw down, ka/llipe left behind, kakkei/ontes lit. lying down, kaua/cais break in pieces, for kavva/cais = kat-va/cais, ka\d de/, kaddu=sai entering into, ka\p pedi/on through the plain, ka\g go/nu on the knee (kag not kang), ka\r r(o/on in the stream; u(bba/llein interrupt, a)ppe/myei will send away. When three consonants collide, the final consonant of the apocopate word is usually lost, as ka/ktane slew, from ka/kktane out of kat（e/）ktane. Apocope occurs rarely in Attic poetry. po/t for poti/ (= pro/s in meaning) is frequent in Doric and Boeotian.
N.—The shorter forms may have originated from elision.

## APHAERESIS (INVERSE ELISION)

§76
Aphaeresis (a)fa|i/resis taking away) is the elision of e at the beginning of a word after a word ending in a long vowel or diphthong. This occurs only in poetry, and chiefly after mh/ not, h)/ or. Thus, mh\ ) ntau=qa, h)\ ) me/, pare/cw ) mauto/n, au)th\ ) ch=lqen. In some texts editors prefer to adopt crasis (62) or synizesis (60). a is rarely elided thus.

## EUPHONY OF CONSONANTS

§77

Assimilation.—A consonant is sometimes assimilated to another consonant in the same word. This assimilation may be either partial, as in e)-pe/mf-qhn I was sent for e)-pemp-qhn (82), or complete, as in e)mme/nw I abide by for e)n-menw (94).
a. A preceding consonant is generally assimilated to a following consonant. Assimilation to a preceding consonant, as in o)/llu_mi I destroy for o)l-nu_-mi, is rare.

## DOUBLING OF CONSONANTS

§78
Attic has tt for ss of Ionic and most other dialects: pra/_ttw do for pra/_ssw, qa/latta sea for qa/lassa, krei/ttwn stronger for krei/sswn.
a. Tragedy and Thucydides adopt ss as an Ionism. On xari/essa see 114 a.
b. tt is used for that ss which is regularly formed by k or x and i (112), sometimes by t, q, and i (114). On tt in ) *attiko/s see 83 a.

§79
Later Attic has rr for rs of older Attic: qa/rros courage = qa/rsos, a)/rrhn male = a)/rshn.
a. But rs does not become rr in the dative plural (r(h/tor-si orators) and in words containing the suffix -sis for -tis (a)/r-sis raising).
b. Ionic and most other dialects have rs. rs in Attic tragedy and Thucydides is probably an Ionism. Xenophon has rs and rr.

§80
An initial r is doubled when a simple vowel is placed before it in inflection or composition. Thus, after the syllabic augment (429), e)/-rrei was flowing from r(e/w; and in kali/-rroos fair flowing. After a diphthong r is not doubled: eu)/-roos fair flowing.
a. This rr, due to assimilation of sr (e)/-rrei, kali/-rroos), or vr (e)rrh/qh was spoken), is strictly retained in the interior of a word; but simplified to single r when standing at the beginning, i.e. r(e/w is for rre/w. In composition (eu)/-roos) single r is due to the influence of the simplified initial sound.
b. A different rr arises from assimilation of rs (79), re (sounded like py, 44, 117), and nr (95).

§80 D
In Hom. and even in prose r may remain single after a vowel: e)/-rece did from r(e/zw, kalli/-roos. So i)so/-rropos and i)so/-ropos (by analogy to r(o/pos) equally balanced. e)k xeirw=n be/lea_ r(e/on M 159 represents be/lea rre/on. Cp. 146 D.

§81

b, g, d are not doubled in Attic (cp. 75 D.). In gg the first g is nasal (19 a). f, x, q are not doubled in Attic; instead, we have pf, kx, tq as in *sapfw/ Sappho, *ba/kxos Bacchus, ) *atqi/s (Atthis) Attic. Cp. 83 a.

§81 D
1. Hom. has many cases of doubled liquids and nasals: e)/llabe took, a)/llhktos unceasing, a)/mmoros without lot in, filommeidh/s fond of smiles, a)ga/nnifos very snowy, a)rgenno/s white, e)/nnepe relate. These forms are due to the assimilation of s and l, m, or n. Thus, a)ga/-nnifos is from a)ga-snifos, cp. sn in snow.
2. Doubled stops: o(/tti that (svod-ti), o(ppo/te as (svod-pote), e)/ddeise feared (e)dveise).
3. ss in me/ssos middle (for meqios medius, 114), o)pi/ssw backward, in the datives of s-stems, as e)/pessi (250 D. 2), and in verbs with stems in s (tre/sse).
4. One of these doubled consonants may be dropped without lengthening the preceding vowel: ) *oduseu/s from ) *odusseu/s, me/sos, o)pi/sw. So in ) *axileu/s from ) *axilleu/s. On dd, bb, see 75 D. Aeolic has many doubled consonants due to assimilation (37 D. 3).

## CONSONANTS WITH CONSONANTS

## STOPS BEFORE STOPS

§82
A labial or a palatal stop (16) before a dental stop （t, d, q） must be of the same order (16).
a. bt, ft become pt: (tetri_b-tai) te/tri_ptai has been rubbed from tri/_b-w rub; (gegraf-tai) ge/graptai has been written from gra/f-w write. gt, xt become kt: (leleg-tai) le/lektai) has been said from le/g-w say; (bebrex-tai) be/brektai has been moistened from bre/x-w moisten.
b. pd, fd become bd: (klep-dhn) kle/bdhn by stealth from kle/p-t-w steal; (grafdhn) gra/bdhn scraping from gra/f-w write (originally scratch, scrape). kd becomes gd: (plek-dhn) ple/gdhn entwined from ple/k-w plait.
c. pq, bq become fq: (e)pemp-qhn) e)pe/mfqhn I was sent from pe/mp-w send; (e)tri_b-qh) e)tri/_fqh it was rubbed (tri/_b-w rub). kq, gq become xq: (e)plek-qh) e)ple/xqh it was plaited (ple/k-w plait); (e)leg-qh) e)le/xqh it was said (le/g-w say).
N. 1.—Cp. e(pta/ seven, e(/bdomos seventh, e(fqh/meros lasting seven days.
N. 2.—But e)k out of remains unchanged: e)kdi/dwmi surrender, e)kqe/w run out (104).

§83
A dental stop before another dental stop becomes s.
a)nusto/s practicable for a)nut-tos from a)nu/tw complete, i)/ste you know for i)d-te, oi)=sqa thou knowest for oi)d-qa, pe/peistai has been persuaded for pepeiq-tai, e)pei/sqhn I was persuaded for e)peiq-qhn.
a. tt, tq remain unchanged in ) *attiko/s, ) *atqi/s Attic, and in katqanei=n die (75 D., 81). So tt for ss (78).

§84
Any stop standing before a stop other than t, d, q, or in other combination than pf, kx, tq (81) is dropped, as in keko/mi（d）-ka I have brought. g before k, g, or x is gamma-nasal (19 a), not a stop.

## STOPS BEFORE M

§85
Before m, the labial stops (p, b, f) become m; the palatal stops k, x become g; g before m remains unchanged.
o)/mma eye for o)p-ma (cp. o)/pwpa), le/leimmai I have been left for leleip-mai from lei/p-w leave, te/tri_mmai for tetri_b-mai from tri/_b-w rub, ge/grammai for gegrafmai from gra/f-w write, pe/plegmai for peplek-mai from ple/k-w plait, te/teugmai for teteux-mai from teu/x-w build.
a. k and x may remain unchanged before m in a noun-suffix: a)k-mh/ edge, drax-mh/ drachma. km remains when brought together by phonetic change (128 a), as in ke/-kmh-ka am wearied (ka/m-nw).

§85 a D
So in Hom. i)/kmenos favoring (i(ka/_nw), a)kaxme/nos sharpened.
b. ggm and mmm become gm and mm. Thus, e)lh/legmai for e)lhlegg-mai from e)lhlegx-mai (e)le/gx-w convict), pe/pemmai for pepemm-mai from pepemp-mai (pe/mp-w send).

§86
A dental stop (t, d, q) before m often appears to become s. Thus, h)/nusmai for h)nut-mai (a)nu/t-w complete), pe/frasmai for pefrad-mai (fra/zw declare), pe/peismai for pepeiq-mai (pei/q-w persuade).

§87
On the other hand, since these stops are actually retained in many words, such as e)retmo/n oar, po/tmos fate, a)riqmo/s number, s must be explained as due to analogy. Thus, h)/nusmai, pe/frasmai, pe/peismai have taken on the ending -smai by analogy to -stai where s is in place (pe/frastai for pefrad-tai). So i)/smen we know (Hom. i)/dmen) follows i)/ste you know (for i)d-te). o)smh/ odor stands for o)d-smh.

## CONSONANTS BEFORE N

§88

b regularly and f usually become m before n. Thus, semno/s revered for seb-nos (se/b-omai), stumno/s firm for stuf-nos (stu/_fw contract).

§89

gi/gnomai become, gignw/skw know become gi/_nomai, gi_nw/skw in Attic after 300 B.C., in New Ionic, late Doric, etc.

§90

ln becomes ll in o)/llu_mi destroy for o)l-nu_mi.
ln is kept in pi/lnamai approach. On sigma before n see 105.

§90 D
Aeolic bo/lla council, attic boulh/ and Doric bwla/_ (with compensatory lengthening), probably for bolna_.

## N BEFORE CONSONANTS

§91

n before p, b, f, y becomes m: e)mpi/_ptw fall into for e)n-pi_ptw, e)mba/llw throw in for e)n-ballw, e)mfai/nw exhibit for e)n-fainw, e)/myu_xos alive for e)n-yu_xos.

§92

n before k, g, x, c becomes g-nasal (19 a): e)gkale/w bring a charge for e)n-kalew, e)ggra/fw inscribe for e)n-grafw, sugxe/w pour together for sun-xew, sugcu/_w grind up for sun-ci_w.

§93

n before t, d, q remains unchanged. Here n may represent m: bron-th/ thunder (bre/m-w roar).

§94

n before m becomes m: e)/mmetros moderate for e)n-metros, e)mme/nw abide by for e)n-menw.
a. Verbs in -nw may form the perfect middle in -smai (489 h); as in pe/fasmai (from fai/nw show) for pefan-mai (cp. pe/fag-ka, pe/fan-tai).
b. Here n does not become s; but the ending -smai is borrowed from verbs with stems in a dental (as pe/frasmai, on which see 87).

§95

n before l, r is assimilated (ll, rr): su/llogos concourse for sun-logos, surre/w flow together for sun-rew.

§96

n before s is dropped and the preceding vowel is lengthened (e to ei, o to ou, 37): me/la_s black for melan-s, ei(=s one for e(n-s, tiqei/s placing for tiqen（t）-s, tou/s for to/n-s.
a. But in the dative plural n before -si appears to be dropped without compensatory lengthening: me/lasi for melan-si, dai/mosi for daimon-si divinities, fresi/ for fren-si mind. But see 250 N.

## CONSONANTS BEFORE *s

§97
With s a labial stop forms y, a palatal stop forms c.

lei/yw shall leave for leip-swkh=ruc herald for khruk-s

tri/_yw shall rub “ tri_b-swa)/cw shall lead “ a)g-sw

gra/yw shall write “ graf-swbh/c cough “ bhx-s
a. The only stop that can stand before s is p or k, hence b, f become p, and g, x become k. Thus, graf-sw, a)g-sw become grap-sw, a)k-sw.

§98
A dental stop before s is assimilated (ss) and one s is dropped.
sw/masi bodies for swmassi out of swmat-si, posi/ feet for possi/ out of pod-si, o)/rni_si birds for o)rni_ssi out of o)rni_q-si. So pa/sxw suffer for passxw out of paq-skw (cp. paq-ei=n and 126).
a. d and q become t before s: pod-si, o)rni_q-si become pot-si, o)rni_t-si.

§98 D
Hom. often retains ss: possi/, da/ssasqai for dat-sasqai (date/omai divide).

§99

k is dropped before sk in dida（k）-skw teach (didak-to/s taught).
p is dropped before sf in bla（p）s-fhmi/a_ evil-speaking.

§100

nt, nd, nq before s form nss (98), then ns, finally n is dropped and the preceding vowel is lengthened (37).
pa=si all for pans-si out of pant-si, tiqei=si placing for tiqens-si out of tiqent-si. So gi/ga_s giant for gigant-s, lu/_ousi loosing for lu_ont-si, spei/sw shall make libation for spend-sw, pei/somai shall suffer for penq-somai (pe/nqos grief).

§101

a. e)n in, su/n with in composition are treated as follows:
e)n before r, s, or z keeps its n: e)/n-ruqmos in rhythm, e)n-skeua/zw prepare, e)nzeu/gnu_mi yoke in.
su/n before s and a vowel becomes sus-: sus-sw/|zw help to save. before s and a consonant or z, becomes su-: su-skeua/zw pack up, su/-zugos yoked together.
b. pa=n, pa/lin before s either keep n or assimilate n to s: pa/n-sofos all-wise, pan-se/lhnos or passe/lhnos the full moon, pali/n-skios thick-shaded, pali/s-sutos rushing back.

§102
On rs see 79 a. ls is retained in a)/lsos precinct. rs, ls may become r, l with lengthening of the preceding vowel: h)/geira I collected, h)/ggeila I announced for h)ger-sa, h)ggel-sa.

§102 D
Hom. has w)=rse incited, ke/rse cut, e)e/lsai to coop up, ke/lsai to put to shore.

## *s BEFORE CONSONANTS

§103
Sigma between consonants is dropped: h)/ggel（s）qe you have announced, gegra/f（s）qai to have written, e(/k（s）mhnos of six months (e(/c six, mh/n month).
a. But in compounds s is retained when the second part begins with s: e)/n-spondos included in a truce. compounds in dus- ill omit s before a word beginning with s: du/sxistos hard to cleave for dus-sxistos (sxi/zw).

§104

e)c out of (= e)ks) drops s in composition before another consonant, but usually retains its k unaltered: e)ktei/nw stretch out, e)kdi/dwmi surrender, e)kfe/rw carry out, e)kqu/_w sacrifice, e)ksw/|zw preserve from danger (not e)cw/|zw), e)kmanqa/nw learn thoroughly. Cp. 82 N. 2, 136.

§105

s before m or n usually disappears with compensatory lengthening (37) as in ei)mi/ for e)s-mi. But sm stays if m belongs to a suffix and in compounds of dus- ill: dus-menh/s hostile.
a. Assimilation takes place in *pelopo/nnhsos for *pe/lopos nh=sos island of Pelops, e(/nnu_mi clothe for e(s-nu_mi (Ionic ei(/nu_mi), e)/rrei was flowing for e)-srei, 80 a.

§105 D

s is assimilated in Aeol. and Hom. e)/mmenai to be for e)s-menai (ei)=nai), a)rgenno/s white for a/rges-nos, e)rebenno/s dark (e)rebes-nos, cp. )/ *erebos), a)/mme we, u)/mmes you (a)sme, u)smes). Cp. 81 D.

§106

sd becomes z in some adverbs denoting motion towards. Thus, ) *aqh/naze for ) *aqh/nas-de Athens-wards (26, 342 a).

§106 D
Aeolic has sd for medial z in u)/sdos branch (o)/zos), meli/sdw make melody (meli/zw).

§107
Two sigmas brought together by inflection become s: be/lesi for be/les-si missiles, e)/pesi for e)/pes-si words (98), tele/sai for tele/s-sai (from tele/w accomplish, stem teles-).
a. ss when = tt (78) never becomes s.

§107 D
Homer often retains ss: be/lessi, e)/pessi, tele/ssai.

§108
Many of the rules for the euphony of consonants were not established in the classical period. Inscriptions show a much freer practice, either marking the etymology, as su/nmaxos for su/mmaxos ally (94), e)nkalei=n for e)gkalei=n to bring a charge (92), or showing the actual pronunciation (phonetic spelling), as to\g (= to\n) kako/n (92), th\m (= th\n) boulh/n (91), to\l (= to\n) lo/gon, e)/gdosis for e)/kdosis surrendering (104), e)xfe/rw, e)xqu/_w for e)kfe/rw, e)kqu/_w (104).

## CONSONANTS WITH VOWELS

## CONSONANTS BEFORE I AND E

§109
Numerous changes occur before the semivowel [iglide] (= y, 20) before a vowel. This y is often indicated by the sign [iglide]. In 110-117 (except in 115) [iglide] is = y.

§110

l[iglide] becomes ll: a)/llos for a)lios Lat. alius, a(/llomai for a(l[iglide]omai Lat. salio, fu/llon for ful[iglide]on Lat. folium.

§111
After an, on, ar, or, [iglide] is shifted to the preceding syllable, forming ain, oin, air, oir. This is called Epenthesis (e)pe/nqesis insertion).
fai/nw show for fan-[iglide]w, me/laina black for melan-[iglide]a, spai/rw gasp for spar-[iglide]w, moi=ra fate for mor-[iglide]a. (So klai/w weep for klav-[iglide]w 38 a.) On i after en, er, in, ir, un, ur, see 37 a.

§112

k[iglide], x[iglide] become tt (= ss 78): fula/ttw guard for fulak-[iglide]w (cp. fulakh/ guard), tara/ttw disturb for tarax-[iglide]w (cp. taraxh/ disorder).

§113
(I) t[iglide], q[iglide] after long vowels, diphthongs, and consonants become s; after short vowels t[iglide], q[iglide] become ss (not = tt 78), which is simplified to s.
ai)=sa fate from ai)t-[iglide]a, pa=sa all from pant-[iglide]a, me/sos middle (Hom. me/ssos) from meq-[iglide]os (cp. Lat. med-ius), to/sos so great (Hom. to/ssos) from tot-[iglide]os (cp. Lat. toti-dem).
a. In the above cases t[iglide] passed into ts. Thus pant-[iglide]a, pantsa, panssa, pa/nsa (Cretan, Thessalian), pa=sa (37 D. 3).

§114
(II) t[iglide], q[iglide] become tt (= ss 78): me/litta bee from melit-ia (cp. me/li, -itos honey), koru/ttw equip from koruq-[iglide]w (cp. ko/rus, -uqos helmet).
a. xari/essa graceful and other feminine adjectives in -essa are poetical, and therefore do not assume the native Attic prose form in tt. But see 299 c.
b. tt from t[iglide], q[iglide] is due to analogy, chiefly of tt from k[iglide].

§115

t before final i often becomes s. Thus, ti/qhsi places for ti/qhti; also in plou/sios rich for plout-ios (cp. plou=tos wealth).
a. nt before final i becomes ns, which drops n: e)/xousi they have for e)/xonti (37).

§115 D
Ioric often retains t (ti/qhti, e)/xonti). se/ is not from (Dor.) te/ (cp. Lat. te), no is soi/ from toi/.

§116

d[iglide] between vowels and g[iglide] after a vowel form z: thus, e)lpi/zw hope for e)lpid-[iglide]w, pezo/s on foot for ped-[iglide]os (cp. ped-i/o-n ground), a(rpa/zw seize for a(rpag-[iglide]w (cp. a(/rpac rapacious). After a consonant g[iglide] forms d: e)/rdw work from e)rg-[iglide]w.

§117

p[iglide] becomes pt, as in xale/ptw oppress from xalep-[iglide]w. r[eglide] becomes rr in *borra=s from *bore/a_s Boreas. Here e was sounded nearly like y (44, 61 a).

## DISAPPEARANCE OF *s AND *v

§118
The spirant s with a vowel before or after it is often lost. Its former presence is known by earlier Greek forms or from the cognate languages.

§119
Initial s before a vowel becomes the rough breathing.
e(pta/ seven, Lat. septem; h(/misus half, Lat. semi-; i(/sthmi put for si-sth-mi, Lat. si-st-o; ei(po/mhn I followed from e)-sep-o-mhn, Lat. sequor.
a. When retained, this s is due to phonetic change (as su/n for cu/n, si_gh/ silence for s[uglide]i_gh Grm. schweigen), or to analogy. On the loss of ( see 125 e.

§120
Between vowels s is dropped.
ge/nous of a race from gene（s）-os, Lat. gener-is, lu/_ei thou loosest from lu/_h| for lu_e-（s）ai, e)lu/_ou from e)lu_e-（s）o thou didst loose for thyself, tiqei=o for tiqei=so, ei)/hn from e)s-ih-n Old Lat. siem, a)lh/qe-ia truth from a)lhqes-ia.
a. Yet s appears in some -mi forms (ti/qesai, i(/staso), and in qrasu/s = qarsu/s 128. s between vowels is due to phonetic change (as s for ss 107, plou/sios for ploutios 115) or to analogy (as e)/lu_sa for e)lu_a, modelled on e)deik-s-a), cp. 35 c.

§121

s usually disappears in the aorist of liquid verbs (active and middle) with lengthening of the preceding vowel (37): e)/steila I sent for e)stel-sa, e)/fhna I showed for e)fan-sa, e)fh/nato for e)fan-sato. Cp. 102.

§122
Digamma (3) has disappeared in Attic.
The following special cases are to be noted:
a. In nouns of the third declension with a stem in au, eu, or on (43). Thus, nau=s ship, gen. new/s from nhv-o/s, basileu/s king, gen. basile/ws from basilh=v-os (34).
b. In the augment and reduplication of verbs beginning with v: ei)rgazo/mhn I worked from e)-vergazomhn, e)/oika am like from vevoika. Cp. 431, 443.
c. In verbs in ew for evw: r(e/w I flow, fut. r(eu/-somai.

§123
Some words have lost initial sv: h(du/s sweet (Lat. sua（d）vis), ou(=, oi(=, e(/ him, o(/s his (Lat. suus), e)/qos custom, h)=qos character (Lat. con-suetus).

§123 D
Hom. eu)/ade pleased stands for e)vvade from e)svade.

## ASPIRATION

§124
A smooth stop (p, t, k), brought before the rough breathing by elision, crasis, or in forming compounds, is made rough, becoming an aspirate (f, q, x). Cp. 16 a.
a)f' ou(= for a)p（o\) ou(=, nu/xq' o(/lhn for nu/kt（a) o(/lhn (82); qa)/_teron the other (69), qoi)ma/tion for to\ i(_ma/tion the cloak (66); meqi/_hmi let go for met（a/) i(/_hmi, au)qa/_dhs selfwilled from au)to/s self and a(dei=n please.
a. A medial rough breathing, passing over r, roughens a preceding smooth stop: frouro/s watchman from pro-o(ros, frou=dos gone from pro/ and o(do/s, te/qrippon four-horse chariot (tetr + i(/ppos).

§124 D
New Ionic generally leaves p, t, k before the rough breathing: a)p' ou(=, meti/hmi, tou)/teron. But in compounds (9 D.) f, q, x may appear: me/qodos method (meta/ after + o(do/s way).

§125
Two rough stops beginning successive syllables of the same word are avoided in Greek. A rough stop is changed into a smooth stop when the following syllable contains a rough stop.
a. In reduplication (441) initial f, q, x are changed to p, t, k. Thus, pe/feuga for fe-feu-ga perfect of feu/gw flee, ti/-qh-mi place for qi-qh-mi, ke/-xh-na for xe-xh-na perf. of xa/skw gape.
b. In the first aorist passive imperative -qi becomes -ti after -qh-, as in lu/-qh-ti for lu-qh-qi; elsewhere -qi is retained (gnw=qi).
c. In the aorist passive, qe- and qu- are changed to te- and tu- in e)-te/-qhn was placed (ti/qhmi) and e)-tu/-qhn was sacrificed (qu/_w).
d. From the same objection to a succession of rough stops are due a)mpe/xw a)mpi/sxw clothe for a)mf-, e)ke-xeiri/a_ truce for e)xe-xeiria_ (from e)/xw and xei/r).
e. The rough breathing, as an aspirate (16 a), often disappeared when either of the two following syllables contains f, q, or x. e)/xw have stands for e)/xw = sexw (119, cp. e)/-sxon), the rough changing to the smooth breathing before a rough stop. The rough breathing reappears in the future e(/cw. Cp. i)/sxw restrain for i(sxw from si-sx-w, e)/deqlon foundation, but e(/dos seat, Lat. sedes.
f. In qri/c hair, gen. sing. trix-o/s for qrixos, dat. pl. qrici/; taxu/s swift, comparative taxi/_wn (rare) or qa/_ttwn (qa/_sswn) from qaxi_wn (112).
g. In taf- (ta/fos tomb), pres. qa/p-t-w bury, fut. qa/yw, perf. te/qam-mai (85); tre/fw nourish, fut. qre/yw, perf. te/-qram-mai; tre/xw run, fut. qre/comai; truf- (trufh/ delicacy), pres. qru/ptw enfeeble, fut. qru/yw; tu/_fw smoke, perf. te/-qu_m-mai.
N.—The two rough stops remain unchanged in the aorist passive e)qre/fqhn was nourished, e)qru/fqhn was enfeebled, e)fa/nqhn was shown forth, w)rqw/qhn was set upright, e)qe/lxqhn was charmed, e)kaqa/rqhn was purified; in the perfect inf. pefa/nqai, kekaqa/rqai, teqa/fqai; in the imperatives gra/fhqi be written, stra/fhqi turn about, fa/qi say.

§126

Transfer of Aspiration.—Aspiration may be transferred to a following syllable: pa/sxw for paq-skw (cp. 98).

§126 D
Hdt. has e)nqau=ta there (e)ntau=qa), e)nqeu=ten thence (e)nteu=qen), kiqw/n tunic (xitw/n).

§127
Some roots show variation between a final smooth and a rough stop; de/xomai receive, dwrodo/kos bribe-taker; a)lei/fw anoint, li/pos fat; ple/kw weave, ploxuo/s braid of hair; and in the perfect, as h)=xa from a)/gw lead.

§127 D
Hom. and Hdt. have au)=tis again (au)=qis), ou)ki/ not (ou)xi/). All the dialects except Attic have de/komai.

## VARIOUS CONSONANT CHANGES

§128

Metathesis (transposition).—A vowel and a consonant often exchange places: *pnu/c the Pnyx, gen. *pukno/s, ti/ktw bear for ti-tk-w (cp. tek-ei=n).
a. Transposition proper does not occur where we have to do with ar, ra = ṛ (20, 35 b) as in qa/rsos and qra/sos courage; or with syncope (44 b) due to early shifting of accent, as in pe/t-omai fly, pte-ro/n wing; or where a long vowel follows the syncopated root, as in te/m-nw te/-tmh-ka I have cut.
In be/blhka I have thrown (ba/llw throw), blh is formed from bele found in be/le-mnon missile.

§128 D
Hom. kradi/h, kardi/h heart, ka/rtistos best (kra/tistos), ba/rdistos slowest (bradu/s), drato/s and -dartos from de/rw flay, e)/-drakon saw from de/rkomai see.

§129

Dissimilation.—a. l sometimes becomes r when l appears in the same word: a)rgale/os painful for a)lgaleos (a)/lgos pain).
b. A consonant (usually r) sometimes disappears when it occurs also in the adjoining syllable: dru/faktos railing for dru-fraktos (lit. fenced by wood).
c. Syllabic dissimilation or syncope occurs when the same or two similar syllables containing the same consonant succeed each other: a)mforeu/s a jar for a)mfi-foreus, qa/rsunos bold for qarso-sunos. This is often called haplology.
d. See also under 99, 125 a, b.

§130

Development.—d is developed between n and r, as in a)ndro/s of a man for a)nros from a)nh/r (cp. cinder with Lat. cineris); b is developed between m and r (or l), as in meshmbri/a_ midday, south from mes-hmria_ for mes-hmeria_ from me/sos middle and h(me/ra_ day (cp. chamber with Lat. camera).

§130 D
So in Hom. me/-mblw-ka have gone from mlw from mol- in e)/-mol-o-n (128 a). At the beginning of words this m is dropped; thus, blw/skw go, broto/s mortal for mbro-tos (root mro-, mor-, as in mor-tuus). In composition m remains, as in a)/-mbrotos immortal; but a)/-brotos immortal is formed from broto/s.

§131
Labials and dentals often correspond: poinh/ and ti/sis retribution; fo/nos murder, qei/nw strike. p and k: ai)po/los goat-herd, bouko/los ox-herd. pt for t is found in pto/lemos war, pto/lis city for po/lemos, po/lis. Cp. Neoptolemus and Ptolemy. So xq and x in xqw/n ground, xamai/ on the ground.

§132
The dialects often show consonants different from Attic in the same or kindred words.

§132 D

t for s: Doric tu/, toi/, te/, dia_kati/oi (dia_ko/sioi), vi/_kati (ei)/kosi), *poteida/_n (*poseidw/n).
s “ t: Doric sa/_meron to-day (th/meron Attic, sh/meron Ionic).
k “ p: Ionic (not Hom.) ko/te when, ko/teros which of two? o(/kws, ko/sos, kh=.

p “ t: Hom. pi/sures, Aeol. pe/ssures four (te/ttares); Aeol. ph/lui far off (cp. thlo/se), pe/mpe five (pe/nte).

f “ q: Hom. fh/r centaur (qh/r beast).
