## FINAL CONSONANTS

§133
No consonant except n, r, or s (including c and y) can stand at the end of a Greek word. All other consonants are dropped.
a. Exceptions are the proclitics (179) e)k out of, derived from e)c (cp. 104, 136), and ou)k not, of which ou) is another form (137).
b. Examples of dropped final consonants: sw=ma body for swmat (gen. sw/matos); pai= oh boy for paid (gen. paid-o/s); ga/la milk for galakt (gen. ga/lakt-os); fe/ron bearing for feront (gen. fe/ront-os); kh=r heart for khrd, cp. kard-i/a_; a)/llo for a)l[iglide]od (110), cp. Lat. aliud; e)/fere- (t) was carrying, e)/fero-n (t) were carrying (464 c, e).
c. An original final m preceded by a vowel becomes n, cp. i(/ppon with Lat. equum. So e(/n one from e(m (349 a), Lat. sem-el, a(/ma once.

## MOVABLE CONSONANTS

§134

Movable N may be added at the end of a word when the next word begins with a vowel. Movable n may be annexed to words ending in -si; to the third person singular in -e; and to e)sti/ is.
Thus, pa=sin e)/legen e)kei=na he said that to everybody (but pa=si le/gousi tau=ta), le/gousin e)moi/ they speak to me (but le/gousi/ moi), e)/stin a)/llos there is another (187 b), ) *aqh/nhsin h)=san they were at Athens.
a. Except e)sti/, words that add n do not elide their final vowel (73).
b. Verbs in -ew never (in Attic) add -n to the 3 sing. of the contracted form: eu)= e)poi/ei au)to/n he treated him well. But h)/ei went and pluperfects (as h)/|dei knew) may add n.
N.—Movable n is called n e)felkustiko/n (dragging after).

§134 D
Hom. has e)gw/ (n) I, a)/mmi (n) to us, u)/mmi (n) to you, sfi/ (n) to them. The suffixes -fi and -qe vary with -fin and -qen: qeo/fi（n), pro/sqe（n). Also ke/（n) = Attic a)/n, nu/ (n) now. The Mss. of Hdt. avoid movable n, but it occurs in Ionic inscriptions. Hdt. often has -qe for -qen (pro/sqe before, o)/pisqe behind).

§135
Movable n is usually written at the end of clauses, and at the end of a verse in poetry. To make a syllable long by position (144) the poets add n before words beginning with a consonant. Prose inscriptions frequently use n before a consonant.

§136

Movable *s appears in ou(/tws thus, e)c out of, before vowels, ou(/tw, ek/ before consonants. Thus, ou(/tws e)poi/ei he acted thus but ou(/tw poiei= he acts thus; e)c a)gora=s but e)k th=s a)gora=s out of the market-place.
a. eu)qu/s means straightway, eu)qu/ straight towards.

§136 D
Several adverbs often omit s without much regard to the following word: a)mfi/ about, a)mfi/s (poet.), me/xri, a)/xri until (rarely me/xris, a)/xris), a)tre/mas and a)tre/ma quietly, polla/kis often (polla/ki Hom., Hdt.).

§137

ou)k not is used before the smooth breathing, ou)x (cp. 124) before the rough breathing: ou)k o)li/goi, ou)x h(du/s. Before all consonants ou) is written: ou) polloi/, ou) r(a/|dios. Standing alone or at the end of its clause ou) is written ou)/ (rarely ou)/k), as pw=s ga\r ou)/; for how not? Cp. 180 a.
a. A longer form is ou)xi/ (Ion. ou)ki/) used before vowels and consonants.
b. mhke/ti no longer derives its k from the analogy of ou)ke/ti no longer.

## SYLLABLES AND THEIR QUANTITY

§138
There are as many syllables in a Greek word as there are separate vowels or diphthongs: thus, a)-lh/-qei-a truth.

§139
The last syllable is called the ultima; the next to the last syllable is called the penult (paen-ultima almost last); the one before the penult is called the antepenult (ante-paen-ultima).

§140
In pronouncing Greek words and in writing (at the end of the line) the rules commonly observed are these:
a. A single consonant standing between two vowels in one word belongs with the second vowel: a)/-gw, so-fi/-zw.
b. Any group of consonants that can begin a word, and a group formed by a stop with m or n, and by mn, belongs with the second vowel: tu/-ptw, o)/-gdoos, a)/-stron, e)/-xqos; pra=-gma, e)/-qnos, li/-mnh.
c. A group of consonants that cannot begin a word is divided between two syllables: a)/n-qos, e)l-pi/s, e)/r-gma. Doubled consonants are divided: qa/lat-ta.
d. Compounds divide at the point of union: ei)s-fe/rw, pros-fe/rw; a)n-a/gw, ei)sa/gw, sun-e/xw. (But the ancients often wrote a)-na/gw, ei)-sa/gw, pro-selqei=n, e)-ca/gw, du-sa/restos.)
e. s, when followed by one or more consonants, is either attached to the preceding vowel (a)/-ris-tos), or, with the consonant, begins the following syllable (a)/-ri-stos). (The ancients were not consistent, and there is evidence for the pronunciation a)/-ris-stos.)
f. The ancients divided e)k tou/tou as e)-k tou/-tou. This practice is now abandoned.

§141
A syllable ending in a vowel is said to be open; one ending in a consonant is closed. Thus, in mh/-thr mother the first syllable is open, the second closed.

## QUANTITY OF SYLLABLES

§142
A syllable is short when it contains a short vowel followed by a vowel or a single consonant: qe-o/s god, e)-no/-mi-sa I thought.

§143
A syllable is long by nature when it contains a long vowel or a diphthong: xw/-ra_ country, dou=-los slave.

§144
A syllable is long by position when its vowel precedes two consonants or a double consonant: i(/ppos horse, e)c out of.
a. One or both of the two consonants lengthening a final syllable by position may belong to the next word: a)/llo_s poli/_ths, a)/llo_ kth=ma.
b. Length by position does not affect the natural quantity of a vowel. Thus, both le/-cw I shall say and lh/-cw I shall cease have the first syllable long by position; but the first vowel is short in le)cw, long in lh/cw.

§144 D

v may be one of the two consonants: pro/s (v) oi)=kon (¯ ¯ ˘).

§145
A stop with a liquid after a short vowel need not make the preceding syllable long by position. A syllable containing a short vowel before a stop and a liquid is common (either short or long). When short, such syllables are said to have weak position.
Thus, in da/kru, patro/s, o(/plon, te/knon, ti/ dra=| the first syllable is either long or short as the verse requires. In Homer the syllable before a stop with a liquid is usually long; in Attic it is usually short.
a. The stop and the liquid making weak position must stand in the same word or in the same part of a compound. Thus, in e)k-lu/_w I release the first syllable is always long, but in e)/-klue he heard it is common.
b. b, g, d before m, or n, and usually before l, make the preceding syllable long by position. Thus, a(gno/s (¯˘) pure, bibli/on (×˘˘) book.
N.—‘Common’ quantity has been explained as due to a difference in syllabic division. Thus, in te/_knon, the first syllable is closed (te/k-non); while in te^/knon the first syllable is open (te/-knon). Cp. 141.

§146
The quantity of most syllables is usually apparent. Thus, syllables
a. with h, w, or a diphthong, are long.
b. with e, o, before a vowel or a single consonant, are short.
c. with e, o, before two consonants, or a double consonant, are long.
d. with a, i, u, before two consonants, or a double consonant, are long.
N.—But syllables with e, o, or a, i, u before a stop and a liquid may be short (145). Cp. also 147 c.

§146 D
In Hom. an initial liquid, nasal, and digamma (3) was probably doubled in pronunciation when it followed a short syllable carrying the rhythmic accent. Here a final short vowel appears in a long syllable: e)ni\ mega/roisi (˘[macrdot]˘˘[macrdot]˘), cp. 28 D. The lengthening is sometimes due to the former presence of s or v before the liquid or nasal: o(/te lh/ceiev (˘[macrdot]¯[macrdot]˘) (cp. a)/llhktos unceasing for a)-slhktos), te r(h/cein ([macrdot]¯[macrdot]) (cp. a)/rrhktos unbroken for a)-vrhktos). (Cp. 80 a, 80 D., 81 D.)

§147
The quantity of syllables containing a, i, u before a vowel or a single consonant must be learned by observation, especially in poetry. Note, however, that a, i, u are always long
a. when they have the circumflex accent: pa=s, u(_mi=n.
b. when they arise from contraction (59) or crasis (62): ge/ra_ from ge/raa, a)_rgo/s idle from a)-ergos (but a^)rgo/s bright), ka)_gw/ from kai/ e)gw/.
c. i and u are generally short before c (except as initial sounds in augmented forms, 435) and a, i, u before z. Thus, kh=ru^c, e)kh/ru^ca, pni^/cw, a(rpa^/zw, e)lpi^/zw.
d. as, is, and us are long when n or nt has dropped out before s (96, 100).
e. The accent often shows the quantity (163, 164, 170).

§147 D

a, i, u in Hom. sometimes show a different quantity than in Attic. Thus, Att. ka^lo/s, ti^/nw, fqa^/nw, lu/_w, i(/_hmi, Hom. ka_lo/s, ti/_nw, fqa/_nw (28), and lu^/w and i(/^hmi usually.

§148
A vowel standing before another vowel in a Greek word is not necessarily short (as it usually is in classical Latin).

§148 D
1. In Hom., and sometimes in the lyric parts of the drama, a syllable ending in a long vowel or diphthong is shortened before an initial vowel: a)/cw e(lw/n ([macrdot]˘˘[macrdot]), eu)/xetai ei)=nai ([macrdot]˘˘[macrdot]¯), klu=qi/ meu a)rguro/toc' ([macrdot]:˘˘[macrdot]˘˘[macrdot]). Here i and u have become semivowels (20, 43); thus, eu)/xeta | yei)=nai, cp. 67. -a|, -h|, -w| were shortened like a_, h, w. Thus, a)spe/tw| o)/mbrw| ([macrdot]˘˘[macrdot]¯).
2. This shortening does not occur when the rhythmic accent falls upon the final syllable: a)ntiqi/w| ) *odush=i ([macrdot]˘˘[macrdot]˘˘[macrdot]˘), w(=| e)/ni ([macrdot]˘˘).
3. The shortening rarely occurs in the interior of a word. Thus, Hom. h(/rwos (¯˘˘), ui(o/n (˘˘), in the Attic drama au(thi+/ (¯˘¯), toiou=tos (˘:¯˘), poiw= (˘¯), often written pow= in inscriptions (cp. 43).

## ACCENT: GENERAL PRINCIPLES

§149
There are three accents in Greek. No Greek accent can stand farther back than the antepenult.
1. Acute (/): over short or long vowels and diphthongs. It may stand on ultima, penult, or antepenult: kalo/s, dai/mwn, a)/nqrwpos.
2. Circumflex (=): over vowels long by nature and diphthongs. It may stand on ultima or penult: gh=, qeou=, dw=ron, tou=to.
3. Grave (\): over short or long vowels and diphthongs. It stands on the ultima only: to\n a)/ndra, th\n tu/xhn, oi( qeoi\ th=s ( *ella/dos.

§150
The acute marks syllables pronounced in a raised tone. The grave is a low-pitched tone as contrasted with the acute. The circumflex combines acute and grave.

§151
Accented syllables in Ancient Greek had a higher pitch (to/nos) than unaccented syllables, and it was the rising and falling of the pitch that made Ancient Greek a musical language. The Greek word for accent is prosw|di/a_ (Lat. accentus: from ad-cano), i.e. ‘song accompanying words.’ Musical accent (elevation and depression of tone) is to be distinguished from quantity (duration of tone), and from rhythmic accent (stress of voice at fixed intervals when there is a regular sequence of long and short syllables).
N.—The accent heard in Modern Greek and English is a stress-accent. Stress is produced by strong and weak expiration, and takes account of accented syllables to the neglect of the quantity of unaccented syllables. Thus, shortly after Christ, a)/nqrwpos was often pronounced like a dactyl, fi/los like a trochee; and pro/swpon, e)nne/a, were even written pro/sopon, e/nnh/a.

§152
The marks of accent are placed over the vowel of the accented syllable. A diphthong has the accent over its second vowel (tou=to), except in the case of capital a|, h|, w| (as (/ *aidhs, 5), where the accent stands before the first vowel.

§153
A breathing is written before the acute and grave (oi(/, h)/), but under the circumflex (w)=, ou(=tos). Accents and breathings are placed before capitals: (/ *omhros, (= *wrai. The accent stands over a mark of diaeresis (8): klhi+=di.

§154
The grave is written in place of a final acute on a word that is followed immediately by another word in the sentence. Thus, meta\ th\n ma/xhn after the battle (for meta/ th/n ma/xhn). It is also sometimes placed on ti\s, ti\ (334), to distinguish these indefinite pronouns from the interrogatives ti/s, ti/.
a. An oxytone (157) changes its acute to the grave when followed by another word, except: (1) when the oxytone is followed by an enclitic (183 a); (2) in ti/s, ti/ interrogative, as ti/s ou(=tos; who's this? (3) when an elided syllable follows the accented syllable: nu/xq' o(/lhn (124), not nu\xq' o(/lhn (174 a); (4) when a colon or period follows. (Usage varies before a comma.)

§155
The ancients regarded the grave originally as belonging to every syllable not accented with the acute or circumflex; and some Mss. show this in practice, e.g. pa\gkra\th/s. Later it was restricted to its use as a substitute for a final acute.

§156
The circumflex is formed from the union of the acute and the grave (/\ = ^), never from \/. Thus, pai=s = pa/i\s, eu)= = e)/u\. Similarly, since every long vowel may be resolved into two short units (morae), tw=n may be regarded as = to/o\n. The circumflex was thus spoken with a rising tone followed by one of lower pitch. mou=sa, dh=mos are thus = mo/u\sa, de/e\mos; mou/shs, dh/mou are = mo\u/shs, de\e/mou. In didou=sa (i.e. dido/u\sa) compared with didou/s the accent has receded (159) one mora.
a. The whole vowel receives the acute when the second short unit of a vowel long by nature is accented: *di/_ = *di\i/.

§157
Words are named according to their accent as follows:
Oxytone (acute on the ultima): qh/r, kalo/s, lelukw/s.
Paroxytone (acute on the penult): lu/_w, lei/pw, leluko/tos.
Proparoxytone (acute on the antepenult): a)/nqrwpos, paideu/omen.
Perispomenon (circumflex on the ultima): gh=, qeou=.
Properispomenon (circumflex on the penult): pra=cis, mou=sa.
Barytone (when the ultima is unaccented, 158): mou=sa, mh/thr, po/lemos.

§158
A word is called barytone (baru/-tonos deep-toned, low-toned) when it has no accent on the ultima. All paroxytones, proparoxytones, and properispomena are also barytones.

§159
An accent is called recessive when it moves back as far from the end of the word as the quantity of the ultima permits (166). The quantity of the penult is here disregarded (tre/pwmen). Cp. 178.

§160

Oxytone (o)cu/s, sharp + to/nos) means ‘sharp-toned,’ perispomenon (perispw/menos) ‘turned-around’ (circumflectus, 156). Paroxytone and proparoxytone are derived from o)cu/tonos with the prepositions para/ and pro/ respectively. Acute corresponds to Lat. acutus (o)cei=a, scil. prosw|di/a_).

§161
The invention of the marks of accent is attributed to Aristophanes of Byzantium, librarian at Alexandria about 200 B.C. The use of signs served to fix the correct accentuation, which was becoming uncertain in the third century B.C.; marked the variation of dialect usage; and rendered the acquisition of Greek easier for foreigners. The signs for the accents (and the breathings) were not regularly employed in Mss. till after 600 A.D.

§162
The position of the accent has to be learned by observation. But the kind of accent is determined by the following rules.

§162 D
1. Aeolic has recessive (159) accent in all words except prepositions and conjunctions. Thus, so/fos, *zeu=s, i.e. *ze/u\s, au)=tos, li/pein (= lipei=n), li/pontos (= lipo/ntos), a)/mmes (= h(mei=s).
2. Doric regarded final -oi (169) as long (a)nqrw/poi), and probably -ai in nouns (xw/rai); made paroxytones the 3 pl. act. of the past tenses (e)fe/ron, e)lu/_san) and such words as pai/des, gunai/kes, ptw/kas; made perispomena the gen. masc. pl. of pronouns (toutw=n, a)llw=n) and the gen. fem. pl. of adj. in -os (a)mfotera=n). The substitution, in the accus. pl., of -a^s and -os for -a_s and -ous, caused no change in the accent (pa/_sa^s, a)mpe/los).

§163
The antepenult, if accented, can have the acute only (a)/nqrwpos, basi/leia queen, oi)kofu/lakos of a house-guard). If the ultima is long, either by nature or by position (144), the antepenult cannot take an accent: hence a)nqrw/pou (176 a), basilei/a_ kingdom, oi/kofu/lac.
a. Some nouns in -ews and -ewn admit the acute on the antepenult. Thus, the genitive of nouns in -is and -us (po/lews, po/lewn, a)/stews), the forms of the Attic declension, as i(/_lews (289). So the Ionic genitive in -ew (poli/_tew); also some compound adjectives in -ws, as du/serws unhappy in love, u(yi/kerws lofty antlered. On w(=ntinwn see 186.

§164
The penult, if accented and long, takes the circumflex when the ultima is short by nature (nh=sos, tau=ta). In all other cases it has the acute (fo/bos, leluko/tos, tou/tou).
a. Apparent exceptions are w(/ste, ou)/tis, h(/de (properly h(=de). See 186.
b. A final syllable containing a vowel short by nature followed by c or y does not permit the acute to stand on the antepenult (oi)kofu/lac); but the circumflex may stand on the penult (kh=ruc).

§165
The ultima, if accented and short, has the acute (potamo/s); if accented and long, has either the acute (lelukw/s), or the circumflex (*periklh=s).

§166
When the ultima is long, the acute cannot stand on the antepenult, nor the circumflex on the penult. Thus, a)/nqrwpou and dw=rou are impossible.

§167
When the ultima is short, a word, if accented
a. on the ultima, has the acute: sofo/s.
b. on a short penult, has the acute: no/mos.
c. on a long penult, has the circumflex: dw=ron.
d. on the antepenult, has the acute: a)/nqrwpos.

§168
When the ultima is long, a word, if accented
a. on the ultima, has the acute or the circumflex: e)gw/, sofw=s.
b. on the penult, has the acute: le/wn, dai/mwn.

§169
Final -ai and -oi are regarded as short: mou=sai, bou/lomai, pro/palai, a)/nqrwpoi. But in the optative -ai and -oi are long (lu/_sai, bouleu/oi), as in contracted syllables. So also in the locative oi)/koi at home (but oi)=koi houses).
a. The difference in the quantitative treatment of -ai and -oi depends on an original difference of accentuation that may have vanished in Greek. -ai and -oi, when short, were pronounced with a clipped, or simple, tone; when long, with a drawled, or compound, tone.

§170
The quantity of a, i, u (147) may often be learned from the accent. Thus, in qa/latta, h(/misus, ph=xus, du/namis, mh=nis, the vowel of the last syllable must be short; in fi/los the i must be short (otherwise fi=los). Cp. 163.

## ACCENT AS AFFECTED BY CONTRACTION, CRASIS, AND ELISION

§171

Contraction.—If either of the syllables to be contracted had an accent, the contracted syllable has an accent. Thus:
a. A contracted antepenult has the acute: fileo/menos = filou/menos.
b. A contracted penult has the circumflex when the ultima is short; the acute, when the ultima is long: file/ousi = filou=si, fileo/ntwn = filou/ntwn.
c. A contracted ultima has the acute when the uncontracted form was oxytone: e(staw/s = e(stw/s; otherwise, the circumflex: file/w = filw=.
N. 1.—A contracted syllable has the circumflex only when, in the uncontracted form, an acute was followed by the (unwritten) grave (155, 156). Thus, *perikle/h\s = *periklh=s, ti_ma/w\ = ti_mw=. In all other cases we have the acute: file\o/ntwn = filou/ntwn, beba\w/s = bebw/s.
N. 2.—Exceptions to 171 are often due to the analogy of other forms (236 a, 264 e, 279 a, 290 c, 309 a).

§172
If neither of the syllables to be contracted had an accent, the contracted syllable has no accent: fi/lee = fi/lei, ge/nei+ = ge/nei, peri/ploos = peri/plous. For exceptions, see 236 b.

§173

Crasis.—In crasis, the first word (as less important) loses its accent: ta)_gaqa/ for ta\ a)gaqa/, ta)_n for ta\ e)n, ka)_gw/ for kai\ e)gw/.
a. If the second word is a dissyllabic paroxytone with short ultima, it is uncertain whether, in crasis, the paroxytone remains or changes to properispomenon. In this book tou)/rgon, ta)/_lla are written for to\ e)/rgon, ta\ a)/lla; but many scholars write tou)=rgon, ta)=lla.

§174

Elision.—In elision, oxytone prepositions and conjunctions lose their accent: par' (for para\) e)mou=, a)ll' (for a)lla\) e)gw/. In other oxytones the accent is thrown back to the penult: po/ll' (for polla\) e)/paqon.
a. Observe that in po/ll' e)/paqon the acute is not changed to the grave (154 a, 3). A circumflex does not result from the recession of the accent. Thus, fh/m' (not fh=m') e)gw/ for fhmi\ e)gw/. tina/ and pote/, after a word which cannot receive their accent (183 d), drop their accent: ou(/tw pot' h)=n.

## ANASTROPHE

§175
Anastrophe (a)nastrofh/ turning-back) occurs in the case of oxytone prepositions of two syllables, which throw the accent back on the first syllable.
a. When the preposition follows its case: tou/twn pe)ri (for peri\ tou/twn) about these things. No other preposition than peri/ follows its case in prose.
N. 1.—In poetry anastrophe occurs with the other dissyllabic prepositions (except a)nti/, a)mfi/, dia/). In Homer a preposition following its verb and separated from it by tmesis (1650) also admits anastrophe (lou/sh| a)/po for a)polou/sh|).
N. 2.—When the final vowel of the preposition is elided, the accent is dropped if no mark of punctuation intervenes: xersi\n u(f' h(mete/rh|sin B 374.
b. When a preposition stands for a compound formed of the preposition and e)sti/. Thus, pa/ra for pa/resti it is permitted, e)/ni for e)/nesti it is possible (e)ni/ is a poetic form of e)n).
N.—In poetry, pa/ra may stand for pa/reisi or pa/reimi; and a)/na arise! up! is used for a)na/sthqi. Hom. has e)/ni = e)/neisi.

## CHANGE OF ACCENT IN DECLENSION, INFLECTION, AND COMPOSITION

§176
When a short ultima of the nominative is lengthened in an oblique case
a. a proparoxytone becomes paroxytone: qa/latta qala/tths, a)/nqrwpos a)nqrw/pou.
b. a properispomenon becomes paroxytone: mou=sa mou/shs, dw=ron dw/ron.
c. an oxytone becomes perispomenon in the genitive and dative of the second declension: qeo/s qeou= qew=| qew=n qeoi=s.

§177
When, for a long ultima, a short ultima is substituted in inflection
a. a dissyllabic paroxytone (with penult long by nature) becomes properispomenon: lu/_w lu=e.
b. a polysyllabic paroxytone (with penult either long or short) becomes proparoxytone: paideu/w pai/deue, ple/kw ple/komen.

§178
In composition the accent is usually recessive (159) in the case of substantives and adjectives, regularly in the case of verbs: ba/sis a)na/basis, qeo/s a)/qeos, lu=e a)po/lu_e.
a. Proper names having the form of a substantive, adjective, or participle, usually change the accent: *)/elpis (e)lpi/s), *glau=kos (glauko/s), *ge/lwn (gelw=n).
b. Special cases will be considered under Declension and Inflection.

## PROCLITICS

§179
Ten monosyllabic words have no accent and are closely connected with the following word. They are called proclitics (from prokli/_nw lean forward). They are:
The forms of the article beginning with a vowel (o(, h(, oi(, ai(); the prepositions e)n, ei)s (e)s), e)c (e)k); the conjunction ei) if; w(s as, that (also a preposition to); the negative adverb ou) (ou)k, ou)x, 137).

§180
A proclitic sometimes takes an accent, thus:
a. ou) at the end of a sentence: fh/|s, h)\ ou)/; do you say so or not? pw=s ga\r ou)/; for why not? Also ou)/ no standing alone.
b. e)c, e)n, and ei)s receive an acute in poetry when they follow the word to which they belong and stand at the end of the verse:

kakw=n e)/c out of evils
*c 472.
c. w(s as becomes w(/s in poetry when it follows its noun: qeo\s w(/s as a god. w(s standing for ou(/tws is written w(/s even in prose (ou)d' w(/s not even thus).
d. When the proclitic precedes an enclitic (183 e): e)/n tisi.
N.—o( used as a relative (for o(/s, 1105) is written o(/. On o(/ demonstrative see 1114.

## ENCLITICS

§181
Enclitics (from e)gkli/_nw lean on, upon) are words attaching themselves closely to the preceding word, after which they are pronounced rapidly. Enclitics usually lose their accent. They are:
a. The personal pronouns mou=, moi/, me/; sou=, soi/, se/; ou(=, oi(=, e(/, and (in poetry) sfi/si.
b. The indefinite pronoun ti\s, ti\ in all cases (including tou=, tw=| for tino/s, tini/, but excluding a)/tta = tina/); the indefinite adverbs pou/ (or poqi/), ph/|, poi/, poqe/n, pote/, pw/, pw/s. When used as interrogatives these words are not enclitic (ti/s, ti/, pou= (or po/qi), ph=|, poi=, po/qen, po/te, pw=, pw=s).
c. All dissyllabic forms of the present indicative of ei)mi/ am and fhmi/ say (i.e. all except ei)= and fh/|s).
d. The particles ge/, te/, toi/, pe/r; the inseparable -de in o(/de, toso/sde, etc.
N.—Enclitics, when they retain their accent, are called orthotone. See 187.

§181 D
Also enclitic are the dialectic and poetical forms meu=, se/o, seu=, toi/, te/, and tu/ (accus. = se/), e(/o, eu(=, e(/qen, mi/n, ni/n, sfi/, sfi/n, sfe/, sfwe/, sfwi/_n, sfe/wn, sfe/as, sfa^/s and sfa=s, sfe/a; also the particles nu/ or nu/n (not nu=n), Epic ke/ (ke/n), qh/n, r(a/; and Epic e)ssi/, Ion. ei)=s, thou art.

§182
The accent of an enclitic, when it is thrown back upon the preceding word, always appears as an acute: qh/r te (not qh=r te) from qh/r + te/.

§183
The word preceding an enclitic is treated as follows:
a. An oxytone keeps its accent, and does not change an acute to a grave (154 a): do/s moi, kalo/n e)sti.
b. A perispomenon keeps its accent: filw= se, ti_mw=n tinwn.
c. A proparoxytone or properispomenon receives, as an additional accent, the acute on the ultima: a)/nqrwpo/s tis, a)/nqrwpoi/ tines, h)/kousa/ tinwn; sw=so/n me, pai=de/s tines.
d. A paroxytone receives no additional accent: a monosyllabic enclitic loses its accent (xw/ra_ tis, fi/los mou), a dissyllabic enclitic retains its accent (xw/ra_s tino/s, fi/loi tine/s) except when its final vowel is elided (174 a).
N.—Like paroxytones are treated properispomena ending in c or y when followed by a dissyllabic enclitic: kh=ruc e)sti/; and so probably kh=ruc tis.
e. A proclitic (179) takes an acute: e)/n tini, ei)/ tines.

§184
Since an enclitic, on losing its accent, forms a part of the preceding word, the writing a)/nqrwpos tis would violate the rule (149) that no word can be accented on a syllable before the antepenult. A paroxytone receives no additional accent in order that two successive syllables may not have the acute (not fi/lo/s e)stin).

§185
When several enclitics occur in succession, each receives an accent from the following, only the last having no accent:

ei)/ pou/ ti/s tina i)/doi e)xqro/n if ever any one saw an enemy anywhere
T. 4.47.

§186
Sometimes an enclitic unites with a preceding word to form a compound (cp. Lat. -que, -ve), which is accented as if the enclitic were still a separate word. Thus, ou)/te (not ou)=te), w(/ste, ei)/te, kai/toi, ou(=tinos, w(=|tini, w(=ntinwn; usually per (e(/sper); and the inseparable -de in o(/de, tou/sde, oi)/kade; and -qe and -xi in ei)/qe (poetic ai)/qe), nai/xi. ou)/te, w(=|tini, etc., are not real exceptions to the rules of accent (163, 164).
a. oi(=o/s te able is sometimes written oi(=o/ste. ou)k ou)=n is usually written ou)/koun not therefore , and not therefore? in distinction from ou)kou=n therefore. e)gw/ ge and e)moi/ ge may become e)/gwge, e)/moige.

§187
An enclitic retains its accent (is orthotone, cp. 181 N.):
a. When it is emphatic, as in contrasts: h)\ soi\ h)\ tw=| patri/ sou either to you or to your father (e)mou=, e)moi/, e)me/ are emphatic: ei)pe\ kai\ e)moi/ tell me too), and at the beginning of a sentence or clause: fhmi\ ga/r I say in fact.
b. e)sti/ is written e)/sti at the beginning of a sentence; when it expresses existence or possibility; when it follows ou)k, mh/, ei), w(s, kai/, a)lla/ (or a)ll'), tou=to (or tou=t'); and in e)/stin oi(/ some, e)/stin o(/te sometimes. Thus, ei) e)/stin ou(/tws if it is so, tou=to d e)/sti that which exists.
c. In the phrases pote\ me\n . . . pote\ de/, tine\s me\n . . . tine\s de/.
d. After a word suffering elision: polloi\ d' ei)si/n (for de/ ei)sin), tau=t' e)sti/.
e. When a dissyllabic enclitic follows a paroxytone (183 d).
N. 1.—When they are used as indirect reflexives in Attic prose (1228), the pronouns of the third person ou(= and sfi/si are orthotone, oi(= is generally enclitic, while e(/ is generally orthotone.
N. 2.—After oxytone prepositions and e(/neka enclitic pronouns (except ti\s) usually keep their accent (e)pi\ soi/, not e)pi/ soi; e(/neka sou=, not e(/neka/ sou; e(/neka/ tou, not e(/neka tou=). e)mou=, e)moi/, e)me/ are used after prepositions (except pro/s me; and in the drama a)mfi/ moi).

## MARKS OF PUNCTUATION

§188
Greek has four marks of punctuation. The comma and period have the same forms as in English. For the colon and semicolon Greek has only one sign, a point above the line (.):

oi( de\ h(de/ws e)pei/qonto: e)pi/steuon ga\r au)tw=| and they gladly obeyed; for they trusted him
X. A. 1.2.2. The mark of interrogation (;) is the same as our semicolon: pw=s ga\r ou)/; for why not?

## Part II: Inflection

## Parts of Speech

§189

Parts of Speech.—Greek has the following parts of speech: substantives, adjectives, pronouns, verbs, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, and particles. In this Grammar noun is used to include both the substantive and the adjective.

§190

Inflection is the change in the form of nouns, pronouns, and verbs which indicates their relation to other words in the sentence. Declension is the inflection of substantives, adjectives (including participles), and pronouns; conjugation is the inflection of verbs.

§191

Stems.—Inflection is shown by the addition of endings to the stem, which is that part of a word which sets forth the idea; the endings fit the word to stand in various relations to other words in the sentence. The endings originally had distinct meanings, which are now seldom apparent. In verbs they represent the force of the personal pronouns in English; in nouns they often correspond to the ideas expressed by of, to, for, etc. Thus, the stem logo- becomes lo/go-s word, the stem lego- becomes le/go-men we say. Whether a stem is used as a noun or a verb depends solely on its signification; many stems are used both for nouns and for verbs, as ti_ma_- in ti_mh/ honour, ti_ma- in ti_ma/-w I honour; e)lpid- in e)lpi/（d）-s hope, e)lpi/zw I hope (e)lpid-iw). The pure stem, that is, the stem without any ending, may serve as a word; as xw/ra_ land, le/ge speak! lo/ge oh word!

§192
The stem often changes in form, but not in meaning, in nouns and verbs. Thus, the stem of lo/go-s word is logo- or loge-, of path/r father is pater- (strong stem) or patr- (weak stem); of lei/po-men we leave is leipo-, of e)-li/pomen we left is lipo-. The verbal stem is also modified to indicate change in time: ti_mh/-so-men we shall honour.

§193

Roots.—The fundamental part of a word, which remains after the word has been analyzed into all its component parts, is called a root. When a stem agrees in form with a root (as in pod-o/s, gen. of pou/s foot) it is called a root-stem. A root contains the mere idea of a word in the vaguest and most abstract form possible. Thus, the root leg, and in another form log, contains the idea of saying simply. By the addition of a formative element o we arrive at the stems lego- and logo- in le/go-men we say, lo/go-s word (i.e. what is said). Words are built by adding to the root certain formative suffixes by which the stem and then the word, ready for use, is constructed. Thus, from the root lu are formed lu/-si-s loosing, lu/-tro-n ransom, lu-ti-ko/-s able to loose, lu-qh=-nai to have loosed. The formation of the stem by the addition of suffixes to the root is treated in Part III. The root itself may assume various forms without change of meaning, as leg in le/g-o-men we say, log in lo/g-o-s word.
N.—Since Greek is connected with the other Indo-European languages, the roots which we establish in Greek by analysis of a word into its simplest form often reappear in the connected languages (p. 1, A). Thus, the root fer of fe/rw I bear is seen in Sanskrit bhárāmi, Lat. fero, Germ. ge-bären. The assumption of roots is merely a grammatical convenience in the analysis of word-forms, and their determination is part of comparative grammar. Roots and suffixes as such never existed as independent words in Greek, or indeed in any known period of the parent language from which Greek and the other Indo-European tongues are derived. The theory that all roots are monosyllables is ill supported. As far back as we can follow the history of the Indo-European languages we find only complete words; hence their analysis into component morphological elements is merely a scientific device for purposes of arrangement and classification.

## DECLENSION

§194
Declension deals with variations of number, gender, and case.

§195

Number.—There are three numbers: singular, dual, and plural. The dual speaks of two or a pair, as tw\ o)fqalmw/ the two eyes; but it is not often used, and the plural (which denotes more than one) is frequently substituted for it (oi( o)fqalmoi/ the eyes).

§196

Gender.—There are three genders: masculine, feminine, and neuter.
a. Gender strictly marks sex-distinction. But in Greek, as in German and French, many inanimate objects are regarded as masculine or feminine. Such words are said to have ‘grammatical’ gender, which is determined only by their form. Words denoting objects without natural gender usually show their grammatical gender by the form of the adjective, as makro\s lo/gos a long speech, makra\_ nh=sos a long island, makro\n tei=xos a long wall.
b. The gender of Greek words is usually indicated by means of the article: o( for masculine, h( for feminine, to/ for neuter.

§197

Rule of Natural Gender.—Nouns denoting male persons are masculine, nouns denoting female persons are feminine. Thus, o( nau/ths seaman, o( stratiw/ths soldier, h( gunh/ woman, h( ko/rh maiden.
a. A whole class is designated by the masculine: oi( a)/nqrwpoi men, i.e. men and women.
b. EXCEPTIONS TO THE RULE OF NATURAL GENDER.—Diminutives in -ion are neuter (199 d), as to\ a)nqrw/pion manikin (o( a)/nqrwpos man), to\ paidi/on little child (male or female, o( or h( pai=s child), to\ gu/naion little woman (h( gunh/ woman). Also the words te/knon, te/kos child (strictly ‘thing born’), a)ndra/podon captive.

§198

Common Gender.—Many nouns denoting persons are either masculine or feminine. Thus, o( pai=s boy, h( pai=s girl, o( qeo/s god, h( qeo/s (h( qea/_ poet.) goddess. So with names of animals: o( bou=s ox, h( bou=s cow, o( i(/ppos horse, h( i(/ppos mare.
a. Some names of animals have only one grammatical gender without regard to sex, as o( lagw/s he-hare or she-hare, h( a)lw/phc he-fox or she-fox.

§199

Gender of Sexless Objects.—The gender of most nouns denoting sexless objects has to be learned by the endings (211, 228, 255) and by observation. The following general rules should be noted.
a. Masculine are the names of winds, months, and most rivers. Thus, o( *bore/a_s the North Wind, o( *(ekatombaiw/n Hecatombaeon, o( *khfisso/s Cephissus.
N.—The gender of these proper names is made to correspond to o( a)/nemos wind, o( mh/n month, o( potamo/s river. In the case of winds and rivers the gender may be due in part to personification.
b. Feminine are the names of almost all countries, islands, cities, trees, and plants. Thus, h( *)attikh/ Attica, h( *dh=los Delos, h( *ko/rinqos Corinth, h( pi/tus pine, h( a)/mpelos vine. The gender here follows that of h( gh= or h( xw/ra_ land, country, h( nh=sos island, h( po/lis city, h( dru=s, originally tree in general, but later oak (to\ de/ndron is the ordinary word for tree).
c. Feminine are most abstract words, that is, words denoting a quality or a condition. Thus, h( a)reth/ virtue, h( eu)/noia good-will, h( taxu/ths swiftness, h( e)lpi/s hope.
d. Neuter are diminutives (197 b), words and expressions quoted, letters of the alphabet, infinitives, and indeclinable nouns. Thus, to\ u(_mei=s the word ‘you,’ to\ gnw=qi seauto/n the saying ‘learn to know thyself,’ to\ a)/lfa alpha, to\ paideu/ein to educate, to\ xrew/n necessity.
N.—But some names of women end in -ion (197 b): h( *gluke/rion Glycerium.

§200

Remarks.—a. Most of the exceptions to 199 a-b are due to the endings; e.g. h( *lh/qh Lethe, h( *stu/c Styx (rivers of the Lower World), to\ *)/argos Argos, o( *kaludw/n Calydon, to\ *)/i_lion Ilium, oi( *delfoi/ Delphi, o( lwto/s lotus.
b. Change in gender is often associated with change in form: o( lu/kos he-wolf, h( lu/kaina she-wolf, o( poihth/s poet, h( poih/tria poetess, o( bi/otos and h( bioth/ life, o( tro/pos manner, h( troph/ rout.
c. The gender of one word may influence that of another word of like meaning. Thus h( nh=sos island and h( li/qos stone are feminine probably because of h( gh= land and h( pe/tra_ rock.

§201

Cases.—There are five cases: nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, and vocative. The genitive denotes from as well as of, the dative denotes to or for and also by, with, on, in, at, etc. The other cases are used as in Latin.
a. The genitive, dative, and accusative are called oblique cases to distinguish them from the nominative and vocative.

§202
The vocative is often like the nominative in the singular; in the plural it is always the same. Nominative, vocative, and accusative have the same form in neuter words, and always have a in the plural. In the dual there are two forms, one for nominative, accusative, and vocative, the other for genitive and dative.

§203

Lost Cases.—Greek has generally lost the forms of the instrumental and locative cases (which have become fused with the dative) and of the ablative. The Greek dative is used to express by, as in bi/a|, Lat. ui_ ; with, as in li/qois with stones; and in, on, as in gh=| on the earth. From may be expressed by the genitive: po/rrw *spa/rths far from Sparta. When the genitive and dative do duty for the ablative, prepositions are often used. Instances of the forms of the lost cases are given in 341.

§204

Declensions.—There are three declensions, which are named from the stems to which the case endings are attached.
1. First or Â-declension, with stems in a_) Vowel Declension.
2. Second or O-declension, with stems in o)
3. Third or Consonant declension, with stems in a consonant or in i and u.
The nominative and accusative are alike in the singular and plural of all neuter nouns. The nominative and vocative are alike in the plural.

## GENERAL RULES FOR THE ACCENT OF NOUNS

§205
Substantives and adjectives accent, in the oblique cases, the same syllable as is accented in the nominative, provided the ultima permits (163); otherwise the following syllable receives the accent.
1 decl. qa/latta, qala/tths, qala/tth|, qa/lattan, qa/lattai (169), qala/ttais, qala/tta_s.
2 decl. a)/nqrwpos, a)nqrw/pou, a)nqrw/pw|, a)/nqrwpon, a)/nqrwpoi (169), a)nqrw/pwn, a)nqrw/pois, a)nqrw/pous.
3 decl. le/wn, le/ontos, le/onti, le/onta, le/ontes, leo/ntwn.
Adj.: a)/cios (287), a)ci/a_, a)/cion, a)ci/ou, a)ci/a_s, a)ci/w|, a)ci/a|, a)ci/wn, a)ci/ois. xari/eis (299), xari/entos, xari/enti, xari/enta, xarie/ntwn.

§206
The character of the accent depends on the general laws (167, 168, 176). Thus, ni/_kh, vi=kai (169); dw=ron, dw/rou, dw=ra; sw=ma, sw/matos, swma/twn, sw/mata.

§207
Oxytones of the first and second declensions are perispomena in the genitive and dative of all numbers: skia/_, skia=s, skia=|, skiw=n, skiai=s; qeo/s, qeou=, qew=|, qew=n, qeoi=s; fanero/s, fanerou=, fanerw=|, fanerw=n, faneroi=s.

§208
The genitive plural of all substantives of the first declension has the circumflex on the w of -wn. Thus, ni/_kh ni_kw=n; qa/latta qalattw=n; poli/_ths poli_tw=n; nea_ni/a_s nea_niw=n.

§209
The fem. gen. plural of adjectives and participles in -os has the same accent and form as the masculine and neuter. Thus, di/kaios, gen. pl. dikai/wn (in all genders); luo/menos, gen. pl. luome/nwn (in all genders).

## SUBSTANTIVES

## FIRST DECLENSION (STEMS IN a_）

§211
Stems in a_ are masculine or feminine. The feminine nominative singular ends in -a_, -a^, or -h; the masculine nominative singular adds -s to the stem, and thus ends in -a_s or -hs.

§212
Table of the union of the case endings (when there are any) with the final vowel of the stem.

FEM. SING.MASC. SING.MASC. FEM. PL.MASC. FEM. DUAL

Gen. a_-s or h-s h-sa_-io (Hom. a_-o）w=n (for e/-wn, a/_-wn）G. D. a-in

Dat. a_-i or h-i h-ia_-ih-ia-is or a-isi（n）

Acc. a_-n or a^-n h-na_-nh-na_s (for a-ns）

Voc. a_ or a^ ha_a^ or ha-i
Observe the shortening of the stem in vocative singular and plural, in nominative and dative plural, and genitive and dative dual.

§213

Accent.—For special rule of accent in the genitive plural, see 208. The genitive plural is always perispomenon since -w=n is contracted from -e/-wn derived from original (and Hom.) -a/_-wn (51). Final -ai is treated as short (169).
a. The form of the gen. pl. is taken from the pronominal adjective, i.e. (Hom.) qea/_wn goddesses follows the analogy of (Hom.) ta/_wn (332 D.) for ta_- (s）wn, cf. Lat. istā-rum deā-rum.

§214
The dialects show various forms.

§214 D
1. For h, Doric and Aeolic have original a_; thus, ni/_ka_, vi/_ka_s, vi/_ka|, ni/_ka_n; poli/_ta_s, krita/_s, *)atrei/da_s.
2. Ionic has h for the a_ of Attic even after e, i, and r; thus, geneh/, oi)ki/h, a)gorh/, moi/rhs, moi/rh| (nom. moi=ra^), nehni/hs. Thus, a)gorh/, -h=s, -h=|, -h/n; nehni/hs, -ou, -h|, -hn. But Hom. has qea/_ goddess, *(ermei/a_s Hermes.
3. The dialects admit -a^ in the nom. sing. less often than does Attic. Thus, Ionic pru/mnh stern, kni/_sh savour (Att. pru/mna, kni=sa), Dor. to/lma_ daring. Ionic has h for a^ in the abstracts in -ei/h, -oi/h (a)lhqei/h truth, eu)noi/h good-will). Hom. has nu/mfa^ oh maiden from nu/mfh.
4. Nom. sing. masc.—Hom. has -ta for -ths in i(ppo/ta horseman, i(pphla/ta driver of horses, nefelhgere/ta cloud-collector, ku_anoxai=ta dark-haired; and, with recessive accent, mhti/eta counsellor. So in the adj. eu)ru/opa far-sounding. Cp. Lat. poeta, scriba.
5. Gen. sing. masc.—(a) -a_o, the original form from a_-（i）o, is used by Hom. (*)atrei/da_o). It contracts in Aeolic and Doric to -a_ (*)atrei/da_).
(b) -ew, from ho (= a_o) by 34, is also used by Hom., who makes it a single syllable by synizesis (60), as in *)atrei/dew. Hdt. has -ew, as poli/_tew (163 a).
(c) -w in Hom. after a vowel, *bore/w (nom. *bore/hs).
6. Accus. sing. masc.—In proper names Hdt. often has -ea borrowed from s stems (264), as *miltia/dea for *miltia/dh-n.
7. Dual.—Hom. has the nom. dual of masculines only. In the gen. and dat. Hom. has -ain and also -aiin.
8. Gen. plur.—(a) -a/_wn, the original form, occurs in Hom. (mousa/_wn, a)gora/_wn). In Aeolic and Doric -a/_wn contracts to (b) -a=n (a)gora=n). The Doric -a=n is found also in the choral songs of the drama (petra=n rocks). (c) -e/wn, the Ionic form, appears in Homer, who usually makes it a single syllable by synizesis (60) as in boule/wnn, from boulh/ plan. -e/wn is from -h/wn, Ionic for -a/_wn. (d) -w=n in Hom. generally after vowels (klisiw=n, from klisi/h hut).
9. Dat. plur.: -h|si（n), -h|s, generally before vowels, and (rarely) -ais in Hom. Ionic has -h|si, Aeolic -aisi（n), -ais, Doric -ais.
10. Accus. plur.: -ans, -a^s, a_s in various Doric dialects, -ais in Aeolic.

§215

Dative Plural.—The ending -aisi（n) occurs in Attic poetry (di/kaisi from di/kh right, despo/taisi from despo/ths lord).
a. Attic inscriptions to 420 B. C. have -h|si (written -hisi), -hsi, and (after e, i, r) -a|si (written -aisi) and -a_si. Thus, draxmh=|si and draxmh=si drachmas, tami/a|si and tami/a_si stewards. -hsi and -a_si are properly endings of the locative case (341).

§217
RULES.—a. If the nominative singular ends in alpha preceded by a vowel (skia/_ shadow) or r (moi=ra), alpha is kept throughout the singular.
b. If the nominative singular ends in alpha preceded by a consonant not r, alpha is changed to h in the genitive and dative singular.
c. If the nominative singular ends in h, h is kept in all the cases of the singular.
d. When the genitive singular has -hs, final a of the nominative singular is always short; when the genitive singular has -a_s, the final a is generally long.
Feminines fall into two classes:

§218
(I) Feminines with a_ or h in all the cases of the singular.
After e, i, or r, a_ appears in all the cases of the singular, as in genea/_ race, oi)ki/a_ house, xw/ra_ land. Otherwise, h throughout the singular, as ni/_kh victory.
a. After o, we find both a_ and h, as stoa/_ porch, boh/ shout, a)koh/ hearing, o(|oh/ current, r(o/a_ pomegranate. After r we have h in ko/rh girl, de/rh neck (31).

§219
(II) Feminines with a^ in the nominative, accusative, and vocative singular. The quantity of the vowel is generally shown by the accent (163, 164).
In this class are included:
1. Substantives having s (c, y, tt, or ss), z, ll, or ain before the final a show a^ in nom., accus., and voc. sing., and h in gen. and dat. sing. Thus, mou=sa muse, mou/shs, mou/sh|, a(/maca wagon, tra/peza table, glw=tta tongue, r(i/za root, a(/milla contest, le/aina lioness. Others are to/lma daring, di/aita mode of life, a)/kanqa thorn, mui=a fly.
2. Substantives in a^ in nom., accus., and voc. sing., and a_ in gen. and dat. sing.
a. Substantives in -eia and -tria denoting females, as basi/leia queen (but basilei/a_ kingdom), ya/ltria female harper; so the fem. of adj. in -us, as gluku/s, glukei=a sweet.
b. Abstracts in -eia and -oia from adjectives in -hs and -oos, as a)lh/qeia truth (from a)lhqh/s true), eu)/noia good will (from eu)/nous, eu)/noos kind, 290).
c. Most substantives in -ra after a diphthong or u_, as moi=ra fate, ge/fu_ra bridge.

§220
Exceptions to 219, 1: ko/rsh temple (later ko/rrh), e(/rsh dew; to 2 b: in Attic poetry, a)lhqei/a_, eu)noi/a_, a)gnoi/a_ ignorance, which owe their a_ to the influence of the genitive and dative a)lhqei/a_s, a)lhqei/a|, etc.

§221
Most, if not all, of the substantives in a^ are formed by the addition of the suffix [iglide]a or ia (20); thus, glw=tta from glwx-[iglide]a (cp. glwxi=n-es points), ge/fu_ra from gefur-[iglide]a, do/teira giver from doter-[iglide]a (and so fe/rousa bearing from feront[iglide]a), moi=ra from mor-[iglide]a, ya/ltr-ia.

## SECOND DECLENSION (STEMS IN o）

§228
O stems in the nominative add -s to the stem in masculines and feminines; -n in neuters. The feminines, of which there are few, are declined like the masculines. In the neuters, nominative, vocative, and accusative singular have the same form (in -o-n); in the plural these cases end in -a.

The dialects show various forms.

§230 D

## ATTIC DECLENSION

§237
Some substantives ending in -ews are placed under the Second Declension because they are derived from earlier o stems preceded by a long vowel (-ews from -hos, 34). A few others have a consonant before -ws. The vocative has no special form.
N.—This declension is called “Attic” because the words in question generally show -ws in Attic and -os in the Koinè dialect (p. 3, F).

§238
o( new/s temple

b. There are no neuter substantives belonging to the Attic declension in standard classical literature; but neuter adjectives (289) end in -wn.
c. new/s and most words of this declension owe their forms to transfer of quantity (34) or to shortening (39). Thus, new/s is from nho/s ( = Doric na_o/s), new/n from nho/n; new/| is from nhw=|. lagw/s is contracted from lagwo/s.
d. In the accusative singular some words end in -w or -wn, as lagw/ or lagw/n hare. So o( *)/aqws, h( *ke/ws, h( *te/ws, h( *kw=s, o( *mi/_nws. h( e(/ws dawn always has e(/w.

§238 D
Hom. has nho/s temple, la_o/s people, ka/los cable, lagwo/s hare, ga/lows sister-in-law, *)aqo/ws, *ko/ws; Hdt. has lew/s, lago/s, *ke/os. Hom. and Hdt. have h)w/s, gen. h)ou=s, dawn, whence Att. e(/ws by 39. Hom. has *petew=-o, the original form of the genitive, from *petew/s. new/ is from newo out of nhoo.

§239

Accent.—a. The accent of the nominative is kept in all cases. *mene/0ews (163 a) retains the accent of the earlier *mene/la_os.
b. The genitive and dative are oxytone when the final syllable is accented.
N.—The accentuation of the words of this declension is doubtful. Some of the ancients accented lagw/s, lagw/n, others lagw=s, lagw=n, etc.

## THIRD DECLENSION

§240
This declension includes stems ending in a consonant, in i, u, or a diphthong, and some in w and o, representing wv and oi.
N.—To determine whether a noun belongs to the third declension it is necessary in most cases to know the stem, which is usually found by dropping -os of the genitive singular. Stems in i and u are classed under the consonant declension because neither of these vowels admits contraction with the case endings beginning with a vowel, herein being like a consonant.

## FORMATION OF CASES: NOMINATIVE SINGULAR

§241
Masculine and feminine stems not ending in n, r, s and ont, add s.
a. A labial (p, b, f) + s becomes y (97).
b. A dental (t, d, q) + s becomes ss (98), which is reduced to s (107).
c. A palatal (k, g, x) or kt + s becomes c (97).
(The same changes occur in the dative plural.)
gu/_y vulture gu_p-o/s, *)/aray Arab *)/arab-os; kako/ths baseness kako/tht-os, e)lpi/s hope e)lpi/d-os, o)/rni_s bird o)/rni_q-os; fu/lac guard fu/lak-os, ma/sti^c scourge ma/sti_g-os, sa/lpigc trumpet sa/lpigg-os, o)/nuc nail o)/nux-os, nu/c night nukt-o/s; a(/l-s salt a(l-o/s, i)xqu/_s fish i)xqu/-os; e)le/fa_s elephant e)le/fant-os.

§242
Masculine and feminine stems ending in n, r, and s reject s and lengthen a preceding vowel if short (e to h, o to w).
dai/mwn divinity dai/mon-os, xeimw/n winter xeimw=n-os, limh/n harbour lime/n-os, *(/ellhn Greek *(/ellhn-os; r(h/twr orator r(h/tor-os, a)h/r air a)e/r-os, fw/r thief fwr-o/s, trih/rhs trireme (stem trihres-, 263 b), ai)dw/s shame (stem ai)dos-, 266). On mh/n see 259 end. For stems in es, nominative -os, see 263 c.

§243
Masculine stems in ont drop t (133) and lengthen o to w: ge/rwn old man ge/ront-os, le/wn lion le/ont-os.

§243 D
Hdt. has o)dw/n tooth o)do/nt-os. Attic o)dou/s has the inflection of a participle in -ous (307).

§244
Neuters show the pure stem, from which final t and other consonants not standing at the end of a word (133) are dropped: a(/rma chariot a(/rmat-os, pra=gma thing pra/_gmat-os, ga/la milk ga/lakt-os (133 b).

§245

Summary.—s is added to stems ending in a labial, dental, palatal, and in ant, ent, unt; to some stems in n (as ei(=s one e(n-o/s, me/la_s black me/lan-os); to stems in eu, au, ou; and to masc. and fem. stems in i and u. s is not added to most stems ending in n, nor to those in ont, r, es, as, os, u (neut.), w（v), o（i).

## ACCUSATIVE SINGULAR

§246
Masculines and feminines usually add a to stems ending in a consonant; n to stems ending in i or u.
gu=p-a, o)/nux-a, e)le/fant-a, lime/n-a, r(h/tor-a, le/ont-a; po/li-n, i)xqu/_-n, bou=-n from po/li-s city, i)xqu/_-s fish, bou=-s ox, cow. Stems in eu take a (275).

§247
Barytone stems of two syllables ending in it, id, i_q usually drop the dental and add n.
xa/ris grace (stem xarit-) xa/rin, e)/ris strife (e)rid-) e)/rin, o)/rni_s bird (o)rni_q-) o)/rni_n. So eu)/elpis hopeful (eu)elpid-) eu)/elpin (292). Oxytones end in a: e)lpi/d-a, sfra_gi=da (sfra_gi/_s seal).
a. klei=s key (kleid-), Old Att. klh/|s, has klei=n (late klei=da), acc. pl. klei=s (late klei=das).

§247 D
The acc. in a (xa/rita, e)/rida, o)/rni_qa) occurs in Hom., Hdt., and in Attic poetry. So ko/ruqa and ko/run (ko/rus helmet) in Hom.

## VOCATIVE SINGULAR

§248
The vocative of masculines and feminines is usually the pure stem.
po/li (po/li-s city), bou= (bou=-s ox, cow), *sw/krates (*swkra/ths). Stems in id and nt cannot retain final d and t (133), hence *)/artemi from *)/artemis (*)artemid-), pai= from pai=s boy, girl (paid-), nea=ni from nea=nis maiden (nea_nid-); ge/ron from ge/rwn old man (geront-), gi/gan from gi/ga_s giant (gigant-).

§249
The vocative is the same as the nominative:
a. In stems ending in a stop (16) consonant (except those in it, id, i_q; nt in nouns): w)= fu/lac watchman. (*ai)/a_s Ajax (*ai)ant-) is nom. and voc.)
b. In oxytone stems ending in a liquid and not taking s to form their nominative (242): w)= poimh/n shepherd (poimen-); but a)nh/r man, path/r father have a)/ner, pa/ter (262). Barytones use the stem as the vocative: dai=mon, r(h+tor from dai/mwn divinity, r(h/twr orator.
c. In all participles.

§249 D
Hom. has a)/na oh king as well as a)/nac (a)nakt-); *ai)=an from *ai)ant-. *pouluda/ma_, *la_oda/ma_ (from stems in ant) are later forms due to analogy.

## DATIVE DUAL AND PLURAL

§250
The dative plural adds -si to the stem.
*)/aray (*)arab-) *)/arayi, ma/sti^c (masti_g-) ma/stici, fu/lac (fulak-) fu/laci, sw=ma (swmat-) sw/masi (98), e)lpi/s (e)lpid-) e)lpi/si (98), o)/rni_s (o)rni_q-) o)/rni_si (98), e)le/fa_s (e)lefant-) e)le/fa_si, qh/r (qhr-) qhrsi/.
a. Stems in nt drop nt and lengthen the preceding vowel (100): le/wn (leont-) le/ousi, gi/ga_s (gigant-) gi/ga_si.
b. Stems in n drop n without lengthening the preceding vowel (if short): dai/mwn (daimon-) dai/mosi, poimh/n (poimen-) poime/si, frh/n mind (fren-) fresi/.
N.—Strictly n is not dropped, but since the stem of the dat. pl. is weak in form (253 a) the n stood originally between two consonants and should become a (35 b). Thus, frasi/ in Pindar is for frṇsi. Attic fresi/ borrows its e from fre/nes, frenw=n, etc. So poime/si, for poimasi from poimṇsi, because of poime/nes, etc.
c. rs is not changed to rr (79 a).

§250 D
1. Hom. has only -oiin in the gen. and dat. dual.
2. In the dat. pl. Hom. has -si (be/les-si, de/pas-si), and in a few cases -esi, reduced from -essi (a)na/kt-esi); -ssi occurs after vowels (ge/nu-ssi; for ge/nu_si?). -essi was added both to stems not ending in s (po/d-essi, bo/-essi, a)/ndr-essi, o)i+/-essi, 274 D.), and even to stems in s (e/pe/-essi). Hom. has also possi/, posi/; Pind. xari/tessi, qe/missi. Tragedy has this -essi (koru/q-essi), and so Aeolic, and the Doric of Corinth.

## ACCUSATIVE PLURAL

§251

a. The ending -as is produced by adding ns to the stem (n becoming a between two consonants by 35 b). Thus fu/lak-as is from fulak-ṇs. This -as may be added even to i and u stems: Hom. po/li-as, i)xqu/-as, Hdt. ph/xe-as. Hom. po/li_s is from po/li-ns (Cretan).
b. The nominative pl. masc. or fem. is sometimes used instead of the accusative pl.: trih/reis 264, po/leis and ph/xeis 268.

## ACCENT, STEM FORMATION, QUANTITY, GENDER

§252

Accent.—Stems of one syllable accent the case ending in the genitive and dative of all numbers; and -wn and -oin take the circumflex accent. Thus, fle/y vein, fleb-o/s, fleb-w=n; qh/r wild beast, qhr-o/s, qhr-oi=n, qhr-w=n; qri/c hair, trix-o/s, trix-w=n.
a. Exceptions. The ending of the gen. dual and pl. is not accented in the case of o(, h( pai=s boy, girl, o( dmw/s slave, o( qw/s jackal, o( *trw/s Trojan, h( da/|s torch, to\ fw=s light, to\ ou)=s ear. Thus, pai/dwn (but paisi/), *trw/wn, w)/twn, etc. So w)/n being, o)/ntwn (305).
b. A trisyllabic form, if contracted, does not show the accent on the case ending: h)=r-os for e)/ar-os, h)=r-i for e)/ar-i, from to\ e)/ar spring.

§253

Variation of Stem Formation.—Many words of the third declension show traces of an original variation of stem that is due to the influence of a shifting accent which is seen in some of the cognate languages. In Greek this variation has often been obscured by the analogy of other forms. Thus pate/rwn, in comparison with Hom. patrw=n, Lat. patrum, gets its e from pate/res.
a. Variation of stem is seen in wn, on (259); hr, er, ra (262); hs, es- (264); in stems in i, ei (270); u, eu (270); eu, hu (278); oi, w (279), etc. Words in wn, hn show a middle form on, en, and a weak form in n (250 N.).
b. Several words ending in r show a parallel stem in t; thus, u(/dwr water u(/dat-os, h(=par liver h(/pat-os, fre/a_r tank fre/a_t-os (but poet. da/ma_r wife da/mart-os). The reason for this change is uncertain, but at is derived from nt after a consonant (35 b): u(dntos, h(pntos, cp. Lat. jecinoris, nom. jecur. h(=par is probably derived from h(part (133).
c. -atos was transferred from such genitives as o)no/matos, h(/patos to other neuter words: go/natos from go/nu knee, instead of gonv-os, whence Hom. gouno/s. fw=s light, for fa/os (stem faes-), has taken on the t inflection (fwt-o/s, etc.).
d. Neuter stems in -es show -os in the nominative. Cp. e)/tos year (stem e)tes-) with Lat. vetus, veter-is (for vetes-is).

§254

Variation of Quantity.—a. In poetry the quantity of i in words in -is may differ from that of prose; as in tragedy o)/rni^s bird, ko/ni_s dust, o)/fi_s serpent (in prose o)/rni_s, ko/ni^s, o)/fi^s); so in Pind. i)xqu^/s (prose i)xqu/_s) fish.
b. kh=ru^c herald, *foi=ni^c Phoenician, ma/sti^c whip have long u and i in the oblique cases except the dat. pl. (kh/ru_kos, *foi/ni_ki, ma/sti_ga, etc.). a)lw/phc fox has e in the gen. a)lw/pekos, etc., by analogy to such words as poimh/n, poime/nos (a)lwph/kwn occurs in Ionic). pu=r fire has pu^ro/s, pu^ri/, etc. (285, 25).

§255

Gender.—The gender of substantives of the third declension is frequently known by the last letters of the stem.
1. Masculine are stems ending in
a. nt: o)dou/s tooth (o)dont-), dra/kwn serpent (drakont-).
b. ht, wt: pe/nhs day-labourer (penht-), ge/lws laughter (gelwt-).
Exceptions. Stems in -tht (2, b): h( e)sqh/s dress (e)sqht-), to\ fw=s light (fwt-).
c. n: leimw/n meadow (leimon-).
Exceptions. Fem.: stems in gon, don (2, a), and frh/n mind (fren-), i)/_s strength (i)_n-), r(i/_s nose (r(i_n-), a)kti/_s ray (a)kti_n-), glwxi/_s arrow-point (glwxi_n-), w)di/_s birth-pang (w)di_n-), ei)kw/n image (ei)kon-), h)i+w/n shore (h)i+on-), xqw/n earth (xqo/n-), xiw/n snow (xion-), a)lkuw/n halcyon (a)lkuon-), etc., o(, h( xh/n goose (xhn-).
d. r: qh/r wild beast (qhr-), fw/r thief (fwr-).
Exceptions. Fem.: xei/r hand (xer-), kh/r fate (khr-), gasth/r belly (gaster-); neut.: stems in ar (3, a), pu=r fire (pur-), and the indeclinable pe/lwr monster, te/kmwr (Hom) token, etc.
e. eu: goneu/s parent, foneu/s murderer.
2. Feminine are stems ending in
a. gon, don: stagw/n drop (stagon-), xeli_dw/n swallow (xeli_don-).
b. tht, d, q: kako/ths baseness (kakotht-), e)/ris strife (e)rid-), e)lpi/s hope (e)lpid-).
Exceptions. Masc.: pou/s foot (pod-), o(, h( o)/rni_s bird (o)rni_q-).
c. i, u with nom. in -is, -us: po/li-s city, i)sxu/_-s strength.
Exceptions. Masc.: o)/fi-s serpent, e)/xi-s viper, o)/rxi-s testicle; bo/tru-s cluster of grapes, i)xqu/_-s fish, mu=-s mouse, ne/ku-s corpse, sta/xu-s ear of corn, pe/leku-s axe, ph=xu-s fore-arm; and o(, h( su=-s or u(=-s swine.
d. oi: h)xw/ echo, peiqw/ pèrsuasion.
3. Neuter are stems ending in
a. at, ar: pra=gma thing (pra_gmat-), ne/ktar nectar (nektar-). But o( ya/_r starling.
b. as, es (with nom. in -os): kre/as flesh (kreas-), genos race (genes-).
c. i, u with nom. in -i, -u: si/na_pi mustard, a)/stu city.
N.—No stem ending in p, b, f or k, g, x is neuter.

## STEMS IN SIGMA (es, as, os）

§263
Stems in sigma are contracted where s falls out between the vowel of the stem and the vowel of the ending (120). Thus, ge/nos race, gen. gene（s）-os ge/nous, dat. gene（s）-i ge/nei, cp. Lat. genus gener-is (for genes-is), gener-i.
a. The masculine and feminine accusative plural, when it is contracted, borrows the form of the contracted nominative plural. -eis is not derived from -eas. In the dative plural the union of s of the stem and s of the ending produces ss, which is reduced to s without lengthening the preceding vowel (107).
b. Masculine stems in es with the nominative in -hs are proper names; the feminine trih/rhs trireme is an adjective used substantively (properly, triply fitted; h( trih/rhs (nau=s) ‘ship with three banks of oars’).
c. Neuters with stems in es have -os in the nominative, accusative, and vocative singular; neuters with stems in as have -as in these cases.
d. Some stems in as have also a stem in at or a_t (258).

§268 D
1. i stems. a. Doric, Aeolic, and New Ionic retain the i stem without variation in all cases: po/lis, po/lios, po/li_ (from poli-i) and rarely po/lei in Hdt., po/lin, po/li, po/lies, poli/wn, po/lisi, po/li_s from po/lins (Cretan), and po/lias.

b. The gen. pl. has the regular accent (phxe/wn, a)ste/wn). On the dat. pele/kessi, ne/kussi, pi/tussi (some would read ne/ku_si, pi/tu_si), neku/essi, see 250 D. 2. Hom. has accus. i)xqu=s and i)xqu/as, Hdt. has i)xqu/as very rarely.

§269

Stems in i and u are of two kinds:—
1. a. Stems in i, with genitive in -ews, as (masc.) ma/ntis seer, e)/xis viper; (fem.) po/lis city, poi/hsis poetry, du/namis power, sta/sis faction, u(/bris outrage. Neuter nominatives in -i are not used in classical prose.
b. Stems in i, with genitive in -ios, as o( ki/_s weevil, gen. ki_-o/s, dat. ki_-i/; and so in proper names in -is, as *lu/gdamis Lygdamis, gen. *lugda/mios.
2. a. Stems in u, with genitive in -uos; as (masc.) mu=s mouse, bo/trus cluster of grapes, i)xqu/_s fish; (fem.) dru=s oak, o)fru/_s eyebrow, i)sxu/_s force.
b. Stems in u, with genitive in -ews: (masc.) ph=xus forearm, pe/lekus axe; (neut.) a)/stu town.
N. 1.—In the nom., acc., and voc. sing. barytone stems in u have short u; oxytone substantives (usually) and monosyllables have u_; and monosyllables circumflex the u_ (su=s, su=n, su=).
N. 2.—h( e)/gxelus eel follows i)xqu/_s in the singular (e)gxe/lu-os, etc.), but ph=xus in the plural (e)gxe/leis, etc.). But this does not hold for Aristotle.

§270
Stems in i and u vary with stronger stems, of which e in the cases other than nom., acc., and voc. sing. is a survival. Thus:
a. i, u, as in po/li-s, ph=xu-s.
b. ei, eu, which before vowels lost their i and u (43), as in pole（[iglide]）-i, pole（[iglide]）-es, phxe（[uglide]）-es; which contract to po/lei, po/leis, ph/xeis.
c. There is also a stem in h, as in Hom. po/lh-os (268 D. 1, c), whence po/le-ws.
N. 1.—po/le-os in Attic poetry for the sake of the metre is due to the analogy of u stems with gen. in -e-os (h(de/-os, 297). Hom. ph/xe-os is the regular form (from phxe（[uglide]）-os). Attic ph/xe-ws follows po/lews. po/le-si and ph/xe-si for po/li-si and ph/xu-si are due to the analogy of forms from stems in ei, eu (po/le-wn, ph/xe-wn, etc.).
N. 2.—The dual po/lee occurs in some Mss.

§271

Accent.—Final -ws of the genitive singular does not prevent the acute from standing on the antepenult (163 a). Thus po/le-ws, ph/xe-ws, a)/ste-ws. po/le-ws retains the accent of the earlier po/lh-os, which, by transference of quantity (34), became po/le-ws. The accent of the gen. pl. follows that of the gen. sing.

§272

Accusative plural.—po/leis, ph/xeis are borrowed from the nominative. i)xqu=s is from i)xqun-s. i)xqu/as occurs in late Greek. Cp. 251 a.

§273

Contraction.—i)xqu= (once) for i)xqu/e and i)xqu=s for i)xqu/es occur in comedy. i)xqu= is not a legitimate contraction, as u cannot contract with e (51 c). i)xqu=s (for i)xqu/es) is the accus. form used as the nom. (251 b).

§274

oi)=s sheep is declined as follows: oi)=s, oi)-o/s, oi)-i/, oi)=-n, oi)=; dual, oi)=-e, oi)-oi=n; pl. oi)=-es, oi)-w=n, oi)-si/, oi)=-s. Here the stem is oi', representing o)vi, which is properly an i stem: o)vi-s, Lat. ovi-s.

§274 D
Hom. has o)/i+s, o)i+/os and oi)o/s, o)/i+n, o)/i+es, o)i+/wn and oi)w=n, o)i+/essi (oi)/essi o 386) and o)/essi, o)/i+s（i_).

§276
Substantives in -eu/s preceded by a vowel may contract in the gen. and acc. sing. and pl. Thus, a(lieu/s fisherman has gen. a(lie/ws or a(liw=s, acc. a(lie/a_ or a(lia=, gen. pl. a(lie/wn or a(liw=n, acc. pl. a(lie/a_s or a(lia=s. All other forms are regular. The contracted forms were in use in the fifth century, but in the fourth (especially after 350 B.C.) the open forms are common. So are declined *eu)boeu/s Euboean from *eu)boieu/s, *pairaieu/s Peiraeus, *plataieu/s Plataean.

§277

Other Forms.—a. In the drama from words in -eu/s we find rarely -e/a^ in acc. sing., -e/a^s in acc. pl. -e/os and -h=os, -h=es, -h=as are occasionally found.
b. The nom. pl. in older Attic ended in -h=s (basilh=s), derived either from -h=es by contraction or from -e/hs (once on an inscription) by 34. -h=s occurs on inscriptions till about 350 B.C., and is the form to be adopted in the texts of authors of the fifth century and in Plato. -e/es occurs rarely, but is suspected. basilei=s (regular on inscriptions after 329 B.C.) is from analogy to h(dei=s.
c. The acc. pl. basilei=s was not used till the end of the fourth century. -h=s (the nom. form) is used for the acc. in a few passages (251 b).

§278

Stem Variation.—Stems ending in eu, au, ou lose u before case endings beginning with a vowel, [uglide] passing into v (43). Stems in eu show the pure form only in the vocative; other forms are derived from the stronger stem hu. hu and a_u before a consonant become eu, a^u (40) as in basileu/s, basileu=si, nau=s, nausi/ from basilhus, na_us, etc. From basilh=（v）-os, -h=（v）-i, -h=（v）-a, -h=（v）-as come, by transfer of quantity (34), the Attic forms. So new/s is derived from nh（v）-o/s. In basile/wn, new=n, e is shortened from the h of basilh/wn, nhw=n by 39. bo-o/s, etc. are from the stem bou- bov-, cp. Lat. bovis.

## STEMS IN oi

§279
Stems in oi, with nominative in -w/, turn i into unwritten [iglide] (y) (43) before the endings beginning with a vowel. h( peiqw/ persuasion is thus declined:
N. peiqw/. G. peiqou=s (peiqo/-os). D. peiqoi= (peiqo/-i). A. peiqw/ (peiqo/-a). V. peiqoi=. Dual and plural are wanting.
So h)xw/ echo, eu)estw/ well-being, feidw/ sparing, *sapfw/, *lhtw/, *kaluyw/. oi stems are chiefly used for women's names.
a. A stronger form of the stem is wi, seen in the earlier form of the nominative (*sapfw/|, *lhtw/|). The accusative has the accent of the nominative.
b. When dual and plural occur, they are of the second declension: nom. lexoi/ (late) from lexw/ woman in child-bed, acc. gorgou/s from gorgw/ gorgon.
c. h( ei)kw/n image, h( a)hdw/n nightingale, properly from stems in on, have certain forms from this declension (ei)kou=s, ei)kw/, voc. a)hdoi=).

§279 D
In Ionic the forms are contracted (peiqou=s, etc.). Hdt. has acc. *)i_ou=n from *)i_w/, *lhtou=n, but also peiqw/.

## CASES IN -fi（n）

§280

Cases in -fi（n).—-fi（n) is often added to noun stems in Hom. to express the relations of the lost instrumental, locative, and ablative, both singular and (more commonly) plural; rarely to express the relations of the genitive and dative cases. From a_ stems are made singulars, from o stems singulars or plurals, from consonant stems almost always plurals. Except in qeo/-fin with the gods -fi（n) is not added to a stem denoting a person. (a) Instrumental: bi/h-fi by might, e(te/rh-fi with the other (hand), dakruo/-fin with tears; (b) Locative: qu/rh-fi at the door, o)/res-fi on the mountains; (c) Ablative: kefalh=-fin from off the head; especially with prepositions, as e)k ponto/-fin from off the sea, a)po\ nau=-fin from the ships.

## IRREGULAR DECLENSION

§281
The gender in the singular and in the plural may not be the same: o( si=tos grain, ta\ si=ta; o( desmo/s chain, ta\ desma/ chains (oi( desmoi/ cases of imprisonment); to\ sta/dion stade, race-course, pl. ta\ sta/dia and oi( sta/dioi.

§282
Usually the irregularity consists in a word having two different stems.
a. Both stems have a common nominative singular: sko/tos darkness, sko/tou sko/tw|, etc. (like i(/ppou i(/ppw|) or sko/tous sko/tei (like ge/nous ge/nei). So to\n *)/aqw, and to\n *)/aqwn from *)/aqws (238 d), to\n *swkra/th and to\n *swkra/thn (264 b). These are called heteroclites (e(tero/klita differently declined).
N. Many compound proper names in -hs (especially names of foreigners) have forms of the 1 and 3 decl., as *tissafe/rnhs, -nous, -nh| and -nei. So *qeokri/_nh (voc.) in Demosth., *lewni/dhn and *lewni/dea in Hdt.
b. Certain cases are formed from another stem than that of the nom. singular: o( o)/neiro-s dream, gen. o)nei/rat-os (as if from to\ o)/neirar), or (less freq.) o)nei/rou; so to\n *)apo/llwna and to\n *)apo/llw (260), tou= ui(e/os and tou= ui(ou= (285, 27). These are called metaplastic forms (metaplasmo/s change of formation).

§283

Defectives are substantives having, by reason of their meaning or use, only one number or only certain cases. Thus, sing. only: o( a)h/r air, o( ai)qh/r upper air; plur. only: ta\ *dionu/_sia, ta\ *)olu/mpia the Dionysiac (Olympic) festival, oi( e)thsi/ai annual winds; in some cases only: w)= me/le my good sir or madam; o)/nar dream; o)/felos use only in nom.; libo/s li/ba from *li/y stream, libation.

§284

Indeclinables are substantives having one form for all cases: to\ xrew/n, tou= xrew/n, etc. fatality, to\ a)/lfa alpha, to\ le/gein to speak, most cardinal numbers (to\ de/ka ten), several foreign words, as *)iakw/b Jacob, *dabi/d David.

## ADJECTIVES

## ADJECTIVES OF THE FIRST AND SECOND DECLENSIONS

§286

Adjectives of Three Endings.—Most adjectives of the vowel declension have three endings: -os, -h (or -a_), -on. The masculine and neuter are declined according to the second declension, the feminine according to the first.
a. When e, i, or r (30, 218) precedes -os the feminine ends in -a_, not in -h. But adjectives in -oos (not preceded by r) have h. Thus, o)/gdoos, o)gdo/h, o)/gdoon eighth, a)qro/os, a)qro/a_, a)qro/on crowded. See 290 e.

## ADJECTIVES OF THE CONSONANT DECLENSION

§291
Such adjectives as belong only to the consonant declension have two endings. Most such adjectives have stems in es (nominative -hs and -es) and on (nominative -wn and -on). Under on stems fall comparative adjectives, as belti/_wn, be/lti_on better.
a. There are some compounds with other stems: M. F. a)pa/twr, N. a)/pator fatherless, G. a)pa/toros; a)/polis a)/poli without a country, a)po/lidos; au)tokra/twr au)tokra/tor independent, au)tokra/toros; a)/rrhn (older a)/rshn) a)/rren male, a)/rrenos; eu)/xaris eu)/xari agreeable, eu)xa/ritos; eu)/elpis eu)/elpi hopeful, eu)e/lpidos. For the acc. of stems in it and id see 247. Neut. eu)/xari and eu)/elpi for eu)xarit, eu)elpid (133).

## CONSONANT AND VOWEL DECLENSION COMBINED

§294
Adjectives of the consonant declension having a separate form for the feminine inflect the feminine like a substantive of the first declension ending in -a^ (216).

§295
The feminine is made from the stem of the masculine (and neuter) by adding the suffix -[iglide]a (ya), which is combined with the preceding syllable in different ways. The genitive plural feminine is always perispomenon (cp. 208). For the feminine dual, see 287 b.

§296

Stems in u (-us, -eia, -u).—The masculine and neuter have the inflection of ph=xus and a)/stu, except that the genitive singular masculine and neuter ends in -os (not -ws) and -ea in the neuter plural remains uncontracted.

§296 D
Hom. has usually -ei=a, -ei/hs, -ei/h|, etc.; sometimes -e/a, -e/hs, -e/h|, etc. The forms without i (43) are regular in Hdt. For -u/n Hom. has -e/a in eu)re/a po/nton the wide sea. h(du/s and qh=lus are sometimes feminine in Hom.

## DECLENSION OF PARTICIPLES

§300
Like a)gaqo/s, -h/, -o/n are inflected all the participles of the middle, and the future passive participle.

§301
Participles of the active voice (except the perfect, 309), and the aorist passive participle have stems in nt. The masculine and neuter follow the third declension, the feminine follows the first declension.
a. Most stems in ont make the nom. sing. masc. without s, like ge/rwn (243). But stems in ont in the present and second aorist of mi-verbs (didou/s, dou/s), and all stems in ant, ent, unt, add s, lose nt (100), and lengthen the preceding vowel (-ous, -a_s, -eis, -u_s, 37). In like manner the dat. pl. is formed: -ont-si = -ousi, etc.
N.—The stem of participles in -wn, -ontos was originally wnt. ge/rwn was orignally a participle.
b. The nominative neuter of all participles drops final t of the stem (133).
c. The perfect active participle (stem ot) has -ws in the masculine, -os in the neuter. -ws and -os are for -vwt-s, -vot-s.
d. The feminine singular is made by adding [iglide]a to the stem. Thus, lu/_ousa (lu_ont-[iglide]a), ou(=sa (o)nt-[iglide]a), i(sta=sa (i(stant-[iglide]a), tiqei=sa (tiqent-[iglide]a). The perfect adds -u（s）-[iglide]a, as in ei)d-ui=a.

§302
The vocative of all participles is the same as the nominative.

§303
Participles in -wn, -a_s, -eis, -ous, -u_s frequently use the masculine for the feminine in the dual.

§304
The accent of monosyllabic participles is an exception to 252: w)/n, o)/ntos (not o)nto/s), sta/_s, sta/ntos.

## ADJECTIVES OF ONE ENDING

§312
Adjectives of one ending have the same termination for masculine and feminine. The neuter (like masc. and fem.) sometimes occurs in oblique cases. Examples: a)gnw/s a)gnw=t-os unknown or unknowing, a)/pais a)/paid-os childless, a)rgh/s a)rgh=t-os white, a(/rpac a(/rpag-os rapacious, ma/kar ma/kar-os blessed, a)ka/ma_s a)ka/mant-os unwearied. Here belong also certain other adjectives commonly used as substantives, as gumnh/s gumnh=t-os light armed, pe/nhs pe/nht-os poor, fuga/s fuga/d-os fugitive, h(=lic h(/lik-os comrade, a)lazw/n a)lazo/n-os flatterer. Some are masculine only, as e)qelonth/s (-ou=) uolunteer. Adj. in -i/s -i/dos are feminine only. *(ellhni/s Greek, patri/s (scil. gh=) fatherland, summaxi/s (po/lis) an allied state.

## COMPARISON OF ADJECTIVES

§313

Comparison by -teros, -tatos.—The usual endings are:
For the comparative: -teros m. -tera_ f. -teron n.
For the superlative: -tatos m. -tath f. -taton n.
The endings are added to the masculine stem of the positive. Comparatives are declined like a)/cios, superlatives like a)gaqo/s (287).
dh=los (dhlo-) clear, dhlo/-teros, dhlo/-tatos; i)sxu_ro/s (i)sxu_ro-) strong, i)sxu_ro/teros, i)sxu_ro/-tatos; me/la_s (melan-) black, mela/n-teros, mela/n-tatos; baru/s (baru-) heavy, baru/-teros, baru/-tatos; a)lhqh/s (a)lhqes-) true, a)lhqe/s-teros, a)lhqe/s-tatos; eu)kleh/s (eu)klees-) famous, eu)klee/s-teros, eu)klee/s-tatos.
a. xarie/steros, -e/statos are from xariet-teros, -tatos (83, 299 b), from xari/eis graceful. Compounds of xa/ris grace add o to the stem (xarit-o-), whence e)pixaritw/teros more pleasing. pe/nhs poor has pene/s-teros from penet-teros, with e for h.
b. Originally -teros had no other force than to contrast one idea with another, and this function is retained in deci/teros right) (a)ri/steros left, h(me/teros our) ( u(_me/teros your. Hom. has several such words: a)gro/teros wild) (tame, qhlu/terai gunai=kes) (men, cp. Arcadian a)rre/nteros from a)/rrhn male. Cp. 1082 b.

§314
Adjectives in -os with a short penult lengthen o to w: ve/o-s new, vew/-teros, new/-tatos, xalepo/-s difficult, xalepw/-teros, xalepw/-tatos. An undue succession of short syllables is thus avoided.
a. If the penult is long either by nature or by position (144), o is not lengthened: lepto/s lean, lepto/teros, lepto/tatos. A stop and a liquid almost always make position here (cp. 145); as pikro/s bitter, pikro/teros, pikro/tatos. keno/s empty and steno/s narrow were originally kenvos, stenvos (Ionic keino/s, steino/s, 37 D. 1), hence keno/teros, steno/teros.

§314 a. D
Hom. o)izu_rw/tatos (but cp. Att. oi)zu^ro/s), la_rw/tatos (la^erw/tatos?).

§315
The following drop the stem vowel o: geraio/-s aged, gerai/-teros, gerai/tatos; palaio/-s ancient, palai/-teros, palai/-tatos; sxolai=o-s slow, sxolai/-teros, sxolai/-tatos; fi/lo-s dear, fi/l-teros (poetic), fi/l-tatos (319, 11).
a. Some other adjectives reject the stem vowel o and end in -aiteros, -aitatos, as h(/suxos quiet, i)/sos equal, o)/rqrios early. These, like sxolai/teros and gerai/teros, imitate palai/teros, which is properly derived from the adverb pa/lai long ago. So mesai/teros, -ai/tatos imitate mesai- in Hom. mesai-po/lios middle-aged.

§316

-esteros, -estatos.—By imitation of words like a)lhqe/s-teros, a)lhqe/statos (313), -esteros, -estatos are added to stems in on and to some in oo (contracted to ou). Thus, eu)dai/mwn happy, eu)daimon-e/steros, -e/statos; a(plou=s simple, a(plou/steros (for a(plo-esteros), a(plou/statos; eu)/nous well-disposed, eu)nou/steros, -ou/statos, and so in all others in -nous from nou=s mind. (Others in -oos have -owteros: a)qrow/teros more crowded from a)qro/os.)
a. Some stems in on substitute o for on; as (from e)pilh/smwn forgetful, e)pilhsmone/s-teros) e)pilhsmo/-tatos; pi/_wn fat, pi_o/teros, pi_o/tatos; pe/pwn ripe has pepai/teros, pepai/tatos. Cp. 315 a.
b. Other cases: (with loss of o) e)rrwme/no-s strong, e)rrwmene/steros, -e/statos, a)/kra_to-s unmixed, a)kra_te/statos, a)/smeno-s glad, a)/fqono-s abundant.

§317

-isteros, -istatos.—By imitation of words like a)xari/steros for a)xaritteros (83) from a)/xaris disagreeable, -isteros, -istatos are used especially with adjectives of a bad meaning, as klept-i/statos (kle/pths thief, 321), kakhgori/steros (kakh/goros abusive), lal-i/steros (la/los talkative).

§318

§321
In poetry and sometimes in prose comparatives and superlatives are formed from substantives and pronouns. Hom. has basileu/teros more kingly, -tatos (basileu/s king), e(tairo/tatos a closest companion (e(tai=ros comrade), ku/nteros more doglike, -tatos (ku/wn dog), kouro/teros more youthful (kou=ros a youth). Aristophanes has klepti/statos most thievish (kle/pths thief, 317), and au)to/tatos his very self, ipsissimus.

§322

Double Comparison.—A double comparative occurs sometimes to produce a comic effect, as kunterw/teros (321). A double superlative is prw/tistos.

§323

Comparison by ma=llon, ma/lista.—Instead of the forms in -teros, -tatos or -i_wn, -istos the adverbs ma=llon more, ma/lista most, may be used with the positive; as ma=llon fi/los more dear, dearer, ma/lista fi/los most dear, dearest. This is the only way of comparing participles and words that do not take the comparative and superlative endings (ma=llon e(kw/n more willing).
a. Comparison by ma=llon, ma/lista is common in the case of compound adjectives, adjectives with a prepositional prefix, verbal adjectives in -to/s, and adjectives in -ios.

§324
To express equality or inferiority ou(/tw as (often in correlation with w(/sper), h(=tton less, may be placed before the positive. Thus, as good as handsome may be expressed by ou(/tws a)gaqo\s w(/sper kai\ kalo/s, w(/sper a)gaqo\s ou(/tw kai\ kalo/s, ou)=x h(=tton kalo\s h)\ kai\ a)gaqo/s.

§328

au)to/s is a definite adjective and a pronoun. It has three meanings:
a. self: standing by itself in the nominative, au)to\s o( a)nh/r or o( a)nh\r au)to/s the man himself, or (without the article) in agreement with a substantive or pronoun; as a)ndro\s au)tou= of the man himself.
b. him, her, it, them, etc.: standing by itself in an oblique case (never in the nominative). The oblique cases of au)to/s are generally used instead of ou(=, oi(=, e(/, etc., as o( path\r au)tou= his father, oi( pai=des au)tw=n their children.
c. same: when it is preceded by the article in any case: o( au)to\s a)nh/r the same man, tou= au)tou= a)ndro/s of the same man.
N.—The article and au)to/s may unite by crasis (68 a): au(to/s, au(th/, tau)to/ or tau)to/n; tau)tou=, tau)th=s; tau)tw=|, tau)th=|, etc. Distinguish au(th/ the same f. from au(/th this f.; tau)ta/ the same n. from tau=ta these things n.; tau)th=| from tau/th|.
