## ADVERBS

§341

Origin.—Adverbs, like prepositions and conjunctions, were originally case forms, made from the stems of nouns and pronouns. Some of these nominal and pronominal stems have gone out of common use, so that only petrified forms are left in the adverbs. Some of these words were still felt to be live cases; in others no consciousness of their origin survived. Many adverbs show old suffixes joined to the stem or to a case form (342). It is sometimes uncertain whether we should speak of adverbs or of nouns with local endings.
Nominative (rare): pu/c with clenched fist, a(/pac once, a)nami/c pell-mell.
Genitive: e(/nhs day after to-morrow, e(ch=s next, pou=, ou(= where, au)tou= in the very place, e)kpodw/n out of the way (e)k + podw=n); by analogy, e)mpodw/n in one's way.
Dative: dhmosi/a| at public cost, la/qra| in secret, koinh=| in common, etc. (1527 b), a)/llh| otherwise, ph=| how.
Accusative: very common, especially such adverbs as have the form of the accusative of neuter adjectives, as polu/ much, mi_kro/n a little, prw=ton at first, th/meron to-day, polla/ often. See 1606-1611.
Locative: oi)/ko-i at home (oi)=ko-s house), *)isqmo-i= at the Isthmus, poi= whither, and all adverbs in -oi. The -i of the consonantal declension is properly the ending of the locative, as in *maraqw=n-i at Marathon; -oisi (234) in O stems, in contrast to -ois; -a_si (-hsi) in Ā stems (215): qu/ra_si at the doors, *plataia=si at Plataea, *)aqh/nhsi at Athens; further in pa/lai long ago, e)kei= there, pandhmei/ in full force.
Instrumental: a)/nw above, ka/tw below, ou)/pw not yet, w(=-de thus (but the forms in -w may be ablatives); krufh= and la/qra_ in secret.
Ablative: all adverbs in -ws, as w(s as, ou(/tws thus, e(te/rws otherwise. Here, e.g. original e(terwd (cp. Old Lat. altoōd, abl. of altus) became e(terw (133), which took on -s from the analogy of such words as a)mfi/s parallel to a)mfi/.

§342

Place.—To denote place the common endings are:—
-i, -qi, -si at, in to denote place where (locative). -ou, the sign of the genitive, is also common.
-qen from to denote the place whence (ablative).
-de (-ze), -se to, toward to denote place whither.
In the following examples poetical words are bracketed.

oi)/ko-i (oi)/ko-qi) at homeoi)/ko-qen from homeoi)/kade (oi)=ko/nde) homeward

（oi)ka- is an old accusative form.)

*)olumpi/a_-si at Olympia*)olumpi/a_-qen from Olympia*)olumpi/aze to Olympia
a. In -aze, -de is added to the accusative (1589), and stands for -a（n）s, the old acc. pl.,+-de (Eng. TO). Cp. 26, 106. The other endings are added to the stem. -se is usually added only to pronominal stems. -si forms a locative plural. o sometimes takes the place of a_ of the first declension (r(i/zoqen from the root, stem r(iza_-), or is added to consonant stems. Words in -tero- lengthen o to w. Between stem and ending ax is often inserted.
b. -qen may take the form -qe in poetry, and especially when the idea of whence is lost, as pro/sqe in front (134 D.). -qa is found in e)/nqa in all dialects. -qa for -qen occurs in Aeolic and Doric.
c. Some local adverbs are made from prepositions, as a)/nw above, e)/cw outside, e)/sw within, ka/tw below, pro/sqen in front.

§348

Notation.—The system of alphabetic notation came into use after the second century B.C. The first nine letters stand for units, the second nine for tens, the third nine for hundreds (27 letters). In addition to the 24 letters of the alphabet, three obsolete signs are employed: s, a form identical with the late abbreviation for st, in place of the lost v (3), once used for 6; ϟ (koppa), in the same order as Lat. q, for 90; for 900, [sampi ] sampi, probably for san, an old form of sigma, + pi. From 1 to 999 a stroke stands above the letter, for 1000's the same signs are used but with the stroke below the letter (a# = 1, [tnum ]a = 1000). Only the last letter in any given series has the stroke above: rnz# 157, ua# 401, [tnum ]a[sampi ]i# 1910. a+ is sometimes used for 10,000; b+ for 20,000, etc.
a. In the classical period the following system was used according to the inscriptions: *i = 1, *i*i*i*i = 4, *g (pe/nte) = 5, *g*i = 6, *d (de/ka) = 10, *d*d = 20, *h (e(kato/n) = 100, *h*h = 200, *x = 1000, *m = 10,000, *i (penta/kis de/ka) = 50, *gx*x (penta/kis xi/_lioi + xi/_lioi) = 6000.
b. For the numbers from 1 to 24 the letters, used in continuous succession, are frequently used to designate the books of the Iliad (*a, *b, *g, etc.) and of the Odyssey (a, b, g, etc.).

## VERBS

## INFLECTION: PRELIMINARY REMARKS (355-380）

§355
The Greek verb shows distinctions of voice, mood, verbal noun, tense, number, and person.

§356

Voices.—There are three voices: active, middle, and passive.
a. The middle usually denotes that the subject acts on himself or for himself, as lou/omai wash myself, a)mu/_nomai defend myself (lit. ward off for myself).
b. The passive borrows all its forms, except the future and aorist, from the middle.
c. Deponent verbs have an active meaning but only middle (or middle and passive) forms. If its aorist has the middle form, a deponent is called a middle deponent (xari/zomai gratify, e)xarisa/mhn); if its aorist has the passive form, a deponent is called a passive deponent (e)nqu_me/omai reflect on, e)nequ_mh/qhn). Deponents usually prefer the passive to the middle forms of the aorist.

§357

Moods.—Four moods, the indicative, subjunctive, optative, imperative, are called finite, because the person is defined by the ending (366). The infinitive, strictly a verbal noun (358), is sometimes classed as a mood.

§358

Verbal Nouns.—Verbal forms that share certain properties of nouns are called verbal nouns. There are two kinds of verbal nouns.
1. Substantival: the infinitive.
N.—The infinitive is properly a case form (chiefly dative, rarely locative), herein being like a substantive.
2. Adjectival (inflected like adjectives):
a. Participles: active, middle, and passive.
b. Verbal adjectives:
In -to/s, denoting possibility, as filhto/s lovable, or with the force of a perfect passive participle, as grapto/s written.
In -te/os, denoting necessity, as grapte/os that must be written.

§359

Tenses.—There are seven tenses in the indicative: present, imperfect, future, aorist, perfect, pluperfect, and future perfect. The future perfect commonly has a passive force, but it may be active or middle in meaning (see 581).
The subjunctive has three tenses: present, aorist, and perfect.
The optative and infinitive have five tenses: present, future, aorist, perfect, and future perfect.
The imperative has three tenses: present, aorist, and perfect.

§359 D
Hom. does not use the future or future perfect in the optative.

§360

Primary and Secondary Tenses.—There are two classes of tenses in the indicative: (1) Primary (or Principal) tenses, the present and perfect expressing present time, the future and future perfect expressing future time; (2) Secondary (or Historical) tenses, the imperfect, pluperfect, and aorist expressing past time. The secondary tenses have an augment (428) prefixed.

§361

Second Aorists, etc.—Some verbs have tenses called second aorists (active, middle, and passive), second perfects and pluperfects (active only), and second futures (passive). The meaning of these tenses ordinarily corresponds to that of the first aorist, etc.; but when a verb has both forms in any tense (which is rarely the case), the two forms usually differ in meaning. Sometimes one form is poetical, the other used in prose.

§362
No single Greek verb shows all the tenses mentioned in 359 and 361; and the paradigms are therefore taken from different verbs.

§363

Number.—There are three numbers: the singular, dual, and plural.

§364

Person.—There are three persons (first, second, and third) in the indicative, subjunctive, and optative. The imperative has only the second and third persons.
a. Except in a few cases in poetry (465 c) the first person plural is used for the first person dual.

§365

Inflection.—The inflection of a verb consists in the addition of certain endings to the different stems.

§366

Endings.—The endings in the finite moods (357) show whether the subject is first, second, or third person; and indicate number and voice. See 462 ff.
a. The middle has a different set of endings from the active. The passive has the endings of the middle except in the aorist, which has the active endings.
b. The indicative has two sets of endings in the active and in the middle: one for primary tenses, the other for secondary tenses.
c. The subjunctive uses the same endings as the primary tenses of the indicative; the optative uses the same as those of the secondary tenses.

## STEMS

§367
A Greek verb has two kinds of stems: (1) the tense-stem, to which the endings are attached, and (2) a common verb-stem (also called theme) from which all the tense-stems are derived. The tense-stem is usually made from the verb-stem by prefixing a reduplication-syllable (439), and by affixing signs for mood (457, 459) and tense (455). A tense-stem may be identical with a verbstem.

§368

The Tense-stems.—The tenses fall into nine classes called tense-systems. Each tense-system has its own separate tense-stem.

SYSTEMS.TENSES.

I.Present,includingpresent and imperfect.

II.Future,“future active and middle.

III.First aorist,“first aorist active and middle.

IV.Second aorist,“second aorist active and middle.

V.First perfect,“first perfect, first pluperfect, and fut. perf., active.

VI.Second perfect,“second perfect and second pluperfect active.

VII.Perfect middle,“perfect and pluperfect middle (pass.), future perfect.

VIII.First passive,“first aorist and first future passive.

IX.Second passive,“second aorist and second future passive.
The tense-stems are explained in detail in 497-597.
a. Since few verbs have both the first and second form of the same tense (361), most verbs have only six of these nine systems; many verbs do not even have six. Scarcely any verb shows all nine systems.
b. There are also secondary tense-stems for the future passive, the pluperfect, and the future perfect.
c. The tense-stems assume separate forms in the different moods.

§369
The principal parts of a verb are the first person singular indicative of the tense-systems occurring in it. These are generally six: the present, future, first aorist, first (or second) perfect active, the perfect middle, and the first (or second) aorist passive. The future middle is given if there is no future active. The second aorist (active or middle) is added if it occurs. Thus:
lu/_w loose, lu/_sw, e)/lu_sa, le/luka, le/lumai, e)lu/qhn.
lei/pw leave, lei/yw, le/loipa, le/leimmai, e)lei/fqhn, 2 aor. e)/lipon.
gra/fw write, gra/yw, e)/graya, ge/grafa, ge/grammai, 2 aor. pass. e)gra/fhn.
skw/ptw jeer, skw/yomai, e)/skwya, e)skw/fqhn.

§370
The principal parts of deponent verbs (356 c) are the present, future, perfect, and aorist indicative. Both first and second aorists are given if they occur.
bou/lomai wish, boulh/somai, bebou/lhmai, e)boulh/qhn (passive deponent).
g/gnomai become, genh/somai, gege/nhmai, 2 aor. e)geno/mhn (middle deponent).
e)rga/zomai work, e)rga/somai, ei)rgasa/mhn, ei)/rgasmai, ei)rga/sqhn.

§371

Verb-stem (or Theme).—The tense-stems are made from one fundamental stem called the verb-stem (or theme).
This verb-stem may be a root (193) as in ti/_-w honour, or a root to which a derivative suffix has been appended, as in ti_-ma/-w honour.

§372
A verb forming its tense-stems directly from a root is called a primitive verb. A denominative verb forms its tense-stems from a longer verb-stem, originally a noun-stem; as doulo/w enslave from dou=los slave. Verbs in mi (379), and verbs in w of two syllables (in the present indicative active, as le/g-w speak) or of three syllables (in the middle, as de/xomai receive) are generally primitive. Others are denominative.

§373
The verb-stem may show numerous modifications in form.
Thus, corresponding to the gradations in sing, sang, sung (35), the verb lei/p-w leave shows the stems leip-, loip- (2 perf. le/-loip-a), lip- (2 aor. e)/-lip-o-n); the verb feu/g-w flee shows feug- and fug- (2 aor. e)/-fug-o-n). In r(h/gnu_mi break we find the three stems r(hg, r(wg (2 perf. e)/rrwga), r(ag (2 aor. pass. e)rra/ghn). ste/ll-w send has the stems stel- and stal- (perf. e)/-stal-ka, 2 fut. pass. stal-h/somai).
a. When the fundamental stem shows modifications, it is customary for convenience to call its shorter (or shortest) form the verb-stem, and to derive the other forms from it. The student must, however, beware of assuming that the short forms are older than the other forms.

§374
The verb-stem may also show modifications in quantity, as present lu/_-w loose, perfect le/-lu^-ka.
N.—Various causes produce this variation. lu/_w has u_ from analogy to lu/_-sw, e)/-lu_-sa where the verb-stem lu^ has been regularly lengthened (534, 543). For Attic fqa/nw anticipate Hom. has fqa/_nw for fqanvw (28, 147 D.).

§375

w Inflection and mi Inflection.—There are two slightly different methods of inflecting verbs, the first according to the common, the second according to the mi system. The names w-verbs and mi verbs (a small class) refer to the ending of the first person singular active of the present tense indicative only: lu/_-w loose, ti/qh-mi place.
a. In the w inflection the tense-stem ends in the thematic vowel. To this form belong all futures, and the presents, imperfects, and second aorists showing the thematic vowel.

§376
According to the ending of the verb-stem, w-verbs are termed:
1. Vowel (or pure) verbs:
a. Not contracted: those that end in u or i, as lu/_-w loose, paideu/-w educate, xri/_-w anoint. Such verbs retain the final vowel of the stem unchanged in all their forms.
b. Contracted: those that end in a, e, o, as ti_mw= honour from ti_ma/-w, poiw= make from poie/-w, dhlw= manifest from dhlo/-w.
2. Consonant verbs, as:
Liquid or nasal verbs: de/r-w flay, me/n-w remain.
Verbs ending in a stop (or mute), as a)/g-w lead, pei/q-w persuade.
N.—Verbs ending in a stop consonant are called labial, dental, or palatal verbs. Consonant verbs do not retain the final consonant of the stem unchanged in all their forms. The final consonant may be assimilated to a following consonant, or may form with it a double consonant.

§377

Thematic Vowel.—Some tense-stems end in a vowel which varies between o and e (or w and h) in certain forms. This is called the thematic (or variable) vowel. Thus lu/_o-men lu/_e-te, lu/_w-men lu/_h-te, lu/_so-men lu/_se-te. The thematic vowel is written o/e or w/h, as lu_o/e-, grafw/h-. See 456.

§378

o is used before m or n in the indicative, and in the optative, w before m or n in the subjunctive, elsewhere e is used in the indicative (h in the subjunctive).

§379
In the mi inflection no thematic vowel is employed, and the endings are attached directly to the tense-stem. The mi form is used only in the present, imperfect, and second aorist. In the other tenses, verbs in mi generally show the same inflection as w-verbs. For further explanation of the w and the mi inflection see 602ff., 717ff.

§380

Meanings of the Tenses and Moods.—In the synopsis (382) meanings are given wherever these are not dependent on the use of the various forms in the sentence. The meanings of the subjunctive and optative forms and the difference between the tenses can be learned satisfactorily only from the syntax. Some of these meanings may here be given:
a. Subjunctive: lu/_wmen or lu/_swmen let us loose, (e)a\_n) lu/_w or lu/_sw (if) I loose, (i(/na) gra/fw (that) I may write.
b. Optative: (ei)/qe) lu/_oimi or lu/_saimi (would) that I may loose! (ei)) lu/_oimen or lu/_saimen (if) we should loose.

§381

## I. (B) VOWEL VERBS: CONTRACTED VERBS

§385
Verbs in -aw, -ew, -ow are contracted only in the present and imperfect. The principles of contraction are explained in 49-55. ti_ma/w (ti_ma-) honour, poie/w (poie-) make, and dhlo/w (dhlo-) manifest are thus inflected in the present and imperfect of the active, middle and passive.

Attic prose always, and Attic poetry usually, use the contracted forms.
N. 1.—The open forms of verbs in -aw are sometimes found in Homer. Verbs in -ew often show the uncontracted forms in Homer; in Herodotus contraction properly takes place except before o and w. Verbs in -ow never appear in their uncontracted forms in any author.
N. 2.—poie/w sometimes loses its i (43) except before o sounds.

Examples of Contracted Verbs.

1. Verbs in -aw:

a)pata/w deceive (a)pa/th deceit）o(rma/w set in motion (o(rmh/ impulse）

meleta/w practise (mele/th practice）teleuta/w finish (teleuth/ end）

ni_ka/w conquer (ni/_kh victory）tolma/w dare (to/lma daring）

2. Verbs in -ew:

a)dike/w do wrong (a)/dikos unjust）oi)ke/w inhabit (oi)=kos housë, poetic)

bohqe/w assist (bohqo/s assisting）poleme/w make war (po/lemos war）

kosme/w order (ko/smos order）fqone/w envy (fqo/nos envy）

mi_se/w hate (mi=sos hate）file/w love (fi/los friend）

3. Verbs in -ow:

a)cio/w think worthy (a)/cios worthy）ku_ro/w make valid (ku=ros authority）

doulo/w enslave (dou=los slave）polemo/w make an enemy of (po/lemos war）

e)leuqero/w set free (e)leu/qeros free）stefano/w crown (ste/fanos crown）

zugo/w put under the yoke (zugo/n yoke）tapeino/w humiliate (tapeino/s humbled）

## REMARKS ON THE CONTRACTED VERBS

§393
In the present optative active there are two forms: (1) that with the modal sign -ih-, having -n in the 1 sing., and -san in the 3 pl.; (2) that with the modal sign -i_-, having -mi in the 1 sing., and -en in the 3 pl. The first form is more common in the singular, the second in the dual and plural.
ti_mw/|hn (rarely ti_mw=|mi), ti_mw=|ton (rarely ti_mw/|hton), ti_mw=|men (rarely ti_mw/|hmen), poioi/hn (rarely poioi=mi), poioi=ton (rarely poioi/hton), poioi=men (rarely poioi/hmen), dhloi/hn (rarely dhloi=mi), dhloi=ton (rarely dhloi/hton), dhloi=men (rarely dhloi/hmen).

§394
Ten verbs in -aw show h where we expect a_. These are diyw= thirst, zw= live, peinw= hunger, knw= scrape, nw= spin (rare), smw= wash, xow= give oracles, xow= am eager for (rare), xrw=mai use, and yw= rub. See 641,

kai/w burn, klai/w weep, do not contract the forms in which i has disappeared (38). Thus, ka/_w, ka/_eis, ka/_ei, ka/_omen, ka/_ete, ka/_ousi.

§397
Verbs in -ew of two syllables do not contract e with o or w. The present and imperfect indicative of ple/w sail are inflected as follows.

## I. (C) CONSONANT VERBS

§400
Verbs whose stems end in a consonant are in general inflected like non-contracting w-verbs in all tenses. The future active and middle of liquid and nasal verbs are inflected like contracted ew-verbs.

## PERFECT AND PLUPERFECT MIDDLE (AND PASSIVE)

§403
In the perfect and pluperfect middle (and passive) of stems ending in a consonant certain euphonic changes (409) occur upon the addition of the personal endings.

§404
Several verbs with stems ending in a short vowel retain that vowel in the perfect (and in other tenses); such stems originally ended in s; as tele/-w finish, from te/los end (teles-). This s appears in the perfect middle stem (tete/le-s-mai, tete/le-s-tai). In the second person singular and plural but one s is found: tete/le-sai, tete/le-sqe. By analogy some other verbs have a s at the end of the verbal stem.

§405
In the perfect and pluperfect middle the third person plural of stems ending in a consonant or of stems adding s consists of the perfect middle participle with ei)si/ are (in the perfect) and h)=san were (in the pluperfect).

## EXPLANATION OF THE PERFECT AND PLUPERFECT FORMS

§408
The periphrastic third plural is used instead of the forms derived directly from the union of the stem with the ending.
Thus, gegramme/noi ei)si/ is used for gegraf-ntai which would become gegra/fatai by 35 b, n between consonants passing into a. The periphrastic form is also used in verbs adding s to their stems, as tetele-s-me/noi ei)si/ for tetele-s-ntai. Stems in n that drop n in the perfect system form their perfect and pluperfect regularly; thus, kri/_nw (krin-) judge has ke/krintai, e)ke/krinto.
N.—On the retention of -atai, -ato see 465 f.

§409

Euphonic Changes.—For the euphonic changes in these forms see 82-87, 103.
a. Labial Stems.—le/leim-mai is for leleip-mai, le/leif-qon is for leleip-sqon, le/leifqe is for leleip-sqe (103). In the same manner are inflected other labial stems, as tri/_bw (tri_b-) rub, r(i/_ptw (r(i_p-) throw: te/tri_m-mai for tetri_b-mai, te/tri_yai for tetri_b-sai, etc. Stems ending in mp drop p before m, but retain it before other consonants. Thus,

pepemp-maibecomespe/pemmaipepemp-meqabecomespepe/mmeqa

pepemp-sai“pe/pemyaipepemp-sqe“pe/pemfqe (103）

pepemp-tai“pe/pemptai
b. Dental Stems.—pe/peis-tai is for pepeiq-tai (83), pe/peis-qon is for pepeiqqon (83), pe/peisqe is for pepeiq-（s）qe (83, 103). The s thus produced was trans ferred to the first persons pe/peismai, pepei/smeqa (86, 87). Like pe/peismai, etc., are formed and inflected e)/yeusmai from yeu/dw (yeud-) deceive, pe/frasmai from fra/zw (frad-) declare, e)/speismai (100) from spe/ndw (spend-) pour a libation.

§409 b. D
Hom. has the original forms pefradme/nos, kekoruqme/nos.
c. Paltal Stems.—pe/pra_cai is for pepra_g-sai (97), pe/pra_ktai is for pepra_gtai (82 a), pe/pra_xqe is for pepra_g-sqe (103). Like pe/pra_gmai are inflected ple/kw (plek-) weave pe/pleg-mai, a)/gw (a)g-) lead h)=gmai, a)lla/ttw (a)llag-) exchange h)/llagmai, tara/ttw (tarax-) confuse teta/ragmai. Stems in -gx change x before m to g and drop one g (as in e)lh/leg-mai for e)lhlegg-mai, 85 and 85 b), but keep the second palatal before other consonants (as in e)lh/legcai for e)lhlegx-sai, 97; e)lh/legk-tai for e)lhlegx-tai, 82). On the reduplication see 446.
d. Liquid and Nasal Stems.—Stems in l or r are inflected like h)/ggelmai, as ste/llw (stel-, stal-) send e)/stalmai, ai)/rw (a)r-) raise h)=rmai, e)gei/rw (e)ger-) wake e)gh/germai (446). Stems in n retaining the nasal are inflected like pe/fasmai, as shmai/nw (shman-) signify sesh/masmai. (For -smai see 94 a and b.) Stems in n dropping the nasal (559 a) are inflected like le/lumai, as kri/_nw (krin-) judge ke/krimai.
e. Vowel Stems adding s.—Here the stem ends in a vowel except before m and t; thus, tete/le-sai, tete/le-sqon, tete/le-sqe: but tete/le-s-mai, tetele/-s-meqa, tete/le-s-tai.
N.—Since the stem of tele/w is properly teles- (teles-[iglide]w, 624), the original inflection is teteles-sai, whence tete/le-sai (107); tete/les-tai; teteles-sqon, teteles-sqe, whence tete/lesqon, tete/lesqe (103). tete/lesmai and tetele/smeqa are due to the analogy of the other forms.

§410
The forms pe/fansai, e)pe/fanso, and pe/fanso are not attested. Cp. 707 a.

§411
The principal parts of the verbs in 406-407 are as follows:
a)gge/llw announce (a)ggel-), a)ggelw=, h)/ggeila, h)/ggelka, h)/ggelmai, h)gge/lqhn.
gra/fw write (graf-), gra/yw, e)/graya, ge/grafa, ge/grammai, 2 aor. pass. e)gra/fhn.

## CONJUGATION OF mi-VERBS

§412
The conjugation of mi-verbs differs from that of w-verbs only in the present, imperfect, and second aorist active and middle; and (rarely) in the second perfect. The mi forms are made by adding the endings directly to the tense-stem without any thematic vowel, except in the subjunctive of all verbs, and in the optative of verbs ending in -nu_mi.

§413
Verbs having second aorists and second perfects of the mi form are, as a rule, w-verbs, not mi-verbs, in the present. Thus, the second aorists: e)/bhn (bai/nw go), e)/gnwn (gignw/skw know); the second perfect: te/qnamen (qnh/|skw die).

§414
There are two main classes of mi-verbs.
A. The root class. This class commonly ends in -h-mi or -w-mi (from stems in e, a, or o). The present stem is usually reduplicated, but may be the same as the verb-stem, which is a root.

Verb-stemPresent StemPresent

qe-, qh-tiqe-, tiqh- (for qiqe, qiqh, 125 a)ti/qhmi place

e(-, h(-i(_e-, i(_h- (for sise, sish）i(/_hmi send

sta-, sth-i(sta-, i(sth- (for sista, sisth, 119）i(/sthmi set

do-, dw-dido-, didw-di/dwmi give

fa-, fh-fa-, fh-fhmi/ say
B. The -nu_mi class. This class adds nu (nu_), after a vowel nnu (nnu_), to the verb-stem. In the subjunctive and optative regularly, and sometimes in the indicative, verbs in -nu_mi are inflected like verbs in -w.

Verb-stemPresent StemPresent

deik-deiknu-, deiknu_-dei/knu_mi show

zeug-zeugnu-, zeugnu_-zeu/gnu_mi yoke

kera-kerannu-, kerannu_-kera/nnu_mi mix

r(hg-r(hgnu-, r(hgnu_-r(h/gnu_mi break

sbe-sbennu-, sbennu_-sbe/nnu_mi extinguish
C. There are some (mostly poetic) verbs in -nhmi, which add na-, nh- to form the present stem; as da/m-nh-mi I subdue, da/m-na-men we subdue.

§415
All the possible mi forms do not occur in any single verb. ti/qhmi and di/dwmi are incomplete and irregular in the second aorist active; and e)/sbhn went out from sbe/nnu_mi is the only second aorist formed from nu_mi-verbs. e)pria/mhn I bought, second aorist middle (from the stem pria- with no present), is given in the paradigms in place of the missing form of i(/sthmi; and e)/du_n I entered from du/_w (but formed as if from du=mi) in place of a second aorist of the nu_mi-verbs.

§416
(A) Root Class.—Inflection of ti/qhmi place, i(/sthmi set, di/dwmi give, in the present, imperfect, and second aorist tenses; and of e)pria/mhn I bought.

## ACCENT

§423
Simple or compound verbs usually throw the accent as far back as the quantity of the last syllable permits (recessive accent, 159).
lu/_w, lu/_omen, e)lu_o/mhn; paideu/w, paideu/ousi, e)paideue/thn; a)poba/llw, a)po/balle; a)polu/_w, a)pe/lu_on; a)/peimi, su/nesmen, su/mfhmi, pa/resti.

§424
To this general rule there are exceptions.
a. Enclitics.—All the forms of fhmi/ say, and ei)mi/ am, except fh/|s and ei)=.
b. Imperatives.—(1) The second person sing. of the second aorist active imperative of five verbs is oxytone: ei)pe/ say, e)lqe/ come, eu(re/ find, i)de/ see, labe/ take. Their plurals are accented ei)pe/te, e)lqe/te, etc.; compounds have recessive accent: ka/teipe, a)/pelqe, e)/feure, para/labe.
(2) The second aorist middle (2 sing.) is perispomenon, as labou=, parabalou=, kaqelou=.
c. Contracted verbs are only apparent exceptions: thus, e.g., ti_ma=| for ti_ma/ei, dhlou=si for dhlo/ousi, filei=n for file/ein. So the subjunctive of the first and second aorist passive luqw= for luqe/w, fanw= for fane/w; the optatives luqei=men from luqe/-i_-men, didoi=men from dido/-i_-men; the futures fanw= for fane/w, fanoi=mi for fane/oimi, fanei=n for fane/ein, fanw=n for fane/wn; lipei=n for lipe/en; and the present and second aorist active and middle subjunctive of most mi-verbs, as tiqw= for tiqe/w, i(stw=mai, qw=mai, perf. kektw=mai. On didou=si, tiqei=si, see 463 d.
N. 1.—In athematic optatives the accent does not recede beyond the diphthong containing -i_-, the sign of the optative mood: i(stai=o, i(stai=men, i(stai=to, didoi=to; and so in luqei=men, luqei=en.
N. 2.—du/namai am able, e)pi/stamai understand, kre/mamai hang, o)ni/nhmi profit, and e)pria/mhn bought (749 b, 750 b, 757 a) have recessive accent in the subjunctive and optative (du/nwmai, e)pi/stwmai, du/naito, kre/maito).
d. Poetic forms sometimes fail to follow the rule, as e)w/n being.

§425
Infinitives, participles, and verbal adjectives are verbal nouns (358), and hence do not regularly show recessive accent.
a. Infinitives.—The following infinitives accent the penult: all infinitives in -nai, as leluke/nai, luqh=nai, i(sta/nai, sth=nai (except Epic -menai, as sth/menai); in verbs in w the first aorist active, as lu=sai, paideu=sai, the second aorist middle, as lipe/sqai, the perfect (middle) passive, as lelu/sqai, pepaideu=sqai, pepoih=sqai.

§425 a. D
The 2. aor. mid. inf. in Hom. is recessive in a)ge/resqai (a)gei/rw assemble); so the perf. a)la/lhsqai (a)la/omai wander), a)ka/xhsqai (a)/xnumai am distressed).
N.—The present inf. of contracted verbs and the second aorist active inf. of w-verbs have the perispomenon by 424 c.
b. Participles.—(1) Oxytone: the masculine and neuter sing. of the second aorist active, as lipw/n, lipo/n; and of all participles of the third declension ending in -s in the masculine (except the first aorist active), as luqei/s luqe/n, lelukw/s leluko/s, e(stw/s e(sto/s, tiqei/s tiqe/n, didou/s dido/n, i(sta/_s i(sta/n, deiknu/_s deiknu/n (but lu/_sa_s, poih/sa_s). Also i)w/n going from ei)=mi.
(2) Paroxytone: the perfect middle (passive): lelume/nos.
N.—Participles are accented like adjectives, not like verbs. The fem. and neuter nom. accent the same syllable as the masc. nom. if the quantity of the ultima permits, thus paideu/wn, paideu/ousa, paideu=on (not pai/deuon); poih/sa_s, poih/sa_sa, poih=san (not poi/hsan); filw=n, filou=sa, filou=n (from file/on).

§425 b (2) D
But Hom. has a)lalh/menos (a)la/omai wander), a)kaxh/menos or a)khxe/menos (a)/xnumai am distressed), e)ssu/menos (seu/w drive).
c. Verbal Adjectives.—The verbal adjective in -tos is accented on the ultima (luto/s); that in -teos on the penult (lute/os).
N.—Prepositional compounds in -tos denoting possibility generally accent the last syllable and have three endings (286), as dialuto/s dissoluble, e)caireto/s removable. Such compounds as have the force of a perfect passive participle accent the antepenult and have two endings, as dia/lutos dissolved, e)cai/retos chosen. All other compounds in -tos accent the antepenult and have two endings, as a)/batos impassable, xeiropoi/htos artificial.

§426

Exceptions to the recessive accent of compound verbs.—a. The accent cannot precede the augment or reduplication: a)/peimi am absent, a)ph=n was absent, ei)s-h=lqon they entered, a)p-h=san they were absent; a)f-i=ktai arrived (cp. i(=ktai).
N.—A long vowel or diphthong not changed by the augment receives the accent: u(p-ei=ke was yielding (indic. u(p-ei/kw, imper. u(/p-eike).
b. The accent cannot precede the last syllable of the preposition before the simple verb nor move back to the first of two prepositions: peri/qes put around, sune/kdos give up together (not su/nekdos), sugka/qes put down together (not su/gkaqes). Compounds of the second aorist active imperatives do/s, e(/s, qe/s, and sxe/s are thus paroxytone: e)pi/qes set on, peri/qes put around, e)pi/sxes hold on.
c. When compounded with a monosyllabic preposition, monosyllabic second aorist middle imperatives in -ou= from mi-verbs retain the circumflex: prodou= betray, e)nqou= put in. But the accent recedes when these imperatives prefix a dissyllabic preposition: a)po/dou sell, kata/qou put down. The open forms always have recessive accent, as e)/nqeo, kata/qeo.
d. The accent of uncompounded infinitives, participles, aorist passive, perfect passive, and of the second aorist middle imperative (2. p. sing., but see 426 c) is retained in composition.
e. a)pe/stai will be far from, e)pe/stai will be upon do not have recessive accent.
f. Compound subjunctives are differently accentuated in the Mss.: a)podw=mai and a)po/dwmai, e)piqh=tai and e)pi/qhtai; the aorist of i(/_hmi has prow=mai and pro/wmai. a)pe/xw has a)po/sxwmai. Compound optatives retain the accent of the primitives: a)podoi=to, as doi=to. For sunqoi=to, prosqoi=sqe (746 c) the Mss. occasionally have su/nqoito, pro/sqoisqe; and so pro/oito.

§427
Final -ai (and -oi) are regarded as long in the optative (169), elsewhere as short. Hence distinguish the forms of the first aorist.

## AUGMENT

§428
The augment (increase) denotes past time. It appears only in the secondary or past tenses of the indicative mood, namely, imperfect, aorist, and pluperfect. The augment has two forms, the syllabic and the temporal.

§429

Syllabic Augment.—Verbs beginning with a consonant prefix e as the augment, which thus increases the word by one syllable. In the pluperfect e is prefixed to the reduplication.

lu/_wloosee)/-lu_one)/-lu_sae)-lelu/kh

paideu/weducatee)-pai/deuone)-pai/deusae)-pepaideu/kh
a. Verbs beginning with r double the r after the augment. r(i/_ptw throw, e)/-rri_pton, e)/-rri_ya, e)-rri/_fqhn; r(h/gnu_mi break, e)/-rrhca, e)-rra/ghn.
N.—rr is here due to assimilation of vr, as in Hom. e)/rreca did (and e)/reca); of sr in e)/rreon flowed. Cp. 80 a.

§429 a. D
Hom. has e)/llabe took (for e)-slabe), e)/nneon swam (for e)-sneon), e)ssei/onto shook (for e)-tveionto), e)/ddeise feared (for e)-dveise). e)/mmaqe learned is due to analogy.

§430

a. These forms seem to be due to parallelism with h)/qelon (from e)qe/lw wish) and e)/qelon (from qe/lw).

§431 D
Syllabic augment in Homer before a vowel is a sure proof of initial v in e)/eipon and some other verbs. Similar Ionic and poetic forms occur from ei)=don, ei)/lw, ei)/rw, e)/lpw, e(/nnu_mi, e)/rdw, oi)noxoe/w, etc.

§432
Some forms of some verbs in 431 are augmented as if no consonant had preceded the first vowel, as h)rgazo/mhn (and ei)rgazo/mhn).

§433
Since v disappeared early, many augmented forms show no trace of its existence, as, w)/|koun from oi)ke/w dwell (voi=kos). Besides e, h was also used as the syllabic augment. This appears in Hom. h)-ei/deis (-hs?), Attic h)/|deis you knew.

§434
The verbs a)/gnu_mi, a(li/skomai, (a)n）oi/gnu_mi, o(ra/w, which began originally with v, show forms that appear to have a double augment; as e)a/_ghn, e(a/_lwn, (a)n）e)w|gon (rarely h)/noigon), e(w/rwn, e(w/ra_ka (and e(o/ra_ka). These forms appear to be due to transference of quantity (34) from h)-va^ghn, h)-voigon, h)-vorwn (cp. 433).

§435

Temporal Augment.—Verbs beginning with a vowel take the temporal augment by lengthening the initial vowel. The temporal augment is so called because it usually increases the time required to pronounce the initial syllable. Diphthongs lengthen their first vowel.

§435 D
Initial a becomes a_ in Doric and Aeolic; initial ai and au remain.

§436
Initial a| becomes h|: a)/|dw sing, h)=|don. Initial h, i_, u_, w remain unchanged. Initial a_ usually becomes h: a)_rista/w breakfast, h)ri/sthsa. a)na_li/skw and a)na_lo/w expend form a)na/_lwsa and a)nh/lwsa, a)na_lw/qhn and a)nhlw/qhn.

§437
Initial diphthongs are sometimes unaugmented: au in au(ai/nomai dry; ei: ei)/kazon, h)/|kazon; eu: eu(re/qhn and hu(re/qhn from eu(ri/skw find, eu)ca/mhn and hu)ca/mhn from eu)/xomai pray; ou is never augmented, since it is never a pure diphthong when standing at the beginning of a verb-form.

§438

Omission of the Augment.—a. In Attic tragedy the augment is sometimes omitted in choral passages, rarely in the dialogue parts (messengers' speeches), which are nearer akin to prose.
b. In xrh=n (from xrh\ + h)=n) the augment is strictly unnecessary, but is often added (e)xrh=n) since the composition of xrh=n was forgotten.
c. In Homer and the lyric poets either the syllabic or the temporal augment is often absent; as fa/to and e)/fato, bh=n and e)/bhn, e)/xon and ei)=xon. Iteratives (495) in Hom. usually have no augment (e)/xeskon).
N.—In Homer the absence of the augment represents the usage of the parent language, in which the augment was not necessarily added to mark past time. It is therefore erroneous, historically, to speak of the omission of the augment in Homer.
d. In Herodotus the syllabic augment is omitted only in the case of pluperfects and iteratives in skon; the temporal augment is generally preserved, but it is always omitted in verbs beginning with ai, au, ei, eu, oi, and in a)gi_ne/w, a)eqle/w, a)nw/gw, e)/rdw, e)a/w, o(rme/w, etc.; in others it is omitted only in some forms (as a)goreu/w, a)/gw, e(/lkw, o(rma/w), and in others it is variable (a)gge/llw, a(/ptw, a)/rxw, e)pi/stamai, a)ne/xomai); in cases of Attic reduplication the augment is never added. Hdt. omits the augment for the reduplication in the above verbs.

## REDUPLICATION

§439
Reduplication is the doubling of the sound standing at the beginning of a word. It is used in the perfect, pluperfect, and future perfect tenses in all the moods, to denote completed action. It is sometimes found also in the present and second aorist.

§439 D
Reduplication (or the augment for the reduplication) is generally retained in Hom. Exceptions are e)/rxatai and e)/rxato from e)/rgw shut, a)/nwga order, e(/stai from e(/nnu_mi clothe. On de/xatai await, e)de/gmhn was expecting cp. 634.

§440
Verbs beginning with a simple consonant (except r) or with a stop and a liquid (l, m, n, r) place the initial consonant with e before the stem. lu/_w loose, le/-luka, le-luke/nai, le/-lumai, le-lu/_somai; gra/fw write, ge/-grafa; kli/_nw incline, ke/-klika; bla/ptw injure, be/-blafa; pri/_w saw, pe/-pri_smai.
a. Exceptions: verbs beginning with gn, most of those with gl, and some with bl. Thus, gnwri/zw recognize, e)-gnw/rika; gi-gnw/skw know, e)/-gnwka; glu/fw carve, e)/-glufa; blasta/nw sprout, e)-bla/sthka (usu. bebla/sthka).

§441
An initial aspirate is reduplicated by the corresponding smooth stop: foneu/w murder, pe-fo/neuka; qu/_w sacrifice, te/-quka; xoreu/w dance, ke-xo/reuka.

§442
In all other cases the reduplication is formed like the augment.
a. Verbs beginning with a short vowel lengthen the vowel, as a)/gw lead, h)=xa; o)rqo/w set upright, w)/rqwka; a)gge/llw announce, h)/ggelka.
b. Verbs beginning with two or more consonants (except a stop with a liquid), a double consonant, and r simply prefix e. r is here doubled (cp. 429 a). Thus, kti/zw found, e)/-ktika; spei/rw sow, e)/-sparmai; strathge/w am general, e)-strath/ghka; zhte/w seek, e)-zh/thka; yau/w touch, e)/-yauka; r(i/_ptw throw, e)/rri_fa.
N.—mimnh/|skw remind and kta/omai acquire are exceptions: me/-mnhmai, e)-memnh/mhn; ke/-kthmai, e)-ke-kth/mhn.

§442. b. D
Hom. has r(e-rupwme/nos (r(upo/w soil), e)/mmore (mei/romai obtain) for e)-smore 445 a, e)/ssumai (seu/w urge) for e)-k[iglide]u-mai; Ionic has e)/kthmai.

§443
The verbs mentioned in 431 which originally began with a consonant now lost, reduplicate regularly. Since the reduplicated consonant has disappeared only e is left, and this often contracts with the initial vowel of the theme. Thus, e)/a_ga for ve-va_ga from va/gnu_mi break; e)/wsmai for ve-vwsmai from vwqe/w push; e(/sthka for sesthka from i(/sthmi set; ei(=ka for seseka from i(/_hmi (si-shmi) send.

§444

Pluperfect.—The pluperfect prefixes the syllabic augment e to the reduplicated perfect beginning with a consonant; when the perfect stem begins with a vowel the pluperfect retains the prefix of the perfect.
Thus perf. le/luka, le/lumai, plup. e)-lelu/kh, e)-lelu/mhn; perf. e)/-stalka, e)/-stalmai, plup. e)-sta/lkh, e)-sta/lmhn from ste/llw send; perf. h)go/reuka, plup. h)goreu/kh from a)goreu/w harangue; perf. h(/|rhka, plup. h(|rh/kh from ai(re/w seize.
a. Verbs showing ‘Attic’ reduplication (446), in almost all cases augment the pluperfect.
b. The verbs of 431 follow the perfects of 443; as e)a/_gh (a)/gnu_mi), e)w/smhn (w)qe/w), ei(/mhn (i(/_hmi), e)rrw/gh from (v）rh/gnu_mi. i(/sthmi forms ei(sth/kh ( = e)-（s）esthkh), Ion. and poet. e(sth/kh (rare in Att. prose). e)/oika am like forms e)w/|kh.

§444 b. D
Hdt. has oi)=ka (for e)/oika), e)/wqa, e)w/qea; Hom. has e)/wqen and ei)/wqe.

§445
Some verbs beginning with a liquid or m take ei instead of the reduplication: lamba/nw (lab-) take, ei)/-lhfa, ei)/-lhmmai, ei)-lh/fh; lagxa/nw (lax-) obtain by lot, ei)/-lhxa, ei)-lh/xh; le/gw collect (in composition) -ei)/-loxa, -ei)-lo/xh, -ei)/-legmai (rarely le/-legmai); mei/romai receive a share, ei(/-martai it is fated, ei(/-marto with rough breathing; also the stems ep, rh say, ei)/-rhka, ei)-rh/kh.

§445 D
Hom. dei/dw fear stands for de-dvw from de-dvo（[iglide]）a (cp. dve/os). So dei/doika for de-dvoika. For dei/dekto greeted we should read dh/dekto with h-reduplication. Hdt. has lela/bhka and -lelamme/nos. le/lhmmai occurs in tragedy.
a. ei)/lhfa is from se-slhfa by 37 (cp. Hom. e)/llabon for e)-slabon), ei(/martai is from se-smartai (cp. Hom. e)/mmore). The other forms are probably analogues of ei)/lhfa.

§446

Attic Reduplication.—Some verbs whose themes begin with a, e, or o, followed by a single consonant, reduplicate by repeating the initial vowel and the consonant and by lengthening a and e to h, o to w. Thus a)gei/rw collect, a)g-h/gerka, a)g-h/germai; e)gei/rw awaken, e)g-h/germai; e)le/gxw confute, e)l-h/legmai; o)ru/ttw dig, o)r-w/ruxa, o)r-w/rugmai; o)/m-nu_mi swear, o)m-w/moka; o)/l-lu_mi destroy, o)l-w/leka. So also fe/rw bear, e)n-h/noxa, e)n-h/negmai.
a. The name ‘Attic’ was given by the Greek grammarians to this form of reduplication though it occurs in Homer and in the other dialects.
b. a)kou/w hear has a)k-h/koa for a)k-h/ko（[uglide]）a; a)/gw has a)g-h/oxa for a)g-h/（g）oxa. The pluperfect augments except in the case of verbs with initial e: h)k-hko/h, w)m-wmo/kh, a)pwlw/lh; but e)l-hlu/qh, e)n-hne/gmhn.

§446 D

—In Hom. ‘Attic’ reduplication is even more frequent than in Attic; thus, e)dhdw/s from e)/dw eat, e)rh/ripa have fallen, e)re/ripto (without lengthening) from e)rei/pw overthrow, o)rwre/xatai from o)re/gw reach. For other poetical forms see in the List of Verbs a)gei/rw, ai(re/w, a)la/omai, a)rari/skw, e)rei/dw, e)ri/zw, e)/xw, o)/zw, o(ra/w, o)/rnu_mi.

§447

Reduplication in the Present.—A few verbs reduplicate in the present by prefixing the initial consonant and i, as gi/-gnomai, gi-gnw/skw, mi-mnh/|skw, ti/-ktw for ti-t（e）kw, pi/_-ptw for pi-p（e）tw, i(/-sthmi for si-sthmi, ti/-qhmi for qi-qhmi (125 a), di/-dwmi. pi/m-plh-mi fill (pla-, plh-) and pi/mprhmi burn (pra-, prh-) insert m.
a. In some verbs the reduplication belongs to the verbal stem: biba/zw make go e)bi/basa, dida/skw teach e)di/daca.

§448

Reduplication in the Second Aorist.—a)/gw lead forms the second aorist h)/g-agon, a)g-a/gw, a)g-a/goimi, a)g-agei=n, middle h)g-ago/mhn. So also h)/n-egka and h)/n-egkon from fe/rw.

§448 D
Hom. has many reduplicated second aorists, as pe/-piqon from pei/qw (piq-) persuade, keklo/mhn, ke-klo/menos from ke/lomai command, le-laqe/sqai from lanqa/nw (laq-) escape the notice of, pe-fide/sqai from fei/domai (fid-) spare, h)/r-aron from a)rari/skw (a)r-) join, w)/r-oron from o)/rnu_mi arouse. The indicative forms may take the syllabic augment, as in e)-pe/-fradon from fra/zw (frad-) tell. From e)ni/ptw chide and e)ru/_kw check come h)ni/_papon and e)ne/ni_pon, and h)ru/_kakon.

## POSITION OF AUGMENT AND REDUPLICATION IN COMPOUND VERBS

§449
In verbs compounded with a preposition, augment and reduplication stand between the preposition and the verb.
Thus, u(perbai/nw pass over, u(pere/bainon, u(perbe/bhka; ei)sba/llw throw into, ei)se/ballon, ei)sbe/blhka.
a. Before e of the augment e)k regains its fuller form e)c (133 a), and e)n and su/n reappear in their proper forms which were modified in the present. Thus e)kba/llw throw out, e)ce/ballon, e)kbe/blhka; e)mba/llw throw into, e)ne/ballon; sulle/gw collect, sune/legon, sunei/loxa; surri/_ptw throw together, sune/rri_ya, sune/rri_fa; suskeua/zw pack together, suneskeu/azon, suneskeua/sqhn.
b. Prepositions (except peri/ and pro/) drop their final vowel: a)poba/llw throw away, a)p-e/ballon; but periba/llw throw around, perie/ballon, probai/nw step forward, proe/bhn. But pro/ may contract with the augment (prou)/bhn).

§450
But some verbs, which are not often used except as compounds, are treated like uncompound verbs and take the augment before the preposition, as e)kaqh/mhn sat from ka/qhmai, e)ka/qizon set, sat from kaqi/zw, h)mfi/esa clothed from a)mfie/nnu_mi, e)ka/qeudon (and kaqhu_don) slept from kaqeu/dw, h)pista/mhn, h)pisth/qhn from e)pi/stamai understand. i(/_hmi forms a)fi/_ei and h)fi/_ei. The simple verbs occur mostly in poetry. But a)polau/w enjoy makes a)pole/lauka, e)ceta/zw review e)ch/taka.

§451

Double Augment.—Some verbs take two augments, one before and the other after the preposition, as h)n-eixo/mhn, h)n-esxo/mhn from a)n-e/xomai endure, h)n-w/xloun from e)noxle/w annoy, e)phnw/rqwmai from e)panorqo/w set upright. So also, by analogy to the foregoing, a few verbs derived from compound words: h)mfesbh/toun from a)hfisbhte/w dispute, h)ntede/kei from a)ntidike/w go to law (a)nti/dikos).

§452
Compounds of dus- ill and eu)= well. (1) dustuxe/w am unhappy, e)-dustu/xoun, de-dus-tu/xhka. dus-hre/stoun, dus-hre/sthka from dus-areste/w do not occur. (2) eu)ergete/w do good, eu)erge/thsan, eu)erge/thka (inscrip.) eu)hrge/thka (texts).

§453
Verbs derived from compound nouns take the augment and the reduplication at the beginning; as e)mu_qolo/goun, memu_qolo/ghka from mu_qologe/w tell legends (mu_qolo/gos teller of legends); w)|kodo/moun, w)|kodo/mhka from oi)kodome/w build (oi)kodo/mos house-builder); h)mpo/lwn, h)mpo/lhka from e)mpola/w traffic in (e)mpolh/ traffic).
a. e)kklhsia/zw hold an assembly (e)kklhsi/a_) makes h)k-klhsi/azon or e)c-e-klhsi/azon. e)ggua/w pledge makes e)negu/wn, e)negu/hsa and (better) h)ggu/wn, h)ggu/hsa.

§454
Verbs derived from compound nouns whose first part is a preposition are commonly treated as if compounded of a preposition and a simple verb; as kathgore/w accuse (kath/goros), kathgo/roun, kathgo/rhka; e)nqu_me/omai ponder (e)/nqu_mos) e)nequ_mh/qhn, e)ntequ_mh=sqai; e)piorke/w swear falsely (e)pi/orkos), e)piw/rkhka; e)gxeiri/zw entrust (e)n xeiri/), e)nexei/risa.
a. But several verbs are not treated as compounds, such as a)pata/w deceive, a)piste/w distrust, a)pore/w am in difficulty, parrhsia/zomai speak freely.

## TENSE-SUFFIXES, THEMATIC VOWEL, MOOD-SUFFIXES

§455

Tense-Suffixes.—The tense-suffixes, which are added to the verb-stem to form the tense-stems, consist of the thematic vowel and certain other letters. No tense-suffixes are added to the verb-stem (1) in the second aorist active and middle, and second perfect and pluperfect, of mi-verbs; (2) in the perfect and pluperfect middle of verbs in -w and -mi. The tense-suffixes are as follows:—
1. Present system, -o/e-, -to/e-, -[iglide]o/e-, -no/e-, -ano/e-, -neo/e-, -na-, -nu-, -（i）sko/e; or none, as in fa-me/n.
2. Future system, -so/e-.
3. First aorist sytem, -sa-.
4. Second aorist system, -o/e-; or none, as in e)/-sth-n.
5. First perfect system, -ka- (plupf. -kh- from -kea-; -kei- from -kee-; -ke-).
6. Second perfect system, -a- (plupf. -h-, -ei-, or -e-); or none, as in e(/-sta-te.
7. Perfect middle system, none (future perfect -so/e-).
8. First passive system, qh-, -qe- (future passive -qhso/e-).
9. Second passive system, h, -e- (future passive -hso/e-).
N.—-a in the aorist is properly a relic of the personal ending (666).

§455. D
For the Doric future -seo/e-, see 540.—For the Epic first aorist -so/e-, see 542 D.—For the doubling of s in the future and first aorist, see 534 b. D., 544 b. D.

§456

Thematic Vowel.—The thematic, or variable, vowel appears at the end of the tense-stems in the present, imperfect, and second aorist active and middle of w-verbs, and in all futures and future perfects. The thematic vowel in the indicative is o before m or n (and in the optative of the tenses mentioned); elsewhere it is e. Thus, lu_o/e-, lipo/e-, lu_so/e-, luqhso/e-, lelu_so/e-; lu/_o-i_-mi. In the subjunctive it is w/h.
a. Attic inscriptions have both -esqwn and -osqwn in the imperative.

§457

Subjunctive.—In the subjunctive of all verbs the thematic vowel is w/h-. Thus, lu/_w-men, lu/_h-te, lu/_sw-men, stei/lh-te.
a. Verbs in -nu_mi form their subjunctive like w-verbs.

§457 D
Hom. has -o/e- instead of -w/h-, especially in the 1 aor., 2 aor. of mi- verbs, and 2 aor. pass. (e)ru/ssomen, dw/omen, trapei/omen; also in i)/omen, ei)/domen). These forms do not occur in the sing. or 3 pl. active. Verbs in w rarely show this o/e in the present. (Other examples 532, 667 D., 682 D.)

§458
In the present and second aorist of mi-verbs, and in the aorist passive, w/h is added to the tense stem. Thus tiqw=men from tiqe/-w-men, qw= from qe/-w, tiqh=te from tiqe/-h-te, luqw= from luqe/-w.

§459

Suffix of the Optative.—The optative adds the mood suffix -i_-, or -ih- which contracts with the final vowel of the tense-stem: lu/_oimi for lu/_o-i_-mi, filoi/hn for fileo-i/h-n, tiqei/hn for tiqe-i/h-n. -ih- occurs only before active endings. When the suffix is -ih-, the 1 pers. sing. ends in -n; as ti_mao-i/h-n = ti_mw/|hn; when it is -i_-, the 1 pers. sing. ends in -mi, as ti_ma/o-i_-mi = ti_mw=|mi.

§460

ih is used as follows (in all other cases -i_-):—
a. In contracted verbs in the singular, rarely in the dual and plural. -i_- appears in the dual and plural, rarely in the singular.
b. In liquid verbs in the future active singular: fanoi/h-n for faneo-i/h-n. In the dual and plural -i_-: fanoi=ton, fanoi=men for faneo/-i_-ton, faneo/-i_-men.
c. In the singular of mi-verbs: tiqei/hn for tiqe-i/h-n, didoi/hn for dido-i/h-n, qei/hn for qe-i/h-n. Here the modal sign is added to the tense-stem without any thematic vowel. -i_- is more common in the dual and plural: tiqei=men for tiqe/-i_-men, didoi=men for dido/-i_-men, qei=te for qe/-i_-te. Verbs in -nu_mi make their optatives like lu/_w.
d. In the aorist passive: luqei/hn for luqe-i/h-n, fanei/hn for fane-i/h-n. In the dual and plural -i_- is more common: luqei=men for luqe/-i_-men, fanei=te for fane/-i_-te.
e. In some second perfects, as proelhluqoi/hs, and in the second aorist sxoi/hn from e)/xw (but -sxoi=mi in composition).
N.—In the 3 pl. -ie- is regular before -n: lu/_o-ie-n, tiqe-i=e-n, luqe-i=e-n.

§460 D

-ih- is very rare in Hom. in the dual and plural.

§461

a. In the 1 aor. opt. act. of w-verbs the endings -eias, -eie, and -eian are more common than -ais, -ai, -aien.
b. In the aor. opt. passive of all verbs and in the opt. of mi-verbs and of contract verbs -iton, -ithn, -imen, -ite, -ien are commoner than -ihton, -ihthn, -ihmen, -ihte, -ihsan. Prose writers use either the shorter or the longer forms; poets use only the shorter forms. Except in contract verbs -ihte is very common in the 2 pl. and is sometimes the only form in the Mss., as doi/hte, qei/hte, gnoi/hte, -bai/hte, luqei/hte, fanei/hte; but the forms in question occur in prose writers and their genuineness is therefore unsupported by metrical evidence.

§463
PRIMARY ENDINGS OF THE ACTIVE (IND. AND SUBJ.)
a. 1 Sing.—-mi is found only in mi-verbs. Verbs in -w have no ending and simply lengthen the thematic vowel (lu/_w, lei/pw). The perfect has no personal ending, -a taking the place of a thematic vowel.

§463 a. D
The Hom. subj. e)qe/lwmi, tu/xwmi, a)ga/gwmi, are new formations. Aeolic has fi/lhmi, doki/mwmi (indic.).
b. 2 Sing.—(1) -si is found in Hom. e)ssi/ thou art from the mi-verb ei)mi/ I am; possibly also in fh/|s thou sayest. Attic ei)= thou art is derived from e)-si. ti/qh-s is obscure. lu/_eis is probably for lu_e-si, lu_ei+, lu_ei, to which s has been added. Subj. lu/_h|-s follows the analogy of the indicative, but with long thematic vowel. tiqh=|s for tiqe/-h|s. In the perfect -s (not for -si) has been added.
b. (1) ei)=s or ei)/s in Hom. and Hdt. is derived from ei)= + s. For this form e)ss（i/) may be read in Hom. Theocr. has -es for -eis (a)me/lges, etc.) and perf. pepo/nqeis (557. 2. D.).
(2) -qa is a perfect ending, as in oi)=sqa knowest for oi)d + qa (83). From the perfect it spread to the imperfects h)=sqa wast, h)/eisqa wentst, e)/fhsqa saidst, and to h)/|dhsqa or h)/|deisqa knewest. The perfect has commonly -a-s. oi)=sqas and h)=sqas are late.
b. (2) -sqa in Hom. indic. fh=sqa, ti/qhsqa, h)/|dhsqa; subj. e)qe/lh|sqa also written e)qe/lhsqa; opt. (rarely) klai/oisqa, ba/loisqa. -sqa occurs also occasionally in Doric (poqorh=sqa) and Aeolic (e)/xeisqa, fi/lhsqa).
c. 3 Sing.—-ti is found in mi-verbs: e)s-ti/, ti/qhsi for ti/qh-ti (Doric) by 115. lu/_ei is obscure, but it cannot be derived from lu_e-si for lu_e-ti. lu/_h|, tiqh=| (for tiqe/h|) follow lu/_ei, but with long thematic vowel. In the perfect, -e with no personal ending.
c. Aeolic has ti/qh, poi/h, stefa/noi, but h)=si says. Subj.: Hom. e)qe/lh|si (also written e)qe/lhsi; cp. Arcad. e)/xh), fore/h|si, qe/h|si.
d. 3 Pl.—Original -nti is retained in Doric lu/_onti, whence Attic lu/_ousi (115 a); e)nti/, Attic ei)si/. Subj. lu/_wsi from lu/_w-nti, tiqw=si from tiqe/w-nti, poiw=si from poiw=nti (Dor.). Many mi forms are derived from -anti, as tiqe/a_si (tiqe/-anti), dido/a_si (dido/-anti), e(sta=si (e(sta/-anti), i(sta=si (from i(sta/-anti), the accent of which has been transferred to tiqei=si (747 D. 1), didou=si from (Dor.) ti/qe-nti, di/do-nti. -a^ti from -ṇti (35 b), properly the ending of the perfect after a consonant, appears as -a^si in Hom. pefu/ka^si; but it has been replaced by -a_si out of -anti, as in tetra/f-a_si.
d. Hom. has -a_si in i)/a_si they go, e)/a_si they are, and in beba/a_si, gega/a_si. Aeolic has lu/_oisi, fi/leisi, ti/_maisi.

§464
SECONDARY ENDINGS OF THE ACTIVE (IND. AND OPT.)
The optative usually has the endings of the secondary tenses of the indicative.
a. 1 Sing.—-n stands for m (133 c), cp. e)/fero-n, Skt. ábhara-m. After a consonant m (sonant nasal, 20 b, 35 c) became a: e)/lu_sa for e)lu_sṃ, Epic h)=a was for h'（s）a from h)sṃ. In the pluperfect -h is from e-a (467). -n is found in the optative when the mood suffix is -ih-; elsewhere the optative has -mi.

§464 a. D

-n for -mi is very rare (tre/foin in Eur., a(ma/rtoin in Cratinus).
b. 2 Sing.—On -sqa see 463 b (2).
c. 3 Sing.—-t dropped (133 b) in e)/lu_e, e)ti/qh, and in the opt. lu/_oi, ei)/h (cp. Old Lat. sied). e)/lu_se has its -e from the perfect (cp. oi)=de) and shows no personal ending.
c. Doric h)=s was for h)s（t).
d. Dual.—-thn is rarely found for -ton in the 2 dual (eu(re/thn in Plato). Hom. has e)teu/xeton as 3 dual.
e. 3 Pl.—-n for -nt by 133 b. -san (taken from the 1 aorist) is used (1) in the imperf. and 2 aor. of mi-verbs, as e)ti/qe-san, e)/qe-san; (2) in the aor. pass. e)lu/qh-san, e)fa/nh-san (here -n preceded by a short vowel occurs in poetry, 585 a. D.); (3) in the pluperf. e)lelu/ke-san; (4) in the opt. when -ih- is the modal suffix (460). In the opt. -san is rare.
e. -n is regular in Doric and common in Hom. and later poetry; as e)/sta^-n (e)/sth-san), e)/dido-n (e)di/do-san), fi/lhqen (e)filh/qh-san), tra/fen (e)tra/fh-san). The short vowel before n（t) is explained by 40. Hom. h)=e-n were became h)=n, used in Dor. as 3 pl.; in Attic it was used as 3 sing.

§465
ENDINGS OF THE MIDDLE (INDIC., SUBJ., OPT.)
a. 2 Sing.—Primary -sai retains its s in the perfect of all verbs (le/lu-sai), and in the pres. of mi-verbs (ti/qe-sai). Elsewhere s drops between vowels, as in lu/_h| or lu/_ei from lu/_e-sai, luqh/sh| or -ei, fanh=| from fane/e-sai, ti_ma=| from ti_ma/e-sai; subj. lu/_h| from lu/h-sai, fh/nh| from fh/nh-sai, qh=| from qh/e-sai, dw=| from dw/h-sai, h(=| from e(/h-sai, filh=| from file/h-sai, dhloi= from dhlo/h| = dhlo/h-sai.
N. 1.—The forms -h| and -ei are found in the present, future, and future perfect. See 628.
N. 2.—du/na| and du/nh| for du/nasai, e)pi/sta| and e)pi/sth| for e)pi/stasai, e)fi/_ei for e)fi/_esai, are poetic and dialectic or late.

§465 a. D
Hom. has bou/leai, perf. me/mnhai, but pres. du/nasai, pari/stasai; o)/yei is unique (for o)/yeai); subj. du/nhai. Doric often contracts, as oi)/h| for oi)/e-ai. Aeolic generally leaves eai open (kei/se-ai). Hdt. has open -eai, -hai.
b. 2 Sing.—-so stays in all plups. and in the imperf. of mi-verbs. Elsewhere it loses its s, as in e)lu/_ou from e)lu/_e-so, e)lu/_sw from e)lu/_sa-so, e)fh/nw from e)fh/na-so, e)li/pou from e)li/pe-so, e)/qou from e)/qe-so, e)pri/w from e)pri/a-so, e)ti_mw= from e)ti_ma/e-so, e)filou= from e)file/e-so. In the optative, lu/_oio, li/poio, tiqei=o, ei(=o, lu/_saio, from lu/_oi-so, etc.; ti_mw=|o from ti_ma/oi-so.
N. 1.—e)du/nw or h)du/nw and h)pi/stw are commoner than e)du/naso and h)pi/staso from du/namai am able and e)pi/stamai understand.
N. 2.—After a diphthong or a long vowel in the 2 aor. indic. mid. -so is retained, as ei(=so (i(/_hmi send), w)/nhso (o)ni/nhmi benefit).
b. Hom., Doric, and Aeolic have generally open forms, as Hom. ba/lle-o (rarely ba/lleu), w)du/sa-o. e)/reio, spei=o are from -eeo. Hom. has e)ma/rnao for Attic e)ma/rnaso, and may drop s even in the pluperfect (e)/ssuo). When Doric contracts ao we have a_. In Hdt. ao, eo are open, but the writing eu for eo is found.
c. Dual.—The 1 pl. is used for the 1 dual except in the three poetic forms peridw/meqon, lelei/mmeqon, o(rmw/meqon. Hom. has -sqon for -sqhn in qwrh/ssesqon.
d. 1 Pl.—In epic and dramatic poetry -mesqa is often used for -meqa for metrical reasons (boulo/mesqa, e)pista/mesqa).
e. 2 Pl.—On the loss of s in sqe (e)/stalqe), see 103.
f. 3 Pl.—After vowel stems -ntai, -nto are preserved. After stems ending in a consonant -ntai, -nto became -atai, -ato by 35 b. These forms were retained in prose till about 400 B.C. (e.g. teta/xatai, e)teta/xato).
f. -atai, -ato occur in Hom. regularly in the perfect and pluperfect of consonant stems, as tetra/fatai, e(/atai for e(s-ntai, h(/ato for h(s-nto from h(=mai (h(smai); also in stems ending in -i, as e)fqi/ato. -atai, -ato were transferred to vocalic stems, as beblh/atai, beblh/ato, Hdt. dune/atai. Hom. has -d-atai in e)lhla/datai from e)lau/nw drive. In the opt. -ato always (genoi/ato for ge/nointo). In Hdt. h before -atai, -ato is shortened, as perf. h(ge/atai for h(gh/-atai = h(/ghntai, e)beble/ato for -hato. For kei=ntai, Hom. kei/atai and ke/atai, Hdt. has ke/atai. In the opt. Hdt. has -ato: bouloi/ato, decai/ato. In Hdt. -atai, -ato occur even in the present system, tiqe/atai, dune/atai, i(_ste/ato.

§466
ENDINGS OF THE IMPERATIVE
1. Active.
a. 2 Sing.—lu=e, li/pe, ti/qei (for ti/qe-e) have not lost -qi. -qi is found in 2 aor. pass. fa/nh-qi; in sth=-qi and e(/sta-qi; in some 2 aorists, like gnw=-qi, tlh=-qi, pi=-qi, which are mi forms though they have presents of the w form (687). Also in i)/s-qi be or know, i)/qi go, fa/qi or faqi/ say. lu/qhti is for luqhqi by 125 b.

§466 a. D

-qi is not rare in Hom., pres. di/dwqi = di/dou, o)/rnuqi, aor. klu=qi, perf. te/tlaqi. Aeolic has i)/sta_, fi/lh. pi/ei, de/xoi, di/doi (Pindar) are very rare.
b. -s occurs in qe/s, e(/s, do/s, sxe/s (and in the rare qi/ges, pi/eis). This -s is not derived from -qi.
c. lu=s-on aor. act. and lu=s-ai aor. mid. are obscure in origin.
2. Middle.
a. 2 Sing.—-so retains its s in the (rare) perf. of all verbs and in the pres. of mi-verbs (le/luso, ti/qeso, i(/staso). Elsewhere s is dropped, as in lu/_ou from lu/_e-so, lipou= from lipe/-so, qou= from qe/-so, ou(= from e(/-so, pri/w from pri/a-so, ti_mw= from ti_ma/e-so.
N.—ti/qou, i(/stw, di/dou are poetic or late.
3. 3 Pl.—For -ntwn and -sqwn we find -twsan and -sqwsan in prose after Thucydides, in Euripides, and in inscriptions after 300 B.C. Thus, lu_e/twsan, lu_sa/twsan, lu_e/sqwsan, lu_sa/sqwsan, luqh/twsan, lipe/twsan, lipe/sqwsan, fhna/sqwsan, fanh/twsan, ti_ma/sqwsan, filei/sqwsan, gegra/fqwsan, pepei/sqwsan, tiqe/twsan, dido/twsan, qe/twsan, tiqe/sqwsan, qe/sqwsan, -e(/twsan, -e(/sqwsan.
N.—e)/stwn for o)/ntwn is rare. Attic inscriptions have (very rarely) -ntwsan.
3. Doric has also -ntw, as in parexo/ntw; Aeolic -nton, as fe/ronton. Doric has -sqw (pl.) and -sqwn.

## ENDINGS OF THE PLUPERFECT, ENDINGS IN sq

§467

Endings of the Pluperfect Active.—-h, -hs, -ei（n) are derived from -e（s）a, -e（s）as, -e（s）e. In later Greek the endings are -ein, -eis, -ei（n), -eiton, -eithn, -eimen, -eite, and very late -eisan.

§467 D
Hom. has -ea, -hs, -ei or ei-n (-ee only in h)/|dee), -esan, and rarely -on, -es, -e; Hdt. has -ea, -eas, -ee (-ei?), -eate, -esan.

§468

The Endings -sqe, etc.—The s of the endings -sqe, -sqw, -sqon, -sqwn, -sqai (409 N.) has no exact parallel in cognate languages, and seems to have spread in Greek from forms like tete/les-qe, e)/zws-qe, etc., where a sigma-stem was followed by original -qe.

## ENDINGS OF THE INFINITIVE, PARTICIPLE, AND VERBAL ADJECTIVE

§469

Infinitive.—The following are the endings added to the tense-stem to make the infinitive.
a. -en: in present and 2 aorist active of w-verbs, all futures active. Thus, lu/_ein, ti_ma=n, lipei=n, lu/_sein, fanei=n from lu/_e-en, ti_ma/e-en, lipe/-en, lu/_se-en, fane/e-en.
b. -ai: in 1 aor. active, as lu=sai, paideu=sai, dei=cai.
c. -nai: (1) present, 2 perf. of mi-verbs, the two passive aorists, as tiqe/-nai, e(sta/nai, luqh=-nai, fanh=-nai; (2) perfect active, leluke/-nai, and ei)de/-nai from ei)d-e (oi)=da).
N. 1.—The ending enai appears in the 2 aor. of mi-verbs, as dou=nai from do/-enai, qei=nai from qe/-enai.
d. -sqai: in other cases.
N. 2.—The infinitives are old cases of substantives, those in -ai being datives, the others locatives.

§469 D

-en appears also in Hom. i)de/en (miswritten i)de/ein). Hom. has no case of -enai (for i)e/nai write i)/menai). For -en or -nai Hom. often uses -menai (also Aeolic) and -men (which is also Doric); both endings show the accent on the preceding syllable, as zeugnu/menai, e)/mmenai ( = ei)=nai), filh/menai, sth/menai, e(sta/menai, a)ce/menai, o(moiwqh/menai, dah/menai; tiqe/men, e)/mmen, i)/men, qe/men, e)lqe/men, a)ce/men. Doric has -men in the aorist passive, as ai)sxunqh=men. -men is preceded by a short syllable and generally stands before a vowel. -nai always follows a long vowel. Doric has -hn and -en in the present. Aeolic has -hn in the present and 2 aorist.

§470

Participles.—The stem of the participle is formed by adding the following endings to the tense stem.
a. -nt-: in all active tenses except the perfect, and in 1 and 2 aor. passive (301).
b. -ot-: in the perfect active (for -vot-); masc. -w/s, fem. -ui=a, neut. -o/s (301 c).
c. -meno-: in the middle, and in the passive except in the aorist.

§471

Verbal Adjectives.—Most of the verbals in -to/s and -te/os are formed by adding these suffixes to the verbal stem of the aorist passive (first or second). Thus, filhto/s, -te/os (e)-filh/-qhn); peisto/s, -te/os (e)-pei/s-qhn); telesto/s, -te/os (e)-tele/s-qhn); stalto/s, -te/os (e)-sta/l-hn); blhto/s, -te/os (e)-blh/-qhn). On the accent of compound verbals, see 425 c.
a. Some are derived from other stem forms (pres. and fut.), as fer-to/s, i/-te/on, duna-to/s; meneto/s (cp. mene/-w = menw= fut.).

§472
Verbals in -to/s, -th/, -to/n either (1) have the meaning of a perfect passive participle, as krupto/s hidden, paideuto/s educated, or (2) express possibility, as nohto/s thinkable, o(ra_to/s visible. Many have either signification, but some are passive only, as poihto/s done. See 425 c. N.
a. Usually passive in meaning are verbals from deponent verbs, as mi_mhto/s imitated.
b. Usually active in meaning are compounds derived from transitive active verbs; but some intransitive verbs make active verbals, as r(uto/s flowing.
c. Many are active or passive, others only active: mempto/s blamed, blamable, blaming, pisto/s trusting in (rare), trusted, a)/pra_ktos doing nothing, not done, fqegkto/s sounding.

§473
Verbals in -te/os, -te/a_, -te/on express necessity (cp. the Lat. gerundive in -ndus), as dote/os that must be given, paideute/os educandus.

## FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)

## CHANGES IN THE VERB-STEM

§474
From the verb-stem (or theme) each tense-stem is formed by the addition of a tense-suffix (455) or of a prefix, or of both. In 475-495 certain modifications of the verb-stem are considered.

§475

Variation in Quantity.—Many verbs of the first class (498 ff.) show variation in the quantity of the vowel of the verb-stem, which is commonly long in the present but fluctuates in other tenses, as lu/_-w, lu/_-sw, e)/lu_-sa, but le/lu^-ka, le/lu^-mai, e)lu^/-qhn. (Other examples, 500.)
a. Some verbs of the Fourth Class (523 c) lengthen a short vowel of the present in some other tenses. Thus, lamba/nw (lab-) take, lh/yomai, ei)/lhfa, ei)/lhmmai, e)lh/fqhn, but 2 aor. e)/labon.

§476

Vowel Gradation (35, 36).—Verbs of the first class show a variation between a strong grade (or two strong grades) and a weak grade. The weak grades, i^, u^, a^, appear especially in the second aorist and second passive systems; the corresponding strong grades, ei (oi), eu (ou), h (w), appear usually in the other systems (oi, ou, w, in the second perfect).
a. Expulsion of a short vowel between consonants (so-called syncope 493) produces a weak form of the stem of the same grade as i, u, a (36). Cp. gi/-gn-omai become (aor. e)-gen-o/-mhn), e)-pt-o/-mhn (pres. pe/t-o-mai fly) with e)/-lip-o-n, e)/-fug-o-n, e)-ta/k-h-n (477 c). So e)/-sx-o-n got from e)/x-w have.
b. a is the weak form of h (a_), as in th/kw e)ta/khn; and of e, when e has l, m, n, r before or after it, as in tre/pw, e)tra/phn (479).

§477
The following examples illustrate the principles of 476.
a. ei oi i: lei/pw leave, lei/yw, 2 perf. le/loipa, le/leimmai, e)lei/fqhn, 2 aor. e)/lipom
N.—The weak form appears when the verb undergoes Attic reduplication (446); as in a)lei/fw anoint, 2 perf. a)lh/lifa, a)lh/limmai; e)rei/kw tear (Ionic and poetic), 2 perf. e)rh/rigmai, 2 aor. h)/rikon; e)rei/pw overthrow, Epic e)rh/ripa; but e)rei/dw prop, e)rh/reismai.
b. eu ou u: e)leu/（q）somai I shall go, 2 perf. e)lh/luqa (Epic e)lh/louqa), 2 aor. (Epic h)/luqon); feu/gw flee, feu/comai or feucou=mai, 2 perf. pe/feuga, 2 aor. e)/fugon; r(e/w flow (for r(eu-w, 43), r(eu/somai, e)rru/hka (r(ue-), 2 aor. pass. e)rru/hn.
N.—xe/w pour (for xeu-w, 43), e)/xea (for e)/xeua), has u in ke/xuka, ke/xumai, e)xu/qhn; seu/w (poetic) urge, e)/sseua, e)/ssumai, e)ssu/qhn or e)su/qhn rushed. See also teu/xw in the List of Verbs.
c. h w a: r(h/g-nu_mi break, r(h/cw, e)/rrhca, 2 perf. e)/rrwga, 2 aor. pass. e)rra/ghn; th/k-w melt, th/cw, e)/thca, te/thka, e)th/xqhn, 2 aor. pass. e)ta/khn.
N.—Verbs of class c usually have a^ in the 2 aorist, w in the 2 perfect (if there is one), elsewhere h. w occurs in the present in trw/gw gnaw, 2 aor. e)/tragon.

§478

Change of e to o in the Second Perfect.—In the second perfect e of the verb-stem is changed to o.
kle/p-t-w steal ke/klofa, (a)po-) ktei/nw kill (kten-, 519) -e/ktona, le/g-w collect ei)/loxa, pa/sxw, fut. pei/somai (from penqsomai, 100) pe/ponqa, pe/mp-w send pe/pomfa, ste/rg-w love e)/storga, ti/ktw beget te/toka, tre/p-w turn te/trofa, tre/f-w nourish te/trofa, fqei/r-w corrupt e)/fqora. §479

Change of e to a.—In verb-stems containing l, m, n, r, an e is usually changed to a in the first perfect, perfect middle, and second passive systems.
tre/p-w turn, te/trammai, e)tra/phn (1 aor. e)tre/fqhn); tre/f-w feed, te/qrammai, e)tra/fhn (1 aor. e)qre/fqhn); spei/rw (sper-) sow, e)/sparmai, e)spa/rhn; fqei/rw (fqer-) destroy, e)/fqarmai, e)fqa/rhn; ste/llw (stel-) send, e)/stalka, e)/stalmai, e)sta/lhn; tei/nw (ten-) stretch, te/taka, te/tamai, e)ta/qhn (1 aor.).
a. Also in the 2 aor. pass. of kle/ptw steal (e)kla/phn), ple/kw weave (e)pla/khn), te/rpw gladden (Epic e)ta/rphn). Many of these verbs also show o in the second perfect (478).

§480

§481

e in the perfect middle in ke/klemmai (kle/ptw steal), pe/plegmai (ple/kw weave) is introduced from the present.

§482
The a^ in 479, 480 is developed from a liquid or nasal brought between two consonants (35 b). Thus, e)/stalmai, te/tamai from e)stḷmai, tetṇmai, e)ta/qhn from e)tṇqhn (20 b). Here stl, tn represent weak grades of the stem.

§483

a. The variations e, o, a, w appear in tre/pw turn, tre/yw, e)/treya, 2 perf. te/trofa, te/trammai, e)tre/fqhn, 2 aor. pass. e)tra/phn; frequentative trwpa/w (867).

§484

h, a in the Second Perfect.—In the second perfect a^ of the verb-stem is lengthened to h (a_): qa/llw (qal-) bloom, te/qhla; fai/nw (fan-) show, pe/fhna; mai/nw (man-) madden, me/mhna; kra/_zw (krag-) cry out, ke/kra_ga.

§485

Addition of e.—a. To the verb-stem e is added to make the present stem in doke/w seem, fut. do/cw, aor. e)/doca (dok-); so in game/w marry, w)qe/w push. Usually e is added in some stem other than the present.
b. In many verbs e is added to the verb-stem to form the tense-stems other than present, second aorist, and second perfect, e.g. ma/xomai (max-) fight, maxou=mai ( = maxe（s）omai), e)maxesa/mhn, mema/xhmai. So a)/xqomai am grieved, bou/louai wish, gi/gnomai become, de/w want, (e'）qe/lw wish, me/llw intend, me/lei is a care, oi)/omai think.
c. In some verbs e is added to form one or more tense-stems, as me/nw (men-) remain, meme/nhka (mene-) to avoid -n-ka in the perfect. So, ne/mw distribute, e)/xw have, oi)/xomai am gone. So also darqa/nw, o)sfai/nomai, r(e/w, stei/bw (poetic), tugxa/nw.
d. Some verbs have alternative presents with or without e. Here sometimes one is used in prose, the other in poetry, sometimes both are poetic or both used in prose. Thus, e(/lkw draw (Hom. also e(lke/w), i)a/xw i)axe/w sound (both poetic), me/dw mede/w (both poetic), r(i/_ptw and r(i_pte/w throw (both in prose).

§485 D
Some Ionic and poetic verbs adding e are a)le/cw, a)/lqomai, gegwne/w, ghqe/w, doupe/w, ei)/romai, ei)le/w, e)paure/w, kelade/w, ke/lomai, kente/w, kh/dw, ktupe/w, kure/w, la/skw, me/domai, mu/zw, pate/omai, r(i_ge/w, stuge/w, tore/w, xa/zw, file/w (poetic forms), xra<*> sme/w; a)mplaki/skw, a)pafi/skw; Epic e)dida/skhsa (dida/skw), piqh/sw, pepiqh/sw<*> piqh/sa_s (pei/qw), pefidh/somai (fei/domai).

§486 D

§487

Lengthening of Short Final Vowel.—Verb-stems ending in a short vowel generally lengthen that vowel before the tense-suffix in all tenses (except the present and imperfect) formed from them. Here a (except after e, i, and r) and e become h, o become w.
ti_ma/-w (ti_ma-) honour, ti_mh/-sw, e)ti/_mh-sa, teti/_mh-ka, teti/_mh-mai, e)ti_mh/-qhn; qhra/-w (qhra-) hunt, qhra/_-sw, e)qh/ra_-sa, etc. (389); poie/w (poie-) make, poih/-sw, e)poi/h-sa, pepoi/h-ka, pepoi/h-mai, e)poih/-qhn; dhlo/w (dhlo-) manifest, dhlw/-sw, e)dh/lw-sa, etc.; e)a/w permit, e)a/_sw, etc.
a. Note a)kroa/_somai, h)kroa_sa/mhn, etc., from a)kroa/omai hear; xrh/sw, e)/xrhsa from xra/w give oracles; xrh/somai, e)xrhsa/mhn from xra/omai use; trh/sw and e)/trhsa from tetrai/nw bore are from tre-.
b. Verb-stems adding e or o (486), and stems apparently receiving a short final vowel by metathesis (128), lengthen the short final vowel, as bou/lomai (boul-) wish, boulh/-somai (boule-, 485), ka/mnw (kam-) am weary, ke/kmh-ka (kma-).

§488

gela^/-w laugh, gela^/somai, e)ge/la^sa, e)gela^/sqhn; tele/w finish, telw= from tele/-w, e)te/lesa, tete/leka, tete/lesmai, e)tele/sqhn; a)nu/w accomplish, a)nu^/sw, h)/nu^sa, h)/nu^smai.

b. So ai(re/w, bai/nw (ba-), bu_ne/w (bu-), di/dwmi (do-, dw-), du/na-mai, du/_w (du^-, du_-), eu(ri/skw (eu(r-e-), e)/xw (sex-, sxe-), qu/_w (qu^-, qu_-), i(/hmi (e(-, h(-), i(/sthmi (sta^-, sth-), lu/_w (lu^-, lu_-), ti/qhmi (qe-, qh-), ti/nw (ti-), fu/_w (fu^-, fu_-), and the root e)r-, r(e- (ei)=pon).

§488 D
Here belong Epic a)khde/w, kote/w, loe/w, neike/w, and the forms a)/asa, -a/mhn, a)/esa. e)ru/w shows e)ru_- and e)ru^-.

§489

Insertion of s.—In the perfect middle and first aorist passive systems, verbs which retain a short final vowel and some others usually insert s before the personal ending.
Thus, tele/w (488 d), tete/lesmai, e)tele/sqhn; spa/w draw, e)/spasmai, e)spa/sqhn; keleu/w order, keke/leusmai, e)keleu/sqhn; gignw/skw know, e)/gnwsmai, e)gnw/sqhn.
a. If the aorist passive ends in -qhn and not in -sqhn, the perfect middle does not insert s. Thus -qhn, not -sqhn, occurs in all verbs in -euw except leu/w stone to death, in all verbs in -ew which have -qhn preceded by h, in all verbs in -ow except xo/w heap up, and in all verbs in -aw except those that retain a^. Stems originally ending in s (624) properly show s.
b. If the aorist passive ends in -sqhn, the perfect middle may or may not insert s. Verbs in -azw and -izw (stems -ad, -id) regularly have s by 83, 587. In the case of other verbs some always show s, some never show s, and some are doubtful. In many cases the later usage with s has crept into the Mss. of the classical authors (so with the perfect of a)le/w, bai/nw, dra/w, zw/nnu_mi, klei/w (klh/|w), sw/|zw, xri/_w, and with the aorist of pau/w).
c. The following verbs show an inserted s both in the perfect middle and the aorist passive in classical Greek: ai)de/omai, gignw/skw, e(lku/w, qla/w, qrau/w, keleu/w, kla/w, kna（i/）w, kore/nnu_mi, kuli/_w, cu/_w, pi/mplhmi, pri/_w, pti/ttw, sbe/nnu_mi, sei/w, skeda/nnu_mi, spa/w, tanu/w, tele/w, ti/nw, u(/_w, fla/w, xo/w, xrw/|zw.
d. The following form only the perfect middle with s in classical Greek: bu_ne/w, e(/nnu_mi (ei(=mai, but e(/sto Hom.), e)ru/w, zw/nnu_mi, ce/w, *o)du/ssomai, ple/w, fleu/w (Hdt.).
e. The following form only the aorist passive with s in classical Greek: a)/gamai, a)kou/w, a)nu/w, a)re/skw, a)/xqomai, gela/w, dai/nu_mi, dra/w, e)lu/w, e)/ramai, e)ra/w, i(_la/skomai, klei/w (klh/|w), leu/w, mequ/skw, mimnh/|skw, o)i/_w, o)/nomai (Hdt.), pai/w, palai/w, peta/nnu_mi, pi/mprhmi, r(ai/w, r(w/nnu_mi, sto/rnu_mi, xala/w, xra/omai, xra/w, xri(_w.
f. Only in post-classical Greek is s attested both in the perfect middle and aorist passive in a)rke/w, ze/w, klai/w, (a)po) lau/w, lo/w, o)/llu_mi, pne/w, ptai/w, sa/w, yau/w. —Only in the perfect middle: a)/gamai, a)kou/w, a)nu/w, gela/w, dra/w, e)me/w, e)/ramai, kera/nnu_mi, kolou/w, mequ/skw, nai/w, na/w spin, o)pui/w, pai/w, palai/w, peta/nnu_mi (and in Ionic), pi/mprhmi (Aristotle; earlier perf. pe/prhmai), sto/rnu_mi, xala/w, yau/w. When the perfect middle is not attested in classical Greek some at least of the s forms from the above verbs may represent classical usage, provided the aorist passive has -sqhn.—Only in the aorist passive: a)ke/omai, a)le/w, a)ru/w, bai/nw, bu_ne/w, yeu/w, ei)lu/w, e)lau/nw, e)/rumai, e)ru/w, zw/nnu_mi, kai/w, ce/w, ma/xomai, ne/w heap up, *o)du/ssomai, ple/w, ptu/w, sw/|zw, fqa/nw.
g. Some verbs have double forms (one of which may be disputed) in the classical period: du/namai: e)dunh/qhn and e)duna/sqhn (chiefly Ionic and poetic); ke<*>a/nnu_mi: e)kra/_qhn and e)kera/sqhn; krou/w: ke/kroumai better than ke/krousmai; ne/w: ne(nhmai and ne/nhsmai; o)/mnu_mi: o)mw/momai (and o)mw/mostai), w)mo/qhn and w)mo/sqhn.— Dialectal or dialectal and late are e)bw/sqhn for e)boh/qhn (boa/w), e)lh/lasmai h)la/sqhn (e)lau/nw), keko/rhmai for keko/resmai (kore/nnu_mi), pepe/tasmai (peta/nnu_mi).
h. Some verb-stems ending in n show -s-mai in the perfect middle: h(du/_nw, miai/nw, paxu/_nw, perai/nw, u(fai/nw, fai/nw. Thus pe/fasmai, h(/dusmai, memi/asmai. Dialectal or late: qhlu/_nw, koilai/nw, leptu/_nw, lu_mai/nomai, cai/nw, chmai/nw, shmai/nw. On -mmai see 579.
i. Observe that some vowel verbs inserting s do not lengthen the final vowel of the verb-stem in any tense (gela/w, tele/w); and that some not inserting s (de/w, qu/_w, lu/_w) do not lengthen the final vowel in some tenses. e)p-aine/w commend and par-aine/w exhort do not insert s and have the short vowel in all tenses.
j. The insertion of s in the perfect middle started in the 3 sing. and 2 pl. Before the endings -tai and -sqe, s was retained in the case of verbs with stems originally ending in s (as tele/w), or where s developed from t, d, q (98) before -tai, -sqe (pe/peistai from pepeiqtai). See 409 b, 624. In all cases where the verb-stem did not originally end in s, the sigma forms are due to analogy; as in keke/leusmai (keleu/w), pe/plhsmai (pi/mplhmi), e)/gnwsmai (gignw/skw).

§489 D
Hom. has original forms in pefradme/nos (frazw), kekoruqme/nos (koru/ttw), e)pe/piqmen (pei/qw).

§490

Addition of q.—The present stems of some poetical verbs are made by the addition of q; as nh/-q-w spin, plh/-q-w am full (pi/m-plh-mi). Cp. 832.
a. Most of the indicative forms seem to be imperfects, but since some have the force of aorists (e.g., Soph. O. C. 862, 1334, O. T. 650), in certain editions they are regarded as second aorists, and the infinitives and participles are accented (against the Mss.) on the ultima (diwkaqei=n, ei)kaqw/n).

§490 D
A few verbs make poetic forms by adding -qo/e- to the present or the 2 aorist tense-stem, in which a or e (u once) takes the place of the thematic vowel of the simple verb. Such forms are chiefly Homeric, but occur sometimes in Attic poetry, very rarely in prose. Thus, flege/qw (fle/gw burn), e)diw/kaqoi (diw/kw pursue), e)/sxeqon (e)/xw have). q-forms are found in moods other than the indicative (ei)ka/qw, ei)ka/qoimi, a)mu_na/qate, diwka/qein, ei)ka/qwn).

§491

Omission of n.—Some verbs in -nw drop the n of the verbal stem in the first perfect, perfect middle, and first passive systems.
kri/_nw (krin-), judge, ke/kri-ka, ke/kri-mai, e)kri/-qhn. So also kli/_nw incline, plu/_nw wash.

§492

§493

§494

Reduplication.—The verb-stem may be reduplicated.
a. In the present with i: gi-gnw/-skw (gnw-) know, ti/-qh-mi place, i(/-sth-mi set, di/-dw-mi give. The present reduplication may be carried over to other tenses: dida/ (k) skw teach (99), dida/cw. With e: te-trai/nw bore.
