a. iw for eo is a diphthong. eu for eo is common in Theocritus. In Cretan i ( = y) for e is often expelled (kosmo/ntes = kosme/ontes).

§655
Verbs in -ow contract oo and oe to w in Severer Doric and to ou in Milder Doric.

§656

Aeolic.—In Aeolic contract verbs commonly pass into the mi-conjugation: ti/_maimi, -ais, -ai, ti/_ma_men, ti/_ma_te, ti/_maisi, imperfect, e)ti/_ma_n, e)ti/_ma_s, e)ti/_ma_, etc. inf. ti/_ma_n, part. ti/_mais, -antos, mid. ti/_ma_mai, inf. ti_ma/_menai. So fi/lhmi, fi/lhmen, fi/lhte, fi/leisi, e)fi/lhn, inf. fi/lhn, part. fi/leis, -entos. Thus o)/rhmi from o)re/w = Att. o(ra/w, ka/lhmi, ai)/nhmi. So also dh/lwmi, 3 pl. dh/loisi, inf. dh/lwn. Besides these forms we find a few examples of the earlier inflection in -aw, -ew, -ow, but these forms usually contract except in a few cases where e is followed by an o sound (pote/ontai). From other tenses, e.g. the fut. in -hsw, h has been transferred to the present in a)dikh/w, poqh/w.

§657
Hom. has several cases of contract verbs inflected according to the mi- conjugation in the 3 dual: su_lh/-thn (su_la/w spoil), prosaudh/-thn (prosauda/w speak to), a)peilh/-thn (a)peile/w threaten), o(marth/-thn (o(marte/w meet); also sa/w 3 sing. imperf. (sao/w keep safe). In the infinitive -hmenai, as goh/menai (goa/w), peinh/menai (peina/_w, 641), filh/menai (file/w), forh/menai and forh=nai (fore/w). But a)gi_ne/w has a)gi_ne/menai.

## FUTURE ACTIVE AND MIDDLE (532 ff.). FUTURE PERFECT (580 ff.)

§658
All vowel and consonant verbs in -w inflect the future alike.

§659

Indicative.—The future active and middle add the primary endings, and are inflected like the present; as lu/_sw, lu/_somai. On the two endings of the second singular middle, see 628. Liquid verbs, Attic futures (538), Doric futures (540) are inflected like contract verbs in -ew; thus fanw= fanou=mai, kalw= kalou=mai, and pesou=mai, follow poiw= poiou=mai (385).
a. The only future perfect active from an w-verb is teqnh/cw shall be dead (584), which is inflected like a future active. Ordinarily the periphrastic formation is used: leleukw\s e)/somai shall have loosed. The future perfect passive (lelu/_somai shall have been loosed) is inflected like the future middle. The periphrastic forms and the future perfect passive rarely occur outside of the indicative.

§660

Optative.—The inflection is like the present: lu/_so-i_-mi, lu_so-i/_-mhn. In the optative singular of liquid verbs, -ih-n, -ih-s, -ih, in the dual and plural -i_-ton, -i_-thn, -i_-men, -i_-te, -ie-n, are added to the stem ending in the thematic vowel o; thus faneo-i/hn = fanoi/hn, fane/o-i_-men = fanoi=men. So in Attic futures in -a/zw, as biba/zw (539 d) cause to go: bibw/|hn, -w/|hs, -w/|h, pl. bibw=|men.

§661

Infinitive.—The future infinitive active adds -en, as lu/_sein from lu/_se-en, fanei=n from fane/（s）e-en. The infinitive middle adds -sqai, as lu/_se-sqai, fanei=sqai, from fane/（s）e-sqai.

§661 D
Hom. has a)ce/menai, a)ce/men, a)/cein. Doric has -hn, -ein; Aeolic has -hn.

§662

Participle.—The future participle has the same endings as the present: lu/_swn lu/_sousa lu=son, fanw=n fanou=sa fanou=n; middle, lu_so/menos, fanou/menos.

## FIRST AND SECOND FUTURE PASSIVE (589, 597）

§663
All verbs inflect the first and second future passive alike, that is, like the future middle.

§664
The indicative adds -mai to the stem ending in -qhso- or -hso-, as luqh/so-mai, fanh/-so-mai. For the two forms of the second person singular see 628. The optative adds -i_-mhn, as luqhso-i/_-mhn, fanhso-i/_-mhn. The infinitive adds -sqai, as luqh/-se-sqai, fanh/-se-sqai. The participle adds -menos, as luqhso/-menos, fanhso/-menos.

## FIRST AORIST ACTIVE AND MIDDLE (542）

§665
All vowel and consonant w-verbs inflect the first aorist alike.

§666

Indicative.—The secondary endings of the first aorist active were originally added to the stem ending in -s-; thus, e)lu_sṃ, e)lu_s-s, e)lu_s-t, e)lu_s-men, e)lu_s-te, e)lu_s-nt. From e)lu_sṃ came e)/lu_sa (by 35 c), the a of which spread to the other forms except in the 3 sing., where e was borrowed from the perfect.
a. In the middle the secondary endings are added to the stem ending in -sa-. For the loss of s in -so, see 465 b.

§667

Subjunctive.—In the subjunctive the long thematic vowel -w/h- is substituted for the a of the indicative, and these forms are inflected like the present subjunctive: lu/_sw lu/_swmai, fh/nw fh/nwmai. For the loss of s in -sai see 465 a.

§667 D
Hom. has forms with the short thematic vowel, as e)ru/ssomen, a)lgh/sete, nemesh/sete; mu_qh/somai, e)fa/yeai, i(_laso/mesqa, dhlh/setai. In such forms aorist subjunctive and future indicative are alike (532). Pindar has ba/_somen, au)da/_somen (457 D.).

§668

Optative.—To the stem ending in a the mood-suffix i_ is added, making ai, to which the same endings are affixed as in the present: lu/_sa-i_-mi = lu/_saimi, lu_sa-i/_-mhn = lu_sai/mhn, fh/na-i_-mi = fh/naimi. The inflection in the middle is like that of the present. For the loss of s in -so see 465 b.—In the active -eias, -eie, -eian are more common than -ais, -ai, -aien.

§668 D
Hom. has both sets of endings, but that in ai is rarer. In the drama -eias is very much commoner than -ais. -ais is most frequent in Plato and Xenophon, less common in poetry, and very rare in the orators. Neither Thuc. nor Hdt. has -ais. -ai is rare in prose, most examples being in Plato and Demosthenes. Hdt. has no case. In Aristotle -ai is as common as -eie. -ai=en is very rare in poetry, in Thuc. and Hdt., but slightly better represented in Xenophon and the orators. -eian is probably the regular form in the drama.—The forms in -eias, -eie, -eian are called “Aeolic,” but do not occur in the remains of that dialect.

§669

Imperative.—The regular endings (462) are added to the stem in -sa (or -a in liquid verbs) except in the active and middle 2 sing., in which -on and -ai take the place of -a: lu=son lu_sa/tw, lu=sai lu_sa/sqw, fh=non fhna/tw, fh=nai fhna/sqw.

§670

Infinitive.—The aorist active infinitive ends in -ai, which is an old dative: the middle ends in -sqai: lu=sai lu/_sa-sqai, fh=nai fh/na-sqai, ple/cai ple/ca-sqai.

§671

Participle.—The active participle adds -nt like the present: masc. lu/_sa_s from lu_sant-s, fem. lu/sa_sa from lusa_nt-[iglide]a, neut. lu=san from lu_san（t). See 301. The middle ends in -menos: lu_sa/-menos, fhna/-menos.

§671 D
Aeolic has -ais, -aisa, -an (37 D. 3).

## FIRST AND SECOND AORIST PASSIVE (585, 590）

§672
All vowel and consonant verbs in -w inflect the aorists passive alike, that is, according to the mi-conjugation, except in the subjunctive.
a. Vowel verbs rarely form second aorists that are passive in form, as r(e/w flow, e)rru/hn (803). But r(e/w is properly not a vowel verb (see 503).

§673

Indicative.—The indicative adds the active secondary endings directly to the tense stem ending in -qh- (first aorist) or -h- (second aorist). The inflection is thus like that of the imperfect of a verb in -mi.

e)lu/qh-ne)ti/qh-ne)lu/qh-mene)ti/qe-men

e)lu/qh-se)ti/qh-se)lu/qh-tone)ti/qe-tone)lu/qh-tee)ti/qe-te

e)lu/qhe)ti/qhe)luqh/-thne)tiqe/-thne)lu/qh-sane)ti/qe-san
a. For -san we find -n from -n（t) in poetical and dialectic forms before which h has been shortened to e (40), thus w(/rmhqen for w(rmh/qhsan from o(rma/w urge.

§674

Subjunctive.—The subjunctive adds -w/h- to the tense stem ending in -qe- or -e- and contracts: luqw=, -h=|s, -h=|, etc., from luqe/w, -e/h|s, -e/h|, etc.; fanw=, -h=|s, -h=| from fane/w, -e/h|s, -e/h|, etc.

§674 D
Hdt. leaves ew open (ai(reqe/w, fane/wsi) but contracts eh, eh| (fanh=|). Hom. has some forms like the 2 aor. subj. of mi-verbs. Thus, from damna/w (da/mnhmi) subdue: damh/w, -h/h|s, -h/h|, -h/ete. So also dah/w (da- learn), saph/h| (sh/pw cause to rot), fanh/h| (fai/nw show), traph/omen (te/rpw amuse). The spellings with ei (e.g. damei/w, daei/w) are probably incorrect.

§675

Optative.—The optative adds -i_- or -ih- to the tense-stem ending in -qe- or -e-, and contracts. In the singular -ih- is regular; in the dual and plural -i_- is generally preferred. Thus luqei/hn from luqe-i/h-n, fanei/hn from fane-i/h-n, luqei=ton from luqe/-i_-ton, fanei=ton from fane/-i_-ton, luqei=men from luqe/-i_-men, fanei=en from fane/-ie-n. The inflection is like that of the present optative of a mi-verb.

luqe-i/h-ntiqe-i/h-nluqe-i=-mentiqe-i=-men

luqe-i/h-stiqe-i/h-sluqe-i=-tontiqe-i=-tonluqe-i=-tetiqe-i=-te

luqe/-i/htiqe-i/hluqe-i/-thntiqe-i/-thnluqe-i=e-ntiqe-i=e-n
a. -ei/hmen is used only in prose (but Plato and Isocrates have also -ei=men). -ei/hte is almost always found in the Mss. of prose writers; -ei=te occurs only in poetry (except from mi-verbs). -ei=en is more common in prose than -ei/hsan.

§676

Imperative.—The endings of the imperative are added to the tense-stem ending in -qh- or -h-. Before -ntwn, -qh- and -h- become -qe- and -e- (luqe/ntwn, fane/ntwn). For -ti instead of -qi in the first aorist (lu/qhti) see 125 b.

§677

Infinitive.—-nai is added to the tense-stem in -qh- or -h-: luqh=-nai, fanh=-nai.

§677 D
Hom. has -menai, as o(moiwqh/menai, dah/menai (and dah=nai). Doric has -men, Aeolic -n (mequ/sqhn = mequsqh=nai).

§678

Participle.—The participle adds -nt, as masc. luqei/s from luqent-s, fem. luqei=sa from luqent-[iglide]a, neut. luqe/n from luqen（t). See 301. So fanei/s, etc.

The following w-verbs have in poetry (especially in Homer) second aorists of the mi form: a(/llomai (a)=lso, a)=lto), a)paura/w (a)pou/ra_s), a)rari/skw (a)/rmenos), a)/w (a)/_menai), ba/llw (cumblh/thn, e)/blhto), bibrw/skw (e)/brwn), root gen- (ge/nto grasped), de/xomai (de/kto), Epic kixa/_nw (e)ki/xhn, kixh/w, kixei/h, kixh=nai and kixh/menai, kixei/s and kixh/menos; properly from ki/xhmi), kla/w (a)po/kla_s), klu/w (klu=qi, ke/kluqi), kti/zw (kti/menos), root lex- (e)/lekto laid himself to rest), lu/_w (lu/to), ou)ta/w (ou)=ta, ou)ta/menos), pa/llw (pa/lto), pela/zw (e)plh/mhn), pe/rqw (pe/rqai = perq-sqai), plw/w (e)/plwn), pnu_- (a)/mpnu_to revived), pth/ssw (katapth/thn), seu/w (e)ssu/mhn, e)/suto, su/menos), fqi/nw (e)fqi/mhn), xe/w (e)xu/mhn, xu/menos).
e)/lekto, pa/lto are properly first aorists (for e)lek-s-to, pal-s-to), s being lost between two consonants (103).

## FIRST AND SECOND PERFECT AND PLUPERFECT ACTIVE (555, 561）

§689
All vowel and consonant verbs in -w inflect the first perfect alike. Some verbs in -w inflect the second perfect according to the w-conjugation, others inflect it according to the mi-conjugation.

§690

Indicative.—Originally the endings were added to the stem without any thematic vowel. Of this unthematic formation a few traces survive (573). In the 2 p. sing. the ending is -s, but originally -qa; in the 3 pl. -ka_si stands for ka-nsi out of ka-nti (100). Thus le/luka, -as, -e, pe/pomfa, -as, -e, etc. The periphrastic combination occurs in the indicative (599 a).

§691

Subjunctive.—The perfect subjunctive is commonly formed periphrastically by the perfect active participle and w)=, h)=|s, h)=|, etc. Thus lelukw\s (gegrafw\s) w)=, etc., leluko/tes (gegrafo/tes) w)=men, etc. Of the periphrastic forms only the 1 and 3 sing., 2 and 3 plur. are attested.

§692
Instances of the simple perfect subjunctive (lelu/kw, gegra/fw) are very rare. The simple form is made by substituting the thematic vowel w/h for a in the tense-stem. Only the sing. and the 3 plur. are attested from w-verbs.

§693
Besides ei)dw= (oi)=da) and e(sth/kh|, etc., Attic prose has only about 16 occurrences of the simple perf. subj., and from the following verbs only: bai/nw, de/dia, e)gei/rw, e)/oika, qnh/|skw, lamba/nw, lanqa/nw, pa/sxw, poiw=, fu/_w. Hippocr. has forms from bibrw/skw, ponw=, teu/xw. There are about 30 occurrences in the poetry. Attic prose writers show about 25 cases of the periphrasis from all w-verbs.

§694

Optative.—The perfect optative is commonly formed periphrastically by the perfect active participle and ei)/hn, ei)/hs, ei)/h, etc. Thus lelukw\s (gegrafw\s) ei)/hn, etc., leluko/tes (gegrafo/tes) ei)=men, etc. The dual is exceedingly rare.

§695
Occasionally the simple forms are used (lelu/koimi, gegra/foimi). These are formed by adding the mood-sign i_, and the endings, to the tense-stem with the thematic vowel (o). All the -ih-forms are attested; of the -i_-forms only the 3 sing. and 1 and 3 plur.

§696
Of the simple optative there are about 25 occurrences in Attic prose, and from the following verbs only: a)poxwrw=, e)capatw=, ei)sba/llw, paradi/dwmi, e)/oika, -e(sth/koi, u(phretw=, qnh/|skw, lanqa/nw, katalei/pw, poiw=, pa/sxw, proe/rxomai, e)mpi/_ptw, fu/_w. In the poets there are about 16 occurrences. Prose writers show about 106 occurrences of the periphrastic forms.

§697

Imperative.—The usual form of the first perfect imperative is periphrastic: lelukw\s i)/sqi, e)/stw, etc. No classical Attic writer uses the simple forms.

§698
The second perfect is rare, and occurs only in the case of verbs which have a present meaning. From active verbs inflected according to the w- conjugation there occur kexh/nete gape, Ar. Ach. 133 (xa/skw, xan-), and kekra/_gete screech, Vesp. 415 (kra/_zw). Most second perfects show the mi form and have present meaning, as te/qnaqi (Hom.) teqna/tw from qnh/|skw die, de/diqi from de/dia fear, and ke/kra_xqi from kra/_zw in Aristophanes. Most such second perfects are poetical.

§699

Infinitive.—The perfect infinitive adds -e/-nai, as leluke/nai, leloipe/nai.

§699 D
Doric has -hn and -ein, as dedu/khn = deduke/nai, gega/_kein = gegone/nai. Aeolic has -hn, as teqna/khn.

§700

Participle.—The suffixes of the perfect participle in the nominative are -(v）w/s, -ui=a, -(v）o/s, as lelukw/s, leloipw/s. See 301 c, d, 309.

§700 D
In the 2 perf. Hom. sometimes has -w=t-os for -o/t-os, as kekmhw/s, -w=tos (ka/mnw am weary). In the 2 perf. Hom. sometimes has a for Attic h in the feminine, as a)rhrw/s a)rarui=a from a)/rhra (a)rari/skw fit). See 573. Aeolic inflects the perfect participle as a present in -wn, -ontos. Thus Hom. keklh/gontas for keklhgo/tas (kla/zw scream), Pind. pefri/_kontas (fri/_ttw shudder).

§701

Pluperfect Active.—The pluperfect is formed by adding -ea, -eas, -ee, -eton, -ethn, -emen, -ete, -esan to the reduplicated stem. By contraction from e)lelukea, -eas, -ee come the forms e)lelu/kh, -hs -ei (n). In the later language ei spread from the 3 sing. and was used throughout, as e)lelu/kein, -eis, -ei, -eiton, -ei/thn, -eimen, -eite, and very late -eisan. The best Mss. of Demosthenes have -ein in 1 sing. Instead of the simple pluperfect we find periphrastic forms, 599 a.

Other verbs with second perfects of the mi-form (chiefly Homeric) are: a)/nwga (a)/nwxqi), bibrw/skw (bebrw=tes), e)gei/rw (e)grh/gora), e)/rxomai (ei/lh/luqmen), me/mona (memaw/s), pa/sxw (pe/posqe), pei/qw (e)pe/piqmen), pi(_ptw (peptw/s), root da- learn (dedaw/s), root tla- (te/tlamen, tetlai/hn, te/tlaqi, tetla/menai and tetla/men, tetlhw/s).

## PERFECT AND PLUPERFECT MIDDLE AND PASSIVE (574）

§706
All vowel and consonant verbs in -w inflect the perfect middle according to the mi-conjugation.

§707

Indicative.—The perfect middle is inflected by adding the primary middle endings directly to the tense-stem, herein agreeing with the mi-conjugation. The pluperfect adds the secondary middle endings. In vowel verbs the formation is simple, as in le/lu-mai, e)lelu/-mhn. But in consonant verbs, the consonant at the end of the stem comes into collision with the consonant at the beginning of the ending; hence certain euphonic changes described in 409. The periphrastic form occurs in the 3 pl. and sometimes in the 3 sing. (599 d, e).
a. Stems in n avoid the forms -n-sai, -n-so; thus, from fai/nw, instead of pe/fansai, e)pe/fanso the periphrastic pefasme/nos ei)=, h)=sqa were probably used.

§708

Subjunctive.—The perfect middle subjunctive is commonly formed by periphrasis of the perfect middle participle and w)=, h)=|s, h)=|, etc. Thus lelume/nos w)=.

§708 D
Hdt. has memnew/meqa, and this form may be read in
c 168.

§709
From two verbs, whose perfect stem ends in h-（a), the simple forms are constructed. kta/omai (kta-) acquire, perf. ke/kthmai possess (1946), forms its subjunctive by adding the thematic vowel -w/h- to ke-kta; thus ke-kta/-w-mai = kektw=mai, ke-kta/-h-sai = kekth=|, ke-kta/-h-tai = kekth=tai, etc.—mimnh/|skw (mna- remind, perf. me/mnhmai remember (1946): me-mna/-w-mai = memnw=mai, memnh-w/-meqa = memnw/meqa. With kektw=mai, memnw=mai, cp. i(stw=mai, p. 137. The periphrastic kekthme/nos w)=, memnhme/nos w)= occur.

§710

Optative.—The perfect middle optative is commonly formed by the periphrasis of the perfect middle participle and ei)/hn, ei)/hs, ei)/h, etc. Thus lelume/nos ei)/hn, etc.

§711
Some verbs add -i/_-mhn, -o-i/_-mhn to the tense-stem (709).—a. kta/omai (kta-) acquire, perf. ke/kthmai possess (1946): opt. kekth-i/_-mhn = kekth/|mhn, kekth/i_-so = kekth=|o, kekth/-i_-to = kekth=|to. Less frequent and doubtful are kektw/|mhn, -w=|o, -w=|to, -w/|meqa from kekth-o-i/_-mhn, etc.
b. mimnh/|skw (mna-) remind, perf. me/mnhmai remember; opt. memnh-i/_-mhn = memnh/|mhn, memnh/-i_-so = memnh=|o, memnh/-i_-to = memnh=|to, etc. The forms memnw/|mhn, -w=|o, -w=|to, etc., from memnh-o-i/_-mhn, etc., are uncommon and suspected.
c. kale/w (kale-, klh-) call, perf. ke/klhmai am called (1946); opt. keklh-i/_-mhn, etc. = keklh/|mhn, keklh=|o, keklh=|to, keklh/|meqa.
d. ba/llw (bal-, blh-) throw, perf. diabe/blhmai, opt. diabeblh=|sqe.
N.—The forms in -h/|mhn, etc., have the mi-form; the doubtful -w/|mhn, etc., belong to the w-conjugation.

§711 D
Hom. has lelu=to s 238 = lelu/-i_to (cp. dai/nhu_to). Pind. has memnai/ato. me/mnoio in Xen. is from me/mnomai.

§712

Imperative.—In the third person singular the perfect meaning is regularly retained, as ei)rh/sqw let it have been said. The 2 sing. and pl. are generally found only in the case of perfects with a present meaning, as me/mnhsqe remember! mh\ pefo/bhsqe do not be afraid! pe/pauso stop! See 698.
a. The dual and 3 pl. are apparently wanting. The 2 sing. in -nso from stems in -n does not occur. For pe/fanso, pefasme/nos i)/sqi was probably used.

§713
Attic prose writers have a)nabeblh/sqw, a)pokekri/sqw, ei)rh/sqw, e)kth/sqw, e)yeu/sqw, kei=so, -kei/sqw, ke/kthso, me/mnhsqe, pepai/sqw, pepera/nqw, pepoi/hso, pepra/_sqw, pefa/sqw, pefo/bhsqe, teta/xqw, tetolmh/sqw.

§714
Instead of the simple forms of the imperative we find the periphrastic use of the perfect participle and i)/sqi, e)/stw, etc. (599 g). Thus ei)rhme/non e)/stw = ei)rh/sqw.

§715

Infinitive.—The perfect infinitive adds -sqai, as lelu/-sqai. Consonant stems lose the s by 103, as lelei=fqai, pepra=xqai (406), e)lhle/gxqai, pefa/nqai (407).

§716

Participle.—The perfect participle adds -me/nos, as lelume/nos, leleimme/nos, pepra_gme/nos (406, 407). On the s of pefasme/nos see 409 d.

## SECOND CONJUGATION OR VERBS IN MI

§717
Verbs in -mi usually have no thematic vowel between the tense-stem and the personal endings in the present system (except in the subjunctive). The name “mi-conjugation,” or “non-thematic” conjugation,” is applied to all verbs which form the present and imperfect without the thematic vowel.

§718
Of verbs ending in -mi the following tenses are inflected according to the mi-conjugation (except in the subjunctive): all non-thematic presents and imperfects; all aorists passive; all perfects and pluperfects middle; those second aorists active and middle in which the tense-stem does not end with the thematic vowel; one verb (i(/sthmi) in the second perfect and pluperfect active.

§719
Certain tenses of verbs ending in -mi in the first person present indicative active, or in -mai in the present middle (and passive) when not preceded by the thematic vowel, are inflected according to the w-conjugation. These tenses are: all futures, all first aorists active and middle, most perfects and pluperfects active, and all subjunctives. Verbs in -nu_mi regularly inflect the subjunctive and the optative according to the w-conjugation. Furthermore, the 2 sing. in the present and 2 and 3 sing. in the imperfect active of certain verbs, and some other forms, follow the w-conjugation (746).

§720
Verbs in -mi add the endings directly either to the verb-stem (here a root) or after the suffixes nu or nh. Hence three classes are to be distinguished.
A. Root class; as fh-mi/ say, verb-stem (and root) fa-, fh-. This class often shows reduplication in the present and imperfect, as di/dw-mi give.
N.—Two verbs have verb-stems ending in a consonant: ei)mi/ am (e)s-mi) and h(=mai sit (h(s-mai).
B. -nu- class; as dei/k-nu_-mi show, verb-stem deik-, present stem deiknu_^-.
C. A few verbs, mainly poetical, add na-, nh-; as ski/d-nh-mi ski/d-namen scatter, da/m-nh-mi da/m-na-men, subdue.

§721
Deponent verbs without the thematic vowel are inflected according to the mi-conjugation.

## PRESENT SYSTEM

§722
Verbs in -mi belong to the first or simple class (504) or to the fourth class (523).

## FIRST OR SIMPLE CLASS

§723
The present is made by adding the personal endings directly to the verb-stem, which is a root. This verb-stem may be used in its pure form or it may be reduplicated.
a. Some verbs of this class with no active have a verb-stem of more than one syllable (usually two syllables).

§724

Unreduplicated Presents: ei)mi/ (e)s-) am, ei)=mi (i)-, ei)-) go, h(=mai (h(s-) sit, h)mi/ say (h)= said, 3 sing.), kei=mai (kei-) lie, fhmi/ (fa-, fh-) say, xrh/ it is necessary (793); and poet. a)/hmi (a)h-) blow.

§725

Deponents.—a)/ga-mai (and a)ga/omai) admire, de/a-mai appear, di/e-mai flee, make flee (cp. di/w), du/na-mai am able (737 a), e)pi/-sta-mai understand, e)/ra-mai love (poet. for e)ra/w), i(/ptamai fly (late, see 726 a), kre/ma-mai hang (intrans.), o)/no-mai insult, pe/ta-mai (poet. by-form of pe/tomai) fly, e)pria/mhn bought a second aorist, steu=mai affirm.
a. Other such forms are Hom. i(/_emai (vi/_emai) strive, ei)/rumai and e)/rumai rescue, Ion. la/zumai take. e)pi/sthtai II 243 owes its h to such non-present forms as e)pisth/somai.

§726

Reduplicated Presents.—di/dhmi bind (rare for de/w), di/dwmi (do-, dw-) give, i(/_hmi (e(-, h(-) send, i(/sthmi (sta-, sth-) set, ki/xrhmi (xra-, xrh-) lend, o)ni/nhmi (o)na-, o)nh-) benefit, pi/mplhmi (pla-, plh-) fill, pi/mprhmi (pra-, prh-) burn, ti/qhmi (qe-, qh-) place.
a. Also poetic bi/bhmi (ba-, bh-) go, in Hom. biba/_s striding, di/-zhmai (also Ion.) seek, for di-d[iglide]h-mai by 116 (cp. zhte/w seek), i(/lhmi (i(_la-, i(_lh- for sisla-, sislh-) am propitious. i(/ptamai (late) for pe/tomai fly is an analogue of i(/stamai and is not properly reduplicated. ti/trhmi bore is late.

§727
Verbs in -mi reduplicate with i in the present. See 414, 447. pi/-m-plhmi and pi/-m-prhmi may lose the inserted nasal in compounds of e)n, but only when e)n- takes the form e)m-; as e)mpi/plhmi, but e)nepi/mplasan. Doric has ki/gxhmi. In o)-ni/-nh-mi the reduplication takes place after a vowel (verb-stem o)na-, o)nh-).
a. Reduplication is in place only in present and imperfect; but Hom. has didw/somen.

## FOURTH CLASS

§728
Most mi-verbs of the fourth class add -nu- (after a vowel, -nnu-) to the verb-stem.

§729
Verb-stems in -a: kera/-nnu_mi mix, krema/-nnu_mi hang (intrans.), peta/nnu_mi spread, skeda/-nnu_mi scatter.

§730
Verb-stems in e (for es): e(/-nnu_mi (in prose a)mfie/-nnu_mi) clothe, kore/nnu_mi satiate, sbe/-nnu_mi extinguish.

§731
Verb-stems in w: zw/-nnu_mi gird, r(w/-nnu_mi strengthen, strw/-nnu_mi spread.

§732
All the forms in -nnu_mi started from verb-stems ending in s: e(/nnu_mi from e(s-nu_-mi, sbe/nnu_mi from sbes-nu_-mi, zw/nnu_mi from zws-nu_-mi. All the other verbs are analogues of these.

§733
Verb-stems in a consonant: a)/g-nu_mi break, a)/r-numai earn, dei/k-nu_mi show, ei)/rg-nu_mi ( = ei)/rgw) shut in, zeu/g-nu_mi yoke (a)po）ktei-nu_mi often written -kti/nnu_mi ( = ktei/nw) kill, mei/g-nu_mi (miswritten mi/_g-nu_mi) mix, -oi)g-nu_mi ( = -oi)/gw) open, o)/llu_mi (o)l-e) destroy, o)/m-nu_mi (o)m-e-, o)m-o) swear, o)mo/rg-nu_mi wipe off, o)/r-nu_mi rouse, ph/g-nu_mi (pag-, phg-) fix, plh/g-nu_mi (once, in e)kplh/gnusqai Thuc. 4. 125; cp. plh/ttw), pta/r-numai sneeze, r(h/g-nu_mi (r(ag-, r(hg-, r(wg-) break, sto/rnu_mi spread, fra/g-nu_mi ( = fra/ttw) inclose.

§734
Poetic verbs: ai)/-numai take, a)/-nu_mi complete (a)nu/w), a)/x-numai am troubled, ga/-numai rejoice, dai/-nu_mi entertain, kai/-numai excel, ki/_-numai move myself (cp. ki_ne/w), o)re/g-nu_mi reach, ta/-numai stretch, with nu carried into other tenses (tanu/w), ti/_-numai (cp. Epic ti/_nw from ti-nv-w) better tei/numai, chastise.

§735
The verbs whose verb-stem ends in a liquid or nasal often form the tenses other than the present by adding e or o, as o)/llu_mi (from o)lnu_mi) w)/lesa, o)lw/leka (o)l-e-), o)/mnu_mi w)/mosa (o)m-o-).

§736

nu_mi-verbs form only the present and imperfect according to the mi- conjugation; with the exception of sbe/-nnu_mi, which has 2 aor. e)/sbhn. The 2 aorist passive and 2 future passive are rare, as r(h/gnu_mi e)rra/ghn e)kragh/somai, zeu/gnu_mi e)zu/ghn.

§736 D
From verbs in -nu_mi second aorists middle are formed in Hom. by only three verbs: mei/gnu_mi (commonly written mi/_gnu_mi) mix e)/mikto, o)/rnu_mi rouse w)=rto, ph/gnu_mi fix kate/phkto.

§737

-nhmi class. A few verbs add nh- in the singular, na- in the plural, to the verb-stem. These verbs are almost entirely poetical or dialectical; and show by-forms in -naw. They are:
da/mnhmi (damna/w) subdue, ki/rnhmi (kirna/w also Epic) mix, kri/mnhmi (miswritten krh/mnhmi) suspend, pe/rnhmi sell, pi/tnhmi (petna/w) spread, ski/dnhmi (and ki/dnhmi) scatter.
a. Only in the middle: ma/rnamai fight, pi/lnamai (pilna/w) approach. In du/namai am able, na has grown fast (cp. dunato/s).

§738

Stem Gradation.—Verbs of the root class show in the stem vowel a variation between strong and weak grades in the present and imperfect indicative active. The singular has the strong grade, the dual and plural have the weak grade. The optative active and most middle forms have the weak grade.
a. h strong (original and Dor. a_), a weak; fhmi/ fame/n, e)/fhn e)/famen; i(/sthmi i(/stamen, i(/_sthn i(/_stamen; da/mnhmi da/mnamen.
b. h strong, e weak: ti/qhmi ti/qemen, e)ti/qhn e)ti/qemen; i(/_hmi i(/_emen.
c. w strong, o weak: di/dwmi di/domen.
d. ei strong, i weak (cp. lei/pw e)/lipon): ei)=mi will go, i)/men. The grades ei, oi, i appear in ei)dw=, subjunctive of oi)=da know, pl. i)/smen for i)/dmen (799).

§739
In the second aorist e)/sthn I stood the strong form has been carried from the singular through the dual and plural of the indicative. The strong stem occurs also in the imperative (sth=qi, sth=te) and infinitive (sth=nai).

§740
The second aorist infinitive shows the weak stem: qei=nai from qe/-enai, dou=nai from do/-enai. Cp. 469 N. dth=nai is, however, from sth/-enai (469 c. N.).

§741
A few root verbs retain the strong grade h throughout. Thus, poet. a)/hmi blow a)/hmen; a)e/ntes is from a)hntes by 40; di/zhmai seek (poet. di/zesqai is from di/zomai); pi/mplhmi fill 2 aor. e)neplh/mhn, opt. e)mplh/|mhn.

§742
Verbs adding nu show the strong form of the verb-stem in the present. r(h/g-nu_-mi break 2 aor. pass. e)rra/ghn, mei/g-nu_-mi (miswritten mi/_gnu_mi) mix 2 aor. pass. e)mi/ghn, zeu/g-nu_-mi yoke 2 aor. pass. e)zu/ghn.

§743
The ending nu varies between strong nu_ and weak nu^. Thus dei/knu_mi dei/knu^men, e)dei/knu_n e)dei/knu^men.

## INFLECTION OF MI-VERBS

§744
Verbs in -mi differ in inflection from verbs in -w in the present and second aorist systems and (rarely) in the second perfect system. Verbs in -mi have the following peculiarities of inflection:
a. The endings -mi and -si (for original -ti) occur in the present indicative active: ti/qh-mi, ti/qh-si; fh-mi/ fh-si/.
b. The 3 plural present indicative active has generally the ending -a_si, from a-anti, as tiqe/a_si, i(sta=si. So in the 2 perf. active e(sta=si.
c. The 3 plural of active past tenses has -san: e)ti/qe-san.
d. The imperative ending -qi is sometimes retained: fa-qi/, sth=-qi; some forms never had it: ti/qei, i(/sth.
e. The middle endings -sai and -so regularly retain s: ti/qe-sai, e)ti/qe-so.
N.—But not in the subjunctive or optative; and usually not in the second aorist; as tiqh=| for tiqe/h-sai, tiqei=o for tiqe/-i_-so, e)/qou for e)/qe-so.
f. The infinitive active has -nai: tiqe/-nai, dido/-nai; the 2 aorist active has -enai rarely: qei=nai for qe/-enai, dou=nai for do/-enai.
g. Active participles with stems in -ont- have the nominative sing. masc. in -ou/s (301 a, 307 a): didou/s, dido/-nt-os.

§745
Forms of -mi verbs which are inflected according to the thematic conjugation are included under the Second Conjugation.

§746

mi-verbs may pass into the w inflection elsewhere than in the subjunctive. a. Verbs in -nu_mi often inflect the present and imperfect active (not the middle) from a present in -nu/w; as deiknu/w (but usually dei/knu_mi), deiknu/eis, deiknu/ei, imperf. e)dei/knuon, -es, -e, etc.,; imper. dei/knue, inf. deiknu/ein, part. deiknu/wn.
b. ti/qhmi, i(/sthmi, di/dwmi, i(/_hmi, etc., show some w-forms in pres. (and imperf.) indic. opt. imper. and infin.; but the forms tiqe/w, i(ste/w, dido/w, i(_e/w, do not occur in the 1 sing.
c. In the present and second aorist optative of ti/qhmi and i(/_hmi there is a transition to the w-conjugation but not in the 1 and 2 singular. The accent is differently reported: (1) as if the presents were tiqe/w, i(_e/w; (2) as if the presents were ti/qw, i(/_w. Thus:
Active: a)fi/_oite for a)fi_ei=te, a)fi/_oien for a)fi_ei=en.—Middle: tiqoi=to, e)piqoi/meqa, sunqoi=to, e)piqoi=nto (also accented ti/qoito, e)pi/qointo); prooi=to, prooi=sqe, prooi=nto (also accented pro/oito, pro/ointo). Hdt. has -qe/oito and -qei=to. The form in -oi=to for -ei=to occurs especially in Plato.
d. The Mss. vary between tiqw=mai and ti/qwmai, a)poqw=mai and a)po/qwmai (426 f).
e. Some other mi-verbs show alternative w-forms, as pimpla/w, -ew (pi/mplhmi), pipra/w (pi/mprhmi), Hom. a)ga/omai (a)/gamai), and i(_la/omai (i(/_lhmi). So often with -nhmi verbs (737), as damna=| and da/mnhsi, e)ki/rna_ and kirna/_s.

§746 D
The tragic poets never have the w-forms; the poets of the Old Comedy seldom; those of the New Comedy often have the w-forms.—Plato usually has -nua_si. Hom. has zeu/gnuon (and zeu/gnusan, w)/rnuon, w)/mnue, o)mnue/tw, etc.). Hdt. usually keeps the mi-forms, but has some w-forms in 2, 3 sing. 3 pl. present indic. and part., and 1 sing., 3 pl. imperfect. Doric usually has the w-forms; Aeolic has zeu/gnu_, and o)/mnu_n infin.

## PRESENT AND IMPERFECT ACTIVE AND MIDDLE (PASSIVE)

§747

Present Indicative.—a. The primary personal endings are added to the stem with the strong form in the singular and the weak form in the dual and plural.
b. In the 2 sing. ti/qhs, i(/_hs, i(/sths, dei/knu_s, etc., s has been added to the stem. This s is obscure in origin, but cannot be derived from -si. tiqei-s is rare.
c. 3 sing. ti/qhsi, i(/sthsi, etc., with -si for -ti (463 c).
d. 3 plur. tiqe/a_si, i(sta=si, etc., from tiqe/-anti, i(sta/-anti (463 d).
e. For the retention of s in ti/qe-sai, etc., see 465 a, b, and N. 2.
f. di/domai in the middle present and imperfect is used only in composition, as a)podi/domai. But the simple form occurs in the passive.

§747 D
1. Hom. has ti/qhsqa, ti/qhsi and tiqei=, tiqei=si; didoi=s and didoi=sqa, di/dwsi (usually) and didoi=, didou=si, r(hgnu=si from r(hgnu-nti, i)/a_si they go and e)/a_si they are. On i(/_staske see 495. Mid. e)ma/rnao from ma/rnamai.
2. Hdt. has tiqei= tiqei=si; i(sta=| is doubtful; didoi=s, didoi=, didou=si, i)/a_si e)/a_si, -nu=si and -nu/ousi. Middle: -atai and -ato (imperf.) for -ntai, -nto in tiqe/atai e)tiqe/ato, i(ste/atai i(_ste/ato, dune/atai e)dune/ato. -atai, -ato have been transferred from the perfect and pluperfect of consonant stems, such as gegra/fatai, e)gegra/fato (465 f).
3. Doric has i(/sta_mi, and a_ for h in all tenses (sta/_sw, e)/sta_sa, e)/sta_n); -ti in 3 sing. ti/qhti; -nti in 3 pl. ti/qenti, di/donti.
4. Aeolic has ti/qhs, ti/qh, ti/qeisi; i)/sta_s, i)/sta_; di/dws, di/dw; da/mna_s.

§748

Imperfect.—e)ti/qeis e)ti/qei, e)di/doun e)di/dous e)di/dou (for e)didwn, -ws, -w) are thematic forms (746 b). For the imperfect of du/namai and e)pi/stamai see 465 b, N. 1. For the retention of s in e)ti/qeso see 465 b.

§748 D
Hom. has e)ti/qei, e)di/dous, e)di/dou.—Hdt. has u(pereti/qea 1 sing., e)di/doun, e)di/dou, i(/_sta_ and a)ni/_sth (both in Mss.).—In poetry -n occurs for -san as ti/qen, i(/_sta^n, di/don (464 e. D.).

§749

Subjunctive.—Attic tiqw=, etc., are derived by contraction from the forms of the weak stem to which the thematic vowel w/h has been added. Thus tiqe/w, -e/h|s, -e/h|, tiqe/wmen, -e/hte, -e/wsi; dido/w, -o/h|s, -o/h|, dido/wmen, -o/hte, -o/wsi. i(stw= is derived from i(ste/w. See 746 b. Verbs in -nu_mi regularly inflect the subjunctive like w-verbs: deiknu/w, -u/h|s, -u/h|.
a. Similarly the middle (passive) forms are derived from tiqe/w-mai tiqe/h-（s）ai, etc., dido/w-mai dido/h-（s）ai, i(ste/w-mai i(ste/h-（s）ai, etc. For the loss of s in -sai see 465 a. -nu_mi verbs inflect the mid. subj. like lu/_wmai.
b. du/namai am able, e)pi/stamai understand, kre/mamai hang, and a)/gamai admire put w/h in place of the stem-vowel so that there is no contraction: du/nwmai, du/nh|, du/nhtai, dunw/meqa, etc. So, too, e)pria/mhn, pri/wmai (757 a).
c. Traces of -u_tai in -nu_mi verbs are very rare: r(h/gnu_tai Hipponax 19; cp. diaskeda/nnu_tai
P. Ph. 77b.

§749 D
Dor. has tiqe/w, -e/wmen, but contracts e + h to h; pl. didw=nti (and ti/qhnti). Dor. has du/na_mai, i(/sta_tai; Hdt. e)ni/sthtai, e)piste/wntai, dune/wntai.

§750

Present Optative.—The optative active has the secondary endings and the mood sign -ih- in the singular, -i_- (-ie- 3 pl.) in the dual and plural. In the dual and plural the longer (-ih-) forms are rare. Thus tiqei/hn (tiqe-i/h-n), tiqei=men (tiqe/-i_-men), i(stai/hn (i(sta-i/h-n) i(stai=en (i:sta/-ie-n). The shorter forms in dual and plural occur in poetry and prose, the longer forms only in prose.
a. The middle (passive) has the secondary endings and the mood sign -i_- throughout: tiqei/mhn (tiqe-i/_-mhn), i(stai/mhn (i(sta-i/_-mhn), i(stai/meqa (i(sta-i/_-meqa), didoi=nto (dido/-i_-nto). On tiqoi=to, etc., see 746 c.
b. The accent follows 424 c, N. 1 (tiqei=to not ti/qeito). But the verbs of 749 b are exceptional: du/naio du/naito; and so o)/naio o)/naito from o)ni/nhmi benefit (424 c, N. 2).

§750 D
Hom. has the mi-forms dainu=to and dainu/_ato, Plato has phgnu=to.

§751

Present Imperative.—ti/qei and di/dou are formed (cp. poi/ei and dh/lou) from ti/qe-e, di/do-e. i(/sth and dei/knu_ show the stronger stem forms.
For the middle endings and the retention of s, see 466. 2. a.—On the forms tiqe/twsan for tiqe/ntwn, tiqe/sqwsan for tiqe/sqwn, see 466. 2. b.

§751 D
Hom. has i(/sth and kaqi/sta_, di/dwqi, e)mpi/plhqi, o)/mnuqi, o)/rnuqi, i(/staso and i(/stao. ti/qou, i(/stw occur in the drama. Pind. has di/doi (active).

§752

Present Infinitive.—The active adds -nai, the middle -sqai. dei/knu_mi admits the form deiknu/ein.

§752 D
Hom. has -menai or -nai preceded by h in a)h/menai a)h=nai from a)/hmi blow, tiqh/menai, kixh/menai and kixh=nai as from ki/xhmi. Also i(sta/menai (and i(sta/men), zeugnu/menai (and zeugnu/men, once zeugnu=men). -men after a short vowel, as tiqe/men, dido/men (once didou=nai). Doric has tiqe/men, dido/men. Theognis has tiqei=n, suniei=n.

§753

Present Participle.—The active adds -nt-, the middle -menos. Thus tiqei/s (tiqe-nt-s), tiqei=sa (tiqe-nt-[iglide]a); tiqe/-menos. For deiknu/_s we find deiknu/wn.

§753 D
Hom. has tiqh/menos K 34.

## THE FUTURES

§754
The futures of verbs in -mi do not differ in formation and inflection from those of verbs in -w.
ti/qhmi: qh/sw, qh/somai, teqh/somai; i(/sthmi: sth/sw, sth/somai, staqh/somai, e(sth/cw; i(/_hmi: h(/sw, -h)/somai, -e(qh/somai; di/dwmi: dw/sw, -dw/somai, doqh/somai; dei/knu_mi: dei/cw, dei/comai, deixqh/somai, dedei/comai (late) or dedeigme/nos e)/somai; mei/gnu_mi: mei/cw, -mixqh/somai, migh/somai (poet.), memei/comai (poet.); ph/gnu_mi: ph/cw, pagh/somai.
a. e(sth/cw is the only future perfect from a mi-verb (584).

## FIRST AORIST ACTIVE AND MIDDLE

§755
The verbs ti/qhmi, i(/_hmi, di/dwmi form the singular active of the first aorist in -k-a, thus, e)/qhka, e)/dwka, h(=ka. The forms of the second aorist (756) are generally used in the dual and plural and in the other moods.
a. The form in k rarely appears outside of the singular, chiefly in the 3 pl., as e)/dwkan ( = e)/dosan), less frequently in the 1 and 2 pl., as e)dw/kamen, -ate.
b. That k was not a suffix but a part of an alternative root appears from a comparison of qhk- in e)/qhka and perf. te/qhka with fēc- in fēci.
c. i(/sthmi has e)/sthsa I set, placed (mid. e)sthsa/mhn), to be distinguished from 2 aor. e)/sthn I stood.
d. e)qhka/mhn is un-Attic; h(ka/mhn (in comp.) is rare and probably found only in the indic.; e)dwka/mhn is very late.

§755 D
Hom. has e)/qhkan, e)/dwkan, e)nh/kamen, qh/kato; Hdt. sunqh/kanto; Pind. qhka/menos.

## SECOND AORIST ACTIVE AND MIDDLE

§756

Indicative.—ti/qhmi, i(/_hmi, di/dwmi use the short grade forms in dual and plural active: e)/-qe-ton, e)/-qe-men, e)/qe-san; ei(=-ton, ei(=-men, ei(=-san (for e)-e(-ton, etc.); e)/-do-men, e)/-do-san. In the singular the k-forms, e)/qhka, h(=ka, e)/dwka, are used. i(/sthmi has e)/sthn, e)/sths, e)/sth (for e)stht, 464 c), e)/sthmen, etc. (p. 138).
a. sbe/nnu_mi extinguish is the only verb in -nu_mi forming a second aorist (e)/sbhn, sbw=, sbei/hn, sbh=qi, sbh=nai, sbei/s).
b. The middle uses the weak stems -qe-, -e(-, -do- in e(-qi/-mhn, -ei(/mhn (for e)-e(-mhn), e)-do/-mhn (only in composition). For the loss of s in -so (e)/qou, e)/dou) see 465 b.
c. In prose the only uncompounded second aorists middle are e)pria/mhn bought (pres. w)ne/omai) and w)nh/mhn derived benefit (o)ni/nhmi). w)nh/mhn keeps h (poet. o)/nhso, o)nh/menos). i(/sthmi does not make the form e)stamhn.

§756 D
Hom. has older -n for -san in e)/sta^n (he uses e)/sthsan also), Dor. has e)/qen, e)/sta^n, e)/don. For the iterative sta/-ske, do/-skon see 495.
c. D. In poetry: e)pta/mhn (prose -e)pto/mhn) from pe/tamai fly; Hom. plh=to approached, e)/blhto was hit (others, 688).

§757

Second Aorist Subjunctive.—All the forms of the 2 aor. subj. are due to contraction of the thematic vowel with the weak stem-vowel. Thus qw=, etc., from qe/w, qe/h|s, qe/h|, qe/wmen, etc.; w(=, etc., from e(/w, e(/h|s, e(/wsi; dw=, etc., from do/w, do/h|s, do/h|; stw=, etc., from ste/w, ste/h|s, etc., with e from h before a vowel. Cp. 682.
a. e)pria/mhn has pri/wmai with w/h in place of the final vowel of the stem (749 b).

§757 D
The subjunctive shows traces of an earlier double form of inflection:
1. With short thematic vowel: qh/eis, qh/ei, qh/eton, qh/omen, qh/ete, qh/ousi. Homer: qh/omen, sth/omen, -sth/eton, kixh/omen, dw/omen, a)poqh/omai.
2. With long thematic vowel: qh/w, qh/h|s, qh/h|, qh/hton, qh/wmen, qh/hte, qh/wsi. Hom. qh/w, qh/h|s, qh/h|, sth/h|s, sth/h|, a)nh/h|, dw/h| or dw/h|si, peristh/wsi, dw/wsi.
By shortening of the long vowel of the stem we obtain a third form:
3. qe/w, qe/h|s, qe/h|, qe/hton, qe/wmen, qe/hte, qe/wsi. Hom. a)fe/h|, qe/wmen, ste/wmen, Hdt. qe/w, qe/wmen, qe/wsi, qe/wmai, ste/wmen, a)poste/wsi, Aeolic qe/w.
4. From 3 are derived the contracted forms qw=, qh=|s, qh=|, etc. Hom. a)nasth=|, dw=|s, dw=| or dw=|si, dw=men; Dor. dw=nti; Hdt. -qh=|, -qh=tai; dw=men, -dw=te, dw=si.
N.—In Hom. the Mss. often have ei for h of the stem, as qei/w, bei/w, qei/omen, kixei/omen.

§758

Second Aorist Optative.—The forms of the optative of the second aorist are made and inflected like those of the present except for the reduplication. Thus, in the active: qei/hn (qe-i/h-n), stai/hn (sta-i/h-n), doi=men (do/-i_-men), doi=en (do/-ie-n). The shorter forms are preferred in the dual and plural, and poetry has only these; prose admits either the longer or the shorter forms.
a. In the 2 pl. cases of -ih-te (doi/hte) are more numerous than -i-te; but they usually lack metrical warrant.
b. Second aorists of stems in u lack the optative in Attic.
c. In the middle: qei/mhn (qe-i/_-mhn), doi/mhn (do-i/_-mhn), -ei(/mhn (e(-i/_-mhn). For qoi/meqa see 746 c. For the accent of pri/aio see 424 c, N. 2.

§758 D
Hom. has stai/hsan P 733, the only case of -ih- outside of the singular; du/_h (for du-i/h), e)kdu=men (for -du/-i_-men), and fqi=to (for fqi/-i_-to) from fqi/_nw perish.

§759

Second Aorist Imperative.—On qe/-s, do/-s, e(/-s, see 466. 1. b. These verbs show the weak form of the stem (qe/-tw, qe/-ntwn). i(/sthmi and sbe/nnu_mi have -qi in sth=-qi, sbh=-qi. For sth=-qi the poets may use -sta_ in composition, as a)po/sta_ stand off.
a. The middle adds -so, which loses its s after a short vowel, as in qou= for qe/-so, dou= for do/-so, pri/w (and poet. pri/a-so). s is not dropped after a long vowel (o)/nhso). Cp. 465 b, N. 2.
b. In composition peri/qes, a)po/dos, para/sthqi, e)nqou=, prodou=; but kata/qou, peridou, peri/dosqe (426 b-c).
c. For the 3 pl. qe/twsan, do/twsan, e(/sqwsan, see 466. 2. b.

§759 D
Hom. has qe/o and e)/nqeo.

§760

Second Aorist Infinitive.—The active adds -enai in qei=nai (qe/-enai), sth=nai (sth/-enai), dou=nai (do/-enai), ei(=nai (e(/-enai). The middle adds -sqai, as qe/-sqai.

§760 D
Hom. has qe/menai, qe/men; sth/menai; do/menai, do/men; and qei=nai, sth=nai, dou=nai. Dor. has qe/men, do/men, sta=men.

§761

Second Aorist Participle.—The active adds -nt- like the present: qei/s (qe-nt-s), qei=sa (qe-nt-[iglide]a), qe/n (qe-nt); sta/_s (sta-nt-s), sta=sa (sta-nt-[iglide]a), sta/n (sta-nt). The middle adds -menos, as qe/-menos.

## FIRST AND SECOND PERFECT (AND PLUPERFECT) ACTIVE

§762

Indicative.—The perfect of ti/qhmi is te/qhka. A later form te/qeika, not found on Attic inscriptions till after 200 B.C. and due to the analogy of ei(=ka, still appears in some texts. te/qeka is Doric. For kaqe/staka Attic used katasth/sa_s e)/xw (cp. 599 b).
a. The dual and plural of the second perfect and pluperfect of i(/sthmi (417) are formed without k: e(/staton, e(/stamen (without augment in the pluperf.), e(sta=si from e(-sta-anti, pluperf. e(/sta-san. The singular is supplied by the 1 perf. e(/sthka I stand.

§763

Subjunctive.—e(sth/kw and e(stw= appear in prose and poetry, e(sthkw\s w)= in prose.

§764

Optative.—e(sth/koimi occurs in comp. in prose, a)festw=tes ei)=en in Plato, teqhkw\s ei)/hs and dedwko/tes ei)=en in Demosthenes. e(stai/hn is poetical.

§765

Imperative.—e(/staqi is poetical.

§766

Infinitive and Participle.—e(sta/nai and e(stw/s are much more common than e(sthke/nai and e(sthkw/s.

§766 D
Hom. has e(sta/menai and e(sta/men, e(staw/s, -ao/tos. Hdt. has e(stew/s, -ew=tos. Doric has -ei=a for -ui=a (e(sta_kei=a).

## PERFECT MIDDLE (PASSIVE)

§767

te/qeimai even in composition is rare and is unknown on Attic inscriptions. For the pass. perf. kei=mai (791) was used. Doric has te/qemai.

## PECULIARITIES IN THE USE OF THE VOICE-FORMS, ETC.

§800
Some verbs in the present appear in classical Greek in the active voice only, as bai/nw go, e(/rpw creep, tre/w tremble; others in the middle only, as a(/llomai leap, bou/lomai wish, ka/qhmai sit, kei=mai lie.

§801
Outside of the present some active verbs show middle forms especially in the future, as bh/somai shall go, a)kou/somai shall hear (805); and some verbs exclusively or chiefly deponent show active forms especially in the perfect, as gi/gnomai become ge/gona, mai/nomai rage me/mhna, de/rkomai poet., 2 aor. e)/drakon, perf. d<*>dorka.

§802
For the passive voice the middle forms sufficed in most cases; many middle futures are still used passively (807, as a)dikh/so- mai shall be wronged; and traces of the passive use of the aorist middle appear in Hom., as e)/blhto was hit. This use was largely abandoned when -hn and -qhn came to be used as special marks of the passive. Originally neither -hn nor -qhn was passive in meaning.

§802 D
Hom. has e)kta/mhn was killed, e)sxo/mhn was stayed. Cp. also h)|desa/mhn and ai)/desqen (ai)de/omai respect), o)i(_sato and w)i/sqhn (oi)/omai think), e)xolwsa/mhn and e)xolw/qhn (xolo/w enrage).

§803
The second aorist in -hn is primarily intransitive and shows active inflection (as e)/sthn stood). Many so-called passive forms are in fact merely intransitive aorists of active verbs, as e)rru/hn from r(e/w flow, katekli/nhn from katakli/_nw lie down, and do not differ in meaning from the aorists of deponent verbs, as e)ma/nhn from mai/nomai rage.

§804
The aorists in -qhn that are called passive are often active or middle in meaning, as h(/sqhn took pleasure in from h(/domai, h)|sxu/nqhn felt ashamed from ai)sxu/_nw disgrace, ai)sxu/_nomai am ashamed; w)rgi/sqhn became angry from o)rgi/zw anger.

## FORMS OF ONE VOICE IN THE SENSE OF ANOTHER

§805

Future Middle with Active Meaning.—Many verbs have no active future, but use instead the future middle in an active sense: lamba/nw take lh/yomai, gignw/skw know gnw/somai.
a. Most such verbs denote a physical action, as the action of the vocal organs; the action of the organs of sight, hearing, smell, touch; the action of throat, mouth, lips; bodily activity in general, voluntary or involuntary; and other aspects of the physical side of human organism.

Verbs denoting praise or blame usually have both an active and a middle future.

§810

Middle Deponents.—Deponent verbs whose aorists have an active or middle meaning with middle forms are called middle deponents. The aorist passive of such verbs, when it occurs, has a passive force. Thus ai)tia/omai accuse, h)|tia_sa/mhn accused, h)|tia/_qhn was accused. Others 813 c.

§811

Passive Deponents.—Deponent verbs whose aorists have the passive form but the active or middle meaning are called passive deponents; as bou/lomai wish, aor. e)boulh/qhn. The future is usually middle in form. Most passive deponents express mental action of some sort.

§813

Deponents with Passive Meaning.—Some deponent verbs have a passive meaning. This is avoided by good writers in the present and imperfect or future passive, is not frequent in the aorist, but is common in the perfect and pluperfect passive. Thus a)pekri/netai (a)pekri/qh) tau=ta this answer is (was) made is not good Greek. Few verbs show the passive meaning in most of these tenses; as w)ne/omai buy, am bought, e)wnh/qhn was bought, e)w/nhmai have bought, have been bought.
a. Present and Imperfect: a)gwni/zomai contend, am contended for, bia/zomai force, am forced, lu_mai/nomai maltreat, am maltreated, w)ne/omai buy, am bought.
b. Future Passive: a)parne/omai deny, a)parnhqh/somai, e)rga/zomai work, do, e)rgasqh/somai.
c. Aorist Passive: These verbs (middle deponents, 810) have also an aorist middle; the aorist passive is used in a passive sense: a)gwni/zomai contend, ai)ki/zomai harass, ai)ni/ttomai speak darkly, ai)tia/omai accuse, a)ke/omai heal, bia/zomai force, de/xomai receive, dwre/omai present, e)rga/zomai work, do, h(ge/omai lead, qea/omai behold, i)_a/omai heal, kta/omai acquire, lu_mai/nomai maltreat, lwba/omai abuse, mi_me/omai imitate, o)lofu/_romai lament, profasi/zomai feign an excuse, xra/omai use, w)ne/omai buy. a)pokri/_nomai has a)pekri/_nato answered, a)pekri/qhn usu. means was separated.
d. Perfect and Pluperfect: These verbs use the perfect middle in the middle or the passive sense: a)gwni/zomai contend, ai)ni/ttomai speak darkly, ai)tia/omai accuse, a)pokri/_nomai answer, a)pologe/omai make a defence, bia/zomai force, e)nqu_me/omai consider, e)rga/zomai work, do, eu)/xomai pray, h(ge/omai lead, kta/omai acquire, lwba/omai abuse, mhxana/omai devise, mi_me/omai imitate, parrhsia/zomai speak boldly, poli_teu/omai act as (discharge the duties of) a citizen, pra_gmateu/omai am engaged in, ske/ptomai view, xra/omai use, w)ne/omai buy.

§814

Active Verbs with Aorist Passive in a Middle Sense.—The aorist passive of some active verbs has a reflexive or middle sense, either sometimes or always. Thus eu)frai/nw gladden, hu)fra/nqhn rejoiced, ki_ne/w move, e)ki_nh/qhn was moved or moved myself, fai/nw show, e)fa/nhn showed myself, appeared (e)fa/nqhn usually was shown).
a. These verbs are often called middle passives.
b. The middle and the passive form of the future of such verbs is often found, the middle being frequently preferred.

## Part III: Formation of Words

§822
Inflected words generally consist of two distinct parts: a stem and an inflectional ending (191):

dw=ro-ngift,stem dwro-,inflectional ending n;

lu/_o-menwe loose,stem li_o-,inflectional ending men.
a. The inflectional endings of nouns and verbs, and the formation of verbal stems, have been treated under Inflection. The formation of words, as discussed here, deals primarily with the formation of noun-stems, of verbal stems derived from nouns, and of compound words. Uninflected words (adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, and particles) are mostly of pronominal origin and obscure; such adverbs as show case forms are mentioned in 341 ff.

§823
Some stems are identical with roots (root-stems, 193) to which only an inflectional ending, or no ending at all, has been added.

bou=-s ox, cowmu=-s mouseu(=-s hog, sow

ei(=s one (stem e(n-）nau=-s shipflo/c flame (fle/g-w burn）

qh/r wild beast (gen. qhr-o/s）o)/y voice (stem o)p-）xei/r hand (gen. xeir-o/s）

klw/y thief (kle/p-t-w steal）pou/s foot (stem pod-）xqw/n earth (stem xqon-）

§824
Most stems are derived from roots by the addition of one or more formative suffixes.

dw=-ro-ngift,stem dwro-,root dw (di/-dw-mi give),suffix ro-.

gram-mat-eu/-sscribe,stem grammateu-,root graf,suffixes mat and eu.
a. Most words are therefore built up from root, suffix, and inflectional ending by a process of composition analogous to that seen in compounds (869 ff.), in which the union of the various elements yields an idea different from that seen in each of the parts.

§825
A stem is primary if only one suffix is added to the root (dw=-ro-n); secondary, when more than one suffix is added to the root (gram-mat-eu/-s).

§826
There are two kinds of stems: noun-stems (substantive and adjective) and verb-stems.

§827
Words containing a single stem are called simple words, as lo/go-s speech; words containing two or more stems are called compound words, as logo-gra/fo-s speech-writer.

§828
According to the character of the suffix words are called:
a. Primitive (or Primary): formed by the addition of a suffix either to a root or to a verb-stem to which a vowel, usually e, has been added (485, 486).
Root graf: gra/f-w write, graf-h/ writing, graf-eu/-s writer, gra/m-ma something written, gram-mh/ line.
Verb-stem gen-e in gene/-sqai become (e)geno/mhn, gi/-gn-omai): ge/ne-si-s genesis, origin; ter-e (te/rw bore): te/re-tro-n gimlet, instrument for boring.
b. Denominative (or Secondary): formed from a noun-stem (substantive or adjective) or adverb.
gram-mat-eu/s writer (stem grammat-, nom. gra/mma); eu)daimon-i/a_ happiness (stem eu)daimon-, nom. eu)dai/mwn); dikaio-su/nh justice, di/ka-io-s just (di/kh right); fi/l-io-s friendly (fi/lo-s dear); doulo/-w enslave (dou=lo-s slave); palai-o/-s ancient, of old date, from the adverb pa/lai long ago.

§829
Suffixes forming primitive words are called primary suffixes; suffixes forming denominative words are called secondary suffixes.
a. The distinction between primary and secondary suffixes is not original and is often neglected. Thus, in deino/s terrible (dei- fear), no is a primary suffix; in skoteino/s dark (sko/tos, 858. 11), it is secondary. So English -able is both primary (readable) and secondary (companionable).
b. It is often difficult to determine whether a suffix is added to a verb-stem or to a noun-stem: i)sxu_-ro/s strong (i)sxu/_-s strength, i)sxu/_-w am strong).
c. A primitive word may be formed from a verb-stem which is itself denominative: toceu-th/s bowman from toceu/-w shoot with the bow, derived from to/co-n bow. A primitive may be formed with a suffix derived from a denominative: fleg-uro/-s burning (fle/g-w burn) with uro from ligu-ro/-s (ligu/-s) shrill.
d. A denominative often has no corresponding primitive; sometimes the latter has been lost, sometimes it was presumed for the purpose of word-formation by the imitative process always at work in the making of language. Thus, de/m-n-io-n bed, from dem-no-n (de/m-w build, construct).

§830
To determine the root all suffixes must be removed from the stem until only that part remains which contains the fundamental idea.
a. Most roots are noun-roots or verb-roots; but originally a root was neither noun or verb (193). Some roots are pronominal, and express direction or position. Greek has many words whose roots cannot be discovered. The form of a root in Greek is not necessarily that which Comparative Grammar shows was common to the cognate languages.
b. Since the origin of many words, even with the help of the cognate languages, is uncertain, we are often at a loss where to make the dividing line between root and suffix. Suffixes are often preceded by a vowel which may be regarded as a part of the suffix or as an expansion of the root (by some scholars regarded as a part of the root itself).

§831

Changes of the root-vowel.—a. The root-vowel is sometimes strong, sometimes weak: ei, oi (weak i); eu, ou (weak u); h or w (weak a or e). lei=m-ma remnant, loip-o/-s remaining, cp. lei/p-w, e)/-lip-on; zeu=g-os team, cp. zeu/g-nu_-mi, zug-o/n yoke; spoud-h/ zeal, speu/d-w hasten; lh/q-h forgetfulness, lanqa/nw (laq-) forget; h)=q-os disposition, e)/q-os custom, habit; r(wx-mo/s cleft, r(h/g-nu_-mi break (r(ag-, r(hg-, r(wg-). Cp. 36.
b. e often varies with o, sometimes with a; h sometimes varies with w. go/n-o-s offspring, gi/-gn-omai (gen-); to/n-o-s tone, tei/nw (ten-) stretch; traf-ero/s well-fed, trof-h/ nourishment, tre/f-w nourish; a)rwg-o/-s helping, a)rh/g-w help. Cp. 36.

§832

Root-determinatives.—A consonant standing between root and suffix (or ending), and not modifying the meaning of the root, is called a root-determinative.
ba/-q-ro-n pedestal, from bai/nw go (ba-); e)/s-q-w (poetical for e)sqi/w) eat, for ed-q-w, cp. Ionic e)/d-w; plh/-q-w (poet.) am full, plh=-q-os crowd, plh-q-w/rh satiety, cp. pi/m-plh-mi; sta-q-mo/s day's journey, sta/-q-mh a rule, from i(/sthmi (sta-); smh/-x-w wipe, cp. sma/w wipe.—On the insertion of s, see 836.
a. The origin of root-determinatives is obscure. In part they may be relics of roots, in part due to the analogy of words containing the consonants in question.

§833

Suffixes.—A suffix is a formative element added to a root (or to a stem) and standing between the root and the ending. Suffixes limit or particularize the general meaning of the root; but only in a few cases is the distinct meaning of the suffix known to us.
a. The origin of the Greek suffixes is often obscure; of those inherited from the parent language only some were employed to make new words; others were formed by Greek itself (productive suffixes). From the analogy of the modern languages we infer that some suffixes were once independent words, which, on becoming a part of a compound, lost their signification. Thus -hood, -head in childhood, godhead are derived from Old Eng. ‘hād,’ Gothic ‘haidus’ character, nature; -ship in ownership, courtship, comes from a lost word meaning ‘shape’; -ly in friendly from Old Eng. ‘līc’ body. So -w/dhs meaning smelling (o)/zw), as in eu)w/dhs fragrant, acquired a range of meaning originally inappropriate to it by passing into the general idea of ‘full of,’ ‘like,’ as in poiw/dhs grassy (poi/a_), loimw/dhs pestilential (loimo/s), sfhkw/dhs wasp-like (sfh/c). This suffix is distinct from -eidh/s having the form of, like (898 a).
Conversely, many suffixes, themselves insignificant, acquired a definite meaning by reason of the root with which they were associated.—Irrespective of its meaning, one word may serve as a model for the creation of another word; as starvation, constellation, etc., are modelled on contemplation, etc.
b. Many dissyllabic suffixes, due to a combination of the final letter or letters of the stem and an original monosyllabic suffix, adapt themselves to independent use. Cp. ego-tism for ego-ism because of patriot-ism, -able in laughable and probable (from proba-bilis). Thus, patronymics in -a/dhs, -ia/dhs 845. 2, 3; words in -aina 843 b, 5; -ai=os 858. 2 a; -ei=on 851. 1; -e/steros 316; -e/ths 843 a, N.; -h/eis 858. 3; -h/i+os 858. 2 b; -ei=os 858. 2 a; -o/eis 858. 3; -i/dion 852. 2; -i/_ths 843 a, N., 844. 2 a; -simos 858. 9; -w/ths 843 a, N., 844. 2 a; and many others.
c. Simple suffixes are often added to case forms or adverbs, thus producing, by contamination, dissyllabic suffixes; as a)rxai=-o-s ancient 858. 2 a; palai-o/-s of old date 828 b, e)ari-no/-s vernal 858. 12; fusi-ko/-s natural 858. 6 b; cp. e)n-a/li-o-s marine (a(/ls).
d. Many compound suffixes are formed by the union of two suffixes, new stems being created by the addition of a suffix to a stem, as: thr-io 851. 2, isk-io 852. 6, isk-idio 854. See 854.
e. Suffixes often show gradations: thr, twr, ter, tr (36 N. 1) as in do-th/r, dw/-twr, do/teira (out of doter-i=a) giver; ya/l-tr-ia harp-player; mhn mn: li-mh/n harbour, li/-mn-h lake; mwr mar: te/k-mwr, te/k-mar goal; wr r: u(/d-wr water, u(/d-ra_ hydra; wn an: te/kt-wn carpenter, fem. te/ktaina, from tektan-i=a; and in le/wn lion, fem. le/aina (843 b. 5).

§834

Changes in stems.—Various changes occur when a suffix is added to a stem.
a. The final vowel of a stem is contracted with the initial vowel of a suffix: o)fi/_dion small snake (o)/fi- + idion from o)/fi-s). So when a consonant is dropped at the end of a stem: ai)do-i=o-s venerable (ai)dw/s reverence, stem ai)dos-), basile-i/a_ kingdom (basileu/-s king, stem basilev- for basileu=-. 43), a)ste-i=o-s refined (a)/stu city, stem a)stev- for a)steu=-, 43). Cp. 858. 2.
b. A long final vowel of a stem may be shortened before the initial vowel of a suffix: di/ka^-io-s just, di/kh right, stem dika_-. (Properly di/kai is an old case form, 833 c, to which -o-s is added.)
c. A final vowel or diphthong may be dropped before the initial vowel of a suffix: sof-i/a_ wisdom (sofo/-s wise), ti/_m-io-s honoured, costly (ti_mh/ honour, stem ti_ma_-), basil-iko/-s royal (basileu/-s king), poli_t-iko/-s civic (poli/_ths citizen, stem poli_ta_-).
d. The final letter or letters of a consonant stem may be dropped: swfro-su/nh temperance, moderation (sw/frwn temperate, stem swfron-), mel-u/drion little song (me/l-os song, meles-), a)lhq-ino/-s genuine (a)lhqh/s -e/s true). So apparently in the case of a vowel stem in despo/-sunos belonging to the master (despo/ths).
e. The final consonant of a stem undergoes regular euphonic change before the initial consonant of a suffix: ble/m-ma glance (ble/p-w look), dikas-th/s a judge (dikad-ths, from dika/zw judge, stem dikad-), pi/s-ti-s faith ( = piq-ti-s, from pei/q-w persuade, stem piq-), le/cis style ( = leg-si-s, from le/g-w speak).
f. Stems in o have an alternative in e (cp. i(/ppo-s, voc. i(/ppe; 229 b). This e often appears in denominatives: oi)ke/-w dwell, oi)ke/-ths house-servant, oi)ke-i=o-s domestic (oi)=ko-s house).
g. Derivatives of a_ stems may apparently show w in place of a_; as stratiw/-ths soldier (stratia/_ army), *)i_taliw/-ths an Italiote, Greek inhabitant of Italy (*)i_tali/a_ Italy). See 843 a, N. Stems in a_ have h in ti_mh/-eis honoured (ti_mh/, stem ti_ma_-).
h. Vowel stems, especially those derived from verbs, often lengthen a final short vowel before a suffix beginning with a consonant: poi/h-ma poem, poi/h-si-s poetry, poih-th/-s poet, poih-ti-ko/-s creative, poetical (poie/-w make); desmw/-th-s prisoner (desmo/-s, desma/ fetters). Verbs with stems in a, e, o usually show in derivatives the stem vowel as found in the tenses other than the present; as dhlo/-w manifest, fut. dhlw/-sw, dh/lw-si-s manifestation; a)ro/w plough, fut. a)ro/-sw, a)/ro-si-s arable land, a)ro-th/r ploughman; eu(r-i/sk-w find out, fut. eu(r-h/-sw, eu(/r-h-ma discovery, but eu(/r-e-sis discovery, eu(r-e-th/s discoverer.
i. Vowel stems sometimes insert a vowel before a suffix beginning with a consonant: poli-h/-th-s, Ionic for poli/_-th-s citizen, ptoli/-e-qro-n (poetic) city.
j. Consonant stems, and vowel stems not ending in o, often show o before a suffix in denominatives; a stem in -on is thus replaced by one in -o: swfrosu/nh temperance (sw/frwn temperate, swfron-); ai(mat-o/-eis bloody (ai(=ma, -atos blood) and ski-o/-eis shadowy (skia/_ shadow) by analogy to dolo/-eis wily, 858. 3. Cp. 873-875.

§835
Several substantives are formed by reduplication: a)g-wg-h/ training (a)/g-w lead), e)d-wd-h/ food (Ionic e)/d-w eat), gi/-ga_s, -antos giant. Some, by metathesis (128 a): tmh=-si-s cutting (te/m-n-w cut).

§836

Insertion of sigma.—Between root (or stem) and suffix s is often found, and in some cases it has become attached to the suffix. This parasitic letter spread from the perfect middle, where it is properly in place only in stems in t, d, q, or s; as in sxi-s-mo/-s cleaving with s from e)/-sxi-s-mai by analogy to e)/-sxis-tai for e)-sxid-tai (sxi/zw cleave). In -s-ths the transference was made easier by words like sxis-to/s cloven for sxid-tos. This s appears before many suffixes, and usually where the perfect middle has acquired it (489).
ma: spa/-s-ma spasm (spa/w rend, e)/spasmai), ke/leu-s-ma command (keleu/-w command, keke/leusmai), mi/a-s-ma stain (miai/nw stain, memi/asmai).—mo: spa-s-mo/s = spa/-s-ma, keleu-s-mo/s command.—mh: du/-s-mh setting (du/_w set).—ths: keleus-th/s signal-man, o)rxh-s-th/s dancer (o)rx-e/-omai dance), duna/-s-ths lord (du/na-mai am able). Also in dra-s-th/rios efficacious (dra/-w do), o)rxh/-s-tra_ dancing-place, plh-s-mo/nh fulness. -s-m has displaced dm, -q-m (832) in o)smh/ odour (earlier o)dmh/), r(u-s-mo/s (and r(u-q-mo/s) rhythm.

§837

Insertion of tau.—In a few words t is inserted before the suffixes mo, ma, mh, mhn. Thus, e)f-e-t-mh/ command (e)fi/_hmi, root e(, h(), lai=-t-ma depth of the sea, a)u+-t-mh/ and a)u+-t-mh/n breath (a)/hmi blow). In e)ret-mo/-n oar the t may be part of the verb-stem (e)re/ssw, 515), and have spread thence to the other words.

## FORMATION OF SUBSTANTIVES

§838
Some suffixes have a special significance; of these the most important are given in 839-856. But suffixes commonly used with a special function (such as to denote agency, action, instrument, etc.) are not restricted to this function. Only a few have one function, as tero to denote comparison.
a. The instrument may be viewed as the agent, as in r(ai-s-th/r hammer, lit. smasher, from r(ai/-w smash. tro (863. 16) may express the agent, instrument, or place. Suffixes used to denote actions or abstract ideas often make concrete words, as trof-h/ nurture and nourishment, a)ggel-i/a_ message (cp. Eng. dwelling, clothing). porqmei=on means ferry, ferry-boat, ferryman's fee. Words originally denoting an agent have lost that meaning, as pa-th/r father (orig. protector), and in many cases the original force is changed.

§839

§840
NAMES OF ACTIONS AND ABSTRACT SUBSTANTIVES
a. Substantives denoting actions often express abstract idea and names of actions and verbal abstracts are often used co<*> cretely. The following suffixes (except mo, nominative -mo/-s, an es, nominative -os) form feminines; all are primary except ia_ i<*> some words.
1. ti (nom. -ti-s): pi/s-ti-s faith (pei/q-w persuade, piq-), fa/-ti-s rumour (fh<*> say, fa-).
2. si (nom. -si-s): le/cis style (le/g-w speak), poi/h-si-s poetry (poie/-w make) fqi/-si-s decay (fqi/-n-w decay), do/-si-s act of giving or gift (di/-dw-mi giv<*> do-, dw-), qe/-si-s placing (ti/-qh-mi place, qe-, qh-), ta/-si-s tension (fo<*> tṇ-si-s 35 b, from tei/nw stretch, ten-). si is derived from ti after vowel (115).
3. sia_ (nom. -si/a_): in substantives from verbs in -azw out of -ad-i=w; a<*> dokimasi/a_ examination (dokima/zw examine, dok mad-).
4. tu (nom. -tu/_-s 863 a. 17): rare, poetic and dialectic, e)d-h-tu/_s eating (poet<*> e)/d-w eat), boh-tu/_-s shouting (boa/-w shout).
5. mo (nom. -mo/-s, masc.): diwg-mo/-s pursuit (diw/k-w pursue), ptar-mo/-s sneez<*> ing (pta/r-nu-mai sneeze). On q-mo see 832, s-mo 836, t-mo 837. Cp 861. 1.
6. ma_ (nom. -mh): gnw/-mh knowledge (gi-gnw/-skw know), fh/-mh report, omen (fh-mi/ say), ti_-mh/ honour (poet. ti/_-w honour), mnh/-mh memory (mi-mnh/|-skw remind). See also 861. 1.
7. ma_ (nom. -ma^): to/l-ma daring (tlh=-nai dare).
8. es (nom. -os, neut.): de/-os fear, r(i=g-os cold.
9. ia_ (nom. -i/a_): primitive, from verb-stems, as man-i/a_ madness (mai/nomai rage, man-). Denominative: h(gemon-i/a_ sovereignty (h(gemw/n leader), eu)ergesi/a kind service (eu)erget-ia from eu)erge/ths doer of good deeds). Without any noun-stem: poliorki/a_ siege (poliorke/w besiege). Verbs in -euw derived from substantives, as paideu/-w educate (pai=s child), show abstracts in -ei/a_ for e（u=）-ia_ (43): paidei/a_ education, stratei/a_ campaign (strateu/omai take the field), basilei/a_ reign, kingdom (basileu/-w am king).
10. o, a: see 859. 1, 2.
b. Many feminine substantives expressing the abstract notion of the adjective are derived from adjective stems (a few from substantive or verb stems). Many of these denominatives express quality, cp. Eng. -ness, -hood.
1. ia_ (nom. -ia^): from adjectives in -hs and -oos, -ous, as a)lh/qeia truth for a)lhqes-ia from a)lhqh/s true; e)/ndeia want for e)nde（e）s-ia from e)ndeh/s needy, 44 a, 292 d; eu)/noia kindness for eu)no（o）-ia from eu)noo-s eu)/nous kind.
2. ia_ (nom. -i/a_): eu)daimon-i/a_ happiness (eu)dai/mwn happy), summaxi/a_ alliance (su/mmaxos fighting along with), sof-i/a_ wisdom (sofo/-s wise). Since t becomes s before ia_ we have a)qanasi/a_ immortality (a)qa/nato-s immortal). Cp. 859. 6.
3. suna_ (nom. -su/nh): dikaio-su/nh justice (di/kaio-s just). Abstracts in -sunh are properly fem. of adj. in -sunos, as ghqo-su/nh joy (ghqo/-sunos joyful). -osu/nh by analogy in mant-osu/nh art of divination (ma/nti-s seer). See 865. 7.
4. tht (nom. -ths): filo/-ths, -thtos friendship (fi/lo-s friend), i)so/-ths, -thtos equality (i)/so-s equal), neo/-ths youth (ne/o-s young), paxu/-ths thickness (paxu/-s thick).
5. ad (nom. -a/s): abstract substantives of number, as tri-a/s, -a/dos triad (trei=s). mon-a/s, -a/dos unit (mo/no-s alone, single). See also 863 b. 8.
c. Some neuter abstracts express quality: ta/x-os speed (tax-u/-s swift), eu)=r-os width (eu)r-u/-s broad). See 840 a. 8.
d. A feminine adjective is used substantively in poet. pinuth/ wisdom from pinuto/-s wise; with recessive accent in e)/xqra_ enmity from e)xqro/-s hostile, qe/rmh warmth from qermo/-s warm.
e. Some compound adjectives in -h/s yield (by analogy) abstracts in -ia_ not in -eia^; as a)tuxi/a_ misfortune from a)-tux-h/s unfortunate. Fluctuation often occurs, as in kakoh/qeia kakohqi/a_ malignity from kako-h/qhs ill-disposed; Old Attic a)lhqei/a_ ( = Ion. a)lhqei/h) for a)lh/qeia.

§841
RESULT OF ACTION
The result or effect of an action is expressed by the primary suffixes
1. es (nom. -os, neut.): ge/n-os race, family, stem gen-es- (gi/-gn-omai am born, e)-gen-o/mhn, gen-), te/k-os child, stem tek-es- (ti/ktw bring forth, tek-), yeu=d-os lie, stem yeud-es- (yeu/d-w deceive).
2. mat (nom. -ma, neut.): gra/m-ma thing written (gra/f-w write), no/h-ma thought (noe/w think), poi/h-ma poem (poie/-w make), de/r-ma hide (de/r-w flay), tmh=-ma section (te/m-nw cut, tem-, tmh-, 128 a).

§842

The instrument or means of an action is expressed by the primary suffixes
1. tro (nom. -tro-n, neut.): a)/ro-tro-n plough (a)ro/-w plough), lu/-tro-n ransom (lu/_-w release, lu_^-), sei=-s-tro-n rattle (sei/-w shake, 624 a), di/-dak-tro-n teacher's pay (dida/skw teach, didax-), lou-tro/-n bath (bathing-water; lou/-w wash).
2. q-ro (nom. -qro-n, neut.): klei=-qro-n bar for closing a door (klei/-w shut, 832).
3. tra_ (nom. -tra_, fem.): ma/k-tra_ kneading-trough (ma/ttw knead, mag-), r(h/-tra_ compact (e)re/w e)rw= shall say, e)r-, r(e-), xu/-tra_ pot (xe/w pour, xu-).
4. thr-io- (nom. -thr-io-n, neut.): in a few words, as po-th/r-io-n cup (pi/_nw drink, po- 529); qelk-th/r-io-n spell, charm (qe/lg-w charm). See 858. 14.
