§843
THE PERSON CONCERNED
a. The person concerned or occupied with anything is denoted by a denominative formed by one of the following secondary suffixes:
1. eu (nom. -eu/-s, masc.): gram-mat-eu/-s secretary (gra/mma, -atos anything written), i(er-eu/-s priest (i(ero/-s sacred), i(pp-eu/-s horseman (i(/ppo-s horse), xalkeu/-s coppersmith (xalko/-s copper).
2. ta_ (nom. -th-s, masc.): nau/-th-s sailor (nau=-s ship), toco/-ths bowman (to/co-n bow), oi)ke/-ths house-servant (oi)=ko-s house, 834 f), desmw/-th-s prisoner (834 h).
N.—By analogy are formed: eu)n-e/th-s bed-fellow (eu)nh/ bed), following oi)ke/th-s; o(pl-i/_th-s heavy-armed soldier (o(/plo-n, o(/pla armour) following poli/_-th-s from older po/li_-s; strati-w/th-s soldier (stratia/_ army) following desmw/-th-s. See 834 g.
b. The following secondary suffixes form feminine substantives:
1. ia_ (nom. -ia^): corresponding to masculines in -eu/-s, as i(e/reia priestess for i(er-eu=-ia (i(er-eu/-s priest), basi/leia queen (basil-eu/-s king). See -aina below.
2. id (nom. -i/s): farmak-i/s sorceress (fa/rmako-n charm, poison, farmak-eu/-s sorcerer), kaphl-i/s female huckster (kaphlo/-s huckster), fulak-i/s female guard (fu/lac).
3. tid (nom. -tis): corresponding to masculines in -th-s: oi)ke/-tis house-maid (oi)ke/-ths), poli=-tis female citizen (poli/_-ths).
4. itta_, issa_ (nom. -itta, -issa): from i=a added to stems in t or k (112, 114), as qh=tta female serf from qht-i=a (qh/s, qht-o/s serf), *ki/lissa Cilician woman from *kilik-i=a (*ki/lic Cilician); later, by analogy, basi/lissa queen.
5. aina_ (nom. -aina) corresponding to masculines in -wn: le/-aina lioness (le/-wn lion), qera/p-aina handmaid (qera/p-wn attendant), *la/k-aina woman of Laconia (*la/k-wn a Laconian). By analogy, in o stems: lu/k-aina she-wolf (lu/ko-s). -aina stands for -an-i=a, -an being a weak form of -wn (833 e, 35 b).
N.—Names of dealers in anything usually end in -pw/lhs, -ou; fem. -pwlis, -idos (pwle/w sell), as biblio-pw/lhs bookseller (bibli/o-n book), si_to-pw/lhs graindealer (si=to-s grain), a)rto/-pwlis bread-woman (a)/rto-s bread). Cp. also kaphli/s under id.

§844
GENTILES OR PLACE NAMES
Gentiles are denominative nouns denoting belonging to or coming from a particular country, nation, or city. Gentiles are formed from proper nouns by secondary suffixes.
1. eu (nom. -eu/s, gen. -e/ws, masc.), id (nom. -i/s, gen. i/d-os, fem.):
*plataieu/s -e/ws, *plataii+/s -i/dos a Plataean (h( *pla/taia); *)eretrieu/s an Eretrian (h( *)ere/tria); *megareu/s, *megari/s a Megarian (ta\ *me/gara); *ai)oleu/s Aeolian (*ai)/olos, mythical ancestor of the Aeolians).
a. -i/s (-i/dos) may denote a land or a dialect: h( *dwri/s (gh=) Doris; h( *ai)oli/s (glw=tta) the Aeolic dialect.
2. ta_ (nom. -th-s, masc.), tid (nom. -tis, fem.): *tegea/_-ths, *tegea=-tis of Tegea (h( *tege/a_); *spart-ia/_-ths, *spart-ia=-tis of Sparta (h( *spa/rta_); *ai)gi_nh/-ths, *ai)gi_nh=-tis of Aegina (h( *ai)/gi_na); *subar-i/_-ths, *subar-i=-tis Sybarite (h( *su/baris); *sikeli-w/-ths, *sikeli-w=-tis Siciliote (h( *sikeli/a_).
a. The endings -i_ths, -wths are due to analogy; see 843 a. N.
3. Other gentiles, properly adjectives, end in -ios, -ia_, as *)aqhnai=o-s, -ai/a_ of Athens (ai( *)aqh=nai), *mi_lh/s-io-s for *mi_lht-io-s of Miletus (*mi/_lhtos), *)opou/ntio-s of Opus (*)opou=s); (i）ko/s, (i）ka/_, as *)iwn-iko/s Ionic (*)/iwn-es Ionians); no/-s, nh/ preceded by a_（h), i_, as *sardi-a_no/-s of Sardis (*sa/rdeis), *lamyak-hno/-s of Lampsacus (*la/myakos), *buzant-i=no-s Byzantine (*buza/ntion). See 863 b. 12.

§845
PATRONYMICS
Patronymics, or denominative proper names denoting descent from a father or ancestor, are formed from proper names of persons by means of the following suffixes:
1. da_ (nom. -dh-s, masc.), d (nom. -s, fem.):

*borea^/-dh-sson of Boreasfem. *borea^/-s, -dosfrom *bore/a_-s
Stems in a_ shorten a_ to a; from such forms arose
2. ada_ (nom. -a/dh-s, masc.), ad (nom. -a/s, fem.):

*qesti-a/dh-sson of Thestiusfem. *qesti-a/s, -a/dosfrom *qe/stio-s
From this type arose a new formation:
3. iada_ (nom. -ia/dh-s, masc.), iad (nom. -ia/s, fem.):

*ferht-ia/dh-sson of Pheresfem. *ferht-ia/s, -ia/d-osfrom *fe/rhs (-htos）

*persh-i+a/dh-sson of Perseus(fem. *persh-i+/s, -i/d-os）from *perseu/-s

*telamwn-ia/dh-sson of Telamonfrom *telamw/n (-w=nos）
4. ida_ (nom. -i/dh-s, masc.), :id (nom. -i/s, fem.):

*tantal-i/dh-sson of Tantalusfem. *tantal-i/s, -i/d-osfrom *ta/ntalo-s

*kekrop-i/dh-sson of Cecropsfem. *kekrop-i/s, -i/d-osfrom *ke/kroy (-opos）

*oi)ne-i/dh-sson of Oeneusfem. *oi)nh-i+/s, -i/d-osfrom *oi)neu/-s

*lhto-i+/dh-sson of Letofem. *lhtw-i+/s, -i/d-osfrom *lhtw/ (279）
Stems in o drop o; stems in eu (hu) drop u; stems in oi (wi) drop i.
5. i_on or i^wn (poetic and rare; nom. -i/_wn, masc.):
*kron-i/_wn son of Cronus (also *kron-i/dh-s), gen. *kron-i/_on-os or *kron-i^/wn-os according to the metre, from *kro/no-s.
6. iwna_ or i_na_ (poetic and rare; nom. -iw/nh or i/_nh, fem.):

*)akris-iw/nh daughter of *)akri/sio-s*)adrhst-i/_nh daughter of *)/adrhsto-s

§846
Variations occur especially in poetry: a. Hom. *phle-i/dh-s, *phle-i+/dh-s, *phlh-i+a/dh-s, and *phle-i+/wn, son of *phleu/-s; *)atre-i/dh-s, *)atre-i+/dh-s, and *)atre-i+/wn, son of *)atreu/-s.
b. Two patronymic endings: *tala-i+_on-i/dh-s son of *talao/-s.
c. The stem drops or adds a syllable: *deukal-i/dh-s son of *deukali/wn, -i/wn-os; *lamp-et-i/dh-s son of *la/mpo-s.
d. -idhs is used in comic formations: klept-i/dh-s son of a thief.
e. -nda_s occurs in the dialects, as *)epameinw/nda_-s Epaminondas.
f. -ios, -eios, may indicate descent, as *telamw/nie pai= oh son of Telamon, *tundarei/a_ quga/thr daughter of Tyndareus; cp. Tennyson's “Niobean daughter.”

§847
A patronymic may include the father, as *peisistrat i/dai the Peisistratidae (Peisistratus and his sons).

§848
Most genuine patronymics are poetical and belong to the older language. In the classical period patrony mics rarely indicate descent in the case of historical persons; as *eu)ri_pi/dhs, *)aristei/dhs.

§849
Metronymics denote descent from the mother, as *da_na-i+/dh-s son of *da^na/h, *fi_lur-i/dh-s son of *fi^lu/ra_.

§850
Relationship is sometimes denoted by the suffixes ideo (nom. -idou=-s son of) and idea_ (nom. -idh= daughter of); as a)delf-idou=-s nephew, a)delf-idh= niece (a)delfo/-s brother).

## PLACE

§851
Place may be expressed by the secondary suffixes
1. io (nom. -io-n, neut.): *dionu/_sion (scil. i(ero/n) temple of Dionysus, *(/hraion Heraeum.
Also -e-io (nom. -ei=o-n, neut.): from substantives in -eu/-s and by extension in others; as xalke-i=o-n forge (xalk-eu/-s coppersmith), *qhse-i=on Thesēum (*qhseu/-s), log-ei=o-n place for speaking (lo/go-s speech), mous-ei=o-n seat of the Muses (mou=sa muse), *)olumpi-ei=o-n Olympiēum (*)olu/mpio-s Olympian Zeus).
2. thr-io (nom. -th/r-io-n, neut.): derived from substantives in -th/r (or -th/s); as a)kroa_th/r-io-n auditorium (a)kroa_th/r or a)kroa_th/s hearer), e)rgasth/r-io-n workshop (e)rgasth/r workman), bouleuth/rion senate house (bouleuth/r or bouleuth/s councillor, senator). See 863 a. 8.
3. wn (nom. -w/n, gen. -w=n-os, masc.): a)ndr-w/n apartment for men (a)nh/r, a)ndr-o/s man), i(pp-w/n stable (i(/ppo-s horse), parqen-w/n maiden's apartment, Parthenon, temple of Pallas (parqe/no-s maiden), oi)n-w/n wine-cellar (oi)=no-s wine), a)mpel-w/n vineyard (a)/mpelo-s vine). Forms in -ew/n occur, as perister-ew/n dove-cote (peristera/_ dove), oi)new/n.
4. i_tid (nom. -i=tis, fem.): added to wn, a)ndrwn-i=tis apartment for men, gunaikwni=tis apartment for women.
5. wnia_ (nom. -wnia/_, fem.): r(od-wnia/_ rose-bed (r(o/do-n rose).
6. tra_ (rare; nom. -tra_, fem.): o)rxh/-s-tra_ dancing-place (o)rxe/-omai dance), palai/-s-tra_ wrestling-ground (palai/-w wrestle). Cp. 836.

## DIMINUTIVES

§852
Diminutives are denominatives formed from the stems of substantives by various secondary suffixes.
1. io (nom. -io-n, neut.): paid-i/o-n little child (pai=s, paid-o/s), o)rni/_q-io-n small bird (o)/rni_s, o)/rni_qos), a)spi/d-io-n small shield (a)spi/s, a)spi/d-os).
N.—Trisyllabic words are paroxytone if the first syllable is long by nature or position.
2. id-io (nom. -i/dio-n, neut.): derived from such words as a)spi/d-io-n; as cif-i/dio-n dagger (ci/fos sword, stem cifes-), bo-i/dio-n small cow (bou=-s), oi)ki/_dio-n small house, oi)ki + idion (oi)ki/a_), i)xqu/_dio-n small fish (i)xqu/_s). See 833 b.
3. ar-io (nom. -a/rion, neut.): paid-a/rio-n little child.
4. ud-rio (nom. -u/drion, neut.): mel-u/drio-n little song (me/los).
5. ullio (nom. -u/llion, neut.): e)p-u/llio-n little epic or cersicle (e)/pos).
6. isko, iska_ (nom. -i/skos, masc., -i/skh, fem.): a)nqrwp-i/sko-s manikin, paid-i/sko-s young boy, paid-i/skh young girl. From this comes -isk-io in a)spid-i/skio-n small shield.

§853
Many other diminutives occur, as akna_: in piqa/knh wine-jar (pi/qos); id, i_d: in a(maci/s, -i/dos small wagon (a(/maca), nhsi/_s, -i=dos islet (nh=so-s); id-eu: of the young of animals, as luk-ideu/s wolf's whelp (lu/ko-s), also u(i+deu/s son's son, grandson (ui(o/s); ixo: o)rta/lixos young bird (o)rtali/s) chick; ixna_: kuli/xnh (and kuli/xnion, kulixni/s) small cup (ku/lic). Rare or late are -a_ki/dion, -a/_sion, -a/fion, -ida/rion, -iska/rion, ion, 861. 19, -u/los, and over 25 others. See lo, 860. 1.

§854
Diminutives are often combined: paid-isk-a/rion stripling, meira/k-ion, meirak-i/skos, meirak-u/ll-ion, meirak-ull-i/dion stripling (mei=rac lass), xlan-isk-i/dion cloaklet (xlani/s), zw|da/rion insect (zw=|on animal).

§855
Some words, especially such as denote parts of the body, are diminutive in form, but not in meaning; as kra_ni/on skull, qhri/on beast ( = qh/r), pedi/on plain (pe/don ground), all in Homer, who has no diminutives. Diminutives often employed tend to lose their diminutive value.

§856
Diminutives may express affection, familiarity, daintiness, and sometimes pity or contempt (cp. dar-ling, lord-ling). See the examples under 852, and also patr-i/dion daddy (path/r), a)delf-i/dio-n dear little brother, *swkrat-i/dion dear Socky, a)nqrw/p-ion manikin. Some endings often have an ironical force, as plou/t-a_c rich churl, ga/str-wn fat-belly.

## FORMATION OF ADJECTIVES

§857
Adjectives are formed by the same suffixes as are used in substantives, the same formation producing in one case a substantive, in another an adjective. Many words formed with certain suffixes (io, mo, no, ro, to) are used as adjectives or as abstract substantives (usually feminine or neuter). Thus fili/a_ friendly or friendship; so ste/f-ano-s crown (ste/f-w encircle) was originally an adjective. Many suffixes have no characteristic signification.
Adjectives are either primitive (from roots or verb-stems) or denominative (from substantives or other adjectives). But this distinction is often obliterated and difficult to determine.

§858
The following are the chief adjectival suffixes:
1. o, a_ (nom. -o-s, -h or -a_, -o-n): primary: loip-o/-s remaining (lei/p-w leave, lip-, leip-, loip-), leuk-o/-s bright (leu/ssw shine, leuk-i=w).
2. io, ia_: a common suffix expressing that which pertains or belongs in any way to a person or thing. By union with a preceding stem vowel we have aio, eio, oio, w|o, uio.
Primary (rare): a(/g-io-s sacred (a(/gos expiation); with a comparative force: a)/llos other (a)l-i=o-s alius), me/sos middle (meq-i=o-s medius, 113).
Secondary in ti/_m-io-s worthy, costly (ti_mh/ honour); fi/l-io-s friendly (fi/lo-s dear); o)/rq-io-s steep (o)rqo/-s straight); plou/s-io-s rich (plou=to-s riches, 115); di/ka-io-s just (di/k-h right, 834 b); oi)ke-i=o-s domestic (oi)=ko-s house, 834 f); pa/tr-io-s hereditary (path/r father, patr-, 262); basi/leio-s royal (basileu/-s king); qe/re-io-s of summer (qe/ros, stem qeres-); ai)do-i=o-s venerable (ai)dw/s shame, stem ai)dos-, 266); h(rw=|os heroic (h(/rws hero, h(rwv-, 267); ph/xu-io-s a cubit long (ph=xu-s, 268). The feminines are often abstract substantives, as fil-i/a_ friendship.
a. The ending -ai=os has been transferred from a_ stems, as in xers-ai=o-s of or from dry land (xe/rs-os). The form i-ai=os occurs: draxm-iai=o-s worth a drachma (draxmh/). -ei=os has become independent in a)ndr-ei=os manly (a)nh/r). On gentiles in -ios, see 844. 3.
b. Ionic h-i+o (nom. -hi+os), properly from stems in eu (hu), as Hom. xalkh/-i+o-s brazen (pertaining to a xalkeu/-s brazier; Attic xa/lkeos, -ou=s, see 858. 4), basilh/-i+o-s royal; and transferred in Ionic to other stems, as in polemh/i+o-s warlike, a)nqrwp-h/i+o-s human (Attic a)nqrw/peio-s), a)ndr-h/i+o-s manly.
3. ent for vent (nom. -eis) forms denominative adjectives denoting fulness or abundance (mostly poetic).
ti_mh/-eis (ti_mh=s) honoured, and by analogy dendr-h/eis woody (de/ndro-n tree); xari/-eis graceful (xa/ri-s), dolo/-eis wily (do/lo-s), and by analogy ai(mat-o/-eis bloody (ai(=ma, -at-os blood, 834 j), i)xqu-o/-eis full of fish, kru-o/-eis chilling (kru/-os chill). Also in eu)rw/-eis mouldy (eu)rw/s, -w=tos).
4. eo (nom. -eo-s, -ou=s, 290) forms denominative adjectives denoting material: xru/_seos, xru_sou=s golden (xru_so/-s gold).
a. eo is derived from e-i=o, seen in xru/_seios (poetic). Here e is part of the stem (834 f). On -hi+os see 858. 2 b.
5. es (nom. -h/s, -e/s): primitive: yeud-h/s false (yeu/d-w deceive), saf-h/s clear, prhn-h/s prone, u(gi-h/s healthy. Very common in compounds, as a)-sfal-h/s unharmed, secure (a)-priv. + sfal- in sfa/llw trip).
6. ko, ako, iko (nom. -kos, very common, cp. 864. 1): many denominatives formed by these suffixes denote relation, many others fitness or ability.
a. Denominatives: manti-ko/-s prophetic (ma/nti-s prophet); fusi-ko/-s natural (fu/si-s nature); qhlu-ko/-s feminine (qh=lu-s female); *da_rei-ko/-s Daric (*da_rei=o-s Darius).
b. From fusi-ko/ s, etc., iko was taken as an independent suffix in mous-iko/-s musical (mou=sa muse); barbar-iko/-s barbaric (ba/rbaro-s barbarian, foreigner); didaskal-iko/-s able to teach (dida/skalo-s teacher); maqhmatiko/-s fond of learning (ma/qhma, -matos thing learnt); *kerame-iko/-s Potters' quarter, Ceramīcus (kerameu/-s potter); basil-iko/-s royal (basileu/-s king); h(rw-i+ko/-s heroic, from h(/rw（v), -os hero; *)axai-iko/-s or *)axa_-iko/-s (38) Achaean (*)axaio/-s Achaean).
N.—a)rx-iko/-s able to rule (a)rx-h/), graf-iko/-s able to write or draw (graf-h/), need not be derived directly from the root.
c. *korinqi-ako/-s Corinthian (*kori/nq-io-s Corinthian); spondei-ako/-s consisting of spondees (spond-ei=o-s spondee).
d. t-iko/ represents iko/ added to the verbal in to/- (cp. also maqhmat-iko/-s). Thus, lek-tiko/-s suited to speaking (le/g-w speak); ai)sqh-tiko/-s capable of feeling (ai)sq-a/nomai feel); a)riqmh-tiko/-s skilled in numbering (a)riqme/w to number); pra_k-tiko/-s practical, able to do (pra/_ttw do); skeptiko/-s reflective (ske/p-t-omai look carefully, consider). Added to a noun-stem: nau-tiko/-s nautical (nau=-s ship).
7. lo (nom. -lo-s): primary (usually active) and secondary. Cp. 860. 1. Primary in dei-lo/-s cowardly (de/doi-ka fear, di-, dei-, doi-); streb-lo/-s twisted (stre/f-w turn); tuf-lo/-s blind (tu/_f-w raise a smoke); koi=los hollow ( = kov-ilo-s, Lat. cav-us); trox-alo/-s running (tre/x-w run); ei)/k-elo-s like (e)/oika am like, ei)k-); kamp-u/lo-s bent (ka/mp-t-w bend); feid-wlo/-s sparing (fei/d-omai spare). a)pat-h-lo/s deceitful (a)pa/th deceit, a)pata/-w deceive) may be a primitive or a denominative. Cp. 860. 1.
a-leo denoting quality in a(rp-ale/o-s attractive, ravishing (a(rpa/zw seize), qars-ale/o-s bold (qa/rs-os boldness).
8. mo (nom. -mo-s, 861. 1): primary: qer-mo/-s warm (qe/r-w warm); secondary in e(/bd-o-mo-s seventh.
9. i-mo, s-imo (nom. -imo-s, -simo-s): often denoting able to or fit to. Adjectives in imo are primitive or denominative, and are derived from i-stems; those in -simo are denominative and come mostly from stems in si + mo (as xrh/-si-mo-s useful, from xrh=-si-s use); but simo has thence been abstracted as an independent suffix.
do/k-imo-s approved (dok-e/-w seem good); ma/x-imo-s warlike (ma/xh battle); no/m-imo-s conformable to law (no/mo-s); e)|d-w/d-imo-s eatable (e)d-wd-h/ food, poet. e)/d-w eat); kau/si-mo-s combustible (ka/_w burn, kau=-si-s burn- ing); lu/si-mo-s able to loose (lu/-si-s loosing); i(ppa/-simo-s fit for riding (i(ppa/zomai ride); a(lw/-simo-s easy to take (a(li/skomai, e(a/_lwn).
10. mon (nom. -mwn, -mon): primary in mnh/-mwn mindful (mi-mnh/|-skomai remember), tlh/-mwn enduring, wretched (e)/-tlh-n endured). Cp. 861. 8.
11. no (nom. -no-s, 861. 11): primary (usually passive) and secondary (829 a). Sometimes denoting that which may, can, or must be done.
Primary in dei-no/-s fearful (de/-doi-ka fear, di-, dei-, doi-); sem-no/-s to be revered (se/b-omai revere); piq-ano/-s persuasive (pei/q-w persuade, piq-, peiq-, poiq-); pi/s-uno-s trusting (pei/q-w). Secondary in skotei-no/-s dark ( = skotes-no-s from sko/t-os darkness).
12. ino (nom. -ino-s, 861. 11): forms denominative adjectives of material, as li/q-ino-s of stone (li/qo-s), cu/l-ino-s wooden (cu/lo-n); to denote time, and derived from such forms as e)ari-no/-s vernal (e)/ar spring), as in h(mer-ino/-s by day (h(me/ra_), xqes-ino/-s of yesterday (xqe/s); other uses: a)nqrw/p-ino-s human (a)/nqrwpo-s man), a)lhq-ino/-s genuine (a)lhqh/s true).
ineo in la-i+/neo-s = la/-i+no-s stony (la=s stone). On -hnos, -i_nos in gentiles, see 844. 3.
13. ro, ra_ (nom. -ro/-s, -ra/_): primary, and secondary. Primary, in e)xq-ro/-s hated, hostile (e)/xq-w hate), lamp-ro/-s shining (la/mp-w shine), xala-ro/-s slack (xala/-w slacken). Secondary, in fobe-ro/-s fearful (fo/bo-s fear, fobo/e-, 834 f), krat-ero/-s mighty (kra/t-os might); primary or secondary in a)nia_-ro/-s grievous (a)ni/a_ grief, a)nia/-w grieve). See 860. 3.
14. thr-io (nom. -th/rio-s): in denominatives, derived from substantives in -thr (or -ths) by the suffix io; but the substantive is not always found.
sw-th/r-io-s preserving (sw-th/r saviour), whence the abstract swthri/a_ (858. 2) safety; qelk-th/r-io-s enchanting (qelk-th/r charmer, qe/lg-w enchant), whence qelkth/rion (842. 4), lu-th/r-io-s delivering (lu-th/r), o(rmhth/rion starting-place (o(rma/w, o(rmw=mai start).
15. u (nom. -u/-s, -ei=a, -u/): primitives are h(du/-s sweet (h(/d-omai am pleased), tax-u/-s swift (ta/x-os swiftness), baq-u/-s deep (ba/q-os depth). Cp. 859. 8.
16. wdes (nom. -w/dhs, -w=des): in primitives (rare), as prep-w/dhs proper (pre/p-w beseem); usually in denominatives denoting fulness or similarity: poi-w/dhs grassy (poi/a_), ai(mat-w/dhs looking like blood (ai(=ma). See 833 a.
17. Suffixes of Degree: i_on and isto (318) usually form primitives; tero and tato (313 ff.), denominatives. tero occurs also in po/-tero-s which of two? pro/-tero-s earlier, u(/s-tero-s later, e(ka/-tero-s each. On the suffix tero apparently without comparative force, see 1066, 1082 b. e)/n-tero-n is substantivized (bowel); from e)n in.
18. Suffixes of Participles and Verbal Adjectives (primary): active nt, ot, 301 a, c; middle and passive meno. Verbal adjectives denoting completion (usually passive) to; possibility and necessity to, teo (471-473).
On the formation of ADVERBS, see 341 ff.

## LIST OF NOUN SUFFIXES

The list includes the chief suffixes used in substantives and adjectives. Separation of a suffix from the root is often arbitrary and uncertain.

§859
VOWEL SUFFIXES
1. o: nom. -o-s masc., fem., -o-n neut. A common suffix in primitives denoting persons (usually male agents) or things (often abstracts).
a)rx-o/-s leader from a)/rx-w lead; zug-o/-n yoke from zeu/g-nu_-mi yoke (zug-, zeug-); lo/g-o-s speech from le/g-w speak; no/m-o-s custom, law from ne/m-w distribute; sto/l-o-s expedition from ste/llw (stel-) send; trof-o/-s (o(, h() nurse from tre/f-w nourish; fo/r-o-s tribute from fe/r-w bear, bring.
a. The roots of some words appear only in other languages: oi)=k-o-s house, Lat. vīc-u-s.
b. The suffix has the accent when the agent is denoted. e of the root varies with o (831 b).
2. a_: nom. -a_ or -h fem. A common suffix in primitives, usually to denote things, often abstracts (action).
a)rx-h/ beginning from a)/rx-w begin; loib-h/ pouring from lei/b-w pour; ma/x-h fight from ma/x-omai fight; spoud-h/ haste from speu/d-w hasten; ste/g-h roof from ste/g-w shelter; trof-h/ nourishment from tre/f-w nourish; tu/x-h chance from tugxa/nw happen (tux-); for-a/_ crop from fe/r-w bear; fug-h/ flight from feu/gw flee (fug-, feug-).
a. The roots of some words appear only in other languages: gun-h/ woman (Eng. queen).
b. Most substantives accent the suffix; but many accent the penult.
3. a_: nom. -a_s, -hs, in a few masculines, usually compounds: paido-tri/b-h-s trainer of boys in gymnastics (tri/_bw rub).
4. i^, i_: primary, in o)/f-i-s snake, poet. tro/x-i-s runner (tre/x-w run), po/l-i-s city (originally po/l-i_-s), h)/n-i_-s yearling. Many words with the i-suffix have taken on d or t; as e)lp-i/-s hope e)lpi/-d-os (e)/lp-omai hope), xa/r-i-s grace xa/ri-t-os (xai/rw rejoice, xar-).
5. io: in a few primitive verbal adjectives (a(/g-io-s 858. 2), but common in denominate adjectives (858. 2), rare in substantives: numf-i/o-s bridegroom (nu/mfh bride); in names of things more concrete than those ending in -ia_: martu/r-io-n a testimony (cp. martu/r-ia_ testimony); in gentiles (844. 3); in diminutives (852. 1), often in combination with other diminutive suffixes (ario, idio, ullio, etc. 852); often in combination with a final stem vowel (851. 1, 858. 2).
6. ia^, ia_: rarely primary, in fu/za flight (feu/g-w flee); in verbal abstracts: mani/a_ madness (840 a. 9); usually secondary in the fem. of adj. in -u/s: barei=a = bareu=-ia, pi/tta pitch (= pik-i=a, cp. Lat. pic-us), glw=tta tongue = glwx-ia (cp. glwx-i/_-s point, glw=x-es beards of corn), qh=tta serf (843 b. 4); in the nom. fem. of participles in nt, ot (lu/_ousa from lu_ont-i=a, leluku-i=a); in denominative abstracts expressing quality (840 b. 1, 2); in names of persons: tam-i/a_-s steward (te/m-n-w cut, e)/-tam-on), *ni_k-i/a_-s Nicias (ni/_kh victory).—Often in combination with other suffixes: aina 843 b. 5; -e-ia 840 a. 9; issa 843 b. 4; tria, teira_ 839 b. 2, 3.
7. *vo, *va_: primary, in o(/ros for o(/r（v）os boundary, ken（v）o/s empty, la_i（v）o/s left (Lat. laevus), kal（v）o/s beautiful; (probably) secondary in verbals in -te/os (lute/os that must be loosed) and in adj. in -ale/os (860. 1).
8. u (eu): primary, in adjectives (858. 15), in substantives: ge/n-u-s chin, ph=x-u-s fore-arm.—9. u_: primary, in feminines: i)sx-u/_-s strength, o)fr-u=-s eye-brow, ne/k-u_-s (Hom.) corpse, cf. ## DENOMINATIVE VERBS

The formation of primitive verbs (372) is treated in 496-529, 607-624, 722-743.

§866
Denominative verbs are formed from the stems of nouns (substantives or adjectives). Verbs lacking such a noun-stem are made on the model of the ordinary denominative verb. The principal terminations are as follows:
1. -aw: derived chiefly from words with a_ stems (a few from words of the second declension). Verbs in -aw denote to do, to be , or to have, that which is expressed by the stem.
ti_ma/-w honour (ti_mh/, stem ti_ma_-), a)_rista/-w breakfast (a)/_risto-n breakfast), tolma/-w dare (to/lma daring, stem tolma_-), koma/-w wear long hair (ko/mh hair). koima/-w, lull to sleep, has no primitive noun.
On -iaw and -aw denoting a desire or a bodily condition, see 868 b.
2. -ew: derived chiefly from o/e- stems (834 f), and thence extended to all kinds of stems. Verbs in -ew denote a condition or an activity, and are often intransitive.
oi)ke/-w dwell (oi)=ko-s house, oi)ko/e-), file/-w love (fi/lo-s dear, filo/e-), u(phrete/w serve (u(phre/ths servant, u(phreta_-), eu)tux-e/-w am fortunate (eu)tuxh/s fortunate, eu)tuxes-), mi_s-e/-w hate (mi=sos hate, mi_ses-), swfron-e/-w am temperate (sw/frwn), martur-e/-w bear witness (ma/rtus, -ur-os).
a. Some ew-verbs from es-stems have older forms in -ei/w (624 a).
3. -ow: chiefly derived from o-stems. Verbs in -ow are usually factitive, denoting to cause or to make.
dhlo/-w manifest, make clear (dh=lo-s), doulo/-w enslave (dou=lo-s), zhlo/-w emulate (zh=lo-s emulation), zhmio/-w punish (zhmi/a_ damage), masti_go/-w whip (ma/stic, -i_gos whip). a)ro/w plough has no primitive.
On the formation of the present stem of verbs in -aw, -ew, -ow, see 522.
4. -euw: derived from substantives from eu-stems (607) and thence extended to other stems. euw-verbs usually denote a condition, sometimes an activity.
basileu/-w am king, rule (basileu/-s), bouleu/-w counsel (boulh/), kindu_neu/-w venture, incur danger (ki/ndu_no-s), paideu/-w educate (pai=s boy, girl), qerapeu/-w attend (qera/pwn attendant).
5. -u_w (rare): from u-stems, as dakru/_-w weep (da/kru tear). Cp. 608.
6. -ozw, -izw: derived originally from stems in d or g (as e)lpi/zw hope = e)lpid-i=w, a(rpa/zw seize = a(rpag-iw), and thence widely extended to other stems (cp. 623 d, g). Such verbs denote action.
gumna/zw exercise (gumna/s, -a/d-os stripped, naked); a)nagka/zw compel (a)na/gkh necessity); a)ti_ma/zw dishonour (a)/ti_mos); bia/zomai use force (bi/a_ force); qauma/zw wonder (qau=ma); fronti/zw take care (fronti/s); u(bri/zw insult (u(/bri-s outrage); nomi/zw consider (no/mo-s custom, law); teixi/zw fortify (tei=x-os wall, stem teixes-); xari/zomai do a favour (xa/ris, -itos favour).
a. Verbs in -izw and -iazw derived from proper names express an adoption of language, manners, opinions, or politics:
e(llhni/zw speak Greek (*(/ellhn), bakxia/zw act like a bacchante (bakxia/s), lakwni/zw imitate Laconian manners (*la/kwn), mhdi/zw side with the Medes (*mh=dos).
b. Verbs in -ezw, -ozw, and -uzw are rare (pie/zw press, poet. despo/zw am lord, kokku/zw cry cuckoo).
7. -ainw: originally from stems in -an + [iglide]w (518), but usually extended to other stems. See 620, III.
melai/nw blacken (me/la_s black, melan-), eu)frai/nw gladden (eu)/frwn glad, eu)fron-), shmai/nw signify (sh=ma, sh/mat-os sign), xalepai/nw am angry (xalepo/-s hard, angry).
8. -u_nw: from stems in un + i=w (519). The primitive words often show stems in u. See 620, III.
baqu/_nw deepen (baqu/-s deep), taxu/_nw hasten (taxu/-s swift), ai)sxu/_nw disgrace (ai)=sx-os shame), qarru/_nw encourage (qa/rr-os courage).
9. On other denominatives in lw, nw, rw, see 620, III; on inceptives see 526-528.
10. Parallel formations are frequent, often with different meanings.
a)_rista/w take a midday meal, a)_risti/zw give a midday meal; a)tima/w, (poet.) a)ti_mo/w, a)ti_ma/zw dishonour; doulo/w enslave, douleu/w am a slave; eu)daimone/w am happy, eu)daimoni/zw account happy, congratulate; qarre/w am courageous, qarru/_nw encourage; o(rko/w, o(rki/zw make one swear an oath; o(rma/w urge on, o(rmai/nw (poet.) ponder; o(rme/w lie at anchor, o(rmi/zw anchor trans. (o(/rmos anchorage); poleme/w (polemi/zw Epic) wage war, polemo/w make hostile; skhna/w put in shelter, mid. take up one's abode, skhne/w am in camp, skhno/w encamp, go into quarters; swfrone/w am temperate, swfroni/zw chasten; turanne/w, turanneu/w am absolute ruler, turanni/zw take the part of absolute ruler, turannia/w (late) smack of tyranny. Cp. 531.

§867

Frequentatives and Intensives.—These are mostly poetical. -aw in strwfa/w turn constantly (stre/fw turn), trwxa/w gallop (tre/xw run), pota/omai, pwta/omai, and pote/omai, fly about (pe/tomai fly). -strew in e)lastre/w drive (e)la/w, e)lau/nw). -taw in skirta/w spring (skai/rw skip). -tazw in e(lkusta/zw drag about (e(/lkw drag). With reduplication, often with change of the stem-vowel, in poipnu/w puff (pne/w breathe, pnu-), porfu/_rw gleam darkly (fu/_rw mix), pamfai/nw shine brightly (fai/nw bring to light, make appear).

§868
Desideratives express desire. Such verbs end in -seiw, -iaw, and rarely in -aw. Thus, polemhsei/w desire to wage war (poleme/w), a)pallacei/w wish to get rid of (a)lla/ttw exchange), gelasei/w wish to laugh (gela/w); strathgia/w wish to be general (strathgo/s); fona/w wish to shed blood (fo/nos murder).
a. Verbs in -iaw and -aw are formed from substantives. Those in -seiw may come from the future stem.
b. -iaw and -aw may denote a bodily affection: o)fqalmia/w suffer from ophthalmia (o)fqalmi/a_), bragxa/w am hoarse (bragxo/s hoarse). Some verbs in -wttw (-wssw) have a similar meaning: tuflw/ttw am blind (tuflo/s), and even li_mw/ssw am hungry (li_mo/s hunger).

## COMPOUND WORDS

§869
A compound word is formed by the union of two or more parts; as logo-gra/fo-s speech-writer, di-e/c-odo-s outlet (lit. way out through).
a. Compounds of three or more parts usually fall into two separate units; as batraxo-mu_o-maxi/a_ battle of the frogs-and-mice. Such compounds are common in comedy; as streyo-diko-pan-ourgi/a_ rascally perversion of justice.
b. In a compound word two or more members are united under one accent; as in bláckberry contrasted with black berry. Most compounds in Greek, an inflected language, are genuine compounds, not mere word-groups such as are common in English, which is for the most part devoid of inflections.
c. Every compound contains a defining part and a defined part. The defining part usually precedes: eu)-tuxh/s fortunate, as opposed to dus-tuxh/s unfortunate. The parts of a compound stand in various syntactical relations to each other, as that of adjective or attributive genitive to a substantive, or that of adverb or object to a verb, etc. Compounds may thus be regarded as abbreviated forms of syntax. Cp. 895 a, 897 N. 1.

## FIRST PART OF A COMPOUND

§870
The first part of a compound may be a noun-stem, a verbstem, a numeral, a preposition or adverb, or an inseparable prefix.
a. The use of stems in composition is a survival of a period in the history of language in which inflections were not fully developed.

## FIRST PART A NOUN-STEM

§871

First Declension (a_-stems).—The first part may
a. end in a_ or h (rarely): a)gora_-no/mo-s clerk of the market (a)gora/_), ni_kh-fo/ro-s bringing victory (ni/_kh).
b. end in o: diko-gra/fo-s writer of law-speeches (di/kh justice). Here o is substituted for a_ of the stem by analogy to o-stems.
N.—Compounds of gh= earth have gew- (for gho- by 34); as gew-me/trhs surveyor (land-measurer; metre/w measure). Doric has ga_-me/trhs. Cp. 224 a.
c. lose its vowel before a vowel: kefal-algh/s causing head-ache (kefalh/ head, a)/lg-os pain).

§872

Second Declension (o-stems).—The first part may
a. end in o: logo-gra/fo-s speech-writer.
b. end in a_ or h (rarely): e)lafh-bo/lo-s deer-shooting (e)/lafos, ba/llw). Here h is due to the analogy of a_-stems.
c. lose o before a vowel: mo/n-arxo-s monarch (sole ruler: mo/no-s alone, a)/rx-w rule).
N.—Words of the ‘Attic’ declension may end in w, as new-ko/ro-s custodian of a temple (new/s).

§873

Third Declension (consonant stems).—The first part may
a. show the stem (i, u, au, ou): manti-po/lo-s inspired (ma/nti-s seer, pe/l-w, cp. -kolos), i)xqu-bo/lo-s catching-fish (i)xqu/_s, ba/llw), bou-ko/lo-s ox-herd (bou=-s, -kolo-s, cp. Lat. colo, and 131).
N.—A few consonant stems retain the consonant: mela/g-xolos dipped in black bile (me/la_s, xolh/). See also 876.
b. add o to the stem: swmat-o-fu/lac body-guard (sw=ma body, fula/ttw guard), mhtr-o/-polis mother-city, metropolis (mh/thr, po/lis), fusi-o-lo/gos natural philosopher (fu/si-s nature), i)xqu-o-pw/lhs fishmonger (i)xqu/_s, pwle/w sell).
c. add a^ (rarely h): pod-a/-niptro-n water for washing the feet (pou=s, ni/ptw), lampad-h-dromi/a_ torch-race.

§874
Compounds of pa=s all usually show pa^n-, as pa/n-sofo-s (and pa/s-sofos 101 b) all-wise, par-rhsi/a_ frankness (‘all-speaking’); but also pant- in pa/ntarxos all-ruling; and pant-o- in pant-o-pw/lio-n bazaar (pwle/w sell).

§875
Neuter stems in mat usually show mat-o, as a)galmat-o-poio/-s sculptor (a)/galma statue, poie/w make). Some have ma, as o)noma-kluto/-s of famous name; some show mo for mato, as ai(mo-rragi/a_ hemorrhage (ai(=ma, -atos blood, r(h/gnu_mi break, 80).

§876
Stems in es (nom. -hs or -os) usually drop es and add o; as yeud-o marturi/a_ false testimony (yeud-h/s); and so stems in as, as kreo-fa/go-s flesh-eating (kre/as, fagei=n 529. 5). Some stems in es and as retain es and as (in poetry), as sakes-pa/lo-s wielding a shield (sa/kos, pa/llw), selas-fo/ro-s light-bringing (se/las, fe/rw); some add i (for sake of the metre), as o)res-i/-trofos mountain-bred (o)/ros, tre/fw); these may belong to 879.

§877
Other abbreviations: gala-qhno/-s nurse (galakt- milk, qh=-sqai give suck), meli-hdh/s honey-sweet (melit-), kelai-nefh/s black with clouds from kelaino/-s black (cp. 129 c) and ne/fos cloud.

§878

Words once beginning with *v or s.—When the second part consists of a word beginning with digamma, a preceding vowel is often not elided: kako-ergo/s (Epic) doing ill (later kakou=rgos) from ve/rgo-n work; mhno-eidh/s crescent-shaped (mh/nh moon, vei=dos shape); ti_ma/_-oros (later ti_mwro/s) avenging (ti_mh/ honour, vora/w observe, defend).—Compounds of -oxos, from e)/xw have (orig. se/xw, -soxos) contract: klhrou=xos holding an allotment of land (klh=ro-s lot), poli-ou=xos protecting a city (for poli-o-oxos).

§879

Flectional Compounds.—A compound whose first part is a case form, not a stem, is called a flectional compound (cp. sportsman, kinsfolk): (1) nominative: treis-kai/-deka thirteen; (2) genitive: *dio/s-kouroi Dioscuri (sons of Zeus), *(ellh/s-pontos Helle's sea, *pelopo/n-nhsos (for *pelopos-nhsos, 105 a) Pelops' island; (3) dative: dori/-lhptos won by the spear; (4) locative: o(doi-po/ros wayfarer, *puloi-genh/s born in Pylus.—From such compounds derivatives may be formed, as *(ellhspo/ntios of the Hellespont, qeoisexqri/a_ hatred of the gods.

## FIRST PART A VERB-STEM

§880
Some compounds have as their first part a verb-stem (cp. break-water, pick-pocket, catch-penny). Such compounds are usually poetic adjectives. The verb-stem is usually transitive and has the form that appears in the present or aorist.

§881
Before a vowel the verb-stem remains unchanged or drops a final vowel; before a consonant it adds e, o, or i: fe/r-aspis shield-bearing, mi_s-a/nqrwpos man-hating (mi_se/-w), e)k-e-xeiri/a_ (125 d) holding of hands, truce, lip-o-strati/a_ desertion of the army, ni_k-o/-boulos prevailing in the Senate, a)rx-i-te/ktwn masterbuilder.

§882
The verb-stem adds si (before a vowel, s). Some insert e before si (s): sw-si/-polis saving the state (sw/|zw), r(i/_y-aspis craven, lit. throwing away a shield (r(i/_p-t-w), dhci/-qu_mos (and dak-e/-qu_mos) heart-eating (da/k-n-w), e(lk-e-si/peplos with long train, lit. trailing the robe (cp. e(lk-e-xi/twn)
a. This e is the vowel added in many verb-stems (485).

## FIRST PART A NUMERAL

§883
The first part of a compound is often a numeral: di/-pous biped, tri/-pous tripod (having three feet), te/qr-ippon four-horse chariot, pe/nt-a_qlon contest in five events.

## FIRST PART A PREPOSITION OR ADVERB

§884
A preposition or adverb is often the first part of a compound: ei)/s-odos entrance, a)po-feu/gw flee from, eu)-tuxh/s happy, a)ei/mnhstos ever to be remembered.
a. Except when the substantive is treated as a verbal (as in ei)/s-odos entrance, cp. ei)s-ie/nai enter), prepositions are rarely compounded with substantives. Thus, su/n-doulos fellow-slave, u(po-dida/skalos (= o( u(po/ tini d.) under-teacher; also u(po/-leukos whitish.
b. The ordinary euphonic changes occur. Observe that pro/ before may contract with o or e to ou: proe/xw or prou)/xw hold before (cp. 449 b). See 124 a.
c. h sometimes is inserted after a preposition or takes the place of a final vowel: u(per-h/-fanos conspicuous, e)p-h/-bolos having achieved.
d. Akin to adverbial compounds are some in fil-o, as filo-maqh/s one who gladly learns.

## FIRST PART AN INSEPARABLE PREFIX

§885
Several prefixes occur only in composition:
1. a'（n)- (a)n- before a vowel, a)- before a consonant; alpha privative) with a negative force like Lat. in-, Eng. un- (or -less): a)n-a/cios unworthy (= ou)k a)/cios), a)n-o/moios unlike, a)n-w/dunos anodyne (o)du/nh pain, cp. 887), a)/-nous silly, a)/-ti_mos unhonoured, a)/-qeos godless, ga/mos a)/gamos marriage that is no marriage. a)- is also found before words once beginning with digamma or sigma: a)-hdh/s unpleasant (vhdu/s), a)-o/ra_tos unseen (vora/w), a)/-oplos without shields (soplon), and, by contraction with the following vowel, a)/_kwn (a)-ve/kwn unwilling). But a)n- often appears: a)n-e/lpistos (and a)/-elptos) unhoped for (velpi/s), a)/n-oplos without shield.
a. a)-, a)n- (for ṇ, 35 b) represent weak forms of I. E. ne ‘not.’
2. h(mi- half (Lat. sēmi-): h(mi-ku/klios semi-circular (ku/klos), h(mi-o/lios half as much again (o(/los whole), h(mi-qnh/s half-dead.
3. dus- (opposed to eu)= well) ill, un-, mis-, denoting something difficult, bad, or unfortunate, as dus-tuxh/s unfortunate, dus-xerh/s hard to manage, dusdai/mwn of ill fortune (contrast eu)-tuxh/s, eu)-xerh/s, eu)-dai/mwn), dus-a/restos ill-pleased, *du/s-paris ill-starred Paris.
4. a)- (or a(-) copulative denotes union, likeness (cp. Lat. con-); a)-ko/louqos attendant, agreeing with (ke/leuqos path: i.e. going on the same road), a)-ta/lantos of the same weight, a(/-pa_s all together. A variation of a)-copulative is a)- intensive: a)-tenh/s stretched (tei/nw stretch), a)/-pedos level (pe/don ground).
a. a)- copulative stands for sa- (from sṃ 20, 35 c), and is connected with a(/ma, o(mou=, and o(mo- together.
5. nh- (poetic) with the force of a negative (cp. Lat. nē): nh/-poinos unavenged (poinh/ punishment), nh-penqh/s freeing from pain and sorrow (pe/nqos). In some cases nh- may be derived from n (not) and the h of the second part, as n-h=stis not eating (poetic e)/d-w, cp. 887).
6. a)ri-, e)ri- (poetic) with intensive force (cp. a)/ri-stos best), a)ri-preph/s very distinguished (pre/pw), e)ri/-ti_mos precious.
7. a)ga- (poetic) intensive (cp. a)/gan very): a)ga/-stonos loud wailing (ste/nw groan).
8. za-, da- (poetic) intensive (for d[iglide]a = dia- very, 116): za-menh/s very courageous (me/nos courage), da/-skios thick-shaded (skia/_).

## LAST PART OF A COMPOUND

§886

Compound Substantives and Adjectives.—The last part of a noun-compound consists of a noun-stem or of a verb-stem with a noun-suffix.

§887
Nouns beginning with a^, e, o lengthen these vowels (a^ and e to h, o to w) unless they are long by position. strat-hgo/s army-leading, general (strato/s, a)/gw), eu)-h/nemos with fair wind (eu)= well, a)/nemos), cen-hlasi/a_ driving out of foreigners (ce/nos, e)lau/nw), a)n-w/numos nameless (a)n-, o)/noma), a)n-w/malos uneven (a)n-, o(malo/s).
a. Some compounds of a)/gw lead show a_: lox-a_go/s captain (lo/xos company).
b. By analogy to the compound the simple form sometimes assumes a long vowel: h)nemo/essa windy. Cp. 28 D.
c. Lengthening rarely occurs when a preposition or pa=s precedes: sun-wmosi/a_ conspiracy (o)/mnu_mi swear), pan-h/guris general assembly (a)/guris = a)gora/_).
d. The lengthening in 887 is properly the result of early contraction (strato + agos). On the pattern of such contracted forms irrational lengthening occurs when the first part of the compound ends in a consonant, as dus-hlegh/s (for dus-alegh/s) cruel from a)le/gw care for.

§888
A noun forming the last part of a compound often changes its final syllable.
N. Masculine or feminine nouns of the second or third declensions usually remain unaltered: e)/n-qeos inspired, a)/-pais childless.
a. -os, -h, -on: form compound adjectives from nouns of the first declension, neuters of the second declension, nouns of the third declension, and from many verb-stems. a)/-ti_mos dishonoured (ti_mh/), su/n-deipnos companion at table (dei=pno-n meal), a)/n-aimos bloodless (ai(=ma, 875), e(kato/g-xeiros hundred-handed (xei/r), dasmofo/ros bringing tribute (fe/r-w), gew-gra/fos geographer 871 b. N. (gra/f-w), i)xquo-fa/gos fish-eating (fagei=n 529. 5).
b. -hs, -es: form compound adjectives from nouns of the first and third declensions, and from many verb-stems: a)-tuxh/s unfortunate (tu/xh), deka-eth/s of ten years (ve/tos), eu)-eidh/s beautiful in form (ei)=dos), eu)-maqh/s quick at learning (manqa/nw, maq-), a)-fanh/s invisible (fai/nw, fan-).
c. Other endings are -hs (gen. -ou), -ths, -thr: gew-me/trhs surveyor (871 b. N.), nomo-qe/ths law-giver (no/mos, ti/qhmi, qe-), mhlo-both/r shepherd (mh=lon, bo/-skw feed).
d. Neuters in -ma make adjectives in -mwn: pra=gma thing, a)-pra/_gmwn inactive. frh/n mind becomes -frwn: eu)/-frwn well-minded, cheerful.—path/r father becomes -pa/twr: a)-pa/twr fatherless, filo-pa/twr loving his father.
e. Compounds of gh= land end in -geios, -gews: kata/-geios subterranean, lepto/-gews of thin soil.—Compounds of nau=s ship, ke/ras horn, gh=ras old age end in -ws, as peri/-news supercargo, u(yi/-kerws lofty-antlered (163 a), a)-gh/rws free from old age.

§889
The last member of a compound is often a verbal element that is not used separately: a)galmat-o-poio/s statue-maker, sculptor, u(p-h/koos subject (a)kou/w hear, a)kh/koa), logo-gra/fos speech-writer. -foros bringing, -domos building, -dromos running are used separately in the meanings tribute, building, race.

§890
An abstract word can enter into composition only by taking a derivative ending (usually -ia_) formed from a real or assumed compound adjective: nau=-s ship, ma/xh fight = nau/-maxos, whence nau-maxi/a_ naval battle; eu)= well, boulh/ counsel = eu)/-boulos, whence eu)-bouli/a_ good counsel; a)n-neg., a)rxh/ rule = a)/n-arxos, whence a)n-arxi/a_ anarchy; eu)= well, pra=cis doing = *eu)pra_cos, whence eu)-pra_ci/a_ well-doing. Contrast eu)-bouli/a_ with pro-boulh/ forethought, eu)-logi/a_ eulogy with pro/-logos prologue.
a. Only after a preposition does an abstract word remain unchanged: proboulh/ forethought. Exceptions are rare: misqo-fora/_ receipt of wages (misqo/s, fora/_).

§891

Compound Verbs.—Verbs can be compounded directly only by prefixing a preposition, as sum-ma/xomai fight along with.
a. A preposition (pro/-qesis) derived its name from this use as a prefix. Originally all prepositions were adverbs modifying the verb, and in Homer are partly so used. See 1638, 1639. Cp. upheave and heave up.

§892
All compound verbs not compounded with prepositions are denominatives (ending in -ew) and formed from real or assumed compound nouns. From nau=s ship and ma/xh fight comes nau/maxos fighting in ships, whence naumaxe/w fight in ships; so oi)kodome/w build a house from oi)ko-do/mos house-builder (oi)=kos, de/mw). Contrast a)na-pei/qw bring over, convince with a)-piste/w disbelieve (a)/-pistos); a)nti-le/gw speak against with o(mo-loge/w agree (o(mo/logos agreeing).—eu)= a)gge/llw announce good news cannot form a verb eu)aggellw.
a. a)ti_ma/w (a)ti/w) dishonour, dakruxe/w shed tears are exceptions. a)n-omoio/w make unlike is not from a)n- and o(moio/w but from a)n-o/moios unlike.

## ACCENT OF COMPOUNDS

§893
Compounds generally have recessive accent, as filo/-ti_mos loving-<*> (ti_mh/). But there are many exceptions, e.g.—
a. P<*>tives in -a/_, -h/, -h/s, -eu/s, -mo/s, and -e/os usually keep their accent when compoun<*>; except dissyllabic words in -a/_, -h/, -h/s whose first part is not a preposition. Thus, krith/s judge, u(pokrith/s actor, o)neirokri/ths interpreter of dreams.
b. Compound adjectives in -hs, -es are usually oxytone: eu)-genh/s well-born.

§894
Compounds in -os (not -tos or -kos) formed by the union of a noun or adverb and the stem of a transitive verb are:
a. <*> when they have a long penult and an active meaning: strat-hgo/s general.
b. <*> when they have short penult and an active meaning: patrokt<*> <*>icide, liqo-bo/los throwing-stones, laimo-to/mos throat-cutting, u(drofo<*> <*>ter-carrier.
c. propar<*>, when they have a short penult and passive meaning: patro/kto<*> <*>ain by a father, liqo/-bolos pelted with stones, laimo/-tomos with thr<*> out, au)to/-grafos written with one's own hand.
N.—A<*> compounds of -oxos (e)/x-w, 878), -arxos (a)/rx-w), -su_los (su_la/-w rob<*> -po<*> (pe/rq-w destroy) are proparoxytone; h(ni/-oxos (rein-holder) charioteer, <*> commander of horses, i(ero/-su_los temple-robber, ptoli/-porqos sacking cities. <*> staff-bearer (r(abdo/s) is contracted from r(abdo/-oxos.

## MEANING OF COMPOUNDS

§895
Compound nouns (substantives and adjectives) are divided, according to their meaning, into three main classes: determinative, possessive, and prepositional-phrase, compounds.
a. The <*>ical relation of the parts of compounds varies so greatly that boundary-lines between the different classes are difficult to set up, and a complete formal division is impossible. The poets show a much wider range of usage than the pro<*>-writers.

§896

Determinative Compounds.—In most determinative compounds the first part modifies or determines the second part: the modifier stands first, the principal word second.
Thus by hand-work a particular kind of work is meant, as contrasted with machine-work; cp. speech-writer and letter-writer, race-horse and horse-race.
a. The first part may be an adjective, an adverb, a preposition, an inseparable prefix, or, in a few cases, a substantive.

§897
There are two kinds of determinative compounds.
(1) Descriptive determinative compounds.—The first part defines or explains the second part in the sense of an adjective or adverb. (This class is less numerous than the second class.)
a)kro/-polis upper city, citadel (a)/kra_ po/lis), o(mo/-doulos fellow-slave (o(mou= douleu/wn, cp. 885. 4 a), o)yi/-gonos late-born (o)ye\ geno/menos), pro-boulh/ forethought, a)mfi-qe/a_tron amphitheatre (a place-for-seeing round about), a)/-grafos not written (ou) gegramme/nos).
a. Copulative compounds are formed by the coördination of two substantives or adjectives: i)_a_tro/-mantis physician and seer, gluku/-pikros sweetly-bitter. Similar is deaf-mute. So also in numerals: dw/-deka two (and) ten = 12.
b. Comparative compounds (generally poetic) are meli-hdh/s honey-sweet (me/li, h(du/s), pod-h/nemos *)=iris Iris, with feet swift as the wind. Cp. eagle-eyed, goldfish, blockhead. Such compounds are often possessive (898), as r(odo-da/ktulos rosy-fingered, xru_so-ko/mhs golden-haired.
(2) Dependent determinative compounds.—A substantive forming either the first or the second part stands in the sense of an oblique case (with or without a preposition) to the other part.
Accusative: logo-gra/fos speech-writer (lo/gous gra/fwn), strat-hgo/s armyleading, general (strato\n a)/gwn), fil-a/nqrwpos loving mankind (filw=n a)nqrw/pous), deisi-dai/mwn superstitious (dediw\s tou\s dai/monas); cp. pickpocket, sightseer, painstaking, soothsayer, laughter-loving.
Genitive: strato/-pedon camp (stratou= pe/don ground on which an army is encamped). In a)cio/-logos worthy of mention (a)/cios lo/gou) the defining part stands second (869 c) and is governed by the adjective part like a preposition (cp. 899). Cp. ringmaster, law-offcer, jest-book.
(Ablative): a)nemo-skeph/s sheltering from the wind; cp. land-breeze, sea-breeze.
Dative: i)so/-qeos godlike (i)/sos qew=|); cp. churchgoer, blood-thirsty.
(Instrumental): xeir-o-poi/htos made by hand (xersi\ poihto/s), xru_so/-detos bound with gold (xru_sw=| deto/s); cp. thunder-struck, storm-swept, star-sown.
(Locative): oi)ko-genh/s born in the house (e)n oi)/kw| geno/menos), o(doi-po/ros wayfarer (879); cp. heart-sick.
N. 1.—The Greeks did not think of any actual case relation as existing in these compounds, and the case relation that exists is purely logical. The same form may be analysed in different ways, as fila/nqrwpos = filw=n a)nqrw/pous or = fi/los a)nqrw/pwn.
N. 2.—Such compounds may often be analysed by a preposition and a dependent noun: qeo/-dmhtos god-built (u(po\ tw=n qew=n dmhto/s).

§898

Possessive Compounds.—In possessive compounds the first part defines the second as in determinatives; but the whole compound is an adjective expressing a quality, with the idea of possession understood. In most possessive compounds the idea of having (e)/xwn) is to be supplied.
So, in English, redbreast is a bird having a red breast, the first part being an attribute of the second.
a)rguro/-tocos having a silver bow; makro/-xeir having long arms, long-armed; qeo-eidh/s having the appearance (ei)=dos) of a god, godlike; sw/-frwn having sound mind, temperate; te/qr-ippos having four horses; o(mo/-tropos of like character (o(mo-occurs only in compounds, but note o(/moios like); polu-ke/falos many-headed; eu)-tuxh/s having good fortune, fortunate; deka-eth/s lasting ten years (cp. a twoyear-old); a)mfi-ki/_wn having pillars round about; e)/n-qeos inspired (having a god within: e)n e(autw=| qeo\n e)/xwn).
a. Adjectives in -eidh/s from ei)=dos form (a)ster-o-eidh/s star-like, i)xqu-o-eidh/s fish-like, mhn-o-eidh/s crescent, polu-eidh/s of many kinds, sfair-o-eidh/s spherical) are to be distinguished from those in -w/dhs derived from o)/zw smell (833 a).
b. English possessive compounds in -ed apply that ending only to the compound as a whole and not to either member. In Milton: deep-throated, whitehanded, open-hearted; in Keats: subtle-cadenced. Besides those in -ed there are others such as Bluebeard.
c. Many possessive compounds begin with a'（n)-negative or dus- ill; as a)/-pais childless (having no children or not having children, pai=das ou)k e)/xwn), a)/-ti_mos dishonoured (having no honour), du/s-boulos ill advised (having evil counsels).

§899

Prepositional-phrase Compounds.—Many phrases made of a preposition and its object unite to form a compound and take on adjectival inflection. Such compounds are equivalent to the phrases in question with the idea of being or the like added.
a)/p-oikos colonist (away from home: a)p' oi)/kou); e)gxeiri/dios in the hand, dagger (e)n xeiri/); e)gxw/rios native (in the country: e)n xw/ra|); e)piqala/ttios dwelling on the coast (e)pi\ qala/tth|); e)fe/stios on the hearth (e)f' e(sti/a|); kata/geios underground, cp. subterranean (kata\ gh=s); para/-docos contrary to opinion (para\ do/can); para/-frwn out of one's mind, Lat. de-mens (para\ th\n fre/na); u(p-eu/qu_nos under liability to give account (u(p' eu)qu/_nais); so frou=dos gone (= pro\ o(dou= geno/menos, cp. 124 a).
a. From such phrases are derived verbs and substantives: e)gxeiri/zw put into one's hands, entrust, diaxeiri/zw have in hand, manage (dia\ xeirw=n), diapa_sw=n octave-scale (h( dia\ pa_sw=n xordw=n sumfwni/a_ the concord through all the notes). By analogy to e)kpodw/n out of the way (e)k podw=n) come e)mpodw/n in the way and e)mpo/dios impeding, e)mpodi/zw impede.
b. The compounds of 899 represent bits of syntax used so frequently together that they have become adherent.

## Part IV: Syntax

## DEFINITIONS

§900
A sentence expresses a thought. Syntax (su/ntacis arranging together) shows how the different parts of speech and their different inflectional forms are employed to form sentences.

§901
Sentences are either complete or incomplete (904).

§902
Every complete sentence must contain two members:
1. The Subject: the person or thing about which something is said.
2. The Predicate: what is said about the subject.
Thus, to\ qe/ros (subj.) e)teleu/ta_ (pred.) the summer | came to an end
T. 3.102, h)=lqe (pred.) kh=ruc (subj.) a herald | came 3. 113.

§903
Complete sentences are simple, compound, or complex. In the simple sentence subject and predicate occur only once. A compound sentence (2162) consists of two or more simple sentences coördinated:

th=| d' u(sterai/a| e)poreu/onto dia\ tou= pedi/ou, kai\ *tissafe/rnhs ei(/peto but on the next day they marched through the plain and Tissaphernes kept following them
X. A. 3.4.18. A complex sentence (2173) consists of a main sentence and one or more subordinate sentences: o(po/te de/oi ge/fu_ran diabai/nein, e)/speuden e(/kastos whenever it was necessary to cross a bridge, every one made haste 3. 4. 20.

§904
Incomplete sentences consist of a single member only. Such sentences stand outside the structure of the sentence. The chief classes of incomplete sentences are
a. Interjections, such as w)=, feu=, ai)ai=, oi)/moi.
b. Asseverations which serve as a predicate to a sentence spoken by another: nai/ yes, surely, ou)/ no, ma/lista certainly, kalw=s very well!
c. Headings, titles: *ku/_rou *)ana/basis the Expedition of Cyrus, *)antigo/nh the Antigone,

summaxi/a_ *)aqhnai/wn kai\ *qettalw=n the Alliance of the Athenians and Thessalians
C.I.A. /lref>b.
d. Vocatives (1283), and nominatives used in exclamation (1288).
e. Exclamations without a verb: deu=ro hither!
N.—Examples of such incomplete sentences in English are oh, assuredly, no wonder, right about face, away, fire!

§905
True impersonal verbs (932) have a grammatical subject in the personal ending; but the real subject is properly an idea more or less vague that is present to the mind of the speaker. Similar in nature are infinitives used in commands (2013).

## SYNTAX OF THE SIMPLE SENTENCE

§906
The most simple form of sentence is the finite verb: e)s-ti/ he-is, le/go-men we-say, e(/pe-sqe you-follow.
Here the subject is in the personal ending, the predicate in the verbal stem. No other single word than a verb can of itself form a complete sentence.

§907
The subject of a sentence is a substantive or one of its equivalents.

§908

Equivalents of the Substantive.—The function of the substantive may be assumed by a pronoun, adjective (in masculine and feminine more frequently with the article), numeral, participle, relative clause (

oi(\ e)lh/fqhsan tw=n polemi/wn tau)ta\ h)/ggellon those of the enemy who were captured made the same report
X. A. 1.7.13); by the article with an adverb (oi( to/te the men of that day), or with the genitive (ta\ th=s tu/xhs the incidents of fortune, fortune (1299)); by a prepositional phrase (oi( a)mfi\ to\n *swkra/th Socrates and his followers; e)pi\ me/ga a great part), a preposition with a numeral (

e)/fugon peri\ o)ktakosi/ous about eight hundred took to flight
X. H. 6.5.10); by an infinitive with or without the article (1984, 2025); and by any word or phrase viewed merely as a thing (to\ u(_mei=s o(/tan le/gw, th\n po/lin le/gw when I say You, I mean the State
D. 18.88). Cp. 1153 g. (Furthermore, by a clause in a complex sentence, 2189. 1.)

§909
The predicate of a sentence is always a verb. The verb may either stand alone, as in *periklh=s a)ph=lqe Pericles departed; or it may have certain modifiers, called complements to the predicate (nouns, participles, adverbs), as *periklh=s a)ph=lqe prw=tos first (o)rgizo/menos in anger; to/te then). Cp. 924.

§910

Predicate Nouns.—Nouns (substantival or adjectival) are often used as complements to the predicate. Thus,
a. A predicate substantive is a substantive forming part of the predicate and asserting something of its substantive: *periklh=s h(|re/qh strathgo/s Pericles was elected general,

ei(/lesqe e)kei=non presbeuth/n you elected him envoy
L. 13.10.
b. A predicate adjective is an adjective forming part of the predicate and asserting something of its substantive: o( a)nh\r di/kaio/s e)sti the man is just, e)no/misan *perikle/a_ eu)tuxh= they thought Pericles fortunate.

§911
A predicate substantive or adjective may often be distinguished from an attributive (912) in that the former implies some form of ei)=nai be. Thus, presbeuth/n and eu)tuxh= in 910. After verbs signifying to name or call, ei)=nai is sometimes expressed (1615).

§912

Attributive Adjective.—An attributive adjective is an adjective simply added to a noun to describe it, and not forming any part of an assertion made about it: o( di/kaios a)nh/r the just-man.

§913
All adjectives that are not attributive are predicate. So prw=toi a)fi/_<*>onto they were the first to arrive (1042 b), tou/tw| fi/lw| xrw=mai I treat this man <*>s a friend (= ou(=tos, w(=| xrw=mai, fi/los e)sti/).

§914
Under adjectives are included participles: o( me/llwn (attrib.) po/lemos the future war, tau=ta ei)pw\n (pred.) a)ph/|ein saying this he went off, o(rw= se kru/ptonta (pred.) I see you hiding.

§915
Predicate substantives, adjectives, and participles, in agreement either with subject or object, are more common in Greek than in English, and often call for special shifts in translation:

metew/rous e)ceko/misan ta\_s a(ma/ca_s they lifted the wagons and carried them out
X. A. 1.5.8. Cp. 1579.

§916

Appositive.—An appositive is a noun added to another noun or to a pronoun to describe or define it: *miltia/dhs o( strathgo/s Miltiades, the general, u(_mei=s oi( i(erei=s you, the priests, tou=to, o(\ su\ ei)=pes, a)_ei\ pa/resti, sxolh/ this, which you mentioned, is always present, (I mean) leisure
P. Th. 172d.

§917

Copula.—An indeterminate verb that serves simply to couple a predicate substantive or adjective to the subject is called a copula: *cenofw=n h)=n *)aqhnai=os Xenophon was an Athenian.
a. The most common copulative verbs are ei)=nai be and gi/gnesqai become. Many other verbs serve as copulas: kaqi/stasqai become, pefu_ke/nai, u(pa/rxein, pe/lein (poetical) be, dokei=n seem, fai/nesqai appear. kalei=sqai, o)noma/zesqai, a)kou/ein, klu/ein (poetical) be called, tugxa/nein, kurei=n (poet.) happen, turn out, ai(rei=sqai be chosen, nomi/zesqai be regarded, kri/_nesqai be judged, and the like.

§918

a. The copula is strictly the predicate or is a part of the predicate with its supplements.
b. The above verbs may also be complete predicates: e)/sti qeo/s there is a god.
c. For the omission of the copula, see 944.
d. A predicate substantive or adjective stands in the same case as the subject when coupled to it by a copulative verb (939).
e. For ei)=nai added to a copulative verb, see 1615.

§919

Object.—A verb may have an object on which its action is exerted. The object is a substantive (or its equivalent, 908) in an oblique case. An object may be direct (in the accusative) or indirect (in the genitive or dative): *ku=ros dw/sei e(\c mna=s (direct) tw=| dou/lw| (indirect) Cyrus will give six minae to the slave, e)/labon th=s zw/nhs (indirect) to\n *)oro/nta_n (direct) they took hold of Orontas by the girdle
X. A. 1.6.10.

§920

Transitive and Intransitive Verbs.—Verbs capable of taking a direct object are called transitive because their action passes over to an object Other verbs are called intransitive.
a. But many intransitive verbs, as in English, are used transitively (1558, 1559), and verbs usually transitive often take an indirect object (1341 ff., 1460 ff., 1471 ff.).

## KINDS OF SIMPLE SENTENCES

§921
Simple sentences have six forms: Statements; Assumptions, Commands, Wishes; Questions; and Exclamations. Of these, Assumptions, Commands, and Wishes express will. See 2153 ff.

## EXPANSION OF THE SIMPLE SENTENCE

§922
The subject and the predicate may be expanded by amplification or qualification:

§923

Expansion of the Subject.—The subject may be expanded: A. By amplification: *ceni/a_s kai\ *pa_si/wn a)pe/pleusan Xenias and Pasion sailed away. B. By qualification: 1. By an attributive adjective, o( a)gaqo\s a)nh/r the good man, an attributive substantive denoting occupation, condition , or age, a)nh\r strathgo/s a captain (986), an adjective pronoun or numeral: h(me/teros fi/los a friend of ours, du/o pai=des two children. 2. By the genitive of a noun or substantive pronoun (adnominal or attributive genitive): ste/fanos xru_sou= a crown of gold, o( path\r h(mw=n our father. 3. By a prepositional phrase: o(do\s kata\ tou= ghlo/fou a way down the hill. 4. By an adverb: oi( nu=n a)/nqrwpoi the men of the present day. 5. By an appositive (916). A substantive in any case may be qualified like the subject.

§924

Expansion of the Predicate.—The predicate may be expanded: A. By amplification: oi( loxa_goi\ a)ph=lqon kai\ e)poi/oun ou(/tw the captains departed and did so. B. By qualification: 1. By the oblique case of a noun, a substantive pronoun, or a numeral. This is called the object (919, 920). Thus: o(rw= to\n a)/ndra I see the man, fwnh=s a)kou/w I hear a voice, ei(/peto tw=| h(gemo/ni he followed the guide, a)gapa=| h(ma=s he loves us, e)ni/_khse th\n ma/xhn he won the battle (cognate accusative, 1567), e)/dwka de/ka I gave ten. The oblique case may be followed by an adnominal genitive or a dative: o(rw= pollou\s tw=n poli_tw=n I see many of the citizens. 2. By a preposition with its appropriate case: h)=lqon e)pi\ ta\_s skhna/_s they went to their tents. 3. By an infinitive: e)qe/lei a)pelqei=n he wishes to depart. 4. By a participle: a)/rcomai le/gwn I will begin my speech. 5. By an adverb or adverbial expression: eu)= i)/stw let him know well, th=s nukto\s h)=lqe he came during the night, a)ph=lqe tritai=os he departed on the third day (1042). On complements to the predicate, see 909.

## AGREEMENT: THE CONCORDS

§925
There are three concords in simple sentences:
1. A finite verb agrees with its subject in number and person (949).
2. A word in apposition with another word agrees with it in case (976).
3. An adjective agrees with its substantive in gender, number, and case (1020).
(For the concord of relative pronouns, see 2501.)

§926
Apparent violation of the concords is to be explained either by
a. Construction according to sense, where the agreement is with the real gender or number (e.g. 949 a, 950-953, 958, 996, 997, 1013, 1044, 1050, 1055 a, 1058 b); or by
b. Attraction, when a word does not have its natural construction because of the influence of some other word or words in its clause (e.g. 1060 ff., 1239, 1978, 2465, 2502, 2522 ff.). This principle extends to moods and tenses (2183 ff.).

## THE SUBJECT

§927
The subject of a finite verb is in the nominative: *ku=ros e)bo/a_ Cyrus called out.

§928
The subject nominative may be replaced
a. By a prepositional phrase in the accusative:

e)nqu_mei=sqe kaq' e(ka/stous te kai\ cu/mpantes consider individually and all together
T. 7.64.
b. By a genitive of the divided whole (1318):

*pellhnei=s de\ kata\ *qespie/a_s geno/menoi e)ma/xonto/ te kai\ e)n xw/ra| e)/pi_pton e(kate/rwn the Pellenians who were opposed to the Thespians kept up the contest and several on both sides fell on the spot
X. H. 4.2.20.

## OMISSION OF THE SUBJECT

§929
An unemphatic pronoun of the first or second person is generally omitted: le/ge to\n no/mon read the law (spoken to the clerk of the court)
D. 21.8.

§930
An emphatic pronoun is generally expressed, as in contrasts:

su\ me\n kei=non e)kde/xou, e)gw\ d' a)/peimi do thou wait for him, but I will depart
S. Ph. 123. But often in poetry and sometimes in prose the pronoun is expressed when no contrast is intended. The first of two contrasted pronouns is sometimes omitted: a)lla/, ei) bou/lei, me/n' e)pi\ tw=| strateu/mati, e)gw\ d' e)qe/lw poreu/esqai but, if you prefer, remain with your division, I am willing to go
X. A. 3.4.41. Cp. 1190, 1191.

§931
The nominative subject of the third person may be omitted
a. When it is expressed or implied in the context:

o( so\s path\r fobei=tai mh\ ta\ e)/sxata pa/qh| your father is afraid lest he suffer death
X. C. 3.1.22.
b. When the subject is indefinite, especially when it is the same person or thing as the omitted subject of a preceding infinitive (937 a): h( tou= oi)/esqai ei)de/na/i (a)maqi/a_), a(\ ou)k oi)=den the ignorance of thinking one knows what one does not know
P. A. 29b. Often in legal language: o( no/mos, o(\s keleu/ei ta\ e(autou= e)cei=nai diaqe/sqai o(/pws a)\n e)qe/lh| the law, which enjoins that a man has the right to dispose of his property as he wishes
Is. 2.13.
c. When a particular person is meant, who is easily understood from the situation: tou\s no/mous a)nagnw/setai he (the clerk) will read the laws
Aes. 3.15.
d. When it is a general idea of person, and usually in the third person plural of verbs of saying and thinking:

w(s le/gousin as they say
D. 5.18. So fa_si/ they say, oi)/ontai people think; cp. aiunt, ferunt, tradunt.
e. In descriptions of locality: h)=n de\ krhmnw=des for it (the place) was steep
T. 7.84.
f. In impersonal verbs (932, 934).

§932

Impersonal Verbs (905).—The subject of a true impersonal verb is a vague notion that cannot be supplied from the context: o)ye\ h)=n it was late, kalw=s e)/xei it is well,

h)/dh h)=n a)mfi\ a)gora\_n plh/qousan it was already about the time when the market-place is full
X. A. 1.8.1, au)tw=| ou) prouxw/rei it (the course of events) did not go well with him
T. 1.109.

§933
An impersonal verb the subject of which may be derived from the context is called quasi-impersonal.
a. When the indefinite it anticipates an infinitive or subordinate proposition which forms the logical subject (1985). So with dokei= it seems, sumbai/nei it happens, e)/cesti it is permitted, pre/pei, prosh/kei it is fitting, fai/netai it appears, e)ge/neto it happened, ei)sh/|ei me venit me in mentem, dhloi= it is evident, etc. Thus,

u(_ma=s prosh/kei proqu_mote/rous ei)=nai it behooves you to be more zealous
X. A. 3.2.15, ei)sh/|ei au)tou\s o(/pws a)\n oi)/kade a)fi/kwntai it came into their thoughts how they should reach home 6. 1. 17.
b. So also with xrh/, dei= it is necessary; as, dei= s' e)lqei=n you ought to go (lit. to go binds you). The impersonal construction with -te/on is equivalent to dei= (2152 a):

bohqhte/on e)sti\ toi=s pra/_gmasin u(_mi=n you must rescue the interests at stake
D. 1.17.

§934
In some so-called impersonal verbs the person is left unexpressed because the actor is understood or implied in the action. So
a. In expressions of natural phenomena originally viewed as produced by a divine agent: bronta=| tonat, u(/_ei pluit, nei/fei ningit, xeima/zei it is stormy, e)/seise it shook, there was an earthquake. The agent (*zeu/s, o( qeo/s) is often (in Hom. always) expressed, as *zeu\s a)stra/ptei Iuppiter fulget.
b. When the agent is known from the action, which is viewed as alone of importance: salpi/zei the trumpet sounds (i.e. o( salpigkth\s salpi/zei the trumpeter sounds the trumpet), e)kh/ruce proclamation-was made (scil. o( kh=ruc), shmai/nei the signal is given (scil. o( kh=ruc or o( salpigkth/s).

§935
In impersonal passives the subject is merely indicated in the verbal ending: le/getai/ te kai\ gra/fetai speeches (lo/goi) and writings (gra/mmata) are composed
P. Phae. 261b. This construction is relatively rare, but commonest in the perfect and pluperfect:

ou)k a)/llws au)toi=s pepo/nhtai their labour has not been lost
P. Phae. 232a,

e)pei\ au)toi=s pareskeu/asto when their preparations were completed
X. H. 1.3.20.

§936

Subject of the Infinitive.—The subject of the infinitive is in the accusative:

e)ke/leuon au)tou\s poreu/esqai they ordered that they should proceed
X. A. 4.2.1.
a. See 1975. On the nominative subject of the infinitive, see 1973.

§937

Omission of the Subject of the Infinitive.—The subject of the infinitive is usually not expressed when it is the same as the subject or object (direct or indirect) of the principal verb:

e)/fh e)qe/lein he said he was willing
X. A. 4.1.27 (contrast dixit se velle), pa/ntes ai)tou=ntai tou\s qeou\s ta\ fau=la a)po-

tre/pein everybody prays the gods to avert evil
X. S. 4. 47,

do/s moi trei=s h(me/ra_s a)/rcai au)tou= grant me the control of him for three days
X. C. 1.3.11. Cp. 1060, 1973.
a. An indefinite subject of the infinitive (tina/, a)nqrw/pous) is usually omitted. Cp. 931 b, 1980.

## CASE OF THE SUBJECT: THE NOMINATIVE

§938
The nominative is the case of the subject; the oblique cases, with the exception of the adnominal genitive (1290 ff.) and adnominal dative (1502), are complements of the predicate.

§939
The nominative is the case of the subject of a finite verb and of a predicate noun in agreement with the subject.

*pro/cenos parh=n Proxenus was present
X. A. 1.2.3, *kle/arxos fuga\s h)=n Clearchus was an exile 1. 1. 9.
a. On the nominative subject of the infinitive, see 1973; in exclamations, 1288.

§940

Independent Nominative.—The nominative may be used independently in citing the names of persons and things: prosei/lhfe th\n tw=n ponhrw=n koinh\n e)pwnumi/a_n su_kofa/nths he received the common appellation of the vile, i.e. ‘informer’
Aes. 2.99, to\ d' u(_mei=s o(/tan le/gw, le/gw th\n po/lin when I say You, I mean the State
D. 18.88. Cp. 908. (The accus. is also possible.) So in lists (cp. 904 c):

ti/qhmi du/o poihtikh=s ei)/dh: qei/a_ me\n kai\ a)nqrwpi/nh I assume two kinds of poetry: the divine and the human
P. Soph. 266d.

§941
A sentence may begin with the nominative as the subject of the thought in place of an oblique case: oi( de\ fi/loi, a)/_n tis e)pi/sthtai au)toi=s xrh=sqai, ti/ fh/somen au)tou\s ei)=nai; but as for friends, if one knows how to treat them, what shall we call them?
X. O. 1.14 (for tou\s de\ fi/lous . . . ti/ fh/somen ei)=nai).
a. On the nominative in suspense see under Anacoluthon (Index).

§942
In referring to himself in letters a man may use his own name in the nominative, either in apposition to the first person contained in the verb (976), or as subject of a verb in the third person: *qemistoklh=s h(/kw para\ se/ I, Themistocles, have come to you
T. 1.137,

*)artace/rchs nomi/zei Artaxerxes thinks
X. H. 5.1.31.
a. A speaker referring to himself in the third person usually soon reverts to the first person (
D. 18.79).

§943
When there is no danger of obscurity, the subject may shift without warning: mi/an me\n nau=n lamba/nousin, ta\_s d' a)/lla_s ou)k e)dunh/qhsan, a)ll' a)pofeu/gousin they captured one ship; the rest they were unable to capture; but they (the ships) escaped
T. 7.25, tw=n no/mwn au)tw=n a)kou/ete ti/ keleu/ousi kai\ ti/ parabebh/ka_sin hear what the laws themselves command and what transgressions they (my opponents) have committed
D. 59.115.

## THE PREDICATE

## Omission of the Verb

§944

Ellipsis of the Copula.—The copulative verb ei)=nai is often omitted, especially the forms e)sti/ and ei)si/. This occurs chiefly
a. In general or proverbial statements:

koinh\ h( tu/xh kai\ to\ me/llon a)o/ra_ton chance is common to all and the future cannot be scanned
I. 1.29; b. in expressions of necessity, duty, etc.:

a)na/gkh fula/ttesqai it is necessary to be on our guard
D. 9.6. So with w(/ra_, kairo/s, ei)ko/s, xrew/n, de/on, verbals in -te/on (2152), as

qerapeute/on tou\s qeou/s we must serve the gods
X. M. 2.1.28; c. with various adjectives: a)/cios, dunato/s, pro/qu_mos, di/kaios, oi(=os, frou=dos, e(/toimos; thus,

h( yu_xh\ douleu/ein e(toi/mh the soul is ready to be a servant
P. Phae. 252a,

ei)/ tis e)perwtw/|h po/teron krei=tton if anybody should ask whether it is better
X. M. 1.1.9.

§945
Other forms of ei)=nai are less commonly omitted: koinwnei=n e(/toimos (scil. ei)mi/), oi)=mai de\ kai\ *la/xhta to/nde (scil. e(/toimon ei)=nai) I am ready to assist you and I think that Laches here is also ready
P. Lach. 180a, ou) su\ logogra/fos (scil. ei)=); are you not a speech-writer?
D. 19.250, nu\c e)n me/sw| (scil. h)=n) the night was half gone
Aes. 3.71, a)/topa le/geis kai\ ou)damw=s pro\s sou= (scil. o)/nta) you are talking absurdly and not at all like yourself
X. M. 2.3.15, toi=s qeoi=s megi/sth xa/ris (scil. e)/stw) to the gods let our heartiest thanks be given
X. C. 7.5.72. Cp. 1041.

§946
In lively discourse the form of a verb signifying to do, speak, come, go, etc., may be omitted for brevity. The ellipsis is often unconscious and it is frequently uncertain what is to be supplied to complete the thought. Thus, ti/ a)/llo (scil. e)poi/hsan) h)\ e)pebou/leusan; what else did they do except plot against us?
T. 3.39, ou)de\n a)/llo (scil. poiw=n) h)\ po/lin th\n au(tou= a)polei/pwn doing nothing else except leaving his native city 2. 16, i(/na ti/ (scil. ge/nhtai); to what purpose?
D. 19.257, peri\ me\n tou/tou kata\ sxolh/n (scil. le/cw) about this by and by 24. 187, mh/ moi/ ge mu/_qous (scil. le/chte) none of your legends for me!
Ar. Vesp. 1179, a)ll' (ske/yasqe) e(/teron but consider another point
L. 13.79, w)= fi/le *fai=dre, poi= dh\ (scil. ei)=) kai\ po/qen (scil. h(/keis); my dear Phaedrus whither, I beg of you, are you going and whence do you come?
P. Phae. 227a, ou)k e)s ko/rakas (scil. e)rrh/seis); will you not be off to the crows?
Ar. Nub. 871, pro/s se (scil. i(keteu/w) gona/twn I entreat thee by thy knees
E. Med. 324. Cp. 1599.

§947

*kai\ tau=ta and that too takes up a preceding expression:

a)griwte/rous au)tou\s a)pe/fhne . . . kai\ tau=t' ei)s au(to/n he made them more savage and that too towards himself
P. G. 516c; often with concessive participles (2083): *me/nwna d' ou)k e)zh/tei, kai\ tau=ta par' *)ariai/ou w)\n tou= *me/nwnos ce/nou he did not ask for Menon and that too although he came from Ariaeus, Menon's guest-friend
X. A. 2.4.15. Cp. 1246, 2083.

§948
A verb that may easily be supplied from the context is often omitted. Thus, e)a\n ma/qw, pau/somai (scil. poiw=n) o(/ ge a)/_kwn poiw= if I learn better, I shall leave off doing what I do unintentionally
P. A. 26a, a)melh/sa_s w(=nper oi( polloi/ (scil. e)pimelou=ntai) not caring for what most men care for 36 b, e)a\_n au)=qis zhth/sete tau=ta, ou(/tws (scil. e)/xonta) eu(rh/sete if you inquire about this later, you will find that it is so 24 b. See under Brachylogy (Index).

## CONCORD OF SUBJECT AND PREDICATE

§949
A finite verb agrees with its subject in number and person.
Thus,

tou=to to\ yh/fisma e)ge/neto this bill was passed
L. 13.56,

o(\ de/doik' e)gw\ mh\ pa/qhq' u(_mei=s which I fear lest you may suffer
D. 9.65, h)\n d' a)poyhfi/swntai oi( a)/lloi, a)/pimen a(/pantes tou)/mpalin but if the rest vote against (following), we shall all return back again
X. A. 1.4.15,

tw\ ce/nw tw/de fi/lw e)sto\n e)mw/ these two strangers are friends of mine
P. G. 487a.
a. The verbal predicate, when a copulative verb (917), may be attracted to the number of a predicate noun, which often stands between subject and verb:

to\ xwri/on tou=to, o(/per pro/teron *)enne/a o(doi\ e)kalou=nto this place which was formerly called Nine Ways
T. 4.102,

a(/pa_n to\ me/son tw=n teixw=n h)=san sta/dioi trei=s the entire space between the walls was three stades
X. A. 1.4.4. So with the participles of such copulative verbs: th\n h(donh\n diw/kete w(s a)gaqo\n o)/n (for ou)=san) you chase after pleasure as if it were a good
P. Pr. 354c.

## WITH ONE SUBJECT

## Subject in the Singular, Verb in the Plural

§950
With singular collective substantives (996) denoting persons and with like words implying a plural, the verb may stand in the plural.
Thus,

to\ strato/pedon e)n ai)ti/a| e)/xontes to\n *)=agin a)nexw/roun the army returned holding Agis at fault
T. 5.60,

toiau=ta a)kou/sa_sa h( po/lis *)a_ghsi/la_on ei(/lonto basile/a_ the city, after hearing such arguments, chose Agesilaus king
X. H. 3.3.4. So with boulh/ senate, me/ros part, plh=qos multitude, dh=mos people, o)/xlos throng.

§951
So with e(/kastos: tw=n e(autou= e(/kastos kai\ pai/dwn kai\ xrhma/twn a)/rxousi every man is master of his own children and property X. R.
L. 6.1.

§952
If e(/kastos, e(ka/teros, a)/llos are added in apposition to a plural subject, the verb generally remains plural:

e)gw/ te kai\ su\ makro\n lo/gon e(ka/teros a)petei/namen both you and I have carried on a long controversy
P. Pr. 361a. If the verb follows the apposition, it may be singular: ou(=toi me\n a)/llos a)/lla le/gei these say, some one thing, some another
X. A. 2.1.15. Cp. 982.

§953
A subject in the singular, followed by a clause containing the preposition meta/ with, rarely takes a plural verb:

*)alkibia/dhs meta\ *mantiqe/ou i(/ppwn eu)porh/santes a)pe/dra_san Alcibiades and Mantitheus escaped because they were well provided with horses
X. H. 1.1.10.

## Subject in the Dual, Verb in the Plural

§954
The first person dual agrees in form with the first person plural (462).

§955
A dual subject may take a plural verb:

*cenofw=nti prose/trexon du/o nea_ni/skw two youths ran up to Xenophon
X. A. 4.3.10. In the orators the dual verb is almost always used.

§956
The dual and plural verb may alternate: ai(/resin ei(le/thn te kai\ diepra/_canto the two souls have made their choice and put it into effect
P. Phae. 256c.

§957
The neuter dual may be followed by the dual, the plural, or the singular verb (A 104, 200, M 466).

## Subject in the Plural, Verb in the Singular

§958
A neuter plural subject is regarded as a collective (996), and has its verb in the singular:

kala\ h)=n ta\ sfa/gia the sacrifices were propitious
X. A. 4.3.19.
N.—The neuter plural seems to have been originally in part identical in form with the feminine singular in a_, and to have had a collective meaning.

§959
A plural verb may be used when stress is laid on the fact that the neuter plural subject is composed of persons or of several parts:

ta\ te/lh tw=n *lakedaimoni/wn au)to\n e)ce/pemyan the Lacedaemonian magistrates despatched him
T. 4.88,

fanera\ h)=san kai\ i(/ppwn kai\ a)nqrw/pwn i)/xnh polla/ many traces both of horses and of men were plain
X. A. 1.7.17.
a. With the above exception Attic regularly uses the singular verb. Homer uses the singular three times as often as the plural, and the plural less frequently with neuter adjectives and pronouns than with substantives. In some cases (B 135) the metre decides the choice.

§960
Following the construction of dokei= tau=ta, we find

do/can tau=ta when it had been thus decided
X. A. 4.1.13, and also do/canta tau=ta
X. H. 3.2.19. See 2078 a.

§961

Pindaric Construction. A masculine or feminine plural subject occasionally is used with e)/sti, h)=n, gi/gnetai, as:

e)/sti kai\ e)n tai=s a)/llais po/lesin a)/rxonte/s te kai\ dh=mos there are in the other cities too rulers and populace
P. R. 462e. The verb usually precedes, and the subject is still undetermined; hence the plural is added as an afterthought. (Cp. Shakesp. “far behind his worth | Comes all the praises.”) In Greek poetry this construction is rarely used with other verbs. On e)/stin oi(/, see 2513.
a. h)=n was originally plural (464 e. D), and seems to survive in that use.

## Subject in the Plural, Verb in the Dual

§962
A plural subject may take a dual verb when the subject is a pair or two pairs: ai( i(/ppoi drame/thn the span of mares ran *y 392.
a. This is common when du/o, a)/mfw, a)mfo/teroi are used with a plural subject:

du/o a)/ndres proselqo/nte *)/a_gidi dielege/sqhn mh\ poiei=n ma/xhn two men coming to Agis urged him not to fight
T. 5.59. But even with these words the plural is preferred. The neuter plural with du/o rarely takes the dual verb (
P. Tim. 56e).

## WITH TWO OR MORE SUBJECTS

§963
(I) When the subjects are different individuals or things and stand in the third person

§964
With two subjects in the singular, the verb may be dual or plural: *kriti/a_s kai\ *)alkibia/dhs e)duna/sqhn e)kei/nw| xrwme/nw summa/xw| tw=n e)piqu_miw=n kratei=n Critias and Alcibiades were able to keep control of their appetites by the help of his example
X. M. 1.2.24,

*eu)rume/dwn kai\ *sofoklh=s a)fiko/menoi e)s *ke/rku_ran e)stra/teusan on their arrival in Corcyra Eurymedon and Sophocles proceeded to make an attack
T. 4.46.

§965
In Homer the verb may intervene between the subjects (Alcmanic Construction):

ei)s *)axe/ronta *puriflege/qwn te r(e/ousin *kw/ku_to/s te Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus flow into Acheron
k 513.

§966
The verb may agree with the nearest or most important of two or more subjects. The verb may be placed
a. Before both subjects:

h(=ke me\n o( *qersago/ra_s kai\ o( *)ech/kestos ei)s *le/sbon kai\ w)/|koun e)kei= Thersagoras and Execestus came to Lesbos and settled there
D. 23.143.
b. After the first subject:

o(/ te *pole/marxos h(=ke kai\ *)adei/mantos kai\ *nikh/ratos kai\ a)/lloi tine/s Polemarchus came and Adimantus and Niceratus and certain others
P. R. 327b,

*fali=nos w)/|xeto kai\ oi( su\n au)tw=| Phalinus and his companions departed
X. A. 2.2.1.
c. After both subjects:

to\ bouleuth/rion kai\ o( dh=mos parora=tai the senate and the people are disregarded
