Aes. 3.250. (Cp. Shakesp. “my mistress and her sister stays.”）

§967
(II) With several subjects referring to different persons the verb is in the plural; in the first person, if one of the subjects is first person; in the second person, if the subjects are second and third person:

u(_mei=s de\ kai\ e)gw\ ta/de le/gomen but you and I say this
P. L. 661b, h(mei=s kai\ oi(/de ou)k a)/llhn a)/n tina dunai/meqa w)|dh\n a)/|dein we and these men could not sing any other song 666 d, ou) su\ mo/nos ou)de\ oi( soi\ fi/loi prw=toi tau/thn do/can e)/sxete not you alone nor your friends are the first who have held this opinion 888 b.

§968
But the verb may be singular if it refers to the nearer or more important or more emphatic subject: pa/reimi kai\ e)gw\ kai\ ou(=tos *fru_ni/skos kai\ *polukra/ths. I am present and so are Phryniscus here and Polycrates
X. A. 7.2.29.

§969
The verb may agree in person with the nearer or more important subject:

su/ te ga\r *(/ellhn ei)= kai\ h(mei=s for you are a Greek and so are we
X. A. 2.1.16.

§970
With subjects connected by the disjunctives h)/ or, h)/—h)/ either—or, ou)/te—ou)/te neither—nor, the verb agrees in number with the nearer subject when each subject is taken by itself:

oi)/te su\ ou)/t' a)\n a)/llos ou)dei\s du/nait' a)nteipei=n neither you nor anybody else could reply
X. M. 4.4.7.

§971
When the subjects are taken together, the plural occurs:

a(\ *dhmofw=n h)\ *qhrippi/dhs e)/xousi tw=n e)mw=n what Demophon or Therippides have of my property
D. 27.12. This is unusual.

§972
When h)/ than unites two subjects, if the verb follows h)/, it agrees with the second subject:

tu/xh a)ei\ be/lti_on h(\ h(mei=s h(mw=n au)tw=n e)pimelou/meqa fortune always takes better care of us than we do of ourselves
D. 4.12.

## CONCORD OF PREDICATE SUBSTANTIVES

§973
A predicate substantive agrees with its subject in case: *miltia/dhs h)=n strathgo/s Miltiades was a general.

§974
A predicate substantive may agree in gender and number with its subject; but this is often impossible: tu/xh ta\ qnhtw=n pra/_gmata the affairs of mortals are chance Trag. frag. p. 782,

pa/nt' h)=n *)ale/candros Alexander was everything
D. 23.120.

§975
A predicate substantive or adjective agrees with the subject of the governing verb when the subject of the infinitive is omitted because it is the same as that of the governing verb (937):

ou)x o(mologh/sw a)/klhtos h(/kein I shall not admit that I have come uninvited
P. S. 174d,

ei)/per a)ciou=men e)leu/qeroi ei)=nai if indeed we claim to be free
X. C. 8.1.4.
On the agreement of demonstrative and relative pronouns with a predicate substantive, see 1239, 2502 e.

## APPOSITION

§976

Concord.—An appositive (916) agrees in case with the word it describes:

ko/laki, deinw=| qhri/w| kai\ megi/sth| bla/bh| to a flatterer, a terrible beast and a very great source of injury
P. Phae. 240b. An appositive also agrees in case with the pronoun contained in a verb: *talqu/bios, h(/kw, *dana+/dwn u(phre/ths I, Talthybius, have come, the servant of the Danaids
E. Hec. 503. Cp. 942.

§977
An appositive to a possessive pronoun stands in the genitive, in agreement with the personal pronoun implied in the possessive: to\n e)mo\n ( = e)mou=)

tou= talaipw/rou bi/on the life of me, wretched one
Ar. Plut. 33, ta\ u(_me/ter' ( = u(_mw=n)

au)tw=n komiei=sqe you will regain your own
D. 4.7. Cp. 1200. 2. b, 1202. 2. b.

§978
An appositive in the genitive may follow an adjective equivalent to a genitive: *)aqhnai=os ( = *)aqhnw=n) w)/n, po/lews th=s megi/sths being an Athenian, a citizen of the greatest city
P. A. 29d.

§979
Agreement in number between the appositive and its noun is unnecessary and often impossible: *qh=bai, po/lis a)stugei/twn Thebes, a neighbouring city
Aes. 3.133. So with dw=ra in poetry: ga/mos, xru_sh=s *)afrodi/_ths dw=ra, marriage, gift of golden Aphrodite Theognis 1293.

§980
An appositive to two substantives is dual or plural:

qa/rros kai\ fo/bos, a)/frone cumbou/lw daring and fear, two unintelligent counsellors
P. Tim. 69d,

u(/pnos po/nos te, ku/_rioi sunwmo/tai sleep and toil, supreme conspirators
A. Eum. 127.

§981

Partitive Apposition (sxh=ma kaq' o(/lon kai\ me/ros, construction of the whole and part). The parts are represented by the appositives, which stand in the same case as the whole, which is placed first to show the subject or object of the sentence: tw\ o(dw/, h( me\n ei)s maka/rwn nh/sous, h( d' ei)s ta/rtaron two roads, the one to the Islands of the Blest, the other to Tartarus
P. G. 524a (distributive apposition). The appositives are generally in the nominative (o( me/n, h( de/; oi( me/n, oi( de/), rarely in the accusative.
a. The whole may stand in the singular: le/getai yu_xh\ h( me\n nou=n e)/xein, h( de\ a)/noian; with regard to the soul, is one said to have intelligence, the other folly?
P. Ph. 93b.

§982
To the word denoting the whole the appositive may be a collective singular (adjunctive apposition):

ou(=toi me\n a)/llos a)/lla le/gei these say, some one thing, some another
X. A. 2.1.15 (cp. h)rw/twn de\ a)/llos a)/llo
P. Charm. 153c),

oi( strathgoi\ braxe/ws e(/kastos a)pelogh/sato each of the generals defended himself briefly
X. H. 1.7.5. Cp. 952.

§983
The apposition may be limited to one or more parts:

*peloponnh/sioi kai\ oi( cu/mmaxoi ta\ du/o me/rh two-thirds of the Peloponnesians and the allies
T. 2.47. Often with participles: (oi( *)aqhnai=oi) a)nemnh/sqhsan kai\ tou=de tou= e)/pous, fa/skontes oi( presbu/teroi pa/lai a)/|desqai the Athenians bethought themselves of this verse too, the old men saying that it had been uttered long before
T. 2.54.

§984
In partitive apposition emphasis is laid on the whole, which is stated at once as the subject or object of the sentence. In the genitive of the divided whole (1306) emphasis is laid on the parts; thus, tw=n po/lewn ai( me\n turannou=ntai, ai( de\ dhmokratou=ntai, ai( de\ a)ristokratou=ntai of states some are despotic, others democratic, others aristocratic
P. R. 338d.

§985

Construction of the Whole and Part in Poetry.—In Homer and later poets a verb may take two objects, one denoting the person, the other the part especially affected by the action:

to\n d' a)/ori plh=c' au)xe/na him he smote in the neck with his sword
*l 240,

h(/ se po/das ni/yei she will wash thy feet
t 356. But the accusative of the part, often explained as an appositive, was an external object (1554 b) that became an accusative of respect (1601 a). In

*)axaioi=sin de\ me/ga sqe/nos e)/mbal' e(ka/stw| kardi/h| and she set mighty strength in the heart of each of the Achaeans
*l 11, e(ka/stw| is a partitive appositive, kardi/h| is local dative and grammatically independent of *)axaioi=sin. The construction is very rare in prose:

toi=s vi(e/sin au)tw=n a)reth\ paragenome/nh tai=s yu_xai=s if virtue is imparted in the souls of their sons
P. Lach. 190b.

§986

Attributive Apposition.—A substantive may be used as an attributive to another substantive. This is common with substantives denoting occupation, condition , or age (usually with a)nh/r, a)/nqrwpos, gunh/): a)nh\r r(h/twr a public speaker, a)nh\r tu/rannos a despot, presbu=tai a)/nqrwpoi old men, grau=s gunh/ an old woman. So also

peltastai\ *qra=|kes Thracian targeteers
X. A. 1.2.9,

o)/leqros *makedw/n a scoundrel of a Macedonian
D. 9.31, *(/ellhn (for *(ellhniko/s), as

oi( *(/ellhnes peltastai/ the Greek targeteers
X. A. 6.5.26.
a. In standard prose *(/ellhn is used as an adjective only of persons (in poetry also of things).
b. The addition of a)nh/r often implies respect:

a)/ndres stratiw=tai fellow soldiers
X. A. 1.3.3, w)= a)/ndres dikastai/ jurymen, gentlemen of the jury
D. 27.1. (Cp. foemen.) The addition of a)/nqrwpos often implies contempt:

a)/nqrwpos go/hs a juggling fellow
Aes. 2.153.
c. Many of the substantives thus qualified by an attributive substantive were originally participles, as

ge/rwn a)nh/r an old man
P. Lys. 223b.

§987

Descriptive Apposition.—Here the appositive describes something definite that has just been mentioned:

h( h(mete/ra_ po/lis, h( koinh\ katafugh\ tw=n *(ellh/nwn our city, the common refuge of the Greeks
Aes. 3.134.

§988

Explanatory Apposition.—Here the appositive explains a general or vague statement:

tou/tou ti_mw=mai, e)n prutanei/w| si_th/sews I propose this as the penalty, maintenance in the Prytaneum
P. A. 37a, megi/stou kakou= a)pallagh/, ponhri/a_s deliverance from the greatest of evils, vice
P. G. 478d. So in geographical statements: *ku/pron i(/ka_ne . . . e)s *pa/fon she came to Cyprus, to Paphos
*q 362; cp.

e)s *dwria=s, *boio/n to the territory of the Dorians in which Boeum lies
T. 1.107.

§989
In Homer the substantival article at the beginning of a sentence may be followed by an appositive noun at or near the end: h( d' a)e/kous' a(/ma toi=si gunh\ ki/en but she, the woman, went unwillingly with them A 348.

§990

tou=to, au)to\ tou=to, au)to/, e)kei=no often introduce emphatically a following substantive (or an equivalent, 908): e)kei=no kerdai/nein h(gei=tai, th\n h(donh/n this (namely) pleasure it regards as gain
P. R. 606b. Cp. 1248.

§991

Apposition to a Sentence.—A noun in the nominative or accusative may stand in apposition to the action expressed by a whole sentence or by some part of it.
a. The appositive is nominative when a nominative precedes: e)me/quon: i(kanh\ pro/fasis I was tipsy, a sufficient excuse Philemon (Com. frag. 2. 531).
b. The appositive is accusative, and states a reason, result, intention, effect, or the like: r(i/_yei a)po\ pu/rgou, lugro\n o)/leqron will hurl thee from the battlement, a grievous death
*w 735, *(ele/nhn kta/nwmen, *mene/lew| lu/_phn pikra/_n let us slay Helen and thus cause a sore grief to Menelaus
E. Or. 1105,

eu)daimonoi/hs, misqo\n h(di/stwn lo/gwn blest be thou—a return for thy most welcome tidings
E. El. 231.
N.—The appositive accusative is often cognate (1563 f.): o(ra=|s *eu)rusqe/a_, a)/elpton o)/yin thou beholdest Eurystheus, an unexpected sight E. Heracl. 930.

§992
An effect or result may be denoted by an appositive in other cases:

e)pw|dw=n prosdei=sqai/ moi dokei= mu/_qwn e)/ti tinw=n we need, it seems, some further words to act as a spell
P. L. 903b.

§993
From the construction in 991 b arose many adverbial accusatives (1606 ff.) such as xa/rin on account of, pro/fasin in pretence, dwrea/_n gratis; as o(/s tis de\ *trw/wn e)pi\ nhusi\ fe/roito . . . xa/rin *(/ektoros whoever of the Trojans rushed at the ships as a favour to Hector (for Hector's sake) O 744.

§994
Many neuter words are used in apposition to a sentence or clause, which they usually precede. Such are a)mfo/teron, a)mfo/tera both, to\ deino/taton the most dreadful thing, duoi=n qa/_teron or qa/_tera one or the other, to\ e)nanti/on the contrary, to\ kefa/laion the chief point, to\ lego/menon as the saying is, ou)de/teron neither thing, shmei=on de/ sign, tekmh/rion de/ evidence, to\ teleutai=on the last thing, to\ th=s paroimi/a_s as the proverb runs, au)to\ tou=to this very thing, tau)to\ tou=to this same thing. Thus,

tous a)mfo/tera tau=ta, kai\ eu)/nous th=| po/lei kai\ plousi/ous those who are both loyal to the State and rich
D. 18.171, ei)=pen o(/ti dei= duoi=n qa/_teron, h)\ kei/nous e)n *olu/nqw| mh\ oi)kei=n h)\ au(to\n e)n *makedoni/a| he said that one of two things was necessary—either that they should not live at Olynthus or he himself in Macedon 9. 11,

to\ de\ me/giston, po/lemon a)nt' ei)rh/nhs e)/xontes and what is worst of all, having war instead of peace
T. 2.65, a)ll' h)=, to\ lego/menon, kato/pin e(orth=s h(/komen; but have we come ‘after a feast’ as the maying is?
P. G. 447a,

tou=to au)to\ to\ tou= *(omh/ron in these very words of Homer
P. A. 34d.

§995
Very common are introductory relative clauses forming a nominative predicate of the sentence that follows:

o(\ de\ pa/ntwn deino/taton but what is most terrible of all
L. 30.29. e)sti/ is regularly omitted (944). Such relative clauses are followed by an independent sentence, a clause with o(/ti, by o(/te ga/r, o(/tan, o(/tan ga/r, <*>. Similarly

to\ d' e)/sxaton pa/ntwn, o(/ti but what is worst of all
P. Ph. 66d, etc.

## PECULIARITIES IN THE USE OF NUMBER

§996

Collective Singular.—A noun in the singular may denote a number of persons or things:

o( *mh=dos the Medes
T. 1.69, to\ *(ellhniko/n the Greeks 1. 1, to\ barbariko/n the barbarians 7. 29, h( pli/nqos the bricks 3. 20,

i(/ppon e)/xw ei)s xi_li/a_n I have about a thousand horse
X. C. 4.6.2,

mu_ri/a_ a)spi/s ten thousand heavy armed
X. A. 1.7.10. On the plural verb with collectives, see 950. Cp. 1024, 1044.
a. So with the neuter participle: to\ maxo/menon almost =

oi( maxo/menoi the combatants
T. 4.96.
b. The name of a nation with the article may denote one person as the representative (King, etc.) of a class: o( *makedw/n the Macedonian (Philip)
D. 7.6.

§997
The inhabitants of a place may be implied in the name of the place:

*le/sbos a)pe/sth boulhqe/ntes kai\ pro\ tou= pole/mou Lesbos revolted, having wished to do so even before the war
T. 3.2.

§998

Distributive Singular.—The singular of abstract nouns may be used distributively (rarely with concrete substantives):

o(/soi di/kaioi e)ge/nonto e)n tw=| e(autw=n bi/w| all who proved themselves just in their lives
P. A. 41a,

dia/foroi to\n tro/opon different in character
T. 8.96. The distributive plural (1004) is more common than the distributive singular: cp.

nea_ni/ai ta\_s o)/yeis youths in appearance
L. 10.29 with

h(dei=s th\n o)/yin pleasing in appearance
P. R. 452b.

§999

Dual.—The dual is chiefly employed of two persons or things which, by nature or association, form a pair: o)fqalmw/ the eyes (both eyes), xei=re the hands, i(/ppw a span of horses. The addition of a)/mfw both indicates that the two things belong together: du/o emphasizes the number. Both a)/mfw and du/o were early used with the plural. The dual died out in the living speech of Attica by 300 B.C. Aeolic has no dual, and Ionic lost it very early. In Hom. the dual is used freely, and often in conjunction with the plural.

§1000

Plural.—The plural of proper names, of materials, and of abstracts is used to denote a class. (1) of proper names:

*qhse/es men like Theseus
P. Th. 169b. (2) of materials: here the plural denotes the parts, the different kinds of a thing, a mass, etc.:

to/ca bow
Hdt. 3.78, pu_roi/, kri_qai/ wheat, barley
X. A. 4.5.26, oi)=noi wines 4. 4. 9,

kre/a_ meat
Ar. Ran. 553 (kre/as piece of meat),

h(/lioi hot days
T. 7.87,

cu/la timber
T. 7.25. (3) of abstracts: here the plural refers to the single kinds, cases, occasions, manifestations of the idea expressed by the abstract substantive; or is referred to several persons:

a)gnwmosu/nai misunderstandings
X. A. 2.5.6,

qa/lph degrees of heat
X. M. 1.4.13. Used in the plural, abstract nouns may become concrete, as

tafai/ funeral
T. 2.34 (tafh/ sepulture),

eu)frosu/nai good cheer
X. C. 7.2.28 (eu)frosu/nh mirth),

xa/rites proofs of good will, presents
D. 8.53,

eu)/noiai cases of benevolence, presents
D. 8.25.
a. Many concrete substantives are commonly used only in the plural: pu/lai gate, qu/rai door, ta\ *)olu/mpia the Olympic festival; and in poetry dw/mata house, kli/_makes ladder, le/ktra bed; cp. 1006.
b. The plural, especially in poetry, may correspond to the English indefinite singular: e)pi\ nausi/ by ship.

§1001
In Homer the plural denotes the various forms in which a quality is manifested:

tektosu/nai the arts of the carpenter
e 250. In poetry, often of feelings, emotions, etc.: mani/ai (attacks of) madness
A. Pr. 879.

§1002

ou)de/nes (mhde/nes) denotes classes of men, states, nations (
D. 5.15).

§1003
The neuter plural is often used even in reference to a single idea or thought in order to represent it in its entirety or in its details, as ta\ a)lhqh= the truth. This is very common with neuter pronouns: e)xeirono/moun de/: tau=ta ga\r h)pista/mhn but I waved my arms, for I knew how to do this
X. S. 2. 19,

dia\ taxe/wn quickly
P. A. 32d.
a. Thucydides is fond of the neuter plural of verbal adjectives used impersonally:

e)yhfi/santo polemhte/a ei)=nai they voted that it was necessary to make war
T. 1.88, a)du/nata h)=n it was impossible 4. 1. Cp. 1052.

§1004

Distributive Plural.—Abstract substantives are often used distributively in the plural:

si_gai\ tw=n newte/rwn para\ presbute/rois the silence of the younger men in the presence of their elders
P. R. 425a.

§1005
Names of towns and parts of the body are sometimes plural: *)aqh=nai Athens, *qh=bai Thebes, sth/qh and ste/rna breast (chiefly poetic). The name of the inhabitants is often used for the name of a city: *delfoi/
D. 5.25.

§1006

Plural of Majesty (poetic).—The plural may be used to lend dignity:

qro/noi throne
S. Ant. 1041,

skh=ptra scepter
A. Ag. 1265,

dw/mata dwelling
e 6; paidika/ favourite in prose (only in the plural form).

§1007
Here belongs the allusive plural by which one person is alluded to in the plural number: despotw=n qana/toisi by the death of our lord
A. Ch. 52, paqou=sa pro\s tw=n filta/twn I (Clytaemnestra) having suffered at the hands of my dearest ones (Orestes)
A. Eum. 100.

§1008

Plural of Modesty.—A speaker in referring to himself may use the first person plural as a modest form of statement. In prose, of an author:

e)/nnoia/ poq' h(mi=n e)ge/neto the reflection once occurred to me
X. C. 1.1.1. In tragedy, often with interchange of plural and singular: ei) kwlu_o/mesqa mh\ maqei=n a(\ bou/lomai if I (Creusa) am prevented from learning what I wish
E. Ion 391,

i(keteu/omen a)mfi\ sa\_n geneia/da . . . prospi/tnwn I entreat thee, as I grasp thy beard
E. H. F. 1206. See 1009.

§1009
In tragedy, if a woman, speaking of herself, uses the plural verb (1008), an adjective or participle, in agreement with the subject, is feminine singular or masculine plural:

h(/lion martu_ro/mesqa, drw=s' a(\ dra=n ou) bou/lomai I call the sun to witness, that I am acting against my will
E. H. F. 858, a)rkou=men h(mei=s oi( proqnh/|skontes se/qen it is enough that I (Alcestis) die in thy stead
E. Alc. 383.

§1010

ei)pe/, fe/re, a)/ge may be used as stereotyped formulas, without regard to the number of persons addressed: ei)pe/ moi, w)= *sw/krate/s te kai\ u(_mei=s oi( a)/lloi tell me, Socrates and the rest of you
P. Eu. 283b.

§1011
One person may be addressed as the representative of two or more who are present, or of his family: *)anti/no', ou)/ pws e)/stin . . . meq' u(_mi=n dai/nusqai Antinous, it is in no wise possible to feast with you
b 310,

w)= te/knon, h)= pa/reston; my children, are ye here?
S. O. C. 1102. So in dramatic poetry, the coryphaeus may be regarded as the representative of the whole chorus, as

w)= ce/noi, mh/ m' a)ne/rh| ti/s ei)mi strangers [note: (addressed to the whole chorus)] do not ask [note: (the singular of the coryphaeus)] me who I am
S. O. C. 207.

§1012
Greek writers often shift from a particular to a general statement and vice versa, thus permitting a free transition from singular to plural, and from plural to singular:

ou)de\ to/te sugxai/rei o( tu/rannos: e)ndeeste/rois ga\r ou)=si tapeinote/rois au)toi=s oi)/ontai xrh=sqai not even then does the despot rejoice with the rest; for the more they are in want, the more submissive he thinks to find them
X. Hi. 5.4.

## PECULIARITIES IN THE USE OF GENDER

§1013

Construction according to the Sense (926 a).—The real, not the grammatical, gender often determines the agreement: w)= fi/ltat', w)= perissa\ ti_mhqei\s te/knon O dearest, O greatly honoured child
E. Tro. 735 (this use of the attributive adjective is poetical),

ta\ meira/kia pro\s a)llh/lous dialego/menoi the youths conversing with one another
P. Lach. 180e,

tau=t' e)/legen h( a)naidh\s au(/th kefalh/, e)celhluqw/s this shameless fellow spoke thus when he came out
D. 21.117.

§1014
So in periphrases: i)\_s *thlema/xoio e)s pate/ra i)dw/n mighty Telemachus, gazing at his father
p 476,

to\ de\ tw=n presbute/rwn h(mw=n . . . xai/rontes th=| e)kei/nwn paidia=| we the elders delighting in their sport
P. L. 657d.

§1015
The masculine is used for person in general: ou)k a)ne/cetai ti/ktontai a)/llous, ou)k e)/xous' au)th\ te/kna unfruitful herself, she will not endure that others bear children
E. And. 712,

o(po/teros a)\n h)=| belti/_wn, ei)/q' o( a)nh/r ei)/q' h( gunh/ which ever of the two is superior, whether the man or the woman
X. O. 7.27. So oi( gonei=s parents, oi( pai=des children. See 1055.
See also 1009, 1050.

## PECULIARITIES IN THE USE OF PERSON

§1016

ti\s or pa=s may be used in the drama with the second person of the imperative: i)/tw tis, ei)sa/ggelle go, one of you, announce
E. Bacch. 173.

§1017
The second person singular is used to designate an imaginary person, as in proverbs:

yu_xh=s e)pimelou= th=s seautou= care for thy own soul
Men. Sent. 551, and in such phrases as ei)=des a)/n you would have seen (1784 a), h(gh/saio a)/n you might think, as credideris (1824).
a. Hdt. uses the second person in directions to travellers (2. 30).
See also 942.

## ADJECTIVES

§1018
Adjectives modify substantives (including words used substantively, 908), and substantive pronouns. Adjectives are either attributive (912) or predicate (910).

§1019
The equivalents of an adjective are: a participle (oi( paro/ntes poli=tai the citizens who are present); a noun in apposition (*dhmosqe/nhs o( r(h/twr Demosthenes the orator, i.e. not *dhmosqe/nhs o( strathgo/s, u(_mei=s oi( *)aqhnai=oi you Athenians); an oblique case (ste/fanos xru_sou= a crown of gold, th=s au)th=s gnw/mhs e)gw/ I am likeminded); an oblique case with a preposition (ai( e)n th=| *)asi/a| po/leis the cities in Asia); an adverb (oi( pa/lai the ancients). (Furthermore, a clause in a complex sentence: to\ tei/xisma, o(\ h)=n au)to/qi, ai(rou=si they captured the fortress which was there; cp. 2542.)

§1020

Concord.—An adjective agrees with its substantive in gender, number, and case. This holds true also of the article, adjective pronouns, and participles: thus, A. Attributive: o( di/kaios a)nh/r the just man, tou= dikai/ou a)ndro/s, tw\ dikai/w a)/ndre, oi( di/kaioi a)/ndres, etc., ou(=tos o( a)nh/r this man, tou/tou tou= a)ndro/s, etc., h( filou=sa quga/thr the loving daughter. B. Predicate: kalo\s o( a)gw/n the prize is glorious, tau=t' e)sti\n a)lhqh= these things are true,

ai( a)/ristai dokou=sai ei)=nai fu/seis the natures which seem to be best
X. M. 4.1.3.
On the agreement of demonstrative pronouns used adjectively with a predicate substantive, see 1239. For relative pronouns, see 2501.

## ATTRIBUTIVE ADJECTIVES

## ADJECTIVES USED SUBSTANTIVELY

§1021
An attributive adjective (or participle) generally with the article, often dispenses with its substantive, and thus itself acquires the value of a substantive.
a. This occurs when the substantive may be supplied from the context; when it is a general notion; or when it is omitted in common expressions of a definite character, when the ellipsis is conscious.

§1022
Masculine or feminine, when the substantive is a person: o( di/kaios the just man, di/kaios a just man, oi( *)aqhnai=oi the Athenians, oi( polloi/ the many, the rabble, oi( o)li/goi the oligarchical party, oi( boulo/menoi all who will, h( kalh/ the beautiful woman, h( tekou=sa the mother (poet.,
E. Alc. 167), e)kklhsia/zousai women in assembly.

§1023
Neuter, when the substantive idea is thing in general: to\ a)gaqo/n the (highest) good
P. R. 506b (but

ta\ a)gaqa/ good things
L. 12.33),

to\ a)lhqe/s truth
P. G. 473b, to\ koino/n the commonwealth Ant. 3.
b. 3,

to\ e)so/menon the future
Aes. 3.165,

to\ lego/menon as the saying is
T. 7.68,

a)mfi\ me/son h(me/ra_s about mid-day
X. A. 4.4.1,

e)pi\ polu/ over a wide space
T. 1.18.

§1024
In words denoting a collection (996) of persons or facts:

to\ u(ph/koon the subjects
T. 6.69,

to\ barbariko/n the barbarian force
X. A. 1.2.1,

to\ cummaxiko/n the allied forces
T. 4.77 (and many words in -iko/n),

ta\ *(ellhnika/ Greek history
T. 1.97; and in words denoting festivals (

ta\ *)olu/mpia the Olympian games
X. H. 7.4.28).

§1025
With participles, especially in Thucydides:

to\ o)rgizo/menon th=s o)rgh=s their angry feelings
T. 2.59, th=s po/lews to\ ti_mw/menon the dignity of the State 2. 63. The action of the verb is here represented as taking place under particular circumstances or at a particular time. These participles are not dead abstractions, but abstract qualities in action.

§1026
A substantivized adjective may appear in the neuter plural as well as in the neuter singular:

ta\ decia\ tou= ke/ra_tos the right of the wing
X. A. 1.8.4,

th=s *salami=nos ta\ polla/ the greater part of Salamis
T. 2.94, e)pi\ plei=ston a)nqrw/pwn to the greatest part of mankind 1. 1, e)s tou=to dustuxi/a_s to this degree of misfortune 7. 86 (cp. 1325).
a. On the construction of

th=s gh=s h( pollh/ the greater part of the land
T. 2.56, see 1313.

§1027
In common expressions a definite noun is often implied (such as h(me/ra_ day, o(do/s way, xei/r hand).
a. Masculine: ko/lpos gulf, o( *)io/nios the Ionian gulf
T. 6.34, strato/s force, o( pezo/s the land force 1. 47.
b. Feminine: gh= land (xw/ra_ country）—a)po\ th=s e(autw=n from their own country
T. 1.15; ou)/q' h( *(ella\s ou)/q' h( ba/rbaros neither Greece nor barbaric land
D. 9.27; gnw/mh judgment: kata\ th\n e)mh/n according to my opinion
Ar. Eccl. 153, e)k th=s ni_kw/shs according to the prevailing opinion
X. A. 6.1.18; di/kh suit:

e)rh/mhn kathgorou=ntes bringing an accusation in a case where there is no defence
P. A. 18c; h(me/ra_ day:

th\n u(sterai/a_n the next day
X. C. 1.2.11,

th=| proterai/a| the day before
L. 19.22; ke/ras wing: to\ eu)w/numon the left wing
T. 4.96; meri/s part: ei)kosth/ a twentieth 6. 54; moi=ra portion: h( peprwme/nh (
I. 10.61) or h( ei(marme/nh (
D. 18.205) the allotted portion, destiny; nau=s ship: h( trih/rhs the ship with three banks of oars; o(do/s way: eu)qei/a| by the straight road
P. L. 716a, th\n taxi/sthn by the shortest way
X. A. 1.3.14; te/xnh art: mousikh/ the art of music
P. L. 668a; xei/r hand: e)n decia=| on the right hand
X. A. 1.5.1, e)c a)riste/ra_s on the left 4. 8. 2; yh=fos vote:

th\n e)nanti/a_n *ni_ki/a| e)/qeto he voted in opposition to Nicias
P. Lach. 184d.

§1028
The context often determines the substantive to be supplied: tou=ton a)ne/kragon w(s o)li/ga_s (plhga\_s) pai/seien they shouted that he had dealt him (too, 1063) few blows
X. A. 5.8.12, tri/a ta/lanta kai\ xi_li/a_s (draxma/_s) three talents and a thousand drachmas
D. 27.34; cp. a dollar and twenty (cents). Cp. 1572.

§1029
From such substantivized adjectives arose many prepositional and adverbial expressions of whose source the Greeks themselves had probably lost sight. Many of these seem to be analogues of phrases once containing o(do/s:

th\n a)/llws yhfi/zesqe you vote to no purpose
D. 19.181 (i.e. the way leading elsewhere than the goal),

a)po\ th=s prw/ths at the very beginning
T. 7.43, a)po\ th=s i)/shs on an equality 1. 15, e)c e)nanti/a_s from an opposite direction, facing 7. 44.

## AGREEMENT OF ATTRIBUTIVE ADJECTIVES

§1030
An attributive adjective belonging to more than one substantive agrees with the nearest:

to\n kalo\n ka)_gaqo\n a)/ndra kai\ gunai=ka eu)dai/mona ei)=nai/ fhmi the perfect man and woman are happy I maintain
P. G. 470e. In some cases it is repeated with each substantive (often for emphasis):

e(\n sw=m' e)/xwn kai\ yu_xh\n mi/an having one body and one soul
D. 19.227.

§1031
But occasionally the adjective agrees with the more important substantive:

o( si/glos du/natai e(pta\ o)bolou\s kai\ h(miwbo/lion *)attikou/s the siglus is worth seven and a half Attic obols
X. A. 1.5.6.

§1032
Of two adjectives with one substantive, one may stand in closer relation to the substantive, while the other qualifies the expression thus formed:

po/lis e)rh/mh mega/lh a large deserted-city
X. A. 1.5.4.

§1033
If one substantive has several attributive adjectives, these are sometimes added without a conjunction (by Asyndeton): kre/a_ a)/rneia, e)ri/feia, xoi/reia flesh of lambs, kids, swine
X. A. 4.5.31. This is commoner in poetry, especially when the adjectives are descriptive: e)/gxos bri_qu\ me/ga stibaro/n a spear heavy, huge, stout
*p 141.

§1034
Two adjectives joined by kai/ may form one combined notion in English, which omits the conjunction. So often with polu/s to emphasize the idea of plurality:

polla\ ka)_gaqa/ many blessings
X. A. 5.6.4,

polla\ kai\ deina/ many dreadful sufferings
D. 37.57.
a. kalo\s ka)_gaqo/s means an aristocrat (in the political sense), or is used of a perfect quality or action (in the moral sense) as
T. 4.40,
P. A. 21d.

§1035
An attributive adjective is often used in poetry instead of the attributive genitive: bi/h *(hra_klhei/h B 658 the might of Heracles (cp. “a Niobean daughter” Tennyson); rarely in prose:

potamo/s, eu)=ros pleqriai=os a river, a plethron in width
X. A. 4.6.4.

§1036
An attributive adjective belonging logically to a dependent genitive is often used in poetry with a governing substantive:

nei=kos a)ndrw=n cu/naimon kindred strife of men
S. A. 793 (for strife of kindred men). Rarely in prose in the case of the possessive pronoun:

e)n tw=| u(_mete/rw| a)sqenei= th=s gnw/mhs in the weakness of your purpose
T. 2.61.

§1037
An attributive adjective may dispense with its substantive when that substantive is expressed in the context: mete/xei th=s kalli/sths (te/xnhs)

tw=n texnw=n he shares in the fairest of the arts
P. G. 448c.

§1038
A substantivized participle may take the genitive rather than the case proper to the verb whence it is derived:

basile/ws prosh/kontes relations of the king
T. 1.128; contrast

*periklh=s o( e)moi\ prosh/kwn Pericles my relation
X. H. 1.7.21.

§1039
Adjectives used substantively may take an attributive:

oi( u(_me/teroi dusmenei=s your enemies
X. H. 5.2.33.

## PREDICATE ADJECTIVES

§1040
The predicate adjective is employed
a. With intransitive verbs signifying to be, become, and the like (917):

h( de\ xa/ris a)/dhlos gege/nhtai the favour has been concealed
Aes. 3.233. So with active verbs which take a preposition:

no/mous e)/qesqe e)p' a)dh/lois toi=s a)dikh/sousi you have enacted laws with regard to offenders who are unknown
D. 21.30.
b. With transitive verbs: (1) to qualify the object of the verb directly and immediately:

tou\s kakou\s xrhstou\s nomi/zein to judge bad men good
S. O. T. 609, (2) to express the result of the action (the proleptic use, 1579). So with au)/cein grow, ai)/rein raise with me/gas great, mete/wros on high, u(yhlo/s high, makro/s large.

§1041
With verbs of saying and thinking the predicate adjective is usually connected with its noun by ei)=nai, with verbs of perceiving, showing, by w)/n (2106):

ou)de/na ga\r oi)=mai daimo/nwn ei)=nai kako/n for I think no one of the gods is base
E. I. T. 391,

dhloi= yeudh= th\n diaqh/khn ou)=san it shows that the will is false
D. 45.34. But ei)=nai is sometimes omitted (945), as

ta\_s ga\r kala\_s pra/_ceis a(pa/_sa_s a)gaqa\_s w(mologh/samen for we have agreed that all honourable actions are good
P. Pr. 359e. On the omission of w)/n, see 2117. For ei)=nai with verbs of naming and calling, see 1615.

§1042
Several adjectives of time, place, order of succession, etc., are used as predicates where English employs an adverb or a preposition with its case:

a)fiknou=ntai tritai=oi they arrive on the third day
X. A. 5.3.2, kate/bainon skotai=oi they descended in the dark 4. 1. 10. In such cases the adjective is regarded as a quality of the subject; whereas an adverb would regard the manner of the action.
a. Time, place: xro/nios late, o)/rqrios in the morning, deuterai=os on the second day, postai=os how many days? u(pai/qrios in the open air.
b. Order of succession: prw=tos, pro/teros first, u(/steros later, me/sos in the midst, teleutai=os last, u(/statos last.
N.—When one action is opposed to another in order of sequence, the adverbs prw=ton, pro/teron, u(/staton, etc., not the adjectives prw=tos, etc.. must be used:

prw=ton me\n e)da/kru_e polu\n xro/non . . . ei)=ta de\ e)/lece toia/de first he wept for a long time, then he spoke as follows
X. A. 1.3.2. Hence distinguish

prw=tos th=| po/lei prose/balehe was the first to attack the city.

prw/th| th=| po/lei prose/balethe city was the first place he attacked.

prw=ton th=| po/lei prose/balehis first act was to attack the city.
The same rule applies in the case of mo/nos, mo/non, as mo/nhn th\n e)pistolh<*> e)/graya this is the only letter I wrote, mo/non e)/graya th\n e)pistolh/n I only wrote (but did not send) the letter. But this distinction is not always observed (
Aes. 3.69).

§1043
So also with adjectives of degree, mental attitude, manner, etc.:

fe/rontai oi( li/qoi polloi/ the stones are thrown in great numbers
X. A. 4.7.7,

tou\s nekrou\s u(pospo/ndous a)pe/dosan they restored the dead under a truce
T. 1.63,

oi( qeoi\ eu)menei=s pe/mpousi/ se the gods send you forth favourably
X. C. 1.6.2. So with me/gas high, a)/smenos gladly, e(kou/sios, e(kw/n willingly, o(/rkios under oath, ai)fni/dios suddenly. On a)/llos, see 1272.

## AGREEMENT OF PREDICATE ADJECTIVES (AND PARTICIPLES)

## WITH ONE SUBJECT

§1044
A circumstantial participle (2054) referring to a collective noun (996) may be plural:

to\ stra/teuma e)pori/zeto si=ton ko/ptontes tou\s bou=s the army provided itself with provisions by killing the cattle
X. A. 2.1.6. So after ou)dei/s, as ou)dei\s e)koimh/qh ( = pa/ntes e)n a)grupni/a| h)=san)

tou\s a)polwlo/tas penqou=ntes no one slept because they were all bewailing the dead
X. H. 2.2.3. Cp. 950.

§1045
A plural participle may be used with a dual verb:

e)gelasa/thn a)/mfw ble/yantes ei)s a)llh/lous both looked at each other and burst out laughing
P. Eu. 273d. A dual participle may be used with a plural verb: pou= pot' o)/nq' hu(rh/meqa; where in the world are we?
E. I. T. 777.

§1046
A dual subject may be followed by a plural predicate adjective or participle:

ei) ga/r tis fai/h tw\ po/lei tou/tw plei/stwn a)gaqw=n ai)ti/a_s gegenh=sqai if any one should assert that these two cities have been the cause of very many blessings
I. 12.156.

§1047
A predicate adjective is neuter singular when the subject is an infinitive, a sentence, or a general thought:

h(du\ pollou\s e)xqrou\s e)/xein ; is it pleasant to have many enemies?
D. 19.221, dh=lon d' o(/ti tau=t' e)sti\n a)lhqh= it is clear that these things are true 2. 19.

§1048
A predicate adjective referring to a masculine or feminine singular subject is often neuter singular and equivalent to a substantive. This occurs chiefly in statements of a general truth, where the subject refers to a whole class, not to an individual thing. Thus,

kalo\n ei)rh/nh peace is a fine thing
D. 19.336, a)/piston tai=s poli_- tei/ais h( turanni/s despotism is an object of mistrust to free states 1. 5,

mei=zon po/lis e(no\s a)ndro/s the state is larger than the individual
P. R. 368e. So also in the plural (1056).

§1049
So with names of places:

e)/sti de\ h( *xairw/neia e)/sxaton th\s *boiwti/a_s Chaeronea is on the frontier of Boeotia
T. 4.76.

§1050
A predicate superlative agrees in gender either with the subject or (usually) with a dependent genitive: no/swn xalepw/tatos fqo/nos envy is the most fell of diseases Men. fr. 535, su/mboulos a)gaqo\s xrhsimw/taton a(pa/ntwn tw=n kthma/twn a good counsellor is the most useful of all possessions
I. 2.53.

§1051
For a predicate adjective used where English has an adverb, cp. 1042.

§1052
A predicate adjective is often used in the neuter plural (especially with verbal adjectives in -to/s and -te/os in Thucydides and the poets): e)peidh\ e(toi=ma h)=n, a)nh/geto when (all) was ready, he put out to sea
T. 2.56, a)du/nata h)=n tou\s *lokrou\s a)mu/_nesqai it was impossible to resist the Locrians 4. 1, e)do/kei e)pixeirhte/a ei)=nai they decided to make the attempt 2. 3. Cp. 1003 a.

## WITH TWO OR MORE SUBJECTS

§1053
With two or more substantives a predicate adjective is plural, except when it agrees with the nearer subject:

fo/bos kai\ no/mos i(kano\s e)/rwta kwlu/_ein fear and the law are capable of restraining love
X. C. 5.1.10,

pollw=n de\ lo/gwn kai\ qoru/bou gignome/nou there arising much discussion and confusion
D. 3.4. See 968.

§1054
With substantives denoting persons of like gender, a predicate adjective is of the same gender: *)aga/qwn kai\ *swkra/ths loipoi/ Agathon and Socrates are left
P. S. 193c.

§1055
When the persons are of different gender, the masculine prevails:

w(s ei)=de pate/ra te kai\ mhte/ra kai\ a)delfou\s kai\ th\n e(autou= gunai=ka ai)xmalw/tous gegenhme/nous, e)da/kru_se when he saw that his father and mother and brothers and wife had been made prisoners of war, he burst into tears
X. C. 3.1.7.
a. But persons are sometimes regarded as things:

e)/xw au)tw=n kai\ te/kna kai\ gunai=kas frourou/mena I have their children and wives under guard
X. A. 1.4.8.

§1056
With substantives denoting things of like gender a predicate adjective is of the same gender and plural. A neuter plural with the singular verb is often preferred:

eu)ge/neiai/ te kai\ duna/meis kai\ ti_mai\ dh=la/ e)stin a)gaqa\ o)/nta noble birth and power and honour are clearly good things
P. Eu. 279b.

§1057
When the things are of different gender, a predicate adjective is neuter plural with singular verb:

li/qoi te kai\ pli/nqoi kai\ cu/la kai\ ke/ramos a)ta/ktws e)rri_mme/na ou)de\n xrh/sima/ e)stin stones and bricks and pieces of wood and tiles thrown together at random are useless
X. M. 3.1.7.

§1058
When the substantives denote both persons and things, a predicate adjective is—a. plural, and follows the gender of the person, if the person is more important, or if the thing is treated as a person: gra/|dia kai\ gero/ntia kai\

pro/bata o)li/ga kai\ bou=s kataleleimme/nous old women and old men and a few sheep and oxen that had been left behind
X. A. 6.3.22,

h( tu/xh kai\ *fi/lippos h)=san tw=n e)/rgwn ku/_rioi Fortune and Philip were masters of the situation
Aes. 2.118,
b. or is neuter plural if the person is treated like a thing:

h( kalli/sth poli_tei/a_ te kai\ o( ka/llistos a)nh\r loipa\ a)\n h(mi=n ei)/h dielqei=n we should still have to treat of the noblest polity and the noblest man
P. R. 562a.

§1059
The verbal and the adjective predicate may agree with the first of two subjects as the more important:

*bra_si/da_s kai\ to\ plh=qos e)pi\ ta\ mete/wra th=s po/lews e)tra/peto boulo/menos kat' a)/kra_s e(lei=n au)th/n Brasidas with the bulk of his troops turned to the upper part of the city wishing to capture it completely
T. 4.112.
For further uses of predicate adjectives, see 1150 ff., 1168 ff., 2647.

## ATTRACTION OF PREDICATE NOUNS WITH THE INFINITIVE TO THE CASE OF THE OBJECT OF THE GOVERNING VERB

§1060
When the subject of the infinitive is the same as a genitive or dative depending on the governing verb, it is often omitted.

§1061
A predicate adjective referring to a genitive regularly stands in the genitive, but a predicate substantive or participle generally stands in the accusative in agreement with the unexpressed subject of the infinitive:

*ku/_rou e)de/onto w/s proqu_mota/tou gene/sqai they entreated Cyrus to show himself as zealous as possible
X. H. 1.5.2,

u(po\ tw=n deome/nwn mou prosta/thn gene/sqai by those who begged me to become their chief
X. C. 7.2.23, de/omai u(_mw=n e)qelh=sai/ mou a)kou=sai, u(pologizome/nous to\ plh=qos tw=n ai)tiw=n I beg of you that you be willing to listen to me, paying heed to the number of charges
Aes. 2.1.

§1062
A predicate substantive, adjective, or participle referring to a dative stands in the dative or in the accusative in agreement with the unexpressed subject of the infinitive:

nu=n soi e)/cestin a)ndri\ gene/sqai now it is in your power to prove yourself a man
X. A. 7.1.21,

*lakedaimoni/ois e)/cestin u(_mi=n fi/lous gene/sqai it is in your power to become friends to the Lacedaemonians
T. 4.29,

e)/docen au)toi=s . . . e)coplisame/nois proi+_e/nai they decided to arm themselves fully and to advance
X. A. 2.1.2, e)/docen au)toi=s profulaka\_s katasth/santas sugkalei=n tou\s stratiw/ta_s they decided to station pickets and to assemble the soldiers 3. 2. 1,

sumfe/rei au)toi=s fi/lous ei)=nai ma=llon h)\ polemi/ous it is for their interest to be friends rather than enemies
X. O. 11.23.
For predicate nouns in the nominative or accusative in agreement with omitted subject of the infinitive, see 1973-1975.

## COMPARISON OF ADJECTIVES (AND ADVERBS）

## POSITIVE

§1063
The positive, used to imply that something is not suited or inadequate for the purpose in question, is especially common before an infinitive with or without w(/ste (w(s): (to\ u(/dwr) yu_xro/n e)stin w(/ste lou/sasqai the water is too cold for bathing
X. M. 3.13.3, nh=es o)li/gai a)mu/_nein ships too few to defend
T. 1.50, makro\n a)\n ei)/h moi le/gein it would take too long for me to state
And. 2.15.

§1064
A positive adjective followed by the genitive of the same adjective has, in poetry, the force of a superlative:

kaka\ kakw=n woe of woe
S. O. C. 1238.

§1065

ma=llon h)/ rather than, more . . . than may be used after a positive:

proqu/_mws ma=llon h)\ fi/lws more prompt than kindly
A. Ag. 1591.

## COMPARATIVE

§1066
The comparative expresses contrast or comparison. Thus, deci/teros is right in contrast to its opposite, a)ristero/s left. Cp. 1082 b. Usually comparison is expressed, as

eu)= te kai\ xei=ron well or ill
T. 2.35.
a. When the positive precedes, ma=llon alone may stand for the comparative; as in e)kei=noi/ te a)/cioi e)pai/nou kai\ e)/ti ma=llon (i.e. a)ciw/teroi)

oi( pate/res they are worthy of praise and still more worthy are our fathers
T. 2.36.
b. The persons or things with which comparison is made may include all others of the same class: h(mw=n o( gerai/teros the elder (= eldest) of us
X. C. 5.1.6.

§1067
The comparative is sometimes used merely as an intensive and does not differ essentially from the positive: tou/twn katadee/steros at a disadvantage with (inferior to) these men
D. 27.2.

§1068
For the use of ma=llon instead of the comparative, and ma/lista instead of the superlative, see 323. When either form can be used, that with ma=llon or ma/lista is more emphatic. Thucydides sometimes uses ple/on (ti), to\ ple/on instead of ma=llon.

§1069
The comparative degree may be followed by the genitive (1431) or by h)/ than: sofw/teros e)mou= or sofw/teros h)\ e)gw/ wiser than I. The genitive may precede or follow the comparative. With h)/, the persons or things compared usually stand in the same case, and always so when they are connected by the same verb:

filw= ga\r ou) se\ ma=llon h)\ do/mous e)mou/s for I do not love thee more than my own house
E. Med. 327.
a. The genitive is usual if two subjects would have the same verb in common; as oi( *krh=tes braxu/tera tw=n *persw=n e)to/ceuon the Cretans shot a shorter distance than the Persians ( = h)\ oi( *pe/rsai)
X. A. 3.3.7.
b. When two objects have the same verb in common: if the object stands (1) in the accusative, the genitive is preferred, as

e)moi\ dokei= *ku=ros, ou(/stinas a)\n o(ra=| a)gaqou/s, filei=n ou)de\n h(=tton e(autou= Cyrus seems to me to love all whom he finds excellent quite as much as he loves himself
X. C. 2.3.12, but the accusative is not uncommon, as
E. Med. 327 quoted above; (2) in the dative, the genitive is frequent, as

prosh/kei moi ma=llon e(te/rwn . . . a)/rxein it behooves me rather than others to rule
T. 6.16; (3) in the genitive, the genitive is very rare (
X. M. 4.3.10). Here h)/ is preferred to the genitive for the sake of euphony: oi( ga\r ponhroi\ polu\ pleio/nwn eu)ergesiw=n h)\ oi( xrhstoi\ (not tw=n xrhstw=n)

de/ontai for the wicked need more favours than the good
X. M. 2.6.27.
c. The genitive is often used where h)/ would be followed by some other case than nominative or accusative, or by a preposition: tau=ta toi=s o(pli/_tais ou)x h(=sson tw=n nautw=n ( = h)\ toi=s nau/tais)

parakeleu/omai I address these exhortations to the hoplites not less than to the sailors
T. 7.63, (dei= ble/pein) ei)s th\n e)mpeiri/a_n ma=llon th=s a)reth=s ( = h)\ ei)s th\n a)reth/n) we must look at skill more than (at) courage Aristotle, Politics 1309 b 5.
d. e)la/_ttwn (xei/rwn, e)ndee/steros, u(/steros, etc.) ou)deno/s inferior to none, greater than all; here h)/ is not used). Thus,

douleu/ein doulei/a_n ou)demia=s h(=tton ai)sxra/_n to endure a most disgraceful slavery
X. M. 1.5.6.

§1070
The word following h)/ may be the subject of a new verb (expressed or understood): h(mei=s u(po\ krei/ttonos didaska/lou pepaideu/meqa h)\ ou(=toi we have been educated by a better teacher than they (have been)
X. C. 2.3.13; but this word is more often attracted into the case of the preceding word: tine\s kai\ e)k deinote/rwn h)\ toiw=nde ( = h)\ toia/de e)sti/n)

e)sw/qhsan some have been rescued from dangers even greater than these
T. 7.77. The genitive is also common without h)/:

le/gwn o(/ti ou)/pw . . . tou/tou h(di/_oni oi)/nw| e)pitu/xoi saying that he had never met with sweeter wine than this
X. A. 1.9.25.

§1071

w(s for h)/ is rare, and suspected by some. But cp.
A. Pr. 629,
P. A. 30b, 36 d, R. 526 c.

§1072

ma=llon h)/ may be used though a comparative precedes: ai(retw/tero/n e)sti maxome/nous a)poqnh/|skein ma=llon h)/ feu/gontas sw/|zesqai it is more desirable for men to die fighting (rather) than to save themselves by running away
X. C. 3.3.51. Here ma=llon h)/ is to be taken with the verb.

§1073
Instead of the genitive or h)/, the prepositions a)nti/, pro/ (w. gen.) or pro/s, para/ (w. accus.) are sometimes used with the comparative: katerga/sasqai ai(retw/teron ei)=nai to\n kalo\n qa/naton a)nti\ tou= ai)sxrou= bi/ou to make a noble death more desirable than (instead of) a shameful life X. R.
L. 9.1, mh\ pai=das peri\ plei/onos poiou= pro\ tou= dikai/ou do not consider children of more account than (before) justice
P. Cr. 54b, xeimw\n mei/zwn para\ th\n kaqesthkui=an w(/ra_n a cold too severe for (in comparison with) the actual time of year
T. 4.6.

§1074
In statements of number and measure h)/ may be omitted after the adverbial comparatives ple/on (plei=n) more, e)/la_tton (mei=on) less, which do not alter their case and number: pe/mpei ou)k e)/la_tton de/ka fe/rontas pu=r he sends not less than ten men carrying fire
X. H. 4.5.4, po/lis ple/on pentakisxi_li/wn a)ndrw=n a city of more than 5000 men 5. 3. 16. Even when h)/ is kept, ple/on (plei=n), etc., remains unchanged: e)n plei=n ( = plei/osin)

h)\ dia_kosi/ois e)/tesin in more than 200 years
D. 24.141,

toco/ta_s plei=n h)\ ei)/kosi mu_ria/das more bowmen than 20 myriads
X. C. 2.1.6.
a. In place of the adverbial ple/on, etc., we find also the adjectival forms with or without h)/ or with the genitive:

toco/ta_s plei/ous h)\ tetrakisxi_li/ous more bowmen than 4000
X. C. 2.1.5, e)/th gegonw\s plei/w e(bdomh/konta more than 70 years old
P. A. 17d,

i:ppe/a_s plei/ous tria_kosi/wn more than 300 horse
X. H. 1.3.10.

§1075
The genitive sometimes occurs together with h)/, and either when the genitive has a separate construction, or is a pronoun to which the h)/ clause stands as an appositive, or of which it is explanatory. Thus,

proh/|ei ple/on . . . h)\ de/ka stadi/wn he advanced more than ten stades
X. H. 4.6.5 (here ple/on is treated as a substantive), ti/s ga\r a)\n ge/noito tau/ths mani/a_ mei/zwn h)\ . . . h(ma=s kakw=s poiei=n; for what madness could be greater than (this) . . . to use us ill?
Is. 1.20. Cp. 1070.

§1076

Compendious Comparison.—The possessor, rather than the object possessed, may be put in the genitive after a comparative: ei) d' h(mei=s i(ppiko\n kthsai/meqa mh\ xei=ron tou/twn ( = tou= tou/twn i(ppikou=) but if we should raise a cavalry-force not inferior to theirs
X. C. 4.3.7.

§1077

Comparison with a Noun representing a clause.—When one person or thing is to be compared, not with another person or thing in regard to its quality, but with an entire idea expressed by a clause (e.g. h)\ w(/ste with the infinitive, h)\ w(s with the potential optative, or h)/ and a finite verb), this clause may be abridged into a substantive or a participle. Thus, pra=gma e)lpi/dos krei=sson an event beyond our expectations (too great to be expected)
T. 2.64, proswte/rw tou= kairou= proi+o/ntes advancing further than the proper measure (i.e. further than they should have gone)
X. A. 4.3.34, w(s tw=n ge paro/ntwn ou)k a)\n pra/_cantes xei=ron in the belief that they could not fare worse than at present (h)\ ta\ paro/nta e)sti/n)
T. 7.67.

§1078

Reflexive Comparison.—The comparative followed by the reflexive pronoun in the genitive is used to denote that an object displays a quality in a higher degree than usual. The degree of increase is measured by comparison with the subject itself. au)to/s is often added to the subject:

au)toi\ au(tw=n eu)maqe/steroi gi/gnontai they learn more easily than before
I. 15.267,

plousiw/teroi e(autw=n gigno/menoi becoming richer than they were before
T. 1.8. Cp. 1093.

§1079

Proportional Comparison.—After a comparative, h)\ kata/ with the accusative (1690. 2 c), or h)\ w(/ste, h)\ w(s, rarely h)/ alone, with the infinitive (not with the indicative), denote too high or too low a degree:

o(/pla e)/ti plei/w h)\ kata\ tou\s nekrou\s e)lh/fqh more arms were taken than there were men slain
T. 7.45,

fobou=mai mh/ ti mei=zon h)\ w(/ste fe/rein du/nasqai kako\n th=| po/lei sumbh=| I fear lest there should befall the State an evil too great for it to be able to bear
X. M. 3.5.17 (2264).

§1080

Double Comparison.—Two adjectives (or adverbs) referring to the same subject, when compared with each other, are both put in the comparative; h)/ is always used:

h( ei)rh/nh a)nagkaiote/ra_ h)\ kalli/_wn a peace inevitable rather than honourable
Aes. 3.69,

suntomw/teron h)\ safe/steron dialexqh=nai to discourse briefly rather than clearly
I. 6.24.
a. ma=llon may be used with the first adjective in the positive (cp. 1065), and h)/ before the second:

pro/qu_mos ma=llon h)\ sofwte/ra_ with more affection than prudence
E. Med. 485.

§1081
A comparative may follow a positive to mark the contrast with it: kai\ mi_kra\ kai\ mei/zw both small and great(er)
D. 21.14.

§1082
The comparative may stand alone, the second part being implied.
a. That which is exceeded is indicated by the sense only: oi( sofw/teroi the wiser (those wiser than the rest); e)n ei)rh/nh| ai( po/leis a)mei/nous ta\_s gnw/ma_s e)/xousin in time of peace States are actuated by higher convictions (than in time of war)
T. 3.82. So ti new/teron something new (more recent than that already known)
P. Pr. 310a (often = a calamity or a revolutionary movement);

u(/steron h(=kon they came too late
T. 7.27; and often where we supply is usual (right, fitting, etc.).
b. The Hom. qhlu/terai gunai=kes implies a comparison with men. In *ku=ros . . . e)gego/nei mhtro\s a)mei/nonos, patro\s de\ u(podeeste/rou Cyrus was born of a mother of superior, but of a father of inferior race (
Hdt. 1.91) the comparison is between the qualities of mother and father respectively. Cp. 313 b.
c. The comparative denotes excess:

mei/zosin e)/rgois e)pixeirou=ntes ou) mi_kroi=s kakoi=s peripi/_ptousi by entering upon undertakings too great they encounter no slight troubles
X. M. 4.2.35.
d. The comparative is used to soften an expression (rather, somewhat):

a)groiko/teron somewhat boorishly
P. G. 486c,

a)mele/steron e)poreu/eto he proceeded rather carelessly
X. H. 4.8.36. Here the quality is compared with its absence or with its opposite.

§1083
The comparative is often used where English requires the positive:

ou) ga\r xei=ron polla/kis a)kou/ein for 'tis not a bad thing to hear often
P. Ph. 105a.

§1084

Strengthened forms.—The comparative may be strengthened by e)/ti, pollw=|, makrw=| (1513), polu/ (1609), polu\ e)/ti, etc. ma=llon is sometimes used with the comparative:

ai)sxunthrote/rw ma=llon tou= de/ontos more bashful than they ought to be
P. G. 487b. So the correlative o(/sw|, o(/son:

o(/sw| mei/zous ei)si\ ta\_s o)/yeis, tosou/tw| ma=llon o)rgh=s a)/cioi/ ei)si the braver they are to appearances, the more they deserve our anger
L. 10.29.

## SUPERLATIVE

§1085
The superlative expresses either the highest degree of a quality (the relative superlative: o( sofw/tatos a)nh/r the wisest man) or a very high degree of a quality (the absolute superlative, which does not take the article: a)nh\r sofw/tatos a very wise man). The relative superlative is followed by the genitive of the person or thing surpassed (1315, 1434). On the agreement, see 1050.
a. The class to which an individual, marked by the superlative, belongs, may be designated by a genitive of the divided whole (1315): o( sofw/tatos tw=n *(ellh/nwn the wisest of the Greeks. So often by pa/ntwn: pa/ntwn a)nqrw/pwn a)gnwmone/statoi the most senseless of all men Lyc. 54. On the superlative with a)/llwn, see 1434.
b. With two the comparative exhausts all the degrees of comparison: hence pro/teros and prw=tos, u(/steros and u(/statos, e(ka/teros each of two, and e(/kastos each of several, are carefully to be distinguished.

§1086

Strengthened Forms.—The superlative may be strengthened by prefixing o(/ti or w(s, rarely h(=| (also o(/son or o(/pws in poetry): o(/ti plei=stoi as many men as possible, o(/ti ta/xista as quickly as possible,

h(=| a)/riston the very best way
X. C. 7.5.82 (o(/pws a)/rista
A. Ag. 600). o(/ti or w(/s is always added when a preposition precedes the superlative:

w(s ei)s stenw/taton into as narrow compass as possible
X. O. 18.8. w(s and o(/ti may be used together:

w(s o(/ti be/ltiston e)me/ gene/sqai for me to become as good as may be
P. S. 218d.
a.With w(s and h)=|, rarely with o(/ph| (not with o(/ti), a form of du/namai or oi(=o/s te/ ei)mi, may be employed:

dihgh/somai u(_mi=n w(s a)\n du/nwmai dia\ braxuta/twn I will relate to you in the briefest terms I can
I. 21.2.

§1087

o(=ios may strengthen the superlative:

o(rw=ntes ta\ pra/_gmata ou)x oi(=a be/ltista e)n th=| po/lei o)/nta observing that affairs are not in the very best state in the city
L. 13.23. If o)/sos or o(po/sos take the place of oi(=os, a form, or a synonym, of du/namai is usually added:

h)/gagon summa/xous o(po/sous plei/stous e)duna/mhn I brought the very largest number of allies I could
X. C. 4.5.29. o(poi=os is rare (Thuc., Plato).

§1088

ei(=s a)nh/r in apposition to the person designated may be added to strengthen the superlative: *)antifw=n plei=sta ei(=s a)nh\r duna/menos w)felei=n Antiphon being able to render (most aid as one man) aid beyond any other man
T. 8.68.

§1089

e)n toi=s is used before the superlative in all genders and numbers (esp. in Hdt., Thuc., Plato):

w)mh\ h( sta/sis . . . e)/doce ma=llon, dio/ti e)n toi=s prw/th e)ge/neto the revolution seemed the more cruel since it was the first
T. 3.81, e)n toi=s plei=stai dh' nh=es a(/m' au)toi=s e)ge/nonto they had the very largest number of ships 3. 17.

§1090

ma/lista, or plei=ston, me/giston, occurs with the superlative:

oi( ma/lista a)nohto/tatoi the very stupidest
P. Tim. 92a. In poetry baqu- has the effect of a superlative:

baqu/ploutos exceeding rich
A. Supp. 555.

§1091

kai/ even, pollw=|, makrw=| (1513), polu/ (1609), para\ polu/, pa/nta (ta\ pa/nta), the correlative o(/sw| also strengthen the superlative.

§1092
In poetry (rarely in prose) a superlative may be strengthened by the addition of the genitive of the same adjective in the positive: w)= kakw=n ka/kiste oh, vilest of the vile
S. O. T. 334.

§1093
Reflexive comparison (cp. 1078) occurs with the superlative:

a)mblu/tata au)to\s au(tou= o(ra=| his sight is at its dullest
P. L. 715d.

## ADVERBS

§1094
Adverbs are of two kinds
a. Ordinary adverbs, denoting manner, degree, time, place, etc. Ordinary adverbs qualify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs, and (rarely) substantives:

o)/pisqen geno/menos getting behind
X. A. 1.8.24, eu)qu\s e)bo/a_ straightway he shouted 1. 8. 1,

fanero\n h)/dh already clear
L. 4.6,

polu\ qa=tton much more quickly
X. A. 1.5.2, eu)= ma/la very easily 6. 1. 1,

ei)ko/tws tro/pon tina/ in a way reasonably
D. 8.41,

ma/la sumfora/_ a great misfortune
X. C. 4.2.5,

ma/la strathgo/s an excellent general
X. H. 6.2.39.
b. Sentence adverbs (or particles) are adverbs that affect the sentence as a whole or give emphasis to particular words of any kind. Greek has many sentence adverbs, some of which are treated more fully under Particles.
Such are words of interrogation (h)=, a)=ra, mw=n); of affirmation and confidence (dh/ now, indeed, dh=ta surely, ge/ at least, even, h)= really, mh/n in truth, nh/ surely, toi/ surely); of uncertainty (i)/sws, pou/, ta/xa perhaps); of negation (ou), mh/, ou)/toi, mh/toi, etc.); of limitation (a)/n 1761 ff.).

§1095
The equivalents of an ordinary adverb are: an oblique case (e)basi/leuen ei)/kosin e)/th he reigned for twenty years, 1581, 1582; a)kou/ein spoudh=| to listen attentively, th=| u(sterai/a| e)poreu/onto they proceeded on the next day, and many other datives, 1527 b; h(=ke th\n taxi/sthn he came in the quickest way, and many other accusatives, 1606-1611); an oblique case with a preposition (dia\ ta/xous h)=lqe he came quickly = taxe/ws, a)p' oi)/kou o(rmw=mai I start from home = oi)/koqen, e)n tw=| e)mfanei= clearly, e)di/dou pro\s th\n a)ci/a_n he gave according to merit = a)ci/ws, pro\s bi/a_n forcibly = biai/ws); a participle (gelw=n ei)=pe he said with a laugh, laughingly). (Furthermore, a clause in a complex sentence, as

ei)sphdh/santes . . . qa=tton h)\ w(/s tis a)\n w)/|eto leaping in more quickly than one would have thought
X. A. 1.5.8; cp. 2189. 3.)

§1096
In the attributive position an ordinary adverb may serve as an adjective:

e)n tw=| plhsi/on paradei/sw| in the neighbouring park
X. A. 2.4.16,

o( e)kei=qen a)/ggelos the messenger from that quarter
P. R. 619b,

taraxh\ h( to/te the confusion of that time
L. 6.35. See 1153 e. N.

§1097

a. An ordinary adverb qualifying a verb is often so used that it may be referred to the subject or object of the sentence where an adjective could stand. Thus, w(/ste . . . u(polamba/nesqai meizo/nws h)\ kata\ th\n a)ci/a_n so as to be regarded as greater (lit. in a greater way) than (according to) their deserts
I. 11.24.
b. di/xa and xwri/s apart, e(ka/s far, e)ggu/s near and some other ordinary adverbs supply, with ei)=nai or gi/gnesqai, the place of missing adjectives. Thus,

xwri\s sofi/a_ e)sti\n a)ndrei/a_s wisdom is different from courage
P. Lach. 195a.

§1098
For adjectives used adverbially, see 1042; for degrees of comparison, 345, 1068; for the genitive or dative after adverbs, 1437 ff., 1499 ff.; for adverbs used as prepositions, 1700 ff.; for a relative adverb used with names of things as an equivalent of a relative pronoun preceded by e)n, ei)s, e)c, see 2499.

## THE ARTICLE—ORIGIN AND DEVELOPMENT

§1099
The article o(, h(, to/, was originally a demonstrative pronoun, and as such supplied the place of the personal pronoun of the third person. By gradual weakening it became the definite article. It also served as a relative pronoun (1105). (Cp. Germ. der, demonstrative article and relative; French le from ille.) o( as a demonstrative is still retained in part in Attic prose (1106), while the beginnings of its use as the article are seen even in Homer (1102).

## o(, h(, to/ IN HOMER

§1100
In Homer o(, h(, to/ is usually a demonstrative pronoun and is used substantively or adjectively; it also serves as the personal pronoun of the third person:

a)lla\ to\ qauma/zw but I marvel at this
d 655, to\n lwbhth=ra e)pesbo/lon this prating brawler B 275, th\n d' e)gw\ ou) lu/_sw but her I will not release A 29.

§1101
In its substantival use o( either marks a contrast or recalls the subject (the anaphoric use). But with a)lla/, de/, au)ta/r the subject is generally changed. It often precedes an explanatory relative clause: tw=n oi(\ nu=n brotoi/ ei)si of those who are now mortal men A 272.

§1102

o(, h(, to/ often approaches to its later use as the definite article or is actually so used: to\n me/n . . . to\n d' e(/teron E 145 (cp. 1107). a. The substantive often stands in apposition, and is added, as an afterthought, to the demonstrative (especially o( de/) which is still an independent pronoun:

au)ta\r o( toi=si ge/rwn o(do\n h(gemo/neuen but he, the old man, was leading the way for them
w 225. In some cases the appositive is needed to complete the sense:

e)pei\ to/ ge kalo\n a)koue/men e)sti\n a)oidou= since this—to listen to a minstrel—is a good thing
a 370. b. Often with adjectives and participles used substantively, with pronouns, and adverbs; especially when a contrast or distinction is implied:

oi( a)/lloi the others
*f 371, ta\ e)sso/mena the things that are to be A 70, to\ pa/ros formerly N 228. The attributive adj. before the noun:

tou\s sou/s thy
*y 572,

ta\ me/gista a)/eqla the greatest prizes
*y 640; and in apposition: *)=iron to\n a)lh/thn Irus, the beggar
s 333. Hom. has path\r ou(mo/s *q 360 (but does not use o( path\r o( e)mo/s).

§1103
In Hom. o( contrasts two objects, indicates a change of person, or a change of action on the part of the same person. Attic o( defines.

§1104
The transition from the demonstrative to the article is so gradual that it is often impossible to distinguish between the two. Ordinarily Homer does not use the article where it is required in Attic prose. The Epic use is adopted in general by the lyric poets and in the lyric parts of tragedy. Even in tragic dialogue the article is less common than in prose. Hdt. has o( de/ and he, o( ga/r for he.

## o(, h(, to/ AS A RELATIVE

§1105
The demonstrative o(, h(, to/ is used as a relative pronoun in Homer only when the antecedent is definite (cp. that): teu/xea d' e)cena/rice, ta/ oi( po/re xa/lkeos *)/arhs he stripped off the arms that brazen Ares had given him H 146. The tragic poets use only the forms in t-, and chiefly to avoid hiatus or to produce position:

ktei/nousa tou\s ou) xrh\ ktanei=n slaying those whom it is not right to slay
E. And. 810. (o(/ = o(/s
E. Hipp. 525.) On the use in Herodotus, see 338 D. 3.

## o(, h(, to/ AS A DEMONSTRATIVE IN ATTIC PROSE

§1106
The demonstrative force of o(, h(, to/ survives chiefly in connection with particles (me/n, de/, ge/, toi/; and with kai/ preceding o().

§1107

o( is a demonstrative commonly before me/n, de/, and especially in contrasted expressions: o( me/n . . . o( de/ the one, this . . . the other, that, as in

oi( me\n e)poreu/onto, oi( d' ei(/ponto the one party proceeded, the other followed
X. A. 3.4.16.

§1108
The reference may be indefinite; in which case ti\s is often added:

tou\s me\n a)pe/kteine, tou\s d' e)ce/balen some he put to death, and others he expelled
X. A. 1.1.7, oi( me/n tines a)pe/qnh|skon, oi( d' e)/feugon some were killed, but others escaped C. 3. 2. 10.

§1109
With prepositions the order is usually inverted: e)k me\n tw=n, ei)s de\ ta/ (1663 a).

§1110
In late writers (but in Demosthenes) the relative is used as in 1107: po/leis, a_<*>s me\n a)nairw=n, ei)s a_<*>s de\ tou\s fuga/das kata/gwn destroying some cities, into others bringing back their exiles
D. 18.71 (the first instance).

§1111
Note the adverbial expressions: to\ (ta\) me/n . . . to\ (ta\) de/ on the one hand . . . on the other hand, partly . . . partly (so also tou=to me/n . . . tou=to de/ 1256); to\ de/ ti partly, th=| me/n . . . th=| de/ in this way . . . in that way, to\ de/ whereas (1112), tw=| toi therefore.

§1112

o( de/, h( de/, to\ de/ (without a preceding me/n clause) often mean but (or and) he, she, this. In the nominative the person referred to is usually different from the subject of the main verb: *ku=ros di/dwsin au)tw=| mu_ri/ous da_reikou/s: o( de\ labw\n to\ xru_si/on k.t.l. Cyrus gives him (Clearchus) 10,000 darics; and he taking the money, etc.
X. A. 1.1.9, tau=ta a)pagge/llousi toi=s stratiw/tais: toi=s de\ u(poyi/a_ h)=n o(/ti a)/goi pro\s basile/a_ they report this to the soldiers; and they had a suspicion that he was leading (them) against the king
X. A. 1.3.21,

to\ d' ou)k e)/sti toiou=ton whereas this is not so
P. A. 37a.

## VARIOUS USES OF o( (o(/s), h( (h(/), to/ DEMONSTRATIVE

§1113
As a personal pronoun, chiefly after kai/, and in the nominative: kai\ o(/s (h(/) and he (she):

kai\ oi(\ ei)=pon and they said
X. A. 7.6.4. Also in

h)= d' o(/s and he said
P. R. 327c (792). So kai\ to/n (th/n) used as the accusative of kai\ o(/s, as subject of a following infinitive in indirect discourse: kai\ to\n ei)pei=n and (he said that) he said
P. S. 174a.

§1114
In the nominative o(/s, h(/, are usually thus written. Some write o(/, h(/, oi(/, ai(/ when these words are used as demonstratives; but o(\ me/n . . . o(\ de/ is rare.
a. The forms o(/s, h(/, here apparently relatives with an older demonstrative force, may be in reality demonstratives, o(/s being the demonstrative (article) o( to which the nominative sign -s has been added. From this o(/s may be derived, by analogy, the demonstrative use of o(/, and of oi)=s, ou(/s in fixed expressions (1110).

§1115
Also in

to\n kai\ to/n this one and that one
L. 1.23,

to\ kai\ to/ this and that
D. 9.68, ta\ kai\ ta/
D. 21.141,

ou)/te toi=s ou)/te toi=s neither to these nor to those
P. L. 701e. In the nom.

o(\s kai\ o(/s such and such an one
Hdt. 4.68.

§1116
In an oblique case before the relatives o(/s, o(/sos, oi)=os:

to/n te *eu)qu/kriton . . . kai\ to\n o(\s e)/rh despo/ths tou/tou ei)=nai, ma/rturas pare/comai and as witness I will produce both Euthycritus and the man who said he was his master
L. 23.8,

o)re/getai tou= o(\ e)/stin i)/son he aims at that which is equal
P. Ph. 75b, and often in Plato in defining philosophical terms.

§1117
Rarely with prepositions, except in pro\ tou= (or protou=) before this time
T. 1.118. On e)n toi=s with the superlative, see 1089.

## o/, h(, to/ AS AN ARTICLE (the) IN ATTIC (ESPECIALLY IN PROSE)

§1118
The article o(, h(\, to/ marks objects as definite and known, whether individuals (the particular article) or classes (the generic article). The context must determine the presence of the generic article.
a. There is no indefinite article in Greek, but a, an is often represented by ti\s (1267).

## THE PARTICULAR ARTICLE

§1119
The particular article denotes individual persons or things as distinguished from others of the same kind. Thus, mai/netai a(/_nqrwpos the man is mad (a definite person, distinguished from other men)
P. Phae. 268c.

§1120
Special uses of the particular article. The particular article defines
a. Objects well known: o( tw=n e(pta\ sofw/tatos *so/lwn Solon the wisest of the Seven (Sages)
P. Tim. 20d.
b Objects already mentioned or in the mind of the speaker or writer (the anaphoric article): ei)=pon o(/ti ta/lanton a)rguri/ou e(/toimos ei)/hn dou=nai . . . o( de\ labw\n to\ ta/lanton k.t.l. I said that I was ready to give him a talent of silver . . . and he taking the talent, etc.
L. 12.9-10.
c. Objects specially present to the senses or mind (the deictic article):

labe to\ bibli/on take the book
P. Th. 143c,

boulo/menos th\n ma/xhn poih=sai wishing to fight the battle
T. 4.91. Hence the article is regularly used with demonstrative pronouns (1176).
N.—The foregoing (a - c) uses recall the old demonstrative force of the article. Words that ordinarily have no article may receive the article when this older force is present.
d. Objects particularized by an attributive or by a following description:

o( dh=mos o( *)aqhnai/wn the people of the Athenians
Aes. 3.116,

le/ge th\n e)pistolh/n, h(\n e)/pemyen read the letter that he sent
D. 18.39. Cp. 1178 d.
e. Objects marked as usual or proper under the circumstances: to\ me/ros tw=n yh/fwn o( diw/kwn ou)k e)/laben the prosecutor did not get the (requisite) part of the votes
D. 18.103.
f. Objects representative of their class (the distributive article, which resembles the generic use; often translated by a, each):

u(pisxnei=tai dw/sein tri/a h(mida_reika\ tou= mhno\s tw=| stratiw/th| he promises to give each soldier three half-darics a month
X. A. 1.3.21. But the article may be omitted: kai\ ei(/lonto de/ka, e(/na a)po\ fu_lh=s and they chose ten, one from (each) tribe
X. H. 2.4.23.

§1121
The article often takes the place of an unemphatic possessive pronoun when there is no doubt as to the possessor.

*ku=ros kataphdh/sa_s a)po\ tou= a(/rmatos to\n qw/ra_ka e)ne/du_ Cyrus leaped down from his chariot and put on his breastplate
X. A. 1.8.3.

## THE GENERIC ARTICLE

§1122
The generic article denotes an entire class as distinguished from other classes. Thus, o( a)/nqrwpos man (as distinguished from other beings), oi( ge/rontes the aged; dei= to\n stratiw/thn fobei=sqai ma=llon to\n a)/rxonta h)\ tou\s polemi/ous the (a) soldier should fear his commander rather than the enemy
X. A. 2.6.10,

ponhro\n o( su_kofa/nths the informer is a vile thing
D. 18.242.

§1123
In the singular the generic article makes a single object the representative of the entire class; in the plural it denotes all the objects belonging to a class. The generic article is especially common, in the plural, with adjectives used substantively:

ou)k a)/n tis ei)/poi w(s tou\s kakou/rgous kai\ a)di/kous ei)/a_ katagela=n no one could say that he permitted the malefactor and the wrongdoer to deride him
X. A. 1.9.13.

§1124

The Article with Participles.—A participle with the article may denote an entire class: o( boulo/menos any one who wishes. Cp. 2050, 2052.
o( tuxw/n any chance comer, o( h(ghso/menos a guide,

ou)k a)porh/sete tw=n e)qelhso/ntwn u(pe\r u(_mw=n kindu_neu/ein you will not be in want of those who will be willing to encounter danger for you
D. 20.166, oi( logopoiou=ntes newsmongers 4. 49. The same sense is expressed by pa=s o( with a participle or adjective. On the article with a participle in the predicate, see 1152.
a. When the reference is to a particular occasion, the article may be particular (2052); as o( le/gwn the speaker on a definite occasion.

## THE ARTICLE WITH NUMERALS

§1125
The article may be used with cardinal numerals
a. When the numeral states the definite part of a whole (expressed or understood): a)ph=san tw=n lo/xwn dw/deka o)/ntwn oi( trei=s of the companies, numbering twelve (in all), there were absent three
X. H. 7.5.10, ei(=s para\ tou\s de/ka one man in (comparison with) ten
X. O. 20.16,

tw=n pe/nte ta\_s du/o moi/pa_s two fifths
T. 1.10, du/o me/rh two thirds 3. 15. (The genitive is omitted when the denominator exceeds the numerator by one.)
b. When the numeral is approximate:

e)/meinan h(me/ra_s a)mfi\ ta\_s tria/_konta they remained about thirty days
X. A. 4.8.22,

gegono/tes ta\ penth/konta e)/th about fifty years of age
X. C. 1.2.13.
c. When the number is used abstractly (without reference to any definite object):

o(/pws mh\ e)rei=s o(/ti e)/stin ta\ dw/deka di\s e(/c beware of saying 12 is twice 6
P. R. 337b.
N. Ordinals usually omit the article and regularly do so in statements of time in the dative (1540):

deute/rw| mhni\ th\n po/lin e)tei/xizon in the second month they fortified the city
T. 8.64.

## FLUCTUATION IN THE USE OF THE ARTICLE: OMISSION OF THE ARTICLE

§1126
The article is often omitted (1) in words and phrases which have survived from the period when o(, h(, to/ was a demonstrative pronoun; (2) when a word is sufficiently definite by itself; (3) when a word expresses a general conception without regard to its application to a definite person. The generic article is frequently omitted, especially with abstracts (1132), without appreciable difference in meaning. Its presence or absence is often determined by the need of distinguishing subject from predicate (1150), by the rhythm of the sentence, etc.

§1127
The article is omitted in many adverbial designations of time, mostly with prepositions (except h(me/ra_s by day, nukto/s by night).
Thus, peri\ me/sa_s nu/ktas about midnight, a(/ma e(/w| just before daylight, w(/ra| e(/tous at the season of the year. So with o)/rqros daybreak, dei/lh afternoon, e(spe/ra_ evening, e)/ar spring; and e)k pai/dwn from childhood. Most of the above cases are survivals of the older period when the article had a demonstrative force.

§1128
The article is very often omitted in phrases containing a preposition:

e)n a)rxh=| tou= lo/gou in the beginning of the speech
D. 37.23,

e)/cw belw=n out of reach of the missiles
X. A. 3.4.15,

*)hio/na th\n e)pi\ *stru_mo/ni Eion on the Strymon
T. 1.98.

§1129
Words denoting persons, when they are used of a class, may omit the article. So a)/nqrwpos, strathgo/s, qeo/s divinity, god (o( qeo/s the particular god). Thus,

pa/ntwn me/tron a)/nqrwpo/s e)stin man is the measure of all things
P. Th. 178b.

§1130
Adjectives and participles used substantively have no article when the reference is general:

me/son h(me/ra_s midday
X. A. 1.8.8, yu_xro/n cold,

qermo/n heat
P. S. 186d, pe/myai prokatalhyome/nous ta\ a)/kra to send men to preoccupy the heights
X. A. 1.3.14. Rarely when an adverb is used adjectively:

tw=n e)xqrw=n a)/rdhn o)/leqros the utter destruction of the enemy
D. 19.141.

## THE ARTICLE WITH ABSTRACT SUBSTANTIVES

§1131
Abstract substantives generally have the article:

h( a)reth\ ma=llon h)\ h( fugh\ sw/|zei ta\_s yu_xa/_s valour rather than flight saves men's lives
X. C. 4.1.5.

§1132
The names of the virtues, vices, arts, sciences, occupations often omit the article: ti/ swfrosu/nh, ti/ mani/a_; what is temperance, what is madness?
X. M. 1.1.16, a)rxh\ fili/a_s me\n e)/painos, e)/xqra_s de\ yo/gos praise is the beginning of friendship, blame of enmity
I. 1.33. Similarly mousikh/ music, gewrgi/a_ agriculture. So also with do/ca opinion, nou=s mind, te/xnh art, no/mos law.

§1133
The article must be used when reference is made to a definite person or thing or to an object well known:

h( tw=n *(ellh/nwn eu)/noia the goodwill of the Greeks
Aes. 3.70, (u(_mi=n)

h( sxolh/ your usual idleness
D. 8.53.

§1134
The article may be omitted in designations of space; as ba/qos depth, u(/yos height; also me/geqos size, plh=qos size, amount. ge/nos and o)/noma, used as accusatives of respect (1600), may omit the article.

§1135
The article may be omitted with some concrete words conveying a general idea, as yu_xh/ soul, sw=ma body (but the parts of the body regularly have the article).

## THE ARTICLE WITH PROPER NAMES

§1136
Names of persons and places are individual and therefore omit the article unless previously mentioned (1120 b) or specially marked as well known:

*qouku_di/dhs *)aqhnai=os Thucydides an Athenian
T. 1.1, tou\s stratiw/ta_s au)tw=n, tou\s para\ *kle/arxon a)pelqo/ntas, ei)/a_ *ku=ros to\n *kle/arxon e)/xein their soldiers who seceded to Clearchus, Cyrus allowed Clearchus to retain
X. A. 1.4.7, o( *so/lwn
D. 20.90, oi( *(hra_<*>le/es the Heracleses
P. Th. 169b.

§1137
Names of deities omit the article, except when emphatic (nh\ to\n *di/a by Zeus) or when definite cults are referred to: to\ th=s *)aqhna=s e(/dos the sanctuary of Athena (at Athens)
I. 15.2. Names of festivals vary in prose writers (no article in inscriptions): *panaqh/naia the Panathenaea (but

*panaqhnai/ois toi=s mi_kroi=s at the Lesser Panathenaea
L. 21.4). Names of shrines have the article.

§1138
Names of nations may omit the article, but oi( *(/ellhnes is usual when opposed to oi( ba/rbaroi the barbarians. When nations are opposed, the article is usually absent: o( po/lemos *)aqhnai/wn kai\ *peloponnhsi/wn
T. 2.1 (but o( po/lemos tw=n *peloponnhsi/wn kai\ *)aqhnai/wn 1. 1). The name of a nation without the article denotes the entire people. Names of families may omit the article: *)asklhpia/dai
P. R. 406a.

§1139

Continents: h( *eu)rw/ph Europe, h( *)asi/a_ Asia. Other names of countries, except those originally adjectives (as h( *)attikh/ Attica), omit the article (*libu/h Libya). gh= and xw/ra_ may be added only to such names as are treated as adjectives: h( *boiwti/a_ (gh=) Boeotia. The names of countries standing in the genitive of the divided whole (1311) usually omit the article only when the genitive precedes the governing noun:

*sikeli/a_s to\ plei=ston the most of Sicily
T. 1.12. The article is generally used with names of mountains and rivers; but is often omitted with names of islands, seas (but o( *po/ntos the Pontus), and winds. Names of cities usually omit the article. Names of cities, rivers, and mountains often add po/lis, potamo/s, o)/ros (1142 c). The article is omitted with proper names joined with au)to/s used predicatively (1206 b):

au)tou\s *)aqhnai/ous the Athenians themselves
T. 4.73.

§1140
Several appellatives, treated like proper names, may omit the article: basileu/s the king of Persia (o( basileu/s is anaphoric (1120 b) or refers expressly to a definite person). Titles of official persons: pruta/neis the Prytans, strathgoi/ the Generals. Names of relationship, etc.: path/r father, a)nh/r husband, gunh/ wife (but the article is needed when a definite individual is spoken of). Thus:

h)=kon de\ tw=| me\n mh/thr, tw=| de\ gunh\ kai\ pai=des to one there came his mother, to another his wife and children
And. 1.48. So also patri/s fatherland.

§1141
Similarly in the case of words forming a class by themselves, and some others used definitely: h(/lios sun, ou)rano/s heaven, w(=rai seasons, kerauno/s thunder, qa/natos death; a)/stu, po/lis city, a)kro/polis citadel, a)gora/_ market-place, tei=xos city-wall, prutanei=on prytaneum, nh=sos island (all used of definite places), qa/latta sea as opposed to the mainland, but h( qa/latta of a definite sea; similarly gh= earth, land.

§1142
When the name of a person or place is defined by an appositive (916) or attributive, the following distinctions are to be noted:
a. Persons: *perdi/kka_s *)aleca/ndrou Perdiccas, son of Alexander
T. 2.99: the official designation merely stating the parentage. *dhmosqe/nhs o( *)alkisqe/nous (the popular designation) distinguishes Demosthenes, the son of Alcisthenes (
T. 3.91) from other persons named Demosthenes. (Similarly with names of nations.)
b. Deities: the article is used with the name and with the epithet or (less often) with neither:

tw=| *dii\ tw=| *)olumpi/w| to Olympian Zeus
T. 5.31, *dii\ e)leuqeri/w| to Zeus guardian of freedom 2. 71.
c. Geographical Names are usually treated as attributives, as

o( *eu)fra/_ths potamo/s the river Euphrates
X. A. 1.4.11,

h( *bo/lbh li/mnh lake Bolbe
T. 4.103. In a very few cases (six times in Thuc.) o( is omitted with the name of a river when potamo/s is inserted; but Hdt. often omits o(. With the names of mountains the order is

to\ *ph/lion o)/ros Mt. Pelion
Hdt. 7.129 when the gender agrees, but otherwise

e)s to\ o)/ros th\n *)istw/nhn to Mt. Istone
T. 3.85 (rarely as

u(po\ th=| *ai)/tnh| tw=| o)/rei at the foot of Mt. Aetna
T. 3.116). With names of islands, towns, etc., the order varies:

to\ *parqe/nion po/lisma the town of Parthenium
X. A. 7.8.21;

h( *yutta/leia nh=sos the island of Psyttalea
Hdt. 8.95;

*tragi/a_ h( nh=sos the island of Tragia
T. 1.116;

tou= *peiraiw=s tou= lime/nos of the harbour of Peiraeus
T. 2.93; to\ frou/rion to\ *la/bdalon fort Labdalon 7. 3. The city of Mende would be *me/ndh po/lis, h( *me/ndh h( po/lis, *me/ndh h( po/lis.

## OTHER USES OF THE ARTICLE

§1143
A single article, used with the first of two or more nouns connected by and, produces the effect of a single notion: oi( strathgoi\ kai\ loxa_goi/ the generals and captains (the commanding officers)
X. A. 2.2.8, ta\_s megi/sta_s kai\ e)laxi/sta_s nau=s the largest and the smallest ships (the whole fleet)
T. 1.10,

h( tw=n pollw=n diabolh/ te kai\ fqo/nos the calumniation and envy of the multitude
P. A. 28a. Rarely when the substantives are of different genders:

peri\ ta\_s e(aut w=n yu_xa\_s kai\ sw/mata concerning their own lives and persons
X. A. 3.2.20.

§1144
