A repeated article lays stress on each word:

o( *qra=|c kai\ o( ba/rbaros the Thracian and the barbarian
D. 23.132 (here the subject remains the same),

oi( strathgoi\ kai\ oi( loxa_goi/ the generals and the captains
X. A. 7.1.13.

§1145
Instead of repeating a noun with the article it may suffice to repeat the article:

o( bi/os o( tw=n i)diwteuo/ntwn h:\ o( tw=n turanneuo/ntwn the life of persons in a private station or that of princes
I. 2.4.

§1146
A substantive followed by an attributive genitive and forming with it a compound idea, usually omits the article: teleuth\ tou= bi/ou (the) end of his life (‘life-end’ as life-time)
X. A. 1.1.1. (Less commonly h( teleuth\ tou= bi/ou
X. A. 1.9.30.) Cp. 1295 a.

§1147
When the genitive dependent on a substantive is a proper name:

meta\ *eu)boi/a_s a(/lwsin after the capture of Euboea
T. 2.2, and meta\ th\n *le/sbou a(/lwsin after the capture of Lesbos 3. 51. A preceding genitive thus often takes the place of the article:

dia\ xro/nou plh=qos by reason of the extent of time
T. 1.1.

§1148
Concrete coördinated words forming a copulative expression may omit the article:

pro\s ou)=n pai/dwn kai\ gunaikw=n i(keteu/w u(_ma=s by your children and wives I beseech you
L. 4.20,

po/lin kai\ oi)ki/a_s h(mi=n para/dote surrender to us your city and houses
T. 2.72,

i(e/reiai kai\ i(erei=s priestesses and priests
P. R. 461a. Cp. man and wife, horse and rider.

§1149
An appositive to the personal pronouns of the first and second persons has the article when the appositive would have it (as third person) with the pronoun omitted: u(_mei=s oi( h(gemo/nes pro\s e)me\ pa/ntes sumba/llete do you, captains, all confer with me (oi( h(gemo/nes sumba/lloi<*>)
X. C. 6.2.41, ou) sfo/dra xrw/meqa oi( *krh=tes toi=s cenikoi=s poih/masin we Cretans do not make very much use of foreign poems
P. L. 680c, xai/rw a)kou/wn u(_mw=n tw=n sofw=n I delight in listening to you <*> P. Ion 532 d.

## THE ARTICLE AND A PREDICATE NOUN

§1150
A predicate noun has no article, and is thus distinguished from the subject: kalei=tai h( a)kro/polis e)/ti u(p' *)aqhnai/wn po/lis the acropolis is still called ‘city’ by the Athenians
T. 2.15.

§1151
Predicate comparatives and superlatives, possessive pronouns, and ordinals have no article: w)/|mhn th\n e)mautou= gunai=ka pa_sw=n swfronesta/thn <*> I thought that my wife was (the) most virtuous of all
L. 1.10, *xairefw=n <*> e(tai=ros h)=n Chaerephon was a friend of mine
P. A. 21a. Cp. 1125 d.

§1152
Even in the predicate the article is used with a noun referring to a definite object (an individual or a class) that is well known, previously mentioned or hinted at, or identical with the subject: oi( d' a)/lloi e)pixeirou=si ba/llein <*> *de/cippon a)nakalou=ntes to\n prodo/thn the rest try to strike Dexippus calling him ‘the traitor’
X. A. 6.6.7, ou(=toi h)=san oi( feu/gontes to\n e)/legxon these men were those who (as I have said) avoided the inquiry
Ant. 6.27. oi( tiqe/menoi tou\s no/mons <*> a)sqenei=s a)/nqrwpoi/ ei)si kai\ oi( polloi/ the enactors of the laws are the weak men and the multitude
P. G. 483b,

u(pw/pteue de\ ei)=nai to\n diaba/llonta *me/nwna he suspected that it was Menon who traduced him
X. A. 2.5.28 (here subject and predicate could change places). So also with o( au)to/s the same (1209 a), qa)/_teron one of two (69), tou)nanti/on the opposite.

## SUBSTANTIVE-MAKING POWER OF THE ARTICLE

§1153
The article has the power to make substantival any word or words to which it is prefixed.
a. Adjectives: o( sofo/s the wise man, to\ di/kaion justice.
b. Participles (with indefinite force): o( boulo/menos whoever wills, the first that offers. Cp. 1124.
N. 1.—Such participial nouns appear in active, middle, and passive forms, and admit the distinctions of tense:

oi( e)qelh/sontes me/nein those who shall be willing to remain
X. H. 7.5.24.
N. 2.—Thucydides often substantivizes the neuter participle to form abstract expressions: th=s po/lews to\ ti_mw/menon the dignity of the State 2. 63. Such participial nouns denote an action regulated by time and circumstance. Contrast to\ dedio/s fear (in actual operation) 1. 36 with to\ de/os (simply fear in the abstract).
c. Preposition and case:

oi( e)pi\ tw=n pra_gma/twn those in power, the government
D. 18.247,

oi( e)n th=| h(liki/a| those in the prime of life
T. 6.24.
d. With the genitive, forming a noun-phrase (1299):

ta\ tw=n stratiwtw=n the condition of the soldiers
X. A. 3.1.20,

ta\ th=s o)rgh=s the outbursts of wrath
T. 2.60.
e. Adverbs:

oi(/ t' e)/ndon sunelamba/nonto kai\ oi( e)kto\s kateko/phsan those who were inside were arrested and those outside were cut down
X. A. 2.5.32. Similarly oi( to/te the men of that time, oi( e)kei= the dead, oi( pa/lai the ancients.
N.—An adverb preceded by the article may be used like an adjective:

o( o)rqw=s kubernh/ths the good pilot
P. R. 341c. The article is rarely omitted.
f. Infinitives:

kalou=si/ ge a)kolasi/a_n to\ u(po\ tw=n h(donw=n a)/rxesqai they call intemperance being ruled by one's pleasures
P. Ph. 68e.
g. Any single word or clause: to\ u(_mei=s o(/tan le/gw, th\n po/lin le/gw when I say You, I mean the State
D. 18.88, u(perba\_s to\ di/ka_s u(pexe/tw tou= fo/nou omitting (the words) ‘let him submit to judgment for the murder’
D. 23.220.

## POSITION OF THE ARTICLE

## Attributive Position of the Article

§1154
A word or group of words standing between the article and its noun, or immediately after the article if the noun, with or without the article, precedes, is an attributive. Thus, o( sofo\s a)nh/r, o( a)nh\r o( sofo/s, or a)nh\r o( sofo/s (cp. 1168).

§1155
This holds true except in the case of such post-positive words as me/n, de/, ge/, te/, ga/r, dh/, oi)=mai, ou)=n, toi/nun; and ti\s in Hdt.: tw=n tis *perse/wn one of the Persians 1. 85. In Attic, ti\s intervenes only when an attributive follows the article:

tw=n barba/rwn tine\s i(ppe/wn some of the barbarian cavalry
X. A. 2.5.32.

§1156
Adjectives, participles, adverbs, and (generally) prepositions with their cases, if preceded by the article, have attributive position.

§1157
(1) Commonly, as in English, the article and the attributive precede the noun: o( sofo\s a)nh/r the wise man. In this arrangement the emphasis is on the attributive. Thus,

th=| prw/th| h(me/ra| on the first day
T. 3.96,

e)n tw=| pro\ tou= xro/nw| in former times
D. 53.12,

to\n e)k tw=n *(ellh/nwn ei)s tou\s barba/rous fo/bon i)dw/n seeing the terror inspired by the Greeks in the barbarians
X. A. 1.2.18.

§1158
(2) Less often, the article and the attributive follow the noun preceded by the article: o( a)nh\r o( sofo/s the wise man. Thus,

to\ stra/teuma to\ tw=n *)aqhnai/wn the army of the Athenians
T. 8.50,

e)n th=| porei/a| th=| me/xri e)pi\ qa/lattan on the journey as far as the sea
X. A. 5.1.1. In this arrangement the emphasis is on the noun, as something definite or previously mentioned, and the attributive is added by way of explanation. So tou\s ku/nas tou\s xalepou\s dide/a_si they tie up the dogs, the savage ones (I mean)
X. A. 5.8.24.

§1159
(3) Least often, the noun takes no article before it, when it would have none if the attributive were dropped: a)nh\r o( sofo/s the wise man (lit. a man, I mean the wise one). Thus,

ma/xais tai=s plei/osi in the greater number of battles
T. 7.11, su/neimi me\n qeoi=s, su/neimi de\ a)nqrw/pois toi=s a)gaqoi=s I associate with gods, I associate with good men
X. M. 2.1.32. In this arrangement the attributive is added by way of explanation; as in the last example: with men, the good (I mean).

§1160
A proper name, defining a preceding noun with the article, may itself have the article: o( a)delfo\s o( *)areqou/sios (his) brother Arethusius
D. 53.10. Cp. 1142 c. An appositive to a proper name has the article when it designates a characteristic or something well known:

o( *so/lwn o( palaio\s h)=n filo/dhmos Solon of ancient times was a lover of the people
Ar. Nub. 1187, *pa_si/wn o( *megareu/s Pasion, the Megarian
X. A. 1.4.7.

§1161
The genitive of a substantive limiting the meaning of another substantive may take any one of four positions:—
a. to\ tou= patro\s bibli/on the father's book (very common). Thus, h( <*> teqnew/twn a)reth/ the valour of the dead
L. 12.36.
b. to\ bibli/on to\ tou= patro/s (less common). Thus,

h( oi)ki/a_ h( *si/mwnos the house of Simon
L. 3.32.
c. tou= patro\s to\ bibli/on (to emphasize the genitive or when a genitive has just preceded). Thus,

th=s vi/_khs to\ me/geqos the greatness of the victory
X. H. 6.4.19.
d. to\ bibli/on tou= patro/s (very common). Thus,

h( to/lma tw=n lego/ntwn the effrontery of the speakers
L. 12.41. The genitive of the divided whole (1306) is so placed or as in c.
N. 1.—A substantive with no article is sometimes followed by the article and the attributive genitive: e)pi\ skhnh\n i)o/ntes th\n *cenofw=ntos going to the ten<*> (namely, that) of Xenophon
X. A. 6.4.19. Cp. 1159.

§1162
The order bringing together the same forms of the article (peri\ tou= t<*> patro\s bibli/ou) is avoided, but two or three articles of different form may stand together:

to\ th=s tou= cai/nontos te/xnhs e)/rgon the work of the art of the wool-carder
P. Pol. 281a.

§1163
The attributive position is employed with the possessive pronouns and the possessive genitives of the reflexive and demonstrative pronouns (1184), au)to<*> meaning same (1173), and pa=s expressing the sum total (1174).

§1164
Two or more attributives of a substantive are variously placed: (1)

ei)s ta\_s a)/lla_s *)arkadika\_s po/leis to the other Arcadian cities
X. H. 7.4.38. (2)

to\ e)n *)arkadi/a| to\ tou= *dio\s tou= *lukai/ou i(ero/n the sanctuary of Lycean Zeus in Arcadia
P. R. 565d. (3)

e)s to\n e)pi\ tw=| sto/mati tou= lime/nos stenou= o)/ntos to\n e(/teron pu/rgon to the other tower at the mouth of the harbour which was narrow
T. 8.90. (4)

e)n th=| oi)ki/a| th=| *xarmi/dou th=| para\ to\ *)olumpiei=on in the house of Charmides by the Olympieum
And. 1.16. (5)

a)po\ tw=n e)n th=| *)asi/a| po/lewn *(ellhni/dwn from the Greek cities in Asia
X. H. 4.3.15. (6)

pro\s th\n e)k th=s *sikeli/a_s tw=n *)aqhnai/wn mega/lhn kakopra_gi/a_n with regard to the great failure of the Athenians in Sicily
T. 8.2. (7)

to\ tei=xos to\ makro\n to\ no/tion the long southern wall
And. 3.7.

§1165
A relative or temporal clause may be treated as an attributive:

*so/lwn e)mi/_sei tou\s oi(=os ou(=tos a)nqrw/pous Solon detested men like this man here
D. 19.254.

§1166
Position of an attributive participle with its modifiers (A = article, N = noun, P = participle, D = word or words dependent on P): (1) APND:

to\n e)festhko/ta ki/ndu_non th=| po/lei the danger impending over the State
D. 18.176. (2) APDN: tou\s periesthko/tas th=| po/lei kindu/_nous
D. 18.179. (3) ADPN: to\n to/te th=| po/lei perista/nta ki/ndu_non
D. 18.188. (4) NADP:

e(/toimon e)/xei du/namin th\n . . . katadoulwsoue/nhn a)/pantas he has in readiness a force to enslave all
D. 8.46.

§1167

a. Especially after verbal substantives denoting an action or a state an attributive prepositional phrase is added without the article being repeated:

th\n mega/lhn stratei/a_n *)aqhnai/wn kai\ tw=n cumma/xwn e)s *ai)/gupton the great expedition of the Athenians and their allies to Egypt
T. 1.110.
b. A word defining a substantivized participle, adjective, or infinitive may be placed before the article for emphasis:

kai\ tau=ta tou\s ei)do/tas kalou=men and we will summon those who have knowledge of this
D. 57.65,

tou/twn toi=s e)nanti/ois with the opposite of these
T. 7.75.

## Predicate Position of Adjectives

§1168
A predicate adjective either precedes or follows the article and its noun: sofo\s o( a)nh/r or o( a)nh\r sofo/s the man is wise.
Thus,

a)telei= th=| ni/_kh| a)ne/sthsan they retired with their victory incomplete
T. 8.27,

yi_lh\n e)/xwn th\n kefalh/n with his head bare
X. A. 1.8.6,

ta\_s trih/reis a)fei/lkusan kena/_s they towed off the ships without their crews
T. 2.93.
a. This is called the predicate position, which often lends emphasis.

§1169
A predicate adjective or substantive may thus be the equivalent of a clause of a complex sentence:

a)qa/naton th\n peri\ au(tw=n mnh/mhn katalei/yousin they will leave behind a remembrance of themselves that will never die
I. 9.3, e)ph/reto po/son ti a)/goi to\ stra/teuma he asked about how large the force was that he was leading ( = po/son ti ei)/h to\ stra/teuma o(\ a)/goi 2647)
X. C. 2.1.2, par' e(ko/ntwn tw=n cumma/xwn th\n h(gemoni/a_n e)/labon they received the leadership from their allies (being willing) who were willing to confer it
I. 1.17.

§1170
A predicate expression may stand inside an attributive phrase: o( deino\s (pred.)

lego/menos gewrgo/s he who is called a skilful agriculturist
X. O. 19.14. This is common with participles of naming with the article.

§1171
The predicate position is employed with the demonstratives ou(=tos, o(/de, e)kei=nos, and a)/mfw, a)mfo/teros, e(ka/teros, and e(/kastos; with the possessive genitives of personal and relative pronouns (1185, 1196) and of au)to/s (1201); with au)to/s meaning self (1206 b); with the genitive of the divided whole (1306), as

tou/twn oi( plei=stoi the most of these
X. A. 1.5.13, oi( a)/ristoi tw=n peri\ au)to/n the bravest of his companions 1. 8. 27; and with pa=s meaning all (1174 b).
a. This wise man is ou(=tos o( sofo\s a)nh/r, o( sofo\s a)nh\r ou(=tos (and also o( sofo\s ou(=tos a)nh/r).

## PECULIARITIES OF POSITION WITH THE ARTICLE

§1172

Adjectives of Place.—When used in the predicate position (1168) a)/kros (high) means the top of, me/sos (middle) means the middle of, e)/sxatos (extreme) means the end of. Cp. summus, medius, extremus.

Attributive PositionPredicate Position

to\ a)/kron o(/ros the lofty mountaina)/kron to\ o)/ros )the top of

to\ o)/ros a)/kron )the mountain

h( me/sh a)gora/_ the central marketme/sh h( a)gora/_ )the centre of

h( a)gora\_ me/sh )the market

h( e)sxa/th nh=sos the farthest islande)sxa/th h( nh=sos )the verge of

h( nh=sos e)sxa/th )the island
Thus, peri\ a)/krais tai=s xersi\ xeiri=des gloves on the fingers (points of the hands)
X. C. 8.8.17,

dia\ me/sou tou= paradei/sou r(ei= flows through the middle of the park
X. A. 1.2.7. The meaning of the predicate position is also expressed by (to\) a)/kron tou= o)/rous, (to\) me/son th=s a)gora=s, etc.

§1173

mo/nos, h(/misus.—(1) Attributive: o( mo/nos pai=s the only son, ai( h(mi/seiai xa/rites half-favours. (2) Predicate: mo/nos o( pai=s (or o( pai=s mo/nos) pai/zei the boy plays alone, h(/misus o( bi/os (or o( bi/os h(/misus) half of life, ta\ a(/rmata ta\ h(mi/sea half of the chariots.
au)to/s: (1) Attributive: o( au)to\s a)nh/r the same man. (2) Predicate: au)to\s o( a)nh/r or o( a)nh\r au)to/s the man himself.

§1174

pa=s (and in the strengthened forms a(/pa_s, su/mpa_s all together). a. In the attributive position pa=s denotes the whole regarded as the sum of all its parts (the sum total, the collective body): oi( pa/ntes poli=tai the whole body of citizens, h( pa=sa *sikeli/a_ the whole of Sicily,

a)poktei=nai tou\s a(/pantas *mutilhnai/ous to put to death the entire Mitylenean population
T. 3.36.
N.—Hence, with numbers, oi( pa/ntes, ta\ su/mpanta in all:

e(cako/sioi kai\ xi/_lioi oi( pa/ntes 1600 in all
T. 1.60.
b. In the predicate (and usual) position pa=s means all: pa/ntes oi( poli=tai or (often emphatic) oi( poli=tai pa/ntes all the citizens (individually),

peri\ pa/ntas tou\s qeou\s h)sebh/ka_si kai\ ei)s a(/pa_san th\n po/lin h(marth/ka_sin they have committed impiety towards all the gods and have sinned against the whole State
L. 14.42.
c. Without the article: pa/ntes poli=tai all (conceivable) citizens,

misqwsa/menoi pa/ntas a)nqrw/pous hiring every conceivable person
L. 12.60.
N. 1.—In the meaning pure, nothing but, pa=s is strictly a predicate and has no article: ku/klw| frourou/menos u(po\ pa/ntwn polemi/wn hemmed in by a ring of guards all of whom are his enemies ( = pa/ntes u(f' w(=n frourei=tai pole/mioi/ ei)si)
P. R. 579b. So pa=sa kaki/a_ utter baseness.
N. 2.—The article is not used with pa=s if the noun, standing alone, would have no article.
N. 3.—In the singular, pa=s often means every:

su\n soi\ pa=sa o(do\s eu)/poros with you every road is easy to travel
X. A. 2.5.9,

pa=sa qa/lassa every sea
T. 2.41.

§1175

o(/los: (1) Attributive: to\ o(/lon stra/teuma the whole army; (2) Predicate: o(/lon to\ stra/teuma (or to\ stra/teuma o(/lon) the army as a whole, th\n nu/kta o(/lhn the entire night. With no article: o(/lon stra/teuma a whole army, o(/la strateu/mata whole armies.

§1176
The demonstrative pronouns ou(=tos, o(/de, e)kei=nos, and au)to/s self, in agreement with a noun, usually take the article, and stand in the predicate position (1168): ou(=tos o( a)nh/r or o( a)nh\r ou(=tos (never o( ou(=tos a)nh/r) this man, au)to\s o( a)nh/r or o( a)nh\r au)to/s the man himself (o( au)to\s a)nh/r the same man 1173).

§1177
One or more words may separate the demonstrative from its noun:

o( tou/tou e)/rws tou= a)nqrw/pou the love of this man
P. S. 213c. Note also tw=n oi)kei/wn tine\s tw=n e)kei/nwn some of their slaves (some of the slaves of those men)
P. A. 33d.

§1178

ou(=tos, o(/de, e)kei=nos sometimes omit the article.
a. Regularly, when the noun is in the predicate:

au(/th e)/stw i(kanh\ a)pologi/a_ let this be a sufficient defence
P. A. 24b,

oi)=mai e)mh\n tau/thn patri/da ei)=nai I think this is my native country
X. A. 4.8.4.
b. Usually, with proper names, except when anaphoric (1120 b): e)kei=nos *qouku_di/dhs that (well-known) Thucydides
Ar. Ach. 708.
c. Usually, with definite numbers:

tau/ta_s tria/_konta mna=s these thirty minae
D. 27.23.
d. Optionally, when a relative clause follows:

e)pi\ gh=n th/nde h)/lqomen, e)n h(=| oi( pate/res h(mw=n *mh/dwn e)kra/thsan we have come against this land, in which our fathers conquered the Medes
T. 2.74.
e. In the phrase (often contemptuous) ou(=tos a)nh/r
P. G. 505c; and in other expressions denoting some emotion: a)/nqrwpos ou(tosi/_
D. 18.243.
f. Sometimes, when the demonstrative follows its noun: e)pi/gramma to/de
T. 6.59. So often in Hdt.
g. Frequently, in poetry.

§1179

a)/mfw, a)mfo/teros both, e(ka/teros each (of two), e(/kastos each (of several) have the predicate position. But with e(/kastos the article is often omitted: kata\ th\n h(me/ra_n e(ka/sthn (day by day and) every day, kaq' e(ka/sthn h(me/ra_n every day.

§1180
The demonstratives of quality and quantity, toiou=tos, toio/sde, tosou=tos, toso/sde, thlikou=tos, when they take the article, usually follow it:

tw=n tosou/twn kai\ toiou/twn a)gaqw=n of so many and such blessings
D. 18.305, tou=to to\ toiou=ton e)/qos such a practice as this 21. 123. o( dei=na such a one (336) regularly takes the article.
a. But the predicate position occurs:

tosau/th h( prw/th paraskeuh\ pro\s to\n po/lemon die/plei so great was the first armament which crossed over for the war
T. 6.44.

§1181
An attributive, following the article, may be separated from its noun by a pronoun:

h( pa/lai h(mw=n fu/sis our old nature
P. S. 189d, h( stenh\ au(/th o(do/s (for au(/th h( stenh\ o(do/s) this narrow road
X. A. 4.2.6.

§1182
Possessive pronouns take the article only when a definite person or thing is meant, and stand between article and noun: to\ e)mo\n bibli/on my book, ta\ h(me/tera bibli/a our books.
a. But names of relationship, po/lis, patri/s, etc., do not require the article (1140).

§1183
The article is not used with possessive pronouns or the genitive of personal and reflexive pronouns (cp. 1184, 1185):
a. When no particular object is meant: e)mo\n bibli/on or bibli/on mou a book of mine.
b. When these pronouns belong to the predicate:

maqhth\s ge/gona so/s I have become a pupil of yours
P. Euth. 5a,

ou) lo/gous e)mautou= le/gwn not speaking words of my own
D. 9.41.

## POSITION OF THE GENITIVE OF PRONOUNS AND THE ARTICLE

§1184
In the attributive position (1154) stands the genitive of the demonstrative, reflexive, and reciprocal pronouns. to\ tou/tou bibli/on or to\ bibli/on to\ tou/tou his book, to\ e)mautou= bibli/on or to\ bibli/on to\ e)mautou= my own book;

metepe/myato th\n e(autou= qugate/ra kai\ to\n pai=da au)th=s he sent for his daughter and her child
X. C. 1.3.1.
a. The type to\ bibli/on tou/tou is rare and suspected except when another attributive is added: th=| nu=n u(/brei tou/tou
D. 4.3. The types to\ bibli/on e)mautou= (
Hdt. 6.23) and to\ au)tou= bibli/on (
T. 6.102) are rare.

§1185
In the predicate position stands
a. The genitive of the personal pronouns (whether partitive or not): to\ bibli/on mou (sou, au)tou=, etc.), or mou sou, au)tou=. etc.) to\ bibli/on when other words precede, as

o(\s e)/xei sou th\n a\delohn who has your sister to wife
And. 1.50.
b. The genitive of the other pronouns used partitively.
N. 1.—Homer does not use the article in the above cases, and often employs the orthotone forms (

sei=o me/ga kle/os thy great fame
p 241). Even in Attic e)mou= for mou occurs (

e)mou= ta\ forti/a my wares
Ar. Vesp. 1398).
N. 2.—The differences of position between 1184 and 1185 may be thus illustrated:

My book is pretty:kalo/n e)sti/ to\ bibli/on mou.

kalo/n e)sti/ mou to\ bibli/on.

My pretty book:to\ kalo/n mou bibli/on.

They read their books:ta\ e/autw=n <*>bibli/a a)nagignw/skousi.

## INTERROGATIVES, a)/llos, polu/s, o)li/gos WITH THE ARTICLE

§1186
The interrogatives ti/s, poi=os may take the article when a question is asked about an object before mentioned: *s*w. nu=n d<*> e)ke <*>na, w)= *fai=dre, duna/meqa kri/_nein. *f*a*i. ta\ poi=a; SOCR. Now at last we can decide those questions. PH. The what questions?
P. Phae. 277a.

§1187
So even with a personal pronoun: A. deu=ro dh\ eu)qu\ h(mw=n . . . B. poi= le/geis kai\ para\ ti/nas tou\s u(_ma=s; A. Come hither straight to us. B. Whither do you mean and who are you that I am to come to (you being who)?
P. Lys. 203b.

§1188

a)/llos other.—o( a)/llos in the singular usually means the rest (h( a)/llh *(ella/s the rest of Greece); in the plural. the others (oi( a)/lloi *(/ellhnes the other (ceteri) Greeks, but a)/lloi *(/ellhnes other <*>lii) Greeks). A substantivized adjective or participle usually has the article when it stands in apposition to oi( a)/lloi:

ta)=lla ta\ poli_tika/ the other civic affairs
X. Hi. 9.5. On a)/llos, o( a)/llos (sometimes e(/teros) besides, see 1272.

§1189

polu/s, o)li/gos: to\ polu/ usually means the great（er) part, oi( polloi/ the multitude, the vulgar crowd; plei/ones several, oi( plei/ones the majority, the mass; plei=stoi very many, oi( plei=stoi the most; o(li/goi few, oi( o)li/goi the oligarchs (as opposed to oi( polloi/). Note polu/s predicative:

e)pei\ e(w/ra_ polla\ ta\ kre/a_ when he saw that there was abundance of meat
X. C. 1.3.6.

## PRONOUNS

## THE PERSONAL PRONOUNS

§1190
The nominative of the personal pronoun is usually omitted except when emphatic, e.g. in contrasts, whether expressed or implied: e)pei\ u(_mei=s e)moi\ ou) qe/lete pei/qesqai, e)gw su\n u(_mi=n e(/yomai since you are not willing to obey me, I will follow along with you
X. A. 1.3.6. In contrasts the first pronoun is sometimes omitted (930).

§1191
Where there is no contrast the addition of the pronoun may strengthen the verb:

ei) mhde\ tou=to bou/lei a)pokri/_nasqai, su\ de\ tou)nteu=qen le/ge if you do not wish to reply even to this, tell me then
X. C. 5.5.21.

§1192
The forms e)mou=, e)moi/, and e)me/ and the accented forms of the pronoun of the second person (325 a) are used when emphatic and usually after prepositions:

kai\ pei/sa_s e)me\ pista\ e)/dwka/s moi kai\ e)/labes par' e)mou= and after prevailing on me you gave me pledges of faith and received them from me
X. A. 1.6.7. Cp. 187 N. 2. On the reflexive use of the personal pronouns of the first and second persons, see 1222-1224.

§1193

e)gw/, su/ (e)mo/s, so/s) are rarely used of an imaginary person (‘anybody’):
D. 9.17,
X. R. A. 1.11.

§1194
The nominative of the pronoun of the third person is replaced by e)kei=nos (of absent persons), o(/de, ou(=tos (of present persons), o( me/n . . . o( de/ (at the beginning of a sentence), and by au)to/s in contrasts. The oblique cases of the foregoing replace ou(=, etc., which in Attic prose are usually indirect reflexives (1228, 1229). ou(= and e(/ in Attic prose occur chiefly in poetical passages of Plato; in Attic poetry they are personal pronouns. The pronoun of the third person is very rare in the orators.

§1195
Homer uses e(/o, oi(=, etc., as personal pronouns ( = au)tou=, au)tw=|, etc., in Attic), in which case they are enclitic: dia\ mantosu/nhn, th/n oi( po/re *foi=bos by the art of divination, which Phoebus gave to him A 72. Homer also uses e(/o, oi(=, etc., either as direct ( = e(autou=, etc., 1218) or as indirect reflexives ( = au)tou=, etc., 1225). In the former case they are orthotone; in the latter, either enclitic or orthotone. Thus, oi/= pai=da e)oiko/ta gei/nato he begat a son like unto himself E 800, ou)/ tina/ fhsin o(moi=on oi)= e)/menai *danaw=n he says there is no one of the Danaans like unto himself I 306. Hdt. agrees with Hom. except that eu(=, oi(= are not direct reflexives and orthotone; sfi/si (not sfi/) is reflexive.

## THE POSSESSIVE PRONOUNS

For the article with a possessive pronoun see 1182-1183.

§1196
The possessive pronouns (330) of the first and second persons are the equivalents of the possessive genitive of the personal pronouns: e)mo/s = mou, so/s = sou, h(me/teros = h(mw=n, u(_me/teros = u(_mw=n.
a. When the possessives refer to a definite, particular thing, they have the article, which always precedes (1182); the personal pronouns have the predicate position (1185). Distinguish o( e)mo\s fi/los, o( fi/los o( e)mo/s, o( fi/los mou my friend from fi/los e)mo/s, fi/los mou a friend of mine.
b. A word may stand in the genitive in apposition to the personal pronoun implied in a possessive pronoun. See 977.

§1197
A possessive pronoun may have the force of an objective genitive (cp. 1331) of the personal pronoun:

fili/a| th=| e)mh=| out of friendship for me
X. C. 3.1.28. (fili/a_ h( e)mh/ usually means my friendship (for others)).

§1198
The possessive pronouns of the first and second persons are sometimes reflexive (when the subject of the sentence and the possessor are the same person), sometimes not reflexive.

§1199
FIRST AND SECOND PERSONS SINGULAR
1. Not reflexive (adjective my, thy (your); pronoun mine, thine (yours)).
e)mo/s, so/s: o(ra=| to\n e)mo\n fi/lon he sees my friend, o(ra=| to\n so\n pate/ra she sees your father, ste/rgei to\n e)mo\n pate/ra he loves my father (or to\n pate/ra to\n e)mo/n or pate/ra to\n e)mo/n; or to\n pate/ra mou or mou to\n pate/ra),

oi( e)moi\ o)fqalmoi\ kalli/_ones a)\n tw=n sw=n ei)/hsan my eyes will prove to be more beautiful than yours
X. S. 5. 5.
2. Reflexive (my own, thine (your) own).
a. e)mautou=, seautou=, in the attributive position (very common): e)/labon to\n e)mautou= misqo/n (or to\n misqo\n to\n e)mautou=) I received my (own) pay, to\n a)delfo\n to\n e)mautou= e)/pemya I sent my (own) brother
Aes. 2.94, ka)_pi\ toi=s sauth=s kakoi=si ka)_pi\ toi=s e)moi=s gela=|s; art thou laughing at thine own misery and at mine?
S. El. 879.
b. e)mo/s, so/s (less common): ste/rgw to\n e)mo\n pate/ra I love my (own) father, ste/rgeis th\n sh\n mhte/ra you love your (own) mother,

h( e)mh\ gunh\ my wife
X. C. 7.2.28,

a)delfo\s th=s mhtro\s th=s e)mh=s brother of my mother
And. 1.117.
c. e)mo\s au)tou=, so\s au)tou= (poetical): to\n e)mo\n au)tou= pate/ra (
b 45,
S. O. T. 416).
d. mou, sou (rare): to\n pate/ra mou
Ant. 1.23.
N.—When the possessor is not to be mistaken, the article alone is placed before the substantive and the possessive or reflexive pronoun is omitted (cp. 1121). Thus, ste/rgeis to\n pate/ra you love your (own) father, ste/rgei to\n pate/ra he loves his (own) father, ste/rgousi to\n pate/ra they love their (own) father.

§1200
FIRST AND SECOND PERSONS PLURAL
1. Not reflexive (adjective our, your; pronoun ours, yours).
a. h(me/teros, u(_me/teros: o( h(me/teros fi/los our friend (more common than o( fi/lo<*> h(mw=n), o( u(_me/teros fi/los your friend (more common than o( fi/los u(_mw=n),

zh/thsin poiou/menoi h)\ u(_mw=n h)\ tw=n u(_mete/rwn tino/s making a search for you or for anything of yours

a. h(me/teros, u(_me/teros (common): ste/rgomen to\n h(me/teron fi/lon we love our own friend, ste/rgete to\n u(_me/teron fi/lon you love your own friend.
b. Usually the intensive au)tw=n is used with h(me/teros, u(_me/teros in agreement with h(mw=n (u(_mw=n) implied in the possessive forms. This gives a stronger form of reflexive. Thus:
h(me/teros au)tw=n, u(_me/teros au)tw=n: ste/rgomen to\n h(me/teron au)tw=n fi/lon we love our own friend,

oi)kodo/mhma h)\ tw=n fi/lwn tini\ h)\ h(me/teron au)tw=n a house either for some one of our friends or our own

§1201

P. Pr. 310d.

a)fiknou=ntai par' *)ariai=on kai\ th\n e)kei/nou stratia/_n they come up with Ariaeus and his army

c. o(\s au)tou=, au)th=s (poetical): o(\n au)tou= pate/ra (K 204).

## THE PRONOUN au)to/s

§1204

au)to/s is used as an adjective and as a pronoun. It has three distinct uses: (1) as an intensive adjective pronoun it means self (ipse). (2) As an adjective pronoun, when preceded by the article, it means same (idem). (3) In oblique cases as the personal pronoun of the third person, him, her, it, them (eum, eam, id, eos, eas, ea).

§1205
Only the first two uses are Homeric. In Hom. au)to/s denotes the principal person or thing, in opposition to what is subordinate, and is intensive by contrast: au)to\n kai\ qera/ponta the man himself and his attendant Z 18 (cp. sw/sa_s' au)to\n kai\ pai=das
P. G. 511e and see 1208 d). On au)to/s as a reflexive, see 1228 a; on au)to/s emphatic with other pronouns, see 1233 ff.

§1206

au)to/s is intensive (self)
a. In the nominative case, when standing alone: au)toi\ th\n gh=n e)/sxon they (the Athenians) seized the land themselves
T. 1.114. Here au)to/s emphasizes the word understood and is not a personal pronoun.
b. In any case, when in the predicate position (1168) with a substantive, or in agreement with a pronoun: au)to\s o( a)nh/r, o( a)nh\r au)to/s the man himself, au)tou= tou= a)ndro/s, tou= a)ndro\s au)tou=, etc.

§1207
With a proper name or a word denoting an individual, the article is omitted:

au)to\s *me/nwn Menon himself
X. A. 2.1.5, pro\ au)tou= basile/ws in front of the Great King himself 1. 7. 11.

§1208
The word emphasized may be an oblique case which must be supplied: e)/lege de\ kai\ au)to\s o( *bra_si/da_s th=| *qessalw=n gh=| kai\ au)toi=s (scil. toi=s *qessaloi=s) fi/los w)\n i)e/nai and Brasidas himself also said that he came as a friend to the country of the Thessalians and to the Thessalians themselves
T. 4.78, dei= toi/nun tou=t' h)/dh skopei=n (scil. h(ma=s)

au)tou/s we must forthwith consider this matter ourselves
D. 2.2.

§1209
Special renderings of the emphatic au)to/s:
a. By itself, in itself, unaided, alone, etc.:

au)th\ h( a)lh/qeia the naked truth
Aes. 3.207, to\ ple/on tou= xwri/ou au)to\ kartero\n u(ph=rxe the greater part of the place was strong in itself (without artificial fortification)
T. 4.4. On au)toi=s a)ndra/si men and all, see 1525. au)to/ with a noun of any gender is used by Plato to denote the abstract idea of a thing: au)to\ to\ kalo/n ideal beauty R. 493 e, au)to\ dikaiosu/nh ideal justice 472 c.
b. Just, merely:

au)to\ to\ de/on just what we want
X. A. 4.7.7,

au)ta\ ta/de merely this
T. 1.139.
c. Voluntarily:

a)/ndras oi(\ kai\ toi=s mh\ e)pikaloume/nois au)toi\ e)pistrateu/ousi men who uninvited turn their arms even against those who do not ask their assistance
T. 4.60.
d. The Master (said by a pupil or slave): *au)to\s e)/fa_ the Master (Pythagoras) said it (ipse dixit)
Diog. Laert. 8.1. 46,

ti/s ou(=tos; *au)to/s. ti/s *au)to/s; *swkra/ths Who's this? The Master. Who's the Master? Socrates
Ar. Nub. 220.
e. With ordinals: h(|re/qh presbeuth\s de/katos au)to/s he was chosen envoy with nine others (i.e. himself the tenth)
X. H. 2.2.17.

§1210
After the article, in the attributive position (1154), au)to/s in any case means same.
Thus o( au)to\s a)nh/r, rarely (o() a)nh\r o( au)to/s the same man;

tou= au)tou= qe/rous in the same summer
T. 4.58,

ta\ au)ta\ tau=ta these same things
X. A. 1.1.7,

oi( tou\s au)tou\s ai)ei\ peri\ tw=n au)tw=n lo/gous le/gontes the people who are continually making the same speeches about the same things
Ant. 5.50.
a. So as a predicate: e)gw\ me\n o( au)to/s ei)mi, i(_mei=s de\ metaba/llete I am the same, it is you who change
T. 2.61.

§1211
In Hom. au)to/s, without the article, may mean the same:

h)=rxe de\ tw=| au)th\n o(do/n, h(/nper oi( a)/lloi and he guided him by the same way as the others had gone
q 107.

§1212

au)to/s when unemphatic and standing alone in the oblique cases means him, her, it, them.

e)ke/leuon au)th\n a)pie/nai they ordered her to depart
L. 1.12.

§1213
Unemphatic au)tou=, etc., do not stand at the beginning of a sentence.

§1214

au)tou=, etc., usually take up a preceding noun (the anaphoric use): kale/sa_s de\ *da/mnippon le/gw pro\s au)to\n ta/de summoning Damnippus, I speak to him as follows
L. 12.14. But an oblique case of au)to/s is often suppressed where English employs the pronoun of the third person: e)mpipla\_s a(pa/ntwn th\n gnw/mhn<*> a)pe/pempe having satisfied the minds of all he dismissed them
X. A. 1.7.8.

§1215

au)tou=, etc., may be added pleonastically;

peira/_somai tw=| pa/ppw|, kra/tistos w)\n i(ppeu/s, summaxei=n au)tw=| I will try, since I am an excellent horseman, to be an ally to my grandfather
X. C. 1.3.15.

§1216

au)tou=, etc., are emphatic (= au)tou= tou/tou, etc.) in a main clause when followed by a relative clause referring to au)tou=, etc.: ei)/rhkas au)to/, di' o(/per e)/gwge

ta\ e)ma\ e)/rga plei/stou a)/cia nomi/zw ei)=nai you have mentioned the very quality for which I consider my work worth the highest price
X. M. 3.10.14. But when the relative clause precedes, au)tou=, etc., are not emphatic:

ou(\s de\ mh\ eu(/riskon, kenota/fion au)toi=s e)poi/hsan they built a cenotaph for those whom they could not find
X. A. 6.4.9.

§1217

au)tou=, etc., are often used where, after a conjunction, we expect the oblique case of a relative pronoun:

o(\ mh\ oi)=de mhd' e)/xei au)tou= sfra_gi=da which he does not know nor does he have the seal of it
P. Th. 192a.

## THE REFLEXIVE PRONOUNS

§1218

Direct Reflexives.—The reflexive pronouns are used directly when they refer to the chief word (usually the subject) of the sentence or clause in which they stand.

gnw=qi seauto/n learn to know thyself
P. Charm. 164e,

sfa/ttei e(auth/n she kills herself
X. C. 7.3.14, kaq' e(autou\s bouleusa/menoi ta\ o(/pla pare/dosan kai\ sfa=s au)tou/s after deliberating apart by themselves they surrendered their arms and themselves (their persons)
T. 4.38. Less commonly the reference is to the object, which often stands in a prominent place:

tou\s de\ perioi/kous a)fh=ken e)pi\ ta\_s e(autw=n po/leis but the perioeci he dismissed to their own cities
X. H. 6.5.21.

§1219
The direct reflexives are regular in prose if, in the same clause, the pronoun refers emphatically to the subject and is the direct object of the main verb: e)mauto\n (not e)me\) e)painw= I praise myself. The usage of poetry is freer:

ste/nw se\ ma=llon h)\ )me/ I mourn thee rather than myself
E. Hipp. 1409.

§1220
The reflexives may retain or abandon their differentiating force. Contrast the third example in 1218 with pare/dosan sfa=s au)tou/s they surrendered (themselves)
T. 7.82.

§1221
The reflexives of the first and second persons are not used in a subordinate clause to refer to the subject of the main clause.

§1222
The personal pronouns are sometimes used in a reflexive sense:

qrhnou=nto/s te/ mou kai\ le/gontos polla\ kai\ a)na/cia e)mou= wailing and saying much unworthy of myself
P. A. 38e (contrast

a)kou/sei polla\ kai\ a)na/cia sautou= you will hear much unworthy of yourself
P. Cr. 53e), dokw= moi a)du/natos ei)=nai I (seem to myself to be) think I am unable
P. R. 368b (less usually dokw= e)mautw=|). So in Hom.: e)gw\n e)me\ lu/_somai I will ransom myself K 378. Cp. 1195.

§1223

e)me/, se/, not e)mauto/n, seauto/n, are generally used as subject of the infinitive:

e)gw\ oi)=mai kai\ e)me\ kai\ se\ to\ a)dikei=n tou= a)dikei=sqai ka/ki_on h(gei=sqai I think that both you and I believe that it is worse to do wrong than to be wronged
P. G. 474b.

§1224
The use in 1222, 1223 generally occurs when there is a contrast between two persons, or when the speaker is not thinking of himself to the exclusion of others. Cp. 1974.

§1225

Indirect Reflexives.—The reflexive pronouns are used indirectly when, in a dependent clause, they refer to the subject of the main clause.
*)ore/sths e)/peisen *)aqhnai/ous e(auto\n kata/gein Orestes persuaded the Athenians to restore him (self)
T. 1.111,

e)bou/leto o( *kle/arxos a(/pan to\ stra/teuma pro\s e(auto\n e)/xein th\n gnw/mhn Clearchus wished the entire army to be devoted to himself
X. A. 2.5.29. Cp. sibi, se.

§1226
When the subject of the leading clause is not the same as the subject of the subordinate clause or of the accusative with the infinitive (1975), the context must decide to which subject the reflexive pronoun refers: (o( kath/goros) e)/fh . . . a)napei/qonta tou\s ne/ous au)to\n . . . ou(/tw diatiqe/nai tou\s e)autw=| suno/ntas k.t.l. the accuser said that, by persuading the young, he (Socrates) so disposed his (i.e. Socrates') pupils, etc.
X. M. 1.2.52.

§1227

e(autou=, etc., are rarely used as indirect reflexives in adjectival clauses: ta\ naua/_gia, o(/sa pro\s th=| e(autw=n (gh=|)

h)=n, a)nei/lonto they took up the wrecks, as many as were close to their own land
T. 2.92.

§1228
Instead of the indirect e(autou=, etc., there may be used
a. The oblique cases of au)to/s:

e)peira=to tou\s *)aqhnai/ous th=s e)s au)to\n o)rgh=s paralu/_ein he tried to divert the Athenians from their anger against himself
T. 2.65. When e(autou=, etc. precede, au)tou=, etc. are usual instead of the direct reflexive:

th\n e(autou= gnw/mhn a)pefai/neto *swkra/ths pro\s tou\s o(mi_lou=ntas au)tw=| Socrates was wont to set forth his opinion to those who conversed with him
X. M. 4.7.1.
b. Of the forms of the third personal pronoun, oi(= and sfi/si (rarely ou(=, sfei=s, sfw=n, and sfa=s). Thus,

h)rw/ta_ au)th\n ei) e)qelh/soi dia_konh=sai/ oi( he asked her if she would be willing to do him a service
Ant. 1.16,

tou\s pai=das e)ke/leuon tou= *ku/_rou dei=sqai diapra/_casqai sfi/sin they ordered their boys to ask Cyrus to get it done for them
X. C. 1.4.1,

keleu/ousi ga\r h(ma=s koinh=| meta\ sfw=n polemei=n for they urge us to make war in common with them
And. 3.27, e)/fh de/, e)peidh\ ou(= e)kbh=nai th\n yu_xh\n . . . . . . a)fiknei=sqai sfa=s ei)s to/pon tina\ daimo/nion he said that when his soul had departed out of him, they (he and others) came to a mysterious place
P. R. 614b. See 1195.
N. 1.—sfei=s may be employed in a dependent sentence if the pronoun is itself the subject of a subordinate statement, and when the reference to the subject of the leading verb is demanded by way of contrast or emphasis:

ei)sagagw\n tou\s a)/llous strathgou\s . . . le/gein e)ke/leuen au)tou\s o(/ti ou)de\n a)\n h(=tton sfei=s a)ga/goien th\n stratia\_n h)\ *cenofw=n after bringing in the rest of the generals he urged them to say that they could lead the army just as well as Xenophon
X. A. 7.5.9. Here au)toi/ (ipsi) is possible. In the singular au)to/s is necessary.
N. 2.—Thucydides often uses the plural forms in reference to the nearest subject: tou\s cumma/xous e)de/disan sfw=n they were afraid of their own allies ( = sfw=n au)tw=n) 5. 14.
N. 3.—e(autou=, etc., are either direct or indirect reflexives, oi(= and sfi/si are only indirect reflexives.

§1229

ou(=, sfi/si, etc., and the oblique cases of au)to/s are used when the subordinate clause does not form a part of the thought of the principal subject. This is usual in subordinate indicative clauses, and very common in o(/ti and w(s clauses, in indirect questions, and in general in subordinate clauses not directly dependent on the main verb: tw=n pre/sbewn, oi(\ sfi/si (1481) peri\ tw=n spondw=n e)/tuxon a)po/ntes, h)me/loun they thought no more about their envoys, who were absent on the subject of the truce
T. 5.44, e)fobou=nto mh\ e)piqoi=nto au)toi=s oi( pole/mioi they were afraid lest the enemy should attack them (selves)
X. A. 3.4.1.

§1230
The reflexive pronoun of the third person is sometimes used for that of the first or second:

dei= h(ma=s a)nere/sqai e(autou/s we must ask ourselves
P. Ph. 78b,

para/ggelle toi=s e(autou= give orders to your men
X. C. 6.3.27.
a. In Homer o(/s his is used for e)mo/s or so/s:

ou)/toi e)/gwge h(=s gai/hs du/namai glukerw/teron a)/llo i)de/sqai I can look on nothing sweeter than my own land
i 28.

§1231

Reciprocal Reflexive.—The plural forms of the reflexive pronouns are often used for the reciprocal a)llh/lwn, a)llh/lois, etc.: h(mi=n au)toi=s dialeco/meqa we will converse with (ourselves) one another
D. 48.6.

§1232
But the reciprocal must be used when the idea ‘each for or with himself’ is expressed or implied: ma=llon xai/rousin e)pi\ toi=s a)llh/lwn kakoi=s h)\ toi=s au(tw=n i)di/ois a)gaqoi=s ( = h)\ e)pi\ toi=s au(tou= e(/kastos a)gaqoi=s) they take greater pleasure in one another's troubles than each man in his own good fortune
I. 4.168,

ou)/te ga\r e(autoi=s ou)/te a)llh/lois o(mologou=sin they are in agreement neither with themselves nor with one another
P. Phae. 237c. Reciprocal and reflexive may occur in the same sentence without difference of meaning (
D. 48.9). The reflexive is regularly used when there is a contrast (expressed or implied) with a)/lloi: fqonou=sin e(autoi=s ma=llon h)\ toi=s a)/llois a)nqrw/pois they envy one another more than (they envy) the rest of mankind
X. M. 3.5.16.

## au)to/s EMPHATIC OR REFLEXIVE WITH OTHER PRONOUNS

§1233
Of the plural forms, h(mw=n au)tw=n, etc. may be either emphatic or reflexive; au)tw=n h(mw=n, etc. are emphatic only; but sfw=n au)tw=n is only reflexive (au)tw=n sfw=n is not used). In Hom. au)to/n may mean myself, thyself , or himself, and e(\ au)to/n, oi(= au)tw=|, etc. are either emphatic or reflexive.

§1234

h(mw=n (u(_mw=n, sfw=n) au)tw=n often mean ‘their own men,’ ‘their own side’: fulakh\n sfw=n te au)tw=n kai\ tw=n cumma/xwn katalipo/ntes leaving a garrison (consisting) of their own men and of the allies
T. 5.114.

§1235

au)to/s, in agreement with the subject, may be used in conjunction with a reflexive pronoun for the sake of emphasis:

au)toi\ e)f' e(autw=n e)xw/roun they marched by themselves
X. A. 2.4.10,

au)to\s . . . e(auto\n e)n me/sw| kateti/qeto tou= stratope/dou he located himself in the centre of the camp
X. C. 8.5.8.

§1236

au)to/s may be added to a personal pronoun for emphasis. The forms e)me\ au)to/n, au)to/n me, etc. are not reflexive like e)mauto/n, etc. Thus,

tou\s pai=das tou\s e)mou\s h)/|sxu_ne kai\ e)me\ au)to\n u(/_brise he disgraced my children and insulted me myself
L. 1.4. Cp. au)tw=| moi e)pe/ssuto he sprang upon me myself E 459. Cp. 329 D.

§1237
The force of au)to/s thus added is to differentiate. Thus e)me\ au)to/n means myself and no other, e)mauto/n means simply myself without reference to others. u(_ma=s au)tou/s is the usual order in the reflexive combination; but the differentiating you yourselves (and no others) may be u(_ma=s au)tou/s or au)tou\s u(_ma=s.

## THE DEMONSTRATIVE PRONOUNS

§1238
The demonstrative pronouns are used substantively or adjectively: ou(=tos, or ou(=tos o( a)nh/r, this man.

§1239
A demonstrative pronoun may agree in gender with a substantive predicated of it, if connected with the substantive by a copulative verb (917) expressed or understood: au(/th (for tou=to)

a)ri/sth didaskali/a_ this is the best manner of learning
X. C. 8.7.24, ei) de/ tis tau/thn (for tou=to)

ei)rh/nhn u(polamba/nei but if any one regards this as peace
D. 9.9.
a. But the unattracted neuter is common, especially in definitions where the pronoun is the predicate: tou=t' e)/stin h( dikaiosu/nh this is (what we call) justice
P. R. 432b. So ou)x u(/bris tau=t' e)sti/; is not this insolence?
Ar. Ran. 21.

§1240

ou(=tos and o(/de this usually refer to something near in place, time, or thought; e)kei=nos that refers to something more remote. ou(tosi/_ and o(di/_ are emphatic, deictic (333 g) forms (this here).

§1241

Distinction between ou(=tos and o(/de.—o(/de hic points with emphasis to an object in the immediate (actual or mental) vicinity of the speaker, or to something just noticed. In the drama it announces the approach of a new actor. o(/de is even used of the speaker himself as the demonstrative of the first person (1242). ou(=tos iste may refer to a person close at hand, but less vividly, as in statements in regard to a person concerning whom a question has been asked. When o(/de and ou(=tos are contrasted, o(/de refers to the more important, ou(=tos to the less important, object. Thus,

a)ll' o(/de basileu\s xwrei= but lo! here comes the king
S. Ant. 155, au(/th pe/las sou= here she (the person you ask for) is near thee
S. El. 1474,

kai\ tau=t' a)kou/ein ka)/_ti tw=nd' a)lgi/_ona so that we obey both in these things and in things yet more grievous
S. Ant. 64. See also 1245. ou(=tos has a wider range of use than the other demonstratives.

§1242

o(/de is used in poetry for e)gw/: th=sde/ ( = e)mou=)

ge zw/shs e)/ti while I still live
S. Tr. 305. Also for the possessive pronoun of the first person:

ei)/ tis tou/sd' a)kou/setai lo/gous if any one shall hear these my words
S. El. 1004.

§1243

ou(=tos is sometimes used of the second person: ti/s ou(tosi/_; who's this here? ( = who are you?)
Ar. Ach. 1048. So in exclamations: ou(=tos, ti/ poiei=s; you there! what are you doing?
Ar. Ran. 198.

§1244

ta/de, ta/de pa/nta (tau=ta pa/nta) are used of something close at hand:

ou)k *)/iwnes ta/de ei)si/n the people here are not Ionians
T. 6.77.

§1245

ou(=tos (toiou=tos, tosou=tos, and ou(/tws) generally refers to what precedes, o(/de (toio/sde, toso/sde, thliko/sde, and w(=de) to what follows.
Thus, toia/de e)/lecen he spoke as follows, but toiau=ta (tosau=ta) ei)pw/n after speaking thus. Cp.

o( *ku=ros a)kou/sa_s tou= *gwbru/ou toiau=ta toia/de pro\s au)to\n e)/lece Cyrus after hearing these words of Gobryas answered him as follows
X. C. 5.2.31.

§1246

kai\ ou(=tos meaning (1) he too, likewise; (2) and in fact, and that too, points back:

*)agi/a_s kai\ *swkra/ths . . . kai\ tou/tw a)peqane/thn Agias and Socrates . . . they too were put to death
X. A. 2.6.30; a)po/rwn e)sti\ . . . kai\ tou/twn ponhrw=n it is characteristic of men without resources and that too worthless 2. 5. 21 (cp. 1320). On kai\ tau=ta see 947.

§1247
But ou(=tos, etc. sometimes (especially in the neuter) refer to what follows, and o(/de, etc. (though much less often) refer to what precedes:

meta\ de\ tou=ton ei)_pe tosou=ton but after him he spoke as follows
X. A. 1.3.14,

toiou/tous lo/gous ei)=pen he spoke as follows
T. 4.58, toia/de parakeleuo/menos exhorting them thus (as set forth before) 7. 78, w(=de qa/ptousin they bury them thus (as described before) 2. 34, ou(/tws e)/xei the case is as follows (often in the orators).

§1248

ou(=tos (especially in the neuter tou=to) may refer forward to a word or sentence in apposition: w(s mh\ tou=to mo/non e)nnow=ntai, ti/ pei/sontai that they may not consider this alone (namely) what they shall suffer
X. A. 3.1.41. So also ou(/tws. e)kei=nos also may refer forward: e)kei=no kerdai/nein h(gei=tai th\n h(donh/n this (namely) pleasure, it regards as gain
P. R. 606b. Cp. 990.

§1249

ou(=tos (toiou=tos, etc.) is regularly, o(/de (toio/sde, etc.) rarely, used as the demonstrative antecedent of a relative:

o(/tan toiau=ta le/gh|s, a(\ ou)dei\s a)\n fh/seien a)nqrw/pwn when you say such things as no one in the world would say
P. G. 473e. ou(=tos is often used without a conjunction at the beginning of a sentence.

§1250
When o(/de retains its full force the relative clause is to be regarded as a supplementary addition:

ou(= dh\ ou)=n e(/neka le/gw tau=ta pa/nta to/d' e)sti/ but here's the reason why I say all this!
P. Charm. 165a.

§1251
The demonstratives ou(=tos, etc., when used as antecedents, have an emphatic force that does not reproduce the (unemphatic) English demonstrative those, e.g. in you released those who were present. Here Greek uses the participle (tou\s paro/ntas a)pelu/_sate
L. 20.20) or omits the antecedent.

§1252

ou(=tos (less often e)kei=nos) may take up and emphasize a preceding subject or object. In this use the pronoun generally comes first, but may be placed after an emphatic word: poih/santes sth/lhn e)yhfi/santo ei)s tau/thn a)nagra/fein tou\s a':lithri/ous having made a slab they voted to inscribe on it the (names of the) offenders Lyc. 117,

a(\ a)\n ei)/ph|s, e)/mmene tou/tois whatever you say, hold to it
P. R. 345b. The anaphoric au)to/s in its oblique cases is weaker (1214).

§1253

tou=to, tau=ta (and au)to/) may take up a substantive idea not expressed by a preceding neuter word: oi(\ th\n *(ella/da h)leuqe/rwsan: h(mei=s de\ ou)d' h(mi=n au)toi=s bebaiou=men au)to/ (i.e. th\n e)leuqeri/a_n) who freed Greece; whereas we cannot secure this (liberty) even for ourselves
T. 1.122.

§1254

ou(=tos (less frequently e)kei=nos) is used of well known persons and things. Thus, *gorgi/a_s ou(=tos this (famous) Gorgias
P. Hipp. M. 282b (cp. ille), tou/tous tou\s su_kofa/nta_s these (notorious) informers
P. Cr. 45a (cp. iste), to\n *)aristei/dhn e)kei=non that (famous) Aristides
D. 3.21, *kalli/a_n e)kei=non that (infamous) Callias 2. 19. e)kei=nos may be used of a deceased person (
P. R. 368a).

§1255
When, in the same sentence, and referring to the same object, ou(=tos (or e)kei=nos) is used more than once, the object thus designated is more or less emphatic: o( qeo\s e)cairou/menos tou/twn to\n nou=n tou/tois xrh=tai u(phre/tais the god deprives them of their senses and employs them as his ministers P. Ion 534 c. For the repeated ou(=tos (e)kei=nos) an oblique case of au)to/s is usual.

§1256

tou=to me/n . . . tou=to de/ first . . . secondly, partly . . . partly has, especially in Hdt., nearly the sense of to\ me/n . . . to\ de/ (1111).

§1257

e)kei=nos refers back (rarely forward, 1248), but implies remoteness in place, time, or thought.

*ku=ros kaqora=| basile/a_ kai\ to\ a)mf' e)kei=non sti=fos Cyrus perceives the king and the band around him
X. A. 1.8.26, nh=es e)kei=nai e)piple/ousin yonder are ships sailing up to us
T. 1.51.

§1258

e)kei=nos may refer to any person other than the speaker and the person addressed; and may be employed of a person not definitely described, but referred to in a supposed case. It is even used of the person already referred to by au)to/s in an oblique case:

a)\_n au)tw=| didw=|s a)rgu/rion kai\ pei/qh|s e)kei=non if you give him money and persuade him
P. Pr. 310d. e)kei=nos, when so used, usually stands in a different case than au)to/s. The order e)kei=nos . . . au)to/s is found:

pro\s me\n e)kei/nous ou)k ei=pen h(\n e)/xoi gnw/mhn, a)ll' a)pe/pemyen au)tou/s he did not tell them the plan he had, but dismissed them
X. H. 3.2.9.

§1259
When used to set forth a contrast to another person, e)kei=nos may even refer to the subject of the leading verb (apparent reflexive use): o(/tan e)n th=| gh=| o(rw=sin h(ma=s dh|ou=nta/s te kai\ ta)_kei/nwn fqei/rontas when they (the Athenians) see us (the Dorians) in their land plundering and destroying their property ( = ta\ e(autw=n)
T. 2.11, e)/lece toi=s *xaldai/ois o(/ti h(/koi oi)/te a)pole/sai e)piqu_mw=n e)kei/nous ou)/te polemei=n deo/menos he said to the Chaldaeans that he had come neither with the desire to destroy them (e)kei/nous is stronger than au)tou/s) nor because he wanted to war with them
X. C. 3.2.12.

§1260
In the phrase o(/de e)kei=nos, o(/de marks a person or thing as present, e)kei=nos a person or thing mentioned before or well known:

o(/d' e)kei=nos e)gw/ lo! I am he
S. O. C. 138. Colloquial expressions are tou=t' e)kei=no there it is! (lit. this is that)
Ar. Ach. 41, and

to/d' e)kei=no I told you so
E. Med. 98.

§1261

Distinction between ou(=tos and e)kei=nos.—When reference is made to one of two contrasted objects, ou(=tos refers to the object nearer to the speaker's thought, or to the more important object, or to the object last mentioned. Thus, w(/ste polu\ a)\n dikaio/teron e)kei/nois toi=s gra/mmasin h)\ tou/tois pisteu/oite so that you must with more justice put your trust in those lists (not yet put in as evidence) than in these muster-rolls (already mentioned)
L. 16.7,

ei) de\ tou=to/ soi dokei= mi_kro\n ei)=nai, e)kei=no katano/hson but if this appear to you unimportant, consider the following
X. C. 5.5.29. e)kei=nos may refer to an object that has immediately preceded: kai\ (dei=) to\ be/ltiston a)ei/, mh\ to\ r(a=|ston, a(/pantas le/gein: e)p' e)kei=no me\n (i.e. to\ r(a=|ston) ga\r h( fu/sis au)th\ badiei=tai, e)pi\ tou=to de\ (to\ be/ltiston)

tw=| lo/gw| dei= proa/gesqai dida/skonta to\n a)gaqo\n poli/_thn it is necessary that all should speak what is always most salutary, not what is most agreeable; for to the latter nature herself will incline; to the former a good citizen must direct by argument and instruction
D. 8.72.

## THE INTERROGATIVE PRONOUNS

§1262
The interrogative pronouns are used substantively ti/s; who? or adjectively ti/s a)nh/r; what man?

§1263
The interrogatives (pronouns and adverbs, 340, 346) are used in direct and in indirect questions. In indirect questions the indefinite relatives o(/stis, etc., are generally used instead of the interrogatives.
ti/ bou/letai h(mi=n xrh=sqai; for what purpose does he desire to employ us?
X. A. 1.3.18, ou)k oi)=da o(/ ti a)/n tis xrh/saito au)toi=s I do not know for what service any one could employ them 3. 1. 40, A. phni/k' e)sti\n a)/ra th=s h(me/ras; B. o(phni/ka; A. What's the time of day? B. (You ask), what time of day it is?
Ar. Av. 1499.
N.—For peculiarities of Interrogative Sentences, see 2666, 2668.

§1264

ti/ is used for ti/na as the predicate of a neuter plural subject when the general result is sought and the subject is considered as a unit: tau=ta de\ ti/ e)stin; but these things, what are they?
Aes. 3.167. ti/na emphasizes the details: ti/n' ou)=n e)sti tau=ta;
D. 18.246.

§1265

ti/s asks a question concerning the class, ti/ concerning the nature of a thing:

ei)pe\ ti/s h( te/xnh say of what sort the art is
P. G. 449a, ti/ swfrosu/nh, ti/ poli_tiko/s; what is temperance, what is a statesman?
X. M. 1.1.16, fqo/non de\ skopw=n o(/ ti ei)/h considering what envy is (quid sit invidia)
X. M. 3.9.8.

## THE INDEFINITE PRONOUNS

§1266
The indefinite pronoun ti\s, ti\ is used both substantively (some one) and adjectively (any, some). ti\s, ti\ cannot stand at the beginning of a sentence (181 b).

§1267
In the singular, ti\s is used in a collective sense: everybody (for anybody); cp. Germ. man, Fr. on:

a)lla\ mi_sei= tis e)kei=non but everybody detests him
D. 4.8. e(/kasto/s tis, pa=s tis each one, every one are generally used in this sense. ti\s may be a covert allusion to a known person: dw/sei tis di/khn some one (i.e. you) will pay the penalty
Ar. Ran. 554. It may also stand for I or we. Even when added to a noun with the article, ti\s denotes the indefiniteness of the person referred to: o(/tan d' o( ku/_rios parh=| tis, u(_mw=n o(/stis e)sti\n h(gemw/n ktl. but whenever your master arrives, whoever he be that is your leader, etc.
S. O. C. 289. With a substantive, ti\s may often be rendered a, an, as in

e(/tero/s tis duna/sths another dignitary
X. A. 1.2.20; or, to express indefiniteness of nature, by a sort of, etc., as in ei) me\n qeoi/ tine/s ei)sin oi( dai/mones if the ‘daimones’ are a sort of gods
P. A. 27d.

§1268
With adjectives, adverbs, and numerals, ti\s may strengthen or weaken an assertion, apologize for a comparison, and in general qualify a statement:

deino/s tis a)nh/r a very terrible man
P. R. 596c,

mu/wy tis a sort of gad-fly
P. A. 30e,

sxedo/n ti pretty nearly
X. O. 4.11,

tria/_konta/ tines about 30
T. 8.73. But in parege/nonto/ tines du/o nh=es the numeral is appositional to tine/s (certain, that is, two ships joined them)
T. 8.100.

§1269

ti\s, ti\ sometimes means somebody , or something, of importance:

to\ dokei=n tine\s ei)=nai the seeming to be somebody
D. 21.213,

e)/doce/ ti le/gein he seemed to say something of moment
X. C. 1.4.20.

§1270

ti\ is not omitted in

qaumasto\n le/geis what you say is wonderful
P. L. 657a. h)/ tis h)\ ou)dei/s means few or none
X. C. 7.5.45,

h)/ ti h)\ ou)de/n little or nothing
P. A. 17b.

## THE ADJECTIVE PRONOUNS a)/llos AND e(/teros

§1271

a)/llos strictly means other (of several), e(/teros other (of two). On o( a)/llos, oi( a)/lloi see 1188.
a. e(/teros is sometimes used loosely for a)/llos, but always with a sense of difference; when so used it does not take the article.

§1272

a)/llos, and e(/teros (rarely), may be used attributively with a substantive, which is to be regarded as an appositive. In this sense they may be rendered besides, moreover, as well: oi( a)/lloi *)aqhnai=oi the Athenians as well (the others, i.e. the Athenians)
T. 7.70,

tou\s o(pli/_ta_s kai\ tou\s a)/llous i(ppe/a_s the hoplites and the cavalry besides
X. H. 2.4.9, ge/rwn xwrei= meq' e(te/rou nea_ni/ou an old man comes with (a second person, a young man) a young man besides
Ar. Eccl. 849. Cp. “And there were also two other malefactors led with him to be put to death” St. Luke 23. 32.

§1273

a)/llos other, rest often precedes the particular thing with which it is contrasted: ta/ te a)/lla e)ti/_mhse kai\ mu_ri/ous e)/dwke da_reikou/s he gave me ten thousand darics besides honouring me in other ways (lit. he both honoured me in other ways and etc.)
X. A. 1.3.3,

tw=| me\n a)/llw| stratw=| h(su/xazen, e(kato\n de\ peltasta\_s prope/mpei with the rest of the army he kept quiet, but sent forward a hundred peltasts
T. 4.111.

§1274

a)/llos followed by another of its own cases or by an adverb derived from itself (cp. alius aliud, one . . . one, another . . . another) does not require the second half of the statement to be expressed: a)/llos a)/lla le/gei one says one thing, another (says) another
X. A. 2.1.15 (lit. another other things). So a)/lloi a)/llws, a)/lloi a)/lloqen.
a. Similarly e(/teros, as sumfora\_ e(te/ra_ e(te/rous pie/zei one calamity oppresses one, another others
E. Alc. 893.

§1275
After o( a)/llos an adjective or a participle used substantively usually requires the article:

ta)=lla ta\ me/gista the other matters of the highest moment
P. A. 22d. Here ta\ me/gista is in apposition to ta)=lla (1272). oi( a)/lloi pa/ntes oi(, ta)=lla pa/nta ta/ sometimes omit the final article.

§1276

o( a)/llos often means usual, general: para\ to\n a)/llon tro/pon contrary to my usual disposition Ant. 3.
b. 1.

## THE RECIPROCAL PRONOUN

§1277
The pronoun a)llh/loin expresses reciprocal relation:

w(s d' ei)de/thn a)llh/lous h( gunh\ kai\ o( *)abrada/ta_s, h)spa/zonto a)llh/lous when Abradatas and his wife saw each other, they mutually embraced
X. C. 6.1.47.

§1278
To express reciprocal relation Greek uses also (1) the middle forms (1726); (2) the reflexive pronoun (1231); or (3) a substantive is repeated: a)nh\r e(/len a)/ndra man fell upon man O 328.
On Relative Pronouns see under Complex Sentences (2493 ff.).

## THE CASES

§1279
Of the cases belonging to the Indo-European language, Greek has lost the free use of three: instrumental, locative, and ablative. A few of the forms of these cases have been preserved (341, 1449, 1535); the syntactical functions of the instrumental and locative were taken over by the dative; those of the ablative by the genitive. The genitive and dative cases are therefore composite or mixed cases.
N.—The reasons that led to the formation of composite cases are either (1) formal or (2) functional. Thus (1) xw/ra| is both dat. and loc.; lo/gois represents the instr. lo/gois and the loc. lo/goisi; in consonantal stems both ablative and genitive ended in -os; (2) verbs of ruling may take either the dat. or the loc., hence the latter case would be absorbed by the former; furthermore the use of prepositions especially with loc. and instr. was attended by a certain indifference as regards the form of the case.

§1280
Through the influence of one construction upon another it often becomes impossible to mark off the later from the original use of the genitive and dative. It must be remembered that since language is a natural growth and Greek was spoken and written before formal categories were set up by Grammar, all the uses of the cases cannot be apportioned with definiteness.

§1281
The cases fall into two main divisions. Cases of the Subject: nominative (and vocative). Cases of the Predicate: accusative, dative. The genitive may define either the subject (with nouns) or the predicate (with verbs). On the nominative, see 938 ff.

§1282
The content of a thought may be expressed in different ways in different languages. Thus, pei/qw se, but persuadeo tibi (in classical Latin): and even in the same language, the same verb may have varying constructions to express different shades of meaning.

## VOCATIVE

§1283
The vocative is used in exclamations and in direct address:

w)= *zeu= kai\ qeoi/ oh Zeus and ye gods
P. Pr. 310d,

a)/nqrwpe my good fellow
X. C. 2.2.7. The vocative forms an incomplete sentence (904 d).
a. The vocative is never followed immediately by de/ or ga/r.

§1284
In ordinary conversation and public speeches, the polite w)= is usually added. Without w)= the vocative may express astonishment, joy, contempt, a threat, or a warning, etc. Thus a)kou/eis *ai)sxi/nh; d'ye hear, Aeschines?
D. 18.121. But this distinction is not always observed, though in general w)= has a familiar tone which was unsuited to elevated poetry.

§1285
The vocative is usually found in the interior of a sentence. At the beginning it is emphatic. In prose e)/fh, in poetry w)=, may stand between the vocative and an attributive or between an attributive and the vocative; in poetry w)= may be repeated for emphasis.

§1286
In late poetry a predicate adjective may be attracted into the vocative: o)/lbie kw=re ge/noio blessed, oh boy, mayest thou be Theocr. 17. 66. Cp. Matutine pater seu Iane libentius audis Hor. S. 2. 6. 20.

§1287
By the omission of su/ or u(_mei=s the nominative with the article may stand in apposition to a vocative: w)= a)/ndoes oi( paro/ntes you, gentlemen, who are present
P. Pr. 337c,

w)= *ku=re kai\ oi( a)/lloi *pe/rsai Cyrus and the rest of you Persians
X. C. 3.3.20; and in apposition to the pronoun in the verb: o( pai=s, a)kolou/qei boy, attend me
Ar. Ran. 521.

§1288
The nominative may be used in exclamations as a predicate with the subject unexpressed:

w)= pikro\s qeoi=s oh loathed of heaven
S. Ph. 254,

fi/los w)= *mene/la_e ah dear Menelaus
*d 189; and connected with the vocative by and:

w)= po/lis kai\ dh=me oh city and people
Ar. Eq. 273. In exclamations about a person:

w)\ gennai=os oh the noble man
P. Phae. 227c.
a. ou(=tos is regular in address: ou(=tos, ti/ pa/sxeis, w)= *canqi/a_; ho there, I say, Xanthias, what is the matter with you?
Ar. Vesp. 1; w)= ou(=tos, *ai)/a_s ho there, I say, Ajax
S. Aj. 89.

## GENITIVE

§1289
The genitive most commonly limits the meaning of substantives, adjectives, and adverbs, less commonly that of verbs.
Since the genitive has absorbed the ablative it includes (1) the genitive proper, denoting the class to which a person or thing belongs, and (2) the ablatival genitive.
a. The name genitive is derived from casus genitivus, the case of origin, the inadequate Latin translation of genikh\ ptw=sis case denoting the class.

## THE GENITIVE PROPER WITH NOUNS: (ADNOMINAL GENITIVE)

§1290
A substantive in the genitive limits the meaning of a substantive on which it depends.

§1291
The genitive limits for the time being the scope of the substantive on which it depends by referring it to a particular class or description, or by regarding it as a part of a whole. The genitive is akin in meaning to the adjective and may often be translated by an epithet. Cp. ste/fanos xru_si/ou with xru_sou=s ste/fanos, fo/bos polemi/ou with pole/mios fo/bos, to\ eu)=ros ple/qrou with to\ eu)=ros pleqriai=on (1035). But the use of the adjective is not everywhere parallel to that of the genitive.

§1292
In poetry a genitive is often used with bi/a_, me/nos, sqe/nos might, etc., instead of the corresponding adjective: bi/h *diomh/deos mighty Diomede E 781.

§1293
In poetry de/mas form, ka/ra_ and kefalh/ head, etc., are used with a genitive to express majestic or loved persons or objects: *)ismh/nhs ka/ra_
S. Ant. 1.

§1294

xrh=ma thing is used in prose with a genitive to express size, strength, etc.:

sfendonhtw=n pa/mpolu/ ti xrh=ma a very large mass of slingers
X. C. 2.1.5. Cp. 1322.

§1295
The genitive with substantives denotes in general a connection or dependence between two words. This connection must often be determined (1) by the meaning of the words, (2) by the context, (3) by the facts presupposed as known (1301). The same construction may often be placed under more than one of the different classes mentioned below; and the connection between the two substantives is often so loose that it is difficult to include with precision all cases under specific grammatical classes.
a. The two substantives may be so closely connected as to be equivalent to a single compound idea: teleuth\ tou= bi/ou ‘life-end’ (cp. life-time)
X. A. 1.1.1. Cp. 1146.
b. The genitive with substantives has either the attributive (1154), or, in the case of the genitive of the divided whole (1306), and of personal pronouns (1185), the predicate, position (1168).

§1296
Words denoting number, especially numerals or substantives with numerals, often agree in case with the limited word instead of standing in the genitive:

fo/ros te/ssara ta/lanta a tribute of four talents
T. 4.57 (cp. 1323), e)s ta\_s nau=s, ai(\ e)frou/roun du/o, katafugo/ntes fleeing to the ships, two of which were keeping guard 4. 113. So with oi( me/n, oi( de/ in apposition to the subject (981).

## GENITIVE OF POSSESSION OR BELONGING

§1297
The genitive denotes ownership, possession, or belonging:

h( oi)ki/a_ h( *si/mwnos the house of Simon
L. 3.32,

o( *ku/_rou sto/los the expedition of Cyrus
X. A. 1.2.5. Cp. the dative of possession (1476).

§1298
Here may be classed the genitive of origin:

oi( *so/lwnos no/moi the laws of Solon

§1299
The possessive genitive is used with the neuter article (singular or plural) denoting affairs, conditions, power, and the like:

§1300
The genitive of possession may be used after a demonstrative or relative pronoun:

tou=to/ mou diaba/llei he attacks this action of mine

§1301
With persons the genitive may denote the relation of child to parent, wife to husband, and of inferior to superior: *qouku_di/dhs o( *)olo/rou Thucydides, the son of Olorus

h( *smi_kuqi/wnos *melisti/xh Melistiche wife of Smicythion

oi( *me/nwnos the troops of Menon

a. In poetry we may have an attributive adjective: *telamw/nios *ai)/a_s ( = *ai)/a_s o( *telamw=nos) B 528. Cp. 846 f.

§1302
The word on which the possessive genitive depends may be represented by the article: a)po\ th=s e(autw=n from their own country (gh=s)

e)n *)ari/fronos at Ariphron's

e)k *patrokle/ous e)/rxomai I come from Patroclus's

§1303

Predicate Use.—The genitive may be connected with the noun it limits by means of a verb.

*(ippokra/ths e)sti\ oi)ki/a_s mega/lhs Hippocrates is of an influential house

*boiwtw=n h( po/lis e)/stai the city will belong to the Boeotians

§1304
The genitive with ei)mi/ may denote the person whose nature, duty, custom, etc., it is to do that set forth in an infinitive subject of the verb: peni/a_n fe/rein ou) panto/s, a)ll' a)ndro\s sofou= 'tis the sage, not every one, who can bear poverty

§1305
With verbs signifying to refer or attribute, by thought, word, or action, anything to a person or class. Such verbs are to think, regard, make, name, choose, appoint, etc.

logi/zou . . . ta\ d' a)/lla th=s tu/xhs deem that the rest belongs to chance

## GENITIVE OF THE DIVIDED WHOLE (PARTITIVE GENITIVE)

§1306
The genitive may denote a whole, a part of which is denoted by the noun it limits. The genitive of the divided whole may be used with any word that expresses or implies a part.

§1307

Position.—The genitive of the whole stands before or after the word denoting the part:

tw=n *qra|kw=n peltastai/ targeteers of the Thracians
T. 7.27,

oi( a)/poroi tw=n poli_tw=n the needy among the citizens
D. 18.104; rarely between the limited noun and its article:

oi( tw=n a)di/kwn a)fiknou/menoi those of the unrighteous who come here
P. G. 525c. Cp. 1161 N. 1.

§1308
When all are included there is no partition: so in ou(=toi pa/ntes all of these, all these, te/ttares h(mei=s h)=men there were four of us,

to\ pa=n plh=qos tw=n o(pli_tw=n the entire body of the hoplites
T. 8.93, o(/soi e)ste\ tw=n o(moi/wn as many of you as belong to the ‘peers’
X. A. 4.6.14.

§1309
The idea of division is often not explicitly stated. See third example in 1310.

§1310
(I) The genitive of the divided whole is used with substantives.

me/ros ti tw=n barba/rwn some part of the barbarians
T. 1.1, oi( *dwrih=s h(mw=n those of us who are Dorians 4. 61. The governing word may be omitted: *)arxi/a_s tw=n *(hra_kleidw=n Archias (one) of the Heraclidae
T. 6.3. To an indefinite substantive without the article may be added a genitive denoting the special sort: *ferau/la_s *pe/rshs tw=n dhmotw=n Pheraulas, a Persian, one of the common people
X. C. 2.3.7.

§1311

Chorographic Genitive.—

th=s *)attikh=s e)s *oi)no/hn to Oenoë in Attica
T. 2.18 (or e)s *oi)no/hn th=s *)attikh=s, not e)s th=s *)attikh=s *oi)no/hn), th=s *)itali/a_s *aokroi/ the Locrians in Italy 3. 86. The article, which is always used with the genitive of the country (as a place well known), is rarely added to the governing substantive (

to\ *kh/naion th=s *eu)boi/a_s Cenaeum in Euboea
T. 3.93).

§1312
(II) With substantive adjectives and participles.

oi( a)/dikoi tw=n a)nqrw/pwn the unjust among men
D. 27.68 (but always oi( qnhtoi\ a)/nqrwpoi),

mo/nos tw=n pruta/newn alone of the prytans
P. A. 32b,

o)li/goi au)tw=n few of them
X. A. 3.1.3,

tw=n a)/llwn *(ellh/nwn o( boulo/menos whoever of the rest of the Greeks so desires
T. 3.92. So

to\ katantikru\ au)tw=n tou= sphlai/ou the part of the cavern facing them
P. R. 515a. For nihil novi the Greek says ou)de\n kaino/n.

§1313
Adjectives denoting magnitude, and some others, may conform in gender to the genitive, instead of appearing in the neuter:

e)/temon th=s gh=s th\n pollh/n they ravaged most of the land
T. 2.56, th=s gh=s h( a)ri/sth the best of the land 1. 2. This construction occurs more frequently in prose than in poetry.

§1314
But such adjectives, especially when singular, may be used in the neuter:

tw=n *)argei/wn loga/dwn to\ polu/ the greater part of the picked Argives
T. 5.73, e)pi\ polu\ th=s xw/ra_s over a great part of the land 4. 3.

§1315
(III) With comparatives and superlatives.

h(mw=n o( gerai/teros the elder of us
X. C. 5.1.6 (1066 b),

oi( presbu/tatoi tw=n strathgw=n the oldest of the generals
X. A. 3.3.11,

si/_tw| pa/ntwn a)nqrw/pwn plei/stw| xrw/meq' e)peisa/ktw| we make use of imported grain more than all other people
D. 18.87. So with a superlative adverb:

h( nau=s a)/rista/ moi e)/plei panto\s tou= stratope/dou my ship was the best sailer of the whole squadron
L. 21.6.

§1316
In poetry this use is extended to positive adjectives: a)ridei/ketos a)ndrw=n conspicuous among men A 248,

w)= fi/la_ gunaikw=n oh dear among women
E. Alc. 460. In tragedy an adjective may be emphasized by the addition of the same adjective in the genitive:

a)/rrht' a)rrh/twn horrors unspeakable
S. O. T. 465. Cp. 1064.

§1317
(IV) With substantive pronouns and numerals.

oi( me\n au)tw=n, oi( d' ou)/ some of them and not others
P. A. 24e,

oi(\ u(/steron e)lh/fqhsan tw=n polemi/wn those of the enemy who were taken later
X. A. 1.7.13,

ou)dei\s a)nqrw/pwn no one in the world
P. S. 220a,

ti\ tou= tei/xous a part of the wall
T. 7.4,

ti\s qew=n one of the gods
E. Hec. 164 (

ti\s qeo/s a god
X. C. 5.2.12),

e(\n tw=n pollw=n one of the many things
P. A. 17a; rarely after demonstrative pronouns: tou/tois tw=n a)nqrw/pwn to these (of) men
T. 1.71.
a. With o)li/goi and with numerals a)po/ and e)c are rarely added:

e)k triw=n e(/n one of three
S. Tr. 734. e)c with superlatives is also rare. See also 1688. 1 c.

§1318
The genitive of the divided whole may do duty as the subject of a finite verb (928 b) or of the infinitive: (e)/fasan) e)pimeignu/nai sfw=n pro\s e)kei/nous they said that some of their number associated with them
X. A. 3.5.16.

§1319

Predicate Use.—

h)=n d' au)tw=n *fali=nos and among them was Phalinus
X. A. 2.1.7, *so/lwn tw=n e(pta\ sofistw=n e)klh/qh Solon was called one of the Seven Sages
I. 15.235,

tw=n a)topwta/twn a)\n ei)/h it would be very strange
D. 1.26; and often with verbs signifying to be, become, think, say, name, choose. With some of these verbs ei(=s with the genitive may be used instead of the genitive alone.

## GENITIVE OF QUALITY

§1320
The genitive to denote quality occurs chiefly as a predicate.

e)w\n tro/pou h(suxi/ou being of a peaceful disposition
Hdt. 1.107,

oi( de/ tines th=s au)th=s gnw/mhs o)li/goi kate/fugon but some few of the same opinion fled
T. 3.70,

tau=ta pampo/llwn e)sti\ lo/gwn this calls for a thorough discussion
P. L. 642a, qewrh/sat' au)to/n, mh\ o(pote/rou tou= lo/gou, a)ll' o(pote/rou tou= bi/ou e)sti/n consider, not the manner of his speech, but the manner of his life
Aes. 3.168,

ei) dokei= tau=ta kai\ dapa/nhs mega/lhs kai\ po/nwn pollw=n kai\ pra_gmatei/a_s ei)=nai if these matters seem to involve great expense and much toil and trouble
D. 8.48.
a. The attributive use occurs in poetry:

xo/rtwn eu)de/ndrwn *eu)rw/pa_s Europe with its pastures amid fair trees
E. I. T. 134, leukh=s xio/nos pte/ruc a wing white as snow (of white snow)
S. Ant. 114.

§1321
The use of the genitive to express quality, corresponding to the Latin genitive, occurs in the non-predicate position, only when age or size is exactly expressed by the addition of a numeral (genitive of measure, 1325). The Latin genitive of quality in mulier mirae pulchritudinis is expressed by gunh\ qaumasi/a_ ka/llos (or tou= ka/llous), gunh\ qaumasi/a_ i)dei=n, gunh\ e)/xousa qauma/sion sxh=ma, etc.

## GENITIVE OF EXPLANATION (APPOSITIVE GENITIVE)

§1322
The genitive of an explicit word may explain the meaning of a more general word.
*)i_li/ou po/lis E 642, as urbs Romae,

a)/ellai pantoi/wn a)ne/mwn blasts formed of winds of every sort
e 292. This construction is chiefly poetic, but in prose we find u(o\s me/ga xrh=ma a monster (great affair, 1294) of a boar
Hdt. 1.36,

to\ o)/ros th=s *)istw/nhs Mt. Istone

a)maqi/a_ h( tou= oi)/esqai ei)de/nai a:\ ou)k oi)=den the ignorance of thinking one knows what one does not know

a. But with o)/noma the person or thing named is usually in apposition to o)/noma:

tw=| de\ newta/tw| e)qe/mhn o)/noma *kalli/straton I gave the youngest the name Callistratus

## GENITIVE OF MEASURE

§1325
The genitive denotes measure of space, time, or degree.

o)ktw\ stadi/wn tei=xos a wall eight stades long
T. 7.2, pe/nte h(merw=n si_ti/a provisions for five days 7. 43 (cp. fossa pedum quindecim, exilium decem annorum Less commonly with a neuter adjective or pronoun: e)pi\ me/ga e)xw/rhsan duna/<*> they advanced to a great pitch of power

ei)s tou=to th=s h(liki/a_s to this stage of life
