§1326
Under the head of measure belongs amount:

duoi=n mnai=n pro/sodos an income of two minae
X. Vect. 3.10. Cp. 1296, 1323.

§1327

Predicate Use.—

e)peida\n e)tw=n h)=| tis tria/_konta when a man is thirty years old
P. L. 721a,

ta\ tei/xh h)=n stadi/wn o)ktw/ the walls were eight stades long
T. 4.66.

## SUBJECTIVE AND OBJECTIVE GENITIVE

§1328
With a verbal noun the genitive may denote the subject or object of the action expressed in the noun.
a. Many of these genitives derive their construction from that of the kindred verbs:

tou= u(/datos e)piqu_mi/a_ desire for water
T. 2.52 (1349), xo/los ui(o/s anger because of his son O 138 (1405). But the verbal idea sometimes requires the accusative, or (less commonly) the dative.

§1329
In poetry an adjective may take the place of the genitive:

no/stos o( basi/leios the return of the king
A. Pers. 8. Cp. 1291.

§1330
The Subjective Genitive is active in sense: tw=n barba/rwn fo/bos the fear of the barbarians (which they feel: oi( ba/rbaroi fobou=ntai)
X. A. 1.2.17, h( basile/ws e)piorki/a_ the perjury of the king (basileu\s e)piorkei=) 3. 2. 4,

to\ o)rgizo/menon th=s gnw/mhs their angry feelings
T. 2.59 (such genitives with substantive participles are common in Thucydides; cp. 1153 b, N. 2).

§1331
The Objective Genitive is passive in sense, and is very common with substantives denoting a frame of mind or an emotion: fo/bos tw=n *ei(lw/twn the fear of the Helots (felt towards them: fobou=ntai tou\s *ei(/lwtas)
T. 3.54, h( tw=n *(ellh/nwn eu)/noia good-will towards the Greeks (eu)noei= toi=s *(/ellhsi)
X. A. 4.7.20, h( tw=n kalw=n sunousi/a_ intercourse with the good (su/neisi toi=s kaloi=s)
P. L. 838a.
a. The objective genitive often precedes another genitive on which it depends:

meta\ th=s cummaxi/a_s th=s ai)th/sews with the request for an alliance
T. 1.32.

§1332
Various prepositions are used in translating the objective genitive:

o( qew=n po/lemos war with the gods
X. A. 2.5.7,

o(/rkoi qew=n oaths by the gods
E. Hipp. 657,

qew=n eu)xai/ prayers to the gods
P. Phae. 244e,

a)dikhma/twn o)rgh/ anger at injustice
L. 12.20,

e)gkra/teia h(donh=s moderation in pleasure
I. 1.21,

h( tw=n h(donw=n ni/_kh victory over pleasures
P. L. 840c,

tro/paia barba/rwn memorials of victory over barbarians
X. A. 7.6.36,

paraine/seis tw=n cunallagw=n exhortations to reconciliation
T. 4.59,

mu=qos fi/lwn tidings about friends
S. Ant. 11,

sou= mu=qos speech with thee
S. O. C. 1161. In

qana/tou lu/sis release from death
i 421, metapauswlh\ pole/moio respite from war T 201, it is uncertain whether the genitive is objective or ablatival (1392).

§1333
The objective genitive is often used when a prepositional expression, giving greater precision, is more usual: to\ *megare/wn yh/fisma the decree relating to (peri/) the Megarians
T. 1.140, a)po/basis th=s gh=s a descent upon the land (e)s th\n gh=n) 1. 108, a)po/stasis tw=n *)aqhnai/wn revolt from the Athenians (a)po\ tw=n *)aqhnai/wn) 8. 5.

§1334
For the objective genitive a possessive pronoun is sometimes used:

sh\n xa/rin for thy sake
P. Soph. 242a,

diabolh\ h( e)mh/ calumniation of me
P. A. 20e. o( e)mo\s fo/bos is usually objective: the fear which I inspire. (But

sou= mu=qos speech with thee
S. O. C. 1161.)

§1335

Predicate Use.—ou) tw=n kakou/rgwn oi)=ktos, a)lla\ th=s di/khs compassion is not for wrong-doers, but for justice E. fr. 270.

## GENITIVE OF VALUE

§1336
The genitive expresses value.

i(era\ triw=n tala/ntwn offerings worth three talents
L. 30.20,

xi_li/wn draxmw=n di/khn feu/gw I am defendant in an action involving a thousand drachmas
D. 55.25.

§1337

Predicate Use:

tou\s ai)xmalw/tous tosou/twn xrhma/twn lu/_esqai to ransom the captives at so high a price
D. 19.222, triw=n draxmw=n ponhro\s w)/n a threepenny rogue 19. 200.

## TWO GENITIVES WITH ONE NOUN

§1338
Two genitives expressing different relations may be used with one noun.

oi( a)/nqrwpoi dia\ to\ au(tw=n de/os tou= qana/tou katayeu/dontai by reason of their fear of death men tell lies
P. Ph. 85a,

*dionu/_sou presbu_tw=n xoro/s a chorus of old men in honour of Dionysus
P. L. 665b,

h( tou= *aa/xhtos tw=n new=n a)rxh/ Laches' command of the fleet
T. 3.115, h( *faia/_kwn proenoi/khsis th=s *kerku/_ra_s the former occupation of Corcyra by the Phaeacians 1.25.

## GENITIVE WITH VERBS

§1339
The genitive may serve as the immediate complement of a verb, or it may appear, as a secondary definition, along with an accusative which is the immediate object of the verb (920, 1392, 1405).

§1340
The subject of an active verb governing the genitive may become the subject of the passive construction: *ni_kh/ratos e)rw=n th=s gunaiko\s a)ntera=tai Niceratus, who is in love with his wife, is loved in return
X. S. 8. 3. Cp. 1745 a.

## THE GENITIVE PROPER WITH VERBS

## THE PARTITIVE GENITIVE

§1341
A verb may be followed by the partitive genitive if the action affects the object only in part. If the entire object is affected, the verb in question takes the accusative.
*)adrh/stoio d' e)/ghme qugatrw=n he married one of Adrastus' daughters
*c 121, tw=n pw/lwn lamba/nei he takes some of the colts
X. A. 4.5.35, labo/ntes tou= barbarikou= stratou= taking part of the barbarian force 1. 5. 7, kle/ptontes tou= o)/rous seizing part of the mountain secretly 4. 6. 15 (cp. tou= o)/rous kle/yai ti 4. 6. 11), th=s gh=s e)/temon they ravaged part of the land
T. 2.56 (cp. th\n gh=n pa=san e)/temon 2. 57 and e)/temon th=s gh=s th\n pollh/n 2. 56), katea/_gh th=s kefalh=s he had a hole knocked somewhere in his head
Ar. Vesp. 1428 (

th\n kefalh\n katea_ge/nai to have one's head broken
D. 54.35).

§1342
With impersonals a partitive genitive does duty as the subject:

pole/mou ou) meth=n au)th=| she had no share in war
X. C. 7.2.28,

e)moi\ ou)damo/qen prosh/kei tou/tou tou= pra/_gmatos I have no part whatever in this affair
And. 4.34. Cp. 1318.

§1343
The genitive is used with verbs of sharing.

pa/ntes metei=xon th=s e(orth=s all took part in the festival
X. A. 5.3.9, metedi/dosan a)llh/lois w(=n (= tou/twn a(\) ei)=xon e(/kastoi they shared with each other what each had 4. 5. 6,

to\ a)nqrw/pinon ge/nos metei/lhfen a)qanasi/a_s the human race has received a portion of immortality
P. L. 721b,

si/_tou koinwnei=n to take a share of food
X. M. 2.6.22,

dikaiosu/nhs ou)de\n u(_mi=n prosh/kei you have no concern in righteous dealing
X. H. 2.4.40,

poli_tei/a_, e)n h(=| pe/nhsin ou) me/testin a)rxh=s a form of government in which the poor have no part in the management of affairs
P. R. 550c. So with metalagxa/nein get a share (along with somebody else), sunai/resqai and koinou=sqai take part in, metaitei=n and metapoiei=sqai demand a share in.

§1344
The part received or taken, if expressed, stands in the accusative. oi( tu/rannoi tw=n megi/stwn a)gaqw=n e)la/xista mete/xousi tyrants have the smallest por- tion in the greatest blessings
X. Hi. 2.6,

tou/twn metaitei_ to\ me/ros he demands his share of this
Ar. Vesp. 972.
a. With me/testi the part may be added in the nominative:

me/testi xu)_mi=n tw=n pepra_gme/nwn me/ros ye too have had a share in these doings
E. I. T. 1299.

§1345
The genitive is used with verbs signifying to touch, take hold of, make trial of.
（h( no/sos)

h(/yato tw=n a)nqrw/pwn the plague laid hold of the men
T. 2.48, th=s gnw/mhs th=s au)th=s e)/xomai I hold to the same opinion 1. 140,

e)n th=| e)xome/nh| e)mou= kli/_nh| on the couch next to me
P. S. 217d,

a)ntila/besqe tw=n pra_gma/twn take our public policy in hand
D. 1.20, o(/pws peirw=|nto tou= tei/xous to make an attempt on (a part of) the wall
T. 2.81. So with yau/ein touch (rare in prose), a)nte/xesqai cling to, e)pilamba/nesqai and sullamba/nesqai lay hold of.

§1346
The genitive of the part, with the accusative of the person (the whole) who has been touched, is chiefly poetical:

to\n de\ peso/nta podw=n e)/labe but him as he fell, he seized by his feet
*d 463,

e)/labon th=s zw/nhs to\n *)oro/nta_n they took hold of Orontas by the girdle
X. A. 1.6.10 (but

mou= labo/menos th=s xeiro/s taking me by the hand
P. Charm. 153b),

a)/gein th=s h(ni/a_s to\n i(/ppon to lead the horse by the bridle
X. Eq. 6.9 (cp.

bou=n d' a)ge/thn kera/wn they led the cow by the horns
g 439).

§1347

Verbs of beseeching take the genitive by analogy to verbs of touching: e)me\ lisse/sketo gou/nwn she besought me by (clasping) my knees I 451 (cp. genei/ou a(ya/menos li/ssesqai beseech by touching his chin K 454).

§1348
The genitive is used with verbs of beginning.
a. Partitive:

e)/fh *ku=ron a)/rxein tou= lo/gou w(=de he said that Cyrus began the discussion as follows
X. A. 1.6.5, tou= lo/gou h)/rxeto w(=de he began his speech as follows 3. 2. 7. On a)/rxein as distinguished from a)/rxesqai see 1734. 5.
b. Ablatival (1391) denoting the point of departure: se/o d' a)/rcomai I will make a beginning with thee I 97. In this sense a)po/ or e)c is usually added: a)rca/menoi a)po\ sou=
D. 18.297,

a)/rcomai a)po\ th=s i)_a_trikh=s le/gwn I will make a beginning by speaking of medicine
P. S. 186b.

§1349
The genitive is used with verbs signifying to aim at, strive after, desire (genitive of the end desired).

a)nqrw/pwn stoxa/zesqai to aim at men
X. C. 1.6.29,

e)fi_e/menoi tw=n kerdw=n desiring gain
T. 1.8,

pa/ntes tw=n a)gaqw=n e)piqu_mou=sin all men desire what is good
P. R. 438a,

to\ e)ra=n tw=n kalw=n the passionate love of what is noble
Aes. 1.137,

peinw=si xrhma/twn they are hungry for wealth
X. S. 4. 36,

po/lis e)leuqeri/a_s diyh/sa_sa a state thirsting for freedom
P. R. 562c. So with o)i+steu/ein shoot at (poet.), lilai/esqai desire (poet.), gli/xesqai desire. filei=n love, poqei=n long for take the accusative.

§1350
The genitive is used with verbs signifying to reach, obtain (genitive of the end attained).

th=s a)reth=s e)fike/sqai to attain to virtue
I. 1.5,

oi( a)kontistai\ braxu/tera h)ko/ntizon h)\ w(s e)ciknei=sqai tw=n sfendonhtw=n the javelin-throwers did not hurl far enough to reach the slingers
X. A. 3.3.7, spondw=n e)/tuxe he obtained a truce 3. 1. 28. So with kurei=n obtain (poet.), klhronomei=n inherit, a)potugxa/nein fail to hit. tugxa/nein, when compounded with e)n, e)pi/, para/, peri/, and su/n, takes the dative. lagxa/nein obtain by lot usually takes the accusative.
a. This genitive and that of 1349 form the genitive of the goal.

§1351
The genitive of the thing obtained may be joined with an ablatival genitive (1410) of the person:

ou(= de\ dh\ pa/ntwn oi)o/meqa teu/cesqai e)pai/nou in a case where we expect to win praise from all men
X. A. 5.7.33. But where the thing obtained is expressed by a neuter pronoun, the accusative is employed.

§1352
It is uncertain whether verbs signifying to miss take a partitive or an ablatival genitive:

ou)dei\s h(ma/rtanen a)ndro/s no one missed his man
X. A. 3.4.15,

sfale/ntes th=s do/chs disappointed in expectations
T. 4.85.

§1353

Verbs of approaching and meeting take the genitive according to 1343 or 1349. These verbs are poetical. Thus, a)ntio/wn tau/rwn for the purpose of obtaining (his share of) bulls
a 25, a)nth/sw tou=d' a)ne/ros I will encounter this man II 423,

pela/sai new=n to approach the ships
S. Aj. 709. In the meaning draw near to verbs of approaching take the dative (1463).

§1354
The genitive is used with verbs of smelling.

o)/zw mu/rou I smell of perfume
Ar. Eccl. 524. So pnei=n mu/rou to breathe (smell of) perfume S. fr. 140.

§1355
The genitive is used with verbs signifying to enjoy, taste, eat, drink.

a)polau/omen pa/ntwn tw=n a)gaqw=n we enjoy all the good things
X. M. 4.3.11,

eu)wxou= tou= lo/gou enjoy the discourse
P. R. 352b,

o)li/goi si/_tou e)geu/santo few tasted food
X. A. 3.1.3. So (rarely) with h(/desqai take pleasure in.
a. Here belong e)sqi/ein, pi/_nein when they do not signify to eat up or drink up:

w)mw=n e)sqi/ein au)tw=n to eat them alive
X. H. 3.3.6,

pi/_nein oi)/noio drink some wine
x 11, as boire du vin (but

pi/_nein oi)=non drink wine
*c 5, as boire le vin). Words denoting food and drink are placed in the accusative when they are regarded as kinds of nourishment.

§1356
The genitive is used with verbs signifying to remember, remind, forget, care for , and neglect.

tw=n a)po/ntwn fi/lwn me/mnhso remember your absent friends
I. 1.26,

bou/lomai d' u(_ma=s a)namnh=sai tw=n e)moi\ pepra_gme/nwn I desire to remind you of my past actions
And. 4.41,

de/doika mh\ e)pilaqw/meqa th=s oi)/kade o(dou= I fear lest we may forget the way home
X. A. 3.2.25, e)pimelo/menoi oi( me\n u(pozugi/wn, oi( de\ skeuw=n some taking care of the pack animals, others of the baggage 4. 3. 30,

th=s tw=n pollw=n do/chs dei= h(ma=s fronti/zein we must pay heed to the world's opinion
P. Cr. 48a, ti/ h(mi=n th=s tw=n pollw=n do/chs me/lei; what do we care for the world's opinion? 44 c,

toi=s spoudai/ois ou)x oi(=o/n te th=s a)reth=s a)melei=n the serious cannot disregard virtue
I. 1.48, mhdeno\s o)ligwrei=te mhde\ katafronei=te (cp. 1385) tw=n prostetagme/nwn neither neglect nor despise any command laid on you 3. 48.

§1357
So with mnhmoneu/ein remember (but usually with the accus., especially of things), a)mnhmonei=n not to speak of, kh/desqai care for, e)ntre/pesqai give heed to, e)nqu_mei=sqai think deeply of, proora=n make provision for (in Hdt.), metame/lei moi it repents me, katamelei=n neglect.

§1358
Many of these verbs also take the accusative. With the accus. memnh=sqai means to remember something as a whole, with the gen. to remember something about a thing, bethink oneself. The accus. is usually found with verbs of remembering and forgetting when they mean to hold or not to hold in memory, and when the object is a thing. Neuter pronouns must stand in the accus. e)pilanqa/nesqai forget takes either the genitive or the accusative, lanqa/nesqai (usually poetical) always takes the genitive. me/lei it is a care, e)pime/lesqai care for, memnh=sqai think about may take peri/ with the genitive. oi)=da generally means I remember when it has a person as the object (in the accusative).

§1359

Verbs of reminding may take two accusatives:

tau=q' u(pe/mnhs' u(_ma=s I have reminded you of this
D. 19.25 (1628).

§1360
With me/lei, the subject, if a neuter pronoun, may sometimes stand in the nominative (the personal construction):

tau=ta qew=| melh/sei God will care for this
P. Phae. 238d. Except in poetry the subject in the nominative is very rare with other words than neuter pronouns: xoroi\ pa=si me/lousi
P. L. 835e.

§1361
The genitive is used with verbs signifying to hear and perceive: a)kou/ein, klu/ein (poet.) hear, a)kroa=sqai listen to, ai)sqa/nesqai perceive, punqa/nesqai hear, learn of, suni_e/nai understand, o)sfrai/nesqai scent. The person or thing, whose words, sound, etc. are perceived by the senses, stands in the genitive; the words, sound, etc. generally stand in the accusative.

tino\s h)/kous' ei)po/ntos I heard somebody say
D. 8.4,

a)kou/santes th=s sa/lpiggos hearing the sound of the trumpet
X. A. 4.2.8, a)kou/santes to\n qo/rubon hearing the noise 4. 4. 21,

a)krow/menoi tou= a)/|dontos listening to the singer
X. C. 1.3.10,

o(/soi a)llh/lwn cuni/_esan all who understood each other
T. 1.3,

e)peida\n suni_h=| tis ta\ lego/mena when one understands what is said
P. Pr. 325c (verbs of understanding, suni_e/nai and e)pi/stasqai, usually take the accus.),

krommu/wn o)sfrai/nomai I smell onions
Ar. Ran. 654.
a. A supplementary participle is often used in agreement with the genitive of the person from whom something is heard:

le/gontos e)mou= a)kroa/_sontai oi( ne/oi the young men will listen when I speak
P. A. 37d.
b. The accusative is almost always used when the thing heard is expressed by a substantivized neuter adjective or participle, but the genitive plural in the case of ou(=tos, o(/de, au)to/s, and o(/s is frequent.

§1362
A double genitive, of the person and of the thing, is rare with a)kou/ein:

tw=n u)pe\r th=s grafh=s dikai/wn a)kou/ein mou to listen to my just pleas as regards the indictment
D. 18.9.

§1363

a)kou/ein, ai)sqa/nesqai, punqa/nesqai, meaning to become aware of, learn, take the accusative (with a participle in indirect discourse, 2112 b) of a personal or impersonal object: oi( de/ *plataih=s, w(s h)/|sqonto e)/ndon te o)/ntas tou\s *qhbai/ous kai kateilhmme/nhn th\n po/lin but the Plataeans, when they became aware that the Thebans were inside and that the city had been captured
T. 2.3, puqo/menoi *)artace/rchn teqnhko/ta having learned that Artaxerxes was dead 4. 50.
a. To hear a thing is usually a)kou/ein ti when the thing heard is something definite and when the meaning is simply hear, not listen to.

§1364

a)kou/ein, a)kroa=sqai, punqa(nesqai, meaning to hear from, learn from, take the genitive of the actual source (1411).

§1365

a)kou/ein, klu/ein, punqa/nesqai/tinos may mean to hear about, hear of:

ei) de/ ke teqnhw=tos a)kou/sh|s but if you hear that he is dead
a 289,

klu/wn sou= hearing about thee
S. O. C. 307,

w(s e)pu/qonto th=s *pu/lou kateilhmme/nhs when they heard of the capture of Pylos
T. 4.6. For the participle (not in indirect discourse) see 2112 a. peri/ is often used with the genitive without the participle.

§1366
In the meaning heed, hearken, obey, verbs of hearing generally take the genitive: a)/koue pa/ntwn, e)kle/gou d' a(\ sumfe/rei listen to everything, but choose that which is profitable
Men. Sent. 566,

tw=n polemi/wn a)kou/ein to submit to enemies
X. C. 8.1.4. pei/qesqai takes the genitive, instead of the dative, by analogy to this use (
Hdt. 6.12,
T. 7.73). (On the dative with a)kou/ein obey see 1465.)

§1367

ai)sqa/nesqai takes the genitive, or (less frequently) the accusative, of the thing immediately perceived by the senses:

th=s kraugh=s h)/|sqonto they heard the noise
X. H. 4.4.4,

h)/|sqeto ta\ gigno/mena he perceived what was happening
X. C. 3.1.4. The genitive is less common than the accusative when the perception is intellectual:

w(s h)/|sqonto teixizo/ntwn when they heard that they were progressing with their fortification
T. 5.83. Cp. 1363.

§1368
Some verbs, ordinarily construed with the accusative, take the genitive by the analogy of ai)sqa/nesqai, etc.:

e)/gnw a)/topa e)mou= poiou=ntos he knew that I was acting absurdly
X. C. 7.2.18,

a)gnoou=ntes a)llh/lwn o(/ ti le/gomen each of us mistaking what the other says
P. G. 517c. This construction of verbs of knowing (and showing) occurs in Attic only when a participle accompanies the genitive.

§1369
The genitive is used with verbs signifying to fill, to be full of. The thing filled is put in the accusative.

ou)k e)mplh/sete th\n qa/lattan trih/rwn ; will you not cover the sea with your triremes?
D. 8.74,

a)naplh=sai ai)tiw=n to implicate in guilt
P. A. 32c,

trofh=s eu)porei=n to have plenty of provisions
X. Vect. 6.1,

trih/rhs sesagme/nh a)nqrw/pwn a trireme stowed with men
X. O. 8.8,

u(/brews mestou=sqai to be filled with pride
P. L. 713c. So with plh/qein, plhrou=n, ge/mein, ploutei=n, bri/_qein (poet.), bru/ein (poet.).
a. Here belong also

xei\r sta/zei quhlh=s *)/areos his hand drips with sacrifice to Ares
S. El. 1423,

mequsqei\s tou= ne/ktaros intoxicated with nectar
P. S. 203b,

h( phgh\ r(ei= yu_xrou= u(/o=atos the spring flows with cold water
P. Phae. 230b. The instrumental dative is sometimes used.

§1370
The genitive is used with verbs signifying to rule, command, lead.

qei=on to\ e)qelo/ntwn a)/rxein it is divine to rule over willing subjects
X. O. 21.12,

th=s qala/tths e)kra/tei he was master of the sea
P. Menex. 239e,

*)/erws tw=n qew=n basileu/ei Love is king of the gods
P. S. 195c,

h(gei=to th=s e)co/dou he led the expedition
T. 2.10, strathgei=n tw=n ce/nwn to be general of the mercenaries X. A. 2. 6. 28. So with turannei=n be absolute master of, a)na)ssein be lord of (poet.), h(gemoneu/ein be commander of. This genitive is connected with that of 1402.

§1371
Several verbs of ruling take the accusative when they mean to conquer, overcome (so kratei=n), or when they express the domain over which the rule extends; as

th\n *pelopo/nnhson peira=sqe mh\ e)la/_ssw e)chgei=sqai try not to lessen your dominion over the Peloponnese
T. 1.71. h(gei=sqai/ tini means to be a guide to any one, show any one the way. Cp. 1537.

## GENITIVE OF PRICE AND VALUE

§1372
The genitive is used with verbs signifying to buy, sell, cost, value, exchange. The price for which one gives or does anything stands in the genitive.

a)rguri/ou pri/asqai h)\ a)podo/sqai i(/ppon to buy or sell a horse for money
P. R. 333b,

*qemistokle/a_ tw=n megi/stwn dwrew=n h)ci/wsan they deemed Themistocles worthy of the greatest gifts
I. 4.154,

ou)k a)ntallakte/on moi th\n filoti_mi/a_n ou)deno\s ke/rdous I must not barter my public spirit for any price
D. 19.223. So with ta/ttein rate, misqou=n let, misqou=sqai hire, e)rga/zesqai work, and with any verb of doing anything for a wage, as

oi( th=s par' h(me/ra_n xa/ritos ta\ me/gista th=s po/lews a)polwleko/tes those who have ruined the highest interests of the State to purchase ephemeral popularity
D. 8.70,

po/sou dida/skei; pe/nte mnw=n for how much does he teach? for five minae
P. A. 20b,

oi( *xaldai=oi misqou= strateu/ontai the Chaldaeans serve for pay
X. C. 3.2.7.
a. The instrumental dative is also used. With verbs of exchanging, a)nti/ is usual (1683).

§1373

To value highly and lightly is peri\ pollou= (plei/onos, plei/stou) and peri\ o)li/gou (e)la/_ttonos, e)laxi/stou) ti_ma=sqai or poiei=sqai:

ta\ plei/stou a)/cia peri\ e)laxi/stou poiei=tai, ta\ de\ faulo/tera peri\ plei/onos he makes least account of what is most important, and sets higher what is less estimable
P. A. 30a. The genitive of value, without peri/, is rare:

pollou= poiou=mai a)khkoe/nai a(\ a)kh/koa *prwtago/rou I esteem it greatly to have heard what I did from Protagoras
P. Pr. 328d.
a. The genitive of cause is rarely used to express the thing bought or that for which pay is demanded:

ou)de/na th=s sunousi/a_s a)rgu/rion pra/_ttei you charge nobody anything for your teaching
X. M. 1.6.11,

trei=s mnai= difri/skou three minae for a small chariot
Ar. Nub. 31.

§1374
In legal language ti_ma=n tini qana/tou is to fix the penalty at death (said of the jury, which is not interested in the result), ti_ma=sqai/ tini qana/tou to propose death as the penalty (said of the accuser, who is interested), and tima=sqai/ tinos to propose a penalty against oneself (said of the accused). Cp.

ti_ma=tai/ moi o( a)nh\r qana/tou the man proposes death as my penalty
P. A. 36b, a)lla\ dh\ fugh=s ti_mh/swmai; i)/sws ga\r a)/n moi tou/tou ti_mh/saite but shall I propose exile as my penalty? for perhaps you (the jury) might fix it at this 37 c. So qana/tou with kri/_nein, diw/kein, u(pa/gein. Cp. 1379.

## GENITIVE OF CRIME AND ACCOUNTABILITY

§1375
With verbs of judicial action the genitive denotes the crime, the accusative denotes the person accused.

ai)tia=sqai a)llh/lous tou= gegenhme/nou to accuse one another of what had happened
X. Ages. 1.33,

diw/kw me\n kakhgori/a_s, th=| d' au)th=| yh/fw| fo/nou feu/gw I bring an accusation for defamation and at the same trial am prosecuted for murder
L. 11.12,

e)me\ o( *me/lhtos a)sebei/a_s e)gra/yato Meletus prosecuted me for impiety
P. Euth. 5c,

dw/rwn e)kri/qhsan they were tried for bribery
L. 27.3. On verbs of accusing and condemning compounded with kata/, see 1385.

§1376
So with a)mu/_nesqai and kola/zein punish, ei)sa/gein and proskalei=sqai summon into court, ai(rei=n convict, ti_mwrei=sqai take vengeance on. With ti_mwrei=n avenge and lagxa/nein obtain leave to bring a suit, the person avenged and the person against whom the suit is brought are put in the dative. So with dika/zesqai/ tini/ tinos to go to law with a man about something.

§1377
Verbs of judicial action may take a cognate accusative (di/khn, grafh/n), on which the genitive of the crime depends:

grafh\n u(/brews kai\ di/khn kakhgori/a_s feu/cetai he will be brought to trial on an indictment for outrage and on a civil action for slander
D. 21.32. From this adnominal use arose the construction of the genitive with this class of verbs.

§1378

a(li/skesqai (a(lw=nai) be convicted, o)fliska/nein lose a suit, feu/gein be prosecuted are equivalent to passives:

e)a/_n tis a(lw=| kloph=s . . . ka)\_n a)stratei/a_s tis o)/flh| if any one be condemned for theft . . . and if any one be convicted of desertion
D. 24.103,

a)sebei/a_s feu/gonta u(po\ *melh/tou being tried for impiety on the indictment of Meletus
P. A. 35d. o)fliska/nein may take di/khn as a cognate accus. (

w)flhke/nai di/khn to be cast in a suit
Ar. Av. 1457); the crime or the penalty may stand in the genitive (with or without di/khn), or in the accusative:

o(po/soi kloph=s h)\ dw/rwn o)/floien all who had been convicted of embezzlement or bribery
And. 1.74, u(f' u(_mw=n qana/tou di/khn o)flw/n having incurred through your verdict the penalty of death,

u(po\ th=s a)lhqei/a_s w)flhko/tes moxqhri/a_n condemned by the truth to suffer the penalty of wickedness
P. A. 39b.

§1379
With verbs of judicial action the genitive of the penalty may be regarded as a genitive of value:

qana/tou kri/_nousi they judge in matters of life and death
X. C. 1.2.14. So

u(pa/gein tina\ qana/tou to impeach a man on a capital charge
X. H. 2.3.12; cp. ti_ma=n qana/tou 1374.
a. With many verbs of judicial action peri/ is used.

## GENITIVE OF CONNECTION

§1380
The genitive may express a more or less close connection or relation, where peri/ is sometimes added.
With verbs of saying or thinking: ti/ de\ i(/ppwn oi)/ei; but what do you think of horses?
P. R. 459b. Often in poetry:

ei)pe\ de/ moi patro/s but tell me about my father
l 174, tou= kasignh/tou ti/ fh/|s; what dost thou say of thy brother?
S. El. 317.

§1381
The genitive is often used loosely, especially at the beginning of a construction, to state the subject of a remark: i(/ppos h)\n kakourgh=|, to\n i(ppe/a_ kaki/zomen: th=s de\ gunaiko/s, ei) kakopoiei= ktl. if a horse is vicious, we lay the fault to the groom; but as regards a wife, if she conducts herself ill, etc.
X. O. 3.11,

w(sau/tws de\ kai\ tw=n a)/llwn texnw=n and so in the case of the other arts too
P. Charm. 165d, ti/ de\ tw=n pollw=n kalw=n; what about the many beautiful things?
P. Ph. 78d.

## GENITIVE WITH COMPOUND VERBS

§1382
The genitive depends on the meaning of a compound verb as a whole (1) if the simple verb takes the genitive without a preposition, as u(pei/kein withdraw, paralu/_ein release, paraxwrei=n surrender (1392), e)fi/_esqai desire (1349); or (2) if the compound has acquired through the preposition a signification different from that of the simple verb with the preposition: thus

a)pogno/ntes th=s e)leuqeri/a_s despairing of freedom
L. 2.46 cannot be expressed by gno/ntes a)po\ th=s e)leuqeri/a_s. But it is often difficult to determine whether the genitive depends on the compound verb as a whole or on the preposition contained in it.

§1383
A verb compounded with a preposition taking the dative or accusative may take the genitive by analogy of another compound verb whose preposition requires the genitive: so

e)mbai/nein o(/rwn to set foot on the boundaries
S. O. C. 400 by analogy to e)pibai/nein tw=n o(/rwn
P. L. 778e.

§1384
Many verbs compounded with a)po/, pro/, u(pe/r, e)pi/, and kata/ take the genitive when the compound may be resolved into the simple verb and the preposition without change in the sense:

tou\s summa/xous a)potre/yantes th=s gnw/mhs dissuading the allies from their purpose
And. 3.21,

proapesta/lhsan th=s a)posta/sews they were despatched before the revolt
T. 3.5,

polloi=s h( glw=tta protre/xei th=s dianoi/a_s in many people the tongue outruns the thought
I. 1.41, (oi( pole/mioi)

u(perka/qhntai h(mw=n the enemy are stationed above us
X. A. 5.1.9,

tw=| e)piba/nti prw/tw| tou= tei/xous to the first one setting foot on the wall
T. 4.116. This use is most frequent when the prepositions are used in their proper signification. Many compounds of u(pe/r take the accusative.
a. This use is especially common with kata/ against or at:

mh/ mou katei/ph|s don't speak against me
P. Th. 149a,

kateyeu/sato/ mou he spoke falsely against me
D. 18.9,

yeudh= kateglw/ttize/ mou he mouthed lies at me
Ar. Ach. 380. The construction in 1384 is post-Homeric.

§1385
The verbs of accusing and condemning (cp. 1375) containing kata/ in composition (katagignw/skein decide against, katadika/zein adjudge against, katayhfi/zesqai vote against, katakri/_nein give sentence against) take a genitive of the person, and an accusative of the penalty. kathgorei=n accuse, katagignw/skein and katayhfi/zesqai take a genitive of the person, an accusative of the crime:

katagnw=nai dwrodoki/a_n e)mou= to pronounce me guilty of bribery
L. 21.21, tou/tou deili/a_n katayhfi/zesqai to vote him guilty of cowardice 14. 11,

tw=n diafugo/ntwn qa/naton katagno/ntes having condemned the fugitives to death
T. 6.60; person, crime, and penalty:

pollw=n oi( pate/res mhdismou= qa/naton kate/gnwsan our fathers passed sentence of death against many for favouring the Persians
I. 4.157. The genitive is rarely used to express the crime or the penalty:

parano/mwn au)tou= kathgorei=n to accuse him of proposing unconstitutional measures
D. 21.5; cp.

a)nqrw/pwn katayhfisqe/ntwn qa/naton men who have been condemned to death
P. R. 558a.

§1386
In general, prose, as distinguished from poetry, repeats the preposition contained in the compound; but kata/ is not repeated.

§1387

Passive.—qa/natos au)tw=n kategnw/sqh sentence of death was passed on them
L. 13.39 (so

kateyhfisme/nos h)=n mou o( qa/natos
X. Ap. 27),

kathgorei=to au)tou= ou)x h(/kista mhdismo/s he was especially accused of favouring the Persians
T. 1.95.

## FREE USES OF THE GENITIVE

§1388
Many verbs ordinarily construed with the accusative are also followed by a genitive of a person, apparently dependent on the verb but in reality governed by an accusative, generally a neuter pronoun or a dependent clause. Thus,

ta/d' au)tou= a(/gamai I admire this in him
X. Ages. 2.7, tou=to e)painw= *)a_ghsila/_ou I praise this in Agesilaus 8. 4,

au)tw=n e(\n e)qau/masa I was astonished at one thing in them
P. A. 17a.

*)aqhnai=oi sfw=n tau=ta ou)k a)pode/contai the Athenians will not be satisfied with them in this
T. 7.48, o)\ me/mfontai ma/lista h(mw=n which they most censure in us 1. 84, ei) a)/gasai tou= patro\s o(/sa pe/pra_xe if you admire in my father what he has done (the actions of my father)
X. C. 3.1.15,

diaqew/menos au)tw=n o(/shn xw/ra_n e)/xoien contemplating how large a country they possess
X. A. 3.1.19, qauma/zw tw=n strathgw=n o(/ti ou) peirw=ntai h(mi=n e)kpori/zein si_thre/sion I wonder that the generals do not try to supply us with money for provisions 6. 2. 4,

e)neno/hse de\ au)tw=n kai\ w(s e)phrw/twn a)llh/lous he took note also how they asked each other questions
X. C. 5.2.18. So with qewrei=n observe, u(ponoei=n feel suspicious of, e)nqu_mei=sqai consider, etc.

§1389
From such constructions arose the use of the genitive in actual dependence on the verb without an accusative word or clause:

a)/gasai au)tou= you admire him
X. M. 2.6.33,

qauma/zw tw=n u(pe\r th=s i)di/a_s do/chs a)poqnh/|skein e)qelo/ntwn I wonder at those who are willing to die in defence of their personal opinions
I. 6.93. The use in 1389 recalls that with ai)sqa/nesqai (1367). On a)/gasqai, qauma/zein with the genitive of cause, see 1405.

§1390
A form of the genitive of possession appears in poetry with verbal adjectives and passive participles to denote the personal origin of an action (cp. 1298):

kei/nhs didakta/ taught of her
S. El. 344,

e)kdidaxqei\s tw=n kat' oi)=kon informed by those in the house
S. Tr. 934,

plhgei\s qugatro/s struck by a daughter
E. Or. 497. Cp. dio/sdotos given of God; and “beloved of the Lord.”
On the genitive absolute, see 2070.

## THE ABLATIVAL GENITIVE WITH VERBS

§1391
The same verb may govern both a true genitive and an ablatival genitive. So a)/rxesqai to begin (1348 a) and to start from, e)/xesqai to hold to (1345) and to keep oneself from. In many cases it is difficult to decide whether the genitive in question was originally the true genitive or the ablatival genitive, or whether the two have been combined; e.g. in kune/h r(i_nou= poihth/ a cap made of hide K 262,

ku/pellon e)de/cato h(=s a)lo/xoio he received a goblet from his wife
*w 305. So with verbs to hear from, know of (1364, 1411), and verbs of emotion (1405), the partitive idea, cause, and source are hard to distinguish. Other cases open to doubt are verbs of missing (1352), being deceived (1392), and the exclamatory genitive (1407).

## GENITIVE OF SEPARATION

§1392
With verbs signifying to cease, release, remove, restrain, give up, fail, be distant from, etc., the genitive denotes separation.

lh/gein tw=n po/nwn to cease from toil
I. 1.14,

e)pisth/mh xwrizome/nh dikaiosu/nhs knowledge divorced from justice
P. Menex. 246e,

metasta\_s th=s *)aqhnai/wn cummaxi/a_s withdrawing from the alliance with the Athenians
T. 2.67,

pau/santes au)to\n th=s strathgi/a_s removing him from his office of general
X. H. 6.2.13,

ei)/rgesqai th=s a)gora=s to be excluded from the forum
L. 6.24,

sw=sai kakou= to save from evil
S. Ph. 919,

e)kw/lu_on th=s porei/a_s au)to/n they prevented him from passing
X. Ages. 2.2,

pa=s a)sko\s du/o a)/ndras e(/cei tou= mh\ katadu=nai each skin will keep two men from sinking
X. A. 3.5.11,

lo/gou teleuta=n to end a speech
T. 3.59,

th=s e)leuqeri/a_s paraxwrh=sai *fili/ppw| to surrender their freedom to Philip
D. 18.68, ou) po/nwn u(fi/_eto, ou) kindu/_nwn a)fi/_stato, ou) xrhma/twn e)fei/deto he did not relax his toil, stand aloof from dangers, or spare his money
X. Ages. 7.1,

yeusqe/ntes tw=n e)lpi/dwn disappointed of their expectations
I. 4.58 (but cp. 1352),

h( nh=sos ou) polu\ die/xousa th=s h)pei/rou the island being not far distant from the mainland
T. 3.51.

§1393
Several verbs of separation, such as e)leuqerou=n (especially with a personal subject), may take a)po/ or e)c when the local idea is prominent. Many take also the accusative.

§1394
The genitive, instead of the accusative (1628), may be used with verbs of depriving:

a)posterei= me tw=n xrhma/twn he deprives me of my property
I. 17.35,

tw=n a)/llwn a)fairou/menoi xrh/mata taking away property from others
X. M. 1.5.3.

§1395
The genitive of the place whence is employed in poetry where a compound verb would be used in prose:

ba/qrwn i(/stasqe rise from the steps
S. O. T. 142 (cp.

u(pani/stantai qa/_kwn they rise from their seats
X. S. 4. 31),

xqono\s a)ei/ra_s raising from the ground
S. Ant. 417.

§1396
The genitive with verbs signifying to want, lack, empty, etc. may be classed with the genitive of separation.

tw=n e)pithdei/wn ou)k a)porh/somen we shall not want provisions
X. A. 2.2.11,

e)pai/nou ou)/pote spani/zete you never lack praise
X. Hi. 1.14,

a)ndrw=n ta/_nde po/lin kenw=sai to empty this city of its men
A. Supp. 660. So with e)llei/pein and ste/resqai lack, e)rhmou=n deliver from.

§1397

de/w I lack (the personal construction) usually takes the genitive of quantity:

pollou= ge de/w nothing of the sort
P. Phae. 228a,

mi_krou= e)/deon e)n xersi\ tw=n o(pli_tw=n ei)=nai they were nearly at close quarters with the hoplites
X. H. 4.6.11,

tosou/tou de/w zhlou=n I am so far from admiring
D. 8.70 (also tosou=ton de/w).

§1398

de/omai I want, request may take the genitive, or the accusative (regularly of neuter pronouns and adjectives), of the thing wanted; and the genitive of the person: e)rwtw/menos o(/tou de/oito, *)askw=n, e)/fh, disxi_li/wn deh/somai being asked what he needed, he said ‘I shall have need of two thousand skins’
X. A. 3.5.9,

tou=to u(_mw=n de/omai I ask this of you
P. A. 17c. The genitive of the thing and of the person is unusual:

deo/menoi *ku/_rou a)/llhs a)/llhs pra/_cews petitioning Cyrus about different matters
X. C. 8.3.19.

§1399

dei= (impersonal) is frequently used with genitives of quantity:

pollou= dei= ou(/tws e)/xein far from that being the case
P. A. 35d, ou)de\ pollou= dei=
D. 8.42 (only in D.) and ou)d' o)li/gou dei= no, far from it
D. 19.184. dei=n may be omitted (but not with pollou=), leaving o)li/gou and mi_krou= in the sense of almost, all but; <*>li/gou pa/ntes almost all
P. R. 552d,

o)li/gou ei(=lon th\n po/lin they all but. took the city
T. 8.35. On dei=n used absolutely, see 2012 d; on de/wn with numerals, 350 c.

§1400

dei= moi/ tinos means I have need of something. In place of the dative (1467) an accusative of the person is rarely allowed in poetry on the analogy of dei= with the infinitive (1985):

ou) po/nou pollou= me dei= I have need of no great toil
E. Hipp. 23 (often in E.). The thing needed is rarely put in the accusative:

ei)/ ti de/oi tw=| xorw=| if the chorus need anything
Ant. 6.12 (here some regard ti\ as nominative). Cp. 1562.

## GENITIVE OF DISTINCTION AND OF COMPARISON

§1401
The genitive is used with verbs of differing.

a)/rxwn a)gaqo\s ou)de\n diafe/rei patro\s a)gaqou= a good ruler differs in no respect from a good father
X. C. 8.1.1.

§1402
With verbs signifying to surpass, be inferior to, the genitive denotes that with which anything is compared.

ti_mai=s tou/twn e)pleonektei=te you had the advantage over them in honours
X. A. 3.1.37,

h(ttw=nto tou= u(/datos they were overpowered by the water
X. H. 5.2.5,

u(sterei=n tw=n e)/rgwn to be too late for operations
D. 4.38,

h(mw=n leifqe/ntes inferior to us
X. A. 7.7.31. So with presbeu/ein hold the first place, a)risteu/ein be best (poet.), meiou=sqai fall short of, meionektei=n be worse off, e)lattou=sqai be at a disadvantage. nika=sqai/ tinos is chiefly poetic. h(tta=sqai often takes u(po/. Akin to this genitive is that with verbs of ruling (1370), which are often derived from a substantive signifying ruler.

§1403
Many verbs compounded with pro/, peri/, u(pe/r denoting superiority take the genitive, which may depend on the preposition (1384):

ta/xei periege/nou au)tou= you excelled him in speed
X. C. 3.1.19,

gnw/mh| proe/xein tw=n e)nanti/wn to excel the enemy in spirit
T. 2.62, toi=s o(/plois au)tw=n u(perfe/romen we surpass them in our infantry 1. 81. So with periei=nai, u(pere/xein. proti_ma=n, prokri/_nein, and proairei=sqai prefer, proesthke/nai be at the head of certainly take the genitive by reason of the preposition. u(perba/llein and u(perbai/nein surpass take the accusative.

§1404
The object compared may be expressed by pro/, a)nti/ with the genitive, or by para/, pro/s with the accusative. See under Prepositions. That in which one thing is superior or inferior to another usually stands in the dative (1513, 1515).

## GENITIVE OF CAUSE

§1405
With verbs of emotion the genitive denotes the cause. Such verbs are to wonder at, admire, envy, praise, blame. hate, pity, grieve for, be angry at, take vengeance on, and the like.

e)qau/masa th=s to/lmhs tw=n lego/ntwn I wondered at the hardihood of the speakers
L. 12.41,

tou=ton a)gasqei\s th=s pra|o/thtos admiring him for his mildness
X. C. 2.3.21, zhlw= se tou= nou=, th=s de\ deili/a_s stugw= I envy thee for thy prudence, I hate thee for thy cowardice
S. El. 1027, se\ hu)daimo/nisa tou= tro/pou I thought you happy because of your disposition
P. Cr. 43b,

sugxai/rw tw=n gegenhme/nwn I share the joy at what has happened
D. 15.15,

a)ne/xesqai tw=n oi)kei/wn a)meloume/nwn to put up with the neglect of my household affairs
P. A. 31b,

to\n ce/non di/kaion ai)ne/sai proqu_mi/a_s it is right to praise the stranger for his zeal
E. I. A. 1371,

ou)/pot' a)ndri\ tw=|de khru_keuma/twn me/myh| never wilt thou blame me for my tidings
A. Sept. 651,

tou= pa/qous w)/|kti_ren au)to/n he pitied him for his misery
X. C. 5.4.32,

ou)d' ei)ko\s xalepw=s fe/rein au)tw/n nor is it reasonable to grieve about them
T. 2.62, ou)ke/ti w(=n ou(=toi kle/ptousin o)rgi/zesqe, a)ll' w(=n au)toi\ lamba/nete xa/rin i)/ste you are no longer angry at their thefts, but you are grateful for what you get yourselves
L. 27.11,

ti_mwrh/sasqai au)tou\s th=s e)piqe/sews to take revenge on them for their attack
X. A. 7.4.23. Here belongs, by analogy,

suggignw/skein au)toi=s xrh\ th=s e)piqu_mi/a_s it is necessary to forgive them for their desire
P. Eu. 306c (usually suggignw/skein th\n e)piqu_mi/a_n tini/ or th=| e)piqu_mi/a| tino/s).
a. The genitive of cause is partly a true genitive, partly ablatival.

§1406
With the above verbs the person stands in the accusative or dative. Some of these verbs take the dative or e)pi/ and the dative (e.g. a)lgei=n, ste/nein, a)/xqesqai, fqonei=n) to express the cause of the emotion. See the Lexicon.

§1407
The genitive of cause is used in exclamations and is often preceded by an interjection:

feu= tou= a)ndro/s alas for the man!
X. C. 3.1.39, th=s tu/xhs my ill luck! 2. 2. 3. In tragedy, the genitive of a pronoun or adjective after oi)/moi or w)/moi refers to the second or third person. For the first person the nominative is used (

oi)/moi ta/laina ah me, miserable!
S. Ant. 554).

§1408
Allied to the genitive of cause is the genitive of purpose in tou= with the infinitive (esp. with mh/, 2032 e), and in expressions where e(/neka is usually employed, as

h( pa=s' a)pa/th suneskeua/sqh tou= peri\ *fwke/a_s o)le/qrou the whole fraud was contrived for the purpose of ruining the Phocians
D. 19.76.

§1409
Closely connected with the genitive of cause is the genitive with verbs of disputing:

ou) basilei= a)ntipoiou/meqa th=s a)rxh=s we have no dispute with the king about his empire
X. A. 2.1.23,

h)mfisbh/thsen *)erexqei= th=s po/lews he disputed the possession of the city with Erechtheus
I. 12.193, a)=r' ou)=n mh\ h(mi=n e)nantiw/setai th=s a)pagwgh=s; well then he will not oppose us about the removal (of the army), will he?
X. A. 7.6.5. a)ntipoiei=sqai claim may follow 1349 (

th=s po/lews a)ntepoiou=nto they laid claim to the city
T. 4.122). Verbs of disputing are sometimes referred to 1343 or 1349.

## GENITIVE OF SOURCE

§1410
The genitive may denote the source.

pi/qwn h)fu/sseto oi)=nos wine was broached from the casks
y 305,

*da_rei/ou kai\ *parusa/tidos gi/gnontai pai=des du/o of Darius and Parysatis are born two sons

§1411
With verbs of hearing from and the like the genitive is probably ablatival rather than partitive (1364):

e)mou= a)kou/sesqe pa=san th\n a)lh/qeian from me you shall hear the whole truth

S. El. 668.
a. Usually (except with punqa/nesqai) we have para/ (a)po/ rarely), e)c or pro/s (in poetry and Hdt.) with verbs of hearing from.
b. The genitive with ei)=nai in

patro\s d' ei)/m' a)gaqoi=o I am of a good father
*f 109,

toiou/twn me/n e)ste progo/nwn of such ancestors are you
X. A. 3.2.13 is often regarded as a genitive of source, but is probably possessive.

## GENITIVE WITH ADJECTIVES

§1412
The genitive is used with many adjectives corresponding in derivation or meaning to verbs taking the genitive.

§1413
The adjective often borrows the construction with the genitive from that of the corresponding verb; but when the verb takes another case (especially the accusative), or when there is no verb corresponding to the adjective, the adjective may govern the genitive to express possession, connection more or less close, or by analogy. Many of the genitives in question may be classed as objective as well as partitive or ablatival. Rigid distinction between the undermentioned classes must not be insisted on.

§1414

Possession and Belonging (1297).—

o( e)/rws koino\s pa/ntwn a)nqrw/pwn love common to all men
P. S. 205a (cp. koinwnei=n 1343),

i(ero\s tou= au)tou= qeou= sacred to the same god
P. Ph. 85b,

oi( ki/ndu_noi tw=n e)festhko/twn i)/dioi the dangers belong to the commanders
D. 2.28. So with oi)kei=os and e)pixw/rios peculiar to. koino/s (usually), oi)kei=os inclined to, appropriate to, and i)/dios also take the dative (1499).

§1415

X. C. 2.1.31,

P. S. 181c. So <*>klhros without lot in, a)me/toxos not sharing in.

P. L. 724b,

§1428

Compounds of alpha privative.—In addition to the adjectives with alpha privative which take the genitive by reason of the notion expressed in the verb, or by analogy, there are many others, some of which take the genitive because of the idea of separation, especially when the genitive is of kindred meaning and an attributive adjective is added for the purpose of more exact definition. Thus, a)/ti_mos deprived of, a)paqh/s not suffering, a)telh/s free from (1392): as

ti_mh=s a)/ti_mos deprived of honour

a)/fwnos th=sde th=s a)ra=s without uttering this curse
S. O. C. 865. This is more frequent in poetry than prose.
a. So when the adjectives are passive:

S. Ant. 847, cp.

kakw=n dusa/lwtos ou)dei/s no one is hard for evil fortune to capture
S. O. C. 1722. The genitive with adjectives in alpha privative is sometimes called the genitive of relation.

§1431

Comparison (1402).—Adjectives of the comparative degree or implying comparison take the genitive. The genitive denotes the standard or point of departure from which the comparison is made, and often expresses a condensed comparison when actions are compared. Thus,

h)/ttwn a)maqh\s sofou=, deilo\s a)ndrei/ou an ignorant man is inferior to a wise man, a coward to a brave man
P. Phae. 239a,

krei=tto/n e)sti lo/gou to\ ka/llos th=s gunaiko/s the beauty of the woman is too great for description
X. M. 3.11.1,

*)epu/aca prote/ra_ *ku/_rou pe/nte h(me/rais a)fi/_keto Epyaxa arrived five days before Cyrus
X. A. 1.2.25,

katadeeste/ra_n th\n do/can th=s e)lpi/dos e)/laben the reputation he acquired fell short of his expectation
I. 2.7. So with deu/teros, u(sterai=os, peritto/s. Comparatives with h)/, 1069.

§1432

§1433
The genitive with the comparative often takes the place of h)/ with another construction: a)_qliw/tero/n e)sti mh\ u(giou=s sw/matos ( = h)\ mh\ u(giei= sw/mati)

mh\ u(giei= yu_xh=| sunoikei=n it is more wretched to dwell with a diseased soul than a diseased body

parh=san they came with more ships than the Athenians
T. 8.52.

§1434
The superlative with the genitive is both partitive and ablatival; the latter, when a thing is compared with many things taken singly. Thus, sofw/tatos a)nqrw/pwn
P. A. 22c means wisest among men (part.) and wiser than any other single man. The partitive idea is the stronger. The comparative and the superlative idea are both expressed in a)nh\r e)pieikh\s ui(o\n a)pole/sa_s oi)/sei r(a=|sta tw=n a)/llwn a reasonable man will bear the loss of a son more easily than other men (and most easily of all men)
P. R. 603e,

stratei/a_ megi/sth tw=n pro\ au)th=s an expedition greater than any preceding it
T. 1.10,

tw=n a)/llwn u(/statoi the last among nations
D. 8.72. Cp. mo/nos tw=n a)/llwn = alone of all
D. 21.223.

§1435

eu)dai/mwn tou= tro/pou happy because of his disposition

§1436

Free Use.—a. Compound adjectives formed of a preposition and substantive may take a genitive dependent on the substantive:

skhnh=s u(/paulos under the shelter of the tent
S. Aj. 796 ( = u(po\ au)lh=|). Frequent in poetry.
b. Some adjectives are freely used with the genitive in poetry, as

la/moi *pa/ridos o)le/qrioi fi/lwn the marriage of Paris bringing ruin on his friends
A. Ag. 1156. This is rare in prose:

to\ pu=r e)pi/kouron yu/_xous fire that protects against cold
X. M. 4.3.7, kakou=rgos me\n tw=n a)/llwn, e(autou= de\ kakourgo/teros doing evil to the others but more to himself 1. 5. 3,

o( th=s *(ella/dos a)lith/rios the curse and destroyer of Greece
Aes. 3.157. These adjectives are practically equivalent to substantives. Cp. amans patriae.

## GENITIVE OF TIME AND PLACE

§1444

Time.—The genitive denotes the time within which, or at a certain point of which, an action takes place. As contrasted with the accusative of time (1582), the genitive denotes a portion of time. Hence the genitive of time is partitive. Cp. to\n me\n xeimw=na u(/_ei o( qeo/s, tou= de\ qe/reos xrhi/skontai tw=| u(/dati during the (entire) winter the goo<*>rains, but in (a part of) summer they need the water
Hdt. 3.117.
h(me/ra_s by day, nukto/s at or by night, meshmbri/a_s at midday, dei/lhs in the afternoon, e(spe/ra_s in the evening, qe/rous in summer, xeimw=nos in winter, h)=ros in spring, o)pw/ra_s in autumn, tou= loipou= in the future. The addition of article or attributive usually defines the time more exactly. Thus, ou)kou=n h(du\ me\n qe/rous yu_xeinh\n e)/xein, h(du\ de\ xeimw=nos a)leeinh/n; is it not pleasant to have (a house) cool in summer, and warm in winter?
X. M. 3.8.9,

w)/|xeto th=s nukto/s he departed during the night
X. A. 7.2.17, kai\ h(me/ra_s kai\ nukto\s a)/gwn e)pi\ tou\s polemi/ous both by day and by night leading against the enemy 2. 6. 7, e)/legon tou= loipou= mhke/ti e)cei=nai a)nomi/a_s a)/rcai they said that for the future (at any time in the future) it should no longer be permitted to set an example of lawlessness 5. 7. 34. (Distinguish to\ loipo/n for the (entire) future 3. 2. 8.) e)nto/s within is sometimes added to the genitive.

§1445
The addition of the article may have a distributive sense:

draxmh\n e)la/mbane th=s h(me/ra_s he received a drachm a day
T. 3.17.

§1446
The genitive may denote the time since an action has happened or the time until an action will happen:

ou)dei/s me/ pw h)rw/thke kaino\n ou)de\n pollw=n e)tw=n for many years nobody has put a new question to me
P. G. 448a,

basileu\s ou) maxei=tai de/ka h(merw=n the king will not fight for ten days
X. A. 1.7.18.

§1447
The genitive may or may not denote a definite part of the time during which anything takes place; the dative fixes the time explicitly either by specifying a definite point in a given period or by contracting the whole period to a definite point; the accusative expresses the whole extent of time from beginning to end: cp.

th=| de\ u(sterai/a| oi( me\n *)aqhnai=oi to/ te proa/steion ei(=lon kai\ th\n h(me/ra_n a(/pa_san e)dh/|oun th\n gh=n, oi(/ te tria_ko/sioi tw=n *skiwnai/wn th=s e)piou/shs nukto\s a)pexw/rhsan on the next day the Athenians captured the suburb and laid waste the land for that entire day, while the three hundred Scionaeans departed in the course of the following night
T. 4.130; h(me/ra| de\ a)rca/menoi tri/th| w(s oi)/koqen w(/rmhsan, tau/thn te ei)rga/zonto kai\ th\n teta/rthn kai\ th=s pe/mpths me/xri a)_ri/stou beginning on the third day after their departure, they continued their work (all) this day and the fourth, and on the fifth until the mid-day meal 4. 90.
a. The genitive of time is less common than the dative of time (1539) with ordinals, or with o(/de, ou(=tos, e)kei=nos; as tau/ths th=s nukto/s
T. 6.97,
P. Cr. 44a,

e)kei/nou tou= mhno/s in the course of that month
X. M. 4.8.2. For qe/rous we find e)n qe/rei rarely and, in poetry, qe/rei.
T. 4.133 has both tou= au)tou= qe/rous and e)n tw=| au)tw=| qe/rei in the course of the same summer; cp. i)=sos r(e/ei e)/n te qe/rei+ kai\ xeimw=ni o( *)/istros
Hdt. 4.50 and *)/istros i)=sos r(e/ei qe/reos kai\ xeimw=nos 4. 48 (the Ister flows with the same volume in summer and winter).

§1448

Place.—The genitive denotes the place within which or at which an action happens. This is more frequent in poetry than in prose.
pedi/oio diwke/men to chase over the plain E 222, i(=zen toi/xou tou= e(te/roio he was sitting by the other wall (lit. in a place of the wall) I 219, leloume/nos *)wkeanoi=o having bathed in Oceanus E 6,

ou)/te *pu/lou i(erh=s ou)/t' *)/argeos ou)/te *mukh/nhs neither in sacred Pylos nor in Argos nor in Mycenae
f 108,

to/nd' ei)sede/cw teixe/wn thou didst admit this man within the walls
E. Phoen. 451,

i)e/nai tou= pro/sw to go forward
X. A. 1.3.1,

e)peta/xu_non th=s o(dou= tou\s sxolai/teron prosio/ntas they hastened on their way those who came up more slowly
T. 4.47;

laia=s xeiro\s oi)kou=si they dwell on the left hand
A. Pr. 714 (possibly ablatival).

§1449
Many adverbs of place are genitives in form (au)tou= there, pou= where? ou)damou= nowhere). Cp. 341.

## DATIVE

§1450
The Greek dative does duty for three cases: the dative proper, and two lost cases, the instrumental and the locative.
a. The dative derives its name (h( dotikh\ ptw=sis, casus dativus) from the use with dido/nai (1469).

§1451
The dative is a necessary complement of a verb when the information given by the verb is incomplete without the addition of the idea expressed by the dative. Thus, pei/qetai he obeys, calls for the addition of an idea to complete the sense, as toi=s no/mois the laws.

§1452
The dative as a voluntary complement of a verb adds something unessential to the completion of an idea. Thus, au)toi=s oi( ba/rbaroi a)ph=lqon the barbarians departed—for them (to their advantage). Here belongs the dative of interest, 1474 ff.

§1453
But the boundary line between the necessary and the voluntary complement is not always clearly marked. When the idea of the action, not the object of the action, is emphatic, a verb, usually requiring a dative to complete its meaning, may be used alone, as pei/qetai he is obedient.

§1454
With many intransitive verbs the dative is the sole complement. With transitive verbs it is the indirect complement (dative of the indirect or remoter object, usually a person); that is, it further defines the meaning of a verb already defined in part by the accusative.

§1455
Many verbs so vary in meaning that they may take the dative either alone or along with the accusative (sometimes the genitive). No rules can be given, and English usage is not always the same as Greek usage.

§1456
The voice often determines the construction. Thus, pei/qein tina/ to persuade some one, pei/qesqai/ tini to persuade oneself for some one (obey some one), <*>leu/ein tina\ tau=ta poiei=n to order some one to do this, parakeleu/esqai/ tini tau=ta toiei=n to exhort some one to do this.

## DATIVE PROPER

§1457
The dative proper denotes that to or for which something is or is done.

§1458
It is either (1) used with single words (verbs, adjectives, and sometimes with adverbs and substantives) or (2) it serves to define an entire sentence; herein unlike the genitive and accusative, which usually modify single members <*> a sentence. The connection between dative and verb is less intimate than that between genitive or accusative and verb.

§1459
The dative proper is largely personal, and denotes the person who is interested in or affected by the action; and includes 1461-1473 as well as 1474 ff. The dative proper is not often used with things; when so used there is usually personification or semi-personification.

keleu/ein command (strictly impel) may be followed in Attic by the accusative and (usually) the infinitive; in Hom. by the dative either alone or with the infinitive. X. A. 3.1.31. e)/cesti/ moi it is in my power does not take the genitive. For the accusative instead of the dative, see 1400. Cp. 1344.

§1468
An intransitive verb taking the dative can form a personal passive, the dative becoming the nominative subject of the passive. Cp. 1745.

## DATIVE AS INDIRECT COMPLEMENT OF VERBS

§1469
Many verbs take the dative as the indirect object together with an accusative as the direct object. The indirect object is commonly introduced in English by to.

§1470

Passive.—The accusative of the active becomes the subject of the passive, the dative remains:

§1473
For the dative of purpose (to what end?), common in Latin with a second dative (dono dare), Greek uses a predicate noun:
