## DATIVE AS A MODIFIER OF THE SENTENCE

## DATIVE OF INTEREST

§1474
The person for whom something is or is done, or in reference to whose case an action is viewed, is put in the dative.
a. Many of the verbs in 1461 ff. take a dative of interest. 1476 ff. are special cases.

§1475
After verbs of motion the dative (usually personal) is used, especially in poetry:

xei=ras e)moi\ o)re/gontas reaching out their hands to me
m 257, yu_xa\_s *)/ai+di proi+/ayen hurled their souls on to Hades (a person) A 3; rarely, in prose, after verbs not compounded with a preposition: sxo/ntes (scil. ta\_s nau=s)

*(phgi/w| putting in at Rhegium
T. 7.1. Cp. 1485.

§1476

Dative of the Possessor.—The person for whom a thing exists is put in the dative with ei)=nai, gi/gnesqai, u(pa/rxein, fu=nai (poet.), etc., when he is regarded as interested in its possession.

a)/llois me\n xrh/mata/ e)sti, h(mi=n de\ cu/mmaxoi a)gaqoi/ others have riches, we have good allies
T. 1.86,

tw=| dikai/w| para\ qew=n dw=ra gi/gnetai gifts are bestowed upon the just man by the gods
P. R. 613e,

u(pa/rxei h(mi=n ou)de\n tw=n e)pithdei/wn we have no supply of provisions
X. A. 2.2.11,

pa=si qna_toi=s e)/fu_ mo/ros death is the natural lot of all men
S. El. 860.

§1477
So with verbs of thinking and perceiving: to\n a)gaqo\n a)/rxonta ble/ponta no/mon a)nqrw/pois e)no/misen Cyrus considered that a good ruler was a living law to man
X. C. 8.1.22,

qarrou=si ma/lista pole/mioi, o(/tan toi=s e)nanti/ois pra/_gmata punqa/nwntai the enemy are most courageous when they learn that the forces opposed to them are in trouble
X. Hipp. 5.8.

§1478
In the phrase o)/noma/ (e)sti/) tini the name is put in the same case as o)/noma. Thus,

e)/doca a)kou=sai o)/noma au)tw=| ei)=nai *)aga/qwna I thought I heard his name was Agathon
P. Pr. 315e. o)/noma/ moi/ e)sti and o)/noma (e)pwnumi/a_n) e)/xw are treated as the passives of o)noma/zw. Cp. 1322 a.

§1479
Here belong the phrases (1) ti/ (e)stin) e)moi\ kai\ soi/; what have I to do with thee?; cp. ti/ tw=| no/mw| kai\ th=| basa/nw|; what have the law and torture in common?
D. 29.36. (2) ti/ tau=t' e)moi/; what have I to do with this?
D. 54.17. (3) ti/ e)moi\ ple/on; what gain have I?
X. C. 5.5.34.

§1480
The dative of the possessor denotes that something is at the disposal of a person or has fallen to his share temporarily. The genitive of possession lays stress on the person who owns something. The dative answers the question what is it that he has?, the genitive answers the question who is it that has something? The uses of the two cases are often parallel, but not interchangeable. Thus, in *ku=ros, ou(= su\ e)/sei to\ a)po\ tou=de Cyrus, to whom you will henceforth belong
X. C. 5.1.6, w(=| would be inappropriate. With a noun in the genitive the dative of the possessor is used (tw=n e(kate/rois cumma/xwn
T. 2.1); with a noun in the dative, the genitive of the possessor (toi=s e(autw=n cumma/xois 1. 18).

§1481

Dative of Advantage or Disadvantage (dativus commodi et incommodi).—The person or thing for whose advantage or disadvantage, anything is or is done, is put in the dative. The dative often has to be translated as if the possessive genitive were used; but the meaning is different.
e)peidh\ au)toi=s oi( ba/rbaroi e)k th=s xw/ra_s a)ph=lqon after the barbarians had departed (for them, to their advantage) from their country
T. 1.89,

a)/llo stra/teuma au)tw=| sunele/geto another army was being raised for him
X. A. 1.1.9,

a)/llw| o( toiou=tos ploutei=, kai\ ou)x e(autw=| such a man is rich for another, and not for himself
P. Menex. 246e,

stefanou=sqai tw=| qew=| to be crowned in honour of the god
X. H. 4.3.21,

*filisti/dhs e)/pra_tte *fili/ppw| Philistides was working in the interest of Philip
D. 9.59, ta\ xrh/mat' ai)/ti' a)nqrwpoi=s kakw=n money is a cause of misery to mankind E. Fr. 632, oi( *qra=|kes oi( tw=| *dhmosqe/nei u(sterh/santes the Thracians who came too late (for, i.e.) to help Demosthenes
T. 7.29, h(/de h( h(me/ra_ toi=s *(/ellhsi mega/lwn kakw=n a)/rcei this day will be to the Greeks the beginning of great sorrows 2. 12,

a)/_n ti/s soi tw=n oi)ketw=n a)podra=| if any of your slaves runs away
X. M. 2.10.1.
a. For the middle denoting to do something for oneself, see 1719.
b. In the last example in 1481, as elsewhere, the dative of a personal pronoun is used where a possessive pronoun would explicitly denote the owner.

§1482
A dative, dependent on the sentence, may appear to depend on a substantive:

soi\ de\ dw/sw a)/ndra th=| qugatri/ to you I will give a husband for your daughter
X. C. 8.4.24. Common in Hdt.

§1483
With verbs of depriving, warding off, and the like, the dative of the person may be used: to\ sustrateu/ein a)felei=n sfi/sin e)deh/qhsan they asked him to relieve them (lit. take away for them) from serving in the war
X. C. 7.1.44, *danaoi=sin loigo\n a)/mu_non ward off ruin from (for) the Danai A 456. So a)le/cein tini/ ti (poet.). Cp. 1392, 1628.

§1484
With verbs of receiving and buying, the person who gives or sells may stand in the dative. In de/xesqai/ ti/ tini (chiefly poetic) the dative denotes the interest of the recipient in the donor: *qe/misti de/kto de/pas she took the cup from (for, i.e. to please) Themis O 87. So with po/sou pri/wmai/ soi ta\ xoiri/dia; at what price am I to buy the pigs of you?
Ar. Ach. 812.

§1485
With verbs of motion the dative of the person to whom is properly a dative of advantage or disadvantage: h)=lqe toi=s *)aqhnai/ois h( a)ggeli/a_ the message came to (for) the Athenians
T. 1.61. Cp. 1475.

§1486

Dative of Feeling (Ethical Dative).—The personal pro nouns of the first and second person are often used to denote the interest of the speaker, or to secure the interest of the person spoken to, in an action or statement.

me/mnhsqe/ moi mh\ qorubei=n pray remember not to make a disturbance
P. A. 27b,

a)mouso/teroi genh/sontai u(_mi=n oi( ne/oi your young men will grow less cultivated
P. R. 546d,

toiou=to u(_mi=n e)sti h( turanni/s such a thing, you know, is despotism
Hdt. 5.92 h, *)artafe/rnhs u(_mi=n *(usta/speo/s e)sti pai=s Artaphernes, you know, is Hystaspes' son 5. 30. The dative of feeling may denote surprise:

w)= mh=ter, w(s kalo/s moi o( pa/ppos oh mother, how handsome grandpa is
X. C. 1.3.2. With the dative of feeling cp. “knock me here” Shakesp. T. of Sh. 1. 2. 8, “study me how to please the eye” L. L. L. i. 1. 80. toi\ surely, often used to introduce general statements or maxims, is a petrified dative of feeling (= soi/).
a. This dative in the third person is very rare (au)th=| in
P. R. 343a).
b. This construction reproduces the familiar style of conversation and may often be translated by I beg you, please, you see, let me tell you, etc. Sometimes the idea cannot be given in translation. This dative is a form of 1481.

§1487

e)moi\ boulome/nw| e)sti/, etc.—Instead of a sentence with a finite verb, a participle usually denoting inclination or aversion is added to the dative of the person interested, which depends on a form of ei)=nai, g<*>gnesqai, etc.
tw=| plh/qei tw=n *plataiw=n ou) boulome/nw| h)=n tw=n *)aqhnai/wn a)fi/stasqai the Plataean democracy did not wish to revolt from the Athenians (= to\ plh=qos ou)k e)bou/leto a)fi/stasqai)
T. 2.3 (lit. it was not for them when wishing), a)\_n boulome/nois a)kou/ein h)=| toutoisi/_, mnhsqh/somai if these men (the jury) desire to hear it, I shall take the matter up later (= a)\_n ou(=toi a)kou/ein bou/lwntai)
D. 18.11,

e)pane/lqwmen, ei)/ soi h(dome/nw| e)sti/n let us go back if it is your pleasure to do so
P. Ph. 78b,

ei) mh\ a)sme/nois u(_mi=n a)fi=gmai if I have come against your will
T. 4.85, *ni_ki/a| prosdexome/nw| h)=n ta\ para\ tw=n *)egestai/wn Nicias was prepared for the news from the Egestaeans 6. 46,

h)=n de\ ou) tw=| *)a_ghsila/_w| a)xqome/nw| this was not displeasing to Agesilaus
X. H. 5.3.13. Cp. quibus bellum volentibus erat.

§1488

Dative of the Agent.—With passive verbs (usually in the perfect and pluperfect) and regularly with verbal adjectives in -to/s and -te/os, the person in whose interest an action is done, is put in the dative. The notion of agency does not belong to the dative, but it is a natural inference that the person interested is the agent.
e)moi\ kai\ tou/tois pe/pra_ktai has been done by (for) me and these men
D. 19.205,

e)peidh\ au)toi=s pareskeu/asto when they had got their preparations ready
T. 1.46,

tosau=ta/ moi ei)rh/sqw let so much have been said by me
L. 24.4,

e)yhfi/sqai th=| boulh=| let it have been decreed by the senate
C.I.A. /lref>
a. With verbal adjectives in -to/s and -te/os (2149):

toi=s oi)/koi zhlwto/s envied by those at home
X. A. 1.7.4,

h(mi=n g' u(pe\r th=s e)leuqeri/a_s a)gwniste/on we at least must struggle to defend our freedom
D. 9.70. For the accus. with -te/on, see 2152 a.

§1489
The usual restriction of the dative to tenses of completed action seems to be due to the fact that the agent is represented as placed in the position of viewing an already completed action in the light of its relation to himself (interest, advantage, possession).

§1490
The dative of the agent is rarely employed with other tenses than perfect and pluperfect:

le/getai h(mi=n is said by us
P. L. 715b, toi=s *kerku_rai/ois ou)x e(wrw=nto the ships were not seen by (were invisible to) the Corcyraeans
T. 1.51; present,
T. 4.64, 109; aorist
T. 2.7.

§1491
The person by whom (not for whom) an action is explicitly said to be done, is put in the genitive with u(po/ (1698. 1. b).

§1492
The dative of the personal agent is used (1) when the subject is impersonal, the verb being transitive or intransitive, (2) when the subject is persal and the person is treated as a thing in order to express scorn (twice only in the orators:
D. 19.247, 57. 10).

§1493

u(po/ with the genitive of the personal agent is used (1) when the subject is a person, a city, a country, or is otherwise quasi-personal, (2) when the verb is intransitive even if the subject is a thing, as

tw=n teixw=n u(po\ tw=n barba/rwn peptwko/twn the walls having been destroyed by the barbarians
Aes. 2.172, (3) in a few cases with an impersonal subject, usually for the sake of emphasis, as

w(s e(tai/ra_ h)=n . . . u(po\ tw=n a)/llwn oi)kei/wn kai\ u(po\ tw=n geito/nwn memartu/rhtai that she was an hetaera has been testified by the rest of his relatives and by his neighbours
Is. 3.13.
a. ni_ka=sqai, h(tta=sqai to be conquered may be followed by the dative of a person, by u(po/ tinos, or by the genitive (1402).

§1494
When the agent is a thing, not a person, the dative is commonly used whether the subject is personal or impersonal. If the subject is personal, u(po/ may be used; in which case the inanimate agent is personified (see 1698. 1. N. 1). u(po/ is rarely used when the subject is impersonal. u(po/ is never used with the impersonal perfect passive of an intransitive verb.

## DATIVE OF RELATION

§1495
The dative may be used of a person to whose case the statement of the predicate is limited.

feugein au)toi=s a)sfale/stero/n e)stin h)\ h(mi=n it is safer for them to flee than for us
X. A. 3.2.19, trih/rei e)sti\n ei)s *(hra/_kleian h(me/ra_s makra=s plou=s for a trireme it is a long day's sail to Heraclea 6. 4. 2. Such cases as

dro/mos e)ge/neto toi=s stratiw/tais the soldiers began to run
X. A. 1.2.17 belong here rather than under 1476 or 1488.
a. w(s restrictive is often added: makra\_ w(s ge/ronti o(do/s a long road (at least) for an old man
S. O. C. 20, swfrosu/nhs de\ w(s plh/qei ou) ta\ toia/de me/gista; for the mass of men are not the chief points of temperance such as these?
P. R. 389d.

§1496

Dative of Reference.—The dative of a noun or pronoun often denotes the person in whose opinion a statement holds good.

ga/mous tou\s prw/tous e)ga/mei *pe/rsh|si o( *da_rei=os Darius contracted marriages most distinguished in the eyes of the Persians
Hdt. 3.88,

pa=si ni_ka=n toi=s kritai=s to be victorious in the judgment of all the judges
Ar. Av. 445,

polloi=sin oi)ktro/s pitiful in the eyes of many
S. Tr. 1071. para/ is often used, as in para\ *da_rei/w|

krith=| in the opinion of Darius
Hdt. 3.160.

§1497
The dative participle, without a noun or pronoun, is frequently used in the singular or plural to denote indefinitely the person judging or observing. This construction is most common with participles of verbs of coming or going and with participles of verbs of considering.

h( *qra/|kh e)sti\n e)pi\ decia\ ei)s to\n *po/nton ei)sple/onti Thrace is on the right as you sail into the Pontus
X. A. 6.4.1, e)/legon o(/ti h( o(do\s diaba/nti to\n potamo\n e)pi\ *lu_di/a_n fe/roi they said that, when you had crossed the river, the road led to Lydia 3. 5. 15, ou)k ou)=n a)/topon dialogizome/nois ta\_s dwrea\_s nu_ni\ plei/ous ei)=nai; is it not strange, when we reflect, that gifts are more frequent now?
Aes. 3.179,

to\ me\n e)/cwqen a(ptome/nw| sw=ma ou)k a)/ga_n qermo\n h)=n if you touched the surface the body was not very hot
T. 2.49,

pro\s w)fe/leian skopoume/nw| o( e)paine/ths tou= dikai/ou a)lhqeu/ei if you look at the matter from the point of view of advantage, the panegyrist of justice speaks the truth
P. R. 589c. So (w(s) sunelo/nti ei)pei=n (
X. A. 3.1.38) to speak briefly (lit. for one having brought the matter into small compass), sunelo/nti
D. 4.7.
a. The participle of verbs of coming or going is commonly used in statements of geographical situation.
b. The present participle is more common than the aorist in the case of all verbs belonging under 1497.

§1498

Dative of the Participle expressing Time.—In expressions of time a participle is often used with the dative of the person interested in the action of the subject, and especially to express the time that has passed since an action has occurred (cp. “and this is the sixth month with her, who was called barren” St. Luke i. 36).

a)porou=nti d' au)tw=| e)/rxetai *promhqeu/s Prometheus comes to him in his perplexity
P. Pr. 321c,

*cenofw=nti poreuome/nw| oi( i(ppei=s e)ntugxa/nousi presbu/_tais while Xenophon was on the march, his horsemen fell in with some old men
X. A. 6.3.10. The idiom is often transferred from persons to things: h(me/rai ma/lista h)=san th=| *mutilh/nh| e(a_lwkui/a| e(pta/, o(/t' e)s to\ *)/embaton kate/pleusan about seven days had passed since the capture of Mytilene, when they sailed into Embatum
T. 3.29. This construction is frequent in Hom. and Hdt. The participle is rarely omitted (
T. 1.13.).
a. A temporal clause may take the place of the participle:

th=| stratia=|, a)f' ou(= e)ce/pleusen ei)s *sikeli/a_n, h)/dh e)sti\ du/o kai\ penth/konta e)/th it is already fifty-two years since the expedition sailed to Sicily
Is. 6.14.

## DATIVE WITH ADJECTIVES, ETC.

§1499
Adjectives, adverbs, and substantives, of kindred meaning with the foregoing verbs, take the dative to define their meaning.

basilei= fi/loi friendly to the king
X. A. 2.1.20,

eu)/nous tw=| dh/mw| well disposed to the people
And. 4.16,

toi=s vo/mois e)/noxos subject to the laws
D. 21.35, e)xqro\n e)leuqeri/a| kai\ no/mois e)nanti/on hostile to liberty and opposed to law 6. 25,

cummaxi/a| pi/sunoi relying on the alliance
T. 6.2, fo/rw| u(ph/kooi subject to tribute 7. 57, h)\n poih=te o(/moia toi=s lo/gois if you act in accordance with your words 2. 72, strato\s i)/sos kai\ paraplh/sios tw=| prote/rw| an army equal or nearly so to the former 7. 42,

a)delfa\ ta\ bouleu/mata toi=s e)/rgois plans like the deeds
L. 2.64,

a)llh/lois a)nomoi/ws in a way unlike to each other
P. Tim. 36d. For substantives see 1502.
a. Some adjectives, as fi/los, e)xqro/s, may be treated as substantives and take the genitive. Some adjectives often differ slightly in meaning when they take the genitive.

§1500

With o( au)to/s the same.—

th\n au)th\n gnw/mhn e)moi\ e)/xein to be of the same mind as I am
L. 3.21,

tou= au)tou= e)moi\ patro/s of the same father as I am
D. 40.34, tau)ta\ fronw=n e)moi/ agreeing with me 18. 304.

§1501
With adjectives and adverbs of similarity and dissimilarity the comparison is often condensed (brachylogy) : o(moi/a_n tai=s dou/lais ei)=xe th\n e)sqh=ta she had a dress on like (that of) her servants
X. C. 5.1.4 (the possessor for the thing possessed, = th=| e)sqh=ti tw=n doulw=n), *)orfei= glw=ssa h( e)nanti/a_ a tongue unlike (that of) Orpheus
A. Ag. 1629.
a. After adjectives and adverbs of likeness we also find kai/, o(/sper (w(/sper). Thus,

paqei=n tau)to\n o(/per polla/kis pro/teron pepo/nqate to suffer the same as you have often suffered before
D. 1.8, ou)x o(moi/ws pepoih/ka_si kai\ *(/omhros they have not composed their poetry as Homer did P. Ion 531 d.

§1502
The dative after substantives is chiefly used when the substantive expresses the act denoted by the kindred verb requiring the dative:

e)piboulh\ e)moi/ a plot against me
X. A. 5.6.29, dia/doxos *klea/ndrw| a successor to Cleander 7. 2. 5,

h( e)mh\ tw=| qew=| u(phresi/a_ my service to the god
P. A. 30a. But also in other cases:

fili/a_ toi=s *)aqhnai/ois friendship for the Athenians
T. 5.5,

u(/mnoi qeoi=s hymns to the gods
P. R. 607a,

e)fo/dia toi=s strateuome/nois supplies for the troops
D. 3.20, h(=loi tai=s qu/rais nails for the doors (1473).
a. Both a genitive and a dative may depend on the same substantive:

h( tou= qeou= do/sis u(_mi=n the god's gift to you
P. A. 30d.

## INSTRUMENTAL DATIVE

§1503
The Greek dative, as the representative of the lost instrumental case, denotes that by which or with which an action is done or accompanied. It is of two kinds: (1) The instrumental dative proper; (2) The comitative dative.

§1504
When the idea denoted by the noun in the dative is the instrument or means, it falls under (1); if it is a person (not regarded as the instrument or means) or any other living being, or a thing regarded as a person, it belongs under (2); if an action, under (2).

§1505
Abstract substantives with or without an attributive often stand in the instrumental dative instead of the cognate accusative (1577).

## INSTRUMENTAL DATIVE PROPER

§1506
The dative denotes instrument or means, manner, and cause.

§1507

Instrument or Means.—

e)/balle/ me li/qois he hit me with stones
L. 3.8, i(/_hsi th=| a)ci/_nh| he hurls his ax at him (hurls with his ax)
X. A. 1.5.12, tai=s maxai/rais ko/ptontes hacking them with their swords 4. 6. 26,

ou)de\n h)/nue tou/tois he accomplished nothing by this
D. 21.104, e)zhmi/wsan xrh/masin they punished him by a fine
T. 2.65, u(/_ontos pollw=| (u(/dati) during a heavy rain
X. H. 1.1.16 (934). So with de/xesqai: tw=n po/lewn ou) dexome/nwn au)tou\s a)gora=| ou)de\ a)/stei, u(/dati de\ kai\ o(/rmw| as the cities did not admit them to a market nor even into the town, but (only) to water and anchorage
T. 6.44. Often with passives:

w)|kodomhme/non pli/nqois built of bricks
X. A. 2.4.12.
a. The instrumental dative is often akin to the comitative dative:

a)lw/menos nhi/ te kai\ e(ta/roisi wandering with his ship and companions
l 161,

nhusi\n oi)xh/sontai they shall go with their ships
*w 731,

qu_mw=| kai\ r(w/mh| to\ ple/on e)nauma/xoun h)\ e)pisth/mh| they fought with passionate violence and brute force rather than by a system of tactics
T. 1.49.
b. Persons may be regarded as instruments:

fulatto/menoi fu/laci defending themselves by pickets
X. A. 6.4.27. Often in poetry (
S. Ant. 164).
c. Verbs of raining or snowing take the dative or accusative (1570 a).

§1508
Under Means fall:
a. The dative of price (cp. 1372):

me/rei tw=n a)dikhma/twn to\n ki/ndu_non e)cepri/anto they freed themselves from the danger at the price of a part of their unjust gains
L. 27.6.
b. Rarely, the dative with verbs of filling (cp. 1369):

da/krusi pa=n to\ stra/teuma plhsqe/n the entire army being filled with tears
T. 7.75.
c. The dative of material and constituent parts:

kateskeua/sato a(/rmata troxoi=s i)sxu_roi=s he made chariots with strong wheels
X. C. 6.1.29.

§1509

xrh=sqai use (strictly employ oneself with, get something done with; cp. uti), and sometimes nomi/zein, take the dative. Thus, ou)/te tou/tois (toi=s nomi/mois)

xrh=tai ou)/q' oi(=s h( a)/llh *(ella\s nomi/zei neither acts according to these institutions nor observes those accepted by the rest of Greece
T. 1.77. A predicate noun may be added to the dative:

tou/tois xrw=ntai dorufo/rois they make use of them as a body-guard
X. Hi. 5.3. The use to which an object is put may be expressed by a neuter pronoun in the accus. (1573); ti/ xrhso/meqa tou/tw|; what use shall we make of it?
D. 3.6.

§1510
The instrumental dative occurs after substantives:

mi/_mhsis sxh/masi imitation by means of gestures
P. R. 397b.

§1511
The instrumental dative of means is often, especially in poetry, reinforced by the prepositions e)n, su/n, u(po/:

e)n lo/gois pei/qein to persuade by words
S. Ph. 1393,

oi( qeoi\ e)n toi=s i(eroi=s e)sh/mhnan the gods have shown by the victims
X. A. 6.1.31;

su\n gh/ra| barei=s heavy with old age
S. O. T. 17; po/lis xersi\n u(f' h(mete/rh|sin a(lou=sa a city captured by our hands B 374.

§1512

Dative of Standard of Judgment.—That by which anything is measured, or judged, is put in the dative: cunemetrh/santo tai=s e)pibolai=s tw=n pli/nqwn they measured the ladders by the layers of bricks.
T. 3.20,

tw=|de dh=lon h)=n it was plain from what followed
X. A. 2.3.1,

oi(=s pro\s tou\s a)/llous pepoi/hke dei= tekmai/resqai we must judge by what he has done to the rest
D. 9.10, ti/ni xrh\ kri/_nesqai ta\ me/llonta kalw=s kriqh/sesqai; a)=r' ou)k e)mpeiri/a| te kai\ fronh/sei kai\ lo/gw|; by what standard must we judge that the judgment may be correct? Is it not by experience and wisdom and reasoning?
P. R. 582a. With verbs of judging e)k and a)po/ are common.

§1513

Manner (see also 1527).—The dative of manner is used with comparative adjectives and other expressions of comparison to mark the degree by which one thing differs from another (Dative of Measure of Difference).
kefalh=| e)la/_ttwn a head shorter (lit. by the head)
P. Ph. 101a,

ou) pollai=s h(me/rais u(/steron h)=lqen he arrived not many days later
X. H. 1.1.1,

i)o/ntes de/ka h(me/rais pro\ *panaqhnai/wn coming ten days before the Panathenaic festival
T. 5.47,

tosou/tw| h(/di_on zw= o(/sw| plei/w ke/kthmai the more I possess the more pleasant is my life
X. C. 8.3.40,

pollw=| mei/zwn e)gi/gneto h( boh\ o(/sw| dh\ plei/ous e)gi/gnonto the shouting became much louder as the men increased in number
X. A. 4.7.23. So with pollw=| by much, o)li/gw| by little, tw=| panti/ in every respect (by all odds).
a. With the superlative:

makrw=| a)/rista by far the best
P. L. 858e.

§1514
With comparatives the accusatives (1586) ti/, ti\, ou)de/n, mhde/n without a substantive are always used:

ou)de\n h(=tton nihilo minus
X. A. 7.5.9. In Attic prose (except in Thuc.) polu/ and o)li/gon are more common than pollw=| and o)li/gw| with comparatives. Hom. has only polu\ mei/zwn.

§1515
Measure of difference may be expressed by e)/n tini; ei)/s ti, kata/ ti; or by e)pi/ tini.

§1516
The dative of manner may denote the particular point of view from which a statement is made. This occurs chiefly with intransitive adjectives but also with intransitive verbs (Dative of Respect). (Cp. 1600.)

a)nh\r h(liki/a| e)/ti ne/os a man still young in years
T. 5.43, toi=s sw/masi to\ ple/on i)sxu/_ousa h)\ toi=s xrh/masin a power stronger in men than in money 1. 121,

a)sqenh\s tw=| sw/mati weak in body
D. 21.165,

th=| fwnh=| tra_xu/s harsh of voice
X. A. 2.6.9,

fronh/sei diafe/rwn distinguished in understanding
X. C. 2.3.5,

tw=n to/te duna/mei prou/xwn superior in power to the men of that time
T. 1.9, o)no/mati spondai/ a truce so far as the name goes 6. 10.
a. The accusative of respect (1600) is often nearly equivalent to the dative of respect.

§1517

Cause.—The dative, especially with verbs of emotion, expresses the occasion (external cause) or the motive (internal cause).
Occasion:

th=| tu/xh| e)lpi/sa_s confident by reason of his good fortune
T. 3.97, qauma/zw th=| a)poklh/|sei mou tw=n pulw=n I am astonished at being shut out of the gates 4. 85,

tou/tois h(/sqh he was pleased at this
X. A. 1.9.26, h)xqo/meqa toi=s gegenhme/nois we were troubled at what had occurred 5. 7. 20, xalepw=s fe/rw toi=s parou=si pra/_gmasin I am troubled at the present occurrences 1. 3. 3. Motive:

fili/a| kai\ eu)noi/a| e(po/menoi following out of friendship and good will
X. A. 2.6.13. Occasion and motive: oi( me\n a)pori/a| a)kolou/qwn, oi( de\ a)pisti/a| some (carried their own food) because they lacked servants, others through distrust of them
T. 7.75,

u(/brei kai\ ou)k oi)/nw| tou=to poiw=n doing this out of insolence and not because he was drunk
D. 21.74.

§1518
Some verbs of emotion take e)pi/ (with dat.) to denote the cause; so always me/ga fronei=n to plume oneself, and often xai/rein rejoice, lu_pei=sqai grieve, a)ganaktei=n be vexed, ai)sxu/_nesqai be ashamed. Many verbs take the genitive (1405).

§1519
The dative of cause sometimes approximates to a dative of purpose (1473): *)aqhnai=oi e)f' h(ma=s w(/rmhntai *leonti/_nwn katoiki/sei the Athenians have set out against us (with a view to) to restore the Leontines
T. 6.33. This construction is common with other verbal nouns in Thucydides.

§1520
Cause is often expressed by dia/ with the accusative, u(po/ with the genitive, less frequently by a)mfi/ or peri/ with the dative (poet.) or u(pe/r with the genitive (poet.).

## COMITATIVE DATIVE

§1521
The comitative form of the instrumental dative denotes the persons or things which accompany or take part in an action.

§1522
Prepositions of accompaniment (meta/ with gen., su/n) are often used, especially when the verb does not denote accompaniment or union.

§1523

Dative of Association.—The dative is used with words denoting friendly or hostile association or intercourse. This dative is especially common in the plural and after middle verbs.
a.

kakoi=s o(mi_lw=n kau)to\s e)kbh/sh| kako/s if thou associate with the evil, in the end thou too wilt become evil thyself
Men. Sent. 274,

a)llh/lois dieile/gmeqa we have conversed with each other
P. A. 37a,

tw=| plh/qei ta\ r(hqe/nta koinw/santes communicating to the people what had been said
T. 2.72, deo/menoi tou\s feu/gontas cunalla/cai sfi/si asking that they reconcile their exiles with them 1. 24,

ei)s lo/gous soi e)lqei=n to have an interview with you
X. A. 2.5.4,

metesxh/kamen u(_mi=n qusiw=n we have participated in your festivals
X. H. 2.4.20, a)llh/lois sponda\_s e)poih/santo they made a truce with one another 3. 2. 20,

au)toi=s dia\ fili/a_s i)e/nai to enter into friendship with them
X. A. 3.2.8. So with verbs of meeting: prose/rxesqai, prostugxa/nein and e)ntugxa/nein, a)panta=n.
b.

polloi=s o)li/goi maxo/menoi few fighting with many
T. 4.36, *ku/_rw| polemou=ntes waging war with Cyrus 1. 13, a)mfisbhtou=si me\n di' eu)/noian oi( fi/loi toi=s fi/lois, e)ri/zousi de\ oi( dia/foroi a)llh/lois friends dispute with friends good-naturedly, but adversaries wrangle with one another
P. Pr. 337b,

di/ka_s a)llh/lois dika/zontai they bring lawsuits against one another
X. M. 3.5.16,

diafe/resqai tou/tois to be at variance with these men
D. 18.31 (and so many compounds of dia/),

ou)k e)/fh tou\s lo/gous toi=s e)/rgois o(mologei=n he said their words did not agree with their deeds
T. 5.55. So also tini\ dia\ pole/mou (dia\ ma/xhs, ei)s xei=ras) i)e/nai, tini\ o(mo/se xwrei=n, etc.
N. 1.—polemei=n (ma/xesqai) su/n tini (meta/ tinos) means to wage war in conjunction with some one.
N. 2.—Verbs of friendly or hostile association, and especially periphrases with poiei=sqai (po/lemon, sponda/_s), often take the accusative with pro/s.

§1524

Dative of Accompaniment.—The dative of accompaniment is used with verbs signifying to accompany, follow, etc.

a)kolouqei=n tw=| h(goume/nw| to follow the leader
P. R. 474c, e(/pesqai u(_mi=n bou/lomai I am willing to follow you
X. A. 3.1.25. meta/ with the genitive is often used, as are su/n and a(/ma with the dative.

§1525

With au)to/s.—The idea of accompaniment is often expressed by au)to/s joined to the dative. This use is common when the destruction of a person or thing is referred to. Thus,

tw=n vew=n mi/a au)toi=s a)ndra/sin one of the ships with its crew
T. 4.14,

ei)=pen h(/kein ei)s ta\_s ta/ceis au)toi=s stefa/nois he bade them come to their posts, crowns and all
X. C. 3.3.40. The article after au)to/s is rare; and su/n is rarely added (
X. C. 2.2.9). Hom. has this dative only with lifeless objects.

§1526

Dative of Military Accompaniment.—The dative is used in the description of military movements to denote the accompaniment (troops, ships, etc.) of a leader:

e)celau/nei tw=| strateu/mati panti/ he marches out with all his army
X. A. 1.7.14. su/n is often used with words denoting troops (
T. 6.62).
a. An extension of this usage occurs when the persons in the dative are essentially the same as the persons forming the subject (distributive use):

h(mi=n e)fei/ponto oi( pole/mioi kai\ i(ppikw=| kai\ peltastikw=| the enemy pursued us with their cavalry and peltasts
X. A. 7.6.29.
b. The dative of military accompaniment is often equivalent to a dative of means when the verb does not denote the leadership of a general.

§1527

Dative of Accompanying Circumstance.—The dative, usually of an abstract substantive, may denote accompanying circumstance and manner.
a. The substantive has an attribute:

pollh=| boh=| prose/keinto they attacked with loud shouts
T. 4.127, panti\ sqe/nei with all one's might 5. 23,

tu/xh| a)gaqh=| with good fortune
C.I.A. /lref>So panti\ (ou)deni\, a)/llw|, tou/tw| tw=|) tro/pw|. Manner may be expressed by the adjective, as biai/w| qana/tw| a)poqnh/|skein to die (by) a violent death
X. Hi. 4.3 (= bi/a|).
b. Many particular substantives have no attribute and are used adverbially:

qei=n dro/mw| to run at full speed
X. A. 1.8.19, bi/a| by force, di/kh| justly, do/lw| by craft, (tw=|) e)/rgw| in fact, h(suxh=| quietly, komidh=| (with care) entirely, ko/smw| in order, duly, ku/klw| round about, (tw=|) lo/gw| in word, profa/sei ostensibly, si_gh=|, siwph=| in silence, spoudh=| hastily, with difficulty, th=| a)lhqei/a| in truth, tw=| o)/nti in reality, o)rgh=| in anger, fugh=| in hasty flight.
N.—When no adjective is used, prepositional phrases or adverbs are generally employed: su\n kraugh=|, su\n di/kh|, meta\ di/khs, pro\s bi/a_n (or biai/ws).
c. Here belongs the dative of feminine adjectives with a substantive (o(dw=|, etc.) omitted, as tau/th| in this way, here, a)/llh| in another way, elsewhere, ph=|, h(=| in what (which) way. So dhmosi/a| at public expense, i)di/a| privately, koinh=| in common, pezh=| on foot.
N.—Some of these forms are instrumental rather than comitative, e.g. tau/th|.

§1528

Space and Time.—The dative of space and time may sometimes be regarded as comitative.
a. Space: the way by which (qua), as e)poreu/eto th=| o(dw=| h(\n pro/teron e)poih/sato he marched by the road (or on the road?) which he had made before
T. 2.98; b. Time: kathgo/rei w(s e)kei/nh tw=| x<*>o/nw| peisqei/h she charged that she had been persuaded in (by) the course of time
L. 1.20. Some of these uses are instrumental rather than comitative.

## WITH ADJECTIVES, ETC.

§1529
Many adjectives and adverbs, and some substantives, take the instrumental dative by the same construction as the corresponding verbs.

su/mmaxos au)toi=s their ally
D. 9.58, xw/ra_ o(/moros th=| *lakedaimoni/wn a country bordering on that of the Lacedaemonians 15. 22, a)ko/louqa tou/tois conformable to this 18. 257. So koino/s (cp. 1414), su/mfwnos, suggenh/s, metai/tios, and dia/foros meaning at variance with.—

e(pome/nws tw=| no/mw| conformably to the law
P. L. 844e,

o( e(ch=s no/mos tou/tw| the law next to this
D. 21.10. Many of the adjectives belonging here also take the genitive when the idea of possession or connection is marked.—a(/ma chiefly in the meaning at the same time.—

koinwni/a_ toi=s a)ndra/si intercourse with men
P. R. 466c,

e)pidromh\ tw=| teixi/smati attack on the fort
T. 4.23.

## LOCATIVE DATIVE

§1530
The dative as the representative of the locative is used to express place and time.
a. On the instrumental dative of space and time, see 1528.

§1531

Dative of Place.—In poetry the dative without a preposition is used to denote place.
a. Where a person or thing is:

sta\_s me/sw| e(/rkei+ taking his stand in the middle of the court
*w 306,

gh=| e)/keito she lay on the ground
S. O. T. 1266, nai/ein o)/resin to dwell among the mountains O. T. 1451. Often of the parts of the body (Hom. qu_mw=|, kardi/h|, etc.). With persons (generally in the plural): a)ripreph\s *trw/essin conspicuous among the Trojans Z 477. toi=si d' a)ne/sth A 68 may be rose up among them or a dative proper (for them).
b. Place whither (limit of motion): pedi/w| pe/se fell on the ground E 82,

kolew=| a)/or qe/o put thy sword into its sheath
k 333.

§1532
After verbs of motion the dative, as distinguished from the locative, denotes direction towards and is used of persons (1485), and is a form of the dative of interest.

§1533
Many verbs capable of taking the locative dative in poetry, require, in prose, the aid of a preposition in composition. The limit of motion is usually (1589) expressed by the accusative with a preposition (e.g. ei)s, pro/s).

§1534
In prose the dative of place (chiefly place where) is used only of proper names: *pu_qoi= at Pytho, *)isqmoi= at the Isthmus, *salami=ni at Salamis, *)olumpi/a_si at Olympia, *)aqh/nhsi at Athens (inscr.); especially with the names of Attic demes, as *falhroi=, *qorikoi=, *maraqw=ni. But e)n *maraqw=ni and e)n *plataiai=s occur. Some deme-names require e)n, as e)n *koi/lh|.

§1535
Many adverbs are genuine locatives, as oi)/koi, pa/lai, pandhmei/, *falhroi=; *)aqh/nhsi, *plataia=si; others are datives in form, as ku/klw|, *plataiai=s.

§1536
With names of countries and places, e)n is more common than the locative dative, and, with the above exceptions, the place where is expressed in Attic prose with e)n.

§1537

Verbs of ruling often take the dative, especially in Homer: *murmido/nessin a)/nasse
*a 180, *giga/ntessin basi/leuen h 59, h)=rxe d' a)/ra sfin *)agame/mnwn *c 134. Rarely in prose: h(gei=sqai/ tini to serve as guide (leader) to some one, e)pistatei=n tini to be set over one; a)/rxein tini/ means only = to be archon (*pu_qodw/rou a)/rxontos *)aqhnai/ois
T. 2.2). Cp. 1371.
a. Only when stress is not laid on the idea of supremacy is the dative, instead of the genitive (1370), used with verbs of ruling.

§1538
It is not clear whether the dative with verbs of ruling is a dative proper (for), a locative (among; cp. e)n *fai/hcin a)/nasse h 62), or an instrumental (by). a)/rxein, h(gei=sqai may take the dative proper, a)na/ssein, basileu/ein, kratei=n may take the locative dative.

§1539

Dative of Time.—The dative without a preposition is commonly used to denote a definite point of time (chiefly day, night, month, year, season) at which an action occurred. The dative contrasts one point of time with another, and is usually accompanied by an attributive.

§1540
The dative denotes the time at which an action takes place and the date of an event.
tau/thn me\n th\n h(me/ra_n au)tou= e)/meinan, th=| de\ u(sterai/a| ktl. throughout that day they waited there, but on the day following, etc.
X. H. 1.1.14. So th=| proterai/a| the day before, th=| deute/ra| the second day, *)elafhboliw=nos mhno\s e(/kth| (h(me/ra|)

fqi/nontos on the sixth of waning Elaphebolion
Aes. 2.90,

e(/nh| kai\ ve/a| on the last of the month
D. 18.29;

tri/tw| mhni/ in the third month
L. 21.1,

periio/nti tw=| qe/rei when summer was coming to an end
T. 1.30, e)chkostw=| e)/tei in the sixtieth year 1. 12; also with w(/ra| (

xeimw=nos w(/ra| in the winter season
And. 1.137).

§1541
The names of the regular recurring festivals which serve to date an <*>ccurrence stand in the dative:

*panaqhnai/ois at the Panathenaea
D. 21.156, <*>oi=s *dionu_si/ois at the Dionysia 21. 1, tai=s pompai=s at the processions 21. 171, toi=s <*>oagw|doi=s at the representations of the tragedies
Aes. 3.176. e)n is rarely added.

§1542

e)n is added:
a. To words denoting time when there is no attributive:

e)n tw=| xeimw=ni in winter
X. O. 17.3; cp. 1444. b. When the attributive is a pronoun (sometimes): (e)n) e)kei/nh| th=| h(me/ra|. c. To statements of the time within the limits of which an event may take place (where e)nto/s with the genitive is common); to statements of how much time anything takes; with numbers, o)li/gos, polu/s, etc. Thus, e)n trisi\n h(me/rais for (during) three days
X. A. 4.8.8,

ou) r(a/|dion ta\ e)n a(/panti tw=| xro/nw| pra_xqe/nta e)n mia=| h(me/ra| dhlwqh=nai it is not easy to set forth in a single day the acts of all time
L. 2.54,

e)cele/sqai th\n diabolh\n e)n ou(/tws o)li/gw| xro/nw| to clear myself of calumny in so brief a time
P. A. 19a. e)n is rarely omitted in prose, and chiefly when there is an attributive: mia=| nukti\
T. 6.27. d. Always with adjectives or adverbs used substantively: e)n tw=| paro/nti, e)n tw=| to/te. e. To words denoting the date of an event, not a point of time:

e)n th=| prote/ra| presbei/a| in the first embassy
Aes. 2.123. Thuc. employs e)n, as e)n th=| u(sterai/a| e)kklhsi/a| in the assembly held the day after 1. 44, but usu. the simple dative, as ma/xh| in the battle 3. 54, e)kei/nh| th=| e)sbolh=| in that incursion 2. 20, th=| prote/ra| e)kklhsi/a| in the first assembly 1. 44.

§1543
The dative and genitive of time are sometimes employed with only a slight difference (1447 a).

## DATIVE WITH COMPOUND VERBS

§1544
Many compound verbs take the dative because of their meaning as a whole. So a)nte/xein hold out against, a)mfisbhtei=n dispute with (1523 b).

§1545
The dative is used with verbs compounded with su/n (regularly), with many compounded with e)n, e)pi/, and with some compounded with para/, peri/, pro/s, and u(po/, because the preposition keeps a sense that requires the dative.

e)mble/ya_s au)tw=| looking at him
P. Charm. 162d,

e)lpi/das e)mpoiei=n a)nqrw/pois to create expectations in men
X. C. 1.6.19,

au)toi=s e)pe/pese to\ *(ellhniko/n the Greek force fell upon them
X. A. 4.1.10, e)pe/keinto au)toi=s they pressed hard upon them 5. 2. 5, sunadikei=n au)toi=s to be their accomplice in wrong-doing 2. 6. 27, cuni/sa_si *melh/tw| yeudome/nw| they are conscious that Meletus is speaking falsely (i.e. they know it as well as he does)
P. A. 34b,

ou(=toi ou) parege/nonto basilei= these did not join the king
X. A. 5.6.8, pare/stw u(_mi=n o( kh=ruc let the herald come with us 3. 1. 46, *cenofw=nti prose/trexon du/o nea_ni/skw two youths ran up to Xenophon 4. 3. 10,

u(pokei=sqai tw=| a)/rxonti to be subject to the ruler
P. G. 510c.
a. So especially with verbs of motion and rest formed from i)e/nai, pi/_ptein, tiqe/nai, tre/xein, ei)=nai, gi/gnesqai, kei=sqai, etc.

§1546
Some verbs of motion compounded with para/, peri/, u(po/ take the accusative (1559).

§1547
Some verbs have an alternative construction, e.g. periba/llein: tini/ ti <*>nvest a person with something, ti/ tini surround something with something.

§1548
Compounds of su/n take the instrumental, compounds of e)n take the locative dative.

§1549
When the idea of place is emphatic, the preposition may be repeated:

e)mmei/nantes e)n th=| *)attikh=| remaining in Attica
T. 2.23; but it is generally not repeated when the idea is figurative:

toi=s o(/rkois e)mme/nwn abiding by one's oath
I. 1.13. meta/ may be used after compounds of su/n:

met' e)mou= sune/plei he sailed in company with me
L. 21.8.

§1550
The prepositions are more frequently repeated in prose than in poetry.

## ACCUSATIVE

§1551
The accusative is a form of defining or qualifying the verb.
a. The accusative derives its name from a mistranslation (casus accusativus) of the Greek (h( ai)tia_tikh\ ptw=sis, properly casus effectivus, 1554 a).

§1552
A noun stands in the accusative when the idea it expresses is most immediately (in contrast to the dative) and most completely (in contrast to the genitive) under the influence of the verbal conception (in contrast to the nominative).

§1553
The accusative is the case of the direct object (919). The accusative is used with all transitive verbs (and with some intransitive verbs used transitively), with some verbal nouns, and with adjectives.

§1554
The direct object is of two kinds:
a. The internal object (object effected): o( a)nh\r tu/ptei polla\_s plhga/_s the man strikes many blows.
N. 1.—Here the object is already contained (or implied) in the verb, and its addition is optional. The accusative of the internal object is sometimes called the accusative of content. The object stands in apposition to the result of the verbal action. The effect produced by the verb is either (1) transient, when the object is a nomen actionis, and disappears with the operation of the verb, as in ma/xhn ma/xesqai to fight a battle, or (2) permanent, and remains after the verbal action has ceased, as in tei=xos teixi/zein to build a wall. The latter form is the accusative of result (1578).
N. 2.—Almost any verb may take one of the varieties of the internal object.
b. The external object (object affected): o( a)nh\r tu/ptei to\n pai=da the man strikes the boy.
N.—Here the object is not contained in the verb, but is necessary to explain or define the character of the action in question. The external object stands outside the verbal action.

§1555
Many verbs may take an accusative either of the external or of the internal object: te/mnein u(/_lhn fell timber, te/mnein ta\_s tri/xas cut off the hair, te/mnein o(do/n open a road, but sponda\_s or o(/rkia te/mnein, with a specialized verbal idea, to make a treaty by slaying a victim (pass. o(/rkia e)tmh/qh), te/mnein o(do/n make one's way (poet.), teixi/zein xwri/on fortify a place, but teixi/zein tei=xos build a wall. Cp.
E. Supp. 1060: A. ni_kw=sa ni/_khn ti/na; maqei=n xrh/|zw se/qen. B. pa/_sa_s gunai=kas, ktl. A. Victorious in what victory? This I would learn of thee. B. Over all women. Here the construction shifts from the internal to the external object.

§1556
The direct object of an active transitive verb becomes the subject of the passive: o( pai=s u(po\ tou= a)ndro\s tu/ptetai the boy is struck by the man.
a. The object of a verb governing the genitive or dative as principal object may also become the subject of the passive (1340).

§1557
In Greek many verbs are transitive the ordinary English equivalents of which are intransitive and require a preposition. So siwpa=n ti, si_ga=n ti to keep silence about something.

§1558
Many verbs that are usually intransitive are also used transitively in Greek. Thus, a)sebei=n sin against, dusxerai/nein be disgusted at, xai/rein rejoice at, h(/desqai be pleased at, dakru/_ein weep for. Cp. 1595 b.
a. Poetical: a)/|ssein agitate,

pera=n po/da pass on her way
E. Hec. 53, plei=n sail, krotali/zein rattle along (

krotei=n strike
Hdt. 6.58), la/mpein make shine, xoreu/ein qeo/n, e(li/ssein qeo/n celebrate the god by choruses, by dancing.

§1559
Many intransitive verbs are used transitively when compounded with a preposition, e.g. a)nama/xesqai fight over again.—a)poma/xesqai drive off, a)postre/fesqai abandon, a)poxwrei=n leave.—diabai/nein pass over, diaplei=n sail across, diece/rxesqai go through.—ei)sie/nai come into the mind, ei)splei=n said into.—e)kbai/nein pass, e)ktre/pesqai get out of the way of, e)canaxwrei=n shun, e)ci/stasqai avoid.— e)pistrateu/ein march against.—katanaumaxei=n beat at sea, katapolemei=n subdue completely, katapoli_teu/esqai reduce by policy.—mete/rxesqai seek, pursue, metie/nai go in quest of.—parabai/nein transgress.—periie/nai go round, perii/stasqai surround.—prosoikei=n dwell in, prospai/zein sing in praise of.—u(perbai/nein omit.— u(pece/rxesqai escape from.—u(pe/rxesqai fawn on, u(podu/_esqai withstand, u(poxwrei=n shun, u(fi/stasqai withstand.

§1560
Conversely, many verbs that are usually transitive are used intransitively (with gen., dat., or with a preposition). Some of these are mentioned in 1591, 1592, 1595. Sometimes there is a difference in meaning, as a)re/skein = satisfy, with accus., = please, with dat.

§1561
The same verb may be used transitively or intransitively, often with little difference of signification. Cp. 1709. This is generally indicated in the treatment of the cases, e.g. ai)sqa/nesqai/ ti or tinos perceive something, e)nqu_mei=sqai/ ti or tini consider something, me/mfesqai/ tina or tini blame some one.

§1562
On dei= moi/ tinos and dei= me/ tinos see 1400. With the inf. the accus. is usual (dat. and inf.
X. A. 3.4.35). xrh/ me/ tinos is poetical; with the inf. xrh/ takes the accus. (except
L. 28.10, where some read dikai/ous). (xrh/ is an old noun; cp. xrew/, xrei/a need and 793.)
