## COGNATE ACCUSATIVE

§1563
The cognate accusative is of two kinds, of which the second is an extension of the first.

§1564
(I) The substantive in the accusative is of the same origin as the verb.

pollh\n flua_ri/a_n flua_rou=nta talking much nonsense
P. A. 19c, cune/fuge th\n fugh\n tau/thn he shared in the recent exile 21 a,

th\n e)n *salami=ni naumaxi/a_n naumaxh/santes victorious in the sea-fight at Salamis
D. 59.97, ta\_s u(posxe/seis a(\_s ou(=tos u(pi_sxnei=to the promises which he made 19. 47,

h( ai)ti/a_ h(\n ai)tiw=ntai the charge they bring
Ant. 6.27.
a. Sometimes the verb may be suppressed, as h(mi=n me\n eu)xa\_s ta/_sde (eu)/xomai) for us these prayers
A. Ch. 142.

§1565
The cognate accusative occurs even with adjectives of an intransitive character:

mh/te ti sofo\s w)\n th\n e)kei/nwn sofi/a_n mh/te a)maqh\s th\n a)maqi/a_n being neither at all wise after the fashion of their wisdom nor ignorant after the fashion of their ignorance
P. A. 22e, a)ti/_mous e)poi/hsan a)ti_mi/a_n toia/_nde w(/ste ktl. they disfranchised them in such a way that, etc.
T. 5.34 (a)ti/_mous e)poi/hsan = h)ti/_mhsan, cp. 1598).

§1566

Passive:

po/lemos e)polemei=to war was waged
X. H. 4.8.1.

§1567
(II) The substantive in the accusative is of kindred meaning with the verb.

e)ch=lqon a)/lla_s o(dou/s they went forth on other expeditions
X. H. 1.2.17,

to\n i(ero\n kalou/menon po/lemon e)stra/teusan they waged what is called the Sacred War
T. 1.112,

h)sqe/nhse tau/thn th\n no/son he fell ill of this disease
I. 19.24,

a)nqrw/pou fu/sin blastw/n born to man's estate
S. Aj. 760.

§1568

Passive:

po/lemos e)tara/xqh war was stirred up
D. 18.151.

§1569
An extension of the cognate accusative appears in poetry with kei=sqai, sth=nai, kaqi/zein and like verbs:

to/pon, o(/ntina kei=tai the place in which he is situated
S. Ph. 145, ti/ e(/sthke pe/tra_n; why stands she on the rock?
E. Supp. 987,

tri/poda kaqi/zwn sitting on the tripod
E. Or. 956.

§1570
An attributive word is usually necessary (but not in Hom.); otherwise the addition of the substantive to the verb would be tautologous. But the attribute is omitted:
a. When the nominal idea is specialized:

fulaka\_s fula/ttein to stand sentry
X. A. 2.6.10, fo/ron fe/rein to pay tribute 5. 5. 7.
b. When the substantive is restricted by the article:

to\n po/lemon polemei=n to wage the present war
T. 8.58, th\n pomph\n pe/mpein to conduct the procession 6. 56.
c. When a plural substantive denotes repeated occurrences:

e)trihra/rxhse trihrarxi/a_s he performed the duty of trierarch
D. 45.85.
d. In various expressions:

*)olu/mpia ni_ka=n to win an Olympian victory
T. 1.126,

th\n naumaxi/a_n ni_kh=sai to be victorious in the sea-fight
L. 19.28,

qu/_ein ta\ eu)agge/lia to offer a sacrifice in honour of good news
X. H. 1.6.37.
e. In poetry the use of a substantive to denote a special form of the action of the verb is much extended: sta/zein ai(=ma to drip (drops of) blood
S. Ph. 783,

*)/arhpnei=n to breathe war
A. Ag. 375, pu=r dedorkw/s looking (a look of) fire
t 446. This use is common, especially in Aristophanes, with verbs signifying the look of another than the speaker: ble/pein na=pu to look mustard Eq. 631, ble/pein a)pisti/a_n to look unbelief Com. fr. 1. 341 (No. 309); cp. “looked his faith”: Holmes.

§1571
The substantive without an attribute is (rarely) added to the verb as a more emphatic form of statement: lh=ron lhrei=n to talk sheer nonsense Ar. Pl. 517,

u(/brin u(bri/zein to insult grievously
E. H. F. 708. Often in Euripides.

§1572
The substantive may be omitted, leaving only the adjectival attribute: pai=son diplh=n (scil. plhgh/n) strike twice (a double blow)
S. El. 1415, tou=ton a)ne/kragon w(s o)li/ga_s (scil. plhga\_s) pai/seien they called out that he had dealt him too (1063) few blows
X. A. 5.8.12. Cp. 1028.

§1573
Usually an adjective, pronoun, or pronominal adjective is treated as a neuter substantive. Cp.

mega/l' a(marta/nein to commit grave errors
D. 5.5 with me/gista a(marth/mata a(marta/nousi
P. G. 525d. The singular adjective is used in certain common phrases in prose, but is mainly poetical; the plural is ordinarily used in prose.
h(du\ gela=n poet. (= h(du\n ge/lwta gela=n) to laugh sweetly, me/ga (yeu=dos) yeu/detai he is a great liar,

me/ga fronh/sa_s e)pi\ tou/tw| highly elated at this
X. A. 3.1.27, mei=zon fronei= he is too proud 5. 6. 8,

ta\ tw=n *(ellh/nwn fronei=n to be on the side of the Greeks
D. 14.34,

me/giston e)du/nanto had the greatest influence
L. 30.14,

deina\ u(bri/zein to maltreat terribly
X. A. 6.4.2,

tau)ta\ e)presbeu/omen we fulfilled our mission as ambassadors in the same way
D. 19.32, ti/ bou/letai h(mi=n xrh=sqai; what use does he wish to make of us?
X. A. 1.3.18 (= ti/na bou/letai xrei/a_n xrh=sqai, cp. xrh=sqai/ tini xrei/an
P. L. 868b).

§1574

Passive:

tou=to ou)k e)yeu/sqhsan they were not deceived in this
X. A. 2.2.13,

tau=ta ou)dei\s a)\n peisqei/h no one would be persuaded of this
P. L. 836d.

§1575
For a cognate accusative in conjunction with a second object, see 1620.

§1576
Note the expressions dika/zein di/khn decide a case, dika/zesqai di/khn tini/ go to law with somebody, diw/kein grafh/n tina indict somebody, feu/gein di/khn tino/s be put on one's trial for something; gra/fesqai/ tina grafh/n indict one for a public offence, feu/gein grafh/n be put on one's trial for a public offence. Also a)gwni/zesqai sta/dion (= a)gw=na stadi/ou) be a contestant in the race-course, ni_ka=n sta/dion be victorious in the race-course, ni_ka=n di/khn win a case, ni_ka=n gnw/mhn carry a resolution (pass. gnw/mhn h(tta=sqai), o)flei=n di/khn lose a case.

§1577
The (rarer) dative (fo/bw| tarbei=n, biai/w| qana/tw| a)poqnh/|skein, feu/gein fugh=|) expresses the cause (1517), manner (1513), or means (1507).

## ACCUSATIVE OF RESULT

§1578
The accusative of result denotes the effect enduring after the verbal action has ceased.
e(/lkos ou)ta/sai to smite (and thus make) a wound E 361 (so ou)lh\n e)lau/nein y 74), presbeu/ein th\n ei)rh/nhn to negotiate the peace (go as ambassadors (pre/sbeis) to make the peace)
D. 19.134, but presbeu/ein presbei/a_n to go on an embassy Dinarchus 1. 16,

no/misma ko/ptein to coin money
Hdt. 3.56, sponda\_s, or o(/rkia, te/mnein (1555).

§1579
Verbs signifying to effect anything (ai)/rein raise, au)/cein exalt, dida/skein teach, tre/fein rear, paideu/ein train) show the result of their action upon a substantive or adjective predicate to the direct object:

se\ *qh=bai/ g' ou)k e)pai/deusan kako/n Thebes did not train thee to be base
S. O. C. 919,

tou=ton tre/fein te kai\ au)/cein me/gan to nurse and exalt him into greatness
P. R. 565c,

e)poikodomh/santes au)to\ u(yhlo/teron raising it higher
T. 7.4. Such predicate nouns are called proleptic. Passive:

me/gas e)k mi_krou= *fi/lippos hu)/chtai Philip has grown from a mean to be a mighty person
D. 9.21. Cp. 1613.

## ACCUSATIVE OF EXTENT

§1580
The accusative denotes extent in space and time.

§1581

Space.—The accusative denotes the space or way over which an action is extended, and the measure of the space traversed.
a)/gein (stratia\_n)

stena\_s o(dou/s to lead an army over narrow roads
X. C. 1.6.43, e)celau/nei staqmou\s trei=s, parasa/gga_s ei)/kosi kai\ du/o he advances three stages, twenty- two parasangs
X. A. 1.2.5,

a)pe/xei h( *pla/taia tw=n *qhbw=n stadi/ous e(bdomh/konta Plataea is seventy stades distant from Thebes
T. 2.5.
a. This use is analogous to the cognate accusative after verbs of motion (e)co/dous e)celqei=n, plei=n qa/lattan).

§1582

Time.—The accusative denotes extent of time.

e)/meinen h(me/ra_s e(pta/ he remained seven days
X. A. 1.2.6,

cummaxi/a_n e)poih/santo e(kato\n e)/th they made an alliance for a hundred years
T. 3.114.

§1583
The accusative of time implies that the action of the verb covers the entire period. When emphasis is laid on the uninterrupted duration of an action, para/ with the accusative (1692. 3. b) and dia/ with the genitive (1685. 1. b) are used. The accusative of time is rarely employed where the dative (1540) is properly in place: th/nde th\n h(me/ra_n
Aes. 3.7.

§1584
Duration of life may be expressed by gegonw/s:

e)/th gegonw\s e(bdomh/konta seventy years old
P. A. 17d. (Also by ei)=nai and the genitive, 1327.)

§1585
To mark (a) how long a situation has lasted or (b) how much time has elapsed since something happened, an ordinal is used without the article, but often with the addition of ou(tosi/_. The current day or year is included. Thus (a)

th\n mhte/ra teleuth/sa_san tri/ton e)/tos touti/_ my mother who died two years ago
L. 24.6,

e)pidedh/mhke tri/thn h)/dh h(me/ra_n he has been in the city since day before yesterday
P. Pr. 309d. (b)

a)phgge/lqh *fi/lippos tri/ton h)\ te/tarton e)/tos touti\_ *(hrai=on tei=xos poliorkw=n this is the third or fourth year since it was announced that Philip was besieging fort Heraeum
D. 3.4.

§1586
On the accusative of extent in degree, see 1609. With a comparative we find polu/ and o)li/gon as well as pollw=| and o)li/gw| (1514); and always ti/, ti\, ou)de/n with the comparative.

§1587
Time and degree are often expressed by prepositions with the accusative. See Prepositions under a)mfi/, a)na/, dia/, e)pi/, kata/, para/, pro/s, u(po/.

## TERMINAL ACCUSATIVE (IN POETRY)

§1588
In poetry after verbs of motion the accusative may be used without a preposition to express the goal.

a)/stu *kadmei=on molw/n having come to the city of Cadmus
S. O. T. 35,

pe/myome/n nin *(ella/da we will convey her to Greece
E. Tro. 883. Of persons in Hom. (especially with i(kne/omai, i(/kw, i(ka/_nw = reach) and in the lyric parts of the drama:

mnhsth=ras a)fi/_keto came unto the suitors
a 332. Cp. “arrived our coast”: Shakesp. In
Hdt. 9.26 fame\n h(me/as i(kne/esqai means we declare that it befits us.

§1589
The limit of motion is also expressed by -de (a)/stude Hom., in prose, *)aqh/naze = *)aqh/na_s + de; xama=ze or xama/ze = xama_s + de, cp. xama-i/; oi)/kade) and, regularly in prose, by ei)s, e)pi/, para/, pro/s, w(s (with a person) with the accusative.

## EXTERNAL OBJECT (OBJECT AFFECTED）

§1590
Of the many transitive verbs taking this accusative the following deserve mention:

§1591
(I) To do anything to or say anything of a person.
a. eu)= (kalw=s) poiei=n, dra=n (rarely with pra/_ttein), eu)ergetei=n, o)nina/nai, w)felei=n (also with dat.), qerapeu/ein, kakw=s poiei=n, kakou=n, kakourgei=n, bla/ptein, a)dikei=n, u(bri/zein, bia/zesqai, a)mei/besqai requite, ti_mwrei=sqai punish, lu_mai/nesqai (also with dat.), lwba=sqai (also with dat.).
b. eu)= (kalw=s) le/gein, eu)logei=n, kolakeu/ein, qwpeu/ein, proskunei=n, kakw=s le/gein, kakologei=n, kakhgorei=n, loidorei=n.

§1592

sumfe/rein and lu_sitelei=n profit, bohqei=n help, loidorei=sqai rail at take the dat., a)dikei=n injure and u(bri/zein insult also take ei)/s tina or pro/s tina.

§1593

eu)= (kakw=s) a)kou/ein, pa/sxein are used as the passives of eu)= (kakw=s) le/gein, poiei=n. Cp. 1752.

§1594
Many of the above-mentioned verbs take a double accusative (1622).

§1595
(II) Verbs expressing emotion and its manifestations.
a. fobei=sqai, dedie/nai, trei=n, e)kplh/ttesqai, kataplh/ttesqai fear, pth/ssein crouch before, eu)labei=sqai beware of, qarrei=n have no fear of (have confidence in), ai)dei=sqai stand in awe of, ai)sxu/_nesqai feel shame before, dusxerai/nein be disgusted at, e)leei=n pity, penqei=n, qrhnei=n, dakru/_ein, kla/_ein (klai/ein) lament, weep over.
b. xai/rein rejoice at and h(/desqai be pleased to hear take the accus. of a person only in the poets and only with a predicate participle (2100). ai)sxu/_nesqai, xai/rein, h(/desqai, dusxerai/nein usually take the dat. in prose. qarrei=n may take the instr. dat. (
Hdt. 3.76).

§1596
(III) Verbs of swearing.
o)mnu/nai swear by (tou\s qeou/s, pass. *zeu\s o)mw/motai) and swear to (to\n o(/rkon, pass. o( o(/rkos o)mw/motai). So e)piorkei=n swear falsely by.
a. o)mnu/nai tou\s qeou/s may be an abbreviation of o)mnu/nai o(/rkon (internal object) tw=n qew=n.
b. The accusative is used in asseverations with the adverbs of swearing ma/, ou) ma/, nai\ ma/, nh/.
Nay, by Zeus: ma\ (to\n) *di/a, ou) ma\ (to\n) *di/a.
Yea, by Zeus: nai\ ma\ (to\n) *di/a, nh\ (to\n) *di/a.
ma/ is negative, except when preceded by nai/. ma/ may stand alone when a negative precedes (often in a question) or when a negative follows in the next clause: ma\ to\n *)apo/llw, ou)/k
Ar. Thesm. 269. ma/ is sometimes omitted after ou), and after nai/: ou) to\n *)/olumpon
S. O. T. 1088, nai\ ta\_n ko/ra_n
Ar. Vesp. 1438.
c. The name of the deity may be omitted in Attic under the influence of sudden scrupulousness: ma\ to\n—ou' su/ ge not you, by—
P. G. 466e.

§1597
(IV) Various other verbs.
feu/gein flee from, a)podidra/_skein escape from, e)nedreu/ein lie in wait for, fqa/nein anticipate, fula/ttesqai guard oneself against, a)mu/_nesqai defend oneself against, lanqa/nein escape the notice of, me/nein wait for, e)klei/pein and e)pilei/pein give out, fail (

to\ stra/teuma o( si=tos e)pe/lipe corn failed the army
X. A. 1.5.6).

§1598
The accusative is rarely found after verbal nouns and adjectives, and in periphrastic expressions equivalent to a transitive verb. (This usage is post-Homeric and chiefly poetical.)
xoa\_s propompo/s (= prope/mpousa) escorting the libations
A. Ch. 23,

ta\ mete/wra frontisth/s a speculator about things above the earth
P. A. 18b,

e)pisth/mones h)=san ta\ prosh/konta they were acquainted with their duties
X. C. 3.3.9, po/lemos a)/pora po/rimos war providing difficulties (things for which there is no provision)
A. Pr. 904, polla\ suni/stwr (a house) full of guilty secrets
A. Ag. 1090,

se\ fu/cimos able to escape thee
S. Ant. 787; e)/carno/s ei)mi (= e)carnou=mai) ta\ e)rwtw/mena say ‘no’ to the question
P. Charm. 158c,

teqna=si tw=| de/ei tou\s a)posto/lous they are in mortal fear of the envoys
D. 4.45; other cases 1612.

§1599

Elliptical Accusative.—The accusative is sometimes used elliptically.
ou(=tos, w)= se/ toi (scil. kalw=) ho! you there, I am calling you!
Ar. Av. 274, mh/, pro/s se qew=n tlh=|s me prodou=nai (= mh/, pro\s qew=n se ai)tw=) do not, I implore thee by the gods, have the heart to leave me!
E. Alc. 275, mh/ moi pro/fasin (scil. pa/rexe) no excuse!
Ar. Ach. 345. Cp. 946.

## FREE USES OF THE ACCUSATIVE

## ACCUSATIVE OF RESPECT

§1600
To verbs denoting a state, and to adjectives, an accusative may be added to denote a thing in respect to which the verb or adjective is limited.
a. The accusative usually expresses a local relation or the instrument. The word restricted by the accusative usually denotes like or similar to, good or better, bad or worse, a physical or a mental quality, or an emotion.

§1601
The accusative of respect is employed
a. Of the parts of the body:

o( a)/nqrwpos to\n da/ktulon a)lgei= the man has a pain in his finger
P. R. 462d,

tuflo\s ta/ t' w)=ta to/n te nou=n ta/ t' o)/mmat' ei)= blind art thou in ears, and mind, and eyes
S. O. T. 371, po/das w)ku\s *)axilleu/s Hom.
N.—The accusative of the part in apposition to the whole (985) belongs here, as is seen by the passive. Cp.

to\n plh=c' au)xe/na him he smote on the neck
*l 240 (ba/le qou=ron *)/arha kat' au)xe/na *f 406) with be/blhai kenew=na thou art smitten in the abdomen E 284.
b. Of qualities and attributes (nature, form, size, name, birth, number, etc.):

diafe/rei gunh\ a)ndro\s th\n fu/sin woman differs from man in nature
P. R. 453b,

ou)de\ e)/oiken qnhta\_s a)_qana/th|si de/mas kai\ ei)=dos e)ri/zein nor is it seemly that mortal women should rival the immortals in form and appearance
e 213, potamo/s, *ku/dnos o)/noma, eu)=ros du/o ple/qrwn a river, Cydnus by name, two plethra in width
X. A. 1.2.23 (so with u(/yos, ba/qos, me/geqos), plh=qos w(s disxi/_lioi about two thousand in number 4. 2. 2,

le/con o(/stis ei)= ge/nos tell me of what race thou art
E. Bacch. 460.
c. Of the sphere in general:

deinoi\ ma/xhn terrible in battle
A. Pers. 27,

ge/nesqe th\n dia/noian transfer yourselves in thought
Aes. 3.153,

to\ me\n e)p' e)moi\ oi)/xomai, to\ d' e)pi\ soi\ se/swsmai so far as I myself was concerned I was lost, but through you am saved
X. C. 5.4.11. Often of indefinite relations:

pa/nta kako/s base in all things
S. O. T. 1421,

tau=ta a)gaqo\s e(/kastos h(mw=n, a(/per sofo/s, a(\ de\ a)maqh/s, tau=ta de\ kako/s each one of us is good in matters in which he is skilled, but bad in those in which he is ignorant
P. Lach. 194d.

§1602
Very rarely after substantives: xei=ras ai)xmhth/s a warrior valiant with (thy) arm
p 242,

nea_ni/ai ta\_s o)/yeis youths by their appearance
L. 10.29.

§1603
For the acccusative of respect the instrumental dative (1516) is also employed, and also the prepositions ei)s, kata/, pro/s, e.g. diafe/rein a)reth=| or ei)s a)reth/n.

§1604
Not to be confused with the accusative of respect is the accusative after intransitive adjectives (1565) or after the passives of 1632.

§1605
The accusative of respect is probably in its origin, at least in part, an accusative of the internal object.

## ADVERBIAL ACCUSATIVE

§1606
Many accusatives marking limitations of the verbal action serve the same function as adverbs.

§1607
Most of these adverbial accusatives are accusatives of the internal object: thus, in te/los de\ ei)=pe but at last he said, te/los is to be regarded as standing in apposition to an unexpressed object of the verb—words, which were the end. Many adverbial accusatives are thus accusatives in apposition (991) and some are accusatives of respect (1600). It is impossible to apportion all cases among the varieties of the accusatives; many may be placed under different heads. The use of adjectives as adverbs (me/ga plou/sios very rich) is often derived from the cognate accusative with verbs (me/ga ploutei=n).

§1608

Manner.—tro/pon tina/ in some way, ti/na tro/pon in what way? to/nde (tou=ton) to\n tro/pon in this way, pa/nta tro/pon in every way (also panti\ tro/pw|), th\n taxi/sthn (o(do/n) in the quickest way, th\n eu)qei=an (o(do/n) straightforward, proi=ka, dwrea/_n gratis (1616), di/khn after the fashion of (

di/khn toco/tou like an archer
P. L. 705e), pro/fasin in pretence (

e)/plee pro/fasin e)p' *(ellhspo/ntou he sailed professedly for the Hellespont
Hdt. 5.33), xa/rin for the sake of (lit. favour）:

ou) th\n *)aqhnai/wn xa/rin e)strateu/onto did not engage in the expedition out of good will to the Athenians
Hdt. 5.99,

tou= xa/rin for what reason?
Ar. Plut. 53,

th\n sh\n h(/kw xa/rin for thy sake I have come
S. Ph. 1413. Cp. 993.

§1609

Measure and Degree.—me/ga, mega/la greatly, polu/, polla/ much, to\ polu/, ta\ polla/ for the most part, o(/son as much as, ou)de/n, mhde/n not at all, tosou=ton so much, ti\ somewhat, a)rxh/n or th\n a)rxh/n at all with ou) or mh/ (

e)n tw=| paraxrh=ma ou)k e)/stin a)rxh\n o)rqw=s bouleu/esqai it is utterly impossible to deliberate correctly offhand
Ant. 5.73).

§1610

Motive.—ti/ why? tou=to, tau=ta for this reason (cognate accus.): ti/ h)=lqes quid (cur) venisti = ti/na i(=cin h)=lqes; tou=to xai/rw ( = tau/thn th\n xara\_n xai/rw) therefore I rejoice,

au)ta\ tau=ta h(/kw for this very reason have I come
P. Pr. 310e,

tou=t' a)/xqesqe for this reason you are vexed
X. A. 3.2.20.

§1611

Time and Succession (1582): to\ nu=n now, to\ pa/lai of old, pro/teron before, to\ pro/teron the former time, prw=ton first, to\ kat' a)rxa/_s in the beginning, to\ prw=ton in the first place, to\ teleutai=on in the last place (for to\ deu/teron in a series use e)/peita or e)/peita de/), to\ loipo/n for the future, a)kmh/n at the point, just, kairo/n in season.

## TWO ACCUSATIVES WITH ONE VERB

§1612
A compound expression, consisting of the accusative of an abstract substantive and poiei=sqai, ti/qesqai, e)/xein, etc., is often treated as a simple verb; and, when transitive, governs the accusative: th\n xw/ra_n katadromai=s lei/a_n e)poiei=to ( = e)lh/|zeto) he ravaged the country by his incursions
T. 8.41, *)i_li/ou fqora\_s yh/fous e)/qento ( = e)yhfi/santo) they voted for the destruction of Ilium
A. Ag. 814, momfh\n e)/xw e(\n me\n prw=ta/ soi ( = e(\n me/mfomai) I blame thee first for one thing
E. Or. 1069, ta\ d' e)n me/sw| lh=stin i)/sxeis ( = e)pilanqa/nei) what lies between thou hast no memory of
S. O. C. 583. See 1598. So with other periphrases in poetry: te/kna mhku/_nw lo/gon ( = makro/teron prosfwnw=) I speak at length to my children
S. O. C. 1120, ei) de/ m' w(=d' a)ei\ lo/gous e)ch=rxes ( = h)/rxou le/gein) if thou didst always (begin to) address me thus
S. El. 556.

## EXTERNAL OBJECT AND PREDICATE ACCUSATIVE

§1613
Verbs meaning to appoint, call, choose, consider, make, name, show, and the like, may take a second accusative as a predicate to the direct object.

strathgo\n au)to\n a)pe/deice he appointed him general
X. A. 1.1.2, pate/ra e)me\ e)kalei=te you were wont to call me father 7. 6. 38,

ai(rei=sqai au)to\n to\n *)indw=n basile/a_ dikasth/n to choose the king of the Indians himself to be arbitrator
X. C. 2.4.8,

ou) ga\r di/kaion ou)/te tou\s kakou\s ma/thn xrhstou\s nomi/zein ou)/te tou\s xrhstou\s kakou/s for it is not just to consider bad men good at random, or good men bad
S. O. T. 609,

*ti_mo/qeon strathgo\n e)xeiroto/nhsan they elected Timotheus general
X. H. 6.2.11,

th\n si_gh/n sou cugxw/rhsin qh/sw I shall consider your silence as consent
P. Crat. 435b,

e(auto\n despo/thn pepoi/hken he has made himself master
X. C. 1.3.18,

e)a\_n e)me\ so\n qera/ponta poih/sh| if you make me your servant
X. O. 7.42,

ei)s tou\s *(/ellhnas sauto\n sofisth\n pare/xwn showing yourself a sophist before the Greeks
P. Pr. 312a,

eu)maqh= pa/nta pare/xein to render everything easy to learn
X. O. 20.14. Cp. 1579.

§1614
The absence of the article generally distinguishes the predicate noun from the object:

e)phgge/lleto tou\s ko/lakas tou\s au(tou= plousiwta/tous tw=n poli_tw=n poih/sein he promised to make his flatterers the richest of the citizens
L. 28.4.

§1615
Especially in Plato and Herodotus, after verbs signifying to name, to call, the predicate noun may be connected with the external object by (a redundant) ei)=nai (911);

sofisth\n o)noma/zousi to\n a)/ndra ei)=nai they call the man a sophist
P. Pr. 311e,

e)pwnumi/a_n e)/xei smi_kro/s te kai\ me/gas ei)=nai he is called both short and tall
P. Ph. 102c. This is due to the analogy of verbs signifying to think or say (1041).

§1616
A predicate accusative may stand in apposition to the object: e)/dwka dwreia\_n ta\ lu/tra I gave them the price of their ransom as a free gift
D. 19.170.

§1617
This use is the source of many adverbial accusatives (993, 1606 ff.).

§1618

Passive: both the object and the predicate accusative of the active construction become nominative (1743) in the passive construction: au)to\s stra-

thgo\s h(|re/qh he himself was chosen general
L. 12.65,

au)toi\ nomoqe/tai klhqh/sontai they shall themselves be called lawgivers
P. L. 681d.

## INTERNAL AND EXTERNAL OBJECT WITH ONE VERB

§1619
Many verbs take both an internal and an external object.

§1620
The external object refers to a person, the internal object (cognate accusative, 1563 ff.) refers to a thing. Here the internal object stands in closer relation to the verb.

o( po/lemos a)ei/mnhston paidei/a_n au)tou\s e)pai/deuse the war taught them a lesson they will hold in everlasting remembrance
Aes. 3.148,

tosou=ton e)/xqos e)xqai/rw se I hate thee with such an hate
S. El. 1034,

*me/lhto/s me e)gra/yato th\n grafh\n tau/thn Meletus brought this accusation against me
P. A. 19b, e(/lkos, to/ min ba/le the wound that he dealt him E 795 (1578),

*miltia/dhs o( th\n e)n *maraqw=ni ma/xhn tou\s barba/rous ni_kh/sa_s Miltiades who won the battle at Marathon over the barbarians
Aes. 3.181, to\n a)/ndra tu/ptein ta\_s plhga/_s to strike the man the blows Ant. 4.
g. 1,

kalou=si/ me tou=to to\ o)/noma they give me this appellation
X. O. 7.3.

§1621

Passive (1747):

pa=san qerapei/a_n qerapeuo/menos receiving every manner of service
P. Phae. 255a,

tu/ptesqai penth/konta plhga/_s to be struck fifty blows
Aes. 1.139, h( kri/sis, h(\n e)kri/qh the sentence that was pronounced upon him
L. 13.50,

ta\_s ma/xa_s, o(/sa_s *pe/rsai h(tth/qhsan e)w= I omit the battles in which the Persians were defeated
I. 4.145,

o)/noma e(\n keklhme/noi *sikeliw=tai called by the one name of Sicilians
T. 4.64.

§1622
So with verbs signifying to do anything to or say anything of a person (1591):

polla\ a)gaqa\ u(_ma=s e)poi/hsen he did you much good
L. 5.3,

tauti/_ me poiou=si that's what they are doing to me
Ar. Vesp. 696,

ta\ toiau=ta e)painw= *)a_ghsi/la_on I praise Agesilaus for such merits
X. Ages. 10.1, tou\s *korinqi/ous polla/ te kai<*> kaka\ e)/lege he said many bad things about the Corinthians
Hdt. 8.61. For the accusative of the thing, eu)= (kalw=s), kakw=s may be substituted; and ei)s and pro/s with the accusative occur.

§1623
The accusative of the person may depend on the idea expressed by the combination of verb and accusative of the thing (1612); as in

tou\s polemi/ous ei)rga/sqai kaka/ to have done harm to the enemy
L. 21.8 (here ei)rga/sqai of itself does not mean to do anything to a person).

§1624
When the dative of the person is used, something is done for (1474), not to him:

pa/nta e)poi/hsan toi=s a)poqanou=sin they rendered all honours to the dead
X. A. 4.2.23. ei)s or pro/s with the accusative is also employed.

§1625

Passive of 1622:

o(/sa a)/lla h( po/lis h)dikei=to all the other wrongs that the State has suffered
D. 18.70.

§1626

Verbs of dividing (ne/mein, katane/mein, diairei=n, te/mnein) may take two accusatives, one of the thing divided, the other of its parts (cognate accus.). Thus,

*ku=ros to\ stra/teuma kate/neime dw/deka me/rh Cyrus divided the army into twelve divisions
X. C. 7.5.13. ei)s or kata/ may be used with the accusative of the parts.

§1627

Passive:

dih/|rhtai h( a)gora\_ te/ttara me/rh the Agora is divided into four parts
X. C. 1.2.4. ei)s and kata/ may be used with the accusative of the parts.

## DOUBLE OBJECT WITH VERBS SIGNIFYING TO ASK, DEMAND, ETC.

§1628
Verbs signifying to ask, clothe or unclothe, conceal, demand, deprive, persuade, remind, teach, take two objects in the accusative, one of a person, the other of a thing.

ou) tou=t' e)rwtw= se that's not the question I'm asking you
Ar. Nub. 641;

xitw=na to\n e(autou= e)kei=non h)mfi/ese he put his own tunic on him
X. C. 1.3.17,

i)dou\ d' *)apo/llwn au)to\s e)kdu/_wn e)me\ xrhsthri/a_n e)sqh=ta lo Apollo himself divests me of my oracular garb
A. Ag. 1269;

th\n qugate/ra e)/krupte to\n qa/naton tou= a)ndro/s he concealed from his daughter her husband's death
L. 32.7;

*ku=ron ai)tei=n ploi=a to ask Cyrus for boats
X. A. 1.3.14,

w(s e)gw/ pote/ tina h)\ e)pra_ca/mhn misqo\n h)\ h)/|thsa that I ever exacted or asked pay of any one
P. A. 31c;

tou/twn th\n ti_mh\n a)posterei= me he deprives me of the value of these things
D. 28.13;

u(_ma=s tou=to ou) pei/qw I cannot persuade you of this
P. A. 37a;

a)namnh/sw u(_ma=s kai\ tou\s kindu/_nous I will remind you of the dangers also
X. A. 3.2.11;

ou)dei\s e)di/dace/ me tau/thn th\n te/xnhn nobody taught me this art
X. O. 19.16.

§1629
Both person and thing are equally governed by the verb. The accusative of the person is the external object; the accusative of the thing is sometimes a cognate accusative (internal accusative).

§1630
Some of these verbs also take the genitive or dative, or employ prepositions. Thus e)rwta=n tina peri/ tinos, ai)tei=n (ai)tei=sqai/) ti para/ tinos, a)posterei=n or a)fairei=sqai/ tina/ tinos (tino/s ti) (1394), or tini/ ti (1483); a)namimnh/|skein tina/ tinos (1356); paideu/ein tina/ tini or tina\ ei)s (or pro/s) with the accusative.

§1631
The poets employ this construction with verbs of cleansing (a form of depriving):

xro/a ni/zeto a(/lmhn he was washing the brine from his skin
z 224, ai(=ma ka/qhron *sarphdo/na cleanse the blood from Sarpedon II 667. And with other verbs (in tragedy), e.g. ti_mwrei=sqai avenge on, metelqei=n seek to avenge on, metie/nai execute judgment on, e)piskh/ptein charge.

§1632

Passive (1747):

u(po\ basile/ws pepra_gme/nos tou\s fo/rous having had the tribute demanded of him by the king
T. 8.5,

o(/soi i(/ppous a)peste/rhntai all who have been deprived of their horses
X. C. 6.1.12,

ou)k e)pei/qonto ta\ e)saggelqe/nta they would not credit the news
Hdt. 8.81,

mousikh\n paideuqei/s having been instructed in music
P. Menex. 236a (here mousikh=| is possible),

ou)de\n a)/llo dida/sketai a)/nqrwpos h)\ e)pisth/mhn man is taught nothing else except knowledge
P. Men. 87c.

§1633
The accusative of extent (1580) is freely used in the same sentence with other accusatives, as

u(perenegko/ntes to\n *leukadi/wn i)sqmo\n ta\_s nau=s having hauled the ships across the isthmus of Leucas
T. 3.81.
On the accusative of the whole and part, see 985; on the accusative subject of the infinitive, see 1972 ff.; on the accusative absolute, see 2076. See also under Anacoluthon.

## TWO VERBS WITH A COMMON OBJECT

§1634
The case of an object common to two verbs is generally that demanded by the nearer:

ou) dei= toi=s paidotri/bais e)gkalei=n ou)d' e)kba/llein e)k tw=n po/lewn we must not accuse the trainer or banish him from the cities
P. G. 460d.
a. The farther verb may contain the main idea:

e)piti_ma=| kai\ a)podokima/zei tisi/ he censures some and rejects them at the scrutiny
L. 6.33.

§1635
The construction is usually ruled by the participle, not by the finite verb, when they have a common object but different constructions, and especially when the object stands nearer the participle:

tou/tw| dou\s h(gemo/nas poreu/esqai e)ke/leusen h(su/xws having given him guides he ordered him to proceed quietly
X. C. 5.3.53; and when the common object stands between, as

prospeso/ntes toi=s prw/tois tre/pousi falling upon the foremost they put them to flight
T. 7.53.
a. Sometimes the finite verb regulates the construction, as

kale/sa_s parekeleu/eto toi=s *(/ellhsi he summoned the Greeks and exhorted them
X. A. 1.8.11.

## PREPOSITIONS

§1636
Prepositions define the relations of a substantival notion to the predicate.
a. All prepositions seem to have been adverbs originally and mostly adverbs of place; as adverbs they are case-forms. Several are locatives, as peri/.

§1637
The prepositions express primarily notions of space, then notions of time, and finally are used in figurative relations to denote cause, agency, means, manner, etc. Attic often differs from the Epic in using the prepositions to denote metaphorical relations. The prepositions define the character of the verbal action and set forth the relations of an oblique case to the predicate with greater precision than is possible for the cases without a preposition. Thus,

meta\ de\ mnhsth=rsin e)/eipe he spake among the suitors
r 467 specifies the meaning with greater certainty than mnhsth=rsin e)/eipe. So o( *(ellh/nwn fo/bos may mean the fear felt by the Greeks or the fear caused by the Greeks; but with e)c or para/ (cp.
X. A. 1.2.18, Lyc. 130) the latter meaning is stated unequivocally. The use of a preposition often serves to show how a construction with a composite case (1279) is to be regarded (genitive or ablative; dative, instrumental, or locative).

§1638

Development of the Use of Prepositions.—
a. Originally the preposition was a free adverb limiting the meaning of the verb but not directly connected with it: kat' a)/r' e(/zeto down he sate him A 101. In this use the preposition may be called a ‘preposition-adverb.’
b. The preposition-adverb was also often used in sentences in which an oblique case depended directly on the verb without regard to the prepositionadverb. Here the case is independent of the preposition-adverb, as in blefa/rwn a)/po da/krua pi/_ptei from her eyelids, away, tears fall
c 129. Here blefa/rwn is ablatival genitive and is not governed by a)po/, which serves merely to define the relation between verb and noun.
c. Gradually the preposition-adverb was brought into closer connection either (1) with the verb, whence arose compounds such as a)popi/_ptein, or (2) with the noun, the preposition-adverb having freed itself from its adverbial relation to the verb. In this stage, which is that of Attic prose, the noun was felt to depend on the preposition. Hence arose many syntactical changes, e.g. the accusative of the limit of motion (1588) was abandoned in prose for the preposition with the accusative.
Prepositions have three uses.

§1639
(I) Prepositions appear as adverbs defining the action of verbs.

§1640
The preposition-adverb usually precedes the verb, from which it is often separated in Homer by nouns and other words: h(mi=n a)po\ loigo\n a)mu=nai to ward off destruction from (for) us A 67, pro\ ga\r h(=ke qea/_ the goddess sent her forth A 195, e)/xen ka/ta gai=a the earth held him fast B 699.

§1641
So, as links connecting sentences, pro\s de\ kai/ and kai\ pro/s and besides, e)pi\ de/ and besides, meta\ de/ and next, thereupon (both in Hdt.), e)n de/ and among the number (Hdt.).

§1642
The verb (usually e)sti/ or ei)si/, rarely ei)mi/) may be omitted:

ou) ga/r tis me/ta toi=os a)nh/r for no such man is among them
f 93. Cp. 944.

§1643
The preposition-adverb may do duty for the verb in parallel clauses: a)/ndres a)ne/stan, a)\n me\n a)/r' *)atrei+/dhs . . . a)\n d' a)/ra *mhrio/nhs the men rose up, rose up Atreides, rose up Meriones
*y 886. So in Hdt.

§1644
(II) Prepositions connect verbs and other words with the oblique cases of nouns and pronouns.

§1645
It is often impossible to decide whether the preposition belongs to the verb or to the noun. Thus, e)k de\ *xru_shi\s nho\s bh= A 439 may be Chryseïs went out of the ship or Chryseïs went-out-from (e)ce/bh) the ship. When important words separate the prep.-adv. from the noun, the prep.-adv. is more properly regarded as belonging with the verb, which, together with the prep.-adv., governs the noun: a)mfi\ de\ xai=tai w)/mois a)_i+/ssontai and his mane floats-about his shoulders Z 509. The Mss. often vary: toi=sin e)gw\ meq' o(mi/_leon (or meqomi/_leon) with these I was wont to associate A 269.

§1646
(III) Prepositions unite with verbs (less frequently with nouns and other prepositions) to form compounds. Cp. 886 ff.
a. From this use as a prefix the name ‘preposition’ (pro/qesis praepositio) is derived. The original meaning of some prepositions is best seen in compounds.

§1647

Improper prepositions (1699) are adverbs used like prepositions, but incapable of forming compounds. The case (usually the genitive) following an improper preposition depends on the preposition alone without regard to the verb; whereas a true preposition was attached originally, as an adverb, to a case depending directly on the verb.

§1648
The addition of a preposition (especially dia/, kata/, su/n) to a verbal form may mark the completion of the action of the verbal idea (perfective action). The local force of the preposition is here often lost. So diafeu/gein succeed in escaping, katadiw/kein succeed in pursuing, suntelei=n accomplish, carry into effect (telei=n do, perform).

§1649
Two or more prepositions may be used with one verb, either sepa rately, as adverbs, or in composition with the verb. Thus, sth= de\ pare/c (or par' e)c) he stood forth beside him
*l 486. When two prepositions of like meaning are used in composition, that preposition precedes which has the narrower range: summete/xein take part in with, a)mfiperiste/fesqai to be put round about as a crown. When two prepositions are used with one noun, the noun usually depends on the second, while the first defines the second adverbially; as a)mfi\ peri\ krh/nhn round about a spring B 305. It is often uncertain whether or not two prepositions should be written together.
a. Such compound prepositions are a)mfiperi/, pare/c, u(pe/k, a)pe/k, die/k, a)popro/, diapro/, peripro/. Improper prepositions may be used with true prepositions, as me/xri ei)s to\ strato/pedon as far as (into) the camp
X. A. 6.4.26.

§1650

Tmesis (tmh=sis cutting) denotes the separation of a preposition from its verb, and is a term of late origin, properly descriptive only of the post-epic language, in which preposition and verb normally formed an indissoluble compound. The term ‘tmesis’ is incorrectly applied to the language of Homer, since in the Epic the prep.-adv. was still in process of joining with the verb.

§1651
In Attic poetry tmesis occurs chiefly when the preposition is separated from the verb by unimportant words (particles, enclitics), and is employed for the sake of emphasis or (in Euripides) as a mere ornament. Aristophanes uses tmesis only to parody the style of tragic choruses.

§1652
Hdt. uses tmesis frequently in imitation of the Epic; the intervening words are w)=n ( = ou)=n), enclitics, de/, me\n . . . de/, etc.

§1653
In Attic prose tmesis occurs only in special cases: a)nt' eu)= poiei=n (pa/sxein) and su\n eu)= (kakw=s) poiei=n (pa/sxein). Thus,

o(/sous eu)= poih/santas h( po/lis a)nt' eu)= pepoi/hken all whom the city has requited with benefits for the service they rendered it
D. 20.64. Here eu)= pepoi/hken is almost equivalent to a single notion.

§1654
The addition of a preposition to a verb may have no effect on the construction, as in e)kbh=nai th=s new/s, whereas bh=nai th=s new/s originally, and still in poetry, can mean go from-the-ship; or it may determine the construction, as in

perigene/sqai e)mou= to surpass me
D. 18.236. Prose tends to repeat the prefixed preposition: e)kbh=nai e)k th=s new/s
T. 1.137.

§1655
A preposition usually assumes the force of an adjective when compounded with substantives which do not change their forms on entering into composition, as su/nodos a national meeting (o(do/s). Otherwise the compound usually gets a new termination, generally -on, -ion neuter, or -i/s feminine, as e)nu/pnion dream (u(/pnos), e)pigouni/s thigh-muscle (go/nu).

§1656
The use of prepositions is, in general, more common in prose than in poetry, which retained the more primitive form of expression.

§1657
A noun joined by a preposition to its case without the help of a verb has a verbal meaning:

a)po\ pa_sw=n a)rxw=n e)leuqeri/a_ freedom from all rule
P. L. 698a (cp. e)leuqerou=n a)po/ tinos).

§1658
In general, when depending on prepositions expressing relations of place, the accusative denotes the place (or person) toward which or the place over which, along which motion takes place, the dative denotes rest in or at, the genitive (ablative) passing from. Thus,

h(/kw para\ se/ I have come to you
T. 1.137,

oi( par' e(autw=| ba/rbaroi the barbarians in his own service
X. A. 1.1.5, para\ basile/ws polloi\ pro\s *ku=ron a)ph=lqon many came over from the king to Cyrus 1. 9. 29. The true genitive denotes various forms of connection.

§1659

Constructio Praegnans.—a. A verb of motion is often used with a preposition with the dative to anticipate the rest that follows the action of the verb: e)n tw=| potamw=| e)/peson they fell (into and were) in the river
X. Ages. 1.32. This use is common with tiqe/nai, i(dru/_ein, kaqista/nai, etc., and with tenses of completed action which imply rest; as oi( e)n th=| nh/sw| a)/ndres diabebhko/tes the men who had crossed to (and were in) the island
T. 7.71.
b. A verb of rest is often followed by a preposition with the accusative to denote motion previous to or following upon the action of the verb: parh=san ei)s *sa/rdeis (they came to Sardis and were in the city) they arrived at Sardis
X. A. 1.2.2,

e)s *ku_^rh/nhn e)sw/qhsan they were saved by reaching Cyrene
T. 1.110, h(|re/qh presbeuth\s ei)s *lakedai/mona he was chosen ambassador (to go) to Lacedaemon
X. H. 2.2.17. Cp. 1692. 1. a.

§1660
Stress is often laid on (a) the starting-point or (b) the goal of an action.
a. katadh/sa_s a)po\ de/ndrwn tou\s i(/ppous tying his horses to (from) trees
X. H. 4.4.10. By anticipation of the verbal action (attraction of the prep. with the article):

th\n a)po\ stratope/dou ta/cin e)/lipen he deserted his post in the army
Aes. 3.159, oi( e)k th=s a)gora=s katalipo/ntes ta\ w)/nia e)/fugon the market-people (oi( e)n th=| a)gora=|) left their wares and fled
X. A. 1.2.18.
b. With verbs of collecting (a)qroi/zein, sulle/gein) and enrolling (e)ggra/fein): ei)s pedi/on a)qroi/zontai they are mustered in（to) the plain
X. A. 1.1.2, ei)s a)/ndras e)ggra/yai to enrol in（to) the list of men
D. 19.230.

§1661
So with adverbs: o(/pon e)lhlu/qamen where ( = whither, o(/poi) we have gone
X. C. 6.1.14, o(/qen a)peli/pomen, e)pane/lqwmen let us return to the point whence ( = where, o(/pou) we left off
P. Ph. 78b, a)gnoei= to\n e)kei=qen po/lemon deu=ro h(/conta he does not know that the war in that region will come hither ( = to\n e)kei= po/lemon e)kei=qen)
D. 1.15.

§1662
Some adverbs and adverbial phrases meaning from are used with reference to the point of view of the observer: e(kate/rwqen on either side, e)/nqen kai\ e)/nqen on this side and that, e)k decia=s on the right (a dextra), oi( a)po\ th=s skhnh=s the actors, to\ e)k tou= i)sqmou= tei=xos, to\ e)s th\n *pallh/nhn tei=xos the wall (seen) from the isthmus, the wall toward (looking to) Pallene
T. 1.64 (of the same wall).

§1663

Position.—The preposition usually precedes its noun. It may be separated from it
a. By particles (me/n, de/, ge/, te/, ga/r, ou)=n) and by oi)=mai I think: e)n ou)=n th=| po/lei
P. R. 456d, ei)s de/ ge oi)=mai ta\_s a)/lla_s po/leis to the other cities I think 568 c.
Note that the order th\n me\n xw/ra_n (1155) usually becomes, e.g. pro\s me\n th\n xw/ra_n or pro\s th\n xw/ra_n me/n. Demonstrative o( me/n and o( de/, when dependent on a preposition, regularly follow the preposition, and usually with order reversed (1109): e)n me\n a)/ra toi=s sumfwnou=men, e)n de\ toi=s ou)/ in some things then we agree, but not in others
P. Phae. 263b.
b. By attributives:

ei)s *kau+/strou pedi/on to the plain of the Cayster
X. A. 1.2.11.
c. By the accusative in oaths and entreaties (with pro/s): pro/s se th=sde mhtro/s by my mother here I implore thee
E. Phoen. 1665; cp. per te deos oro and see 1599.
N.—A preposition is usually placed before a superlative and after w(s or o(/ti qualifying the superlative:

w(s e)pi\ plei=ston tou= o(mi/_lou over the very greatest part of the throng
T. 2.34. polu/, pa/nu, ma/la may precede the preposition and its case:

polu\ e)n plei/oni ai)ti/a| with far better reason
T. 1.35.

§1664
In poetry a preposition is often placed between an adjective and its substantive; very rarely in prose (

toia=|de e)n ta/cei in the following manner
P. Criti. 115c).

§1665

peri/ is the only true preposition that may be placed after its case in Attic prose:

sofi/a_s pe/ri about wisdom
P. Phil. 49a,

w(=n e)gw\ ou)de\n ou)/te me/ga ou)/te mi_kro\n pe/ri e)pai+/w about which I understand nothing either much or little
P. A. 19c. When used with two substantives pe/ri is placed between them:

tou= o(si/ou te pe/ri kai\ tou= a)nosi/ou concerning both that which is holy and that which is unholy
P. Euth. 4e. pe/ri occurs very often in Plato, only once in the orators and possibly twice in Xenophon. On anastrophe, see 175.
a. e(/neka and xa/rin (usually) and a)/neu (sometimes) are postpositive. The retention of the postpositive use of peri/ may be due to the influence of e(/neka. In poetry many prepositions are postpositive.

## VARIATION OF PREPOSITIONS

§1666
The preposition in the second of two closely connected clauses may be different from that used in the first clause either (1) when the relation is essentially the same or (2) when it is different. Thus (1)

e)/k te th=s *kerku/_ra_s kai\ a)po\ th=s h)pei/rou from Corcyra and the mainland
T. 7.33, and (2) ou)/te kata\ gh=n ou)/te dia\ qala/sshs neither by land nor by (the help of the, the medium of the) sea 1. 2. Cp. 1668.

## REPETITION AND OMISSION OF PREPOSITIONS, ETC.

§1667

a. For the sake of emphasis or to mark opposition and difference, a preposition is repeated with each noun dependent on the preposition:

kata/ te po/lemon kai\ kata\ th\n a)/llhn di/aitan in the pursuit of war and in the other occupations of life
P. Tim. 18c.
b. A preposition is used with the first noun and omitted with the second when the two nouns (whether similar or dissimilar in meaning) unite to form a complex: peri\ tou= dikai/ou kai\ a)reth=s ‘concerning the justice of our cause and the honesty of our intentions’
T. 3.10.
c. In poetry a preposition may be used only with the second of two nouns dependent on it:

*delfw=n ka)_po\ *dauli/a_s from Delphi and Daulia
S. O. T. 734.

§1668
In contrasts or alternatives expressed by h)/, h)\ . . . h)/, kai\ . . . kai/, etc., the preposition may be repeated or omitted with the second noun:

kai\ kata\ gh=n kai\ kata\ qa/lattan both by land and by sea
X. A. 1.1.7,

pro\s e)xqro\n h)\ fi/lon to foe or friend
D. 21.114.

§1669
When prepositions of different meaning are used with the same noun, the noun is repeated; thus neither upon (the earth) nor under the earth is ou)/t' e)pi\ gh=s ou)/q' u(po\ gh=s
P. Menex. 246d.

§1670
In explanatory appositional clauses (988) the preposition may be repeated for the sake of clearness or emphasis; as

e)k tou/twn oi( o)nomastoi\ gi/gnontai, e)k tw=n e)pithdeusa/ntwn e(/kasta the men of mark come from those who have practised each art
P. Lach. 183c, and commonly after demonstratives. The preposition is not repeated when such an appositional clause is closely connected with what precedes: ei)ko\s mhde\ nomi/sai peri\ e(no\s mo/nou, doulei/a_s a)nt' e)leuqeri/a_s, a)gwni/zesqai nor should you think that you are contending for a single issue alone: to avert slavery instead of maintaining your freedom
T. 2.63. A preposition is usually not repeated before descriptive appositional clauses (987): peri\ xrhma/twn lalei=s, a)bebai/ou pra/_gmatos you are talking about wealth, an unstable thing Com. frag. 3. 38 (No. 128).

§1671
Before a relative in the same case as a noun or pronoun dependent on a preposition, the preposition is usually omitted:

kata\ tau/thn th\n h(liki/a_n h)=n h(\n e)gw\ nu=n he was at that age at which I now am
D. 21.155, filei=tai u(po\ w(=n ( = tou/twn w(=n)

filei=tai is loved by whom it is loved
P. Euth. 10c. But the preposition is repeated if the relative precedes:

pro\s o(/ tis pe/fu_ke, pro\s tou=to e(/na pro\s e(\n e(/kaston e)/rgon dei= komi/zein it is necessary to set each individual to some one work to which he is adapted by nature
P. R. 423d.

§1672
In Plato a preposition is often omitted in replies: h(ttw/menos—u(po\ ti/nos; fh/sei. tou= a)gaqou=, fh/somen overcome—by what? he will say. By the good, we shall say Pr. 355 c.

§1673
The preposition is usually omitted with the main noun or pronoun when it is used in a clause of comparison with w(s (rarely w(/sper) as:

dei= w(s peri\ mhtro\s kai\ trofou= th=s xw/ra_s bouleu/esqai they ought to take thought for their country as their mother and nurse
P. R. 414e; so, usually, when the two members are closely united:

w(s pro\s ei)do/t' e)me\ su\ ta)_lhqh= le/ge speak the truth to me as to one who knows
Ar. Lys. 993. The preposition is often omitted in the clause with w(s (w(/sper) as, h)/ than:

oi(\ par' ou)de\n ou(/tws w(s to\ toiau=ta poiei=n a)polw/la_sin who owe their ruin to nothing so much as to such a course of action
D. 19.263,

peri\ tou= me/llontos ma=llon bouleu/esqai h)\ tou= paro/ntos to deliberate about the future rather than the present
T. 3.44.

§1674
A preposition with its case may have the function of the subject, or the object, of a sentence; or it may represent the protasis of a condition.
Subject:

e)/fugon peri\ o)ktakosi/ous about eight hundred took to flight
X. H. 6.5.10; (gen. absol.) suneilegme/nwn peri\ e(ptakosi/ous, labw\n au)tou\s katabai/nei when about seven hundred had been collected he marched down with them 2. 4. 5. Object:

die/fqeiran e)s o)ktakosi/ous they killed about eight hundred
T. 7.32. Protasis:

e)pei\ dia/ g' u(_ma=s au)tou\s pa/lai a)\n a)pwlw/leite for had it depended on your selves you would have perished long ago
D. 18.49 (cp. 2344).

## ORDINARY USES OF THE PREPOSITIONS

§1675

Use of the Prepositions in Attic Prose.—
With the accusative only: a)na/, ei)s.
With the dative only: e)n, su/n.
With the genitive only: a)nti/, a)po/, e)c, pro/.
With the accusative and genitive: a)mfi/, dia/, kata/, meta/, u(pe/r.
With accusative, genitive, and dative: e)pi/, para/, peri/, pro/s, u(po/.
a. With the dative are also used in poetry: a)na/, a)mfi/ (also in Hdt.), meta/. a)po/ (a)pu/), e)c (e)s) take the dative in Arcadian and Cyprian.
b. The genitive is either the genitive proper (of the goal, 1349, 1350, etc.) or the ablatival genitive.
c. The dative is usually the locative or the instrumental, rarely the dative proper (as with e)pi/ and pro/s of the goal).

§1676

Ordinary Differences in Meaning.—

GENITIVEACCUSATIVE

a)mfi/, peri/concerninground about, near

dia/throughowing to

kata/againstalong, over, according to

meta/withafter

u(pe/rabove, in behalf ofover, beyond

GENITIVEDATIVEACCUSATIVE

e)pi/ononto, toward, for

para/fromwith, nearto, contrary to

pro/son the side ofat, besidesto, toward

u(po/by, underunderunder

§1677
Certain prepositions are parallel in many uses; e.g. a)na/ and kata/, a)nti/ and pro/, a)po/ and e)k, a)mfi/ and peri/, u(pe/r and peri/, e)pi/ and pro/s, su/n and meta/.

§1678
The agent is expressed by different prepositions with the genitive:
u(po/ of persons and things personified (1698. 1. N. 1): the normal usage in Attic prose.
para/: here the agent is viewed as the source. The action is viewed as starting near a person, or on the part of a person.
dia/ through: the intermediate agent.
a)po/: indirect agent and source (rare) to mark the point of departure of the action. Chiefly in Thuc.
e)c: chiefly in poetry and Hdt. In Attic prose of emanation from a source.
pro/s: to mark the result as due to the presence (before) of a person; chiefly in poetry and Hdt.

§1679

Means is expressed by dia/ with the genitive (the normal usage in Attic prose), a)po/, e)c, e)n, su/n. Motive is expressed by u(po/ (gen.), dia/ (accus.), e(/neka.

§1680
Prepositions in composition (chiefly a)po/, dia/, kata/, su/n) may give an idea of completion to the action denoted by the verb (1648).
a. For the usage after compound verbs see 1382 ff., 1545 ff., 1559.

## LIST OF PREPOSITIONS

## a)mfi/

§1681

a)mfi/ (cp. a)/mfw, a)mfo/teros, Lat. ambi-, amb-, am-) originally on both sides (either externally only, or inside and outside), hence about. Cp. the use of peri/ (1693) throughout. Chiefly poetic, Ionic, and Xenophontic. In Attic prose chiefly with the accusative.

## 1. a)mfi/ with the Genitive

Local (very rare and doubtful):

oi( a)mfi\ tau/ths oi)ke/ontes th=s po/lios dwellers round about this city
Hdt. 8.104 (only here). Cause: about, concerning:

a)mfi\ sh=s le/gw paido/s I speak about thy child
E. Hec. 580,

a)mfi\ w(=n ei)=xon diafero/menoi quarrelling about what they had
X. A. 4.5.17.

## 2. a)mfi/ with the Dative

Local:

a)mf' w)/moisin e)/xei sa/kos he has a shield about his shoulders
*l 527. Cause:

fobhqei\s a)mfi\ th=| gunaiki/ afraid on account of his wife
Hdt. 6.62, a)mfi\ fo/bw| by reason of (encompassed by) terror
E. Or. 825; Means: a)mfi\ sofi/a| ‘with the environment of poetic art’ Pind. P. 1. 12. Often in Pindar.

## 3. a)mfi/ with the Accusative

Local:

a)mfi\ *mi/_lhton about Miletus
X. A. 1.2.3,

e)/dramon a)mf' *)axilh=a they ran around Achilles
*s 30; temporal:

a)mfi\ dei/lhn towards evening
X. A. 2.2.14. Number: a)mfi\ tou/s disxi_li/ous about two thousand 1. 2. 9; of occupation with an object:

a)mfi\ dei=pnon ei)=xen he was busy about dinner
X. C. 5.5.44.
a. oi( a)mfi/ tina the attendants, followers of a person, or the person himself with his attendants, etc.:

a)nh\r tw=n a)mfi\ *ku=ron pistw=n one of the trusty adherents of Cyrus
X. A. 1.8.1, oi( a)mfi\ *xeiri/sofon Chirisophus and his men 4. 3. 21,

oi( a)mfi\ *prwtago/ra_n the school of Protagoras
P. Th. 170c. This last phrase contains the only use of a)mfi/ in Attic prose outside of Xenophon.

## 4. a)mfi/ in Composition

Around, about' a)mfiba/llein throw around (on both sides), a)mfile/gein dispute (speak on both sides).

## a)na/

§1682

a)na/ (Lesb. o)n, Lat. an- in anhelare, Eng. on): originally up to, up (opposed to kata/). Cp. a)/nw.

## 1. a)na/ with the Dative

Local only (Epic, Lyric, and in tragic choruses): a)na\ skh/ptrw| upon a staff A 15.

## 2. a)na/ with the Accusative

Up along; over, through, among (of horizontal motion). Usually avoided by Attic prose writers except Xenophon (three times in the orators).
a. Local: To a higher point:

a)na\ to\n potamo/n up stream
Hdt. 1.194 (cp. kata\ to\n potamo/n). Extension: a)na\ strato/n through the camp A 10, a)na\ pa=san th\n gh=n over the whole earth X. Ag. 11. 16, basilh=as a)na\ sto/m' e)/xwn having kings in thy mouth B 250 (cp. dia\ sto/matos e)/xein).
b. Extension in Time:

a)na\ nu/kta through the night
*c 80. See c.
c. Other relations: Distributively:

a)na\ e(kato\n a)/ndras by hundreds
X. A. 3.4.21,

a)na\ pa=san h(me/ra_n daily
X. C. 1.2.8. Manner: a)na\ kra/tos with all their might (up to their strength)
X. A. 1.10.15 (better Attic kata\ kra/tos),

a)na\ lo/gon proportionately
P. Ph. 110d.

## 3. a)na/ in Composition

Up (a)ni/stasqai stand up, a)nastre/fein turn upside down), back (a)naxwrei=n go back, a)namimnh/|skein remind), again (a)napnei=n breathe again, a)napeira=sqai practise constantly), often with a reversing force force (a)nalu/_ein unlcose).

## a)nti/

§1683

a)nti/: originally in the face of, opposite to; cp. a)/nta, e)nanti/os, Lat. ante (with meaning influenced by post), Germ. Antwort, ‘reply.’

## 1. a)nti/ with the Genitive only

Local: a)nq' w(=n e(sthko/tes standing opposite to (from the point of view of the speaker, i.e. behind) which (pine-trees)
X. A. 4.7.6. In other meanings: Instead of, for, as an equivalent to:

a)nti\ pole/mou ei)rh/nh peace instead of war
T. 4.20,

ta\ par' e)moi\ e(le/sqai a)nti\ tw=n oi)/koi to prefer what I have to offer you here instead of what you have left at home
X. A. 1.7.4,

th\n teleuth\n a)nti\ th=s tw=n zw/ntwn swthri/a_s h)lla/canto they exchanged death for the safety of the living
P. Menex. 237a; in return for, hence

a)nq' o(/tou wherefore
S. El. 585; for pro/s in entreaty:

s' a)nti\ pai/dwn tw=nde i(keteu/omen we entreat thee by these children here
S. O. C. 1326.

## 2. a)nti/ in Composition

Instead, in return (a)ntidido/nai give in return), against, in opposition to (a)ntile/gein speak against).

## a)po/

§1684

a)po/ (Lesb. etc. a)pu/) from, off, away from; originally of separation and departure. Cp. Lat. ab, Eng. off, of.

## 1. a)po/ with the Genitive only

a. Local:

kataphdh/sa_s a)po\ tou= i(/ppou leaping down from his horse
X. A. 1.8.28, e)qh/reuen a)po\ i(/ppou he used to hunt (from a horse) on horseback 1. 2. 7,

a)po\ qala/sshs at a distance from the sea
T. 1.7. Figuratively:

a)po\ qew=n a)rxo/menoi beginning with the gods
X. A. 6.3.18.
b. Temporal: a)f' e(spe/ra_s after evening began (after sundown)
X. A. 6.3.23, a)po\ tou= au)tou= shmei/ou on the same signal 2. 5. 32, a)po\ tw=n si/_twn after meals X. R.
L. 5.8, a)f' ou(= since.
c. Other relations: (1) Origin, Source: in prose of more remote ancestry: tou\s me\n a)po\ qew=n, tou\s d' e)c au)tw=n tw=n qew=n gegono/tas some descended (remotely) from gods, others begotten (directly) of the gods themselves
I. 12.81. (This distinction is not always observed.) Various other relations may be explained as source.
(2) Author: as agent with passives and intransitives, when an action is done indirectly, through the influence of the agent (u(po/ of the direct action of the agent himself). Not common, except in Thuc. (chiefly with pra)_ttesqai, le/gesqai, and verbs of like meaning):

e)pra/_xqh a)p' au)tw=n ou)de\n e)/rgon nothing was done under their rule
T. 1.17. The startingpoint of an action is often emphasized rather than the agent:

a)po\ pollw=n kai\ pro\s pollou\s lo/goi gigno/menoi speeches made by many and to many
T. 8.93.
(3) Cause (remote):

a)po\ tou/tou tou= tolmh/matos e)ph|ne/qh he was praised in consequence of this bold deed
T. 2.25,

tau=ta ou)k a)po\ tu/xhs e)gi/gneto, a)ll' a)po\ paraskeuh=s th=s e)mh=s this happened not from chance but by reason of the preparations I made
L. 21.10.
(4) Means, Instrument:

stra/teuma sune/lecen a)po\ xrhma/twn he raised an army by means of money
X. A. 1.1.9; rarely of persons:

a)p' au)tw=n bla/yai to do injury by means of them
T. 7.29.
(5) Manner:

a)po\ tou= profanou=s openly
T. 1.66.
(6) Conformity:

a)po\ tou= i)/sou on a basis of equality
T. 3.10, a)po\ cummaxi/a_s au)to/nomoi independent by virtue of (according to) an alliance 7. 57.
N.—a)po/ with gen. is sometimes preferred to the simple gen., often for emphasis:

oi( lo/goi a)f' u(_mw=n the words that proceed from you
T. 6.40, o)li/goi a)po\ pollw=n a few of the many 1. 110 (cp. 1317 a). Thuc. has many free uses of a)po/.

## 2. a)po/ in Composition

From, away, off (a)pie/nai go away, a)poteixi/zein wall off), in return, back (a)podido/nai give back what is due, a)paitei=n demand what is one's right). Separation involves completion (hence a)pana_li/skein utterly consume, a)poqu/_ein pay off a vow), or privation and negation (a)pagoreu/ein forbid, a)potugxa/nein miss). Often almost equivalent to an intensive (a)pofa/nai speak out, a)podeiknu/nai point out, a)potolma=n dare without reserve).

## dia/

§1685

dia/ (Lesb. za/) through, originally through and out of, and apart (separation by cleavage), a force seen in comp. (cp. Lat. dis-, Germ. zwi-schen).

## 1. dia/ with the Genitive

a. Local: through and out of (cp. Hom. die/k, diapro/), as

di' w)/mou e)/gxos h)=lqen the spear went clear through his shoulder
*d 481, a)kou=sai dia\ te/lous to listen from beginning to end Lyc. 16. Through, but not out of: dia\ polemi/a_s (gh=s)

poreu/esqai to march through the enemy's country
X. Hi. 2.8 and often in figurative expressions:

dia\ xeiro\s e)/xein to control
T. 2.13, dia\ sto/matos e)/xein to have in one's mouth (be always talking of)
X. C. 1.4.25 (also a)na\ sto/ma).
b. Temporal: of uninterrupted duration, as

dia\ nukto/s through the night
X. A. 4.6.22,

dia\ panto/s constantly
T. 2.49.
c. Intervals of Space or Time:

dia\ de/ka e)pa/lcewn at intervals of ten battlements
T. 3.21,

dia\ xro/nou after an interval
L. 1.12, intermittently
Aes. 3.220,

dia\ pollou= at a long distance
T. 3.94.
d. Other relations: Means, Mediation (per):

au)to\s di' e(autou= ipse per se
D. 48.15,

dia\ tou/tou gra/mmata pe/mya_s sending a letter by this man
Aes. 3.162. State or feeling: with ei)=nai, gi/gnesqai, e)/xein, of a property or quality:

dia\ fo/bou ei)si/ they are afraid
T. 6.34, di' h(suxi/a_s ei)=xen he kept in quiet 2. 22, e)lqei=n h(mi=n dia\ ma/xhs to meet us in battle 2. 11,

au)toi=s dia\ fili/a_s i)e/nai to enter into friendship with them
X. A. 3.2.8. Manner:

dia\ taxe/wn quickly
T. 4.8.

## 2. dia/ with the Accusative

a. Local: of space traversed, through, over (Epic, Lyric, tragic choruses): dia\ dw/mata through the halls A 600; dia\ nu/kta *q 510 is quasi-temporal.
b. Cause: owing to, thanks to, on account of, in consequence of (cp. propter, ob):

dia\ tou\s qeou\s e)sw|zo/mhn I was saved thanks to the gods
D. 18.249, ti_mw/menos mh\ di' e(auto/n, a\lla\ dia\ do/can progo/nwn honoured, not for himself, but on account of the renown of his ancestors
P. Menex. 247b. So in ei) mh\ dia/ tina (ti) had it not been for in statements of an (unsurmounted) obstacle:

fai/nontai krath/santes a)\n tw=n basile/ws pra_gma/twn, ei) mh\ dia\ *ku=ron it seems they would have got the better of the power of the king, had it not been for Cyrus
I. 5.92.
c. dia/ is rarely used (in place of e(/neka) to denote a purpose or object:

dia\ th\n sfete/ra_n do/can for the sake of their honour
T. 2.89,

di' e)ph/reian for spite
D. 39.32 (cp.

dia\ no/son e(/neka u(giei/a_s on account of disease in order to gain health
P. Lys. 218e).
d. dia/ with gen. is used of direct, dia/ with accus. of indirect, agency (fault, merit, of a person, thing, or situation). dia/ with gen. is used of an agent employed to bring about an intended result; dia/ with accus. is used of a person, thing, or state beyond our control (accidental agency). (1) Persons:

e)/pra_can tau=ta di' *eu)ruma/xou they effected this by the mediation of Eurymachus
T. 2.2, ta\ dia\ tou/tous a)polwlo/ta what has been lost by (the fault of) these men
D. 6.34. The accus. marks a person as an agent not as an instrument. (2) Things: no/moi, di' w(=n e)leuqe/rios o( bi/os paraskeuasqh/setai laws, by means of which a life of freedom will be provided
X. C. 3.3.52, dia\ tou\s no/mous belti/_ous gigno/menoi a)/nqrwpoi men become better thanks to the laws 8. 1. 22. Sometimes there is little difference between the two cases: di' w(=n a(/pant' a)pw/leto
D. 18.33, di' ou(\s a(/pant' a)pw/leto 18. 35.
N.—dia/ with gen. ( = through) is distinguished from the simple dative ( = by): di' ou(= o(rw=men kai\ w(=| a)kou/omen
P. Th. 184c.
e. For dia/ with accus. to express the reason for an action, the dative is sometimes used (1517):

toi=s pepra_gme/nois fobou/menos tou\s *)aqhnai/ous fearing the Athenians by reason of what had happened
T. 3.98. The dative specifies the reason less definitely than dia/ with the accusative.
f. When used in the same sentence, the dative may express the immediate, dia/ with the accus. the remoter, cause:

a)sqenei/a| swma/twn dia\ th\n si_todei/a_n u(pexw/roun they gave ground from the fact that they were weak through lack of food
T. 4.36.
g. dia/ with accus. contrasted with u(po/ with gen.: fh/somen au)to\ di' e)kei=na u(po\ th=s au(tou= kaki/a_s a)polwle/nai we shall say that it (the body) is destroyed on account of those (remoter) causes (as badness of food) by its own evil (immediately)
P. R. 609e.

## 3. dia/ in Composition

Through, across, over (diabai/nein cross), apart, asunder (diako/ptein cut in two, diakri/_nein discernere, diafe/rein differ, diazugnu/nai disjoin), severally (diadido/nai distribute).
dia- often denotes intensity, continuance, or fulfilment (diame/nein remain to the end, diafqei/rein destroy completely). dia- is common in the reciprocal middle (1726), as in diale/gesqai converse; often of rivalry (oi( diapoli_teuo/menoi rival statesmen, diakonti/zesqai contend in throwing the javelin).

## ei)s, e)s

§1686

ei)s, e)s into, to, opposed to e)c; from e)n + s (cp. Lat. abs from ab + s). See on e)n. On ei)s with the genitive by ellipsis, see 1302.

## 1. ei)s with the Accusative only

In the Old Attic alphabet (2 a), generally used in Attica in the fifth century, *e*s was written, and this may be either ei)s or e)s. In the fourth century *e*i*s was generally written. In Thuc. e)s is printed, but its correctness may be doubted; other Attic prose writers use ei)s, the poets ei)s or (less frequently) e)s. It is not true that in poetry e)s is used only before consonants, ei)s only before vowels.
a. Local: of the goal:

*sikeloi\ e)c *)itali/a_s die/bhsan e)s *sikeli/a_n the Sicels crossed over out of Italy into Sicily
T. 6.2; with a personal object: h)=lqen e)k th=s *)asi/a_s e)s a)nqrw/pous a)po/rous he came from Asia to (a land of) poor men
T. 1.9, e)spe/mpei gra/mmata e)s (v. l. pro\s) basile/a_ he dispatches a letter to (the palace of) the king 1. 137 (of sending, etc., to individuals w(s or pro/s is used); against:

e)stra/teusan e)s th\n *)attikh/n they invaded Attica
T. 3.1, po/lemos toi=s *korinqi/ois e)s tou\s *)aqhnai/ous war between the Corinthians and the Athenians 1. 55; with verbs of rest, 1659 b. The idea of motion holds where Eng. uses in or at:

teleuta=n ei)/s ti to end in
T. 2.51. Extension:

*peloponnhsi/ous diabalei=n e)s tou\s *(/ellhnas to raise a prejudice against the Peloponnesians among the Greeks
T. 3.109; in the presence of (coram): e)s to\ koino\n le/gein to speak before the assembly 4. 58.
b. Temporal: of the goal: up to, until:

ei)s to\n loipo\n xro/non in all future time
L. 16.2.
c. Measure and Limit with numerals: ei)s xi_li/ous to the number of (up to) a thousand
X. A. 1.8.5, ei)s du/o two abreast 2. 4. 26,

e)s draxmh/n to the amount of a drachma
T. 8.29.
d. Other relations: Goal, Purpose, Intention:

h( sh\ patri\s ei)s se\ a)poble/pei your country looks for help to you
X. H. 6.1.8,

xrh=sqai ei)s ta\_s sfendo/na_s to use for the slings
X. A. 3.4.17,

paideu/ein ei)s a)reth/n to train with a view to virtue
P. G. 519e. Relation to:

kalo\n ei)s stratia/_n excellent for the army
X. C. 3.3.6, often in Thuc. ( = pro/s with accus.). Manner:

ei)s kairo/n in season
X. C. 3.1.8, ei)s du/namin to the extent of one's powers 4. 5. 52.

## 2. ei)s in Composition

Into, in, to (ei)sbai/nein enter, ei)spra/_ttein get in, exact a debt).

## e)c, e)k

§1688

e)c, e)k out, out of, from, from within, opposed to e)n, ei)s; cp. Lat. ex, e. As contrasted with a)po/ away from, e)c denotes from within.

## 2. e)c, e)k in Composition

## e)pi/

§1689

e)pi/ (cp. Lat. ob) upon, on, on the surface of; opposed to u(po/ under, and to u(pe/r when u(pe/r means above the surface of.

## 1. e)pi/ with the Genitive

a. Local: upon:

ou)/t' e)pi\ gh=s ou)/q' u(po\ gh=s neither upon the earth nor under the earth
P. Menex. 246d,

e)pi\ qro/nou e)kaqe/zeto he seated himself on a throne
X. C. 6.1.6; of the vehicle (lit. or figur.) upon which: e)pi\ tw=n i(/ppwn o)xei=sqai to ride on horseback 4. 5. 58 (never e)pi/ with dat.),

e)pi\ th=s e)mh=s new/s on my ship
L. 21.6; in the direction of:

e)pi\ *sa/rdewn e)/feuge he fled toward Sardis
X. C. 7.2.1; in the presence of (cp. para/ with dat.): e)pi\ martu/rwn before witnesses Ant. 2.
g. 8. e)pi/ is rarely used of mere proximity in poetry or standard prose.
N.—In expressions of simple superposition e)pi/ with the gen. denotes familiar relations and natural position; whereas e)pi/ with the dat. gives clear and emphatic outlines to statements of the definite place of an object or action, is used in detailed pictures, and marks the object in the dative as distinct from the subject of the verbal action. e)pi/ with the gen. is colourless and phraseological, and often makes, with the verb or the subject, a compound picture. Even in contrasting two objects e)pi/ with gen. is used since no special point is made of position. With (unemphatic) pronouns of reference (au)tou=) e)pi/ with gen. is much more frequent than e)pi/ with dat. The distinction between the two cases is often the result of feeling; and certain phrases become stereotyped, now with the gen., now with the dat.
b. Temporal, usually with personal gen.: in the time of:

e)pi\ tw=n progo/nwn in the time of our ancestors
Aes. 3.178,

e)p' e)mou= in my time
T. 7.86,

e)pi\ tou= *dekeleikou' pole/mou in the Decelean war
D. 22.15.
c. Other relations:

menei=n e)pi\ th=s a)noi/a_s th=s au)th=s to persist in the same folly
D. 8.14,

a(\ e)pi\ tw=n a)/llwn o(ra=te, tau=t' e)f' u(_mw=n au)tw=n a)gnoei=te what you see in the case of others, that you ignore in your own case
I. 8.114,

e)f' e(autw=n e)xw/roun they proceeded by themselves
X. A. 2.4.10, e)pi\ tetta/rwn four deep 1. 2. 15,

oi( e)pi\ tw=n pra_gma/twn the men in power
D. 18.247.

## 2. e)pi/ with the Dative

a. Local: on, by:

oi)kou=sin e)pi\ tw=| i)sqmw=| they dwell on the isthmus
T. 1.56, to\ e)pi\ qala/ssh| tei=xos the wall by the sea 7. 4. The dat. with e)pi/ denotes proxim ity much more frequently than the gen. with e)pi/; but denotes superposition less often than the gen. with e)pi/.
b. Temporal (rare in prose):

h)=n h(/lios e)pi\ dusmai=s the sun was near setting
X. A. 7.3.34.
c. Other relations: Succession, Addition:

P. A. 27b,

a)ne/sth e)p' au)tw=| he rose up after him

e)pi\ tw=| si/_tw| o)/yon relish with bread
X. M. 3.14.2. Supervision:

a)/rxwn e)pi\ tou/tois h)=n there was a commander over them
X. C. 5.3.56. Dependence:

kaq' o(/son e)sti\n e)p' e)moi/ as far as is in my power
