## THE VERB: VOICES

## ACTIVE VOICE

§1703
The active voice represents the subject as performing the action of the verb: lou/w I wash.
a. Under action is included being, as h( o(do\s makra/_ e)sti the way is long.

§1704
Active verbs are transitive or intransitive (920).

§1705
The action of a transitive verb is directed immediately upon an object, as tu/ptw to\n pai=da I strike the boy.

§1706
The object of a transitive verb is always put in the accusative (1553).

§1707
The action of an intransitive verb is not directed immedi-ately upon an object. The action may be restricted to the subject, as a)lgw= I am in pain, or it may be defined by an oblique case or by a preposition with its case, as a)lgw= tou\s po/das I have a pain in my feet, a)fi/_keto ei)s th\n po/lin he arrived at the city.

§1708
Many verbs are used in the active voice both transitively and intransitively. So, in English, turn, move, change. Cp. 1557 ff.
a. The distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs is a grammatical convenience, and is not founded on an essential difference of nature.

§1709
Active verbs ordinarily transitive are often used intransitively:
a. By the ellipsis of a definite external object, which in some cases may be employed, as a)/gein (to\ stra/teuma) march, ai)/rein (th\n a)/gku_ran) hoist the anchor, (ta\_s nau=s) get under sail, start, a)pai/rein (ta\_s nau=s, to\n strato/n) sail away, march away, dia/gein (to\n bi/on) live, e)lau/nein (to\n i(/ppon) ride, (to\ a(/rma) drive, (to\n strato/n) march, katalu/_ein (tou\s i(/ppous, ta\ u(pozu/gia) halt, kate/xein (th=n nau=n) put in shore, prose/xein (to\n nou=n) pay attention, teleuta=n (to\n bi/on) die. The original sense has often been so completely forgotten that it becomes possible to say

ai)/rein tw=| stratw=| set out with the army
T. 2.12,

e)lau/nwn i(drou=nti tw=| i(/ppw| riding with his horse in a sweat
X. A. 1.8.1.
b. pra/_ttein, e)/xein with adverbs often mean to keep, to be: eu)= pra/_ttein fare well, kalw=s e)/xein be well (bene se habere), e)/xein ou(/tws be so. So when a reflexive pronoun is apparently omitted:

e)/x' au)tou= stop there!
D. 45.26.
c. Many other transitive verbs may be used absolutely, i.e. with no definite object omitted, as ni_ka=n be a victor, a)dikei=n be guilty. Cp. ‘amare’ be in love, ‘drink’ be a drunkard. This is especially the case in compounds, e.g. of a)lla/ttein, a)nu/ein, dido/nai, kli/_nein, lamba/nein, lei/pein, meignu/nai.
d. In poetry many uncompounded transitive verbs are used intransitively. Many intransitive verbs become transitive when compounded with a prep., especially when the compound has a transferred sense, 1559. In some verbs 1st aorist and 1st perfect are transitive, 2d aorist and 2d perfect are intransitive.

§1710
Instead of the active, a periphrasis with gi/gnesqai may be used, often to express solemnity.

mhnu_tai\ gi/gnontai they turned informers
T. 3.2, mh\ u(bristh\s ge/vh| ‘do not be guilty of outrage’
S. Aj. 1092.

§1711

Causative Active.—The active may be used of an action performed at the bidding of the subject: *ku=ros ta\ basi/leia kate/kausen Cyrus burnt down the palace (i.e. had it burnt down)
X. A. 1.4.10. So with a)poktei/nein put to death, qa/ptein bury, oi)kodomei=n build, paideu/ein instruct, a)nakhru+/ttein publicly proclaim.

§1712
An infinitive limiting the meaning of an adjective is usually active where English employs the passive (cp. 2006).

## MIDDLE VOICE

§1713
The middle voice shows that the action is performed with special reference to the subject: lou=mai I wash myself.

§1714
The middle represents the subject as doing something in which he is interested. He may do something to himself, for himself, or he may act with something belonging to himself.

§1715
The future middle is often (807), the first aorist middle is almost never, used passively.

§1716
The object of the middle (1) may belong in the sphere of the subject, as his property, etc.: lou/omai ta\_s xei=ras I wash my hands, or (2) it may be brought into the sphere of the subject: tou\s o(pli/_ta_s metepe/myanto they sent for the hoplites, or (3) it may be removed from the sphere of the subject: a)podi/doma\i th\n oi)ki/a_n I sell my house (lit. give away). Here the object is also the property of the subject.

§1717
The Direct Reflexive Middle represents the subject as acting directly on himself. Self is here the direct object. So with verbs expressing external and natural acts, as the verbs of the toilet: a)lei/fesqai anoint oneself, lou=sqai wash oneself; and kosmei=sqai adorn oneself, stefanou=sqai crown oneself; gumna/zesqai exercise oneself.
a. The direct reflexive idea is far more frequently conveyed by the active and a reflexive pronoun, 1723.
b. The part affected may be added in the accusative:

e)pai/sato to\n mhro/n he smote his thigh
X. C. 7.3.6.

§1718
So with many other verbs, as i(/stasqai stand (place oneself), tre/pesqai turn (lit. turn oneself), dhlou=sqai show oneself, ta/ttesqai post oneself, a)pologei=sqai defend oneself (argue oneself off), fai/nesqai show oneself, appear, paraskeua/zesqai prepare onself, a)po/llusqai destroy oneself, perish.

§1719
The Indirect Reflexive Middle represents the subject as acting for himself, with reference to himself, or with something belonging to himself. Self is often here the indirect object. So pori/zesqai provide for oneself (pori/zein provide), fula/ttesqai guard against (fula/ttein keep guard), ai(rei=sqai choose (take for oneself), pare/xesqai furnish (pare/xein offer, present).

§1720
Cases in which the object is to be removed from the sphere of the subject may be resolved into the dative for oneself (1483）:

th\n r(a|qu_mi/a_n a)poqe/sqai to lay aside your indolence
D. 8.46,

e)tre/yanto tou\s i(ppe/a_s they routed the cavalry
T. 6.98, tou\s e)xqrou\s a)mu/_nesqai to ward off the enemy for themselves, i.e. to defend themselves against the enemy 1. 144.

§1721
The middle often denotes that the subject acts with something belonging to himself (material objects, means, powers). It is often used of acts done willingly. Thus, pare/xesqai furnish from one's own resources, e)pagge/llesqai promise, make profession of, ti/qesqai th\n yh=fon give one's vote, ti/qesqai ta\ o(/pla ground arms, a)podei/casqai gnw/mhn set forth one's opinion, lamba/nesqai/ tinos put one's hand on (seize) something. Thus,

e)spasme/noi ta\ ci/fh having drawn their swords
X. A. 7.4.16,

pai=das e)kkekomisme/noi h)=san they had removed their children
T. 2.78,

tropai=on sthsa/menoi having set up a trophy
X. H. 2.4.7,

o(/pla pori/sasqai to procure arms for themselves
T. 4.9, o(pli/_ta_s metepe/myato he sent for hoplites 7. 31,

gunai=ka h)gago/mhn I married
L. 1.6.

§1722
Under the indirect middle belong the periphrases of poiei=sqai with verbal nouns instead of the simple verb (cp. 1754). poiei=n with the same nouns means to bring about, effect, fashion, etc.
ei)rh/nhn poiei=sqai make peace (of one nation at war with another).
ei)rh/nhn poiei=n bring about a peace (between opponents, nations at war: of an individual).
qh/ra_n poiei=sqai ( = qhra=n hunt, qh/ra_n poiei=n arrange a hunt.
lo/gon poiei=sqai ( = le/gein) deliver a speech, lo/gon poiei=n compose a speech.
naumaxi/a_n poiei=sqai ( = naumaxei=n) fight a naval battle.
naumaxi/a_n poiei=n bring on a naval battle (of the commander).
o(do\n poiei=sqai ( = o(deu/ein) make a journey, o(do\n poiei=n build a road.
po/lemon poiei=sqai wage war, po/lemon poiei=n bring about a war.
sponda\_s poiei=sqai conclude (make) a treaty , or truce.
sponda\_s poiei=n bring about a treaty , or truce.

§1723

Active and Reflexive.—Instead of the direct middle the active voice with the reflexive pronoun is usually employed; often of difficult and unnatural actions (especially with au)to\s e(auto/n, etc.).

ta\ o(/pla pare/dosan kai\ sfa=s au)tou/s they surrendered their arms and themselves
T. 4.38,

misqw/sa_s au(to/n hiring himself out
D. 19.29 (not misqwsa/menos, which means hiring for himself),

katale/luke th\n au)to\s au(tou= dunastei/a_n he himself has put an end to his own sovereignty
Aes. 3.233,

h)ti/_mwken e(auto/n he has dishonoured himself
D. 21.103. But regularly a)pa/gxesqai hang oneself (1717).
a. The active and a reflexive pronoun in the gen. or dat. may be used for the simple middle when the reflexive notion is emphatic:

katalei/pein suggra/mmata e(autw=n to leave behind them their written compositions
P. Phae. 257d.

§1724

Middle and Reflexive.—The reflexive pronoun may be used with the middle:

e(auto\n a)pokru/ptesqai to hide himself
P. R. 393c; often for emphasis, as in contrasts: oi( me/n fa_si basile/a_ keleu=sai/ tina e)pisfa/cai au)to\n *ku/_rw|, oi( d' e(auto\n e)pisfa/casqai some say that the king issued orders for some one to slay him (Artapates) over (the body of) Cyrus, while others say that he slew himself with his own hand
X. A. 1.8.29, cp. also ti/ th\n po/lin prosh=ke poiei=n, a)rxh\n kai\ turanni/da tw=n *(ellh/nwn o)rw=san e(autw=| kataskeuaco/menon *fi/lippon; what did it beseem the city to do when it saw Philip compassing for himself dominion and despotic sway over the Greeks?
D. 18.66.

§1725

The Causative Middle denotes that the subject has something done by another for himself:

e)gw\ ga/r se tau=ta e)didaca/mhn for I had you taught this
X. C. 1.6.2, parati/qesqai si=ton to have food served up 8. 6. 12, o(/soi o(/pla a)fh/|rhntai, taxu\ a)/lla poih/sontai all who have had their arms taken from them will soon get others made 6. 1. 12, e(autw=| skhnh\n kateskeua/sato he had a tent prepared for himself 2. 1. 30.
a. This force does not belong exclusively to the middle; cp. 1711.

§1726

Reciprocal Middle.—With a dual or plural subject the middle may indicate a reciprocal relation. So with verbs of contending, conversing (questioning, replying), greeting, embracing, etc. The reciprocal middle is often found with compounds of dia/.

oi( a)_qlhtai\ h)gwni/zonto the athletes contended
T. 1.6, katasta/ntes e)ma/xonto when they had got into position they fought 1. 49, a)nh\r a)ndri\ diele/gonto they conversed man with man 8. 93,

e)pimei/gnusqai a)llh/lois to have friendly intercourse with one another
X. C. 7.4.5,

tau=ta dianemou=ntai they will divide this up among themselves
L. 21.14. So ai)tia=sqai accuse, lu_mai/nesqai maltreat, me/mfesqai blame, a(milla=sqai vie, parakeleu/esqai encourage one another.
a. The active may also be employed, as polemei=n wage war.
b. Some of these verbs have a passive aorist form, as diele/xqhn (812).

§1727
The reciprocal relation may also be expressed (1) by the use of the reflexive pronoun (cp. 1724) with the active:

fqonou=sin e(autoi=s they are mutually envious
X. M. 3.5.16; (2) by the use of a)llh/lwn, etc., with the active:

a)mfisbhtou=men a)llh/lois we are at variance with one another
P. Phae. 263a; (3) by repetition of the noun: ptwxo\s ptwxw=| fqone/ei = beggars envy each other Hesiod W. D. 26. The reflexive pronouns and a)llh/lwn, etc., may also be added to the middle.

§1728

Differences between Active and Middle.—As contrasted with the active, the middle lays stress on the conscious activity, bodily or mental participation, of the agent.
In verbs that possess both active and middle: bouleu/esqai deliberate, bouleu/ein plan, staqma=n measure, staqma=sqai calculate, skopei=n look at, skopei=sqai consider, e)/xesqai cling to, pau/esqai cease (1734. 14). The force of the middle often cannot be reproduced in translation (a)kou/esqai, ti_ma=sqai, a)riqmei=sqai, a)porei=sqai), and in some other cases it may not have been felt, as in o(ra=sqai in poetry (proora=sqai occurs in prose).
a. Many such verbs form their futures from the middle: a)kou/somai, a)/|somai, a(marth/somai. See 805.
b. In verbs in -euw, the middle signifies that the subject is acting in a manner appropriate to his state or condition: poli_teu/ein be a citizen, poli_teu/esqai act as a citizen, perform one's civic duties; presbeu/ein be an envoy, presbeu/esqai negotiate as envoy or send envoys (of the State in its negotiations). But this force of the middle is not always apparent.

§1729

Middle Deponents (810) often denote bodily or mental action (feeling and thinking): a(/llesqai jump, pe/tesqai fly, o)rxei=sqai dance, oi)/xesqai be gone, de/rkesqai look; bou/lesqai wish, ai)sqa/nesqai perceive, a)kroa=sqai listen, me/mfesqai blame, oi)/esqai conjecture, think (lit. take omens for oneself, from o)vis, Lat. avis, auspicium), h(gei=sqai consider; o)lofu/_resqai lament.
a. Some of the verbs denoting a functional state or process have the middle either in all forms or only in the future.
b. Verbs denoting bodily activity regularly have a middle future, 805-806.

§1730
Deponent verbs are either direct or indirect middles; direct: u(pisxnei=sqai undertake, promise (lit. hold oneself under); indirect: kta=sqai acquire for oneself, a)gwni/zesqai contend (with one's own powers).

§1731
The middle may denote more vigorous participation on the part of the subject than the active: seu/esqai dart, but qe/ein run.

§1732
The active is often used for the middle when it is not of practical importance to mark the interest of the subject in the action. The active implies what the middle expresses. So with

metape/mpein send for
T. 7.15, dhlw/santes th\n gnw/mhn setting forth their opinion 3. 37, tropai=on sth/santes setting up a trophy 7. 5.

§1733
The passive form may have reflexive force, as ki_nhqh=nai set oneself in motion, a)pallagh=nai remove oneself, e)nantiwqh=nai oppose oneself, swqh=nai save oneself (

sw/qhti save yourself
P. Cr. 44b). Some of these middle passives may take the accusative, as ai)sxunqh=nai be ashamed before, fobhqh=nai be afraid of, kataplhgh=nai/ tina be amazed at some one. See 814 ff.

§1734
List of the chief verbs showing important differences of meaning between active and middle. It will be noted that the active is often transitive, the middle intransitive.
1. ai(rei=n take; ai(rei=sqai choose.
2. a)mu/_nein ti/ tini ward off something from some one, a)mu/_nein tini/ help some one; a)mu/_nesqai/ ti defend oneself against something, a)mu/_nesqai/ tina requite some one.
3. a)podou=nai give back; a)podo/sqai sell (give away for one's profit).
4. a(/ptein attach; a(/ptesqai/ tinos touch.
5. a)/rxein begin, contrasts one beginner of an action with another, as a)/rxein pole/mou take the aggressive, strike the first blow (bellum movere), a)/rxein lo/gou be the first to speak,

h)=rxe xeirw=n a)di/kwn he began an unprovoked assault
L. 4.11; a)/rxesqai make one's own beginning, as contrasted with the later stages, as a)/rxesqai pole/mou begin warlike operations (bellum incipere), a)/rxesqai tou= lo/gou begin one's speech.

pole/mou ou)k a)/rcomen, a)rxome/nous de\ a)mu_nou/meqa we shall not take the initiative in the war, but upon those who take it up we shall retaliate
T. 1.144.
6. gamei=n marry (of the man, ducere); gamei=sqai marry (of the woman, nubere).
7. gra/fein no/mon propose a law (said of the maker of a law whether or not he is himself subject to it); gra/fesqai grafh/n draw up an indictment for a public offence, gra/fesqai/ tina bring suit against some one (have him written down in the magistrates' records).
8. danei/zein (make of anything a da/nos loan) i.e. put out at interest, lend; danei/zesqai (have a da/nos made to oneself) have lent to one, borrow at interest.
9. dika/zein give judgment; dika/zesqai (di/khn tini/) go to law with a person, conduct a case (properly get some one to give judgment).
10. e)piyhfi/zein put to vote (of the presiding officer); e)piyhfi/zesqai vote, decree (of the people).
11. e)/xein hold; e)/xesqai/ t<*>nos hold on to, be close to.
12. qu/_ein sacrifice; qu/_esqai take auspices (of a general, etc.).
13. misqou=n (put a misqo/s, rent, on anything) i.e. let for hire (locare); misqou=sqai (lay a misqo/s upon oneself) i.e. hire (conducere). Cp. 1723.
14. pau/ein make to cease, stop (trans.); pau/esqai cease (intr.). But pau=e le/gwn stop talking.
15. pei/qein persuade; pei/qesqai obey (persuade oneself); pe/poiqa I trust.
16. tiqe/nai no/mon frame or propose a law for others (said of the lawgiver, legem ferre or rogare); ti/qesqai no/mon make a law for one's own interest, for one's own State (said of the State legislating, legem sciscere or iubere). au)tou\s (a)gra/fous no/mous)

oi( a)/nqrwpoi e)/qento . . . qeou\s oi)=mai tou\s no/mous tou/tous toi=s a)nqrw/pois qei=nai men did not make the unwritten laws for themselves, but I think the gods made these laws for men
X. M. 4.4.19.
17. ti_mwrei=n tini avenge some one, ti_mwrei=n tina/ tini punish A for B's satisfaction; ti_mwrei=sqai/ tina avenge oneself on (punish) some one.
18. ti/nein di/khn pay a penalty (poenas dare); ti/nesqai di/khn exact a penalty (poenas sumere).
19. fula/ttein tina/ watch some one; fula/ttesqai/ tina be on one's guard against some one.
20. xra=n give an oracle , and lend; xra=sqai consult an oracle , and use.

## PASSIVE VOICE

§1735
The passive voice represents the subject as acted on: e)w/qoun, e)wqou=nto, e)/paion, e)pai/onto they pushed, were pushed, they struck, were struck
X. C. 7.1.38.
a. The passive has been developed from the middle. With the exception of some futures and the aorist, the middle forms do duty as passives: ai(rei=tai takes for himself, i.e. chooses, and is chosen. (For this development of the passive, cp. the reflexive use in se trouver, sich finden.) So ke/xutai has poured itself, has been poured. In Homer there are more perfect middles used passively than any other middle tenses. Cp. 802.
b. Uncompounded e)sxo/mhn sometimes retained its use as a passive. e)sxe/qhn is late.

§1736
The passive may have the sense allow oneself to be, get oneself:

e)ca/gonte/s te kai\ e)cago/uenoi carrying and allowing ourselves to be carried across the border
P. Cr. 48d,

a)pexqh/sei *gorgi/a| you will incur the hatred of Gorgias
P. Phil. 58c.

§1737
Many future middle forms are used passively (807 ff.).

§1738
The future middle forms in -somai are developed from the present stem, and express durative action; the (later) future passives in -h/somai, -qh/somai are developed from the aorists in -hn and -qhn, and are aoristic. This difference in kind of action is most marked when the future middle forms are used passively, but it is not always found. toi=s a)/llois cumma/xois para/deigma safe\s katasth/sate, o(\s a)\n a)fi/sthtai, qana/tw| zhmiwso/menon give to the rest of the allies a plain example that whoever revolts shall be punished (in each case) with death
T. 3.40, e)a\_n a(lw=|, qana/tw| zhmiwqh/setai if he is convicted, he will be punished (a single occurrence) with death
D. 23.80, o( di/kaios masti_gw/setai, streblw/setai, dedh/setai, e)kkauqh/setai tw)fqalmw/ the just man will be scourged, racked, fettered, will have his eyes burnt out
P. R. 361e, ti_mh/somai I shall enjoy honour, ti_mhqh/somai I shall be honoured (on a definite occasion), w)felh/somai I shall receive lasting benefit, w)felhqh/somai I shall be benefited (on a definite occasion). Cp. 808, 809, 1911.

§1739
The second aorist passive was originally a second aorist active (of the -mi form) that was used intransitively to distinguish it from the transitive first aorist, as e)/fhna showed, e)fa/nhn appeared; e)/fqeira destroyed, e)fqa/rhn am destroyed; e)ce/plhca was terrified, e)cepla/ghn was alarmed. So e)da/hn learned, e)rru/hn flowed. Cp. e)/sthsa placed, e)/sthn stood (819).

§1740
In Hom. all the second aorist forms in -hn are intransitive except e)plh/ghn and e)tu/phn was struck. Most of the forms in -qhn are likewise intransitive in Hom., as e)fa/nqhn appeared (in Attic was shown).

§1741
The perfect passive in the third singular with the dative of the agent (1488) is often preferred to the perfect active of the first person. Thus pe/pra_ktai/ moi it has been done by me is more common than pe/pra_ga or pe/pra_xa I have done.

§1742
The passive may be passive of the middle as well as passive of the active: ai(rei=tai is taken or is chosen, bia/zetai does violence or suffers violence (is forced), h(|re/qh was taken or was chosen, e)gra/fh was written or was indicted (ge/grammai is commonly middle). The use of the passive as passive of the middle is post-Homeric.
a. When deponent verbs have a passive force, the future and aorist have the passive form: e)bia/sqhn I suffered violence (was forced), but e)biasa/mhn I did violence. This holds when there was once an active form. Cp. also ti_mwrei=sqai, metape/mpesqai, yhfi/zesqai, kuklei=sqai.
b. The aorist passive may have a middle sense (814).

§1743
The direct object of an active verb becomes the subject of the passive: h( e)pistolh\ u(po\ tou= didaska/lou gra/fetai the letter is written by the teacher (active o( dida/skalos gra/fei th\n e)pistolh/n).

§1744
The cognate accusative may become the subject of the passive:

po/lemos e)polemh/qh war was waged
P. Menex. 243e (po/lemon polemei=n, 1564).

§1745
Active or middle verbs governing the genitive or dative may form (unlike the Latin use) a personal passive, the genitive or dative (especially if either denotes a person) becoming the subject of the passive.
a. With the genitive: a)/rxein, h(gemoneu/ein, katafronei=n, katagela=n, katayhfi/zein (katayhfi/zesqai), a)melei=n.
b. With the dative: a)peilei=n, a)pistei=n, e)gkalei=n, e)pibouleu/ein, e)piti_ma=n, o)neidi/zein, pisteu/ein, polemei=n, fqonei=n.
c. Examples:

ou)k h)ci/oun ou(=toi h(gemoneu/esqai u(f' h(mw=n they did not think it right to be governed by us
T. 3.61,

e)kei=nos kateyhfi/sqh he was condemned
X. H. 5.2.36, but

qa/natos au)tw=n kategnw/sqh the penalty of death was pronounced against them
L. 13.39 (pass. of katagnw=nai qa/naton au)tw=n),

w(/ra_ h(mi=n bouleu/esqai u(pe\r h(mw=n au)tw=n mh\ katafronhqw=men it is time for us to take counsel for ourselves that we may not be brought into contempt
X. A. 5.7.12,

polemou=ntai me\n u(po\ tw=n th\n xw/ra_n au)tw=n perioikou/ntwn, a)pistou=ntai d' u(f' a(pa/ntwn they are warred against by those who dwell around their country, and are distrusted by all
I. 5.49, pw=s a)\n e)pebou/leusa/ ti au)tw=|, o(/ ti mh\ kai\ e)pebouleu/qhn u(p' au)tou=; how could I have plotted against him, unless I had been plotted against by him? Ant. 4.
b. 5,

fqonhqei\s u(po\ tou=) *odusse/ws envied by Odysseus
X. M. 4.2.33 (contrast Lat. invidetur mihi ab aliquo).
N.—The above principle does not hold when the accusative of an external object intervenes between the verb and the dative.

§1746
A verb governing an oblique case rarely forms in Greek (unlike Latin) an impersonal passive:

e)moi\ beboh/qhtai tw=| te teqnew=ti kai\ tw=| no/mw| my aid has been given to the deceased and to the law
Ant. 1.31. The tense used is one from the perfect stem.

§1747
An active verb followed by two accusatives, one of a person, the other of a thing, retains, when transferred to the passive, the accusative of the thing, while the accusative of the person becomes the nominative subject of the passive. Examples 1621, 1625, 1627, 1632.

§1748
An active verb followed by an accusative of the direct object (a thing) and an oblique case of a person, retains, when transferred to the passive, the accusative of the direct object, while the indirect object becomes the nominative subject of the passive. Cp. I have been willed a large estate.
a. With verbs signifying to enjoin, entrust:

oi( *boiwtoi\ tau=ta e)pestalme/noi a)nexw/roun the Boeotians having received these instructions withdrew
T. 5.37 (pass. of e)piste/llein tau=ta toi=s *boiwtoi=s), a)/llo ti mei=zon e)pitaxqh/sesqe you will have some greater command laid upon you 1. 140 (pass. of e)pita/ttein a)/llo ti mei=zon u(_mi=n). Both accusatives are internal; and so, in

oi( tw=n *)aqhnai/wn e)pitetramme/noi th\n fulakh/n those of the Athenians who had been entrusted with the watch
T. 1.126, fulakh/n is equivalent to an internal accusative. The nominative of the thing and the dative of the person sometimes occur (

*)/iwnes, toi=si e)pete/trapto h( fulakh/ the Ionians to whom the guard had been entrusted
Hdt. 7.10). The dative is common when an inf. is used with the pass. verb:

e)pete/takto toi=s skeuofo/rois i)e/nai the baggage-carriers had been commanded to go
X. C. 6.3.3.
b. With other verbs: a)potmhqe/ntes ta\_s kefala/_s having been decapitated (had their heads cut off)
X. A. 2.6.1 (pass. of a)pote/mnein ta\_s kefala/_s tisi or tinwn).

§1749
A passive may be formed in the case of verbs ordinarily intransitive but allowing a cognate accusative in the active:

i(kana\ toi=s polemi/ois hu)tu/xhtai the enemy has had enough good fortune
T. 7.77 (eu)tuxei=n i(kana/, 1573),

kekindu_neu/setai the risk will have been run
Ant. 5.75. See 1746. This is common with neuter passive participles:

ta\ h)sebhme/na au)tw=| the impious acts committed by him
L. 6.5,

ta\ soi\ ka)_moi\ bebiwme/na the life led by you and by me
D. 18.265, ta\ pepoli_teume/na au)toi=s their political acts 1. 28,

a(marthqe/nta errors committed
X. A. 5.8.20.
a. Some verbs describing the action of the weather may be used in the passive:

neifo/menoi a)ph=lqon ei)s to\ a)/stu they returned to the city covered with snow
X. H. 2.4.3.

§1750
The cognate subject may be implied, as in the case of impersonal passives, in the perfect and tenses derived from the perfect. Thus,

e)peidh\ au)toi=s pareskeu/asto when their preparations were complete
T. 1.46. le/getai it is said, e)dhlw/qh it was made known, followed by the logical subject are not impersonal:

e)dhlw/qh tw=| tro/pw| a)pwlw/lei ta\ xrh/mata it was shown how the money had been lost
Ant. 5.70. See 935.

§1751
Greek uses impersonals from intransitives (corresponding to Lat. ambulatur, itur, curritur) only when the active is itself intransitive; as de/doktai it has seemed good (cp. dokei=).

§1752
The active or the middle deponent of a transitive verb used transitively or of an intransitive verb may replace the passive of a transitive verb.
a)kou/ein (poet. klu/ein) be called; be well (eu)=, kalw=s) or ill (kakw=s) spoken of, = pass. of le/gein:

nu=n ko/lakes a)kou/ousin now they are called flatterers
D. 18.46, ti/s u(p' e)mou= kakw=s a)kh/koen h)\ pe/ponqe; who has been ill spoken of or suffered at my hands?
L. 8.3. Cp. bene, male audire; Milton: “England hears ill abroad.”
a(li/skesqai be caught = pass. of ai(rei=n, as

e)a\_n a(lw=|s tou=to pra/_ttwn if you are caught doing this
P. A. 29c.
a)poqnh/skein (die) be killed = pass. of a)poktei/nein, as

a)pe/qnh|skon u(po\ i(ppe/wn they were killed by the cavalry
X. C. 7.1.48. But not in the perfect, where the uncompounded te/qnhka is used.
gi/gnesqai be born = pass. of ti/ktein beget, bring forth:

pai=des au)tw=| ou)k e)gi/gnonto e)k tau/ths he had no children by her
X. H. 6.4.37.
di/khn dou=nai be punished = pass. of zhmiou=n, as

u(p' au)tw=n tou/twn di/khn e)/dosan they were punished by these very men
X. C. 1.6.45.
h(tta=sqai be defeated = pass. of ni_ka=n conquer, as

u(po\ tw=n summa/xwn h(ttw/menoi worsted by their allies
And. 4.28.
katie/nai (kate/rxesqai) return from exile = pass. of kata/gein restore from exile, as

u(p o)ligarxi/a_s katelqei=n to be restored by an oligarchy
T. 8.68.
kei=sqai (lie) be placed = pass. of the perfect of tiqe/nai:

pei/qou toi=s no/mois toi=s u(po\ tw=n basile/wn keime/nois obey the laws established by kings
I. 1.36.
lagxa/nein (obtain by lot) be drawn by lot = pass. of klhrou=n:

e)/laxon i(ereu/s I became priest by lot
D. 57.47.
pa/sxein (suffer) be treated well (eu)=) or ill (kakw=s) = pass. of poiei=n (eu)=, kakw=s):

eu)= paqo/ntes u(p' au)tw=n well treated by them
P. G. 519c.
pi/_ptein in e)kpi/_ptein (fall out) be expelled = pass. of e)kba/llein: oi( e)kpeptwko/tes <*> tou= dh/mou those who had been expelled by the people
X. H. 4.8.20.
feu/gein (flee) be prosecuted = pass. of diw/kein (be indicted = gra/fesqai passive); <*>iled = pass. of e)kba/llein. So a)pofeu/gein be acquitted = pass. of a)polu/_ein. Thus.

a)sebei/a_s feu/gwn u(po\ *melh/tou prosecuted for impiety by Meletus
P. A. 35d.

§1753
Other equivalents of passive forms are e)/xein, tugxa/nein, lamba/nein, used with a substantive of like meaning with the active verb: o)/noma e)/xein = o)no<*>sqai, suggnw/mhn e)/xein or suggnw/mhs tugxa/nein = suggignw/skesqai, e)/painon lamba/<*> or e)pai/nou tugxa/nein = e)painei=sqai. So with middle deponents: ai)ti/a_n e)/xein = <*>tia=sqai.

§1754
The passive of the periphrasis with poiei=sqai (1722) is made with <*>esqai: so ei)rh/nh gi/gnetai peace is made.

§1755
The agent of the passive is regularly expressed by u(po/ and the genitive; sometimes by a)po/, dia/, e)k, para/, pro/s with the genitive, or by u(po/ with the dative (in poetry). See 1678.

§1756
The instrument of an action, when regarded as the agent, is personified, and may be expressed by u(po/ with the genitive: a<*>li/sketai u(po\ trih/rous he is captured by a trireme
D. 53.6.

§1757
The dative, or a prepositional phrase, is regularly used with the passive to denote the instrument, means, or cause (1506). The agent may be viewed as the instrument: in prose, when persons are regarded as instruments, the dative is usually that of military accompaniment (1526).

§1758
The dative of the agent used with the perfect passive and verbal adjective is a dative of interest (1488); on u(po/ with the genitive used instead of the dative, see 1493, 1494.

## THE MOODS

§1759
Mood designates by the form of the verb the mode or manner (modus) in which the speaker conceives of an assertion concerning the subject.

§1760
There are four moods proper in Greek: indicative, subjunctive, optative, and imperative. The infinitive (strictly a verbal noun) and the participle (strictly an adjective form of the verb) may be classed with the moods.

## THE PARTICLE a)/n

§1761
The particle a)/n (Hom. ke/n, ke/) limits the meaning of the moods. It has two distinct uses:
a. In independent clauses: with the past tenses of the indicative and with the optative; also with the infinitive and participle representing the indicative or optative.
b. In dependent clauses: with the subjunctive.

§1762
No separate word can be used to translate a)/n by itself; its force varies as it modifies the meaning of the moods. In general a)/n limits the force of the verb to particular conditions or circumstances (‘under the circumstances,’ ‘in that case,’ ‘then’).

§1763
In Homer a)/n is preferred in negative, ke/n, ke/ in relative, sentences.

§1764

Position of a)/n.—a)/n does not begin a sentence or a clause, except after a weak mark of punctuation, as ti/ ou)=n, a)/n tis ei)/poi, tau=ta le/geis h(mi=n nu=n; why then (some one might say) do you tell us this now?
D. 1.14. In independent sentences with a)/n (indic. and opt.) the particle is often separated from its verb for emphasis, and is attached to negatives (ou)k a)/n), interrogatives (ti/s a)/n, pw=s a)/n), or to any emphatic modifier. It is commonly attached to verbs of saying or thinking: su\n u(_mi=n me\n a)\n oi)=mai ei)=nai ti/_mios if I should remain with you, I think I should be esteemed
X. A. 1.3.6.
a. So with ou)k oi)=d' a)\n ei) (or ou)k a)\n oi)=da ei)) followed by a verb to which a)/n belongs:

ou)k oi)=d' a)\n ei) pei/saimi I do not know whether I could persuade
E. Med. 941 (for pei/saimi a)/n).

§1765

Repetition of a)/n.—a)/n may be repeated once or twice in the same sentence.
a. a)/n is placed early in a sentence which contains a subordinate clause, in order to direct attention to the character of the construction:

dokou=men d' a)/n moi tau/th| prospoiou/menoi prosbalei=n e)rhmote/rw| a)\n tw=| o)/rei xrh=sqai if we should make a feint attack here it seems to me we should find the mountain to have fewer defenders
X. A. 4.6.13.
b. For rhetorical emphasis a)/n is added to give prominence to particular words: ti/s ga\r toiau=t' a)\n ou)k a)\n o)rgi/zoit' e)/ph klu/wn; and who would not be angered upon hearing such words?
S. O. T. 339, pw=s a)\n ou)k a)\n e)n di/kh| qa/noim' a)/n; how should I not justly die? S. fr. 673.

§1766

a)/n without a Verb.—a)/n sometimes stands without a verb, which is to be supplied from the context. So in the second member of a sentence with coördinate clauses: oi)=da o(/ti pollou\s me\n h(gemo/nas a)\n doi/h, pollou\s d' a)\n (doi/h)

o(mh/rous I know that he would give many guides and many hostages
X. A. 3.2.24. Often with pw=s a)/n (ei)/h); how can (could) it be?
P. R. 353c,

ta/x' a)/n perhaps
P. Soph. 255c.
a. So with w(s a)/n, w(/sper a)\n ei) (2480): parh=n o( *gada/_ta_s dw=ra polla\ fe/rwn, w(s a)\n (scil. fe/roi tis)

e)c oi)/kou mega/lou Gadatas came with many gifts, such as one might offer from large means
X. C. 5.4.29, fobou/menos w(/sper a)\n ei) pai=s fearing like a child (w(/sper a)\n e)fobei=to, ei) pai=s h)=n)
P. G. 479a.
b. ka)\_n ei) is often used for the simple kai\ ei) (2372) and without regard to the mood of the following verb; sometimes there is no verb in the apodosis to which the a)/n may be referred, as

e)/stin a)/ra th=| a)lhqei/a|, ka)\_n ei) mh/ tw| dokei=, o( tw=| o)/nti tu/rannos tw=| o)/nti dou=los the very tyrant is then in truth a very slave even if he does not seem so to any one
P. R. 579d (here kai\ ei) mh\ dokei=, ei)/h a)/n is implied). ka)\_n ei) may be also so used that a)/n belongs to the apodosis, while kai/, though going with ei) in translation (even if), affects the whole conditional sentence. Thus, nu=n de/ moi dokei=, ka)\n a\se/beian ei) (tis) katagignw/skoi, ta\ prosh/konta poiei=n but as it is, it seems to me that, even if any one should condemn his wanton assault, he would be acting properly
D. 21.51 (here a)/n goes with poiei=n, i.e. poioi/h a)/n). ka)/_n if only, followed by a limiting expression, may generally be regarded as kai\ a)/_n ( = e)a/_n) with a subjunctive understood; as a)lla/ moi pa/res ka)\_n smi_kro\n ei)pei=n yet permit me to say but a word ( = kai\ e)a\_n parh=|s)
S. El. 1482.

§1767

Omission of a)/n.—a)/n is sometimes omitted when it may be supplied from the preceding sentence or clause. So often with the second of two verbs that are connected or opposed: ti/ e)poi/hsen a)/n; h)\ dh=lon o(/ti w)/mose (a)/n); what would he have done? is it not clear that he would have taken an oath?
D. 31.9,

ou)/t' a)\n ou(=tos e)/xoi le/gein ou)/q' u(_mei=s peisqei/hte neither can he assert nor can you be made to believe
D. 22.17. By retention of earlier usage the subjunctive is sometimes used without a)/n where it is commonly employed in the later language (2327, 2339, 2565 b, 2567 b). Here the difference is scarcely appreciable except that the omission gives an archaic tone.

## DEPENDENT CLAUSES WITH a)/n

§1768

Subjunctive with a)/n.—Conditional, relative, and temporal clauses requiring the subjunctive must have a)/n, which is more closely attached to the conditional, relative, and temporal words than it is to the subjunctive.
a. Hence the combinations e)a/_n (h)/n, a)/_n) on which cp. 2283; o(/tan, o(po/tan, e)ph/n (e)pa/_n), e)peida/n from ei), o(/te, o(po/te, e)pei/, e)peidh/ + a)/n. When the particle does not thus coalesce, it is usually separated only by such words as me/n, de/, te/, ga/r.
b. The force of a)/n with the subjunctive cannot usually be expressed in English. For a)/n in final clauses with w(s, o(/pws, and o)/fra, see 2201. In Hom. a)/n (ke/n) is found in dependent clauses, 2334 c.

## THE MOODS IN SIMPLE SENTENCES

§1769

§§ 1770-1849 treat of the use of the moods in independent sentences and principal clauses. The dependent construction of the moods was developed from their independent use. The use of the moods in subordinate clauses was not originally different from that in independent sentences and in the principal clauses of complex sentences. For the uses of the indicative, see also 1875-1958.

## INDICATIVE WITHOUT a)/n

§1770
The indicative mood makes a simple, direct assertion of fact; or asks a question anticipating such an assertion: h)=lqe he came, ou)k h)=lqe he did not come, e)leu/setai he will come, po/te tau=ta poih/sei; when will he do this?

§1771
The indicative states particular or general suppositions, makes affirmative or negative assertions, which may or may not be absolutely true. Thus, in assumptions, e)ch/marte/ tis a)/_kwn: suggnw/mh a)nti\ ti_mwri/a_s tou/tw| suppose some one involuntarily committed an offence; for him there is pardon rather than punish- ment
D. 18.274, and often after kai\ dh/, as

kai\ dh\ teqna=si and suppose they are dead
E. Med. 386.

§1772
The indicative may be used to express a doubtful assertion about a present or past action (negative mh/ or mh\ ou)): a)ll' a)/ra . . . mh\ o( *kth/sippos h)=n o( tau=t' ei)pw/n but I suspect (i.e. perhaps) after all it was Ctesippus who said this
P. Eu. 290e,

a)lla\ mh\ tou=to ou) kalw=s w(mologh/samen but perhaps we did not do well in agreeing to this
P. Men. 89c. Such sentences are often regarded as questions with the effect of doubtful affirmation.

§1773
The indicative may be used alone where in English we employ an auxiliary verb: pisteu/wn de\ qeoi=s pw=s ou)k ei)=nai qeou\s e)no/mizen; since he trusted in the gods how could (or should) he believe there were no gods?
X. M. 1.1.5,

o)li/gou ei(=lon th\n po/lin a little more and they would have taken the city
T. 8.35, a)pwllu/meqa we might have perished (we were in danger of perishing)
X. A. 5.8.2. Cp. 2319.

§1774

Unfulfilled Obligation (Propriety, Possibility).—With the imperfect indicative of impersonal expressions denoting obligation, propriety, necessity, or possibility, the action of a dependent infinitive is usually not realized. (Examples 1775-1776.)
Such expressions are e)/dei, xrh=n (or e)xrh=n), prosh=ke, kairo\s h)=n, a)/cion h)=n, ei)ko\s h)=n, di/kaion h)=n, ai)sxro\n h)=n, e)ch=n, kalw=s ei)=xen, verbals in -to/n or -te/on with h)=n, etc.
a. For the use of these expressions (also with a)/n) in the apodosis of unreal conditions, see 2313, 2315.

§1775

Present.—Thus, e)/dei se tau=ta poiei=n you ought to be doing this (but are not doing it),

tou/sde mh\ zh=n e)/dei these men ought not to be alive
S. Ph. 418,

ti/ si_ga=|s; ou)k e)xrh=n si_ga=n why art thou silent? Thou shouldst not be silent
E. Hipp. 297,

ei)ko\s h)=n u(_ma=s . . . mh\ malakw=s, w(/sper nu=n, cummaxei=n you should not be slack in your alliance, as you are at present
T. 6.78.

§1776

Past.—e)/dei se tau=ta poih=sai (or poiei=n) you ought to have done this (but did not do it), e)ch=n soi e)lqei=n you might have gone (but did not go), e)nh=n au)tw=| tau=ta poih=sai he could have done this (almost equivalent to the potential indicative tau=ta e)poi/hsen a)/n, 1784),

e)/dei ta\ e)ne/xura to/te labei=n I ought to have taken the pledges then
X. A. 7.6.23,

a)/cion h)=n a)kou=sai it would have been worth hearing
P. Eu. 304d,

me/nein e)ch=n he might have remained
D. 3.17.

§1777
The Greek usage simply states the obligation (propriety, possibility) as a fact which existed in the past (and may continue to exist in the present). In English we usually express the non-fulfilment of the action.

§1778
Present or past time is denoted when the present infinitive is used. When the reference is to present time, the action of the present infinitive is always denied. Past time is denoted when the aorist infinitive is used.

§1779
The expressions in 1774 may also refer to simple past obligation (propriety, possibility) and have the ordinary force of past indicatives: e)/dei me/nein he had to remain (and did remain)
D. 19.124. The context determines the meaning; thus ti/ to\n su/mboulon e)xrh=n poiei=n; (
D. 18.190) by itself might mean either what was it the duty of the statesman to do or what was it the duty of the statesman to have done?

§1780

Unattainable Wish.—A wish, referring to the present or past, which cannot be realized, is expressed by a past tense of the indicative with ei)/qe or with ei) ga/r (negative mh/). The imperfect refers to present time, the aorist to past time (cp. 2304, 2305).
ei)/q' ei)=xes belti(_ous fre/nas would that thou hadst (now) a better heart
E. El. 1061,

ei)/qe soi to/te sunegeno/mhn would that I had then been with thee
X. M. 1.2.46.

§1781
An unattainable wish may also be expressed by w)/felon (ought) with the present or aorist infinitive: w)/fele *ku=ros zh=n would that Cyrus were (now) alive (Cyrus ought to be alive)
X. A. 2.1.4 (1775). The negative is mh/:

mh/pot' w)/felon lipei=n th\n *sku=ron would that I had never left Scyros
S. Ph. 969. ei)/qe or ei) ga/r (poet. ai)/qe, w(s) may be used before w)/felon: ei) ga\r w)/felon oi(=oi/ te ei)=nai oi( polloi\ kaka\ e)rga/zesqai would that the multitude were able to do evil Pl. Cr. 44 d.

§1782

e)boulo/mhn followed by an infinitive may express an unattainable wish: e)boulo/mhn me\n ou)k e)ri/zein e)nqa/de I would that I were not contending here (as I am)
Ar. Ran. 866. (e)boulo/mhn a)/n vellem, 1789.)

§1783
The indicative is also used in other than simple sentences: in final sentences (2203); in object sentences after verbs of effort (2211), of caution (2220 a), of fearing (2231, 2233); in consecutive sentences with w(/ste so that (2274), in conditional sentences (2300, 2303, 2323, 2326); in temporal sentences (2395); in object sentences after o(/ti and w(s with a verb of saying, etc. (2577 ff.).

## INDICATIVE WITH a)/n

§1784

Past Potential.—The past tenses (usually the aorist, less commonly the imperfect) of the indicative with a)/n (ke/n) denote past potentiality, probability (cautious statement), or necessity:

o(\ ou)k a)\n w)/|onto which they could not have expected
T. 7.55, ti/s ga\r a)\n w)|h/qh tau=ta gene/sqai; for who would have expected these things to happen?
D. 9.68 (note that a)/n does not go with gene/sqai by 1764), e)/gnw a)/n tis one might (could, would) have known
X. C. 7.1.38,

u(po/ ken talasi/frona/ per de/os ei(=len fear might have seized even a man of stout heart
*d 421.
a. This is especially frequent with ti\s and with the ideal second person (cp. putares, crederes): e)pe/gnws a)/n you would (could, might) have observed
X. C. 8.1.33.
b. The potential optative (1829) in Homer refers also to the past.

§1785
A protasis may often be extracted from a participle, or is intimated in some other word; but there is no reference to any definite condition, hence a definite ellipsis is not to be supplied.

§1786

Unreal Indicative.—The indicative of the historical tenses with a)/n (ke/n) may denote unreality:

to/te d' au)to\ to\ pra=gm' a)\n e)kri/_neto e)f' au(tou= but the case would then have been decided on its own merits
D. 18.224,

kai/ ken polu\ ke/rdion h)=en and in that case it were far better
*g 41.

§1787
This use of the indicative with a)/n to denote unreality is not inherent in the meaning of the past tenses of that mood, but has been developed from the past potential with which the unreal indicative is closely connected. On the common use of this construction in the apodosis of unreal conditions see 2303. On e)/dei a)/n, etc., see 2315.

§1788
The imperfect refers to the present or the past, the aorist to the past (rarely to the present), the pluperfect to the present (less commonly to the past).

§1789

e)boulo/mhn a)/n (vellem) I should like or should have liked may express an unattainable wish: e)boulo/mhn a)\n *si/mwna th\n au)th\n gnw/mhn e)moi\ e)/xein I should have liked Simon to be (or I wish Simon were) of the same mind as myself
L. 3.21. On e)boulo/mhn without a)/n, see 1782.

§1790

Iterative Indicative (repeated action).—The imperfect and aorist with a)/n are used to express repeated or customary past action (post-Homeric):

dihrw/twn a)/n I used to ask
P. A. 22b,

a)\n e)/lecen he was wont to say
X. C. 7.1.10.

§1791
This construction is connected with the past potential and denoted originally what could or would take place under certain past circumstances. Thus, a)nalamba/nwn ou)=n au)tw=n ta\ poih/mata . . . dihrw/twn a)\n au)tou\s ti/ le/goien accordingly, taking up their poems, I used to (would) ask them (as an opportunity presented itself) what they meant
P. A. 22b. In actual use, since the action of the verb did take place, this construction has become a statement of fact.

§1792
In Herodotus this construction is used with the iterative forms: klai/eske a)/n she kept weeping 3. 119, oi( de\ a)\n *pe/rsa<*> la/beskon ta\ pro/bata the Persians were wont to seize the cattle 4. 130.

§1793
Homer and the early poets use a)/n (ke/n) with the future indicative with a conditional or limiting force: kai/ ke/ tis w(=d' e)re/ei and in such a case some one will (may) say thus
*d 176. This use is found also in conditional relative sentences (2565 b). In Attic a)/n is found with the future in a few passages which are now generally emended. In
P. A. 29c there is an anacoluthon.

§1794

a)/n is not used with the present and perfect indicative.

## SUBJUNCTIVE WITHOUT a)/n

§1795
The chief uses of the independent subjunctive are the hortatory (1797), the prohibitive (1800), and the deliberative (1805).
a. The name subjunctive is due to the belief of the ancient grammarians that the mood was always subordinate. Thus, ei)/pw shall I speak? (1805) was explained as due to the omission of a preceding bou/lei, i.e. do you wish that I speak?

§1796
The independent subjunctive refers to future time. It has three main uses: (1) the voluntative, expressing the will of the speaker. This is akin to the imperative. (2) The deliberative. This is possibly a form of the voluntative. (3) The anticipatory (or futural). This anticipates an action as an immediate future possibility. Whether the anticipatory is a form of the voluntative is uncertain (cp. ich will sehen, je veux voir, dialectal il veut pleuvoir).

§1797

Hortatory Subjunctive.—The hortatory subjunctive (present or aorist) is used to express a request or a proposal (negative mh/).
a. Usually in the first person plural: nu=n i)/wmen kai\ a)kou/swmen tou= a)ndro/s let us go now and hear the man P. Prot. 314 b, mh/pw e)kei=se i)/wmen let's not go there yet 311 a. a)/ge, fe/re (dh/), in Hom. a)/ge (dh/), sometimes precedes, as a)/ge skopw=men come, let us consider
X. C. 5.5.15. i)/qi (dh/) rarely precedes.
b. Less frequently in the first person singular, which is usually preceded (in affirmative sentences) by fe/re (dh/), in Hom. by a)/ge (dh/):

fe/re dh\ peri\ tou= yhfi/smatos ei)/pw let me now speak about the bill
D. 19.234.

§1798
The first person singular in negative exhortations (rare and poetic) may convey a warning or a threat: mh/ se, ge/ron, koi/lh|sin para\ nhusi\ kixei/w old man, let me not find thee by the hollow ships A 26. This use is often regarded as prohibitive (1800).

§1799
The hortatory use of the subjunctive compensates for the absence of an imperative of the first person.

§1800

Prohibitive Subjunctive.—The subjunctive (in the second and third persons of the aorist) is often used to express prohibitions (negative mh/).
a. Usually in the second person:

mhde\n a)qu_mh/shte do not lose heart
X. A. 5.4.19. For the aorist subjunctive the present imperative may be employed (1840): mh\ poih/sh|s (or mh\ poi/ei) tau=ta do not do this (not mh\ poih=|s).
b. Less commonly in the third person, which usually represents the second:

u(pola/bh| de\ mhdei/s and let no one suppose
T. 6.84 ( = mh\ u(pola/bhte do not suppose).
c. The third person of the present subjunctive is rare: mh\ toi/nun tis oi)/htai ( = mh\ oi)w/meqa) let not any one think P. L. 861 E.
N.—ou) mh/ with the subjunctive of the second person in the dramatic poets occasionally expresses a strong prohibition:

ou) mh\ lhrh/sh|s don't talk nonsense
Ar. Nub. 367.

§1801

Doubtful Assertion.—The present subjunctive with mh/ may express a doubtful assertion, with mh\ ou) a doubtful negation. The idea of apprehension or anxiety (real or assumed) is due to the situation. A touch of irony often marks this use, which is chiefly Platonic. With mh/ (of what may be true): mh\ a)groiko/teron h)=| to\ a)lhqe\s ei)pei=n I suspect it's rather bad form (lit. too rude) to tell the truth
P. G. 462e. With mh\ ou) (of what may not be true):

a)lla\ mh\ ou)x ou(/tws e)/xh| but I rather think this may not be so
P. Crat. 436b,

mh\ ou)k h)=| didakto\n a)reth/ virtue is perhaps not a thing to be taught
P. Men. 94e.

§1802
In Hom. mh/ with the independent subjunctive is used to indicate fear and warning, or to suggest danger: mh/ ti xolwsa/menos r(e/ch| kako\n ui(=as *)axaiw=n may he not (as I fear he may) in his anger do aught to injure the sons of the Achaeans B 195. Usually with the aorist, rarely with the present subjunctive (
o 19). The constructions of 1801, 1802 are used as object clauses after verbs of fearing (2221).

§1803

o(/pws mh/ is occasionally so used with the aorist subjunctive, and with an idea of command: o(/pws mh\ fh/sh| tis may no one say (as I fear he may)
X. S. 4. 8. See 1921.

§1804
From the use in 1801 is probably developed the construction of ou) mh/ with the aorist (less often the present) subjunctive to denote an emphatic denial; as

ou) mh\ pau/swmai filosofw=n I will not cease from searching for wisdom
P. A. 29d,

ou)ke/ti mh\ du/nhtai basileu\s h(ma=s katalabei=n the king will no longer be able to overtake us
X. A. 2.2.12.

§1805

Deliberative Subjunctive.—The deliberative subjunctive (present or aorist) is used in questions when the speaker asks what he is to do or say (negative mh/).
a. Usually in the first person: ei)/pwmen h)\ si_gw=men; shall we speak or keep silence?
E. Ion 758, ti/ dra/_sw; poi= fu/gw; what am I to do? whither shall I fly?
E. Med. 1271, mh\ fw=men; shall we not say?
P. R. 554b.
b. The (rare) second person is used in repeating a question: A. ti/ soi piqw/meqa; B. o(/ ti pi/qhsqe; A. In what shall we take your advice? B. In what shall you take my advice?
Ar. Av. 164.
c. The third person is generally used to represent the first person; commonly with ti\s, as ti/ tis ei)=nai tou=to fh=|; how shall anyone say this is so? ( = ti/ fw=men;)
D. 19.88.
N.—The subjunctive question does not refer to a future fact, but to what is, under the present circumstances, advantageous or proper to do or say.

§1806

bou/lei, bou/lesqe (poet. qe/leis, qe/lete) do you wish often precede the subjunctive: bou/lei soi ei)/pw; do you wish me to say to you?
P. G. 521d. This is a fusion of two distinct questions: bou/lei do you wish? and ei)/pw shall I say?

§1807
The deliberative subjunctive may be replaced by a periphrasis with dei= or xrh/ and the infinitive, or by the verbal adjective in -te/on e)sti/. Thus, h(mei=s de\ prosme/nwmen; h)\ ti/ xrh\ poiei=n; and shall we wait? or what must we do?
S. Tr. 390, ti/ poihte/on; ( = ti/ poiw=men;) what are we to do?
Ar. P. 922.
a. For the deliberative future see 1916.

§1808
Deliberation in the past may be expressed by e)/dei, xrh=n (e)xrh=n), e)/mellon with the infinitive, and by -te/on (verbal adj.) h)=n.

§1809

The Negative in Questions.—The use of mh/ (not ou)) in questions is due to the fact that the construction of 1805 is simply the interrogative form of the hortatory subjunctive: fw=men let us say, mh\ fw=men; are we not to say? Distinguish po/teron bi/a_n fw=men h)\ mh\ fw=men ei)=nai; shall we say that it is force or that it is not?
X. M. 1.2.45, from fw=men tau=t' o)rqw=s le/gesqai h)\ ou)/ shall we say that this is well said or not? (ou)/ = ou)k o)rqw=s le/gesqai)
P. G. 514c.

§1810

Anticipatory Subjunctive (Homeric Subjunctive).—In Homer the subjunctive is often closely akin to the future indicative, and refers by anticipation to a future event (negative ou)): ou) ga/r pw toi/ous i)/don a)_ne/ras, ou)de\ i)/dwmai for never yet saw I such men, nor shall I see them A 262,

kai/ nu/ tis w(=d' ei)/ph|si and one will say
c 275. a)/n (ke/n) usually limits this subjunctive in Hom. (1813).
a. This futural subjunctive is retained in Attic only in subordinate clauses (2327), and in ti/ pa/qw (1811).

§1811
The subjunctive is used in ti/ pa/qw; what will become of me; what am I to do? (lit. what shall I undergo?) as
P. Eu. 302d. So ti/ ge/nwmai; quid me fiet? Thus, w)/ moi e)gw/, ti/ pa/qw; ti/ nu/ moi mh/kista ge/nhtai; ah, woe's me! what is to become of me? what will happen unto me at the last?
e 465. The subjunctive here is not deliberative, but refers to a future event.

§1812
The subjunctive without a)/n is also used in dependent clauses of purpose (2196), after verbs of fearing (2225), in the protasis of conditional (2327, 2339) and conditional relative sentences (2567 b).

## SUBJUNCTIVE WITH a)/n

§1813
The subjunctive with a)/n (more commonly ke/n) is used in Homer in independent sentences and clauses (negative ou)). Cp. 1810. Thus, e)gw\ de/ k' a)/gw *bri_shi/da but in that case I will take Briseis A 184,

ou)k a)/n toi xrai/smh| bio/s of no avail to thee shall be thy bow
*l 387.

## OPTATIVE WITHOUT a)/n

§1814

Optative of Wish.—In independent sentences the optative without a)/n is used to express a wish referring to the future (negative mh/): w)= pai=, ge/noio patro\s eu)tuxe/steros ah, boy, mayest thou prove more fortunate than thy sire
S. Aj. 550. From this use is derived the name of the mood (Lat. opto wish).
a. So even in relative sentences:

e)a/_n pote, d\ mh\ ge/noito, la/bwsi th\n po/lin if ever they capture the city, which Heaven forbid
L. 31.14.
b. Under wishes are included execrations and protestations:

e)coloi/mhn may I perish
Ar. Ach. 324,

kai/ s' e)pidei/cw, h)\ mh\ zw/|hn, dwrodokh/santa and I will prove that you took bribes, or may I not live
Ar. Eq. 833.

§1815
The optative of wish is often introduced by ei) ga/r, ei)/qe (Hom. ai' ga/r, ai)/qe), or by ei), w(s (both poetical):

ei) ga\r ge/noito would that it might happen
X. C. 6.1.38,

w(s o)/loito may he perish
S. El. 126. (w(s is properly an exclamation: how.)

§1816
The optative introduced by ei) ga/r, etc. is sometimes explained as a protasis with the conclusion omitted: ei)/qe fi/los h(mi=n ge/noio oh, if you would become our friend
X. H. 4.1.38. Cp. 2352 e.

§1817
An unattainable wish, referring to the present, may be expressed by the present optative in Homer: ei)/q' h(bw/oimi would that I were young again H 157.

§1818
Unattainable wishes, when they refer to the future, may be expressed by the optative:

ei)/ moi ge/noito fqo/llos e)n braxi/_osi would that I had a voice in my arms
E. Hec. 836. Wishes represented as hopeless are expressed in the postHomeric language by the past tenses of the indicative (1780) or by w)/felon (1781).

§1819
Hom. often uses the optative with a concessive or permissive force: e)/peita de\ kai/ ti pa/qoimi after that I may (lit. may I) suffer come what will
*f 274.

§1820

Imperative Optative.—The optative may express a command or exhortation with a force nearly akin to the imperative:

*xeiri/sofos h(goi=to let Chirisophus lead
X. A. 3.2.37.

§1821
Potential Optative.—The potential optative, which in Attic regu larly takes a)/n (1824), is occasionally found in Homer and later poetry in an earlier form, without that particle:

r(ei=a qeo/s g' e)qe/lwn kai\ thlo/qen a)/ndra saw/sai easily might a god, if he so willed, bring a man safe even from afar
g 231,

qa=sson h)\ le/goi tis quicker than a man could speak
E. Hipp. 1186. This construction is suspected in prose.
a. Usually in negative sentences or in questions expecting a negative answer (with ou)): ou) me\n ga/r ti kakw/teron a)/llo pa/qoimi for I could not (conceivably) suffer anything worse T 321, tea/_n, *zeu=, du/nasin ti/s a)ndrw=n u(perbasi/a_ kata/sxoi; thy power, oh Zeus, what trespass of man can check?
S. Ant. 604.

§1822
The optative after ou)k e)/stin o(/stis (o(/pws, o(/poi) in the dramatists is probably potential:

ou)k e)/sq' o(/pws le/caimi ta\ yeudh= kala/ I could not call false tidings fair
A. Ag. 620. a)/n is usually employed in this construction.

§1823
The optative without a)/n (ke/n) is also used elsewhere, as in purpose clauses (2196) and clauses of fearing (2225) after a secondary tense; in the apodosis of conditional sentences (2300 d, 2326 d, 2333), in relative sentences (2566, 2568); and as the representative of the indicative (2615) or subjunctive (2619) in indirect discourse after secondary tenses.

## OPTATIVE WITH a)/n

§1824

Potential Optative.—The potential optative with a)/n states a future possibility, propriety, or likelihood, as an opinion of the speaker; and may be translated by may, might, can (especially with a negative), must, would, should (rarely will, shall). So in Latin velim, videas, cognoscas, credas.

gnoi/hs d' a)\n o(/ti tou=q' ou(/tws e)/xei you may see that this is so
X. C. 1.6.21,

a(/pantes a)\n o(mologh/seian all would agree
I. 11.5, h(de/ws a)\n e)roi/mhn I (would gladly ask) should like to ask
D. 18.64,

ou)k a)\n la/bois thou canst not take
S. Ph. 103,

le/goim' a)\n ta/de I will tell this
A. Supp. 928. The second person singular is often indefinite (one), as gnoi/hs a)/n (cognoscas) = gnoi/h tis a)/n.
a. The potential optative ranges from possibility to fixed resolve. The aorist optative with a)/n and a negative is very common.
b. When stress is laid on the idea of possibility and power, necessity and obligation, Greek uses du/namai, dei= or xrh/ with the infinitive (statement of fact).
c. The potential optative with a)/n is also used in dependent sentences; in purpose clauses (2202 b), in object clauses after verbs of effort (2216) and verbs of fearing (2232), in causal clauses (2243), in result clauses (2278), in the apodosis of conditional (see 2356) and conditional relative sentences (2566). In indirect discourse the infinitive with a)/n or the participle with a)/n may represent the optative with a)/n (1845 ff.).

§1825
Usually these optatives are not limited by any definite condition present to the mind, and it is unnecessary to supply any protasis in thought. In some cases a protasis is dormant in a word of the sentence (such as dikai/ws, ei)ko/tws). Thus, in

ou(\s a)xari/stous ei)=nai dikai/ws a)\n u(polamba/noite whom you would justly consider to be ungrateful
Aes. 3.196, dikai/ws may stand for ei) dikai/ws u(polamba/noite: if you should consider the matter justly. So ou)/te e)sqi/ousi plei/w h)\ du/nantai fe/rein: diarragei=en ga\r a)/n ktl. they neither eat more than they can bear, for otherwise (if they should eat more: ei) e)sqi/oien plei/w) they would burst
X. C. 8.2.21. The potential optative is also used as the main clause of less vivid conditions (2329) in which the protasis has the optative by assimilation to the mood of the apodosis.

§1826
The potential optative with a)/n is used to soften the statement of an opinion or fact, or to express irony: e(/tero/n ti tou=t' a)\n ei)/h this is (would be) another matter
D. 20.116, nosoi=m' a)/n, ei) no/shma tou\s e)xqrou\s stugei=n I must be mad, if it is madness to hate one's foes
A. Pr. 978. So often with i)/sws or ta/xa perhaps.
a. With a negative, the potential optative may have the force of a strong assertion:

ou) ga\r a)\n a)pe/lqoim', a)lla\ ko/yw th\n qu/ra_n for I will not go away, but I will knock at the door
Ar. Ach. 236.

§1827

bouloi/mhn a)/n (velim) is often used as a softened optative of wish: bouloi/mhn a)\n tou=to ou(/tw gene/sqai I could wish that this might be the result (ou(/tw ge/noito may it result thus)
P. A. 19a. For e)boulo/mhn a)/n see 1789.

§1828
The present and aorist are used of what will be, or what will prove to be, true (future realization of a present fact): a)reth\ a)/ra, w(s e)/oiken, u(gi/eia/ tis a)\n ei)/h virtue then, it seems, will (prove to) be a kind of health
P. R. 444d. The perfect is used of what will prove to be the case as regards a completed action: pw=s a)\n lelh/qoi; how can it have escaped my knowledge?
X. S. 3. 6. Usually the perfect is here equivalent to the present.

§1829
The present and aorist are rarely used of the past: (a) in Hom. of past possibility: kai/ nu/ ken e)/nq' a)po/loito and now he might have perished E 311 (Attic a)pw/leto a)/n, 1784), a)lla\ ti/ ken r(e/caimi; but what could I do? T 90. (b) in Hdt. of a mild assertion: tau=ta me\n kai\ fqo/nw| a)\n ei)/poien they may have said this out of envy 9. 71, ei)/hsan d' a)\n ou)=toi *krh=tes these would prove to be (might be, must have been) Cretans 1. 2. Both uses are doubtful in Attic prose.

§1830
The potential optative with a)/n may be used, in a sense akin to that of the imperative, to express a command, exhortation, or request: le/gois a)\n th\n de/hsin tell me (you may tell) your request
P. Par. 126a,

proa/gois a)/n move on
P. Phae. 229b. This courteous formula is used even where a harsh command might be expected:

xwroi=s a)\n ei)/sw su\n ta/xei go within with all speed
S. El. 1491.
a. In poi= dh=t' a)\n trapoi/mhn; whither pray shall I turn?
Ar. Ran. 296 the use is akin to the deliberative subjunctive (1805) or deliberative future (1916).

§1831
The potential optative with a)/n is used in questions: ti/s ou)k a)\n o(mologh/seien; who would not agree? (ou)dei/s: scil. ou)k a)\n o(mologh/seie)
X. M. 1.1.5. So even the optative of wish: ti/ d' o(/rkw| tw=|de mh\ )mme/nwn pa/qois; but if thou dost not abide by thy oath what dost thou invoke upon thyself?
E. Med. 754 (lit. mayest thou suffer what?).

§1832

pw=s a)/n, ti/s a)/n with the potential optative may be used to express a wish (especially in the tragic poets): pw=s a)\n o)loi/ma_n oh, would that I might die
E. Med. 97, ti/s a)\n e)n ta/xei mo/loi moi=ra oh, that some fate would speedily come
A. Ag. 1448. Properly this usage is not a wish, but is simply a question how the wish may be fulfilled.

§1833
The potential optative with a)/n (especially with negatives) may ex change with the indicative:

fhmi\ kai\ ou)k a)\n a)rnhqei/hn I assert and cannot deny
D. 21.191. It is often stronger, though more courteous, than the future indicative:

ou)k a)\n pe/ra_ fra/saimi I will speak no more
S. O. T. 343.

§1834
The future optative with a)/n occurs only in a few suspected passages.

## IMPERATIVE

§1835
The imperative is used in commands and prohibitions (negative mh/). All its tenses refer to the future.
a. Under commands are included requests, entreaties, summons, prescriptions, exhortations, etc.
b. For the tenses of the imperative, see 1840; for the infinitive used as an imperative, see 2013.

## POSITIVE (COMMANDS）

§1836
In exhortations a)/ge, fe/re, i)/qi (usually with dh/, sometimes with nu/n), often precede the imperative:

a)/ge dh\ a)kou/sate come listen
X. Ap. 14,

a)/gete deipnh/sate go now, take your supper
X. H. 5.1.18,

a)ll' i)/qi ei)pe/ but come, say
P. G. 489e.

§1837

pa=s is sometimes used with the second person in poetry: a)/koue pa=s hear, every one
Ar. Thesm. 372.

§1838
The third person may be used in questions: ou)kou=n kei/sqw tau=ta; shall these points be established?
P. L. 820e. Cp. 1842 a.

§1839
The imperative may be used in assumptions (hypothetical imperative), to make a concession, or to grant permission:

e)mou= g' e(/nek' e)/stw let it be assumed as far as I am concerned
D. 20.14,

ou(/tws e)xe/tw w(s su\ le/geis assume it to be as you say
P. S. 201c. So even as a protasis:

deica/tw, ka)_gw\ ste/rcw let him set it forth and I will be content
D. 18.112.

## NEGATIVE (PROHIBITIONS）

§1840
Prohibitions are expressed by mh/ with the present or aorist subjunctive in the first person plural; by mh/ with the present imperative or the aorist subjunctive in the second and third person singular or plural (cp. 1800). The aorist imperative is rare in prohibitions.
A. I Person.—mh\ gra/fwmen (mh\ gra/ywmen):

mh\ mainw/meqa mhd' ai)sxrw=s a)polw/meqa let us not act like madmen nor perish disgracefully
X. A. 7.1.29.
B. 2 Person.—mh\ gra/fe (mh\ gra/fete):

mh\ qau/maze don't be astonished
P. G. 482a,

mh\ qorubei=te don't raise a disturbance
P. A. 21a,

ta\ me\n poi/ei, ta\ de\ mh\ poi/ei do this and refrain from doing that
P. Pr. 325d,

mh\ me/ga le/ge don't boast so
P. Ph. 95b.—mh\ gra/yh|s (mh\ gra/yhte):

mhde\ qauma/sh|s to/de and do not wonder at this
A. Ag. 879,

mh\ qorubh/shte don't raise a disturbance
P. A. 20e,

mh\ a)/llws poih/sh|s don't do otherwise
P. Lach. 201b, mhdamw=s a)/llws poih/sh|s
Ar. Av. 133.
N.—The type mh\ gra/fh|s is never used. mh\ gra/yon occurs rarely in poetry (
*d 410,
*s 134.—
w 248, S. fr. 453 parodied in
Ar. Thesm. 870).
C. 3 Person.—mh\ grafe/tw (mh\ grafo/ntwn):

mhdei\s didaske/tw let no one tell me
T. 1.86,

mhdei\s tou=t' a)gnoei/tw let no one be ignorant of this fact
Aes. 3.6. mh\ graya/tw (mh\ graya/ntwn):

mhdei\s nomisa/tw let no one think
X. C. 7.5.73,

mh/t' a)pognw/tw mhde\n mh/te katagnw/tw let him neither acquit nor condemn in any way
Aes. 3.60; and in five other passages giving the actual usage of the orators. In the third person the aorist imperative is much less common than the present imperative.
N.—The type mh\ gra/fh| is used only when the third person represents the first person (1800 c). mh\ gra/yh| is much more common than mh\ graya/tw in the orators, e.g.

mhdei\s qauma/sh| let no one be astonished
D. 18.199,

mhdei\s nomi/sh| let no one think
T. 3.13,
D. 23.1.
D. The perfect imperative is rare in prohibitions (mh\ pefo/bhsqe T 6. 17) and is usually poetical. Cp. 698, 712.

§1841

a. mh\ gra/fe, like don't write, is ambiguous and may mean, according to the situation, either cease writing or abstain from writing. Commonly mh\ gra/fe means do not go on writing, write no more, and is an order to stop an action already begun. In many cases, however, mh/ with the present imperative does not refer to the interruption of an action already begun, but to an action still in the more or less distant future against which the speaker urges resistance. Sometimes the reference to the future is directly or indirectly indicated by the context.
b. mh\ gra/yh|s usually has the force of (I beg that) you will not write, (take care that you) don't write, and is commonly a complete prohibition against doing something not already begun. Sometimes, and especially in expressions of a colloquial character, mh/ with the aorist subjunctive marks the speaker's interruption, by anticipation, of a mental (less often of a physical) action that is being done by the person he addresses; as mh\ qauma/sh|s (
P. L. 804b) in reply to an exclamation of surprise. Here the type mh\ gra/yh|s often expresses impatience.
c. If mh\ gra/fe elicits a reply, it is (a)ll') ou) gra/fw, while mh\ gra/yh|s is answered by (a)ll') ou) gra/yw. Thus,

mh/ m' e)kdi/daske toi=s fi/lois ei)=nai kakh/n. a)ll' ou' dida/skw do not teach me to be base to my friends. But I do not
S. El. 395, ei) ou)=n e)/xeis e)narge/steron h(mi=n e)pidei=cai w(s didakto/n e)stin h( a)reth/, mh\ fqonh/sh|s a)ll' e)pi/deicon. a)ll' . . . ou) fqonh/sw now if you can show us more clearly that virtue is capable of being taught, don't refuse, but show us. Well, I will not refuse
P. Pr. 320c. So mh\ gra/fe commonly answers gra/fw, as qauma/zw, h)=n d' e)gw/, kai\ au)to/s. a)lla\ mh\ qau/maz', e)/fh I myself am astonished, said I. Cease your astonishment, said she
P. S. 205b, cp.
S. El. 395. So mh\ gra/yh|s answers gra/yw, as in
Hdt. 3.140,
Ar. Lys. 1036.
d. mh\ gra/fe and mh\ gra/yh|s are often found in closely connected clauses, as

mhdamw=s qu/_maine/ moi, mhde/ m' e)pitri/_yh|s don't be angry with me at all, nor ruin me
Ar. Nub. 1478,

mh/t' o)knei=te mh/t' a)fh=t' e)/pos kako/n do not shrink from me nor utter any harsh words
S. O. C. 731. The second prohibition may be more specific than the first, as

siw/pa_: mhde\n ei)/ph|s nh/pion be silent, don't say anything childish
Ar. Nub. 105. Less often mh\ gra/yh|s is followed by mh\ gra/fe, as mh\ bohqh/sate tw=| peponqo/ti deina/: mh\ eu)orkei=te (they will say) ‘do not come to the aid of one who has suffered grievously; have no regard for your oath’
D. 21.211.
e. The difference between mh\ gra/fe and mh\ gra/yh|s is virtually a difference of tenses, the present denoting an action continuing, in process; the aorist, an action concluded, summarized. So mh\ fobou= don't be fearful, mh\ fobhqh=|s don't be frightened. In maxims mh/ with the present imperative is preferred: mh\ kle/pte don't be a thief, mh\ kle/yh|s don't steal this or that. mhke/ti may be used in either construction. The distinction is often immaterial, often a difference of tone rather than of meaning; sometimes too subtle for dogmatic statement.

§1842
The imperative may be used in subordinate clauses: kra_th=re/s ei)sin . . . w(=n kra=t' e)/reyon there are mixing-bowls, the brims of which thou must crown
S. O. C. 473.
a. Especially after oi)=sqa interrogative in dramatic poetry: oi)=sq' o(\ dra=son; do you know what you are to do?
E. Hec. 225, oi)=sq' w(s poi/hson; do you know how I bid you act?
S. O. T. 543. oi)=sq' o(/ has become a partially fossilized expression, and can be used as subject or be governed by a verb: oi)=sqa/ nun a(/ moi gene/sqw; do you know what I must have done for me?
E. I. T. 1203.

§1843
The use of the imperative is to be explained as equivalent to dei= or xrh/ with the infinitive.

§1844

a)/n is not used with the imperative.

## INFINITIVE AND PARTICIPLE WITH a)/n

§1845
The infinitive or participle with a)/n represents either a past tense of the indicative with a)/n or the optative with a)/n. The context determines whether the indicative or the optative is meant. The participle with a)/n is post-Homeric.

§1846
The present infinitive or participle with a)/n represents the imperfect indicative with a)/n or the present optative with a)/n.
a. (inf.) a)kou/w *lakedaimoni/ous a)\n a)naxwrei=n e)p' oi)/kou I hear the Lacedaemonians used to return home ( = a)\n a)nexw/roun, 1790)
D. 9.48, oi)/esqe ga\r to\n pate/ra ou)k a)\n fula/ttein; for do you think my father would not have taken care? ( = ou)k a)\n e)fu/latten, 1786)
D. 49.35; nomi/zontes a)\n ti_mh=s tugxa/nein in the belief that they would obtain reward ( = a)\n tugxa/noimen)
X. A. 1.9.29.
b. (part.) o(/per e)/sxe mh\ kata\ po/leis au)to\n e)piple/onta th\n *pelopo/nnhson porqei=n, a)duna/twn a)\n o)/ntwn . . . a)llh/lois e)pibohqei=n which prevented him from sailing against the Peloponnese and laying it waste city by city when the Peloponnesians would have been unable to come to the rescue of one another ( = a)du/natoi a)\n h)=san)

sofi/a_ legome/nh dikaio/tat' a)/n that might most justly be called wisdom

§1847
The future infinitive and participle with a)/n are rare and suspected.

§1848
The aorist infinitive or participle with a)/n represents the aorist indicative with a)/n or the aorist optative with a)/n.
a. (inf.) *ku=ro/s ge, ei) e)bi/wsen, a)/ristos a)\n dokei= a)/rxwn gene/sqai it seems probable that Cyrus, if he had lived, would have proved himself a most excellent ruler ( = a)\n e)ge/neto)
X. O. 4.18, w(/ste kai\ i)diw/thn a)\n gnw=nai so that even a common man could have understood ( = a)\n e)/gnw)

§1849
The perfect infinitive with a)/n represents the pluperfect indicative with a)/n or the perfect optative with a)/n: oi)=d' o(/ti (a)\n) fh/seien pa/nta tau=q' u(po\ tw=n barba/rwn a)\n h(lwke/nai I know that he would say that all this would have been captured by the barbarians ( = a)\n h(lw/kesan)
D. 19.312, h(gei=to tou\s a)gnoou=ntas a)ndrapodw/deis a)\n dikai/ws keklh=sqai he thought that those who did not know this might justly be deemed servile in nature ( = keklhme/noi a)\n ei)=en)
X. M. 1.1.16.
For the infinitive and participle without a)/n see 1865 ff., 1872 ff., and under Infinitive and Participle.

## THE TENSES

§1850
By the tenses (‘tense’ from tempus) are denoted:
1. The time of an action: present, past, future.
2. The stage of an action: action continued or repeated (in process of development), action simply brought to pass (simple occurrence), action completed with a permanent result.
a. The time of an action is either absolute or relative. Time that is absolutely present, past, or future is reckoned from the time of the speaker or writer. Time that is relatively present, past, or future in dependent clauses is reckoned from the time of some verb in the same sentence. In dependent clauses Greek has no special forms to denote the temporal relation of one action to another (antecedent, coincident, subsequent), but leaves the reader to infer whether one action happened before, at the same time as, or after another action. The aorist is thus often used where English has the pluperfect (1943). See 1888, 1944. Unless special reference is made to relative time, the expressions “kind of time,” “time of an action,” in this book are used of absolute time.
b. In independent clauses only the tenses of the indicative denote absolute time; in dependent clauses they express relative time. The tenses of the subjunctive, optative, imperative, infinitive and participle do not refer to the differences in kind of time. Thus gra/fein and gra/yai to write, gegrafe/nai to finish writing, may be used of the present, the past, or the future according to the context. On the tenses of the optative, infinitive, and participle in indirect discourse see 1862, 1866, 1874. The future infinitive may be used, outside of indirect discourse, to lay stress on the idea of futurity (1865 d).
c. Even in the indicative the actual time may be different from that which would seem to be denoted by the tense employed. Thus the speaker or writer may imagine the past as present, and use the present in setting forth an event that happened before his time (1883); or may use the aorist or perfect of an event that has not yet occurred (1934, 1950).
d. In the subjunctive, optative (except in indirect discourse), and imperative the kind of time is implied only by the mood-forms, not by the tenses. The relation of the time of one action to the time of another usually has to be inferred in all the moods.
e. The stage of an action is expressed by all the tenses of all the different moods (including the participle and infinitive).
f. The action of the verb of a subordinate clause may overlap with that of the verb of the main clause. See 2388.

## KIND OF TIME

§1851
Only in the indicative do the tenses show time absolutely present, past, or future.
a. Present time is denoted by
1. The Present: gra/fw I write, am writing.
2. The Perfect: ge/grafa I have written.
b. Past time is denoted by
1. The Imperfect: e)/grafon I wrote, was writing.
2. The Aorist: e)/graya I wrote.
3. The Pluperfect: e)gegra/fh I had written.
N.—The only past tenses are the augmented tenses.
c. Future time is denoted by
1. The Future: gra/yw I shall write.
2. The Future Perfect: gegra/yetai it will have been written, teqnh/cw I shall be dead (shall have died).

## STAGE OF ACTION

§1852
Every form of the verb denotes the stage of the action.
a. Continued action is denoted by the present stem:
1. Present: gra/fw I am writing, pei/qw I am persuading (trying to persuade), a)nqei= is in bloom.
2. Imperfect: e)/grafon I was writing, e)/peiqon I was persuading (trying to persuade), h)/nqei was in bloom.
3. Future: gra/yw I shall write (shall be writing), basileu/sei he will reign.
N.—Continued action is incomplete: hence nothing is stated as to the conclusion. Thus feu/gei he flees does not state whether or not the subject succeeded in escaping.
b. Completed action with permanent result is denoted by the perfect stem:
1. Perfect: ge/grafa e)pistolh/n I have written a letter (and it is now finished), h)/nqhke has bloomed (and is in flower).
2. Pluperfect: e)gegra/fh e)pistolh/n I had written a letter (and it was then finished), h)nqh/kei had bloomed (and was in flower).
3. Future Perfect: gegra/yetai it will have been written, teqnh/cei he will be dead.
c. Action simply brought to pass (simple attainment) is denoted by the
1. Aorist: e)/graya I wrote, e)/peisa I persuaded (succeeded in persuading), e)basi/leuse he became king or he was king, h)/nqhse burst into flower or was in flower.
2. Future: gra/yw I shall write, basileu/sei he will become king.
N.—The aorist tense (a)o/ristos xro/nos from o(ri/zw define; unlimited, indefinite, or undefined time) is so named because it does not show the limitation (o(/ros) of continuance (expressed by the imperfect) or of completion with permanent result (expressed by the perfect).

§1853
The present stem may denote the simple action of the verb in present time without regard to its continuance; as qauma/zw I am seized with astonishment, a)stra/ptei it lightens (once or continually), di/dwmi I make a present. This is called the aoristic present. On inceptive verbs, see 526.

§1854
The future stem may denote either continued action (as in the present) or simple occurrence of the action of the verb (as in the aorist). Thus gra/yw I shall be writing or I shall write. See 1910 b.

§1855
Some verbs are, by their meaning, restricted to the tenses of continued action, as o(ra=n behold, fe/rein carry; others are exclusively aoristic, as i)dei=n properly glance at, e)negkei=n bring. Verbs expressing different kinds of action in their several tenses (as o(ra=n, i)dei=n) unite to form a verbal system.

§1856
The difference between the present stem (present and imperfect) and the aorist stem may be compared to the difference between a line and a point (both starting point and end). Thus, e)/rxesqai go, e)lqei=n come, arrive; fe/rein carry, e)negkei=n bring; a)/gein accompany, lead, a)gagei=n bring to a goal.

§1857
For the ‘progressive’ tenses of English (is walking, has been giving, etc.) Greek has no exact equivalent. The periphrasis of the present participle with e)sti/, etc. is employed to adjectivize the participle or to describe or characterize the subject like an adjective, i.e. the subject has a quality which it may display in action. Thus,

a)re/skonte/s e)smen we are acceptable
T. 1.38,

kai\ pa/nt' a)nadexo/menos kai\ ei)s au(to\n poiou/menos ta\ tou/twn a(marth/mat' e)sti/n and he takes upon himself and adopts all their misdeeds
D. 19.36. e)sti/ may be emphatic:

e)/sti pou di/xa diairou/menon there exists a twofold division
P. L. 895d. Some participles have become completely adjectivized: sumfe/rwn useful, diafe/rwn superior. Cp. 1961.

§1858

Primary and Secondary Tenses.—The primary tenses refer to present and future time (present, future, perfect, and future perfect), the secondary or historical tenses refer to past time (imperfect, aorist, pluperfect).
a. The gnomic aorist (1931 b) is regarded as a primary tense, as is the aorist when used for the perfect (1940), and the imperfect indicative referring to present time (1788); the historical present (1883), as a secondary tense. The subjunctive, optative, and imperative moods in their independent uses point to the future, and all their tenses therefore count as primary.

## THE TENSES OUTSIDE OF THE INDICATIVE

§1859
The tenses of the moods except the indicative do not express time in independent sentences.

§1860

Subjunctive.—The subjunctive mood as such refers to the future. The tenses do not refer to differences of time, and denote only the stage of the action (continuance, simple occurrence, completion with permanent result).
Present (continuance):

ta\ au(tw=n a(/ma e)kporizw/meqa let us at the same time keep developing our resources
T. 1.82; Aorist (simple occurrence):

porisw/meqa ou)=n prw=ton th\n dapa/nhn let us procure the money first
T. 1.83; Perfect (completion with permanent result): i(/na, h)\n mh\ u(pakou/wsi, teqnh/kwsin that, in case they do not submit, they may be put to death (lit. may be dead at once)
T. 8.74. The aorist commonly replaces the more exact perfect because the perfect is rarely used.
a. The future time denoted by present or aorist (ti/ poiw=men; or ti/ poih/swmen; what shall we do?) may refer, according to the sense, either to the next moment or to some later time. Greek has no subjunctive form denoting an intention to do this or that.
