In dependent constructions (including general conditions) the action of the present is generally coincident (rarely subsequent), that of the aorist is generally anterior (rarely coincident), to the action of the leading verb:

xalepai/nousi, e)peida\n au)toi=s paragge/llw pi/_nein to\ fa/rmakon they are angry whenever I bid them drink the poison
P. Ph. 116c, e)peida\n a(/pant' a)kou/shte, kri/_nate when you (shall) have heard everything, decide
D. 4.14. The use of the aorist of time relatively anterior to the action of the leading verb ( = Lat. future perfect) is, like its other references to relative time, only an inference from the connection of the thought (1850 a).
b. Present and aorist subjunctive are occasionally used in the same sentence without any great difference in sense (
X. C. 1.2.6-7, 5. 5. 13).
c. An independent or dependent subjunctive may be ingressive (1924): h)\n ga\r o( *plou=tos nuni\ ble/yh| for if now Plutus recovers his sight Ar. Pl. 494.
d. In general conditions (2336) the subjunctive refers to general time, denoting what holds true now and at all times.

§1861

Optative (not in indirect discourse).—The reference is always to future time. The tenses do not refer to differences of time, and denote only the stage of the action.
Present (continuance): plou/sion de\ nomi/zoimi to\n sofo/n may I (always) count the wise man wealthy
P. Phae. 279b; Aorist (simple occurrence):

ei) ga\r ge/noito would that it might happen
X. C. 6.1.38; Perfect (completion with permanent result): teqnai/hs die (lit. may you be dead)
*z 164.
a. In general conditions (2336) the optative is used of past time.
b. In dependent constructions (including general conditions) the action of the present is generally coincident (rarely anterior), that of the aorist generally anterior (rarely coincident), to the action of the leading verb: ei)/ tis ta/de parabai/noi, e)nagh\s e)/stw tou=) *apo/llwnos if any one violates this, let him be accurst of Apollo
Aes. 3.110, e)peidh\ de\ a)noixqei/h (to\ desmwth/rion), ei)sh=|men para\ to\n *swkra/th whenever the prison was opened, we (always) went in to Socrates
P. Ph. 59d. The aorist is often preferred to the more exact perfect because the perfect was rarely used.
c. An independent or dependent optative may be ingressive (1924): ei) polemh/saimen di' *)wrwpo/n, ou)de\n a)\n h(ma=s paqei=n h(gou=mai if we should enter upon a war on account of Oropus, I think we should suffer nothing
D. 5.16.

§1862

Optative (in indirect discourse).—When the optative in indirect discourse represents the indicative after a past tense of a verb of saying or thinking, each tense does denote time (as well as stage of action) relatively to that of the leading verb.
a. The present optative represents the imperfect as well as the present indicative.
b. The future optative (first in Pindar) occurs only in indirect discourse after verbs of saying and thinking, in object clauses after o(/pws, 2212, and in other indirect expressions of thought.
c. When the optative in indirect discourse represents the subjunctive (2619 b), its tenses denote only stage of action.

§1863

a. Present opt. = present indic.: a)nhrw/ta_ ti/ bou/lointo he demanded what they wanted ( = ti/ bou/lesqe;)
X. A. 2.3.4.
b. Present opt. = imperf. indic.: dihgou=nto o(/ti e)pi\ tou\s polemi/ous ple/oien they explained that they kept sailing against the enemy ( = e)ple/omen)
X. H. 1.7.5.
c. Future opt. = future indic.: o(/ ti poih/soi ou)de\ tou/tois ei)=pe he did not tell even these what he would do ( = poih/sw)
X. A. 2.2.2.
d. Aorist opt. = aorist indic.: h)rw/ta_ ti/ pa/qoien he asked what had happened to them ( = ti/ e)pa/qete;)
X. C. 2.3.19.
e. Perfect opt. = perfect indic.: e)/legon o(/ti oi( meta\ *dhmosqe/nous paradedw/koien sfa=s au)tou/s they said that the troops of Demosthenes had surrendered ( = paradedw/ka_si)
T. 7.83.

§1864

Imperative.—The imperative always implies future time. The tenses do not refer to differences of time, and denote only the stage of the action.
a. Present (continuance):

tou\s gonei=s ti(_ma_ honour thy parents
I. 1.16, pa/nta ta)_lhqh= le/ge tell (go on and tell in detail) the whole truth
L. 1.18,

tou\s i(/ppous e)kei/nois di/dote offer the horses to them
X. C. 4.5.47.
b. Aorist (simple occurrence): ble/yon pro\s ta\ o)/rh look (cast a glance) toward the mountains
X. A. 4.1.20, ei)pe/ state (in a word)
P. A. 24d,

h(mi=n tou\s i(/ppous do/te give the horses to us
X. C. 4.5.47.
c. Perfect (completion with permanent result): teta/xqw let him take his place (and stay there)
P. R. 562a, ei)rh/sqw let it have been said (once for all) 503 b.
N.—The perfect active and middle are generally used as presents (

teqna/tw let him be put to death
P. L. 938c,

me/mnhsqe remember
D. 40.30). The perfect passive (in the third person) is used of a fixed decision concerning what is to be done or has been done.

§1865

Infinitive (not in indirect discourse).—The tenses of the infinitive (without a)/n) not in indirect discourse have no time of themselves and express only the stage of the action; their (relative) time depends on the context and is that of the leading verb (present, past, or future). The infinitive may have the article (2025 ff.).
a. Present (continuance):

ou)de\ bouleu/esqai e)/ti w(/ra_, a)lla\ bebouleu=sqai it is time no longer to be making up one's mind, but to have it made up
P. Cr. 46a.
b. Aorist (simple occurrence):

tou= piei=n e)piqu_mi/a_ the desire of obtaining drink
T. 7.84, h)/rcato gene/sqai began to be 1. 103, but h)/rxeto gi/gnesqai 3. 18 (the tense of gi/gnomai depends on that of a)/rxomai; not h)/rcato gi/gnesqai), dei= tou\s u(pe\r au)tou= le/gontas mi_sh=sai (ingressive) one must conceive an aversion for those who speak in his behalf
D. 9.53.
c. Perfect (completion with permanent result): see a. Often of certainty of action.
d. Future.—When the context shows that stress is laid on the idea of futurity, the future infinitive, referring to future time relative to the main verb, is sometimes used instead of the present or aorist:

ou)k a)pokwlu/_sein dunatoi\ o)/ntes not being able to prevent
T. 3.28,

pollou= de/w kat' e)mautou= e)rei=n I am far from intending to speak to my own disadvantage
P. A. 37b. On the future infinitive with me/llw see 1959.
N. 1.—The action set forth by a dependent present or aorist infinitive (without a)/n) not in indirect discourse has no time except that which is implied by the context. With verbs signifying to advise or to command, and when the infinitive expresses purpose, the reference is to future time. Usually the action of the present and aorist is coincident with or antecedent to that of the main verb. The action of an aorist infinitive with the article and a subject is not always relatively past. The perfect (without a)/n) has no time apart from the context; its action is usually antecedent.
N. 2.—On the use of the present and aorist with verbs of promising, etc., see 1868; with me/llw, see 1959.
N. 3.—Observe that verbs denoting continuance (as me/nw remain) often appear in the aorist, while verbs of transitory action (as i(_e/nai send, hurl) often appear in the present.
N. 4.—Present and aorist occasionally occur in close conjunction without any great difference in meaning, as

prosh/kei u(_mi=n tou/tou katayhfi/zesqai . . ., dei= u(_ma=s qa/naton au)tou= katayhfi/sasqai it is fitting that you vote against him, it is necessary that you pass a vote of death against him
L. 13.69; cp. naumaxh=sai and naumaxei=n
T. 2.83, basanisth\s gi/gnesqai and gene/sqai
Ant. 1.10, 1. 11.

§1866

Infinitive (in indirect discourse).—The tenses of the infinitive in indirect discourse denote the same time relative to that of the leading verb (present, past, or future) as was denoted by the corresponding tenses of the indicative in direct discourse which they represent.
a. The present infinitive represents also the imperfect, the perfect infinitive represents also the pluperfect indicative.
b. The action of the present is usually coincident, that of the aorist anterior, to the action of the leading verb.
c. The future infinitive is found chiefly in indirect discourse and in analogous constructions. With me/llw, see 1959. It may have the article (2026).

§1867

a. Present = pres. indic.: fhmi\ tau=ta me\n flua_ri/a_s ei)=nai I say this is nonsense ( = e)sti/)
X. A. 1.3.18.
b. Present = imperf. indic: *kthsi/a_s i)_a=sqai au)to\s to\ trau=ma/ fhsi Ktesias asserts that he himself cured the wound ( = i)_w/mhn)
X. A. 1.8.26. With a)/n, 1846 a.
c. Future = fut. indic.: e)/fh h)\ a)/cein *lakedaimoni/ous h)\ au)tou= a)poktenei=n he said that he would either bring the Lacedaemonians or kill them on the spot ( = a)/cw, a)poktenw=)
T. 4.28.
d. Aorist = aor. indic.: e)ntau=qa le/getai *)apo/llwn e)kdei=rai *marsu/a_n there Apollo is said to have flayed Marsyas ( = e)ce/deire)
X. A. 1.2.8. With a)/n, 1848 a.
e. Perfect = perf. ind.: fhsi\ e)gkw/mion gegrafe/nai he says that he has written an encomium ( = ge/grafa)
I. 10.14, e)/fasan teqna/nai to\n a)/ndra they said the man was dead ( = te/qnhke)
Ant. 5.29.
f. Perfect = pluperf. ind.: le/getai a)/ndra tina\ e)kpeplh=xqai it is said that a certain man had been fascinated ( = e)cepe/plhkto)
X. C. 1.4.27. With a)/n, 1849.

§1868

The construction of verbs of hoping, etc.—Verbs signifying to hope, expect, promise, threaten, swear, with some others of like meaning, when they refer to a future event, take either the future infinitive (in indirect discourse), or the aorist, less often the present, infinitive (not in indirect discourse). The use of the aorist and present is due to the analogy of verbs of will or desire (1991) which take an object infinitive not in indirect discourse. The same analogy accounts for the use of mh/ instead of ou) (2725). The present or aorist infinitive with a)/n, representing the potential optative with a)/n, occurs occasionally.
a.

e)n e)lpi/di w)\n ta\ tei/xh tw=n *)aqhnai/wn ai(rh/sein hoping that he would capture the walls of the Athenians
T. 7.46,

e)lpi\s . . . e)ktrafh=nai hope of being brought up
L. 19.8,

e)lpi/zei dunato\s ei)=nai a)/rxein he expects to be able to rule
P. R. 573c, e)/xeis tina\ e)lpi/da mh\ a)\n . . . th\n nau=n a)pole/sai; have you any expectation that you would not shipwreck the vessel?
X. M. 2.6.38. e)lpi/zw with the present infinitive may mean I feel sure that I am.
b.

ta/xista ou)de/na ei)ko\s su\n au)tw=| boulh/sesqai ei)=nai it is probable that very soon no one will wish to be with him
X. C. 5.3.30,

h(ma=s ei)ko\s e)pikrath=sai it is likely that we shall succeed
T. 1.121, ou)k ei)ko\s au)tou\s periousi/a_n new=n e)/xein it is not likely that they will continue to have ships to spare 3. 13. With ei)ko/s the aorist is preferred.
c.

u(pe/sxeto tau=ta poih/sein he promised that he would do this
L. 12.14, u(pe/sxeto bouleu/sasqai (most Mss.) he promised to deliberate
X. A. 2.3.20. The aorist infinitive is especially common with verbs of promising and must refer to the future. With the present infinitive u(pisxnou=mai means I assure, profess, pledge my word that I am.
d. a)pei/lei e)ktri/_yein he threatened that he would destroy them
Hdt. 6.37,

h)pei/lhsan a)poktei=nai a(/pantas they threatened to kill everybody
X. H. 5.4.7.
e.

dika/sein o)mwmo/kate you have sworn that you will give judgment
D. 39.40, a)nagka/zei to\n *kersoble/pthn o)mo/sai . . . ei)=nai me\n th\n a)rxh\n koinh\n . . ., pa/ntas d' u(_mi=n a)podou=nai th\n xw/ra_n he compelled Cersobleptes to swear that the kingdom should be in common and that they should all restore to you the territory
D. 23.170.
f. With o)/mnu_mi a dependent infinitive may refer to the present, past, or future (e). Thus,

o)mnu/ntes ble/pein . . . *)axille/a_ pa/lin swearing that they see Achilles again
S. Ph. 357, o)mnu/ousi mh\ )kpiei=n they swear they did not drink Pherecrates 143 (Com. fr. I. 187), w)/mnue mhde\n ei)rhke/nai he swore that he had said nothing (direct = ou)de\n ei)/rhka)
D. 21.119.

§1869

Verbs of will or desire (1991) regularly take the present or aorist infinitive not in indirect discourse; but in some cases we find the future infinitive by assimilation to indirect discourse through the analogy of verbs of promising, etc. (1868). So with bou/lomai, e)qe/lw wish, le/gw meaning command, de/omai ask, e)fi/_emai desire and some others (even du/namai am able) that have a future action as their object. Thus,

e)fi_e/menoi a)/rcein being desirous to gain control
T. 6.6,

a)du/natoi e)pimelei=s e)/sesqai unable to be careful
X. O. 12.12. dianoou=mai may follow the analogy of me/llw (1959):

to\n po/lemon dienoou=nto proqu/_mws oi)/sein they intended to carry on the war with zeal
T. 4.121. In these and similar cases the future is employed to stress the future character of the action. Some editors would emend many of these futures.

§1870
Verbs signifying to foretell by oracle usually take the present or aorist infinitive like verbs signifying to command.

§1871
A few cases stand in our texts of an aorist infinitive referring to the future after a verb of saying or thinking, e.g. e)no/misan r(a|di/ws krath=sai they thought they would easily master them
T. 2.3. Many editors change to the future or insert a)/n.

§1872

Participle (not in indirect discourse).—The participle, as a verbal adjective, is timeless. The tenses of the participle express only continuance, simple occurrence, and completion with permanent result. Whether the action expressed by the participle is antecedent, coincident, or subsequent to that of the leading verb (in any tense) depends on the context. The future participle has a temporal force only because its voluntative force points to the future.
a. Present (continuative). The action set forth by the present participle is generally coincident (rarely antecedent or subsequent) to that of the leading verb:

e)rgazo/menai me\n h)ri/stwn, e)rgasa/menai de\ e)dei/pnoun the women took their noonday meal while they continued their work, but took their supper when they had stopped work
X. M. 2.7.12.
1. Antecedent action ( = imperf.):

oi( *ku/_reioi pro/sqen su\n h(mi=n tatto/menoi nu=n a)festh/ka_sin the forces of Cyrus that were formerly marshalled with us have now deserted
X. A. 3.2.17,

tou\s to/te paro/ntas ai)tia/_sontai sumbou/lous they will accuse those who were their counsellors at that time
P. G. 519a, oi( *kori/nqioi me/xri tou/tou proqu/_mws pra/_ssontes a)nei=san th=s filoneiki/a_s the Corinthians, who up to that time had been acting zealously, now slackened in their vehemence
T. 5.32. An adverb (pro/teron, pro/sqen, to/te, pote/) often accompanies the participle, which is sometimes called the participle of the imperfect.
2. Subsequent action (especially when the leading verb denotes motion): e)/pemyan pre/sbeis a)gge/llontas th\n tou= *plhmuri/ou lh=yin they despatched messengers to announce the capture of Plemyrium
T. 7.25. An attributive present part. w. nu=n may refer to the absolute present, though the main verb is past:

th\n nu=n *boiwti/a_n kaloume/nhn w)/|khsan they settled in the country now called Boeotia
T. 1.12.
3. The present participle denotes that an action is in process, is attempted, or is repeated.
b. Future (chiefly voluntative):

ou) sunh/lqomen w(s basilei= polemh/sontes we have not come together for the purpose of waging war with the king
X. A. 2.3.21.
c. Aorist (simple occurrence). The action set forth by the aorist participle is generally antecedent to that of the leading verb; but it is sometimes coincident or nearly so, when it defines, or is identical with, that of the leading verb, and the subordinate action is only a modification of the main action.
1. Antecedent:

deipnh/sa_s e)xw/rei after supper he advanced
T. 3.112, tou\s e)leuqe/rous a)poktei/nantes a)nexw/rhsan after killing the free men they withdrew 5. 83.

e)pomo/sa_s e)/fh he took an oath and said
X. C. 4.1.23,

h)/dh d' e)pi\ tau=ta poreu/somai tosou=ton au)to\n e)rwth/sa_s I shall at once proceed to this matter after having put to him certain questions
D. 18.124. The aorist participle is often thus used when it takes up the preceding verb:

nu=n me\n deipnei=te: deipnh/santes de\ a)pelau/nete take your supper now, and when you have done so, depart
X. C. 3.1.37.
2. Coincident:

mh/ ti e)cama/rthte e)mou= katayhfisa/menoi do not commit the error of condemning me
P. A. 30d,

eu)= g' e)poi/hsas a)namnh/sa_s me you did well in reminding me
P. Ph. 60c ( = a)ne/mnhsa/s me eu)= poiw=n). So also when an aorist participle is used with a future finite verb, as

a)pallaxqh/somai bi/ou qanou=sa by dying I shall be delivered from life
E. Hipp. 356. See also 2103.
3. The action of an attributive aorist participle is rarely subsequent to that of the leading verb. When this is the case, the action of the participle is marked as past from the point of view of the present (like the aor. indic.):

oi( *(/ellhnes u(/steron klhqe/ntes ou)de\n pro\ tw=n *trwi+kw=n a(qro/oi e)/pra_can the people later called Hellenes carried out no joint enterprise prior to the Trojan war
T. 1.3, *sa/turos kai\ *xre/mwn, oi( tw=n tria/_konta geno/menoi, *kleofw=ntos kathgo/roun Satyrus and Chremon, who (afterwards) became members of the Thirty, accused Cleophon
L. 30.12; cp. geno/menos
T. 2.49, 4. 81.
4. The aorist participle is often ingressive or complexive (1924, 1927).
d. Perfect (completion with permanent result): katalamba/nousi *bra_si/da_n e)pelhluqo/ta they found (historical present) that Brasidas had arrived
T. 3.69. A perfect participle may have the force of a pluperfect if accompanied by an adverb like pro/sqen (cp. 1872 a. 1):

o( pro/sqe kekthme/nos he who possessed it before
S. Ph. 778.

§1873

Construction of lanqa/nw, fqa/nw, tugxa/nw.—A supplementary aorist participle with any tense, except the present or imperfect, of lanqa/nw escape the notice of, fqa/nw anticipate, tugxa/nw happen usually coincides in time with the leading verb:

e)/laqon e)mauto\n ou)de\n ei)pw/n I was unconsciously talking nonsense
P. Ph. 76d,

lh/somen e)pipeso/ntes we shall fall on them unawares
X. A. 7.3.43. But the action of an aorist participle with the present or imperfect is generally prior to that of the leading verb:

o(/stis a)nteipw/n ge e)tu/gxane who chanced to have spoken in opposition
L. 12.27. See 2096.

§1874

Participle (in indirect discourse). The tenses of the participle in indirect discourse after verbs of intellectual perception denote the same time relative to that of the leading verb (present, past, or future) as was denoted by the corresponding tenses of the indicative in direct discourse which they represent. See 2106, 2112 b.
a. Present = pres. indic.: the action is generally coincident: e)peida\n gnw=sin a)pistou/menoi when they find out that they are distrusted ( = o(/ti a)pistou/meqa)
X. C. 7.2.17; rarely antecedent (when the present = the imperf. ind.): oi)=da/ se le/gonta a)ei/ I know that you always used to say ( = o(/ti e)/leges) 1. 6. 6.
b. Future = fut. indic.: a)gnoei= to\n po/lemon deu=r' h(/conta he is ignorant that the war will come here ( = o(/ti o( po/lemos h(/cei)
D. 1.15.
c. Aorist = aor. indic.: to\n *mh=don i)/smen e)pi\ th\n *pelopo/nnhson e)lqo/nta we know that the Mede came against the Peloponnese ( = o(/ti o( *mh=dos h)=lqe)
T. 1.69.
d. Perfect = perf. indic.: ou) ga\r h)/|desan au)to\n teqnhko/ta for they did not know that he was dead ( = o(/ti te/qnhke)
X. A. 1.10.16. The perfect may also represent the pluperfect (cp. 1872 d).

## TENSES OF THE INDICATIVE

## PRESENT INDICATIVE

§1875
The present represents a present state, or an action going on at the present time:

a)lhqh= le/gw I am telling the truth
L. 13.72.
a. On the present without any idea of duration, see 1853.

§1876

Present of Customary Action.—The present is used to express a customary or repeated action:

ou(=tos me\n ga\r u(/dwr, e)gw\ d' oi)=non pi/_nw for this man drinks water, whereas I drink wine
D. 19.46.

§1877

Present of General Truth.—The present is used to express an action that is true for all time:

a)/gei de\ pro\s fw=s th\n a)lh/qeian xro/nos time brings the truth to light
Men. Sent. 11.
a. The present is an absolute tense in such sentences. The future, aorist, and perfect may also express a general truth.

§1878

Conative Present.—The present may express an action begun, attempted, or intended.

th\n do/can tau/thn pei/qousin u(_ma=s a)pobalei=n they are trying to persuade you to throw away this renown
I. 6.12,

di/dwmi/ soi au)th\n tau/thn gunai=ka I offer you this woman herself as a wife
X. C. 8.5.19,

prodi/doton th\n *(ella/da they are trying to betray Greece
Ar. P. 408.
a. This use is found also in the infinitive and participle:

*fili/ppou e)pi\ *buza/ntion pario/ntos when Philip is preparing to advance against Byzantium
D. 8.66.
b. The idea of attempt or intention is an inference from the context and lies in the present only so far as the present does not denote completion.

§1879

Present for the Future (Present of Anticipation).—The present is used instead of the future in statements of what is immediate, likely, certain, or threatening.
metacu\ to\n lo/gon katalu/_omen; shall we break off in the middle?
P. G. 505c, kai\ ei) bou/lei, paraxwrw= soi tou= bh/matos, e(/ws a)\n ei)/ph|s and if you wish, I will yield you the floor until you tell us
Aes. 3.165,

a)po/llumai I am on the verge of ruin
Ant. 5.35 (so a)pw/lluto 5. 37 of past time),

ei) au(/th h( po/lis lhfqh/setai, e)/xetai kai\ h( pa=sa *sikeli/a_ if this city is taken, the whole of Sicily as well is in their power
T. 6.91.
a. Sometimes in questions to indicate that the decision must be made on the spot: h)\ pw=s le/gomen; or how shall we say? (what must we say?)
P. G. 480b.

§1880

ei)=mi is regularly future (I shall go) in the indicative present. In the subjunctive it is always future; in the optative, infinitive, and participle it may be either future or present. Cp. 774. In i)w\n tau=ta le/ge go and say this (
X. C. 4.5.17) i)w/n is used of time relatively past. In Hom. ei)=mi means both I go and I shall go.

§1881

e)/rxomai, poreu/omai, ne/omai (poet.) may be used in a future sense. xe/w means either I pour or I shall pour. e)/domai I shall eat, pi/_omai I shall drink, are present in form. Cp. 541.

§1882

Oracular Present.—In prophecies a future event may be regarded as present: xro/nw| a)grei= *pria/mou po/lin a(/_de ke/leuqos in time this expedition will capture Priam's city
A. Ag. 126.

§1883

Historical Present.—In lively or dramatic narration the present may be used to represent a past action as going on at the moment of speaking or writing. This use does not occur in Homer.
o( de\ *qemistoklh=s feu/gei e)s *ke/rku_ran . . . diakomi/zetai e)s th\n h)/peiron Themistocles fled (flees) to Corcyra . . . was (is) transported to the mainland
T. 1.136.
a. The historical present may represent either the descriptive imperfect or the narrative aorist.
b. The historical present may be coördinated with past tenses, which may precede or follow it:

a(/ma de\ th=| h(me/ra| th=| po/lei prose/keito kai\ ai(rei= at daybreak he assaulted the town and took it
T. 7.29,

ou(/tw dh\ a)pogra/fontai pa/ntes a)ne/labo/n te ta\ o(/pla accordingly they all enrolled themselves and took the arms
X. C. 2.1.19.
c. The historical present is less frequent in subordinate clauses (
T. 2.91. 3).

§1884

Annalistic Present.—Closely connected with the historical present is the annalistic present, which is used to register historical facts or to note incidents.
*da_rei/ou kai\ *parusa/tidos gi/gnontai pai=des du/o of Darius and Parysatis were (are) born two sons
X. A. 1.1.1, pro\ *aeutuxi/dew ga\r (*zeuci/dhmos) teleuta=| . . . *aeutuxi/dhs game/ei *eu)ruda/mhn, e)k th=s oi( . . . gi/_netai quga/thr for Zeuxidemus died before Leutychides . . . L. married Eurydame, from her was born to him a daughter
Hdt. 6.71,

kai\ o( e)niauto\s e)/lhgen, e)n w(=| *karxhdo/nioi ai(rou=si du/o po/leis *(ellhni/das and the year came to an end in which the Carthaginians captured two Greek cities
X. H. 1.1.37.

§1885

Present of Past and Present Combined.—The present, when accompanied by a definite or indefinite expression of past time, is used to express an action begun in the past and continued in the present. The ‘progressive perfect’ is often used in translation. Thus, pa/lai qauma/zw I have been long (and am still) wondering
P. Cr. 43b. Cp. iamdudum loquor. So with pa/ros, pote/. This use appears also in the other moods.
a. So with verbs of hearing, saying, learning, whose action commenced in the past, but whose effect continues into the present: e)c w(=n a)kou/w from what I hear (have heard)
X. A. 1.9.28,

o(/per le/gw as I said
P. A. 21a. So with ai)sqa/nomai, gignw/skw, manqa/nw, punqa/nomai. a)/rti just is often found with these verbs.
b. The perfect is used instead of the present when the action is completed in the present.

§1886

Present for Perfect.—h(/kw I am come, I have arrived, oi)/xomai I am gone, have a perfect sense; as also e)/rxomai, a)fiknou=mai. Thus,

*qemistoklh=s h(/kw para\ se/ I Themistocles have come to you
T. 1.137,

oi)=da o(/ph| oi)/xontai I know where they have gone
X. A. 1.4.8.
a. h(/kw may be used in connection with the gnomic aorist (
P. S. 188a).

§1887
The present of certain verbs often expresses an enduring result, and may be translated by the perfect: a)dikw= I am guilty (a)/diko/s ei)mi), I have done wrong, ni_kw=, kratw=, I am victorious, I have conquered, h(ttw=mai I am conquered, feu/gw I am the defendant or I am an exile (oi( feu/gontes the fugitives and the exiles), prodi/dwmi I am a traitor, a(li/skomai I am captured, ste/romai I am deprived, gi/gnomai I am a descendant.

h(/kw ei)s th\n sh\n oi)ki/a_n, a)dikw= d' ou)de/n I am come to thy house, but have done no wrong
L. 12.14,

a)pagge/llete *)ariai/w| o(/ti h(mei=s ge ni_kw=men basile/a_ report to Ariaeus that we at least have conquered the king
X. A. 2.1.4.
a. So, in poetry, gennw=, fu/_w, ti/ktw, qnh/|skw, o)/llumai. Thus, h(/de ti/ktei se this woman (has born thee = ) is thy mother
E. Ion 1560.

§1888
In subordinate clauses, the action expressed by the present may be (a) contemporaneous, (b) antecedent, or (c) subsequent to that set forth by the main verb. The context alone decides in which sense the present is to be taken: (a)

e)/legen o(/ti e(/toimos ei)/h h(gei=sqai au)toi=s he said that he was ready to lead them
X. A. 6.1.33; (b) when the present states an action begun in the past and continued in the present: e)pei/te de\ *pe/rsai e)/xousi to\ kra/tos, (to\ pedi/on)

e)sti\ tou= basile/os from the time that the Persians began to hold sway, it belongs to the king
Hdt. 3.117; and with the historical present:

w(s de\ gi/gnontai e)p' au)tw=|, e)spi/_ptousin when they came to it, they rushed in
T. 7.84; (c)

e)ge/neto r(h/tra_ . . . ei) para\ tau=ta poioi=en, kola/zein an ordinance was passed . . if they act contrary to this, to punish them
X. C. 1.6.33.

## IMPERFECT

§1889
The imperfect represents an action as still going on, or a state as still existing, in the past: *ku=ros ou)/pw h(=ken, a)ll' e)/ti prosh/laune Cyrus had not yet arrived (1886), but was still marching on
X. A. 1.5.12,

e)basi/leuen *)anti/oxos Antiochus was reigning
T. 2.80. The conclusion of the action is usually to be inferred from the context.

§1890

Imperfect of Continuance.—The imperfect thus represents an action as continuing in the past: die/fqeiran *)aqhnai/wn pi/nte kai\ ei)/kosi, oi(\ cunepoliorkou=nto they put to death twenty-five of the Athenians who were besieged (i.e. from the beginning to the end of the siege)
T. 3.68.

§1891
The imperfect of verbs of sending, going, saying, exhorting, etc., which imply continuous action, is often used where we might expect the aorist of concluded action. Thus, in e)/pempon, the action is regarded as unfinished since the goal is not reached:

a)/ggelon e)/pempon kai\ tou\s nekrou\s u(pospo/ndous a)pe/dosan they sent a messenger and surrendered the dead under a truce
T. 2.6. In e)ke/leuon gave orders, urged, requested the command, etc., is regarded as not yet executed. In

e)/legen au)toi=s toia/de he spoke to them as follows
X. H. 1.6.4 (followed by the speech and e)pei\ de\ tau=t' ei)=pen 1. 6. 12) the speech is not thought of as a finished whole, but as developed point by point, as in e)pe)idh\ de\ ou(=tos tau=ta e)/legen, e)/leca but when he had said this, I said
Ant. 6.21.
a. In messenger's speeches the speaker may go back to the time of receiving a command:

i)e/nai s' e)ke/leuon oi( strathgoi\ th/meron the generals order you to depart to-day
Ar. Ach. 1073.

§1892
The imperfect, when accompanied by an expression of past time, is used of actions which had been in progress for some time and were still in progress (cp. 1885):

to\ *(ph/gion e)pi\ polu\n xro/non e)stasi/aze Rhegium had been for a long time in a state of faction
T. 4.1. If the action is regarded as completed the pluperfect is used.

§1893

Imperfect of Customary Action.—The imperfect is used to express frequently repeated or customary past actions:

e)pei\ ei)=don au)to\n oi(/per pro/sqen proseku/noun, kai\ to/te proseku/nhsan when they caught sight of him, the very men who before this were wont to prostrate themselves before him, prostrated themselves on this occasion also
X. A. 1.6.10, (*swkra/ths) tou\s e(autou= e)piqu_mou=ntas ou)k e)pra/_tteto xrh/mata Socrates was not in the habit of demanding money from those who were passionately attached to him
X. M. 1.2.5. See also 2340.
a. The repetition of a simple act in the past is expressed by polla/kis with the aorist (1930).

§1894

Iterative Imperfect.—a)/n may be used with this imperfect (1790): e)pequ/_mei a)/n tis e)/ti plei/w au)tou= a)kou/ein people would (used to) desire to hear still more from him
X. C. 1.4.3.

§1895

Conative Imperfect.—The imperfect may express an action attempted, intended, or expected, in the past.
e)/peiqon au)tou/s, kai\ ou(\s e)/peisa, tou/tous e)/xwn e)poreuo/mhn I tried to persuade them, and I marched away with those whom I succeeded in persuading
X. C. 5.5.22, *(alo/nnhson e)di/dou: o( d' a)phgo/reue mh\ lamba/nein Philip offered (proposed to give) Halonnesus, but he (Demosthenes) dissuaded them from accepting it
Aes. 3.83,

*qhbai=oi katedoulou=nt' au)tou/s the Thebans tried to enslave them
D. 8.74,

h)pei/gonto e)s th\n *ke/rku_ran they were for pushing on to Corcyra
T. 4.3.
a. Here may be placed the imperfect equivalent in sense to e)/mellon with the infinitive. Thus, foneu\s ou)=n au)tw=n e)gigno/mhn e)gw\ mh\ ei)pw\n u(_ui=n a(\ h)/kousa. e)/ti de\ tria_kosi/ous *)aqhnai/wn a)pw/lluon I was on the point of becoming their murderer (interfecturus eram) had I not told you what I heard. And besides I threatened three hundred Athenians with death
And. 1.58. So a)pwllu/mhn I was threatened with death.

§1896

Imperfect of Resistance or Refusal.—With a negative, the imperfect often denotes resistance or refusal (would not or could not). The aorist with a negative denotes unrestricted denial of a fact.

th\n pro/klhsin ou)k e)de/xesqe you would not accept the proposal
T. 3.64 (th\n i(ketei/a_n ou)k e)de/canto they did not receive the supplication 1. 24),

o( me\n ou)k e)ga/mei, o( de\ e)/ghmen the one would not marry, the other did
D. 44.17,

ou)de\ fwnh\n h)/kouon, ei)/ tis a)/llo ti bou/loito le/gein they would not even listen to a syllable if ever any one wished to say anything to the contrary
D. 18.43. So ou)k ei)/a_ he would not allow (he was not for allowing).

§1897
If simple positive and negative are contrasted, the aorist is preferred with the latter: ta\ u(pa/rxonta/ te sw/|zein (positive with present) kai\ e)pignw=nai mhde/n (negative with aorist) to preserve what you have, and to form no new plans
T. 1.70. But where the verb itself contains or implies a negative idea, the present is used:

parei=nai kai\ mh\ a)podhmei=n to be present and not to be abroad
Aes. 2.59.

§1898

Imperfect of Description.—The imperfect describes manners and customs; the situation, circumstances, and details, of events; and the development of actions represented as continuing in past time.
e)kei=no/s te tou\s u(f' e(autw=| w(/sper e(autou= pai=das e)ti/_ma_, oi(/ te a)rxo/menoi *ku=ron w(s pate/ra e)se/bonto he (Cyrus) treated his subjects with honour as if they were his own children, and his subjects reverenced Cyrus like a father
X. C. 8.8.2, eu)qu\s a)nebo/hsa/n te pa/ntes kai\ prospeso/ntes e)ma/xonto, e)w/qoun, e)wqou=nto, e)/paion, e)pai/onto immediately all raised a shout and falling upon each other fought, pushed and were pushed, struck and were struck 7. 1. 38, e)pei\ de\ tau=ta e)rrh/qh, e)poreu/onto: tw=n de\ a)pantw/ntwn oi( me\n a)pe/qnh|skon, oi( de\ e)/feugon pa/lin ei)/sw, oi( de\ e)bo/wn and when these words had been spoken, they proceeded to advance; and of those who met them some were killed, others fled back indoors, and others shouted 7. 5. 26,

e)strath/gei de\ au)tw=n *)aristeu/s Aristeus was their commander
T. 1.60; cp.
X. C. 4.2.28, X. Ag. 2. 12,
X. A. 4.3.8-25, Isocr. 1. 9, 7. 51-53,
D. 18.169 ff.,
Aes. 3.192.
N.—The imperfect often has a dramatic or panoramic force: it enables the reader to follow the course of events as they occurred, as if he were a spectator of the scene depicted.

§1899
The imperfect is thus often used to explain, illustrate, offer reasons for an action, and to set forth accompanying and subordinate circumstances that explain or show the result of the main action. Descriptive adverbs are often used with the imperfect.
e)ntau=qa e)/meinen h(me/ra_s pe/nte: kai\ toi=s stratiw/tais w)fei/leto misqo\s ple/on h)\ triw=n mhnw=n, kai\ polla/kis i)o/ntes e)pi\ ta\_s qu/ra_s a)ph/|toun: o( de\ e)lpi/das le/gwn dih=ge kai\ dh=los h)=n a)niw/menos there he remained for five days; and the soldiers whose pay was in arrears for more than three months kept going to headquarters and demanding their dues; but he kept expressing his expectation (of making payment) and was plainly annoyed
X. A. 1.2.11. See also 1907 a.

§1900

Inchoative Imperfect.—The imperfect may denote the beginning of an action or of a series of actions: e)peidh\ de\ kairo\s h)=n, prose/ballon but when the proper time arrived, they began an (proceeded to) attack
T. 7.51.

§1901

Imperfect for Present.—In descriptions of places and scenery and in other statements of existing facts the imperfect, instead of the present, is often used by assimilation to the time of the narrative (usually set forth in the main verb).

a)fi/_konto e)pi\ to\n potamo\n o(\s w(/rize th\n tw=n *makrw/nwn xw/ra_n kai\ th\n tw=n *skuqhnw=n they came to the river which divided the country of the Macrones from that of the Scytheni
X. A. 4.8.1, e)celau/nei e)pi\ potamo\n plh/rh i)xqu/wn, ou(\s oi( *su/roi qeou\s e)no/mizon he marched to a river full of fish, which the Syrians regarded as gods 1. 4. 9.

§1902

—Imperfect of a Truth Just Recognized.—The imperfect, usually some form of ei)=nai, with a)/ra, is often used to denote that a present fact or truth has just been recognized, although true before: ou)de\n a)/r' h)=n pra=gma it is, as it appears, no matter after all
P. S. 198e,

tou=t' a)/r' h)=n a)lhqe/s this is true after all
E. I. T. 351,

a)/ra h)pi/stw you know, sure enough
X. H. 3.4.9. a)/ra sure enough, after all appears with other tenses (
P. Cr. 49a,
P. Ph. 61a,
D. 19.160).

§1903
The imperfect may refer to a topic previously discussed: h)=n h( mousikh\ a)nti/strofos th=s gumnastikh=s ei) me/mnhsai music is (as we have seen) the counterpart of gymnastics, if you remember the discussion
P. R. 522a. This is called the philosophical imperfect.

§1904
The epistolary imperfect is rare in Greek. See 1942 b.

§1905

e)/dei, e)xrh=n.—The imperfect of verbs expressing obligation or duty may refer to present time and imply that the obligation or duty is not fulfilled:

si_gh/sa_s h(ni/k' e)/dei le/gein keeping silence when he ought to speak
D. 18.189. So with e)xrh=n it were proper, ei)ko\s h)=n it were fitting (1774). But the imperfect may also express past obligation without denying the action of the infinitive, as e)/dei me/nein he was obliged to remain (and did remain)
D. 19.124, o(/per e)/dei dei=cai quod erat demonstrandum Euclid 1. 5 (1779).

§1906

Imperfect for Pluperfect.—The imperfect has the force of the pluperfect in the case of verbs whose present is used in the sense of the perfect (1886).
Thus, h(=kon I had come (rarely I came), w)|xo/mhn I had departed, as e)ni/_kwn I was victorious, h(ttw/mhn I was defeated (1752). So (*)olu/mpia) oi(=s *)androsqe/nhs pagkra/tion e)ni/_ka_ the Olympic games, at which Androsthenes was the victor (= had won) in the pancratium
T. 5.49.

§1907
In subordinate clauses, the action expressed by the imperfect may be (a) contemporaneous with or (b) antecedent to that set forth by the main verb: (a)

tosou=toi h)=san oi( cu/mpantes o(/te e)s th\n poliorki/a_n kaqi/_stanto this was their total number when they began to be besieged
T. 2.78; (b) to\ ploi=on h(=ken, e)n w(=| e)ple/omen the vessel arrived in which we (had) sailed
Ant. 5.29. Greek has no special form to express time that is anterior to the past.

§1908

Imperfect and Aorist.—The imperfect and aorist often occur in the same passage; and the choice of the one or the other often depends upon the manner in which the writer may view a given action. The imperfect may be represented by a line, along which an action progresses; the aorist denotes a point on the line (either starting point or end), or surveys the whole line from beginning to end.
a. The imperfect of ‘continuance’ or ‘duration’ implies nothing as to the absolute length of the action; cp.

pa/lin kata\ ta/xos e)ko/mize th\n stratia/_n he took the army back as quickly as possible
T. 1.114 with kata\ ta/xos a)nexw/rhse he retreated as quickly as possible 1. 73. The imperfect does not indicate ‘prolonged’ action in contrast to ‘momentary’ action of the aorist.
b. The imperfect puts the reader in the midst of the events as they were taking place, the aorist simply reports that an event took place: e)/peita yi_loi\ dw/deka a)ne/bainon, w(=n h(gei=to *)amme/a_s, kai\ prw=tos a)ne/bh then twelve light-armed men proceeded to climb up under the leadership of Ammeas, who was the first to mount
T. 3.22. Cp.
T. 2.49, 3. 15. 1-2, 4. 14,
X. H. 4.4.1,
I. 5.53-54, 8. 99-100.

§1909
The following statement presents the chief differences between imperfect and aorist as narrative tenses.

ImperfectAorist

circumstances, details, course ofmere fact of occurrence, general state-

actionment

progress, enduring condition, con-consummation (culmination, final is-

tinued activitysue, summary process)

general descriptionisolated points, characteristic examples

endeavourattainment

actions subordinate to the mainmain actions, without reference to

actionother actions
Cp. cunestra/teuon they served with them in the war, cunestra/teusan they took the field with them (both in
T. 7.57). e)/peiqon I tried to persuade, e)/peisa I succeeded in persuading (both in
X. C. 5.5.22).

## FUTURE INDICATIVE

§1910
The future denotes an action that will take place at some future time:

lh/yetai misqo\n ta/lanton he shall receive a talent as his reward
X. A. 2.2.20.
a. The action is future according to the opinion, expectation, hope, fear, or purpose of the speaker or the agent.
b. The action of the future is either continuative (like the present) or, like that of the aorist, expresses simple attainment. Thus pei/sw means I shall try to persuade , or I shall convince (resultative), basileu/sw I shall be king, shall reign or I shall become king (ingressive).

§1911
When a verb has two futures, that formed from the same stem as the present is properly continuative, that formed from the aorist stem marks simple attainment: thus, e(/cw I shall have, sxh/sw I shall get; as kai\ tau=t' ei)ko/tws ou(/tws

u(pela/mbanon e(/cein and I supposed with reason that this would continue so
D. 19.153, *qhbai=oi e)/xousi me\n a)pexqw=s, e)/ti d' e)xqrote/rws sxh/sousin the Thebans are hostile and will become still more so 5. 18. (But e(/cw usually does duty for sxh/sw.) So, a)xqe/somai shall be angry, a)xqesqh/somai shall get angry, fobh/somai shall continue fearful, fobhqh/somai shall be terrified, ai)sxunou=mai shall feel (continued) shame, ai)sxunqh/somai shall be ashamed (on a single occasion). Cp. 1738.

§1912
The future represents both our shall and will. When voluntative (will), the action of the subject may be (1) the result of his own decision, as

ou) dh\ poih/sw tou=to that I never will do
D. 18.11, or (2) dependent on the will of another, as

h( boulh\ me/llei ai(rei=sqai o(/stis e)rei= e)pi\ toi=s a)poqanou=si the Senate is about to choose some one to speak over the dead
P. Menex. 234b. The use of the future is often similar to that of the subjunctive, especially in dependent clauses.

§1913

Verbs of wishing, asking, and other voluntative verbs may appear in the future where English has the present: tosou=ton ou)=n sou tugxa/nein boulh/somai I (shall) wish to obtain only so much at thy hands
E. Med. 259, paraith/somai d' u(_ma=s mhde\n a)xqesqh=nai/ moi I (shall) beg you not to take any offence at me
D. 21.58. Cp. Lat. censebo.
a. In many cases the use of the future indicates that the wish remains unchanged; and there is no reference to a future act. Sometimes the future appears to be a more modest form of statement than the present.

§1914

Gnomic Future.—The future may express a general truth: a)nh\r e)pieikh\s ui(o\n a)pole/sa_s r(a=|sta oi)/sei tw=n a)/llwn a reasonable man, if he loses a son, will (is expected to) bear it more easily than other men
P. R. 603e (cp. 1434).
a. Hdt. uses the future in descriptions of customs and in directions to travellers (1. 173, 2. 29).

§1915

Future for Present.—The future may be used instead of the present of that which is possible at the moment of speaking:

eu(rh/somen tou\s filoti/_mous tw=n a)ndrw=n . . . a)nti\ tou= zh=n a)poqnh/|skein eu)klew=s ai(roume/nous we shall find that ambitious men choose a glorious death in preference to life
I. 9.3.
a. The future may denote present intention:

ai)=re plh=ktron, ei) maxei= raise your spur if you mean to fight
Ar. Av. 759 (in this use me/llw is more common (1959)). So in the tragic ti/ le/ceis; what do you mean?
E. Med. 1310.

§1916

Deliberative Future.—The future is often used in deliberative questions: ti/ e)rou=men h)\ ti/ fh/somen; what shall we say or what shall we propose?
D. 8.37.
a. The deliberative future may occur in connection with the deliberative subjunctive (1805): ei)/pwmen h)\ si_gw=men; h)\ ti/ dra/_somen; shall we speak or keep silent? or what shall we do?
E. Ion 758.

§1917

Jussive Future.—The future may express a command, like the imperative; and, in the second person, may denote concession or permission. The negative is ou). The tone of the jussive future (which is post-Homeric) is generally familiar.

w(\s ou)=n poih/sete you will do thus
P. Pr. 338a, a)nagnw/setai to\n no/mon—a)nagi/gnwske the clerk will read the law—read
D. 24.39,

au)to\s gnw/sei you will judge for yourself
P. Phil. 12a,

spoudh\ e)/stai th=s o(dou= you will have to hurry on the march
T. 7.77, u(_mei=s ou)=n, e)a\_n swfronh=te, ou) tou/tou a)ll' u(_mw=n fei/sesqe now, if you are wise, you will spare, not him, but yourselves
X. H. 2.3.34.

§1918
The future with ou) interrogative is used in questions in an imperative sense to express urgency, warning, or irony: ou)k e)/cimen . . . ou)k e)pi\ th\n e)kei/nou pleuso/meqa; shall we not go forth . . . shall we not set sail against his country?
D. 4.44, ou) fula/cesqe; will you not be on your guard? 6. 25. In exhortations addressed to oneself: ou)k a)pallaxqh/somai qu_mou=; shall I not cease from my passion?
E. Med. 878.
a. mh/ with the future in a prohibitive sense is used in a few suspected passages (
L. 29.13,
D. 23.117).

§1919

ou) mh/ with the second person singular of the future in the dramatic poets denotes a strong prohibition; as ou) mh\ diatri/_yeis don't dawdle (you shall not dawdle)
Ar. Ran. 462. ou) mh/ with any person of the future indicative occasionally denotes an emphatic future denial; as

tou\s ponhrou\s ou) mh/ pote belti/_ous poih/sete you will never make the bad better
Aes. 3.177.

§1920

o(/pws and o(/pws mh/ are used with the future in urgent exhortations and prohibitions:

o(/pws ou)=n e)/sesqe a)/cioi th=s e)leuqeri/a_s prove yourselves then worthy of freedom
X. A. 1.7.3,

o(/pws toi/nun peri\ tou= pole/mou mhde\n e)rei=s say nothing therefore about the war
D. 19.92. For the fuller form of this use after sko/pei, skopei=te. see 2213.

§1921

o(/pws mh/ (negative o(/pws mh\ ou)) may express the desire to avert something; as o(/pws mh\ ai)sxroi\ fainou/meqa mind we don't appear base
X. C. 4.2.39, a)ll' o(/pws mh\ ou)x oi(=o/s t' e)/somai but (I fear that) I shall not be able
P. R. 506d. Cp. 1802, 1803, 2229.

§1922
On a)/n (ke/) with the future indicative, see 1793. On the periphrastic future see 1959; on the future in dependent clauses, see 2203, 2211, 2220 a, 2229, 2231, 2328, 2549-2551, 2554, 2558, 2559, 2565 a, 2573 c.

## AORIST INDICATIVE

§1923
The aorist expresses the mere occurrence of an action in the past. The action is regarded as an event or single fact without reference to the length of time it occupied.

e)ni/_khsan oi( *kerku_rai=oi kai\ nau=s pe/nte kai\ de/ka die/fqeiran the Corcyraeans were victorious and destroyed fifteen ships
T. 1.29,

*paiw/nios e)poi/hse Paeonius fecit
I.G.A. /lref>, e)/docen th=| boulh=| it was voted by (seemed good to) the Senate
C.I.A. /lref>
a. The uses of the aorist may be explained by the figure of a point in time:
1. The starting point (ingressive aorist, 1924); 2. The end point (resultative aorist, 1926); 3. The whole action (beginning to end) concentrated to a point (complexive aorist, 1927).

§1924

Ingressive Aorist.—The aorist of verbs whose present denotes a state or a continued action, expresses the entrance into that state or the beginning of that action.
a. This holds true of the other moods. Greek has no special form to denote entrance into a state in present time (1853).

§1925
Most of the verbs in question are denominatives, and the forms are chiefly those of the first aorist:—

a)/rxw ruleh)=rca became ruler

basileu/w am king, rulee)basi/leusa became king, ascended the throne

ble/pw look ate)/bleya cast a glance

dakru/_w weepe)da/kru_sa burst into tears

douleu/w am a slavee)dou/leusa became a slave

e)rw= loveh)ra/sqhn fell in love

qarrw= am courageouse)qa/rrhsa plucked up courage

nosw= am ille)no/shsa fell ill

ploutw= am riche)plou/thsa became rich

polemw= make ware)pole/mhsa began the war

si_gw= am silente)si/_ghsa became silent
a. Rarely with the second aorist: e)/sxon took hold, took possession of, got, as

*peisistra/tou teleuth/santos *(ippi/a_s e)/sxe th\n a)rxh/n when Peisistratus died Hippias succeeded to his power
T. 6.54. So h)|sqo/mhn became aware, e)/sthn took my stand (perfect e(/sthka am standing).
b. The aorist of these verbs denotes also a simple occurrence of the action as an historical fact: e)basi/leusa was king, ruled, e)no/shsa was ill. Thus,

e)kei=noi pe/nte kai\ tettara/konta e)/th tw=n *(ellh/nwn h)=rcan they held the supremacy over Greece for forty-five years
D. 3.24 (cp. 1927 b).

§1926

Resultative Aorist.—In contrast to the imperfect (and present) the aorist denotes the result, end, or effect of an action.
Thus, h)/gagon I brought, e)bou/leusa I decided (e)bou/leuon I was deliberating), e)/qhca I sharpened, e)/peson I struck in falling (e)/pi_pton I was in the act of falling), e)/peisa I succeeded in persuading (1895).
a. The same verb may be a resultative aorist or an ingressive aorist. Thus, e)/balon I let fly a missile (ingressive), and I hit (resultative); kate/sxon I got possession of (ingressive), and I kept back (resultative).
b. e)/kteina/ se
E. Ion 1291 means I tried to kill you, since ktei/nw denotes properly only the act of the agent, and does not, like kill, also connote the effect of the action upon another.

§1927

Complexive Aorist.—The complexive aorist is used to survey at a glance the course of a past action from beginning to end:

tou/tw| tw=| tro/pw| th\n po/lin e)tei/xisan it was in this manner that they fortified the city
T. 1.93. It may sum up the result of a preceding narrative (often containing imperfects, as
T. 2.47. 4; 3. 81). The complexive aorist appears also in other moods than the indicative.
a. This is often called the ‘concentrative’ aorist, because it concentrates the entire course of an action to a single point. When used of rapid or instantaneous action this aorist is often called ‘momentary.’
b. The complexive aorist is used either of a long or of a short period of time:

te/ssara kai\ de/ka e)/th e)ne/meinan ai( spondai/ the peace lasted fourteen years
T. 2.2, o)li/gon xro/non cune/meinen h( o(maixmi/a_ the league lasted a short time 1. 18, h)=lqon, ei)=don, e)ni/_khsa veni, vidi, vici (“Caesar's brag of came, and saw, and conquered”) Plutarch, Caes. 50.

§1928
The aorist is commonly used with definite numbers. The imperfect is, however, often employed when an action is represented as interrupted or as proceeding from one stage to another. Thus,

e)ntau=qa e)/meine *ku=ros h(me/ra_s tria/_konta Cyrus remained thirty days there
X. A. 1.2.9;

te/ttaras mh=nas o(/lous e)sw/|zonto oi( *fwkei=s tou\s u(/steron, h( de\ tou/tou yeudologi/a_ meta\ tau=q' u(/steron au)tou\s a)pw/lesen for the four whole ensuing months the Phocians remained safe, but the falsehood of this man afterwards effected their ruin
D. 19.78.

§1929
The aorist enumerates and reports past events. It may be employed in brief continuous narration (
X. A. 1.9.6). As a narrative tense it is often used to state the chief events and facts, while the other past tenses set forth subordinate actions and attendant circumstances.

§1930

Empiric Aorist.—With adverbs signifying often, always, sometimes, already, not yet, never, etc., the aorist expressly denotes a fact of experience (e)mpeiri/a_).

polloi\ polla/kis meizo/nwn e)piqu_mou=ntes ta\ paro/nt' a)pw/lesan many men often lose what they have from a desire for greater possessions
D. 23.113,

a)qu_mou=ntes a)/ndres ou)/pw tropai=on e)/sthsan faint heart never yet raised a trophy
P. Criti. 108c. So with polu/s:

h( glw=ssa pollou\s ei)s o)/leqron h)/gagen the tongue brings many a man to his ruin
Men. Sent. 205. From this use proceeds 1931.
a. The empiric aorist is commonly to be translated by the present or perfect. The statement in the aorist is often based upon a concrete historical fact set forth in the context, and the reader is left to infer that the thought holds good for all time.

§1931

Gnomic Aorist (gnw/mh maxim, proverb).—The aorist may express a general truth. The aorist simply states a past occurrence and leaves the reader to draw the inference from a concrete case that what has occurred once is typical of what often occurs: paqw\n de/ te nh/pios e)/gnw a fool learns by experience Hesiod, Works and Days, 218,

ka/llos me\n ga\r h)\ xro/nos a)nh/lwsen h)\ no/sos e)ma/ra_ne for beauty is either wasted by time or withered by disease
I. 1.6.
a. The gnomic aorist often alternates with the present of general truth (1877): ou) ga\r h( plhgh\ pare/sthse th\n o)rgh/n, a)ll' h( a)ti_mi/a_: ou)de\ to\ tu/ptesqai toi=s e)leuqe/rois e)sti\ deino/n . . . a)lla\ to\ e)f' u(/brei for it is not the blow that causes anger, but the disgrace; nor is it the beating that is terrible to freemen, but the insult
D. 21.72. Cp.
P. R. 566e.
b. The gnomic aorist is regarded as a primary tense (1858):

oi( tu/rannoi plou/sion o(\n a)\n bou/lwntai paraxrh=m' e)poi/hsan tyrants make rich in a moment whomever they wish
D. 20.15.

§1932
Akin to the gnomic aorist is the aorist employed in general descritions. So in imaginary scenes and in descriptions of manners and custom Thus, e)peida\n a)fi/kwntai oi( teteleuthko/tes ei)s to\n to/pon, oi(= o( dai/mwn e(/kaston komi/z prw=ton me\n diedika/santo oi(/ te kalw=s kai\ o(si/ws biw/santes kai\ oi( mh/ when the de<*> reach the place whither each is severally conducted by his genius, first of all the have judgment pronounced upon them as they have lived well and devoutly not
P. Ph. 113d, fa=ros de\ au)thmero\n e)cufh/nantes oi( i(_re/es kat' w)=n e)/dhsan e(no\s au)t<*> mi/trh| tou\s o)fqalmou/s after having woven a mantle on the same day the pries bind the eyes of one of their number with a snood
Hdt. 2.122.

§1933

Iterative Aorist.—With a)/n the aorist may denote repetition (1790)

ei)=pen a)/n he used to say
X. C. 7.1.14. Distinguish 2303.

§1934

Aorist for Future.—The aorist may be substituted for the futur when a future event is vividly represented as having actually occurred: a)pwl<*> mhn a)/r', ei)/ me dh\ lei/yeis I am undone if thou dost leave me
E. Alc. 386.

§1935

Aorist in Similes.—The aorist is used in similes in poetry, and usually contains the point of comparison. It may alternate with the present. Thus

h)/ripe d' w(s o(/te tis dru=s h)/ripen he fell as falls an oak
*p 482, oi(=os d' e)k nefe/wn a)na fai/netai ou)/lios a)sth\r | pamfai/nwn, to/te d' au)=tis e)/du_ ne/fea skio/enta, | w(\s *(/ektwr ktl and as from out of the clouds all radiant appears a baneful star, and then again sinks within the shadowy clouds, so Hector, etc.
*a 62.
a. The aorist in 1931, 1935 is used of time past (in 1934 of the future), from the point of view of an assumed or ideal present.

§1936

Aorist for Present.—The aorist is used in questions with ti/ ou)=n ou and ti/ ou) to express surprise that something has not been done. The question is here equivalent to a command or proposal: ti/ ou)=n ou)xi\ kai\ su\ u(pe/mnhsa/s me, why don't you recall it to my mind?
X. Hi. 1.3. The (less lively) present, and the future, may also be used.

§1937

Dramatic Aorist.—The first person singular of the aorist is used in the dialogue parts of tragedy and comedy to denote a state of mind or an act expressing a state of mind (especially approval or disapproval) occurring to the speaker in the moment just passed. This use is derived from familiar discourse, but is not found in good prose. In translation the present is employed. Thus, h(/sqhn, e)ge/lasa I am delighted, I can't help laughing
Ar. Eq. 696,

e)deca/mhn to\ r(hqe/n I welcome the omen
S. El. 668 (prose de/xomai to\n oi)wno/n). So e)ph/|nesa I approve, cunh=ka I understand. Sometimes this use appears outside of dialogue (

a)pe/ptusa I spurn
A. Pr. 1070, Ag. 1193).

§1938
With verbs of swearing, commanding, saying , and advising the aorist may denote a resolution that has already been formed by the speaker and remains unalterable: se\ . . . ei)=pon th=sde gh=s e)/cw pera=n I command thee (once and for all) to depart from out this land
E. Med. 272, a)pw/mosa I swear ‘nay’
S. Ph. 1289. This use is not confined to dialogue.

§1939
So in other cases: pw=s tou=t' e)/lecas; ou) ka/toid' o(/pws le/geis how saidst thou (what dost thou mean）? I do not know how thou meanest
S. Aj. 270. Cp. nu=n with the aorist (B 113,
*g 439).

§1940

Aorist for Perfect.—In Greek the aorist, which simply states a past occurrence, is often employed where English uses the perfect denoting a present condition resulting from a past action. Thus, pareka/lesa u(_ma=s, a)/ndres fi/loi I (have) summoned you, my friends
X. A. 1.6.6, o( me\n toi/nun po/lemos a(pa/ntwn h(ma=s tw=n ei)rhme/nwn a)peste/rhken: kai\ ga\r peneste/rous e)poi/hse kai\ pollou\s kindu/_nous u(pome/nein h)na/gkase kai\ pro\s tou\s *(/ellhnas diabe/blhke kai\ pa/ntas tro/pous tetalaipw/rhken h(ma=s now the war has deprived us of all the blessings that have been mentioned; for it has made us poorer, compelled us to undergo many dangers, has brought us into reproach with the Greeks, and in every possible way has caused us suffering
I. 8.19. Sometimes the aorist is chosen because of its affinity to the negative, as tw=n oi)ketw=n ou)de/na kate/lipen a)ll' a(/pantas pe/pra_ke he (has) left not one of his servants, but has sold them all
Aes. 1.99. This aorist is sometimes regarded as a primary tense.
a. Where an active transitive perfect is not formed from a particular verb, or is rarely used, the aorist takes its place:

*ferai/wn me\n a)fh/|rhtai th\n po/lin kai\ froura\_n e)n th=| a)kropo/lei kate/sthsen he has deprived the Pheraeans of their city and established a garrison in the acropolis
D. 7.32 (kaqe/sta^ke transitive is not classic). So h)/gagon is used for h)=xa.
b. In Greek of the classical period the aorist and perfect are not confused though the difference between the two tenses is often subtle. Cp.
D. 19.72 with 19. 177.

§1941
The aorist may be translated by the perfect when the perfect has the force of a present (1946, 1947): e)kthsa/mhn I have acquired (ke/tkhmai I possess), e)qau/masa I have wondered (teqau/maka I admire). Thus,

e)/kthso au)to\s ta/ per au)to\s e)kth/sao keep thyself what thyself hast gained
Hdt. 7.29.

§1942

Epistolary Tenses.—The writer of a letter or book, the dedicator of an offering, may put himself in the position of the reader or beholder who views the action as past: met' *)artaba/zou, o(/n soi e)/pemya, pra=sse negotiate with Artabazus whom I send (sent) to you
T. 1.129, *troi/a_n e(lo/ntes *)argei/wn sto/los la/fu_ra tau=ta . . . e)passa/leusan the Argive armament having captured Troy hang (hung) up these spoils
A. Ag. 577. Cp. 1923 (last two examples).
a. The perfect is also used: a)pe/stalka/ soi to/nde to\n lo/gon I send (have sent) you this discourse
I. 1.2.
b. The imperfect (common in Latin) occurs rarely: *mnhsi/ergos e)pe/steile toi=s oi)/koi xai/rein kai\ u(giai/nein kai\ au)to\s ou(/tws e)/faske [e)/xein] Mnesiergus sends greetings and wishes for good health to his friends at home and says that he himself is well Jahresheft des oesterreichischen Archaeol. Inst. 7 (1904), p. 94, tw=n de\ tau=ta pra_ca/ntwn a)/xri ou(= o(/de o( lo/gos e)gra/feto *teisi/fonos presbu/tatos w)\n tw=n a)delfw=n th\n a)rxh\n ei)=xe up to the date of this portion of my work, Tisiphonus, as the eldest of the brothers who wrought this deed, maintained control of the government
X. H. 6.4.37.

§1943

Aorist for Pluperfect.—The aorist with many temporal and causal conjunctions, and in relative clauses, has the force of the Eng. pluperfect. So with e)pei/, e)peidh/ after that, since, o(/te, w(s when, o(/ti because; regularly with pri/n before, e(/ws, me/xri until: e)pei\ e)sa/lpigce, e)ph=|san after the trumpeter had given the signal, they advanced
X. A. 1.2.17,

e)pei\ de\ sunh=lqon, e)/lece toia/de and when they had come together, he spoke as follows
X. C. 5.1.19, e)ke/leuse/ me th\n e)pistolh\n h(\n

e)/graya oi)/kade dou=nai he requested me to give him the letter which I had written home
X. C. 2.2.9. So often in other moods than the indicative.

§1944
In subordinate clauses the action expressed by the aorist may be (a) contemporaneous, (b) antecedent, or (c) subsequent to that set forth by the main verb. The context alone decides in which sense the aorist is to be taken. (a)

e)n tw=| xro/nw| o(\n e)pe/sxe o(/sa e)du/nato kateno/hse during the time he waited he learned all he could
T. 1.138; (b) e)tra/ponto e)s to\n *pa/normon, o(/qenper a)nhga/gonto they turned toward Panormus, the very place from which they had put out
T. 2.92 (see 1943); (c)

e)ma/xonto me/xri oi( *)aqhnai=oi a)pe/pleusan they kept fighting until the Athenians had sailed away
X. H. 1.1.3.

## PERFECT INDICATIVE

§1945
The perfect denotes a completed action the effects of which still continue in the present: ta\ oi)kh/mata w)|kodo/mhtai the rooms have been constructed (their construction is finished)
X. O. 9.2, ta\_s po/leis au)tw=n parh/|rhtai he has taken away (and still holds) their cities
D. 9.26, u(pei/lhfa I have formed (hold) the opinion 18. 123, bebou/leumai I have (am) resolved
S. El. 947, ti/ bouleu/esqon poiei=n; ou)d<*>n, e)/fh o( *xarmi/dhs, a)lla\ bebouleu/meqa what are you conspiring to do? Nothing, said Charmides; we have already conspired
P. Charm. 176c.
a. The effects of a completed action are seen in the resulting present state. The state may be that of the subject or of the object:

e)fobh/qhn, kai\ e)/ti kai\ nu=n teqoru/bhmai I was struck with fear, and even at the present moment am still in a state of agitation
Aes. 2.4, oi( pole/mioi ta\_s sponda\_s lelu/ka_sin the enemy have broken the truce (which is now broken)
X. A. 3.2.10.

§1946

Perfect with Present Meaning.—When the perfect marks the enduring result rather than the completed act, it may often be translated by the present.
Thus, ke/klhmai (have received a name) am called, my name is, ke/kthmai (have acquired) possess, me/mnhmai (have recalled) remember, te/qnhka (have passed away) am dead, ei)/qismai (have accustomed myself) am accustomed, h)mfi/esmai (have clothed myself in) have on, pe/poiqa (have put confidence) trust, e(/sthka (have set myself) stand, be/bhka (have stepped) stand and am gone, e)/gnwka (have recognized) know, pe/fu_ka (natus sum) am by nature, oi)=da (have found out) know.
a. These perfecta praesentia do not in nature differ from other perfects.

§1947

‘Intensive’ Perfect.—Many perfects seem to denote an action rather than a state resulting from an action, and to be equivalent to strengthened presents. These are often called intensive perfects.
Such are: verbs of the senses (de/dorka gaze, pe/fri_ka shudder), of sustained sound (ke/kra_ga bawl, le/lhka shout, be/bru_xa roar), of emotion (pefo/bhmai am filled with alarm, ge/ghqa am glad, me/mhle cares for), of gesture (ke/xhna keep the mouth agape), and many others (sesi/_ghka am still, etc.).
a. But most if not all of the verbs in question may be regarded as true perfects, i.e. they denote a mental or physical state resulting from the accomplishment of the action; thus, pe/fri_ka I have shuddered and am now in a state of shuddering.
b. Certain verbs tend to appear in the perfect for emphasis: te/qnhka am dead, a)po/lwla perish, pe/pra_ka sell (have sold).

§1948

Empiric Perfect.—The perfect may set forth a general truth expressly based on a fact of experience:

h( a)taci/a_ pollou\s h)/dh a)polw/leken lack of discipline ere now has been the ruin of many
X. A. 3.1.38. Cp. 1930.

§1949

Perfect of Dated Past Action.—The perfect is sometimes used of a past action whose time is specifically stated:

u(/brismai to/te I was insulted on that occasion
D. 21.7. This use approaches that of the aorist.

§1950

Perfect for Future Perfect.—The perfect may be used vividly for the future perfect to anticipate an action not yet done: ka)\_n tou=to ni_kw=men, pa/nq' h(mi=n pepoi/htai and if we conquer in that quarter, everything has been (will have been) accomplished by us
X. A. 1.8.12.
a. Especially with the phrase to\ e)pi/ tini, the perfect anticipates the certain occurrence of an event:

to\ e)pi\ tou/tw| a)polw/lamen for all he could do, we had perished
X. A. 6.6.23.

§1951
In subordinate clauses, the action of the perfect is usually (a) contemporaneous, but may be (b) antecedent to that of the main verb. The context alone decides in which sense the perfect is to be taken. (a) oi( de\ qera/pontes, e)peidh\ e)s a)nti/pala kaqesth/kamen, au)tomolou=si while our attendants desert, now that we have been brought down to a level with the Syracusans
T. 7.13. (b) a(/ soi tu/xh ke/xrhke, tau=t' a)fei/leto Fortune has taken back what she has lent you Men. fr. 598.
On the epistolary perfect see 1942 a.

## PLUPERFECT

§1952
The pluperfect is the past of the perfect, hence it denotes a past fixed state resulting from a completed action: e)bebouleu/mhn I had (was) resolved.
a. When the perfect is translated by the present, the pluperfect is rendered by the imperfect: e)kekth/mhn was in possession, e)teqnh/kei he was dead, h)/|dh knew, e)memnh/mhn remembered. Cp. 1946.

§1953

Pluperfect of Immediate Occurrence.—The pluperfect may denote that a past action occurred so immediately or suddenly that it was accomplished almost at the same moment as another action: w(s de\ e)lh/fqhsan, e)le/lunto ai( spondai/ and when they were captured the truce was (already) at an end
T. 4.47 (the fact of their capture was equivalent to the immediate rupture of the truce).

§1954
In subordinate clauses the pluperfect is rarely used to mark an action as anterior to an action already past:

h)=lqon oi( *)indoi\ e)k tw=n polemi/wn ou(\s e)pepo/mfei *ku=ros e)pi\ kataskoph/n the Indians returned whom Cyrus had sent to get news of the enemy
X. C. 6.2.9. The aorist is usually employed (1943, 1944 b).

## FUTURE PERFECT

§1955
The future perfect denotes a future state resulting from a completed action: a)nagegra/yomai I shall stand enrolled, dedh/setai he shall be kept in prison;

h( qu/ra_ keklh/|setai the door will be kept shut
Ar. Lys. 1071.
a. Most future perfects are middle in form, passive in meaning (581).
b. The active future perfect is usually periphrastic (600):

ta\ de/ont' e)so/meqa e)gnwko/tes we shall have determined on our duty
D. 4.50.

§1956
When stress is laid upon complete fulfilment, the future perfect may imply rapidity, immediate consequence, or certainty, of action accomplished in the future: fra/ze, kai\ pepra/_cetai speak, and it shall be done instanter Ar. Pl. 1027, eu)qu\s *)ariai=os a)festh/cei: w(/ste fi/los h(mi=n ou)dei\s lelei/yetai Ariaeus will soon withdraw, so that we shall have no friend left
X. A. 2.4.5.

§1957
The future perfect may have an imperative force (1917): ei)rh/setai ga\r ta)_lhqe/s for the truth shall (let it) be spoken
I. 7.76.

§1958
When the perfect has the force of a present, the future perfect is used like a simple future (1946): keklh/somai I shall bear the name, memnh/somai shall remember, kekth/somai shall possess. So in the two active forms: teqnh/cw I shall be dead, e(sth/cw I shall stand.
a. The aorist subjunctive with a)/n (2324), not the future perfect, is used to denote a past action in relation to an action still in the future.

## PERIPHRASTIC TENSES

On the periphrastic forms of perfect, pluperfect, and future perfect, see 599, 600.

§1959

Periphrastic Future.—A periphrastic future is formed by me/llw I am about to, intend to, am (destined) to, am likely to (strictly think) with the present or future (rarely the aorist) infinitive. Thus,

a(\ me/llw le/gein soi\ pa/lai dokei= what I am going to say has long been your opinion
X. C. 3.3.13 (cp. 1885),

*kle/andros me/llei h(/cein Cleander is on the point of coming
X. A. 6.4.18, qh/sein e)/mellen a)/lgea he purposed to inflict suffering B 39,

e)/mellon o)/lbios ei)=nai I was destined to be happy
s 138, ei)/ pote poreu/oito kai\ plei=stoi me/lloien o)/yesqai, proskalw=n tou\s fi/lous e)spoudaiologei=to if ever Cyrus was on the march and many were likely to catch sight of him, he summoned his friends and engaged them in earnest talk
X. A. 1.9.28.
a. The present infinitive usually occurs with me/llw as a verb of will, the future infinitive with me/llw as a verb of thinking.
b. The aorist is used when it is important to mark the action as ingressive, resultative, or complexive:

o(/per me/llw paqei=n what I am doomed to suffer
A. Pr. 625.
c. me/llw I delay usually takes the present, rarely the aorist, infinitive.
d. pw=s ou) me/llw and ti/ ou) me/llw mean why should I not? Thus, ti/ d' ou' me/llei geloi=on ei)=nai; how should it not be ridiculous?
P. R. 530a.

§1960

e)/mellon is used of past intention in

e)/melle katalu/_ein he was about to stop for the night
X. A. 1.8.1,

tou\s e)/splous klh/|sein e)/mellon they intended to close the entrances
T. 4.8. e)/mellon with the infinitive denoting an unfulfilled past intention is a periphrasis for an aorist indicative with a)/n. Thus,

ou) sustrateu/ein e)/mellon they would not have joined forces
D. 19.159 (= ou)k a)\n sunestra/teusan). Cp. recturus eram, etc.

§1961

With ei)mi/.—The present and perfect participle are freely used with the forms of ei)mi/ to form a periphrasis, especially when the participle has an adjectival character (1857): h(gei= diafqeirome/nous tina\s ei)=nai; do you think that some are being ruined?
P. R. 492a,

ai( te/xnai diefqarme/nai e)/sontai the arts will be ruined
X. C. 7.2.13,

h)=n tou=to sumfe/ron this was advantageous
Ant. 5.18; h)=| qe/lousa is stronger than qe/lh|,
S. O. T. 580.

§1962
The aorist participle is rarely so used, since it denotes a single act, not a characteristic:

h)=san de/ tines kai\ geno/menoi tw=| *ni_ki/a| lo/goi pro/teron pro/s tinas and communications between Nicias and some persons had actually been held before
T. 4.54.
a. With e)/somai the aorist participle equals the future perfect: ou) siwph/sa_s e)/sh|; be silent, won't you, once and for all?
S. O. T. 1146.

§1963

With e)/xw.—The periphrasis with e)/xw and the aorist participle is analogous to the perfect in meaning, and emphasizes the permanence of the result attained (chiefly in Hdt. and the drama):

khru/_ca_s e)/xw I have proclaimed
S. Ant. 192.
a. In Attic prose e)/xw usu. has a separate force:

*fera\_s prw/hn e)/xei katalabw/n he lately seized and now occupies Pherae
D. 9.12. So with the (rare) perfect: ta\ e)pith/deia ei)=xon a)nakekomisme/noi they had carried up to the forts the provisions and kept them there
X. A. 4.7.1.

§1964

With gi/gnomai.—The forms of gi/gnomai often combine with a participle to form periphrases. Thus,

mh\ sauto\n . . . ktei/na_s ge/nh| lest thou destroy thyself
S. Ph. 773; in prose this periphrasis has the tone of tragedy. On gi/gnomai with a substantive, see 1710, 1754.

§1965

With fai/nomai.—The aorist participle is used periphrastically with forms of fai/nomai. Thus,

ou)x u(pe\r u(_mw=n ou)de\ tw=n no/mwn fronti/sa_s ou)d' a)ganakth/sa_s fanh/setai it will appear that he took no heed, nor felt any resentment, concerning you or the laws
D. 21.39.

## VERBAL NOUNS

1. The Infinitive. 2. The Participle. 3. The Verbal Adjectives in -to/s and -te/os.

## THE INFINITIVE

§1966
The infinitive is in part a verb, in part a substantive.
a. Many substantives are closely related to verbs, but not all verbs can form substantives. All verbs can, however, form infinitives.
b. The word infinitive denotes a verbal form without any limitations (finis) of number and person.

§1967
The infinitive is like a verb herein:
a. It shows the distinctions of voice and tense (but not those of number and person). Having tenses, it can express different stages of action (action simply occurring, continuing, or finished); whereas the corresponding substantive sets forth the abstract idea without these distinctions. Contrast poiei=n, poih/sein, poih=sai, pepoihke/nai with poi/hsis making.
b. It can have a subject before it and a predicate after it, and it can have an object in the genitive, dative, or accusative like the corresponding finite verb. Infinitives scarcely ever stand in the subjective genitive; and the object of an infinitive never stands in the objective genitive.
c. It is modified by adverbs, not by adjectives.
d. It may take a)/n and with that particle represent a)/n with the indicative (1784 ff.) or a)/n with the optative (1824).
e. It forms clauses of result with w(/ste, and temporal clauses with pri/n, etc.

§1968
The infinitive is like a substantive herein:
a. It may be the subject or object of a verb.
b. With the (neuter) article it shows all the case forms (except the vocative): to\ (tou=, tw=|, to\) lu/_ein, lu/_sein, etc.
c. It may be governed by prepositions: pro\ tou= lu/_ein.

§1969
The infinitive was originally a verbal noun in the dative (in part possibly also in the locative) case. The use to express purpose (2008) is a survival of the primitive meaning, from which all the other widely diverging uses were developed in a manner no longer always clear to us. But the to or for meaning seen in manqa/nein h(/komen we have come to learn (for learning) can also be discerned in du/namai i)dei=n I have power for seeing, then I can see. Cp. 2000, 2006 a. As early as Homer, when the datival meaning had been in part obscured, the infinitive was employed as nominative (as subject) and accusative (as object). After Homer, the infinitive came to be used with the neuter article, the substantive idea thus gaining in definiteness. The article must be used when the infinitive stands as an object in the genitive or dative, and when it depends on prepositions.

§1970
The infinitive is used as subject, as predicate, and to supplement the meaning of words and clauses.

§1971
The negative of the infinitive is mh/; but ou), used with a finite mood in direct discourse, is retained when that mood becomes infinitive in indirect discourse. Sometimes, however, mh/ is used in place of this ou) (2723 ff.).

## SUBJECT AND PREDICATE NOUN WITH THE INFINITIVE

§1972
In general the subject of the infinitive, if expressed at all, stands in the accusative; when the subject of the infinitive is the same as the subject or object of the governing verb, or when it has already been made known in the sentence, it is not repeated with the infinitive.

§1973
When the subject of the infinitive is the same as that of the governing verb, it is omitted, and a predicate noun stands in the nominative case.

oi)=mai ei)de/nai I think that I know
P. Pr. 312e,

*pe/rshs e)/fh ei)=nai he said he was a Persian
X. A. 4.4.17,

e)gw\ ou)x o(mologh/sw a)/klhtos h(/kein I shall not admit that I have come uninvited
P. S. 174d, o(mologei=s peri\ e)me\ a)/dikos gegenh=sqai; do you admit that you have been guilty as regards me?
X. A. 1.6.8 (cp. 4.2.27 in 2263).
a. The nominative is used when the infinitive, expressing some action or state of the subject of the main verb, has the article in an oblique case. Thus, tou/twn a)ciwqei\s dia\ to\ patriko\s au)tw=| fi/los ei/=nai justifying these requests on the ground that he was his hereditary friend
Aes. 3.52,

tou=to d' e)poi/ei e)k tou= xalepo\s ei)=nai this he effected by reason of his being severe
X. A. 2.6.9, e)pi\ tw=| o(moi=oi toi=s leipome/nois ei)=nai e)kpe/mpontai (colonists) are sent out to be the equals of those who stay at home
T. 1.34.
b. The nominative stands usually in sentences with dei=n, xrh=nai etc., dependent on a verb of saying or thinking. Thus,

h(gou/mhn . . . periei=nai dei=n au)tw=n kai\ megaloyu_xo/teros fai/nesqai I thought I ought to surpass them and to show myself more magnificent
D. 19.235. Here h(gou/mhn dei=n is equivalent to I thought it proper.
c. When the governing verb is a participle in an oblique case, a predicate noun usually agrees with the participle, and rarely stands in the nominative. Thus,

a)pallagei\s tou/twn tw=n fasko/ntwn dikastw=n ei)=nai being rid of those who profess to be judges
P. A. 41a,

ta\_s a)rxa\_s di/dwsi . . . toi=s a)ei\ do/ca_sin a)ri/stois ei)=nai it dispenses the offices to those who always seem to be the most deserving
P. Menex. 238d.

§1974
A pronoun subject of the infinitive, if (wholly or partially) identical with the subject of the main verb, is generally expressed when emphatic, and stands in the accusative (cases of the nominative are rare and suspected); but the indirect reflexive sfei=s stands in the nominative or accusative.

oi)=mai e)me\ plei/w xrh/mata ei)rga/sqai h)\ a)/llous su/nduo I think I have made more money than any two others together
P. Hipp. M. 282e, h(ghsa/menos e)mauto\n e)pieike/steron ei)=nai (emphatic for h(ghsa/menos e)pieike/steros ei)=nai) deeming myself to be too honest
P. A. 36b,

tou\s de\ *qhbai/ous h(gei=to . . . e)a/_sein o(/pws bou/letai pra/_ttein e(auto/n he thought the Thebans would let him have his own way
D. 6.9, ou) sfei=s a)dikei=sqai, a)ll' e)kei/nous ma=llon he said that not they (the speaker and the other Lacedaemonians), but they (the Toroneans) rather had been wronged 4. 114 (but sfa=s in 1228 b).
a. After a preceding accusative with the infinitive, a second pronoun referring to a different person, and also subject of an infinitive, must also stand in the accusative whether or not it denotes the same person as the subject of the governing verb. Thus, a)lla\ nomi/zeis h(ma=s me\n a)ne/cesqai/ sou, au)to\s (see below) de\ tuph/sein; kai\ h(ma=s me\n a)poyhfiei=sqai/ sou, de\ (not su\) d' ou' pau/sesqai but do you think that we are going to put up with you, while you strike us yourself? and that we are going to acquit you, while you will not cease your outrageous conduct?
D. 21.204. au)to/s, above and in *kle/wn ou)k e)/fh au)to/s, a)ll' e)kei=non strathgei=n Cleon said that not he himself, but that Nicias was in command
T. 4.28, is not the expressed subject of the infinitive, but au)to/s of direct discourse (au)to\s tuph/seis, au)to\s ou) strathgw=); hence au)to/s is not used here for seauto/n (e(auto/n).

§1975
When the subject of the infinitive is different from that of the governing verb, it stands in the accusative; and a predicate noun stands also in the accusative.

nomi/zw ga\r u(_ma=s e)moi\ ei)=nai kai\ patri/da kai\ fi/lous for I think you are to me both fatherland and friends
X. A. 1.3.6,

to\n ga\r kalo\n ka)_gaqo\n a)/ndra eu)dai/mona ei)=nai/ fhmi for I maintain that the noble and good man is happy
P. G. 470e.

§1976
A predicate noun takes the case of the subject of an infinitive itself dependent on a subjectless infinitive. Thus,

h(mi=n de\ poiou=si dokei=n sfa=s pantodapou\s fai/nesqai they manage it so that they seem to us to appear in various forms
P. R. 381e.

§1977
Several infinitives may be used in succession, one infinitive being the subject of another:

peri\ pollou= poiou/menos mhdeni\ do/cai u(bri/zein bou/lesqai regarding it of great importance not to seem to any one to wish to behave outrageously
L. 23.5.

§1978
When the subject of the infinitive is the same as the object (in the genitive or dative) of the governing verb, it is often omitted, and a predicate noun is either attracted into the genitive or dative, or stands in the accusative in agreement with the omitted subject of the infinitive. See 1060-1062.
e)/cestin h(mi=n a)gaqoi=s ei)=nai or e)/cestin h(mi=n a)gaqou\s ei)=nai it is in our power to be good (lit. to be good is possible for us). Thus, deo/meq' ou)=n u(_mw=n . . . a)kroa/_sasqai tw=n legome/nwn, e)nqu_mhqe/ntas o(/ti ktl. we ask you therefore to listen to what is said, considering that, etc. 1. 14. 6. Cp. nu=n soi e)/cestin a)ndri\ gene/sqai quoted in 1062 with

*lakedaimoni/ois e)/cestin u(_mi=n fi/lous gene/sqai it is in your power to become friends to the Lacedaemonians
T. 4.29. The latter construction may be explained as abbreviated for e)/cestin u(_mi=n (u(_ma=s) fi/lous gene/sqai.

§1979
The subject of the infinitive is often retained when it is the same as the (omitted) oblique object of the governing verb. Thus,

parh/ggeile ta\ o(/pla ti/qesqai tou\s *(/ellhnas he issued orders that the Greeks should get under arms
X. A. 2.2.21.

§1980
An indefinite or general subject of the infinitive (tina/, tina/s, a)nqrw/pous) is commonly omitted; and a predicate noun stands in the accusative. Thus, fila/nqrwpon ei)=nai dei= one (tina/) must be humane
I. 2.15 (cp. 1984), r(a=|on parainei=n h)\ paqo/nta karterei=n it is easier for a man to give advice than to endure suffering
Men. Sent. 471,

drw=ntas ga\r h)\ mh\ drw=ntas h(/di_on qanei=n for it is preferable to die in action rather than doing nothing
E. Hel. 814.

§1981
The construction of the accusative with the infinitive seems to have originated from the employment of the infinitive to complement the meaning of transitive verbs; as in keleu/w se a)pelqei=n I command you to depart. Here the accusative was separated from the transitive verb and felt to be the independent subject of the infinitive (I command that you depart). Gradually the accusative with the infinitive was used even after verbs incapable of taking an object-accusative.

## PERSONAL AND IMPERSONAL CONSTRUCTION

§1982
