Instead of an impersonal passive verb with the accusative and infinitive as subject, Greek often uses the personal passive construction, the accusative becoming the nominative, subject to the leading verb.
Thus, *ku=ros h)gge/lqh ni_kh=sai Cyrus was reported to have conquered instead of h)gge/lqh *ku=ron ni_kh=sai it was reported that Cyrus had conquered, and di/kaio/s ei)mi a)pelqei=n I am justified in going away instead of di/kaio/n e)stin e)me\ a)pelqei=n it is right for me to go away. English sometimes has to use the impersonal construction in place of the Greek personal construction (cp. 2107).
a. The personal construction is more common with le/getai, a)gge/lletai, o(mologei=tai and other passive verbs of saying (regular with passive verbs of thinking); with sumbai/nei it happens; with a)nagkai=os necessary, a)/cios worthy, di/kaios just, dunato/s possible, e)pith/deios fit, etc., followed by a form of ei)=nai, instead of a)nagkai=on, a)/cion, etc. Thus,

o( *)assu/rios ei)s th\n xw/ra_n au)tou= e)mbalei=n a)gge/lletai the Assyrian is reported to be about to make an incursion into his country
X. C. 5.3.30,

pollh/ tis a)logi/a_ cumbai/nei gi/gnesqai much absurdity would result
P. Phil. 55a,

di/kaios ei)= ei)pei=n it is right for you to speak
P. S. 214c,

th\n ai)ti/a_n ou(=to/s e)sti di/kaios e)/xein it is right for him to bear the blame
D. 18.4. Both constructions together: soi\ ga\r dh\ le/getai pa/nu ge teqerapeu=sqai o( *)apo/llwn, kai/ se pa/nta e)kei/nw| peiqo/menon pra)_ttein for Apollo is said to have been greatly served by you, and (it is said) that you do everything in obedience to him
X. C. 7.2.15. Cp. 2104.
N.—dh=lo/s e)sti and fanero/s e)sti take o(/ti or the participle (2107); dh=lo/n e)sti and fanero/n e)sti take o(/ti, not the infinitive.

§1983
The personal constructions dokw=, e)/oika (2089 c), de/w are regular instead of dokei=, e)/oike it seems, dei= it lacks (much or little). So with fai/nomai for fai/netai.

dokw= ga/r moi a)/dunatos ei)=nai for I seem to be unable
P. R. 368b,

dokou=me/n moi kaqh=sqai it seems to me that we are encamped
X. A. 1.3.12,

nu=n ge h(mw=n e)/oikas basileu\s ei)=nai now at least you seem to be our king
X. C. 1.4.6,

pollou= de/w e)gw\ u(pe\r e)mautou= a)pologei=sqai I am far from speaking in my own defence
P. A. 30d, mi_krou= e)de/hsen *ku/pron a(/pa_san katasxei=n he almost (lacked a little) occupied the whole of Cyprus
I. 9.62,

eu)= su\ le/gein fai/nei you seem to speak well
Ar. Nub. 403.
a. dokei= moi/ tina e)lqei=n for dokei= ti/s moi e)lqei=n it seems to me that some one came is very rare. dokei= meaning it seems good, it is decreed always takes the infinitive (1984, 1991). dokw= believe has the construction of 1992 c. Cp. 1998.

## THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE

§1984

As Subject.—The infinitive may be used as subject, especially with quasi-impersonal verbs and expressions (933 a).

gra/mmata maqei=n dei= to learn to read is necessary
Men. Sent. 96, ti/ xrh\ poiei=n; what must be done?
X. A. 2.1.16, ko/smos (e)sti\)

kalw=s tou=to dra=n to perform this well is a credit
T. 1.5, pa=sin a(dei=n xalepo/n (e)sti) to please everybody is difficult Solon 7,

e)/docen au)toi=s proi+e/nai it seemed best to them to proceed
X. A. 2.1.2,

sumfe/rei au)toi=s fi/lous ei)=nai it is for their interest to be friends
X. O. 11.23. Cp. 1062, 1978.

§1985
Such quasi-impersonal verbs and expressions are dei= it is necessary, xrh/ (properly a substantive with e)sti/ omitted, 793) it is necessary, dokei= it seems good, e)/sti it is possible, e)/cesti it is in one's power, oi(=o/n te/ e)sti it is possible, pre/pei and prosh/kei it is fitting, sumbai/nei it happens; and many expressions formed by e)sti/ and a predicate noun, as a)/cion it is right, di/kaion it is just, a)nag- kai=on it is necessary, dunato/n it is possible, a)du/naton (or a)du/nata) it is impossible, ai)sxro/n it is disgraceful, kalo/n it is honourable, w(/ra_ and kairo/s it is time. With the last two expressions the old dative use of the infinitive is clear:

w(/ra_ bouleu/esqai it is time for considering
P. Soph. 241b.
a. On the personal a)/cio/s ei)mi, di/kaio/s ei)mi, dokw=, see 1982. For dei= me tou=to le/gein we find the personal de/omai tou=to le/gein. Note the attraction in

to\ plh=qos tw=n e)no/ntwn ei)pei=n the number of the things it is possible to mention
I. 5.110 (for tou/twn a(\ e)/nestin).
b. dei= and xrh/ regularly take the accusative and infinitive (cp. 1562); a)na/gkh it is necessary takes the accusative or dative with the infinitive.
c. The subject of the infinitive is expressed or omitted according to the sense.
d. Homer shows only the beginnings of the use of the infinitive as a real subject, i.e. not a grammatical subject, as in 1984.

§1986

As Predicate.—In definitions the infinitive may be used as a predicate noun with e)sti/.

to\ ga\r gnw=nai e)pisth/mhn labei=n e)stin for to learn is to get knowledge
P. Th. 209e.

§1987

As an Appositive.—The infinitive may stand in apposition to a preceding substantive, pronoun, or adverb.
ei(=s oi)wno\s a)/ristos, a)mu/_nesqai peri\ pa/trhs one omen is best, to fight for our country M 243, ei)=pon . . . tou=to mo/non o(ra=n pa/ntas, tw=| pro/sqen e(/pesqai I told all to pay heed to this only, viz., to follow their leader
X. C. 2.2.8, kai\ u(_ma=s de\ ou(/tws, w)= pai=des, . . . e)pai/deuon, tou\s me\n geraite/rous proti_ma=n, tw=n de\ newte/rwn proteti_mh=sqai and I have instructed you, too, my children (to this effect) to honour your elders in preference to yourselves and to receive honour from the younger in preference to them
X. C. 8.7.10.

§1988
The infinitive not in indirect discourse, and in indirect discourse, is often used as the object of a verb.

## THE INFINITIVE NOT IN INDIRECT DISCOURSE

§1989
The infinitive as object not in indirect discourse is used after almost any verb that requires another verb to complete its meaning. The tenses of this infinitive are timeless, and denote only stage of action.

§1990
The infinitive may be the only expressed object, or it may be one of two expressed objects, of the leading verb.

pai/deusis kalh\ dida/skei xrh=sqai no/mois a good education teaches obedience to the laws
X. Ven. 12.14,

diagignw/skein se tou\s a)gaqou\s kai\ tou\s kakou\s e)di/dacen he taught you to distinguish the good and the bad
X. M. 3.1.9.
a. Verbs signifying to ask, bid, forbid, permit, teach, etc., allow an infinitive as one of two objects.
b. Many verbal expressions, formed by a substantive and a verb, take the infinitive. Thus, tou\s a)/llous dida/skein te/xnhn e)/xousin they possess the skill to teach (the) others
I. 16.11. Cp. 2000.

## A. Object Infinitive after Verbs of Will or Desire

§1991

Verbs of will or desire (and their opposites) are often followed by an infinitive. The infinitive with a subject accusative denotes that something should (may) be or be done. The negative is mh/ (see 2719-2721).

h)/qelon au)tou= a)kou/ein they were willing to listen to him
X. A. 2.6.11,

e)bouleu/onto e)klipei=n th\n po/lin they planned to leave the city
Hdt. 6.100,

ta\ h(/dista . . . zhtei= poiei=n he seeks to do what he likes best
X. M. 4.5.11,

basileu\s a)cioi= se\ a)poplei=n the king asks that you sail away
X. H. 3.4.25, i(_ke/teue mh\ a)poktei=nai he entreated that they should not put him (self) to death
L. 1.25, pe/mpousin . . . strateu/esqai e)pi\ *ka_ri/a_n they send orders that he shall march upon Caria
X. H. 3.1.7,

e)/doce plei=n to\n *)alkibia/dhn it was decided that Alcibiades should sail
T. 6.29.
a. Verbs of will or desire with an accusative subject of the infinitive form one of the classes of substantive clauses introduced in English by that, though the infinitive in English is often more idiomatic.

§1992
Of verbs of will or desire that take the infinitive some have an object
a. In the accusative (or are intransitive), e.g.: ai(rou=mai choose, ai)tw=, ai)tou=mai ask, a)ciw= claim, ask, bouleu/omai resolve, bou/lomai wish, will, dikaiw= deem right, dianoou=mai intend, e)qe/lw (poet. qe/lw), wish, will, ei)/wqa am wont to, e)pixeirw= attempt, e)w= permit, zhtw= seek, keleu/w command, suggest, invite, me/llw delay, peirw=mai try, pe/mpw send, proqu_mou=mai am zealous, prokalou=mai invite, protre/pw urge, speu/dw hasten, am eager, spouda/zw am eager, tolmw= dare, filw= am wont to, yhfi/zomai vote.
b. In the genitive, e.g.: de/omai ask, e)piqu_mw= and o)re/gomai desire.
c. In the dative, e.g.: eu)/xomai pray, paragge/llw and prosta/ttw command, e)pibouleu/w purpose, sumbouleu/w advise, e)pitre/pw and sugxwrw= permit, parainw= exhort, dokw= moi I have a mind to; and le/gw, ei)=pon, fwnw=, fra/zw tell (and bow= shout) in the sense of command.
N.—pei/qw urge to a course of action, takes the infinitive, pei/qw convince generally has w(s, rarely the accusative with the infinitive. Thus,

e)/peiqen au)to\n kaq' au(to\n poreu/esqai he urged him to go by himself
X. A. 6.2.13,

ou) ga\r pei/sontai oi( polloi/, w(s su\ au)to\s ou)k h)qe/lhsas a)pie/nai for most people will not be convinced that of your own free will you did not desire to go away
P. Cr. 44c (infinitive
X. M. 1.1.20).

§1993
Verbs of will or desire not to do anything are e.g.: de/doika, fobou=mai fear, feu/gw avoid, o)knw= scruple, ai)sxu/_nomai, ai)dou=mai (2126) feel shame to, a)pagoreu/w forbid, kwlu/_w hinder, a)pe/xomai abstain from, eu)labou=mai, fula/ttomai beware of. Thus,

fobou=mai diele/gxein se I fear to refute you
P. G. 457e,

ai)sxu/_nomai u(_mi=n ei)pei=n ta)_lhqh= I am ashamed to tell you the truth
P. A. 22b.

§1994
Under verbs of will or desire are included verbs expressing an activity to the end that something shall or shall not be done. Thus, di/dwmi offer, give, diama/xomai struggle against, poiw=, diapra/_ttomai, katerga/zomai manage, effect, pare/xw offer (others in 1992, 1993).

§1995
Several verbs of will or desire take o(/pws with the future or the subjunctive (verbs of effort, 2211, 2214); or mh/ with the subjunctive (verbs of fear, 2225); some take the participle (2123 ff.).

§1996
The infinitive may be used with the
a. Genitive or dative when the expression of desire is addressed to a person and the genitive or dative depends on the leading verb. Here the sentence is simple. Thus,

de/omai u(_mw=n . . . ta\ di/kaia yhfi/sasqai I ask you to render a just verdict
I. 19.51,

toi=s a)/llois pa=si parh/ggellen e)copli/zesqai he ordered all the rest to arm themselves
X. A. 1.8.3.
b. Accusative when the action of a person is desired (example in 1979). Such sentences are complex.
N.—Verbs of commanding allow either a or b; but only keleu/w with the accusative permits either meaning: keleu/w se\ tau=ta mh\ poiei_n I tell you not to do this and I command that you shall not do this. Cp. 1981.

§1997
Several verbs signifying to say are also used as verbs of will and then mean command. The agent commanded usually stands in the accusative subject of the infinitive. So with le/gw, ei)=pon, fra/zw, fwnw=. Thus

le/gw s' e)gw\ do/lw| *filokth/thn labei=n I say that thou shalt take Philoctetes by craft
S. Ph. 101,

tou/tois e)/legon plei=n I told them that they should sail
D. 19.150,

pa/ntes e)/legon tou\s tou/twn a)/rcantas dou=nai di/khn all said that the ringleaders should suffer punishment
X. A. 5.7.34, ei)=pon th\n qu/ra_n keklei=sqai they commanded that the door should be shut (and stay shut)
X. H. 5.4.7, basileu\s e)/graye pa/_sa_s ta\_s e)n th=| *(ella/di po/leis au)tono/mous ei)=nai the king issued a written order that all the cities in Greece should be independent (not: wrote that they were independent)
X. H. 6.3.12.
a. The agent may stand in the dative as

xala=n le/gw soi I bid thee let go
S. O. C. 840.

§1998
The present and aorist infinitive (both timeless) are the usual tenses of the infinitive after verbs of will or desire (see 1869). The perfect is rare; as ei)=pon th\n qu/ra_n keklei=sqai (1997). dokw= and dokw= moi signifying I have a mind to or I am determined to take the present or aorist like

dokei=: to\n o)/non e)ca/gein dokw= I have a mind to bring out the ass
Ar. Vesp. 177, e)gw\ ou)=n moi dokw= . . . u(fhgh/sasqai ktl. now I have a mind to show, etc.
P. Eu. 288c. Cp. 1983 a. When it is clearly denoted that the action resolved on is to follow without delay the future is used; as in

a)lla/ moi dokw= . . . ou) pei/sesqai au)tw=| but I am determined that I will not accept his opinion
P. Th. 183d.
a. Some verbs, as keleu/w, which might be held to introduce indirect discourse, are classed under ver<*>s of will or desire, because, like these verbs, they do not regularly take the future infinitive; and because, unlike verbs of saying and thinking (which admit all the tenses of the infinitive) they introduce infinitives which do not show differences of time. The future infinitive does not express a command. For a few cases of the future after verbs of will or desire, see 1869.

§1999
Verbs signifying to hope, expect, promise, threaten , and swear, when followed by the aorist (less often the present) infinitive (1868), have the construction of verbs of will or desire. When such verbs take the future infinitive they have the construction of indirect discourse.

## B. Infinitive after Other Verbs

§2000
The infinitive follows many verbs, especially such as denote ability, fitness, necessity, etc. (and their opposites).

ou)ke/ti e)du/nato . . . bioteu/ein he was no longer able to live
T. 1.130,

nei=n e)pista/menos knowing how to swim
X. A. 5.7.25,

pefu/_ka_si/ te a(/pantes . . . a(marta/nein and all men are by nature prone to err
T. 3.45,

manqa/nousin a)/rxein te kai\ a)/rxesqai they learn how to govern and be governed
X. A. 1.9.4; also after the impersonals of 1985.
a. e)/xw I can is derived from the meaning I have especially with a verb of saying. Thus,

*dio\s pla_ga\_n e)/xousin ei)pei=n they can proclaim a stroke of Zeus
A. Ag. 367.

## C. Infinitive after Adjectives, Adverbs, and Substantives

§2001
The infinitive serves to define the meaning of adjectives, adverbs, and substantives, especially those denoting ability, fitness, capacity, etc. (and their opposites), and generally those analogous in meaning to verbs which take the infinitive (2000). Here the datival meaning (purpose, destination) is often apparent. Cp. 1969.

§2002

Adjectives and Adverbs.—

i(kanoi\ h(ma=s w)felei=n able to assist us
X. A. 3.3.18,

deino\s le/gein, kako\s biw=nai skilled in speaking, evil in life
Aes. 3.174,

oi(=oi filei=n able to love
D. 25.2,

e(/toimoi/ ei)si ma/xesqai they are ready to fight
X. C. 4.1.1,

a)/rxein a)ciw/tatos most worthy to govern
X. A. 1.9.1, o(do\s . . . a)mh/xanos ei)selqei=n strateu/mati a road impracticable for an army to enter 1. 2. 21, xalepo\n diabai/nein hard to cross 5. 6. 9,

e)pinoh=sai o)cei=s quick to conceive
T. 1.70. So also after r(a/|dios easy, h(du/s pleasant, di/kaios just, a)nagkai=os necessary, e)pith/deios suitable, a)gaqo/s good, ai)/tios responsible for, malako/s incapable of; cp. o)li/gos 1063. After adverbs:

ka/llista i)dei=n most splendid to behold
X. C. 8.3.5.
a. Some of these adjectives take the infinitive by analogy to the related verbs, as pro/qu_mos zealous (proqu_mou=mai), e)pisth/mwn knowing how (e)pi/stamai).

§2003

oi(=os fit, o(/sos sufficient take the infinitive like the fuller expressions toiou=tos oi(=os, tosou=tos o(/sos. Thus,

ou) ga\r h)=n w(/ra_ oi(/a_ to\ pedi/on a)/rdein for it was not the proper season to irrigate the plain
X. A. 2.3.13,

o(/son a)pozh=n sufficient to live off of
T. 1.2,

toiou=tos oi(=os . . . pei/qesqai the kind of a man to be convinced
P. Cr. 46b. On tosou=tos w(/ste (w(s) see 2263. Hom. has the infinitive after toi=os, to/sos, etc.

§2004

Substantives.—As,

oi( pai=des u(_mi=n o)li/gou h(liki/a_n e)/xousi paideu/esqai your children are almost of an age to be educated
P. Lach. 187c. With e)sti/ omitted:

sxolh/ ge h(mi=n manqa/nein we have leisure to learn
X. C. 4.3.12,

a)na/gkh pei/qesqai there is need to obey
X. H. 1.6.8,

perai/nein h)/dh w(/ra_ it is high time to finish
X. A. 3.2.32. Cp. 1985.

§2005
The infinitive is added, like an accusative of respect (1601, 1602), to intransitive verbs (especially in poetry), to adjectives (more frequently in poetry), and to substantives (rarely). Thus, toi=os i)dei=n such in aspect (lit. to look on) Theognis 216,

o(ra=n stugno/s of a repulsive expression
X. A. 2.6.9, a)kou=-

sai pagka/lws e)/xei it is very fine to hear
D. 19.47,

qau=ma kai\ a)kou=sai a marvel even to hear of
P. L. 656d.

§2006
The infinitive limiting the meaning of an adjective is commonly active (or middle) in cases where the passive is more natural in English. Thus,

lo/gos dunato\s katanoh=sai a speech capable of being understood
P. Ph. 90c,

a)/cios qauma/sai worthy to be admired
T. 1.138 (but a)/cios qauma/zesqai
X. C. 5.1.6).
a. The active use is due to the old datival function of the infinitive: dunato\s katanoh=sai capable for understanding.

§2007
The infinitive, with or without w(/ste or w(s, may be used with h)/ than after comparatives, depending on an (implied) idea of ability or inability. h)\ w(/ste is more common than h)/ or h)\ w(s. Cp. 2264.

to\ ga\r no/shma mei=zon h)\ fe/rein for the disease is too great to be borne
S. O. T. 1293,

fobou=mai mh/ ti mei=zon h)\ w(/ste fe/rein du/nasqai kako\n th=| po/lei sumbh=| I fear lest some calamity befall the State greater than it can bear
X. M. 3.5.17,

braxu/tera h)\ w(s e)ciknei=sqai too short to reach
X. A. 3.3.7.
a. The force of h)\ w(/ste may be expressed by the genitive; as, krei=sson lo/gou (
T. 2.50) = krei=sson h)\ w(/ste le/gesqai. Cp. 1077.
b. Words implying a comparison may take the infinitive with w(/ste or w(s (1063).

## D. Infinitive of Purpose and Result

§2008

Infinitive of Purpose.—The infinitive may express purpose (usually only with verbs taking the accusative).

tau/thn th\n xw/ra_n e)pe/treye diarpa/sai toi=s *(/ellhsin he gave this land over to the Greeks to plunder
X. A. 1.2.19, to\ h(/misu (tou= strateu/matos) kate/lipe fula/ttein to\ strato/pedon he left half (of the army) behind to guard the camp 5. 2. 1, i)e/nai e)pi\ basile/a_ ou)k e)gi/gneto ta\ i(era/ the sacrifices did not turn out (favourable) for going against the king 2. 2. 3,

*)arista/rxw| . . . e)/dote h(me/ra_n a)pologh/sasqai you granted a day to Aristarchus to make his defence
X. H. 1.7.28, h( qu/ra_ h( e)mh\ a)ne/w|kto . . . ei)sie/nai tw=| deome/nw| ti e)mou= my door stood open for any petitioner of mine to enter 5. 1. 14,

pare/xw e)mauto\n e)rwta=n I offer myself to be questioned
P. A. 33b, ta\_s gunai=kas piei=n ferou/sa_s the women bringing (something) to drink
X. H. 7.2.9. Cp. also 2032 e.

§2009
The infinitive of purpose is used in prose especially after verbs meaning to give, entrust, choose, appoint, take, receive. Verbs signifying to send, go, come usually take the future active participle (2065); but
T. 6.50 has de/ka tw=n new=n prou/pemyan e)s to\n me/gan lime/na pleu=sai they sent ahead ten ships to sail into the great harbour; and in poetry the infinitive often denotes purpose after these verbs, and after ei)=nai in Homer (
*l 20) and Hdt. (5. 25).

§2010
After verbs meaning to have (or be) at one's disposition:

oi( stratiw=tai a)rgu/rion ou)k ei)=xon e)pisi_ti/zesqai the soldiers did not have money by means of which they could provision themselves
X. A. 7.1.7,

e)kei= skia/_ t' e)sti\ kai\ po/a_ kaqi/zesqai there is shade and grass to sit down in
P. Phae. 229b.

§2011

Infinitive of Result.—The infinitive may be used with w(/ste (sometimes with w(s) to denote a result, often an intended result. See 2260 ff.
a. Several verbs, substantives, and adjectives usually taking the infinitive also admit w(/ste with the infinitive (2271); and the infinitive is found where w(/ste with the infinitive might be expected: mnhmoneu/ousin a)feqe/nta tou=ton e)leu/qeron ei)=nai they recall that he was emancipated (lit. released so as to be free)
D. 29.25. Here the redundant infinitive expresses an intended result.
N.—This redundant use of ei)=nai is common in Hom. and Hdt.

## E. Absolute Infinitive

§2012
Certain idiomatic infinitives are used absolutely in parenthetical phrases to limit the application of a single expression or of the entire sentence.
a. Verbs of Saying.—w(s e)/pos ei)pei=n, w(s ei)pei=n so to speak, almost; (w(s) a(plw=s ei)pei=n, w(s sunelo/nti (1497) ei)pei=n, w(s (e)n braxei= or) sunto/mws ei)pei=n to speak briefly, concisely; w(s e)pi\ pa=n ei)pei=n, to\ su/mpan ei)pei=n speaking generally; sxedo\n ei)pei=n so to say, almost (paene dixerim); su\n qew=| ei)pei=n in God's name; and so w(s with le/gein, fra/zein, ei)rh=sqai, as w(s e)n tu/pw| ei)rh=sqai in general. Examples: a)lhqe/s ge w(s e)/pos ei)pei=n ou)de\n ei)rh/ka_sin not one word of truth, I may say, did they utter
P. A. 17a, a)gaqo\n me\n a(plw=s ei)pei=n ou)de\n ge/gone th=| po/lei in a word the State gained no advantage Dinarchus 1.33.
b. w(s (e)/pos) ei)pei=n is often used to limit too strict an application of a general statement, especially pa=s or ou)dei/s. Thus, pa/ntes w(s e)/pos ei)pei=n nearly every one, ou)dei\s w(s e)/pos ei)pei=n almost no one. It is thus used like paene dixerim; rarely, like ut ita dicam, to soften the strength of a metaphor.
c. Especially common is the absolute ei)=nai in e(kw\n willingly, intentionally, if you can help it, usually in negative or quasi-negative statements (e(kw/n may be inflected). Also in to\ kata\ tou=ton (e)pi\ tou/tw|) ei)=nai as far as he is concerned, w(s . . . ei)=nai as far as . . . is concerned, to\ nu=n ei)=nai at present. Examples:

ou)de\ ce/nois e(kw\n ei)=nai ge/lwta pare/xeis nor do you intentionally cause strangers to laugh
X. C. 2.2.15,

e(kou=sa ei)=nai ou)k a)polei/petai it is not willingly separated
P. Phae. 252a, to/ ge e)p' e)kei=non ei)=nai e)sw/qhs (a)/n) so far, at least, as it depended on him you would have been saved
L. 13.58.
d. Other expressions: e)moi\ dokei=n, w(s e)moi\ dokei=n, w(s e)moi\ kri=nai as it seems to me, in my opinion, (w(s) ei)ka/sai to make a guess, (w(s) sumba/llein to compare, (w(s) a)kou=sai to the ear, w(s u(momnh=sai to recall the matter, o(/son ge/ m' ei)de/nai as far as I know, etc.; o)li/gou dei=n, mi_krou= dei=n almost, all but (dei=n may be omitted, 1399). Examples: o( ga\r *kth/sippos e)/tuxe po/rrw kaqezo/menos tou= *kleini/ou, e)moi\ dokei=n for Ctesippus, it seems to me, happened to be sitting at a distance from Clinias
P. Eu. 274b,

mi_krou= dei=n tri/a ta/lanta almost three talents
D. 27.29.
e. Some of these absolute infinitives may be explained by reference to the idea of purpose (2008) or result. Thus, sunelo/nti ei)pei=n for one compressing the matter to speak (cp. ut paucis dicam), mi_krou= dei=n so as to lack little. Others recall the adverbial accusative (1606); cp. e)moi\ dokei=n with gnw/mhn e)mh/n.

## F. Infinitive in Commands, Wishes, and Exclamations

§2013

Infinitive in Commands.—The infinitive may be used for the second person of the imperative. The person addressed is regarded as the subject. This infinitive is commoner in poetry than in prose (where it has a solemn or formal force).
qarsw=n nu=n, *dio/mhdes, e)pi\ *trw/essi ma/xesqai with good courage now, Diomed, fight against the Trojans E 124, su\ de/, *kleari/da_ . . . ta\_s pu/la_s a)noi/ca_s e)pekqei=n but do you, Clearidas, open the gates and sally forth
T. 5.9.
a. This infinitive may be used in conjunction with an imperative:

a)kou/ete lew/|: kata\ ta\ pa/tria tou\s xo/as pi/_nein hear ye, good people! drink the Pitchers as our sires drank!
Ar. Ach. 1000.
b. The infinitive for the third person of the imperative often occurs in legal language (laws, treaties, etc.), and does not necessarily depend on the principal verb. Thus,

e)/th de\ ei)=nai ta\_s sponda\_s penth/konta and the treaty shall continue for fifty years
T. 5.18. In this construction the infinitive has the force of an infinitive dependent on e)/doce (it was voted that) or the like. So in medical language, as pi/_nein de\ u(/dwr it is well for the patient to drink water Hippocrates 1. 151.
c. The infinitive (with subject accusative) is rarely used for the third person of the imperative when there is an unconscious ellipsis of a word like do/s grant, or eu)/xomai I pray. Thus, teu/xea su_lh/sa_s fere/tw koi/la_s e)pi\ nh=as, sw=ma de\ oi)/kad' e)mo\n do/menai pa/lin let him strip off my arms and carry them to the hollow ships, but let him give back my body to my home H 78.
d. In negative commands (prohibitions) mh/ with the infinitive is poetic and Ionic: oi(=s mh\ pela/zein do not approach these ( = mh\ pe/laze)
A. Pr. 712,

mhde\ kalei=n pw o)/lbion and do not call him happy yet
Hdt. 1.32.

§2014

Infinitive in Wishes.—The infinitive with a subject accusative may be used in the sense of the optative of wish, usually with the same ellipsis as in 2013 c.

qeoi\ poli=tai, mh/ me doulei/a_s tuxei=n ye gods of my country, may bondage not be my lot!
A. Sept. 253, w)= *zeu=, e)kgene/sqai moi *)aqhnai/ous tei/sasqai oh Zeus, that it be granted to me to punish the Athenians!
Hdt. 5.105 (cp. w)= *zeu=, do/s me tei/sasqai mo/ron patro/s oh Zeus, grant that I may avenge my father's murder!
A. Ch. 18). This construction is very rare in Attic prose:

to\n kunhge/thn e)/xonta e)cie/nai . . . e)lafra\_n e)sqh=ta the hunter should go forth in a light dress
X. Ven. 6.11. Here no definite verb can be supplied.
a. The nominative with the infinitive (instead of the optative) after ai' ga/r occurs in Homer (
h 311,
w 376).

§2015

Infinitive in Exclamations.—The infinitive is often used in exclamations of surprise or indignation. The subject stands in the accusative.

e)me\ paqei=n ta/de that I should suffer this!
A. Eum. 837,

toioutoni\_ tre/fein ku/na to keep a dog like that!
Ar. Vesp. 835.
On the infinitive with e)f' w(=| (e)f' w(=|te) see 2279; with pri/n, see 2453.

## INFINITIVE AS OBJECT IN INDIRECT DISCOURSE

§2016
The infinitive is used as the object of verbs of saying and thinking. Such infinitives denote both time and stage of action (cp. 1866).
a. The finite verb of a sentence placed in dependence on a verb of saying or thinking that requires the infinitive, becomes infinitive, which infinitive stands in the relation of a substantive as subject or object of the leading verb. Commonly as object: thus, *ku=ros ni_ka=| Cyrus is victorious, when made the object of fhsi/ he says, becomes a part of a new sentence fhsi\ *ku=ron ni_ka=n, in which *ku=ron nika=n is the object of fhsi/. As subject, when the verb of saying is passive: thus, in le/getai *ku=ron ni_ka=n, the last two words form the subject of le/getai.

§2017

Verbs of saying are e.g.: say fhmi/, fa/skw, le/gw; confess o(mologw=; promise u(pisxnou=mai, u(pode/xomai, e)pagge/llomai, u(fi/stamai; pretend prospoiou=mai; swear o)/mnu_mi; deny a)parnou=mai; gainsay a)ntile/gw; dispute a)mfisbhtw=, etc.
Some verbs of saying admit other constructions than the infinitive, and especially o(/ti or w(s (2579). le/gw, ei)=pon, fra/zw, fwnw= with o(/ti or w(s mean say, with the infinitive command (1997).
a. fhmi/ say, assert, express the opinion that in classical Greek is almost always followed by the infinitive, but by o(/ti very often in the later language. fhmi\ o(/ti occurs in
X. A. 7.1.5 (fhmi\ w(s in
L. 7.19,
X. H. 6.3.7;
D. 4.48, 27. 19 by anacoluthon).
b. le/gw state (impart a fact) takes either the infinitive or o(/ti or w(s. The infinitive occurs usually with the passive (le/getai, etc.) either in the personal or impersonal construction (1982 a). The active forms of le/gw with the infinitive mean command (1997).
c. ei)=pon said usually takes o(/ti or w(s; with the infinitive, it commonly means commanded (1997). Cp. the double use of told.
N.—ei)=pon meaning said with the infinitive is rare, but occurs in good Attic prose:
And. 1.57, 80; Thuc. 7. 35; Lys. 10. 6, 10. 9, 10. 12; Xen. H. 1. 6. 7, 2. 2. 15, C. 5. 5. 24, S. 2. 13;
Is. 2.29; Lyc. 50;
Aes. 3.37, 3. 59; Dem. 15. 18; Plato, G. 473 a, 503 d, Lach. 192 b, Charm. 174 a, Hipp. Maj. 291 b, Pol. 263 c, 290 b, L. 654 a, Clitoph. 409 a, 410 b. In poetry this use is frequent.

§2018

Verbs of thinking almost always take the infinitive. Such are: think h(gou=mai, oi)/omai, dokw=, nomi/zw; hope e)lpi/zw; suppose u(polamba/nw; suspect u(popteu/w; guess ei)ka/zw; feel confident pisteu/w; disbelieve a)pistw=. The use of w(s is rare, while o(/ti is very rare (2580).
a. Verbs of perceiving sometimes take the infinitive by analogy to verbs of thinking; as a)kou/w, ai)sqa/nomai, punqa/nomai (2144).

§2019
Each tense of direct discourse is retained (with its proper meaning as regards stage of action) when it becomes infinitive in indirect discourse; but an imperfect is represented by the present infinitive; a pluperfect, by the perfect infinitive. See 1866, 1867.

§2020
An original ou) of direct discourse is generally, an original mh/ is always, retained in indirect discourse. But in some cases ou) becomes mh/ (2723 ff.).

§2021
The infinitive is the subject of the passive of verbs of saying and thinking (1982 a). So with dokei= it seems, fai/netai it is plain, etc.

§2022
The infinitive represents a finite verb after verbs of saying and thinking.
a.

eu)=noi/ fa_sin ei)=nai they assert that they are loyal
L. 12.49, ou)dei\s e)/fasken gignw/skein au)to/n nobody said that he knew him 23. 3, oi( h(gemo/nes ou)/ fa_sin (2692)

ei)=nai a)/llhn o(do/n the guides say there is no other road
X. A. 4.1.21,

pa/ntes e)rou=si to\ loipo\n mhde\n ei)=nai kerdalew/teron th=s a)reth=s everybody in time to come will say that there is nothing more profitable than bravery
X. C. 7.1.18. Other examples 1867.
b. basileu\s ni_ka=n h(gei=tai the king thinks he is victorious ( = ni_kw=, cp. 1887)
X. A. 2.1.11, oi)/omai be/ltiston ei)=nai I think it is best 5. 1. 8, u(pw/pteuon e)pi\ basile/a_ i)e/nai they suspected that they were to go against the king 1. 3. 1, (*swkra/ths)

to\ a)gnoei=n e(auto\n e)gguta/tw . . . mani/a_s e)logi/zeto ei)=nai Socrates was of the opinion that for a man not to know himself was very near to madness
X. M. 3.9.6.
c. When a word of saying is expressed or implied in what precedes, several infinitives may be used where the indicative is employed in translation. So in the narration in
X. C. 1.3.5-6.

§2023
The infinitive with a)/n represents an indicative with a)/n or a potential optative with a)/n. See 1846, 1848, 1849, 2270.

§2024
Verbs signifying to hope, expect, promise, threaten , and swear take the future infinitive in indirect discourse, and the aorist (less often the present) infinitive not in indirect discourse (like verbs of will or desire, 1868, 1999). e)lpi/zw tau=ta poih/sein I hope that I shall do this, e)lpi/zw tau=ta poih=sai or poiei=n I hope to do this.

## THE INFINITIVE WITH THE ARTICLE (ARTICULAR INFINITIVE)

§2025
The articular infinitive, while having the character of a substantive, retains the functions of a verb. In its older use the articular infinitive is a subject or object; the nearest approach to this use in Homer is

a)ni/_h kai\ to\ fula/ssein to watch is also trouble
u 52. In the tragic poets the genitive and dative are rarely used; in the speeches in Thucydides and in Demosthenes all of its four cases appear with great frequency. The articular infinitive may take dependent clauses.

§2026
The articular infinitive admits the constructions of an ordinary substantive.
Nom. to\ poiei=n making or to make, to\ poih/sein, to\ poih=sai, to\ pepoihke/nai
Gen. tou= poiei=n of making, tou= poih/sein, tou= poih=sai, etc.
Dat. tw=| poiei=n for making, by making, tw=| poih/sein, tw=| poih=sai, etc.
Acc. to\ poiei=n, to\ poih/sein, to\ poih=sai, etc.

§2027
The articular infinitive is treated as subject, predicate noun, and object like the simple infinitive (1984-1986).

§2028
The negative of the articular infinitive is mh/.

§2029
The articular infinitive may indicate time (after verbs of saying or thinking, 2034 g), or may be timeless.

§2030
The articular infinitive is in general used like the infinitive without the article, and may take a)/n; as regards its constructions it has the value of a substantive. The article is regularly used when the connection uniting the infinitive to another word has to be expressed by the genitive, the dative, or a preposition.
a. The articular infinitive is rarely used, like a true substantive, with the subjective genitive:

to/ g' eu)= fronei=n au)tw=n mi_mei=sqe imitate at least their wisdom
D. 19.269.

§2031
NOMINATIVE OF THE ARTICULAR INFINITIVE
Subject (1984):

ne/ois to\ si_ga=n krei=tto/n e)sti tou= lalei=n in the young silence is better than speech
Men. Sent. 387,

to\ *peloponnhsi/ous au)toi=s mh\ bohqh=sai pare/sxen u(_mi=n . . . *sami/wn ko/lasin the fact that the Peloponnesians did not come to their assistance enabled you to punish the Samians
T. 1.41.

§2032
GENITIVE OF THE ARTICULAR INFINITIVE
a. The genitive of the articular infinitive is used to limit the meaning of substantives, adjectives, and verbs.
b. Adnominal (1290):

tou= piei=n e)piqu_mi/a| from desire to drink

tou= qarsei=n to\ plei=ston ei)lhfo/tes having gained the greatest amount of courage
T. 4.34. After comparatives (1431): ti/ ou)=n e)stin . . . tou= toi=s fi/lois a)rh/gein ka/lli_on; what then is nobler than to help one's friends?

d. After verbs:

e)pe/sxomen tou= dakru/_ein we desisted from weeping

e)teixi/sqh *)atala/nth . . . tou= mh\ lh|sta\_s . . . kakourgei=n th\n *eu)/boian Atalante was fortified to prevent pirates from ravaging Euboea
T. 2.32. More common is the use with u(pe/r (2032 g) or e(/neka.

T. 3.12.

X. H. 3.4.12,

a)/neu tou= swfronei=n without exercising self-control
X. M. 4.3.1. To express purpose the genitive with u(pe/r is very common:

u(pe\r tou= tou/twn gene/sqai ku/_rios . . . pa/nta pra_gmateu/etai he devotes his every effort that he may become master of these
D. 8.45, u(pe\r tou= mh\ to\ keleuo/menon poih=sai in order not to do what was commanded 18. 204. Furthermore, after a)po/, pro/, dia/, meta/, peri/, u(po/, e(/neka, xa/rin, xwri/s, plh/n, me/xri; and after adverbs. In Hdt. tou= may be omitted after a)nti/.

§2033
DATIVE OF THE ARTICULAR INFINITIVE
a. With verbs, adjectives, and adverbs: thus,

i(/na . . . a)pistw=si tw=| e)me\ teti_mh=sqai u(po\ daimo/nwn that they may distrust my having been honoured by divine powers

ou)deni\ tw=n pa/ntwn ple/on kekra/thke *fi/lippos h)\ tw=| pro/teros pro\s toi=s pra/_gmasi gi/gnesqai Philip has conquered us by nothing so much as by being beforehand in his operations

P. R. 468e,

i)/son de\ tw=| proste/nein equal to sorrowing beforehand

o( me\n pro\s tw=| mhde\n e)k th=s presbei/a_s labei=n, tou\s ai)xmalw/tous . . . e)lu/_sato the one, in addition to gaining nothing from the embassy, ransomed the prisoners of war

§2034
ACCUSATIVE OF THE ARTICULAR INFINITIVE
a. Object (cp. 1989):

dei/sa_s to\ zh=n fearing to live

mei=zon me/n famen kako\n to\ a)dikei=n, e)/la_tton de\ to\ a)dikei=sqai we call doing wrong a greater evil, being wronged a lesser
P. G. 509c.
b. After prepositions: e.g.

X. M. 1.2.1, pw=s e)/xeis pro\s to\ e)qe/lein a)\n i)e/nai a)/klhtos e)pi\ dei=pnon; how do you feel about being willing to go uninvited to supper?
P. S. 174a (cp. e)qe/lois a)\n i)e/nai). Furthermore, after dia/, e)pi/, kata/, meta/, peri/.
c. The accusative of the infinitive with to/ appears after many verbs and verbal expressions which usually take only the simple infinitive. Such verbal expressions may be followed also by a genitive of a noun. Thus,

to\ speu/dein de/ soi parainw= I commend speed to thee
S. Ph. 620, kardi/a_s d' e)ci/stamai to\ dra=n I withdraw from my resolution so as to ( = and) do this thing
S. Ant. 1105, maqw\n ga\r ou)k a)\n a)rnoi/mhn to\ dra=n when I am informed, I will not refuse the deed
S. Ph. 118,

to\ proqu_mei=sqai de\ sunau/cein to\n oi)=kon e)paideu/omen au)th/n we trained her to show zeal in assisting to increase our estate
X. O. 9.12 (cp. 1628),

to\ e)ra=n e)/carnos ei)= you refuse to love
P. Lys. 205a.
d. So after adjectives. Thus, makro\s to\ kri=nai tau=ta xw( loipo\s xro/nos the future is long (i.e. time enough) to decide this
S. El. 1030.
e. This object infinitive after verbs is often an internal accusative. The accusative after verbs and nouns is, in many cases, like an accusative of respect (1600); as

to\ dra=n ou)k h)qe/lhsan they refused to do it
S. O. C. 442,

ai)sxu/_nontai to\ tolma=n they are ashamed to dare

ou)d' e)moi/ toi tou)canista/nai e)sti\ qa/rsos nor have I courage to remove thee

e)sba/llein . . . i(kanoi/ ei)si they are able to make an inroad into our country

X. C. 5.1.25.
f. Some verbs take the articular infinitive as an object when the simple infinitive could not be used:

mo/non o(rw=n to\ pai/ein to\n a(lisko/menon taking heed only to strike any one he caught

th=s e)lpi/dos ga\r e)/rxomai dedragme/nos, to\ mh\ paqei=n a)\n a)/llo plh\n to\ mo/rsimon for I come with good grip on the hope that I can suffer nothing save what is my fate
