h. On the use of the object infinitive with to\ mh/ and to\ mh\ ou), see 2744 and 2749.
i. The accusative with the infinitive may stand in the absolute construction: e)pei/ ge to\ e)lqei=n tou=ton, oi)=mai qeo/n tina au)to\n e)p' au)th\n a)gagei=n th\n ti_mwri/a_n as for his coming, I believe that some god brought him to his very punishment Lyc. 91.

## OTHER USES OF THE ARTICULAR INFINITIVE

§2035

Apposition (cp. 1987). The articular infinitive, in any case, is often used in apposition to a preceding word, especially a demonstrative.

tou=to/ e)sti to\ a)dikei=n, to\ ple/on tw=n a)/llwn zhtei=n e)/xein injustice is this: to seek to have more than other people
P. G. 483c, ti/ ga\r tou/tou makariw/teron, tou= gh= mixqh=nai ktl. for what is more blessed than this: to be commingled with the earth, etc.
X. C. 8.7.25,

dokei= tou/tw| diafe/rein a)nh\r tw=n a)/llwn zw/|wn, tw=| ti_mh=s o)re/gesqai man differs herein from other creatures that he aspires after honour
X. Hi. 7.3.

§2036

In Exclamation (cp. 2015).—Thus,

th=s tu/xhs: to\ e)me\ nu=n klhqe/nta deu=ro tuxei=n my ill-luck! that I should happen now to have been summoned hither!
X. C. 2.2.3.

§2037

With Adjuncts.—The articular infinitive may take various adjuncts including dependent clauses, the whole forming one large substantival idea.

to\ me\n ga\r po/ll' a)polwleke/nai kata\ to\n po/lemon the fact that we have lost much in the war
D. 1.10, pe/peismai . . . ta\ plei/w tw=n pra_gma/twn h(ma=s e)kpefeuge/nai tw=| mh\ bou/lesqai ta\ de/onta poiei=n, h)\ tw=| mh\ suni_e/nai I am persuaded that more of your advantages have escaped you from your not being willing to do your duty than from your ignorance 3. 3, kai\ ga\r pa/nu moi dokei= a)/fronos a)nqrw/pou ei)=nai to\ (mega/lou e)/rgou o)/ntos tou= e(autw=| ta\ de/onta paraskeua/zein)

mh\ a)rkei=n tou=to, a)lla\ prosanaqe/sqai to\ kai\ toi=s a)/llois poli/_tais w(=n de/ontai pori/zein and in fact, since it is a serious business to provide for one's own necessities, it seems to me to be the part of an utter fool not to rest content with that, but in addition to take upon himself the burden of providing for the needs of the rest of the community
X. M. 2.1.8.

## CONSTRUCTIONS OF THE INFINITIVE WITH VERBS OF hindering

§2038
Verbs signifying (or suggesting) to hinder take both the simple infinitive and the articular infinitive. Such verbs may take the strengthening but redundant negative mh/ (2739); and some, when themselves negatived or appearing in a question expecting a negative answer, admit the addition of the sympathetic ou) (2742). Hence we have a variety of constructions (described in 2744 ff.)

## THE PARTICIPLE

§2039
The participle (metoxh/ participation) is a verbal adjective, in part a verb, in part an adjective.

§2040
The participle is like a verb herein:
a. It shows the distinctions of voice and tense. Its tenses mark action simply occurring, continuing, and completed.
b. It can have an object in the same case (genitive, dative, accusative) as the finite forms.
c. It is modified by adverbs, not by adjectives.
d. It may take a)/n, and, with that particle, represents a)/n with the indicative or a)/n with the optative (1845 ff.).

§2041
The participle shows its adjectival nature by being inflected and by admitting the article before it, both of which characteristics give it the character of a noun. It follows the rules of agreement like other adjectives (1020). Unlike the adjective, it represents a quality in action (cp. 1857).

§2042
The participle is always used in connection with a substantive or a substantive pronoun, which may be contained in a verbal form, as dia/gousi manqa/nontes they spend their time in learning.

§2043
The tenses of the participle (except the future) not in indirect discourse are timeless, and denote only stage of action (1872). When they stand in indirect discourse and represent the indicative, they denote time relatively to that of the main verb.

§2044
The future participle marks an action as in prospect at the time denoted by the leading verb. Since it expresses an idea of will, it shows that an action is purposed, intended, or expected. With the article it denotes the person or thing likely (or able) to do something ( = me/llwn with inf. 1959). The nearest approach to mere futurity appears in general only after verbs of knowing and perceiving (2106, cp. 2112 b).

o( d' a)nh\r au)th=s lagw\s w)/|xeto qhra/_swn but her husband had gone to hunt hares
X. A. 4.5.24, o( h(ghso/menos ou)dei\s e)/stai there will be no one to guide us 2. 4. 5, polla\ . . . dei= to\n eu)= strathgh/sonta ( = to\n me/llonta eu)= strathgh/sein) e)/xein he who intends to be a good general must have many qualifications
X. M. 3.1.6, qanoume/nh ga\r e)ch/|dh for I knew that I should (or must) die
S. Ant. 460 (cp. 2106).

§2045
The negative of the participle is ou), except when the participle has a general or conditional force, or occurs in a sentence which requires mh/. See 2728.

§2046
The participle has three main uses.
A. Attributive: as an attributive to a substantive.
B. Circumstantial (or Adverbial): denoting some attendant circumstance and qualifying the main verb like an adverbial phrase or clause.
C. Supplementary: as a supplement to a verbal predicate, which, without such a supplement, would be incomplete.

§2047
The circumstantial and supplementary participles are predicate participles.

§2048
The attributive and circumstantial participles are commonly not necessary to the construction; but the removal of a supplementary participle may make the construction incomplete. The circumstantial participle is used by way of apposition to the subject of the verb and, though strictly predicative, may agree attributively with a noun or pronoun. An attributive participle may be circumstantial, as oi( mh\ duna/menoi diatele/sai th\n o(do\n e)nukte/reusan a)/si_toi those who (i.e. if any) were unable to complete the march passed the night without food
X. A. 4.5.11. A participle may be both circumstantial and supplementary, as a)dikou/menoi o)rgi/zontai (
T. 1.77) they are enraged at being wronged or because (when, if) they are wronged. Circumstantial and supplementary participles often cannot be sharply distinguished; as with verbs signifying to be angry, ashamed, content, pleased (2100), inferior to, do wrong (2101), endure (2098), come and go (2099). Thus, a)dikw= tau=ta poiw=n I do wrong in doing this or I am guilty in doing this: in the first case tau=ta poiw=n is appositive to the subject of the verb; in the second these words define the predicate adjective a)/dikos contained in a)dikw= ( = a)/diko/s ei)mi).

## THE ATTRIBUTIVE PARTICIPLE

§2049
The attributive participle (with any modifier), with or without the article, modifies a substantive like any other adjective.

o( e)festhkw\s ki/ndu_nos th=| po/lei the danger impending over the State
D. 18.176, oi( o)/ntes e)xqroi/ the existing enemies 6. 15, o( parw\n kairo/s the present crisis 3. 3,

to\ *kotu/laion o)nomazo/menon o)/ros the mountain called Cotylaeum
Aes. 3.86,

ai( *ai)o/lou nh=soi kalou/menai the so-called islands of Aeolus
T. 3.88 (cp. 1170). For the position of an attributive participle with its modifiers, see 1166.

§2050
The substantive with which the attributive participle (with the article) agrees directly, may be omitted, the participle thus becoming a substantive (1153 b, and N. 1); as,

o( oi)/kade boulo/menos a)pie/nai whoever wants to go home
X. A. 1.7.4. Neuter participles are often substantival, as ta\ de/onta duties.
a. Substantives or relative clauses must often be used to translate such par ticiples, as o( feu/gwn the exile or the defendant, to\ me/llon the future, oi( ni_kw=ntes the victors, o( kle/ptwn the thief, oi( qano/ntes the dead, o( swqei/s the man who has been saved, oi( dedio/tes those who are afraid, oi( a)dikou/menoi those who are (being) wronged,

o( th\n gnw/mhn tau/thn ei)pw/n the one who gave this opinion
T. 8.68,

o( e)ntau=q' e(auto\n ta/ca_s th=s poli_tei/a_s ei)/m' e)gw/ the man who took this position in the State was I
D. 18.62. The participle with the article may represent a relative clause of purpose or result, as
X. A. 2.4.5 cited in 2044.

§2051
A participle may be modified by adjectives or take a genitive, when its verbal nature has ceased to be felt:

ta\ mi_kra\ sumfe/ronta th=s po/lews the petty interests of the State
D. 18.28. Cp. sumfe/ron h)=n th=| po/lei it was advantageous to the State 19. 75 (here the participle is used like a predicate). Thucydides often uses in an abstract sense a substantival neuter participle where the infinitive would be more common, e.g., to\ dedio/s fear, to\ qarsou=n courage (for to\ dedie/nai, to\ qarsei=n) 1. 36. See 1153 b, N. 2. In poetry many participles are used substantively, as o( tekw/n father, h( tekou=sa mother, oi( teko/ntes parents.

§2052
The article with the participle is either generic or particular (1124). Thus, o( le/gwn the definite speaker on a particular occasion, or orator in general. So o( ou) dra/_sa_s the definite person who did not do something, o( mh\ dra/_sa_s any one who did not do something (a supposed case),

o( mh\ gamw=n a)/nqrwpos ou)k e)/xei kaka/ the unmarried man has no troubles
Men. Sent. 437. Generic are o( tuxw/n, o( boulo/menos, 2050 a.
a. Participles having an indefinite force may, especially in the plural number, be used without the article. Thus,

kataskeyome/nous e)/pempe he sent men to reconnoitre
X. C. 3.1.2,

a)dikou=nta peira_so/meqa . . . a)mu/_nasqai we shall endeavour to avenge ourselves on any one who injures us
X. A. 2.3.23.

§2053
A participle and its substantive often correspond to a verbal noun with the genitive or to an articular infinitive. Cp. post urbem conditam and Milton's “Since created man.”
tw=| si/_tw| e)pilei/ponti e)pie/zonto they suffered from the failure of the crops ( = th=| tou= si/_tou e)pilei/yei)
T. 3.20, di' u(_ma=s mh\ cummaxh/santas by reason of your not joining the alliance ( = dia\ to\ u(_ma=s mh\ cummaxh=sai) 6. 80, meta\ *sura_kou/sa_s oi)kisqei/sa_s after the foundation of Syracuse 6. 3,

e)lu/_pei au)to\n h( xw/ra_ porqoume/nh the ravaging of the country grieved him
X. A. 7.7.12,

h( o)rgh\ su\n tw=| fo/bw| lh/gonti a)/peisi his wrath will disappear with the cessation of his fear
X. C. 4.5.21.
a. Except in expressions of time, such as

a(/ma h)=ri a)rxome/nw| at the beginning of spring
T. 2.2, e)pi\ *ko/drou basileu/ontos in the reign of Codrus Lyc. 84 (cp. 1689 b), this construction is in place only when the part. is necessary to the sense. In poetry:

*zeu\s geloi=os o)mnu/menos swearing by Zeus is ridiculous
Ar. Nub. 1241; in Hom. A 601, I 682.

## THE CIRCUMSTANTIAL PARTICIPLE

§2054
The circumstantial participle is added, without the article, to a noun or pronoun to set forth some circumstance under which an action, generally the main action, takes place.
a. The circumstantial participle thus qualifies the principal verb of the sentence like an adverbial clause or supplementary predicate. Cp. meta\ tau=ta ei)=pe afterwards he said with gelw=n ei)=pe he said laughingly. Such participles usually have the force of subordinate clauses added to the main verb by conjunctions denoting time, condition, cause, etc.; but may often be rendered by adverbial phrases or even by a separate finite verb, which brings out distinctly the idea latent in the participle.
b. The circumstantial participle has no article. In agreement with a noun and its article, it stands before the article or after the noun (i.e. in the predicate position). By the agreement of the participle with a noun or pronoun, the predicate of the sentence is more exactly defined.

§2055
The circumstantial participle has two main constructions each equivalent in meaning to a clause of time, condition, cause, etc.

§2056
(I) The subject of the participle is identical with the noun or pronoun subject or object of the leading verb, and agrees with it in gender, number, and case.
（oi( a)/nqrwpoi) lipo/ntes th\n o(do\n feu/gontes o)li/goi a)pe/qnh|skon by leaving the road and making off only a few were killed
X. A. 4.2.7,

prope/myantes kh/ru_ka po/lemon proerou=nta having sent a herald in advance to proclaim war
T. 1.29.

§2057
(II) Absolute participial clauses, in which a participle, and not a finite verb, forms the predicate. These are of two kinds.

§2058
A. Genitive Absolute.—A participle agreeing in the genitive with its own subject, which is not identical with the subject of the leading verb, is said to stand in the genitive absolute. Cp. 2070.

*ku=ros a)ne/bh e)pi\ ta\ o)/rh ou)deno\s kwlu/_ontos Cyrus ascended the mountains without any one preventing him
X. A. 1.2.22.
N.—The English nominative absolute is represented by the Greek genitive absolute. Cp. Tennyson: “we sitting, as I said, the cock crew loud” = h(mw=n kaqhme/nwn, o(/per e)/legon, me/ga h)=|sen o( a)lektruw/n.

§2059
B. Accusative Absolute.—When the participle has no definite subject (i.e. with impersonal verbs), the accusative absolute is used instead of the genitive absolute. Cp. 2076.
sundo/can tw=| patri\ kai\ th=| mhtri\ gamei= th\n *kuaca/rou qugate/ra on the approval of (lit. it seeming good to) his father and mother he married the daughter of Cyaxares
X. C. 8.5.28.

§2060
The circumstantial participle expresses simply circumstance or manner in general. It may imply various other relations, such as time, manner, means, cause, purpose, concession, condition, etc. But it is often impossible to assign a participle exclusively to any one of these relations (which are purely logical), nor can all the delicate relations of the participle be set forth in systematic form.

§2061

Time.—The time denoted by the participle is only relative to that of the governing verb, and is to be inferred from the context. Each participial form in itself expresses only stage of action (1850).
a)kou/sa_si toi=s strathgoi=s tau=ta e)/doce to\ stra/teuma sunagagei=n on hearing this i<*> seemed best to the generals to collect the troops
X. A. 4.4.19.
a. Several temporal participles have an adverbial force: a)rxo/menos in the beginning, at first, teleutw=n at last, finally, dialipw\n (or e)pisxw\n) xro/non after a while, dialei/pwn xro/non at intervals, xroni/zwn for a long time. Thus,

a(/per kai\ a)rxo/menos ei)=pon as I said at the outset
T. 4.64,

teleutw=n e)xale/painen at last he became angry
X. A. 4.5.16. Note a)rca/menos a)po/ tinos beginning with or especially.

§2062

Manner.—

parh/launon tetagme/noi they marched past in order
X. A. 1.2.16, kraugh\n pollh\n e)poi/oun kalou=ntes a)llh/lous they made a loud noise by calling to each other 2. 2. 17,

proei/leto ma=llon toi=s no/mois e)mme/nwn a)poqanei=n h)\ paranomw=n zh=n he preferred rather to abide by the laws and die than to disobey them and live
X. M. 4.4.4,

fate\ me\n eu)tuxei=s ei)=nai, w(s kai\ e)ste\ kalw=s poiou=ntes you claim to be favoured by fortune as happily you are in fact
Aes. 3.232. To characterize a preceding statement with the participle in apposition to the subject of the preceding sentence; thus, o)rqw=s ge tau=ta le/gontes yes, and saying this correctly
X. O. 16.2.
a. Several participles of manner have an idiomatic meaning, e.g. a)nu/sa_s quickly (lit. having accomplished), e)/xwn continually, persistently (lit. holding on), laqw/n secretly, klai/wn to one's sorrow (lit. weeping), xai/rwn with impunity (lit. rejoicing), fe/rwn hastily (lit. carrying off), fqa/sa_s before (lit. anticipating). Thus,

a)/noig' a)nu/sa_s hurry up and open
Ar. Nub. 181,

e)/kploun poiei=tai laqw\n th\n fulakh/n he sailed out unobserved by the guard
T. 1.65 (cp. 2096 f),

flua_rei=s e)/xwn you keep trifling
P. G. 490e, tou=ton ou)dei\s xai/rwn a)dikh/sei no one will wrong him with impunity 510 d, a)ne/w|ca/s me fqa/sa_s you opened the door before I could knock
Ar. Plut. 1102 (cp. 2096 e).

§2063

Means (often the present participle).—

lh|zo/menoi cw=si they live by pillaging
X. C. 3.2.25, mh\ kri=n' o(rw=n to\ ka/llos, a)lla\ to\n tro/pon judge by regarding not beauty, but (by regarding) character
Men. Sent. 333.

§2064

Cause.—

*paru/satis . . . u(ph=rxe tw=| *ku/_rw|, filou=sa au)to\n ma=llon h)\ to\n basileu/onta *)artace/rchn Parysatis favoured Cyrus because she loved him more than she did Artaxerxes the king
X. A. 1.1.4,

a)pei/xonto kerdw=n ai)sxra\ nomi/zontes ei)=nai they held aloof from gains because they thought them disgraceful
X. M. 1.2.22, ti/ ga\r dedio/tes sfo/dra ou(/tws e)pei/gesqe; for what are you afraid of, that you are so desperately in haste?
X. H. 1.7.26.
a. ti/ maqw/n what induced him to (lit. having learned what?), ti/ paqw/n what possessed him to (lit. having experienced what?) are used with the general sense of wherefore? in direct (with o(/ ti in indirect) questions expressing surprise or disapprobation; as ti/ maqo/ntes e)marturei=te u(_mei=s; what put it into your heads to give evidence?
D. 45.38, ti/ paqo/nte lela/smeqa; what possessed us to forget?
*l 313. Cp. ti/ boulo/menos.
b. ti/ e)/xwn; what's the matter with you? (lit. having what?）

§2065

Purpose or Object.—The future (sometimes the present) participle is used to denote purpose, especially after verbs denoting to come, go, send, summon, etc. Thus,

prope/myantes kh/ru_ka po/lemon proerou=nta having sent a herald in advance to proclaim war
T. 1.29, o( ba/rbaros e)pi\ th\n *(ella/da doulwso/menos h)=lqen the barbarians proceeded against Greece with the purpose of enslaving it 1. 18, suneka/lesan a)po\ tw=n po/lewn a(pa_sw=n a)kousome/nous (2052 a) th=s para\ basile/ws e)pistolh=s they summoned from all the cities men to listen to the letter from the king
X. H. 7.1.39. Present: e)/pempon . . . le/gontas o(/ti ktl. they sent men to say that, etc.
X. H. 2.4.37.

§2066

Opposition or Concession.—ou)de\n e)rw= pro\s tau=ta e)/xwn ei)pei=n I will make no reply to this though I might (speak) do so
P. Lach. 197c,

polloi\ ga\r o)/ntes eu)genei=s ei)sin kakoi/ for many, albeit noble by birth, are ignoble
E. El. 551.

§2067

Condition (negative always mh/).—su\ de\ klu/wn ( = e)a\_n klu/h|s)

ei)/sei ta/xa but if you listen you shall soon know
Ar. Av. 1390, ou)k a)\n du/naio mh\ kamw\n ( = ei) mh\ ka/mois) eu)daimonei=n you cannot be happy unless you work E. fr. 461.

§2068

Any Attendant Circumstance.—

sulle/ca_s stra/teuma e)polio/rkei *mi/_lhton having collected an army he laid siege to Miletus
X. A. 1.1.7, paragge/llei tw=| *klea/rxw| labo/nti h(/kein o(/son h)=n au)tw=| stra/teuma he gave orders to Clearchus to come with all the force he had 1. 2. 1.
a. e)/xwn having, a)/gwn leading, fe/rwn carrying (mostly of inanimate objects), xrw/menos using, labw/n taking are used where English employs with. Thus,

e)/xwn stratia\_n a)fiknei=tai he arrives with an army
T. 4.30, boh=| xrw/menoi with a shout 2. 84, e)ke/leuse labo/nta a)/ndras e)lqei=n o(/ti plei/stous he ordered him to come with all the men he could (or to take . . . and come)
X. A. 1.1.11.
b. In poetry participles (especially) of verbs denoting motion are often added to verbs of giving, setting to make the action more picturesque (H. 304,
S. Aj. 854).

§2069
The force of these circumstantial participles does not lie in the participle itself, but is derived from the context. Unless attended by some modifying adverb, the context often does not decide whether the participle has a temporal, a causal, a conditional, a concessive force, etc.; and some participles may be referred to more than one of the above classes. Thus, path\r d' a)peilw=n ou)k e)/xei me/gan fo/bon (Men. fr. 454) may mean: a father by threatening ( = when or because or if or though, he threatens) does not excite much fear.

## GENITIVE ABSOLUTE. ACCUSATIVE ABSOLUTE

§2070

Genitive Absolute.—A circumstantial participle agreeing with a genitive noun or pronoun which is not in the main construction of the sentence, stands in the genitive absolute. Like other circumstantial participles, the genitive absolute expresses time, cause, condition, concession, or simply any attendant circumstance.
a. Time:

tau=t' e)pra/_xqh *ko/nwnos strathgou=ntos these things were effected while Conon was in command
I. 9.56,

tou/twn lexqe/ntwn a)ne/sthsan this said, they rose
X. A. 3.3.1,

*)hi+o/na . . . *mh/dwn e)xo/ntwn poliorki/a| ei(=lon they blockaded and captured Eïon which was held by the Medes
T. 1.98.
b. Cause:

tw=n swma/twn qhlu_nome/nwn kai\ ai( yu_xai\ a)rrwsto/terai gi/gnontai by the enfeebling of the body, the spirit too is made weaker
X. O. 4.2.
c. Opposition or Concession: kai\ metapempome/nou au)tou= ou)k e)qe/lw e)lqei=n even though he is sending for me, I am unwilling to go
X. A. 1.3.10. kai/per is usually added (2083).
d. Condition: oi)/omai kai\ nu=n e)/ti e)panorqwqh=nai a)\n ta\ pra/_gmata tou/twn gignome/- nwn if these measures should be taken, I am of the opinion that even now our situation might be rectified
D. 9.76.
e. Attendant Circumstance: *ku=ros a)ne/bh e)pi\ ta\ o)/rh ou)deno\s kwlu/_ontos Cyrus ascended the mountains without opposition (lit. no one hindering)
X. A. 1.2.22 (or since no one opposed him).

§2071

e(kw/n willing, a)/_kwn unwilling are properly participles and are treated as such (cp. 2117 c). Thus,

e)mou= ou)x e(ko/ntos without my consent
S. Aj. 455.
a. a)/_kwn, a)ekaco/menos, a)frone/wn, a)elpte/wn, a)na/rmenos, a)nomologou/menos, a)ti/cwn are the only cases in Greek showing the earlier method of negativing the participle with alpha privative. Elsewhere ou) or mh/ is used.

§2072
The genitive of the participle may stand without its noun or pronoun
a. When the noun or pronoun may easily be supplied from the context. Thus, oi( de\ pole/mioi, prosio/ntwn (tw=n *(ellh/nwn, previously mentioned),

te/ws me\n h(suxi/azon the enemy, as they were approaching, for a while remained quiet
X. A. 5.4.16, e)rw/ta_, e)/fh, w)= *ku=re, . . . w(s (e)mou=) ta)_lhqh= e)rou=ntos put your question (said he), Cyrus, on the supposition that I will speak the truth
X. C. 3.1.9.
b. When the noun or pronoun may easily be supplied otherwise; here, e.g., a)nqrw/pwn or pra_gma/twn is said to be supplied grammatically. Thus, i)o/ntwn ei)s ma/xhn when (men) are going into battle
X. C. 3.3.54, tou=ton to\n tro/pon pra_xqe/ntwn th=s po/lews gi/gnetai ta\ xrh/mata when (things) have happened in this way, the property belongs to the State
D. 24.12; and in u(/_ontos (*dio/s, 934 a)

pollw=| when it was raining hard
X. H. 1.1.16. Quasi-impersonal verbs (933) thus take the genitive rather than the accusative absolute:

ou(/tws e)/xontos in this state of things
P. R. 381c, influenced by ou(/tws e)xo/ntwn
X. A. 3.1.40.
c. When a subordinate clause with o(/ti follows upon the participle in the passive. Thus,

e)saggelqe/ntwn o(/ti *foi/nissai nh=es e)p' au)tou\s ple/ousin it having been announced that Phoenician ships were sailing against them
T. 1.116, dhlwqe/ntos o(/ti e)n tai=s nausi\ tw=n *(ellh/nwn ta\ pra/_gmata e)ge/neto it having been shown that the salvation of the Greeks depended on their navy 1. 74. The plural is used when the subject of the subordinate clause is plural, or when several circumstances are mentioned.

§2073
Exceptionally, the subject of the genitive absolute is the same as that of the main clause. The effect of this irregular construction is to emphasize the idea contained in the genitive absolute. Thus,

bohqhsa/ntwn u(_mw=n proqu/_mws po/lin proslh/yesqe nautiko\n e)/xousan me/ga if you assist us heartily, you will gain to your cause a State having a large navy
T. 3.13. The genitive absolute usually precedes the main verb.
a. The genitive absolute may be used where the grammatical construction demands the dative. Thus,

diabebhko/tos *perikle/ous . . . h)gge/lqh au)tw=| o(/ti *me/gara a)fe/sthke when Pericles had already crossed over, news was brought to him that Megara had revolted
T. 1.114 (in Latin: Pericli iam transgresso nuntiatum est).
b. The subject of the genitive absolute may be identical with the object of the leading verb:

h(=lqon e)pi\ th\n *)epi/dauron w(s e)rh/mou ou)/shs . . . ai(rh/sontes they came against Epidaurus expecting to capture it undefended
T. 5.56.

§2074
Observe that the genitive absolute differs from the Latin ablative abso lute herein: 1. The subject need not be expressed (2072). 2. The subject may appear in the leading clause (2073 a). 3. With a substantive the participle w)/n is always added in prose, whereas Latin has to omit the participle. Thus,

pai/dwn o)/ntwn h(mw=n nobis pueris
P. S. 173a. On e)mou= a)/_kontos me invito, see 2071. 4. Because it has a present participle passive and an aorist and perfect participle active, Greek can use the genitive absolute where Latin, through lack of a past participle active, has to use a clause with dum, cum, etc. Thus,

o(/lhs th=s po/lews e)n toi=s polemikoi=s kindu/_nois e)pitrepome/nhs tw=| strathgw=| cum bellicis in periculis universa respublica imperatori committatur
X. M. 3.1.3, tou= paido\s gela/santos cum puer risisset. Latin uses the absolute case more frequently than Greek because it employs the perfect participle passive where Greek uses the aorist participle active. Thus, *ku=ros sugkale/sa_s tou\s strathgou\s ei)=pen Cyrus, convocatis ducibus, dixit
X. A. 1.4.8.

§2075
The genitive absolute took its rise from such cases as *sarph/donti d' a)/xos ge/neto *glau/kou a)pio/ntos but sorrow came on Sarpedon for Glaucus—departing M 392. The genitive, here properly dependent on a)/xos ge/neto, ceased to be felt as dependent on the governing expression, and was extended, as a distinct construction, to cases in which the governing expression did not take the genitive. Cp. the development of the accusative with the infinitive (1981).

§2076

Accusative Absolute.—A participle stands in the accusative absolute, instead of the genitive, when it is impersonal, or has an infinitive as its subject (as under C). When impersonal, such participles have no apparent grammatical connection with the rest of the sentence.
A. Impersonal verbs: de/on, e)co/n, meto/n, paro/n, prosh=kon, me/lon, metame/lon, pare/xon, parasxo/n, tuxo/n, dokou=n, do/can, or do/canta (tau=ta), geno/menon e)p' e)moi/ as it was in my power.
ou)dei\s to\ mei=zon kako\n ai(rh/setai e)co\n to\ e)/la_tton (ai(rei=sqai) no one will choose the greater evil when it is possible to choose the less
P. Pr. 358d, h(=s (boulh=s)

nu=n a)cioi= tuxei=n ou) meto\n au)tw=| to which he now claims admission though he has no right
L. 31.32,

dh=lon ga\r o(/ti oi)=sqa me/lon ge/ soi for of course you know because it concerns you
P. A. 24d, meteme/lonto o(/ti meta\ ta\ e)n *pu/lw|, kalw=s parasxo/n, ou) cune/bhsan they repented that after what had occurred at Pylos, although a favourable occasion had presented itself, they had not come to terms
T. 5.14. Cp. 2086 d, 2087.
N.—Apart from do/can, tuxo/n, the accusative absolute of the aorist participle of impersonal verbs is very rare.
B. Passive participles used impersonally: gegramme/non, dedogme/non, ei)rhme/non, prostaxqe/n, prostetagme/non. Cp. Eng. granted this is so, this done, which said.

ei)rhme/non d' au)tai=s a)panta=n e)nqa/de . . . eu(/dousi kou)x h(/kousin though it was told them to meet here, they sleep and have not come
Ar. Lys. 13, prostaxqe/n moi u(po\ tou= dh/mou *me/nwna a)/gein ei)s *(ellh/sponton a command having been given (it having been commanded) me by the people to convey Menon to the Hellespont
D. 50.12.
N.—The aorist participle passive is rarely used absolutely: a)melhqe/n, a)porrhqe/n, kataxeirotonhqe/n, ku_rwqe/n, o(risqe/n, peranqe/n, prostaxqe/n, xrhsqe/n.
C. Adjectives with o)/n: a)/dhlon o)/n, dunato\n o)/n, a)du/naton o)/n, ai)sxro\n o)/n, kalo\n o)/n, xrew/n (xrew/ + o)/n), etc.

se\ ou)xi\ e)sw/samen . . . oi(=o/n te o)\n kai\ dunato/n we did not rescue you although it was both feasible and possible
P. Cr. 46a, w(s ou)k a)nagkai=on (o)/n)

to\ kle/ptein, ai)tia=| to\n kle/ptonta on the ground that stealing is not necessary you accuse the thief
X. C. 5.1.13.

§2077
The impersonal character of the above expressions would not be shown by the genitive since the participle in that case marks a distinction between masculine (neuter) and feminine. The accusative absolute, which occurs first in Herodotus and the Attic prose writers of the fifth century, is probably in its origin an internal accusative, developed, at least in part, by way of apposition (991-994), the neuter of a participle or of an adjective standing in apposition to an idea in the leading clause. Thus, prostaxqe\n au)toi=s ou)k e)to/lmhsan ei)sagagei=n (
Is. 1.22) they did not dare to bring him in—a duty that was enjoined (although it was enjoined) upon them. Cp. pei/qei d' *)ore/sthn mhte/ra . . . ktei=nai, pro\s ou)x a(/pantas eu)/kleian fe/ron he persuaded Orestes to slay his mother, a deed that brings not glory in the eyes of all
E. Or. 30.

§2078
The participle of a personal verb may be used absolutely if it is preceded by w(s or w(/sper. Thus, hu)/xeto pro\s tou\s qeou\s ta)_gaqa\ dido/nai, w(s tou\s qeou\s ka/llista ei)do/tas o(poi=a a)gaqa/ e)sti (Socrates) prayed to the gods that they would give him good things, in the belief that the gods know best what sort of things are good
X. M. 1.3.2,

siwph=| e)dei/pnoun, w)/sper tou=to prostetagme/non au)toi=s they were supping in silence just as if this had been enjoined upon them
X. S. 1. 11.
a. Cases without w(s or w(/sper are rare. Thus,

do/canta u(_mi=n tau=ta ei(/lesqe a)/ndras ei)/kosi on reaching this conclusion you chose twenty men
And. 1.81; cp. do/can tau=ta
X. A. 4.1.13 (by analogy to e)/doce tau=ta) and doca/ntwn tou/twn
X. H. 1.7.30. Neuter participles so used come chiefly from impersonal verbs, but
T. 4.125 has ku_rwqe\n ou)de\n oi( *makedo/nes e)xw/roun e)p' oi)/kou the Macedonians proceeded homewards, nothing having been accomplished. The neuter subject is a pronoun, very rarely a substantive (
I. 5.12).

## ADVERBS USED IN CONNECTION WITH CIRCUMSTANTIAL PARTICIPLES

§2079
Adverbs are often used to set forth clearly the relations of time, manner, cause, concession, etc., that are implied in the participle. They occur also with the genitive and accusative absolute. These adverbs modify either the principal verb or the participle itself.

## ADVERBIAL ADJUNCTS OF THE PRINCIPAL VERB

§2080
The adverbs e)/peita thereupon, to/te, ei)=ta (less often e)ntau=qa) then, h)/dh already, ou(/tw so, when used with the verb of the sentence which contains a temporal participle, emphasize the temporal relation: (u(_mw=n de/omai) a)kroa_same/nous dia\ te/lous th=s a)pologi/a_s to/te h)/dh yhfi/zesqai ktl. (I beg you) when you have heard my defence to the end, then and not till then to vote, etc.
And. 1.9, u(pe\r megi/stwn

kai\ kalli/stwn kindu_neu/santes ou(/tw to\n bi/on e)teleu/thsan they incurred danger for a great and noble cause, and so ended their lives
L. 2.79.

§2081

a(/ma at the same time, au)ti/ka immediately, eu)qu/s straightway, metacu/ between, in the midst, though strictly modifying the main verb, are often placed close to a temporal participle which they modify in sense:

a(/ma tau=t' ei)pw\n a)ne/sth saying this, he rose
X. A. 3.1.47, tw=| deciw=| ke/ra| tw=n *)aqhnai/wn eu)qu\s a)pobebhko/ti . . . e)pe/keinto they fell upon the right wing of the Athenians as soon as it had disembarked (lit. upon the right wing when it had disembarked)
T. 4.43,

e)canasta/ntes metacu\ deipnou=ntes getting up in the middle of supper
D. 18.169, pollaxou= me e)pe/sxe le/gonta metacu/ it often checked me when the words were on my lips (in the very act of speaking)
P. A. 40b.

§2082
A participle implying opposition or concession (2066) may have its meaning rendered explicit by o(/mws yet, nevertheless (with or without kai/per, 2083), ei)=ta then or e)/peita afterwards to express censure or surprise (then, for all that): su\n soi\ o(/mws kai\ e)n th=| polemi/a| o)/ntes qarrou=men with you, though we are in the enemies' country, nevertheless we have no fear
X. C. 5.1.26, e)/peit' a)polipw\n tou\s qeou\s e)nqa/de menei=s; and then, though you desert the gods, will you remain here? Ar. Pl. 1148. o(/mws may attach itself more closely to the participle, though belonging with the principal verb:

pei/qou gunaici/, kai/per ou) ste/rgwn o(/mws take the advice of women none the less though thou likest it not
A. Sept. 712.

§2083
With participles of opposition or concession (2066): kai/per although, kai/ (infrequent), although kai\ tau=ta (947) and that too. Thus,

sumbouleu/w soi kai/per new/teros w)/n I give you advice though I am your junior
X. C. 4.5.32, a)poplei= oi)/kade kai/per me/sou xeimw=nos o)/ntos he sailed off home though it was midwinter X. Ag. 2. 31,

*kle/wnos kai/per maniw/dhs ou)=sa h( u(po/sxesis a)pe/bh Cleon's promise, insane though it was, was fulfilled
T. 4.39, kai\ dou=los w)/n ga\r ti/_mios ploutw=n a)nh/r for, slave though he be, the man of wealth is held in esteem E. fr. 142,

a)dikei=s o(/ti a)/ndra h(mi=n to\n spoudaio/taton diafqei/reis gela=n a)napei/qwn, kai\ tau=ta ou(/tw pole/mion o)/nta tw=| ge/lwti you do wrong in that you corrupt the most earnest man we have by tempting him to laugh, and that though he is such an enemy to laughter
X. C. 2.2.16. On kai/toi see 2893 b.
a. In Homer the parts of kai/per are often separated by the participle or an emphatic word connected with it: kai\ a)xnu/menoi/ per although distressed M 178. pe/r may stand alone without kai/: a)na/sxeo khdome/nh per bear up, though vexed A 586. Both uses occur in tragedy. The part. with pe/r is not always concessive.
b. In a negative sentence, ou)de/ (mhde/), with or without pe/r, takes the place of kai/; as gunaiki\ pei/qou mhde\ ta)_lhqh= klu/wn listen to a woman, though thou hearest not the truth E. fr. 440.

§2084
With participles of cause (2064): ou(/tws, dia\ tou=to (tau=ta), e)k tou/tou. Thus, a)nelo/menoi ta\ naua/_gia . . . kai\ o(/ti au)toi=s . . . ou)k a)ntepe/pleon, dia\ tau=ta tropai=on e)/sthsan because they had picked up the wrecks and because they (the enemy) did not sail against them, (for this reason) they set up a trophy
T. 1.54.

§2085
With participles of cause (2064): a(/te (a(/te dh), oi(=a or oi(=on (oi(=on dh/) inasmuch as, state the cause as a fact on the authority of the speaker or writer. Thus, o( *ku=ros, a(/te pai=s w)/n, . . . h(/deto th=| stolh=| Cyrus, inasmuch as he was a child, was pleased with the robe
X. C. 1.3.3, h(/komen e(spe/ra_s a)po\ tou= stratope/dou, oi(=on de\ dia\ xro/nou a)fi_gme/nos h)=| e)pi\ ta\_s sunh/qeis diatriba/_s I returned in the evening from the camp, and, as I arrived after a long absence, I proceeded to my accustomed haunts
P. Charm. 153a,

oi(=a dh\ a)pio/ntwn pro\s dei=pnon . . . tw=n peltastw=n, . . . e)pelau/nousi inasmuch as the peltasts were going off to supper, they rode against them
X. H. 5.4.39. w(/ste has the same force in Hdt.

§2086
With participles of cause or purpose, etc. (2064, 2065): w(s. This particle sets forth the ground of belief on which the agent acts, and denotes the thought, assertion, real or presumed intention, in the mind of the subject of the principal verb or of some other person mentioned prominently in the sentence, without implicating the speaker or writer.
a. Thus, a)ph=lqon w(s ni_kh/santes may mean either they departed under the impression that they had been victorious (though as a matter of fact they may have been defeated) or pretending that they had been victorious (when they knew they had been defeated). The use of w(s implies nothing as to the opinion of the speaker or writer. On the other hand a)ph=lqon ni_kh/santes means that, as a matter of fact, and on the authority of the writer, they had been victorious.
b. w(s may be rendered as if (though there is nothing conditional in the Greek use, as is shown by the negative ou), not mh/), by in the opinion (belief) that, on the ground that, under pretence of, under the impression that, because as he said (or thought）; in the hope of, with the (avowed) intention of (with the future participle).
c.

e)ntau=q' e)/menon w(s to\ a)/kron kate/xontes : oi( d' ou' katei=xon, a)lla\ masto\s h)=n u(pe\r au)tw=n there they remained in the belief that they were occupying the summit; but in fact they were not occupying it, since there was a hill above them
X. A. 4.2.5, tau/thn th\n xw/ra_n e)pe/treye diarpa/sai toi=s *(/ellhsin w(s polemi/a_n ou)=san he turned this country over to the Greeks to ravage on the ground that it was hostile 1. 2. 19, th\n pro/fasin e)poiei=to w(s *pi_si/da_s boulo/menos e)kbalei=n he made his pretence as if he wished (i.e. he gave as his pretext his desire) to expel the Pisidians 1. 2. 1, pareskeua/zonto w(s polemh/sontes they made preparations to go to war (with the avowed intention of going to war)
T. 2.7, sullamba/nei *ku=ron w(s a)poktenw=n he seized Cyrus for the purpose (as he declared) of putting him to death
X. A. 1.1.3, and often with the future participle. After verbs of motion w(s is rarely used.
d. w(s with the absolute participle:

ou) dei= a)qu_mei=n w(s ou)k eu)ta/ktwn o)/ntwn *)aqhnai/wn we must not be discouraged on the ground that the Athenians are not well disciplined
X. M. 3.5.20,

e)/lege qarrei=n w(s katasthsome/nwn tou/twn e)s to\ de/on he bade him be of good cheer in the assurance that this would arrange itself in the right way
X. A. 1.3.8,

w(s e)co\n h)/dh poiei=n au)toi=s o(/ ti bou/lointo, pollou\s a)pe/kteinon in the belief that it was already in their power to do what they pleased, they put many to death
X. H. 2.3.21. Cp. also 2078, and 2122.

§2087

w(/sper as, just as, as it were, an adverb of comparison, denotes that the action of the main verb is compared with an assumed case. Thus,

katakei/meq' w(/sper e)co\n h(suxi/a_n a)/gein we lie inactive just as if it were possible to take one's ease
X. A. 3.1.3, w)rxou=nto . . . w(/sper e)pideiknu/menoi they danced as it were making an exhibition 5. 4. 34, oi( de\ w(s h)/kousan, w(/sper suo\s a)gri/ou fane/ntos, i(/_entai e)p' au)to/n but when they heard him, just as though a wild boar had appeared, they rushed against him 5. 7. 24. Cp. 2078.
a. Where a condition is meant, we have w(/sper a)\n ei) (w(speranei/). Cp. 2480 a.
b. Hom. uses w(/s te, w(s ei), w(s ei)/ te like w(/sper or w(s. w(s ei), w(s ei)/ te occur also in tragedy, and do not have a conditional force. Thus,

o)lofu_ro/menoi w(s ei) qanato/nde kio/nta bewailing him as if he were going to death
*w 328. Cp. 2481.

## THE SUPPLEMENTARY PARTICIPLE

§2088
The supplementary participle completes the idea of the verb by showing that to which its action relates.

§2089
The supplementary participle agrees either with the subject or with the object of the main verb; with the subject when the verb is intransitive or passive, with the object when the verb is transitive.

ou)/pot' e)pauo/mhn h(ma=s oi)kti/_rwn I never ceased pitying ourselves
X. A. 3.1.19,

tou\s pe/nhtas e)/paus' a)dikoume/nous I put a stop to the poor being wronged
D. 18.102, e(w/rwn ou) katorqou=ntes kai\ tou\s stratiw/ta_s a)xqome/nous they saw that they (themselves) were not succeeding and that the soldiers were indignant
T. 7.47,

a)dikou=nta fi/lippon e)ch/legca I proved that Philip was acting unjustly
D. 18.136,

eu)qu\s e)legxqh/setai geloi=os w)/n he will straightway be proved to be ridiculous
X. M. 1.7.2.
a. When the object is the same as the subject, it is commonly suppressed, and the participle agrees with the subject. Thus,

o(rw= e)camarta/nwn I see that I err
E. Med. 350,

i)/sqi a)no/htos w)/n know that you are a fool
X. A. 2.1.13, ou)k ai)sqa/nesqe e)capatw/menoi; do you not perceive that you are being deceived?
X. H. 7.1.12,

e)dh/lwse tw=n no/mwn katafronw=n he showed that he despised the laws
And. 4.14.
b. For the sake of emphasis or contrast (and to secure greater symmetry) the object may be expressed by the reflexive pronoun. Thus,

oi)=da e)mauto\n dikai/ws kexrhme/non au)toi=s I know that I have presented my case honestly
I. 15.321,

dei=con ou) pepoihko/ta tau=ta sauto/n show that you did not do this yourself
D. 22.29,

a)mfo/ter' ou)=n oi)=de, kai\ au(to\n u(_mi=n e)pibouleu/onta, kai\ u(_ma=s ai)sqanome/nous now he knows both—that he is himself plotting against you and that you are aware of it
D. 6.18. Observe e)la/nqanon au(tou\s e)pi\ tw=| lo/fw| geno/menoi (agreeing with the subject) without knowing it they found themselves on the hill
X. A. 6.3.22. On the use with su/noida, see 2108.
c. e)/oika (the personal use for the impersonal e)/oike, 1983) usually takes the participle in the dative; as,

e)/oikas o)knou=nti le/gein you seem reluctant to speak
P. R. 414c; but also in the nominative (see 2133).

§2090
Many verbs supplementing their meaning by the participle admit of the construction with the infinitive (often with a difference of meaning; see 2123 ff.) or with a substantive clause with o(/ti or w(s.

§2091
The present or perfect participle is often used as a simple predicate adjective, especially with ei)mi/ and gi/gnomai. The aorist participle is chiefly poetic.

h)=san a)pistou=nte/s tines fili/ppw| there were some who distrusted Philip
D. 19.53, (*kle/arxos) filoki/ndu_no/s t' h)=n kai\ h(me/ra_s kai\ nukto\s a)/gwn e)pi\ tou\s polemi/ous Clearchus was both fond of danger and by day and by night led his men against the enemy
X. A. 2.6.7, e)gw\ to\ pra=gm' ei)mi\ tou=q' o( dedra_kw/s I am the one who has done this deed
D. 21.104, h)\ tou=to ou)k e)/sti gigno/menon par' h(mi=n; or is not this something that takes place in us?
P. Phil. 39c. So with adjectivized participles (1857), as

sumfe/ron h)=n th=| po/lei it was advantageous to the State
D. 19.75. So with u(pa/rxw am, am assumed (
D. 18.228).
a. Here the participle has the article when it designates the subject itself (third example; cp. 1152). But the article is not used when the participle marks a class in which the subject is included.

§2092
The supplementary participle after certain verbs represents a dependent statement.
In h)/kouse *ku=ron e)n *kiliki/a| o)/nta he heard that Cyrus was in Cilicia o)/nta stands for e)sti/, what was heard being “*ku=ros e)n *kiliki/a| e)sti/.” This is shown by the fact that the sentence might have been, according to the principles of indirect discourse, h)/kousen o(/ti *ku=ros e)n *kiliki/a| ei)/h (or e)sti/, 2615). With verbs not introducing indirect discourse, however, there is no such indirect statement; as in

e)pau/santo maxo/menoi they ceased fighting
L. 23.9.

§2093
Accordingly, from this point of view, the uses of the supplementary participle are two: (1) not in indirect discourse, and (2) in indirect discourse.
a. Some verbs take the participle either in indirect discourse or not in indirect discourse (2112). It is sometimes impossible to decide whether a participle stands in indirect discourse or not (2113); and the difference, especially after verbs of perceiving (2112 a, b), may be of no great importance to the sense.

## THE SUPPLEMENTARY PARTICIPLE NOT IN INDIRECT DISCOURSE

§2094
The supplementary participle not in indirect discourse is often like an object infinitive, the tenses denoting only stage of action and not difference of time (cp. 1850). Thus, compare pau/ome/n se le/gonta we stop you from speaking (of continued action) with kwlu/_ome/n se le/gein we prevent you from speaking (also of continued action).

§2095
With verbs denoting being in some modified way (2096-2097).

§2096

tugxa/nw (poet. kurw=) happen, am just now, lanqa/nw escape the notice of, am secretly, fqa/nw anticipate, am beforehand.
a. With these verbs the participle contains the main idea, and is often represented in translation by the finite verb with an adverbial phrase; thus, parw\n e)tu/gxane he happened to be there, or he was there by chance
X. A. 1.1.2.
b. The action of fqa/nw and lanqa/nw usually coincides with that of the supplementary participle (present with present, aorist with aorist). But the aorist of a finite verb is occasionally followed by the present participle when it is necessary to mark an action or a state as continuing. ou)k e)/laqon is like an imperfect and may take the present participle. The aorist of tugxa/nw very often takes the present participle. With a present or imperfect of tugxa/nw, lanqa/nw, fqa/nw, the (rare) aorist participle refers to an action or state anterior to that of the present or imperfect. Many of the cases of the present of tugxa/nw with the aorist participle are historical presents; and in some cases the aorist participle is used for the perfect. With other tenses than present or imperfect, an aorist participle with these verbs refers to an action or state coincident in time (cp. 1873).
c. tugxa/nw often loses the idea of chance, and denotes mere coincidence in time (I am just now, I was just then) or simply I am (was).
d. Examples. tugxa/nw:

procenw=n tugxa/nw I happen to be proxenus
D. 52.5,

I. 4.79. Without regard to its mood, the present and imperfect of fqa/nw are followed by the present participle (rarely by the perfect); the future, aorist, and historical present are followed by the aorist participle.

## THE SUPPLEMENTARY PARTICIPLE IN INDIRECT DISCOURSE

§2106

Verbs of Knowing and Showing.—After verbs signifying to know, be ignorant of, learn (not learn of), remember, forget, show, appear, prove, acknowledge, and announce, the participle represents a dependent statement, each tense having the same force as the corresponding tense of the indicative or optative with o(/ti or w(s, the present including also the imperfect, the perfect including also the pluperfect.
Such verbs are: oi)=da, gignw/skw, e)pi/stamai, e)nnow=, manqa/nw (2136), (ou)k) a)gnow=, me/mnhmai, e)pilanqa/nomai (2134), dhlw=, (e)pi) dei/knu_mi, fai/nw, a)pofai/nw, fai/nomai (2143), e)/oika (2089 c, 2133), (e)c-) e)le/gxw, o(mologw= (rarely), a)gge/llw, poiw= represent (2115).
ou) ga\r h)/|desan au)to\n teqnhko/ta (= te/qnhke) for they did not know that he was dead
X. A. 1.10.16, e)/gnw th\n e)sbolh\n e)some/nhn (= e)/stai) he knew that the invasion would take place
T. 2.13, dn u(_mei=s e)pi/stasqe h(ma=s prodo/nta (= prou)/dwke) you know that he betrayed us
X. A. 6.6.17, ti/s ou(/tws eu)h/qhs e)sti\n u(_mw=n o(/stis a)gnoei= to\n e)kei=qen po/lemon deu=r' h(/conta (= h(/cei); who of you is so simple-minded as not to know that the war will come hither from that quarter?

P. Charm. 156a, e)pilelh/smesq' h(de/ws ge/rontes o)/ntes (= e)sme/n) we have gladly forgotten that we are old
E. Bacch. 188, dei/cw (au)to\n) pollw=n qana/twn o)/nt' (= e)sti/)

a)/cion I will show that he deserves to die many times

a. Except with a)gge/llw announce (what is certain), verbs of saying or thinking rarely take the participle in prose, e.g. pa=si tau=ta dedogme/na h(mi=n no/mize (= eu)= i)/sqi) think that this is our unanimous opinion
P. R. 450a.

§2107
The personal constructions dh=lo/s ei)mi, fanero/s ei)mi I am plainly (impersonal dh=lo/n and fanero/n e)stin o(/ti) are followed by a dependent statement in the participle. Thus, dh=los h)=n oi)o/menos (= dh=lon h)=n o(/ti oi)/oito) it was clear that he thought
X. A. 2.5.27, qu/_wn fanero\s h)=n polla/kis (= fanero\n h)=n o(/ti qu/_oi) it was evident that he often sacrificed
X. M. 1.1.2, a)nia_qei\s dh=los h)=n (= dh=lon h)=n o(/ti a)nia_qei/h) he showed his dissatisfaction
X. C. 2.2.3.

§2108
The participle with su/noida or suggignw/skw am conscious, accompanied by the dative of the reflexive pronoun, may stand either in the nominative agreeing with the subject, or in the dative agreeing with the reflexive. Thus, suneidw\s au)to\s au(tw=| e)/rgon ei)rgasme/nos conscious (to himself) that he had done the deed
Ant. 6.5,

e)mautw=| cunh/|dh ou)de\n e)pistame/nw| I was conscious of knowing nothing
P. A. 22c.
a. When the subject is not the same as the object, the latter, with the participle, may stand in the dative, or (rarely) in the accusative. Thus, cuni/sa_si *melh/tw| me\n yeudome/nw|, e)moi\ de\ a)lhqeu/onti they know as well as Meletus that he is lying, and (as well as I do) that I am speaking the truth
P. A. 34b,

suneidw\s tw=n a)_qlhma/twn dou/lous mete/xontas knowing that slaves participate in the contests
D. 61.23. (The force of su/n at times almost disappears.)

§2109
The use of the participle to represent a dependent statement comes from its circumstantial use. Thus, in ou) ga\r h)/|desan au)to\n teqnhko/ta (2106), teqnhko/ta agrees with the object of h)/|desan; and from they did not know him as dead the thought passes into they did not know (the fact) that he was dead.

## CONSTRUCTION OF VERBS OF PERCEIVING AND OF FINDING

§2110

Verbs of Perception.—Verbs signifying to see, perceive, hear, learn (i.e. learn by inquiry, hear of), when they denote physical (actual) perception take the participle. When they denote intellectual perception they may take the participle or o(/ti or w(s with a finite verb. (The Homeric usage is less strict.)

§2111
Such verbs are, in Attic, o(rw= see, ai)sqa/nomai perceive, a)kou/w hear, punqa/nomai learn.

§2112
The participle may stand either not in indirect discourse or in indirect discourse.
a. Not in Indirect Discourse.—Here verbs of perceiving denote physical perception—the act perceived or heard of. With a)kou/w and punqa/nomai the participle stands in the genitive; with ai)sqa/nomai it usually stands in the accusative (as with o(rw=), but sometimes in the genitive. (See 1361, 1367.)

ei)=de *kle/arxon dielau/nonta he saw Clearchus riding through
X. A. 1.5.12;

ai)sqo/menos *lamprokle/a_ pro\s th\n mhte/ra xalepai/nonta perceiving Lamprocles angry with his mother
X. M. 2.2.1, h)/|sqhsai pw/pote/ mou h)\ yeudomarturou=ntos h)\ su_kofantou=ntos; have you ever noticed me either bearing false witness or playing the part of an informer? 4. 4. 11;

h)/kousan au)tou= fwnh/santos they heard him speaking
X. S. 3. 13;

w(s e)pu/qonto th=s *pu/lou kateilhmme/nhs when they learned of the capture of Pylos
T. 4.6.
N. Verbs of physical perception, o(rw= (especially) and a)kou/w, regularly take the present participle in Attic prose, which usually refuses to distinguish between I see a house burning and I see a house burn. The complexive aorist, summing up the action, does however occur, as

w(s ei)=den e)lafon e)kphdh/sa_san . . . e)di/wken when he saw a hind break cover he gave chase
X. C. 1.4.8. Cp. peso/nta ei)=don
Hdt. 9.22.
b. In Indirect Discourse.—Here verbs of perceiving denote intellectual perception—the fact that something is perceived or heard of. With a)kou/w and punqa/nomai the participle stands in the accusative (as with o(rw=, ai)sqa/nomai). Cp. 1363, 1365, 2144, 2145.

o(rw=men pa/nta a)lhqh= o)/nta a(\ le/gete we see that everything you say is true
X. A. 5.5.24,

ai)sqa/nomai tau=ta ou(/tws e)/xonta I perceive that this is so
X. M. 3.5.5,

h)/kouse *ku=ron e)n *kiliki/a| o)/nta he heard that Cyrus was in Cilicia
X. A. 1.4.5,

o(/tan klu/h| tino\s h(/cont' *)ore/sthn when she hears from any one that Orestes will return
S. El. 293,

puqo/menoi *)artace/rchn teqnhko/ta having learned that Artaxerxes was dead
T. 4.50.

§2113

Verbs of Finding.—Verbs of finding and detecting (eu(ri/skw, (kata）lamba/nw; pass. a(li/skomai) in their capacity as verbs of perceiving take the participle (a) not in indirect discourse, of the act or state in which a person or thing is found; or (b) in indirect discourse, of the fact that a person or thing is found in an act or state.
a. kh=ruc a)fiko/menos hu(=re tou\s a)/ndras diefqarme/nous the herald, on his arrival, found the men already put to death
T. 2.6,

eu(/rhtai pistw=s pra/_ttwn he has been found to have dealt faithfully
D. 19.332,

a)\_n a)/r' a)/llon tina\ lamba/nh| yeudo/menon if then he catch anybody else lying
P. R. 389d, h)\n e)pibouleu/wn a(li/skhtai if he be detected in plotting X. Ag. 8. 3.
b.

dia\ th\n *)i_li/ou a(/lwsin eu(ri/skousi sfi/si e)ou=san th\n a)rxh\n th=s e)/xqrhs they conclude that the beginning of their enmity was on account of the capture of Ilium
Hdt. 1.5.

§2114
It is often difficult to distinguish the two constructions of 2113. Thus, katalamba/nousi newsti\ sta/sei tou\s tw=n *)aqhnai/wn e)nanti/ous e)kpeptwko/tas (
T. 7.33) may mean they found that the anti-Athenian party had been recently expelled by a revolution (ind. disc.) or them recently expelled (not in ind. disc.). So

katalamba/nousi . . . ta)=lla a)festhko/ta they found the other cities in a state of revolt
T. 1.59 (that they had revolted would be possible). In the meaning discover, find katalamba/nw does not take the aorist participle.

§2115

poiw= meaning represent has the construction of the verbs of 2113. Thus, plhsia/zontas tou\s qeou\s toi=s a)nqrw/pois oi(=o/n t' au)toi=s poih=sai it is possible for them (poets) to represent the gods as drawing nigh to men
I. 9.9. Cp. 2142.

## OMISSION OF w)/n

§2116
The participle w)/n is often omitted.

§2117
After a(/te, oi(=a, w(s, or kai/per, w)/n is often omitted in prose with predicate adjectives: sundei/pnous e)/laben a)mfote/rous pro\s e(auto\n w(s fi/lous h)/dh (o)/ntas) he took both to supper with him since they were now friends
X. C. 3.2.25. Such omission is rare in prose except after these particles: ei) h(/ttous (o)/ntes)

tw=n polemi/wn lhfqhso/meqa if we shall be caught at the mercy of our enemies
X. A. 5.6.13. With predicate substantives, even after these particles, w)/n is very rarely omitted (
P. R. 568b).
a. In the genitive and accusative absolute the particles of 2117 usually precede when w)/n is omitted. With the genitive absolute the omission is very rare in prose: w(s e(toi/mwn (o)/ntwn) xrhma/twn just as though the property was at their disposal
X. A. 7.8.11; but h(me/ra_s h)/dh (ou)/shs) it being already day
T. 5.59. In poetry the substantive usually suggests the verb: u(fhghth=ros ou)deno\s (o)/ntos) fi/lwn with no friend to guide him
S. O. C. 1588. Accusative absolute: w(s kalo\n (o)\n) a)goreu/esqai au)to/n on the ground that it is admirable for it (the speech) to be delivered
T. 2.35. Without the particles of 2117, the omission of o)/n is poetical (
S. Ant. 44). The omission of o)/n with adjectives ending in -on aids euphony.
b. e(kw/n willing, a)/_kwn unwilling are treated like participles (2071):

e)mou= me\n ou)x e(ko/ntos against my will
S. Aj. 455.
c. w)/n must be used when it has the force of in the capacity of.

§2118
A predicate substantive or adjective, coördinated with a participle in the same construction, may omit w)/n; as

ou) r(a/|dion h)=n mh\ a(qro/ois kai\ a)llh/lous perimei/na_si dielqei=n th\n polemi/a_n it was not easy for them to pass through the enemy's country except in a body and after having waited for one another
T. 5.64.

§2119

w)/n may be omitted with verbs taking a supplementary participle; so with verbs meaning to perceive (2111 ff.), know, show, announce, find, discover, etc.; especially with fai/nomai, tugxa/nw (poet. kurw=), diatelw=, diagi/gnomai, rarely with periorw= and sumbai/nw. Thus, o(rw= me/gan (o)/nta)

## *(ws WITH A PARTICIPLE IN INDIRECT DISCOURSE

§2120

w(s is often used with a participle in indirect discourse to mark the mental attitude of the subject of the main verb or of some other person mentioned prominently in the sentence (cp. 2086); sometimes, to denote emphasis, when that mental attitude is already clearly marked.
w(s mhde\n ei)do/t' i)/sqi me be assured that I know nothing (lit. understand that you are to assume that I know nothing)
S. Ph. 253, dh=los h)=n *ku=ros w(s speu/dwn Cyrus was plainly bent on haste (Cyrus showed that it was his intention to make haste)
X. A. 1.5.9.

§2121
A participle with w(s may follow a verb of thinking or saying though the verb in question does not take the participle in indirect discourse without w(s. Thus,

w(s ta\ be/ltista bouleu/ontes i)_sxu_ri/zonto they kept insisting in the belief that they were recommending the best course
T. 4.68, w(s strathgh/sont' e)me\ tau/thn th\n strathgi/a_n mhdei\s u(_mw=n lege/tw let no one of you say (i.e. speak of me in the belief) that I will assume this command
X. A. 1.3.15.

§2122
So after verbs admitting the supplementary participle in indirect discourse we may have the genitive or accusative absolute with w(s instead of the participle or a clause with o(/ti or w(s. Thus, w(s pole/mou o)/ntos par' u(_mw=n a)paggelw=; shall I report from you (on the assumption) that there is war?
X. A. 2.1.21, w(s e)mou= ou)=n i)o/ntos, o(/ph| kai\ u(_mei=s, ou(/tw th\n gnw/mhn e)/xete make up your minds (on the assumption) that I am going wherever you go (= be sure that I am going, etc.) 1. 3. 6 (here th\n gnw/mhn e)/xete could not take the participle without w(s); w(s pa/nu moi dokou=n, ou(/tws i)/sqi rest assured that it is my decided opinion (lit. on the assumption that this seems so to me, understand accordingly)
X. M. 4.2.30. For w(s with the absolute participle not in indirect discourse, see 2086 d.

## VERBS TAKING EITHER THE PARTICIPLE OR THE INFINITIVE

§2123
Some verbs admit either the supplementary participle or the infinitive, sometimes with only a slight difference in meaning. Cases where the difference is marked are given below. (Most of the verbs in question admit also a substantive clause with o(/ti or w(s, 2577).

§2124
Infinitive and participle here differ greatly when the infinitive expresses purpose or result. Where the infinitive shows only its abstract verbal meaning it differs but little from the participle (cp. 2144).

§2125
A participle or infinitive standing in indirect discourse is indicated in 2126-2143 by O (ratio) O (bliqua); when not standing in O. O. this fact is ordinarily not indicated.

§2126

ai)sxu/_nomai and ai)dou=mai with part. (2100) = I am ashamed of doing something which I do; with inf. = I am ashamed to do something which I have refrained from doing up to the present time and may never do. Thus,

tou=to me\n ou)k ai)sxu/_nomai le/gwn: to\ de\ . . . ai)sxu_noi/mhn a)\n le/gein I am not ashamed of saying this; but the following I should be ashamed to say
X. C. 5.1.21,
