## THE PARTICIPLE WITH a)/n

§2146
The participle with a)/n represents the indicative with a)/n (1784 ff.) or the potential optative with a)/n (1824). The present participle with a)/n thus represents either the imperfect indicative with a)/n or the present optative with a)/n; the aorist participle with a)/n represents either the aorist indicative with a)/n or the aorist optative with a)/n. Cp. 1845 ff.

## REMARKS ON SOME USES OF PARTICIPLES

§2147
The abundance of its participles is one of the characteristic features of Greek. Their use gives brevity to the sentence (cp. 2050), enabling the writer to set forth in a word modifications and amplifications of the main thought for which we require cumbersome relative clauses. But an excessive use of participles, especially in close conjunction, marked a careless style.
a. The participle may contain the leading thought, the finite verb the subordinate thought, of a sentence. Thus, to\ yh/fisma tou=to gra/fw . . . tou\s o(/rkous th\n taxi/sthn a)polamba/nein, i(/n' e)xo/ntwn tw=n *qra|kw=n . . . tau=ta ta\ xwri/a, a(\ nu=n ou)=tos die/su_re . . ., ou(/tw gi/gnoinq' oi( o(/rkoi I moved this bill that the envoys should with all speed receive Philip's oaths in order that when the oaths were taken the Thracians might be in possession of the places which the plaintiff has just now been ridiculing (lit. while the Thracians were in possession, etc. . . . the oaths might under these circumstances be ratified)
D. 18.27, bou/lomai o)li/ga e(kate/rous a)namnh/sa_s katabai/nein I wish to recall a few things to the memory of each party and then sit down (descend from the bema)
L. 12.92. Cp. also 2096, 2099.
b. The participle may repeat the stem and meaning of the finite verb. Thus, kai\ eu)xo/menos a)/n tis tau=ta eu)/caito and some one might (praying) utter this prayer
Ant. 6.1.
c. A participial construction may pass over into a construction with a finite verb. Thus, ma/rtura me\n . . . ou)de/na parasxo/menos . . . parekeleu/eto de/ ktl. lit. producing on the one hand no witness . . . on the other hand he exhorted, etc.
D. 57.11, prose/balon tw=| teixi/smati, a)/llw| te tro/pw| peira/_santes kai\ mhxanh\n prosh/gagon lit. they attacked the rampart both making trial in other ways, and they brought up an engine (i.e. and after trying other devices brought up an engine)
T. 4.100.
d. A participle may be used in close connection with a relative or interrogative pronoun. Thus,

ou)d' u(pe\r oi(=a pepoihko/twn a)nqrw/pwn kindu_neu/sete dialogisa/menoi not even calculating what had been the conduct of the men for whom you were going to risk your lives
D. 18.98, e)launome/nwn kai\ u(brizome/nwn kai\ ti/ kako\n ou)xi\ pasxo/ntwn pa=s' h( oi)koume/nh mesth\ ge/gone the whole civilized world is filled with men who are harried to and fro and insulted, nay, what misery is there which they do not suffer? 18. 48.
e. In contrasts, two subjects may, by anacoluthon, belong to one participle in the nominative, though the participle belongs to only one subject (
T. 3.34. 3).
f. Two or more participles may be coördinated without any connective. This is common in Homer when one participle forms a contrast to, or intensifies, another participle. Cp. h)= kai\ e)pw=rt' *)axilh=i kukw/menos u(yo/se qu/_wn, mormu/_rwn a)frw=| ktl. he spake, and swelling in tumult rushed upon Achilles, raging on high, roaring with foam, etc.
*f 324. This is very rare in prose (
Aes. 3.94).
g. In prose such coördination without any connective is incomplete, one participle, e.g., often defining another, as in o( *ku=ros u(polabw\n tou\s feu/gontas sulle/ca_s stra/teuma e)polio/rkei *mi/_lhton taking the exiles under his protection, Cyrus collected an army, and laid siege to Miletus
X. A. 1.1.7. So even when the participles are connected, as chra/_na_s th\n diw/ruxa kai\ paratre/ya_s a)/llh| to\ u(/dwr by draining the canal and (i.e. in consequence of) diverting the water elsewhere
T. 1.109. One participle may be appositive to another. Thus,

e)ce/tasin poih/santes e)n toi=s i(ppeu=si, fa/skontes ei)de/nai bou/lesqai po/soi ei)=en . . ., e)ke/leuon a)pogra/fesqai pa/ntas by making a review in the presence of the cavalry, alleging that they wished to find out how many they were, they ordered all to inscribe themselves
X. H. 2.4.8.
h. A participle with case absolute may be coördinated with a participle not in an absolute case. Thus,

oi( de\ a)fikome/nhs th=s new\s kai\ a)ne/lpiston th\n eu)tuxi/a_n a)kou/santes . . . polu\ e)perrw/sqhsan they were much encouraged on the arrival of the ship and on hearing of the success which was unhoped for
T. 8.106,

metapemfqe/ntes h)/lqomen h)\ ou)deno\s kale/santos we came summoned or at no one's call
L. 4.11.
i. A finite verb may have two or more participles attached to it in different relations. Thus,

oi( peltastai\ prodramo/ntes . . . diaba/ntes th\n xara/dra_n, o(rw=ntes pro/bata polla\ . . . prose/ballon pro\s to\ xwri/on the light-armed troops after running forward and crossing the ravine, proceed to attack the stronghold on seeing quantities of sheep
X. A. 5.2.4. Of several aorist participles, one may be relatively earlier in time than another.
j. A participle may be added predicatively to another participle, and often follows the article belonging to the main participle. Thus,

oi( zw=ntes kataleipo/menoi those who were being left behind alive
T. 7.75.
k. A participle is often omitted when it can be supplied from the context. Thus, w(rmi/santo kai\ au)toi\ . . . e)peidh\ kai\ tou\s *)aqhnai/ous (o(rmisame/nous)

ei)=don they too came to anchor when they saw that the Athenians had done so
T. 2.86.

§2148
The participle often agrees with the logical, and not with the grammatical, subject. The participle thus often agrees with the subject of the finite verb which the writer had in mind when he began the sentence, but for which he later substitutes another verb; or the participle may later be used as if in agreement with the subject of another finite verb than the one actually employed.
a. A participle in the nominative may belong to a finite verb requiring an oblique case. Thus, a)poble/ya_s pro\s tou=ton to\n sto/lon . . ., e)/doce/ moi pa/gkalos ei)=nai (= h(ghsa/mhn pa/gkalon ei)=nai) on looking at this expedition, it seemed to me to be very admirable
P. L. 686d, e)/xontes . . . a)rxh\n megi/sthn . . ., o(/mws ou)de\n tou/twn h(ma=s e)ph=re (= ou)deni\ tou/twn e)ph/rqhmen)

e)camartei=n although we possessed the greatest empire . . . levertheless none of these reasons induced us to do wrong
I. 4.108, e)/docen au)tois (= e)bouleu/santo) ou) tou\s paro/ntas mo/non a)poktei=nai a)lla\ kai\ tou\s a(/pantas *mutilhnai/ous . . . e)pikalou=ntes th\n a)po/stasin ktl. they decided to put to death not merely those who were there but also all the Mytilenaeans, urging against them their revolt, etc.
T. 3.36.
b. Two or more substantives or pronouns with their participles may stand in partitive apposition (981) to the logical subject. Thus, ta\ peri\ *pu/lon u(p' a)mfote/rwn kata\ kra/tos e)polemei=to (= a)mfo/teroi e)pole/moun),

*)aqhnai=oi me\n . . . th\n nh=son periple/ontes . . ., *peloponnh/sioi de\ e)n th=| h(pei/rw| stratopedeuo/menoi the war at Pylus was vigorously waged by both sides, the Athenians on their part by sailing around the island . . . the Peloponnesians by encamping on the mainland
T. 4.23. Cp.

lo/goi d' e)n a)llh/loisin e)rro/qoun kakoi/, fu/lac e)le/gxwn fu/laka bitter words flew loud from one to another, watchman accusing watchman
S. Ant. 259. As the sentence stands, we expect fu/lakos e)le/gxontos fu/laka, but the first clause is equivalent to kakou\s lo/gous ei)/pomen a)llh/lous. Cp.

qauma/zontes a)/llos a)/llw| e)/legen one spoke to the other in astonishment
P. S. 220c. Cp. 982.
c. Without regard to the following construction, a participle may stand in the nominative. The use of the genitive absolute would here be proper, but would cause the main subject of the thought to occupy a subordinate position. Thus, e)pipesw\n th=| *farnaba/zou stratopedei/a|, th=s me\n profulakh=s au)tou= *mu_sw=n o)/ntwn polloi\ e)/peson attacking the camp of Pharnabazus, he slew a large number (= pollou\s a)pe/kteine) of Mysians who constituted his advance guard
X. H. 4.1.24.
N. The nominative participle is sometimes found in clauses without a finite verb, but only when some finite verb is to be supplied (cp.
*y 546), as with ei), e)a/_n, o(/tan (
X. M. 2.1.23); with o(/sa mh/ as far as is possible (
T. 1.111); in replies in dialogue, where it stands in apposition to the subject of the preceding sentence (
P. Ph. 74b); or is interposed as a parenthesis (eu)= poiou=n in
D. 23.143).
d. Likewise a participle may stand in the accusative or (rarely) in the dative when the construction demands another case. Thus, soi\ de\ suggnw/mh (= suggnw/mh e)sti\ se\)

le/gein ta/d' e)sti/, mh\ pa/sxousan w(s e)gw\ kakw=s it is excusable for thee to speak thus, since thou dost not suffer cruelly as I do
E. Med. 814, h)=n h( gnw/mh tou= *)ariste/ws (= e)/doce tw=| *)aristei=),

to\ me\n meq' e(autou= strato/pedon e)/xonti e)n tw=| i)sqmw=| e)pithrei=n tou\s *)aqhnai/ous Aristeus decided to keep his own forces at the Isthmus and watch for the Athenians
T. 1.62.

## VERBAL ADJECTIVES IN -te/os

On verbal adjectives in -to/s, -th/, -to/n, see 425 c, 472, 473.

§2149
Verbal adjectives in -te/os express necessity. They admit two constructions:
1. The personal construction (-te/os, -te/a_, -te/on), passive in meaning, and emphasizing the subject.
2. The (more common) impersonal construction (-te/on, -te/a^, 1052), practically active in meaning, and emphasizing the action.
Both constructions are used with the copula ei)mi/, which may be omitted. The agent—the person on whom the necessity rests— is expressed, if at all, by the dative (never by u(po/ and the genitive).

§2150
Verbal adjectives from transitive verbs take the personal construction when the subject is emphasized; but the impersonal construction, when the emphasis falls on the verbal adjective itself. Verbal adjectives from intransitive verbs (that is, such as are followed by the genitive or dative) take only the impersonal construction.
a. Oblique cases of verbal adjectives are rare. Thus,

peri\ tw=n u(_mi=n pra_kte/wn concerning what need be done by us
D. 6.28.

§2151

The Personal (Passive) Construction.—The personal verbal in -te/os is used only when the verb from which it is derived takes the accusative. The verbal agrees with the subject in gender, number, and case. The agent, if expressed, must always stand in the dative.

potamo/s tis h(mi=n e)sti diabate/os a river must be crossed by us
X. A. 2.4.6,

w)felhte/a_ soi h( po/lis e)sti/ the State must be benefited by you
X. M. 3.6.3, e)moi\ tou=to ou) poihte/on this must not be done by me (I must not do this)
X. A. 1.3.15,

oi( summaxei=n e)qe/lontes eu)= poihte/oi those who would be allies must be well treated
X. M. 2.6.27, ou) . . . tosau=ta o)/rh o(ra=te u(_mi=n o)/nta poreute/a; do you not see such high mountains that must be traversed by you?
X. A. 2.5.18.

§2152

The Impersonal (Active) Construction.—The impersonal verbal stands in the neuter nominative, usually singular (-te/on), rarely plural (-te/a^). Its object stands in the case (genitive, dative, or accusative) required by the verb from which the verbal adjective is derived; verbs taking the genitive or dative have the impersonal construction only. The agent, if expressed, must always stand in the dative.

tw=| a)dikou=nti dote/on di/khn the wrong-doer must suffer punishment
P. Euth. 8c,

pista\ kai\ o(mh/rous dote/on kai\ lhpte/on we must give and receive pledges and hostages
X. H. 3.2.18,

to\n qa/naton h(mi=n met' eu)doci/a_s ai(rete/on e)sti/n we must prefer death with honour
I. 6.91,

peiste/on patro\s lo/gois I must obey my father's commands
E. Hipp. 1182, peiste/on ta/de (soi/) thou must obey in this
S. Ph. 994 (distinguish peiste/on e)sti/ se one must persuade thee),

fhmi\ dh\ bohqhte/on ei)=nai toi=s pra/_gmasin u(_mi=n I say that you must render assistance to the interests at stake
D. 1.17, tou\s fi/lous eu)ergethte/on, th\n po/lin w)felhte/on . . ., tw=n boskhma/twn e)pimelhte/on you must do good to your friends, benefit your State, take care of your flocks
X. M. 2.1.28,

h(mi=n cu/mmaxoi a)gaqoi/, ou(\s ou) paradote/a toi=s *)aqhnai/ois e)sti/n we have serviceable allies, whom we must not abandon to the Athenians
T. 1.86, e)yhfi/santo . . . polemhte/a ei)=nai they voted that they must go to war 1. 88.
a. Since the impersonal construction is virtually active, and hence equivalent to dei= with the accusative and infinitive (active or middle), the agent sometimes stands in the accusative, as if dependent on dei=. The copula is (perhaps) always omitted when the agent is expressed by the accusative. Thus, to\n boulo/menon eu)dai/mona ei)=nai swfrosu/nhn diwkte/on kai\ a)skhte/on (= dei= diw/kein kai\ a)skei=n) it is necessary that the man who desires to be happy should pursue and practice temperance
P. G. 507c.

## SUMMARY OF THE FORMS OF SIMPLE SENTENCES

§§ 906-2152 deal, in general, with the simple sentence. The following summary shows the chief forms of simple sentences (921) used in Attic.

§2153
STATEMENTS
1. Statements of Fact (direct assertions) as to the present, past, or future are made in the indicative mood (negative ou)), 1770.
A. Statements of fact include statements of present, past, or future possibility, likelihood, or necessity, which are expressed by the indicative of a verb denoting possibility, likelihood, or necessity, and an infinitive (1774-1779).
B. Statements of customary or repeated past action are made in the imperfect or aorist indicative with a)/n (negative ou)), 1790.
2. Statement of Opinion (usually cautious, doubtful, or modest assertions) as to what may be (might be), can be (could be), may (might, could, would) have been, etc., are made:
A. In reference to the present or past: by e)boulo/mhn a)/n I should like or I should have liked (negative ou)), 1789. (Rarely by the indicative without a)/n, negative mh/ or mh\ ou), 1772.)
B. In reference to the past: by the aorist or imperfect indicative with a)/n (negative ou)), 1784, cp. 1786.
C. In reference to the present (statement of present opinion the verification of which is left to the future): by the optative with a)/n (negative ou)), 1824.
D. In reference to the future: by the present subjunctive with mh/ or mh\ ou) (1801); by ou) mh/ with the aorist subjunctive to denote an emphatic denial (1804).

§2154
ASSUMPTIONS
Assumptions, including concessions, are usually expressed by the imperative (negative mh/), 1839. Other forms occur, as kai\ dh/ with the indicative (negative ou)), 1771; a verb of assuming with the accu sative and infinitive, etc.

§2155
COMMANDS (INCLUDING EXHORTATIONS)
1. Positive Commands are expressed by the
A. Imperative, except in the first person (1835).
B. Subjunctive, in the first person (1797).
C. Future indicative (negative ou)) 1917, 1918; with o(/pws (1920).
D. Optative without a)/n (1820); potential optative with a)/n (negative ou), 1830).
E. Infinitive used independently (2013).
2. Negative Commands (Prohibitions, 1840), including Exhortations, are expressed by mh/ with the
A. Present imperative (1840) or aorist subjunctive (second or third person), 1800.
B. Present or aorist subjunctive in the first person plural (1840).
C. Aorist imperative in the third person (rare), 1840.
D. Future indicative with o(/pws mh/ (1920); with ou) mh/ (1919).
E. Aorist subjunctive with o(/pws mh/ (rare), 1803; with ou) mh/ (rare), 1800, N.
F. Infinitive used independently (2013).

§2156
WISHES
1. mh/ is the negative of a direct expression of a wish, and of all indirect expressions of wish except pw=s a)/n with the optative and a form of bou/lomai with the infinitive.
2. Wishes for the future, whether the object of the wish is reasonable or unreasonable, attainable or unattainable, are expressed by the optative with or without ei)/qe or ei) ga/r (1814, 1815). Indirect expressions are: pw=s a)/n with the optative (1832); bouloi/mhn a)/n with the infinitive (1827).
3. Wishes for the present: that something might be otherwise than it now is, are expressed by the imperfect with ei)/qe or ei) ga/r (1780). Indirect expressions are: w)/felon (with or without ei)/qe or ei) ga/r) and the present or aorist infinitive (1781); e)boulo/mhn (with or without a)/n) with the infinitive (1782, 1789).
4. Wishes for the past: that something might have been otherwise than it then was, are expressed by the aorist indicative with ei)/qe or ei) ga/r (1780). Indirect: w)/felon (with or without ei)/qe or ei) ga/r) with the present or aorist infinitive (1781).
5. Unattainable wishes for the present or past may be entirely reasonable.

§2157
QUESTIONS
A simple question results from making any form of statement interrogative. Direct and indirect questions are treated in 2636 ff. See also the Index.

§2158
EXCLAMATIONS
Exclamations form complete or incomplete (904) sentences. Direct and indirect exclamatory sentences are treated in 2681 ff. See also the Index.

## COMPOUND AND COMPLEX SENTENCES: COÖRDINATION AND SUBORDINATION

§2159
All sentences other than simple sentences are formed by combining simple sentences either by coördination or subordination.

§2160
Coördination produces compound sentences, subordination produces complex sentences. Complex sentences have been developed out of coördinate independent sentences, one of which has been subordinated in form, as in thought, to another.

§2161
Comparative Grammar shows that, historically, coördination was preceded by simple juxtaposition and followed by subordination. Thus the simplest form of associating the two ideas night fell and the enemy departed was nu\c e)ge/neto: oi( pole/mioi a)ph=lqon (or in reverse order). From this was developed a closer connection by means of coördinating conjunctions, e.g. nu\c (me\n) e)ge/neto, oi( de\ pole/mioi a)ph=lqon or oi( de\ pole/mioi a)ph=lqon: nu\c e)ge/neto (or nu\c ga\r e)ge/neto), or nu\c e)ge/neto kai\ oi( pole/mioi a)ph=lqon. Finally it was recognized that one of these ideas was a mere explanation, definition, or supplement of the other, and hence dependent or subordinate. This stage is represented by the complex sentence: e)pei\ (o(/te) nu\c e)ge/neto, oi( pole/mioi a)ph=lqon or nu\c e)ge/neto, w(/ste oi/ pole/mioi a)ph=lqon, and so on to express various other relations. Since Greek inherited from the parent Indo-European language both the subordinate and the coördinate sentence, it must be clearly understood that the above examples of the process of development of sentence-building, though taken from Greek, illustrate an earlier period of the history of language than Greek as we have it. Though it may be possible to reconstruct the form of the earlier, coördinate sentence out of the later, subordinate sentence, and though we have examples of parallel coördinate and subordinate sentences in Greek, the subordinate sentence did not in Greek regularly go through the previous stages of simple juxtaposition and coördination. A subordinate construction produced by analogy to another subordinate construction may not be resolved into the coördinate form.

## SYNTAX OF THE COMPOUND SENTENCE

§2162
A compound sentence consists of two or more simple sentences, grammatically independent of one another and generally united by a coördinating conjunction. Thus,

th=| de\ u(sterai/a| e)poreu/onto dia\ tou= pedi/ou | kai\ | *tissafe/rnhs ei(/peto but on the next day they proceeded through the plain and Tissaphernes kept following them
X. A. 3.4.18.
a. Abbreviated compound sentences, i.e. sentences containing a compound subject with a single verbal predicate or a single subject with a compound verbal predicate, are treated in this book as expanded simple sentences (923, 924).

§2163
Greek has, among others, the following coördinating conjunctions, the uses of which in connecting sentences, clauses, phrases, and single words are described under Particles.
A. Copulative conjunctions: te/ (enclitic), kai/ and, te\. te/, te\ . . kai/, kai\ . . . kai/ both . . . and, ou)de/ (mhde/) and not, nor, ou)/te . . . ou)/te (mh/te . . . mh/te) neither . . . nor.
B. Adversative conjunctions: a)lla/ but, de/ (postpositive, often with me/n in the preceding clause) but, and, a)ta/r but, yet, however, me/ntoi (postpositive) however, yet, kai/toi and yet.
C. Disjunctive conjunctions: h)/ or, h)\ . . . h)/ either . . . or, ei)/te . . . ei)/te (without a verb) either . . . or.
D. Inferential conjunctions: a)/ra then, accordingly, ou)=n therefore, then, nu=n (in the poetic and enclitic forms nun and nu_n) then, therefore, toi/nun now, then, toiga/r (poetic), toiga/rtoi, toigarou=n so then, therefore.
E. Causal conjunction: ga/r for.

§2164
Compound sentences are divided into Copulative, Adversative, Disjunctive, Inferential, and Causal sentences.

## ASYNDETON

§2165
Two or more sentences (or words) independent in form and thought, but juxtaposed, i.e. coördinated without any connective, are asyndetic (from a)su/ndeton not bound together), and such absence of connectives is called asyndeton.
a. The absence of connectives in a language so rich in means of coördination as is Greek is more striking than in other languages. Grammatical asyndeton cannot always be separated from rhetorical asyndeton. Grammatical asyndeton is the absence of a conjunction where a connective might have been used without marked influence on the character of the thought; as especially in explanatory sentences (often after a preparatory word, usually a demonstrative) which take up the matter just introduced; also where, in place of a conjunction, a resumptive word, such as ou(=tos, toiou=tos, tosou=tos, e)ntau=qa, ou(/tw, etc., is employed. Rhetorical asyndeton is the absence of a conjunction where the following sentence contains a distinct advance in the thought and not a mere formal explanation appended to the foregoing sentence. Rhetorical asyndeton generally expresses emotion of some sort, and is the mark of liveliness, rapidity, passion, or impressiveness, of thought, each idea being set forth separately and distinctly. Thus, ou)k a)sebh/s; ou)k w)mo/s; ou)k a)ka/qartos; ou) su_kofa/nths; is he not impious? is he not brutal? is he not impure? is he not a pettifogger?
D. 25.63.

§2166
Asyndeton is frequent in rapid and lively descriptions.

sumbalo/ntes ta\_s a)spi/das e)wqou=nto, e)ma/xonto, a)pe/kteinon, a)pe/qnh|skon interlocking their shields, they shoved, they fought, they slew, they were slain
X. H. 4.3.19, prospeso/ntes e)ma/xonto, e)w/qoun e)wqou=nto, e)/paion e)pai/onto falling upon them, they fought; pushed (and) were pushed; struck (and) were struck
X. C. 7.1.38. Also with anaphora (2167 c), as in

e)/xeis po/lin, e)/xeis trih/reis, e)/xeis xrh/mata, e)/xeis a)/ndras tosou/tous you have a city, you have triremes, you have money, you have so many men
X. A. 7.1.21. Cp.
T. 7.71,
D. 19.76, 19. 215,
P. S. 197d.

§2167
Asyndeton also appears when the unconnected sentence
a. Summarizes the main contents, or expresses the result, of the preceding. Thus,

pa/nt' e)/xeis lo/gon you have the whole story
A. Ag. 582,

a)khko/ate, e(wra(_kate, pepo/nqate, e)/xete: dika/zete you have heard, you have seen, you have suffered, you have the evidence; pronounce your judgment
L. 12.100, fulakh=| me/ntoi pro\ tw=n pulw=n e)nteuco/meqa: e)/sti ga\r a)ei\ tetagme/nh. ou)k a)\n me/llein de/oi, e)/fh o( *ku=ros, a)ll' i)e/nai however, we shall meet with a guard in front of the gates, for one is always stationed there. We must not delay, but advance, said Cyrus
X. C. 7.5.25. This is often the case when a demonstrative takes up the foregoing thought (as e)/doce tau=ta
X. A. 1.3.20) or continues the narrative, as in a)kou/sa_si toi=s strathgoi=s tau=ta e)/doce to\ stra/teuma sunagagei=n 4. 4. 19 (cp. 2061).
b. Expresses a reason or explains the preceding. Thus, mi_kro\n d' u(/pnou laxw\n ei)=den o)/nar: e)/docen au)tw=| . . . skhpto\s pesei=n ktl. when he had snatched a little sleep, he saw a vision; a bolt of lightning seemed to him to fall, etc.
X. A. 3.1.11,

i(kou= pro\s oi)/kous: pa=s se *kadmei/wn lew\s kalei= come home; all the Cadmean folk calls thee
S. O. C. 741. Here ga/r or a)/ra might have been used. So often after a preparatory word (often a demonstrative); as tau)to\n dh/ moi dokei= tou=t' a)/ra kai\ peri\ th\n yu_xh\n ei)=nai: e)/ndhla pa/nta e)sti\n e)n th=| yu_xh=| e)peida\n gumnwqh=| tou= sw/matos ktl. now it seems to me that this is the same with regard to the soul too; everything in the soul is open to view when a man is stripped of his body
P. G. 524d.

e(ni\ mo/nw| proe/xousin oi( i(ppei=s h(ma=s: feu/gein au)toi=s a)sfale/stero/n e)stin h)\ h(mi=n in one point alone has the cavalry the advantage of us: it is safer for them to run away than for us
X. A. 3.2.19, and so when w(/sper is followed by ou(/tw kai/ (
P. R. 557c). Also when me/n ge . . . de/ take up what precedes, as o(/moio/s ge *so/lwn nomoqe/ths kai/ *ti_mokra/ths: o( me/n ge . . . o( de/
D. 24.106. Furthermore after tekmh/rion de/ (994), as
T. 2.50.
c. Repeats a significant word or phrase of the earlier sentence (anaphora). Thus,

kai\ o(/tw| dokei= tau=ta, a)nateina/tw th\n xei=ra: a)ne/teinan a(/pantes and let him who approves this, hold up his hand; they all held up their hands
X. A. 3.2.33. In poetry a thought is often repeated in a different form by means of a juxtaposed sentence (
S. Tr. 1082).
d. Sets forth a contrast in thought to the preceding. This is commoner in poetry than in prose. Thus,

me/llonta tau=ta: tw=n prokeime/nwn ti xrh\ pra/_ssein this lies in the future; the present must be thy care
S. Ant. 1334.
e. Introduces a new thought or indicates a change to a new form of expression. Thus, a)ll' i)te/on, e)/fh. prw=to/n me u(pomnh/sate a(\ e)le/gete but we must proceed, said he. First recall to my mind what you were saying
P. Ph. 91c.
f. Is introduced by a word stressed by emotion, as tau=ta
D. 3.32, e)gw/ 4. 29.
On juxtaposition of participles, see 2147.

## COÖRDINATION IN PLACE OF SUBORDINATION—PARATAXIS

§2168
The term parataxis (para/tacis arranging side by side), as here employed, is restricted to the arrangement of two independent sentences side by side, though one is in thought subordinate to the other.
a. In Greek, para/tacis means simply coördination in general, as u(po/tacis means subordination.

§2169
In many cases parataxis is a common form of expression not only in the earlier language of Homer, but also in Attic prose and poetry.
So frequently in Attic prose with kai/, te\ . . . kai/, a(/ma . . . kai/, eu)qu\s . . . kai/, and with de/ meaning for. Thus, h)/dh de\ h)=n o)ye\ . . . kai\ oi( *kori/nqioi pru/mnan e)krou/onto it was already late and (for when) the Corinthians started to row astern
T. 1.50, kai\ h)/dh te h)=n peri\ plh/qousan a)gora\_n kai\ e)/rxontai . . . kh/ru_kes and it was already about the time when the market-place fills and ( = when) heralds arrived
X. A. 2.1.7,

kai\ a(/ma tau=t' e)/lege kai\ a)ph/|ei and as soon as he said this, he departed
X. H. 7.1.28, e)pi/stasqe mo/noi tw=n *(ellh/nwn tou\s a)gaqou\s a)/ndras ti_ma=n: eu(rh/sete de\ . . . par' u(_mi=n strathgou\s a)gaqou\s (a)nakeime/nous) you alone among the Greeks know how to honour men of merit; for you will find statues of brave generals set up among you Lyc. 51. Cp. ske/yasqe de/
T. 1.143.
a. Temporal conjunctions, as h(ni/ka, are rarely used to introduce such clauses, which often indicate a sudden or decisive occurrence or simultaneous action.
b. Thucydides is especially fond of kai/ or te/ to coördinate two ideas, one of which is subordinate to the other.

§2170
Parataxis often occurs when a thought naturally subordinate is made independent for the sake of emphasis or liveliness. Such rhetorical parataxis occurs chiefly in the orators and in Pindar. So especially when me/n and de/ are used to coördinate two contrasted clauses, the former of which is logically subordinate and inserted to heighten the force of the latter. Here English uses whereas, while. Thus,

ai)sxro/n e)sti, ei) e)gw\ me\n ta\ e)/rga tw=n u(pe\r u(_mw=n po/nwn u(pe/meina, u(_mei=s de\ mhde\ tou\s lo/gous au)tw=n a)ne/cesqe it is a shame that, whereas I have undergone the toil of exertions in your cause, you will not endure even their recital
D. 18.160.

§2171
There exist many traces in Greek of the use of the older coördination in place of which some form of subordination was adopted, either entirely or in part, in the later language.
a. Thus several relative pronouns and adverbs were originally demonstrative, and as such pointed either to the earlier or the later clause. So o(, h(, to/ (1105, cp. 1114): teu/xea d' e)cena/rize, ta/ oi( po/re xa/lkeos *)/arhs (H 146) meant originally he stripped him of his arms; these brazen Ares had given him. te/ws so long is properly demonstrative, but has acquired a relative function in

kai\ te/ws e)sti\ kairo/s, a)ntila/besqe tw=n pra_gma/twn and while there is time, take our policy in hand
D. 1.20.

§2172
Homer often places two thoughts in juxtaposition without any regard for logical connection. This is especially common with de/, te/, kai/, au)ta/r, a)lla/. Thus, polu\s d' o)rumagdo\s e)p' au)tw=| a)ndrw=n h)de\ kunw=n, a)po/ te/ sfisin (for oi)=s)

u(/pnos o)/lwlen and there is loud clamour around him of men and of dogs, and sleep is gone from them
*k 185.
a. So also in clauses preceded by a relative word; as ei(=os o( tau=q' w(/rmaine . . ., e)k d' *(ele/nh qala/moio . . . h)/luqen while he was pondering on this, (but) Helen came forth from her chamber
d 120, o(/s ke qeoi=s e)pipei/qhtai, ma/la t' e)/kluon au)tou= whoever obeys the gods, (and) him they hear
*a 218.
b. This use appears even in Attic prose; as oi)kou=|si d' e)n mia=| tw=n nh/swn ou) mega/lh|, kalei=tai de\ (for h(\ kalei=tai) *lipa/ra_ they dwell in one of the islands that is not large, and it (which) is called Lipara
T. 3.88. Cp. also 2837.

## SYNTAX OF THE COMPLEX SENTENCE

§2173
A complex sentence consists of a principal sentence and one or more subordinate, or dependent, sentences. The principal sentence, as each subordinate sentence, has its own subject and predicate. The principal sentence of a complex sentence is called the principal clause, the subordinate sentence is called the subordinate clause. The principal clause may precede or follow the subordinate clause.

§2174
The principal clause may have any form of the simple sentence.
a. Parentheses belonging to the thought of the entire sentence, but standing in no close grammatical relation to it, count as principal clauses. So oi)=mai, dokw=, fhmi/, o(ra=|s; oi)=da, oi)=d' o(/ti certainly (2585), eu)= i)/sqi know well, ai)tou=mai/ se I beseech thee; pw=s (po/son) dokei=s; and pw=s oi)/ei; in the comic poets and Euripides, etc. Some of these expressions are almost adverbial.

§2175
The subordinate clause is always introduced by a subordinating conjunction, as ei) if, e)pei/ since or when, o(/ti that, e(/ws until, etc.

§2176
A finite mood in a subordinate clause may be influenced by the tense of the principal clause. If the verb of the principal clause stands in a secondary tense, the verb of the subordinate clause is often optative instead of indicative or subjunctive, as it would have been after a primary tense. Dependence of mood after a secondary tense is never indicated by the subjunctive.

§2177
Each tense in a subordinate clause denotes stage of action; the time is only relative to that of the leading verb. A subordinate clause may be marked by change of person in verb and pronoun.

§2178
A subordinate clause in English may be expressed in Greek by a predicate adjective or substantive. Cp. 1169, 2647.

§2179
A subordinate clause may be coördinate in structure.

e)pei\ d' h)sqe/nei *da_rei=os kai\ u(pw/pteue teleuth\n tou= bi/ou, e)bou/leto/ oi( tw\ pai=de parei=nai but when Darius was ill and suspected that his end was near, he wished his two sons to be by him
X. A. 1.1.1.
a. So a relative clause, though properly subordinate, may be equivalent to a coördinating clause: ei) d' u(_mei=s a)/llo ti gnw/sesqe, o(\ mh\ ge/noito, ti/n' oi)/esq' au)th\n yu_xh\n e(/cein; but if you decide otherwise, —and may this never come to pass!— what do you think will be her feelings?
D. 28.21. In such cases o(/s is equivalent to kai\ ou(=tos, ou(=tos de/, ou(=tos ga/r.

§2180
A clause dependent upon the principal clause may itself be followed by a clause dependent upon itself (a sub-dependent clause).
oi( d' e)/legon (principal clause) o(/ti peri\ spondw=n h(/koien a)/ndres (dependent clause) oi(/tines i(kanoi\ e)/sontai . . . a)paggei=lai (sub-dependent clause) and they said that they had come with regard to a truce and were men who were competent to . . . report
X. A. 2.3.4.

§2181
A verb common to two clauses is generally placed in one clause and omitted from the other (so especially in comparative and relative clauses).
h(/per (tu/xh) a)ei\ be/lti_on (scil. e)pimelei=tai) h)\ h(mei=s h(mw=n au)tw=n e)pimelou/meqa fortune, which always cares better for us than we for ourselves
D. 4.12. Also as in English: o(/ ti de\ me/llete (pra/_ssein), . . . eu)qu\s . . . pra/_ssete but whatever you intend, do it at once
T. 7.15. In comparative clauses with ou)x w(/sper (or w(s) the main and the subordinate clause are sometimes compressed, the predicate of the clause with ou)x being supplied from the w(/sper clause, which is made independent; as ou)x (ou)de\n a)\n e)gi/gneto)

w(/sper nu=n tou/twn ou)de\n gi/gnetai peri\ au)to/n it would not be as now, when none of these things is done for him
P. S. 189c.

## ANTICIPATION (OR PROLEPSIS)

§2182
The subject of the dependent clause is often anticipated and made the object of the verb of the principal clause. This transference, which gives a more prominent place to the subject of the subordinate clause, is called anticipation or prolepsis (pro/lhyis taking before).

de/doika d' au)th\n mh/ ti bouleu/sh| ne/on but I fear lest she may devise something untoward
E. Med. 37,

h)/|dei au)to\n o(/ti me/son e)/xoi tou= *persikou= strateu/matos he knew that he held the centre of the Persian army
X. A. 1.8.21,

e)peme/leto au)tw=n o(/pws a)ei\ a)ndra/poda diateloi=en he took care that they should always continue to be slaves
X. C. 8.1.44. Note o(ra=|s to\n eu)tra/pezon w(s h(du\s bi/os thou seest how sweet is the luxurious life E. fr. 1052. 3.
a. Anticipation is especially common after verbs of saying, seeing, hearing, knowing, fearing, effecting.
b. When a subordinate clause defines a verbal idea consisting of a verb and a substantive, its subject may pass into the principal clause as a genitive depending on the substantive of that clause:

h)=lqe de\ kai\ toi=s *)aqhnai/ois eu)qu\s h( a)ggeli/a_ tw= po/lewn o(/ti a)festa=si and there came straightway to the Athenians also the report that the cities had revolted
T. 1.61 (= o(/ti ai( po/leis a)festa=si).
c. The subject of the dependent clause may be put first in its own clause:

e)pixeirh/swmen ei)pei=n, a)ndrei/a_ ti/ pot' e)sti/n let us try to say what courage is
P. Lach. 190d.
d. The object of the subordinate clause may be anticipated and made the object of the principal clause. Thus,

ei)rw/ta_ o( *da_rei=os th\n te/xnhn ei) e)pi/staito Darius asked if he understood the art
Hdt. 3.130.
e. A still freer use is seen in e)qau/mazen au)to\n o( *lu/_sandros w(s kala\ ta\ de/ndra ei)/h Lysander marvelled at the beauty of his trees (for ta\ de/ndra au)tou= w(s ktl.) X. O. 4. <*>.

## ASSIMILATION OF MOODS

§2183
The mood of a subordinate clause which is intimately connected with the thought of the clause on which it depends, is often assimilated to the mood of that clause. Such subordinate clauses may be simply dependent or sub-dependent (2180).
a. This idiom is most marked in Unreal and Less Vivid Future conditions where the mood of the protasis is the same as that of the principal clause. It is also very common when a past indicative or an optative attracts the mood of a subordinate clause introduced by a relative word referring to indefinite persons or things or to an indefinite time or place. But subordinate clauses standing in a less close relation to the main clause, because they do not continue the same mental attitude but present a new shade of thought, retain their mood unassimilated; e.g. a relative clause, or a temporal clause expressing purpose, after an unreal condition may stand in the optative (
Is. 4.11,
P. R. 600e). On the other hand, there are many cases where the writer may, or may not, adopt modal assimilation without any great difference of meaning. The following sections give the chief occurrences of mood-assimilation apart from that found in Unreal and Less Vivid Future conditions (2302, 2329):

§2184
An indicative referring simply to the present or past remains unassimilated.

cunene/gkoi me\n tau=ta w(s boulo/meqa may this result as we desire
T. 6.20,

ni_kw/|h d' o(/ ti pa=sin me/llei sunoi/sein but may that prevail which is likely to be for the common weal
D. 4.51, e)peida\n diapra/_cwmai a(\ de/omai, h(/cw when I shall have transacted what I want, I will return
X. A. 2.3.29.

§2185

Assimilation to the Indicative.—The subordinate clause takes a past tense of the indicative in dependence on a past tense of the indicative (or its equivalent) denoting unreality.
a. Conditional relative clauses: ei) me\n ga\r h)=n moi xrh/mata, e)ti_mhsa/mhn a)\n xrhma/twn o(/sa e)/mellon e)ktei/sein for if I had money, I should have assessed my penalty at the full sum that I was likely to pay
P. A. 38b,

ei) . . . katemartu/roun a(\ mh\ safw=s h)/|dh a)koh=| de\ h)pista/mhn, deina\ a)\n e)/fh pa/sxein u(p' e)mou= if I brought in as evidence against him matters which I did not know certainly but had learned by hearsay, he would have said that he was suffering a grave injustice at my hands
Ant. 5.74.
b. Temporal clauses:

ou)k a)\n e)pauo/mhn . . ., e(/ws a)pepeira/_qhn th=s sofi/a_s tauthsi/_ I would not have ceased until I had made trial of this wisdom
P. Crat. 396c,

e)xrh=n . . . mh\ pro/teron peri\ tw=n o(mologoume/nwn sumbouleu/ein, pri\n pri\n peri\ tw=n a)mfisbhtoume/nwn h(ma=s e)di/dacan they ought not to have given advice concerning the matters of common agreement before they instructed us on the matters in dispute
I. 4.19.
c. Final clauses: here the principal clause is an unfulfilled wish, an unfulfilled apodosis, or a question with ou); and the indicative in the final clause denotes that the purpose was not or cannot be attained, and cannot be reached by the will of the speaker. Thus, ei) ga\r w)/felon oi(=oi/ te ei)=nai oi( polloi\ ta\ me/gista kaka\ e)rga/zesqai, i(/na oi(=oi/ te h)=san kai\ a)gaqa\ ta\ me/gista would that the many were able to work the greatest evil in order that they might be able (as they are not) to work also the greatest good
P. Cr. 44d,

e)boulo/mhn a)\n *si/mwna th\n au)th\n gnw/mhn e)moi\ e)/xein i(/na . . . r(a|di/ws e)/gnwte ta\ di/kaia I should have liked Simon to be of the same opinion as myself in order that you might easily have rendered a just verdict
L. 3.21,

e)/dei ta\ e)ne/xura to/te labei=n, w(s mhd' ei' e)bou/leto e)du/nato e)capata=n I ought to have taken security at the time in order that he could not have deceived us even if he wished
X. A. 7.6.23, ti/ dh=t' ou)k e)/rri_y' e)mauto\n th=sd' a)po\ pe/tra_s, o(/pws tw=n pa/ntwn po/nwn a)phlla/ghn; why indeed did I not hurl myself from this rock, that I might have been freed from all these toils?
A. Pr. 747.
N. 1.—In this (post-Homeric) construction, i(/na is the regular conjunction in prose; w(s and o(/pws are rare. a)/n is very rarely added and is suspected (
Is. 11.6,
P. L. 959e).
N. 2.—Assimilation does not take place when the final clause is the essential thing and sets forth a real future purpose of the agent of the leading verb, or does not show whether or not the purpose was realized. This occurs especially after i(/na = eo consilio ut, rarely after o(/pws (
X. A. 7.6.16); after w(s only in poetry and Xenophon. The subjunctive or optative is used when the purpose of the agent, and not the non-fulfilment of the action, is emphasized. Thus,

kai/toi xrh=n se . . . h)\ tou=ton mh\ gra/fein h)\ e)kei=non lu/_ein, ou)x, i(/n' o(\ bou/lei su\ ge/nhtai, pa/nta ta\ pra/_gmata suntara/cai you ought either not to have proposed this law or to have repealed the other; not to have thrown everything into confusion to accomplish your desire
D. 24.44.
d. Causal clauses (rarely, as
D. 50.67). Modal assimilation never takes place in indirect questions or in clauses dependent on a verb of fearing.

§2186

Assimilation to the Optative.—When an optative of the principal clause refers to future time (potential optative and optative of wish), the subordinate clause takes the optative by assimilation in the following cases.
a. Conditional relative clauses (regularly): pw=s ga\r a)/n (1832) tis, a(/ ge mh\ e)pi/staito, tau=ta sofo\s ei)/h; for how could any one be wise in that which he does not know?
X. M. 4.6.7, ti/s mi_sei=n du/nait' a)/n u(f' ou(= ei)dei/h kalo/s te kai\ a)gaqo\s nomizo/menos; who could hate one by whom he knew that he was regarded as both beautiful and good?
X. S. 8. 17,

e)/rdoi tis h(\n e(/kastos ei)dei/h te/xnhn would that every man would practise the craft that he understood
Ar. Vesp. 1431, ti/s a)\n . . . mo/loi (1832),

o(/stis diaggei/leie ta)_m' ei)/sw kaka/ would that some one would come to report within my tale of woe
E. Hel. 435.
N. 1.—If the relative has a definite antecedent, assimilation does not take place; but not all relative clauses with an indefinite antecedent are assimilated. Cp.

w(/sper a)\n u(_mw=n e(/kastos ai)sxunqei/h th\n ta/cin lipei=n h(\n a)\n taxqh=| e)n tw=| pole/mw| as each one of you would be ashamed to leave the post to which he may be appointed in war
Aes. 3.7.
N. 2.—A relative clause depending on an infinitive rarely takes the optative:

a)lla\ tou= me\n au)to\n le/gein a(\ mh\ safw=s ei)dei/h ei(/rgesqai dei= one should abstain from saying oneself what one does not know for certain
X. C. 1.6.19. (See 2573.)
b. Temporal clauses (regularly): teqnai/hn, o(/te moi mhke/ti tau=ta me/loi may I die when these things no longer delight me Mimnermus 1. 2,

o( me\n e(kw\n peinw=n fa/goi a)\n o(po/te bou/loito he who starves of his own free will can eat whenever he wishes
X. M. 2.1.18, ei) de\ pa/nu spouda/zoi fagei=n, ei)/poim' a)\n o(/ti para\ tai=s gunaici/n e)stin, e(/ws paratei/naimi tou=ton ktl. but if he was very desirous of eating, I would tell him that “he was with the women” until I had tortured him, etc.
X. C. 1.3.11,

o)/loio mh/pw, pri\n ma/qoimi perish not yet . . . until I learn
S. Ph. 961. But

ou)k a)\n a)pe/lqoimi pri\n a)\n panta/pa_sin h( a)gora\_ luqh=| I shall not be leaving until the gathering in the market-place is quite dispersed
X. O. 12.1.
c. Final and object clauses (rarely in prose, but occasionally after an optative of wish in poetry): peirw/|mhn (a)\n) mh\ pro/sw u(_mw=n ei)=nai, i(/na, ei)/ pou kairo\s ei)/h, e)pifanei/hn I will try to keep not far away from you, in order that, if there should be any occasion, I may show myself
X. C. 2.4.17 (and five other cases in Xen.);

e)/lqoi o(/pws ge/noito tw=nd' e)moi\ luth/rios may she come to prove my liberator from this affliction
A. Eum. 297. Ordinarily the subjunctive or future indicative is retained, as

o)knoi/hn a)\n ei)s ta\ ploi=a e)mbai/nein a(\ *ku=ros h(mi=n doi/h mh\ h(ma=s . . . katadu/_sh| I should hesitate to embark on the vessels which Cyrus might give us lest he sink us
X. A. 1.3.17,

teqnai/hn, di/khn e)piqei\s tw=| a)dikou=nti, i(/na mh\ e)nqa/de me/nw katage/lastos let me die, when I have punished him who has done me wrong, that I may not remain here a laughing-stock
P. A. 28d.
d. Indirect questions, when the direct question was a deliberative subjunctive:

ou)k a)\n e)/xois e)celqw\n o(/ ti xrw=|o sautw=| if you should escape, you would not know what to do with yourself
P. Cr. 45b ( = ti/ xrw=mai;). But when a direct question or a direct quotation stood in the indicative, that mood is retained, as

ei) a)podeixqei/h ti/nas xrh\ h(gei=sqai tou= plaisi/ou if it should be settled who must lead the square
X. A. 3.2.36.
e. Very rarely in relative clauses of purpose (
P. R. 578e possibly); after w(/ste (
X. C. 5.5.30), and in dependent statements with o(/ti or w(s (
X. C. 3.1.28).
f. Assimilation and non-assimilation may occur in the same sentence (
E. Bacch. 1384 ff.)

§2187
An optative referring to general past time in a general supposition usually assimilates the mood of a conditional relative or temporal clause depending on that optative.
e)/xairen o(po/te ta/xista tuxo/ntas w(=n de/ointo a)pope/mpoi but he was wont to rejoice whenever he dismissed without delay his petitioners with their requests granted (lit. obtaining what they wanted) X. Ag. 9. 2. But the indicative may remain unassimilated, as

e)ka/lei de\ kai\ e)ti/_ma_ o(po/te tina\s i)/doi toiou=to/n ti poih/santas o(\ au)to\s e)bou/leto poiei=n and he was wont to honour with an invitation any whom he saw practising anything that he himself wished them to do
X. C. 2.1.30.
So when the optative refers to past time through dependence on a verb of past time, as

proskalw=n tou\s fi/lous e)spoudaiologei=to w(s dhloi/h ou(\s ti_ma=| summoning his friends he used to carry on a serious conversation with them in order to show whom he honoured
X. A. 1.9.28 (here ti_mw/|h would be possible).

§2188

Assimilation to the Subjunctive.—Conditional relative clauses and temporal clauses referring to future or general present time, if dependent on a subjunctive, take the subjunctive.
a. In reference to future time: tw=n pra_gma/twn tou\s bouleuome/nous (h(gei=sqai dei=),

i(/n' a(\_n e)kei/nois dokh=|, tau=ta pra/_tthtai men of counsel must guide events in order that what they resolve shall be accomplished
D. 4.39.
b. In reference to general present time:

ou)d', e)peida\n w(=n a)\n pri/htai ku/_rios ge/nhtai, tw=| prodo/th| sumbou/lw| peri\ tw=n loipw=n e)/ti xrh=tai nor when he has become master of what he purchases, does he any longer employ the traitor to advise him concerning his plans for the future
D. 18.47. But the indicative may occur (
D. 22.22).

## CLASSES OF SUBORDINATE CLAUSES

§2189
Subordinate clauses are of three classes:
1. Substantival clauses: in which the subordinate clause plays the part of a substantive and is either the subject or the object:

dh=lon h)=n | o(/ti e)ggu/s pou basileu\s h)=n it was plain that the king was somewhere hard by
X. A. 2.3.6, ou)k i)/ste | o(/ ti poiei=te you do not know what you are doing 1. 5. 16.
2. Adjectival (attributive) clauses: in which the subordinate clause plays the part of an adjective, and contains a relative whose antecedent (expressed or implied) stands in the principal clause:

le/ge dh\ th\n e)pistolh\n | h(\n e)/pemye *fi/lippos come read the letter which Philip sent
D. 18.39 ( = th\n u(po\ *fili/ppou pemfqei=san).
3. Adverbial clauses: in which the subordinate clause plays the part of an adverb or adverbial expression modifying the principal clause in like manner as an adverb modifies a verb.

kraugh\n pollh\n e)poi/oun kalou=ntes a)llh/lous, w(/ste kai\ tou\s polemi/ous a)kou/ein they made a loud noise by calling each other so that even the enemy heard them
X. A. 2.2.17 (here w(/ste . . . a)kou/ein may be regarded as having the force of an adverb: and in a manner audible even to the enemy); pw=s a)\n ou)=n o)rqw=s dika/saite peri\ au)tw=n; ei) tou/tous e)a/_sete to\n nomizo/menon o(/rkon diomosame/nous kathgorh=sai ktl. how then would you judge correctly about them? if you permit (i.e. by permitting) them to make their accusations after having sworn the customary oath, etc.
Ant. 5.90. Cp. 1095 end.

§2190
Accordingly all complex sentences may be classified as Substantival sentences, Adjectival sentences, and Adverbial sentences. This division is, in general, the basis of the treatment of complex sentences in this book, except when, for convenience, closely connected constructions are treated together; as in the case of (adverbial) pure final clauses and (substantival) object clauses after verbs of effort and of fearing.
a. Some sentences may be classed both as substantival and adverbial, as clauses with w(/ste and o(/pws. An adverbial or adjectival clause may assume a substantival character (2247, 2488).
Complex sentences are considered in the following order: Adverbial, Adjectival, Substantival.

## ADVERBIAL COMPLEX SENTENCES (2193-2487）

§2191
In an adverbial complex sentence the subordinate clause denotes some one of the following adverbial relations: purpose (2193), cause (2240), result (2249), condition (2280), concession (2369), time (2383), comparison (2462).

§2192
An adverbial sentence is introduced by a relative conjunction denoting purpose, cause, result, etc.

## PURPOSE CLAUSES (FINAL CLAUSES）

§2193
Final clauses denote purpose and are introduced by i(/na, o(/pws, w(s in order that, that (Lat. ut); negative i(/na mh/, o(/pws mh/, w(s mh/, and mh/ alone, lest (Lat. ne).
a. Also by o)/fra, strictly while, until, in Epic and Lyric; and e(/ws in Epic (2418). i(/na is the chief final conjunction in Aristophanes, Herodotus, Plato, and the orators. It is the only purely final conjunction in that it does not limit the idea of purpose by the idea of time (like o)/fra and e(/ws), or of manner (like o(/pws and w(s); and therefore never takes a)/n (ke/n), since the purpose is regarded as free from all conditions (2201 b). o(/pws is the chief final conjunction in Thucydides, and in Xenophon (slightly more common than i(/na). w(s often shows the original meaning in which way, how, as (cp. 2578, 2989). It is rare in prose, except in Xenophon, and does not occur on inscriptions; rare in Aristophanes, but common in tragedy, especially in Euripides. mh/ is very rare in prose, except in Xenophon and Plato (mh\ ou) is very rare in Homer and in Attic:
X. M. 2.2.14).
b. In order that no one is i(/na (etc.) mhdei/s or mh/ tis, in order that . . . never is i(/na (etc.) mh/pote or mh/ pote, and in order that . . . not is mhde/ after mh/.

§2194
Final clauses were developed from original coördination.

qa/pte me o(/tti ta/xista: pu/la_s *)ai/da_o perh/sw bury me with all speed; let me pass the gates of Hades
*y 71, where we have a sentence of will added without any connective; and (negative) a)po/stixe mh/ ti noh/sh| *(\hrh depart lest Hera observe aught A 522 (originally let Hera not observe anything, 1802). Even in Attic, where subordination is regular, the original form of coördination can be (theoretically) restored, as in

kai/ se pro\s . . . qew=n i(knou=mai mh\ prodou\s h(ma=s ge/nh| and I entreat thee by the gods | do not forsake us
S. Aj. 588. We can no longer trace the original coördination with i(/na and w(s.

§2195
A final clause stands in apposition to tou/tou e(/neka or dia\ tou=to expressed or understood. Thus, e)kklhsi/a_n tou/tou e(/neka cunh/gagon o(/pws u(pomnh/sw I have convened an assembly for this reason that I may remind you
T. 2.60. Here tou/tou e(/neka might be omitted.

§2196
The verb of a final clause stands in the subjunctive after an introductory primary tense, in the optative (sometimes in the subjunctive, 2197) after a secondary tense.
gra/fw i(/na e)kma/qh|s I write (on this account) that you may learn.
gra/fw i(/na mh\ e)kma/qh|s I write (on this account) that you may not learn.
e)/graya i(/na e)kma/qois (or e)kma/qh|s) I wrote (on this account) that you might learn.
e)/graya i(/na mh\ e)kma/qois (or e)kma/qh|s) I wrote (on this account) that you might not learn.

kata/mene i(/na kai\ peri\ sou= bouleusw/meqa remain behind that we may consider your case also
X. A. 6.6.28,

basileu\s ai(rei=tai ou)x i(/na e(autou= kalw=s e)pimelh=tai, a)ll' i(/na kai\ oi' e(lo/menoi di' au)to\n eu)= pra/_ttwsi a king is chosen, not that he may care for his own interest however nobly, but that those who choose him may prosper through him
X. M. 3.2.3,

parakalei=s i)_a_trou\s o(/pws mh\ a)poqa/nh| you call in physicians in order that he may not die
X. M. 2.10.2. fu/lakas sumpe/mpei (hist. pres., 1883) . . .

o(/pws a)po\ tw=n dusxwriw=n fula/ttoien au)to/n he sent guards along in order that they might guard him from the rough parts of the country
X. C. 1.4.7.

kai\ a(/ma tau=t' ei)pw\n a)ne/sth w(s mh\ me/lloito a)lla\ perai/noito ta\ de/onta and with these words on his lips he stood up in order that what was needful might not be delayed but be done at once
X. A. 3.1.47,

mh\ speu=de ploutei=n mh\ taxu\s pe/nhs ge/nh| haste not to be rich lest thou soon become poor
Men. Sent. 358. For the optative after an optative, see 2186 c.

§2197
After a secondary tense, the subjunctive may be used in place of the optative.
a. In the narration of past events, the subjunctive sets forth a person's previous purpose in the form in which he conceived his purpose. Thus (ta\ ploi=a) *)abroko/ma_s . . . kate/kausen i(/na mh\ *ku=ros diabh=| Abrocomas burned the boats in order that Cyrus might (may) not cross
X. A. 1.4.18. Here the thought of A. was ‘I will burn the boats that Cyrus may not cross’ (i(/na mh\ diabh=|), and is given in a kind of quotation.
N.—Thucydides and Herodotus prefer this vivid subjunctive; the poets, Plato, and Xenophon, the optative. In Demosthenes, the subjunctive and optative are equally common.
b. When the purpose (or its effect) is represented as still continuing in the present. See the example in 2195. This use is closely connected with a.
c. After ti/ ou), ti/ ou)=n ou), and the aorist indicative: ti/ ou)=n ou)xi\ ta\ me\n tei/xh fulakh=| e)xura\ e)poih/samen o(/pws a)/n (2201) soi sa= h)=| ktl.; why then do we not make your walls strong by a garrison that they may be safe for you, etc.?
X. C. 5.4.37. Here the sentence with e)poih/samen is practically equivalent to one with poih/swmen.

§2198
The alternative construction of final clauses with subjunctive or optative is that of implicit indirect discourse (2622). The subjunctive is always possible instead of the optative. Observe that the subjunctive for the optative is relatively past, since the leading verb is past.

§2199
After a secondary tense both subjunctive and optative may be used in the same sentence.
nau=s oi( *kori/nqioi . . . e)plh/roun o(/pws naumaxi/a_s te a)popeira(_swsi . . ., kai\ ta\_s o(lka/das au)tw=n h)=sson oi<*> e)n th=| *naupa/ktw| *)aqhnai=oi kwlu/_oien a)pai/rein the Corinthians manned . . . ships both to try a naval battle and that the Athenians at Naupactus might be less able to prevent their transports from putting out to sea
T. 7.17.
a. In some cases, especially when the subjunctive precedes, the subjunctive may express the immediate purpose, the realization of which is expected; while the optative expresses the less immediate purpose conceived as a consequence of the action of the subjunctive or as a mere possibility.

§2200
The optative is very rare after a primary tense except when that tense implies a reference to the past as well as to the present.

oi)/xontai i(/na mh\ doi=en di/khn they have gone away that they might not suffer punishment
L. 20.21. Here oi)/xontai is practically equivalent to e)/fugon, and the optative doi=en shows that the purpose was conceived in the past. On the optative (without a)/n) by assimilation after an optative, see 2186 c.

§2201

o(/pws with the subjunctive sometimes takes a)/n in positive clauses.

tou=t' au)to\ nu=n di/dasx', o(/pws a)\n e)kma/qw tell me now this very thing, that I may learn
S. O. C. 575,

a)/ceis h(ma=s o(/pws a)\n ei)dw=men you will guide us in order that we may know
X. C. 5.2.21.
a. w(s and o)/fra with a)/n or ke/ occur in poetry, especially in Homer. w(s a)/n (first in Aeschylus) is very rare in Attic prose, but occurs eight times in Xenophon; as

w(s d' a)\n ma/qh|s . . ., a)nta/kouson but that you may learn, hear me in turn
X. A. 2.5.16. This use must not be confused with w(s a)/n in conditional relative clauses (2565).—o(/pws a)/n is more common than simple o(/pws in Aristophanes and Plato, far less common in Xenophon. It is regular in official and legal language. —i(/na a)/n is not final, but local (wherever, 2567). The original meaning of i(/na was local and denoted the end to be reached.
b. a)/n (ke/) does not appreciably affect the meaning. Originally these particles seem to have had a limiting and conditional force (1762): w(s a)/n in whatever way, that so (cp. so = in order that so) as in “Teach me to die that so I may Rise glorious at the awful day” (Bishop Ken), and cp. w(s with o(/tw| tro/pw| in

i(_ko/mhn to\ *pu_qiko\n mantei=on, w(s ma/qoim' o(/tw| tro/pw| patri\ di/ka_s a)roi/mhn I came to the Pythian shrine that I might learn in what way I might avenge my father
S. El. 33. With o(/pws a)/n cp. e)a/_n pws. Both o(/pws and w(s were originally relative adverbs denoting manner (how, cp. 2578), but when they became conjunctions (in order that), their limitation by a)/n ceased to be felt.

§2202

w(s a)/n and o(/pws a)/n with the optative occur very rarely in Attic prose (in Xenophon especially), and more frequently after secondary than after primary tenses.

e)/dwke xrh/mata *)antalki/da| o(/pws a)\n plhrwqe/ntos nautikou= . . . oi(/ te *)aqhnai=oi . . . ma=llon th=s ei)rh/nhs prosde/ointo he gave money to Antalcidas in order that, if a fleet were manned, the Athenians might be more disposed to peace
X. H. 4.8.16. w(s a)/n final must be distinguished from w(s a)/n consecutive (2278).
a. Homer has a few cases of w(s a)/n (ke/) and o)/fr' a)/n (ke/); i(/na ken once (
m 156). Hdt. has w(s a)/n, o(/kws a)/n rarely.
b. After primary tenses the optative with a)/n is certainly, after secondary tenses probably, potential. Its combination with the final conjunction produces a conditional relative clause in which the relative and interrogative force of o(/pws and w(s comes to light. With o(/pws a)/n the final force is stronger than with w(s a)/n. In the example quoted above, plhrwqe/ntos nautikou= represents the protasis (ei) nautiko\n plhrwqei/h) to a)\n prosde/ointo.

§2203
The future indicative is used, especially in poetry, after o(/pws (rarely after w(s, o)/fra, and mh/) in the same sense as the subjunctive.
ou)de\ di' e(\n a)/llo tre/fontai h)\ o(/pws maxou=ntai nor are they maintained for any other single purpose than for fighting (lit. how they shall fight)
X. C. 2.1.21, si_ga=q', o(/pws mh\ peu/setai/ (fut.) tis . . . glw/sshs xa/rin de\ pa/nt' a)paggei/lh| (subj.)

ta/de keep silence, lest some one hear and report all this for the sake of talk
A. Ch. 265. In prose the future occurs with o(/pws in Xenophon and Andocides. This usage is an extension of that after verbs of effort (2211).

§2204
The principal clause is sometimes omitted.

i(/n' e)k tou/twn a)/rcwmai to begin with this
D. 21.43. i(/na ti/, originally to what end (cp. 946), and w(s ti/ are also used colloquially: i(/na ti/ tau=ta le/geis; why do you say this?
P. A. 26d.

§2205
By assimilation of mood, final clauses may take a past tense of the indicative without a)/n (2185 c) or the optative without a)/n (2186 c.)

§2206

Equivalents of a Final Clause.—The common methods of expressing purpose may be illustrated by the translations (in Attic) of they sent a herald to announce:
e)/pemyan kh/ru_ka i(/na (o(/pws) a)pagge/lloito (2196).
e)/pemyan kh/ru_ka o(/stis (o(\s) a)paggelei=tai (2554).

e)/pemyan kh/ru_ka a)pagge/llein (rare in prose, 2009).

## OBJECT CLAUSES

§2207
Two types of object (substantival) clauses are closely connected in construction with final clauses.
1. Object clauses after verbs of effort.
2. Object clauses after verbs of fearing.
Both stand in apposition to a demonstrative expressed or implied.
ou)de/na dei= tou=to mhxana=sqai, o(/pws a)pofeu/cetai pa=n poiw=n qa/naton no man ought to contrive (this) how he shall escape death at any cost
P. A. 39a,

mhxana=sqai o(/kws to\ sw=ma . . . komiei= to contrive how he might bring home the body
Hdt. 2.121 g, au)to\ tou=to fobou=mai, mh\ . . . ou) dunhqw= dhlw=sai peri\ tw=n pra_gma/twn I am afraid of this very thing, namely, that I may not be able to make the case plain
D. 41.2,

e)fobei=to . . . mh\ ou) du/naito . . . e)celqei=n he was afraid that he could not escape
X. A. 3.1.12.

§2208

Connection of Final with Object Clauses.—(1) Final clauses proper denote a purpose to accomplish or avert a result, which purpose is set forth in a definite action. (2) Object clauses after verbs of effort consider means to accomplish or avert a result; the action of the subordinate clause is the object purposed. Such clauses are incomplete final clauses, because, though the purpose is expressed, the action taken to effect the purpose is not expressed. (3) Object clauses after verbs of fearing deprecate an undesired result or express fear that a desired result may not be accomplished. According to the form of expression employed, the construction of these three kinds of clauses may differ in varying degree or be identical. Thus compare these usages of Attic prose:
(1) parakalei= i)_a_tro\n o(/pws mh\ a)poqa/nh| (common)
parakalei= i)_a_tro\n o(/pws mh\ a)poqanei=tai (occasionally)
parakalei= i)_a_tro\n mh\ a)poqa/nh| (rare)
he summons a physician in order that he may not die.
(2) e)pimelei=tai o(/pws mh\ a)poqanei=tai (common)
e)pimelei=tai o(/pws mh\ a)poqa/nh| (occasionally)
he takes care that he shall not die.
o(/ra_ mh\ a)poqa/nh|s (occasionally) see to it that you do not die.
(3) fobei=tai mh\ a)poqa/nh| (common)
fobei=tai o(/pws mh\ a)poqa/nh| (occasionally)
fobei=tai o(/pws mh\ a)poqanei=tai (occasionally)
he is afraid lest he die.

## OBJECT CLAUSES AFTER VERBS OF EFFORT

§2209
Object clauses after verbs of effort are introduced by o(/pws, rarely by w(s (Herodotus, Xenophon), scarcely ever by i(/na. The negative is mh/.

§2210

Verbs of effort include verbs denoting to take care or pains, to strive.
e)pimelou=mai, me/lei moi, meletw=, frourw=, pro/noian e)/xw, bouleu/omai, mhxanw=mai, paraskeua/zomai, proqu_mou=mai, pra/_ttw, pa/nta poiw= (poiou=mai), spouda/zw, etc.
a. The same construction follows certain verbs of will signifying to ask, command, entreat, exhort , and forbid, and which commonly take the infinitive (ai)tw=, de/omai, paragge/llw, i(keteu/w, dia- or parakeleu/omai, a)pagoreu/w, etc.).
b. Some verbs take, by analogy, but in negative clauses only, the construction either of verbs of effort or of verbs of fearing. These verbs signify to see to a thing: o(rw=, skopw= (-ou=mai), e)skeya/mhn, skepte/on e)sti/, thrw=; to be on one's guard: eu)labou=mai, fronti/zw, fula/ttw (-omai). See 2220.
These verbs may take mh/ with the infinitive. eu)labou=mai and fula/ttomai take the infinitive when they mean to guard against doing something.

§2211
Object clauses after verbs of effort take the future indicative with o(/pws after primary and secondary tenses (rarely the optative after secondary tenses, 2212).

e)pemelou/mhn o(/pws tau=ta poih/sei (poih/soi) I took care that he should do this.
e)pemelou/mhn o(/pws mh\ tau=ta poih/sei (poih/soi) I took care that he should not do this.

ei) a)na/gkh e)sti\ ma/xesqai, tou=to dei= paraskeua/sasqai o(/pws w(s kra/tista maxou/meqa if it is necessary to fight, we must prepare to fight bravely

§2212
After secondary tenses the future optative occasionally occurs.

e)peme/leto o(/pws mh/te a)/si_toi mh/te a)/potoi/ pote e)/sointo he took care that they should never be without food or drink
X. C. 8.1.43.
a. The future optative occurs especially in Xenophon, and represents a thought that was originally expressed by the future indicative. Here the indicative would present the thought vividly, i.e. as it was conceived in the mind of the subject.

§2213

o(/pws and o(/pws mh/ with the future indicative may be used without any principal clause, to denote an urgent exhortation or a warning. Originally the o(/pws clause depended on sko/pei (skopei=te), o(/ra_ (o(ra=te) see to it; but the ellipsis was gradually forgotten and the construction used independently.

o(/pws ou)=n e)/sesqe a)/ndres a)/cioi th=s e)leuqeri/a_s h(=s h(=s ke/kthsqe be men worthy of the freedom which you possess

o(/pws de\ tou=to mh\ dida/ceis mhde/na but don't tell anybody this

§2214

Verbs of effort sometimes have the construction of final clauses, and take, though less often, o(/pws with the present or second aorist subjunctive or optative (cp. 2196). The subjunctive may be used after secondary tenses.
e)/pra_ssen . . . o(/pws po/lemos ge/nhtai he tried to bring it about that war should be occasioned

a. The object desired by the subject of a verb of effort is here expressed by the same construction as is the purpose in the mind of the subject of a final clause.

§2215

a)/n is sometimes added to o(/pws with the subjunctive to denote that the purpose is dependent on certain circumstances.

o(/pws a)\n . . . oi( stratiw=tai peri\ tou= strateu/esqai bouleu/wntai, tou/tou peira(_somai e)peme/lesqai I will endeavour to make it my care that the soldiers deliberate about continuing the war

§2216

w(s and w(s a)/n with subjunctive and optative and o(/pws a)/n with the optative occur in Xenophon, w(s a)/n and o(/pws a)/n with the optative being used after primary and secondary tenses. Hdt. has o(/kws a)/n after secondary tenses. The optative with w(s a)/n and o(/pws a)/n is potential.

§2217
After verbs meaning to consider, plan , and try o)/pws or w(s with the subjunctive (with or without ke/) or optative is used by Homer, who does not employ the future indicative in object clauses denoting a purpose. Thus,

§2218
Verbs of will or desire signifying to ask, command, entreat, exhort , and forbid, which usually have an infinitive as their object, may take o(/pws (o(/pws mh/) with the future indicative (or optative) or the subjunctive (or optative). The o(/pws clause states both the command, etc. and the purpose in giving it. Between take care to do this and I bid you take care to do this the connection is close. Cp. impero, postulo with ut (ne).

diakeleu/ontai o(/pws ti_mwrh/setai they urge him to take revenge
P. R. 549e,

*lakedaimoni/wn e)de/onto to\ yh/fism' o(/pws metastrafei/h they begged the Lacedaemonians that the decree might be changed

a)phgo/reues o(/pws mh\ tou=to a)pokrinoi/mhn you forbade me to give this answer

§2219

Dawes' Canon.—The rule formulated by Dawes and afterwards extended (that the first aorist subjunctive active and middle after o(/pws, o(/pws mh/, and ou) mh/ is incorrect and should be emended) is applicable only in the case of verbs of effort. After these verbs the future is far more common than subjunctive or optative (except in Xenophon), and some scholars would emend the offending sigmatic subjunctives where they occur in the same sentence with second aorists (as
And. 3.14) or even where the future has a widely different form (as e)kpleusei=tai, subj. e)kpleu/sh|, cp.
X. A. 5.6.21).

## OBJECT CLAUSES WITH VERBS OF FEARING

§2221
Object clauses after verbs of fear and caution are introduced by mh/ that, lest (Lat. ne), mh\ ou) that . . . not, lest . . . not (Lat. ut = ne non).
a. mh/ clauses denote a fear that something may or might happen; mh\ ou) clauses denote a fear that something may not or might not happen. Observe that the verb is negatived by ou) and not by mh/, which expresses an apprehension that the result will take place. mh/ is sometimes, for convenience, translated by whether; but it is not an indirect interrogative in such cases.

§2222
The construction of mh/ after verbs of fearing has been developed from an earlier coördinate construction in which mh/ was not a conjunction (that, lest) but a prohibitive particle. Thus, dei/dw mh/ ti pa/qh|sin (
*l 470) I fear lest he may suffer aught was developed from I fear + may he not suffer aught (1802); fulakh\ de/ tis . . . e)/stw, mh\ lo/xos ei)se/lqh|si po/lin (
*q 521) but let there be a guard, lest an ambush enter the city, where the clause mh\—ei)se/lqh|si meant originally may an ambush not enter. Here mh/ expresses the desire to avert something (negative desire).
a. When mh/ had become a pure conjunction of subordination, it was used even with the indicative and with the optative with a)/n. Some scholars regard mh/ with the indicative as standing for a)=ra mh/ (hence an indirect interrogative). Observe that the character of mh/ after verbs of fearing is different from that in final clauses, though the construction is the same in both cases.

§2223
For the use of the subjunctive, without a verb of fearing, with mh/, see 1801, 1802; with mh\ ou) see 1801, with ou) mh/ see 1804.

§2224
Verbs and expressions of fear are: fobou=mai, de/doika or de/dia, tarbw=, trw= and pe/fri_ka (mostly poetical); deino/s ei)mi, deino/n e)sti, de/os e)sti/, fobero/s ei)mi, fobero/n e)sti, etc.
a. Sometimes it is not actual fear that is expressed but only apprehension, anxiety, suspicion, etc. These are the verbs and expressions of caution: o)knw=, a)qu_mw=, a)pistw=, a)pisti/a_n e)/xw (pare/xw), u(popteu/w, e)nqu_mou=mai, ai)sxu/_nomai (rare), ki/ndu_no/s e)sti, prosdoki/a_ e)sti/. Here belong also, by analogy, o(rw=, skopw=, e)nnow=, eu)labou=mai, fronti/zw, fula/ttw (-omai), which admit also the construction of verbs of effort (2210 b).

## I. FEAR RELATING TO THE FUTURE

§2225
Object clauses after verbs of fear and caution take the subjunctive after primary tenses, the optative (or subjunctive, 2226) after secondary tenses.

e)fobou/mhn mh\ ge/ncito (or ge/nhtai) I feared it might happen.
e)fobou/mhn mh\ ou) ge/noito (regularly ge/nhtai) I feared it might not happen.

X. A. 1.10.9,

## II. FEAR RELATING TO THE PRESENT OR PAST

§2233

b. The aorist occurs in Homer:

## OTHER CONSTRUCTIONS WITH VERBS OF FEARING

§2234

In Indirect Questions.—Here the ideas of fear and doubt are joined. Thus, fo/bos ei) pei/sw de/spoinan e)mh/n (direct pei/sw; 1916) I have my doubts whether I shall (can) persuade my mistress
E. Med. 184, th\n qeo\n d' o(/pws la/qw de/doika (direct pw=s la/qw; 1805) I am fearful how I shall escape the notice of the goddess
E. I. T. 995,

de/doika o(/ ti a)pokrinou=mai I am afraid what to answer
P. Th. 195c.

§2235

In Indirect Discourse with w(s (rarely o(/pws) that.—Verbs of fearing may have the construction of verbs of thinking and be followed by a dependent statement. This occurs regularly only when the expression of fear is negatived. Thus,

a)ndro\s de\ th=| qugatri\ mh\ fobou= w(s a)porh/seis do not fear that you will be at a loss for a husband for your daughter
X. C. 5.2.12. Here mh/ or o(/pws mh/ would be regular. With w(s the idea is fear, thinking that.

§2236

With o(/ti (w(s) Causal.—

e)fobei=to o(/ti a)po\ *dio\s . . . to\ o)/nar e)do/kei au)tw=| ei)=nai he was afraid because the dream seemed to him to be from Zeus
X. A. 3.1.12.

§2237

With a Causal Participle.—ou)/te th\n a)kro/polin . . . prodidou\s e)fobh/qh nor was he terrified at having betrayed the Acropolis Lyc. 17.

§2238

With the Infinitive.—Verbs of fearing often take an object infinitive (present, future or aorist) with or without the article; and with or without mh/ (2741). Thus,

fobh/setai a)dikei=n he will be afraid to injure
X. C. 8.7.15,

ou) fobou/meqa e)lassw/sesqai we are not afraid that we shall be beaten
T. 5.105 (the future infinitive is less common than mh/ with the subjunctive), fulatto/menos to\ lu_ph=sai/ tina ( = mh\ lu_ph/sw) taking care to offend no one
D. 18.258, e)fula/cato mh\ a)/pistos gene/sqai he took precautions not to become an object of distrust X. Ag. 8. 5.
a. ## CAUSAL CLAUSES

§2240
Causal clauses are introduced by o(/ti, dio/ti, dio/per because, e)pei/, e)peidh/, o(/te, o(po/te since, w(s as, since, because. The negative is ou).
a. Also by poetic ou(/neka ( = ou(= e(/neka) and o(qou/neka ( = o(/tou e(/neka) because, eu)=te since (poetic and Ionic; also temporal), and by o(/pou since (
Hdt. 1.68,

D. 1.1,

## RESULT CLAUSES (CONSECUTIVE CLAUSES)

§2249
A clause of result denotes a consequence of what is stated in the principal clause.

§2250
Result clauses are introduced by the relative word w(/ste (rarely by w(s) as, that, so that. In the principal clause the demonstrative words ou(/tws thus, toiou=tos such, tosou=tos so great, are often expressed. w(/ste is from w(s and the connective te/, which has lost its meaning.
a. To a clause with ou(/tws, etc. Herodotus sometimes adds a clause either with te/ or without a connective, where Attic would employ w(/ste; cp. 3. 12.

§2251
There are two main forms of result clauses: w(/ste with the infinitive and w(/ste with a finite verb. With the infinitive, the negative is generally mh/; with a finite verb, ou). On the use in indirect discourse and on irregularities, see 2759.

§2252
Consecutive w(s occurs almost always with the infinitive (chiefly in Herodotus, Xenophon, Aeschylus, and Sophocles); with a finite verb occasionally in Herodotus and Xenophon. With the infinitive, the orators and Thucydides (except 7. 34) have w(/ste.

§2253
Consecutive w(/ste (w(s) with a finite verb does not occur in Homer, who uses coördination instead (cp. de/ in A 10). Two cases of w(/s te occur with the infinitive (I 42;
z 21 may mean and so), where the infinitive might stand alone, since Homer uses the infinitive to denote an intended or possible result.

§2254
A clause with w(/ste and the infinitive is merely added to the clause containing the main thought in order to explain it. The consequence is stated without any distinction of time and only with difference of stage of action.
a. Since the infinitive expresses merely the abstract verbal idea, its use with w(/ste (as with pri/n) outside of indirect discourse cannot explicitly denote a fact. By its datival nature (1969), the infinitive is simply a complement to, or explanation of, the governing word. w(/ste is one of the means to reinforce this explanatory office of the infinitive. The origin of its use is suggested by the comparison with o(/sos sufficient for, oi(=os capable of (2003) and the infinitive, which was not originally dependent on these words.

§2255
A clause with w(/ste and a finite verb contains the main thought, and is often so loosely connected with the leading verb as to be practically independent and coördinate. w(/ste may thus be simply introductory and take any construction found in an independent sentence. The consequence expresses distinctions of time and stage of action.

§2256
Result may also be expressed by relative clauses (2556).

## DIFFERENCE BETWEEN w(/ste WITH THE INDICATIVE AND w(/ste WITH THE INFINITIVE

§2257
A clause of result with w(/ste stating that something actually occurred as a fact must be expressed by the indicative.

§2258
A clause of result with w(/ste stating that something may occur in consequence of an intention, tendency, capacity, and in general in consequence of the nature of an object or action, is regularly expressed by the infinitive. When a consequence is stated without affirming or denying its actual occurrence, the infinitive is in place. The infinitive may therefore denote a fact, but does not explicitly state this to be the case; and is, in general, permissible in all cases where the attainment of the result is expected, natural, or possible, and its actual occurrence is not emphasized; as it is emphasized by the indicative.
a. w(/ste with the infinitive does not state a particular fact. The infinitive is preferred in clauses containing or implying a negative. w(/ste with the indicative is preferred after ei)s tou=to h(/kei and like phrases when affirmative (cp. 2265, 2266, 2274).

§2259
This difference may be illustrated by examples.
e)/xw trih/reis w(/ste e(lei=n to\ e)kei/nwn ploi=on I have triremes (so as) to catch their vessel
X. A. 1.4.8 (w(/ste ei(=lon would mean so that I caught with an essentially different meaning),

pa/ntas ou(/tw diatiqei\s w(/ste au)tw=| ei)=nai fi/lous treating all in such a manner that they should be his friends
X. A. 1.1.5 (an intended result, 2267),

ou(/tw dia/keimai u(f' u(_mw=n w(s ou)de\ dei=pnon e)/xw e)n th=| e)mautou= xw/ra| I am treated by you in such a manner that I cannot even sup in my own country
X. H. 4.1.33 (a fact), w(/ste pa/rodon mh\ ei)=nai para\ pu/rgon, a)lla\ di' au)tw=n me/swn dih=|san so that it was impossible to pass by the side of a tower, but the guards went through the middle of them
T. 3.21,

kraugh\n pollh\n e)poi/oun kalou=ntes a)llh/lous w(/ste kai\ tou\s polemi/ous a)kou/ein: w(/ste oi( me\n e)ggu/tata tw=n polemi/wn kai\ e)/fugon they made a loud noise by calling each other so that even the enemy could hear; consequently those of the enemy who were nearest actually fled
X. A. 2.2.17. Here the fact that some of the enemy fled is proof that they actually heard the cries; but the Greek states merely that the noise was loud enough to be heard. Had the clause w(/ste . . . e)/fugon not been added, we could only have inferred that the noise was heard.

## w(/ste (RARELY w(s) WITH THE INFINITIVE

§2260
The infinitive with w(/ste denotes an anticipated or possible result; but the actual occurrence of the result is not stated, and is to be inferred only. The negative is mh/, but ou) is used when the w(/ste clause depends on a clause itself subordinate to a verb of saying or thinking (2269). Cp. 2759.
a. w(/ste with the infinitive means as to, so as to; but with a subject necessary in English it must often be translated by so that.

§2261
The infinitive with w(/ste is usually present or aorist, rarely perfect (e.g.
D. 18.257). The future is common only in indirect discourse (
D. 19.72).

§2262

w(/ste (w(s) with the infinitive is used when its clause serves only to explain the principal clause. Thus,

## w(/ste (w(s) WITH A FINITE VERB

§2273
Any form used in simple sentences may follow w(/ste (rarely w(s) with a finite verb. w(/ste has no effect on the mood of a finite verb.
a. w(s is found especially in Xenophon.

§2274

w(/ste so that with the indicative states the actual result of the action of the leading verb. This is especially common in narrative statements with the aorist tense. The negative is ou).
