## CONDITIONAL CLAUSES

§2280
A condition is a supposition on which a statement is based. A conditional sentence commonly consists of two clauses:
The protasis: the conditional, or subordinate, clause, expressing a supposed or assumed case (if).
The apodosis: the conclusion, or principal clause, expressing what follows if the condition is realized. The truth or fulfilment of the conclusion depends on the truth or fulfilment of the conditional clause.
a. The protasis has its name from pro/tasis, lit. stretching forward, that which is put forward (in logic, a premiss); the apodosis, from a)po/dosis, lit. giving back, return; i.e. the resuming or answering clause.

§2281
The protasis usually precedes, but may follow, the apodosis.

§2282
The protasis is introduced by ei) if.
a. Homer has also ai', which is an Aeolic (and Doric' form.

§2283
With the subjunctive mood, ei' commonly takes a)/n (Epic ei)/ ke or ei)/ ken, not e)a/_n).
a. There are three forms, e)a/_n, h)/n, a)/_n. e)a/_n is the ordinary form in Attic prose and inscriptions; h)/n appears in Ionic and in the older Attic writers (the tragic poets and Thucydides); a)/_n, generally in the later writers (sometimes together with e)a/_n), very rarely in Attic inscriptions. In Plato a)/_n is commoner than e)a/_n. Xenophon has all three forms.
b. h)/n is from ei) + a)/n, a)/_n from h' (another form of ei)) + a)/n. The etymology of e)a/_n is uncertain: either from h' + a)/n or from ei) + a)/_n.

§2284
The particle a)/n is used in the apodosis: (1) with the optative, to denote possibility (cp. 1824); (2) with the past tenses of the indicative, to denote either the non-fulfilment of the condition (1786) or, occasionally, repetition (1790).

§2285
The apodosis may be introduced by de/ or a)lla/, less often by au)ta/r. See under Particles. nu=n de/ as it is, as it was corrects a supposition contrary to fact. The apodosis sometimes has to/te, to/te dh/, ou(/tws (Hom. tw=|) comparable to Eng. then, in that case in the conclusion of conditional sentences.

§2286
The negative of the protasis is mh/ because the subordinate clause expresses something that is conceived or imagined. mh/ negatives the conditional clause as a whole. On ou) adherescent in protasis, see 2698.
The negative of the apodosis is ou), in case the principal clause states the conclusion as a fact on the supposition that the protasis is true; mh/, when the construction requires that negative (2689).

§2287
The indicative, subjunctive, and optative moods, and the participle may stand in protasis and apodosis. The imperative and infinitive may be used in the apodosis. The future optative is not used in conditional sentences except in indirect discourse. The tenses in conditional sentences, except unreal conditions, have the same force as in simple sentences.

§2288
Instead of a formal conditional sentence the two members may be simply coördinated, the protasis having the form of an independent clause.
smi_kro\n labe\ para/deigma, kai\ pa/nta ei)/sei a(\ bou/lomai take an insignificant example, and you will know what I mean
P. Th. 154c, pra/_ttetai/ ti tw=n u(_mi=n dokou/ntwn sumfe/rein: a)/fwnos *ai)sxi/nhs something is going on (of a kind) that seems to be to your advantage. Aeschines is dumb.
D. 18.198. Cp. “Take with you this great truth, and you have the key to Paul's writings” (Channing); “Petition me, perhaps I may forgive” (Dryden). Cp. 1839.

## CLASSIFICATION OF CONDITIONAL SENTENCES

## A. CLASSIFICATION ACCORDING TO FORM

§2289
Conditional sentences may be classified according to form or function (i.e. with reference to their meaning). Classified according to form, all conditional sentences may be arranged with regard to the form of the protasis or of the apodosis.
Protasis: ei) with the indicative.
e)a/_n (rarely ei)) with the subjunctive.
ei) with the optative.
Apodosis: with a)/n, denoting what would (should) be or have been.
without a)/n, not denoting what would (should) be or have been.

## B. CLASSIFICATION ACCORDING TO FUNCTION

§2290
Greek possesses a great variety of ways to join protasis and apodosis, but certain types, as in English, are more common than others and have clear and distinct meanings. In the case of some of the less usual types the exact shade of difference cannot be accurately known to us; as indeed to the Greeks themselves they were often used with no essential difference from the conventional types. In the following classification only the ordinary forms are given.

## ACCORDING TO TIME

§2291
This is the only functional distinction that characterizes all conditional sentences. Here are included also 2292, 2295, 2296.

## 1. Present

Protasis: a primary tense of the indicative.
Apodosis: any form of the simple sentence.
ei) tau=ta poiei=s, kalw=s poiei=s if you do this, you do well.

## 2. Past

Protasis: a secondary tense of the indicative.
Apodosis: any form of the simple sentence.
ei) tau=ta e)poi/eis, kalw=s e)poi/eis if you were doing this, you were doing well, ei) tau=ta e)poi/hsas, kalw=s e)poi/hsas if you did this, you did well.

## 3. Future

a. Protasis: e)a/_n with the subjunctive.
Apodosis: any form expressing future time.
e)a\_n tau=ta poih=|s (poih/sh|s), kalw=s poih/seis if you do this, you will do well.
b. Protasis: ei) with the future indicative.
Apodosis: any form expressing future time.
ei) tau=ta poih/seis, pei/sei if you do this, you will suffer for it.
c. Protasis: ei) with the optative.
Apodosis: a)/n with the optative.
ei) tau=ta poioi/hs (poih/seias), kalw=s a)\n poioi/hs (poih/seias) if you should (were to) do this, you would do well.

## According to Fulfilment or Non-fulfilment

§2292
Only one class of conditional sentences distinctly expresses non-fulfilment of the action.

## 1. Present or Past

Protasis: ei) with the imperfect indicative.
Apodosis: a)/n with the imperfect indicative.
ei) tau=ta e)poi/eis, kalw=s a)\n e)poi/eis if you were (now) doing this, you would be doing well; if you had been doing this, you would have been doing well.

## 2. Past

Protasis: ei) with the aorist indicative.
Apodosis: a)/n with the aorist indicative.
ei) tau=ta e)poi/hsas, kalw=s a)\n e)poi/hsas if you had done this, you would have done well.
N.—Greek has no special forms to show that an action is or was fulfilled, however clearly this may be implied by the context. Any form of conditional sentence in which the apodosis does not express a rule of action may refer to an impossibility.

## According to Particular or General Conditions

§2293
A particular condition refers to a definite act or to several definite acts occurring at a definite time or at definite times.

§2294
A general condition refers to any one of a series of acts that may occur or may have occurred at any time.

§2295
General conditions are distinguished from particular conditions only in present and past time, and then only when there is no implication as to the fulfilment of the action. General conditions have no obligatory form, as any form of condition may refer to a rule of action or to a particular act; but there are two common types of construction:

1. Present
Protasis: e)a/_n with the subjunctive.
Apodosis: present indicative.
e)a\_n tau=ta poih=|s (poih/sh|s), se\ e)painw= if ever you do this, I always praise you.

2. Past
Protasis: ei) with the optative.
Apodosis: imperfect indicative.
ei) tau=ta poioi/hs (poih/seias), se\ e)ph/|noun if ever you did this, I always praised you.

§2296
But equally possible, though less common, are:
ei) tau=ta poiei=s, se\ e)painw= and ei) tau=ta e)poi/eis, se\ e)ph/|noun.

## PRESENT AND PAST CONDITIONS

## First Form of Conditions: SIMPLE PRESENT AND PAST CONDITIONS

§2298
Simple present or past conditions simply state a supposition with no implication as to its reality or probability. The protasis has the indicative, the apodosis has commonly the indicative, but also any other form of the simple sentence appropriate to the thought.
ei) tau=ta poiei=s, kalw=s poiei=s if you do this, you do well.
ei) tau=ta e)poi/hsas, kalw=s e)poi/hsas if you did this, you did well.
a. This form of condition corresponds to the logical formula if this is so, then that is so; if this is not so, then that is not so; if A = B, then C = D. The truth of the conclusion depends solely on the truth of the condition, which is not implied in any way. In these conditions something is supposed to be true only in order to draw the consequence that something else is true.
b. The conditional clause may express what the writer knows is physically impossible. Even when the supposition is true according to the real opinion of the writer, this form of condition is employed. In such cases ei)/per is often used for ei). Both ei) and ei)/per sometimes have a causal force (2246); cp. si quidem and quia.
c. The simple condition is particular or general. When the protasis has ei)/ tis and the apodosis a present indicative, the simple condition has a double meaning referring both to an individual case and to a rule of action. When a present general condition is distinctly expressed, e)a/_n with the subjunctive is used (2337.)

§2299
There are many possible combinations of present and past conditions with different forms of the protasis and apodosis. Protasis and apodosis may be in different tenses, and present and future may be combined.

§2300
The apodosis may be the simple indicative or any other form of the simple sentence appropriate to the thought.
a. Simple Indicative: ei) tou=t' e)/xei kalw=s, e)kei=no ai)sxrw=s if this is excellent, that is disgraceful
Aes. 3.188, ei) me\n (*)asklhpio\s)

P. R. 408c, ei)/ te/ ti a)/llo . . . e)ge/neto e)piki/ndu_non toi=s *(/ellhsi, pa/ntwn . . . mete/sxomen and if any other danger befell the Greeks, we took our share in all
T. 3.54,

h)= kalo\n . . . te/xnhma a)/ra ke/kthsai, ei)/per ke/kthsai in truth you do possess a noble art, if indeed you do possess it
P. Pr. 319a, ei)/per ge *da_rei/ou . . . e)sti pai=s . . . , ou)k a)maxei\ tau=t' e)gw\ lh/yomai if indeed he is a son of Darius, I shall not gain this without a battle

§2301
If the protasis expresses a present intention or necessity, the future indicative may be used.
ei) de\ kai\ tw=| h(gemo/ni pisteu/somen o(\n a)\n *ku=ros didw=|, ti/ kwlu/_ei kai\ ta\ a)/kra h(mi=n keleu/ein *ku=ron prokatalabei=n; but if we are going to trust any guide that Cyrus may give us, what hinders our also ordering Cyrus to occupy the heights in advance in our behalf?
X. A. 1.3.16, ai)=re plh=ktron, ei) maxei= raise your spur if you mean (are going) to fight
Ar. Av. 759. The future here has a modal force and expresses something besides futurity; hence it is equivalent to me/lleis maxei=sqai (1959), but not to e)a\_n ma/xh| (2323) or to ei) maxei= (a threat, 2328), both of which refer to future time. The periphrasis with me/llw and the present or future infinitive is more common in prose.

## Second Form of Conditions: PRESENT AND PAST UNREAL CONDITIONS

§2302
In present and past unreal conditions the protasis implies that the supposition cannot or could not be realized because contrary to a known fact. The apodosis states what would be or would have been the result if the condition were or had been realized.

§2303
The protasis has ei' with the imperfect, aorist, or pluperfect indicative; the apodosis has a)/n with these past tenses. The protasis and apodosis may have different tenses. Unreal conditions are either particular or general.

§2304
The imperfect refers to present time or (sometimes) to a continued or habitual past act or state. The imperfect may be conative.
ei) tau=ta e)poi/eis, kalw=s a)\n e)poi/eis if you were (now) doing this, you would be doing well , or if you had been doing this, you would have been doing well.
The implied opposite is a present (a)ll' ou' poiei=s but you are not doing this) or an imperfect (a)ll' ou)k e)poi/eis but you were not doing this).
The imperfect of past time emphasizes the continuance of the action.

§2305
The aorist refers to a simple occurrence in the past.
ei) tau=ta e)poi/hsas, kalw=s a)\n e)poi/hsas if you had done this, you would have done well.
The implied opposite is an aorist (a)ll' ou)k e)poi/hsas but you did not do this).

§2306
The (rare) pluperfect refers to an act completed in past or present time or to the state following on such completion.
ei) tau=ta e)pepoih/khs, kalw=s a)\n e)pepoih/khs if you had finished doing this (now or on any past occasion), you would have done well.
The implied opposite is a perfect (a)ll' ou' pepoi/hkas but you have not done this) or a pluperfect (a)ll' ou)k e)pepoih/khs but you had not done this).
a. The pluperfect is used only when stress is laid on the completion of the act or on the continuance of the result of the act, and generally refers to present time. In reference to past time, the aorist is generally used instead of the pluperfect.

§2307
In reference to past time, the imperfect or aorist is used according as either tense would be used in an affirmative sentence not conditional. The pluperfect is commonly used when the perfect would have been used of present time.

§2308
In the form of the protasis and the apodosis of unreal conditions there is nothing that denotes unreality, but, in the combination, the unreality of the protasis is always, and that of the apodosis generally, implied. The past tenses of the indicative are used in unreal conditions referring to present time, because the speaker's thought goes back to the past, when the realization of the condition was still possible, though at the time of speaking that realization is impossible.

§2309

Same Tenses in Protasis and Apodosis.—a. Imperfect of present time:

tau=ta de\ ou)k a)\n e)du/nanto poiei=n, ei) mh\ kai\ diai/th| metri/a| e)xrw=nto but they would not be able to do this, if they were not also following a temperate diet
X. C. 1.2.16.
b. Imperfect of past time:

ou)k a)\n ou)=n nh/swn . . . e)kra/tei, ei) mh/ ti kai\ nautiko\n ei)=xen accordingly he would not have ruled over islands, if he had not possessed also some naval force
T. 1.9. Present and past combined: ei) mh\ to/t' e)po/noun, nu=n a)\n ou)k eu)fraino/mhn if I had not toiled then, I should not be rejoicing now Philemon 153.
c. Aorist of past time:

ou)k a)\n e)poi/hsen *)agasi/a_s tau=ta, ei) mh\ e)gw\ au)to\n e)ke/leusa Agasias would not have done this, if I had not ordered him
X. A. 6.6.15.

§2310

Different Tenses in Protasis and Apodosis.—a. Imperfect and Aorist: ei) me\n pro/sqen h)pista/mhn, ou)d' a)\n sunhkolou/qhsa/ soi if I had known this before, I would not even have accompanied you
X. A. 7.7.11.
N.—With an imperfect of present time in the protasis, ei)=pon a)/n, a)pekri_na/mhn a)/n and like verbs, denote an act in present time (I should at once say). Thus, ei) mh\ path\r h)=sq', ei)=pon a)/n s' ou)k eu)= fronei=n if thou wert not my father, I would say (would have said) thou wast unwise
S. Ant. 755. Often in Plato, as ei) me\n ou)=<*> su/ me h)rw/ta_s ti tw=n nu=n dh/, ei)=pon a)/n ktl. if now you were asking me any one of the questions with which we are now dealing, I should say etc.,
P. Euth. 12d, cp.
P. G. 514d,
X. A. 7.6.23.
b. Imperfect and Pluperfect:

kai\ ta)/ll' a)\n a(/pant' a)kolou/qws tou/tois e)pe/pra_kto, ei)/ tis e)pei/qeto/ moi and everything else would have been effected consistently with what I have said, if my advice had been followed
D. 19.173.
c. Aorist and Imperfect: ei) mh\ u(_mei=s h)/lqete, e)poreuo/meqa a)\n e)pi\ basile/a_ if you had not come, we should now be marching against the king
X. A. 2.1.4.
d. Aorist and Pluperfect: ei) e)gw\ pa/lai e)pexei/rhsa pra/_ttein ta\ poli_tika\ pra/_gmata, pa/lai a)\n a)polw/lh if I had long ago essayed to meddle with politics, I should long ago have perished
P. A. 31d, ei) mi/a yh=fos mete/pesen, u(perw/rist' a)/n if one vote had been transferred to the other side, he would have been transported across the borders (and now be in exile)
Aes. 3.252.
e. Pluperfect and Imperfect:

h( po/lis e)la/mbanen a)\n di/khn, ei)/ ti h)di/khto the State would inflict punishment, if it had been wronged
Ant. 6.10.
f. Pluperfect and Aorist: ou)k a)\n pare/meina, ei) e)lelu/mhn I should not have stayed, if I had been free
Ant. 5.13.

§2311

Homeric Constructions.—In Homer the imperfect in unreal conditions refers only to past time. The apodosis may have ke/ or a)/n with the optative.
a. The present unreal condition with ei) with the optative in the protasis and a)/n with the optative in the apodosis (in form like a less vivid future condition in Attic) is very rare (
*y 274). In B 80,
*w 220 we have a combination of a past protasis (imperfect or aorist indicative) with present apodosis (with ke/n and the optative).
b. Past unreal conditions have, in the protasis, the imperfect or aorist indicative; in the apodosis, either the imperfect or aorist indicative with a)/n or ke/ or the aorist or present optative with ke/. Thus, kai/ nu/ ken e)/nq' a)po/loito . . . *ai)nei/a_s, ei) mh\ a)/r' o)cu\ no/hse . . . *)afrodi/_th and here Aeneas had perished, if Aphrodite had not quickly observed him E 311.

§2312
Unreal conditions with a)/n and the optative in apodosis (cp. 2311) in Attic are rare and some are suspected. Either the common reading is at fault (
X. M. 3.5.8), or we have a simple condition with a potential optative (2300 e), as in
And. 1.57,
L. 6.39,
I. 4.102. In ei) me\n toi/nun tou=t' e)pexei/roun le/gein . . . , ou)k e)/sq' o(/stis ou)k a)\n ei)ko/tws e)piti_mh/seie/ moi if now I were attempting to say this, there would be no one who would not censure me with good reason (
D. 18.206) the implied conclusion is ou)k a)\n h)=n o(/stis ktl.
a. The optative in protasis and apodosis occur in
E. Med. 568 (present unreal). Hdt. uses the potential optative occasionally (e.g. 7. 214) where English uses a past expression.

UNREAL CONDITIONS—APODOSIS WITHOUT a)/n

§2313

a)/n may be omitted in the apodosis of an unreal condition when the apodosis consists of an imperfect indicative denoting unfulfilled obligation, possibility, or propriety. Such are the impersonal expressions e)/dei, xrh=n, e)ch=n, ei)ko\s h)=n, kalo\n h)=n, etc., with the infinitive, the action of which is (usually) not realized.
ei) tau=ta e)poi/ei, e)/dei (e)ch=n) ai)tia=sqai au)to/n if he were doing this (as he is not), one ought to (might) blame him.
ei) tau=ta e)poi/hse, e)/dei (e)ch=n) ai)tia/_sasqai (or ai)tia=sqai) au)to/n if he had done this (as he did not), one ought to (might) have blamed him.
a. Here e)/dei and e)ch=n are auxiliaries and the emphasis falls on the infinitive. The impersonal verb has the effect of a modifying adverb denoting obligation, possibility, or propriety: thus e)/dei ai)tia=sqai au)to/n is virtually equivalent to dikai/ws a)\n h)|tia=to, and ei)ko\s h)=n ai)tia/_sasqai au)to/n to ei)ko/tws a)\n h)|tia/_qh he would properly have been blamed.
b. e)/dei, xrh=n, etc., may be used in simple sentences (1774 ff.) without any protasis either expressed or implied. But a protasis may often be supplied in thought.

§2314
The present infinitive generally expresses what would necessarily, possibly, or properly be done now. The aorist, and sometimes the present, infinitive expresses what would necessarily, possibly, or properly have been done in the past.
a. Present infinitive of present time:

xrh=n dh/pou, ei)/te tine\s au)tw=n presbu/teroi geno/menoi e)/gnwsan o(/ti ne/ois ou)=sin au)toi=s e)gw\ kako\n pw/pote/ ti cunebou/leusa, nu_ni\_ au)tou\s a)nabai/nontas e)mou= kathgorei=n if some of them on growing older had perceived that I ever gave them any bad counsel when they were young, they ought of course now to rise up in person and accuse me
P. A. 33d.
b. Present infinitive of past time: ei)/ tina (proi=ka) e)di/dou, ei)ko\s h)=n kai\ th\n doqei=san u(po\ tw=n paragene/sqai fasko/ntwn marturei=sqai if he had given any dowry, that which was actually delivered would naturally have been attested by those who claimed to have been present
Is. 3.28.
c. Aorist infinitive of past time: ei) e)bou/leto di/kaios ei)=nai peri\ tou\s pai=das, e)ch=n au)tw=| . . . misqw=sai to\n oi)=kon if he had wished to be just in regard to the children, he might properly have let the house
L. 32.23.

§2315
With the same impersonal expressions, a)/n is regularly used when the obligation, possibility, or propriety, and not the action of the verb dependent on e)/dei, etc., is denied. Here the main force of the apodosis falls on the necessity, possibility, or propriety of the act.
ei) tau=ta e)poi/ei, e)/dei (e)ch=n) a)\n ai)tia=sqai au)to/n if he were doing this (as he is not), it would be necessary (possible) to blame him; but, as the case now stands, it is not necessary (possible). Thus, ei) me\n h)pista/meqa safw=s o(/ti h(/cei ploi=a . . . a)/gwn i(kana/, ou)de\n a)\n e)/dei w(=n me/llw le/gein if we knew for certain that he would return with a sufficient number of vessels, there would be no need to say what I am going to say (but there is need)
X. A. 5.1.10, tau=ta ei) me\n di' a)sqe/neian e)pa/sxomen, ste/rgein a)\n h)=n a)na/gkh th\n tu/xhn if we had suffered this because of our weakness, we should have (necessity would compel us) to rest content with our lot
L. 33.4.

§2316
With a)/n, it is implied that the obligation does (or did) not exist; without a)/n, it is implied that the action of the dependent infinitive is (or was) not realized. Thus the first sentence in 2315, without a)/n, would mean: if he were doing this (as he is not), one ought to blame him; but, as the case now stands, one does not blame him.

§2317

e)boulo/mhn, or e)boulo/mhn a)/n, with the infinitive may stand in the apodosis. Cp. 1782, 1789.

§2318

a)/n is regularly omitted in an apodosis formed by the imperfect of me/llw and the infinitive (usually future) to denote an unfulfilled past intention or expectation (cp. the Lat. future participle with eram or fui). Cp. 1895 a, 1960.
h)= ma/la dh\ *)agame/mnonos . . . fqi/_sesqai kako\n oi)=ton e)ni\ mega/roisin e)/mellon, ei) mh\ . . . e)/eipes in sooth I was like to have perished in my halls by the evil fate of Agamemnon, hadst thou not spoken
n 383 (periturus eram, nisi dixisses).

§2319

a)/n may be omitted with the aorist of kindu_neu/w run a risk when the emphasis falls on the dependent infinitive.
ei) mh\ dro/mw| mo/lis e)cefu/gomen ei)s *delfou/s, e)kindu_neu/samen a)pole/sqai if we had not escaped with difficulty to Delphi by taking to our heels, we ran the risk of perishing ( = we should probably have perished: a)\n a)pwlo/meqa)
Aes. 3.123. Contrast

ei) me/ntoi to/te plei/ous sunele/ghsan, e)kindu/_neusen a)\n diafqarh=nai polu\ tou= strateu/matos if they had mustered in larger force at this time, a large part of the troops would have been in danger of being destroyed
X. A. 4.1.11.

§2320
Some expressions containing a secondary tense of the indicative without a)/n, and not followed by a dependent infinitive, are virtually equivalent to the apodosis of an unreal condition.
tou/tw| d' ei' mh\ w(molo/goun a(\ ou(=tos e)bou/leto, ou)demia=| zhmi/a| e)/noxos h)=n but if they had not acknowledged to him what he wished, he would have been (lit. was) liable to no penalty
L. 7.37.
a. Imperfects (not impersonal) without a)/n are often emended, as h)|sxu_no/mhn me/ntoi (some editors me/nta)/n), ei) u(po\ polemi/ou ge o)/ntos e)chpath/qhn I should, however, be ashamed, if I had been deceived by any one who was an enemy
X. A. 7.6.21. Cp. “Tybalt's death was woe enough, if it had ended there” (Shakesp.). Cases like 1895 a do not belong here.

## FUTURE CONDITIONS

§2321
Future conditions set forth suppositions the fulfilment of which is still undecided. There are two main forms of future conditions:
More Vivid Future conditions.
Less Vivid Future conditions.
A variety of the first class is the Emotional Future (2328).
Future conditions may be particular or general (2293, 2294).

§2322
The difference between the More Vivid Future and the Less Vivid Future, like the difference between if I (shall) do this and if I should do this, depends on the mental attitude of the speaker. With the Vivid Future the speaker sets forth a thought as prominent and distinct in his mind; and for any one or more of various reasons. Thus, he may (and generally does) regard the conclusion as more likely to be realized; but even an impossible (2322 c) or dreaded result may be expressed by this form if the speaker chooses to picture the result vividly and distinctly. The More Vivid Future is thus used whenever the speaker clearly desires to be graphic, impressive, emphatic, and to anticipate a future result with the distinctness of the present.
The Less Vivid Future deals with suppositions less distinctly conceived and of less immediate concern to the speaker, mere assumed or imaginary cases. This is a favourite construction in Greek, and is often used in stating suppositions that are merely possible and often impossible; but the form of the condition itself does not imply an expectation of the speaker that the conclusion may possibly be realized. The difference between the two forms, therefore, is not an inherent difference between probable realization in the one case and possible realization in the other. The same thought may often be expressed in either form without any essential difference in meaning. The only difference is, therefore, often that of temperament, tone, or style.
a. e)a/_n with the subjunctive and ei) with the optative are rarely used in successive sentences. In most such cases the difference lies merely in the degree of distinctness and emphasis of the expression used; but where the speaker wishes to show that the conclusion is expected or desired, he uses e)a/_n with the subjunctive rather than the other form. Thus, ei) ou)=n i)/doien kai\ nw\| kaqa/per tou\s pollou\s e)n meshmbri/a| mh\ dialegome/nous, a)lla\ nusta/zontas kai\ khloume/nous u(f' au(tw=n di' a)_rgi/a_<*> th=s dianoi/a_s, dikai/ws a)\n katagelw=|en: . . . e)a\_n d' o(rw=si dialegome/nous . . ., ta/x' a)\n doi=en a)gasqe/ntes if now they should see that we, like the many, are not conversing at noon-day but slumbering and charmed by them because of the indolence of our thoughts, they would rightly laugh at us; but if they see us conversing, they will, perhaps, out of admiration make us gifts
P. Phae. 259a.
b. Cases of both forms in successive sentences are I 135,
Hdt. 8.21, 9. 48;
P. Cr. 51d, Ph. 105 b, Phae. 259 a, Pr. 330 c-331 a,
D. 4.11, 18. 147-148. In
D. 18.178 both the desired and the undesired alternative have e)a/_n with the subjunctive.
c. Impossibilities may be expressed by e)a/_n with the subjunctive. Thus, ti/ ou)=n, a)\_n ei)/pwsin oi( no/moi; what, then, if the laws say?
P. Cr. 50c; cp.
P. Eu. 299b, R. 610 a, 612 b (opt. in 359 c, 360 b), Ar. Aves 1642,
E. Or. 1593, Phoen. 1216. Cp. 2329 a.

## Third Form of Conditions: MORE VIVID FUTURE CONDITIONS

§2323
More vivid future conditions have in the protasis e)a/_n (h)/n, a)/_n) with the subjunctive; in the apodosis, the future indicative or any other form referring to future time.
e)a\_n tau=ta poih=|s (poih/sh|s), kalw=s poih/seis if you do this, you will do well.

§2324
This form of condition corresponds to the use of shall and will in conditional sentences in older English (“if ye shall ask . . . I will do it”: St. John). Modern English substitutes the present for the more exact future in ordinary future conditions of this class; and often uses shall in the protasis with an emotional force. The English present subjunctive, although somewhat rarely used in the modern language, corresponds more nearly to the Greek subjunctive (“if she be there, he shall not need”: Beaumont and Fletcher).—Since if you do this may be expressed in Greek by e)a\_n tau=ta poih=|s or ei) tau=ta poih/seis (2328), and by ei) tau=ta poiei=s (2298), the difference in meaning is made clear only by the apodosis. The form e)a\_n tau=ta poih=|s in vivid future conditions must be distinguished from the same form in present general conditions (if ever you do this, 2337). e)a\_n tau=ta/ soi dokh=|, poi/ei may be particular or general: if (or if ever) this seems good to you, do it.

§2325
The present subjunctive views an act as continuing (not completed); the aorist subjunctive as simply occurring (completed). Neither tense has any time of itself. The aorist subjunctive may mark the action of the protasis as completed before the action of the principal clause (cp. the Lat. future perfect). Ingressive aorists (1924) retain their force in the subjunctive.

§2326
The apodosis of the more vivid future condition is the future indicative or any other form of the simple sentence that refers to future time.
a. Future Indicative:

e)a\_n zhth=|s kalw=s, eu(rh/seis if you seek well, you shall find
P. G. 503d,

e)a\_n d' e)/xwmen xrh/maq', e(/comen fi/lous if we have money, we shall have friends
Men. Sent. 165,

xa/rin ge ei)/somai, e)a\_n a)kou/hte I shall be grateful, if you listen
P. Pr. 310a, a)\_n au)tw=| didw=|s a)rgu/rion kai\ pei/qh|s au)to/n, poih/sei kai\ se\ sofo/n if you give him money and persuade him, he will make you too wise 310 d,

h)\n ga\r tou=to la/bwmen, ou) dunh/sontai me/nein for if we take this, they will not be able to remain
X. A. 3.4.41, e)a\_n ku/klou e)pi\ th=s periferei/a_s lhfqh=| du/o tuxo/nta shmei=a, h( e)pi\ ta\ shmei=a e)pizeugnume/nh eu)qei=a e)nto\s pesei=tai t<*>u= ku/klou if any two points be taken in the circumference of a circle, the straight line which joins them shall fall within the circle Euclid 3. 2.
b. Primary Tenses of the indicative other than the future. Present (1879):

h)\n qa/nh|s su/, pai=s o(/d' e)kfeu/gei mo/ron if thou art slain, yon boy escapes death
E. And. 381, di/dws' e(kw\n ktei/nein e(auto/n, h)\n ta/de yeusqh=| le/gwn freely he offers himself to death, if he lies in speaking thus (di/dwsi = he says that he is ready) S. Phil. 1342. Aorist: see 1934, and cp. ei) me/n k' au)=qi me/nwn *trw/wn po/lin a)mfima/xwmai, w)/leto me/n moi no/stos if I tarry here and wage war about the city of the Trojans, my return home is lost for me I 413. Perfect: see 1950. Cp. “if I shall have an answer no directlier, I am gone”: Beaumont and Fletcher.
c. Subjunctive of exhortation, prohibition, or deliberation, and with mh/ (mh\ ou)) of doubtful assertion (1801). Thus, mhd' a)/_n ti w)nw=mai, e)/fh, h)\n pwlh=| new/teros tria/_konta e)tw=n, e)/rwmai, o(po/sou pwlei=; even if I am buying something, said he, am I not to ask ‘what do you sell it for?’ if the seller is under thirty years of age?
X. M. 1.2.36, ka)\_n fainw/meqa a)/dika au)ta\ e)rgazo/menoi, mh\ ou) de/h| u(pologi/zesqai ktl. and if we appear to do this unjustly, I rather think it may not be necessary to take notice, etc.
P. Cr. 48d.
d. Optative of wish, or potential optative with a)/n (‘something may happen’ instead of ‘something will happen’). Thus, h)/n se tou= loipou= pot' a)fe/lwmai xro/nou, . . .

ka/kist' a)poloi/mhn if ever in the future I take them away from you, may I perish most vilely!
Ar. Ran. 586, e)a\_n kata\ me/ros fula/ttwmen . . ., h(=tton a)\n du/nainto h(ma=s qhra=n oi( pole/mioi if we keep guard by turns, the enemy will (would) be less able to harry us
X. A. 5.1.9. See also 2356 a.
e. Imperative, or infinitive for the imperative (2013):

h)\n po/lemon ai(rh=sqe, mhke/ti h(/kete deu=ro a)/neu o(/plwn if you choose war, do not come here again without your arms
X. C. 3.2.13,

su\ d', a)/_n ti e)/xh|s be/lti_o/n poqen labei=n, peira=sqai kai\ e)moi\ metadido/nai but if you can find anything better from any quarter, try to communicate it to me too
P. Crat. 426b.

§2327

Homeric Constructions.—a. ei) alone without ke/ or a)/n with the subjunctive with no appreciable difference from ei)/ ke (a)/n): ei)/ per ga/r se katakta/nh|, ou)/ s' . . . klau/somai for if he slay thee, I shall not bewail thee X 86. This construction occurs in lyric and dramatic poetry, and in Hdt., as dusta/laina ta)/_r' e)gw/, ei)/ sou sterhqw= wretched indeed shall I be, if I am deprived of thee
S. O. C. 1443. In Attic prose it is very rare and suspected (
T. 6.21).
b. Subjunctive with ke/ in both protasis and apodosis (the anticipatory subjunctive, 1810): ei) de/ ke mh\ dw/h|sin, e)gw\ de/ ken au)to\s e(/lwmai and if he do not give her up, then will I seize her myself A 324.
c. ei)/ (ai)/) ke with the future in protasis (rare): soi\ . . . o)/neidos e)/ssetai, ei)/ k' *)axilh=os . . . e(tai=ron . . . ku/nes e(lkh/sousin it will be a reproach unto thee, if the dogs drag the companion of Achilles P 557. Some read here the subjunctive.

§2328

Emotional Future Conditions.—When the protasis expresses strong feeling, the future indicative with ei) is commonly used instead of e)a/_n with the subjunctive, and may often be rendered by hall. The protasis commonly suggests something undesired, or feared, or intended independently of the speaker's will; the apodosis commonly conveys a threat, a warning, or an earnest appeal to the feelings. The apodosis is generally expressed by the future indicative, but other forms of 2326 are possible.

ei) tau=ta le/ceis, e)xqarei= me\n e)c e)mou= if thou speakest thus, thou wilt be hated by me
S. Ant. 93, ei) mh\ kaqe/ceis glw=ssan, e)/stai soi kaka/ if you won't hold your tongue, there's trouble in store for you E. frag. 5,

a)poktenei=s ga/r, ei)/ me gh=s e)/cw balei=s for thou wilt slay me if thou shalt thrust me out of the land
E. Phoen. 1621,

ei) w(=de strateuso/meqa, ou) dunhso/meqa ma/xesqai if we keep the field thus, we shall not be able to fight
X. C. 6.1.13, a)_qliw/tatos a)\n genoi/mhn (potential optative),

ei) fuga\s a)di/kws katasth/somai I should become most wretched, were I to be driven unjustly into exile
L. 7.41.
a. When ei) with the future indicative is directly contrasted with e)a/_n with the subjunctive, the former usually presents the unfavourable, the latter the favourable, alternative. Thus,
h)\n me\n ga\r e)qe/lwmen a)poqnh/|skein u(pe\r tw=n dikai/wn, eu)dokimh/somen . . ., ei) de\ fobhso/meqa tou\s kindu/_nous, ei)s polla\_s taraxa\_s katasth/somen h(ma=s au)tou/s if we are (shall be) willing to die for the sake of justice, we shall gain renown; but if we are going to fear dangers, we shall bring ourselves into great confusion
I. 6.107. Cp.
X. C. 4.1.15,
Ar. Nub. 586-591,
L. 27.7,
I. 12.237, 15. 130, 17. 9,
D. 8.17, 18. 176, 27. 20-22. Both constructions are rarely used in successive clauses with out any essential difference (
X. Ap. 6). e)a/_n with the subjunctive, when used in threats or warnings, is a milder form of statement than ei) with the future (
Hdt. 1.71). An unfavourable alternative may thus be expressed by e)a/_n with the subjunctive (A 135-137,
Hdt. 3.36,
Aes. 3.254).
b. ei) with the future indicative may have a modal force like that of dei= or me/llw (am to, must) with the infinitive: barei=a (kh/r), ei) te/knon dai+/cw hard is fate, if I must slay my child
A. Ag. 208. The future of present intention (2301) is different.

## Fourth Form of Conditions: LESS VIVID FUTURE CONDITIONS

§2329
Less vivid future conditions (should . . . would conditions) have in the protasis ei) with the optative, in the apodosis a)/n with the optative.
ei) tau=ta poioi/hs, kalw=s a)\n poioi/hs or ei) tau=ta poih/seias, kalw=s a)\n poih/seias if you should do this, you would do well.

ei)/hs forhto\s ou)k a)/n, ei) pra/_ssois kalw=s thou wouldst be unendurable shouldst thou be prosperous
A. Pr. 979, ei) d' a)nagkai=on ei)/h a)dikei=n h)\ a)dikei=sqai, e(loi/mhn a)\n ma=llon a)dikei=sqai h)\ a)dikei=n but if it should be necessary to do wrong or be wronged, I should prefer to be wronged than to do wrong
P. G. 469c,

deina\ a)\n ei)/hn ei)rgasme/nos, . . . ei) li/poimi th\n ta/cin I should be in the state of having committed a dreadful deed, if I were to desert my post
P. A. 28d.
a. Anything physically impossible may be represented as supposable, hence this construction may be used of what is contrary to fact. Thus,

fai/h d' a)\n h( qanou=sa/ g' ei' fwnh\n la/boi the dead would speak if gifted with a voice
S. El. 548. Cp.
A. Ag. 37,
P. Pr. 361a, Eu. 299 d, and see 2311 a, 2322 c.

§2330
Conditional sentences of this class arose partly from optatives of wish (1814, 1815), partly from potential optatives (1824). Cp. ei)/q' w(=s h(bw/oimi . . . tw=| ke ta/x' a)nth/seie ma/xhs . . . *(/ektwr would that I were thus young . . . in that case Hector would soon find his combat H 157; see also
c 193.

§2331
The present optative views an action as continuing (not completed); the aorist optative, as simply occurring (completed). (The future optative is never used except to represent a future indicative in indirect discourse.) The perfect (rare) denotes completion with resulting state. In
Hdt. 7.214 it is used vaguely of the past: ei)dei/h me\n ga\r a)\n . . . tau/thn th\n a)t rapo\n *)onh/ths, ei) th=| xw/ra| polla\ w(mi_lhkw\s ei)/h for Onetes might know of this path . . . if he had been well acquainted with the country.

§2332
English would is equivocal, being used either in the translation of a)/n with the optative or of a)/n with the past indicative (2302). Thus, cp. ei)/ ti/s se h)/reto . . ., ti/ a)\n a)pekri)_nw; if any one had asked you . . ., what would you have replied? with ei) ou)=n tis h(ma=s . . . e)/roito . . ., ti/ a)\n au)tw=| a)pokri_nai/meqa; if then some one should (were to) ask us . . ., what would (should) we reply to him?
P. Pr. 311b, d. If I were may be used to translate both ei) with the optative and ei) with the past indicative. English shows examples of were in the protasis followed by would, shall, will, is (was, etc.). Were occurs also in apodosis (“should he be roused out of sleep to-night, it were not well”: Shelley).

§2333
The apodosis has the optative without a)/n in wishes.

ei) me\n sumbouleu/oimi a(\ be/ltista/ moi dokei=, polla/ moi kai\ a)gaqa\ ge/noito if I should give the advice that seems best to me, may many blessings fall to my lot
X. A. 5.6.4.
On the optative with ei) followed by other forms of the apodosis, see 2359.

§2334

Homeric Constructions.—a. In the protasis, ei)/ ke (ei) a)/n) with the optative with the same force as ei) alone. This use is exclusively Homeric. Thus, ou) me\n ga/r ti kakw/teron a)/llo pa/qoimi, ou)d' ei)/ ken tou= patro\s a)pofqime/noio puqoi/mhn for I could not suffer anything worse, not even if I should learn of my father's death T 321. On ei) a)/n in Attic, see 2353.
b. In the apodosis, a primary tense of the indicative: the present (
h 52), the future (I 388), the future with ke/ (
m 345: but this may be the aorist subjunctive).
c. In the apodosis, the hortatory subjunctive (
*y 893), the subjunctive with a)/n or ke/ (
*l 386).
d. In the apodosis, the optative without a)/n not in a wish, but with the same force as the optative with a)/n. See T 321 in a.
e. For ke/ with the optative in the apodosis where we should expect, in Homeric and Attic Greek, a past indicative with a)/n (ke/) in an unreal condition, see 2311 b.

## GENERAL CONDITIONS

§2335
General conditions refer indefinitely to any act or series of acts that are supposed to occur or to have occurred at any time; and without any implication as to fulfilment.
The if clause has the force of if ever (whenever), the conclusion expresses a repeated or habitual action or a general truth.

§2336
Any simple or unreal condition of present or past time, or any future condition, may refer to a customary or frequently repeated act or to a general truth. But for the present and past only (when nothing is implied as to fulfilment) there are two forms of expression: either a special kind of conditional sentence or (less frequently) the simple condition, as regularly in English and in Latin:
Present. Protasis: e)a/_n (= e)a/_n pote) with the subjunctive; apodosis: the present indicative (2337).
Protasis: ei) ( = ei)/ pote) with the present indicative; apodosis: the present indicative (2298 c, 2342).
Past. Protasis: ei) with the optative; apodosis: the imperfect indicative (2340).
Protasis: ei) with the imperfect; apodosis: the imperfect (2298 c, 2342).
a. By reason of the past apodosis, the optative in the protasis refers to the past. Only in this use (and when the optative in indirect discourse represents a past indicative) does the optative refer distinctly to the past.
b. The present subjunctive and optative view the action as continuing (not completed); the aorist subjunctive and optative, as simply occurring (completed). The tenses of the protasis have no time of themselves, but usually the action of the present is relatively contemporaneous with, the action of the aorist relatively antecedent to, the action of the main verb.
c. The indicative forms in the protasis are more common in temporal and relative sentences. Observe that it is the character of the apodosis alone which distinguishes the special kind of general condition from the two forms of future conditions.

## Fifth Form of Conditions: PRESENT GENERAL CONDITIONS

§2337
Present general conditions have, in the protasis, e)a/_n (h)/n, a)/_n) with the subjunctive; in the apodosis, the present indicative or an equivalent. e)a\_n tau=ta poih=|s (poih/sh|s), se\ e)painw= if ever you do this, I always praise you. The conclusion holds true of any time or of all time.

h)\n d' e)ggu\s e)/lqh| qa/natos, ou)dei\s bou/letai qnh/|skein but if death draws near, no one wishes to die
E. Alc. 671,

gela=| d' o( mw=ros, ka)/_n ti mh\ geloi=on h)=| the fool laughs even if there is nothing to laugh at
Men. Sent. 108, e)a\_n i)/sois i)/sa prosteqh=|, ta\ o(/la e)sti\n i)/sa if equals be added to equals, the wholes are equal Euclid, Ax. 2.

§2338
The gnomic aorist is equivalent to the present indicative in apodosis. h)\n de/ tis tou/twn ti parabai/nh|, zhmi/a_n au)toi=s e)pe/qesan but if any one ever transgresses any one of these regulations, they always impose punishment upon them (him)

§2339
Homer and Pindar prefer ei) to e)a/_n or ei)/ ke (A 81); and this ei) is sometimes found in Attic poetry (
S. Ant. 710). a)/n is more often absent in general conditions than in vivid future conditions.

## VARIATIONS FROM THE ORDINARY FORMS AND MEANINGS OF CONDITIONAL SENTENCES

## MODIFICATIONS OF THE PROTASIS

§2344

Substitutions for the Protasis.—For the protasis with ei) there may be substituted a participle, often in the genitive absolute (2067, 2070), an adverb, a prepositional phrase, a relative clause (2560), or some other single word or phrase. The present participle represents the imperfect, as the perfect represents the pluperfect.
pw=s dh=ta di/khs ou)/shs (= ei) di/kh e)sti/n) o( *zeu\s ou)k a)po/lwlen to\n pate/r' au(tou= dh/sa_s; how, pray, if there is any justice, has Zeus not perished since he bound his own father?

## MODIFICATIONS OF THE APODOSIS

§2350
The apodosis may be expressed in a participle or infinitive with or without a)/n as the construction may require; cp. 1846, 1848.

§2351

Verb of the Apodosis Omitted.—The verb of the apodosis is often omitted, and especially when the protasis has the same verb (cp. 2345). Thus, ei) dh/ tw| sofw/tero/s tou fai/hn ei)=nai, tou/tw| a)/n (fai/hn ei)=nai) if I should say that in any respect I am wiser than any one, (I should say) in this
P. A. 29b. Also in other cases, as ti/ dh=t' a)/n (le/gois), e(/teron ei) pu/qoio *swkra/tous fro/ntisma; what then would (you say), if you should hear another excogitation of Socrates?
Ar. Nub. 154. On w(/sper ei), w(/sper a)\n ei), w(s ei), see 1766 a, 2478, 2484.

§2352

Omission of the Apodosis.—a. When the conclusion is it is well (kalw=s e)/xei) or the like, it is often omitted. So often when the second of alternative opposing suppositions is expressed by ei) de\ mh/ (2346 d, N. 3). Cp. “yet now, if thou wilt forgive this sin, —: and if not, blot me . . . out of thy book” (Exodus 32. 32).
b. When we should introduce the conclusion by know that or I tell you: ei) kai\ oi)/ei me a)dikou=nta/ ti a)/gesqai, ou)/te e)/paion ou)de/na ou)/te e)/ballon if you possibly think that I was taken for some wrong-doing, know that I neither struck nor hit any one
X. A. 6.6.27. Here the apodosis might be introduced by ske/yasqe, e)nqu_mh/qhte, etc.
c. Sometimes when the protasis is merely parenthetical:

o( xru_so/s, ei) bou/loio ta)_lhqh= le/gein, e)/kteine to\n e)mo\n pai=da it was the gold—wouldst thou only tell the truth—that slew my child
E. Hec. 1206.
d. In passionate speech for rhetorical effect (aposiopēsis, 3015): ei)/ per ga/r k' e)qe/lh|sin *)olu/mpios a)sterophth\s e)c e(de/wn stufeli/cai: o( ga\r polu\ fe/rtato/s e)stin for if indeed the Olympian lord of the lightning will to thrust us out from our habitations, thrust us he will; for he is by far the most powerful A 581.
e. There is properly no omission of an apodosis after clauses with ei), ei) ga/r, ei)/qe, etc., in wishes (see 1816). In such clauses it is often possible to find an apodosis in an appended final clause:

potana\_n ei)/ me/ tis qew=n kti/sai, dipo/tamon i(/na po/lin mo/lw if only some one of the gods were to make me winged so that I might come to the city of twin rivers!
E. Supp. 621.

## PROTASIS AND APODOSIS COMBINED

§2353

ei) and a)/n both in Protasis.—The potential optative with a)/n or the unreal indicative with a)/n, standing as the apodosis in the conditional clause with ei), is the apodosis of another protasis expressed or understood.
a. Potential Optative.—a)lla\ mh\n ei)/ ge mhde\ dou=lon a)krath= decai/meq' a)/n, pw=s ou)k a)/cion au)to/n ge fula/casqai toiou=ton gene/sqai; and yet indeed if we would not accept even a slave who was intemperate, how is it not right for a man (the master) to guard against becoming so himself?
X. M. 1.5.3. Here decai/meqa is the protasis with ei); and also, with a)/n, the apodosis to an understood protasis (e.g. if we should think of so doing). The verb of the protasis may be contained in a participle, as ei) de\ mhdei\s a)\n u(_mw=n a)ciw/seie zh=n a)posterou/menos th=s patri/dos, prosh/kei ktl. but if no one of you should think life worth having if he were to be deprived of his country, it is right, etc.
I. 6.25. Such clauses form simple present conditions (if it is true that we would accept, etc.). The verb following the compressed condition stands usually in the present, at times in the future, indicative.
X. C. 3.3.55: qauma/zoimi a)\n . . . ei) a)\n w)felh/seie is an exception.
b. Unreal Indicative.—ei) toi/nun tou=to i)sxu_ro\n h)=n a)\n tou/tw| tekmh/rion . . ., ka)_moi\ gene/sqw tekmh/rion if then this would have been strong evidence for him (if he had been able to bring it forward), let it be evidence for me too
D. 49.58. This is a present condition (if it is true that this would, etc.) except in so far as the unexpressed protasis refers to the past. Such conditions may also be past.
N. 1.—The real protasis is: if it is (or was) the case that something could now (or hereafter) be (or could have been), it follows that.
N. 2.—In some of these cases, ei) has almost the force of e)pei/ since (
D. 49.58).

§2354

ei', e)a/_n, on the chance that.—ei) or e)a/_n may set forth the motive for the action or feeling expressed by the apodosis, and with the force of on the chance that, in case that, in the hope that, if haply.
After primary tenses in the apodosis, we have ei) with the indicative or e)a/_n (pws) with the subjunctive; after secondary tenses, ei) with the optative or, occasionally, e)a/_n (pws) with the subjunctive. Homer has sometimes the optative after primary tenses. The reference is to the future as in final clauses.
The protasis here depends, not on the apodosis proper, but on the idea of purpose or desire suggested by the thought. The accomplishment of the purpose may be desired or not desired, and by the subject either of the apodosis or of the protasis.
nu=n au)=t' e)gxei/h| peirh/somai, ai)/ ke tu/xwmi but now I will make trial with my spear on the chance (in the hope) that I may hit thee E279, a)/kouson kai\ e)mou=, e)a/_n soi e)/ti tau)ta\ dokh=| listen to me too on the chance (in the hope) that you may still have the same opinion
P. R. 358b,

poreuo/menoi e)s th\n *)asi/a_n w(s basile/a_, ei)/ pws pei/seian au)to/n going into Asia to the king in the hope that somehow they might persuade him
T. 2.67, pro\s th\n po/lin, ei) e)pibohqoi=en, e)xw/roun they advanced toward the city on the chance that they (the citizens) should make a sally 6. 100.
N.—This use is to be distinguished from that of ei) a)/ra if perchance, ei) mh\ a)/ra unless perchance (often ironical).
a. This construction should be distinguished from cases like

e)pibouleu/ousin . . . e)celqei=n . . ., h)\n du/nwntai bia/sasqai they planned to get out, if they might make their way by force
T. 3.20, where we have implied indirect discourse (e)ce/lqwmen, h)\n dunw/meqa bia/sasqai).
b. Homer uses this construction as an object clause in dependence on oi)=da, ei)=don, or on a verb of saying. Thus ti/s d' oi)=d', ei)/ ke/n oi( su\n dai/moni qu_mo\n o)ri/_nw pareipw/n; who knows if, perchance, with God's help I may rouse his spirit by persuasion? O 403 (i.e. the chances of rousing his spirit, if haply I may), e)ni/spes, ei)/ pws . . . u(pekprofu/goimi *xa/rubdin tell me if haply I shall (might) escape Charybdis
m 112. Here the apodosis is entirely suppressed. Observe that this construction is not an indirect question.

## LESS USUAL COMBINATIONS OF COMPLETE PROTASIS AND APODOSIS

§2355
In addition to the ordinary forms of correspondence between protasis and apodosis (2297), Greek shows many other combinations expressing distinct shades of feeling. Most of these combinations, though less frequent than the ordinary forms, are no less “regular.” Shift of mental attitude is a known fact of all speech, though the relation of cause to effect must not be obscured. A speaker or writer, having begun his sentence with a protasis of one type, may alter the course of his thought: with the result that he may conclude with an apodosis of another form, in some cases even with an apodosis “unsymmetrical” with the protasis and logically dependent upon a protasis that is only suggested by the form actually adopted. Since either protasis or apodosis may choose the form of expression best suited to the meaning, the student should beware of thinking that conditional sentences invariably follow a conventional pattern, departure from which is to be counted as violation of rule. Some combinations are less usual than others: most of the more common variations from the ordinary type have been mentioned under the appropriate sections, and are here summarized (2356-2358). Special cases are considered in 2359-2365.

§2356
The optative with a)/n (the potential optative) may be used as the apodosis of
ei) with the indicative in Simple Present and Past conditions (2300 e),
ei) with the past indicative in Unreal conditions in Homer (rarely in Attic, 2312),
ei) with the future indicative in Emotional Future conditions (2328),
ei) with the optative in Less Vivid Future conditions (2329). In Present conditions (2353): ei) le/goim' a)/n supposing I would say, whereas ei) le/goimi means supposing I should say.
e)a/_n with the subjunctive in More Vivid Future conditions (2326 d).
a. When the protasis is a future indicative or a subjunctive, the optative with a)/n sometimes seems to be merely a mild future and to have no potential force. Thus, h)\n ou)=n ma/qh|s moi to\n a)/dikon tou=ton lo/gon, ou)k a)\n a)podoi/hn ou)d' a)\n o)bolo\n ou)deni/ if then you learn this unjust reason for me, I will not pay even an obol to anybody
Ar. Nub. 116.

§2357
The subjunctive of exhortation, prohibition, or deliberation, the optative of wish, and the imperative, may be used as the apodosis of
ei) with the indicative in Simple Present and Past conditions (2300 c, d, f),
ei) with the future indicative in Emotional Future conditions (2328),
e)a/_n with the subjunctive in More Vivid Future conditions (2326 c-e).

§2358
The unreal indicative with or without a)/n may be used as the apodosis of
a. ei) with the indicative in Simple Present and Past conditions (2300 b). So after ei) with the future denoting present intention or necessity that something shall be done (2301), as ei) ga\r gunai=kes ei)s to/d' h(/cousin qra/sous . . ., par' ou)de\n au<*>tai=s h)=n a)\n o)llu/nai po/seis for if women are to reach this height of boldness, it would be as nothing for them to destroy their husbands
E. Or. 566.
b. ei) with the past indicative in Present and Past Unreal conditions (2302).

ei) with the Optative, Apodosis a primary tense of the Indicative, etc.

§2359

ei) with the optative (instead of e)a/_n with the subjunctive) is not infrequent in the protasis with a primary tense of the indicative, a subjunctive, or an imperative, in the apodosis. The reference is usually either to general present time (with the present indicative), or to future time. When the apodosis contains a present indicative it frequently precedes the protasis.
a. Compare the analogous usage in English commonly with should, would: “There is some soul of goodness in things evil, would men observingly distil it” (Shakespeare). “If you should die, my death shall follow yours” (Dryden). “I shall scarcely figure in history, if under my guidance such visitations should accrue” (Disraeli). “If he should kill thee . . ., he has nothing to lose” (Sedley). “But if an happy soil should be withheld . . . think it not beneath thy toil” (Philips).

§2360

a)ndrw=n ga\r swfro/nwn me/n e)stin, ei) mh\ a)dikoi=nto, h(suxa/zein for it is the part of prudent men to remain quiet if they should not be wronged

TWO OR MORE PROTASES OR APODOSES IN ONE SENTENCE

§2366
A conditional sentence may have several protases and one apodosis or one protasis and several apodoses. Two such protases or apodoses are coördinate or one of the two is subordinate to the other.

§2367
Two coördinated protases with a single apodosis, or two coördinated apodoses with a single protasis, may refer to the same time or to different times.
ei) de\ mh/t' e)/sti (ti be/lti_on) mh/t' h)=n mh/t' a)\n ei)pei=n e)/xoi mhdei\s mhde/pw kai\ th/meron, ti/ to\n su/mboulon e)xrh=n poiei=n; but if there neither is nor was any better plan, and if yet even to-day no one can suggest any, what was it the duty of the statesman to do?
D. 18.190, kai\ ga\r a)\n kai\ u(perfue\s ei)/h, ei) kata\ me\n tw=n *)olunqi/ous prodo/ntwn polla\ kai\ dei/n' e)yhfi/sasqe, tou\s de\ par' u(_mi=n au)toi=s a)dikou=ntas mh\ kola/zontes fai/noisqe and in fact it would be actually monstrous if, whereas you have passed many severe votes against the betrayers of the Olynthians, you appear not to punish the wrongdoers in your midst
D. 19.267, ei) e)gw\ e)pexei/rhsa pra/_ttein ta\ poli_tika\ pra/_gmata, pa/lai a)\n a)polw/lh kai\ ou)/t' a)\n u(_ma=s w)felh/kh ou)de\n ou)/t' a)\n e)mauto/n if I had tried to engage in politics, I should have long ago perished and benefited neither you nor myself at all
P. A. 31d.

§2368
When two or more protases are not coördinated in the same sentence, one is of chief importance and any other protasis is subordinate to it. Such protases may follow each other or one may be added after the apodosis; and may show the same or a different modal form.
a)ciou=men, ei) me/n tina o(ra=te swthri/a_n h(mi=n (e)some/nhn), e)a\_n diakarterw=men polemou=ntes, dida/cai kai\ h(ma=s ktl. if you see any safety for us if we persist in making war, we beg that you will inform us too what it is
X. H. 7.4.8 (here e)a\_n diakarterw=men depends on ei) o(ra=te); e)a\_n de\ h(de/a pro\s lu_phra/ (i(sth=|s), e)a\_n me\n ta\ a)nia_ra\ u(perba/llhtai u(po\ tw=n h(de/wn, e)a/_n te ta\ e)ggu\s u(po\ tw=n po/rrw e)a/_n te ta\ po/rrw u(po\ tw=n e)ggu/s, tau/thn th\n pra=cin pra_kte/on e)n h(=| a)\n tau=t' e)nh=|: e)a\_n de\ ta\ h(de/a u(po\ tw=n a)nia_rw=n, ou) pra_kte/a but if you weight pleasures against pains, if on the one hand what is painful is exceeded by what is pleasurable (whether the near by the distant or the distant by the near), you must adopt that course of action in which this is the case; if on the other hand the pleasurable (is exceeded) by the painful, the former must not be adopted
P. Pr. 356b (here to e)a\_n h(de/a i(sth=|s are subordinated e)a\_n me/n and e)a\_n de/, and to e)a\_n me/n are subordinated e)a/_n te . . . e)a/_n te); ei) de/ se h)ro/mhn e)c a)rxh=s ti/ e)sti kalo/n te kai\ ai)sxro/n, ei)/ moi a(/per nu=n a)pekri/_nw, a)=r' ou)k a)\n o)rqw=s a)peke/kriso; but if I had asked you at the start what beauty and ugliness is—if you had answered me as you have now done, would you not have answered me rightly?
P. Hipp. M. 289c;

h)\n me\n po/lemon ai(rh=sqe, mhke/ti h(/kete deu=ro a)/neu o(/plwn, ei) swfronei=te if you choose war, come no more hither without arms if you are wise
X. C. 3.2.13, ei) meta\ *qhbai/wn h(mi=n a)gwnizome/nois ou(/tws ei(/marto pra=cai, ti/ xrh=n prosdoka=n ei) mhde\ tou/tous e)/sxomen summa/xous a)lla\ *fili/ppw| prose/qento; if it was decreed by fate that we should fare thus with the Thebans fighting on our side, what ought we to have expected if we had not even secured them as allies but they had joined Philip?
D. 18.195.
a. A second protasis may be added to the first protasis to explain or define it. Thus, kai\ ou) tou=to le/cwn e)/rxomai w(s polu\ me\n e)la/_ttous polu\ de\ xei/ronas e)/xwn o(/mws sune/balen: ei) ga\r tau=ta le/goimi, *)a_ghsi/la_o/n t' a)/n moi dokw= a)/frona a)pofai/nein kai\ e)mauto\n mw=ron, ei) e)painoi/hn to\n peri\ tw=n megi/stwn ei)kh=| kindu_neu/onta and I am not going to say that he made the engagement in spite of having much fewer and inferior troops; for if I should maintain this, I think that I should be proving Agesilaus senseless and myself a fool, if I should praise the man who rashly incurs danger when the greatest interests are at stake X.
