## CONCESSIVE CLAUSES

§2369
Concessive clauses are commonly formed by kai/ in conjunction with the ei) or e)a/_n of conditional clauses: kai\ ei) (kei'), kai\ e)a/_n (ka)/_n) even if, ei) kai/, e)a\_n kai/ although.

§2370
Such concessive clauses are conditional, but indicate that the condition which they introduce may be granted without destroying the conclusion. The apodosis of concessive clauses thus has an adversative meaning, i.e. it states what is regarded as true notwithstanding (o(/mws) what is assumed in the protasis.

§2371
Concessive clauses have the construction of conditional clauses. The protasis, if negative, takes mh/.

§2372

kai\ ei) (even if) clauses.—kai\ ei) commonly implies that the conclusion must be true or must take place even in the extreme, scarcely conceivable, case which these words introduce (even supposing that, even in the case that). In such cases the speaker does not grant that the alleged condition really exists. On ka)\_n ei) see 1766 b.
kei' mh\ pe/poiqa, tou)=rgon e)/st' e)rgaste/on even if I have no confidence, yet the deed must be done
A. Ch. 296, kai\ e)a\_n mh\ h(mei=s parakeleuw/meqa, (h( po/lis), i(kanw=s e)pimelh/setai and even if we do not use exhortations, the city will take sufficient care
P. Menex. 248d, gela=| d' o( mw=ros, ka)/_n ti mh\ geloi=on h<*> the fool laughs even if there is nothing to laugh at
Men. Sent. 108,

*mu_soi=s basileu\s pollou\s me\n h(gemo/nas a)\n doi/h . . ., kai\ ei) su\n teqri/ppois bou/lointo a)pie/nai the king would give many guides to the Mysians even supposing they should want to depart with four-horse chariots
X. A. 3.2.24.

§2373
The kai/ of kai\ ei) may mean simply and, as

kei' ta/d' ei)/setai *kre/wn and if Creon learns this
S. Ant. 229.

§2374
Some scholars hold that the difference between kai\ ei) and ei) kai/ is that kai\ ei) concedes a supposition and is used of an assumed fact, while ei) kai/ concedes a fact and is used of an actual fact. But this distinction cannot be supported. kai\ ei) sometimes differs from ei) kai\ only in being more emphatic. When an actual fact is referred to, we expect ei) kai/; but kai\ ei) sometimes occurs, as i)/sws toi, kei' ble/ponta mh\ )po/qoun, qano/nt' a)\n oi)mw/ceian perhaps, though they did not miss him when alive, they will lament him now that he is dead
S. Aj. 962, cp. peiste/on, kei' mhde\n h(du/ although it is in no wise sweet, I must obey
S. O. T. 1516.

§2375

ei' kai/ (although) clauses.—ei) kai/ commonly admits that a condition exists (granting that), but does not regard it as a hindrance. The condition, though it exists, is a matter of no moment so far as the statement in the principal clause is concerned.

ei) kai\ turannei=s king though thou art
S. O. T. 408,

po/lin me/n, ei) kai\ mh\ ble/peis, fronei=s d' o(/mws oi(/a| no/sw| su/nestin though thou canst not see, thou yet dost feel with what a plague our city is afflicted
S. O. T. 302,

ei) kai/ tw| smi_kro/teron dokei= ei)=nai although it seems too unimportant to some
P. Lach. 182c.

§2376
The verb is omitted in

ei) kai\ geloio/teron ei)pei=n though the expression be ridiculous
P. A. 30c (cp. 944).

§2377
The kai/ of ei) kai/ may go closely with a following word. Here the meaning is either also or indeed; as ei) kai\ dunh/sei ge if thou shalt also be able (besides having the will)
S. Ant. 90, deino/n g' ei)=pas, ei) kai\ zh=|s qanw/n a strange thing truly hast thou uttered, if, though slain, thou indeed livest
S. Aj. 1127. Where trajection is assumed (ei) mh\ kai/ for ei) kai\ mh/) the kai/ is intensive, as ei) mh\ kai\ nu=n . . . a)lla/ if not already . . . at least
T. 2.11. 6, ei) mh\ kai\ de/dra_ken unless he has actually done it 6. 60. 3.

§2378

ei) (e)a\_n) kai/ not infrequently means even if in prose as well as poetry.

ei(/leto ma=llon suneide/nai u(_ma=s, i(/n', ei) kai\ bou/loito kako\s ei)=nai, mh\ e)cei/h au)tw=| he preferred rather that you should know of it, in order that, even if he should wish to be base, it might not be possible
L. 20.23,

a)ll' ei' kai\ mhde\n tou/twn u(ph=rxen h(mi=n, ou)d' w(\s xalepo/n e)sti gnw=nai peri\ au)tw=n o(po/teroi ta)_lhqh= le/gousin but even if I had none of these points to rely on, even so it is not difficult to find out which tells the truth
D. 41.15. Cp. also
Ant. 5.27,
And. 1.21,
L. 31.20;
Is. 11.23,
D. 16.24,
Aes. 3.211. ei) kai/ for kai\ ei) is especially common in Isocrates, who does not use kai\ ei) or kei' except in 21. 11. Demosthenes is not fond of kai\ ei), and often substitutes ka)\_n ei) for it (19. 282, 24. 109, 45. 12). Cp. 1766 b.

§2379

ei) (e)a/_n) sometimes has a concessive force (
X. Eq. 1.17). ei)/per (e)a/_nper) has, rarely in Attic, a sort of concessive meaning (
P. Euth. 4b), and especially when the truth of a statement is implicitly denied or doubted. Cp.
L. 16.8.

§2380

e)pei/, usually with a following ge/, is sometimes translated although, where a speaker is strictly giving the reason for his statement of a fact (or for something in that statement) and not for the fact itself. Here there is a thought in the speaker's mind which is suppressed. Thus, ai)sxu_noi/mhn a)\n e)/gwge tou=to o(mologei=n, e)pei\ polloi/ ge/ fa_si tw=n a)nqrw/pwn for my part I should be ashamed to acknowledge this (and I say this for myself) since there are many men who do assert it
P. Pr. 333c.

§2381
Negative concessive clauses have ou)d' (mhd') ei) or e)a/_n not even if. Here not (ou)-, mh-) belongs to the leading clause, while even (-de/, cp. kai/) belongs to the dependent clause. The negative is frequently repeated in the leading clause.

ou)d' ei' pa/ntes e)/lqoien *pe/rsai, plh/qei ou)x u(perbaloi/meq' a)\n tou\s polemi/ous even if all the Persians should come, we should not exceed the enemy in numbers
X. C. 2.1.8, mh\ qorubh/shte, mhd' e)a\_n do/cw ti u(_mi=n me/ga le/gein do not raise a disturbance, even if I seem to you to be speaking presumptuously
P. A. 20e. Cp. 2382.

§2382
The idea of concession or opposition is often expressed by the participle alone (2066) or by the participle with kai/per or kai\ tau=ta (2083). The negative is ou). In negative concessive sentences we find also the participle with ou)de/ (mhde/), ou)de/ (mhde/) per.

ou)de\ peponqw\s kakw=s e)xqro\n ei)=nai/ moi tou=ton o(mologw= not even though I have been ill-treated do I admit that he is my enemy
D. 21.205, gunaiki\ pei/qou mhde\ ta)_lhqh= klu/wn listen to a woman, even if thou dost not hear the truth E. fr. 440.

## TEMPORAL CLAUSES

§2383
Temporal clauses are introduced by conjunctions or relative expressions having the force of conjunctions
A. Denoting time usually the same as that of the principal verb:
o(/te, o(po/te, h(ni/ka, o(phni/ka when; o(sa/kis as often as; e(/ws, me/xri (rarely a)/xri), o(/son xro/non so long as; e(/ws, e)n w(=| (rarely e)n o(/sw| and e)/ste) while.
N. 1.—e(/ws means so long as in reference to actions that are coëxtensive; while, in reference to actions not coëxtensive.
N. 2.—h(ni/ka, o(phni/ka have the force of what time, at the moment when, when, (rarely while), and are more precise than o(/te.
N. 3.—Poetic or Ionic are eu)=te (= o(/te) when, h)=mos (only with the indicative) when, o(/pws when (o(/kws in Hdt. of antecedent action), o)/fra so long as. Hom. has ei(=os (i.e. h(=os) or ei(/ws for e(/ws.
N. 4.—e)/ste is used (rarely) in lyric, Sophocles, Euripides, Herodotus, Xenophon.
B. Denoting time usually prior to that of the principal verb:
e)pei/, e)peidh/ after, after that (less exactly when); e)pei\ prw=ton, w(s (or e)pei\) ta/xista, e)peidh\ ta/xista (rarely o(/pws ta/xista) as soon as; e)c ou(= (rarely e)c w(=n), e)c o(/tou, a)f' ou(= since, ever since; w(s when, as soon as, since.
N.—e)pei/te after is very common in Herodotus.
C. Denoting time subsequent to that of the principal verb:
e(/ws, e)/ste, me/xri, me/xri ou(= (rarely a)/xri), a)/xri ou(= until: followed by a finite verb.
pri/n, pro/teron h)/ before, until: followed by a finite verb or by an infinitive.
N.—Homer has also o)/fra (also final), ei)s o(/te (ke), ei)s o(/ (ke). Herodotus has e)s o(/, e(/ws ou(=, e)s ou(= until. o(ppo/te with the optative in Homer after a past tense of a verb of waiting or expecting means for the time when (H 414). e)/ste (first in Hesiod) is rare in lyric, tragedy, Herodotus, and Plato, very common in Xenophon.—me/xri is avoided by the orators.—me/xri and a)/xri take the articular infinitive in Demosthenes.—te/ws for e(/ws is rare (2171).

§2384
Demonstrative adverbs in the principal clause often correspond to the relative conjunctions, as o(/te . . . to/te, e)n w(=| . . . e)ntou/tw|, e(/ws . . . te/ws (me/xri tou/tou). So also e)pei\ . . . to/te, w(s (o(/te) . . . e)ntau=qa, etc.

§2385
Some temporal conjunctions also denote cause:
o(/te, o(po/te, e)pei/, eu)=te (poet.), e)peidh/ since, whereas, w(s because. w(s means also as, as to, rarely, in prose, in order that. e(/ws in Homer has in part become a final conjunction (2419); for the Attic use, see 2420.

§2386
A temporal sentence and a conditional sentence may occur in close conjunction without marked difference of signification.
o(/tan de\ nosh/swsin, u(giei=s geno/menoi sw/|zontai: e)a/_n te/ tis a)/llh sumfora\_ katalamba/nh| au)tou/s, ta\ e)nanti/a e)pigigno/mena o)ni/nhsin whenever they fall ill, they are saved by regaining their health; and if ever any other calamity overtakes them, the reversal to prosperity that follows is to their benefit Ant. 2.
b. 1.

§2387
A temporal conjunction is often used in Greek where English employs a conditional or a concessive conjunction.
ou)k a)\n e)/gwge *kroni/_onos a)=sson i(koi/mhn, . . . o(/te mh\ au)to/s ge keleu/oi I would not draw nearer to Cronus' son unless (lit. when not) he should himself bid me
*c 248.

§2388
The time denoted by a temporal clause is not always solely contemporaneous, antecedent, or subsequent to that of the principal clause, but may overlap with the time of the principal clause (before and at the same time, at the same time and after, until and after).

e)pei\ de\ h)sqe/nei *da_rei=os kai\ u(pw/pteue teleuth\n tou= bi/ou, e)bou/leto tw\ pai=de parei=nai when Darius was ill and suspected that his life was coming to an end, he wished his two sons to be with him
X. A. 1.1.1 (here the situation set forth by h)sqe/nei and u(pw/pteue occurred both before and after the time indicated in e)bou/leto), toiau=ta e)poi/ei e(/ws diedi/dou pa/nta a(\ e)/labe kre/a_ he kept doing thus until he saw that (and so long as) he was distributing all the meat he had received
X. C. 1.3.7 (the imperfect is rare with e(/ws or pri/n until),

o( d' e)/n te tw=| paro/nti pro\s ta\ mhnu/_mata a)pelogei=to kai\ e(toi=mos h)=n pri\n e)kplei=n kri/_nesqai he both defended himself then and there against the charges and offered to be tried before he sailed
T. 6.29.
a. Conjunctions of antecedent action usually take the aorist, rarely the imperfect except when that tense represents overlapping action, as in
T. 5.72. 3. Cp.
T. 1.13. 5 with 1. 5. 1.
b. A verb of aoristic action is used: in the temporal clause when complete priority, in the main clause when complete subsequence, is to be clearly marked.

§2389
Clauses introduced by relative adverbs (or conjunctions) of time, have, in general, the same constructions as clauses introduced by relative pronouns (340, 2493 ff.) and by relative adverbs of place and manner. Temporal clauses are treated separately for the sake of clearness.
a. Temporal clauses introduced by a word meaning until differ from ordinary conditional relatives in some respects, as in the use of the optative in implied indirect discourse (2408, 2420); and in the frequency of the absence of a)/n (2402).
b. Strictly o(/te, e)/nqa, w(s, etc., are subordinating conjunctions when the clause introduced by them fixes the time, place, or manner of the main clause; but are relative adverbs when they serve only to define the antecedent and introduce a clause merely supplementary to the main clause.

§2390
Temporal clauses are either definite or indefinite.

§2391
A temporal clause is definite when the action occurs at a definite point of time (negative ou), except when the special construction requires mh/). Definite temporal clauses usually refer to the present or to the past.

§2392
A temporal clause is indefinite when the action (1) occurs in the indefinite future, (2) recurs an indefinite number of times, (3) continues for an indefinite period. The same clause may have more than one of these meanings. (3) is rare. The negative is mh/. Indefinite temporal clauses refer either to the future or to general present or past time.

§2393
The same temporal conjunction may refer either to definite or to indefinite time; sometimes with a difference of meaning.

§2394
When the time is definite, the indicative is used; when indefinite, the subjunctive with a)/n, the optative, or (rarely) the indicative.
Temporal conjunctions with the subjunctive take a)/n. (For exceptions, see 2402, 2412, 2444 b.) a)/n is not used with the optative except when the optative is potential, 2406, 2421 (cp. 2452).

## INDICATIVE TEMPORAL CLAUSES REFERRING TO PRESENT OR PAST TIME

§2395
Present or past temporal clauses take the indicative when the action is marked as a fact and refers to a definite occasion (negative ou)). The principal clause commonly has the indicative, but may take any form of the simple sentence.
A. Temporal clauses denoting the same time as that of the principal verb (2383 A).

o(/te tau=ta h)=n, sxedo\n me/sai h)=san nu/ktes it was about midnight when this was taking place
X. A. 3.1.33, cp. 1. 1. 1, cited in 2388, h(ni/ka de\ dei/lh e)gi/gneto, e)fa/nh koniorto/s but when it was getting to be afternoon, a cloud of dust appeared 1. 8. 8,

me/xri a)po\ tou= i)/sou h(gou=nto, proqu/_mws ei(po/meqa as long as they led on equal terms we followed willingly
T. 3.10,

o(/son xro/non e)kaqe/zeto . . . a)mfi\ th\n peri\ to\ frou/rion oi)konomi/a_n, . . . a)ph=gon i(/ppous as long as he was employed with regulations about the fortress, they kept bringing horses
X. C. 5.3.25,

e)n w(=| w(pli/zonto, h(=kon . . . oi( skopoi/ while they were arming, the scouts came
X. A. 2.2.15, e(/ws e)sti\ kairo/s, a)ntila/besqe tw=n pra_gma/twn ‘while there is opportunity, take our public policy in hand’
D. 1.20.
N. me/mnhmai, oi)=da, a)kou/w often take o(/te when instead of o(/ti that. Thus, me/mnhmai o(/te e)gw\ pro\s se\ h)=lqon I remember when (that) I came to you
X. C. 1.6.12. h(ni/ka (and h)=mos in poetry) has a similar use. oi)=da o(/te, a)kou/w o(/te are probably due to the analogy of me/mnhmai o(/te, originally I remember (the moment) when.
B. Temporal clauses denoting time prior to that of the principal verb (2383 B).

e)pei\ d' e)ch=lqen, e)ch/ggeile toi=s fi/lois th\n kri/sin tou= *)oro/nta_ w(s e)ge/neto but after he came out, he announced to his friends how the trial of Orontas had resulted
X. A. 1.6.5 (observe that the aorist, and not the pluperfect, is commonly used to denote time previous to that of the main verb; cp. 1943), e)peidh\ de\ e)teleu/thse *da_rei=os . . ., *tissafe/rnhs diaba/llei to\n *ku=ron after Darius died Tissaphernes calumniated Cyrus 1. 1. 3, w(s ta/xista e(/ws u(pe/fainen, e)qu/_onto as soon as daylight indistinctly appeared, they sacrificed 4. 3. 9, e)c ou(= fi/los ei)=nai prospoiei=tai, e)k tou/tou u(_ma=s e)chpa/thken ever since Philip pretended to be friendly, from that time on he had deceived you
D. 23.193. (On ever since expressed by the dative of the participle, see 1498.)
C. Temporal clauses denoting time subsequent to that of the principal verb (2383 C).

e)/meinan e(/ws a)fi/_konto oi( strathgoi/ they waited until the generals arrived
X. H. 1.1.29,

loidorou=si to\n *swthri/da_n e)/ste h)na/gkasan . . . poreu/esqai they kept reviling Soteridas until they forced him to march on
X. A. 3.4.49, kai\ tau=ta e)poi/oun me/xri sko/tos e)ge/neto and they kept doing this until darkness came on 4. 2. 4,

tou\s *(/ellhnas a)pelu/_sato doulei/a_s w(/st' e)leuqe/rous ei)=nai me/xri ou(= pa/lin au)toi\ au(tou\s katedoulw/santo she released the Greeks from slavery so as to be free until they enslaved themselves
P. Menex. 245a.

§2396
When the principal verb is a past indicative with a)/n and denotes non-fulfilment, a temporal clause has, by assimilation of mood, a past tense of the indicative denoting non-fulfilment.

o(phni/k' e)fai/neto tau=ta pepoihkw\s . . ., w(mologei=t' a)\n h( kathgori/a_ toi=s e)/rgois au)tou= if it appeared that he had ever done this, his form of accusation would tally with his acts
D. 18.14 (here whenever would make the condition ambiguous), e)basa/nizon a)\n me/xri ou(= au)toi=s e)do/kei they would have kept questioning them under <*>orture as long as they pleased 53. 25,

ou)k a)\n e)pauo/mhn . . . e(/ws a)pepeira/_qhn th=s sofi/a_s tauthsi/_ I would not cease until I had made trial of this wisdom
P. Crat. 396c. See 2185 b.

§2397
The negative is mh/ only when the temporal relation is regarded as conditional.
o(po/te to\ di/kaion mh\ oi)=da, o(/ e)sti, sxolh=| ei)/somai ei)/te a)reth/ tis ou)=sa tugxa/nei ei)/te kai\ ou)/ when (if) I do not know what justice is, I am scarcely likely to know whether it is or is not a virtue
P. R. 354c.

## TEMPORAL CLAUSES REFERRING TO THE FUTURE

§2398
The future indicative is rarely used in temporal clauses; and when used refers to definite time.

thnikau=ta . . . o(/te ou)d' o(/ ti xrh\ poiei=n e(/cete at that time, when you will not be able to do even what is necessary
D. 19.262.
a. The future is rare because that tense does not usually make clear the difference between action continuing and action simply occurring in the future. o(/te with the future indicative has thus been almost entirely displaced by o(/tan with the subjunctive.
b. For the future with ke/ in
q 318 the subjunctive is probably correct.

§2399
Temporal clauses referring indefinitely to the future take either the subjunctive with a)/n or the optative without a)/n.
a. The addition of a)/n produces the forms o(/tan, o(po/tan; e)pa/_n, e)ph/n (both rare in Attic), e)peida^/n. e(/ws a)/n, me/xri a)/n, e)/st' a)/n mean as long as or until. w(s when scarcely ever takes a)/n (for w(s a)/n while e(/ws a)/n is read in
S. Aj. 1117, Ph. 1330).
b. The temporal conjunctions have here, in general, the same constructions as conditional e)a/_n or ei). Thus o(po/tan = e)a/_n pote, o(po/te = ei)/ pote.

§2400
The present marks the action as continuing (not completed), the aorist marks the action as simply occurring (completed). The present usually sets forth an action contemporaneous with that of the leading verb; the aorist, an action antecedent to that of the leading verb.
a. The present may denote time antecedent when the verb has no aorist, and in the case of some other verbs: Thus, (o( po/lemos) d\s lu_ph/sei e(/kaston, e)peida\n parh=| the war which will afflict every one when it comes
D. 6.35, e)peida\n a)kou/h| . . . e(te/rous kri/_nontas, ti/ kai\ poih/sh|; when he hears that they are prosecuting other men, what should he then do? 19. 138.

## FUTURE TEMPORAL CLAUSES WITH THE SUBJUNCTIVE

§2401
Temporal clauses referring to the future take the subjunctive with a)/n in sentences corresponding to more vivid future conditions. The principal clause has the future indicative or any form of the verb referring to the future except the simple optative. The negative is mh/.
h(ni/ka d' a)/n tis u(_ma=s a)dikh=|, h(mei=s u(pe\r u(_mw=n maxou/meqa but when any one wrongs you, we will fight in your defence
X. C. 4.4.11, o(/tan mh\ sqe/nw, pepau/somai when my strength fails, I shall cease
S. Ant. 91,

e)peida\n a(/pant' a)kou/shte, kri/_nate when you have heard everything, decide
D. 4.14, e)moi\ . . . dokei=, e)pa\_n ta/xista a)_risth/swmen, i)e/nai in my judgment we must go as soon as we have breakfasted X. A. 4. 6. 9, me/xri d' a)\n e)gw\ h(/kw, ai( spondai\ meno/ntwn but until I return, let the armistice continue 2. 3. 24,

le/cw . . . e(/ws a)\n a)kou/ein bou/lhsqe I will speak so long as you wish to listen
D. 21.130,

perime/nete e)/st' a)\n e)gw\ e)/lqw wait until I come
X. A. 5.1.4, mh\ a)namei/nwmen e(/ws a)\n plei/ous h(mw=n ge/nwntai let us not wait until the enemy outnumbers us
X. C. 3.3.46, ou)k a)name/nomen (present as emphatic future) e(/ws a)\n h( h(mete/ra_ xw/ra_ kakw=tai we do not wait until our land shall be ravaged 3. 3. 18. The present subjunctive is rare with e(/ws until, and marks overlapping action (here = e(/ws a)\n i)/dwmen kakoume/nhn).

§2402
The subjunctive without a)/n (ke/) is sometimes found in poetry and in Herodotus; in Attic prose only with me/xri, me/xri ou(= until (and pri/n, 2444 b). Thus,

e)bou/leusan desmoi=s au)tou\s fula/ssein me/xri ou(= ti cumbw=sin they decided to guard them in fetters until they should reach some agreement
T. 4.41. The omission of a)/n is more common after temporal conjunctions than after ei) (2327 a) and in writers later than Homer lends an archaic colouring to the style.

§2403
The principal clause may be a potential optative, which is at times nearly equivalent to the future: e)gw\ de\ tau/thn me\n th\n ei)rh/nhn, e(/ws a)\n ei(=s *)aqhnai/wn lei/phtai, ou)de/pot' a)\n sumbouleu/saimi poih/sasqai th=| po/lei so long as a single Athenian is left, I never would recommend the city to make peace
D. 19.14.

## FUTURE TEMPORAL CLAUSES WITH THE OPTATIVE

§2404
Temporal clauses referring to the future in sentences corresponding to less vivid future conditions usually take the optative without a)/n. An optative referring to the future stands in the principal clause (2186 b). The negative is mh/.
teqnai/hn, o(/te moi mhke/ti tau=ta me/loi may I die, when I shall no longer care for these delights Mimnermus 1. 2,

peinw=n fa/goi a)\n o(po/te bou/loito when hungry he would eat whenever he wished
X. M. 2.1.18, ei) de\ bou/loio tw=n fi/lwn tina\ protre/yasqai, o(po/te a)podhmoi/hs, e)pimelei=sqai tw=n sw=n, ti/ a)\n poioi/hs; should you desire to induce one of your friends to care for your interests when you were away from home, what would you do? 2. 3. 12,

de/oito/ g' a)\n au)tou= me/nein, e(/ws a)pe/lqois he would beg him to remain until you should depart
X. C. 5.3.13 (here the temporal clause depends on me/nein, itself dependent on de/oito a)/n).

§2405
The optative with a)/n (ke/) in Homer, where Attic would have the simple optative, is potential or virtually equivalent to a future. Thus, au)ti/ka ga/r me kataktei/neien *)axilleu\s . . ., e)ph\n go/ou e)c e)/ron ei(/hn for let Achilles slay me forthwith, when I have satisfied my desire for lamentation
*w 227. Cp. I 304,
d 222, e(/ws ke b 78 (potential), ei)s o(/ ke *o 70 (elsewhere this expression always takes the subjunctive in Homer).

§2406
The potential optative or indicative (with a)/n) having its proper force may appear in temporal clauses (cp. 2353).
fula/ca_s . . . to\n xeimw=n' e)pixeirei=, h(ni/k' a)\n h(mei=s mh\ dunai/meq' e)kei=s' a)fike/sqai by watching for winter to set in he begins his operations when we are unable (he thinks) to reach the spot
D. 4.31. Cp. 2405.

§2407
The principal clause rarely has the present or future indica tive, when the temporal clause has the optative without a)/n (cp. 2360, 2361, 2573 b, c).
fronh/sews dei= pollh=s pro\s tou\s polu\ plei/ous . . ., o(po/te kairo\s parape/soi when the critical moment arrives, he must have great judgment to cope with forces much more numerous than his own
X. Hipp. 7.4, ai)pu/ oi( e)ssei=tai . . . nh=as e)niprh=sai, o(/te mh\ au)to/s ge *kroni/_wn e)mba/loi ai)qo/menon da_lo\n nh/essi hard will it be for him to fire the ships unless (when . . . not) Kronion himself hurl upon the ships a blazing brand N 317.
a. Homer has a)/n (ke/) with the subjunctive; as

ou)k a)/n toi xrai/smh| ki/qaris . . ., o(/t' e)n koni/h|si migei/hs thy cithern will not avail thee when thou grovellest in the dust
*g 55.

§2408
After a secondary tense introducing indirect discourse (real or implied) the optative may represent the subjunctive with a)/n as the form in which the thought was conceived.
parh/ggeilan, e)peidh\ deipnh/saien . . . pa/ntas a)napau/esqai kai\ e(/pesqai h(ni/k' a)/n tis paragge/llh| they issued orders that, when they had supped, all should rest and follow when any one should give the command ( = e)peida\n deipnh/shte . . . a)napau/esqe)
X. A. 3.5.18, e)pimei=nai keleu/santes e)/ste bouleu/sainto, e)qu/_onto ordering them to wait until they had taken counsel, they proceeded to sacrifice ( = e)pimei/nate e)/st' a)\n bouleusw/meqa) 5. 5. 2, e)/docen au)toi=s . . . proi+e/nai . . ., e(/ws *ku/_rw| summei/ceian they resolved to keep advancing until they should join Cyrus ( = proi+/wmen e(/ws a)\n summei/cwmen) 2. 1. 2.

## TEMPORAL CLAUSES IN GENERIC SENTENCES

§2409
If the leading verb denotes a repeated or customary action or a general truth, a temporal clause takes the subjunctive with a)/n after primary tenses, the optative after secondary tenses. The negative is mh/. Cp. 2336.
a. A present tense denotes action continuing (not completed) and is of the same time as that of the leading verb; an aorist tense denotes action simply occurring (completed) and time usually antecedent to that of the leading verb when the action of the dependent clause takes place before the action of the main clause. In clauses of contemporaneous action the aorist denotes the same time as that of the main verb; in clauses of subsequent action, time later than that of the main verb.
b. w(s is rare in these temporal clauses (
Hdt. 1.17, 4. 172; o(/kws with the optative occurs in 1. 17, 1. 68).
c. On Homeric similes with w(s o(/te, w(s o(po/te, see 2486.

§2410
In temporal sentences of indefinite frequency the temporal clause has the subjunctive with a)/n when the principal clause has the present indicative, or any other tense denoting a present customary or repeated action or a general truth. Cp. 2337.
maino/meqa pa/ntes o(po/tan o)rgizw/meqa we are all mad whenever we are angry Philemon 184, fwnh/ tis, h(/, o(/tan ge/nhtai, a)ei\ a)potre/pei me a kind of voice which, whenever it comes, always deters me
P. A. 31d, o(/tan speu/dh| tis au)to/s, xw( qeo\s suna/ptetai whenever a man is eager himself, God too works with him
A. Pers. 742,

e(/ws a)\n sw/|zhtai to\ ska/fos . . ., xrh\ kai\ nau/thn kai\ kubernh/thn . . . proqu/_mous ei)=nai . . ., e)peida\n d' h( qa/latta u(pe/rsxh|, ma/taios h( spoudh/ as long as the vessel remains in safety, both sailor and pilot should exert themselves; but when the sea has overwhelmed it, their efforts are fruitless
D. 9.69,

poiou=men tau=q' e(ka/stoq' . . . e(/ws a)\n au)to\n e)mba/lwmen e)s kako/n we do this on each occasion until we plunge him into misfortune
Ar. Nub. 1458.

§2411
The verb of the main clause may stand in the participle, or in other tenses than the present indicative: kai/per tw=n a)nqrw/pwn, e)n w(=| me\n a)\n polemw=si, to\n paro/nta (po/lemon)

a)ei\ me/giston kri_no/ntwn although men always consider the present war the greatest so long as they are engaged in it
T. 1.21, o(/tan d' e(te/rw| tau=ta paradw=|, katale/luke th\n au)to\s au(tou= dunastei/a_n but whenever he surrenders these rights to another, he destroys once and for all his own sovereignty
Aes. 3.233,

pole/mioi . . . h)/dh o(/tan . . . katadoulw/swntai/ tinas, pollou\s dh\ belti/_ous h)na/gkasan ei)=nai enemies ere now have forced improvement upon those whom they have enslaved
X. O. 1.23 (cp. 2338), polla/kis e)qau/masa th=s to/lmhs tw=n lego/ntwn u(pe\r au)tou=, plh\n o(/tan e)nqu_mhqw= ktl. I have often marvelled at the effrontery of the speakers in his behalf, except when (ever) I consider, etc.
L. 12.41.

§2412

a)/n (ke/) is frequently omitted in Homer, and occasionally in lyric and dramatic poetry and in Herodotus, e.g.

e)pei\ d' a(ma/rth|, kei=nos ou)ke/t' e)/st' a)nh\r a)/boulos but whenever a man commits an error, that man is no longer heedless
S. Ant. 1025.

§2413
The present indicative is very rarely used instead of the subjunctive with a)/n in temporal clauses of indefinite frequency. Thus, peri\ tw=n a)/llwn tw=n a)dikou/ntwn, o(/te (o(/tou conj.) dika/zontai, dei= para\ tw=n kathgo/rwn puqe/sqai with regard to other malefactors, one has to learn during their trial (lit. when they are tried) from the accusers
L. 22.22. Cp. 2342.

§2414
In temporal sentences of indefinite frequency the temporal clause has the optative when the principal clause has the imperfect or any other tense denoting a past customary or repeated action.
e)qh/reuen a)po\ i(/ppou o(po/te gumna/sai bou/loito e(auto/n he was wont to hunt on horseback, whenever he wanted to exercise himself
X. A. 1.2.7,

o(po/te w(/ra_ ei)/h a)_ri/stou, a)ne/menen au)tou\s e)/ste e)mfa/goie/n ti whenever it was breakfast time, he used to wait until they had eaten something
X. C. 8.1.44, perieme/nomen e(ka/stote e(/ws a)noixqei/h to\ desmwth/rion: e)peidh\ de\ a)noixqei/h, ei)sh=|men we used to wait about on each occasion until the prison was opened; but when (ever) it was opened, we used to go in
P. Ph. 59d. Observe that a)noixqei/h marks a repeated past action (until it was regularly opened) and represents the thought of the subject (until it should be opened, cf. 2420; i.e. direct = e(/ws a)\n a)noixqh=|).

§2415
The optative is rare after a primary tense, and occurs only when that tense includes a reference to the past (
w 254; cp. 2573).—o(/te ken with the optative occurs once (I 525).

§2416
Other tenses than the imperfect in the principal clause: a)ll' o(/te dh\ . . . a)na_i+/ceien *)odusseu/s, sta/sken, u(pai\ de\ i)/deske ktl. (cp. 495) but whenever Odysseus arose, he always kept his position and looked down T 215, o(po/te prosble/yeie/ tinas tw=n e)n tai=s ta/cesin, ei)=pen a)/n ktl. whenever he looked toward any of the men in the ranks, he would say, etc.
X. C. 7.1.10. Cp. 2341.

§2417
The indicative (cp. 2342) is rare in temporal clauses of past indefinite frequency, as

kai\ h)=|don kai\ e)xo/reuon o(po/te oi( pole/mioi au)tou\s o)/yesqai e)/mellon they both sang and danced whenever the enemy were likely to look at them
X. A. 4.7.16. So with o(sa/kis referring to particular events of repeated occurrence, as o(sa/kis kexorh/ghke . . . neni/_khke as often as he has been choregus, he has gained a victory
X. M. 3.4.3.

## TEMPORAL CLAUSES DENOTING PURPOSE

§2418
Temporal conjunctions denoting limit as to duration (so long as, while) or limit as to termination (until, till) may imply purpose.
a. So e(/ws till, against the time when, in order that, pri/n before, in order that not. o)/fra (poet.) is usually final (in order that) rather than temporal (so long as, while, till, up to the time that). Sometimes in post-Homeric Greek e(/ws and the subjunctive (with or without a)/n) has a touch of purpose.

§2419
In the Odyssey e(/ws, usually with the aorist optative after a secondary tense, is almost a final conjunction. Thus, dw=ken . . . e)/laion ei(/ws xutlw/saito she gave olive oil that (against the time when) she might anoint herself
z 79. So
d 799,
e 385,
t 367. In
i 375 the present optative expresses durative action (qermai/noito gradually get hot).

§2420
After a secondary tense e(/ws with the aorist optative sometimes in Attic prose implies an expectation, hope, or purpose on the part of the subject of the main verb that the action of the temporal clause may be attained. Since such optatives are due to the principle of indirect discourse, the subjunctive with a)/n, denoting mere futurity, might have been used instead.
sponda\_s e)poih/santo e(/ws a)paggelqei/h ta\ lexqe/nta they made a truce (which they hoped would last) until the terms should be announced
X. H. 3.2.20 (here we might have had e(/ws a)\n a)paggelqh=|), ta\ a)/lla xwri/a ei)=xon me/nontes e(/ws sfi/si ka)_kei=noi poih/seian ( = a)\n poih/swsi) ta\ ei)rhme/na they retained the other places, waiting until they (the Lacedaemonians) on their part should have performed for them (the Athenians) what had been agreed on
T. 5.35. Compare e(/ws a)\n tau=ta diapra/_cwntai fulakh\n . . . kate/lipe he left a garrison (to remain there) until they should settle these matters
X. H. 5.3.25 (here e(/ws diapra/_cainto might have been used). Other examples are
L. 13.25,
Is. 1.10, 7. 8 (e(/ws ou(=?),
X. H. 4.4.9,
D. 27.5, 29. 43 (te/ws), 33. 8; cp. also
Ar. Eq. 133. Present optative in
T. 3.102,
X. H. 5.4.37.

§2421

e(/ws a)/n with the optative occurs rarely where it might be thought that the simple optative or a)/n with the subjunctive should be used. Many editors emend, but a)/n may generally be defended as potential, expressing the conviction of the agent. Thus, ei(/lesqe a)/ndras ei)/kosi: tou/tous de\ e)pimelei=sqai th=s po/lews, e(/ws a)\n oi( no/moi teqei=en you elected twenty men whose duty it should be to care for the State until such a time as in all probability the laws would be made
And. 1.81. Cp.
S. Tr. 687, I.17, 15,
P. Ph. 101d. So o(/tan
A. Pers. 450, pri\n a)/n
X. H. 2.3.48,2.4.18.

## SUMMARY OF THE CONSTRUCTIONS OF e(/ws AND OF OTHER WORDS MEANING BOTH SO LONG AS AND UNTIL

e(/ws so long as, while: Temporal Limit as to Duration (during the time when）

§2422

Indicative, when the action of the temporal clause denotes definite duration in the present or past. The present often connotes cause (while, now that, because). The imperfect is used of past action: the main clause has the imperfect usually, but the aorist occurs (
T. 5.60).

§2423

Subjunctive (present) with a)/n, when the action lies in the
a. Future, and the verb of the main clause is future indicative or an equivalent form.
b. Present, and the verb of the main clause states a present customary or repeated action or a general truth.

§2424
The present optative (of future time) is very rare: in dependence on a past tense (
X. H. 5.4.37, Aristotle, Athen. Pol. 28 end); by regular assimilation (2186 b) in a less vivid condition (
P. Th. 155a).

e(/ws until, till: Temporal Limit as to Termination (up to the time when）

§2425

Indicative, of a definite present or past action. The present connotes cause. The aorist is normally used of past action: the main verb is usually imperfect, but the aorist occurs (
I. 17.12).
a. Of a future action the future is very rare:
X. C. 7.5.39 (e)s o(/
Hdt. 9.58).

§2426

Subjunctive with a)/n, when the action lies in the
a. Future, and the main clause contains a verb referring to the future (except the optative without a)/n). The tense is usually the aorist: the present marks overlapping.
b. Present, and the verb of the main clause states a present customary or repeated action or a general truth.

§2427

Optative (usually aorist), when the action lies in the
a. Future, and depends on an optative with a)/n.
b. Past, and depends on a secondary tense expressing or implying indirect discourse. Here the optative represents a)/n with the subjunctive after a primary tense.
c. Past, and the verb of the main clause states a past customary or repeated action.
N.—The present optative in b is rare; the future optative occurs only in
X. H. 4.4.9, where some read the aorist.

§2428
Conjunctions meaning until may have, as an implied or expressed antecedent, me/xri tou/tou up to the time. Thus, me/xri tou/tou *la_sqe/nhs fi/los w)noma/zeto, e(/ws prou)/dwken )/ *olunqon Lasthenes was called a friend (up to the time when) until he betrayed Olynthus
D. 18.48.

§2429
With conjunctions meaning until, when the principal clause is affirmative, it is implied that the action of the verb of the principal clause continues only up to the time when the action of the verb of the until clause takes place. Thus, in the passage cited in 2428, it is implied that Lasthenes ceased to be called a friend after he had betrayed Olynthus.
a. When the principal clause is negative, it is implied that the action of the verb of the principal clause does not take place until the action of the until clause takes place; as in

ou) pro/teron e)pau/santo e(/ws th\n po/lin ei)s sta/seis kate/sthsan they did not stop until they divided the city into factions
L. 25.26. In sentences like dei= mh\ perime/nein e(/ws a)\n e)pistw=sin we must not wait until they are upon us (
I. 4.165), by reason of the meaning of perime/nein the action of the principal clause ceases before the action of the until clause takes place.

## GENERAL RULE FOR pri/n BEFORE, UNTIL

§2430

pri/n is construed like other conjunctions meaning until except that it takes the infinitive as well as the indicative, subjunctive, and optative.

§2431
After an affirmative clause pri/n usually takes the infinitive and means before.

§2432
After a negative clause pri/n means until, and usually takes the indicative (of definite time), the subjunctive or optative (of indefinite time).
a. The subjunctive or optative is never used with pri/n unless the principal clause is negative.
b. When the principal clause is negative, pri/n is construed like e(/ws and other words for until (ou) pri/n = e(/ws).

§2433
When the principal clause is affirmative, the clause with pri/n simply adds a closer definition of the time. When the principal clause is negative, pri/n defines the time as before, but the closer definition serves also as a condition that must be realized before the action of the principal clause can be realized. Thus,

mh\ a)pe/lqhte pri\n a)\n a)kou/shte do not go away until you hear
X. A. 5.7.12 (i.e. without hearing = e)a\_n mh\ a)kou/shte). Cp. ou)/te ga\r ei)rh/nhn oi(=o/n te bebai/a_n a)gagei=n, h)\n mh\ koinh=| toi=s barba/rois polemh/swmen, ou)/q' o(monoh=sai tou\s *(/ellhnas, p r i\ n a)\n . . . tou\s kindu/_nous pro\s tou\s au)tou\s poihsw/meqa neither is it possible to make a lasting peace unless we war in common against the barbarians, nor can the Greeks attain unanimity of sentiment until we encounter our perils in the front of the same enemies
I. 4.173.

§2434

pri/n is used with the aorist or (less often) with the imperfect indicative only when pri/n is equivalent to e(/ws until; but, when the verb of the main clause is negatived, pri/n may be translated by before or until. When pri/n must be rendered by before, it takes the infinitive.
tau=ta e)poi/oun pri\n *swkra/ths a)fi/_keto I was doing this until Socrates arrived (rare even in poetry; cp. 2441 c).
ou) tau=ta e)poi/oun pri\n *swkra/ths a)fi/_keto I was not doing this until (or before) Socrates arrived.
tau=ta e)poi/oun pri\n *swkra/thn a)fike/sqai (not *swkra/ths a)fi/_keto) I was doing this before Socrates arrived.

§2435
It is correct to say ou) poih/sw tou=to pri\n a)\n keleu/sh|s, poih/sw (or ou) poih/sw) tou=to pri\n keleu=sai, but incorrect to say poih/sw tou=to pri\n a)\n keleu/sh|s.

§2436
The action of an infinitive introduced by pri/n before may or may not (according to the sense) actually take place at some time later than the action of the leading verb. The clause with pri/n signifies merely that the action of the infinitive had not taken place at the time of the leading verb.

§2437
The clause with pri/n may precede or follow the correlated clause. Cp. 2455.

§2438

pri/n is originally a comparative adverb meaning before, i.e. sooner or formerly; and seems to be connected with pro/, pro/teron before. The adverbial force survives in Attic only after the article, as

e)n toi=s pri\n lo/gois in the foregoing statements
T. 2.62. The adverbial and original use appears also in Homer wherever pri/n occurs with the indicative, the anticipatory (futural) subjunctive (1810), or the optative with ke/. Thus, th\n d' e)gw\ ou) lu/_sw: pri/n min kai\ gh=ras e(/peisin but her I will not release; sooner shall old age come upon her A 29, ou)de/ min a)nsth/seis: pri\n kai\ kako\n a)/llo pa/qh|sqa nor shalt thou recall him to life; sooner (before this) thou wilt suffer yet another affliction
*w 551.—From this early coördination was developed the construction of the conjunction pri/n with the finite moods; but in general only after Homer, who never uses the indicative, and the optative only once (
*f 580), with pri/n. The required sense was given by e(/ws or pri/n g' o(/te dh/. A finite mood was first used of the future, and after negative clauses (ou) pro/teron pri/n like ou) pro/teron e(/ws).—Homer commonly uses the infinitive with pri/n meaning before and until. Here the infinitive (as with w(/ste) simply states the abstract verbal notion, and thus has no reference to differences of time or mood; pri/n being used almost like pro/ before as pri\n i)dei=n = pro\ tou= i)dei=n before seeing (first in Xenophon). This early use with the infinitive was, with some restrictions, retained in Attic, where the infinitive may sometimes be used instead of the finite verb. pri/n came more and more to take the subjunctive with a)/n and to assume conditional relations (cp. 2433); while the use with the infinitive was more and more confined to cases where the leading verb was affirmative.

§2439
The comparative idea in pri/n explains its negative force: an event A happened before another event B, i.e. A occurred when B had not yet (ou)/pw) occurred. Because of its negative force pri/n commonly takes the aorist in all the moods. The aorist has an affinity for the negative because it marks simple and total negation of an action regarded in its mere occurrence; whereas the imperfect with a negative denotes resistance or refusal (1896) in respect of an action regarded as continuing. When pri/n takes the present in any mood the actions of the correlated clauses usually overlap. The present occurs chiefly in the prose writers of the fourth century.

§2440

pro/teron or pro/sqen may be used in the principal clause as a forerunner of pri/n. Examples in 2441, 2444, 2445.
a. Homer has pri\n . . . pri/n B 348. Attic has also fqa/nw . . . pri/n, as

fqh/sontai pleu/santes pri\n th\n cumfora\_n *xi/ous ai)sqe/sqai they will succeed in making their voyage before the Chians hear of the disaster
T. 8.12.

## pri/n WITH THE INDICATIVE

§2441

pri/n in Attic prose takes the indicative of a definite past action when the verb of the principal clause is negative or implies a negative, rarely when it is affirmative.

ou)/te to/te *ku/_rw| i)e/nai h)/qele pri\n h( gunh\ au)to\n e)/peise nor was he willing then to enter into relations with Cyrus until his wife persuaded him
X. A. 1.2.26,

ou) pro/teron e)pau/santo pri\n to/n te pate/r' e)k tou= stratope/dou metepe/myanto kai\ tw=n fi/lwn au)tou= tou\s me\n a)pe/kteinan, tou\s d' e)k th=s po/lews e)ce/balon they did not stop until they sent for his father from the camp, put some of his friends to death and expelled others from the city
I. 16.8,

ou) pro/sqen e)pau/santo pri\n e)cepolio/rkhsan to\n *)/olouron they did not cease from hostilities until they had captured Olurus by siege
X. H. 7.4.18, ou)d' w(\s . . . h)ci/wsan new/tero/n ti poiei=n e)s au)to/n . . . pri/n ge dh\ . . . a)nh\r *)argi/lios mhnu_th\s gi/gnetai (historical present = aorist) not even under these circumstances did they think it right to take any severe measures against him, until finally a man of Argilus turned informer
T. 1.132.
a. The tense in the pri/n clause is usually the aorist (the tense of negation, 2439, and of prior action); rarely the imperfect (of contemporaneous, overlapping action), as
D. 9.61. The historical present is also used as an equivalent of the aorist. The principal clause usually has a secondary tense of the indicative. pri/n with the indicative is not common until Herodotus and the Attic writers.
b. The verb of the principal clause may be virtually negative, as tou\s . . . *)aqhnai/ous lanqa/nousi pri\n dh\ th=| *dh/lw| e)/sxon they escaped the notice of the Athenians (i.e. ou)x o(rw=ntai) until they reached Delos
T. 3.29. Cp.
T. 3.104,
X. A. 2.5.33. Observe that ou) pau/omai (2441) is not regarded as virtually affirmative.
c. The verb of the principal clause is affirmative in prose only in
T. 7.39, 7. 71,
Aes. 1.64. In all of these cases the leading verb is an imperfect, which emphasizes the continuation of the action up to the point of time expressed by the pri/n clause.
d. The use in Herodotus is the same as in Attic prose. Homer has the indicative (after affirmative or negative clauses) only with pri/n g' o(/te until. In the drama pri/n with the indicative is rare. Euripides uses it only after affirmative clauses. When pri/n is = e(/ws it often takes dh/.

§2442
A pri/n clause, depending on a past tense denoting non-fulfilment, itself denotes non-fulfilment and takes a past indicative by assimilation (2185 b).
xrh=n toi/nun *lepti/nhn mh\ pro/teron tiqe/nai to\n e(autou= no/mon pri\n tou=ton e)/lu_se Leptines ought not then to have proposed his own law until (before) he had repealed this
D. 20.96. Cp. 2455 b.

## pri/n WITH THE SUBJUNCTIVE

§2443

pri/n with the subjunctive and a)/n refers to the future or to general present time.

§2444
(I) pri/n takes the subjunctive with a)/n to denote a future action anticipated by the subject of the leading verb. The principal clause is negative, and contains any verb referring to the future except the simple optative.

ou) pro/teron kakw=n pau/sontai ai( po/leis pri\n a)\n e)n au)tai=s oi( filo/sofoi a)/rcwsin States will not cease from evil until philosophers become rulers in them
P. R. 487e, mh\ a)pe/lqhte pri\n a)\n a)kou/shte do not go away until you hear (shall have heard)
X. A. 5.7.12, ou) xrh/ m' e)nqe/nde a)pelqei=n pri\n a)\n dw= di/khn I must not depart hence until I have suffered punishment 5. 7. 5,

mhde/na fi/lon poiou= pri\n a)\n e)ceta/sh|s pw=s ke/xrhtai toi=s pro/teron fi/lois make no one your friend until you have inquired how he has treated his former friends
I. 1.24, mh/ pot' e)painh/sh|s pri\n a)\n ei)dh=|s a)/ndra safhne/ws never praise a man until you have come to know him well Theognis 963. Observe that the last two examples contain a general truth.
a. The aorist subjunctive is usual (the tense of negation, 2439, and of action prior to that of the principal clause); much less common is the present subjunctive (usually of contemporaneous, overlapping action) as
X. C. 2.2.8 (2446).
b. Homer does not use ke/ or a)/n in this construction since pri/n is here adverbial and its clause is simply coördinated. But Hom. has pri/n g' o(/t' a)/n. The subjunctive without a)/n occurs occasionally as an archaism in Hdt. and the dramatic poets. In Attic prose especially in Thuc. (e.g. 6. 10, 29, 38); but a)/n is often inserted by editors.
c. The leading verb is rarely the optative with a)/n (as a form of future expression): ou)k a)\n a)pe/lqoimi pri\n panta/pa_sin h( a)gora\_ luqh=| (cp. b) I will not go away until the market is entirely over
X. O. 12.1.

§2445
(II) After a negative clause of present time that expresses a customary or repeated action or a general truth, pri/n takes the subjunctive with a)/n.
ou) pro/teron pau/ontai pri\n a)\n pei/swsin ou(\s h)di/khsan they do not cease to endure until they have won over those whom they have wronged
P. Ph. 114b.
a. The leading verb may stand in another tense than the present indicative, as ou)dei\s pw/pote e)pe/qeto (empiric aorist, 1930)

pro/teron dh/mou katalu/sei pri\n a)\n mei=zon tw=n dikasthri/wn i)sxu/_sh| no one has ever attempted the subversion of the people until he became superior to the courts of justice
Aes. 3.235.

§2446
After a secondary tense in actual or implied indirect discourse, pri/n with the subjunctive and a)/n is common instead of the optative without a)/n (2449).

ei)=pon mhde/na tw=n o)/pisqen ki_nei=sqai pri\n a)\n o( pro/sqen h(gh=tai I ordered that none in the rear should move until the one before him led the way
X. C. 2.2.8 (here pri\n h(goi=to is possible).

§2447
The principal clause may be affirmative in form, but virtually negative.
ai)sxro\n ( = ou) kalo\n or ou) dei=n) d' h(gou=mai pro/teron pau/sasqai pri\n a)\n u(_mei=s peri\ au)tw=n o(/ ti a)\n bou/lhsqe yhfi/shsqe I consider it base (i.e. I do not consider it to be honourable) to stop until you have voted what you wish
L. 22.4. Cf. Thuc. 6. 38,
D. 38.24, E. Heracl. 179.

## pri/n WITH THE OPTATIVE

§2448

pri/n with the optative is used only in indirect discourse or by assimilation to another optative.

§2449
(I) The optative without a)/n follows pri/n to denote an action anticipated in the past when the principal clause is negative and its verb is in a secondary tense. The optative is here in indirect discourse (actual or implied) and represents a)/n with the subjunctive, which is often retained (2446). Cp. 2420.

a)phgo/reue mhde/na ba/llein pri\n *ku=ros e)mplhsqei/h qhrw=n he forbade any one to shoot until Cyrus should have had his fill of hunting
X. C. 1.4.14 ( = mhdei\s balle/tw pri\n a)\n *ku=ros e)mplhsqh=|), oi( *)hlei=oi . . . e)/peiqon (au)tou\s)

mh\ poiei=sqai ma/xhn pri\n oi( *qhbai=oi parage/nointo the Eleans persuaded them not to engage in battle until the Thebans should have come up
X. H. 6.5.19 ( = mh\ poiei=te ma/xhn pri\n a)\n parage/nwntai).
a. In indirect discourse the infinitive is preferred (2455 d).

§2450
(II) By assimilation of mood, pri/n may take the optative when the negative principal clause has the optative. Cp. 2186 b.
ei) e(/lkoi tis au)to/n . . . kai\ mh\ a)nei/h pri\n e)celku/_seien e)s to\ tou= h(li/ou fw=s ktl. if one should drag him and not let him go until he had dragged him out into the sunlight, etc.
P. R. 515e.

§2451
The optative with pri/n in clauses of customary or repeated action seems not to be used.

§2452

pri\n a)/n with the optative is rare and suspected (cp. 2421).

## pri/n WITH THE INFINITIVE

§2453

pri/n takes the infinitive in Attic especially when the principal clause is affirmative. The infinitive must be used, even with negative clauses, when pri/n must mean only before (and not until).
a. The infinitive is obligatory in Attic when the action of the pri/n clause does not take place or is not to take place (cp. w(/ste mh/ with the infinitive).
b. The infinitive takes the accusative when its subject is different from that of the principal clause.
c. The usual tense is the aorist, the tense of negation (2439) and of the simple occurrence of the action. Less frequent is the present (chiefly in Xenophon), of action continuing, repeated, or attempted (before undertaking to, before proceeding to). The perfect, of action completed with permanent result, is rare.

oi( kai\ pri\n e)me\ ei)pei=n o(tiou=n ei)do/tes who know even before I say anything at all
D. 18.50,

su/niste me\n kai\ pri\n e)me\ le/gein you know as well as I do even before I proceed to set forth in detail the matter of my speech
Aes. 1.116, a)petra/ponto e)s th\n po/lin pri\n u(perbai/nein they turned back to the city before they attempted to scale the wall
T. 3.24.

§2454
When the principal clause is affirmative, pri/n before regularly takes the infinitive.

e)pi\ to\ a)/kron a)nabai/nei *xeiri/sofos pri/n tinas ai)sqe/sqai tw=n polemi/wn Chirisophus ascended the height before any of the enemy perceived him
X. A. 4.1.7, pri\n katalu=sai to\ stra/teuma pro\s a)/_riston basileu\s e)fa/nh before the army halted for breakfast, the king appeared 1. 10. 19, pe/mya_s, pri\n e)n *tege/a| au)to\s ei)=nai, pro\s to\n a)/rxonta tw=n ce/nwn, e)ke/leue ktl. lit. before he himself arrived at Tegea, sending to the commander of the mercenaries, he gave orders, etc.
X. H. 5.4.37 (au)to/s, by attraction to the subject of pe/mya_s).

§2455
When the main clause is negative, pri/n sometimes takes the infinitive in Attic, and generally means before, rarely until. When before and after are contrasted, until is out of place, and the pri/n clause often precedes.
a. In reference to present or past time:

pri\n w(s *)/ afobon e)lqei=n mi/an h(me/ra_n ou)k e)xh/reusen before she came to Aphobus she was not a widow a single day
D. 30.33, pri\n me\n tou=to pra=cai *lewkra/thn a)/dhlon h)=n o(poi=oi/ tines e)tu/gxanon, nu=n de/ ktl. before Leocrates did this, it was uncertain what sort of men they were; but now, etc. Lyc. 135,

pri\n a)na/gesqai/ me ei)s th\n *ai)=non . . . ou)dei\s h)|tia/_sato/ me before I proceeded to set sail for Aenus no one accused me
Ant. 5.25.
b. In reference to action unfulfilled: ou(\s (lo/gous)

ei)/ tis e)pe/deicen au)toi=s pri\n e)me\ dialexqh=nai peri\ au)tw=n, ou)k e)/stin o(/pws ou)k a)\n . . . dusko/lws pro\s se\ diete/qhsan and if any one had shown these words to them before I discussed them, it is inevitable that they would have been discontented with you
I. 12.250.
c. In reference to future time:

ou)x oi(=o/n t' e)sti\n ai)sqe/sqai pri\n kakw=s tinas paqei=n u(p' au)tw=n it is not possible to perceive this before some suffer injury at their hands
I. 20.14,

kai/ moi mh\ qorubh/sh| mhdei\s pri\n a)kou=sai and let no one raise a disturbance before he hears
D. 5.15 (cp. o(/pws mh\ qorubh/sei mhdei\s pri\n a)\n a(/panta ei)/pw D. 13, 14).
N.—With verbs of fearing, the positive being the thing dreaded; as de/doika mh\ pri\n po/nois u(perba/lh| me gh=ras pri\n sa\_n xari/essan prosidei=n w(/ra_n I fear lest old age overcome me with its troubles before I live to behold thy gracious beauty E. fr. 453.
d. Infinitive instead of the optative after a leading verb in a secondary tense:

i(_ke/teuon mhdamw=s a)potre/pesqai pri\n e)mbalei=n ei)s th\n tw=n *lakedaimoni/wn xw/ra_n they entreated them by no means to turn aside until they should invade the territory of the Lacedaemonians
X. H. 6.5.23 (here the optative might stand in indirect discourse to represent the subjunctive with a)/n), ou)/t' au)to/s pote pri\n i(drw=sai dei=pnon h(|rei=to neither was he ever accustomed to take his supper until he got into a sweat by exercise
X. C. 8.1.38 (for i(drw/seie, see 2451).
e. Infinitive after an optative with a)/n in a principal clause: ei)/ ti/s tina mhxanh\n e)/xoi pro\s tou=to . . ., ou)k a)/n pote le/gwn a)pei/poi to\ toiou=ton pri\n e)pi\ te/los e)lqei=n; if ever any lawgiver should have any plan for this, would he ever be weary of discussing such a scheme until he reached the end?
P. L. 769e. Here the subjunctive with a)/n is permitted.

§2456
The lyric poets and Herodotus use pri/n with the infinitive as it is used in Attic prose and poetry. Homer has the infinitive after affirmative or negative clauses alike (before and until), and often where a finite verb would be used in Attic; as nai=e de\ *ph/daion pri\n e)lqei=n ui(=as *)axaiw=n he dwelt in Pedaeon before the sons of the Achaeans came N 172, ou)/ m' a)potre/yeis pri\n xalkw=| maxe/sasqai ( = Attic a)\n maxe/sh|) thou shalt not dissuade me until thou hast fought with the spear
*u 257; often in correspondence with the adverbial pri/n, as ou)de/ tis e)/tlh pri\n pie/ein, pri\n lei=yai nor durst any man (sooner) drink before he had offered a libation H 480.

§2457

h)\ pri/n than before, with a past tense suppressed after h)/, occurs first in Xenophon (C. 5. 2. 36, 7. 5. 77).

## pro/teron h)/, pro/sqen h)/, pri\n h)/, pa/ros

§2458

pro/teron h)/ sooner than, before is used especially in Herodotus and Thucydides. (a) With the indicative:

ou) pro/teron e)ne/dosan h)\ au)toi\ e)n sfi/sin au)toi=s . . . e)sfa/lhsan they did not succumb before they were overthrown by themselves
T. 2.65. (b) With the infinitive: ta\_s d' a)/lla_s po/leis e)/fh a)dikei=n, ai(\ e)s *)aqhnai/ous pro/teron h)\ a)posth=nai a)nh/loun he said the other States were wrong, which, before they revolted, used to pay money into the treasury of the Athenians
T. 8.45. (c) With the subjunctive (without a)/n) rarely (
T. 7.63). Chiefly in Hdt.

§2459
So pro/sqen h)/ sooner than, before: a)pekri/_nato . . . o(/ti pro/sqen a)\n a)poqa/noien h)\ ta\ o(/pla paradoi/hsan he answered that they would die before (sooner than that) they would surrender their arms
X. A. 2.1.10. u(/steron h)/ later than takes, by analogy, the infinitive once in Thuc. (6. 4).

§2460

pri\n h)/ sooner than, before with the infinitive occurs in Homer (only E 288, X 266) and Hdt. (2. 2); and in Hdt. also with the indicative (6. 45) and subjunctive (7. 10 h, without a)/n). pri\n h)/ is rare and suspected in Attic (
X. C. 1.4.23); but is common in late Greek.

§2461

pa/ros before in Homer takes the infinitive (Z 348).

## CLAUSES OF COMPARISON

§2462
Clauses of comparison (as clauses) measure an act or state qualitatively or quantitatively with reference to an act or state in the leading clause.
a. Comparative clauses with h)/ than are used in disjunctive coördinated sentences. See under Particles (2863).

§2463
Comparative clauses of quality or manner are introduced by w(s as, w(/sper, kaqa/per just as, o(/pws, h(=|, o(/ph|, h(=|per as. The principal clause may contain a demonstrative adverb (ou(/tws, w(=de so). w(/sper may be correlated with o( au)to/s.
w(s, etc., are here properly conjunctive relative adverbs of manner, some uses of which fall under conditional relative clauses.
a. Other comparative conjunctive adverbs are w(/ste as (poetic and Ionic), h)u+/te, eu)=te as, like as (Epic). Demonstrative adverbs in Epic are w(/s, tw/s, toi/ws, au)/tws, w(sau/tws.
b. On other uses of w(s, etc., see under Particles (2990 ff.). On w(s, w(/sper with a participle, see 2086, 2087.

§2464
The verb of the comparative clause is commonly omitted if it is the same as the verb of the leading clause. Thus, e)a\_n soi\ cundokh=| w(/sper e)moi/ if it seems good also to you as (it seems) to me
P. Ph. 100c.

§2465
The subject of a comparative clause with w(s or w(/sper, the verb of which is omitted, is often attracted into the case (usually the accusative) of the other member of the comparison. Thus, ou)damou= ga\r e)/stin *)ago/raton *)aqhnai=on ei)=nai w(/sper *qrasu/boulon it is in no wise possible for Agoratus to be an Athenian as Thrasybulus is ( = *qrasu/boulos *)aqhnai=o/s e)sti)
L. 13.72. Attraction into the dative is less common: *ku/_rw| h(/deto . . . w(/sper sku/laki gennai/w| a)nakla/zonti he was delighted with Cyrus, who set up a cry like a young and noble dog ( = sku/lac gennai=os a)nakla/zei)
X. C. 1.4.15.
a. Usually, however, we have the nominative with the verb omitted: pe/peismai/ se ma=llon a)poqanei=n a)\n e(le/sqai h)\ zh=n w(/sper e)gw/ I am persuaded that you would prefer to die rather than live as I live
X. M. 1.6.4.

§2466
Comparative clauses of quality are often fused with the leading clause by the omission of the preposition in the correlated member of the comparison, but only when w(s precedes. Cp. 1673.

§2467
The antecedent clause may contain a wish: ou(/tw (w(/s) . . . w(s (which may be omitted); as ou(/tw ni_kh/saimi/ t' e)gw\ kai\ nomizoi/mhn sofo/s, w(s u(_ma=s h(gou/menos ei)=nai qea_ta\_s deciou\s . . . prw/tous h)ci/ws' a)nageu=s' u(_ma=s as surely as I thought it proper to let you first taste this comedy because I thought you were clever spectators, so surely may I win and be accounted a master
Ar. Nub. 520. Cp. N 825,
Ar. Thesm. 469.

§2468
Comparative clauses of quantity or degree are introduced by o(/sw|, o(/son in proportion as. The principal clause usually contains the corresponding demonstratives tosou/tw|, tosou=ton (to/sw|, to/son are usually poetic).
a. Greek, like Latin, uses the adjective relative pronoun o(/sos (quantus) in the subordinate clause in correlation to tosou=tos agreeing with a substantive. Here English uses the conjunctive adverb as. So with toiou=tos . . . oi(=os.— tosou/tw|, tosou=ton may be followed by w(s, w(/ste.

§2469

tosou=ton . . . o(/son or o(/son . . . tosou=ton denotes that the action of the main clause takes place in the same degree as the action of the subordinate clause. o(/sw| . . . tosou/tw| with a comparative or superlative adjective or adverb is equivalent to the more . . . the more, the less . . . the less.

§2470
The demonstrative antecedent may be omitted, especially when its clause precedes:

kai\ xalepw/teroi e)/sontai o(/sw| new/teroi/ ei)sin and they will be the more severe the younger they are
P. A. 39d.

§2471
One member may contain a comparative, the other a superlative; as o(/sw| ga\r e(toimo/tat' au)tw=| (tw=| lo/gw|)

dokou=men xrh=sqai, tosou/tw| ma=llon a)pistou=si pa/ntes au)tw=| for the more we are thought to excel all others in ability to speak, so much the more do all distrust it
D. 2.12.

§2472

o(/sw| (o(/son) may be used without a comparative or superlative when the correlative clause has a comparative or superlative with or without tosou/tw| (tosou=ton). Thus, w(/sper e)n i(/ppois, ou(/tw kai\ e)n a)nqrw/pois tisi\n e)ggi/gnetai, o(/sw| a)\n e)/kplea ta\ de/onta e)/xwsi, tosou/tw| u(briste/rois ei)=nai as it is in the nature of horses, so it is in the case of certain men: in so far as they have their wants satisfied, the more they are wanton
X. Hi. 10.2. o(/sw| may stand for the logical o(/ti in

tosou/tw| *su/rwn kaki/_wn e)ge/neto, o(/sw| *su/roi e)/fugon he proved himself a greater coward than the Syrians all the more because they fled
X. C. 6.2.19.

§2473
The correlated clauses may be fused when both o(/sw| (o(/son) and tosou/tw| (tosou=ton) are omitted and the predicate of the subordinate clause is a comparative or superlative with a form of ei)=nai. Thus,

e)ndeeste/rois ga\r ou)=si tapeinote/rois au)toi=s oi)/ontai xrh=sqai for the more indigent they are so much the more submissive do they expect to find them
X. Hi. 5.4 ( = o(/sw| e)ndee/steroi/ ei)si, tosou/tw| tapeinote/rois).

## SIMILES AND COMPARISONS

§2481

w(s, w(s ei), w(s ei)/ te as if, w(s o(/te, w(s o(po/te as when are often used in poetry in similes and comparisons.
a. The present and aorist indicative and subjunctive (usually without a)/n) are regularly used. The optative occurs only with w(s ei) or w(s ei)/ te. The verb of the apodosis may sometimes be supplied from the main clause, and the sense may be satisfied in other cases by supplying as happens, as is the case; but as early as Homer the ellipsis was probably unconscious, as it is in English as if, as when. Hence w(s ei), w(s o(/te are scarcely to be distinguished from w(s.
b. The tense of the main clause may be primary or secondary without influence on the construction. Cp. 1935 and 1935 a.

§2482

w(s (w(/s te) is followed by the indicative present (less often aorist) or by the subjunctive. Thus,

w(s de\ path\r ou(= paido\s o)du/_retai o)ste/a kai/wn . . . , w(\s *)axileu\s e(ta/roio o)du/_reto o)ste/a kai/wn and as a father waileth when he burneth the bones of his son, so Achilles wailed as he burned the bones of his comrade
*y 222.

§2483

w(s is common in Homer with the subjunctive (without a)/n) depending on the verb of the introductory clause, which is usually past. The simile may begin with w(s or with a demonstrative (oi( or tou/s) after which w(/s te is placed. Thus, w(s de\ le/wn mh/loisin a)shma/ntoisin e)pelqw/n . . . kaka\ frone/wn e)norou/sh|, w(\s me\n *qrh/ikas a)/ndras e)pw/|xeto *tu_de/os ui(o/s and as a lion, coming on flocks without a shepherd, with evil purpose leaps upon them, so the son of Tydeus attacked the men of Thrace K 485, oi( d', w(/s t' ai)gupioi\ . . . pe/trh| e)f' u(yhlh=| mega/la kla/zonte ma/xwntai, w(\s oi( keklh/gontes e)p' a)llh/loisin o)/rousan and they, like vultures who contend with loud screams on a lofty cliff, even so they rushed screaming against each other II 429. After the subjunctive with w(s or w(s o(/te an independent indicative may follow (M 167, II 296).

§2484

w(s ei), commonly w(s ei)/ te, in Homer is used rarely with the indicative and subjunctive, more frequently with the optative; but usually without any finite verb. Thus, la_oi\ e(/ponq' w(s ei)/ te meta\ kti/lon e(/speto mh=la the soldiers followed as sheep follow after the ram N 492 (the only occurrence in Homer of the indicative), kai/ me fi/lhs' w(s ei)/ te path\r d\n pai=da filh/sh| and he loved me as a father loveth his son I 481 (the only occurrence in Homer of the subjunctive), do/khse d' a)/ra sfi/si qu_mo\s w(\s e)/men, w(s ei) patri/d' i(koi/ato and their feeling seemed to be as (it would be) if they had come to their own country
k 416 (the optative occurs only after a past tense, except
*l 389, a negative present); tw\ de/ oi( o)/sse lampe/sqhn w(s ei)/ te puro\s se/las and his eyes flashed like gleaming fire T 366.

§2485
Attic poetry does not use the Epic and Lyric w(s ei)/ te for w(s ei). In Attic w(s ei) (w(sei/) is practically equivalent to w(s as, like; thus,

a)ll' ou)=n eu)noi/a| g' au)dw=, ma/_thr w(sei/ tis pista/_ but at any rate I speak in good-will at least as some faithful mother
S. El. 234.

§2486

w(s o(/te, w(s o(po/te are used with the indicative (present or aorist) or the subjunctive (as in general conditions). With the subjunctive a)/n is generally absent in Homer; but w(s d' o(/t' a)/n (never ke/n) occurs. The clause with w(s o(/te, w(s o(po/te generally precedes the main clause. w(s o(/te without appreciable difference from w(s in *)erifu/la_n, o(/rkion w(s o(/te pisto/n, do/ntes *oi)klei/da| gunai=ka having given to the son of Oecles Eriphyle to wife, as a sure pledge Pind. Nem. 9. 16.

§2487
A relative pronoun referring to a substantive accompanied by w(/s, w(/ste as often takes the subjunctive (without a)/n). Thus,

o( d' e)n koni/h|si xamai\ pe/sen ai)/geiros w(/s, h(/ r(a/ t' e)n ei(amenh=| e(/leos mega/loio pefu/_kh| lei/h and he fell to the ground amid the dust like a poplar that has grown up smooth in the lowland of a great marsh
*d 483.

## ADJECTIVE CLAUSES (RELATIVE CLAUSES: 2488-2573）

§2488
Relative clauses correspond to attributive adjectives (or participles), since like adjectives they serve to define substantives. Like adjectives, too, they often have the value of substantives and stand in any case.
d\n ga\r qeoi\ filou=sin ( = o( qeofilh/s), a)poqnh/|skei ne/os for whom the gods love, dies young
Men. Sent. 425, h)= qi/gw dh=q' oi(/ m' e)/fu_san; ( = tw=n me fu_sa/ntwn) am I to embrace him who begat me?
E. Ion 560, su\n toi=s qhsauroi=s oi(=s o( path\r kate/lipen ( = toi=s u(po\ tou= patro\s kataleifqei=si) with the treasures which my father left
X. C. 3.1.33, e)n au)toi=s oi(=s e)ti_ma=sqe ( = e)n au)tai=s tai=s ti_mai=s) in the very honours which you received
D. 19.238,

w(=n e)/laben a(/pa_si mete/dwken it shared with all what it received
I. 4.29.

§2489
Relative clauses are introduced by relative pronouns or by relative adverbs of time, place , or manner (cp. 340, 346), and refer to an antecedent expressed or implied in the main clause.
a. Temporal clauses, which are like relative clauses in many respects, have been treated in 2389 ff. On relatives used as indirect interrogatives and as exclamations, see 2668 ff., 2685 ff.

§2490
Many relative clauses are equivalent to coördinate clauses (e.g. 2553). In such cases the relative has the force of a demonstrative or personal pronoun with a connective (kai/, a)lla/, de/, ga/r, ou)=n, a)/ra, etc.). Thus, pw=s ou)=n a)\n e)/noxos ei)/h th=| grafh=|; o(\s ( = ou(=tos ga\r) . . .

fanero\s h)=n qerapeu/wn tou\s qeou/s how then could he be subject to the indictment? For he manifestly worshipped the gods
X. M. 1.2.64. Greek often uses here the demonstrative (contrast tau=ta de\ ei)pw/n with quae cum dixisset).

§2491
A relative must often be resolved into a conjunction and a pronoun (2555).

§2492
A truly subordinate relative clause may precede the main clause or be incorporated into it (2536). The relative clause is often made emphatic by placing after it the main clause with the demonstrative antecedent. Thus, o(/ ti bou/letai, tou=to poiei/tw whatever he wants, that let him do
P. Eu. 285e.

§2493

o(/s who and the other simple relatives (e.g. oi(=os, o(/sos) refer to a particular and individual person or thing.
h)=n tis e)n th=| stratia=| *cenofw=n *)aqhnai=os, o(\s ou)/te strathgo\s ou)/te stratiw/ths w)\n sunhkolou/qei there was in the army one Xenophon, an Athenian, who accompanied it though he was neither general nor soldier
X. A. 3.1.4.
a. On the relation of the relative o(/s to the demonstrative o(/s, see 1113, 1114.
b. o(/s is often used instead of o(/stis (or oi(=os) especially with a)/n or mh/. Cp. 2508. o(/s whoever with the indicative generally adds (in prose) dh/ pote, dh/pot' ou)=n (339 e).

§2494

o(/ (sometimes a(/) at the beginning of a sentence may have the force of as to what (cp. quod), suggesting the matter to which it pertains.

d\ d' e)zh/lwsas h(ma=s, w(s tou\s me\n fi/lous . . . eu)= poiei=n duna/meqa . . ., ou)de\ tau=q' ou(/tws e)/xei as to what excited your envy of us—that we are able to benefit our friends—not even is this as you suppose
X. Hi. 6.12. The postponed antecedent may be omitted (
X. A. 6.1.29).
a. An introductory relative clause with o(/ may stand in apposition to an entire clause that follows. Thus,

o(/ pa/ntwn qaumasto/taton, *swkra/th mequ/onta ou)dei\s pw/pote e(w/ra_ken a)nqrw/pwn what is most wonderful, no one whatsoever ever saw Socrates drunk
P. S. 220a. (So with an infinitive,
I. 14.18.) The main clause, following such a relative clause, may be introduced by o(/ti or ga/r. Thus, d\ me\n pa/ntwn qaumasto/taton a)kou=sai, o(/ti e(\n e(/kaston w(=n e)ph|ne/samen a)po/llu_si th\n yu_xh/n what is most wonderful of all to hear, (that) each one of the things we approved ruins the soul
P. R. 491b. Cp. 994, 995.

§2495

o(/sper the same as (qui quidem) is especially definite and denotes identity (338 c). o(/s ge (quippe qui) is causal (2555 a).

§2496

o(/stis whoever and the other compound relatives (e.g. o(poi=os, o(po/sos) denote a person or thing in general, or mark the class, character, quality, or capacity of a person (less often of a thing).

maka/rios o(/stis ou)si/a_n kai\ nou=n e)/xei happy is the man who possesses property and sense
Men. Sent. 340.
a. After a negative expressed or implied, o(/stis (not o(/s) is used because of its general meaning. So ou)k e)/stin o(/stis, ti/s e)stin o(/stis; ou)dei/s e)stin o(/stis (rarely ou)/tis e)sti\n o(/s), pa=s o(/stis (plural usually pa/ntes o(/soi). Cp. 2557.
b. e)c o(/tou is common for e)c ou(= since. In Ionic (and Thuc. 6. 3) o(/stis is used of a definite object. Cp.
Hdt. 1.7, 2. 99.

§2497

oi(=os of such sort as to, proper for, and o(/sos of such amount as to, enough for, denote result and commonly take the infinitive (negative mh/).
kalo/n te (dokei=) ei)=nai h( e)pisth/mh kai\ oi(=on a)/rxein tou= a)nqrw/pou knowledge seems to be both a noble thing and able to command man P. Prot. 352 c,

o(/son mo/non geu/sasqai e(autw=| katalipw/n leaving himself only enough to taste
X. A. 7.3.22. So oi(=o/s te able to (for toiou=tos oi)=o/s te); thus,
