P. G. 455d.
a. On clauses with oi(=os or o(/sos following a main clause after which we supply a verb of reflection, see 2687.
b. o(/sos is used elliptically in o(/sai h(me/rai (o(shme/rai) daily, o(/sa e)/th yearly.

§2498
Local clauses are introduced by the relative adverbs ou(=, o(/pou, e)/nqa, i(/na (usually poetic, but sometimes in Plato) where, oi(=, o(/poi, e)/nqa whither, o(/qen, o(po/qen, e)/nqen whence, h(=|, o(/ph| which way, where, whither. o(/qi and o(po/qi where are Epic and Lyric, h(=xi where is Epic. e)/nqa and e)/nqen are also demonstratives (there, thence).

§2499
With names of things the relative adverbs e)/nqa, h(=|, o(/qen, oi(=, ou(= are often used instead of the relative pronouns preceded by e)n, ei)s, e)c. Thus, plhsi/on h)=n o( staqmo\s e)/nqa (= ei)s o(\n)

e)/melle katalu/_ein the stopping-place was near where he intended to make a halt
X. A. 1.8.1, e)n tw=| staqmw=| . . . o(/qen (= e)c ou(=) w(rmw=nto at the stopping-place whence they set out 2. 1. 3. A relative adverb may also refer to a personal antecedent, as

katabai/nein pro\s tou\s a)/llous e)/nqa ta\ o(/pla e)/keinto to descend to the others where the armed force was stationed
X. A. 4.2.20.

§2500
On comparative clauses of manner introduced by w(s, w(/sper etc., see 2463 ff.

## CONCORD OF RELATIVE PRONOUNS

§2501
A relative pronoun agrees with its antecedent in gender, number, and person; its case is determined by the construction of the clause in which it stands.
ou(=to/s e)stin o( a)nh\r d\s h)=lqe this is the man who came, au(/th e)sti\n h( gunh\ h)\n e)zhtou=men this is the woman whom we were looking for, labw\n tou\s i(ppe/a_s oi(\ h)=san au)tw=| taking the cavalry which he had, e)/xwn tou\s o(pli(_ta_s w(=n e)strath/gei having the hoplites which he commanded, triw=n qurw=n ou)sw=n, a(\_s e)/dei me dielqei=n there being three doors through which I had to go.
a. If the main clause as a whole is regarded as the antecedent, the relative stands in the neuter singular with or without a demonstrative. Thus,

plei=n e)pi\ *seli_nou=nta pa/_sh| th=| stratia=|, e)f' o(/per ma/lista e)pe/mfqhsan to sail for Selinus with all their force, for which purpose especially they had been sent
T. 6.47.
b. The person of the verb in a relative clause, in which the relative pronoun is the subject, is regularly determined by the person of the antecedent pronoun expressed or implied. Thus,

ou)k oi)=d' o(/stis a)/nqrwpos gege/nhmai I do not know what sort of a person I have become
X. C. 1.4.12, kai\ oi)ki/a_ ge polu\ mei/zwn h( u(_mete/ra_ th=s e)mh=s, oi(/ ge oi)ki/a| xrh=sqe gh=| te kai\ ou)ranw=| and your habitation is much larger than mine since you occupy both heaven and earth as a habitation 5. 2. 15. The third person rarely follows a vocative (P 248).

§2502
Variations from the law of agreement are, in general, the same as in the case of other pronouns (926).
a. The construction according to sense (950, 1013) often occurs, as fi/lon qa/los, d\n te/kon au)th/ my dear child, whom I myself bore X 87; so with collective nouns, as ta\ do/canta plh/qei, oi(/per dika/sousi what is approved by the multitude, who will judge
P. Phae. 260a.
b. A relative in the plural may follow a singular antecedent denoting a whole class: qhsauropoio\s a)nh/r, ou(\s . . . e)painei= to\ plh=qos a man who lays up a store, the class of men which the multitude approves
P. R. 554a. This construction is less common in prose than in poetry; as

h)= ma/la tis qeo\s e)/ndon, oi(\ ou)rano\n eu)ru\n e)/xousin in truth there is within some one of the gods who occupy the wide heaven
t 40.
c. A relative in the singular having a collective force may have its antecedent in the plural; as

tou/tous e)painei=n, d\s a)\n e(kw\n mhde\n kako\n poih=| to commend those who voluntarily do nothing evil
P. Pr. 345d,

w(/|tini e)ntugxa/noien . . . pa/ntas e)/kteinon they slew all whom they met
X. A. 2.5.32. Here o(/s with the indicative is rare.
d. The relative may stand in the neuter, in agreement with the notion implied in the antecedent rather than with the antecedent itself; as dia\ th\n pleoneci/a_n, d\ pa=sa fu/sis diw/kein pe/fu_ken w(s a)gaqo/n for the sake of profit, a thing which every nature is inclined to pursue as a good
P. R. 359c.
e. The relative may agree in gender and number, not with the antecedent but with a following predicate noun. This is common with verbs of naming; as lo/goi mh/n ei)sin e)n e(ka/stois h(mw=n, a(\_s e)lpi/das o)noma/zomen; assuredly there are propositions in each of us which we call hopes?
P. Phil. 40a,

ei)_pen o(/ti . . . diagege/nhtai pra/_ttwn ta\ di/kaia kai\ tw=n a)di/kwn a)pexo/menos, h(/nper nomi/zoi kalli/sthn mele/thn a)pologi/a_s ei)=nai he said that he had continued to do what was just and to refrain from what was unjust, which he thought was the best practice for his defence
X. M. 4.8.4.
f. A relative may agree with a predicate noun when it follows that noun immediately and not its own substantive: kai\ di/kh e)n a)nqrw/pois pw=s ou) kalo/n, o(\ pa/nta h(me/rwke ta\ a)nqrw/pina; and justice among men, how is not that something beautiful, which civilizes all human things?
P. L. 937d.

## THE ANTECEDENT OF RELATIVE CLAUSES

§2503
The demonstrative antecedents of the relative pronouns are commonly: ou(=tos . . . o(/s, toiou=tos . . . oi(=os, tosou=tos . . . o(/sos, thlikou=tos . . . h(li/kos, etc.
a. The antecedent of o(/s is often toiou=tos (1249). The antecedent of o(/s, o(/sper, oi(=os, may be o(/moios, paraplh/sios, i)/sos.

§2504
On comparative clauses of degree with tosou/tw| . . . o(/sw|, etc., see 2468 ff.

§2505

Definite and Indefinite Antecedent.—The antecedent of a relative pronoun or adverb may be definite or indefinite.
a. A definite antecedent refers to a definite or particular person, thing, time, place, or manner. When the antecedent is definite, the relative clause takes any form that occurs in an independent sentence (921); with ou) as the negative, unless the particular construction requires mh/.
b. An indefinite antecedent refers to an indefinite person, thing, time, place, or manner. When the antecedent is indefinite, the relative clause commonly has a conditional force, and, if negative, takes mh/ like the protasis of a conditional sentence.

§2506
In general when the relative clause has the indicative, the antecedent is either definite (negative ou)) or indefinite (negative mh/). When the relative clause has the subjunctive with a)/n or the optative (not in a wish), the antecedent is indefinite (negative mh/).
DEFINITE: tau=ta a(\ bou/letai pra/_ttei he does what he wants (i.e. the particular thing he wants to do). Negative tau=ta a(\ ou) bou/letai pra/_ttei.
INDEFINITE: tau=ta a(/tina bou/letai pra/_ttei he does whatever he wants (i.e. if he wants to do anything, he does it); negative tau=ta a(/tina mh\ bou/letai pra/_ttei. So tau=ta a(/tina a)\n bou/lhtai pra/_ttei whatever he wants to do, that he always does, tau=ta a(/tina bou/loito e)/pra_tte whatever he wanted to do, that he always did, tau=ta a(/tina a)\n bou/lhtai pra/_cei whatever he wants to do, that he will do, tau=ta a(/tina bou/loito, pra/_ttoi a)/n whatever he might want to do, that he would (will) do. In the last four sentences the negative of the relative clause is mh/.

§2507
When the verb of the relative clause stands in the indicative, the distinction between a definite and indefinite antecedent is commonly clear only in negative sentences.
a(\ mh\ oi)=da ou)de\ oi)/omai ei)de/nai whatever I do not know (= ei)/ tina mh\ oi)=da) I do not even think I know
P. A. 21d. Here a(\ ou)k oi)=da would mean the particular things I am ignorant of, and would have no conditional force whatever. So in

ou)k oi)=d': e)f' oi(=s ga\r mh\ fronw= si_ga=n filw= I do not know; for I am wont to be silent in matters which I do not understand
S. O. T. 569.

§2508
When the antecedent is definite, the simple relatives (o(/s, oi(=os, o(/sos, etc.) are used; when indefinite, the compound relatives (o(/stis, o(poi=os, o(po/sos, etc.) are used, but the simple relatives are often employed instead. When the antecedent is indefinite, o(/s usually has the subjunctive with a)/n or the optative; while o(/stis is preferred to o(/s if the verb is indicative (2569).

§2509

Omission of the Antecedent to a Relative.—The demonstrative pronoun antecedent to a relative is often omitted: either when it is in the same case as the relative, or in a different case from the relative. The omission occurs when the antecedent expresses the general idea of person or thing, and often when the relative clause precedes.
e)gw\ de\ kai\ (ou(=toi) w(=n kratw= menou=men but I and those whom I command will remain
X. C. 5.1.26, kalo\n to\ qnh/|skein oi(=s (for tou/tois oi(=s) u(/brin to\ zh=n fe/rei death is sweet to those to whom life brings contumely
Men. Sent. 291, le/gw pa/ntas ei)sfe/rein a)f' o(/swn (for a)po\ tosou/twn o(/sa) e(/kastos e)/xei I say that all must contribute according to the ability of each (from such means as each man has)
D. 2.31.

§2510
In general statements in the subjunctive with a)/n or the indicative, the relative, referring to a person, is often without an antecedent and has the force of ei)/ tis. In such cases the main clause contains a substantive or a neuter adjective with e)sti/ (which is commonly omitted), and the relative is the subject of the sentence or in apposition to it.
sumfora\_ d', d\s a)\n tu/xh| kakh=s gunaiko/s it is a calamity if a man gets a bad wife E. fr. 1056, kai\ tou=to mei=zon th=s a)lhqei/a_s kako/n, o(/stis ta\ mh\ proso/nta ke/kthtai kaka/ and this is a misfortune exceeding the reality, if a man incurs the blame for evils that are not his doing
E. Hel. 271, o(/stis . . . pro\s qew=n kakou=tai, baru/ if a man suffers ill-usage from the gods, it is grievous
E. Hel. 267.
a. The antecedent may be a genitive of quality (1320). Thus, a)po/rwn e)sti\ . . ., oi(/tines e)qe/lousi di' e)piorki/a_s . . . pra/_ttein ti it is the characteristic of men without resources to wish (lit. who wish) to accomplish their purposes by perjury
X. A. 2.5.21 (here e)qe/lein alone might be expected, but oi(/tines e)qe/lousi follows as if a)/poroi/ ei)sin had preceded), tou=to h(gou=mai me/ga tekmh/rion a)/rxontos a)reth=s ei)=nai w(=| a)\n (= e)a/_n tini or au)tw=|) e(ko/ntes e(/pwntai I regard this as striking testimony to the merit of a ruler if men follow one (him) of their own free will
X. O. 4.19.

§2511
The antecedent of a neuter relative is often omitted, leaving the relative with the force of a conjunction. So e)c ou(= and a)f' ou(= since, e)n w(=| while, ei)s <*>(/ till, me/xri (a)/xri) ou(= until. a)nq' w(=n and e)c w(=n because (cp. ou(/neka, o(qou/neka), e)f' w(=|te on condition that (2279).

§2512
A demonstrative adverb may be suppressed: a)/cw u(_ma=s e)/nqa (for e)kei=se e)/nqa) to\ pra=gma e)ge/neto I will bring you to the spot where the affair took place
X. C. 5.4.21, a)poklei/ontes o(/qen (for e)kei=qen o(/qen) a)/n ti labei=n h)=| shutting them out from places whence it may be possible to take anything
X. M. 2.1.16.

§2513

e)/stin o(/stis, ei)si\n oi(/.—The antecedent is omitted in the phrases e)/stin o(/stis (rarely o(/s) there is some one who, somebody, plural ei)si\n oi(/ some (less often e)/stin oi(/), h)=san oi(/ (of the past).
e)/stin ou)=n o(/stis bou/letai u(po\ tw=n suno/ntwn bla/ptesqai; is there then any one who wishes to be harmed by his companions?
P. A. 25d,

ou)/te..e)/stin ou)/t' e)/stai o(/tw| e)gw\ katalei/yw to\n e)mo\n oi)=kon there neither is nor will there be any one to whom I may leave my property
X. C. 5.4.30, ei)si\ de\ kai\ oi(\ . . . feu/gousin some horses too run away
X. Eq. 3.4,

ei)si\ d' au)tw=n ou(\s ou)d' a)\n panta/pa_si diabai/hte and some of them you would not be able even to cross at all
X. A. 2.5.18, h)=san de\ oi(\ kai\ pu=r prose/feron and some brought firebrands too 5. 2. 14, e)/stin o(/tw| . . . plei/w e)pitre/peis h)\ th=| gunaiki/; is there any one to whom you entrust more than to your wife?
X. O. 3.12,

e)/stin oi(/ kai\ e)tu/gxanon kai\ qwra/_kwn kai\ ge/rrwn some hit both the cuirasses and wicker-shields
X. C. 2.3.18. e)/stin oi(/ is not an example of 961, but due to the analogy of e)/stin o(/te (e)ni/ote), e)/stin ou(=, etc.

§2514
The oblique cases of ei)si\n oi(/ there are those who = some (e)/nioi) are regularly formed by e)/stin w(=n, e)/stin oi(=s, e)/stin ou(/s (or ou(/stinas), which are used also of the past and future.

plh\n *)iw/nwn . . . kai\ e)/stin w(=n a)/llwn e)qnw=n except the Ionians and some other nations
T. 3.92, au)xmoi\ e)/sti par' oi(=s mega/loi great droughts among some 1. 23,

e)/sti me\n ou(\s au)tw=n kate/balon some of them they struck down
X. H. 2.4.6,

e)/stin a(\ kai\ poli/smata ei(=len he captured also some towns
T. 1.65.
a. Xenophon also uses h)=n oi(/; thus,

tw=n de\ polemi/wn h)=n ou(\s u(pospo/ndous a)pe/dosan there were some of the enemy whom they restored under a truce
X. H. 7.5.17.

§2515
Here belong certain idiomatic phrases due to the omission of the antecedent: e)/stin ou(= (o(/pou) somewhere, sometimes, e)/stin h(=| in some way, e)/stin o(/te and e)ni/ote (= e)/ni o(/te, cp. 175 b) sometimes, e)/stin o(/pws somehow (in questions = is it possible that?), ou)k e)/stin o(/pws in no way, it is not possible that (lit. there is not how).

e)/sti d' ou(= si_gh\ lo/gou krei/sswn ge/noit' a)/n but sometimes silence may prove better than speech
E. Or. 638, e)/stin o(/te kai\ oi(=s (2514)

be/lti_on teqna/nai h)\ zh=n sometimes and for some people it is better to die than to live
P. Ph. 62a, ou)k e)/sq' o(/pws . . . a)\n h(ma=s e)/ti la/qoi it is not possible that he should elude us again A. Vesp. 212,

ou)k e)/stin o(/pws ou)k e)piqh/setai h(mi=n it is not possible that he will not attack us
X. A. 2.4.3.

§2516

ou)de\n oi(=on (with the inf.) there is nothing like stands for ou)de/n e)sti toiou=ton, oi(=o/n e)sti. Thus,

ou)de\n oi(=on to\ au)to\n e)rwta=n there is nothing like questioning him
P. G. 447c.

§2517

Relative not repeated.—If two or more relative clauses referring to the same antecedent are connected by a copulative conjunction and the second relative would have to stand in a different case from the first, it is either omitted or its place is taken by au)to/s (less frequently by ou(=tos or e)kei=nos) or a personal pronoun. Here, instead of a repeated relative, we have an independent sentence coördinated with the relative clause.
*)ariai=os, o(\n h(mei=s h)qe/lomen basile/a_ kaqista/nai, kai\ (w(=|) e)dw/kamen kai\ (par' ou(=) e)la/bomen pista\ . . . h(ma=s kakw=s poiei=n peira=tai Ariaeus, whom we wished to set up as king, and to whom we gave, and from whom we received pledges, is attempting to injure us
X. A. 3.2.5, pou= dh\ e)kei=no/s e)stin o( a)nh\r d\s suneqh/ra_ h(mi=n kai\ su/ moi ma/la e)do/keis qauma/zein au)to/n; where, pray, is that man who used to hunt with us and whom you seemed to me to admire greatly?
X. C. 3.1.38, kai\ nu=n ti/ xrh\ dra=n; o(/stis e)mfanw=s qeoi=s e)xqai/romai, mi_sei= de/ m' *(ellh/nwn strato/s and now what must I do? Since I (lit. I who) am manifestly hateful to the gods, and the army of the Greeks hates me
S. Aj. 457. Cp. “Whose fan is in His hand, and He shall thoroughly purge His floor.”
a. The relative is sometimes repeated as in English (
X. A. 1.7.3,
T. 2.43. 2, 44. 1).

§2518
If the demonstrative would have to stand in the nominative, it is commonly omitted unless the demands of emphasis require its presence: (te/xnais) a_s e)pisth/ma_s me\n polla/kis prosei/pomen dia\ to\ e)/qos, de/ontai de\ o)no/matos a)/llou arts which we have often called sciences because it is usual to do so, but they require another name
P. R. 533d (here au(=tai, not ai(/, is the subject).

§2519

Preposition not repeated.—A preposition governing a relative pronoun is usually omitted if it stands in the same case as the preceding noun or pronoun before which the preposition has already been used. See 1671.

§2520

Verb omitted.—The verb of a relative clause is often omitted when it belongs also to the main clause.
fi/lous nomi/zous' ou(/sper a)\n po/sis se/qen (nomi/zh| fi/lous) regarding as friends those whom thy husband so regards
E. Med. 1153. Or the verb of the main clause may be omitted: ta\ ga\r a)/lla (e)poi/ei) o(/saper kai\ u(_mei=s e)poiei=te for the rest he did just what you too were doing
X. C. 4.1.3.

§2521
Transition from a relative to an independent clause sometimes occurs.
（i)xqu/wn) ou(\s oi( *su/roi qeou\s e)no/mizon kai\ a)dikei=n ou)k ei)/wn, ou)de\ ta\_s peristera/_s fish which the Syrians regard as gods and which they will not permit to be injured, nor do they permit the doves to be injured
X. A. 1.4.9.

§2522

Attraction.—A relative pronoun is often attracted from its proper case into the case of its antecedent, especially from the accusative into the genitive or dative. A demonstrative pronoun to whose case the relative is attracted, is usually omitted if unemphatic. Cp. “Vengeance is his, or whose he sole appoints:” Milton.
a. Genitive.—a)/cioi th=s e)leuqeri/a_s h(=s (for h(\n)

ke/kthsqe worthy of the freedom which you possess
X. A. 1.7.3, pro\ tw=n kakw=n w(=n (for a(\)

oi)=da instead of the evils which I know
P. A. 29b, a)f' w(=n (for tou/twn a(\)

i)/ste from what you know
D. 19.216, *mh/dwn o(/swn (for o(/sous) e(w/ra_ka . . . o( e)mo\s pa/ppos ka/llistos my grandfather is the handsomest of all the Medes I have seen
X. C. 1.3.2, mh\ u(pokeime/nwn oi(/wn dei= qemeli/wn (for toiou/twn oi(=a dei= u(pokei=sqai) if the foundations were not as they ought to be
X. Eq. 1.2.
b. Dative.—foboi/mhn a)\n tw=| h(gemo/ni w(=| (for d\n)

doi/h e(/pesqai I should fear to follow the leader whom he might give
X. A. 1.3.17, e)painw= se e)f' oi(=s (for e)pi\ tou/tois a(\) le/geis I commend you for what you say 3. 1. 45, oi(=s (for tou/tois a(\)

hu)tuxh/kesan e)n *leu/ktrois ou) metri/ws e)ke/xrhnto they had not used with moderation the success they gained at Leuctra
D. 18.18.

§2523
A relative in the nominative or dative is very rarely attracted. Thus, bla/ptesqai a)f' w(=n (for a)po\ e)kei/nwn a(\)

h(mi=n pareskeu/astai to be harmed by what has been prepared by us
T. 7.67, o)li/goi w(=n (for tou/twn oi(=s)

e)gw\ e)ntetu/xhka a few of those whom I have met with
P. R. 531e.

§2524
The pronouns subject to attraction are o(/s, oi(=os, o(/sos, but not o(/stis (except in 2534). Attraction is not necessary, and takes place only (but not always) when the relative clause is essential to complete the meaning of the antecedent. When the relative clause is added merely as a remark, attraction does not take place. An attracted relative clause virtually has the force of an attributive adjective.

§2525
Predicate nouns follow the case of the relative attracted to an antecedent expressed or omitted (2531 b).

§2526
An omitted antecedent to which the relative has been attracted may afterward be supplied in the main clause. Thus, a)f' w(=n (for a)po\ tou/twn a(\) . . .

prosaitei= kai\ danei/zetai, a)po\ tou/twn dia/gei from what he begs and borrows, from that he lives
D. 8.26.

§2527
Before bou/lei, which with the relative is treated almost like one word (cp. quivis), attraction to various cases from the accusative is rare. Thus, oi(=a tou/twn d\s (for d\n)

bou/lei ei)/rgastai such deeds as any one you please of these has done
P. G. 517a; cp.
P. Crat. 432a, Phil. 43 d.

§2528
Attraction takes place also in the case of relative adverbs; as diekomi/zonto o(/qen (for e)kei=qen oi(=) u(pece/qento pai=das they conveyed their children from the places where (whither) they had deposited them
T. 1.89.

§2529

Case of the Relative with Omitted Antecedent.—When the antecedent is omitted the relative either retains its own case or is attracted.

§2530
When the omitted antecedent is nominative or accusative, the relative retains its own case. Thus, oi(=s ma/lista ta\ paro/nta a)rkei= (ou(=toi)

h(/kista tw=n a)llotri/wn o)re/gontai those who are best satisfied with what they have, covet least what is their neighbour's
X. S. 4. 42, stugw=n me\n h(/ (= e)kei/nhn h(/) m' e)/tikten hating her who bore me
E. Alc. 338.

§2531
When the omitted antecedent is genitive or dative, the relative (if standing in a different case) is usually attracted into the genitive or dative. But a relative in the nominative masculine or feminine (sometimes in the neuter), or a relative depending on a preposition, retains its own case.
a. Genitive: w(=n (for tou/twn oi(=s) e)ntugxa/nw polu\ ma/lista a)/gamai se/ of those whom I meet with, I admire you by far the most
P. Pr. 361e, dhloi=s de\ kai\ e)c w(=n (for e)k tou/twn a(\)

zh=|s you show it also by the life you lead
D. 18.198. But ei)de/nai th\n du/namin (tou/twn) e)f' ou(\s a)\n i)/wsin to discover the strength of those against whom they are to proceed
X. A. 5.1.8. Cp.
E. Ion 560 (in 2488) where oi(/ = tou/twn oi(/).
b. Dative: tou=to d' o(/moio/n e)stin w(=| (for tou/tw| d\)

nu=n dh\ e)le/geto this is like that which was said just now
P. Ph. 69a, e)mme/nomen oi(=s (for tou/tois a(\) w(mologh/samen dikai/ois ou)=sin h)\ ou)/; do we abide by what we agreed was just, or not?
P. Cr. 50a. But dia\ to\ a)nagkai=on au)toi=s ei)=nai diale/gesqai (tou/tois) par' w(=n la/boien to\n misqo/n because it is necessary for them to give lessons to those from whom they expect to receive their fee
X. M. 1.2.6.

§2532
The relatives oi(=os, o(/sos, h(li/kos, o(/stis dh/, o(stisou=n (and some others) and a following nominative with the copula may be attracted to the case of the antecedent. Thus, xarizo/menos toiou/tw| a)ndri\ oi(=os du\ ei)= showing favour to such a man as you are is commonly condensed to xarizo/menos oi(/w| soi a)ndri/ (
X. M. 2.9.3). Here the whole relative clause (with copula omitted) is attracted. The antecedent, if expressed, is often incorporated (2536) in the relative clause.
pro\s a)/ndras tolmhrou\s oi(/ous kai\ *)aqhnai/ous (for oi(=oi kai\ *)aqhnai=oi/ ei)si) to bold men such as the Athenians
T. 7.21, a)ni/sth *)agria=nas . . . kai\ a)/lla o(/sa e)/qnh *paionika/ he called out the Agrianes and all the other Paeonian tribes 2. 96, xeimw=nos o)/ntos

oi(/ou le/geis when the weather is such as you describe
X. A. 5.8.3, a)ne/lamyen oi)ki/a_ . . . o(/tou dh\ e)na/yantos (for e)na/yanto/s tinos o(/stis dh\ h)=n) the house burst into flames, some one or other having set it on fire 5. 2. 24.
a. oi(=os is often attracted with superlatives: o)/ntos pa/gou oi(/ou deinota/tou (for toiou/tou oi(=o/s e)sti deino/tatos) when the frost was tremendous
P. S. 220b. Cp. 1087.
b. The article may appear in this construction with oi(=os and h(li/kos, the relative clause being treated like a substantive:

toi=s oi(/ois h(mi=n to such as we are
X. H. 2.3.25.
c. The subject of the relative clause rarely stands in the nominative, not being attracted along with oi(=os. Thus,

kinai/dous oi(/ousper su/ rascals just like you
Aes. 2.151. This occurs only when the number of the subject is different from that of the attracted relative. When the article precedes, as in *so/lwn e)mi/_sei tou\s oi(=os ou(=tos a)nqrw/pous Solon detested men like him (
D. 19.254), editors generally read tou\s oi(/ous ou(=tos.

§2533

Inverse Attraction.—An antecedent nominative or (oftener) accusative may be attracted to the case of the relative. The attracted antecedent is often prefixed for emphasis to the relative clause, which thus separates it from the verb it governs or by which it is governed. Cp. urbem quam statuo vestra est, and “Him (= he whom) I accuse, By this, the city ports hath enter'd” (Shakespeare), where the antecedent is attracted into the case of the (omitted) relative.
ta/_sde (for ai(/de)

d' a(/_sper ei)sora=|s . . . xwrou=si but the women whom thou seest are coming
S. Tr. 283, poli_tei/a_n (for poli_tei/a_) oi(/a_n ei)=nai xrh/ para\ mo/nois h(mi=n e)stin we alone have an ideal constitution (lit. such as ought to be)
I. 6.48, e)/legon o(/ti *lakedaimo/nioi w(=n de/ontai pa/ntwn (for pa/nta)

pepra_go/tes ei)=en they said that the Lacedaemonians had gained all they asked for
X. H. 1.4.2.
a. The main clause may contain a resumptive demonstrative pronoun; as

to\n a)/ndra tou=ton, d\n pa/lai zhtei=s . . ., ou(=to/s e)stin e)nqa/de this man whom you have long been searching for, this man is here
S. O. T. 449.
b. The rare cases of the inverse attraction of the dative are suspected or admit another explanation (
E. Med. 12,
S. El. 653,
X. Hi. 7.2).
c. So with adverbs: kai\ a)/llose (for a)/lloqi) o(/poi a)\n a)fi/kh| a)gaph/sousi/ de and elsewhere, wherever you go, they will love you
P. Cr. 45c.

§2534

ou)dei\s o(/stis ou) every one (lit. nobody who not) for ou)dei/s e)stin o(/stis ou), commonly shows inverse attraction, is treated like a single pronoun, and inflected ou)deno\s o(/tou ou), ou)deni\ o(/tw| ou), ou)de/na o(/ntina ou).

ou)deno\s o(/tou ou)xi\ a)logw/teron than which there is nothing more irrational
P. Charm. 175c,

ou)deni\ o(/tw| ou)k a)pokri_no/menos replying to every one
P. Men. 70c,

peri\ w(=n ou)de/na ki/ndu_non o(/ntin' ou)x u(pe/meinan oi( pro/gonoi for which our ancestors underwent every danger
D. 18.200.
a. Cp. ou)damw=n *(ellhnikw=n tw=n ou) pollo\n me/zw his power was much greater than any Hellenic power
Hdt. 7.145 (= ou)dama/ e)sti tw=n),

ou)damw=s w(s ou) fh/somen it can in no wise be that we should say no
P. Pol. 308b.

§2535

o(/sos preceded by an Adjective.—Here the subject of the relative clause is identical with that of the main clause, and is omitted together with the copula: xrh/mata e)/labe qaumasta\ o(/sa (for qaumasto/n e)stin o(/sa) he received a wonderful amount of money
P. Hipp. M. 282c, meta\ i(drw=tos qaumastou= o(/sou (for qaumasto/n e)stin meq' o(/sou) with an astonishing amount of sweat
P. R. 350d. So qaumasi/ws w(s (for qaumasto/n e)stin w(s)
P. Ph. 92a.

§2536

Incorporation.—The antecedent taken up into the relative clause is said to be incorporated. The relative and antecedent then stand in the same case, the relative agreeing adjectively with its antecedent. If the antecedent is a substantive, it often stands at the end of the relative clause, and commonly has no article. An antecedent in the nominative or accusative is more frequently incorporated than one in the genitive or dative.

§2537
A nominative, accusative, or vocative antecedent, when incorporated, usually conforms to the case of the relative.
ei) e)/stin, h(\n su\ pro/teron e)/leges a)reth/n, a)lhqh/s (for e)/stin h( a)reth\ a)lhqh/s, h(\n) if the virtue which you were speaking of before, is real
P. G. 503c, ei)s de\ h(\n a)fi/_konto kw/mhn mega/lh h)=n (for h( kw/mh ei)s h(\n) the village at which they arrived was large
X. A. 4.4.2, klu=qi/ meu, d\ xqizo\s qeo\s h)/luqes (for qeo\s d\ or w)= qeo/s) hear me thou that camest yesterday in thy godhead
b 262.
a. An accusative antecedent is incorporated in the accusative when the verb of the relative clause takes the accusative. Thus, ou)k a)pekru/pteto h(\n ei)=xe gnw/mhn (for th\n gnw/mhn h(\n) he did not conceal the opinion he had
X. M. 4.4.1, mhd' . . . a)fe/lhsqe u(_mw=n au)tw=n h(\n dia\ panto\s a)ei\ tou= xro/nou do/can ke/kthsqe kalh/n (for th\n kalh\n do/can h(\n) do not deprive yourselves of the fair fame which you have enjoyed throughout all time
D. 20.142.
b. An accusative antecedent may be incorporated as nominative, genitive, or dative, e.g. ei)/ tina o(rw/|h . . . kataskeua/zonta h(=s a)/rxoi xw/ra_s (for th\n xw/ra_n h(=s a)/rxoi) if ever he saw any one improving the district which he governed
X. A. 1.9.19.

§2538
A genitive or dative antecedent, when incorporated, usually attracts the relative to its own case.
peri\ d' ou(= pro/teron . . . e)/qhke no/mou dielqw/n (for tou= no/mou d\n) dealing in detail with the law which he formerly passed
D. 24.61, e)poreu/eto su\n h(=| ei)=xe duna/mei (for su\n th=| duna/mei h(\n) he advanced with what force he had
X. H. 4.1.23. Even when the antecedent is omitted, the attraction takes place: pro\s w(=| ei)=xe sune/lege . . . stra/teuma (for pro\s tou/tw| tw=| strateu/mati d\) he was collecting an army in addition to that which he had
X. H. 4.1.41.
a. But a genitive or dative antecedent, when incorporated, is attracted into the case of a nominative relative. Thus, e)n dikasthri/ois kai\ o(/soi a)/lloi dhmo/sioi su/llogoi (sc. ei)si/) in courts and all the other public assemblies
P. Phae. 261a (for tosou/tois a)/llois sullo/gois, o(/soi dhmo/sioi/ ei)si).
b. When an antecedent in the genitive or dative is incorporated, the place of the antecedent is usually taken by a demonstrative pronoun in the genitive or dative. Thus,

ou)de/ nu tw=n per me/mnhai, o(/sa dh\ pa/qomen kaka/ nor do you remember all the evils we suffered
*f 441.

## OTHER PECULIARITIES OF RELATIVE CLAUSES

§2539
Appositives to the antecedent may be drawn into the relative clause as the nearest construction or for the sake of emphasis. Thus, eu(rh/sei tou\s . . . dikasta/_s, oi(/per kai\ le/gontai e)kei= dika/zein, *mi/_nws te kai\ *(rada/manqus ktl. he will find the judges, who are said to pronounce judgment there, Minos and Rhadamanthys, etc.
P. A. 41a.

§2540
A substantive, usually with the article, is often taken over into the relative clause, to explain, by a necessary addition, the idea conveyed by that clause; and stands in the same case as the relative. Thus,

ei) manqa/neis o(\ bou/lomai le/gein to\ ei)=dos if you understand the class I wish to describe
P. R. 477c, ou)/te au)toi\ ou)/te ou(/s famen h(mi=n paideute/on ei)=nai tou\s fu/lakas neither ourselves nor the guardians whom we say we must instruct 402 c.

§2541
The antecedent may be reserved for the main clause, which follows the relative clause. Thus,

kaq' ou(\s me\n a)ph/xqhn, ou)k e)/noxo/s ei)mi toi=s no/mois I am not subject to the laws in virtue of which I was arrested
Ant. 5.85.

§2542
An attributive adjective, or an attributive genitive belonging to a substantive standing in the main clause, may be placed either in the relative clause (if either is emphatic) or in the main clause. Two adjectives may be divided between the two clauses. The substantives may remain in the main clause or be transferred to the relative clause. Thus,

to\ tei/xisma d\ h)=n au)to/qi tw=n *sura_kosi/wn ai(rou=si they captured the fort of the Syracusans which was there
T. 7.43,

w(=n e)gw\ h)/qelon tou/tw| tau/thn h(/tis ei)/h megi/sth pi/stis dou=nai of which I was willing to offer to the plaintiff the assurance that was most solemn
D. 52.12, e)pidei=cai . . . th\n dikai/a_n h(/tis e)sti\n a)pologi/a_ to show what the fair line of defence is 19. 203, e)/fri_cen de\ ma/xh . . . e)gxei/h|sin makrh=|s, a(\_s ei)=xon tamesi/xroas and the battle bristled with the long spears, the flesh-piercing spears, which they grasped N 339.
a. From the transference of superlatives to the relative clause arise such expressions as h)/gagon summa/xous o(po/sous plei/stous e)duna/mhn (1087). Similarly w(s ta/xista (scil. du/nasai or the like) as soon as, as soon as possible, e)pei\ (o(/te) ta/xista as soon as.

§2543
A participial or subordinate clause depending on a following main clause may be joined to a preceding clause containing the antecedent of the relative. Thus, e)/fh ei)=nai a)/kron d\ ei) mh/ tis prokatalh/yoito, a)du/naton e)/sesqai parelqei=n he said that there was a height which would be impossible to pass, unless it was seized in advance
X. A. 4.1.25. The case of the relative may be not that required by its own verb, but that of an omitted pronoun dependent on a participle or a subordinate verb inserted in the relative clause. Thus, katalamba/nousi tei=xos . . . o(/ pote *)akarna=nes teixisa/menoi koinw=| dikasthri/w| e)xrw=nto (for w(=| e)xrw=nto teixisa/menoi au)to/) they seized a fortress which the Acarnanians once built and used as a common place of judgment
T. 3.105.

§2544
When the relative clause contains a verb of naming, the main clause is fused with the relative clause. Thus, e)/nqa kalei=tai *)arte/midos te/menos (for e)/nqa te/meno/s e)sti, d\ kalei=tai *)arte/midos) where there is a precinct of Artemis Simonides 107.

## USE OF THE MOODS IN RELATIVE CLAUSES

§2545
The ordinary uses of the moods in relative clauses are as follows:
a. The present and past tenses of the indicative without a)/n express a fact or the assumption of a fact. The future indicative is used to denote purpose, present intention, or an intended result.
b. The indicative with a)/n denotes unreality.
c. The subjunctive with a)/n expresses a possible or supposed fact in future time or a generality in present time. The subjunctive without a)/n is used in indirect questions (1805 b).
d. The optative without a)/n expresses a wish, a possibility less distinctly conceived, or a generality in past time.
e. The optative with a)/n is potential, and is used either in conditional relative clauses with an optative in the main clause, or alone, as

mi/) e)/stin e)lpi/s, h(=| mo/nh| swqei=men a)/n there is one hope by which alone we may be saved
E. Hel. 815.
f. The imperative occurs in relative clauses (1842, 2553).
g. The infinitive occurs in relative clauses in indirect discourse (2631).

## THE USE OF THE MOODS IN CERTAIN RELATIVE CLAUSES

§2546
An extension of the deliberative subjunctive not infrequently occurs in relative clauses after such expressions as ou)k e)/xw, ou)k e)/sti, etc., which usually denote baffled will, the existence of an obstacle to carrying out an act desired by the speaker or some one else. The subjunctive is much less common after the positive e)/xw I have the means. The pronoun or adverb introducing such clause is an interrogative that has taken on the function of a relative.

§2547
The subjunctive here follows primary tenses; the optative follows secondary tenses.
a. ou) tou=to de/doika mh\ ou)k e)/xw o(/ ti dw= e(ka/stw| tw=n fi/lwn . . ., a)lla\ mh\ ou)k e)/xw i(kanou\s oi(=s dw= I do not fear that I shall not have something to give to each of my friends, but that I shall not have enough friends to give to
X. A. 1.7.7, ou)x e(/cousin e)kei=noi o(/poi fu/gwsin they will not have any place whither to escape 2. 4. 20,

ou)ke/t' ei)si\n e)lpi/des o(/poi trapo/menos qa/naton . . . fu/gw I have no longer any hopes to which I may turn and escape death
E. Or. 722,

e(/cei o(/ ti le/gh| he will be able to say something
L. 6.42.
b.

ou)de/na ga\r ei)=xon o(/stis . . . ta\_s e)ma\_s e)pistola\_s pe/myeie for I had no one to bring my letter
E. I. T. 588.
c. Attic never, or rarely, has the positive forms e)/xw o(/ ti a)/n, e)/stin d\s a)/n (K 170), pe/mpw o(/stis a)/n, with the potential optative.

§2548
The subjunctive with ke/ in Homer does not involve will in

ou)k e)/sq' ou(=tos a)nh\r . . . ou)de\ ge/nhtai, o(/s ken *faih/kwn . . . e)s gai=an i(/khtai that man lives not nor will ever be born who shall come to the land of the Phaeacians
z 202; cp.
d 756,
*y 345.
*f 103 involves a different aspect of will from that in 2547 a.

§2549
The deliberative future (1916) occurs in relative clauses; as

o(/pws molou/meq' e)s do/mous ou)k e)/xw I do not know how we are to go home
S. O. C. 1742.
The deliberative subjunctive is more common; as

ou)k e)/xw o(/ ti xrh/swmai toi=s lo/gois I am not able to deal with your argument
P. Eu. 287c.

§2550
In a few cases the future is used like the subjunctives of 2547 a; and may be explained as a dependent deliberative future. Thus, ou) ga/r tis o(/rmos e)/stin, ou)d' o(/poi ple/wn e)cempolh/sei ke/rdos for there is no harbour, nor is there any place to which a man may voyage and sell his wares at a profit
S. Ph. 303,

au)to\n ga/r se dei= promhqe/ws o(/tw| tro/pw| th=sd' e)kkuklisqh/sei tu/xhs for thou thyself hast need of forethought whereby thou shalt extricate thyself from this trouble
A. Pr. 86.

§2551

ou)k e)/stin o(/s (o(/pws, o(/pou, w(s) are used with the future indicative to introduce statements as regards the future. Thus, ou) ga/r tis e)/stin d\s pa/roiq' ai(rh/setai th\n sh\n a)xrei=on du/namin a)nt' *eu)rusqe/ws there is no one who will prefer thy feeble power rather than Eurystheus E. Heracl. 57, ou)k e)/sq' o(/pws o)/yei su\ deu=r' e)lqo/nta me thou wilt in no wise (lit. it is not possible how thou shalt) see me coming here
S. Ant. 329. The indicative present or aorist is also used in statements as regards the present or past. All these indicatives may be dependent deliberatives. Cp. 2557.

§2552
The optative without a)/n (probably potential) occurs in Attic poetry after ou)k e)/stin o(/stis (o(/pws, o(/poi) and the interrogative ti/s e)sti/n o(/s (o(/stis) and e)/sq' o(/pws. Thus,

ou)k e)/stin o(/stis plh\n e)mou= kei/raito/ nin there is no one except myself who could cut it
A. Ch. 172, ou)k e)/sq' o(/pws le/caimi ta\ yeudh= kala/ I could not (lit. there is no way how I could) call false tidings fair
A. Ag. 620, ti/s tw=nd' . . . dwma/twn e)/xei kra/tos, o(/stis ce/nous de/caito; who has authority in this house that might receive guests?
Ar. Thesm. 871, e)/st' ou)=n o(/pws )/ *alkhstis e)s gh=ras mo/loi; is there a way by which Alcestis might reach old age?
E. Alc. 52. The potential optative with a)/n occurs after these expressions (
E. Alc. 80,
S. O. C. 1168,
P. Lach. 184c). Attic does not use the optative with a)/n after the positive form e)/stin o(/pws (o(/stis).

## CLASSES OF RELATIVE CLAUSES

§2553

Ordinary Relative Clauses define more exactly a definite antecedent, and show the mood and the negative of simple sentences.
Indicative:

tau=t' e)sti\n a(\ e)gw\ de/omai this is what I want
X. A. 7.2.34, w)= du/sta_na ge/nh brot w=n, oi(=s mh\ me/trios ai)w/n alas, ill-starred races of men, whose destiny is beyond due measure
S. Ph. 179, o(/qen ou)=n r(a=|sta maqh/sesqe peri\ au)tw=n, e)nteu=qen u(_ma=s kai\ e)gw\ prw=ton peira/_somai dida/skein I will first try to inform you (lit.) from the source from which you will most easily learn about them
D. 27.3,

par' e)me\ a)fiko/menos ou) pei/setai a(/per a)\n e)/paqen a)/llw| tw| suggeno/menos tw=n sofistw=n in coming to me he will not meet with the treatment he would have suffered had he consorted with any other of the sophists
P. Pr. 318d.
Subjunctive: *)/anutos o(/de parekaqe/zeto, w(=| metadw=men th=s zhth/sews Anytus has taken his seat here (lit.) to whom let us give a share in the investigation
P. Men. 80e, klu/wn o(qou/neka . . . mh/thr d' e)n oi)/kois: h(\n su\ mh\ dei/sh|s hearing that our mother is in the house, (lit.) of whom have thou no fear
S. El. 1309.
Optative: oi)/omai a)\n h(ma=s toiau=ta paqei=n, oi(=a tou\s e)xqrou\s oi( qeoi\ poih/seian I think we should endure such things as I pray the gods may inflict upon our enemies
X. A. 3.2.3, do/rata e)/xontes . . . o(/sa a)nh\r a)\n fe/roi mo/lis having spears, such as a man could carry with difficulty 5. 4. 25, a)/rcomai d' e)nteu=qen o(/qen . . . e)gw\ ta/xist' a)\n dida/caimi I will begin at (from) that point where I can most quickly inform you
D. 29.5. The potential optative without a)/n is very rare (2552).
Imperative:

pla/nhn fra/sw, h(\n e)ggra/fou su\ mnh/mosin de/ltois frenw=n I will tell thy wandering, which do thou inscribe in the tablets of thy memory
A. Pr. 788. On oi)=sq' d\ dra=son, see 1842 a.
a. Ordinary relative clauses are explanatory, and (in sense) are equivalent to independent coördinated clauses. See 2490.
b. Homer has ke/ or a)/n with the future: par' e)moi/ ge kai\ a)/lloi, oi(/ ke/ me ti_mh/sousi I have others by my side who will honour me A 175.

§2554

Relative Clauses of Purpose (Final Relative Clauses) regularly take the future indicative, even after past tenses (negative mh/). The antecedent of final relative clauses is usually indefinite. o(/s is commoner than o(/stis. (The construction with the future participle is more frequent: 2065).

fhmi\ dh\ dei=n h(ma=s . . . presbei/a_n pe/mpein, h(\ tou\s me\n dida/cei tau=ta, tou\s de\ parocunei= I say that we must send an embassy, which will inform some of this and incite others
D. 2.11,

pe/myon tin' o(/stis shmanei= send some one who will announce
E. I. T. 1209,

e)/doce tw=| dh/mw| tria/_konta a)/ndras e(le/sqai, oi(\ tou\s patri/ous no/mous suggra/yousi, kaq' ou(\s poli_teu/sousi the people voted to choose thirty men who should codify the ancestral laws by which they were to conduct the government
X. H. 2.3.2. So in local clauses:

kru/yw to/d' e)/gxos . . . e)/nqa mh/ tis o)/yetai I will hide this sword where no one shall see it
S. Aj. 659.
a. After a secondary tense the future optative occurs rarely: oi( de\ tria/_konta h(|re/qhsan me\n e)pei\ ta/xista ta\ makra\ tei/xh . . . kaqh|re/qh: ai(reqe/ntes d' e)f' w(=|te cuggra/yai no/mous, kaq' ou(/stinas poli_teu/sointo ktl. the thirty were chosen as soon as the long walls were destroyed; and having been chosen for the purpose of codifying the laws, according to which they were to conduct the government, etc.
X. H. 2.3.11. In local clauses:
S. O. T. 796.
b. A past purpose may be expressed by e)/mellon and the infinitive. Thus,

nau/arxon prose/tacan' *alki/da_n, d\s e)/mellen e)pipleu/sesqai they appointed Alcidas as admiral who was to sail in command
T. 3.16.
c. Homer uses the subjunctive (with ke/, except
*g 287) after primary tenses, the optative after secondary tenses. Thus,

ma/ntis e)leu/setai, o(/s ke/n toi e)/ph|sin o(do/n a seer will come to tell thee the way
k 538,

a)/ggelon h(=kan d\s a)ggei/leie gunaiki/ they sent a messenger to tell the woman
o 458. The future also occurs (
c 332). The present or aorist optative is rare in Attic (
S. Tr. 903, Ph. 281).

§2555

Relative Clauses of Cause take the indicative (negative ou)). o(/s is more common than o(/stis.
qaumasto\n poiei=s, d\s ( = o(/ti su\)

h(mi=n . . . ou)de\n di/dws you do a strange thing in giving us nothing
X. M. 2.7.13, *loci/a| de\ me/mfomai, o(/stis m' e)pa/_ra_s e)/rgon a)nosiw/taton toi=s me\n lo/gois hu)/fra_ne ktl. I blame Loxias, who after inciting me to a deed most unhallowed, cheered me with words, etc.
E. Or. 285. So when the relative is a dependent exclamation (oi(=os = o(/ti toiou=tos, etc., 2687).
a. ge is often added to o(/s or o(/stis.
b. mh/ is used when there is also an idea of characteristic (of such a sort) or condition (perhaps to avoid a harsher form of statement). Cp. 2705 g.

§2556

Relative Clauses of Result (Consecutive Relative Clauses) usually take the indicative (for oi(=os, o(/sos with the infinitive see 2497). The negative is ou) when the relative clause approximates w(/ste (ou)) with the indicative, as is generally the case when the main clause is negative, expressed or implied. Here o(/stis is commoner than o(/s. The negative is mh/ when the relative clause expresses an intended (2557) or anticipated (2558) result, where w(/ste mh/ with the infinitive would be less precise.
ti/s ou(/tw mai/netai o(/stis ou) bou/letai soi\ fi/los ei)=nai; who is so mad that he does not wish to be a friend to you?
X. A. 2.5.12,

ou)de\n ga\r ou(/tw braxu\ o(/plon e(ka/teroi ei)=xon w(=| ou)k e)ci_knou=nto a)llh/lwn for each side did not have weapons so short that they could not reach each other
X. H. 7.5.17.
a. The indicative with a)/n and the optative with a)/n are rare. Thus, ti/s d' h)=n ou(/tws . . . mi_saqh/naios, o(/stis e)dunh/qh a)\n a)/takton au(to\n u(pomei=nai i)dei=n; who was such a hater of Athens that he could endure to see himself not at his post? Lyc. 39,

ti/s ou(/tws i)sxu_ro/s, d\s . . . r(i(_gei du/nait' a)\n maxo/menos strateu/esqai who is so vigorous that he could carry on war while battling with cold?
X. C. 6.1.15. A potential optative with o(/s follows a potential optative in
P. R. 360b.

§2557
The indicative is normal in consecutive relative clauses introduced by ou)k e)/stin o(/stis (ou)), ou)dei/s e)stin o(/stis (ou)), ou)k e)/stin o(/pws (ou)), ei)si\n oi(/, e)/stin oi(=s, etc.

ou)k e)/stin ou)dei\s o(/stis ou)x au(to\n filei= there is no one who does not love himself
Men. Sent. 407, ou)k e)/stin o(/pws h(/bhn kth/sh| pa/lin au)=qis in no way canst thou regain thy youth E. Heracl. 707. See 2551.
a. The indicative with a)/n and the optative with a)/n also occur. Thus,

ou) ga\r h)=n o(/ ti a)\n e)poiei=te for there was nothing that you could have done
D. 18.43,

w(=n ou)k e)/stin o(/stis ou)k a)\n katafronh/seien whom every one would despise
I. 8.52.
b. On the subjunctive and optative without a)/n, see 2546, 2547, 2552.

§2558
The future indicative is often used to express an intended result (negative mh/).

a)no/hton e)pi\ toiou/tous i)e/nai w(=n krath/sa_s mh\ katasxh/sei tis it is senseless to attack men of such a kind that we shall not hold them in subjection if we conquer them
T. 6.11, ou(=toi de\ toiau=t' . . . u(posxh/sontai, e)c w(=n mhd' a)\n o(tiou=n h)=| ki_nhqh/sontai these men shall make promises in consequence of which the Athenians will not better themselves under any circumstances (lit. even if anything occurs)
D. 19.324.

§2559
The future indicative is especially common when the main clause contains an idea of ability, capacity, or characteristic, and the relative clause denotes what is to be expected of the subject.
i(kanoi/ e)smen . . . u(_mi=n pe/myai nau=s te kai\ a)/ndras oi(/tines summaxou=ntai/ te kai\ th\n o(do\n h(gh/sontai (cp. w(/ste summa/xesqai) we are able to send you ships and men who will fight with you and direct your journey
X. A. 5.4.10, ou)/te ploi=a e)/sti ta\ a)pa/conta ou)/te si=tos w(=| qreyo/meqa me/nontes we have neither ships to convey us away nor provisions to feed us while we remain 6. 5. 20,

dei=tai/ tinos o(/stis au)to\n o)nh/sei he needs some one to improve him
P. Eu. 306d, (e)/dei)

yh/fisma ni_kh=sai toiou=to di' ou(= *fwkei=s a)polou=ntai a bill had to be passed of such a character as to destroy the Phocians
D. 19.43.

§2560

Conditional Relative Clauses may be resolved into if clauses, o(/s (o(/stis) corresponding to ei)/ tis and o(/s (o(/stis) a)/n to e)a/_n tis. The negative is mh/.
a. The antecedent of conditional relative clauses is indefinite (2505 b).
b. Such relative clauses, like temporal clauses, correspond in form to the protases of ordinary conditional sentences. Conditional relative sentences show, in general, the same substitutions permitted in the corresponding conditional sentences. d\s a)/n is always generic, e)a/_n may be particular in prose.

N.—English cannot always, without obscurity, use a relative to translate o(/te or o(/ ti with an unreal indicative; in such cases when (ever) or whatever are best rendered by if ever. Cp. 2396.

## PRESENT AND PAST CONDITIONAL RELATIVE CLAUSES

## First Form: SIMPLE PRESENT AND PAST CONDITIONAL RELATIVES

§2562
Simple present and past conditional relative clauses have the present or past indicative. The main clause has the indicative or any other form of the simple sentence (cp. 2298, 2300).
ou) ga\r a(\ pra/_ttousin oi( di/kaioi, a)ll' a(\ (= ei)/ tina) mh\ pra/_ttousi, tau=ta le/geis for it is not what the just do, but what they do not do, that you keep telling us
X. M. 4.4.11, tw=n *(ellh/nwn oi(\ (= ei)/ tines)

mh\ e)/tuxon e)n tai=s ta/cesin o)/ntes ei)s ta\_s ta/ceis e)/qeon those of the Greeks who happened not to be in rank ran into their ranks
X. A. 2.2.14, die/ballen au)to\n o(/ ti e)du/nato he slandered him all he could 6. 1. 32, a)/ndras tw=n *)aqhnai/wn a)pe/kteinan o(/soi mh\ e)ce/neusan they killed all of the Athenians who had not escaped by swimming
T. 2.90, d\ de/ ge mhde\n kako\n poiei= ou)d' a)/n tinos ei)/h kakou= ai)/tion; and that which produces no evil cannot be the cause of any evil either?
P. R. 379b,

a(\ mh\ prosh/kei mh/t' a)/koue mh/q' o(/ra_ neither hear nor behold that which beseems thee not
Men. Sent. 39,

o(/stis zh=n e)piqu_mei=, peira/_sqw ni_ka=n whoever longs to live, let him strive to conquer
X. A. 3.2.39.
a. Since the antecedent of these clauses is indefinite, simple present conditional relative clauses with the present indicative in the main clause often have the value of general conditions. But general clauses with o(/s (mh/) usually take the subjunctive or optative (2567, 2568), and those with o(/stis (mh/) the indicative (2569).

§2563
If the relative clause expresses a present intention or necessity, the future indicative may be used.
e)n tou/tw| kekwlu=sqai (1950) e)do/kei e(ka/stw| ta\ pra/_gmata w(=| mh/ tis au)to\s pare/stai each thought that progress was surely impeded in any undertaking in which he was not going to take part in person (= e)n tou/tw| kekw/lu_tai w(=| mh\ pare/somai)
T. 2.8. Cp.
P. Th. 186c. More common is me/llw with the present or future infinitive:

e(/loisq' o(/ ti . . . a(/pa_si sunoi/sein u(_mi=n me/llei may you adopt whatever course is likely to be of advantage to you all
D. 3.36.
a. Elsewhere the future indicative is not regular in conditional relative sentences.

## Second Form: PRESENT AND PAST UNREAL CONDITIONAL RELATIVES

§2564
Present and past unreal conditional relative clauses have a secondary tense of the indicative. The main clause has a secondary tense with a)/n (cp. 2303).
ou)/te ga\r a)\n au)toi\ e)pexeirou=men pra/_ttein a(\ (= ei)/ tina) mh\ h)pista/meqa ktl. for (if that were so) neither should we ourselves be undertaking (as we are) to do what we did not understand, etc.
P. Charm. 171e, oi( pai=des u(_mw=n, o(/soi (= ei)/ tines) e)nqa/de h)=san, u(po\ tou/twn a)\n u(_bri/zonto (if that were so) your children, as many of them as were present (but none were present), would be insulted by these men
L. 12.98, o(po/tera tou/twn e)poi/hsen, ou)deno\s a)\n h(=tton plou/sioi h)=san whichever of these things he had done, they would be no less rich than any one 32. 23.

## FUTURE CONDITIONAL RELATIVE CLAUSES

## Third Form: MORE VIVID FUTURE CONDITIONAL RELATIVES

§2565
Conditional relative clauses that vividly anticipate the realization of a future event take the subjunctive with a)/n. The main clause has the future indicative or any other form referring to the future.
tw=| a)ndri\ d\n a)\n (= e)a/_n tina)

e(/lhsqe pei/somai I will obey whatever man you may choose
X. A. 1.3.15, oi(=s (for a(\)

a)\n oi( a)/lloi e)rga/zwntai, tou/tois su\ xrh/sh| whatever others acquire by labour, that you shall enjoy
X. M. 2.1.25,

peira/_somai o(/ ti a)\n du/nwmai u(_ma=s a)gaqo\n poiei=n I will try to do you all the good I can
X. A. 6.1.33,

o(/poi a)\n e)/lqw, le/gontos e)mou= a)kroa/_sontai oi( ne/oi wherever I go the young men will listen to my speaking
P. A. 37d,

a)po/kri_nai o(/ ti a)/n de e)rwtw= answer whatever I ask you
L. 12.24,

e(/pesqe o(/ph| a)/n tis h(gh=tai follow where any one may lead you
T. 2.11, w(s a)\n (= e)a/_n pws) e)gw\ ei)/pw, peiqw/meqa let us all obey as I shall bid B 139. Potential optative:

w(/st' a)pofu/gois a)\n h(/ntin' a)\n bou/lh| di/khn so that you can get off in any suit you please
Ar. Nub. 1151.
a. The future indicative is scarcely ever used in a conditional relative clause of this sort (
T. 1.22 o(/soi boulh/sontai; cp. 1913).
b. Homer has some cases of the subjunctive without ke/ or a)/n (e.g. N 234). Homer sometimes uses the future with ke/ or a)/n in the main clause: o( de/ ken kexolw/setai, o(/n ken i(/kwmai and he will be wroth to whom I shall come A 139.

## Fourth Form: LESS VIVID FUTURE CONDITIONAL RELATIVES

§2566
Conditional relative clauses that set forth less vividly the realization of a future event take the optative. The main clause has the optative with a)/n.
o)knoi/hn a)\n ei)s ta\ ploi=a e)mbai/nein a(\ (= ei)/ tina)

h(mi=n *ku=ros doi/h I should hesitate to embark in the vessels that Cyrus might give us
X. A. 1.3.17,

d\ de\ mh\ a)gapw/|h, ou)d' a)\n filoi= nor could he love what he does not desire
P. Lys. 215b.
a. The main clause has the optative without a)/n in wishes:

dw=ra qew=n e)/xoi, o(/tti didoi=en may he keep the gifts of the gods whatever they may give
s 142.
b. Homer sometimes uses ke/ or a)/n in the relative clause (
f 161).

## GENERAL CONDITIONAL RELATIVE CLAUSES

## Fifth Form PRESENT GENERAL CONDITIONAL RELATIVES

§2567
Present general conditional relative clauses have a)/n with the subjunctive. The main clause has the present indicative or an equivalent.
ne/os d' a)po/lluq' o(/ntin' (= ei)/ tina) a)\n filh=| qeo/s ‘he dieth young, whome'er a god doth love’
Stob. Flor. 120.13, ou(\s (= ei)/ tinas) a)\n o(oa=| filokindu/_nws e)/xontas pro\s tou\s polemi/ous, ti_ma=| whomever he sees zealous of danger in the face of the enemy, these he honours
X. H. 6.1.6,

gamou=si/ te o(po/qen a)\n bou/lwntai, e)kdido/wsi/ te ei)s ou(\s a)\n e)qe/lwsi they both get a wife from whatever family they please and give their daughters in marriage to whomsoever they choose
P. R. 613d,

patri\s ga/r e)sti pa=s' i(/n' a)\n pra/_tth| tis eu)= for every land is a man's own country wheresoever he fares well
Ar. Plut. 1151.
a. Gnomic aorist in the main clause: o(/s ke qeoi=s e)pipei/qhtai, ma/la t' e)/kluon au)tou= whoever obeys the gods, him they most do hear A 218.
b. The subjunctive without a)/n (ke/) is usual in Homer and occurs occasionally in Attic and lyric poetry. Thus,

a)nqrw/pous e)fora=| kai\ ti/_nutai o(/s tis a(ma/rth| he watches over men and punishes whoever transgresses
n 214,

tw=n de\ phmonw=n ma/lista lu_pou=s' ai(\ fanw=s' au)qai/retoi but those griefs pain the most which are seen to be self-sought
S. O. T. 1231. Cases of the sort appear in Hdt., but are very rare in Attic prose, e.g.
T. 4.18. The subjunctive without a)/n (ke/) is much commoner in Homer than in the corresponding clauses with ei) (2339).
c. The apodosis here usually expresses a general truth, less often iterative action. In 2568 the apodosis refers to iterative action, usually on the part of designated individuals.

## Sixth Form PAST GENERAL CONDITIONAL RELATIVES

§2568
Past general conditional relative clauses have the optative. The main clause has the imperfect or an equivalent.
a)ei\ pro\s w(=| (= ei) pro/s tini)

ei)/h e)/rgw|, tou=to e)/pra_tten whatever work he was engaged in, that he always performed

T. 2.67,

e)qh/ra_ o(/pou per e)pitugxa/noien qhri/ois he used to hunt wherever they fell in with large game

X. C. 3.3.67.

X. H. 6.2.28.

## INDICATIVE FORM OF GENERAL CONDITIONAL RELATIVE CLAUSES

§2569
The present indicative instead of the subjunctive with a)/n occurs in general conditional relative clauses (cp. 2342). This occurs chiefly after o(/stis, which is itself sufficiently general in meaning.

oi(/tines pro\s ta\_s cumfora\_s gnw/mh| h(/kista lu_pou=ntai, e)/rgw| de\ ma/lista a)nte/xousin those who in feeling are least depressed at misfortunes, in action resist them most

o(/stis de\ plou=ton h)\ eu)ge/neian ei)sidw\n gamei= ponhra/_n, mw=ro/s e)stin whoever fixes his gaze on wealth or noble lineage and weds a wicked woman, is a fool
E. El. 1097,

o(/ ti kalo\n fi/lon a)_ei/ whatsoever is fair is dear forever
E. Bacch. 881.
a. Cases of the imperfect instead of the optative are rare and generally ill supported: o(/pou w)/|eto th\n patri/da ti w)felh/sein, ou) po/nwn u(fi/_eto whenever he thought that he could benefit his country in any respect, he did not shrink from toil X. Ag. 7. 1. Cp.
X. A. 1.1.5, 1. 9. 27.

§2570
The indicative is generally used in parenthetical or appended relative clauses with o(/stis (o(/stis pote/). Thus,

douleu/omen qeoi=s, o(/ ti pot' ei)si\n oi( qeoi/ we serve the gods, whatever those gods are
E. Or. 418.
a. The subjunctive with a)/n is also used when the reference is to future time or to general present time. Cp.
Aes. 1.127,
D. 4.27.

## LESS USUAL FORMS OF CONDITIONAL RELATIVE SENTENCES

§2571
The potential optative with a)/n in the main clause with the indicative (2562) or subjunctive (2565) in the relative clause.

§2572
Indicative with a)/n or potential optative with a)/n in the relative clause.
o(/ntin' a)\n u(_mei=s ei)s tau/thn th\n ta/cin katesth/sate . . ., ou(=tos . . . tw=n i)/swn a)\n ai)/tios h)=n kakw=n o(/swnper kai\ ou(=tos whomsoever you might have appointed to this post, such a one would have been the cause of as many evils as this man has been

The optative in the relative clause with the present or future indicative or the imperative in the main clause (cp. 2359). With the present this occurs especially in general statements and maxims. The main clause is often introduced by a verb requiring the infinitive.

*y 494.
b. Other examples of the present: Homer P 631 (doubtful); Theognis 689; Aes. Pr. 638; Soph. O. T. 315, 979; Lys. 12. 84; Xen. C. 2. 4. 10, 7. 5. 56, H. 3. 4. 18, 7. 3. 7; Plato Charm. 164 a, Eu. 292 e (doubtful), L. 927 c. Temporal:
S. Tr. 92,
P. R. 332a.
c. The future indicative occurs in
t 510 (temporal N 317); the perfect indicative in
*d 262 and
w 254 (temporal); the aorist imperative in
X. C. 1.4.14.

## DEPENDENT SUBSTANTIVE CLAUSES (2574-2635）

§2574
A subordinate clause may play the part of a substantive in relation to the main clause. Such clauses are generally the object, sometimes the subject, of the verb of the main clause.

ei)=pen o(/ti ou) po/lemon poihso/menoi h(/koien he said that they had not come to wage war
X. A. 5.5.24,

e)/pra_sson o(/pws tis boh/qeia h(/cei they were managing how some reinforcements should come
T. 3.4,

de/doika mh\ . . . e)pilaqw/meqa th=s oi)/kade o(dou= I am afraid lest we may forget the way home
X. A. 3.2.25; e)le/geto o(/ti . . . *pw=los o(/son ou) parei/h it was said that Polus had all but arrived 7. 2. 5.

§2575
There are four main divisions of substantive clauses.

1. Dependent Statements: subordinate clauses stating that something is; as

le/gei w(s ou)de/n e)stin a)dikw/teron fh/mhs he says that nothing is more unjust than talk about a man's character
Aes. 1.125.

2. Dependent Clauses of will or desire: subordinate clauses denoting that something should be or should be done. These clauses have been treated under the following divisions:
a. Dependent clauses after verbs of effort (2209).
b. Dependent clauses after verbs of fearing (2221).
N.—On dependent voluntative clauses with the accusative and infinitive (indirect petition), see 1991 ff.

3. Dependent Questions: subordinate clauses asking a question; both parts of the sentence together forming a statement; as

h)rw/twn o(/ ti e)sti\ to\ pra=gma I asked what the matter was
X. A. 5.7.23.

4. Dependent Exclamations: subordinate clauses setting forth an exclamation; both parts of the sentence together forming a statement; as

diaqew/menos au)tw=n o(/shn me\n xw/ra_n kai\ oi(/a_n e)/xoien observing how great the extent of their territory was and how excellent its quality
X. A. 3.1.19.

## DEPENDENT STATEMENTS

§2576
Dependent statements, or subordinate clauses stating that something is, are expressed in various ways:
1. By an infinitive, with or without an accusative (explained in 1972 ff., 2016 ff.). Thus,

nomi/zw ga\r u(_ma=s e)moi\ ei)=nai kai\ patri/da kai\ fi/lous for I think that you are both fatherland and friends to me
X. C. 1.3.6,

oi)=mai ei)de/nai I think that I know
P. Pr. 312c.
2. By a participle, with or without an accusative (explained in 2106 ff.). Thus,

ou) ga\r h)/|desan au)to\n teqnhko/ta for they did not know that he was dead
X. A. 1.10.16,

me/mnhmai a)kou/sa_s I remember that I heard
X. C. 1.6.6.
3. By o(/ti or w(s (and some other conjunctions) with the indicative or optative. On this form of dependent statement see 2577 ff., and under Indirect Discourse.
a. In any form of substantive clause the subject of the subordinate verb may be made the object of the principal verb (2182).
b. A clause with o(/ti (w(s) may precede the principal clause. Cp. 2586.

## DEPENDENT STATEMENTS INTRODUCED BY o(/ti OR w(s

§2577
The conjunctions o(/ti or w(s that introduce dependent statements in the indicative and optative
After verbs of saying, knowing, perceiving, showing, etc.
After verbs of emotion (rejoicing, grieving, wondering), etc.
Or such dependent statements contain an explanation of the main clause or of a word in that clause, no special verb introducing the conjunction.
tou=to a)/cion e)painei=n tw=n a)ndrw=n tw=n to/te naumaxhsa/ntwn, o(/ti to\n . . . fo/bon die/lu_san tw=n *(ellh/nwn it is right to praise this in the men who engaged in the sea-fight of those days, (namely) that they dispelled the fear felt by the Greeks
P. Menex. 241b.

§2578
The conjunctions introducing dependent statements are o(/t<*> (Homeric also o(/tti, o(/ and o(/te), w(s, dio/ti, o(/pws (rarely), ou(/neka and o(qou/neka (both poetic).
a. o(/ti meaning that was originally, like Hom. o(/, perhaps an accusative of the inner object (cognate): o(rw= s\ nosei=s lit. I see what sickness you are sick (= h(\n no/son nosei=s). But by the time of Homer both o(/ and o(/ti had become mere formal conjunctions. Hom. o(/te that seems to be a weakened o(/te when; but this is disputed.
b. dio/ti originally = dia\ tou=to, o(/ti on account of this, that = because (as
T. 1.52); then = o(/ti that in Hdt. and in Attic after Isocrates, who uses dio/ti for o(/ti to avoid hiatus.
c. w(s strictly an old ablative of o(/s (2989) meaning how, in what way, as in exclamatory clauses and indirect questions. The meaning how (cp. how that) may be seen in oi)=da ga\r w(/s moi o)dw/dustai kluto\s e)nnosi/gaios for I know how (that) the famed earth-shaker has been wroth against me
e 423, and also in Attic (
And. 2.14;
I. 2.3, 3. 10, 16. 11, 16. 15;
Aes. 2.35;
D. 24.139). The development of w(s how to w(s that followed from the use of w(s after verbs signifying to see, perceive, know, and the like. Cp. “he sayed how there was a knight.”
d. o(/pws (2929) that is common in Herodotus (o(/kws), rare in Attic, most used in poetry and Xenophon. From its original use in indirect questions o(/pws how gradually acquired the meaning that. Thus,

a)ll' o(/pws me\n . . . e)gw\ a)/xqomai u(_ma=s tre/fwn, mhd' u(ponoei=te do not even entertain the thought that I am annoyed at maintaining you
X. C. 3.3.20.
e. ou(/neka = ou)= e(/neka, for tou/tou e(/neka, o(/, properly causal: on account of (as regards) this, that, and then = that, even in Homer (Odyssey and
*l 21) and later in poetry. Thus,

e)ca/ggelle . . . ou(/nek' *oi)di/pous toiau=t' e)/neime paisi\ toi=s au(tou= ge/ra_ announce that Oedipus has distributed such honours to his sons
S. O. C. 1393.
f. o(qou/neka = o(/tou e(/neka, for tou/tou e(/neka, o(/ti; and then = that. It is found only in tragedy, as

a)/ggelle . . . o(qou/neka te/qnhk' *)ore/sths report that Orestes is dead
S. El. 47.

§2579
Some verbs of saying are followed either by o(/ti or w(s or by an infinitive (2017). In most cases the choice is optional with the writer. Affirmative clauses usually take the infinitive or o(/ti; but w(s is apparently preferred to o(/ti when a writer wishes to mark a statement as an opinion, a pretext, as untrue, and so when the main clause is negative, or when the subordinate clause is negative (or both are negative). Thus,

nomi/zousin oi( e)kei/nh| a)/nqrwpoi . . . w(s o( *(/hfaistos xalkeu/ei the local belief is that Hephaestus is working at his forge
T. 3.88, diabalw\n au)tou\s w(s ou)de\n a)lhqe\s e)n nw=| e)/xousin slanderously attacking them on the score that their intentions were not sincere 5. 45,

polla/kis e)qau/masa ti/si pote\ lo/gois *)aqhnai/ous e)/peisan oi( graya/menoi *swkra/thn w(s a)/cios ei)/h qana/tou I have often wondered with what possible arguments the accusers of Socrates succeeded in convincing the Athenians that he deserved death
X. M. 1.1.1, ou) tou=to le/gw w(s ou) dei= pote kai\ e)la/_ttoni e)/ti mori/w| i)e/nai I do not say (this) that it is not ever necessary to attack the enemy with a still smaller detachment
X. C. 5.4.20. o(/ti may be used of an untrue statement designed to create belief (
S. El. 43).
a. Dependent statements in the optative in indirect discourse after verbs of saying are chiefly post-Homeric.

§2580

Verbs of thinking almost always take the infinitive (2018) but w(s occurs; as with nomi/zw
T. 3.88 (2579), e)lpi/zw 5. 9, oi)/omai
X. H. 6.3.12, u(polamba/nw
X. C. 8.3.40. o(/ti is very rare (with oi)/omai in
P. Ph. 87c). logi/zomai (o(/ti) is a verb of saying.
a. marturw= with o(/ti (w(s) expresses reality; with the infinitive it denotes uncertainty.

§2581
Verbs of intellectual perception usually take o(/ti (w(s); less often the participle, which is normal after verbs of physical perception. A verb of physical perception, if followed by o(/ti (w(s), virtually becomes a verb of intellectual perception.

§2582
Many verbs take o(/ti (w(s) or the participle either in indirect discourse or not in indirect discourse (2106-2115). Here the construction with the finite verb is less dependent than that with the participle; but the meaning is essentially the same in Attic. Many verbs take o(/ti (w(s), the infinitive, or the participle, often without great difference in meaning in Attic (2123-2145).

§2583

o(/ti (w(s), when separated from its clause by another clause, may be repeated. Thus,

e)/legen o(/ti, ei) mh\ katabh/sontai . . . , o(/ti katakau/sei . . . ta\_s kw/ma_s he said that, if they did not descend, he would burn their villages to the ground
X. A. 7.4.5.

§2584
The personal dh=lo/s ei)mi o(/ti, lanqa/nw o(/ti, etc. are often used instead of the impersonal dh=lo/n e)stin o(/ti, lanqa/nei o(/ti, etc. Thus,

o(/ti ponhro/tatoi/ ei)sin ou)de\ se\ lanqa/nousin not even you fail to perceive that they are the very worst
X. O. 1.19.

§2585

dh=lon o(/ti (dhlono/ti) evidently, oi)=d' o(/ti (eu)= oi)=d' o(/ti) surely, eu)= i)/sqi o(/ti be assured are so often used parenthetically and elliptically as to become mere formal expressions requiring no verb. o(/ti here loses all conjunctive force. Thus,

e)/xei dh\ ou(twsi\_ dh=lon o(/ti tou/twn pe/ri the case then stands clearly thus about these matters
P. G. 487d,

ou)/t' a)\n u(_mei=s oi)=d' o(/ti e)pau/sasqe nor assuredly would you have ceased
D. 6.29, kai\ pa/ntwn oi)=d' o(/ti fhsa/ntwn g' a)/n (for kai\ oi)=d' o(/ti pa/ntes fh/saie/n g' a)/n) and all assuredly would say 9. 1.
a. Plato (Sophistes and Leges) uses dh=lon (e)sti/n) w(s for dh=lon o(/ti.

§2586

o(/ti (and by analogy w(s) are often attached loosely to the main clause with the meaning as a proof (in support) of the fact that. Thus, o(/ti d' ou(/tw tau=t' e)/xei, le/ge moi to\ tou= *kallisqe/nous yh/fisma as a proof of the fact that this is so, read me the bill of Callisthenes
D. 18.37.

§2587

Verbs of emotion (to rejoice, grieve, be angry, wonder, etc.) take o(/ti (w(s) with a finite verb (negative ou)), but more commonly the participle (2100) when the subject is not changed.
a. Hom. prefers o(/ti, w(s to the participle or infinitive.
b. The accusative and infinitive with verbs of emotion are rare; as with qauma/zw
E. Alc. 1130. (qauma/zw may be followed by a dependent question:
D. 37.44).
c. On verbs of emotion with ei) instead of o(/ti, w(s (negative, generally mh/), see 2247. On the use in dependent exclamations, see 2687.

§2588

me/mnhmai, oi)=da, a)kou/w and like verbs, may take o(/te instead of o(/ti (2395 A. N.). Cp., in Homer,
*f 396,
p 424.

## INDIRECT DISCOURSE

§2589
The words or thoughts of a person may be quoted in direct or indirect form after verbs, or other expressions, of saying or thinking.
a. In reporting a speech, in making a quotation, or in dialogue, a verb of saying is often repeated (
P. Pr. 310b, 345 c,
X. A. 7.6.5-6). So also in such cases as *pa/nqeia ei)=pen, a)lla\ qa/rrei, e)/fh, w)= *ku=re
X. C. 7.3.13.

§2590
(I) Direct Discourse (Oratio Recta).—In a direct quotation the words or thoughts quoted are given at first hand in the exact form used by the original speaker or thinker.
*megare/es e)/pempon e)pi\ tou\s strathgou\s tw=n *(ellh/nwn kh/ru_ka, a)piko/menos de\ o( kh=ruc pro\s au)tou\s e)/lege ta/de: “*megare/es le/gousi: ‘h(mei=s, a)/ndres su/mmaxoi, ou) dunatoi/ ei)men th\n *perse/wn i(/ppon de/kesqai mou=noi’” the Megarians sent a herald to the generals of the Greeks, and on his arrival the herald spoke as follows: “The Megarians say: ‘we, oh allies, are not able to sustain the attack of the Persian cavalry by ourselves’”
Hdt. 9.21; and often in Hdt. (cp. 3. 40, 3. 122, 5. 24, 7. 150, 8. 140).
a. Direct quotation may, in prose, be introduced by o(/ti, which has the value of quotation marks. Thus, oi( de\ ei)=pon o(/ti i(kanoi/ e)smen but they said (that) “we are ready”
X. A. 5.4.10. So usually when the finite verb is omitted; as a)pekri/_nato o(/ti ou)/ he answered (that) “no” 1. 6. 7. The use of direct speech introduced by o(/ti is, in general, that of familiar style. The first example is
Hdt. 2.115. w(s for o(/ti is very rare (Dinarchus 1. 12, 1. 102). Cp. “the emperor sends thee this word that, if thou love thy sons, let Marcus . . ., or any one of you, chop off your hand” Shakesp. Tit. Andr. 3. 1. 151.

§2591
(II) Indirect Discourse (Oratio Obliqua). In an indirect quotation the words or thoughts are given at second hand with certain modifications to indicate that the words or thoughts are reported.
a. The original form may be preserved except that there is a change from the first or second person to the third person: so pa/nt' e)qe/lei do/menai H 391 reporting pa/nt' e)qe/lw do/menai H 364. In such cases there is no grammatical dependence.
b. The narrator may report in dependent form the words or thoughts of a person from the point of view of that person. This is the common form of indirect discourse.
c. The narrator may report in dependent form the words or thoughts of a person from his own point of view. See 2624.

§2592
The constructions of indirect discourse are regulated by the character of the leading verb or expression.
a. Verbs of saying take either o(/ti or w(s and a finite verb or the infinitive (2017, 2579).
b. Most verbs of thinking and believing take the infinitive (2018, cp. 2580).
c. Most verbs of knowing, perceiving, hearing, showing take the participle (2106, 2110), but admit the construction with o(/ti or w(s. Some are followed by the infinitive (2123 ff.).
d. On the construction of verbs of hoping, promising , and swearing, see 1868, 1999, 2024.

§2593
Indirect discourse is said to be implied in subordinate clauses dependent on verbs which involve an idea of saying or thinking (2622).

§2594
A speaker may state his own words or thoughts in the form of indirect discourse. Cp. 2614, 2615, etc.

§2595
Clauses standing in indirect discourse are substantive clauses, and usually object of the leading verb; its subject, when that verb is passive or intransitive. The infinitive in substantive clauses after verbs of saying and thinking retains the time of the corresponding finite verb of direct discourse.

§2596
Indirect questions (2677) have the constructions of indirect discourse.

## GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF INDIRECT DISCOURSE

§2597
Simple and compound sentences, and principal clauses of complex sentences, introduced by o(/ti or w(s are treated as follows:

§2598
(I) After primary tenses, the original mood and tense are retained, except that the person of the verb may be changed.

§2599
(II) After secondary tenses, primary tenses of the indicative and all subjunctives may be changed to the same tense of the optative; but an indicative denoting unreality (with or without a)/n) is retained. Imperfects and pluperfects are generally retained (2623 b).

§2600
The verb of simple and compound sentences, and of principal clauses of complex sentences, when introduced by a verb taking the infinitive or participle, passes into the infinitive or participle in the corresponding tense. a)/n is kept, if it was used in the direct form.

§2601

Subordinate clauses of complex sentences introduced by o(/ti or w(s are treated as follows:

§2602
(I) Subordinate clauses of a sentence introduced by a leading verb in a primary tense, must remain unchanged in mood and tense.

§2603
(II) If subordinate clauses are introduced by a leading verb in a secondary tense, all primary tenses of the indicative and all subjunctives (with or without a)/n) may be changed to the corresponding tenses of the optative without a)/n. All secondary tenses of the indicative (with or without a)/n) remain unchanged.

§2604
Verbs standing in subordinate clauses of sentences introduced by a leading verb requiring the participle or the infinitive, follow the rules of 2602, 2603.

§2605
The principal and subordinate clauses of the direct form retain the names principal and subordinate in indirect discourse though the whole clause in which they stand itself depends on the verb introducing the indirect discourse (the leading verb).

§2606
The change from direct to indirect discourse is almost always a change of mood, not of tense. The time of a participle introducing indirect discourse is determined by that of the leading verb. The person of the verb is often changed.

§2607

a)/n of the direct form is retained in indirect discourse except when a dependent subjunctive with a)/n becomes optative after a secondary tense. Here e)a/_n, o(/tan, e)peida/n, e(/ws a)/n, etc., become ei), o(/te, e)peidh/, e(/ws, etc.

§2608
The same negative (ou) or mh/) used in the direct discourse is commonly kept in the indirect form. But in some cases with the infinitive and participle mh/ takes the place of ou) (2723 ff., 2730, 2737).

§2609
No verb ever becomes subjunctive by reason of indirect discourse. The subjunctive (with or without a)/n) may, after a secondary tense, become optative without a)/n.

§2610
No verb can be changed to the optative in indirect discourse except after a secondary tense, and since, even after a secondary tense, indicatives or subjunctives may be retained for vividness, no verb must become optative by reason of indirect discourse.

§2611
All optatives with or without a)/n in the direct form are retained (with or without a)/n) in indirect discourse introduced by o(/ti or w(s. After verbs requiring the participle or infinitive, such optatives in principal clauses become participles or infinitives (with or without a)/n), but remain unchanged in subordinate clauses.
a. The optative in indirect discourse may represent either the indicative or the subjunctive after a secondary tense.
b. A present optative in indirect discourse may represent (1) the present indicative; (2) the imperfect (2623 b) indicative; (3) the present subjunctive with or without a)/n; (4) the present optative.

§2612
The imperative is commonly replaced in indirect discourse by a periphrasis with xrh=nai. Cp. 2633 b.

§2613
The retention of the mood of direct discourse, where either the direct or indirect form is possible, lies solely in the option of the writer or speaker. The vivid form reproduces the time and situation in which the quoted words were used. The vivid form is preferred by some writers, as Thucydides; the indirect form by others, as the orators, Plato, and Xenophon.

## SIMPLE SENTENCES IN INDIRECT DISCOURSE

After primary tenses, the verb of the direct form remains unchanged in mood and tense.

## 2. Infinitive and Participle

§2616
The infinitive and participle are used in indirect discourse to represent the finite verb of direct discourse.

## COMPLEX SENTENCES IN INDIRECT DISCOURSE

§2617
When a complex sentence passes into indirect discourse, its principal verb is treated like the verb of a simple sentence and stands either in a finite mood (after o(/ti or w(s) or in the infinitive or in the participle.

§2618
After primary tenses, all subordinate verbs retain the original mood and tense.

le/gousin w(s, e)peida/n tis a)gaqo\s w)/n teleuth/sh|, mega/lhn moi=ran kai\ ti_mh\n e)/xei they say that, when a good man dies, he enjoys great esteem and honour
