## IMPLIED INDIRECT DISCOURSE

§2622
Indirect discourse is implied in the case of any subordinate clause, which, though not depending formally on a verb of saying or thinking, contains the past thought of another person and not a statement of the writer or speaker. Implied indirect discourse appears only after secondary tenses, and in various kinds of dependent clauses.
a. Conditional clauses, the conclusion being implied in the leading verb. Thus, after a verb of emotion,

oi( d' w)/|kti_ron ei) a(lw/sointo others pitied them if they should be captured
X. A. 1.4.7. The original form was ‘we pity them thinking what they will suffer ei) a(lw/sontai if they shall be captured.’ In other ei) clauses, as

ta\ xrh/mata tw=| dh/mw| e)/dwken, ei)/ pws teleuth/seien a)/pais he gave his property to the people in case he died childless
And. 4.15 (i.e. that the people might have it, in case he should die: direct e)a\_n teleuth/sw, and here e)a\_n teleuth/sh| might have been used).
b. Temporal clauses implying purpose, expectation, or the like (cp. 2420). Thus, sponda\_s e)poih/santo, e(/ws a)paggelqei/h ta\ lexqe/nta they made a truce (which they agreed should continue) until what had been said should have been reported
X. H. 3.2.20 (e(/ws a)\n a)paggelqh=| would be the direct form). Cp. e(/ws d' a)\n tau=ta diapra/_cwntai, fulakh\n . . . kate/lipe he left behind a guard (which he intended should remain) until they should settle these matters 5. 3. 25.
c. Causal clauses. See 2242.
d. Ordinary relative clauses. Thus, ei)/reto pai=da, to\n *eu)a/dna_ te/koi he asked for the child which Evadna had borne Pindar, Ol. 6. 49. Here relative and interrogative are not sharply distinguished.
e. Clauses depending on an infinitive especially when introduced by a verb of will or desire, e.g. command, advise, plan, ask, wish (1991, 1992). Here the infinitive expressing command, warning, wish, is not itself in indirect discourse. The negative is mh/. Thus, a)fiknou=ntai (historical present) w(s *sita/lkhn . . . boulo/menoi pei=sai au)to/n, ei) du/nainto, . . . strateu=sai e)pi\ th\n *potei/daian they came to Sitalces with the desire of persuading him (if they could) to make an expedition against Potidaea
T. 2.67 ( = e)a\_n dunw/meqa), cp. 2633 a.
f. Clauses of purpose and object clauses after verbs of effort admit the alternative constructions of indirect discourse.

## REMARKS ON THE CONSTRUCTIONS OF INDIRECT DISCOURSE

§2623

Past Tenses in Indirect Discourse.—The following rules govern past tenses in indirect discourse.
a. The potential indicative with a)/n, the indicative in a condition denoting unreality with a)/n or without a)/n (as e)xrh=n, e)/dei, etc.), always remain unchanged in order to prevent confusion with the optative of the direct form.

a)pelogou=nto w(s ou)k a)/n pote ou(/tw mw=roi h)=san . . . ei) h)/|desan they pleaded that they never would have been so foolish, if they had known
X. H. 5.4.22 ( = ou)k a)\n h)=men, ei) h)=|smen), (e)/legen)

o(/ti krei=tton h)=n au)tw=| to/te a)poqanei=n he said that it would have been better for him to die then
L. 10.25 ( = krei=tton h)=n moi).
b. The imperfect and pluperfect in simple sentences usually remain unchanged after secondary tenses to prevent ambiguity; but when there is no doubt that a past tense stood in the direct form, the imperfect passes into the present optative, the pluperfect into the perfect optative. In subordinate clauses both tenses are retained unaltered.

h)/kousen o(/ti polla/kis pro\s to\n *)indo\n oi( *xaldai=oi e)poreu/onto he heard that the Chaldaeans often went to the Indian king
X. C. 3.2.27, ei)=xe ga\r le/gein kai\ o(/ti mo/noi tw=n *(ellh/nwn basilei= sunema/xonto e)n *plataiai=s, kai\ o(/ti u(/steron ou)depw/pote strateu/sainto (cp. c)

e)pi\ basile/a_ for he was able to say both that alone of the Greeks they had fought on the side of the king at Plataea and that later they had never at any time taken the field against the king
X. H. 7.1.34 ( = sunemaxo/meqa, e)strateusa/meqa), ta\ pepra_gme/na dihgou=nto, o(/ti au)toi\ me\n . . . ple/oien, th\n de\ a)nai/resin tw=n naua_gw=n prosta/caien they related what had occurred to the effect that they were themselves sailing against the enemy and that they had given orāers for the rescue of the men on the wrecks
X. H. 1.7.5 ( = e)ple/omen, proseta/camen).
N.—The change to the optative is not made when the time of the action of imperfect (and pluperfect) is earlier than that of a coőrdinated verb in the same quoted sentence; as e)/lege/n t' w(s filaqh/naios h)=n kai\ ta)_n *sa/mw| prw=tos katei/poi he said that he both had been a lover of Athens and that (afterwards) he was the first to tell what had happened at Samos
Ar. Vesp. 282.
c. The aorist indicative without a)/n in a simple sentence or in a principal clause may be changed to the aorist optative after a secondary tense; but in subordinate clauses (except those denoting cause, N. 3) it remains unchanged to avoid ambiguity with the aorist optative, which usually represents the aorist subjunctive.

a)pekri_na/mhn au)tw=| o(/ti . . . ou) la/boimi I answered him that I did not take
D. 50.36 ( = ou)k e)/labon),

toi=s i)di/ois xrh/sesqai e)/fh, a(\ o( path\r au)tw=| e)/dwken he said that he would use his own money that his father had given him
X. H. 1.5.3 ( = xrh/somai, e)/dwken).
N. 1.—The retention of the aorist indicative is here the essential point of difference between subordinate clauses and principal clauses or simple sentences.
N. 2.—In a subordinate clause the time of the aorist usually expresses an action prior to that of the leading verb.
N. 3.—In causal clauses with o(/ti or w(s a dependent aorist indicative may become aorist optative; as ei)=xe ga\r le/gein . . . w(s *lakedaimo/nioi dia\ tou=to polemh/seian au)toi=s, o(/ti ou)k e)qelh/saien met' *)a_ghsila/_ou e)lqei=n e)p' au)to/n for he was able to say that the Lacedaemonians had gone to war with them (the Thebans) for the reason that they (the Thebans) had not been willing to attack him (the Persian king) in company with Agesilaus
X. H. 7.1.34 (direct e)pole/mhsan h(mi=n, o(/ti ou)k h)qelh/samen). Rarely in temporal clauses with e)pei/ (
X. C. 5.3.26).

§2624

Inserted Statement of Fact.—When the present or perfect indicative would have stood in the direct discourse, a past tense of historical narration is often used as a statement of fact by the writer from his own point of view, though the rest of the sentence may be given in indirect discourse after a secondary tense from the point of view of the subject of the leading verb.

h)/|dei o(/ti ou)x oi(=o/n t' h)=n au)th=| swqh=nai she knew that it was not possible for her to be saved
Ant. 1.8 ( = ou)x oi(=o/n t' e)sti\ e)moi\ swqh=nai. With h)=n the sentence virtually has the force of ou)x oi(=o/n t' h(=n swqh=nai kai\ h)/|dei she could not be saved and she knew it). So

e)/legon ou) kalw=s th\n *(ella/sa e)leuqerou=n au)to/n, ei) a)/ndras die/fqeiren they said that he was not freeing Greece in the right way if he put men to death
T. 3.32 ( = e)leuqeroi=s, diafqei/reis), tou\s fuga/das e)ke/leuse su\n au)tw=| strateu/esqai, u(posxo/menos au)toi=s, ei) kalw=s katapra/_ceien e)f' a(\ e)strateu/eto, mh\ pro/sqen pau/sesqai pri\n au)tou\s kataga/goi oi)/kade he urged the exiles to make the expedition with him, promising them that, if he should succeed in accomplishing the purposes of his campaign, he would not cease until he had brought them back to their homes
X. A. 1.2.2 ( = h)\n katapra/_cw e)f' a(\ strateu/omai, ou) pau/somai pri\n a)\n kataga/gw),

a)poqanw\n e)dh/lwsen o(/ti ou)k a)lhqh= tau=ta h)=n he showed by his death that this was not true
L. 19.52 ( = e)sti/),

e)/fh ei)=nai par' e(autw=| o(/son mh\ h)=n a)nhlwme/non he said that he had in his possession all that had not been expended
D. 48.16 ( = par' e)moi/ e)stin o(/son mh\ e)/stin a)nhlwme/non), e)n pollh=| dh\ a)pori/a| h)=san oi( *(/ellhnes,

e)nnoou/menoi me\n o(/ti e)pi\ tai=s basile/ws qu/rais h)=san the Greeks were accordingly in great perplexity on reflecting that they were at the king's gates
X. A. 3.1.2 (i.e. they were there in fact and they knew it).
a. The use of past tenses of historical narration instead of present tenses of direct discourse occurs, in simple sentences, especially after verbs of knowing, perceiving, showing, and verbs of emotion (rarely after verbs of saying w. o(/ti).
b. Such inserted statements of fact are often difficult to distinguish from indicatives in indirect discourse; and the two forms of expression may occur in the same sentence (
X. C. 4.2.35-36). The common explanation of the use of the imperfect and pluperfect for the present and perfect is that Greek had the same assimilation of tense as English.
c. Except in indirect questions, the optative of indirect discourse is unknown to Homer. (ei)pei=n w(s e)/lqoi w 237 may be considered as interrogative.) After primary or secondary tenses Homer employs, in the dependent clause, the same past tense that would have been used in an independent clause, from the point of view of the speaker, and not the tense which would have been used in direct discourse from the point of view of the subject of the main clause. Thus, gi/gnwskon d\ ( = o(/ti)

dh\ kaka\ mh/deto I knew that he was planning evil
g 166 (i.e kaka\ e)mh/deto kai\ e)gi/gnwskon he was planning evil and I knew it). In Attic we should commonly have mh/detai or mh/doito. After secondary tenses the future is usually expressed in Homer by e)/mellon and the infinitive, as

ou)de\ to\ h)/|dh, o(\ ou) pei/sesqai e)/mellen nor did he know this, that she had no thought to comply
g 146.
d. That this use of statements of fact standing outside indirect discourse is optional only, is seen from a comparison of the first example in 2624 with

kalw=s ga\r h)/|dein w(s e)gw\ tau/th| kra/tisto/s ei)mi for he knew full well that I am first-rate in this line
Ar. Vesp. 635 and with

h)/|dei au)to\n o(/ti me/son e)/xoi tou= *persikou= strateu/matos he knew that he held the centre of the Persian army
X. A. 1.8.21.

§2625
An optative with or without a)/n is regularly retained after o(/ti (w(s).

e)di/daskon w(s . . . sunestrateu/onto o(/poi h(goi=nto they showed that they always followed them in their campaigns wherever they led
X. H. 5.2.8 ( = sunestrateuo/meqa, o(/poi h(goi=sqe, cp. 2568),

a)pekri/_nato . . . o(/ti pro/sqen a)\n a)poqa/noien h)\ ta\ o(/pla paradoi/hsan he replied that they would sooner die than surrender their arms
X. A. 2.1.10 ( = a)\n a)poqa/noimen, paradoi=men).

§2626
In some cases the optative with a)/n in temporal and relative sentences is used to represent the subjunctive with a)/n; but many scholars expel a)/n.

parh/ggeilan au)toi=s mh\ pro/teron e)piti/qesqai pri\n a)\n tw=n sfete/rwn h)\ pe/soi tis h)\ trwqei/h they gave orders to them that they should not attack before some one of their number had either fallen or been wounded
X. H. 2.4.18. Cp. 2421.

§2627
An optative occasioned by indirect discourse may stand after a primary tense when it is implied that the thought quoted has been expressed in the past.

le/gei o( lo/gos o(/ti *neopto/lemos *ne/stora e)/roito the story goes that Neoptolemus asked Nestor
P. Hipp. M. 286b. This may be expressed by le/getai ei)pei=n o(/ti. Cp.

le/getai ei)pei=n o(/ti bou/loito it is reported that he said that he wished
X. C. 1.4.25.
a. The historical present is a secondary tense:

oi( de\ pemfqe/ntes le/gousi *ku/_rw| o(/ti mi_soi=en tou\s *)assuri/ous and those who had been sent told Cyrus that they hated the Assyrians
X. C. 4.2.4.

§2628
Indirect discourse may be introduced by o(/ti (w(s) and then pass into the infinitive as if the introductory verb had required the infinitive.
h( de\ a)pekri/_nato o(/ti bou/loito me\n a(/panta tw=| patri\ xari/zesqai, a)/_konta me/ntoi to\n pai=da xalepo\n ei)=nai nomi/zein ( = nomi/zoi)

katalipei=n she answered that she wished to do everything to oblige her father, but that she considered it unkind to leave the child behind against his inclination
X. C. 1.3.13.
a. It is unusual to have the infinitive first, and then o(/ti (
T. 5.65).
b. One and the same clause may even begin with o(/ti (w(s) and then (sometimes after a parenthesis) be continued by an infinitive, less often by a participle. Thus, a)kou/w o(/ti (omitted in one Ms.)

kai\ sunqhreuta/_s tinas tw=n pai/dwn soi gene/sqai au)tou= I hear too that some of his sons became your companions in the chase
X. C. 2.4.15. Continuation with a participle in
T. 4.37.

§2629
An optative dependent on o(/ti (w(s) may be followed, in a parenthetical or appended clause (often introduced by ga/r or ou)=n), by an independent optative, which is used as if it itself directly depended on o(/ti (w(s).
e)/legon polloi\ . . . o(/ti panto\s a)/cia le/goi *seu/qhs: xeimw\n ga\r ei)/h kai\ ou)/te oi)/kade a)poplei=n tw=| tau=ta boulome/nw| dunato\n ei)/h ktl. many said that what Seuthes said was of much value; for it was winter and neither was it possible for any one who so desired to sail home, etc.
X. A. 7.3.13 (here we might have had xeimw=na ga\r ei)=nai by 2628).
a. Such an independent optative may also follow an infinitive in indirect discourse (
L. 13.78), an indicative after o(/ti (
Is. 8.22), or a participle (
Is. 9.5). After an optative in indirect discourse the appended clause may contain an indicative (
X. A. 6.2.10,
I. 17.21).

§2630
An infinitive in indirect discourse may follow a sentence which merely involves the idea of indirect statement.
o( de\ au)tou\s ei)s *lakedai/mona e)ke/leuen i)e/nai: ou) ga\r ei)=nai ku/_rios au)to/s he recommended them to go to Lacedaemon; for (he said that) he was not himself empowered to act
X. H. 2.2.12.

§2631
In subordinate temporal and relative clauses the infinitive is often used for the indicative or optative by attraction to an infinitive standing in the principal clause after a verb of saying. In some cases e)/fh may be mentally inserted.
e)/fh . . . e)peidh\ de\ gene/sqai e)pi\ th=| oi)ki/a| th=| *)aga/qwnos, a)new|gme/nhn katalamba/nein th\n qu/ran he said that, when he arrived at the house of Agathon, he found the door open
P. S. 174d ( = e)peidh\ e)geno/mhn, katalamba/nw). See also the sentence quoted in 1228 b, end. So ou(=toi de\ e)/legon o(/ti pollou\s fai/h *)ariai=os ei)=nai *pe/rsa_s e(autou= belti/_ous, ou(\s ou)k a)\n a)nasxe/sqai au)tou= basileu/ontos and they said that Ariaeus said that there were many Persians better than himself, who would not endure his being king
X. A. 2.2.1 ( = polloi/ ei)si e)mautou= belti/_ous, oi(\ ou)k. a)\n a)na/sxointo e)mou= b.). Here the relative is equivalent, in sense, to kai\ tou/tous. The infinitive occurs even in clauses with ei) (
T. 4.98, and often in Hdt.), and with dio/ti (
Hdt. 3.55).
a. The infinitive is rare in such relative clauses as

diori/zousi safw=s e)n oi(=s e)cei=nai a)poktinnu/nai they make a clear distinction in cases where it is permitted to kill
D. 23.74.

§2632
For the sake of variation, a mood of the direct form may be used in the same sentence with a mood of the indirect. The main verb may be kept in the direct form, while the subordinate verb becomes optative, or, less often, the subordinate verb may be retained in the direct form though the main verb becomes optative.

ou(=toi e)/legon o(/ti *ku=ros me\n te/qnhken, *)ariai=os de\ pefeugw\s . . . ei)/h these said that Cyrus was dead but that Ariaeus had fled
X. A. 2.1.3 (here we might have had teqnh/koi or pe/feuge), ai( de\ a)pekri/_nanto o(/ti ou)k e)ntau=qa ei)/h, a)ll' a)pe/xei o(/son parasa/gghn and they replied that he was not there but was a parasang distant 4. 5. 10 (here we might have e)sti/ or a)pe/xoi),

e)do/kei dh=lon ei)=nai o(/ti ai(rh/sontai au)to\n ei)/ tis e)piyhfi/zoi it seemed to be clear that they would elect him if any one should put it to vote
X. A. 6.1.25 (here we might have ai(rh/sointo or e)a\_n e<*>piyhfi/zh|), e)/lecas . . . o(/ti me/giston ei)/h maqei=n o(/pws dei= e)cerga/zesqai e(/kasta you said that it was essential to learn how it is necessary to conduct each process
X. O. 15.2 (here e)sti/ or de/oi might have been used),

parh/ggeilan, e)peidh\ deipnh/saien, . . . a)napau/esqai kai\ e(/pesqai, h(ni/k' a)/n tis paragge/llh| they gave orders that, when they had supped, they should rest and follow when any one gave the command
X. A. 3.5.18 (here we might have had e)peida\n deipnh/swsi or h(ni/ka paragge/lloi). Other examples 2619. Subjunctive (in some Mss.), then optative:
X. A. 7.7.57.

§2633
The idea conveyed by an imperative or a hortatory (or even deliberative) subjunctive of direct discourse may be set forth in the infinitive by a statement as to what ought to be.
a. In an infinitive dependent on a verb of will or desire (such as ask, command, advise, forbid, etc. 1992) which does not properly take the construction of indirect discourse.
ei(=s de\ dh\ ei)=pe (1997) . . .

strathgou\s me\n e(le/sqai a)/llous and some one urged that they choose other generals
X. A. 1.3.14 (cp. e(/lesqe or e(/lwmen),

a)phgo/reue mhde/na ba/llein he forbade any one to shoot
X. C. 1.4.14 (cp. mhdei\s balle/tw).
N.—Here may be placed the infinitive after h(gou=mai, nomi/zw, oi)/omai in the sense of dokw= I think it proper (or necessary); as

w)/|onto a)pie/nai they thought that they should retire
X. H. 4.7.4 (cp. a)pi/wmen).
b. In an infinitive dependent on e)/fh xrh=nai (dei=n), as

e)/fh . . . xrh=nai plei=n e)pi\ *sura_kou/sa_s he said that they ought to sail to Syracuse
T. 4.69.
c. In the simple infinitive, as ta\_s me\n e)pistola\_s . . . a)ne/gnwsan, e)n ai(=s pollw=n a)/llwn gegramme/nwn kefa/laion h)=n pro\s *lakedaimoni/ous ou) gignw/skein o(/ ti bou/lontai . . . ei) ou)=n ti bou/lontai safe\s le/gein, pe/myai meta\ tou= *pe/rsou a)/ndras w(s au)to/n they read the dispatches, in which of much besides therein written to the Lacedaemonians the substance was that the king did not understand what they wanted; if therefore they wished to make explicit statements, let them send men to him in company with the Persian
T. 4.50. Cp.
T. 1.27. 1 me/nein = mene/tw.

§2634
Long sentences (and even some short complex sentences), or a series of sentences, in indirect discourse depending on a single verb of saying or thinking, are uncongenial to the animated character of Greek, which resists the formal regularity of Latin. Some long speeches in indirect discourse do, however, appear, e.g. Andoc. 1. 3842, Thuc. 6. 49, Xen. C. 8. 1. 10-11, Plato R. 614 b (the entire Symposium is given in reported form). To effect variety and to ensure clearness by relieving the strain on the leading verb, Greek has various devices.
a. e)/fh (e)/lece, ei)=pen, h)/reto) is repeated, e.g.
T. 7.48.
b. The indirect form is abandoned for the direct form, e.g.
X. A. 1.3.14, 1. 9. 25, 4. 8. 10; often with a change, or repetition, of the verb of saying (
X. A. 5.6.37,
X. H. 2.1.25).
c. e)/fh xrh=nai (dei=n) or e)ke/leuse is inserted or repeated (
T. 6.49. 4).
N. 1.—Transition from direct to indirect discourse is rare (
X. A. 7.1.39, cp.
X. C. 3.2.25).
N. 2.—An interrogative clause always depends immediately on the introductory verb, hence such clauses do not occur in the course of a long sentence in indirect discourse.

§2635
EXAMPLES OF INDIRECT DISCOURSE

e)/fh ga\r ei)=nai me\n a)ndra/podo/n oi( e)pi\ *lauri/w|, dei=n de\ komi/sasqai a)pofora/_n. a)nasta\_s de\ prw\| yeusqei\s th=s w(/ra_s badi/zein: ei)=nai de\ panse/lhnon. e)pei\ de\ para\ to\ propu/laion tou= *dionu/_sou h)=n, o(ra=n a)nqrw/pous pollou\s a)po\ tou= *)widei/ou katabai/nontas ei)s th\n o)rxh/stra_n: dei/sa_s de\ au)tou/s, ei)selqw\n u(po\ th\n skia\_n kaqe/zesqai metacu\ tou= ki/onos kai\ th=s sth/lhs e)f' h(=| o( strathgo/s e)stin o( xalkou=s. o(ra=n de\ a)nqrw/pous to\n me\n a)riqmo\n ma/lista tria_kosi/ous, e(sta/nai de\ ku/klw| a)na\ pe/nte kai\ de/ka a)/ndras, tou\s de\ a)na\ ei)/kosin: o(rw=n de\ au)t w=n pro\s th\n selh/nhn ta\ pro/swpa tw=n plei/stwn gignw/skein. kai\ prw=ton me/n, w)= a)/ndres, tou=q' u(pe/qeto deino/taton pra=gma, oi)=mai, o(/pws e)n e)kei/nw| ei)/h o(/ntina bou/loito *)aqhnai/wn fa/nai tw=n a)ndrw=n tou/twn ei)=nai, o(/ntina de\ mh\ bou/loito, le/gein o(/ti ou)k h)=n. i)dw\n de\ tau=t' e)/fh e)pi\ *lau/rion i)e/nai, kai\ th=| u(sterai/a| a)kou/ein o(/ti oi( *(ermai= ei)=en perikekomme/noi: gnw=nai ou)=n eu)qu\s o(/ti tou/twn ei)/h tw=n a)ndrw=n to\ e)/rgon. h(/kwn de\ ei)s a)/stu zhthta/_s te h)/dh h(|rhme/nous katalamba/nein kai\ mh/nu_tra kekhru_gme/na e(kato\n mna=s.—Andocides 1. 38. For Dioclides said that he had a slave at Laurium, and that he had to fetch a payment due him. Rising early he mistook the time and set out, and there was a full moon. When he was by the gateway of the sanctuary of Dionysus, he saw a body of men coming down from the Odeum into the orchestra, and through fear of them he betook himself into the shade and sat down between the column and the block on which the Bronze General stands. He saw about three hundred men, some standing round about in groups of fifteen, others in groups of twenty. On seeing them in the moonlight he recognized the faces of most. In the first place, gentlemen, he has concocted this most extraordinary tale, in order, as I believe, that it might be in his power to include among these men any Athenian he wished, or to exclude any he did not wish. On seeing this he said he went to Laurium, and on the day after heard that the statues of Hermes had been mutilated. So he knew forthwith that it was the work of these men. On his return to the city he found that commissioners of inquiry had already been appointed and that a hundred minae had been offered as a reward.

## INTERROGATIVE SENTENCES (QUESTIONS)

§2636
Questions are either direct (independent) or indirect (dependent). Thus, ti/s e)/lece tau=ta; who said this? e)rwtw= o(/stis e)/lece tau=ta I ask who said this.

§2637
Questions may have the assertive form with the interrogation expressed simply by the tone of the voice, or may be introduced by an interrogative pronoun, adjective, adverb, or particle.
a. A question gains in animation and has its emphatic part clearly marked if the interrogative word is placed late in the sentence. Thus, h(de/a de\ kalei=s ou) ta\ h(donh=s mete/xonta; you call pleasant, do you not, that which participates in pleasure?
P. Pr. 351d, to\ peinh=n e)/leges po/teron h(du\ h)\ a)nia_ro\n ei)=nai; did you say that to be hungry was pleasant or painful?
P. G. 496c.

§2638

Yes and No Questions (or sentence-questions) are asked by the verb (whether a given thing is or is done). Such questions are commonly introduced by an interrogative particle. Pronoun-questions (or word-questions) are asked by an interrogative pronoun, adjective, or adverb (who, what, where, when, how).
a. A sentence-question may follow a word-question; as ti/ dokou=sin u(_mi=n, w)= a)/ndres; a)=ra/ ge o(moi/ws u(_mi=n peri\ tw=n a)dikou/ntwn gignw/skein ktl.; what do you think of your ancestors, gentlemen of the jury? Do they seem to entertain the same sentiments with yourselves about wrong-doers? Lyc. 119.

§2639

Deliberative Questions ask what is to be done or what was to be done. Questions asking what is to be done in the present or future are expressed by the deliberative subjunctive (negative mh/, 1805), by dei= or xrh/ and the infinitive, by the verbal in -te/on with e)sti/ (1808) or by the deliberative future (1916). Questions asking what was to be done are expressed by xrh=n (e)xrh=n) or e)/dei with the infinitive, or by the verbal in -te/on with h)=n. In direct questions the optative is not used to denote what was to be done.

§2640

Rhetorical Questions are questions asked for effect and not for information, since the speaker knows the answer in advance and either does not wait for, or himself gives, the answer. Thus, a)ll' ou)k e)/sti tau=ta: po/qen; but this is not so. How can it be?
D. 18.47,

ti/ ou)=n ai)/tion ei)=nai u(polamba/nw; e)gw\ u(_mi=n e)rw= what then do I regard as the explanation? I will tell you
P. A. 40b. Such questions are often introduced by mh/ (2651 b). Other examples 2638 a, 2641.
a. Rhetorical questions awaken attention and express various shades of emotion; and are often used in passing to a new subject. Such questions are very rare in Lysias, somewhat frequent in Plato, common in Isaeus, highly developed in Demosthenes. The rhetorical question is much more favoured in Greek than in English.

## DIRECT (INDEPENDENT) QUESTIONS

§2641
Any form of statement (2153) may be used as a direct question. The interrogative meaning may be indicated only by the context, or it may be expressed by placing an emphatic word first or by the use of certain particles (2650, 2651).
e)gw\ ou)/ fhmi; I say no?
P. G. 446e, ou) ga\r a)pekri_na/mhn o(/ti ei)/h h( kalli/sth; for did I not answer that it was the noblest art? 448 e, *(/ellhnes o)/ntes barba/rois douleu/somen; shall we, who are Greeks, be subject to barbarians? E. fr. 719, h(gou/meqa/ ti to\n qa/naton ei)=nai; do we regard death as anything?
P. Ph. 64c. Cp. 1831, 1832.

§2642
Questions which cannot be answered by yes or no are introduced by interrogative pronouns, adjectives or adverbs (340, 346), usually without any interrogative particle, and may have any form of the simple sentence.
ti/ ou)=n keleu/w poih=sai; what then do I urge you to do?
X. A. 1.4.14, po/son . . . a)/pestin e)nqe/nde to\ stra/teuma; how far distant from here is the army?
X. C. 6.3.10, pw=s ei)=pas; what (lit. how) did you say?
P. G. 447d, ti/ a)\n au)tw=| ei)=pes; what would you have said to him?
P. R. 337c.

§2643
An interrogative pronoun or adverb often depends on a participle and not on the main verb of the sentence. Thus, ti/ ou)=n poih/santos katexeirotonh/sate tou= *eu)a/ndrou; for what act then did you condemn Evander?
D. 21.176, (*)olu/nqioi) oi(\ ti/ pepoihko/tos au)toi=s *fili/ppou pw=s au)tw=| xrw=ntai; for whom what has Philip done and how do they treat him? 23. 107. Cp. 2147 d. On ti/ paqw/n see 2064 a.

§2644
A subordinate clause introduced by a conjunction or a relative pronoun may suddenly change into a direct pronoun-question, though the construction of the clause remains unaltered. Thus, e)peidh\ peri\ ti/nos *)aqhnai=oi dianoou=ntai bouleu/esqai, a)ni/stasai sumbouleu/wn; when the Athenians are intending to deliberate (lit. about what?) do you get up to give them advice? P. Alc. I. 106 c, po/q' a(\ xrh\ pra/_cete; e)peida\n ti/ ge/nhtai; when will you do what you ought to do? in what event? (lit. when what shall have happened?)
D. 4.10.
a. Here belong the elliptical phrases i(/na ti/, w(s ti/ (scil. ge/nhtai, 946), o(/ti ti/ (scil. gi/gnetai). Thus, i(/na ti/ tau=ta le/geis; why (lit. that what shall happen?) do you say this?
P. A. 26d, e)/ti kai\ tou=t' au)tw=| prosqh/sete; o(/ti ti/; will you give him this distinction too in addition? for what reason?
D. 23.214.

§2645
Two questions may be condensed into one in an interrogative sentence by placing an interrogative between the article and its noun. Thus, e)gw\ ou)=n to\n e)k poi/a_s po/lews strathgo\n prosdokw= tau=ta pra/_cein; am I waiting for a general to do this? From what city?
X. A. 3.1.14.

§2646
Two or more interrogative pronouns, without a connective, may occur in the same sentence (question within a question). Thus, a)po\ tou/twn ti/s ti/nos ai)/tio/s e)sti genh/setai fanero/n from this it will become clear who is chargeable with what
D. 18.73, e)peida/n ti/s tina filh=|, po/teros pote/rou fi/los gi/gnetai; whenever one person loves another, which one is the lover of which?
P. Lys. 212a.

§2647
With a substantive and the article or with a demonstrative pronoun an interrogative pronoun may be used as a predicate adjective. Here the interrogative sentence is equivalent to an interrogative clause with a dependent (relative) clause (cp. 1169).
poi=on to\n mu=qon e)/eipes; what is the word that thou hast uttered? A 552 (lit. the word being what? In fuller form = poi=o/s e)stin o( mu=qos d\n e)/eipes;), ti/s o( po/qos au)tou\s i(/_keto; what is this longing that has come upon them?
S. Ph. 601, ou(=tos de\ ti/s . . . kratei=; who is this man who holds sway?
S. O. C. 68, ti/nas tou/sd' ei)sorw=; who are these I see?
E. Or. 1347, dia\ sofi/a_n tina\ tou=to to\ o)/noma e)/sxhka. poi/a_n dh\ sofi/a_n tau/thn; thanks to a kind of wisdom I obtained this name. (Thanks to) this wisdom being what? (that is, what is this wisdom?)
P. A. 20d.

§2648

ti/s, ti/, poi=os referring to something mentioned before may take the article; as A. pa/sxei de\ qaumasto/n. B. to\ ti/; A. A strange thing is happening to him. B. (The) what? Ar. Pax 696, A. nu=n dh\ e)kei=na h)/dh . . . duna/meqa kri/_nein. B. ta\ poi=a; A. Now at last we are able to decide those matters. B. (The) what matters?
P. Phae. 277a.

§2649

ti/s, poi=os as adjective pronouns, and pw=s etc., when followed by ou), have the force of an affirmative assertion. Thus, poi/ous lo/gous ou)k a)nhlw/samen; what arguments did we not expend?
I. 8.67 ( = pa/ntas), ti/ kako\n ou)xi/; = pa=n kako/n in 2147 d.

## QUESTIONS INTRODUCED BY INTERROGATIVE PARTICLES

§2650

h)= and a)=ra introduce questions asking merely for information and imply nothing as to the answer expected (neither yes nor no).
h)= te/qnhken *oi)di/pou path/r; is Oedipus' father really dead?
S. O. T. 943, h)= le/gw (delib. subj.); shall I tell you?
X. C. 8.4.10, h)= kai\ oi)/koi tw=n plousi/wn h)=sqa; were you really one of the rich men when you were at home? 8. 3. 36.
a)=r' ei)mi\ ma/ntis; am I a prophet?
S. Ant. 1212, a)=r' *)odusse/ws klu/w; can it be that I am listening to Odysseus?
S. Ph. 976, a)=ra e)qelh/seien a)\n h(mi=n dialexqh=nai; will he really be willing to talk with us?
P. G. 447b.
a. a)=ra is from h)= + a)/ra. h)= is chiefly poetic. Homer uses h)=, not a)=ra. Both particles denote interest on the part of the questioner (often = really? surely?).

§2651

ou), a)=r' ou', ou)kou=n expect the answer yes (nonne), mh/, a)=ra mh/, mw=n ( = mh\ ou)=n) expect the answer no (num).
a. ou)x ou(/tws e)/leges; did you not say so?
P. R. 334b (i.e. ‘I think you did, did you not?’), a)=r' ou)x u(/bris ta/de; is not this insolence?
S. O. C. 883, ou)kou=n . . . eu)= soi dokou=si bouleu/esqai; do they not then seem to you to plan well?
X. C. 7.1.8. ou)kou=n ou) expects the answer no.
b. mh/ ti new/teron a)gge/lleis; no bad news, I hope?
P. Pr. 310b, a)=ra mh\ ai)sxunqw=men; surely we are not ashamed, are we? (or can it be that we should be ashamed?)
X. O. 4.4, mh\ a)pokri/_nwmai; am I not to answer?
P. R. 337b, mw=n ti/ se a)dikei=; surely he has not wronged you, has he? (or can it be that, etc.)
P. Pr. 310d. mw=n ou) expects the answer yes.
c. mw=n is confined to Attic. Since the fact of its composition was lost, we find mw=n ou)=n (
A. Ch. 177) and mw=n mh/ (
P. Lys. 208e).
d. ou) after mh/ or a)=ra mh/ belongs to a single word, not to the sentence (
P. Men. 89c, Lys. 213 d). On mh/ or mh\ ou) with the subjunctive in half-questions, see 1801.
e. a)=ra placed before ou) or mh/ gives greater distinctness to the question. ou) questions ask concerning facts; mh/ questions imply uncertainty or even apprehension, but sometimes are asked merely for effect.
f. ou)/ pou; ou)/ ti/ pou; ou) dh/; ou) dh/ pou mean surely it is not so? Here the negative belongs to the sentence.

§2652

a)/llo ti h)/; is it anything else than? and a)/llo ti; is it not? are used as direct interrogatives. Thus, a)/llo ti h)\ ou)de\n kwlu/_ei parei=nai; there's nothing to hinder our passing, is there? (lit. is there anything else the case than this that nothing prevents, etc.)
X. A. 4.7.5, a)/llo ti filei=tai u(po\ qew=n; is it not loved by the gods?
P. Euth. 10d. Cp. ti/ ga\r a)/llo h)\ kindu_neu/seis e)pidei=cai ktl.; for what other risk will you run than that of showing, etc.? ( = for what else will you do than that you will very likely show?)
X. M. 2.3.17.

§2653

ei)=ta and e)/peita (more emphatic ka)=|ta, ka)/_peita) introduce questions expressing surprise, indignation, irony, etc.; and often indicate a contrast between what a person has or has not done and what is or was to be expected of him. Thus, ei)=ta pw=s ou)k eu)qu\s e)ph/geira/s me; then why did you not rouse me at once?
P. Cr. 43b.

§2654

a)lla/ (a)ll' h)=) introduces a question opposed to an expressed or implied thought of the speaker (especially an objection). Thus, h)/|toun ti/ se kai\ e)pei/ moi ou)k e)di/dous e)/paion; a)ll' a)ph/|toun; a)lla\ peri\ paidikw=n maxo/menos; a)lla\ mequ/wn e)parw/|nhsa; did I ask anything of you and strike you when you would not give it to me? Or did I demand anything back? Or was I quarreling about an object of affection? Or was I the worse for liquor and did I treat you with drunken violence?
X. A. 5.8.4, a)ll' h)=, to\ lego/menon, kato/pin e(orth=s h(/komen; but have we arrived, as the proverb says, late for a feast?
P. G. 447a. Cp. 2785.

§2655

de/ sometimes introduces a suppressed thought, as an objection. Thus, ei)pe/ moi, su\ de\ dh\ ti/ th\n po/lin h(mi=n a)gaqo\n pepoi/hkas; tell me, (but) what good, pray, have you done the State?
D. 8.70.

## DIRECT ALTERNATIVE QUESTIONS

§2656
Direct alternative questions are usually introduced by po/teron (po/tera) . . . h)/ whether . . . or (Lat. utrum . . . an).
po/teron de/dra_ken h)\ ou)/; has he done it or not?
D. 23.79, po/tero/n se/ tis, *ai)sxi/nh, th=s po/lews e)xqro\n h)\ e)mo\n ei)=nai fh=|; shall I say, Aeschines, that you are the enemy of the State or mine? 18. 124 (tis fh=| = fw=, 1805 c), po/tera d' h(gei= . . . a)/meinon ei)=nai su\n tw=| sw=| a)gaqw=| ta\_s ti_mwri/a_s poiei=sqai h)\ su\n th=| sh=| zhmi/a|; do you think that it is better to inflict the proper punishments in your own interest or to your own loss?
X. C. 3.1.15.

§2657

h)/ often stands alone without po/teron (as an without utrum). Thus, e)/lu_e th\n ei)rh/nhn h)\ ou)/; did he break the peace or not?
D. 18.71, h)\n xrh/mata polla\ e)/xh|, e)a=|s ploutei=n h)\ pe/nhta poiei=s; if he has great wealth, do you let him keep on being rich or do you make him poor?
X. C. 3.1.12. So when the first question expresses uncertainty on the part of the questioner; as a)lla\ ti/s soi dihgei=to; h)\ au)to\s *swkra/ths; but who told you the story? (was it some one else) or was it Socrates himself?
P. S. 173a. Cp. 2860.

§2658
An alternative question may follow upon a simple direct (or indirect) question. Thus, po/qen plei=q' u(gra\ ke/leuqa; h)/ ti kata\ prh=cin h)/ mayidi/ws a)la/lhsqe; whence do ye sail over the watery ways? Or is it perchance on some enterprise or by way of rash adventure that ye rove?
i 252. Cp. E 85 (cited in 2660).

§2659

po/teron (po/tera) may stand alone when the second member of the question is implicit in another sentence. Thus, e)nnoh/sate de\ ka)_kei=no, ti/na pro/fasin e)/xontes a)\n prosioi/meqa kaki/_ones h)\ pro/sqen gene/sqai. po/teron o(/ti a)/rxomen; . . . a)ll' o(/ti eu)daimone/steroi dokou=men nu=n h)\ pro/teron ei)=nai; and consider this too: what pretence should we have for allowing ourselves to become less deserving than heretofore? Is it because we are rulers? Or is it because we seem to be more prosperous than before?
X. C. 7.5.83.

§2660

po/teron (po/tera) was originally the neuter of po/teros which of the two? placed in front of a double question and later made a part of the first question. Thus, e)rwtw= po/teron filei= h)\ mi_sei= se I ask which of the two (is true): does he love or does he hate you? Cp. *tu_dei+/dhn d' ou)k a)\n gnoi/hs pote/roisi metei/h, h)e\ meta\ *trw/essin o(mi_le/oi h)= met' *)axaioi=s you could not tell on which side Tydides was, whether he consorted with Trojans or with Achaeans E 85, ti/nes kath=rcan, po/teron *(/ellhnes, ma/xhs, h)\ pai=s e)mo/s; who began the battle—was it the Greeks or my son?
A. Pers. 351, cp.
X. C. 1.3.2.

§2661

h)\ (h)e\) . . . h)= (h)=e), or h)= (h)=e) alone, occurs in Homer, who does not use po/teron. Thus, h)/ r(a/ ti i)/dmen e)ni\ fresi/n, h)=e kai\ ou)ki/; do we know aught in heart, or do we not?
d 632, yeu/somai h)= e)/tumon e)re/w; shall I speak falsehood or the truth? K 534.
a. All the ancient grammarians attest the accentuation of these particles as given above. Modern editors often adopt other accents. h)e/ and h)=e are derived from h)-ve/ and h)=-ve (whence h)/ and h)=). With this enclitic ve/, cp. Lat. -ve.

## MOODS IN DIRECT QUESTIONS

§2662
The moods used in direct questions are the same as those used in statements.
a. Indicative (examples in 2642): sometimes in a past tense with a)/n, as pw=s de\ pa/ntes e)zh/loun a)\n tou\s tura/nnous; but why should all men envy despotic rulers?
X. Hi. 1.9, ei)/ tis e(/na no/mon . . . e)calei/yeien . . . , a)=r' ou)k a)\n a)pektei/nat' au)to/n; if any one should cancel a single law . . ., would you not have put him to death? Lyc. 66. On ti/ ou) or ti/ ou)=n ou) with the aorist, see 1936.
b. Subjunctive: in deliberative questions (2639). On the anticipatory subjunctive in ti/ pa/qw, see 1811.
c. Optative (potential), as ti/s fra/seien a)/n; who can tell?
E. I. T. 577. Without a)/n this optative is rare, as ti/s le/goi; who can tell?
A. Ch. 595. Cp. 1821 a.

## INDIRECT (DEPENDENT) QUESTIONS

§2663
Indirect questions are introduced by interrogative pronouns, adjectives, and adverbs, indefinite relative pronouns and adverbs (340, 346), or by certain interrogative particles (2671, 2675).

§2664
The interrogatives of the direct question may be retained in an indirect question. But it is more common to use the indefinite relatives which (in interrogative sentences) are employed only in indirect questions.

h)rw/twn au)tou\s ti/nes ei)=en they asked them who they were
X. A. 4.5.10 ( = ti/nes e)ste/;), h)rw/twn o(/ ti e)sti\ to\ pra=gma I asked what the matter was 5. 7. 23 ( = ti/ e)sti;), h)rw/ta_ au)to/n po/son xru_si/on e)/xoi he asked him how much money he had 7. 8. 1 ( = po/son e)/xeis;), h)rw/twn au)to\n to\ stra/teuma o(po/son ei)/h they asked him how large the army was 4. 4. 17 ( = po/son e)sti/;),

a)porw=n poi= tra/poito e)pi\ lo/fon tina\ katafeu/gei being in doubt whither he should turn, he fled to a hill
X. C. 3.1.4 ( = poi= tra/pwmai;),

h)/|dei de\ ou)dei\s o(/poi strateu/ousin but no one knew where they were going to march
T. 5.54 ( = poi= strateu/omen;).

§2665
The use of the direct interrogatives is a relic of original juxtaposition, e.g. ei)pe/ moi, poi=o/n ti nomi/zeis eu)se/beian ei)=nai; tell me, what sort of a thing do you think holiness is?
X. M. 4.6.2. The interrogative force of the indefinite relatives is derived, not from any interrogative idea in these words, but from the connection in which they stand.

§2666
An indirect interrogative is often used in the same sentence after a direct interrogative. Thus,

ou)k oi)=da ou)/t' a)po\ poi/ou a)\n ta/xous ou)/te o(/poi a)/n tis feu/gwn a)pofu/goi ou)/t' ei)s poi=on a)\n sko/tos a)podrai/h ou)/q' o(/pws a)\n ei)s e)xuro\n xwri/on a)postai/h I do not know with what swiftness of foot nor by fleeing to what quarter a man might escape nor into what darkness he might run away nor how he could withdraw into any stronghold
X. A. 2.5.7. The direct form precedes less often, as ou) ga\r ai)sqa/nomai/ sou o(poi=on no/mimon h)\ poi=on di/kaion le/geis for I do not perceive what you mean by ‘conformable to law’ or what you mean by ‘just’
X. M. 4.4.13.

§2667
Two interrogatives may occur in the same sentence without a connective; as pw=s oi)=den o(poi=a o)poi/ois dunata\ koinwnei=n; how does he know what letters are able to unite with what?
P. Soph. 253a. Cp. 2646.

§2668
After verbs of saying, knowing, seeing, making known, perceiving, etc. (but not after verbs of asking) the simple relatives are found where the indefinite relatives (or the interrogatives) might stand in an indirect question. Where o(/s is so used, it has the force of oi(=os (cp. qualis in such questions); and rarely follows a negative clause, because verbs denoting lack of knowledge are allied in meaning to verbs of asking. The usual forms are e.g. oi)=da/ se o(\s ei)= and ou)k oi)=da/ se o(/stis ei)=. But we find oi)=da/ se o(/stis ei)= and ou)k oi)=da/ se o(\s ei)=. Thus,

pe/mpei . . . ei)pw\n o(\s h)=n he sends . . . telling who he was
X. C. 6.1.46 (here h)=n represents the point of view of the writer),

e)ke/leuse . . . dei=cai o(\s ei)/h he ordered him to explain who he was
D. 52.7, mh/pote gnoi/hs o(\s ei)= mayest thou never come to know who thou art
S. O. T. 1068, o(ra=|s h(ma=s, o(/soi e)sme/n; do you see how many there are of us?
P. R. 327c. So with the adverbs e)/nqa, ou(=, h(=|, w(s, o(/qen; as

th\n o(do\n o(do\n e)/frazen h(=| ei)/h he told where the road was
X. A. 4.5.34. In some cases these sentences may be exclamatory (2685).
a. That the simple relatives are never thus used after verbs of asking indicates that such clauses are not true indirect questions (as in Latin), and that the pronouns have their value as relatives. But some scholars allow an indirect question after all these words except o(/s; and others admit no such limitation.
b. Only in late Greek are the pronouns or adverbs of the indirect form used in direct questions.
c. o(/pws is used occasionally (often in poetry) in the sense of w(s. Thus, mh/ moi fra/z' o(/pws ou)k ei)= kako/s tell me not that (lit. how) thou art not vile
S. O. T. 548.
d. The context must sometimes determine whether a sentence is an indirect question or a relative clause. Thus, without the context, ou)k ei)=xon o(/poi a)postai=en (
X. H. 3.5.10) might mean they did not know to whom ( = h)gno/oun pro\s ti/nas) to revolt or they had no allies to whom ( = pro\s ou(/s) to revolt. But the present or aorist optative in relative final clauses is rare; cp. 2554 c.

§2669
An indirect question may depend (especially in poetry) on an ide<*> involved in the principal verb; or may depend on a verb to be supplied. Thus,

w(/ste m' w)di/_nein ti/ fh/|s so that I am in travail to know thy meaning
S. Aj. 794, o(pote/rws ou)=n soi . . . a)re/skei in whatever way it pleases you (scil. h(de/ws a)\n a)kou/saimi)
P. R. 348b.

§2670
The indefinite relative is commonly used when a question is repeated by the respondent before his reply. Here you ask? is supplied in thought. Thus, A. a)lla\ ti/s ga\r ei(=; B. o(/stis; poli/_ths xrhsto/s A. But who are you, pray? B. Who am I? an honest burgher
Ar. Ach. 594, pw=s dh/; fh/sw e)gw/. o(/pws; fh/sei how are you? I will say; How am I? he will say Hippocrates 1. 292 c.

§2671
Simple indirect questions are introduced by ei) whether, less often by a)=ra.

e)rwtw=ntes ei) lh|stai/ ei)sin asking whether they are pirates
T. 1.5, tou=ton oi)=sq' ei' zw=n kurei=; dost thou know whether he is alive?
S. Ph. 444,

h)/reto au)to\n ei) blhqei/h he asked him whether he had been struck
X. C. 8.3.30 ( = e)blh/qhs;), fo/bos ei) pei/sw de/spoinan e)mh/n I am afraid (about the question) whether I can persuade my mistress
E. Med. 184 (2234),

i)/dwmen a)=r' ou(twsi\_ gi/gnetai pa/nta let us see whether everything is thus produced
P. Ph. 70d. With the deliberative subjunctive:

e)panerome/nou *kthsifw=ntos ei) kale/sh| *dhmosqe/nhn when Ctesiphon was asking if he was to call Demosthenes
Aes. 3.202 ( = kale/sw;).
a. ei) has an affirmative force (whether) or a negative force (whether . . . not). The latter is seen e.g. after verbs expressing uncertainty or doubt, as after ou)k oi)=da. Thus,

ei) me\n dh\ di/kaia poih/sw, ou)k oi)=da I don't know whether I shall do what is right
X. A. 1.3.5 (i.e. I may possibly not do what is right). The assumption is affirmative in

ta\ e)kpw/mata . . . ou)k oi)=d' ei' *xru_sa/nta| toutw|i+\ dw= I don't know whether I must not give the cups to Chrysantas here
X. C. 8.4.16 (i.e. I think I shall give them).
b. The interrogative use of ei) is derived from the conditional meaning if, as in su\ de\ fra/sai ei)/ me saw/seis but do thou tell me whether thou wilt save me A 83 (i.e. ‘if thou wilt save me, tell me so’).

§2672

e)a/_n rarely, if ever, means whether, even after verbs of examining, considering (skopw= e)skeya/mhn, kaqorw=), where its use is best explained by 2354. In form such conditional sentences often approach closely to indirect questions. Thus, cp. ske/yai . . . e)a\_n a)/ra kai\ soi\ sundokh=| a(/per e)moi/ consider if (in case that, on the chance that) you too agree with me (
P. Ph. 64c) with ske/yasqe ei) a)/ra tou=to . . . pepoih/ka_sin oi( ba/rbaroi consider whether the barbarians have (not) done this
X. A. 3.2.22. Cp.

a)namimnh/skesqai e)a\_n a)lhqh= le/gw to recall to your recollection if I speak the truth
And. 1.37.
a. Some scholars maintain that, in Greek, if was at an early period confused with whether in such sentences as ei)=mi ga\r e)s *spa/rthn . . . no/ston peuso/menos patro\s fi/lou, h)/n pou a)kou/sw strictly for I will go to Sparta to inquire about the return of my dear father, in the hope that I may hear of it
b 359. When the conditional clause was attached to peuso/menos, h)/n acquired (it is claimed) the force of whether. Cp. w)/|xeto peuso/menos . . . ei)/ (v.l. h)/)

pou e)/t' ei)/hs he had gone to inquire whether you were still living
n 415. Cp. German ob, once meaning if, now whether.

§2673
Homer has h)/n, ei)/ ke, ai)/ ke with the subjunctive after verbs of knowing, seeing, saying (but not after verbs of asking). Such cases belong under 2354 b.

§2674

mh/ is sometimes translated by whether after verbs of fear and caution; but such dependent clauses with mh/ are not indirect questions (2221 a). After verbs of seeing, considering and the like (o(rw=, e)nnoou=mai, e)nqu_mou=mai, skopw=) mh/ is properly a conjunction and not the interrogative particle. In such clauses there is an idea of purpose or desire to prevent something or a notion of fear that something is or may be done. Thus,

fronti/zw mh\ kra/tiston h)=| moi si_ga=n I am considering whether it is not best for me to be silent
X. M. 4.2.39,

o(rw=men mh\ *ni_ki/a_s oi)/etai/ ti le/gein let us see whether Nicias is of the opinion that he is saying something important
P. Lach. 196c. That mh/ does not properly mean whether not (indirect question) is clear from the fact that, in these clauses, it is not used of something that is hoped for. Cp. 2676 b.

## INDIRECT ALTERNATIVE QUESTIONS

§2675
Indirect alternative questions are introduced by the particles signifying whether . . . or: po/teron (po/tera) . . . h)/, ei)/te . . . ei)/te, ei) . . . h)/, ei) . . . ei)/te. See also under Particles.
a. po/teron (po/tera) . . . h)/: Thus,

dihrw/ta_ to\n *ku=ron po/teron bou/loito me/nein h)\ a)pie/nai she asked Cyrus whether he wanted to stay or go away
X. C. 1.3.15,

qauma/zw po/tera w(s kratw=n basileu\s ai)tei= ta\ o(/pla h)\ w(s dia\ fili/a_n dw=ra I wonder whether the king asks for our arms as a conqueror or as gifts on the plea of friendship
X. A. 2.1.10.
N.—po/teron . . . h)/ may denote that the second alternative is more important than the first. po/teron is omitted when the introductory clause contains the adjective po/teros (
X. C. 1.3.2).
b. ei)/te . . . ei)/te gives equal value to each alternative. Thus,

th\n ske/yin poiw/meqa ei)/te w)feli/a_n ei)/te bla/bhn pare/xei let us make the inquiry whether it produces benefit or injury
P. Phae. 237d.
N. 1.—In Homer ei)/te . . . ei)/te (ei)/ te . . . ei)/ te) almost always retains the meaning either . . . or (A 65).
N. 2.—The first ei)/te is rarely omitted in prose, as

po/lis ei)/te i)diw=tai/ tines a State or certain individuals
P. L. 864a; more often in poetry, as

lo/goisin ei)/t' e)/rgoisin by words or deeds
S. O. T. 517.
c. ei) . . . h)/ indicates that the second alternative is preferable or more probable. Thus, h)rw/ta_ ei) au)toi=s toi=s a)ndra/si spe/ndoito toi=s i)ou=si kai\ a)piou=sin, h)\ kai\ toi=s a)/llois e)/sointo spondai/ he asked whether he was making a truce merely with the individual men who were coming and going or whether the truce would be with the rest as well
X. A. 2.3.7.
d. ei) . . . ei)/te is like ei)/te . . . ei)/te. Thus,

ei) d' e)/t' e)sti\n e)/myu_xos gunh\ ei)/t' ou)=n o)/lwlen, ei)de/nai bouloi/meq' a)/n we should like to know whether the lady is still alive or dead
E. Alc. 140.
e. h)\ (h)e\) . . . h)= (h)=e) occurs in Homer, as

o)/fr' e)u\ ei)dw= h)e\ ne/on meqe/peis h)= kai\ patrw/io/s e)ssi cei=nos that I may know well whether thou art newly a visitor or art actually an ancestral guest-friend
a 175. Cp. 2661. h)\ . . . h)/ is doubtful in Attic.

## THE NEGATIVES IN INDIRECT QUESTIONS

§2676
The negative of the direct form is usually preserved in indirect questions.

ei)/somai . . . po/teron o( e)/xwn au)to\ ou)k eu)dai/mwn e)sti\n h)\ eu)dai/mwn I shall know whether its possessor is happy or not
P. R. 354c,

ou)k oi)=d' o(/pws fw= tou=to kai\ mh\ fw= I know not how I am to say this and not to say it
E. I. A. 643 ( = pw=s mh\ fw=;).
a. Indirect single questions introduced by interrogative pronouns, adjectives, and adverbs, usually have ou).
b. mh/ appears after verbs of seeing, considering and the like (skopw=, o(rw=, e)nnoou=mai, e)nqu_mou=mai) when there is an idea of purpose or desire to prevent something. Thus, o(ra=te . . . o(/tw| tro/pw| ka/llista a)munei=sqe au)tou\s kai\ mh/te katafronh/santes a)/farktoi lhfqh/sesqe ktl. consider how you may best defend yourselves and may neither be caught off your guard through contempt, etc.
T. 6.33. So also with the potential optative with a)/n; as ti/ ou)=n ou) skopou=men pw=s a)\n au)tw=n mh\ diamarta/noimen; why then do we not consider how we may avoid mistaking them?
X. M. 3.1.10. Indirect questions with mh/ thus belong under mh/ with verbs of fear and apprehension, where mh/ is the negative of the will. Cp. 2674.
c. Indirect questions introduced by ei) have ou) or mh/. Thus,

h)/reto to\n dh=mon ei) ou)k ai)sxu/_nointo he asked the people whether they were not ashamed
Aes. 1.84, h)/reto/ me . . . ei) mh\ me/mnhmai he asked me whether I did not remember 2. 36.
d. In relative clauses joined by kai/ and standing in an indirect question (what . . . and what not), mh/ must be used when the verb is to be supplied with the second clause; but when the verb is repeated, either mh/, or ou) if the antecedent is definite, may be used. Thus,

diagignw/skousin a(/ te du/nantai kai\ a(\ mh/ they distinguish between what they can do and what they cannot
X. M. 4.2.26, oi)=sqa . . . o(po/soi te frouroi\ i(kanoi/ ei)si kai\ o(po/soi mh/ ei)sin you know how many garrisons are advantageously situated and how many are not 3. 6. 10. The antecedent is definite in

a)pe/deicen ou(\s xrh\ dhmhgorei=n kai\ ou(\s ou) dei= le/gein e)n tw=| dh/mw| he showed who must speak in the assembly and who must not speak before the people
Aes. 1.27.
e. As the second member of an alternative question introduced by ei), or not is either h)\ ou) or h)\ mh/. Thus,

skopw=men ei) h(mi=n pre/pei h)\ ou)/ let us consider whether it is proper for us or not
P. R. 451d, nu=n e)/maqon d\ le/geis: ei) de\ a)lhqe\s h)\ mh/, peira/_somai maqei=n now I have made out what you mean; and I will try to make out whether it is true or not 339 a.
f. A shift from mh/ to ou) in sequent alternative indirect questions appears to be due to the desire to attain variety. Thus,

ou) dei= u(_ma=s e)k tw=n tou= kathgo/rou lo/gwn tou\s no/mous katamanqa/nein, ei) kalw=s u(_mi=n kei=ntai h)\ mh/, a)ll' e)k tw=n no/mwn tou\s tou= kathgo/rou lo/gous, ei) o)rqw=s kai\ nomi/mws u(_ma=s dida/skousi to\ pra=gma h)\ ou)/ you must not start from the pleas of the accuser to learn whether your laws have been established well or not, but you must start from the laws to learn whether his pleas set forth the case fairly and legally or not
Ant. 5.14. Cp.
Ant. 6.2,
Is. 8.9,
D. 20.83. Some scholars hold that ou) here lays stress on a negative fact or on something conceived as a negative fact, and that mh/ puts the question abstractly as a mere conception.

## MOODS IN INDIRECT QUESTIONS

§2677
The moods and tenses of indirect questions follow the same rules as govern clauses in indirect discourse. The person may be changed.
After primary tenses, the mood and tense of the direct question are retained (indicative, past indicative with a)/n, deliberative subjunctive, potential optative with a)/n).
After secondary tenses, the mood and tense of the direct form may be retained or the optative may be used instead. The latter is more common. But a past indicative with a)/n always remains unchanged.
a. Direct Form Retained.—

polla/kis e)sko/pei ti/ diafe/rei mani/a_s a)maqi/a_ he often considered in what respect ignorance differed from madness
X. M. 1.2.50,

h)porei=to ti poih/sei he was uncertain what to do
X. A. 7.3.29 ( = ti/ poih/sw, deliberative future, 1916),

e)bouleu/onto ei)/te katakau/swsin . . . ei)/te ti a)/llo xrh/swntai they deliberated whether they should burn them or dispose of them in some other manner
T. 2.4 ( = katakau/swmen, xrhsw/meqa;),

h)rw/thse . . . pou= a)\n i)/doi *pro/cenon he asked where he could see Proxenus
X. A. 2.4.15 ( = pou= a)\n i)/doimi;).
b. Optative:

h)/reto ei)/ tis e)mou= ei)/h sofw/teros he asked whether any one was wiser than I
P. A. 21a ( = e)sti/;),

o(/ ti de\ poih/soi ou) diesh/mhne he did not announce publicly what he was going to do
X. A. 2.1.23 ( = ti/ poih/sw;),

to\n qeo\n e)phrw/twn ei) paradoi=en *korinqi/ois th\n po/lin they questioned the god whether they should surrender the city to the Corinthians
T. 1.25 ( = paradw=men;). Here paradoi=en might represent the aorist indicative, but that tense is usually retained to avoid confusion (exceptionally h)rw/ta_ ti pa/qoien
X. C. 2.3.19; cp.
X. A. 6.3.25,
D. 50.55). An imperfect relatively anterior to the time of the main verb is retained in
D. 30.19.
c. A dubitative subjunctive in an indirect question, when dependent on an optative, may be attracted into the optative; as

e)/leges . . . o(/ti ou)k a)\n e)/xois e)ceqw\n o(/ ti xow=|o sautw=| you were saying that if you went out you would not know what to do with yourself
P. Cr. 45b ( = ti/ xrw=mai e)mautw=|;).
d. Homer has the optative for the indicative due to indirect discourse only in indirect questions; as

ei)/ronto ti/s ei)/h kai\ po/qen e)/lqoi they asked who he was and whence he had come
r 368. See 2624 c.

§2678
After a secondary tense the mood of a direct question may be retained (usually for vividness) in the same sentence with the mood of an indirect question (cp. 2632). Thus,

o(moi=oi h)=san qauma/zein o(/poi pote\ tre/yontai oi( *(/ellhnes kai\ ti/ e)n nw=| e)/xoien they seemed to be wondering to what direction the Greeks would turn and what they had in mind
X. A. 3.5.13,

h)/reto o(/ ti qauma/zoi kai\ o(po/soi au)tw=n teqna=sin he asked what it was that he was astonished at and how many of them were dead
T. 3.113 ( = ti/ qauma/zeis, po/soi teqna=sin;).
a. In some cases there is no apparent reason (apart from desire for variety) for this use of the indicative and optative in the same sentence. Sometimes the indicative may ask for a statement of fact, the optative request an opinion of the person questioned.

§2679
Parallel to 2624 are cases like

h)/|dei o(/pou e)/keito h( e)pistolh/ he knew where the letter had been put
X. C. 2.2.9.

## ANSWERS TO YES AND NO QUESTIONS

§2680

Yes and No questions may be answered in various ways, e.g.:
a. By repeating the verb or another emphatic word with or without one or more confirmative adverbs. Thus,

fh\|s su\ a)mei/nw poli/_thn ei)=nai, o(\n su\ e)painei=s, h)\ o(\n e)gw/; fhmi\ ga\r ou)=n do you assert that the citizen whom you approve is better than the one I approve? I do say so
X. M. 4.6.14,

oi)=sq' ou)=n a)\ le/cai soi . . . qe/lw; ou)k oi)=da dost thou know what I fain would tell thee? No.
E. Hec. 999.
b. By e)gw/, e)/gwge, ou)k e)gw/, ou)k e)/gwge, sometimes with nh\ *di/a or ma\ *di/a.
c. Yes may be expressed by nai/, nai\ ma\ to\n *di/a, ma/lista, fhmi/, pa/nu ge, pa/nu me\n ou)=n, eu)= ge, e)/sti tau=ta, e)/stin ou(/tws, a)lhqh= le/geis, a)lhqe/stata, o)rqw=s ge, komidh=|, etc.
No may be expressed by ou)/, ou)k e)/stin, ou) dh=ta, ou) ma\ *di/a, ou)damw=s, ou)/ fhmi, mh\ ga/r, h(/kista, h(/kista/ ge, etc.
d. In the form of a question: ti/ mh/n; ti/ ga/r; a)lla\ ti/; pw=s; po/qen; pw=s ga\r ou)/;

## EXCLAMATORY SENTENCES

§2681

Direct (independent) exclamatory sentences with a verb expressed (or easily supplied) are formed

§2682
(I) By the relative pronouns oi(=os, o(/sos, or by the relative adverb w(s in exclamations of wonder. The sentences introduced by these words are commonly associated with vocatives or interjections. Cp. 340.

oi(=a poiei=s, w)= e(tai=re what are you about, my friend!

§2683
(II) By the infinitive (2015, 2036).

§2684
Direct exclamations without a verb may be expressed by the vocative or nominative (1288) or by the genitive of cause (1407).

§2685

Indirect (dependent) exclamations form subordinate clauses in sentences which, taken as a whole, are statements (2575. 4). They are introduced by oi(=os, o(/sos, oi(/ws, w(s, oi(=, i(/na. The negative is ou). It is often difficult to distinguish between indirect exclamations and indirect questions introduced by oi(=os or o(/sos. But observe that dependent exclamations are not introduced by the direct interrogatives poi=os, po/sos, pw=s, etc., nor by the indefinite relatives o(poi=os, o(po/sos, o(/pws, etc., both of which classes of words may stand in indirect questions.
a. o(poi=os in
L. 30.4 and o(po/sos in
P. G. 522a are suspected.
b. The introductory verb is sometimes omitted; as w)= miarw/tatos, i(/n' u(pode/du_ken oh the rascal! (to think) where he crept in!
Ar. Vesp. 188.

§2686
Dependent exclamatory clauses follow, as regards mood and tense, the same rules as govern indirect questions (2677). An original indicative remains unchanged after primary tenses of verbs followed by a finite mood, but may become optative after secondary tenses on the principle of indirect discourse.
a. Indicative:

T. 6.30,

§2687
Verbs and other words of emotion (praise, blame, wonder, etc.) and the expression of its results are often followed by a dependent exclamatory clause with oi(=os, o(/sos, w(s, etc. Here a causal sentence would have o(/ti toiou=tos, o(/ti tosou=tos, o(/ti ou(/tws. ## NEGATIVE SENTENCES

§2688
The simple negative particles are ou) and mh/. ou) is the negative of fact and statement, and contradicts or denies; mh/ is the negative of the will and thought, and rejects or deprecates. The difference between the simple negatives holds true also of their compounds ou)/te mh/te, ou)de/ mhde/, ou)dei/s mhdei/s, etc.
a. ta\ ou)k o)/nta is that which does not exist independently of any opinion of the writer: ta\ ou)k o)/nta logopoiei=n to fabricate what does not actually exist
And. 3.35. ta\ mh\ o)/nta is that which is regarded as not existing, that which is dependent on the opinion of the writer, the whole sum of things that are outside of actual knowledge: ta\ mh\ e)o/nta ou)/te o(ra=tai ou)/te gi_nw/sketai that which does not exist is neither seen nor known Hippocrates, de arte § 2; cp. to\ mh\ o)/n
P. R. 478b.
b. The rarer ou)xi/ (ou)-xi/) denies with greater emphasis than ou). The form mhke/ti no longer is due to the analogy of ou)k-e/ti.

§2689

mh/ as the negative of will and thought is used in various expressions involving emotion, as commands, prohibitions, wishes, hopes, prayers, petitions, promises, oaths, asseverations, and the like; in expressions marking condition, purpose, effort, apprehension, cautious assertion, surmise, and fear; in setting forth ideality, mere conceptions, abstractions as opposed to reality or to definite facts; in marking ideas as general and typical; when a person or thing is to be characterized as conceived of rather than real.—mh/ is used not merely when the above notions are apparent but also when they are latent. Greek often conceives of a situation as marked by feeling where English regards it as one of fact; and hence uses mh/ where we should expect ou).
a. mh/ corresponds to the Sanskrit prohibitive particle mā´, which in the Rig Veda is used with the independent indicative of an augmentless aorist or imper fect which has the force of the subjunctive; rarely with the optative. In later Sanskrit mā´ was used with the subjunctive, optative, and imperative.
b. mh/ was originally used only in independent clauses; but later was employed in subordinate clauses, and with dependent infinitives and participles. On the origin of mh/ as a conjunction, see 2222. In Homer mh/ is used especially with the subjunctive, optative, and imperative (i.e. in commands and wishes); rarely with the indicative (in mh\ w)/fellon, in oaths, in questions, after verbs of fearing referring to a past event); with the infinitive when used for the imperative after a verb of saying, etc. when the infinitive expresses a command or a wish, and when a dependent infinitive is used in an oath; with the participle only in connection with a command (
*c 48) or a wish (
d 684).
c. In later Greek (Polybius, Lucian, Dio Chrysostomus, etc.) mh/ has encroached on ou), generally by extension of usages occurring rarely in the classical language. Thus Lucian has mh/ after causal w(s, o(/ti, dio/ti, e)pei/; in relative clauses (sometimes ou)de/n e)stin o(/ti mh/); with participles of cause (even a(/te mh/) or of concession; with participles without the article following an adjective; with the infinitive after verbs of saying and thinking. o(/ti mh/ appears in indirect discourse (complete or partial) where the classical language would use the infinitive or o(/ti with the optative or w(s with the participle; so after verbs of saying and thinking, after verbs of emotion, and even after verbs of knowing.

## POSITION OF ou) AND mh/

§2690

ou) and mh/ are generally placed before the word they negative; but may follow, when emphasis is laid on a particular word, as in contrasts.
u(pola/bh| de\ mhdei/s but let no one suppose T. C. 84,

oi( de\ strathgoi\ e)ch=gon me\n ou)/, suneka/lesan de/ and the generals did not lead them out, but called them together
X. A. 6.4.20, cu/mmaxoi e)geno/meqa ou)k e)pi\ katadoulw/sei tw=n *(ellh/nwn *)aqhnai/ois, a)ll' e)p' e)leuqerw/sei a)po\ tou= *mh/dou toi=s *(/ellhsin we became allies, not to the Athenians, for the purpose of enslaving the Greeks, but to the Greeks for the purpose of freeing them from the Mede
T. 3.10,

a)po/loito me\n mh/ perish indeed —may he not
E. Med. 83.
a. A contrast must be supplied in thought when the negative precedes the article, a relative, a conjunction, or a preposition. Thus,

ei) de\ peri\ h(mw=n gnw/sesqe mh\ ta\ ei)ko/ta but if you pass upon us a sentence that is unjust
T. 3.57, polemei=n de\ mh\ pro\s o(moi/a_n a)ntiparaskeuh\n a)du/natoi unable to carry on a war against a power dissimilar in character to their own 1. 141, a)munou/meqa tou\s polemi/ous ou)k ei)s makra/_n we shall shortly (lit. in no long time) punish the enemy
X. C. 5.4.21, ou) kata\ ko/smon disorderly B 214.
b. The order of the parts of a negative compound may be reversed for strong emphasis; as e)/t' ou)k w)/n ( = ou)ke/ti w)/n)
S. Tr. 161, mi/an ou)k ( = ou)demi/an)
Hdt. 8.119.
c. The negative may be placed in front of an infinitive when English transfers it to another verb in the sentence; as

ei) boulo/meq' h(mei=s mh\ prospoiei=sqai polemei=n au)to\n h(mi=n if we wish to assume that he is not waging war with us
D. 8.58,

h(ma=s ou)d' e)naulisqh=nai e)pitre/peis you do not permit us even to take up our quarters
X. A. 7.7.8 ( = ou)k e)pitre/peis = kwlu/_eis).

## ou) ADHERESCENT

§2691

ou) adherescent (or privative) placed before a verb (or other single word) not merely negatives the meaning of the simple verb but gives it an opposite meaning, the two expressing a single negative idea; as ou)/ fhmi I deny, I refuse (not I say not). ou)/ fhmi is preferred to fhmi\ ou) as nego is preferred to aio non.

§2692
Adherescent ou) is especially common with verbs of saying or thinking, but occurs also with many verbs of will or desire. In such cases ou) goes closely with the leading verb, forming a quasi- compound; whereas it belongs in sense to a following infinitive if an infinitive depends on the leading verb. In Latin actual composition has taken place in nego, nescio, nequeo, nolo.

ou)k e)/fh i)e/nai he refused to go
X. A. 1.3.8, ou)/ fa_sin ei)=nai a)/llhn o(do/n they say that there is no other road 4. 1. 21 (cp. fh\|s h)\ ou)/; yes or no?
P. A. 27d), ti/nas d' ou)k w)/|eto dei=n le/gein; who were those whom he thought ought not to speak?
Aes. 1.28,

a(\ ou)k e)a=te h(ma=s . . . poiei=n what you forbid us to do
X. C. 1.3.10,

ou)k a)cioi= . . . feu/gonta ti_mwrei=sqai he said that it was not right to avenge himself on an exile
T. 1.136.
a. So with ou)/ fhmi and ou) fa/skw deny, refuse ( = a)parnou=mai), ou)k oi)/omai, ou) nomi/zw, ou) dokw=, ou)k e)w= and ou) keleu/w forbid (veto), ou)k a)ciw= regard as unworthy, do not expect that, refuse, ou)x u(pisxnou=mai refuse, ou) prospoiou=mai dissimulo, ou) sumbouleu/w dissuade, advise not to, ou)k e)qe/lw am unwilling, ou)k e)painw= disapprove. This association often persists in participles, as ou)k e)w=n, ou)k e)qe/lwn. Homer has ou)/ fhmi, fhmi\ ou), and ou)/ fhmi ou).

§2693

ou) with the principal verb may be equivalent in sense to mh/ with a dependent infinitive; as ou) sumbouleu/wn *ce/rch| strateu/esqai e)pi\ th\n *(ella/da advising Xerxes not to march against Greece ( = sumbouleu/wn mh\ strateu/esqai)
Hdt. 7.46.

§2694
Analogous to this use with verbs is the use of ou) with adjectives and adverbs.
ou)k o)li/goi = polloi/, ou)k e)la/xistos = me/gistos, ou)x h(=tton = ma=llon, ou)x h(/kista = ma/lista, ou) kalw=s basely, ou)k a)fanh/s famous, ou)k ei)ko/tws unreasonably, ou) peri\ braxe/wn on important matters (cp. 2690 a), regularly ou) pa/nu not at all, as ou) pa/nu xalepo/n easy.

§2695
The origin of adherescent ou) is to be found partly in the unwillingness of the early language to use the negative particle with the infinitive, partly in the preference for a negative rather than a positive assertion, and to the disinclination to make a strong positive statement (litotes, as in some of the cases of 2694), and partly in the absence of negative compounds, the development of which in adjectives and participles (2071 a) was in turn restricted by the use of adherescent ou).

§2696
Adherescent ou) is often found in a protasis with ei) and in other constructions where we expect mh/.
ei) d' a)posth=nai *)aqhnai/wn ou)k h)qelh/samen . . ., ou)k h)dikou=men but if we refused to revolt from the Athenians, we were not doing wrong
T. 3.55,

ei) ou)k e)a=|s if thou forbiddest
S. Aj. 1131 ( = ei) kwlu/_eis), ei) mh\ *pro/cenon ou)x u(pede/canto, e)sw/qhsan a)/n if it had not been that they did not receive Proxenus, they would have been saved
D. 19.74,

ei) me\n ou) polloi\ h)=san if they were few
L. 13.62 (emended by some to ou)=n mh/). e)a\_n ou) is rare, as

e)a/_n te ou) fh=te e)a/_n te fh=te both if you deny it and if you admit it
P. A. 25b (cp.
L. 13.76,
D. 26.24).

§2697
But mh/ often does not yield to ou), as

a)/_nt' e)gw\ fw= a)/_n te mh\ fw= both if I assent and if I do not
D. 21.205,

ou)k oi)=d' o(/pws fw= tou=to kai\ mh\ fw= I know not how I shall say this and not say it
E. I. A. 643, e)a\_n mh\ . . . e)a=te
D. 16.12, and in many cases where mh/ goes closely with the following word, as

## ou) AFTER ei) (e)a/_n）

§2698

ou) is sometimes found in clauses introduced by ei) (e)a/_n).
a. When ou) is adherescent (2696).
b. When there is an emphatic assertion of fact or probability, as where a direct statement is quoted. Thus, ei) de\ ou)de\n h(ma/rthtai/ moi if (as I have shown) no error has been committed by me

E. El. 336, deino\n a)\n ei)/h, ei) oi( me\n e)kei/nwn cu/mmaxoi e)pi\ doulei/a| th=| au(tw=n (xrh/mata)

Is. 14.52; (3) have the force of e)pei/ in the first member, and that of o(/ti in the second member, as

Aes. 3.242; (4) have the force of o(/ti in both members, as
T. 1.35, 1. 121,

f. A bimembered clause introduced by ei) may contain a negative clause with ou) directly opposed to a positive clause; as ei) de\ tw=| me/n, toi=s d' ou)/

g. ei) whether in simple and alternative indirect questions takes either ou) or mh/ (2676 c, e).

§2699
Homer has ei) and the indicative with ou) (12 times) when the subordinate clause precedes the main clause; but usually ei) mh/, when the subordinate clause follows. Thus, ei) de/ moi ou) tei/sousi bow=n e)pieike/) a)moibh/n, du/_somai ei)s *)ai/da_o but if they will not pay a fitting compensation for the cattle, I will go down to Hades
