a. The Homeric ei) ou) with the indicative has been explained either as a retention of the original use, mh/ with that mood being an extension through the analogy of the subjunctive and optative; or because ou) went with the predicate, whereas mh/ was closely attached to ei).

§2700
Homer has ei) ou) (adherescent) with the subjunctive in ei) d' a)\n . . . ou)k e)qe/lwsin *g 289, ei) de/ k' . . . ou)k ei)w=sin *u 139.

§2701
Herodotus has a few cases of ei) ou) with the indicative, as 6. 9; h)\n ou) with the subjunctive is doubtful (6. 133).

## GENERAL RULE FOR mh/

§2702

mh/ stands
1. With the imperative.
2. In clauses with ei), e)a/_n (exceptions, 2698).
3. With the subjunctive, except after mh/ lest, when ou) is used.
4. With the optative, except after mh/ lest, or when the optative has a)/n or is in indirect discourse.
5. With the infinitive, except in indirect discourse.
6. With participles when they have a conditional or general force.

## ou) AND mh/ WITH THE INDICATIVE AND OPTATIVE

## SIMPLE SENTENCES AND INDEPENDENT CLAUSES

§2703
Statements (2153) expressed by simple sentences and independent clauses take ou). Direct questions take either ou) or mh/ (2651). The independent future indicative has mh/ only in questions.

§2704
In wishes mh/ is used with the indicative (1780-1781) or the optative (1814, cp. 2156).

ei)/qe se mh/pot' ei)do/ma_n would that I had never seen thee
S. O. T. 1218, mh/pot' w)/felon lipei=n th\n *sku=ron would that I had never left Scyrus S. Ph 969.

mh\ zw/|hn may I not live
Ar. Eq. 833,

a)naidh\s ou)/t' ei)mi\ mh/te genoi/mhn I neither am nor may I become shameless
D. 8.68,

ou)/t' a)\n dunai/mhn mh/t' e)pistai/mhn le/gein neither could I tell nor may I be capable of telling
S. Ant. 686.
a. That w)/felon takes mh/, not ou), shows that it has lost to a certain extent its verbal nature. In late Greek it even became a particle like ei)/qe.
b. Indirect expressions of wishing with pw=s a)/n and the optative (1832), bouloi/mhn a)/n (1827), e)boulo/mhn (a)/n) with the infinitive, take ou) (1782, 1789).
c. The use is the same in dependent clauses; as e)peidh\ d' a(\ mh/pot' w)/fele (sumbh=nai)

sune/bh but when that happened which I would had never happened
D. 18.320.

## SUBORDINATE CLAUSES IN THE INDICATIVE OR OPTATIVE

§2705
In subordinate clauses mh/ or ou) is used.
a. Final clauses have mh/, as

fi/los e)bou/leto ei)=nai toi=s me/gista duname/nois, i(/na a)dikw=n mh\ didoi/h di/khn he wished to be on friendly terms with men in power in order that he might not pay the penalty for his wrong-doing
X. A. 2.6.21, e)/dei ta\ e)ne/xura to/te labei=n, w(s mhd' ei' e)bou/leto e)du/nato e)capata=n quoted in 2185 c.
b. Object clauses with o(/pws after verbs of effort have mh/, as

fro/ntiz' o(/pws mhde\n a)na/cion th=s ti_mh=s tau/ths pra/_ceis see to it that you do nothing unworthy of this honour
I. 2.37,

e)peme/leto o(/pws mh/te a)/si_toi mh/te a)/potoi/ pote e)/sointo he took care that they should never be without food or drink
X. C. 8.1.43.
c. Conditional clauses regularly have mh/. Thus,

ei) mh\ u(_mei=s h)/lqete, e)poreuo/meqa a)\n e)pi\ basile/a_ if you had not come, we should be marching against the king
X. A. 2.1.4,

ou)k a)pelei/peto au)tou=, ei) mh/ ti a)nagkai=on ei)/h he never left him unless there was some necessity for it
X. M. 4.2.40. So in concessive clauses (2369). On ou) adherescent in conditional clauses see 2696.
d. Relative Clauses, if conditional, have ou) with a definite antecedent, mh/ with an indefinite antecedent (2505). mh/ is thus used when the case in question is typical of a class (mh/ ‘generic’). Thus,

proshmai/nousin a(/ te xrh\ poiei=n kai\ a(\ ou) xrh/ they signify beforehand what one must do and what not
X. C. 1.6.46, a(\ mh\ oi)=da ou)de\ oi)/omai ei)de/nai what I do not know, I do not even think I know
P. A. 21d.
N. 1.—Homer has o(\s (o(/sos) ou) with the indicative (mh/ B 301).
N. 2.—ou) is regular in relative clauses when an opposition is expressed (
T. 1.11. 2), and when a negative clause precedes; as ou)k e)/stin o(/stis (o(/pws) ou) ou)dei\s o(/stis ou), etc. （
X. C. 1.4.25,
X. A. 2.4.3).
e. The expression toiou=tos, o(/s (o(/stis, etc.), when preceded by a negative, takes ou); as tamiei=on mhdeni\ ei)=nai mhde\n toiou=ton, ei)s o(\ ou) pa=s o( boulo/menos ei)/seisi it is necessary that no one shall have (such) a storehouse that anybody who pleases may not enter it
P. R. 416d. But even when no negative precedes, we have ou), when the relative clause makes an assertion or defines attributively; as

suggrafeu\s tw=n lo/gwn . . . toiou=tos, oi(=os ou)dei\s a)/llos ge/gone such a writer of speeches as no one had been
I. 15.35. When the antecedent is general or is thought of in respect of its character we have mh/; as

boulhqei\s toiou=ton mnhmei=on katalipei=n, o(\ mh\ th=s a)nqrwpi/nhs fu/sew/s e)stin wishing to leave behind him such a memorial as would surpass human nature
I. 4.89; cp. 2705 g.
f. Relative clauses of purpose take mh/, as

qala/ssion e)kri/_yat', e)/nqa mh/pot' ei)so/yesq' e)/ti cast me out into the sea where ye may never see me more
S. O. T. 1411,

kru/ya_s' e(auth/n, e)/nqa mh/ tis ei)si/doi hiding herself where no one might see her
S. Tr. 903.
g. Clauses with a relative pronoun referring to an antecedent thought of in respect of its character (of such a sort) take mh/. The use of mh/ characteristic comes from the generic meaning of mh/, i.e. the antecedent is not regarded simply as a person who does something but as a person of such a nature as, one who typifies a class. In such cases o(\s mh/ may refer to a definite person or thing. So especially in relative clauses of cause and result, which ordinarily take ou). Thus,

talai/pwros a)/ra tis su/ ge a)/nqrwpos ei)= . . ., w(=| mh/te qeoi\ patrw=|oi/ ei)si mh/te i(era/ a wretched being art thou then, who hast neither ancestral gods nor shrines
P. Eu. 302b,

yhfi/sasqe toiau=ta e)c w(=n mhde/pote u(_mi=n metamelh/sei pass such a vote that you will never repent of it
And. 3.41,

toiau=ta le/gein . . ., oi(=s mhdei\s a)\n nemesh/sai to use language at which no one could feel just resentment
D. 21.161, o( . . . mhde\n a)\n o)mo/sa_s the man who would not take an oath 54. 40. Sophocles is especially fond of the generic mh/.
h. Consecutive clauses (and consecutive relative clauses) with w)/ste take ou) with the indicative and optative. Thus, (*lakedaimo/nioi) ei)s tou=t' a)plhsti/a_s h)=lqon w(/st' ou)k e)ch/rkesen au)toi=s e)/xein th\n kata\ gh=n a)rxh/n the Lacedaemonians became so insatiate in their desires that they were not satisfied with their empire on the land
I. 12.103,

w(/st' ou)k a)\n au)to\n gnwri/saim' a)\n ei)sidw/n so that I should not recognize him, if I were to see him
E. Or. 379. On toiou=tos o(\s ou) see 2705 e.
i. Oaths and protestations in the indicative with mh/ express a solemn denial or refusal, or repudiate a charge. Thus, i)/stw nu=n *zeu\s . . . mh\ me\n toi=s i(/ppoisin a)nh\r e)poixh/setai a)/llos let Zeus now know (i.e. I swear by Zeus) that no other man shall mount these horses K 329, ma\ th\n *)afrodi/_thn . . . mh\ )gw/ s' a)fh/sw by Aphrodite, far be it from me that I should release you
Ar. Eccl. 999. Cp. 2716.

## mh/ WITH THE SUBJUNCTIVE AND IMPERATIVE

§2706
The subjunctive is a mood of will, and therefore takes mh/.

§2707

Independent clauses take mh/: the hortatory subjunctive (1797), the prohibitive subjunctive (1800), the deliberative subjunctive (1805), the subjunctive of doubtful assertion (1801).
a. The anticipatory subjunctive in Homer takes ou) (1810, cp. 1813).

§2708

Dependent clauses take mh/: final clauses, as

dokei= moi katakau=sai ta\_s a(ma/ca_s . . . i(/na mh\ ta\ zeu/gh h(mw=n strathgh=| it seems to me advisable to burn the wagons that our baggage-train may not be our general
X. A. 3.2.27. Object clauses after verbs of effort, as ou) fula/cesq' o(/pws mh\ . . . despo/thn eu(/rhte; will you not be on your guard lest you find a master?
D. 6.25. So in conditional clauses with e)a/_n, in conditional relative clauses and in relative clauses referring to indefinite time, place, and manner.
a. After mh/ lest, ou) is used (2221).

§2709
The imperative is a mood of will and therefore takes mh/ in prohibitions (1840).
a. The future indicative after interrogative ou) has an imperative sense (1918).

## NEGATIVES OF INDIRECT DISCOURSE

§2710
The negatives of direct discourse are retained in indirect discourse introduced by o(/ti or w(s.

e)nqu_mhqh=nai xrh\ o(/ti ou)dei/s e)stin a)nqrw/pwn fu/sei ou)/te o)ligarxiko\s ou)/te dhmokratiko/s it must be borne in mind that no man by nature is disposed either to oligarchy or to democracy
L. 25.8.

ei)=pe . . . o(/ti ou) peri\ poli_tei/a_s u(_mi=n e)/stai a)lla\ peri\ swthri/a_s, ei) mh\ poih/saiq' a(\ *qhra_me/nhs keleu/oi he said that the question would not be about your constitution but about your safety, if you did not accept the propositions of Theramenes
L. 12.74.
a. In

proei=pen w(s mhdei\s ki_nh/soito e)k th=s ta/cews he gave orders that no one should move from his position
X. H. 2.1.22 mhdei/s is due to the fact that the main verb denotes a command.
On the negative in indirect discourse with the infinitive see 2722, 2737, 2738; with the participle, 2729, 2737, 2738; and in indirect questions, 2676.

## ou) AND mh/ WITH THE INFINITIVE

§2711
The infinitive not in indirect discourse has mh/; the infinitive in indirect discourse has ou), but sometimes mh/. The articular infinitive has mh/. On the use with mh\ ou) see 2742 ff.
a. The ordinary negative of the infinitive is mh/, which could be so used since the infinitive was employed as early as Homer in an imperative sense. ou) with the infinitive in indirect discourse is probably due to the analogy of ou) with the indicative and optative in clauses of indirect discourse introduced by o(/ti (w(s). ou) became the natural negative of indirect discourse as soon as the infinitive came to represent the indicative or optative.

§2712

mh/ is used with the articular infinitive.

para/deigma tou= mh\ u(_ma=s a)dikei=n a warning not to injure you
L. 27.5,

u(pe\r tou= mh\ to\ keleuo/menon poih=sai in order to avoid doing what was commanded
D. 18.204. On to\ (tou=) mh\ ou), see 2744. 9. 10, 2749 b, d.

## ou) AND mh/ WITH THE INFINITIVE NOT IN INDIRECT DISCOURSE

§2713

mh/ is the regular negative after all verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and substantives, which take an infinitive not in indirect discourse. Thus, after verbs and other words denoting ability, fitness, necessity (and their opposites). Cp. 2000-2007.

ei)ko\s sofo\n a)/ndra mh\ lhrei=n it is proper for a wise man not to talk idly
P. Th. 152b,

ta\_s o(moi/a_s xa/ritas mh\ a)ntidido/nai ai)sxro/n it is disgraceful not to repay like services
T. 3.63.

§2714

xrh/ (xrh=n, e)xrh=n) takes either mh/ or ou).

xrh\ mh\ katafronei=n tou= plh/qous one must not despise the multitude
I. 5.79,

xrh=n ou)/ s' a(marta/nein thou oughtst not to do wrong
E. Hipp. 507, xrh= d' ou)/pot'

ei)pei=n ou)de/n' o)/lbion brotw=n it is not right ever to call any son of man happy
E. And. 100.
a. For original ou) xrh/ was substituted (for emphasis) xrh\ ou), where the ou) was still taken with xrh/; ultimately ou) was felt to belong with the infinitive and hence came to be separated from xrh/.
b. dei= takes mh/, as

mh\ o)knei=n dei= au)tou/s they must not fear
T. 1.120. ou) dei= may be used for dei= mh/ (2693). In

dei= ou)x a(plw=s ei)pei=n one must not speak in a general way
I. 15.117 ou)x is adherescent. Note oi)=mai dei=n ou), fhmi\ xrh=nai ou), oi)=mai xrh=nai mh/.

§2715

mh/ is used with the infinitive in wishes and prohibitions. Thus,

qeoi\ poli=tai, mh/ me doulei/a_s tuxei=n ye gods of my country, may bondage not be my lot
A. Sept. 253,

oi(=s mh\ pela/zein do not approach these
A. Pr. 712.

§2716

mh/ is used with the infinitive in oaths and protestations. Thus, i)/stw nu=n to/de gai=a . . . mh/ ti/ toi au)tw=| ph=ma kako\n bouleuse/men a)/llo let earth now know this (i.e. I swear by earth) that I will not devise any harmful mischief to thine own hurt
e 187. Cp. 2705 i.

§2717

mh/ is used with the infinitive of purpose (cp. 2719) or result (2260). Cp. 2759. On e)f' w(=| mh/ see 2279; on w(/ste ou) see 2269.

§2718

mh/ is used when the infinitive stands in apposition (1987), and hence is like to\ mh/ with the infinitive. Thus,

tou=to e(/n e)stin w(=n fhmi, mhde/na a)\n e)n braxute/rois e)mou= ta\ au)ta\ ei)pei=n this is one of the things I maintain—that no one can say the same things in fewer words than I can
P. G. 449c. Cp.
A. Pr. 173, 431, 435,
P. R. 497b. Such cases are not to be confused with mh/ after verbs of asseveration or belief (2725).

§2719

mh/ is used with the infinitive introduced by verbs of will or desire (1991) or by verbs expressing activity to the end that something shall or shall not be done; as

th\n *ke/rku_ran e)bou/lonto mh\ proe/sqai they wished not to give up Corcyra
T. 1.44,

fulakh\n ei)=xe mh/t' e)kplei=n . . . mhde/na mh/t' e)splei=n he kept guard against any one either sailing out or in
T. 2.69.

§2720

Verbs of commanding and exhorting (keleu/w, le/gw, bow=), asking (ai)tw=, a)ciw=), advising (sumbouleu/w), and other verbs of will or desire of like meaning, take mh/.
e)ke/leue . . . mh\ e)reqi/zein he ordered him not to provoke his wrath
P. R. 393e,

e)/legon au)toi=s mh\ a)dikei=n they told them not to commit injustice
T. 2.5,

e)bo/wn a)llh/lois mh\ qei=n they shouted to each other not to run
X. A. 1.8.19, i(_ke/teue mh\ ktei=nai he besought them not to kill him
L. 1.25,

sumbouleu/w soi . . . mh\ a)fairei=sqai a(\ a)\n dw=|s I advise you not to take away what you may have given
X. C. 4.5.32.

§2721

ou) is used after verbs of will or desire only when it is attached to the leading verb or to some particular word; when it marks a contrast inserted parenthetically; where a compound negative takes up ou) used with the leading verb; and when ou)dei/s may be resolved into ou) and ti\s, ou) going with the leading verb. Examples in 2738.

## ou) AND mh/ WITH THE INFINITIVE IN INDIRECT DISCOURSE

§2722

Verbs of saying and thinking take ou) with the infinitive in indirect discourse. Here ou) is retained from the direct discourse.
h(=| (a)na/gkh|)

famen ou)de/na qew=n ou)/te ma/xesqai ta\ nu=n ou)/te maxei=sqai/ pote we declare that no one of the gods either now contends with necessity, or ever will
P. L. 818e ( = ou)dei\s . . . ma/xetai . . . maxei=tai),

le/gontes ou)k ei)=nai au)to/nomoi saying that they were not independent
T. 1.67, ( = ou)/k e)smen),

oi)=mai ga\r a)\n ou)k a)xari/stws moi e)/xein for I think it would not be unattended with gratitude to me
X. A. 2.3.18 ( = ou)k a)\n e)/xoi),

h(gh/santo h(ma=s ou) perio/yesqai they thought that we should not view it with indifference
T. 1.39 ( = ou) perio/yontai),

e)moi\ de\ dokou=sin ou(=toi ou) to\ ai)/tion ai)tia=sqai but these persons seem to me not to blame the real cause
P. R. 329b,

e)no/misen ou)k a)\n du/nasqai me/nein tou\s poliorkou=ntas he thought the besiegers would not be able to hold their position
X. A. 7.4.22 ( = ou)k a)\n du/nainto).

§2723

Verbs of saying and thinking take mh/ in emphatic declarations and expressions of thought which involve a wish that the utterance may hold good. So with fhmi/, le/gw, h(gou=mai, nomi/zw, oi)=mai. Cp. 2725.

fai/hn d' a)\n e)/gwge mhdeni\ mhdemi/an ei)=nai pai/deusin para\ tou= mh\ a)re/skontos but for my part I would maintain that no one gets any education from a teacher who is not pleasing
X. M. 1.2.39,

pa/ntes e)rou=si . . . mhde\n ei)=nai kerdalew/teron a)reth=s all will say that nothing is more profitable than bravery
X. C. 7.1.18, ti/s d' a)\n a)nqrw/pwn qew=n me\n pai=das h(goi=to ei)=nai, qeou\s de\ mh/; who in the world would think that they were the sons of gods and not gods?
P. A. 27d,

a)ph=|san . . . nomi/santes mh\ a)\n e)/ti . . . i(kanoi\ gene/sqai kwlu=sai to\n e)pi\ th\n qa/lassan teixismo/n they departed in the belief that they would no longer prove able to prevent the building of the wall to the sea
T. 6.102.
a. Cp.
P. Th. 155a (fhmi/),
T. 1.139, 6. 49,
P. R. 346e (le/gw),
X. M. 1.2.41,
D. 54.44 (oi)=mai),
X. C. 7.5.59 (nomi/zw),
P. Soph. 230c (dianoou=mai).
b. Cases where the infinitive is in apposition, or depends on an imperative, or occurs after a condition, do not belong here.

§2724

mh/ with the infinitive is often found after verbs denoting an oracular response or a judicial decision actual or implied. Cp. 2725. Thus,

a)nei=len h( *pu_qi/a_ mhde/na sofw/teron ei)=nai the Pythian prophetess made answer that no one was wiser
P. A. 21a (in direct discourse ou)dei\s sofw/tero/s e)sti). So after kri/_nw, as e)/kri_ne mh\ *)ari/stwnos ei)=nai *dhma/rhton pai=da the Pythian prophetess gave decisior that Demaretus was not the son of Ariston
Hdt. 6.66,

ke/krisqe . . . mo/noi tw=n pa/ntwn mhdeno\s a)\n ke/rdous ta\ koina\ di/kaia tw=n *(ellh/nwn proe/sqai you are adjudged to be the only people who would not betray for lucre the common rights of the Greeks
D. 6.10. So katagignw/skw mh/
T. 7.51,
X. C. 6.1.36.

§2725

mh/ is often used with verbs and other expressions of asseveration and belief, after which we might expect ou) with the infinitive in indirect discourse. Such verbs are those signifying to hope, expect, promise, put trust in, be persuaded, agree, testify, swear, etc. The use of mh/ indicates strong assurance, confidence, and resolve; and generally in regard to the future. Cp. 2723.
e)lpi\s u(_ma=s mh\ o)fqh=nai there is hope that you will not be seen
X. C. 2.4.23,

u(pi_sxnou=nto mhde\n xalepo\n au)tou\s pei/sesqai they promised that they should suffer no harm
X. H. 4.4.5,

pisteu/w . . . mh\ yeu/sein me tau/ta_s ta\_s a)gaqa\_s e)lpi/das I trust that these good hopes will not deceive me
X. C. 1.5.13,

qauma/zw o(/pws e)pei/sqhsan *)aqhnai=oi *swkra/thn peri\ qeou\s mh\ swfronei=n I wonder how the Athenians were persuaded that Socrates did not hold temperate opinions regarding the gods
X. M. 1.1.20,

o(mologei= mh\ metei=nai/ oi( makrologi/a_s he acknowledges that he cannot make a long speech
P. Pr. 336b,

au)to\s e(autou= katamarturei= mh\ e)c e)kei/nou gegenh=sqai he proves by his own testimony that he is not his son
D. 40.47,

w)/mosen h)= mh\n mh\ ei)=nai/ oi( ui(o\n a)/llon mhde\ gene/sqai pw/pote he swore that he had no other son and that none other had ever been born to him
And. 1.126,

w)/mnue . . . mhde\n ei)rhke/nai he swore that he had said nothing
D. 21.119,

o)mou=mai mh/pot' . . . a)lech/sein kako\n h)=mar I will swear that I will never ward off the evil day
*f 373. Cp.
Ar. Vesp. 1047, 1281,
And. 1.90, Lyc. 76. With o)/mnu_mi the infinitive may refer to the present, past, or future.

§2726
Such verbs are hope e)lpi/zw; expect e)lpi/zw, prosdokw=, dokw=, oi)/omai, ei)ko/s e)sti; promise u(pisxnou=mai, e)pagge/llomai; swear o)/mnu_mi; agree o(mologw=, sugxwrw=; pledge e)gguw=mai; put trust in pisteu/w; am persuaded pe/peismai; testify marturw=; repudiate a)nai/nomai; threaten a)peilw=, etc.
a. mh/ is regular after verbs of promising; common after verbs of hoping and swearing. With o)/mnu_mi, pisteu/w, pei/qomai, marturw=, etc. there is an idea of deprecation.

§2727

e)pi/stamai and oi)=da usually take mh/ when they denote confident belief ( = I warrant from what I know; cp. pisteu/w mh/, o)/mnu_mi mh/). Thus,

e)ci/stamai mh/ tou to/d' a)gla/i+sma plh\n kei/nou molei=n I assure you this fair offering has not come from any one save from him
S. El. 908 (cp. Ant. 1092). In tosou=to/n g' oi)=da mh/te m' a)\n no/son mh/t' a)/llo pe/rsai mhde/n so much at least I know—that neither sickness nor aught else can undo me (
S. O. T. 1455) the infinitive may be appositional (2718). Cases of i)/sqi mh/ (be assured = I assure you) may have mh/ by reason of the imperative (2737 a). So
S. Ph. 1329.

## ou) AND mh/ WITH THE PARTICIPLE

§2728
The participle has ou) when it states a fact, mh/ when it states a condition. On mh/ due to the force of the leading verb, see 2737.
ou) pisteu/wn since (as, when, etc.) he does not believe, mh\ pisteu/wn if he does not believe,

a)ne/bh e)pi\ ta\ o)/rh ou)deno\s kwlu/_ontos he went up on the mountains since no one hindered him
X. A. 1.2.22, ou)k a)\n du/naio mh\ kamw\n eu)daimonei=n thou canst not be happy if thou hast not toiled E. fr. 461, w(s h(du\ to\ zh=n mh\ fqonou/shs th=s tu/xhs how sweet is life if fortune is not envious
Men. Sent. 563.
a. mh/ with the articular participle is the abridged equivalent of a conditional relative sentence. Thus, in o( mh\ tau=ta poiw=n a)/diko/s e)sti, o( mh\ poiw=n is virtually the generic o(\s a)\n mh\ poih=| or o(/stis mh\ poiei= compressed into a noun.

§2729

ou) is used with a supplementary participle (in indirect discourse) in agreement with a noun (or pronoun, expressed or unexpressed) depending on a verb of knowing, showing, seeing, perceiving, etc. (2106-2115); and also with such supplementary participles (not in indirect discourse) after verbs of emotion (2100), etc. In most such cases o(/ti ou) might have been used.

ou)de/na ga\r oi)=da mi_sou=nta tou\s e)painou=ntas for I know of no one who dislikes his admirers
X. M. 2.6.33, fanero\n pa=sin e)poi/hsan ou)k i)di/a| polemou=ntes they made it clear to all that they were not waging war for their own interests Lyc. 50,

o(rw=si tou\s presbute/rous ou) . . . a)pio/ntas they see that their elders do not depart
X. C. 1.2.8,

ou)dei\s mh/poq' eu(/rh| . . . ou)de\n e)lleifqe/n no one will ever find that anything has been left undone
D. 18.246;

*ku/_rw| h(/deto ou) duname/nw| si_ga=n he rejoiced that Cyrus was unable to remain silent
X. C. 1.4.15.

§2730

e)pi/stamai and oi)=da denoting confident belief may take mh/ for ou). Thus,

e)/coida fu/sei se mh\ pefu_ko/ta toiau=ta fwnei=n kaka/ well do I know that by nature thou art not adapted to utter such guile
S. Ph. 79; cp.
S. O. C. 656,
T. 1.76, 2. 17. This use of mh/ is analogous to that with the infinitive (2727).

§2731

mh/ is used when the reason for an action is regarded as the condition under which it takes place; as ou) tou= ple/onos mh\ sterisko/menoi xa/rin e)/xousin they are not grateful at not being deprived of the greater part of their rights
T. 1.77 ( = ei) mh\ steri/skonto).

§2732
The participle with w(s, w(/sper, a(/te, oi(=on, oi(=a (2085-2087) has ou); as

e)qorubei=te w(s ou) poih/sontes tau=ta you made a disturbance by way of declaring that you did not intend to do this
L. 12.73. The use of ou) shows that there is nothing conditional in the use of w(s though it is often translated by as if. mh/ occurs only after an imperative or a conditional word (2737).

§2733
Participles of opposition or concession (2083) take ou); as

pei/qou gunaici\ kai/per ou) ste/rgwn o(/mws hearken to women albeit thou likest it not
A. Sept. 712.

§2734
The participle with the article has ou) when a definite person or thing is meant, but mh/ when the idea is indefinite and virtually conditional (whoever, whatever); and when a person or thing is to be characterized (of such a sort, one who; 2705 g). Cp. 2052.

oi( ou)k o)/ntes the dead
T. 2.44, oi( ou)k e)qe/lontes the particular persons (or party) who are unwilling
Ant. 6.26,

oi( ou) boulo/menoi tau=ta ou(/tws e)/xein the party of opposition
And. 1.9;

oi( mh\ duna/menoi any who are unable
X. A. 4.5.11 ( = oi(/tines mh\ du/nantai or o(/soi a)\n mh\ du/nwntai),

o( mh\ darei\s a)/nqrwpos ou) paideu/etai he who gets no flogging gets no training
Men. Sent. 422,

o( mh\ le/gwn a(\ fronei= the man who does not say what he thinks
D. 18.282, o( mhde\n a)dikw=n ou)deno\s dei=tai no/mou he who does no wrong needs no law Antiph. 288.

## ou) AND mh/ WITH SUBSTANTIVES AND ADJECTIVES USED SUBSTANTIVELY

§2735

ou) and mh/ are used with substantives and substantivized adjectives with the same difference as with participles. Here the generic mh/ is much more common than ou).

h( tw=n gefu_rw=n . . . ou) dia/lusis the non-destruction of the bridges
T. 1.137, kata\ th\n tw=n xwri/wn a)llh/lois ou)k a)po/dosin because of their non-surrender of the places to each other 5. 35 ( = o(/ti ou)k a)pe/dosan), dia\ th\n tw=n *korinqi/wn ou)ke/ti e)panagwgh/n because the Corinthians no longer sailed out against them 7. 36. Cp. non-regardance (Shakesp.), nonresidences (Milton). So even with concrete nouns: oi( ou)xi\ dou=loi E. fr. 831.

h( mh\ e)mpeiri/a_ lack of experience
Ar. Eccl. 115, o( mh\ i)_a_tro/s he who is not a physician (the non-physician)
P. G. 459b, oi( mh\ plou/sioi whoever are not rich (the non-rich)
P. R. 330a,

ou)k e)/stin e)n toi=s mh\ kaloi=s bouleu/masin ou)d' e)lpi/s in schemes that are unwise there is no place even for hope
S. Tr. 725.
a. The use of the negative here compensates for the absence of negative compounds. Cp. ai( ou)k a)nagkai=ai po/seis unnecessary potations X. R.
L. 5.4.

## ou)dei/s, mhdei/s

§2736

ou)dei/s, ou)de/n denote that which is actually non-existent or of no account; mhdei/s, mhde/n denote that which is merely thought of as nonexistent or of no account. Both are used as the opposite of ti\s or ti\ (ei)=nai) to be somebody (something, cp. 1269). The neuter forms are often used of persons; to\ mhde/n (indeclinable) is used of persons and things.
w)= nu=n me\n ou)dei/s, au)/rion d' u(pe/rmegas oh thou who art now a nobody (an actual fact), but to-morrow exceeding great
Ar. Eq. 158,

o)/ntes ou)de/nes being nobodies
E. And. 700, ou) ga\r h)ci/ou tou\s mhde/nas for he was not wont to esteem (those whom he regarded as) nobodies
S. Aj. 1114, to\ mhde\n ei)s ou)de\n r(e/pei what was thought to be nothing now inclines (shows itself) to be actually nothing E. fr. 532, o(/t' ou)de\n w)\n tou= mhde\n a)ne/sths u(/per when though naught thyself (a fact) thou hast stood up for him who is as naught
S. Aj. 1231. So to\ ou)de/n zero, actually nothing, to\ mhde/n abstract nonentity.
a. The construction may influence the choice between ou)dei/s and mhdei/s; as e)a\_n dokw=si/ ti ei)=nai mhde\n o)/ntes, o)neidi/zete au)toi=s rebuke them if they think they are something when in reality they are nothing
P. A. 41e. Cp. 2737 b.

## APPARENT EXCHANGE OF ou) AND mh/

§2737
Where mh/ is used when we expect ou) the negative expression usually depends on a verb that either has mh/ or would have it, if negatived.
a. After imperatives. Thus, sa/f' i)/sqi mh/ me qwpeu/sonta/ se know well that I shall not fawn upon thee E. Heracl. 983,

no/mize mhde\n ei)=nai tw=n a)nqrwpi/nwn be/baion ei)=nai consider nothing in human life to be secure
I. 1.42 ( = mh\ no/mize/ ti ktl.),

w(s ou)=n mh\ mo/non kri/_nontes, a)lla\ kai\ qewrou/menoi, ou(/tw th\n yh=fon fe/rete cast your ballots then in the belief not only that you are passing judgment but also that the eyes of the world are upon you
Aes. 3.247 (cp. 2732). See also 2086 b.
b. After conditional expressions. Thus,

ei) de/ tis . . . nomi/zei ti mh\ i(kanw=s ei)rh=sqai but if any one thinks some point has not been sufficiently mentioned

T. 1.35. Cp. 2736 a.
c. Other cases:

keleu/ei mei=nai e)pi\ tou= potamou= mh\ diaba/ntas he ordered them to remain by the river without crossing
X. A. 4.3.28 (here mei=nai, if negatived, would take mh/, 2720),

u(pe/sxeto ei)rh/nhn poih/sein mh/te o(/mhra dou\s mh/te ta\ tei/xh kaqelw/n he promised that he would bring peace about without giving hostages or destroying the walls
L. 12.68 (here poih/sein, if negatived, would take mh/, 2725).
N.—But ou) may assert itself even under the above circumstances; as mh\ o(/ ge ou) xrh\ poi/ei don't do what is really wrong
P. Eu. 307b,

h)\ a)fi/_ete/ me h)\ mh\ a)fi/_ete w(s e)mou= ou)k a)\n poih/santos a)/lla either acquit me or do not acquit me in the knowledge that I should not act otherwise
P. A. 30b (cp. 2732),

ei) nomi/zeis ou)x u(fe/cein th\n di/khn if thou thinkest not to suffer the penalty
S. O. T. 551 ( = ou)x u(fe/cw), ei) gnwsqhso/meqa cunelqo/ntes me/n, a)mu/_nesqai de\ ou) (some Mss.)

tolmw=ntes if we shall be known to have come together, and yet not to have the courage to avenge ourselves
T. 1.124 (it would be said of them: cunh=lqon me/n, a)mu/_nesqai de\ ou)k e)to/lmwn, a contrast, cp. 2690).
d. On mh/ in questions where we might expect ou), see 2676 b.

§2738

ou) is sometimes used where we expect mh/.
a. Where ou) stands in a clause introduced by ei) or other words after which mh/ might be expected (2698). Thus,

o)/fra kai\ ou)k e)qe/lwn tis a)nagkai/h| polemi/zoi that every one must of necessity fight even though he would not
*d 300 (cp. 2692 a).
b. Where ou) goes strictly with the leading verb though it stands with the infinitive. Thus, bouloi/mhn d' a(\n ou)k ei)=nai to/de I would fain it were not so (I should not wish that this were so)

o)mw/moken ou) xariei=sqai . . . a)lla\ dika/sein kata\ tou\s no/mous he has sworn, not that he will show favour, but that he will judge according to the laws

c. Where ou) in a contrast goes closely with a following word or words, or stands in a partial parenthesis. o(mologoi/hn a)\n e)/gwge ou) kata\ tou/tous ei)=nai r(h/twr I should acknowledge that I am an orator, but not after their style

## mh/ AND mh\ ou) WITH THE INFINITIVE

## REDUNDANT OR SYMPATHETIC NEGATIVE

## I. With the Infinitive depending on Verbs of Negative Meaning

§2739
Verbs and expressions of negative meaning, such as deny, refuse, hinder, forbid, avoid, often take the infinitive with a redundant mh/ to confirm the negative idea of the leading verb.
With this compare: “First he denied you had in him no right” (Shakesp., Com. of Er. 4. 2. 7); and “La pluie . . . empêche qu'on ne se promène” (Racine); “Verbot ihnen Jesus, dass sie Niemand sagen sollten” (St. Mark 9. 9).
katarnh=| mh\ dedra_ke/nai ta/de; dost thou deny that thou hast done this?
S. Ant. 442,

a)pokwlu=sai tou\s *(/ellhnas mh\ e)lqei=n to hinder the Greeks from coming
X. A. 6.4.24,

kh/ru=ka proe/pemyen au)toi=s . . . a)perou=nta mh\ plei=n they sent a herald to forbid them to sail
T. 1.29,

eu)labh/sesqe mh\ pollw=n e)nanti/on le/gein you will beware of speaking in public
P. Eu. 304a,

a)pe/sxonto mh\ e)pi\ th\n e(kate/rwn gh=n strateu=sai they abstained from marching upon each other's territory
T. 5.25.

§2740
The redundant mh/ is used after a)mfile/gw and a)mfisbhtw= dispute, a)nati/qemai retract an opinion, a)ntile/gw speak against, a)pagoreu/w and a)peipei=n forbid, a)pistw= doubt, a)pogignw/skw abandon an intention, a)pokru/ptomai conceal, a)polu/_w acquit, a)posterw= deprive, a)postre/fw divert, a)poxeirotonw= and a)poyhfi/zomai vote against, a)rnou=mai (and compounds, and a)/parno/s ei)mi, e)/carno/s ei)mi) deny, diama/xomai refuse, ei)/rgw and e)mpodw/n ei)mi prevent, e)nantiou=mai oppose, eu)labou=mai beware of, e)/xw and a)pe/xw prevent, a)nte/xw, a)pe/xomai, e)pe/xw, kate/xw abstain from, kwlu/_w (and compounds) hinder, metabouleu/omai alter one's plans, metagignw/kw change one's mind, o)/knon pare/xw make hesilate, feu/gw (and compounds) escape, avoid, disclaim, fula/ttomai guard against, etc.

§2741
Also after the following verbs: a)paudw= forbid, a)peu/xomai deprecor, a)podokei= resolve not, a)prosdo/khto/s ei)mi do not expect, a)fairou=mai prevent, a)fi/_hmi acquit, de/doika and fobou=mai fear, e)ru/_kw hinder, katadei= lack, metadokei= moi change one's mind, pau/w put an end to, r(u/omai and sw/|zw save from, u(pektre/xw escape from, u(fi/_emai give up, etc.

§2742
When a verb of denying, refusing, hindering, forbidding, etc., is itself negatived, either directly or by appearing in a question expecting a negative answer, the infinitive has mh\ ou). Here both the introductory clause and the dependent clause have virtually an affirmative sense.
ou)dei\s pw/pot' a)ntei=pen mh\ ou) kalw=s e)/xein au)tou/s (tou\s no/mous) no one ever denied that they (the laws) were excellent
D. 24.24, ti/na oi)/ei a)parnh/sesqai mh\ ou)xi\ kai\ au)to\n e)pi/stasqai ta\ di/kaia; who, think you, will deny that he too understands what is just?
P. G. 461c ( = ou)dei\s a)parnh/setai). But mh\ ou) is not used after ou)/ fhmi, ou)k e)w=, ou)k e)qe/lw (2692 a).
a. mh\ ou) with the infinitive here, and elsewhere, is used only when the introductory word or words has an actual or a virtual negative. Since, in a)rnou=mai mh\ tau=ta doa=sai I deny that I did this, mh/ confirms the negative idea in a)rnou=mai, so in ou)k a)rnou=mai mh\ ou) tau=ta dra=sai I do not deny that I did this, ou) after the strengthening mh/ confirms the ou) prefixed to the leading verb. Cp. “Je ne nie pas que je ne sois infiniment flatté” (Voltaire). In the first sentence mh/ repeats the ‘negative result’ of a)rnou=mai (single sympathetic negative, untranslatable); in the second sentence ou) is repeated with the infinitive to sum up the effect of ou)k a)rnou=mai (double sympathetic negative; both untranslatable). After verbs negative in meaning (deny, etc.) mh/ and mh\ ou) cannot be translated in modern English (see 2739). After verbs not negative in character but preceded by a negative, and after virtually negative expressions, mh/ or mh\ ou) has a negative force (2745, 2746).
b. mh\ ou) with the infinitive regularly indicates a certain pressure of interest on the part of the person involved.

§2743
After deny, speak against, doubt, etc., followed by w(s or o(/ti, a redundant ou) is often inserted. Thus,

w(s me\n ou)k a)lhqh= tau=t' e)sti/n, ou)x e(/cet' a)ntile/gein that this is true you will not be able to deny
D. 8.31.
a. Here the w(s clause is an internal accusative (accusative of content) after a)ntile/gein. Originally the meaning seems to have been ‘you will not be able to deny in this way—this is not true’ where ou) is not redundant.

§2744

Summary of Constructions after Verbs of Hindering, etc.
After verbs signifying (or suggesting) to hinder and the like, the infinitive admits the article to/ or tou= (the ablatival genitive, 1392). Hence we have a variety of constructions, which are here classed under formal types. The simple infinitive is more closely connected with the leading verb than the infinitive with to\ mh/ or to\ mh\ ou), which often denotes the result (cp. w(/ste mh/) of the action of the leading verb and is either an accusative of respect or a simple object infinitive. The genitive of the infinitive is very rare with kwlu/_w and its compounds.
a. Some scholars regard the infinitive with the negative as an internal accusative, not as a simple object infinitive; and the infinitive without the negative as an external accusative.
1. ei)/rgei me mh\ gra/fein (the usual construction: examples 2739).
2. ei)/rgei me gra/fein (less common). Since the redundant mh/ is not obligatory, we have the simple infinitive as object (1989), as ei) tou=to/ tis ei)/rgei dra=n o)/knos if some scruple prevents us from doing this
P. Soph. 242a, d\n qane<*>i=n e)rru_sa/mhn whom I saved from death
E. Alc. 11,

oi( qew=n h(ma=s o(/rkoi kwlu/_ousi polemi/ous ei)=nai a)llh/lois the oaths sworn in the name of the gods prevent our being enemies to each other
X. A. 2.5.7, and so usually with kwlu/_w (cp. 2744. 7).
3. ei)/rgei me to\ mh\ gra/fein (rather common; cp. 1): ei)=rgon to\ mh\ . . . kakourgei=n they prevented them from doing damage
T. 3.1,

oi(=oi/ te h)=san kate/xein to\ mh\ dakru/_ein they were able to restrain their weeping
P. Ph. 117c.
4. ei)/rgei me to\ gra/fein (not uncommon; cp. 2):

e)pe/sxon to\ eu)qe/ws toi=s *)aqhnai/ois e)pixeirei=n they refrained from immediately attacking the Athenians
T. 7.33,

e)/stin tis, o(/s se kwlu/_sei to\ dra=n there is some one who will prevent thee from the deed
S. Ph. 1241.
5. ei)/rgei me tou= mh\ gra/fein, with the ablatival genitive, 1392 (not so common as 3): pa=s ga\r a)sko\s du/o a)/ndras e(/cei tou= mh\ katadu=nai for each skin-bag will pre- vent two men from sinking
X. A. 3.5.11. Other cases are:
Hdt. 1.86,
T. 1.76,
X. C. 2.4.13, 2. 4. 23, 3. 3. 31,
I. 7.17, 12. 80, 15. 122,
P. L. 637c, 832 b,
D. 23.149, 33. 25. Observe that this idiom does not have the logical meaning ‘from not,’ which we should expect. Some write to\ mh/ or mh/ alone.
6. ei)/rgei me tou= gra/fein (not common, and very rare with kwlu/_w, as
X. A. 1.6.2): tou= de\ dra_peteu/ein desmoi=s a)pei/rgousi; do they prevent their slaves from running away by fetters?
X. M. 2.1.16,

e)pe/sxomen tou= dakru/_ein we desisted from weeping
P. Ph. 117e (cp. 3).
7. ou)k ei)/rgei me gra/fein (not very common, but more often with ou) kwlu/_w; cp. 2): ou)de\ diakwlu/_ousi poiei=n w(=n a)\n e)piqu_mh=|s; nor will they prevent you from doing what you desire?
P. Lys. 207e, ti/ kwlu/_ei ( = ou)de\n k.) kai\ ta\ a)/kra h(mi=n keleu/ein *ku=ron prokatalabei=n; what hinders our ordering Cyrus to take also the heights in advance for us?
X. A. 1.3.16,

tau=ta/ tines ou)k e)carnou=ntai pra/_ttein certain people do not deny that they are doing these things
Aes. 3.250.
8. ou)k ei)/rgei me mh\ ou) gra/fein (the regular construction): ou)k a)mfisbhtw= mh\ ou)xi\ se\ sofw/teron h)\ e)me/ I do not dispute that you are wiser than I P. Hipp. Minor 369 d,

ou)de\n e)du/nato a)nte/xein mh\ ou) xari/zesqai he was not able to resist granting the favour
X. C. 1.4.2, ti/ e)mpodw\n ( = ou)de\n e)mpodw/n) mh\ ou)xi\ . . . u(brizome/nous a)poqanei=n; what hinders our being put to death ignominiously?
X. A. 3.1.13, ti/ dh=ta me/lleis mh\ ou) gegwni/skein to\ pa=n; why pray dost thou hesitate to declare the whole?

## II. mh\ ou) with the Infinitive depending on Negatived Verbs

§2745
Any infinitive that would take mh/, takes mh\ ou) (with a negative force), if dependent on a negatived verb. Here ou) is the sympathetic negative and is untranslatable.

ou)k a)\n piqoi/mhn mh\ ou) ta/d' e)kmaqei=n safw=s I cannot consent not to learn this exactly as it is
S. O. T. 1065.

§2746

mh\ ou) with the infinitive thus often follows verbs and other expressions formed by ou) (or a-privative) with a positive word and denoting what is impossible, improbable, wrong, senseless, and the like.

ou)dei\s oi(=o/s t' e)sti\n a)/llws le/gwn mh\ ou) katage/lastos ei)=nai no one by speaking otherwise can avoid being ridiculous
P. G. 509a,

u(pe/sxou zhth/sein w(s ou)x o(/sio/n soi o)\n mh\ ou) bohqei=n dikaiosu/nh| you promised to make the inquiry on the ground that it would not be right for you not to assist justice
P. R. 427e,

pa/nu a)no/hton h(gou=mai ei)=nai/ soi mh\ ou) kai\ tou=to xari/zesqai I think it is utterly senseless for me not to grant you this favour also
P. S. 218c.

§2747
Such expressions are, e.g. ou)x o(/sio/s t' ei)mi/, ou)x o(=o/n t' e)sti/, ou)x i(kano/s ei)mi, ou)k e)/sti, a)du/nato/s ei)mi, ou) di/kaio/n e)sti, ou)x o(/sio/n e)sti, ou) prosdoki/a_ e)sti/, a)/logo/n e)sti, ou)k a)nekto/n e)sti, a)/noia/ e)sti, and many others.

§2748
Some expressions denoting repugnance to the moral sense involve a negative idea, and may have the same construction. Thus, w(/ste pa=sin ai)sxu/_nhn ei)=nai mh\ ou) suspouda/zein so that all were ashamed not (i.e. felt it was not right) to coöperate zealously
X. A. 2.3.11. So with ai)sxro/n e)sti ( = ou) kalo/n e)sti), deino/n e)sti.

§2749
Instead of mh\ ou) we find also mh/, to\ mh/, tou= mh/, to\ mh\ ou) (but not tou= mh\ ou)).
a. mh/ (rarely; cp. 2744. 1):

e)/legon o(/ti . . . ou) dunh/sointo mh\ pei/qesqai toi=s *ohbai/ois they said that they could not help submitting to the Thebans
X. H. 6.1.1,

ai)sxro\n . . . gi/gnetai e)me/ ge mh\ e)qe/lein it is disgraceful for me at least not to be willing
P. G. 458d.
b. to\ mh/ (cp. 2744. 3): e)/fh . . . ou)x oi<*>=o/n t' ei)=nai to\ mh\ a)poktei=nai/ me he said it was not possible not to condemn me to death
P. A. 29c.
c. tou= mh/ (cp. 2744. 5):

h( a)pori/a_ tou= mh\ h(suxa/zein the inability to rest
T. 2.49.
d. to\ mh\ ou) (cp. 2744. 10): ou) me/ntoi e)/peiqe/ ge to\ mh\ ou) megalopa/_gmwn . . . ei)=nai he could not, however, persuade them that he was not a man who entertained grand designs
X. H. 5.2.36,

a)/logon to\ mh\ ou) te/mnein dixh=| it is irrational not to make a two-fold division
P. Soph. 219e.

## mh\ ou) WITH THE PARTICIPLE DEPENDING ON NEGATIVED VERBS

§2750

mh\ ou), instead of mh/, is sometimes found with the participle after expressions preceded by ou) or involving a negative, and usually when such expressions denote impossibility or moral repugnance. mh\ ou) here denotes an exception, and has the force of except, unless (cp. ei) mh/, 2346 a).

ou)k a)/ra e)sti\n fi/lon tw=| filou=nti ou)de\n mh\ ou)k a)ntifilou=n nothing then is beloved by a lover except it love in return
P. Lys. 212d,

dusa/lghtos ga\r a)\n ei)/hn toi/a_nde mh\ ou) katoikti/_rwn e(/dra_n for I should prove hard of heart, did I not pity such a supplication as this
S. O. T. 11 (dusa/lghtos = ou)k oi)kti/rmwn, mh\ ou) katoikti/_rwn = ei) mh\ katoikti/_roimi).

## mh/ AND mh\ ou) WITH THE SUBJUNCTIVE AND INDICATIVE

§2751
The use of mh/ and mh\ ou) with the subjunctive is different from that with the infinitive.
a. In doubtful assertions (1801-1802) expressing anxiety, suspicion, surmise, mh/ is used of that which may be true, mh\ ou) of that which may not be true.
b. After verbs of fear and caution, where mh/ means lest, mh\ ou) means lest not, that not (2221, 2225).

§2752

mh/ and mh\ ou) are used with the indicative in doubtful assertions (1772). In questions with mh\ ou) the ou) belongs to a single word (2651 d).
On o(/pws mh/, o(/pws mh\ ou) with the future, see 1920, 1921, 2203.

## REDUNDANT ou) WITH plh/n, ETC.

§2753
Redundant ou) appears after the negative words plh/n, xwri/s, e)kto/s, a)/neu except, without, and after pri/n (and ma=llon h)/ usually) preceded by a negative, which may be involved in a question.
nu=n de\ fai/netai (h( nau=s) . . .

ple/ousa pantaxo/se plh\n ou)k ei)s *)aqh/na_s but now it seems that the ship is sailing everywhere except to Athens
D. 56.23, pri\n d' ou)de\n o)rqw=s ei)de/nai, ti/ soi ple/on lu_poume/nh| ge/noit' a)/n; before thou knowest the facts, what can sorrow avail thee?
E. Hel. 322,

eu)= d' i)/ste o(/ti ou) peri\ tw=n e)mw=n i)di/wn ma=llon ti_mwrh/sesqe *polukle/a_ h)\ ou)x u(pe/r u(_mw=n au)tw=n but be assured that you will punish Polycles rather for your own good than for my private interests
D. 50.66. Cp. “j'irai vous voir avant que vous ne preniez aucune résolution,” “le bon Dieu est cent fois meilleur qu'on ne le dit.”

## ou' mh/

§2754

ou) mh/, and the compounds of each, are used in emphatic negative predictions and prohibitions.
a. ou) mh/ marks strong personal interest on the part of the speaker. In its original use it may have belonged to colloquial speech and as such we find it in comedy; but in tragedy it is often used in stately language. ou) mh/ is rare in the orators.

§2755
(I) In negative predictions to denote a strong denial.
a. With the (first or second) aorist subjunctive, less often with the present subjunctive (1804). Thus,

h)\n ni_kh/swmen, ou) mh/ pote u(_mi=n *peloponnh/sioi e)sba/lwsin e)s th\n xw/ra_n if we are victorious, the Peloponnesians will never invade your territory
T. 4.95,

ou)dei\s mhke/ti mei/nh| tw=n polemi/wn not one of the enemy will stand his ground any longer
X. A. 4.8.13, ou)/ti mh\ fu/ghte you shall not escape (a threat)
E. Hec. 1039,

ou) mh/ soi du/nwntai a)nte/xein oi( pole/mioi your enemies will not be able to withstand you
X. Hi. 11.15.
b. With the future indicative (first and third person). Thus,

ou)/ soi mh\ meqe/yomai/ pote never will I follow thee
S. El. 1052, ou) mh\ dunh/setai *ku=ros eu(rei=n Cyrus will not be able to find
X. C. 8.1.5. In indirect discourse, the future optative or infinitive; as

e)qe/spisen . . . w(s ou) mh/ pote pe/rsoien he prophesied that they never would destroy
S. Ph. 611,

ei)=pen . . . ou) mh/ pote eu)= pra/_cein po/lin he declared that the city would never prosper
E. Phoen. 1590.

§2756
(II) In strong prohibitions (cp. 1919).
a. With the future indicative (second person singular). Thus,

ou) mh\ katabh/sei don't come down
Ar. Vesp. 397.
b. With the aorist subjunctive rarely (1800 N.). Thus

ou) mh\ lhrh/sh|s don't talk twaddle
Ar. Nub. 367. Many editors change the aorist subjunctive to the future indicative.

§2757
There are two cases in which ou) mh/ is not used in conjunction, but where each negative has its own verb.
a. A positive command in the future indicative (second person) may be joined by a)lla/ or de/ to a prohibition introduced by ou) mh/. Thus,

ou) mh\ lalh/seis a)ll' a)kolouqh/seis e)moi/ don't prattle but follow me
Ar. Nub. 505,

ou) mh\ dusmenh\s e)/sei toi=s fi/lois, pau/sei de\ qu_mou= do not be angry with thy friends, but cease thy wrath
E. Med. 1151. (In
E. Bacch. 343 de/ with the future is followed by mhde/ with the future.) In such sentences the force of ou) continues into the a)lla/ or de/ clause. Such sentences are generally printed as questions.
b. A positive command with ou) and the future indicative (second person) may be followed by the future in a prohibition introduced by mhde/ or kai\ mh/. Here the clause with ou) has the form of a question expecting the answer yes, while the whole sentence has the form of a question expecting the answer no. Thus, ou) si=g' a)ne/cei mhde\ deili/a_n a)rei=; wilt thou not keep silence and not win for thyself the reputation of cowardice? ( = keep silence and do not get the reputation of being a coward)
S. Aj. 75, ou)kou=n kalei=s au)to\n kai\ mh\ a)fh/seis; will you not call him and (will you not) send him away? ( = call him and don't send him away)
P. S. 175a. Here ou) is to be taken also with the following clause. Some scholars make the question in the second clause independent of ou).

§2758
The origin of the use of ou) mh/ is obscure and disputed. See Kvičala Zeitschrift für österreichische Gymnasien 1856, p. 755; Goodwin Moods and Tenses 389; Gildersleeve American Journal of Philology 3. 202, 23. 137; Jebb on Sophocles Ajax 75 (appendix); Chambers Classical Review 10. 150, 11. 109; Wharton o.c. 10. 239; Whitelaw o.c. 10. 239, 16. 277; Sonnenschein o.c. 16. 165; Kühner-Gerth Grammatik der griechischen Sprache 2. § 514. 8.

## NEGATIVES WITH w(/ste AND THE INFINITIVE

§2759

w(/ste with the infinitive shows the following uses of the negatives.
a. mh/ in ordinary result clauses including such as express an intended result; as pa=n poiou=sin w(/ste di/khn mh\ dido/nai mhd' a)palla/ttesqai tou= megi/stou kakou= they use every effort (so as) to avoid being punished and released from the greatest of evils
P. G. 479c.
b. mh/ sympathetic, after verbs of hindering; as

a)pexo/menoi w(/ste mh\ e)mba/llein refraining from attacking
T. 1.49 (cp. 2744. 1).
N.—After verbs of hindering w(/ste is rarely used for w(/ste mh/ (cp. 2744. 2); as

w(/ste ga\r th\n su/ntomon pro\s tou\s *pellhne/a_s a)fike/sqai h( pro\ tou= tei/xous fa/ragc ei)=rge the ravine in front of the walls prevented them from reaching the short cut to the Pellenians
X. H. 7.2.13. Cp.
P. Eu. 305d.
c. ou', when the w(/ste clause depends on a clause itself subordinate to a verb of saying or thinking (2269).
d. mh\ ou) after a negatived verb of hindering (cp. 2744. 8); as

ou)/te sfe/as *eu)rubia/dhs kate/xein dunh/setai . . . w(/ste mh\ ou) diaskedasqh=nai th\n stratih/n neither will Eurybiades be able to prevent the fleet from being scattered
Hdt. 8.57. Also when the w(/ste clause depends on a negatived verb (2745); as

pei/somai ga\r ou) tosou=ton ou)de\n w(/ste mh\ ou) kalw=s qanei=n for I will suffer nothing so much as not to die nobly
S. Ant. 97.
e. ou' mh/ (cp. 2754 a); as

ou(/tws e)petequ/_mhka a)kou=sai w(/ste . . . ou) mh/ sou a)poleifqw= I have conceived such a desire to hear that I shall not fall behind you
P. Phae. 227d.

## ACCUMULATION OF NEGATIVES

§2760
If in the same clause a simple negative (ou) or mh/) with a verb follows a negative, each of the two negatives keeps its own force if they belong to different words or expressions. If they belong to the same word or expression, they make an affirmative.
ou) dia\ to\ mh\ a)konti/zein ou)k e)/balon au)to/n it was not because they did not throw that they did not hit him Ant. 3.
d. 6,

ou)/ toi ma\ th\n *dh/mhtra du/namai mh\ gela=n by Demeter I am not able to help laughing
Ar. Ran. 42, ou)dei\s ou)k e)/pasxe/ ti no one was not suffering something (i.e. everybody suffered)
X. S. 1. 9 (ou)dei\s o(/stis ou) = everybody is commonly used for ou)dei\s ou)), ou)de\ to\n *formi/wn' e)kei=nos ou)x o(ra=| nor does he not see Phormio (i.e. he sees him very well)
D. 36.46, ou)d' ei)/ tis a)/llos sofo/s (e)stin)

ou) filosofei= nor if there is any other man who is wise, does he love wisdom
P. S. 204a,

ou)de/ ge o( i)di/a| ponhro\s ou)k a)\n ge/noito dhmosi/a| xrhsto/s nor can the man who is base in private prove himself noble in a public capacity
Aes. 3.78.

§2761
If in the same clause one or more compound negatives follow a negative with the same verb, the compound negative simply confirms the first negative.

ou)dei\s ou)de\n peni/a| dra/_sei no one will do anything because of want
Ar. Eccl. 605,

mh\ qorubh/sh| mhdei/s let no one raise an uproar
D. 5.15,

kai\ ou)/te e)pe/qeto ou)dei\s ou)damo/qen ou)/te pro\s th\n ge/fu_ran ou)dei\s h)=lqe and neither did any one make an attack from any quarter nor did any one come to the bridge
X. A. 2.4.23, tou/tous fobou/menoi mh/pote a)sebe\s mhde\n mhde\ a)no/sion mh/te poih/shte mh/te bouleu/shte holding them (the gods) in fear never do or intend anything either impious or unholy
X. C. 8.7.22. So ou) . . . ou)de/ non . . . ne . . quidem, ou) mh\n ou)de/ (2768). ou)de\ pollou= dei=, after a negative, means far from it. Cp. “no sonne, were he never so old of years, might not marry” (Ascham's Scholemaster), “We may not, nor will we not suffer this” (Marlowe).
a. In ou)de\ ga\r ou)de/ the first negative belongs to the whole sentence, while the second limits a particular part. Thus,

ou)de\ ga\r ou)de\ tou=to e)yeu/sato for he did not deceive me even in this
X. C. 7.2.20 (cp. neque enim . . . ne . . quidem). Cp. E 22,
q 32. So ou)de\ me\n ou)de/ B 703,
k 551.

§2762
The negative of one clause is often repeated in the same or in another clause either for emphasis or because of lax structure.
d\s ou)k, e)peidh\ tw=|de e)bou/leusas mo/ron, dra=sai to/d' e)/rgon ou)k e)/tlhs who did not, after you had planned his death, dare to do this deed
A. Ag. 1634. The repetition is rhetorical when the negative is repeated directly, as

ou) smi_kro/s, ou)/x, a(_gw\n o(/de not trifling, is this struggle, no in truth
S. O. C. 587.

## SOME NEGATIVE PHRASES

§2763

mh\ o(/ti, ou)x o(/pws, rarely ou)x o(/ti and mh\ o(/pws, not to speak of, to say nothing of, not only, not only not, so far from (Lat. tantum aberat ut) are idiomatic phrases probably due to an (early, and later often unconscious) ellipsis of a verb of saying. Thus, ou) le/gw (or ou)k e)rw=) o(/pws, mh\ ei)/pw (le/ge or ei)/ph|s) o(/ti I do (will) not say that, let me not say that, do not say that. mh\ o(/ti, etc. are often used where these verbal forms cannot be supplied by reason of the form of the sentence.
a. ou)x o(/ti (ou)x o(/pws, mh\ o(/ti) . . . a)lla\ (kai/ not only . . . but (also). Thus,

ou)x o(/ti mo/nos o( *kri/twn e)n h(suxi/a| h)=n, a)lla\ kai\ oi( fi/loi au)tou= not only was Crito in peace, but his friends also
X. M. 2.9.8, oi)=mai a)\n mh\ o(/ti i)diw/thn tina/, a)lla\ to\n me/gan basile/a_ eu(rei=n ktl. I think that not merely any private person but the Great King would find, etc.
P. A. 40d.
b. ou)x o(/pws (rarely ou)x o(/ti) or mh\ o(/ti . . . a)lla\ (kai/) is shown by the context to mean not only not (so far from) . . . but (also). Thus,

ou)x o(/pws xa/rin au)toi=s e)/xeis, a)lla\ misqw/sa_s sauto\n kata\ toutwni\_ poli_teu/ei not only are you not grateful to them, but you let yourself out for hire as a public man to their prejudice
D. 18.131; mh\ o(/ti
P. R. 581e.
c. ou)x o(/pws (rarely ou)x o(/ti) or mh\ o(/ti (mh\ o(/pws) . . . a)ll' ou)de/ (mhde/) or a)ll)ou' (mh/) is shown by the context to mean not only not (so far from) . . . but not even. Thus,

ou)x o(/pws th=s koinh=s e)leuqeri/a_s mete/xomen, a)ll' ou)de\ doulei/a_s metri/a_s tuxei=n h)ciw/qhmen not only do we not share in the general freedom, but we were not thought worthy of obtaining even a moderate servitude
I. 14.5,

nomi/zei e(auto\n mh\ o(/ti *plataie/a_ ei)=nai, a)ll' ou)d' e)leu/qeron he considers himself not only not a Plataean but not even a free man
L. 23.12.
N. When a negative precedes, the meaning may be not only . . . but not even; as

th\n oi)ki/a_n . . . ou)deni\ a)\n mh\ o(/ti proi=ka doi/hs, a)ll' ou)d' e)/la_tton th=s a)ci/a_s labw/n you would offer your house to no one not only gratis, but not even for a lower price than it is worth
X. M. 1.6.11.
d. mh\ o(/ti (less often ou)x o(/pws) in the second of two balanced clauses, after an expressed or implied negative in the first clause, means much less (Lat. nedum）; as ou)de\ plei=n, mh\ o(/ti a)nairei=sqai tou\s a)/ndras dunato\n h)=n it was not possible even to sail, much less to rescue the man (i.e. to say nothing of rescuing)
X. H. 2.3.35. The preceding negative may be contained in a question or be otherwise implicit. Thus, dokei= soi r(a/|dion ei)=nai ou(/tw taxu\ maqei=n . . . o(tiou=n pra=gma, mh\ o(/ti tosou=ton ktl.; does it appear to you to be easy to learn so quickly any subject whatever, much less a subject of so great importance?
P. Crat. 427e; cp.
D. 54.17.
The rare ou)x o(/ti in the second member means though (
P. Pr. 336d).
e. mh/ ti/ ge, in the orators instead of mh\ o(/ti, after a negative means much less, after a positive much more. Cp.
D. 19.137, 8. 27.

§2764

ou' mo/non . . . a)lla\ kai/ (negative a)ll' ou)de/) not only . . . but also (Lat. non solum . . . sed etiam). kai/ may be omitted: usually when the a)lla/ clause either includes the first clause or is strongly contrasted with it. Thus,

i(_ma/tion h)mfi/esai ou) mo/non fau=lon, a)lla/ to\ au)to\ qe/rous te kai\ xeimw=nos you put on a cloak that is not merely wretched but is the same both summer and winter alike
X. M. 1.6.2; cp.
D. 18.26.

§2765

o(/ ti mh/, o(/son mh/ except, unless. o(/ ti (sometimes written o(/ti) mh/, and o(/son mh/, o(/sa mh/ are used, without any verb, to limit a preceding assertion (cp. ei) mh/ 2346 a).

ou) ga\r h)=n krh/nh, o(/ ti mh\ mi/a e)n au)th=| th=| a)kropo/lei for there was no spring, except one on the acropolis itself
T. 4.26, pei/qousa de\ e)k tou/twn me\n a)naxwrei=n, o(/son mh\ a)na/gkh au)toi=s xrh=sqai philosophy persuading the soul to withdraw from them, except so far as she has to make use of them
P. Ph. 83a,

th=s gh=s e)kra/toun o(/sa mh\ proi+o/ntes polu\ e)k tw=n o(/plwn they were masters of the country, so far as they could be without advancing far from their camp
T. 1.111 (o(/sa kratei=n e)du/nanto).

§2766

mo/non ou) (lit. only not), o(/son ou) (of time) almost, all but (Lat. tantum non). Thus,

mo/non ou) diespa/sqhn I was almost torn in pieces
D. 5.5,

e)no/mize . . . o(/son ou)k h)/dh e)/xein th\n po/lin he thought that he already was all but in possession of the city
X. H. 6.2.16.

§2767

ou' mh\n a)lla/, ou) me/ntoi a)lla/ nevertheless, notwithstanding, cp. Lat. uerum tamen; the colloquial ou' ga\r a)lla/ has about the force of nay, for indeed, cp. Lat. non enim . . . sed. These elliptical phrases require a verb or some other word to be supplied from the context or general run of the thought; but they often resist strict analysis since the contrasted idea is too vague to be supplied. Thus, o( i(/ppos . . . mi_krou= ka)_kei=non e)cetraxh/lisen: ou) mh\n (e)cetraxh/lisen) a)lla\ e)pe/meinen o( *ku=ros the horse was within a little of throwing him also over its head; (not that it did throw him however, but = ) nevertheless Cyrus kept his seat
X. C. 1.4.8, a)ei\ me\n ou)=n oi(/ q' h(me/teroi pro/gonoi kai\ *lakedaimo/nioi filoti/_mws pro\s a)llh/lous ei)=xon, ou) mh\n (scil. peri\ kakw=n) a)lla\ peri\ kalli/stwn . . . e)filoni/_khsan while our ancestors and the Lacedaemonians were continually jealous of each other (not indeed about base objects but = ) nevertheless they were rivals about the noblest objects
I. 4.85, kai\ ga\r a)\n do/ceien ou(/tw g' ei)=nai a)/logon: ou) me/ntoi (scil. a)/logo/n e)stin) a)ll' i)/sws e)/xei tina\ lo/gon and in fact put thus it would seem to be unreasonable; (it is not however unreasonable but = ) nevertheless perhaps it has some sense
P. Ph. 62b, mh\ skw=pte/ m', w)=de/lf', ou) ga\r a)ll' e)/xw kakw=s don't mock me, brother; nay, for really I am in a bad way Ar. Ran 58 (lit. for it is not so but, i.e. it is not a case for mocking, but). In these phrases a)lla/ seems to show traces of its original force of otherwise (2775).

§2768

ou' mh\n ou)de/ nor (yet) again, not however that corresponds to the positive ou) mh\n (me/ntoi) a)lla/. Thus,

ou) mh\n ou)de\ barba/rous ei)/rhke nor again has he spoken of barbarians
T. 1.3, ou) ma\_n ou)d' *)axileu/s no, nor even Achilles B 703,

ou) mh\n ou)de\ a)naisqh/tws au)tou\s keleu/w tou\s . . . cumma/xous h(mw=n e)a=n bla/ptein not however that I bid you tamely permit them to injure our allies
T. 1.82.

## PARTICLES

§2769
Under the head of particles are included sentence adverbs (1094) and conjunctions. Many sentence adverbs remained such, some sank to mere enclitics, others became pure conjunctions, while still others fluctuated in function, being now adverbial, now conjunctional, as kai/ even and and, ou)de/ not even and nor, ga/r in fact and for, pri/n sooner and until or before.

§2770
Conjunctions are either coördinating or subordinating. The coördinating conjunctions with their several varieties are given in 2163. The subordinating conjunctions are
Causal: o(/ti, dio/ti, dio/per, e)pei/, e)peidh/, o(/te, o(po/te, w(s (2240).
Comparative: w(s, w(/sper, kaqa/per, o(/pws, h(=|, o(/ph|, h(=|per (2463; cp. 2481).
Concessive: kai\ ei) (kei'), kai\ e)o/_n (ka)/_n), ei) kai/, e)a\_n kai/ (2369).
Conditional: ei), e)a/_n, h)/n, a)/_n (2283).
Consecutive: w(/ste, w(s (2250).
Declarative: o(/ti, dio/ti, ou(/neka, o(qou/neka, w(s (2578).
Final: i(/na, o(/pws, w(s, mh/, etc. (2193; cp. 2209, 2221).
Local: ou(=, o(/pou, oi(=, o(/poi, e)/nqa, o(/qen, o(po/qen, h(=|, o(/ph|, etc (2498).
Temporal: o(/te, o(po/te, h(ni/ka, e)pei/, e)peidh/, w(s, me/xri, e)/ste, e(/ws, pri/n, etc (2383).
Some conjunctions belong to more than one class.

§2771
Greek has an extraordinary number of sentence adverbs (or particles in the narrow sense) having a logical or emotional (rhetorical) value. Either alone or in combination these sentence adverbs give a distinctness to the relations between ideas which is foreign to other languages, and often resist translation by separate words, which in English are frequently over emphatic and cumbersome in comparison to the light and delicate nature of the Greek originals (e.g. a)/ra, ge/, toi/). The force of such words is frequently best rendered by pause, stress, or alterations of pitch. To catch the subtle and elusive meaning of these often apparently insignificant elements of speech challenges the utmost vigilance and skill of the student.

§2772
The particles show different degrees of independence as regards their position. Many are completely independent and may occupy any place in the sentence; some may occur only at the beginning (prepositive particles, as a)ta/r); others find their place only after one or more words at the beginning (postpositive particles, as ga/r, de/); and some are attached closely to a preceding word o<*> even form compounds with that word wherever it may occur (ge/, te/).

§2773
Some verbal forms have virtually become particles, e.g. a)/ge used with the second person plural, o(ra=|s used of several persons, parenthetic oi)=mai, dh=lo<*> o(/ti, eu)= oi)=d' o(/ti, eu)= i)/sq' o(/ti (2585).

§2774
As regards their meaning, particles may be arranged in classes, e.g adversative, affirmative, asseverative, concessive, confirmative, conjunctive, infer ential, intensive, interrogative, limitative, negative, etc. These classes canno<*> always be sharply distinguished: some particles fall under two or more classes Many particles, which serve to set forth the logical relation between clauses, ha<*> originally only an intensive or confirmatory force that was confined to their ow<*> clause. The following sections deal only with the commoner uses of the most noteworthy particles.

## a)lla/

§2775

a)lla/, a strongly adversative conjunction (stronger than de/) connects sentences and clauses, and corresponds pretty closely to but; at times a)lla/ need not or cannot be translated (2781 b). In form (but with changed accent) a)lla/ was originally the same wor<*> as the accusative neuter plural a)/lla other things used adverbially = on the other hand. a)lla/ marks opposition, contrast, protest, dif<*> ference, objection, or limitation; and is thus used both where one notion entirely excludes another and where two notions are no<*> mutually exclusive. a)lla/ is often freely repeated in successive clauses.

§2776

The Antecedent Statement is Negative.—In its simplest use a)ll<*> introduces a positive statement after a negative clause. Thus, ou)k a)ndro\s o(/rko<*> pi/stis, a)ll' o(/rkwn a)nh/r his oath is not the warrant of a man, but the man is war rant of his oath A. fr. 394, ou) ga\r kraugh=| a)lla\ si_gh=| w(s a)nusto\n . . . prosh=|san fo<*> they came on, not with shouts, but with as little noise as possible
X. A. 1.8.11.
a. After a question implying a negative answer or a question to be refute<*> a)lla/ may have the force of (nay) rather, on the contrary. Thus, ti/ dei= se i)e/na . . .; a)lla\ a)/llous pe/myon what's the need of your going? Nay rather send oth<*> ers
X. A. 4.6.19. Here a)ll' ou' (mh/) has the force of and not rather (2781 b) as ti/dei= e)mbalei=n lo/gon peri\ tou/tou, a)ll' ou)xi\ proeipei=n o(/ti ou(/tw poih/seis; why is i<*> necessary to propose a discussion about this and not rather announce that you will have it so?
X. C. 2.2.19.

§2777
After a negative clause, or a question implying a negative answer a)lla/, or more commonly the colloquial a)ll' h)/, may mean except, the combination being equivalent either to a)lla/ or to h)/. In the preceding clause a form of a)/llo or e(/teros is often expressed. Thus,

e)/paise . . . nin ou)/tis a)ll' e)gw/ no one smote him except myself
S. O. T. 1331,

ou)de\n e)qe/lontes e)painei=n a)ll' h)\ to\n plou=ton wishing to praise nothing except wealth
P. R. 330c (here a)ll' h)/ is detached from ou)de/n) ti/na a)/llon e)/xousi lo/gon bohqou=ntes e)moi\ a)ll' h)\ to\n o)rqo/n ktl.; what other reason<*> have they for supporting me except the true reason, etc.?
P. A. 34b.
a. Distinguish the use of a)ll' h)/ except (= ei) mh/) in to\ gou=n shmei=on e(/teron fai/ netai, a)ll' h)\ ou) kaqorw= the device at any rate appears different, unless I can't se<*>
Ar. Eq. 953.

§2778

ou)de\n a)ll' h)/ nothing but is also used elliptically, apparently by a<*> original suppression of a form of poiw= or gi/gnomai; in effect, however, the phras<*> has acquired a purely adverbial sense (merely). Thus, diefqa/rmeqa . . . u(p' a)ndrw= ou)de\n a)ll' h)\ fena_ki/zein duname/nwn we have been ruined by men who are able (to do nothing except deceive (i.e. able merely to deceive)
I. 8.36.
a. With the above use compare ou)de\n a)/llo h)/ nothing else than, used without, and with, ellipse; as oi( mu/_rioi i(ppei=s ou)de\n a)/llo h)\ mu/_rioi/ ei)sin a)/nqrwpoi your ten thousand horse are nothing more (else) than ten thousand men
X. A. 3.2.18, ou)de\n a)/llo h)\ po/lin th\n e(autou= a)po/leipwn e(/kastos doing nothing else than each abandoning his own city
T. 2.16. So also ou)de\n a)/llo . . . h)/
D. 8.27. Cp. a)/llo ou)de\n h)/, as in a)/llo ou)de\n h)\ e)k gh=s e)nauma/xoun they did nothing else than conduct ( = they practically conducted) a sea-fight from the land
T. 4.14. Cp. 946, 2652.

§2779
The origin of a)ll' h)/ is disputed, some scholars regarding a)ll' as a)lla/ (originally a)/lla, 2775), while others derive a)ll' directly from a)/llo, which is thought to have lost its force and consequently its accent. In some passages the Mss. do not distinguish between a)ll' and a)/ll'; and a)ll' h)/ and a)/llo h)/ differ only slightly in meaning. In some of the above cases a)ll' has an adjectival force, in some it hovers between an adjective and a conjunction, and in others it clearly has become a conjunction.

§2780
After a comparative (ma=llon, to\ ple/on) in a negative clause a)lla/ has the force of as. Thus, kai\ e)/stin o( po/lemos ou)x o(/plwn to\ ple/on a)lla\ dapa/nhs and war is not so much (lit. more) a matter of arms as (but rather) of money
T. 1.83. Here the clause with a)lla/ is more emphatic than if h)/ had been used. Cp. “there needed no more but to advance one step”: Steele.

§2781

The Antecedent Statement is Affirmative.—a)lla/ is sometimes found after an affirmative statement.
a. The antecedent clause often has a concessive force, and frequently takes me/n (2900). Thus,

ta\ me\n kaq' h(ma=s e)/moige dokei= kalw=s e)/xein: a)lla\ ta\ pla/gia lu_pei\ me the part where we are seems to me to be well disposed, but the wings cause me uneasiness
X. C. 7.1.16.
b. a)ll' ou' (mh/) after an affirmative statement often has the force of and not, and not rather, instead of (sometimes with a touch of irony). Thus, e)kei=qen a)ll' ou)k e)nqe/nde h(rpa/sqh she was carried off from there and not (or simply not) from here
P. Phae. 229d, e)moi\ o)rgi/zontai a)ll' ou)x au(toi=s they are angry with me instead of (or and not rather with) themselves
P. A. 23c. In such cases kai\ ou) (mh/) would not repudiate the opposition.

§2782

a)lla/ in Apodosis.—After a concession or a condition expressed or implied, the apodosis may be emphatically introduced by a)lla/, a)lla\ . . . ge, a)ll' ou)=n ge still, yet, at least. Thus, ei) sw=ma dou=lon, a)ll' o( nou=s e)leu/qeros if the body is enslaved, the mind at least is free A. fr. 854, ei) d' e)n pa=si tou/tois h(ttw/|meqa, a)lla\ to/ ge/ toi pu=r krei=tton karpou= e)stin but if we should be baffled in all these points, still, as they say, fire is stronger than the fruit of the field
X. A. 2.5.19. So also in clauses other than conditional; as a)ll' e)pei\ . . . pate/ra to/nd' e)mo\n ou)k a)ne/tla_t', . . . a)ll' e)me\ . . . oi)kti/_rate but since ye did not bear with my father, pity me at least
S. O. C. 241.

§2783

a)lla/ attached to Single Words.—a)lla/, attached to a single word in an adverbial sense, may stand in the interior of the sentence (not in Hom.). Thus, a)lla\ nu=n now at least, as in ti/ dh=t' a)\n a)lla\ nu=n s' e)/t' w)feloi=m' e)gw/, how pray, can I serve thee even now?
S. Ant. 552. So with ge/, as

e)a\_n ou)=n a)lla\ nu=n g' e)/ti . . . e)qelh/shte if therefore you still desire even now
D. 3.33 (and often in D.). Here a)lla\ nu=n implies ei) mh\ pro/teron. a)lla/ sometimes apparently implies ei) mh/ ti a)/llo or ei) mh\ a)/llois, etc., as le/g' a)lla\ tou=to say this at least (say but this)
S. El. 415.

§2784

a)lla/ opposing Whole Sentences.—a)lla/ well, well but, nay but, however is often used, especially at the beginning of a speech, in opposition either to something said (or supposed to be meant) by another, or to a latent feeling in the mind of the writer or speaker himself. Thus, a)lla\ prw=ton me\n mnhsqh/somai . . . o(\ teleutai=on kat' e)mou= ei)=pe well, I will first allude to the charge against me which he mentioned last
X. H. 2.3.35, a)ll' w)/fele me\n *ku=ros zh=n: e)pei\ de\ teteleu/thken ktl. well, I would that Cyrus were alive; but since he is dead, etc.
X. A. 2.1.4. Often of remonstrance or protest, as a)ll' a)mh/xanon nay, it is impossible
E. El. 529. a)lla/ is also especially common when a previous train of thought or remark is impatiently interrupted, as a)lla\ tau=ta me\n ti/ dei= le/gein; but what is the need of recounting this?
S. Ph. 11. Similarly in
a. Replies (often in quick, abrupt, or decisive answers): h)/reto o(/ ti ei)/h to\ su/nqhma: o( d' a)pekri(_nato: *zeu\s swth\r kai\ ni(_kh: o( de\ *ku=ros a)kou/sa_s *)alla\ de/xomai/ te, e)/fh, kai\ tou=to e)/stw he asked what the watchword was; and he replied: “Zeus the saviour and Victory;” and Cyrus, on hearing this, said, “Well, I accept it and so let it be”
X. A. 1.8.17.
b. Assent, with an adversative sense implied (cp. oh, well): a)ll' ei' dokei=, xwrw=men well, if it pleases thee, let us be going
S. Ph. 645.
c. Appeals, exhortations, proposals, and commands:

a)ll' i)/wmen but let us go
P. Pr. 311a, a)ll' e)moi\ pei/qou kai\ mh\ a)/llws poi/ei nay, take my advice and don't refuse
P. Cr. 45a. The tone here is often impatient.
d. Wishes and imprecations: a)ll' eu)tuxoi/hs well, my blessings on thee!
S. O. T. 1478.
e. Questions, to mark surprise: pw=s ei)=pas; a)ll' h)= kai\ sofo\s le/lhqas w)/n; what dost thou mean? can it really be that thou art subtle too and without my knowing it?
E. Alc. 58.

§2785

a)lla/ is often used when a speaker introduces a supposed objection (either in his own name or in that of his opponent), and immediately answers it; as a)lla\ nh\ to\n *di/a e)kei=n' a)\n i)/sws ei)/poi pro\s tau=ta ktl. but, by Zeus, he might perhaps say in reply to this, etc.
D. 20.3. a)lla/ may here put the supposed objection and also give the answer. Thus, ti/ ga\r kai\ boulo/menoi metepe/mpesq' a)\n au)tou\s e)n tou/tw| tw=| kairw=|; e)pi\ th\n ei)rh/nhn; a)ll' u(ph=rxen a(/pa_sin: a)ll' e)pi\ to\n po/lemon; a)ll' au)toi\ peri\ th=s ei)rh/nhs e)bouleu/esqe for with what possible desire would you have been sending them at that juncture? With a view to peace? Why (but) peace was open to all. With a view to war? Why (but) you were yourselves deliberating about peace
D. 18.24. Cp. French mais introducing a reply to a question.
a. So in rapid dialogue objections may take the form of questions, in which each a)lla/ after the first may be rendered by or. Cp. 2654.

§2786

a)lla/ with other Particles.—For example:
a)lla\ ga/r 2816; on ou' ga\r a)lla/, see 2767.
a)lla\ . . . ge but at any rate.
a)lla/ ge/ toi (toi/ ge) yet at least, yet be sure.
a)lla\ dh/ well then.
a)ll' h)=; why how? can it really be that? what, can it be true? Here a)lla/ marks surprise, while h)= asks the question.
a)lla\ me/ntoi nay, but; well, however; yet truly. On ou' me/ntoi a)lla/, see 2767.
a)lla\ mh/n nay, but; but then; but surely. Often to introduce an objection, to reject an alternative, often merely to introduce a new idea or to resume an interrupted thought. On ou' mh\n a)lla/, see 2767.
a)ll' o(/mws but still. Often without a verb, to introduce the reply to an objection.
a)ll' ou)de/ is sometimes used elliptically, as in u(pe\r . . . w(=n ou(=tos a)ph/ggeile pro\s u(_ma=s a)ll' ou)de\ mi_kro/n nay, there is not even ever so little (not only not a great deal but not even a little) concerning which he reported to you
D. 19.37. a)ll' ou)de\ me\n dh/ is often used to reject an alternative.
a)ll' ou)=n (ge) but then, well then, well at any rate; stronger than d' ou)=n.

## a)/ra

§2787

a)/ra (Epic a)/ra and enclitic a)/r before a consonant, r(a/ usually after monosyllables; all postpositive), a connective, confirmatory, and inferential particle marking the immediate connection and succession of events and thoughts; the natural, direct, and expected consequence of a previous statement of the existing situation, or of the realization of experience of some sort; and agreement of various kinds, as between assertion and reality, cause and result, premise and conclusion, explanation and what was to be explained.
a. a)/ra marks a consequence drawn from the connection of thought, and expresses impression or feeling; the stronger ou)=n marks a consequence drawn from facts (a positive conclusion).

§2788
The etymology of a)/ra, and hence its original meaning, is obscure. Some derive it from the root a)r, seen in a)r-ar-i/skw fit, join, a)/rti just; and thus regard the proper sense as fittingly, accordingly. Others think the earliest meaning was truly, forsooth and connect a)/ra with a lost adj. a)ri/s, surviving in a)/ri-stos, a)ri/-gnwtos. On this interpretation a)/ra would originally assert the truth of its own clause. a)/ra is found also in a)=ra and ga/r.

§2789

a)/ra is used in Homer much more freely than in Attic, and often so as to defy exact translation. In general a)/ra in Epic marks immediate connection and succession, a natural consequence of something already said or done; gives an explanation of an antecedent statement; or is used in recapitulations and transitions. Thus,

au)ta\r e)pei/ r() h)/gerqen . . ., bh= r() i)/men ei)s a)gorh/n but when they were collected, then he started to go to the assembly
b 9, w(\s e)/faq', oi( d' a)/ra pa/ntes a)kh\n e)ge/nonto siwph=| thus he spake, and all accordingly became hushed in silence H 92, si=ton de/ sfin e)/neime *mesau/lios, o(/n r(a subw/ths au)to\s e)kth/sato and Mesaulius distributed food to them, a slave whom (and this was the reason for his so doing) the swineherd had acquired
c 449,

w(\s a)/r' e)fw/nhsen kai\ a)po\ e(/o to/con e)/qhken thus then he spake and put the bow from him
f 163. So also in the later language; as

e)rwth/shs de\ au)to\n th=s mhtro\s . . . a)pekri/_nato a)/ra o( *ku=ros on his mother's questioning him Cyrus naturally replied
X. C. 1.3.2.

§2790
In Attic, and in part also in Homer, a)/ra marks an inference (conse- quently, so then, therefore, it seems, after all, of course, etc.). Thus, ei)=pen au)tw=| o(/ti basileu\s ou) maxei=tai de/ka h(merw=n: *ku=ros d' ei)=pen: ou)k a)/ra e)/ti maxei=tai, ei) e)n tau/tais ou) maxei=tai tai=s h(me/rais the seer said to him that the king would not fight within ten days. And Cyrus answered: “Well then if he does not fight within that time he will not fight at all”
X. A. 1.7.18, ou)dei\<*> potou= e)piqu_mei=, a)lla\ xrhstou= potou= . . ., pa/ntes ga\r a)/ra tw=n a)gaqw=n e)piqu_mou=sin no one desires drink merely, but good drink, since of course everybody desires good things
P. R. 438a.

§2791

a)/ra is often used of direct logical conclusions in conducting an argument (especially in Plato); as

ti/ ou)=n peri\ yu_xh=s le/gomen; o(ra_to\n h)\ a)o/ra_ton ei)=nai; ou)x o(ra_to/n. a)ide\s a)/ra; nai/. o(moio/teron a)/ra yu_xh\ sw/mato/s e)stin tw=| a)idei=, to\ de\ tw=| o(ra_tw=| what then do we say about the soul? That it is visible or invisible? Not visible. Then it is invisible? Yes. Consequently soul has a closer resemblance to the invisible than the body, and the latter to the visible
P. Ph. 79b.

§2792
In the argument ex contrario set forth in clauses with me/n and de/, a)/ra, usually meaning in sooth, is commonly placed with the second clause (
P. Ph. 80d, R. 445 b), occasionally with the first (
P. Cr. 46d, L. 840 b), or with both (
P. Ph. 97a, R. 600 c).

§2793
In direct questions a)/ra adds liveliness, while at the same time it marks connection or consequence. So ti/s a)/ra who then? pw=s a)/ra how then? In questions of anxiety a)/ra marks increase of feeling. Thus, ti/ m' a)/ra ti/ m' o)le/keis; why then, why dost thou destroy me?
S. Ant. 1285.

§2794

a)/ra occurs in questions in which the admissibility of one opinion is inferred from the rejection of another. Thus, ei)pe/ moi, e)/fh, w)= *oeodo/th, e)/sti soi a)gro/s; ou)k e)/moig', e)/fh. a)ll' a)/ra oi)ki/a_ proso/dous e)/xousa; ‘tell me,’ said he, ‘Theodote, have you an estate?’ ‘Not I indeed,’ said she. ‘But perhaps then you have a house that brings in an income?’
X. M. 3.11.4. Such questions are often ironical (
P. A. 25a).

§2795

a)/ra is often used to indicate new perception, or surprise genuine or affected; as when the truth is just realized after a previous erroneous opinion and one finds oneself undeceived either agreeably or disagreeably. So, especially with the imperfect of ei)=nai, a)/ra means after all, it seems, why then, so then, sure enough. See 1902.

§2796

ei' a)/ra, e)a\_n a)/ra if really, if after all, if indeed, are commonly used of that which is improbable or undesirable; ei' (e)a\_n) mh\ a)/ra unless perhaps (nisi forte, nisi vero) is often ironical. Thus,

ei) a)/ra ge/gonen w(s ou(=toi e)/legon if indeed it did take place as they said
D. 56.28, kai\ mh\n ei) kai\ tou=t' a)/ra dei= m' ei)pei=n and yet if I must after all say this too 18. 317, polla/kis toi=s *)aqhnai/ois parh/|nei, h)\n a)/ra pote\ kata\ gh=n biasqw=si . . . tai=s nausi\ pro\s a(/pantas a)nqi/stasqai he often counselled the Athenians, if after all they should ever be hard pressed on the land side, to fight the world with their fleet
T. 1.93,

pw=s a)\n ou)=n o( toiou=tos a)nh\r diafqei/roi tou\s ne/ous; ei) mh\ a)/ra h( th=s a)reth=s e)pime/leia diafqora/_ e)stin how then could such a man corrupt the young? unless perchance the study of virtue is corruption
X. M. 1.2.8.

§2797

ei) (e)a\_n) a)/ra is common after skopw=, etc. See 2672.

§2798

a)/ra is often used, especially with w(s, to introduce the statement of others which, in the view of the speaker, is (usually) to be rejected. Thus, a)kou/w au)to\n e)rei=n w(s a)/r' e)gw\ pa/ntwn w(=n kathgorw= koinwno\s ge/gona I hear that he is going to say that I forsooth (or if you please) have been a partner in all that I denounced
D. 19.202.

§2799
Attic has, in bimembral clauses, ei)/te a)/ra . . . ei)/te or ei)/te . . . ei)/te a)/ra, as

ei)/t' a)lhqe\s ei)/t' a)/r' ou)=n ma/thn whether truly or after all, it may be, falsely
S. Ph. 345. Hom. has also a similar use with ou)/te . . . ou)/te, and h)\ . . . h)/. Hom. has a)/ra . . . a)/ra (
y 887).

## a)=ra

§2800

a)=ra, a confirmative particle from h)= + a)/ra, is used in lyric and dramatic poetry in the sense of a)/ra. a)=ra is postpositive, except in New Comedy.

so\n a)=ra tou)/rgon, ou)k e)mo\n keklh/setai it shall then be called thy work, not mine
S. Aj. 1368. Often with ti/s, as ti/s a)=r' e)mou= ge/noit' a)\n a+)qliw/teros; who then could be more wretched than I am? Trag. fr. 280. On interrogative a)=ra, see 2650, 2651. Epic h)= r(a is both confirmatory and interrogative.

## a)ta/r

§2801

a)ta/r (prepositive; Hom. also au)ta/r from au)=te + a)/r) usually poetical, but found in Xenophon and Plato, is an adversative conjunction commonly used to introduce a strong or surprising contrast (but, but yet, however); sometimes to introduce a slight contrast (and, and then), but one stronger than that marked by de/. a)ta/r is common as a correlative to me/n. It is often found in lively questions to introduce an objection; in rapid transitions; and sometimes it serves to introduce the apodosis of a conditional sentence. a)ta/r was largely displaced by the stronger a)lla/.

## au)=

§2802

au)= (postpositive), an adversative particle meaning on the other hand, on the contrary (properly again). In Hom. it serves as a correlative to me/n or h)= toi, and to introduce the apodosis of conditional or relative clauses.
au)= is often used with personal pronouns, as

a)lla\ su\ au)= . . . le/ge but do you in turn tell us
X. S. 3. 5; and is often added to de/, as

oi( *(/ellhnes e)ph=|san . . . oi( d' au)= ba/rbaroi ou)k e)de/xonto the Greeks came on, but the barbarians on their part did not wait to receive them
X. A. 1.10.11. Connected in meaning are the derivatives au)=te (poetic) and au)=qis.

## ga/r

§2803

ga/r (postpositive) in fact, indeed , and for, a confirmatory adverb and a causal conjunction. As a conjunction, ga/r usually stands after the first word in its clause; as an adverb, its position is freer. ga/r is especially common in sentences which offer a reason for, or an explanation of, a preceding or following statement. It may be used in successive clauses.
a. ga/r is from ge/ + a)/r ( = a)/ra), ge/ originally giving prominence either to the word it followed or to the whole clause, while a)/ra marked this prominence as due to something previously expressed or latent in the context. The compound ga/r originally emphasized a thought either as the result of existing circumstances or as a patent and well known fact.
