In most uses of the word, however, the force of its component parts cannot be distinguished nor is it clear in many cases whether ga/r is a conjunction or an adverb marking <*>ssurance.

§2804
Adverbial ga/r appears in questions, answers, and wishes; and in many other cases where recourse is had to conscious or unconscious ellipse by those scholars who hold that ga/r is always a conjunction. Ellipse is sometimes natural and easy, but often clumsy and artificial. Though we find in parallel use both incomplete and complete clauses with ga/r, it is improbable that the Greeks were conscious of the need of any supplement to explain the thought. In many uses ga/r has become formulaic, serving only to show the natural agreement with the existing situation.

§2805
In questions, ga/r asks for confirmation of a preceding statement, or expresses assent or dissent; asks whether an act before mentioned was not reasonable; asks a question prompted by some form of emotion; and serves to indicate transition, etc.
a. In questions ga/r often marks surprise or indignation, and may frequently be translated by what, why, then, really, surely. Thus, tauti\_ le/geis su\ strathgo\n ptwxo\s w)/n; e)gw\ ga/r ei)mi ptwxo/s; do you, beggar that you are, address your general thus? what! I a beggar?
Ar. Ach. 593, h)= zh=| ga\r a(_nh/r; is the man really alive?
S. El. 1221, oi)/ei ga/r soi maxei=sqai . . . to\n a)delfo/n; do you really think that your brother is going to fight? X. A. <*> 7. 9. So ti/s ga/r; who then, why who?
b. Brief interrogative for<*>ulae asking for confirmation of a preceding statement are:
ti/ ga/r; what then, how when, how else? ti/ ga/r also serves as a formula of transition (now, well then, now what . . ., furthermore).
h)= ga/r; is it not so? surely this is so? (cp. n'est ce pas). Often of surprise.
ou' ga/r; is it not so? often in indignant questions; when not standing alone, why not?
<*>w=s ga/r; po/qen ga/r; imply that something is impossible (often of surprise). Cp. pw=s ga\r ou)/; in negative rhetorical questions.

§2806
In answers ga/<*> marks assent, assurance, sometimes dissent. Thus,

deino/n ge tou)pi/sagma tou= nosh(matos. deino\n ga\r ou)de\ r(hto/n dread indeed is the burden of one disease. Aye dread indeed and beyond all words
S. Ph. 755,

o(mologei=s ou)=n peri\ e)me\ a)/dikos gegenh=sqai; h)= ga\r a)na/gkh do you then confess that you have proved yourself unjust toward me? In truth I must indeed
X. A. 1.6.8,

mhd' ai( mhte/res ta\ paidi/a e)kdeimatou/ntwn . . . mh\ ga/r, e)/fh nor let mothers frighten their children. No indeed, said he
P. R. 381e, fh\|s ta/d' ou)=n; a(\ mh\ fronw\= ga\r ou) filw= le/gein dost thou then consent to this? No, for I am not wont to utter words I do not mean
S. O. T. 1520.
a. ga/r is common in brief answers, as after ou), dei=, e)/oike, ei)ko/s, le/gw, w(molo/ghtai. So in the rhetorical questions pw=s ga/r; pw=s ga\r ou)/; used as answers.

§2807
In wishes:

ei) ga\r . . . e)n tou/tw| ei)/h would that it depended on that
P. Pr. 310d, kakw=s ga\r e)co/loio oh that you might perish wretchedly E. Cyc. 261. Here ga/r marks the agreement of the wish with the existing situation.

§2808

Explanatory (or prefatory) ga/r has the force of now, namely, that is, for example; but usually is not to be translated, and especially when the preceding sentence contains a verb of saying, showing, etc. It usually introduces, as an explanation, the details of that which was promised in an incomplete or general statement; sometimes, without any such statement, it introduces a new fact. Whether this ga/r is an adverb or a conjunction is uncertain. Thus, dokei= toi/nun moi xarie/steron ei)=nai mu=qon u(_mi=n le/gein. h)=n ga/r pote ktl. I think it will be more interesting to tell you a myth. Once upon a time there was, etc.
P. Pr. 320c,

ou(/tw ga\r skopei=te look at it in this light
L. 19.34 (at the beginning of a new point in the discussion).

§2809
Explanatory ga/r often introduces a clause in apposition to a preceding demonstrative, to such expressions as tekmh/rion de/ or martu/rion de/ now the proof is this, dh=lon de/ (e)stin) it is clear, to\ de\ me/giston but, what is of the greatest importance, or to relative clauses (995). Thus, w(s d' e)/ti ma=llon qarrh=|s, kai\ to/de katano/hson: oi( me\n ga\r (explaining to/de) pole/mioi polu\ me\n e)la/_ttone/s ei)si nu=n h)\ pri\n h(tthqh=nai u(f' h(mw=n and that you may be still more encouraged, consider this fact too. The enemy (namely) are much fewer now than they were before they were beaten by us
X. C. 5.2.36, e)nnoh/swmen de\ kai\ th=|de, w(s pollh\ e)lpi/s e)stin a)gaqo\n au)to\ ei)=nai. duoi=n ga\r qa/_tero/n e)stin to\ teqna/nai ktl. let us consider the matter also in this way and we shall see that there is abundant reason to hope that it is a good: now death must be one of two things, etc.
P. A. 40c, martu/rion de/: *dh/lou ga\r kaqairome/nhs ktl. and this is a proof of it: now when Delos was being purified, etc.
T. 1.8,

d\ de\ pa/ntwn sxetliw/taton: ou(\s ga\r o(mologh/saimen a)\n ponhrota/tous ei)=nai tw=n poli_tw=n, tou/tous pistota/tous fu/lakas h(gou/meqa th=s poli_tei/a_s ei)=nai but the most abominable of all is this: we consider the most trustworthy guardians of the State to be those men whom we should agree were the worst citizens
I. 8.53.

§2810

Causal ga/r is a conjunction: for (nam, enim). It serves to introduce a cause of, or a reason for, an action before mentioned; to justify a preceding utterance; to confirm the truth of a previous statement. Causal ga/r often refers to a thought implied in what has preceded. Thus, lekte/a a(\ gignw/skw: e)/mpeiros ga/r (causal) ei)mi kai\ th=s xw/ra_s tw=n *paflago/nwn kai\ th=s duna/mews. e)/xei ga\r (explanatory) a)mfo/tera, kai\ pedi/a ka/llista kai\ o)/rh u(yhlo/tata I must tell what I know, for I am acquainted with the country of the Paphlagonians and its resources; now the country has very fertile plains and very lofly mountains
X. A. 5.6.6, i)ou/, du/sthne: tou=to ga/r s' e)/xw mo/non proseipei=n alas, ill-fated one! for by this name alone can I address thee
S. O. T. 1071, e)pisteuo/mhn de\ u(po\ tw=n *lakedaimoni/wn: ou) ga\r a)/n me e)/pempon pa/lin pro\s u(_ma=s but I was trusted by the Lacedaemonians; for (otherwise, i.e. ei) mh\ e)pi/steuon) they would not have sent me back to you
P. A. 30c.

§2811

Anticipatory ga/r states the cause, justifies the utterance, or gives the explanation, of something set forth in the main clause which follows. The main clause usually contains an inferential word, a demonstrative pointing backward, or kai/, de/, a)lla/; or stands without a connective. Anticipatory ga/r may often be rendered by since, but is often omitted in translation. Thus, e)/ti toi/nun a)kou/sate kai\ ta/de. e)pi\ lei/a_n ga\r u(_mw=n e)kporeu/sontai/ tines. oi)=mai nu=n be/ltiston ei)=nai ktl. listen therefore to this proposal also. Some of you will be going out to plunder. Now it is my opinion that it is best, etc.
X. A. 5.1.8, e)selqw\n de\ th\n taxi/sthn, h)=n ga/r oi( pai=s ei(=s mou=nos . . ., tou=ton e)kpe/mpei and when he had come in straightway, he sent out his son, for he had one only son
Hdt. 1.119, w)= fi/loi, ou) ga/r t' i)/dmen o(/ph| zo/fos ou)d' o(/ph| h)w/s . . . a)lla\ frazw/meqa ktl. friends, since we do not know where is the place of darkness nor of the dawn, let us consider, etc.
k 190,

w)= fi/ltate, spondai\ ga/r ei)si/ soi mo/nw|, me/trhson ei)rh/nhs ti/ moi my dear fellow, since you alone have got a truce, measure me out a bit of peace
Ar. Ach. 102.
a. In this construction ga/r may be an adverb, not a conjunction. Cases of explanatory ga/r (2808) and of parenthetical ga/r (2812), especially after vocatives, may fall under 2811.

§2812
The clause with ga/r since is often inserted parenthetically in the clause which it is intended to explain; as o( de\ (kri(_nousi ga\r boh=| kai\ ou) yh/fw|) ou)k e)/fh diagignw/skein th\n boh\n pote/ra_ mei/zwn but, since they decide by shouts and not by ballot, he said he could not decide which side shouted the louder
T. 1.87.

§2813

kai\ ga/r has in general two distinct meanings according as ga/r is an adverb or a conjunction. As kai\ ga/r has become a formula, it is often uncertain which of the two words is the adverb, which the conjunction.

§2814
(I) kai\ ga/r and in fact, and indeed, kai/ being a conjunction, and ga/r an adverb. Here the clause in which kai\ ga/r stands is added as a new and important thought; where ga/r alone would state the reason or the explanation with less independence and with slighter emphasis. The negative is ou)de\ ga/r. Thus *ku=ros d' o(rw=n tou\s *(/ellhnas ni_kw=ntas to\ kaq' au(tou\s . . . e)pemelei=to o(/ ti poih/sei basileu/s. kai\ ga\r h)/|dei au)to\n o(/ti me/son e)/xoi tou= *persikou= strateu/matos on seeing the Greeks victorious over the troops opposed to them, Cyrus watched to see what the king would do; and in fact he knew that he commanded the centre of the Persian force
X. A. 1.8.21 (cp. 1. 1. 6, 2. 5. 5, 2. 6. 2). So often in affirmative responses: h)\ ou)k a)gaph/seis tou/twn tugxa/nwn; e)gw\ me\n ga\r a)\n a)gapw/|hn. kai\ ga\r e)gw/, e)/fh or will you not be content if you obtain this? For my part I shall be. And so shall I, he said
P. R. 473b.
a. kai\ ga\r kai/ and even is kai\ ga/r and in fact reënforced by kai/. Thus, kai\ ga\r kai\ a)/deia e)fai/neto au)toi=s and in fact it looked to them as if there was perfect safety in so doing
T. 4.108. The negative is ou)de\ ga\r ou)de/ (2938).

§2815
(II) kai\ ga/r for even, for also. Here kai/ is an adverb affecting a single word, several words, or the whole sentence, and ga/r is a conjunction. The negative is ou)de\ ga/r. Thus,

kai\ ga\r ou(=toi for these too
P. A. 22c,

kai\ ga\r h)dikhme/noi si_ghso/mesqa for even wronged as I am I'll keep silent
E. Med. 314, kai\ ga\r mo/nos h(goi=t' a)\n du/nasqai pei/qein for, though quite unaided, he would think that he was able to persuade
X. M. 1.2.11.
a. kai\ ga\r . . . kai/ for both . . . and: here kai/ is correlated with a second kai/; as

kai\ ga\r u(giai/nousin oi( ta\ sw/mata eu)= e)/xontes kai\ i)sxu/_ousi for those who keep their bodies in good condition are both healthy and strong
X. M. 3.12.4.

§2816

a)lla\ ga/r occurs both in conjunction and separated by one or several words, which are generally emphatic.

§2817

First Form (often but since, since however): here there are two predicates. In prose separation is the rule. Thus,

a)ll', ou) ga\r e)/peiqe, didoi= to\ fa=ros but since he could not persuade her, he gave her the mantle
Hdt. 9.109, a)ll' i)/sws ga\r kai\ a)/lloi tau)ta\ e)nqu_mou=ntai, . . . mh\ a)name/nwmen a)/llous e)f' h(ma=s e)lqei=n ktl. since however others too perhaps entertain the same opinion, let us not wait for others to come to us, etc.
X. A. 3.1.24. In poetry the words are generally not separated. Thus, a)lla\ ga\r *kre/onta leu/ssw to/nde . . . pro\s do/mous stei/xonta, pau/sw tou\s . . . go/ous since however I see Creon yonder coming to the palace, I will cease my lamentations
E. Phoen. 1307. Here the clause coördinated by the conjunction ga/r is parenthetical and gives, by anticipation, the reason for the a)lla/ clause. Cp. a)ll' e)pei/ e 137, and Shakesp. Sonnet 54: “but, for their virtue only is their show, They live unwoo'd.”—The first form is found chiefly in Homer, Pindar, Herodotus, and in the drama.

§2818

Second Form (usually but indeed, but in fact, but the truth is, but be that as it may). Here there is a single predicate. Thus,

kai\ ou)x w(s a)ti_ma/zwn le/gw . . . a)lla\ ga\r e)moi\ tou/twn . . . ou)de\n me/testi and I do not speak in disparagement; but the truth is I have nothing to do with these matters
P. A. 19c, a)lla\ gignw/skw ga\r . . . o(/ti ktl. but indeed I know that, etc.
X. C. 2.1.13,

a)ll' ei)sorw= ga\r to/nde . . . *pula/dhn dro/mw| stei/xonta but indeed I see Pylades yonder coming at full speed
E. Or. 725,

a)ll' ou' ga\r e)/sti ta)_mfanh= kru/ptein but indeed it is impossible to hide what lies open
S. O. C. 755.
a. In this use ga/r may have preserved, or regained, its primitive adverbial (confirmatory) force. Many scholars, however, claim that there was a conscious or unconscious ellipse, after a)lla/, of an idea pertinent to the situation; and thus regard this form as logically equivalent to the form in which ga/r is a causal conjunction. In actual use a)lla\ ga/r was clearly a formula used without any consciousness of an omitted idea.

§2819

a)lla\ ga/r has a great variety of uses, most of which may be classed as follows:
a. In statements of direct opposition: kai\ tau=ta/ se pollou= dei= lelhqe/nai, a)lla\ ga\r oi)=mai d\ a)/rti ou)k e)/fhsqa poiei=n, tou=to poiei=s and you are far from forgetting this, but in fact I think you are doing that which you just denied you were doing
P. Charm. 166c.
N. This use is post-Homeric, rare in the drama, common in the orators and Plato. It is especially frequent in putting and setting aside an objection supposed to be raised by an opponent (hypophora). Cp. b.
b. In real and assumed objections (cp. at enim): kai\ a)lhqh= ge e)/legon, w)= *sw/krates. i)/sws. a)lla\ ga/r, w)= *eu)qu/frwn, kai\ a)lla\ polla\ fh\|s ei)=nai o(/sia yes, and I said what was true, Socrates. Perhaps, but in fact, Euthyphron, you say that many other things too are holy
P. Euth. 6d, a)lla\ ga/r, fh/sei tis, ou) r(a/|dion a)ei\ lanqa/nein kako\n o)/nta yes, but some one will say that it is not easy always to conceal the fact that one is wicked
P. R. 365c.
c. In transitions.—(1) At the close of the discussion of an argument, where the force of a)lla/ is like that of and yet or emphatic but. Thus, a)lla\ ga/r, w)= boulh/, tau=ta me\n e)nqa/de ou)k oi)=d' o(/ ti dei= le/gein but, Senators, I do not know why I should discuss these matters here
L. 7.42,

a)lla\ ga\r h)/dh w(/ra_ a)pie/nai but it is already time to depart
P. A. 42a.
(2) To restrain the expression of emotion; as a)ll' a)/nac ga/r e)st' e)mo/s, si_gw= but no, I am silent for he is my king
E. El. 1245.
(3) When the approach of a new actor is announced. Cp. 2817, 2818.

§2820

Other Combinations.—ga\r a)/ra for sure enough.
ga\r dh/ for of course, for indeed, for you must know, as fame\n ga\r dh/ for of course we say so.
ga\r dh/ pou for I presume, for doubtless.
ga\r ou)=n often of frank assent, as ou) ga\r ou)=n certainly not, le/gw ga\r ou)=n certainly, I do say so; less often to explain (for certainly); kai\ ga\r ou)=n (not very common) is stronger than kai\ ga/r.
ga/r pou for I suppose.
ga/r toi for surely, for mark you; sometimes kai\ ga/r toi.

## ge/

§2821

ge/ (postpositive and enclitic) is an intensive and restrictive particle with the force of at least, at any rate, even, certainly, indeed; but often to be rendered by intonation. ge/ may indicate assent, concession, banter, scorn, deprecation, irony, etc. ge/ emphasizes single words or whole phrases or clauses.
a. Single words. So often with pronouns, as e)/gwge I at least (excluding others), e)me/ ge cp. mi-ch, o(/ ge even he (Hom.), ou(=to/s ge, and with a repeated pronoun (
S. Ph. 117). Other words, as o(/ ti bou/lei ge whatever you like
Ar. Ran. 3,

plh/qei ge ou)x u(perbaloi/meq' a)\n tou\s polemi/ous in numbers at least we should not surpass the enemy
X. C. 2.1.18.
b. With phrases or clauses. Thus,

w(s mh/ m' a)/ti_mon, tou= qeou= ge prosta/thn, ou(/tws a)fh=| me that he may not thus send me away in dishonour—who am the suppliant of the god
S. O. C. 1278, a)nqrw/pous ti/_nusqon, o(/tis g' e)pi/orkon o)mo/ssh| ye who punish men who swear falsely
*g 279.

§2822

ge/ may be used twice in the same sentence. Thus,

e)pei/ g' a)rkou=nq' i(kana\ toi=s ge sw/frosin since indeed that which suffices their wants is enough for the wise
E. Phoen. 545. Cp.
Hdt. 1.187,
Ar. Vesp. 1507.

§2823

ge/ stands between article and noun, as oi(/ g' a)/nqrwpoi (after a preposition, as e)/n ge tw=| fanerw=|); between noun and adjective, or after the adjective, as a)nh/r ge sofo/s, or a)nh\r sofo/s ge; after a possessive pronoun, as e)mo/s ge qu_mo/s; after me/n, de/, te/, as o(/ti de/ ge a)lhqh= le/gw. When ge/ influences a whole clause it stands as near as possible to the introductory conjunction; as ei)/ ge, a)=ra/ ge.

§2824

ge/ in contrasts and alternatives; as su\ d' ou' le/geis ge (ai)sxra/),

dra=|s de/ me thou dost not indeed say, but do shameful things to me
E. And. 239,

h)/toi kru/fa ge h)\ fanerw=s either secretly or openly
T. 6.34,

h)\ sofoi\ h)\ ti/_mioi h)\ ge/ronte/s ge or wise or held in honour aye or old
P. Hipp. M. 301a (here ge/ indicates a change in an alternative series; cp. ou)/te . . . ou)/te . . . ou)de/ ge and kai\ . . . ge 2829).

§2825

ge/ in replies and comments (yes, well). Thus, dokei= pareikaqei=n; o(/son g', a)/nac, ta/xista does it seem best to you that I should give way? Aye, my lord, and with all speed
S. Ant. 1102. Here kai\ . . . ge is common, as kai\ ou)de/n ge a)to/pws yes, and no wonder
P. Th. 142b.

§2826

o(/s ge (rarely o(/stis ge) has a causal force, much like qui quidem, quippe qui. Thus,

a)/topa le/geis . . . o(/s ge keleu/eis e)me\ new/teron o)/nta kaqhgei=sqai you are talking absurdly in bidding me who am the younger take precedence
X. M. 2.3.15. So with other relatives, as oi(=os, o(/sos, w(/sper.

§2827

ge/ sometimes marks an ellipse (
S. Ph. 1409). When the verb of the apodosis is omitted, the protasis often has ge/ (so usually in Aristophanes, e.g. Nub. 267).

§2828
When ge/ is followed by other particles, it belongs with the emphasized word, and the other particles retain their original force; as

tou/s ge me/ntoi a)gaqou/s yet the brave at least
X. A. 1.9.14. So ge dh/, ge me\n dh/, ge/ toi (often used like gou=n in giving a reason for a belief), ge/ toi dh/. With the imperative, ge/ is rare except when it is followed by another particle, as o(/ra_ ge mh/n
S. O. C. 587.

§2829

After other Particles.—For example:
de/ ge: here ge/ usually does not emphasize de/ but either a single word or the whole clause; as h(mi=n de/ ge oi)=mai pa/nta poihte/a but we at least, in my opinion, should adopt every means
X. A. 3.1.35. de\ . . . ge is often used when two things are compared, in order to show that one is more important than the other.
kai\ . . . ge sometimes means yes, and and sometimes ge/ emphasizes the intervening word. Thus, kou)de/n ge qau=ma yes, and no wonder
S. O. T. 1132,

kai\ sti/bou ge ou)dei\s ktu/pos and of footsteps there is no sound
S. Ph. 29. kai\ . . . ge often emphasizes one item in a series, and especially the last item, Here kai\ . . . ge/ pros (kai\ pro/s ge) and besides is common. Cp.
P. G. 450d, 469 b.
me/n ge lends force to a contrast (
P. S. 180d); sometimes it has the force of that is to say, for example (
T. 6.86).
Frequent combinations are a)ll' ou)=n . . . ge, me/ntoi . . . ge, mh\n . . . ge, ou)kou=n . . . ge.

## gou=n

§2830

gou=n (postpositive; first in Aeschylus) is a restrictive particle from ge/ + ou)=n. Its meaning varies according to the prominence of the ge/ or ou)=n; often certainly, at any rate (at all events, at least). gou=n commonly confirms a previous general assertion by giving a special instance of its truth (the special instance may be a seeming exception). gou=n is thus used in bringing forward a reason, which, while not absolutely conclusive, is the most probable explanation of a previous statement.

e)/ti ga\r ou(=toi kaki/_one/s ei)si tw=n u(f' h(mw=n h(tthme/nwn: e)/feugon gou=n pro\s e)kei/nous katalipo/ntes h(ma=s for they are even more cowardly than those who were beaten by us. At any rate they deserted us and sought refuge with them
X. A. 3.2.17.

§2831

gou=n may emphasize a pronoun; as pro\s gou=n e)mou=
S. Aj. 527, ta\ gou=n sa/
S. El. 1499.

§2832
In answers gou=n means well, at least; yes certainly; as ei)ko\s gou=n
X. C. 5.3.14.

§2833

gou=n finds the proof of an assertion in one of several possible facts or occurrences; ga/r gives the reason in general, but gives no particular instance; d' ou)=n has an adversative force: ‘be that as it may, yet at any rate.’

## de/

§2834

de/ (postpositive) was originally an adverb with a force not unlike that of on the other hand, on the contrary; later it became a conjunction commonly represented by but or and, which are, however, mere makeshifts of translation. de/ serves to mark that something is different from what precedes, but only to offset it, not to exclude or contradict it; it denotes only a slight contrast, and is therefore weaker than a)lla/, but stronger than kai/. de/ is adversative and copulative; but the two uses are not always clearly to be distinguished.

§2835

Adversative de/ often marks a silent contrast, as at the beginning of speeches (e)gw\ de\ ou(/tw gignw/skw
X. A. 4.6.10); in questions which imply opposition to something just said (
S. O. C. 57); in answers (
S. O. T. 379); in objections or corrections (
S. Ant. 517); in to\ de/, ta\ de/ on the contrary, whereas really, where a true opinion is opposed to a false one; similarly in nu=n de/ but in fact, but as the case stands. When de/ is balanced by me/n (2904) it is antithetical rather than adversative.
a. de/ after a pronoun following a vocative produces a pause; as *nio/ba_ se\ d' e)/gwge ne/mw qeo/n ah Niobe, thee I regard as divine
S. El. 150.
b. de/ instead of a)lla/ is rare except in the poets and Thucydides. Thus, promhnu/_sh|s ge tou=to mhdeni\ tou)=rgon, krufh= de\ keu=qe make known this plan to no one, but hide it in secret
S. Ant. 85,

ou)k e)pi\ kakw=|, e)p' e)leuqerw/sei de\ tw=n *(ellh/nwn parelh/luqa I have come, not to harm, but to liberate, the Greeks
T. 4.86. Sometimes ou) me/n precedes when de/ is used like a)lla/<*>（
T. 1.50).
c. But not is a)ll' ou' or ou) me/ntoi, not ou) de/, in order to avoid confusion with ou)de/ nor, not even. But ou) and de/ may be separated, as

ou) boulome/nwn de/ . . . prosxwrei=n but since they did not wish to surrender
X. H. 1.6.13.

§2836

Copulative de/ marks transition, and is the ordinary particle used in connecting successive clauses or sentences which add something new or different, but not opposed, to what precedes, and are not joined by other particles, such as ga/r or ou)=n.
Copulative de/ is common in marking continuation, especially when something subordinate is added. Thus, when a new phase of a narrative is developed (
X. A. 1.2.7-8); where attention is called to a new point or person (as in ti/ d' e)/stin;); when an interrupted speech or narrative is resumed (
X. C. 1.6.41,
S. Tr. 281); where a second relationship is added (mh/thr basile/ws, basi/leia d' e)mh/ the mother of the King, and my Queen
A. Pers. 151, *)hio/na . . . *mendai/wn a)poiki/a_n, polemi/a_n de\ ou)=san he seized Eïon, a colony of Mende, and which had been hostile
T. 4.7); when de/ has a force like that of ga/r (
X. C. 6.3.16); and in kai\ . . . de/ and also (Epic kai\ de/), 2891.

§2837

Apodotic de/.—The beginning of the principal clause (apodosis) of conditional and concessive sentences is often marked by de/. Apodotic de/ is found also in the principal clause of causal, temporal, comparative, and relative sentences; and regularly gives greater emphasis to the main clause, which is thus distinctly set off against the subordinate clause. Apodotic de/ is very common in Homer and Herodotus, not rare in Attic poetry, but infrequent in Attic prose, where it is used especially after an emphatic personal or demonstrative pronoun or when a participle represents the antecedent clause. Thus, ei(=os o( tau=q' w(/rmaine . . ., h)=lqe d' *)aqh/nh while he was revolving these things, then came Athene A 193,

ei) ou)=n e)gw\ mh\ gignw/skw mh/te ta\ o(/sia mh/te ta\ di/kaia, u(_mei=s de\ dida/cete/ me accordingly if I have no knowledge either of what is holy or what is just, do you then instruct me
X. H. 4.1.33,

e)pei\ toi/nun ou) du/namai/ se pei/qein mh\ e)kqei=nai, su\ de\ w(=de poi/hson since therefore I am not able to persuade you not to expose it, do you then do as follows
Hdt. 1.112,

e)ka/qeudon . . . w(/sper oi( o(pli=tai ou(/tw de\ kai\ oi( peltastai/ as the hoplites so also the peltasts sleep
X. C. 8.5.12,

e)peidh\ de\ a)fiko/menoi ma/xh| e)kra/thsan . . ., fai/nontai d' ou)d' e)ntau=qa pa/_sh| th=| duna/mei xrhsa/menoi but when on their arrival they had conquered in battle, not even then did they appear to have made use of their entire force
T. 1.11,

kai/ pote o)/ntos pa/gou . . . ou(=tos d' e)n tou/tois e)ch/|ei and once when there was a frost he went out in the midst of this
P. S. 220b.
a. Apodotic de/ often resumes a de/ in the subordinate clause and carries on the opposition expressed by that clause; as ei) de\ bou/lesqe . . . e)kleca/menoi o(/poi a)\n bou/lhsqe katasxei=n . . ., ploi=a d' u(_mi=n pa/restin but if you wish to select some place wherever you please and take possession of it, you have ships at command
X. A. 5.6.20, a(\ d' ai)sxu/_nhn h(mi=n fe/rei . . ., tau=ta de\ kata\ xw/ra_n me/nei but the terms which cause us shame, these remain in force
I. 4.176.
b. The use of apodotic de/ should not be regarded as a survival of original coördination.

§2838

de/ without me/n.—A clause with de/ often has no correlative particle in the clause with which it is contrasted. Here me/n is not used because the opposition in the first clause was too weak, or because the speaker did not intend to announce a following contrast or did not think he was going to use a contrasted de/ clause. Sometimes the entire first clause may have to be supplied in thought from the general connection or from what has gone before. de/ without me/n in such cases is common in poetry, but not rare in prose, even in brief antitheses, as a(\ pa/ntes a)ei\ gli/xontai le/gein, a)ci/ws d' ou)dei\s ei)pei=n dedu/nhtai exploits which everybody continually desires to recount, but which no one has been able to set forth adequately
D. 6.11. See also 2835.
a. When a relative construction passes over into a construction with a personal or demonstrative pronoun, the relative clause usually has no me/n. Cp. Soph. Aj. 457, quoted in 2517.
b. oi( de/, when opposed to a larger number of persons or things, is often used without oi( me/n, as proelhluqo/tes e)pi\ xi_lo/n, oi( d' e)pi\ cu/la having gone for fodder, and some for fuel
X. C. 6.3.9.

§2839

de/ with other Particles.—For example:
d' a)/ra, which sometimes follows me/n.
d' au)= and o(/mws de/ mark stronger opposition than de/ alone.
de\ dh/ but then, but now, well but is often used in passing to a new point. In Aristophanes this collocation is used almost always in questions.

## dh/

§2840

dh/ (postpositive except in Hom. dh\ ga/r and poetic dh\ to/te) marks something as immediately present and clear to the mind, and gives greater precision, positiveness, and exactness. It sets forth what is obvious, acknowledged, and natural, and often corresponds to voilà. dh/ is used with single words (especially adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, and conjunctions) or, as a sentence adverb, with whole clauses. dh/ usually stands after the word it emphasizes, though it may be separated from it by one or more other words.

§2841

dh/ of what is Obvious and Natural.—Thus, i)/ste dh/ you know of course, dei= dh/ it is manifestly necessary. So

ou)x oi(/tws e)/xei; e)/xei dh/ is not this so? Of course it is
P. A. 27c,

nu=n d' o(ra=te dh/ but now you certainly see
X. C. 3.2.12, *paru/satis me\n dh\ h( mh/thr u(ph=rxe tw=| *ku/_rw| Parysatis, his mother, naturally supported Cyrus
X. A. 1.1.4.

§2842

Ironical dh/.—Thus,

*swkra/ths o( sofo\s dh/ Socrates the wise forsooth
P. A. 27a; often w(s dh/, as

w(s dh\ su/ moi tu/rannos *(argei/wn e)/sh| that you forsooth should be the lord and master of the Argives!
A. Ag. 1633.

§2843

Intensive dh/ emphasizes, and makes definite, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, and other words. Thus, a(/pantes dh/ absolutely all, kra/tistoi dh/ the very best, mo/nos dh/ quite alone, o)li/goi dh/ very few; ou(/tw dh/ just so, w(/sper dh/ exactly as, polla/kis dh/ very often, dh=la dh/ quite plain, nu=n dh/ just now, now at once; e)kei=nos dh/ this (and no other), d\s dh/ who indeed. With indefinite pronouns dh/ increases the indefiniteness (339 e); as o(/stis dh/ whoever at all. With other words: ei) dh/ if indeed, ou) dh/ no indeed, i(/na dh/ that in truth.
a. With imperatives and in questions dh/ adds urgency; as a)/koue dh/ pray listen! ti/ dh/; why, pray?

§2844

dh/ may introduce emphatically the conclusion of a temporal sentence or of a narrative on passing to a new topic; as e)ntau=qa dh/, to/te dh/ then indeed, then and not till then, then it was that. Cp.
X. A. 1.10.1.

§2845

Temporal dh/ often, especially with kai/, approximates in meaning to h)/dh already. Thus,

o( de\ qanw\n keu/qei ka/tw dh\ gh=s but he is dead and already is hidden beneath the earth
S. O. T. 967, o(po/te . . . qhrw/|hs kai\ dh\ du/o h(me/ra_s when you have hunted (already) for two days
X. C. 2.4.17, kai\ dh\ le/gw soi well I will tell thee (without further ado)
S. Ant. 245. So also in te/los dh/, nu=n dh/.—Of succession, dh/ means next.—Poetic dau)=te (dh\ au)=te) means now again.

§2846

Consecutive and Resumptive dh/ is used to set forth an inference, draw a conclusion, denote a consequence, and mark a transition (me\n dh\ . . . de/). Here dh/ is a sentence adverb: accordingly, then, of course, clearly, you see, I say. Thus,

e)/legon o(/ti kati/doien nu/ktwr polla\ pura\ fai/nonta. e)do/kei dh\ toi=s strathgoi=s ou)k a)sfale\s ei)=nai diaskhnou=n they said that they had seen many fires visible in the night; accordingly it seemed to the generals to be unsafe to encamp apart
X. A. 4.4.10,

ferau/la_s me\n dh\ ou(/tws ei)=pen: a)ni/_stanto de\ kai\ a)/lloi polloi/ Pherauias then spake thus; and many others also rose to speak
X. C. 2.3.16.

§2847

kai\ dh/: (a) Introduces a climax, as kai\ dh\ to\ me/giston and above all, what is the main thing
P. A. 41b. (b) In replies = well; as ble/yon ka/tw: kai\ dh\ ble/pw look down! Well, I am looking
Ar. Av. 175. This is akin to the temporal use. (c) In assumptions = suppose (1771). On kai\ dh\ kai/ see 2890.

## dai/, dh=qen, dh/pou, dh=ta

§2848

dai/ is used in colloquial Attic after interrogative words to express wonder, indignation, etc. Thus, ti/ dai/; pw=s dai/; what then? how so?

§2849

dh=qen truly, forsooth, is commonly used of apparent or pretended truth, and mostly with an ironical tone. Thus,

e)kerto/mhsas dh=qen w(s pai=d' o)/nta me thou hast mocked me forsooth as though I were a child
A. Pr. 986.

§2850

dh/pou probably, I presume, I should hope, doubtless, you will admit, is stronger than pou/ perhaps, I suppose. dh/pou often has a touch of irony or doubt in stating a case that would seem to be certain; as i)/ste dh/pou o(/qen h(/lios a)ni/sxei you know, I presume, where the sun rises
X. A. 5.7.6. In questions dh/pou expects the answer yes. ou) dh/pou certainly not and is it not so? (with irony).

§2851

dh=ta assuredly, really, in truth, is rare outside of Attic. It occurs: (a) In answers, often when a word is repeated with assent; as

gignw/skeq' u(_mei=s h(/tis e)/sq' h(/d' h( gunh/; gignw/skomen dh=ta do you know who this woman is? Yes indeed we do
Ar. Thesm. 606; ou) dh=ta surely not, in strong or indignant denial. (b) In questions, to mark an inference or consequence, as pw=s dh=ta; how in truth? ti/ dh=ta; what then? kai\ dh=ta e)to/lmas; and didst thou really dare?
S. Ant. 449. (c) In wishes and deprecations (stronger than dh/), as

sko/pei dh=ta only look
P. G. 452b, mh\ dh=ta, qu_me/, mh/ su/ g' e)rga/sh| ta/de no indeed, my heart, do not this deed
E. Med. 1056.

## ei)/te

§2852

ei)/te (from ei) + te/), a disjunctive particle, generally doubled: ei)/te . . . ei)/te whether . . . or (2675), if . . . or (siue . . . siue), giving equal value to each supposition.
a. With the subjunctive we find e)a/_n te (h)/n te, a)/_n te). Hom. has ei)/te . . . ei)/te, but not h)/n te . . . h)/n te, with the subjunctive. In the same sense Hom. has h)\ . . . h)/ and h)/te . . . h)/te with the subjunctive.

§2853
There are various forms of ei)/te clauses:
a. Both ei)/te clauses may have the same finite verb in common, which verb is used only once; as

ei)/te bou/lesqe polemei=n h(mi=n ei)/te fi/loi ei)=nai whether you wish to wage war upon us or to be our friends
X. C. 3.2.13.
b. Each ei)/te clause has its own verb and its own main clause; as e)ke/leuse/ se, ei)/te pa/ntas ai)tia=|, kri/_nanta se\ au)to\n xrh=sqai o(/ ti a)\n bou/lh|, ei)/te e(/na tina\ h)\ du/o . . . ai)tia=|, tou/tous a)ciou=si parasxei=n soi e(autou\s ei)s kri/sin the army requests that, if you accuse all, you pass sentence on them and treat them as you may think best; or, if you accuse one or two, they think it right that these men should surrender themselves to you for judgment
X. A. 6.6.20.
c. One main clause refers to both ei)/te clauses; as

o( a)gaqo\s a)nh\r . . . eu)dai/mwn e)sti\ . . . e)a/_n te me/gas kai\ i)sxu_ro/s, e)a/_n te smi_kro\s kai\ a)sqenh\s h)=| the good man is happy whether he is large and strong or small and weak
P. L. 660e.
d. Neither ei)/te clause has a verb, which is to be supplied from the main clause; as le/gontes, ei)/t' a)lhqe\s ei)/t' a)/r' ou)=n ma/thn (e)/legon) saying, whether truly or after all, it may be, falsely
S. Ph. 345.
e. One ei)/te clause has its own verb, while the other gets its verb from the main clause (rare); as e)moi\ su\ . . . fai/nh| . . . xrhsmw|dei=n, ei)/te par' *eu)qu/fronos e)pi/pnous geno/menos (xrhsmw|dei=s),

ei)/te kai\ a)/llh tis mou=sa pa/lai se e)nou=sa e)lelh/qei you seem to me to utter prophecies, whether you were inspired by Euthyphron or whether some other muse has long been present in you without your knowing it
P. Crat. 428c.

§2854

Variations: ei)/te . . . h)/ (common): ei)/te *lu_si/a_s h)/ tis a)/llos pw/pote e)/grayen h)\ gra/yei ktl. whether Lysias or anybody else whoever wrote or will write, etc.
P. Phae. 277d. h)\ . . . ei)/te: only in poetry (
S. Aj. 175). ei)/te . . . ei) de/: when the second member is more important (
P. L. 952c). On ei' . . . ei)/te see 2675 d. On ei)/te for ei)/te . . . ei)/te see 2675 b, N. 2.

§2855

ei)/te may be strengthened by a)/ra, dh/, kai/, or ou)=n. ou)=n is usually placed after the first ei)/te; like kai/, it may stand after the second also. When kai/ stands only after the second ei)/te, its clause is weaker than the first (
D. 18.57).

## h)/

§2856

Disjunctive h)/ (Epic h)e/) or (uel, aut); and repeated: h)\ . . . h)/ either . . . or (uel . . . uel, aut . . . aut) to connect the two members more closely.

a)gaqo\n h)\ kako/n good or bad
X. A. 1.9.11,

h)/ ti h)\ ou)de/n little or nothing
P. A. 17b. h)/ with the subjunctive is often used when a speaker corrects himself; as nu=n d' au)= tri/tos h)=lqe/ poqen swth/r, h)\ mo/ron ei)/pw; and now, again, the third has come, the deliverer—or shall I call it a deed of death?
A. Ch. 1074. On h)/ in questions, see 2657, 2675.

§2857
Between ascending numbers h)/ has the force of Eng. to, as

e)n e(\c h)\ e(pta\ h(me/rais in six to seven days
X. C. 5.3.28.

§2858

h)/toi may be used instead of the first h)/ when the first member, as is commonly the case, contains the more probable choice. In English the order is often inverted. Thus,

h)/toi klu/ousa paido\s h)\ tu/xh| pa/ra she comes either by chance or because she has heard about her son
S. Ant. 1182. h)/toi may be followed by h)/ several times. h)/toi . . . ge is more emphatic, as

h)/toi kru/fa ge h)\ fanerw=s either secretly or openly
T. 6.34.

§2859

h)/ often indicates that a given result will follow in case the action of the previous clause is not realized: or else (cp. ei) de\ mh/, 2346 d). Thus,

o(/pws . . . u(_mei=s e)me\ e)paine/sete, e)moi\ melh/sei: h)\ mhke/ti me *ku=ron nomi/zete it shall be my concern that you commend me; or else my name is no longer Cyrus
X. A. 1.4.16.

§2860

h)/ often does not introduce an alternative to a previous question, but substitutes instead another question which is more specific and intended to anticipate the answer to the first (or rather, or precisely). Thus, le/ge h(mi=n pw=s me fh\|s diafqei/rein tou\s newte/rous; h)\ dh=lon dh\ o(/ti . . . qeou\s dida/skein mh\ nomi/zein ou(\s h( po/lis nomi/zei; tell us how you mean that I corrupt the young? Or rather clearly you mean that (I corrupt them) by teaching them not to acknowledge the gods which the State acknowledges?
P. A. 26b.

§2861

h)/ often introduces an argument ex contrario (
D. 31.14).

§2862

h)\ kai/ is often used where h)/ would suffice (cp. 2888 a); as h)\ ce/nos h)\ kai/ tis po<*>\i/_ths either an alien or a citizen if you will (or as well)
D. 20.123.

§2863

Comparative h)/ than is used to mark difference. It stands after comparatives where the genitive or a preposition (1069 ff.) is not used, and after words indicating difference or diversity or having a comparative force, e.g., a)/llos or e(/teros other, a)/llws otherwise, dia/foros different, diafe/rein to be different, e)nanti/os contrary, dipla/sios twice as much, pri/n sooner.

a)/lla h)\ ta\ geno/mena things different from what occurred
X. C. 3.1.9, a)/llo ou)de\n h)\ e)k gh=s e)nauma/xoun
T. 4.14 (2778 a), th=| u(sterai/a| dei= me a)poqnh/|skein h)\ h(=| a)\n e)/lqh| to\ ploi=on I must die the day after (that on which) the ship arrives
P. Cr. 44a (here h)/ or h(=| might be omitted), ta)_nanti/a . . . h)\ tou\s ku/nas poiou=si differently from the way they treat dogs
X. A. 5.8.24,

to\n h(/misun si=ton h)\ pro/sqen half as much corn as before
X. H. 5.3.21.
a. After ti/ or a negative, h)/ may be used without a)/llos, as ti/ poiw=n h)\ eu)wxou/menos; doing what else except feasting?
P. Cr. 53e,

ei)=pe mhde/na parie/nai h)\ tou\s fi/lous he said that they should let no one pass except his friends
X. C. 7.5.41.
b. Often after verbs of willing, choosing, etc.; as

qa/naton met' e)leuqeri/a_s ai(rou/menoi h)\ bi/on meta\ doulei/a_s preferring death with freedom rather than life with servitude
L. 2.62. Here we might have ma=llon h)/, which is usually not separated, and especially when ma=llon belongs to the whole sentence.
c. If two clauses connected by h)/ have the same verb it may be omitted in the clause following h)/; as e)/pra_ttes a)lloi=on h)\ oi( polloi/ (pra/_ttousi) you behaved differently from the rest
P. A. 20c.
d. On h)\ w(/ste (w(s), or h)/ alone, than so as to, see 2264.

## h)=

§2864

Asseverative h)= (prepositive) in truth, in sooth, verily, upon my honour, etc.; as h)= kalw=s le/geis
P. G. 447c.

§2865

h)= is usually associated with other particles.
h)= ga/r when used alone in dialogue = is it not so? Cp. n'est ce pas, nicht wahr? Elsewhere it often has the force of am I to understand that asked with surprise. Thus, h)= ga\r noei=s qa/ptein sf', a)po/rrhton po/lei; what, dost thou in truth intend to bury him, when it is forbidden to the citizens?
S. Ant. 44.
h)= dh/ expresses lively surprise.
h)= kai/ is found in animated questions. Here kai/ goes closely with h)=.
h)= mh/n (Hom. h)= me/n, h)= ma/_n) prefaces strong asseverations, threats, and oaths, in direct and indirect discourse. Thus,

h)= mh\n e)gw\ e)/paqo/n ti toiou=ton in truth this was my experience
P. A. 22a,

o)/mnu_mi qeou\s . . . h)= mh\n mh/te me *cenofw=nta keleu=sai a)fele/sqai to\n a)/ndra mh/te a)/llon u(_mw=n mhde/na I swear by the gods upon my honour neither did Xenophon nor any one else among you bid me rescue the man
X. A. 6.6.17.
h)= pou indeed, methinks, in poetry I ween. Here the shade of doubt indicated by pou/ is not real.

§2866

Interrogative h)= (2650) is probably the same as asseverative h)=.

## h)de/ (AND i)de）

§2867

h)de/ and (Epic, lyric, tragic); also in conjunction with te kai/, or de/. h)me/n . . . h)de/ (Epic) is used like te\ . . . te/, kai\ . . . kai/.
i)de/ and (Epic, rare in tragedy) is used where h)de/ does not suit the metre.

## kai/

§2868

kai/ is both a copulative conjunction (and) connecting words, clauses, or sentences; and an adverb meaning also, even.

## Conjunctional kai/

§2869
Copulative kai/ often has an intensive or heightening force; as where it joins a part and the whole, the universal and the particular. Thus, e)n *)aqhnai/ois kai\ toi=s *(/ellhsi
Ar. Nub. 413, w)= *zeu= kai\ qeoi/ Ar. Pl. 1 (qeoi\ kai\ *zeu/s the gods and above all Zeus), e)ntau=qa e)/meinan h(me/ra_s trei=s kai\ h(=ke *me/nwn
X. A. 1.2.6. On kai\ tau=ta, see 947, 2083.
a. Here kai/ often = namely, for example, and so where an antecedent statement is explained either by another word or by an example. Cp.
X. A. 1.9.14, 4. 1. 19, 5. 2. 9, 5. 6. 8.

§2870
The heightening force is also seen where kai/ with corrective force may be rendered by or; often to set forth a climax and not an alternative. Thus,

sofi/a_ o)li/gou tino\s a)ci/a_ kai\ ou)deno/s wisdom worth little or nothing
P. A. 23a,

maxairopoioi\ . . . a)na\ pe/nte mna=s kai\ e(/c sword-cutlers worth five or six minas each
D. 27.9,

proiou=si de\ kai\ a)piou=si po/lemos but war if we advance or retire
X. A. 2.1.21,

kai\ di/kaia ka)/_dika right or wrong
Ar. Nub. 99, so\s (go/nos),

kei' mh\ so/s thy son, or if not thine
S. O. C. 1323.

§2871

kai/ often has an adversative force; as where it joins a negative to an affirmative clause. Here kai\ ou) (mh/) is almost = but not, as in e)m' e)xeiroto/nhsan kai\ ou)x u(_ma=s they elected me and (= but) not you
D. 18.288. So also where kai/ is like kai/toi and yet; as

xai/rwn a)/piqi: kai/ s' a)/_kwn e)gw\ lei/pw fare thee well; and yet I leave thee unwillingly
Ar. Eq. 1250. To connect negative clauses ou)de/ is used.

§2872
In questions, kai/ before an interrogative expression marks an objection occasioned by surprise or indignation; as kai\ ti/s qano/ntwn h)=lqen e)c *(/aidou pa/lin; and, pray, who of the dead has come back from Hades?
E. H. F. 297. So kai\ pw=s; pray, how comes it that? Cp. Eng. and when a speaker is stopped by an abrupt question.
a. After an interrogative expression adverbial kai/ asks for further information concerning a statement assumed to be true. Thus, poi/ou xro/nou de\ kai\ pepo/rqhtai po/lis; but when was the city captured?
A. Ag. 278. Cp. 2884.

§2873
In imperative sentences kai/ often means and now, just. Thus,

kai/ moi a)na/gnwqi to\ yh/fisma and now read me the bill
L. 13.35,

kai/ moi a)po/kri_nai just answer me
P. A. 25a.

§2874

kai/ may mark a result (
P. Th. 154c, quoted in 2288).

§2875
After expressions of sameness and likeness kai/ has the force of as (Lat. ac). Thus,

o( au)to\s u(_mi=n sto/los e)sti\ kai\ h(mi=n your expedition is the same as ours
X. A. 2.2.10,

ou)x o(moi/ws kai\ pri/n not the same as before
T. 7.28, i)/sa kai\ i(ke/tai the same as suppliants 3. 14,

tau)ta\ kai/ the same as
X. C. 1.3.18. This use is commoner in prose than poetry.

§2876
In expressions denoting coincidence of time kai/ often has the force of when. So a(/ma . . . kai/ (2169), h)/dh . . . kai/
X. A. 2.1.7, ou)/pw . . . kai/
P. Eu. 277b, ou)k e)/fqhn . . . kai/ (eu)qu/s) I had not got the start . . . when
I. 19.22,
D. 43.69. Cp. kai\ . . . kai/ in

kai\ h(/komen kai\ h(mi=n e)celqw\n o( qurwro\s . . . ei)=pen perime/nein as soon as we arrived the doorkeeper came out and told us to wait
P. Ph. 59e.

§2877

kai\ . . . kai/ both . . . and, not only . . . but also, as . . . so, as well as . . . as also, sometimes whether . . . or, emphasizes each member separately, and forms a less close combination than te\ kai/. Thus, kai\ to/te kai\ nu=n not only then but also now. So

ti_ma\_s dote/on kai\ zw=nti kai\ teleuth/santi honours must be paid him both when living and after death
P. R. 414a, su\ kai\ de/dorkas kou' ble/peis thou both hast sight and (yet) dost not see
S. O. T. 413,

ka)_pempo/mhn pro\s tau=ta kai\ to\ pa=n fra/sw as I was sent for this purpose so I will tell thee all
S. El. 680,

tolma=n a)na/gkh, ka)\_n tu/xw ka)\_n mh\ tu/xw I must dare whether I succeed or fail
E. Hec. 751.

§2878
In a series of more than two ideas kai/ is used before each, where English would use and only before the last. Thus,

suntugxa/nousin au)tw=| kai\ lamba/nousin au)to\n kai\ gunai=ka kai\ pai=das kai\ tou\s i(/ppous kai\ pa/nta ta\ o)/nta they fell upon him and seized him, his wife, his children, his horses, and all his possessions
X. A. 7.8.22.

§2879
Adjectives of quantity, as polu/s and o)li/gos in the plural, are usually joined to an adjective in the same construction by kai/ or te\ kai/ (also by te/ or te\ . . . te/ in poetry). Thus, polla\ kai\ deina/
D. 37.57 (deina\ kai\ polla/ 37. 57), polla/ te kai\ deina/
X. A. 5.5.8. In polla\ kai\ mega/la a)gaqa/ (
X. C. 1.5.9), the substantive is qualified by two adjectives; whereas in English the second adjec tive is taken with the substantive and treated as a unit modified by the first adjective (many good-things).
a. polloi\ kai\ a)/lloi means many others also (with kai/ adverbial). For many others we find a)/lloi polloi/ (very common) or polloi\ a)/lloi.

§2880
Some combinations of conjunctional kai/ are:
kai\ . . . me/ntoi and however, and of course (in kai\ me/ntoi kai/ the first kai/ may be adverbial: yes indeed and).
kai\ . . . toi/nun and . . . further, in connecting a thought with the preceding.

## Adverbial kai/

§2881
Adverbial kai/ also, even (Lat. etiam) influences single words or whole clauses. Adverbial kai/ stresses an important idea; usually the idea set forth in the word that follows, but sometimes also a preceding word when that word stands first in its clause. kai/ often serves to increase or diminish the force of particular words; sometimes it gives a tone of modesty.

§2882
With single words: a. ka)=|ta then too, kai\ e)gw/ I on my part,

so\n h)\ ka)_mo\n ge/nos offspring from thee or me either
S. El. 965,

boulo/menos de\ kai\ au)to\s lampro/n ti poih=sai desirous of himself too doing something illustrious
X. C. 5.4.15.
b. kai\ pri/n even before, kai\ o)ye/ late though it be, kai\ ou(/tws even so, kai\ e)/ti kai\ nu=n and now too, and still even now, o)knw= kai\ le/gein I fear even to say it,

pollh\ mwri/a_ kai\ tou= e)pixeirh/matos the very attempt is utter folly
P. Pr. 317a. On kai/ though with a participle, see 2083.
c. Often with adverbs of intensity, as kai\ ma/la exceedingly, certainly, kai\ ka/rta very greatly, kai\ pa/nu absolutely. With comparatives and superlatives: kai\ ma=llon yet more,

kai\ mwro/taton altogether the most foolish thing
X. A. 3.2.22.

§2883
With a whole phrase or clause; as a)/mfw ga\r au)tw\ kai\ kataktanei=n noei=s; what, dost thou indeed intend to put them both to death?
S. Ant. 770. Other examples in 2885-2887.

§2884
When kai/ stresses a verb in interrogative and conditional sentences it is often to be rendered by an emphatic auxiliary, often by at all. Thus, polla/kis e)skeya/mhn ti/ kai\ bou/lesqe I have often asked myself the question what you can want
T. 6.38, ti/ kai\ xrh\ prosdoka=n; what on earth is one to expect?
D. 4.46, ti/ ga\r a)/n tis kai\ poioi= a)/llo; for what else could one do?
P. Ph. 61e,

ei) dei= kai\ mu=qon le/gein kalo/n if it is well to tell a fable at all
P. Ph. 110b. Cp. 2872 a.
a. In affirmative independent clauses or sentences kai/ often has an emphasis which is difficult to render; as

o( ki/ndu_nos nu=n dh\ kai\ do/ceien a)\n deino\s ei)=nai the danger must now indeed seem to be dreadful
P. Ph. 107c.

§2885

*kai/ of Balanced Contrast.—In order to mark the connection of thought between antecedent and consequent, kai/ also, too, is often placed in the subordinate clause or in the main clause or in both.
a. Greek has thus the following modes of expression where a comparison is instituted between the parts of such bimembral sentences: “What I do, that you also do” (as in English) or “What I also ( = I on my part) do, that you do” or “What I also do, that you also do.” In the subordinate clause kai/ seems superfluous to English idiom.

§2886

*kai/ of balanced contrast occurs frequently when the subordinate clause sets forth something corresponding to, or deducible from, the main clause; and when an antithesis is to be emphasized. It is found especially in relative, causal, and final clauses, and has the effect of putting such subordinate clauses on a plane with the main clause. A relative word often adds -per or is followed by dh/. Thus,

ta\ de\ th=s po/lews e)/pra_tton, w(=nper e(/neken kai\ *swkra/tei prosh=lqon they devoted themselves to those affairs of state on account of which they had in fact associated with Socrates
X. M. 1.2.47,

kai\ h(mi=n tau)ta\ dokei= a(/per kai\ basilei= we hold exactly the same views as the king
X. A. 2.1.22,

e)peidh\ kai\ h( po/lis e)sw/qh . . . a)ciw= ka)_moi\ swthri/a_n gene/sqai since the city has been saved I beg that safety be granted to me as well
And. 1.143, e)/maqon kai\ e)gw\ w(/sper kai\ oi( a)/lloi I (on my part) learned just as the rest did too
P. Alc. 110d,

ti_mwri/a_ ga\r ou)k eu)tuxei= dikai/ws o(/ti kai\ a)dikei=tai for vengeance is not successful in accordance with justice, because it is taken upon a wrong
T. 4.62.

§2887
In final clauses i(/na kai/ is common, and sometimes, like Eng. just, serves to show that the fact answers to the expectation, or the effect to the cause (or vice versa). Thus, bou/lei ou)=n e(/pesqai i(/na kai\ i)/dh|s tou\s o)/ntas au)to/qi; do you wish to go along then just to see those who are there?
P. Lys. 204a,

a)/rcomai de\ a)po\ th=s i)_a_trikh=s le/gwn i(/na kai\ presbeu/wmen th\n te/xnhn I will begin my speech with medicine in order that we may do honour to our art
P. S. 186b.

§2888

*kai/ of balanced contrast appears also in coördinate clauses; as

h)/dh ga\r e)/gwge kai\ *filola/_ou h)/kousa . . . h)/dh de\ kai\ a)/llwn tinw=n for I have ere now heard Philolaus . . . and ere now certain others besides him
P. Ph. 61e, kata\ polla\ me\n kai\ a)/lla, ou)x h(/kista de\ kai\ kata\ tau=ta as in many other respects also and not least (too) in this
Aes. 1.108,

u(po\ tw=n ta)_ntau=qa dioikh/sein . . . kai\ pri\n u(pesxhme/nwn kai\ nu=n de\ pra_tto/ntwn by those who had promised to manage things there before and are now also doing them
D. 7.5. The negative of kai\ . . . kai\ . . . de/ is ou)de\ . . . ou)de\ . . . de/.
a. So in disjunctive phrases or clauses. Thus,

ei)/te dia\ to\ e)pibo/hma ei)/te kai\ au)tw=| a)/llo ti . . . do/can either because of the exclamation or also because some other thought occurred to him
T. 5.65; and so h)\ kai/ 2862. Cp. e)zhtei=to ou)de/n ti ma=llon u(po\ tw=n a)/llwn h)\ kai\ u(p' e)mou= he was not searched for by the others more than he was by me (on my part)
Ant. 5.23.

§2889
Similarly the kai/ of ei)/ tis kai\ a)/llos is superfluous; as

ei)/per ti kai\ a)/llo kai\ tou=to maqhto/n if any other thing is learnable, this is too
X. S. 2. 6. But kai/ is usually omitted in the main clause; as

e)pi/statai d' ei)/ tis kai\ a)/llos he knows as well as anybody else
X. A. 1.4.15. So

w(/s tis kai\ a)/llos as also any other
X. A. 2.6.8.

§2890

kai\ dh\ kai/ and especially, and in particular, and what is more, lays stress on a particular instance or application of a general statement. Here the second kai/ emphasizes the following word. kai\ dh\ kai/ is usually attached to a preceding te/ or kai/. Thus, kai\ dh\ kai\ to/te prw|ai/teron sunele/ghmen and on that especial occasion we came together somewhat earlier than usual
P. Ph. 59d,

e)n a)/llois te polloi=s kai\ dh\ kai\ e)n toi=s ka/mnousin in the case of many others and particularly in that of the sick
X. C. 1.6.21.

§2891

kai\ . . . de/ and . . . also, and . . . moreover. Here kai/ empha sizes the important intervening word or words, while de/ connects. Thus,

kai\ se\ d' e)n tou/tois le/gw and I count thee also among these
A. Pr. 973. And also not is ou)de\ . . . de/. Hom. has kai\ de/ and further, and even (H 113), not kai\ . . . de/. kai\ . . . de/ (for te/) is different (
S. Ant. 432).

## kai/per

§2892

kai<*>per although is common with participles (2083). As a conjunction (cp. quanquam) without a main clause it is very rare (
P. S. 219c).

## kai/toi<*>

§2893

kai/toi (kai\ + toi<*>), not in Homer, means and yet, although, rarely and so then. Here toi/ marks something worthy of note, which is commonly opposed to what precedes. kai/toi is used in making a correction (sometimes in the form of a question), in passing to a new idea, and in the statement of a conclusion. The common kai/toi . . . ge is stronger than kai/toi.

kai/toi ou)de\n o(/ti ou)k a)lhqe\s ei)/rhka w(=n proei=pon and yet there is nothing untrue in what I said before
P. Euth. 3c.
a. A sentence preceding kai/toi is often restated by a clause introduced by a)lla/ (a)ll' o(/mws), de/, or nu=n de/. Cp.
P. Ph. 77a, Charm. 175 c, A. 40 b, G. 499 c.
b. kai/toi is rarely, if ever, used with the participle in classical Greek. It is best attested in
P. R. 511d; emendation is resorted to in
L. 31.34,
Ar. Eccl. 159.

## ma/

§2894

ma/ asseverative (cp. mh/n, me/n asseverative) with the accusative of the divinity or thing by which one swears. In negative sentences we have ou) ma/ or ma/ alone with the accusative; in affirmative sentences, nai\ ma/, but more commonly nh/. The omission of the accusative may sometimes be due to indecision or to indifference and not always to scrupulousness (1596 c). ma/ means properly in truth, verily; but apparently governs the accusative after the ellipse of such verbs as I call to witness.

## me/n

§2895

me/n was originally an asseverative, emphatic particle (surely, certainly, indeed) and a weaker form of mh/n. Cp. Epic h)= me/n, kai\ me/n, ou) me/n in asseverations and protestations. Asseverative me/n survived as me/n solitarium and in combination with other particles. Antithetical (concessive) me/n owes its origin to the fact that, as emphasis. may indicate a contrast, the clause in which me/n stood was felt as preliminary to an adversative member of the sentence. Through association with this adversative member me/n gradually lost its primitive asseverative force.

§2896

me/n solitarium occurs when a clause with me/n is not followed by a clause with de/. This is especially common when the antithetical clause is to be supplied in thought, as when me/n emphasizes a statement made by a person with reference to himself as opposed to others (often with a tone of arrogance or of credulity). Here any possible opposition or difference of opinion, however justifiable, is left unexpressed. Thus, e)gw\ me\n ou)k oi)=da I for my part do not know (though others may)
X. C. 1.4.12,

a)pe/pleusan, w(s me\n toi=s plei/stois e)do/koun, filoti_mhqe/ntes they sailed away since they were jealous as it seemed to the majority at least
X. A. 1.4.7. So in such phrases as dokw= me/n, h(gou=mai me/n, oi)=mai me/n.

§2897
Sometimes me/n solitarium merely emphasizes a word in its clause and does not imply a contrast. Thus,

e)moi\ me\n oi)ste/a ta/de this must be borne by me on my part
S. O. C. 1360.

§2898

me/n solitarium is commonest after personal pronouns; but occurs also after demonstrative pronouns (
L. 25.16), after relatives (
Aes. 3.209), after substantives without the article (
D. 9.15), or after the article and before its substantive (
L. 29.1), after adjectives (
L. 1.27), after adverbs (
L. 12.91), after verbs (
D. 19.231). In questions me/n alone is rare (
P. Men. 82b).

§2899
In combination with other particles, especially dh/ and ou)=n, asseverative me/n either has a simple confirmatory force or is used adversatively. The following cases must be distinguished from those in which me/n is correlative to de/.

§2900

me\n dh/ expresses positive certainty, especially in conclusions. It is common in summing up and in transitions, and is used either alone or with other particles (sometimes it is followed by a)lla/ or de/). Thus,

tau=ta me\n dh\ toiau=ta so much for that
A. Pr. 500. So also, e.g. a)lla\ me\n dh/ but certainly in fact (a)ll' ou)de\ me\n dh/ in rejecting an alternative); ei' me\n dh/ if indeed in truth; kai\ me\n dh/ and in truth, and in fact (often in transitions); ou' me\n dh/ certainly not at all, nor yet, in truth (often used adversatively).

§2901

me\n ou)=n lit. certainly in fact, me/n being a weaker form of mh/n. me\n ou)=n has two common uses, according as the particles have a compound force, or each has its own force.
a. The compound force of me\n ou)=n is seen in affirmations; as in replies: pa/nu (ma/lista) me\n ou)=n yes, by all means; certainly, by all means; aye truly, eu)= me\n ou)=n oi)=da nay, I am sure of it, ou) me\n ou)=n indeed not,

a)=r' ou' to/de h)=n to\ de/ndron e)f' o(/per h)=ges h(ma=s; tou=to me\n ou)=n au)to/ isn't this the tree to which you were bringing us? To be sure this is it
P. Phae. 230a.
b. The compound force appears also when me\n ou)=n indicates a correction; nay rather (imo vero); as le/ge su/: su\ me\n ou)=n moi le/ge do you say. Nay, rather you
Ar. Eq. 13, a)/topon to\ e)nu/pnion, w)= *sw/krates. e)narge\s me\n ou)=n the dream is strange, Socrates. Nay rather, it was distinct
P. Cr. 44b.
c. Each particle has its own force especially where me\n ou)=n indicates a transition to a new subject. Here me/n points forward to an antithesis to follow and indicated by de/, a)lla/, me/ntoi, while ou)=n (inferential) connects with what precedes. Here so then, therefore may be used in translation. Thus,

*kle/arxos me\n ou)=n tosau=ta ei)=pe. *tissafe/rnhs de\ w(=de a)phmei/fqh such then were the words of Clearthus; and on the other hand Tissaphernes answered as follows
X. A. 2.5.15 Sometimes me\n ou)=n (like igitur) shows that a subject announced in general terms is now to be treated in detail (
P. Ph. 70c).

§2902
Common collocations are a)lla\ me/n (a)lla\ . . . me/n) but for a fact, ge\ me/n, h)= me/n, kai\ me/n.

§2903

Antithetical (concessive) me/n distinguishes the word or clause in which it stands from a following word or clause marked usually by de/ or by other particles denoting contrast, such as a)lla/, a)ta/r, me/ntoi, mh/n; and even by copulative te/, kai/ (Hom. h)de/). me/n never connects words, clauses, or sentences.

§2904

me\n . . . de/ serves to mark stronger or weaker contrasts of various kinds, and is sometimes to be rendered by on the one hand . . . on the other hand, indeed . . . but; but is often to be left untranslated. The me/n clause has a concessive force when it is logically subordinate (while, though, whereas, cp. 2170). Thus,

h( me\n yu_xh\ poluxro/nio/n e)sti, to\ de\ sw=ma a)sqene/steron kai\ o)ligoxroniw/teron the soul lasts for a long time, the body is weaker and lasts for a shorter time
P. Ph. 87d,

kai\ pro/sqen me\n dh\ polloi\ h(mw=n h)=rxon me\n ou)deno/s, h)/rxonto de/: nu=n de\ kateskeu/asqe ou(/tw pa/ntes oi( paro/ntes w(/ste a)/rxete oi( me\n pleio/nwn, oi( de\ meio/nwn and whereas in fact many of us hitherto commanded no one, but were subject to the command of others, now however all of you who are present are so placed that you have command, some over more, others over fewer
X. C. 8.1.4.
a. So a)/llote me\n . . . a)/llote de/, a(/ma me\n . . . a(/ma de/ at once . . . and, partly . . . partly, e)/nqa me\n . . . e)/nqa de/, e)ntau=qa me\n . . . e)kei= de/, prw=ton me\n . . . e)/peita de/ (or e)/peita alone). On o( me\n . . . o( de/ see 1107. Instead of o( (oi() de/ we find e.g. a)/llos de/, e)/nioi de/, e)/sti d' oi(/. So tou=to me\n . . . tou=t' a)/llo (or au)=qis).—me/n may stand with a participle, de/ with a finite verb, in an antithetical sentence. Example in 2147 c.
b. ei), ou) (mh/) standing before me\n . . . de/ exercise their force on both opposed clauses.

§2905
When several verbs referring to the same person or thing are contrasted, or when several attributes are contrasted, the first has me/n, the others de/. Cp. Lyc. 5,
X. A. 3.1.19. But me/n is sometimes omitted.

§2906

me/n . . . de/ is used in successive clauses which contain either the same word (anaphora) or a synonymous word; as e)gw\ de\ su/neimi me\n qeoi=s, su/neimi de\ a)nqrw/pois toi=s a)gaqoi=s quoted in 1159,

h)=lqe me\n kai\ a)po\ th=s *)eruqrai/a_s a)ggeli/a_, a)fi_knei=to de\ kai\ pantaxo/qen news came from the district of Erythrae itself and arrived also from all quarters
T. 3.33. But me/n is sometimes omitted, as

sth/sw s' a)/gwn, sth/sw d' e)mauto/n I will bring thee and stablish thee, and I will stablish myself
S. O. C. 1342.

§2907
If more than two clauses are contrasted, only the first clause has me/n, while each of the following clauses has de/ (
X. A. 1.3.14,
X. C. 4.2.28).

§2908
A contrast indicated by me/n and de/ may stand inside another contrast indicated in the same manner, as o( me\n a)nh\r toiau=ta me\n pepoi/hke, toiau=ta de\ le/gei: u(_mw=n de\ su\ prw=tos, w)= *kle/arxe, a)po/fhnai gnw/mhn o(/ ti soi dokei= the man has acted thus, and speaks thus; but do you, Clearchus, be the first to make known what you think best
X. A. 1.6.9.

§2909
Two relative (or conditional) clauses each with me/n may be followed by two demonstrative clauses each with de/; but the second de/ is usually omitted, and there are other variations. Thus, o(po/soi me\n . . . ou(=toi me\n . . . o(po/soi de\ . . . tou/tous o(rw=
X. A. 3.1.43, cp.
X. O. 4.7,
P. A. 28e.

§2910
A clause with me/n is often followed by a contrasted clause without de/ but with a particle containing an element of opposition, as prw=ton me\n . . . e)/peita . . . ei)=ta.

§2911
A shift in the construction may cause de/ to be omitted (
S. Ant. 1199).

§2912

me/n after an emphatic demonstrative may resume me/n of the antecedent clause (
D. 2.18).

§2913

me\n . . . te (and even kai/) is used where the second clause is merely added instead of being coördinated by means of de/. Thus,

taxu\ me\n o(/poi e)/dei perigigno/meqa a)qro/oi te tw=| a)/rxonti e(po/menoi a)nupo/statoi h)=men we have quickly reached the places to which we had to go, and by following our leader in a compact body we have been invincible
X. C. 8.1.3.

§2914

Position of me/n (and de/).—me/n and de/ are commonly placed next to the words they contrast, and take precedence over other postpositive particles. But when two words belong closely together, me/n and de/ are placed between. Thus, when nouns with the article are contrasted, me/n and de/ stand after the article; if the nouns depend on prepositions me/n and de/ stand after the preposition and before the article.
a. But this rule may be neglected in order to emphasize the preceding word, as ta\ me\n a)nqrw/pina pare/ntes, ta\ daimo/nia de\ skopou=ntes neglecting human affairs, but speculating on things divine
X. M. 1.1.12,

a)na\ to\ skoteino\n me/n in the darkness
T. 3.22.
b. If the noun has no article and is governed by a preposition, de/ usually takes the third place.
c. Postponement of de/ (and some other postpositive particles) to the fourth place is only apparent after an introductory vocative, which is not regarded as forming an integral part of the sentence.

§2915

me/n and de/ are sometimes referred to the entire clause or to the predicate and not to the words that are opposed to each other. This arrangement is often adopted to preserve the symmetry of the juxtaposed clause. me/n and de/ are thus often placed after personal or demonstrative pronouns. Thus, e)/lege me\n w(s to\ polu/, toi=s de\ boulome/nois e)ch=n a)kou/ein Socrates for the most part was wont to talk, while any who chose could listen
X. M. 1.1.10, pw=s a)\n polloi\ me\n e)pequ/_moun turannei=n . . . ; pw=s de\ pa/ntes e)zh/loun a)\n tou\s tura/nnous; why should many desire to possess despotic power? why should everybody envy despotic rulers?
X. Hi. 1.9 (for pa/ntes de\ pw=s e)zh/loun a)/n). Cp. e)n me\n tou/tois . . . e)n e)kei/nois de/ Lyc. 140, peri\ au(tw=n me\n . . . peri\ de\ tw=n despotw=n
L. 7.35, etc.
a. The transposition is often designed to produce a chiastic (3020) order, as

e)/paqe me\n ou)de/n, polla\ de\ kaka\ e)no/mize poih=sai he suffered no loss, but thought that he had done a great deal of damage
X. A. 3.4.2 (here ou)de/n and polla/ are brought close together).

§2916
In poetry me/n and de/ often have a freer position than in prose. de/ may often come third when an emphatic word is placed before it, and even fourth.

## me/ntoi

§2917

me/ntoi (postpositive) from me/n (= mh/n, 2895) + toi/, is an asseverative and adversative particle.

§2918
Asseverative me/ntoi certainly, surely, of course, in truth is very common in replies, where it expresses positive, eager, or reflective assent. Often with nh\ (ma\) *di/a. Thus, e)gw/; su\ me/ntoi I? certainly, you
Ar. Eq. 168, ti/ ga/r, e)/fh, . . . me/mnhsai e)kei=na . . . ; nai\ ma\ *di/a . . . me/mnhmai me/ntoi toiau=ta a)kou/sa_s sou well then, said he, do you recall those matters; Yes, by Zeus, certainly I do recall that I heard things to that effect from you
X. C. 1.6.6, a)lhqe/stata me/ntoi le/geis well, certainly you say what is very true
P. Soph. 245b.
me/ntoi may strengthen asseverations or emphasize questions; as

ou(/tw me/ntoi xrh\ le/gein in truth we must speak thus
P. Th. 187b; often with demonstrative pronouns, as w)= tou=to me/ntoi nh\ *di/a au)toi=sin piqou= oh, by Zeus do oblige them in this Ar. Aves 661.
a. Asseverative me/ntoi in combinations, e.g.:
a)lla\ me/ntoi but surely, but in fact (in a)lla\ . . . me/ntoi, me/ntoi refers to the preceding word).
kai\ . . . me/ntoi and . . . indeed, and . . . in fact, and . . . moreover, as

filoqhro/tatos h)=n kai\ pro\s ta\ qhri/a me/ntoi filokindu_no/tatos he was very fond of hunting and moreover exceedingly fond of danger
X. A. 1.9.6.
ou' me/ntoi no indeed (also adversative: yet not).

§2919
Adversative me/ntoi however, yet often marks a contrast or a transition; as

a)fi/_eme/n se, e)pi\ tou/tw| me/ntoi we let you go, on this condition however
P. A. 29c. me/ntoi ge is stronger. me\n . . . me/ntoi is much stronger than me\n . . . de/, as

filoso/fw| me\n e)/oikas . . . i)/sqi me/ntoi a)no/htos w)/n you resemble a philosopher— know however that you are a fool
X. A. 2.1.13. On ou' me/ntoi a)lla/ (ge) see 2767.

## mh/n

§2920

mh/n (postpositive): (1) asseverative, in truth, surely; (2) adversative, especially after a negative, yet, however. The forms mh/n (Hom., Att.), ma/_n (Hom., Lesb., Dor., lyric parts of tragedy), me/n truly (Hom., Att.) and ma/ in oaths are all connected. mh/n emphasizes either a whole statement or a single word.

w(=de ga\r e)cere/w, kai\ mh\n tetelesme/non e)/stai for thus I will declare, and verily it shall be accomplished
*y 410;

kalo\n me\n h( a)lh/qeia . . ., e)/oike mh\n ou) r(a/|dion pei/qein truth is a fine thing, yet it does not seem an easy thing to persuade
P. L. 663e, ei) d' a)/ge mh/n come now, on then A 302,

ou)de\n mh\n kwlu/_ei but nothing hinders
P. Phae. 268e.

§2921

Combinations of mh/n:
a)lla\ mh/n ( . . . ge) but surely; but yet; nay, indeed; well, in truth. Often used to add something of greater importance, or in transitions when a new idea is opposed to the foregoing. a)lla\ mh/n is often separated by a negative.
h)= mh/n verily, verily. Often to introduce an oath or a threat.
kai\ mh/n and verily or and yet according to the context. kai\ mh/n frequently introduces a new fact or thought and hence often denotes transition, sometimes opposition (further, however, and yet). In tragedy this formula is used to mark the beginning of a new scene, as when the arrival of a newcomer is thus signalized (but here comes); as

kai\ mh\n a)/nac o(/de and lo! here is the king
S. O. C. 549. In replies, kai\ mh/n usually confirms the last remark, accedes to a request, or denotes hearty assent; sometimes there is an adversative sense (and yet; and (yet) surely; oh, but). In enumerations, kai\ mh/n adds a new fact (and besides).
kai mh\n . . . ge in transitions or enumerations marks something of still greater importance; but it is not so strong as kai\ me\n dh/. Here ge/ emphasizes the word or words with which it is immediately connected. In replies, and indeed, and yet or oh, but; as

kai\ mh\n poih/sw ge and yet I will do it
S. El. 1045.
kai\ mh\n kai/ (neg. kai\ mh\n ou)de/) and in truth also.
ou' mh/n surely not, ou' mh\n a)lla/ nevertheless (2767), ou' mh\n ou)de/ nor again (2768), ou)de\ mh/n and certainly not.
ti/ mh/n; lit. what indeed (quid uero), as a)lla\ ti/ mh\n dokei=s; but what in truth is your opinion?
P. Th. 162b. ti/ mh/n; standing alone, has the force of naturally, of course. Thus, le/gousin h(ma=s w(s o)lwlo/tas, ti/ mh/n; they speak of us as dead, and why should they not?
A. Ag. 672. Often in Plato to indicate assent. ti/ mh\n ou)/; (why indeed not=) of course I do.

## nai/, nh/

§2922

nai/ (cp. Lat. nae) asseverative (truly, yea), with the accusative in oaths where it is usually followed by ma/ (1596 b). nai/ yes, in answers, is found only in Attic.

§2923

nh/ (cp. Lat. neē) asseverative (truly, yea), with the accusative in oaths, and only in an affirmative sense. nh/ is found only in Attic. See 1596 b.

## nu=n, nu_ni/_, nu/_n, nu/n, nu/

§2924

nu=n now, at present often has a causal sense, as nu=n de/ but as the case stands, as it is; often to mark reality in contrast to an assumed case.

§2925

nu_ni/_ (nu=n + deictic i_, 333 g) is stronger than nu=n: even now, at this moment; rarely in a causal sense.

§2926

nu^/n (enclitic; lyric, tragic, Herodotus, rare and suspected in Homer), a weakened form of nu=n, is rarely temporal, usually inferential, as now is used for then, therefore. nu/n thus marks the connection of the speaker's thought with the situation in which he is placed. It is commonly used after imperatives, prohibitive and hortatory subjunctives. Thus,

ka/qize nu/n me seat me, then
S. O. C. 21. In Xenophon and Plato nun is written by some editors, where the Mss. have nu=n (
X. C. 4.2.37, H. 4. 1. 39).

§2927

nu/_n (enclitic) is adopted by some scholars in Attic tragedy where a long syllable is required (
S. O. T. 644). Others write nu=n (with the force of nu^/n).

§2928

nu^/ (enclitic; Epic and Cyprian), a still weaker form of nu=n, and less emphatic than dh/. It is common in questions and appeals; less frequent in statements; as ti/s nu; who now? Also after other particles, as kai/ nu/ ke, h)= r(a/ nu.

## o(/pws

§2929

o(/pws, originally a relative adverb meaning how, is derived from the relative particle svod (with which Eng. so is connected), to which the indefinite pw/s has been added. Hom. o(/ppws from svod-pws, as o(/tti from svod-ti (81 D 2).
a. The adverbial meaning of o(/pws is still seen in its use as an indefinite relative and as an indirect interrogative; and by the fact that in its place o(/ph|, o(/tw| tro/pw|, e)c o(/tou tro/pou are sometimes used. By association with the subjunctive o(/pws became a conjunction (cp. mh/ pws) used with or without a)/n in final clauses (see 2196, 2201). On the use as a conjunction in object clauses after verbs of effort and of fear, see 2211, 2228. So in dependent statements o(/pws passed from how into that (2578 d).

## ou)de/, ou)/te （mhde/, mh/te）

§2930

ou)de/ (mhde/) is an adverb and a conjunction, and is to be broken up into the negative ou) (mh/) and de/ meaning and, even, also , or but.

## ou)de/ (mhde/) as an Adverb

§2931
Adverbial ou)de/ (mhde/) not even, not . . . either, also . . . not, nor yet (ne . . quidem). Cp. the use of kai/ even, also in affirmative sentences; as ou)d' w(/s not even in that case (kai\ w(/s even in that case).

a)ll' ou)de\ tou/twn sterh/sontai but no; even of these shall they be deprived
X. A. 1.4.8,

o(/t' ou)d' ou(/tw r(a/|dion h)=n when besides it was not so easy
I. 18.65 (= kai\ ou) also not). With ou)d' ei' (e)a/_n) not even if ou) belongs with the main clause, while de/ even goes with the dependent clause. Thus,

ou)d' a)\n ei) bou/lointo, r(a|di/ws ponhroi\ ge/nointo even if they wished, they could not easily become wicked
X. C. 7.5.86 (= kai\ ei) bou/lointo, ou)k a)\n ge/nointo). Similarly with a participle:

ou)de\ peponqw\s kakw=s e)xqro\n ei)=nai/ moi tou=ton o(mologw= I do not admit that this man is my enemy even though I have been ill-used
D. 21.205.

## ou)de/ (mhde/) as a Conjunction

§2932

ou)de/ (mhde/) as a conjunction (and not, nor) connects two or more whole clauses.

§2933
In Attic prose ou)de/ is used only to join a negative clause to another clause itself negative; as

ou)demi/a e)lpi\s h)=n ti_mwri/a_s ou)de\ a)/llh swthri/a_ e)fai/neto there was no hope of assistance nor did any chance of safety appear
T. 3.20.
a. A negative clause is joined to an affirmative clause by kai\ ou) (mh/). Thus,

e)mmenw= th=| cummaxi/a| . . . kai\ ou) parabh/somai I will abide by the alliance and I will not violate it
T. 5.47. kai\ ou) (mh/) may have an adversative force (but not).
N.—But in poetry and Ionic prose ou)de/ may continue an affirmative clause; as

deino\n ga\r ou)de\ r(hto/n dread indeed and not to be uttered
S. Ph. 756.

§2934

ou)de/ is used by the poets for but not, where Attic prose writers have a)ll' ou' or kai\ ou). Thus, e)/nq' a)/llois me\n pa=sin e(h/ndanen, ou)de/ poq' *(/hrh| ou)de\ *posei-

da/wni then it was pleasing to all the others, but not to Hera or to Poseidon
*w 25,

e)mai=si ou)de\ sai=si dusbouli/ais by my folly but not by thine
S. Ant. 1269 (cp. the negative form

ou)k e)mo\n to/d' a)lla\ so/n this is not my part, but thine
S. El. 1470). Cp.

sou= ta/de kindu_neu/eis, a)ll' ou)k e)mou= a)khkoe/nai you probably heard this from yourself and not from me
P. Alc. 113c.

§2935

ou)de/ may stand in an apodosis corresponding to apodotic de/ (2837). Cp.
S. O. C. 590.

§2936

ou)de/ may negative a preceding word also; as

ai( *foi/nissai nh=es ou)de\ o( *tissafe/rnhs . . . h(=kon the Phoenician ships had not arrived nor had Tissaphernes
T. 8.99. Cp. 2943. In such cases we usually find another negative, which goes with the verb; as

a(plou=n me\n ou)de\ di/kaion ou)de\n a)\n ei)pei=n e)/xoi he could say nothing straightforward nor just
D. 22.4.

## ou)de/ (mhde/) with other Negatives

§2937

ou)de\ . . . ou)de/ commonly means not even . . . nor yet (or no, nor), the first ou)de/ being adverbial, the second conjunctive. ou)de\ . . . ou)de/ is not correlative, like ou)/te . . . ou)/te, and hence never means neither . . . nor. Thus, ou)de\ h(/lion ou)de\ selh/nhn a)/ra nomi/zw qeou\s ei)=nai; do I then hold that not even the sun nor yet the moon are gods?
P. A. 26c,

su/ ge ou)de\ o(rw=n gignw/skeis ou)de\ a)kou/wn me/mnhsai you do not even understand though you see, nor yet do you remember though you hear
X. A. 3.1.27. ou)de\ . . . ou)de/ both copulative (and not . . nor yet) in
X. C. 3.3.50. ou)de\ . . . ou)de\ . . . de/ is the negative of kai\ . . . kai\ . . . de/ in
X. A. 1.8.20.
a. So in both members of comparative sentences (cp. kai/ 2885); as

w(/sper ou)de\ gewrgou= a)_rgou= ou)de\n o)/felos, ou(/tws ou)de\ strathgou= a)_rgou=ntos ou)de\n o)/felos as there is no good in an idle tiller of the soil, so there is no good in an idle general
X. C. 1.3.18.

§2938

ou)de\ ga\r ou)de/ (negative of kai\ ga\r kai/); as

ou)de\ ga\r ou)de\ tou=to e)yeu/sato for neither did he deceive me even in this
X. C. 7.2.20. Here the first ou)de/ negatives the whole sentence, the second ou)de/ negatives tou=to.

§2939

ou' . . . ou)de/: ou)de/ not even as well as nor (2933) may resume a preceding ou). Thus, u(/brin ga\r ou) ste/rgousin ou)de\ dai/mones lit. not even the gods do not love insolence
S. Tr. 280,

ou) me/ntoi e)/fh nomi/zein ou)d' ei' pampo/nhros h)=n *de/cippos bi/a| xrh=nai pa/sxein au)to/n he said however that he did not think that, even if Dexippus was a downright rascal, he ought to suffer by an act of violence
X. A. 6.6.25,

ou) dei= dh\ toiou=ton . . . kairo\n a)fei=nai ou)de\ paqei=n tau)to\n o(/per . . . pepo/nqate we must not let such an opportunity go by nor suffer the same as you have suffered
D. 1.8.
ou' me/ntoi ou)de/ not by any means however. On ou' mh\n ou)de/ see 2768.

§2940

ou)de\ . . . ou): ou)de/ may be resumed by ou); as

ou)de/ ge o( i)di/a| ponhro\s ou)k a)\n ge/noito dhmosi/a| xrhsto/s nor can the man who is bad in his private life prove himself good in a public capacity
Aes. 3.78.

§2941

ou)de\ . . . ou)/te is rare (
P. Charm. 171b).

## ou)/te (mh/te）

§2942

ou)/te (mh/te） is usually repeated: ou)/te . . . ou)/te (mh/te . . . mh/te) neither . . . nor (nec . . . nec). ou)/te . . . ou)/te is the negative of te\ . . . te/, and unites single words or clauses.

ou)/te e)/stin ou)/te pote\ e)/stai neither is nor ever shall be
P. Phae. 241c,

ou)/te *xeiri/sofos h(=ken ou)/te ploi=a i(kana\ h)=n ou)/te ta\ e)pith/deia h)=n lamba/nein e)/ti neither had Chirisophus come nor were there enough boats nor was it possible any longer to secure provisions
X. A. 5.3.1.
After a negative clause:

ou)k e)/peiqen ou)/te tou\s strathgou\s ou)/te tou\s stratiw/ta_s he could not persuade either the generals or the soldiers
T. 4.4.
a. ou)/te . . . mh/te is found when each negative is determined by a different construction, as

a)naidh\s ou)/t' ei)mi\ mh/te genoi/mhn neither am I nor may I become shameless
D. 8.68.
b. When ou)/te . . . ou)/te stands between ou)de\ . . . ou)de/ the members thus correlated are subordinate to those expressed by ou)de\ . . . ou)de/. Cp.
Aes. 1.19.

§2943
Sometimes the first ou)/te is omitted in poetry: no/soi d' ou)/te gh=ras disease nor old age Pindar, Pyth. 10. 41,

e(ko/nta mh/t' a)/_konta willingly nor unwillingly
S. Ph. 771. Cp. “my five wits nor my five senses” (Shakesp.).

§2944
For the first ou)/te the poets sometimes have ou), as

ou) nifeto\s ou)/t' a)\r xeimw/n not snow nor storm
d 566.

§2945

ou)/te . . . te/ on the one hand not . . . but, not only not . . . but (cp. neque . . . et). The te/ clause often denotes the contrary of that set forth in the ou)/te clause (so far from). Thus, ou)/te dienoh/qhn pw/pote a)posterh=sai a)podw/sw te so far from ever thinking to deprive them of their pay I will give it to them
X. A. 7.7.48, w)/mosan . . . mh/te prodw/sein a)llh/lous su/mmaxoi/ te e)/sesqai they swore that they would not betray one another and that they would be allies 2. 2. 8. So ou)/te . . . ou)/te . . . te/. te\ . . . ou)/te is not used.
a. Sometimes the negative may be added in the te/ clause:

ou)/te e)kei=nos e)/ti kateno/hse to/ te mantei=on ou)k e)dh/lou neither did he stop to consider and the oracle would not make it plain
T. 1.126.

§2946

ou)/te . . . te ou)
S. Ant. 763. ou)/te . . . te . . . ou)/te
E. H. F. 1341.

§2947

ou)/te . . . de/ is used when the second clause is opposed to the first; as

ou)/te ploi=a/ e)stin oi(=s a)popleuso/meqa, me/nousi de\ au)tou= ou)de\ mia=s h(me/ra_s e)/sti ta\ e)pith/deia we have no vessels by which we can sail away; on the other hand, if we stay here, we haven't provisions even for a single day
X. A. 6.3.16. Cp.
E. Supp. 223,
P. R. 388e, 389 a.

§2948

ou)/te . . . ou) is rare in prose; as

ou)/te nifeto/s, ou)k o)/mbros neither rain nor snow
Hdt. 8.98. Cp.
S. Ant. 249. ou)/te . . . ou) . . . ou)/te
A. Pr. 479. ou' . . . ou)/te is generally changed to ou) . . . ou)de/ in Attic prose.

§2949

ou)/te . . . ou)de/ corresponds to the sequence of te\ . . . de/ in affirmative clauses. The emphatic ou)de/ here adds a new negative idea as after any other preceding negative; and is most common after ou)/te . . . ou)/te: neither . . . nor . . . no, nor yet (nor . . . either). ou)de/ is often followed by an emphasizing particle, as au)=, ge/, mh/n. Thus,

ou)/te po/lis ou)/te poli_tei/a_ ou)de/ g' a)nh/r neither a State nor a constitution nor yet an individual
P. R. 499b,

mh/te paidei/a_ . . . mh/te dikasth/ria mh/te no/moi mhde\ a)na/gkh mhdemi/a neither education nor courts of justice nor laws, no nor yet restraint
P. Pr. 327d.

§2950
A subordinate clause with ou)de/ may come between ou)/te . . . ou)/te. Thus,

ou)/te ga\r w(s o)fei/lonta/ me kate/leipen o( path\r . . . a)pe/fhnen ou)de\ . . . pare/sxhtai ma/rturas ou)/t' au)= to\n a)riqmo\n . . . e)pane/feren for neither did he show that my father left me in debt, nor yet has he adduced witnesses, nor did he put into the account the sum
