D. 27.49.

## ou)kou=n, ou)/koun

§2951

ou)kou=n interrogative: not therefore? not then? (nonne, igitur? nonne ergo?). Here the stress lies on the inferential ou)=n and an affirmative answer is expected as a matter of course. ou)kou=n stands at the beginning of its clause.
ou)kou=n . . . eu)= soi dokou=si bouleu/esqai; pro/s ge a(\ o(rw=si do you not then think that they lay their plans well? Yes, with regard to what they see
X. C. 7.1.8.
a. When a negative answer is expected we have ou)kou=n ou) (
P. Phil. 43d).
b. ou)kou=n and ou)=n stand in parallel questions in
X. A. 1.6.7-8.
c. Some scholars write ou)/koun or ou)k ou)=n for ou)kou=n interrogative (and inferential).

§2952

ou)kou=n inferential: then, well then, therefore, accordingly (ergo, igitur). Inferential ou)kou=n was developed, probably in colloquial speech, from the interrogative use, the speaker anticipating the affirmative answer to his question and emphasizing only the inference. From the negative question all that was left was an expression of his own opinion on the part of the speaker. ou)kou=n has become so completely equivalent to ou)=n that a negative has to be added if one is required.
ou)kou=n, o(/tan dh\ mh\ sqe/nw, pepau/somai well then, when my strength fails, I shall cease
S. Ant. 91,

h)\ . . . tou\s a)mu/_nesqai keleu/ontas po/lemon poiei=n fh/somen; ou)kou=n u(po/loipon douleu/ein or shall we say that those who bid us defend ourselves make war? Then it is left for us to be slaves
D. 8.59. ou)kou=n is used even with imperatives; as

ou)kou=n . . . i(kanw=s e)xe/tw accordingly let it suffice
P. Phae. 274b.
a. Editors often differ whether, in certain cases, ou)kou=n is interrogative or inferential.

§2953

ou)/koun not then, therefore not, so not, at any rate . . . not, surely not (non igitur, non ergo). Here ou) is strongly emphasized, and ou)=n is either confirmative or inferential. ou)/koun is usually placed at the beginning of its clause.
a. In emphatic negative answers; as

ou)/koun e)/moige dokei= certainly not, in my opinion at least
X. O. 1.9.
b. In continuous discourse (
P. L. 807a).
c. ou)/koun . . . ge returns a negative answer with qualified acquiescence in a preceding statement. Thus, tou/twn a)/ra *zeu/s e)stin a)sqene/steros; ou)/koun a)\n e)kfu/goi

ge th\n peprwme/nhn is Zeus then weaker than these? Fate at least he surely cannot escape
A. Pr. 517.
d. In impatient or excited questions (non? non igitur?). Thus, ou)/koun e)rei=s pot', ei)=t' a)pallaxqei\s a)/pei; wilt thou not speak and so depart and be gone?
S. Ant. 244.

§2954

ou)k (mh\) ou)=n is to be distinguished from ou)kou=n or ou)/koun. Thus,

o(po/te kai\ pei/ra| tou sfalei=en, ou)k ou)=n kai\ th\n po/lin ge th=s sfete/ra_s a)reth=s a)ciou=ntes steri/skein whenever they were foiled in any attempt they did not for this reason think it right to deprive their city of their valour
T. 2.43 (mh\ ou)=n 8. 91).
a. Hdt. has ou)k w)=n (sometimes written ou)/kwn) to emphasize an idea opposed to what goes before (non tamen). Thus, tau=ta le/gontes tou\s *krotwnih/ta_s ou)k w)=n e)/peiqon by these words they did not however persuade the men of Croton 3. 137.

## ou)=n

§2955

ou)=n (Ionic, Lesbic, Doric w)=n), a postpositive particle, is either confirmatory or inferential. ou)=n points to something already mentioned or known or to the present situation.

§2956

Confirmatory ou)=n in fact, at all events, in truth belongs properly to the entire clause, but usually, for purposes of emphasis, attaches itself to some other particle, to a relative pronoun, or at times to other words (
P. A. 22b). On gou=n, see 2830; on me\n ou)=n, 2901; on toigarou=n, 2987. In some of its combinations with other particles ou)=n may be inferential or transitional.

§2957

a)ll' ou)=n or a)ll' ou)=n . . . ge (stronger than d' ou)=n) well, at all events; well, certainly, for that matter; as a)ll' ou)=n ponhroi/ ge faino/menoi well, at all events they look like sorry fellows, that they are
X. C. 1.4.19, a)ll' ou)=n tosou=to/n g' i)/sqi well, at any rate you know this at least
S. Ph. 1305. a)ll' ou)=n may stand in the apodosis to an hypothetical proposition (
P. Ph. 91b).

§2958

ga\r ou)=n (and kai\ ga\r ou)=n) for in fact (indeed, in any case）; as

eu)= ga\r ou)=n ge/geis for indeed thou sayest well
S. Ant. 1255,

o)nh/sesqe a)kou/ontes: me/llw ga\r ou)=n a)/tta u(_mi=n e)rei=n kai\ a)/lla you will profit by listening; for I am certainly going to tell you some other things
P. A. 30c.
Also to mark a consequence (
X. A. 1.9.11), and in replies, as ou) ga\r ou)=n
P. Phae. 277e, and also when the speaker repeats an important word of his interlocutor, as fhmi\ ga\r ou)=n
P. G. 466e.

§2959

d' ou)=n but certainly, at all events, anyhow, be that as it may with or without me/n in the preceding clause. Here ou)=n shows that an unquestionable fact is to be set forth in its own clause; while the adversative de/ marks opposition to what has preceded and implies that the foregoing statement is uncertain and liable to dispute: ‘be that true or not, at any rate what follows is certainly true.’ d' ou)=n is used (a) to set aside conjecture, surmise, or hearsay; (b) to resume the main argument after long digression, and to cut short further discussion and come to the point; (c), with imperatives, to denote assent marked by unwillingness, impatience, or indifference. Thus, (a) ei) me\n dh\ di/kaia poih/sw, ou)k oi)=da: ai(rh/somai d' ou)=n u(_ma=s whether I shall do what is right (or not), I do not know; be that as it may, I will choose you
X. A. 1.3.5, kai\ e)le/geto *ku/_rw dou=nai polla\ xrh/mata. th=| d' ou)=n stratia=| to/te a)pe/dwke *ku=ros misqo\n tetta/rwn mhnw=n and she is said to have given Cyrus a large sum; at any rate Cyrus then gave the army four months' pay 1. 2. 12; (b) cp.
T. 1.3, 6. 15, 8. 81. Resumptive d' ou)=n may also set aside doubtful statements. (c)

su\ d' ou)=n le/ge, ei)/ soi tw=| lo/gw| tis h(donh/ well speak on then, if thou hast delight in speaking
S. El. 891, e)/stw d' ou)=n o(/pws u(_mi=n fi/lon however, be it as you wish
S. O. C. 1205.
ei' d' ou)=n = but if indeed, but if in point of fact; as ei) d' ou)=n ti ka)_ktre/poito tou= pro/sqen lo/gou but if he should deviate at all from his former statement
S. O. T. 851.

§2960

dh\ ou)=n certainly then; cp. ou)=n dh/. Thus, ti/ dh\ ou)=n; or ti/ ou)=n dh/; well then pray? pw=s dh\ ou)=n; how then pray? ou)=n dh=ta really then.

§2961

ei)/te ou)=n, ou)/te ou)=n: in alternative clauses ou)=n (indeed) is added to one or both clauses as emphasis may be desired: ei)/te ou)=n . . . ei)/te whether indeed . . . or, ei)/te . . . ei)/te ou)=n whether . . . or indeed, or ei)/te ou)=n . . . ei)/te ou)=n whether indeed . . . or indeed. So also in exclusive clauses: ou)/te (mh/te) . . . ou)/te (mh/te) ou)=n neither . . . nor yet, ou)/te (mh/te) ou)=n . . . ou)/te (mh/te) neither indeed . . . nor.

§2962

ou)=n often follows interrogative pronouns and adverbs (in dialogue); as ti/s ou)=n; who pray? ti/ ou)=n, generally with the aorist, in impatient questions asks why that which is desired has not been done (2197 c).

§2963

ou)=n affixed to a relative pronoun has a generalizing force and makes it indefinite (339 e). Such indefinite relative pronouns are construed like the indefinite ti\s or demonstratives; and do not introduce relative clauses (unlike whosoever, etc., which are both indefinite and relative).
So with adverbs (346 c), as o(pwsou=n in any way, no matter how (= utique not = utcunque). Thus, ou)d' o(pwsou=n not even in the slightest degree.
a. Simply placed after relatives ou)=n has a strengthening force; as w(/sper ou)=n as in fact (often in parentheses), oi(=o/s per ou)=n just as in fact.

§2964

Inferential ou)=n therefore, accordingly (igitur, ergo), usually classed as a conjunction, signifies that something follows from what precedes. Inferential ou)=n marks a transition to a new thought and continues a narrative (often after e)pei/, e)peidh/, o(/te), resumes an interrupted narration (
T. 3.42,
X. C. 3.3.9), and in general states a conclusion or inference. It stands alone or in conjunction with other particles. Thus, a)narxi/a| a)\n kai\ a)taci/a| e)no/mizon h(ma=s a)pole/sqai. dei= ou)=n polu\ me\n tou\s a)/rxontas e)pimeleste/rous gene/sqai tou\s nu=n tw=n pro/sqen they were of the opinion that we would be overcome through our lack of leaders and discipline. It is imperative therefore that the leaders we have now should be much more watchful than those we had before
X. A. 3.2.29.
a. The inferential and transitional use is derived from the confirmative meaning, and is scarcely marked until Herodotus and the Attic poets. Cp. me\n ou)=n. e)pei\ ou)=n in Hom. is sometimes used in transitions.

## pe/r

§2965

pe/r (postpositive and enclitic) very, just, even. Cp. Epic pe/ri very much, and peri/ in composition. In Attic prose pe/r is common only with relatives (338 c) and conjunctions.
o(/sper the very one who (i.e. none other), oi(=o/s per just such, e)/nqa per just where, w(/sper just as, in the very way in which, (sometimes not very different from w(s, to which it is related as o(/sper to o(/s), ei)/per if really. kai/per (Hom. kai\ . . . per) however much, though, Epic h)e/ per just as.
a. After other words especially in Epic and Lyric and in Aeschylus; as

me/nei to\ qei=on douli/a| per e/n freni/ the divine power remains in the mind though it be enslaved
A. Ag. 1084, ma/xet', a)xnu/meno/s per e(tai/rou he fought, (though) sore grieving for his comrade P 459, o)ye/ per howbeit late Pind. Nem. 3. 80.

## plh/n

§2966

plh/n an adverb, is used (a) as a preposition with the genitive (1700) meaning except, save, when that which is excepted is a single substantival idea; (b) as a conjunction, except, except that, save that, unless, only, but (often almost = a)lla/).
a)feisth/kesan . . . pa=sai plh\n *mi_lh/tou all the Ionic cities had revolted except Miletus
X. A. 1.1.6; ou)dei\s a)ph/|ei pro\s basile/a_, plh\n *)oro/nta_s e)pexei/rhse no one went off to the king save that Orontas made the attempt 1. 9. 29,

plh\n e(\n mo/non de/doika but there is one thing and only one that I fear
Ar. Plut. 199. A substantive-equivalent may follow plh/n, not in the genitive, but in the case required by the verb of the sentence, as

sunh=lqon pa/ntes plh\n oi( *ne/wnos all assembled except the men under Neon
X. A. 7.3.2.
a. plh\n ou) only not, except (2753); plh\n h)/ except, as ou) ga\r a)/llw| g' u(pakou/saimen . . . plh\n h)\ *prodi/kw| we would not listen to any one (else) except Prodicus
Ar. Nub. 361; plh\n o(/ti except that; plh\n ei) except if, cp. ei) mh/ (nisi si), after a negative plh\n ei) mh/; often with the verb omitted, as

ou)dei\s oi)=den . . . plh\n ei)/ tis a)/r' o)/rnis no one knows except perhaps some bird
Ar. Av. 601.
b. plh/n may be followed by the infinitive, as ti/ soi pe/pra_ktai pra=gma plh\n teu/xein kaka/; what hast thou accomplished save to work mischief?
A. Eum. 125.

## te/

§2967

te/ and (postpositive, and enclitic as -que) is generally used with a correlative conjunction.

§2968

te/ alone sometimes in prose links whole clauses or sentences which serve to explain, amplify, supplement, or to denote a consequence of, what precedes (and thus, and therefore, and as a result). Thus, o( d' e)xale/painen . . ., e)ke/leuse/ t' au)to\n e)k tou= me/sou e)ci/stasqai but he was angry and (therefore) ordered him to get out of the way
X. A. 1.5.14. Cp. 2978.
a. This use of te/ (te/ consequential) is quite common in Herodotus and Thucydides, rather rare in Xenophon, and infrequent in other prose writers. It occurs also in poetry.
N.—In poetry te/ alone (cp. -que) often connects single parallel nouns and pronouns so that the two connected ideas form a whole; as

skh=ptron ti_ma/_s te sceptre and prerogatives
A. Pr. 171. In prose, participles and infinitives are occasionally linked by te/; as

kaqarwte/ra_ ou)=sa prepo/ntws te ma=llon h)mfiesme/nh being fairer and dressed more becomingly
X. O. 10.12.

§2969

te/ (or kai/) meaning both may be followed by asyndeton (
S. Ant. 296).

§2970
Homer often, and Herodotus sometimes, adds te/ to relative pronouns and conjunctions introducing subordinate clauses, which are usually postpositive. So after o(/s, o(/sos, oi(=os, w(s, o(/te, e)pei/, e)/nqa, o(/qi, etc. Thus, fi/lhqen e)k *dio/s, o(/s te qeoi=si . . . a)na/ssei they were loved by Zeus, who rules over the gods B 669. This untranslatable te/ is probably connective (not indefinite), and belongs to the whole clause. It has the effect of showing that its clause corresponds in some way to the preceding clause. o(/s te is found in lyric poetry and in the lyric parts of tragedy (rarely in dialogue parts). w(/ste, oi(=o/s te became common.

§2971
This connective force is also seen when te/ stands in the principal clause, sometimes both in the principal and in the subordinate clause, e.g. o(/s ke qeoi=s e)pipei/qhtai, ma/la t' e)/kluon au)tou= whosoever obeys the gods, him especially they hear A 218, o(/pph| t' i)_qu/_sh|, th=| t' ei)/kousi sti/xes a)ndrw=n wheresoever he rushes, there the ranks of men give way M 48.

§2972
Homer has te/ after the coördinating conjunctions kai/, de/, ou)de/, a)lla/, h)/; after h)=, me/n, pe/r, ga/r, and before a)/ra in questions.

§2973

te\ . . . te/ usually serves to connect clauses, less frequently single words. In English and often suffices, but as . . . so is often in place. te\ . . . te/ is more common in poetry than in prose, but in prose more common than te/ standing alone. Thus, path\r a)ndrw=n te qew=n te father of men and gods A 544,

e)moi/ te ga\r pole/mioi *)assu/rioi, soi/ te nu=n e)xqi/_one/s ei)sin h)\ e)moi/ for the Assyrians are enemies to me, and they are now more hostile to you than to me
X. C. 4.5.23,

peri\ w(=n ei)de/nai te ka/lliston mh\ ei)de/nai te ai)/sxiston knowledge of which is most excellent and ignorance most disgraceful
P. G. 472c.
a. One clause may be negative, the other affirmative (
T. 2.22); but we usually have ou)/te instead of te\ ou).

§2974

te\ kai/ or te\ . . . kai/ often serves to unite complements, both similars and opposites. te\ . . . kai/ is not used when one clause is subordinate to another. The two words or clauses thus united may show a contrast, or the second may be stronger than the first. te/ is commonly separated from kai/ by one or more words. te\ . . . kai/ is weaker than kai\ . . . kai/, and will not easily bear the translation both . . . and. It is rare in colloquial Attic. Thus,

a)/rxein te kai\ a)/rxesqai to rule and be ruled
X. A. 1.9.4, ka/llisto/n te kai\ a)/riston fairest and best 2. 1. 9,

to/ t' a)/rxein kai\ to\ douleu/ein to rule and to be a slave
A. Pr. 927,

bi/a| te kou)x e(kw/n by force and not willingly
S. O. C. 935,

gumna/sai . . . e(auto/n te kai\ tou\s i(/ppous to exercise himself and his horses
X. A. 1.2.7. Clauses dissimilar in form may be linked by te\ . . . kai/; as

a)pekri/_nato dia\ braxe/wn te kai\ au)ta\ ta\ e)rwtw/mena he answered briefly and only the questions put to him
P. Pr. 336a.

§2975

te\ . . . kai/ is often used of actions coincident in time, or of actions standing in a causal relation to each other; as h(me/ra_ te sxedo\n u(pe/faine kai\ ei)s to\ me/son h(=kon oi( a)/rxontes day was just breaking and (= when) the officers came into the centre of the camp
X. A. 3.3.1 (temporal parataxis; cp. 2169).

§2976

te\ . . . kai/ is sometimes used of alternatives (for ei)/te . . . ei)/te). Thus,

qeou= te ga\r qe/lontos . . . kai\ mh\ qe/lontos whether God wills or not
A. Sept. 427. Here kai\ . . . kai/ is more common (2877).

§2977
We find te\ . . . kai\ . . . te/, te\ . . . kai\ . . . te\ . . . te/ . . . (te/), te\ . . . te\ . . . kai/, te\ . . . te\ . . . kai\ . . . te/, te\ . . . kai\ . . . kai\ . . . te/. But in prose te/ before and after kai/ is rare.

§2978
When te/ follows te\ . . . kai/, te/ does not point back to kai/, but denotes an addition to the preceding member (and besides). Thus,

tei/xh te perielo/ntes kai\ nau=s parado/ntes fo/ron te taca/menoi both destroying their walls and surrendering their ships and besides assessing tribute on themselves
T. 1.108. Cp. 2968.

§2979

kai/ te is Epic; elsewhere the kai/ of kai\ . . . te belongs to the whole clause (
A. Ch. 252).

§2980

a)/llws te kai/ both in other ways and especially, on other grounds and particularly, or simply especially. This combination usually stands before conditional clauses (or clauses with a conditional participle), causal, and temporal clauses. Thus,

xalepo\n oi)=mai diabai/nein a)/llws te kai\ polemi/wn pollw=n e)/mprosqen o)/ntwn I think it hard to cross, especially when the enemy faces us in full force
X. A. 5.6.9,

pa/ntwn . . . a)posterei=sqai lu_phro/n e)sti . . . , a)/llws te ka)\_n u(p' e)xqrou= tw| tou=to sumbai/nh| it is grievous to be deprived of anything, especially if this happens to any one at the hands of a personal enemy
D. 18.5. Cp.

ta/ t' a)/lla e)ti(_mhse kai\ mu_ri/ous e)/dwke da_reikou/s he both honoured me in other ways and gave me ten thousand darics
X. A. 1.3.3.

§2981

te\ . . . de/ is used when a writer begins as if he were going simply to add the second member (both . . . and), but instead contrasts it with the first. This combination of copulative and adversative particles is often rendered less harsh by the form of the de/ clause and by other reasons. (a) The de/ clause contains a kai/; as a(/ma (e)/peita, e)/ti, pollaxou=, w(sau/tws) de\ kai/; e.g. e)/n te th=| tw=n e)pw=n poih/sei pollaxou= de\ kai\ a)/lloqi, lit. both in the construction of epic poetry but also in many other cases
P. R. 394c. (b) The second clause contains a formula with de/ but not with kai/; as e)/ti de/, ti/ de/, to\ de\ kefa/laion, meta\ de\ tau=ta. Thus, pro/tero/n te . . . nu=n de/ (both) formerly . . . but now
X. H. 7.1.24. Cp.
P. L. 664b, 947 a, 967 d. (c) After a considerable interval occasioned by the extension of the te/ clause, it is natural to resume with de/. So
T. 6.83. 1,
X. A. 7.8.11,
X. C. 2.1.22,
L. 2.17.

§2982
Rare combinations are, e.g.:
h)\ . . . te/ instead of h)\ . . . h)/. Thus, h)\ pai=des nearoi\ xh=rai/ te gunai=kes either young children and (= or) widowed women B 289. te\ . . . h)/ is often emended in
X. O. 20.12,
P. Men. 95b.
te\ . . . ou)de/ (mhde/) with te/ instead of ou)/te (mh/te); as
E. I. T. 697,
P. Pol. 271e. te/ is not followed by ou)/te (mh/te).

§2983

Position of te/.—te/ usually follows the word with which the sentence or sentence-part to be connected is most concerned. Apart from many irregularities there are certain exceptions to this rule which are commonly observed.
a. te/ may come between two words which go closely together, as between article (preposition, attributive genitive) and its noun. Thus,

to/ te barbariko\n kai\ to\ *(ellhniko/n the barbarian and the Greek force
X. A. 1.2.1,

ei)=mi pro/s te loutra\ kai\ leimw=nas I will go to the bathing places and the meadows
S. Aj. 654 (for pro\s loutra/ te). But

h( po/lis. te kai\ h(mei=s oi( no/moi the State and we the laws
P. Cr. 53a.
b. te/ connecting an entire clause stands as near as possible to the beginning. Cp.
X. A. 1.8.3.
c. te/ may stand after a word or expression which, though common to two members of a clause, is placed either at the beginning (especially after a preposition) or in the second member. Thus, a(/ te dei= fi/lia kai\ (a(\ dei=)

pole/mia h(ma=s nomi/zein what we must consider as belonging to our friends and what to our enemies
X. C. 5.2.21,

e)/n te tw=| qermote/rw| kai\ yu_xrote/rw| in the hotter and colder
P. Phil. 24b,

a(/pa_si fi/lon a)/ndra te sofw/taton a man dear to all and most wise
Ar. Vesp. 1277.
d. The freer position of te/ is often due to the fact that several words are taken as forming a single notion. Thus,

h( kalli/sth dh\ poli_tei/a_ te kai\ o( ka/llistos a)nh/r the very noblest constitution and the noblest man
P. R. 562a.

## toi/

§2984

toi/ (postpositive and enclitic) in truth, surely, doubtless, mark you, be assured, you (must) know, was originally the dative of feeling (1486) of su/.
a. This toi/ (Sanskrit tē), found in all dialects, is to be distinguished from Doric toi/ ( = soi/) from tnoi (Skt. tvē´). toi/ may thus occur in the same sentence with soi/; as toiau=ta/ toi/ soi . . . le/gw S. fr. 25.

§2985

toi/ is often used in statements of a general truth and in expressions of personal conviction (sometimes with a tone of hesitation); in remarks of a confidential nature; to introduce an explanation; and in general where the special attention of the person addressed is desired. toi/ often gives an easy and familiar tone to a reply. Thus,

tw=n toi matai/wn a)ndra/sin fronhma/twn h( glw=ss' a)lhqh\s gi/gnetai kath/goros true it is that of men's vain conceits their tongue is the true accuser
A. Sept. 438, a)ei/ toi o( *ke/bhs lo/gous tina\s a)nereuna=| for Cebes, you know, is always investigating some speculation or other
P. Ph. 63a.
a. toi/ may emphasize particular words, as e)gw/ toi, e)moi/ toi, se/ toi; and other words not pronouns.

§2986

toi/ is frequently used after other particles, as a)lla/, ga/r, ge/, dh/ (and ge/ toi dh/, cp. dh/ toi . . . ge), e)pei/ because, mh/, ou) (ou)/toi). On h)/toi, see 2858; on kai/toi, 2893; on me/ntoi, 2917.

§2987
The inferential conjunctions toiga/r, toigarou=n, toiga/rtoi, toi/nun contain toi/, the locative of the demonstrative to/, which case had the meaning of tw=| (tw=) therefore, on this account, so lit. by that, therein. (This tw=| is chiefly Epic, and stands at the beginning of the verse. Cp.

to/ therefore
*g 176,
S. Ph. 142.)
toiga/r (prepositive; Ionic and poetic) therefore, wherefore, so then, that is surely the reason why (often to announce a purpose).
toigarou=n, toiga/rtoi (both prepositive) are more emphatic than toiga/r. The final syllable of toiga/rtoi is the toi/ of 2984.
toi/nun (postpositive and post-Homeric; -nun 2927) is transitional (now then, further) or inferential (therefore, accordingly; less emphatic than toiga/r). toi<*>nun is common when a speaker refers to something present in his mind, when he continues or resumes what he has been saying, and when he passes to a new aspect of a subject. It is often found with imperatives (sko/pei toi/nun
P. Cr. 51c).

## w(/s, w(s

§2988

Demonstrative w(/s (also accented w(s, w(=s) thus, so is originally an ablative from the demonstrative stem o(- (from so-), from which come the article and o(/s he in kai\ o(/s, h)= d' o(/s (1113). For the -s, see 341. Cp. also w(=-de thus.
So kai\ w(/s even so, nevertheless, ou)d' (mhd') w(/s not even thus, in no wise, w(s au)/tws (w(sau/tws) in the same way, just so (ablative of o( au)to/s). w(s e(te/rws (lit. thus otherwise, in that other way) quite otherwise and w(s a)lhqw=s (lit. thus truly) in very truth also probably belong here.
a. In some cases it is uncertain whether w(s is demonstrative or relative; e.g. w(s in exclamatory clauses. Cp. 2998, 3001.

§2989

Relative w(s as, how is originally an ablative (in which way) from the relative stem [iglide]o-, whence come also o(/s, h(/, o(/. For the -s, see 341. Relative w(s has various uses as an adverb or a conjunction, all of which represent the primitive meaning.

## Relative w(s as an Adverb

§2990
In comparative clauses, often correlated with ou(/tws. Thus,

pisto\s h)=n, w(s u(_mei=s e)pi/stasqe I was faithful, as you know
X. A. 3.3.2, e)ke/leuse tou\s *(/ellhnas, w(s no/mos au)toi=s ei)s ma/xhn, ou(/tw taxqh=nai he ordered the Greeks (thus) to be stationed as was their custom for battle 1. 2. 15. Cp. 2462 ff. In similes and comparisons, 2481 ff.

§2991

w(s is rarely used for h)/ after comparatives; as

mh/ mou prokh/dou ma=sson w(s e)moi\ gluku/ care not for me further than I wish
A. Pr. 629. Cp. 1071.

§2992
In adverbial clauses w(s is often used parenthetically; as w(s e)moi\ dokei= as it seems to me. Instead of w(s dokei=, w(s e)/oike the personal construction is often preferred; as

a)pe/pleusan, w(s me\n toi=s plei/stois e)do/koun, filoti_mhqe/ntes they sailed away out of jealousy, as it seemed to most people
X. A. 1.4.7.

§2993

w(s restrictive for (cp. ut), involving the judgment of the observer, occurs often in elliptical phrases; as (*bra_si/da_s) h)=n ou)de\ a)du/natos, w(s *lakedaimo/nios, ei)pei=n Brasidas was, for a Lacedaemonian, not a bad speaker either
T. 4.84, tau=ta a)kou/sa_s *ce/rchs w(s e)k kakw=n e)xa/rh on hearing this Xerxes rejoiced as much <*> could be expected considering his misfortunes
Hdt. 8.101. On w(s restrictive with the dative, cp. 1495 a, 1497; with the absolute infinitive, 2012.

§2994

w(s is often used to heighten a superlative (1086).

§2995
With numerals and words indicating degree w(s means about, nearly, not far from; as

o(pli/_ta_s e)/xwn w(s pentakosi/ous having about five hundred hoplites
X. A. 1.2.3,

w(s e)pi\ polu/ for the most part
P. R. 377b (lit. about over the great（er) part).

§2996

w(s often indicates the thought or the assertion of the subject of the principal verb or of some other person prominent in the sentence. Here w(s expresses a real intention or an avowed plea. So often with participles (2086); and also with the prepositions ei)s, e)pi/, pro/s; as

a)pe/pleon . . . e)k th=s *sikeli/a_s w(s e)s ta\_s *)aqh/na_s they sailed away from Sicily as though bound for Athens
T. 6.61.

§2997

w(s e(/kastos means each for himself; as a)pe/pleusan e)c *(ellhspo/ntou w(s e(/kastoi (a)pe/pleusan)

kata\ po/leis they sailed away from the Hellespont each to his own State
T. 1.89.

§2998

w(s exclamatory (2682) may be the relative adverb w(s how, the relative clause originally being used in explanation of an exclamation. Exclamatory w(s has also been explained as w(s demonstrative (so).

§2999
On w(s in wishes, see 1815.

## Relative w(s as a Conjunction

§3000

w(s conjunctive is found in dependent clauses.
Declarative: that, like o(/ti. Cp. 2577 ff., 2614 ff.
Final: that, in order that; like i(/na, but not used in standard Attic prose. Cp. 2193.
Object clauses after verbs of effort: that, like o(/pws; cp. 2209. Rarely after verbs of fearing: that. Cp. 2235.
Causal: as, inasmuch as, since, seeing that, like o(/ti, e)pei/, etc. Cp. 2240.
Consecutive: so that, like w(/ste. Usually with the infinitive, sometimes with the indicative. Cp. 2260.
Temporal: after, like e)pei/; sometimes when, whenever. Cp. 2383.

§3001

w(s is often found before sentences apparently independent, where it is sometimes explained as a conjunction with the verb suppressed. Thus, w(s th=sd' e(kou=sa paido\s ou) meqh/somai (know) that of my own accord I will not relinquish my child
E. Hec. 400, w(s dh\ su/ moi tu/rannos *)argei/wn e)/sei (do you mean) that you forsooth shall be lord and master of Argives
A. Ag. 1633. Some scholars regard this w(s as causal, others regard it as demonstrative, others as comparative.

## SOME GRAMMATICAL AND RHETORICAL FIGURES

§3004

Anacolūthon (a)nako/louqon inconsequent), or grammatical inconsistency, is inadvertent or purposed deviation in the structure of a sentence by which a construction started at the beginning is not followed out consistently. Anacoluthon is sometimes real, sometimes only slight or apparent. It is natural to Greek by reason of the mobility and elasticity of that language; but in English it could not be tolerated to an equal extent because our tongue—a speech of few inflected forms—is much more rigid than Greek.

§3005
Anacoluthon is, in general, caused either (a) by the choice of some form of expression more convenient or more effective than that for which the sentence was grammatically planned; at times, too, the disturbing influence is the insertion of a brief expression of an additional thought not foreseen at the start. Or (b) by the intrusion of some explanation requiring a parenthesis of such an extent that the connection is obscured or the continuation of the original structure made difficult. In this case the beginning may be repeated, or what has already been said may be summed up in a different grammatical form and sometimes with the addition of a resumptive particle, such as dh/, ou)=n well then, then, as I was saying (
X. A. 1.8.13, 3. 1. 20,
X. C. 3.3.9). So with de/ (
T. 8.29. 2).

§3006
Anacoluthon usually produces the effect of naturalness and liveliness, sometimes of greater clearness (as after long parentheses), or of brevity, force, or concentration.

§3007
Anacoluthon is either natural or artificial. Natural anacoluthon is seen in the loose and discursive style of Herodotus; in the closely packed sentences of Thucydides, who hurries from one thought to another with the least expenditure of words; and in the slovenliness of Andocides. Artificial or rhetorical anacoluthon is the result of a deliberate purpose to give to written language the vividness, naturalness, and unaffected freedom of the easy flow of conversation, and is best seen in the dialogues of Plato. Such anacoluthon is usually graceful and free from obscurity.

§3008
There are very many forms of anacoluthon, e.g.
a. Many cases are due to the fact that a writer conforms his construction, not to the words which he has just used, but to another way in which the antecedent thought might have been expressed: the construction pro\s to\ noou/menon (or shmaino/menon) according to what is thought. Cp. 2148 and
X. H. 2.2.3,
S. O. T. 353,
E. Hec. 970.
b. Some cases are due to changes in the subject, as
T. 1.18. 2.
c. Many cases occur in connection with the use of a participle (2147, 2148).
d. Coördinate clauses connected by te\ . . . kai/, kai\ . . . kai/, ou)/te . . . ou)/te, h)\ . . . h)/ often show anacoluthon, especially when a finite verb takes the place of a participle. Cp. 2147 c, and
T. 5.61. 4, 6. 32. 3, 7. 47. 1-2.
e. The nominative “in suspense” may stand at the head of a sentence instead of another case required by the following construction. This involves a redundant pronoun. Thus, *pro/cenos de\ kai\ *me/nwn, e)pei/per ei)si\n u(_me/teroi eu)erge/tai . . . pe/myate au)tou\s deu=ro (for *pro/cenon kai\ *me/nwna . . . pe/myate deu=ro)
X. A. 2.5.41. Cp. “The prince that feeds great natures, they will slay him:” Ben Jonson.
f. The accusative often stands absolutely when at the head of a sentence. Thus, a)lla\ mh\n kai\ ti_ma/_s ge . . ., tw=n me\n meqe/cei kai\ geu/setai e(kw/n, a_<*>\s a)\n h(gh=tai a)mei/nw au(to\n poih/sein, a(\_s d' . . . feu/cetai but furthermore as regards honours, those he will partake of and be glad to taste which he thinks will make him a better man, but others he will shun
P. R. 591e, *(/ellhnas tou\s e)n th=| *)asi/a| oi)kou=ntas ou)de/n pw safe\s le/getai ei) e(/pontai (for le/gousin ei) e(/pontai or le/getai e(/pesqai) as to the Greeks who dwell in Asia there is as yet no certain intelligence whether they are to accompany the expedition
X. C. 2.1.5.
g. A main clause may take the construction of a parenthetical clause (
T. 4.93. 2). Here belongs the attraction into the relative clause of a verb that should have been principal. So after w(s h)/kousa, w(s oi)=mai, w(s le/gousi, etc. Thus, to/de ge mh/n, w(s oi)=mai, peri\ au)tou= a)nagkaio/taton ei)=nai (for e)sti\) le/gein this indeed is, as I think, most necessary to state about it
P. Phil. 20d. Often in Hdt., as w(s d' e)gw\ h)/kousa . . . ei)=nai au)to\n *)idanqu/rsou . . . pa/trwn but as I have heard he was the uncle of Idanthyrsus on the father's side 4. 76. A construction may be introduced by o(/ti or w(s and then pass to the infinitive, or the infinitive may precede and a finite verb follow (2628).
h. After a subordinate clause with parentheses the main clause sometimes follows in the form of an independent sentence (
P. A. 28c, cp. 36 a).
i. An infinitive may resume the idea set forth by the principal verb; as tou= de\ qeou= ta/ttontos, w(s e)gw\ w)|h/qhn te kai\ u(pe/labon, filosofou=nta/ me dei=n zh=n ktl. whereas when God orders me, as I think and believe, to pass my life in the pursuit of wisdom, etc.
P. A. 28e. Cp.
X. H. 7.4.35.
j. Anacoluthon is sometimes due to the desire to maintain similarity of form between contrasted expressions; as

tou\s me\n ga\r i(ppokentau/rous oi)=mai e)/gwge polloi=s me\n a)porei=n tw=n a)nqrw/pois hu(rhme/nwn a)gaqw=n o(/pws dei= xrh=sqai, polloi=s de\ tw=n i(/ppois pefu_ko/twn h(de/wn pw=s au)tw=n xrh\ a)polau/ein for I think that the horse-centaurs were at a loss how to make use of many conveniences devised for men and how to enjoy many of the pleasures natural to horses
X. C. 4.3.19. Here polloi=s de/ is used as if it were to be governed by xrh=sqai, instead of which au)tw=n a)polau/ein is substituted.

§3009

Anadiplōsis (a)nadi/plwsis doubling) is the rhetorical repetition of one or several words. Cp. “The Isles of Greece, the Isles of Greece, where burning Sappho loved and sung:” Byron.
*qh=bai de/, *qh=bai po/lis a)stugei/twn, meq' h(me/ra_n mi/an e)k me/shs th=s *(ella/dos a)nh/rpastai Thebes, Thebes, a neighbouring city, in the course of one day has been extirpated from the midst of Greece
Aes. 3.133.

§3010

Anaphora (a)nafora/_ carrying back) is the repetition, with emphasis, of the same word or phrase at the beginning of several successive clauses. This figure is also called epanaphora or epanalepsis. Cp. “Strike as I would Have struck those tyrants! Strike deep as my curse! Strike! and but once:” Byron.

ou(=toi ga\r pollou\s me\n tw=n poli_tw=n ei)s tou\s polemi/ous e)ch/lasan, pollou\s d' a)di/kws a)poktei/nantes a)ta/fous e)poi/hsan, pollou\s d' e)piti(_mous o)/ntas a)ti/_mous kate/sthsan many of the citizens they drove out to the enemy; many they slew unjustly and left unburied; many who were in possession of their civic rights they deprived of them
L. 12.21. Cp.
D. 18.48, 75, 121, 310.

§3011

Anastrophe (a)nastrofh/ return) is the use, at the beginning of one clause, of the same word that concluded the preceding clause. Also called epanastrophe. Cp. “Has he a gust for blood? Blood shall fill his cup.”
ou) dh/pou *kthsifw=nta du/natai diw/kein di' e)me/, e)me\ d' ei)/per e)cele/gcein e)no/mizen, au)to\n ou)k a)\n e)gra/yato for surely it cannot be that he is prosecuting Ctesiphon on my account, and yet would not have indicted me myself, if he had thought that he could convict me
D. 18.13.

§3012

Antistrophe (a)ntistrofh/ turning about) is the repetition of the same word or phrase at the end of successive clauses.
o(/stis d' e)n tw=| prw/tw| lo/gw| th\n yh=fon ai)tei= o(/rkon ai)tei=, no/mon ai)tei=, dhmokrati/a_n ai)tei= whoever in his first speech asks for your vote as a favour, asks the surrender of your oath, asks the surrender of the law, asks the surrender of the democratic constitution
Aes. 3.198.

§3013

Antithesis (a)nti/qesis opposition) is the contrast of ideas expressed by words which are the opposite of, or are closely contrasted with, each other. Cp. “Wit is negative, analytical, destructive; Humor is creative:” Whipple.
di' w(=n e)k xrhstw=n fau=la ta\ pra/_gmata th=s po/lews ge/gone, dia\ tou/twn e)lpi/zete tw=n au)tw=n pra/_cewn e)k fau/lwn au)ta\ xrhsta\ genh/sesqai; do you expect that the affairs of state will become prosperous instead of bad by the same measures by which they have become bad instead of prosperous?
D. 2.26.
a. Antithesis is sometimes extended to a parallelism in sense effected (1) by the use of two words of opposite meaning in the expression of one idea, (2) by the opposition of ideas which are not specifically contrasted in words.

§3014

Aporia (a)pori/a_ doubt) is an artifice by which a speaker feigns doubt as to where he shall begin or end or what he shall do or say, etc. Cp. “Then the steward said within himself, What shall I do?” St. Luke 16. 3.

a)porw= tou= prw/tou mnhsqw= I am uncertain what I shall recall first
D. 18.129. When the doubt is between two courses it is often called diaporēsis.

§3015

Aposiopēsis (a)posiw/phsis becoming silent) is a form of ellipse by which, under the influence of passionate feeling or of modesty, a speaker comes to an abrupt halt. Examples 2352 d,
D. 18.3, 22, 195,
S. O. T. 1289,
Ar. Vesp. 1178. Cp. “Massachusetts and her people . . . hold him, and his love . . . and his principles, and his standard of truth in utter—what shall I say? —anything but respect:” Webster.

§3016

Asyndeton (a)su/ndeton not bound together) is the absence of conjunctions in a series of coördinate words or phrases. See 2165 ff.
a. Here is sometimes placed the omission of the verb after mh/ (mh\ su/ ge, mh\ ga/r, etc.); as mh\ triba\_s e)/ti (poiei=sqe) no more delays!
S. Ant. 577, ti/s ou)xi\ kate/ptusen a)\n sou=; mh\ ga\r (ei)pe\) th=s po/lews ge, mhd' e)mou= who would not have reviled you? Do not say the State, nor me
D. 18.200. Cp. 946, 1599.

§3017

Brachylogy (braxulogi/a_ brevity of diction, abbreviated expres. sion or construction) is a concise form of expression by which an element is not repeated or is omitted when its repetition or use would make the thought or the grammatical construction complete. The suppressed element must be supplied from some corresponding word in the context, in which case it often appears with some change of form or construction; or it must be taken from the connection of the thought.
a. Brachylogy and ellipse cannot always be distinguished sharply. In ellipse the suppressed word is not to be supplied from a corresponding word in the context; and, in general, ellipse is less artificial and less dependent on the momentary and arbitrary will of the speaker or writer. Compendious Comparison (1501), Praegnans Constructio (3044), and Zeugma (3048) are forms of brachylogy.

§3018
There are many forms of brachylogy; for example:
a. One verbal form must often be supplied from another; e.g. a passive from an active, an infinitive from a finite verb, a participle from an infinitive. Thus, th\n tw=n pe/las dh|ou=n ma=llon h)\ th\n e(autw=n o(ra=n (dh|oume/nhn) rather to ravage the territory of their neighbours than to see their own (being ravaged)
T. 2.11, tau=ta e)gw/ soi ou) pei/qomai . . ., oi)=mai de\ ou)de\ a)/llon a)nqrw/pwn ou)de/na (pei/qesqai/ soi) of this I am not persuaded by you and I do not believe that any other human being is either
P. A. 25e, ou)/te pa/sxontes kako\n ou)de\n ou)/te me/llontes (pa/sxein) neither suffering, nor being likely (to suffer), any evil
I. 12.103, a)nexw/rhsan de\ kai\ oi( *aqhnai=oi . . . , e)peidh\ kai\ e)kei/nous ei)=don (a)naxwrh/santas) and the Athenians too withdrew when they saw that they (the Lacedaemonians) had done so
T. 3.16.
b. A verb must often be supplied from a coördinate or subordinate clause either preceding or following. Thus, e)/geire kai\ su\ th/nd', e)gw\ de\ se/ do you wake her, as I (wake) you
A. Eum. 140, e)a\_n de\ au)to/xeir me\n mh/ (h)=|),

bouleu/sh| de\ qa/nato/n tis a)/llos e(te/rw| if a person shall not kill with his own hand, but if some one shall suggest murder to another
P. L. 872a; fi/lous nomi/zous' ou(/sper a)\n po/sis se/qen (nomi/zh|) regarding as friends even those whom thy husband (so regards)
E. Med. 1153. A verb is rarely supplied from the subordinate to the main construction.
c. In clauses with dei=, xrh/ etc.: i(/na fai/nhsqe a)mu/_nontes oi(=s dei= (a)mu/_nein) that you may seem to assist those you ought (to assist)
T. 3.13. When a form of tugxa/nw stands in the subordinate clause; a)pe/pleusan w(s e(/kastoi e)/tuxon (a)pople/ontes) they sailed away as each best could
T. 4.25. In conditional clauses when the protasis indicates that the assertion made in the apodosis holds true of a person or a thing more than of any other person or thing (ei)/per tis kai\ a)/llos, ei)/per pou, ei)/per pote/, w(/s tis kai\ a)/llos, etc.); as sumfe/rei d' u(_mi=n, ei)/per tw| kai\ a)/llw|, to\ ni_ka=n victory is of advantage to you, if it (is of advantage) to any
X. C. 3.3.42. Hence ei)/ tis (pou, poqen) is almost = ti\s, etc. (
T. 7.21. 5).
d. Compound verbs (especially those compounded with meta/ and e)c) are often so used that the force both of the compound and of the simple verb is requisite to the meaning. Thus, (oi( *)aqhnai=oi) mete/gnwsan *kerku_rai/ois cummaxi/a_n mh\ poih/sasqai the Athenians changed their minds and decided not to make an alliance with the Corcyraeans
T. 1.44.
e. A compound verb on its second occurrence often omits the preposition (rarely vice versa); as a)perga/zhtai . . . ei)rga/zeto
P. Ph. 104d. Euripides is fond of such collocations as u(pa/kouson a)/kouson Alc. 400. Cp. the difference in metrical value of repeated words in Shakespeare, as “These víolént desires have víolent ends.”
N.—In kai\ cummeti/sxw kai\ fe/rw th=s ai)ti/a_s I share and bear alike the guilt (
S. Ant. 537) fe/rw, though capable of taking the partitive genitive, is influenced by cummeti/sxw and has the force of cumfe/rw.
f. From a following verb of special meaning a verb of more general meaning, such as poiei=n, gi/gnesqai, ei)=nai, must be supplied with the phrases ou)de\n a)/llo h)/, a)/llo ti h)/, ti/ a)/llo h)/. Examples in 946, 2652, 2778.
g. A verb of saying or thinking must often be supplied from a foregoing verb of exhorting, commanding, announcing, or from any other verb that implies saying or thinking. Thus, *krito/boulos kai\ *)apollo/dwros keleu/ousi/ me tria/_konta mnw=n ti_mh/sasqai, au)toi\ de\ e)ggua=sqai Critobulus and Apollodorus urge me to set a penalty of thirty minae, and (say) that they themselves are sureties
P. A. 38b.
h. When two verbs taking the same or different cases have an object in common, that object is expressed only once, and usually is dependent on the nearer verb. See 1634, 1635.
i. A substantive or a verb is often to be supplied from a substantive or a verb related in meaning: naumaxh/santas mi/an (naumaxi/a_n) having fought one (sea-fight)
Ar. Ran. 693, h( me\n e)/peita ei)s a(/la a)=lto . . ., *zeu\s de\ e(o\n pro\s dw=ma (e)/bh) she then sprang into the sea, but Zeus (went) to his abode A 532.
j. The subject of a sentence is often taken from a preceding object or from some other preceding noun in an oblique case without a pronoun of reference to aid the transition. Thus, e)cefo/bhsan me\n tou\s pollou\s ou)k ei)do/tas ta\ pra_sso/mena, kai\ e)/feugon (oi( polloi/) they frightened away most of the citizens, who were in ignorance of the plot and began to fly
T. 8.44. Cp. 943.
k. In general an object is frequently omitted when it can readily be supplied from the context. Thus, e)gxei=n (to\n oi)=non) e)ke/lene he gave orders to pour in (the wine)
X. A. 4.3.13. An unemphatic pronoun in an oblique case is often omitted when it can be supplied from a preceding noun. Cp. 1214.
l. A dependent noun must often be supplied, in a different construction, from one coördinate clause to another. Thus, o(/rkous e)/labon kai\ e)/dosan para\ *farnaba/zou they received oaths from Pharnabazus and gave him theirs
X. H. 1.3.9. So in contrasts where one member is to be supplied from the other, as ou)k e)kei=nos (e)kei/nhn), a)ll' e)kei/nh kei=non e)nqa/d' h)/gagen he did not bring (her) here, but she brought him
E. Or. 742.
m. From a preceding word its opposite must often be supplied, especially an affirmative after a negative. Thus, a)melh/sa_s w(=nper oi( polloi\ (e)pimelou=ntai) neglecting the very things which most people (care for)
P. A. 36b. This laxity of expression is especially frequent in the case of e(/kastos, ti\s, or pa/ntes, to be supplied after ou)dei/s (mhdei/s), as mhdei\s th\n u(perbolh\n qauma/sh|, a)lla\ met' eu)noi/a_s d\ le/gw qewrhsa/tw let no one wonder at the extravagance of my statement, but let (every one) consider kindly what I say
D. 18.199. Cp. “No person held to service or labor in one state . . ., escaping into another, shall . . . be discharged from said service or labor, but shall be delivered up, etc.”: U. S. Constitution.
n. The same word though placed only once may stand in two different constructions; as ai)ne/w de\ kai\ to/nde (no/mon) . . . mh/te tw=n a)/llwn *perse/wn mhde/na tw=n

e(wutou= oi)kete/wn . . . a)nh/keston pa/qos e)/rdein and I approve also this custom that no one of the other Persians shall do irremediable hurt to any one of his own servants
Hdt. 1.137. Here mhde/na is both subject and object of e)/rdein.
o. An assertion may be made concerning an action or a thing when the absence of that action or thing is meant (res pro rei defectu). Thus, ei)/ t' a)/r' o(g' eu)xwlh=s e)pime/mfetai whether then he blames us on account of an (unfulfilled) vow A 65, e)n h(=| kai\ peri\ xrhma/twn kai\ peri\ a)ti_mi/a_s a)/nqrwpoi kindu_neu/ousin on which charge men run the risk both of (loss of) money and civil degradation
D. 29.16. So du/namis powerlessness, fulakh/ neglect of the watch, mele/thma lack of liberal exercise.

§3019

Catachrēsis (kata/xrhsis misuse of a word) is the extension of the meaning of a word beyond its proper sphere; especially a violent metaphor. In English: “a palatable tone,” “to take arms against a sea of troubles.”
daimo/nios extraordinary, qauma/sios decided, strange, capital, a)mhxa/nws and u(perfuw=s decidedly, u(popteu/w expect, naustolei=n xqo/na
E. Med. 682. Such usages are less often occasioned by the poverty of the language than by the caprice of the writer.

§3020

Chiasmus (xi_asmo/s marking with diagonal lines like a X) is the crosswise arrangement of contrasted pairs to give alternate stress. By this figure both the extremes and the means are correlated. Cp. “Sweet is the breath of morn, her rising sweet”: Milton.

e(\n sw=m' e)/xwn kai\ yu_xh\n mi/an having one body and one soul
D. 19.227.
So tosou=ton su\ e)mou= sofw/teros ei)= thlikou/tou o)/ntos thliko/sd' w)/n; are you at your age so much wiser than I at mine?
P. A. 25d, pa=n me\n e)/rgon pa=n d' e)/pos le/gonta/s te kai\ pra/_ttontas lit. doing every deed and uttering every word
P. R. 494e,

douleu/ein kai\ a)/rxesqai . . . a)/rxein kai\ despo/zein to be a slave and be ruled . . . to rule and be a master
P. Ph. 80a.

§3021

Climax (kli=mac ladder) is an arrangement of clauses in succession whereby the last important word of one is repeated as the first important word of the next, each clause in turn surpassing its predecessor in the importance of the thought. Cp. “But we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience . . . and experience, hope; and hope maketh not ashamed”: Romans v. 3-5.

ou)k ei)=pon me\n tau=ta, ou)k e)/graya de/, ou)d' e)/graya me/n, ou)k e)pre/sbeusa de/, ou)d' e)pre/sbeusa me/n, ou)k e)/peisa de\ *qhbai/ous I did not utter these words without proposing a motion; nor did I propose a motion without becoming ambassador; nor did I become ambassador without convincing the Thebans
D. 18.179; cp. 4. 19. This figure is very rare in Greek.

§3022

Ellipse (e)/lleiyis leaving out, defect) is the suppression of a word or of several words of minor importance to the logical expres sion of the thought, but necessary to the construction. Ellipse gives brevity, force, and liveliness; it is usually readily to be supplied, often unconscious, and appears especially in common phrases, constructions, and expressions of popular speech (such as e)c o)nu/xwn le/onta to judge a lion from his claws).
a. Ellipse occurs in the case of substantives and pronouns, subject, object, finite verbs, main clauses, and (less often) subordinate clauses. See the Index under Ellipse.

§3023

Enallage (e)nallagh/ interchange) is the substitution of one grammatical form for another, as plural for singular (1006-1008). Thus: “They fall successive, and successive rise”: Pope.

§3024

Euphemism (eu)fhmismo/s lit. speaking favourably) is the substitution of a less direct expression in place of one whose plainer meaning might be unpleasant or offensive. Thus: “The merchant prince had stopped payment” (for “became bankrupt”).
sumfora/_ occurrence for a)tu/xhma misfortune, e(te/rws otherwise = not well, eu)fro/nh ‘the kindly time’ for nu/c night, eu)w/numos left (lit. of good omen, whereas the left was the unlucky side), ei)/ ti pa/qoi if anything should happen to him = if he should die.

§3025

Hendiadys (e(\n dia\ duoi=n one by two) is the use of two words connected by a copulative conjunction to express a single complex idea; especially two substantives instead of one substantive and an adjective or attributive genitive.
xro/nw| kai\ poliorki/a| by length of time and siege = by a long siege
D. 19.123,

e)n a(li\ ku/_masi/ te in the waves of the sea
E. Hel. 226,

a)spi/dwn te kai\ stratou= = w(plisme/nou stratou= armed force
S. El. 36.

§3026

Homoioteleuton (o(moiote/leutos ending alike) is end-rhyme in clauses or verses.
th\n me\n a)rxh\n ei)s to\n po/lemon kate/sthsan w(s e)leuqerw/sontes tou\s *(/ellhnas, e)pi\ de\ teleuth=s ou(/tw pollou\s au)tw=n e)kdo/tous e)poi/hsan, kai\ th=s me\n h(mete/ra_s po/lews tou\s *)/iwnas a)pe/sthsan, e)c h(=s a)pw/|khsan kai\ di' h(\n polla/kis e)sw/qhsan in the beginning they entered upon the war with the avowed object of liberating the Greeks, at the end they have betrayed so many of them, and have caused the Ionians to revolt from our State, from which they emigrated and thanks to which they were often saved
I. 4.122. Cp.
S. Aj. 62-65. Homoioteleuton is most marked in paromoiosis.

§3027

Hypallage (u(pallagh/ exchange) is a change in the relation of words by which a word, instead of agreeing with the case it logically qualifies, is made to agree grammatically with another case. Hypallage is almost always confined to poetry.

e)ma\ kh/dea qu_mou= the troubles of my spirit
c 197, nei=kos a)ndrw=n cu/naimon kindred strife of men for strife of kindred men
S. Ant. 794. Here the adjective virtually agrees with the rest of the phrase taken as a compound.

§3028

Hyperbaton (u(pe/rbaton transposition) is the separation of words naturally belonging together. Such displacement usually gives prominence to the first of two words thus separated, but sometimes to the second also. In prose hyperbaton is less common than in poetry, but even in prose it is frequent, especially when it secures emphasis on an important idea by placing it at the beginning or end of a sentence. At times hyperbaton may mark passionate excitement. Sometimes it was adopted to gain rhythmical effect. Thus: “Such resting found the sole of unblest feet”: Milton.
su\ de\ au)to/s, w)= pro\s qew=n, *me/nwn, ti/ fh\|s a)reth\n ei)=nai; but what do you yourself, in heaven's name, Meno, say virtue is?
P. Men. 71d, w)= pro/s se gona/twn (946) by thy knees (I entreat) thee
E. Med. 324,

u(f' e(no\s toiau=ta pe/ponqen h( *(ella\s a)nqrw/pou from one man Greece endured such sufferings
D. 18.158, kratw=n tou\s o(poiousdh/poq' u(_mei=s e)cepe/mpete strathgou/s conquering the generals you kept sending out—such as they were 18. 146.
a. The displacement is often caused by the intrusion of a clause of contrast or explanation. Thus

tou\s peri\ *)arxi/a_n . . . ou) yh=fon a)nemei/nate a)ll' . . . e)ti_mwrh/sasqe you did not postpone your vote but took vengeance upon Archias and his company
X. H. 7.3.7.
b. Adverbs and particles may be displaced. Thus,

ou(/tw tis e)/rws deino/s a passion so terrible
P. Th. 169c,

polu\ ga\r tw=n i(/ppwn e)/trexon qa=tton for they ran much faster than the horses
X. A. 1.5.2; so eu)=, ma/la; on a)/n see 1764.
c. Prepositions often cause the displacement (1663, 2690). On displacement in connection with participles see 1166, 1167; with the negatives, see 2690 ff.
d. Similar or contrasted words are often brought into juxtaposition. Here a nominative precedes an oblique case. Thus, a)po\ tw=n u(_mete/rwn u(_mi=n polemei= summa/xwn he wages war on you from the resources of your allies
D. 4.34, ou) ga/r ti/s me bi/h| ge e(kw\n a)e/konta di/htai for no one shall chase me by force, he willing me unwilling H 197. Note a)/llos a)/llo (a)/lloqen, a)/llote, etc.), au)to\s au(tou=.
e. Construction a)po\ koinou=.—In poetry an attributive genitive or an object, common to two coördinate words, is often placed with the second only, as

fra/zwn a(/lwsin *)i_li/ou t' a)na/stasin telling of the capture and overthrow of Ilium
A. Ag. 587.

§3029

Hypophora (u(pofora(_ putting under) is the statement of an objection (together with its refutation) which a speaker supposes to be made by an opponent or makes himself. Both objection and reply often take the form of questions (2654, 2785, 2819). Cp. “But I hear it continually rung in my ears . . . ‘what will become of the preamble, if you repeal this tax?’”: Burke.
ti/ ou)=n, a)/n tis ei)/poi, tau=ta le/geis h(mi=n nu=n; i(/na gnw=t' ktl. why then, some one will say, do you tell us this now? In order that you may know, etc.
D. 1.14.

§3030

Hysteron Proteron (u(/steron pro/teron later earlier) is an arrangement reversing the natural order of time in which events occur. It is used when an event, later in time, is regarded as more important than one earlier in time.
tra/fen h)de\ ge/nonto were bred and born A 251 (so trofh\ kai\ ge/nesis
X. M. 3.5.10; cp. “for I was bred and born”: Shakespeare),

ei(/mata/ t' a)mfie/sa_sa quw/dea kai\ lou/sa_sa having put on fragrant robes and washed
e 264.

§3031

Isocōlon (i)so/kwlon having equal members) is the use of two or more sequent cola (clauses) containing an equal number of syllables.
tou= me\n e)pi/ponon kai\ filoki/ndu_non to\n bi/on kate/sthsen, th=s de\ peri/blepton kai\ perima/xhton th\n fu/sin e)poi/hsen the life of the one he rendered full of toil and peril, the beauty of the other he made the object of universal admiration and of universal contention
I. 10.16.

§3032

Litotes (li_to/ths plainness, simplicity) is understatement so as to intensify, affirmation expressed by the negative of the contrary. Cp. 2694. Meiōsis (mei/wsis lessening) is ordinarily the same as litotes. Thus: “One of the few immortal names That were not born to die”: Halleck.

§3033

Metonymy (metwnumi/a_ change of name) is the substitution of one word for another to which it stands in some close relation. Thus: “We wish that infancy may learn the purpose of its creation from maternal lips”: Webster.
mi=sos loathed object, w)= ka/qarma you scum! summaxi/a_ allies, e)n *boiwtoi=s in Boeotia, qe/a_tron spectators, ma/xh battlefield, i(/ppos cavalry, i)xqu/es fish-market.

§3034

Onomatopoeia (o)nomatopoii/a_ making of a name or word) is the formation of names to express natural sounds.
blhxw=mai bleat, bombw= buzz, bru_xw=mai roar, koa/c quack, kakkabi/zw cackle, ko/kkuc cuckoo, kra/zw croak, ti_ti/zw cheep, pippi/zw chirp. Sometimes the sound of a whole verse imitates an action; as

au)=tis e)/peita pe/donde kuli/ndeto la=as a)naidh/s down again to the plain rolled the shameless stone
l 598 (of the stone of Sisyphus).

§3035

Oxymōron (o)cu/mwron pointedly or cleverly foolish) is the juxtaposition of words apparently contradictory of each other.

no/mos a)/nomos a law that is no law
A. Ag. 1142,

a)/xaris xa/ris a graceless grace
A. Pr. 545,

pi/stis a)pistota/th most faithless faith
And. 1.67,

au)toi\ feu/gontas feu/gousi they themselves are flying from those who fly
T. 7.70.

§3036

Paraleipsis (para/leiyis passing over) is pretended omission for rhetorical effect.
ta\_s d' e)p' *)illuri/ous kai\ *pai/onas au)tou= kai\ pro\s *)aru/bba_n kai\ o(/poi tis a)\n ei)/poi paralei/pw stratei/a_s I omit his expeditions to Illyria and Paeonia and against Arybbas and many others that one might mention (lit. whithersoever one might speak of)
D. 1.13.

§3037

Parechēsis (parh/xhsis likeness of sound) is the repetition of the same sound in words in close or immediate succession. Alliteration is initial rhyme.
a)/gamos, a)/teknos, a)/polis, a)/filos
E. I. T. 220 (cp. “unwept, unhonoured, and unsung”), po/nos po/nw| po/non fe/rei toil upon toil brings only toil
S. Aj. 866, tuflo\s

ta/ t' w)=ta to/n te nou=n ta/ t' o)/mmat' ei)= blind art thou in thy ears, thy reason, and thy eyes
S. O. T. 371,

oi( ou)de\ . . . di\s a)poqano/ntes di/khn dou=nai du/naint' a)/n who would not be able to give satisfaction even by dying twice
L. 12.37, e)/swsa/ s': w(s i)/sa_sin *(ellh/nwn o(/soi ktl. I saved thee; as all of the Greeks know who, etc.
E. Med. 476, qana/tou qa=tton qei= wickedness ‘fleeth faster than fate’
P. A. 39a.

§3038

Parisōsis (pari/swsis almost equal) is approximate equality of clauses as measured by syllables. Parisōsis is sometimes regarded as synonymous with isocōlon.

§3039

Paromoiōsis (paromoi/wsis assimilation) is parallelism of sound between the words of two clauses either approximately or exactly equal in size. This similarity in sound may appear at the beginning, at the end (homoioteleuton), in the interior, or it may pervade the whole.

maxome/nous me\n krei/ttous ei)=nai tw=n polemi/wn, yhfizome/nous de\ h(/ttous tw=n e)xqrw=n by fighting to be superior to our public enemies, and by voting to be weaker than our private enemies
L. 12.79.

§3040

Paronomasia (paronomasi/a_) is play upon words.

ou) ga\r to\n tro/pon a)lla\ to\n to/pon meth/llacen for he changed not his disposition but his position
Aes. 3.78. Often in etymological word-play; as *pro/qoos qoo/s B 758, *me/lhtos . . . e)me/lhsen
P. A. 26a, *pausani/ou pausame/nou
P. S. 185c,

ei)s . . . to/pon . . . a)eidh=, ei)s *ai(/dou to an invisible place, to Hades
P. Ph. 80d. Cp. “Old Gaunt indeed, and gaunt in being old”: Shakespeare. Sometimes this figure deals with the same word taken in different senses (homonyms): a(/ma ga\r h(mei=s te th=s a)rxh=s a)pesterou/meqa kai\ toi=s *(/ellhsin a)rxh\ tw=n kakw=n e)gi/gneto ‘no sooner were we deprived of the first place than the first disaster came upon the Greeks’
I. 4.119.

§3041

Periphrasis (peri/frasis circumlocution) is the use of more words than are necessary to express an idea.

qre/mmata *nei/lou nurslings of the Nile = the Egyptians
P. L. 953e,

Oi)di/pou ka/ra_ Oedipus
S. O. T. 40 (ka/ra_ expresses reverence or affection). The substantive on which another substantive depends often stands for an adjective, as i)\_s *thlema/xoio = mighty Telemach (cp. 1014). For various other periphrases, see the Index.

§3042

Pleonasm (pleonasmo/s excess), or redundancy, is the admission of a word or words which are not necessary to the complete logical expression of the thought. Such words, though logically superfluous, enrich the thought by adding greater definiteness and precision, picturesqueness, vigour and emphasis; and by expressing subtle shadings of feeling otherwise impossible. Cp. “All ye inhabitants of the world, and dwellers on the earth.”
a. Adverbs or adverbial expressions combined: of time, as pa/lin au)=, au)=qis au)= pa/lin, pa/lin meta\ tau=ta u(/steron, e)/peita meta\ tau=ta, dia\ te/lous to\n pa/nta xro/non; of manner, as kata\ tau)ta\ w(sau/tws, ma/thn a)/llws, ei)s dunato\n o(/ti ma/lista; of infer- ence, as toiga/rtoi dia\ tau=ta, e)k tou/tou . . . dia\ tau=ta; of verification, as a)lhqw=s tw=| o)/nti; and various other expressions, as i)/sws ta/x' a)/n, lo/gw| ei)pei=n.
b. Adverb and adjective combined (usually poetical): kei=to me/gas megalwsti/ huge he lay with his huge length II 776.
c. Adjective and verb:

w(s de\ mh\ makrou\s tei/nw lo/gous but not to speak at length
E. Hec. 1177.
d. Adjective and substantive in the dative:

nh=sos mega/qei me\n ou) mega/lh an island not large in size
Hdt. 5.31.
e. Verb with an abstract substantive in the dative or accusative (1516, 1564):

basileu\s . . . fu/sei pefu_ke/nai to be a true-born king
X. C. 5.1.24.
f. Compound verb or substantives with substantives:

oi)=kon kalw=s oi)konomei=n to build a house well
X. M. 4.5.10,

h( tw=n neognw=n te/knwn paidotrofi/a_ the rearing of young children
X. O. 7.21. Here the force of the first member of the compound is quiescent.
g. Compound verb and adverb:

prou/graya prw=ton I wrote first
T. 1.23,

a)pagagw\n d' u(_ma=s a)/pwqen a)po\ tou= kle/mmatos having diverted your attention away from the fraud
Aes. 3.100.
h. Verb and participle (2147 b): ti/ dh\ le/gontes die/ballon oi( diaba/llontes; in what words then did my calumniators calumniate me?
P. A. 19b.
i. Amplification by synonymous doublets (especially common in Demosthenes):

a)ciw= kai\ de/omai I beg and beseech
D. 18.6, e)narge\s kai\ safe/s visible and clear 14. 4.
j. Parallelism of positive and negative:

w(s e)/xw peri\ tou/twn, le/cw pro\s u(_ma=s kai\ ou)k a)pokru/yomai I will tell you and I will not conceal my opinion on these matters
D. 8.73,

ou)k a)/klhtoi, paraklhqe/ntes de/ not unbidden but invited
T. 6.87.
k. A person and a characteristic or quality connected by kai/ or te/; as

katadei/santes tou=ton kai\ to\ tou/tou qra/sos fearing him and his audacity
D. 21.20.
l. A relative clause takes up a preceding expression: kai\ eu)xh\n de/ tines au)tou= e)ce/feron w(s eu)/xoito ktl. and some reported also a prayer he made, etc. (lit. how he prayed)
X. A. 1.9.11.
m. ‘Polar’ expressions may be placed here. These are opposites placed in pairs so as to intensify such ideas as all, no one, at all times, everywhere, everything possible. Thus,

kai\ e)n qeoi=s kai\ e)n a)nqrw/pois both among the gods and among men
P. G. 508a,

ou)de\n ou)/te me/ga ou)/te mi_kro/n nothing either great or small = absolutely nothing
P. A. 19c,

e)n gh=| kai\ qala/tth| on land and sea
D. 18.324,

ou)/te dou=los ou)/t' e)leu/qeros nor bond nor free
T. 2.78,

r(hta\ kai\ a)/rrhta fanda nefanda
D. 18.122. For other cases of pleonasm, see the Index.

§3043

Polysyndeton (cp. Asyndeton) is the repetition of conjunctions in a series of coördinate words or phrases.

kai\ tosou/twn kai\ e(te/rwn kakw=n kai\ ai)sxrw=n kai\ pa/lai kai\ newsti\ kai\ mi_krw=n kai\ mega/lwn ai)ti/ou gegenhme/nou who has shown himself the guilty cause of so many other base and disgraceful acts, both long ago and lately, both small and great
L. 12.78. Cp.
D. 4.36.

§3044

Praegnans Constructio is a form of brachylogy by which two expressions or clauses are condensed into one.
Here belong, apart from 1659 ff., such cases as ei)s to\ balanei=on bou/lomai I want to go to the bath
Ar. Ran. 1279 (cp. “he will directly to the lords”: Milton, Samson Agon. 1250) and fanero\s h)=n oi)/kade paraskeuazo/menos he was evidently preparing to go home
X. A. 7.7.57. In

paragge/llei e)pi\ ta\ o(/pla he ordered them to get under arms
X. A. 1.5.13 the command was e)pi\ ta\ o(/pla to arms!

§3045

Prolēpsis (pro/lhyis taking before) in the case of objective predicate adjectives or nouns is the anticipation of the result of the action of a verb. Examples in 1579.
On the prolepsis of the subject of dependent clauses which is put into the main clause, see 2182. So in “Consider the lilies of the field how they grow.” Prolepsis is also used to designate the anticipation of an opponent's arguments and objections. One variety is prodiorthōsis or preparatory apology (
P. A. 20e,
D. 18.199, 256).

§3046

Symploce (sumplokh/ interweaving) is the repetition, in one or more successive clauses, of the first and last words of the preceding clause.

e)pi\ sauto\n kalei=s, e)pi\ tou\s no/mous kalei=s, e)pi\ th\n dhmokrati/a_n kalei=s it is against yourself that you are summoning him, it is against the laws that you are summoning him, it is against the democratic constitution that you are summoning him
Aes. 3.202.

§3047

Synecdoche (sunekdoxh/ understanding one thing with another) is the use of the part for the whole, or the whole for the part. The name of an animal is often used for that which comes from, or is made from, the animal. Cp. “they sought his blood”; “Belinda smiled, and all the world was gay”: Pope.
do/ru ship for plank, beam, a)lw/phc fox-skin for fox, xelw/nh tortoise-shell for tortoise, porfu/ra_ purple dye for purple-fish, e)le/fa_s ivory for elephant, meli/ssa honey for bee.

§3048

Zeugma (zeu=gma junction, band) is a form of brachylogy by which two connected substantives are used jointly with the same verb (or adjective) though this is strictly appropriate to only one of them. Such a verb expresses an idea that may be taken in a wider, as well as in a narrower, sense, and therefore suggests the verb suitable to the other substantive. Cp. “Nor Mars his sword, nor war's quick fire shall burn The living record of your memory.”

ou)/te fwnh\n ou)/te tou morfh\n brotw=n o)/yei thou shalt know neither voice nor form of mortal man
A. Pr. 21, a)ll' h)\ pnoai=sin h)\ baquskafei= ko/nei kru/yon nin no, either give them to the winds or in the deep-dug soil bury them
S. El. 435, e)/dousi/ te pi(_ona mh=la oi)=no/n t' e)/caiton they eat fat sheep and drink choice wine M 319.
a. Different from zeugma is syllēpsis (su/llhyis taking together), by which the same verb, though governing two different objects, is taken both in its literal and its metaphorical sense; but does not properly change its meaning. Thus,

xrh/mata telou=ntes tou/tois . . . kai\ xa/ritas paying money and rendering thanks to them
P. Cr. 48c.

## Appendix: List of Verbs

THIS List in general includes the common verbs showing any formal peculiarity of tense. The forms printed in heavy-faced type belong to standard Attic, that is, to the language used in common speech and in ordinary prose; others are poetical, doubtful, dialectal or late. Many regular forms are omitted because they do not appear in the classical writers; though their non-appearance in the extant texts may often be accidental. Later forms are usually excluded, but reference is made to Aristotle, and to Hippocrates, though many works ascribed to him are of later date. The determination of the forms of Attic prose as distinguished from those of poetry is often difficult because of insufficient evidence, and in many cases certainty is not to be attained. The tenses employed in the dialogue parts of Aristophanes and other early writers of Attic comedy are usually to be regarded as existing in the spoken language except when the character of the verb in question is such as to indicate borrowing from Epic or tragedy. Sometimes a tense attested only in tragedy and in Attic prose of the latter part of the fourth century may have been used in the best Attic prose. The expression in prose means in Attic prose.

A prefixed hyphen indicates that a form used in prose is attested generally, or only, in composition; and that a poetical form occurs only in composition. Rigid consistency would have led to too great detail; besides, many tenses cited as existing only in composition may have occurred also in the simple form. For the details of usage on this and other points the student is referred to Veitch, Greek Verbs, Irregular and Defective, and to Kühner-Blass, Griechische Grammatik.

The tenses cited are those of the principal parts (369). Tenses inferred from these are omitted, but mention is made of the future perfect, future passive, and of the future middle when it shows a passive sense.

An assumed form is marked by * or has no accent; the abbreviations aor. and perf. denote first aorist and first perfect; of alternative forms in tt or ss (78), that in tt is given when the verb in question belongs to the classical spoken language. In the citation of Epic forms, futures and aorists with ss, and several other Epic peculiarities, are usually not mentioned.

The appended Roman numerals indicate the class (497-529) to which the present system of each verb belongs; all verbs not so designated belong to the first class (498-504).

At the end of an item, "LSJ" marks a link to the verb's definition in the Greek-English Lexicon.
